title: An HIV-positive male with fever, cough, and skin lesions.
history:
An man in his twenties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was admitted to a hospital after developing a one-week illness with dyspnea, cough productive of yellow and occasionally blood-streaked sputum, fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. He also reported a 3-week history of a rash, with the appearance of unusual skin lesions that initially appeared on his face, then involved his extremities.

He had had human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for an unknown duration, and was not adherent with medications. He had formerly used intravenous drugs.
exam_studies:
He was alert and oriented, and appeared mildly ill. The temperature was 99.6 °F (37.6°C); the pulse was 108 beats per minute, and the blood pressure 134/88 mm/Hg. Oral thrush was present. The lungs had diffuse rhonchi and wheezes, and the abdomen was soft without organomegaly. The skin examination is shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.
Figure 1. Physical findings on face.
Figure 2. Physical findings in mouth.
Figure 3. Physical findings on extremity.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 7,300/mm³, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 61 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 66 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 630 U/L, and bilirubin was normal. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was less than 20 cells/mm³.
diagnosis:
Disseminated cryptococcosis with cutaneous, cerebrospinal fluid and pulmonary involvement in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Pathological examination of a biopsy of one of the skin nodules was positive for sheets of yeast-like organisms consistent with Cryptococcus. (See Figure 4 for silver stain of biopsy, Figure 5 for mucicarmine stain.) A test of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for cryptococcal antigen (Ag) was positive. Cultures of the blood and sputum grew Cryptococcus.
Figure 4. Silver stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 5. Mucicarmine stain of biopsy.

The patient received amphotericin B for 23 days, followed by oral fluconazole. The skin lesions began to decrease but were still present upon discharge. He was subsequently lost to follow-up.

title: A 5-month-old with failure-to-thrive and a rash.
history:
A 5-month-old male presented with failure-to-thrive and bacteremia caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. During hospitalization, he developed a pustulo-nodular rash. Pathological examination of a skin biopsy showed a non-specific neutrophilic inflammation. The rash progressed despite a prolonged course of anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

Atopic dermatitis and hepatomegaly had been diagnosed at 5 weeks of age. A liver biopsy showed non-specific inflammation. The infant's mother had had a positive tuberculosis skin test (PPD) during pregnancy; chest radiograph was negative. Isoniazid (INH) therapy was deferred until after pregnancy.

There was no history of travel, sick contacts, or animal exposure. The infant had missed the recommended 4-month immunizations.
exam_studies:
The infant appeared malnourished and without distress. The weight and height were below the 5th percentile for age, the temperature was 98.6°F (37°C). The abdomen was protuberant with the liver extending 10 centimeters below the right costal margin and the spleen 5 centimeters below the left costal margin. Scaling erythroderma, numerous erythematous subcutaneous nodules (3 - 5 mm in diameter) and pustules were present on his lower and upper extremities. (See Figures 1 through 4.)
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding.
Figure 4. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 8,700 cells per cubic millimeter (38% neutrophils, 6% bands, 24% lymphs, 7% monocytes, 25% eosinophils), hematocrit 26%, and platelets 63,000 per cubic millimeter. The levels of T-lymphocyte and B-lymphocyte cell counts were normal, but the CD8 T-lymphocyte cell count was very low. There was a diffuse elevation of immunoglobulin (Ig) G, IgM, IgA and IgE levels. No antibody response to tetanus was seen. Mitogen stimulation showed significantly decreased lymphocyte response to concavalin A, phytohemaglutinin and pokeweed mitogen. The findings were consistent with severe combined immunodeficiency.

Numerous blood cultures were negative. A diagnostic test was performed.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Mycobacterium marinum infection in an infant with severe combined immunodeficiency.

Pathological examination of a skin biopsy revealed mixed granulomatous dermatitis with numerous acid-fast bacilli (AFB) present. Examination of a bone marrow biopsy revealed multiple small non-caseating granulomas. Cultures of the skin and bone marrow grew Mycobacterium marinum.

Mycobacterium marinum is a well-described cause of cutaneous infection. After an exposure to contaminated waters, the infection can disseminate systematically especially in an immunocompromised host. M. marinum grows poorly at temperatures greater than 37°C, which explains the typical distribution of the skin lesions over upper and lower extremities.

title: A 9-day-old infant with fever and hypotension.
history: A 9-day-old infant had an anatomic defect at birth that required abdominal surgery. She then developed fever and hypotension. She had been receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central venous line.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 39°C (102.2°F), blood pressure 104/52 mm Hg, and pulse 148 per minute.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 25,000/mm³. Results of laboratory tests of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) parameters were normal, and the CSF culture was sterile. Blood cultures were positive; colonies that grew on blood agar after 48 hours are shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Culture results.
diagnosis:
Line-related sepsis due to Pseudomonas oryzihabitans (formerly called Flavobacterium oryzihabitans) in an infant.

Pseudomonas oryzihabitans (formerly called Flavobacterium oryzihabitans) was identified. This organism is notable for its unusual yellow, rough colonies that are oxidase-negative.

Pseudomonas oryzihabitans has recently gained recognition as a cause of sepsis in immunodeficient patients with central venous access. This organism has an environmental reservoir similar to other non-fermentative gram negative rods.

title: A man in his fifties with a painful and red finger.
history:
A man in his fifties presented to an Emergency Department with a red painful middle finger on the right hand.
Twelve hours before presentation, he cut down a tree with his left hand, while holding onto the tree with his right hand. He did not recall any trauma. Initial examination revealed a red, swollen finger. There was no drainage after a lateral incision. He was prescribed cephalexin and was discharged.
Twenty-one hours later, he returned to the emergency department with fever, chills, and increasing pain from the palm to the axilla.
exam_studies:
See Figures 1, 2 and 3.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding.

Penicillin, clindamycin and aztreonam were administered emergently.
diagnosis:
Group A Streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis.

The patient was taken to the operating room for incision and debridement, and a diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis was made. Wound culture grew Streptococcus Group A.

The patient recovered completely.

title: A man in his seventies with a leg ulcer.
history:
A man in his seventies presented with a history of an enlarging leg ulcer of one year's duration.
The ulcer was at the site of a previous saphenous vein graft harvest and failed skin graft. He also noted skin nodules on both arms. Steroids were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa, but the nodules persisted. He reported no fevers or other systemic symptoms.

There was a history of atherosclerosis and diabetes mellitus.

He had been born in Ecuador and lived in Texas.
exam_studies:
He was afebrile. The skin findings are shown in Figures 1and 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The chest radiograph showed clear lungs. Radiographs of the foot and leg (from the side of the ulcer) are shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Foot radiograph.
Figure 4. Lower leg radiograph.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium chelonae soft tissue infection and osteomyelitis in a patient with diabetes mellitus and a history of surgical procedures.

Pathological examination of a biopsy of the distal left tibia showed suppurative granuloma with central necrosis, but no acid fast bacilli (AFB) were seen. Skin biopsy from the right forearm showed suppurative granulomatous dermatitis with caseating necrosis; again no AFB were seen. Biopsy of a lesion from the left thigh showed similar suppuration and revealed abundant AFB. This specimen later grew Mycobacterium chelonae.

title: A man in his sixties with confusion and a seizure.
history:
A man in his sixties was brought to an emergency department (ED) by his wife because he appeared confused and had not been himself for several weeks. While in the ED, he had a myoclonic seizure. His wife reported that he had been complaining of a frontal headache, and had had a 10-pound weight loss over the previous 3 months.

There was a history of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, for which he took prednisone and cyclophosphamide; pulmonary hypertension; and non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). Twenty years earlier, he had had a brain abscess and was status post craniotomy.

He had stopped smoking 3 years before presentation. There was no history of alcohol or intravenous drug use. He worked in a foundry, and had had occupational exposure to gases and dust.
exam_studies:
The patient was confused and disoriented. The temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F) and respirations 22 breaths per minute. There was conjunctival injection, a grade II/VI systolic murmur, scrotal edema and erythema, right hemiparesis and a right-sided neglect. Ophthalmologic examination showed a right choroidal abscess. There were no splinter hemorrhages.

The hematocrit was 31%, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 135 millimeters per hour. A radiograph of the chest revealed lingular and left basilar infiltrates. Computed tomography (CT) of the head, with contrast, is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Head CT scan.

A brain biopsy was performed. Gram stain of the pathologic specimen is shown in Figure 2, Fite stain in Figure 3, and Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) stain in Figure 4.
Figure 2. Gram stain.
Figure 3. Fite stain.
Figure 4. GMS stain.
diagnosis:
Nocardiosis with dissemination to the brain, possibly to the epididymis, scrotum, and choroid, in an immunocompromised patient with diabetes mellitus and pulmonary fibrosis.

The GMS stain shows filamentous organisms characteristic of Nocardia. Fite stain is a modified acid-fast stain; Nocardia appears as a weakly acid-fast organism.

Nocardiosis generally affects immunocompromised hosts. This patient was on immunosuppressive medication, which increased his risk for nocardiosis. The organism has a tropism for the central nervous system, and can cause brain abscesses as seen in this case.

title: A man with a fever, cough, arthralgias and abdominal pain.
history:
A man in his thirties from a large Midwestern city presented with the sudden onset of fever to 103°F (39.4°C) and rigors. Also noted headache, extreme myalgias, arthralgias. He complained of non-productive cough with pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath, and reported dark urine, abdominal pain, and nausea with one episode of vomiting.
Two weeks prior, he had returned from a country in Southeastern Africa, and one week prior he had been in Northern Idaho.
Prior to leaving for Africa, he had received hepatitis A virus (HAV), diphtheria-tetanus (dT) toxoid, measles, and polio vaccines. Once there, he took mefloquine prophylaxis, drank bottled water only, wore N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET) and long pants. He denied bites, had been primarily in major cities, but did venture into rural areas. No one else on the trip was ill.
In Idaho, he had stayed in a very modern “log” house on a big lake, and had spent time on the water, in the woods on major trails, covered “head to toe” with clothing as the riding was very dusty. He denied insect bites and contact with animals. No one else was ill.

Refer to the history of the present illness.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C); the abdomen was diffusely tender, and a faint erythematous rash with light desquamation was present over his trunk and extremities.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 65 mm per hour, the white blood cell count (WBC) 6,200 per cubic millimeter, hematocrit 38.8%, and the platelet count was 73,000 per cubic millimeter. Peripheral blood smears are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Thick blood smear.
Figure 2. Thin blood smear.
diagnosis:
Tick-borne relapsing fever due to Borrelia hermsii.

The diagnosis of Tick-borne Relapsing Fever due to Borrelia hermsii was made. The diagnosis was based on the history, clinical findings, and the observance of spirochetes on thick and thin peripheral smears (Figures 1 and 2). Serology is usually not helpful, but IgM was weakly positive for B. hermsii.

The patient received a course of doxycycline, with prompt resolution of his symptoms. No Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction was observed.

Tick-borne Relapsing Fever due to Borrelia hermsii is endemic in Northern Idaho. Its Ornithodoros (soft tick) vector feeds on rodent reservoirs, and inhabits decaying wood and caves. Previous cases have occurred in campers staying in log cabins.

title: A man in his sixties with swollen joints.
history:
A man in his sixties with a history of an inflammatory arthritis presented with a 2-month history of swollen joints, especially the left knee. He received steroid therapy with initial improvement in his symptoms.
However, one week prior to admission he developed fevers, night sweats, increasing dyspnea, and a nonproductive cough. The patient also reported a 20-pound weight loss over the previous 2 months.

Other medical problems included myelodysplasia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, and seronegative inflammatory arthritis. An arthrocentesis 10 weeks before admission had revealed inflammatory fluid without crystals. Cultures for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and fungi were negative. He was status post splenectomy several years previously.

He had taken prednisone for 2 months; methotrexate for 1 month (three weeks previous to admission) and hydroxyurea.
exam_studies:
He was afebrile and appeared frail, but not toxic-appearing. There was a white oral exudate consistent with mild thrush, and diffuse bilateral fine rales in the lungs. The left knee was tender, with a palpable effusion.

Arterial blood gases (ABG) obtained while breathing ambient air revealed pH 7.52, partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) 61, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 32. The white blood cell count (WBC) was 22,500/mm³. A chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph at presentation.

Arthrocentesis of the left knee was performed and analysis of the synovial fluid showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 38,100 cells/mm³ (97% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 3% monocytes) and red blood cell count of 700 cells/mm³. Gram stains of his sputum (Figure 2) and his synovial fluid (Figure 3) are shown.
Figure 2. Gram stain of sputum.
Figure 3. Gram stain of synovial fluid.
diagnosis:
Disseminated blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis in an immunocompromised patient.

Gram stain and Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) stain of sputum and synovial fluid demonstrated abundant broad-based budding yeast forms. Cultures grew Blastomyces dermatitidis. (See Figures 4 and 5 for GMS stain of synovial fluid and synovial fluid culture preparation.)
Figure 4. GMS stain of synovial fluid.
Figure 5. Synovial fluid culture preparation.

Itraconazole was administered as soon as broad-based yeast were identified from sputum and synovial fluid, with improvement.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is endemic in many parts of the United States and appears to be the most common endemic mycosis in East Tennessee. After entering by inhalation, B. dermatitidis can cause both symptomatic pneumonitis and asymptomatic lung masses. Dissemination to the skin, bones, synovium, meninges, and brain can occur in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients.

title: A man with sinusitis.
history:
A man in his twenties presented to a Otolaryngology clinic. He had a history of chronic sinusitis, including previous lengthy treatment courses with amoxicillin-clavulanate and levofloxacin, without resolution of symptoms.

See above.

He worked in an office building and liked to garden, and had no significant travel exposures.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. There was purulent sinus drainage and the examination was otherwise normal.

An aspirate of the sinuses, obtained endoscopically, was sent for bacterial and fungal culture. Growth of the aspirate specimen, from the eighteenth day, is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Culture growth.
diagnosis:
Schizophyllum commune sinusitis.

White, fluffy colonies grew on fungal media without cycloheximide within 2 days; clamp connections were seen, with no conidia. The “mushroom” structure developed after 18 days of incubation. Schizophyllum commune was identified. Figure 1. Culture growth.

The organism Schizophyllum commune is a basidiomycetous fungus that has been rarely reported to be a cause of sinusitis in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. The presentation of sinus disease due to Schizophyllum commune may clinically resemble Aspergillus sinusitis.

title: A man with weakness, weight loss and diarrhea.
history:
A man in his sixties presented with a 4-week history of weakness, difficulty walking and diarrhea. He had lost 20 pounds over the previous 2-3 months. The patient reported no fever, chills, nausea or vomiting.

He had a history of hypertension and had had multiple cerebral infarcts.

He had lived in Florida during the previous 6 months, and had no pets.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 38°C (100.4°F). On examination, there was hepatosplenomegaly; motor strength of the upper and lower extremities was decreased, which was not new.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 3,000 cells per cubic millimeter, hematocrit 29%, and platelets 136,000/mm³. The level of serum urea nitrogen was 61 mg/dL and creatinine 3 mg/dL, and tests of liver function and stool studies were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen showed bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Abdominal MRI scan.

An aspirate of the adrenal was performed; a special stain of the aspirate is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Adrenal gland aspirate.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.

Gomori methenamine silver stain of the adrenal aspirate (seen in Figure 2) showed small budding yeast. Cultures of the bone marrow, blood and adrenal aspirate grew Histoplasma capsulatum.

Histoplasma capsulatum is endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. Subacute progressive disseminated histoplasmosis may present with prolonged symptoms, such as weight loss, fever, and diarrhea.
Conidia are inhaled and convert to yeast inside pulmonary macrophages. Organisms invade the adrenal glands in approximately 80% of subacute progressive histoplasmosis. Overt Addison’s disease occurs in less than 10% of cases.

title: A woman from the Philippines with abdominal pain and fever.
history:
A woman in her thirties from the Philippines reported a three-month history of episodic abdominal discomfort, fever and weight loss of 5 kilograms. Over the three days prior to admission, the patient developed worsening abdominal pain, vomiting and watery diarrhea.

There was a history of jaundice at age 14 years and “pelvic infection” treated 6 years previously by a local physician.

The patient had grown up in a rural area in the Philippines.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98°F (36.7°C). The patient was pale, with no jaundice. The abdomen was distended, with firm hepatosplenomegaly and ascites (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The level of hemoglobin was 10.3 g/dL, albumin 29 g/L; alkaline phosphatase 797 U/L and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 227 U/L (elevated). Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 3. Abdominal CT scan.

Endoscopic examination, performed to evaluate the thickened ileocecum seen in the CT scan, showed an ileocecal mass (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Endoscopy.
diagnosis:
Abdominal tuberculosis with an ileocecal mass and liver involvement.

An ileocecal biopsy of the mass showed caseous granulomas (Figure 5). A core biopsy of the liver showed granulomatous inflammation and a giant cell (Figure 6). Acid fast bacilli (AFB) found on the liver biopsy were consistent with abdominal tuberculosis.
Figure 5. Biopsy of ileocecal mass.
Figure 6. Core biopsy of the liver.

The patient improved on standard 4-drug antituberculous treatment and subsequently returned to the Philippines to continue therapy.

title: A teenager with a sore throat, fever, and malaise.
history:
A teenager presented with a five-day history of a sore throat, fever, nausea, cough and malaise. A rapid strep test was negative. Blood cultures were obtained and oral azithromycin was administered. The next day, her symptoms increased, and she was admitted with fever, emesis, dysphagia and shortness of breath.

No significant past medical history.

She was an active student athlete, and had no history of recent travel.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/68 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, while breathing supplemental oxygen. There was tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy with neck swelling bilaterally, greater on the left than the right. Examination of the chest revealed shallow respirations, guarding upon deep inspiration, and coarse rales bilaterally, with good aeration.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 22,400 cells per cubic millimeter and platelets 820,000 per cubic millimeter. A chest radiograph and head scan were done and are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Head scan.

Doppler ultrasound of left internal jugular is shown in Figure 3, and doppler ultrasound of right internal jugular in Figure 4.
Figure 3. Doppler study of left internal jugular vein.
Figure 4. Doppler study of right internal jugular vein.
diagnosis:
LeMierre’s disease caused by Fusobacterium.

Culture of the blood grew Fusobacterium. Ultrasonography of the neck (Figures 3 and 4) showed complete occlusion of the left internal jugular vein and partial occlusion of the right internal jugular vein.

Lemierre's disease (postanginal septicemia) is the classical presentation of human necrobacillosis. The infection often begins in the throat with spread to the lateral pharyngeal space and internal jugular vein. The resulting septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis can be complicated by septic pulmonary emboli, as in this case. Although Fusobacterium necrophorum is the usual causative organism, polymicrobial bacteremia may occur.

title: A woman in her thirties with abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever.
history:
A woman in her thirties, with a history of leukemia, was in complete remission three months after allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplant when she presented after 4 days of diffuse abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever. She had received azithromycin one week before presentation for bronchitis.

She had had acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML), and was status post allogeneic stem cell transplant as above.

She reported that she drank city water, and had no exposures to animals or travel history.

She had received VP-16 three months before admission, and was taking acyclovir prophylaxis.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 39.4°C (102.9°F), blood pressure 90/60 mm/Hg, pulse 130 beats/minute, and respirations 24 breaths per minute. The examination of the abdomen revealed hypoactive bowel sounds and mild generalized abdominal tenderness.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 22,000 cells per cubic millimeter (88% neutrophils), the serum level of urea nitrogen (BUN) was 32 mg/dL and creatinine 3.1 mg/dL. An abdominal scan is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Abdominal scan.

Sigmoidoscopic examination revealed diffuse bowel wall edema, without pseudomembranes (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Sigmoidoscopy findings.
diagnosis:
Clostridium difficile colitis.

Stool was positive for Clostridium difficile toxin by cytotoxicity assay. Stool for ova and parasites (O & P) was negative; polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for cytomegalovirus (CMV) was negative. Biopsies of the sigmoid colon, descending colon and rectum showed no evidence of viruses, bacteria, fungi and graft-versus-host-disease (GVHD).

title: An infant with a lesion on the nose.
history:
A 5-month-old infant developed small red papules on the nose at three-and-one-half months of age. Three weeks later, the child developed a scab over the lesions. Mupirocin ointment treatment was used with little response.
Fluormetholone ophthalmic ointment and oral cephalexin were given without response.

The patient lived in a city in the Western United States. There was no history of travel or animal contact. The patient had gone to a pumpkin patch 3 weeks after the onset of the lesion and sat in a haystack on the mother’s lap.
exam_studies:
The examination was normal except for the lesion on the nose as shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Sporothrix schenckii infection in an infant.

Potassium hydroxide (KOH) scraping was negative. Culture of the lesion grew Sporothrix schenckii.

The patient was treated with itraconazole for four months. The child's appearance one month after the completion of therapy is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Physical findings at follow-up.

Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus that is ubiquitous and can be isolated from soil, plants, and hay. Sporotrichosis most commonly presents as a cutaneous infection at a site of minor trauma after an average incubation period of 7-30 days.

title: A man was found unresponsive.
history:
A man in his sixties was brought to a hospital in early May after being found unresponsive, lying in bed in his home. Friends at work had activated the Emergency Medical Services (EMS) system after he had not been seen in four days.

He had a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia.

The patient lived alone in rural Alabama. His daughter reported that he walked his dogs in the woods on a daily basis. Ten days before his presentation, he had reported a tick bite to her.

Medications included fosinopril, hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), and simvastatin.
exam_studies:
He was obtunded and obese. The temperature was 103.5°F (39.7°C), respiration 20 breaths per minute, pulse 120 beats/minute and blood pressure 95/63 mm/Hg. The conjunctiva were injected, the neck was supple, and the cardiac rhythm was tachycardic and irregularly irregular. A faint diffuse maculopapular rash was noted on the trunk and proximal portion of the extremities, with no plantar or palmar skin lesions. His speech was unintelligible and he moved all extremities.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,000/mm³ (86% polysmorphonuclear leukocytes, 4% bands, 9% lymphocytes, 1% eosinophils); hematocrit 26% platelets 45,000/mm³, and the INR was 1.3. The level of serum sodium was 128 mmol/L, glucose 95 mg/dL, creatinine 5.7 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 306 U/Lm and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 120 U/L.
Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 57 white cells per cubic millimeter (79% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 12% lymphocytes, and 9% atypical lymphocytes) (Figures 1 and 2); the level of glucose was 39 mg/dL and protein 235. Gram stain of the CSF was negative, and cultures of specimens of blood, CSF and urine were sterile. Testing for toxins was also negative.
A chest radiograph showed a right middle lobe opacity. Computed tomography (CT) of the head, without contrast, showed no acute changes.
Figure 1. Wright stain of the CSF.
Figure 2. Wright stain of the CSF.
diagnosis:
Human monocytic ehrlichiosis, caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis.

Review of the “atypical” lymphocytes identified on the CSF Wright stain (Figures 1 and 2) revealed intracellular “mulberry” inclusions within several mononuclear cells. The titer of immunoglobulin (Ig) G to Ehrlichia chaffeensis on the first hospital day was 1:64, and the Ehrlichia chaffeensis IgG level on the tenth hospital day was 1:2056.

The patient was diagnosed with human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME). He received 14 days of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. He spent 10 days in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) requiring mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and hemodialysis. The patient's multisystem organ failure resolved. He responded to doxycycline and supportive care. His mental status slowly improved. The patient's hospital course was complicated by ventricular tachycardia and pulmonary embolus. He was discharged to a rehabilitation facility.

Human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME) is a tick-borne zoonosis. The clustered inclusion-like entities in vacuoles are known as morula. Morulae are seen in macrophages and monocytes, including macrophages in the CSF, and sometimes may be seen in lymphocytes or neutrophils. Symptoms of HME include fever and headache; about one-third of patients have a rash. Laboratory studies may reveal leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases; about half of the patients have infiltrates on chest radiography.

title: A woman with a skin lesion for four weeks.
history:
A woman in her twenties presented to an emergency department in the Northeast United States with a skin lesion on her right shoulder of four weeks' duration. The patient had noticed the skin lesion two days after she returned to the United States from Peru. The lesion started out as a raised papule that enlarged over several weeks. It did not itch and was not painful. She reported no history of fever, chills or night sweats.

She had spent six weeks in the rainforest of Peru. A companion, who had been with her at the time, had a similar skin lesion.
exam_studies:
She appeared well and was afebrile. There was a skin lesion on her right shoulder (see Figure 1) and the remainder of the examination was normal, with no lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

Results of laboratory tests of the blood were normal.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania braziliensis.

Pathological examination of a skin biopsy included a Giemsa-stained slide of a tissue touch prep, which showed amastigotes inside macrophages consistent with leishmaniasis. (See Figure 2.)
Figure 2. Giemsa stain skin biopsy.

Culture of the specimen developed an overgrowth of yeast, and failed to grow any other organisms. Her colleague’s skin biopsy grew Leishmania braziliensis. The patient was treated intravenously for 20 days with antimony in the form of sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The patient tolerated the medication well. She had mild muscle aches and a transient rise in liver function studies, amylase and lipase developed, all of which normalized after cessation of therapy. The skin lesion markedly decreased in size and subsequently scarred over.

Leishmania braziliensis is transmitted by the bite of an infected female sandfly. Other modes of transmission are congenital and parenteral (by blood transfusion, needle sharing and laboratory accident). Cutaneous leishmaniasis may heal without treatment. Systemic treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis is thought, but not proven, to decrease the already low risk (<5%) of mucosal disease.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man in his forties with extremity and
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man in his forties with extremity and groin lesions.
A man in his forties was well until seven months before admission when he noticed several painless, purplish lesions on his lower extremities. These lesions gradually increased in size and number. One month before admission, a right groin lesion developed and grew rapidly. Three days prior to admission, scrotal and penile edema occurred. There were no systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, shortness of breath, abdominal pain or diarrhea.

The past history included syphilis and gonorrhea 10 years ago, which had been treated.

He was a homosexual male. Eight years earlier, testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. He denied tobacco, alcohol or intravenous drug use.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 98.4°F (36.9°C); other vital signs were stable. There were no oral lesions, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. The lungs were clear, and cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, with a 1/6 systolic ejection murmur at the apex. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, and the spleen was not palpable.
Skin examination revealed scattered violaceous lesions on the lower extremities, toes, sacral area, chest and arms (Figure 1). His right groin revealed a nodular, indurated lesion with some necrosis and yellow exudate, and matted lymph nodes bilaterally (Figure 2). There was 2+ scrotal and penile edema.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 3,300 cells/mm³ (with 65% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 25% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, and 2% eosinophils), hematocrit 39%, and platelet count 266,000/mm³. The serum level of globulin was 4.4g/dL; other laboratory test results for serum electrolytes, liver function and extended chemistries were normal.

A biopsy of the lesion in the groin was performed (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Biopsy findings.
Figure 4. Biopsy findings.
diagnosis:
Kaposi’s sarcoma in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Histopathology of the groin biopsy revealed interweaving proliferation of epithelioid and spindle cells (Figure 3) with multiple mitotic figures (Figure 4). Immunohistochemical stains performed revealed the tumor cells to stain positively for CD31 and CD34 (spindle cell markers) supporting the diagnosis of Kaposi’s Sarcoma (KS).
Computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest, abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple enhancing lymph nodes in the retroperitoneum, pelvis and inguinal region, particularly on the right, consistent with metastatic disease (Figures 5 and 6).
There was no evidence of pulmonary KS. Results of testing for antibodies to HIV were positive (ELISA and Western Blot). The CD4+ T-lymphcyte cell count was 72 cells/mm³; HIV nucleic acid viral load was 116,000 copies/mL by RT-PCR.
Figure 5. CT scan.
Figure 6. Pelvic CT scan.

The patient was started on highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) and paclitaxel every 2 weeks. He required granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) thrice weekly due to leukopenia, but had, after two months of treatment, a dramatic improvement in the size and intensity of his skin lesions (Figure 7).
Figure 7. Two month follow-up.

Bacillary angiomatosis, due to either Bartonella quintana or B. henselae, may present in a similar manner to Kaposi's sarcoma (KS); however, in this case, the biopsy demonstrated KS. Verruga peruana, due to Bartonella bacilliformis, is a geographically restricted infection (South America).
Granuloma inguinale typically presents with bulky inguinal adenopathy, and shingles typically has a vesicular eruption. KS is a vascular tumor associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). It is the most common tumor found in AIDS patients, typically in homosexual men. AIDS-related KS often presents with painless, non-pruritic skin lesions, particularly on the lower extremities and face, but extracutaneous disease can occur in the oral mucosa, lymph nodes, GI tract and lungs. The clinical course is variable ranging from minimal, asymptomatic disease to a fulminant and disseminated process. Treatment consists of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) along with adjuvant radiation or chemotherapy when disease is systemic or morbidly severe.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man in his thirties with acute myelog
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man in his thirties with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and a rash.
A man in his thirties with M4 acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) was receiving salvage chemotherapy with high-dose cytarabine (Ara-C) when he developed scattered pruritic erythematous papules across the trunk, axillae and upper extremities in the setting of profound neutropenia. Recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen had demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions (less than one centimeter in diameter) in the liver and spleen.

The past history included acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD).

The patient was originally from Peru. Family members, including young children, had visited recently.
exam_studies:
There were scattered erythematous papules across the trunk, axillae, and upper extremities (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Scabies infestation, in a patient with acute myelogenous leukemia.

A skin biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of the skin biopsy revealed a scabies mite within a parakeratotic scale (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Biopsy result with scabies mite.

The patient was treated with 5% permethrin cream, with reapplication 1 week later. On further evaluation, the children who had recently visited were also found to have scabies infestation. The subcentimeter lesions in the liver and spleen were determined to be due to leukemic infiltration.

Scabies is an ectoparasitic infestation by the mite, Sarcoptes scabiei. Transmission occurs by contact and nosocomial outbreaks are well described. At the time of this publication, treatment is typically topical with either lindane or permethrin.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with fever and rash after chemoth
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with fever and rash after chemotherapy.
A man in his forties, who was receiving chemotherapy for recurrent lung cancer, presented with one week of nausea, vomiting, profuse diarrhea and fever to 102°F (38.9°). He also noted a transient left arm rash. On presentation to the clinic, he noted new skin rashes on his lower extremity and abdomen.

There was a history of recurrent stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lung.

He was living in New England, and had previously lived in Japan and Vietnam during the 1960's. There was a smoking history of 40 pack years, and no recent animal or travel exposure.

The patient was receiving his third cycle of vinorelbine tartrate.
exam_studies:
There was a serpiginous rash on his right thigh and multiple urticarial lesions on his lower back, abdomen (Figure 1), and thigh.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

At the time of his clinic visit, the white blood cell count was 5400 cells/mm³ with a normal differential. Four weeks earlier, the white cell count had been 9400 cells/mm³, with 14% eosinophils.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis.

Stool examination revealed Strongyloides stercoralis (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Examination of stool.

The patient had disseminated strongyloidiasis with gastrointestinal manifestations precipitated by chemotherapy, but with no clinical manifestations of hyperinfection syndrome. He was treated with ivermectin.

The presumed exposure was thought to have occurred during the patient's travel to Southeast Asia. Of the organisms in the differential, only Strongyloides can maintain a subclinical auto-infection over thirty years. Thus onchocerciasis and gnathostomiasis are unlikely. Swimmer's itch is due to avian cercariasis, typically causing a pruritic rash over the lower extremities and associated with wading in fresh water.
Cutaneous manifestations of chronic strongyloidiasis include urticarial rash and dermatitis due to migration of filariform larvae (larva currens or creeping eruption), as seen in this patient. Immune complex mediated polyarthritis can also be a feature of chronic strongyloidiasis.

title:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with fever and weight loss.
A man
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with fever and weight loss.
A man in his thirties presented with three weeks of fever, night sweats and weight loss.

The patient had recently moved to the United States from Honduras.
exam_studies:
The patient was thin, but in no acute distress. The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C), and other vital signs were normal. There were white lesions on the oral mucosa consistent with oral thrush, a freely mobile non-tender lymph node (2-centimeters in diameter) in the left axilla and shotty inguinal lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 2,900 cells/mm³ and the hematocrit 24%. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed innumerable tiny nodules and axillary lymphadenopathy (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Miliary tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

An induced sputum specimen was obtained. Staining of the sputum for acid fast bacilli (AFB) was positive. Culture of the induced sputum grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The patient was diagnosed with miliary tuberculosis. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was also positive.

Miliary tuberculosis (TB) results from uncontrolled hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The presentation is often non-specific and includes fever, weight loss and night sweats. Hematologic abnormalities, including leukopenia and normocytic anemia, are often seen. Miliary TB is more common in patients with HIV infection.
The other diagnoses in the differential listed above were less likely: Paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis and tuberculosis may all present in the manner seen in this case, but of these, tuberculosis is the most prevalent disease. Candida pneumonia is far more rare, and cryptococcal pneumonia typically presents with a nodular pattern.

title: Summary: A man with rapidly progressive (Tempo of onset and resolution are impor
history:
Summary: A man with rapidly progressive (Tempo of onset and resolution are important clues in the diagnosis of infectious diseases. Most 'ordinary' bacterial infections have a time-course over days, consistent with bacterial growth and host immune response. Illnesses which progress much more slowly or more rapidly suggest particular types of organisms. In particular, rapid progression over hours to minutes can suggest toxin-mediated pathophysiology, sometimes induced by bacterial virulence factors.) arm pain and swelling.
A man in his fifties presented to an outside hospital with severe pain in the right upper extremity of a few hours' duration. The physical examination was normal (The pattern of severe pain with normal or minimally changed surface examination is extremely worrisome and suggests underlying tissue destruction. This sign can be a medical and surgical emergency but is frequently missed.) and he was discharged. Over the next few hours, he developed progressive swelling of the right upper extremity, with ecchymoses and bullae (Terminology: Bullae are large, fluid-filled blisters.); he was re-evaluated and transferred to a tertiary-care hospital.

Non-contributory.
exam_studies:
On examination, the right upper extremity was diffusely swollen with a deep red discoloration; there were several hemorrhagic bullae (The bruising suggests that the pathogen is causing bleeding in the tissues and the bullae suggest a bacterial toxin or enzyme causing layers of the skin to peel apart from one another. Both of these are indications of a very dangerous infection.). No pulses were palpable in the right upper extremity. Figures 1 and 2 show a photograph of the arm and axilla, and a close-up of bullous lesions on the right upper extremity.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 8,900 cells/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000) with 47% polymorphonuclear leukocytes and 38% band forms (Terminology: Newly created neutrophils have a band-like nucleus visible under the microscope. The presence of many bands suggest the immune system is making a large number of new white blood cells, indicating severe infection.). A radiograph revealed extensive air in the soft tissues (Only a small number of bacteria that can infect soft tissues produces gas that can be seen on radiographs and occasionally felt on examination. Notably, anaerobic bacteria such as Clostridium are gas-producers.).

High-dose penicillin (Though penicillin has a relatively narrow spectrum of activity and many current pathogens are resistant to it, it remains the most potent agent for several important infections. The distinction between the breadth of activity against multiple organisms and potency against specific organisms is an important principle in infectious diseases and underlies the difference between empiric and targeted therapy. The availability of resources, including medications, may also play a significant role in treatment decisions.) was administered intravenously and an emergent right forequarter amputation (Rapid removal of the source of infection can be essential and life-saving in severe soft tissue infection. In some circumstances, it is crucial not to lose time with diagnostic maneuvers or medical therapies if it delays necessary excision of involved tissue. In general, when infections have killed significant amounts of tissue, this tissue must be removed for the infection to be cleared.) was performed.
diagnosis:
Spontaneous Clostridium septicum gas gangrene, associated with colonic carcinoma.

An aspirate of one of the bullous lesions revealed gram positive rods. Figure 3 shows a gram stain of the aspirate from a bullous lesion. Figure 4, a tissue gram stain of muscle resected at the time of surgery, reveals many gram-positive rods. Surgical cultures grew Clostridium septicum.
Figure 3. Gram stain of the aspirate.
Figure 4. Tissue gram stain.

In retrospect, the patient also reported a history of bright red blood per rectum of several months' duration, and evaluation revealed an invasive colonic carcinoma (The appearance of an unusual infection should prompt evaluation for possible undiagnosed underlying illness that acted as a predisposing factor. In particular, cryptic gastrointestinal malignancy can increase the risk of several infections, such as this one.).

The features of this case that suggest clostridial gas gangrene are the rapidly progressive course and the presence of gas in the tissue.
Group A Streptococcus can cause a fulminant necrotizing fasciitis (Terminology: Fulminant necrotizing fasciitis is a severe, life-threatening infection of the deep soft tissues where infection causes tissue destruction and cell-death.) with bullous lesions, but the organism does not produce gas in the tissues. Vibrio vulnificus generally causes severe infection in individuals with underlying liver disease; this patient had no such history.
Clostridial gas gangrene is generally divided into traumatic gas gangrene (which occurs after surgery or injury) and spontaneous gas gangrene. Traumatic gas gangrene is most often due to C. perfringens, and is sometimes due to C. septicum, C. novyi, C. sordellii and other Clostridium species. In contrast, and as in this case, spontaneous gas gangrene occurs without any apparent preceding trauma. The most common cause is C. septicum. Preexisting lesions include either gastrointestinal diseases (such as colon tumor, intestinal surgery, mucosal ulceration) or systemic illnesses (such as diabetes mellitus, leukemia, neutropenia or cirrhosis). C. septicum infection has been associated with malignancy. In one series of 162 patients with C. septicum infection, 81% had a malignancy and in 37% the cancer was occult. The most common neoplasms were colorectal cancer (as in this case) and hematologic malignancies.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman developed fever after visiting
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman developed fever after visiting Haiti.
A woman in her sixties, living in the United States, returned for a visit to her family (In Travel Medicine, the setting of people returning to their home country to visit friends and relatives is so common and so important that it has its own acronym: VFR. People in this category often do not obtain recommended vaccines or prophylaxis and sometimes do not even report having traveled. Patients may believe that they are immune to locally prevalent diseases, unaware that immunity wanes with time.) in Haiti. One week following her return to the United States, she developed fevers to 103°F (39.4°C), rigors, lethargy, and shortness of breath.

She had recently traveled to Haiti (Obtaining a detailed travel history is critical for anyone presenting with an unexplained febrile illness. Several studies show how often this is missed. Usually, travel to a tropical climate entails increased risk of mosquito-borne infections such as dengue and water-borne infections such as typhoid fever.).
exam_studies:
Her temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), and the pulse was 100 beats per minute. She was diaphoretic (vocabulary: sweating), oriented but lethargic, and had bilateral crackles (Rales, indicating fluid build up in the lungs) on lung examination.

The hematocrit was 20% (Markedly anemic, suggestive of a process with destruction of red blood cells.). The blood smear is shown in Figure 1. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 1900 U/L. Chest radiography showed bilateral diffuse air space disease.
Figure 1. Blood smear.

She rapidly developed worsening mental status, anuric renal failure, and respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
diagnosis:
Severe malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum.

Examination of the peripheral blood smear showed numerous intra-erythrocytic ring forms including some with double rings (Figure 1), gametocytes (Figure 2), and schizonts (Figure 3) consistent with Plasmodium falciparum. Estimated initial parasitemia was 20%.
Figure 2. Blood smear with gametocyte.
Figure 3. Blood smear with schizont.

Severe malaria is a common cause of fever in returning travelers. In this patient, the high parasitemia and possible cerebral, pulmonary, and renal involvement required intubation, dialysis, blood transfusions, and prolonged support in an intensive care unit. She was treated with intravenous quinidine (Classical treatment for malaria caused by P. falciparum was quinine but this is often not available in hospitals. The related anti-arrhythmic, quinidine is used in its place for severe malaria.) and exchange transfusion.

Common causes of fever in travelers returning from Haiti include malaria, dengue, and typhoid fever. This patient had severe malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum (The distinction between P. falciparum and other species is important because the others are not often life-threatening in otherwise healthy people.). Because P. falciparum can infect red blood cells of all ages, the level of parasitemia may be higher with P. falciparum malaria than with P. vivax or P. ovale, which infect young red blood cells. P. falciparum induces expression of knobs on the red blood cell surface which mediate cytoadherence (For this reason, P. falciparum trophozoites are sequestered in the microvasculature, causing end organ damage and, unlike other malarial species, may not be seen in peripheral blood smears.) to endothelial cells and microvascular disease. The result of this microvascular disease may be cerebral, renal, and pulmonary complications, as seen in this case.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with HIV infection and AIDS and
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with HIV infection and AIDS and profuse watery diarrhea.
A woman in her twenties was diagnosed with Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia (PCP) and thrush ten days after delivering a healthy baby. She was subsequently found to be infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and a diagnosis of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) was made. The level of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells was 20 cells/mm³, and the HIV viral RNA level was 485,000 copies/mL. She completed a 21-day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) for the PCP, and began prophylaxis for PCP, Mycobacterium avium complex, and thrush.
Approximately three weeks later, crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and non-bloody, watery diarrhea developed. She reported that the diarrhea smelled “like rotten eggs” and was slimy in consistency. She denied fever, chest pain, cough, headache, vomiting, poor oral intake or any urinary symptoms.

The past history included HIV, AIDS, hypertension, and mild intermittent asthma.

She owned a cat, and denied travel outside of New England.

She lived with her children and another adult relative, and was thought to have contracted HIV from her male sexual partner.

Medications included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength 1 tab) and fluconazole (100 mg) daily, and azithromycin (1200 mg) weekly.
exam_studies:
She appeared comfortable while breathing room air. A flat affect was noted. The temperature was 101.9°F (38.8°C), pulse 120 beats/minute, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. The abdomen was soft, with bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness, and mild rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant. A rectal exam was notable for brown stool, which was negative for occult blood. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 2,600 cells/mm³ (70% neutrophils, 2% bands, 19% lymphocytes, and 2% atypical lymphocytes). The hematocrit was 29.9%. Laboratory test results of serum electrolytes, renal function, and liver function were normal.
Serologic testing performed during her prior admission for syphilis (RPR), toxoplasmosis, hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis B virus surface antigen and hepatitis B surface antibody was negative; testing for cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin (Ig) G and varicella-zoster virus IgG was positive.
Although she did not appear toxic, the abdominal exam was concerning for peritonitis. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed with both oral and intravenous contrast (Figures 1 and 2). The bowel wall was significantly thickened, suggestive of colitis. Due to her ongoing antibiotic exposure as well her profound immunosuppression, infectious colitis was thought to be likely.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 2. Abdominal CT scan.

She was admitted and given metronidazole as well as intravenous fluid resuscitation. Three stool tests were negative for Clostridium difficile toxin. She underwent a colonoscopy and biopsy. (See Figures 3, 4 and 5.)
Figure 3. Colonoscopy images.
Figure 4. Histopathology stain of biopsy.
Figure 5. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of biopsy.
diagnosis:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Blood cultures and stool cultures were negative. Colonoscopy demonstrated patches of inflammation throughout the colon with friable mucosa, but no pseudomembranes. Histopathology demonstrated a dense inflammatory infiltrate, and hematoxylin-eosin stain of the epithelium revealed viral inclusion bodies (Figures 4 and 5). Immunoperoxidase staining with a monoclonal antibody specific for cytomegalovirus (CMV) confirmed the diagnosis of CMV colitis (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Immunoperoxidase stain of biopsy.

The CMV viral load by hybrid capture was 377 pg/mL (lower limit of detection is 1 pg/mL) and intravenous ganciclovir was begun. After one week, the CMV viral load had decreased to 1.2 pg/mL and ganciclovir was changed to oral valganciclovir. Ganciclovir therapy was complicated by the development of neutropenia, for which granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) was administered. As there was concern that an immune reconstitution syndrome may increase her symptoms, antiretroviral medications were not started until she had recovered clinically and was able to tolerate a normal diet with no abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Following discharge, she did well on antiretroviral therapy, and had an undetectable HIV RNA viral load and a slowly recovering CD4 T-lymphocyte count. She remained on secondary prophylaxis for both Pneumocystis and CMV.

Cytomegalovirus colitis is a potentially life-threatening opportunistic infection in patients with profound immunosuppression. In patients with HIV, gastrointestinal disease with CMV is most common when the CD4 cell count is less than 50/mm³. Esophagitis seems to be the most common manifestation of GI involvement by CMV, but any region of the GI tract can be involved. Diagnosis of CMV colitis is based on pathologic findings.
Intravenous ganciclovir is the best-studied therapy for CMV. Based on clinical data in the treatment of CMV retinitis, valganciclovir is likely to have a significant role in the therapy of end-organ CMV disease.
Over the long-term, antiretroviral therapy and immune reconstitution are likely the most effective therapy. While in the past lifelong secondary prophylaxis was recommended for life after an episode of CMV disease, the advent of highly-active antiretroviral therapy has led to remarkable improvements in immunological and clinical parameters in patients with advanced HIV. Evidence from case series suggest that secondary prophylaxis against CMV can be discontinued when a patient has a sustained CD4 T-lymphocyte count above 100-150 cells/mm³ as long as there is no evidence of active infection and with close follow-up by an ophthalmologist.

title: A boy with a rash, gastrointestinal symptoms and a fever.
history:
A pre-teen adolescent boy presented with two days of rash, emesis and abdominal pain, and a one-day history of fever up to 38.9°C (102°F) with headache. The rash had begun with finger-swelling and non-erythematous papules on the dorsa of the hands. The rash became erythematous and edematous on the second day and spread to his trunk, arms and legs. He was reluctant to walk because of pain in his knees. He reported no diarrhea, sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, or photophobia.

He had developed swollen lips after eating shrimp.

His younger sibling had an upper respiratory illness and his mother was treated two months earlier for severe pharyngitis. He reported eating shrimp 3 days before admission. His only animal exposure was his pet cat (not a kitten). He reported no history of travel, camping, or known insect exposures. He denied sexual activity.

He lived with his mother and sibling.

There was no family history of inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis or other autoimmune disease.

He had no allergies to medications.

He had taken ibuprofen during preceding 2 days.
exam_studies:
He appeared normally-developed boy, and uncomfortable with use of his hands or legs. The temperature was 40°C (104°F). There was mild periorbital edema and erythematous macules on soft and hard palate. The lower lip was swollen with a yellow blister. The neck was supple, with shotty non-tender cervical nodes, and there was a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur. Painful edema and erythema with petechiae were symmetrically present on the palms and soles. There was tender edema and papular erythema on the dorsal aspects of hands and feet and in a periarticular distribution around elbows and knees. Passive movement of his knees produced minimal pain but the periarticular rash was very tender. (See Figures 1 through 5.)
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding.
Figure 4. Physical finding.
Figure 5. Physical finding.

The hematocrit was 33.9%; the serum level of sodium was 129 mmol/L; chloride 95 mmol/L; bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; and glucose 130 mg/dL. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 6 (normal 0-0.5) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 60 mm per hour. A rapid strep antigen test on a throat swab and a monospot test were negative. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was normal.

The patient was empirically treated with ceftriaxone. Temperatures ranged from 39.0-41.0°C (102.2-105.8°F) during the first 3 hospital days. The diastolic blood pressure was low (35mm Hg) but the systolic blood pressure was normal. The rash persisted, with an increase in petechiae including coalescence, particularly on the soles.
diagnosis:
Papulo-Purpuric Gloves and Socks Syndrome (PPGSS) caused by Parvovirus B19 infection with a superimposed streptococcal pharyngitis.

A serum parvovirus B19 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test from the 4th hospital day was positive. Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin (Ig) G and IgM were negative by indirect immunofluorescence on hospital day 2, but results of convalescent serum 16 days later were positive for both IgM and IgG. This was consistent with the diagnosis of Papulo-Purpuric Gloves and Socks Syndrome (PPGSS) due to acute Parvovirus B19 infection. In addition, Group A Streptococcus grew from the throat, and he had an increase in his antistreptolysin O (ASLO) level, consistent with a superimposed streptococcal pharyngitis.

Coincident with defervescence on the 6th day of the illness, the patient's pain and erythema dramatically improved.He developed pruritus and peeling of the rash during the second week. Leukopenia developed, with the white blood cell count decreasing to 2,400/mm³ (15% eosinophils) on the 6th day. The reticulocyte count reached a nadir of 0.0% on the 6th day, before beginning its recovery 2 days later.
The patient was discharged 1 week after admission and completed 10 days of penicillin for treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis. All pain, edema, and rash resolved completely.

Papulo-Purpuric Gloves and Socks Syndrome (PPGSS) is characterized by progressive, symmetric, painful and pruritic swelling and erythema of the distal extremities. Confluent papular or petechial-purpuric lesions develop on the palms and soles. Subsequently, many patients develop an enanthem. The process is self-limited, lasting 1-2 weeks. This syndrome is usually associated with acute parvovirus B19 infection.

title: A man with a history of leukemia and fever, cough, confusion and dizziness.
history:
A man in his forties developed relapsed acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) two years after an autologous transplant, and underwent haplo-identical peripheral blood stem cell transplant.
Because of T-cell depletion of the graft, the lymphocyte count remained severely depleted throughout his subsequent course, although his neutropenia resolved by day 12 after transplant. Following the transplant, intravenous immunoglobulin was administered weekly, and he received monthly pentamidine and itraconazole prophylaxis. On day 132 post-transplant, he was admitted because of fever, with a temperature to 40.5°C (104.9°F), and dry cough, with clear rhinorrhea.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed ground-glass opacity in the left upper lobe (Figure 1).
Blood cultures grew coagulase-negative staphylococci. Vancomycin and cefepime were administered and he defervesced. He continued his prophylactic medications as before.
Six days later, he returned for evaluation because of dizziness, lethargy and intermittent confusion, as well as persistent respiratory symptoms. He had problems with balance and reported nausea and vomiting, with no headaches or focal neurologic deficits.
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.

See above.

He did not smoke or drink alcohol, or have pet or travel exposures.

He was married.

His medications included cefepime, vancomycin, valaciclovir, itraconazole, monthly pentamidine, intravenous immunoglobulin and megestrol acetate.
exam_studies:
The patient was somnolent but arousable. The temperature was 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 139/93 mm Hg, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96%. Neurological examination revealed that he was fully oriented, had slow but appropriate responses to questions, and cranial nerves were intact. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 7,500/mm³ (77% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 13% lymphocytes, 10% monocytes, and 0% eosinophils), hematocrit 35% and platelets 33,000/mm³. Results of laboratory testing of serum chemistries, including liver function tests, were normal. A chest radiograph showed no infiltrates or effusions. CT of the head showed pan-sinusitis and multiple lesions in the cerebellum, and in the deep gray matter and the temporal areas. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the head, with gadolinium, showed multiple enhancing lesions (2 mm to 5 cm in diameter). (See Figure 2.)
He was admitted to the hospital. Liposomal amphotericin was administered for presumptive fungal sinusitis and brain abscess.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan with gadolinium.

The patient developed seizure activity and his mental and respiratory condition progressively deteriorated. Comfort measures were instituted and he expired soon after admission. An autopsy was performed.
Hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stains of brain and lung tissue are shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. H and E stain of brain tissue.
Figure 4. H and E stain of lung tissue.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Acanthamoeba castellanii in a patient status post peripheral blood stem cell transplant for acute myelogenous leukemia.

The autopsy revealed amebic encephalitis and necrotizing amebic pneumonia with granulomatous features. Pathological examination of sections of brain and lung revealed marked perivascular acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate with large “histiocytoid” appearing Acanthamoeba trophozoites. Meningeal involvement was absent. Immunofluorescent staining of the tissue performed at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identified the amebae as Acanthamoeba castellanii (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Fluorescent stain.

Acanthamoeba are ubiquitous in the environment. Portals of entry include upper respiratory tract and skin. The organism can cause encephalitis and disseminated disease in immunosuppressed patients. Disease due to Acanthamoeba may present sub-acutely, as opposed to Naegleria, which usually presents fulminantly. Clinical manifestations of Acanthamoeba infection include sinusitis, skin nodules, pneumonia and encephalitis. Once central nervous system dissemination occurs, clinical deterioration may be rapid.

title: A man with abdominal pain and distension for two days.
history:
A man in his forties living in the Middle East presented with a two-day history of moderate abdominal pain and distention. These symptoms were preceded by anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. He denied any change in bowel habits. His wife had presented three days earlier with a skin lesion over the upper lip. (See Figure 1, which shows a skin lesion over the upper lip of the patient's wife.)
Figure 1. Physical finding for spouse.

Non-contributory.

He did not smoke, or have a history of drug or heavy alcohol use. He worked as a shepherd and was in close contact with animals. Goats were the principal source of meat for his family, and the meat was sometimes consumed raw. The patient did not report any history of travel outside of Lebanon.
exam_studies:
The patient was in shock, with a faint pulse and undetectable blood pressure. The temperature was 38.3°C (100.9°F) and respirations 30 breaths per minute. Abdominal distention was prominent with evidence of ascites. A doughy mass could be felt in the peri-umbilical area.

Laboratory studies, including white blood cell count (WBC) and differential, were normal.

The patient underwent a laparotomy, which revealed massive ascites, enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes and edema in the cecum and the adjacent loop of small bowel (Figure 2). The laparotomy showed extensive edema involving the cecum.
Figure 2. Findings on laparotomy.
diagnosis:
Intestinal anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis.

Gram stain of ascitic fluid revealed gram-positive bacilli with central spores (Figure 3). Pathological examination of an excised mesenteric lymph node revealed gram-positive bacilli (Figure 4).
Ascitic fluid as well as cultures of lymph node tissue yielded large, non-motile, non-hemolytic colonies that stained as gram-positive bacilli and were catalase positive. The organism was susceptible to penicillin, and was identified as Bacillus anthracis. This was confirmed at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention by Dr. Philip S. Brachman.
Figure 3. Gram stain of ascitic fluid.
Figure 4. Mesenteric lymph node.

The patient received intravenous penicillin but despite aggressive resuscitative measures and antibiotic therapy, he expired 24 hours after presentation. His wife was diagnosed with cutaneous anthrax. She received penicillin and had an uneventful recovery.

Intestinal anthrax follows the ingestion of contaminated meat. There are three phases that progress over 2-5 days. The first phase includes non-specific symptoms of anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. This is followed by abdominal pain, hematemesis and bloody diarrhea. Lastly, toxemia, shock, cyanosis, and even death may occur. Lesions are frequently seen in the cecum and large intestine. At laparotomy, massive ascites, bowel edema and mesenteric lymphadenopathy may be seen.

title: A man with AIDS, fever and a cough.
history:
A man in his fifties with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) presented with fever, fatigue and dry cough of two weeks' duration. He had not improved on oral erythromycin. He denied hemoptysis, chest pain or gastrointestinal symptoms.

Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) had been diagnosed 6 months before this presentation, and he had recently had Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia, for which he had received adjunctive steroids.

He consumed 1-2 beers per day, smoked marijuana occasionally and had recently stopped smoking. There was no history of travel, or exposures to tuberculosis, animals or sick contacts.

Medications included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (1 double-strength daily), zidovudine (AZT) and lamivudine (3TC).
exam_studies:
He was cachectic, with mild respiratory distress. The temperature was 100.8°F (38.2°C), blood pressure 96/45mm Hg, pulse 110 beats per minute, and respiration 30 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 91%. There were bronchial sounds in the upper lobes with egophony and inspiratory rales, and non-tender mild hepatomegaly, but no lymphadenopathy.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 2,900/mm³ (70% neutrophils) and CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 46 cells/mm³. The results of serum chemistries testing were normal. A chest radiograph (Figure 1) and computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) are shown.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Pathological examination of tissue from needle aspiration of the right lung showed necrotic material containing narrow, septated hyphae with acute angle branching (Figure 3). Cultures from the lung aspirate grew Aspergillus (Figure 4).
Figure 3. Stain of lung aspirate.
Figure 4. Stain of culture growth from lung aspirate.

The patient was treated first with intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ceftriaxone. Three sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). The antibiotics were changed to itraconazole with poor response; the patient died after three weeks of therapy.

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis occurs most commonly in patients who are significantly immunocompromised, including patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infections who are neutropenic, have CD4 T-lymphocyte levels less than 50 per cubic millimeter, and those who have been receiving corticosteroid therapy. Mortality rates are high. Efforts to improve clinical outcomes include development of better diagnostic tests that can lead to earlier diagnosis and the development of more effective antifungal agents.

title: A man with fever and cough.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with a fever and cough of 10 days' duration. Amoxicillin was administered, with no improvement.

Diabetes mellitus had been diagnosed 5 years earlier, and the level of fasting plasma glucose was 180 mg/dL 3 months before presentation.

He was a farmer and lived in the Northeastern region of Thailand.

Medications included chlorpropamide; however, there was a history of poor compliance.
exam_studies:
He appeared dyspneic. The temperature was 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse 120 beats per minute, respirations 26 breaths per minute. There were coarse crepitations over the right lung field, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 39%, white blood cell count (WBC) 14,300/mm³ (95% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes), and platelets 107,000/mm³. The serum level of blood glucose was 210 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 24 mg/dl, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dl. A chest radiograph revealed pulmonary infiltrates in the right lung (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Blood cultures were sterile. Multiple sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Gram stain of the sputum is shown in Figure 2, and results of sputum culture in Figure 3. The culture had a musty odor.
Figure 2. Sputum gram stain.
Figure 3. Sputum culture.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, in a patient with diabetes mellitus.

The clinical presentation, gram stain and culture are consistent with melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei.

The patient treated with cefazolin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol. The organism was resistant to cefazolin. After 2 additional weeks of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol, he was continued on oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and doxycycline for 3 more months.

Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a gram-negative bacillus and soil parasite. The organism is on the bioterrorism agent list. Melioidosis is prevalent among Australian aboriginal populations and in Southeast Asia. B. pseudomallei can cause pneumonia (sometimes cavitary, similar to tuberculosis), abscesses and septicemia.

title: A man with fever and headaches.
history:
A man in his twenties presented with a three-day history of fever, memory loss, and severe headaches.

He had diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic headaches for 1 year, and end-stage renal disease, and was on hemodialysis.

He was from Mexico, worked in agriculture, and had traveled home during previous year. He reported no animal exposures.

There was no history of smoking, drug use, or alcohol.

Medications included enalapril, atenolol, and calcium acetate.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and tachypneic. The temperature was 38.1°C (100.6°F), blood pressure 225/113 mm Hg, pulse 134 beats per minute, and respirations 35 breaths per minute. He was alert, but oriented to self only. The site of a hemodialysis catheter located in the right subclavian vein appeared normal. There was nystagmus on right lateral gaze and the reflexes were hypoactive throughout.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 15,800/mm³ and the serum level of sodium was 124 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL, and creatinine 6.0 mg/dL. A chest radiograph was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head revealed lepto-meningeal enhancement of the midbrain (Figure 1).

The patient was intubated for respiratory failure. He was treated empirically with four drug anti-tuberculosis therapy and intravenous amphotericin B and 5-fluorocytosine (5-FC). An external ventriculostomy drain was placed.
Analysis of ventricular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 133 white cells per cubic millimeter (51% neutrophils, 26% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes) and 291 red cells/mm³, with a protein level of 44 mg/dl and glucose level of 57 mg/dl. Analysis of the CSF for cryptococcal antigen, Histoplasma antigen, and herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and an acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear were negative, and bacterial cultures were sterile. Serum tests for cryptococcal antigen and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody were negative. A cerebral magnetic resonance (MR) study with angiography showed diffuse bilateral vasculitis and infarctions.
Fungal cultures on blood agar plate (Figure 2) and Sabouraud plate (Figure 3) are shown. Growth in AFB broth culture is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 1. Blood agar plate.
Figure 2. Blood agar plate.
Figure 3. AFB broth culture.
Figure 4. AFB broth culture.
diagnosis:
Coccidioidal meningitis, caused by Coccidioides immitis, with vasculitic infarctions in a patient with diabetes mellitus and end-stage renal disease.

The complement fixation tests for Coccidioides immitis antibody in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum were positive.

He received intravenous itraconazole and intrathecal amphotericin B. Unfortunately, he remained comatose. In consultation with the family, medical support was withdrawn, and he expired.

Meningitis is the most serious complication of Coccidioides infection, and typically involves basilar meninges. Vasculitic strokes are seen on computed tomography (CT) scanning in 40% of patients, and are associated with 70% mortality.
