title: A man with scrotal pain.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with scrotal pain of 12 weeks duration, which had failed to respond to several courses of oral antibiotics. He was hospitalized for refractory epididymitis and hyponatremia. Orchiectomy was performed after he did not improve with intravenous antibiotics. Empiric anti-tuberculous therapy was initiated pending pathology results.
On the third post-operative day, mental status changes developed that were felt to be attributable to pain medication and metabolic abnormalities. Two days later, he developed weakness on his right side. Family members reported he had had recent sweats but no fever.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension.

He lived in Northern California. He had moved to the United States from India 20 years earlier, and had not traveled recently.

He lived with his wife and did not smoke or drink alcohol.

Medications included insulin, atenolol, and hydrocodone-acetaminophen.
exam_studies:
The patient was thin. The temperature was 97.8°F (36.6°C). The neck was supple; the bowel sounds were hypoactive, and there was tenderness in all quadrants of the abdomen, extending into the inguinal regions. On neurologic examination, he was unintelligible and unable to follow commands. There was a right facial droop and right upper and lower extremity weakness.

The level of sodium was 126 mmol/L, glucose 220 mg/dL, white blood cell count (WBC) 8,900 cells/mm³. CD4 T-lymphocytes 224 cells/mm³ (38% of total lymphs). Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed white cells of 353 cells/mm³ (89% lymphocytes), glucose 31 mg/dL, and protein 2,400. A stain for acid fast bacilli (AFB) was negative.
A chest radiograph showed no active disease or scarring. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of spine showed diffuse enhancement of the spinal cord between the T2-T6 thoracic verebrae, that was thought to be consistent with pachymeningitis, with no obstruction or focal defect. Results of a head MRI scan are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Head MRI scan.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan.

Pathological examination of the scrotal tissue is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Pathology of scrotal tissue.
diagnosis:
Disseminated tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis including tuberculous epididymitis, prostatitis, pneumonitis, pachymeningitis and numerous tuberculomas of the brain in a patient with diabetes mellitus.
References:

Wise GJ, Shteynshlyuger A. An update on lower urinary tract tuberculosis. Curr Urol Rep. 2008 Jul;9(4):305-13. PMID: 18765130

Staining of the scrotal tissue for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) is shown in Figure 4. Culture of an induced sputum specimen grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which was resistant to isoniazid (INH).
Figure 4. AFB stain of scrotal tissue.

The patient was treated with anti-tuberculous therapy and steroids, with initial improvement. The subsequent course was notable for lower extremity weakness and a thoracic epidural abscess, urinary retention and evidence of granulomas on prostate biopsy, and worsening mental status and neurologic signs when steroids were tapered.

title: A man with skin nodules on the right arm.
history:
A man in his sixties presented with nodular skin lesions on his right upper arm.
In the spring, he had gone fishing in the Gulf of Mexico. His hook had inadvertently caught a rusty crab trap and, while attempting to free his hook, he had sustained a superficial, right dorsal hand laceration that never completely healed. Though it was not painful, it was mildly erythematous and spontaneously drained yellow purulent material. Over the following two months, four more lesions developed proximal to the initial lesion. He reported no history of fevers, chills or sweats.

Non-contributory.

He owned two dogs. His hobbies include fishing and gardening; he reported no rose bush, hay or sphagnum moss exposures.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.2°F (36.8°C), pulse 61 beats per minute, and blood pressure 125/76 mm Hg. There were 3 erythematous nodular lesions (1-3 cm in diameter) on the right upper arm and 2 smaller subcutaneous nodular lesions, with no erythema (Figures 1 and 2). The examination was otherwise normal, with no lymphangitic streaking or lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

Results of laboratory tests were normal.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium marinum skin infection.

Biopsy of the forearm lesion revealed caseating granulomas; special stains and cultures were negative. An incision and drainage procedure of the dorsal hand lesion was performed. The acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain was negative; however, the culture grew Mycobacterium marinum.

Treatment with doxycycline was initiated. After 10 weeks of therapy, four of the five lesions had almost completely regressed. One lesion persisted, but was markedly decreased in size.

Mycobacterium marinum may cause cutaneous infection after an exposure to contaminated waters. The organism grows poorly at temperatures greater than 37°C, which can contribute to the typical distribution of the skin lesions over upper and lower extremities.

title: A man with skin nodules.
history:
A man in his twenties presented with a one-month history of a nodular exanthem that developed over his right forearm and head. The rash was not tender or pruritic, and had failed to improve after an empiric course of cephalexin. He reported no history of weight loss, fever, loss of appetite, cough, chest pain or diarrhea.

He had immigrated to the United States from an island in the Pacific two years before. There was no history of illicit drug use, or exposures to pets or other animals.
exam_studies:
He appeared well-nourished. The temperature was normal. There were erythematous maculopapular lesions on his forehead and malar areas, right tragus and pinna. A confluent, raised plaque-like area along the right forearm had decreased sensation to pinprick testing. There was a similar nodule on the dorsum of the right second metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, with synovial thickening along the extensor digitorum longus tendons. (See Figures 1, 2, and 3.) The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding.

Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Test results for the complete blood count (CBC) and serum chemistries were normal.
diagnosis:
Lepromatous leprosy.

A skin biopsy was performed, and pathologicial examination of the tissue with Kinyoun stain is shown (Figure 4), revealing organisms consistent with Mycobacterium leprae.
Figure 4. Kinyoun stain of skin biopsy.

The patient was treated with dapsone, rifampin and clofazimine. At one-month follow-up, lesions were regressing in size and erythema, and no new neurologic lesions had developed.

Mycobacterium leprae grows best at 27-33°C, and lesions of leprosy seem to have a predilection for cooler areas of the skin. Lepromatous leprosy is characterized by multibacillary disease, with erythematous macules, papules and/or nodules. Nerve damage results either from direct bacterial invasion or perineural granulomatous inflammation.

title: A man with vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and headaches.
history:
A man in his twenties was transferred from another hospital in spring with a nine-day history of vomiting, diarrhea, fever and headaches. At the first hospital, results of computed tomography (CT) of the head and abdomen, analysis of cerebrospinal fluid from a lumbar puncture, trans-esophageal echocardiogram and three blood cultures had been negative.

Negative.

He had a seven pack-year smoking history, and did not drink alcohol or use drugs. There was no recent travel history or tick bites. He worked in a correctional institution, and lived on a farm with goats, chickens, guinea pigs, turkeys, cats and dogs.
exam_studies:
He was obese and appeared acutely ill. The temperature was 104.4°F (40.2°C), pulse 98 beats/minute, respirations 20 breaths/minute, and blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The level of hemoglobin was 11.6 grams/dL and the white blood cell count (WBC) was normal. The level of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 111 U/L (normal 20-60), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 79 U/L (normal 20-60), and alkaline phosphatase 146 U/L (normal 40-125); the bilirubin level was normal. Serological tests for anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), syphilis (RPR), and exposure to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis viruses A, B, and C, Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) were negative.
A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT) scan showed hepatosplenomegaly and mild fatty infiltration of the liver. Examination of tissue from a bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable.

A liver biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of the tissue from the liver biopsy is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Liver biopsy.
Figure 2. Liver biopsy.
diagnosis:
Q fever caused by Coxiella burnetii.

The pathological examination of the liver biopsy revealed “doughnut” granulomas (Figures 1 and 2). Q fever serology was negative at week 2 and week 4 after the onset of illness, but at week 8, serological testing showed an immunoglobulin (Ig) M titer greater or equal to 1:10 and IgG greater or equal to 1:1280.

The patient was treated with doxycycline and rifampin for a total course of 6 weeks' duration. His fever resolved and the liver enzymes returned to normal levels one month after the onset of the illness. By the second month, he was completely well.

Coxiella burnetii, the agent of Q fever, is contracted through exposure to infected ruminants (parturient goats, cattle, sheep). Transmission mainly occurs by inhalation. Q fever is highly infectious, and may be a possible bioterrorism agent. Acute disease usually presents with high fever, pneumonia or hepatitis. The pathologic finding of "doughnut" granuloma is characteristic of Q fever, but may be seen in Hodgkin's disease, allopurinol hypersensitivity, Epstein-Barr virus infection, cytomegalovirus infection, and Salmonella typhi and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections.

title: A middle-aged man with a low-grade fever and cough.
history:
A man in his fifties with a significant smoking history presented to the emergency department with symptoms of low-grade fever and non-productive cough. A chest radiograph revealed a left lung nodular lesion near the pleura, with no infiltrate. He was subsequently referred for computed tomoraphy (CT) scan of the chest and further evaluation.

He had a history of alcohol abuse.

The patient lived in a rural area of Arkansas. He had several pets including a skunk, a python, and several dogs. His pets did not receive regular veterinary care. He had smoked 2-3 packs of cigarettes per day for decades, and reportedly drank several beers per day. He denied recent travel.
exam_studies:
He was a thin, white male who appeared older than his stated age. The temperature was 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 158/85 mm Hg, pulse 62 beats per minute, and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The lungs were clear, and the remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) and differential were normal, as were the results of other laboratory tests.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a left lung nodule (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.

A thoracotomy with resection of the lung nodule was performed. The pathology results are shown (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Pathology of resected lung nodule.
diagnosis:
Dirofilaria immitis pulmonary nodule.

Pathological examination of the lung tissue revealed a rounded area of coagulative necrosis bordered by a layer of granulomatous inflammation. In the center of the lesion, there was a parasite measuring 200 microns in diameter possessing a thick cuticle (Figure 2). The findings were consistent with a microfilaria of Dirofilaria immitis (dog heartworm).

The patient recovered quickly post-operatively and was discharged home without further treatment, to follow-up with his primary care provider.

Dirofilaria immitis (dog heartworm) is transmitted by the mosquito. Its most common host is the dog; humans are dead-end hosts. The parasites develop in the subcutaneous tissues and migrate to the right side of the heart and pulmonary vessels. In humans, the immature filariae die, causing a local vasculitis and pulmonary infarction. May present with cough, chest pain or hemoptysis. Most patients are asymptomatic with a “coin” lesion discovered incidentally.

title: A woman with confusion and leg pain.
history:
A woman in her fifties from Korea presented with confusion and severe pain in both legs, of one day's duration.

There was a history of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and cirrhosis. She was status post resection of breast cancer more than a decade earlier and status post hemicolectomy for colon cancer 6 months before admission.

She had immigrated to United States more than a decade earlier, and lived alone in suburban New York. She drank alcohol socially, and did not smoke or use intravenous drugs. There was no history of recent travel. She had had lunch in a Chinese restaurant one day before admission, and had no history of recent trauma or exposure to fresh water or salt water.

Lamivudine had been started 3 months earlier.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared drowsy, disoriented, and uncomfortable. The temperature was 104°F (40°C), blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats per minute, and respirations 22 breaths per minute. Sclera and skin were icteric. She was confused, but the neurological examination was otherwise non-focal. Physical findings of the legs are shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 4,200/mm³ (band forms 39%); hematocrit 29% and platelet count 30,000/mm³. The level of bilirubin was 4.8 mg/dL (direct 2.7 mg/dL); aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 29 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 60 U/L, creatine kinase (CPK) 94 U/L, prothrombin time (PT) 15.7 seconds, INR 1.9, partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 47 seconds and fibrin split products (FSP) were greater than 40.
diagnosis:
Vibrio vulnificus infection.

The patient underwent surgical debridement. Cultures from the tissue obtained during debridement grew Vibrio vulnificus. Blood cultures were negative.

The patient responded to treatment with ceftazidime and doxycycline, and was finally discharged after three weeks of therapy.

Over 300 cases of Vibrio vulnificus infections have been reported to the Center for Disease Control (CDC) since 1988, with the majority from the Gulf coast states. Most cases occur during warmer months when water temperature is high enough to allow rapid growth of the organism. Nearly all oysters harvested in the summer from Chesapeake Bay contain the pathogen, as do 10% of crabs. Cirrhosis is the most common predisposing risk factor for septicemia.
Three clinical syndromes have been described: septicemia, wound infection and GI illness. Blood cultures are usually positive in patients with septicemia. Case fatality rates are as high as 40 to 50% in patients with septicemia. Prognosis is usually good in patient with wound infection and gastrointestinal illness with no predisposing condition. Patients with cirrhosis and other chronic illness should be warned of the hazards of eating raw oysters or exposure of wounds to seawater.

title: A woman with left calf pain.
history:
A woman in her twenties from Thailand presented with a two-month history of progressive left calf pain, exacerbated by walking and relieved by rest. She had also developed low-grade fevers, and had black ulcers on the toes of her left foot, moving to dorsum. Intravenous antibiotics failed to bring improvement, and the 2nd toe on the left foot was amputated.

She had beta-thalassemia/HbE, with a history of previous blood transfusions.

There was no history of drug or alcohol use. She worked as a farmer in Thailand.

Medications included oral contraceptives.
exam_studies:
The patient had a mild pallor. The temperature was 39°C (102.2°F). There were gangrenous wounds on the medial side of the left lower leg, 1st toe, 3rd toe, and dorsum of the left foot. The left popliteal and dorsalis pedis pulses were not palpable. There was mild hepatosplenomegaly, and the remainder of examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 18.4%. The hemoglobin (Hb) typing showed HbE 16%, HbA 77%, Bart’s 3%, and HbH 4%. Echocardiography showed mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, but no evidence of vegetations. Blood cultures were sterile. Wound cultures grew mixed aerobic flora.
An angiogram of the leg showed an arterial occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Left leg angiogram.

Because of severe pain, the patient underwent a below-the-knee amputation and resection of superficial artery of the left leg.
Pathological findings included a thrombotic occlusion at the proximal superficial femoral artery. Histopathology of the arterial wall is seen in Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c. Fungal cultures are shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.
Figure 2. Histopathology of the arterial wall.
Figure 3. Culture results on Sabouraud agar.
Figure 4. Culture results by light microscopy.
Figure 5. Culture results by light microscopy.
diagnosis:
Human pythiosis caused by Pythium insidiosum.

An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for pythiosis was positive but the immunodiffusion test was negative. Figure 4. Culture results by light microscopy. Figure 5. Culture results by light microscopy.

The surgeons caring for the patient were concerned that excision may not be adequate, and the patient was immunized with pythium vaccine. No recurrence was seen after 2 years.

Pythium insidiosum causes a rare, occasionally fatal disease. It was first isolated from a horse in 1902. The first human case reported in Thailand, where the organism appears to be endemic, was in 1985. There are three main clinical presentations: a) cutaneous/subcutaneous lesions; b) ocular disease presenting as corneal ulcers or keratitis and c) systemic disease (most common). Systemic pythiosis often affects vascular tissue, resulting in arterial occlusions leading to gangrene, or aneurysm leading to arterial rupture. Hemoglobinopathy and rice-field work are risk factors.

title: A woman with skin lesions for one month.
history:
A woman in her thirties, status post renal transplant as a youth, presented with a 1-month history of skin lesions. The lesions were distributed on the face, upper chest and forearms. They started as skin-colored, circular to oval, raised lesions, 1-2 cm in diameter. They were painless and did not have any discharge. The lesions developed a central hemorrhagic crust and then healed 1-2 weeks later, while simultaneously, new lesions appeared. The patient also reported generalized headache and chills without fever. There was no focal weakness, seizures or visual changes.

See history of the present illness.

The patient lived in the southwestern United States, and had no history of travel, smoking, drug or alcohol use, or animal exposure.

Medications included prednisone (10 mg daily, which had recently been tapered from 60 mg daily), and tacrolimus (1 mg daily). Mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine had recently been discontinued.
exam_studies:
The patient had cushingoid facies but otherwise appeared well. The temperature was normal. Multiple 1-2 cm lesions were present on the face, upper chest and forearms, with central hemorrhagic crusting and minimal surrounding erythema (Figures 1 and 2). There was minimal tenderness and no discharge. Multiple bruises and petechiae were also present on the extremities. The neurological exam revealed decreased motor strength in all four extremities (3 out of 5). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The hematocrit was 27.9%. The serum level of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was elevated at 2586 U/L. Chest radiography was normal, and testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain.
diagnosis:
Disseminated cryptococcosis, caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, including cutaneous involvement, meningitis, cryptococcomas in the brain and cryptococcemia in a renal transplant patient.

A skin biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of the skin biopsy (Figure 4) showed Cryptococcus capsules on hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stain, confirmed by mucicarmine stain. The serum cryptococcal antigen (Ag) was positive. The cryptococcal antigen (Ag) titer of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was 1:4953. Cultures of the blood and CSF grew Cryptococcus neoformans.
The ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia on the MRI of the brain (Figure 3) were thought to represent cryptococcomas.
Figure 4. Skin biopsy.

Treatment was initiated with Amphotericin B. The skin lesions showed dramatic improvement within one week. However, in the second week of treatment, the patient became more somnolent. Repeat head MRI suggested increased size of the central nervous system (CNS) lesions. The patient declined repeat lumbar puncture or a brain biopsy. One week later the patient had a cardiac arrest and died.
On autopsy, the brain lesions were confirmed to be cryptococcomas.

Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast. Cutaneous cryptococcosis may present with papules, pustules, plaques or ulcers. The lesions often predominate on the face and neck. The lesions may resemble molluscum contagiosum, especially in patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

A nursing home resident in her forties was referred for colonoscopy to evaluate guaiac positive stools.

There was a history of intellectual disability.

The patient was a nursing home resident in an urban area in New England.
exam_studies:
Results of a complete blood count and serum levels of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, and liver function tests were normal.

Colonoscopy was performed. An abnormality seen in the cecum is shown in Figure 1.

Summary: An African woman with fever, abdominal pain and eosinophilia.

history:
Summary: An African woman with fever, abdominal pain and eosinophilia.
A woman in her sixties from West Africa presented with fever, malaise, and abdominal pain. She noted poor oral intake for several weeks and had weight loss of several pounds (1-2 kilograms). She reported no history of nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

She had immigrated to an urban area in New England many years before from West Africa. She lived in a tight knit community and participated in many traditional rituals. She did not drink alcohol.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was 100.6ºF (38.1ºC) and there was tender hepatomegaly; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 9600 cells/mm³ with 35% eosinophils and the hematocrit was 25%. The level of alkaline phosphatase was 299 U/L; other tests of liver function were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed complex liver lesions (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
diagnosis:
Fasciola hepatica infection.

A liver biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of the liver biopsy specimen (Figure 2) demonstrated an eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate. A tunnel-like path, seen in Figure 2, was thought to represent a tract of one of the flukes. Serology returned positive for Fasciola at 1:256. Examination of a stool specimen for ova and parasites demonstrated a single Fasciola hepatica egg.
Figure 2. Pathological exam of liver biopsy.

Triclobendazole was administered, with improvement

Trichinosis, toxocariasis, and Fasciola can all cause significant eosinophilia. However, only Fasciola is associated with an eosinophilic hepatitis.

title:
Summary: An African pre-teen girl with abdominal swelling.
An East African pre-t
history:
Summary: An African pre-teen girl with abdominal swelling.
An East African pre-teen girl noted progressive swelling in her abdomen. She had also had early satiety and round worms in her stools. She denied any fevers or night sweats, clumsiness, vision changes, headaches, dysphagia, changes in her urine, or other complaints.

She had a history of malaria.

She lived with her parents and four siblings on a small farm in East Africa with cows, goats, and a dog. She attended secondary school in the morning and tended the tea fields in the afternoon.
An uncle had tuberculosis and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
exam_studies:
She was a thin well-appearing adolescent female. The temperature was 36.6°C (97.9°F), pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 per minute, and blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg. The oropharynx was clear and there was no nystagmus. Examination of the neck and chest was normal. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, and a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. There was a 10-cm, non-tender, non-mobile abdominal mass palpable in the midline, superior to the umbilicus. Neurological exam had intact cranial nerves (2-12 tested), with no dysmetria or asterixis, and normal deep tendon reflexes (DTRs).

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 8,300/mm³, hematocrit 32%, and platelet count 240,000/mm³. Serum levels of electrolytes and tests of liver functions were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed an indistinct, heterogeneous mass anterior to the stomach. It was not clear if the bowel was involved. The liver and kidneys appeared normal.

An exploratory laparotomy was performed, and a large mass was found in the greater omentum (Figure 1). It was separate from the stomach, small bowel and large bowel.
Figure 1. Findings on surgery.
diagnosis:
Echinococcal cyst, caused by tapeworm species of Echinococcus.

Gross pathologic examination revealed a thick rind surrounding the mass. When the mass was incised, multiple small gelatinous masses were found (Figure 1), which were diagnostic of an echinococcal cyst, caused by tapeworm species of Echinococcus.

The pathologic finding of a primary cyst with multiple daughter cysts within is classic for echinococcal disease. It is important to remove cysts completely, as the daughter cysts are potentially infectious if 'spilled' in vivo and the cyst contents can cause an anaphylactic reaction.

title: Summary: A teenaged girl with fever, headaches, upper respiratory symptoms and i
history:
Summary: A teenaged girl with fever, headaches, upper respiratory symptoms and increasing peri-orbital edema.
A teenaged girl experienced intermittent headaches and purulent rhinorrhea over a three-week period. She developed fever, neck pain, and vomiting. She was hospitalized at an outside hospital and given intravenous fluids for dehydration. Over a twenty-four-hour interval, she developed bilateral peri-orbital edema, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia, and was transferred to this hospital.

Non-contributory.

She was a high school student who lived with her mother. She was not sexually active and had no history of illicit drug use.
exam_studies:
She was alert but toxic- and ill-appearing. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C) with no rash seen. Facial swelling, peri-orbital edema, marked proptosis, chemosis, complete ophthalmoplegia and meningismus were noted. The remainder of the examination was normal. (See Figure 1.)
Figure 1. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 19,700 cells/mm³, with 91% polys, 6% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes. A lumbar puncture had an opening pressure of 26 cm of water. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed red blood cells 83 cells/mm³, white blood cells 87 cells/mm³, with 82% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 10% bands, 1% lymphocytes, and 7% monocytes, glucose 20 mg/dL and total protein 396 mg/dL.
diagnosis:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The patient had a computed tomography (CT) scan performed emergently, which revealed extensive right ethmoid and sphenoid sinusitis, minimal left ethmoid disease, and marked proptosis on the left greater than the right (OS>OD). (See Figure 2.) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated bilateral cavernous sinus enlargement and thrombosis. In addition, there was probable left ophthalmic vein thrombosis, bilateral orbital cellulitis with a possible left medial orbital collection, pituitary enhancement and edema, low attenuation of the clivus suggesting osteomyelitis, and leptomeningeal enhancement.
Figure 2. CT scan of the head.

The patient underwent bilateral lateral canthotomies, drainage of a left medial orbital abscess, and subsequent drainage of a right orbital abscess. Sequential MRI studies documented infarction in the right subinsular region, globus pallidus, and posterior limb of the right internal capsule with preservation of flow in the right middle cerebral artery. These findings were felt to be secondary to basilar meningitis.

A classic finding with cavernous sinus thrombosis is proptosis due to obstruction of venous drainage. Tuberculosis typically causes basilar meningitis, however sinus disease would be quite unusual. Fungal sinusitis alone would not explain the ocular findings. Thyroid storm may present with symptoms of systemic toxicity and proptosis; this condition would not explain the findings on imaging.

title: Summary: A woman in her twenties with an intra-abdominal mass during pregnancy.
history:
Summary: A woman in her twenties with an intra-abdominal mass during pregnancy.
A woman in her twenties presented with an abdominal mass. She was in the late third trimester of pregnancy when she began to experience sharp abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant. The pain increased when she lay on the right side.
She had no other symptoms and specifically denied fever, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash. Due to the persistence of symptoms, a sonographic evaluation was performed that revealed a diaphragmatic hernia of the fetus, as well as a right-sided mass with cystic and solid components that was thought to be ovarian in origin.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen confirmed the fetal diaphragmatic hernia, as well as the complex cystic structure, which measured 12 centimeters by 6 cm. The differential diagnosis of the mass suggested by the radiographic appearance included an ovarian cyst versus tumor.

The patient had immigrated to the United States from the Middle East nearly two decades earlier and had last visited there over ten years before. She reported no recent international travel, and did not own dogs or have occupational exposure to agriculture or livestock. There was no family history of malignancy.
exam_studies:
She appeared healthy and in no distress. The temperature was 98.5°F (36.9°C), heart rate 98 beats per minute and blood pressure 108/64 mm Hg. The abdomen was gravid and not tender. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 11,700 cells/mm³ with 80% neutrophils, 14% bands, 5% monocytes and no eosinophils.

Due to the severity of the fetal hernia, she underwent caesarian section within two weeks of her presentation. She delivered an infant who was subsequently placed on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and transferred to a pediatric hospital for further care. There was an additional intraoperative finding of a thick-walled cyst attached to the right lobe of the liver (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Intra-operative findings.
diagnosis:
Echinococcal cyst (hydatid cyst disease) due to Echinococcus granulosus.

The pathology revealed a fibrous laminated cyst with lens-shaped bodies and scolices diagnostic for echinococcal infection. Figure 2 shows the outer laminar layer of the cyst, while Figure 3 confirms presence of scolices consistent with Echinococcus granulosus.
Figure 2. Stain of surgical specimen.
Figure 3. Stain of surgical specimen.

Cyst removal was attempted but unsuccessful due to an episode of transient hypotension during which the systolic pressure decreased to 50 mm Hg. Hydrocortisone and diphenhydramine were administered, and copious irrigation with hypertonic saline was performed. Praziquantel and albendazole were administered immediately post-operatively. She remained stable, without further evidence of hemodynamic or airway compromise. She was treated with praziquantel for three days and albendazole for three months.

Echinococcus granulosus belongs to the Taenidae family of Cestodes. It is a tapeworm that undergoes its lifecycle in two hosts, typically involving canines and livestock. The highest prevalence of echinococcal disease is in Russia, China, North Africa, Australia, and South America, as well as the Middle East.
Humans with hydatid cyst disease often have a solitary cyst, most commonly occurring in the liver. Patients usually present due to mass effect or as an incidental radiographic finding, although rupture may also occur. Leakage of cyst contents may induce an anaphylactic syndrome, as seen in this case.
Treatment depends on the size and location of the cyst(s). Therapeutic options include surgical excision, PAIR procedure (percutaneous aspiration, injection, re-aspiration), and chemotherapy (albendazole with or without praziquantel). The other considerations in the differential diagnosis are unlikely as amebiasis typically presents with a hepatic abscess that has anchovy paste-like contents. Schistosomiasis causes a pre-portal fibrosis and Echinococcus multicularis presents with an exophytic infiltrating mass.

title:
Summary: A woman with breast cancer and leukemia developed skin lesions.
A woman
history:
Summary: A woman with breast cancer and leukemia developed skin lesions.
A woman in her fifties, with a history of breast cancer and secondary M4 acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), developed multiple raised erythematous skin lesions during a hospitalization for chemotherapeutic treatment of AML. The chemotherapy had resulted in significant neutropenia prior to development of the skin lesions.

There was a history of breast cancer, status post lumpectomy and axillary node dissection, and M4 acute myelogenous leukemia (AML).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, and vital signs were within normal limits. The site of a Hickman intravenous catheter appeared benign. Examination of the skin revealed a number of small palpable erythematous nodules with surrounding satellite lesions (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The absolute neutrophil count was 220 cells/mm³. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen revealed multiple tiny enhancing nodules throughout the liver and spleen.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Candida tropicalis infection in a patient with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and neutropenia.

Culture of a punch biopsy of the skin grew Candida tropicalis.

The patient was treated with liposomal amphotericin.

Patients with hematologic malignancies and neutropenia are at special risk for disseminated Candida infection. Most Candida infections result from traversal of the mucosal barrier of the gastrointestinal tract or from intravenous catheters.
Hematogenous spread of Candida results in protean manifestations in virtually all organ systems, including such findings as microabscesses in the liver and spleen and skin lesions as described here. Cutaneous lesions due to disseminated candidiasis are generally nodules that are 0.5-1 cm in diameter and erythematous. The lesions may be single or scattered over the entire skin surface. Although these lesions may resemble those of ecthyma gangrenosum (which also afflicts neutropenic hosts), the presence of hepatosplenic lesions in this case suggested the diagnosis of disseminated candidiasis.

title: Summary: A woman, status post bone marrow transplant, with a non-productive coug
history:
Summary: A woman, status post bone marrow transplant, with a non-productive cough.
A woman in her forties underwent an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for acute myelocytic leukemia (AML) eight months prior to the onset of her symptoms. Her bone marrow transplant was complicated by graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) requiring tacrolimus (FK506), rapamycin, methotrexate and steroids. In addition, she was enrolled in a trial and received either daclizumab or placebo. She began to note fevers to 101.4°F (38.6°C), and a non-productive cough two days before admission.

She had a history of acute myelocytic leukemia (AML), status post autologous bone marrow transplant, and graft versus host disease (GVHD).

There was no history of travel, sick contacts or pets, and no tobacco or alcohol use.

Her immediate family was healthy.

Medications included prednisone (10 mg per day), rapamycin (3 per day), tacrolimus (2.5 daily), dapsone (100 mg daily), and acyclovir (400 three times daily).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and in moderate respiratory distress. The temperature was 100.2°F (37.9°C), heart rate 124 beats/minute, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. The chest was clear to auscultation.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,100/mm³, hematocrit 31%, and platelets 96,000/mm³.
A chest radiograph showed bibasilar opacities (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest delineated bibasilar infiltrates with nodular features (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.

She was admitted to the hospital; vancomycin and levofloxacin were initiated empirically for pneumonia.
diagnosis:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis in a patient after bone marrow transplantation.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) viral load by hybrid capture was positive at 6.6 pg/ml. Bronchoscopy with trans-bronchial biopsy was sent for culture and pathology. Pathological examination of the specimens showed was chronic inflammation, consistent with diffuse alveolar damage and cytomegalovirus inclusions. In addition, immunohistochemical stains confirmed the presence of CMV (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Immunohistochemical stain of biopsy.

Immunocompromised patients, particularly transplant recipients, are at risk for CMV pneumonitis. Median time to presentation after transplant is approximately 45 days. Patients often present with dry cough and dyspnea.
Radiographic studies may be unremarkable, although ground glass opacification, infiltrates or nodules can be observed. Diagnosis often requires bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with transbronchial biopsy to confirm CMV culture and histologic evidence of infection.

title:
Summary: An 18-month-old boy with fever and cough.
An 18-month-old Peruvian boy
history:
Summary: An 18-month-old boy with fever and cough.
An 18-month-old Peruvian boy presented with fever and cough. Although gastric aspirates were smear-negative and culture-negative for acid-fast organisms, a chest radiograph was thought to be consistent with miliary tuberculosis (Figure 1).
The patient therefore began standard four-drug therapy; however, he failed to improve. Over the following months, the patient developed progressive lower-extremity paralysis.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

None

The child was born in an urban area of Peru, and lived with his mother and an uncle, who had chronic tuberculosis. He had never traveled outside of Peru and had no pets.

Medications included isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide.
exam_studies:
He appeared alert and emaciated. He weighed 10 kg, and was tachypneic and oxygen dependent. There were bilateral rhonchi and dense right-sided râles. A vertebral deformity was present at the 6th-7th thoracic vertebrae, with flaccid paralysis of the lower extremities.

Results of liver function tests were normal. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. A chest radiograph showed progression of right-side infiltrate (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine revealed a mass at the T6-7 thoracic vertebrae with a paravertebral abscess (Figure 3).
Figure 2. Worsening chest radiograph.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the spine.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary tuberculosis caused by multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with Pott's disease (tuberculous spondylitis).

Cultures of gastric aspirates were repeated and eventually grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis that, on drug-susceptibility testing, was found to be multidrug-resistant.

Diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) in children can be difficult; gastric aspirates, induced sputum, bronchoscopy and biopsy of suspected extrapulmonary sites may be helpful. In this case, diagnosis was confirmed after multiple gastric aspirates were performed.
Multidrug-resistance (MDR) should be suspected if the epidemiological exposure is suggestive (e.g. contact with patient who had multiple treatments or died while in treatment or from country with high rates of MDR). Treatment of MDR-TB involves the use of first- and second-line drugs based on the infecting isolates’ antibiogram. The safety of many second-line medications for pediatric cases is largely unknown; however, potential risks of therapy must be weighed against the risks of untreated disease.

Summary: An elderly man with fever and lethargy.
An elderly man, who had not see
history:
Summary: An elderly man with fever and lethargy.
An elderly man, who had not seen a physician in forty years, was in his usual active state of health until four days before admission. At that time, he began to complain of back pain. His appetite declined over the following days and he had subjective fevers. On the day of admission, he became extremely lethargic and complained of right eye pain and blurred vision. While in the emergency room, he had a generalized seizure.

He had no significant past medical history.

The patient was originally from Italy and had immigrated to the United States decades before. He had a remote history of travel to Europe.There was no exposure to pets or sick contacts, and he did not use alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs.
exam_studies:
He was lethargic. The temperature was 96.7°F (35.9°C). The right eye had erythematous conjunctiva and a clouded anterior chamber (Figure 1). He was able to count fingers. Neck stiffness was present; the lungs were clear to auscultation. He was tachycardic and had a II/IV holosystolic apical murmur. There was a diffusely tender abdomen, as well as diffuse lower back pain without point tenderness. His joints were benign and his skin had no rash.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 17,700/mm³ and hematocrit 27%. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 1050 white cells per cubic millimeter (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), 1800 red blood cells per cubic millimeter, glucose 96 mg/dL and total protein 296 mg/dL.

The patient was admitted and broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered for empiric meningitis coverage. Ophthalmologic evaluation was consistent with uveitis and endophthalmitis; he received intravitreal ceftazidime and vancomycin.
A trans-thoracic echocardiogram revealed a mitral vegetation (2-cm) with heterogeneous features (Figure 2). A lumbar epidural abscess at the L4-5 vertebrae and a left psoas abscess were additionally identified by computed tomography (CT).
The patient was noted to have guaiac-positive stools and iron-deficiency anemia; a stomach mass was identified on endoscopy.
Figure 2. Echocardiogram.
diagnosis:
Streptococcus pneumoniae endocarditis with endophthalmitis, meningitis, and multiple septic emboli.

Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Disseminated Streptococcus pneumoniae may present as endocarditis with complications of septic emboli. In this case, an underlying malignancy was a likely risk factor for disseminated streptococcal sepsis. Susceptibility testing of pneumococcal strains should be obtained to guide antibiotic choice.
Staphylococcus and Enterococcus are important organisms to consider when endocarditis is suspected. Meningitis is an unusual complication with either of these organisms but may occur as a complication of high-grade bacteremia and embolic events. Streptococcus bovis is an important organism to consider in the setting of colon cancer. Klebsiella pneumoniae endocarditis is extremely rare.

title:
Summary: A man in his fifties with left facial swelling.
A man in his fifties un
history:
Summary: A man in his fifties with left facial swelling.
A man in his fifties underwent an allogeneic bone-marrow transplant (ABT) for refractory non-Hodgkin's lymphoma nine months prior to presentation. His transplant was complicated by severe graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) which was treated with steroids, infliximab (remicade), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), and FK506. Approximately three weeks prior to admission, he noted left facial swelling, in particular periorbital edema, as well as proptosis.

There was a history of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, status post allogeneic bone marrow transplant, with graft versus host disease.

Medications included prednisone and FK506.
exam_studies:
He was afebrile, with mild periorbital edema and quarter-sized hypoesthesia over left cheek. Vision and extraocular movements intact, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

Computerized tomography (CT) scan revealed left ethmoid and maxillary sinusitis, as well as inferior orbital involvement (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Head CT scan.
diagnosis:
Invasive aspergillosis, caused by Aspergillus fumigatus, in a patient with Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and status post bone marrow transplant.

He underwent a left maxillary sinus debridement. Pathology revealed chronic inflammation with invasive fungal forms. Hyphae with acute angle branching are seen in Figure 2 and suggest a diagnosis of Aspergillus. Samples grew Aspergillus fumigatus on culture.
Figure 2. Aspergillus fumigatus.

Invasive aspergillosis most commonly affects immunocompromised hosts; portal of entry is usually via the lungs or sinuses. Most often, the lung or central nervous system is involved. Treatment is surgical debridement, when possible, as well as antifungal therapy and minimization of immunosuppression. Antifungals with activity against Aspergillus include amphotericin products, as well as more novel therapeutics such as caspofungin and voriconazole.
The clinical presentation of mucormycosis may be indistinguishable from aspergillosis. Invasive aspergillosis is substantially more common, however. On biopsy, Mucor appears as broad based hyphae without septations. Recurrent lymphoma may present as a retroorbital mass, however the associated sinus disease seen in this case would be unusual. Mycobacterium chelonae may cause disseminated infection in immunocompromised patients, but this typically presents with soft tissue nodules.

title: Summary: A man presented with progressive dyspnea, non-productive cough and feve
history:
Summary: A man presented with progressive dyspnea, non-productive cough and fevers.
A man in his forties was admitted to hospital for investigation of progressive dyspnea, non-productive cough and fevers. He had been diagnosed with polymyositis one year before and started on a course of immunosuppressive therapy (prednisone and mycophenolate). Six months after starting the immunosuppressive medications, he noted mild exertional dyspnea. This progressed over two months and he also noted a dry cough. He did not lose weight, but had not gained weight despite continuing on an average daily dose of 60 mg prednisone.

There was a history of polymyositis.

He was originally from Pennsylvania, and was living in urban New England. He worked in the construction industry and had recently traveled to Chicago and Nashville. There was no history of intravenous drug use.

Medications included prednisone (up to 100 mg daily) and mycophenolate (1g twice daily).
exam_studies:
He was thin; the temperature was 101°F (38.3°C), and there were bronchial breath sounds in the left upper lobe.

The white blood cell count was 12,400 cells/mm³ with 90% polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Results of renal and liver function tests were normal, and a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody test and a skin test for tuberculosis (PPD) were negative. His chest radiograph showed extensive bilateral interstitial nodular disease with several areas of cavitation, most notably at the left apex (Figure 1).
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed areas of bronchiectasis and extensive nodular lesions, many cavitating. (See Figures 2 and 3.) There was a larger area of consolidation at the left apex with a large cavity.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.

He underwent bronchoscopy. Culture of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (Figure 4) yielded two fungal forms: a light growth of creamy pale colonies subsequently identified as Candida albicans; and heavier growth of granular gray colonies. The predominant gray colonies were further cultured at 37°C for 5 days, and fluorescence microscopy revealed cells shown in Figure 5.
Figure 4. Culture plate.
Figure 5. Fluorescent stain of gray colony growth.
diagnosis:
Blastomycosis, caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis in an immunocompromised patient.

Culture of the gray mycelial growth yielded yeast cells bearing large, broad bases daughter buds typical of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Identity of the organism was confirmed using a hybrid DNA/RNA probe. Figure 5 shows a fluorescent stain of Blastomyces dermatitidis.

The broad based budding is characteristic of Blastomyces dermatitidis, the least common of the mycoses endemic to the USA. Highly endemic areas include the Midwest states bordering the Great Lakes, and infection is acquired through inhalation of conidia from the environment, usually soil. Disease is more severe in the immunocompromised host and is associated with a higher mortality.

title:

history:
Summary: A man with fever and a gangrenous leg.
A man in his thirties with diet-controlled type II diabetes mellitus had three days of left foot pain and presented to the emergency room where he was diagnosed with left foot cellulitis and hyperosmolar non-ketotic state. Vancomycin, sulbactam and ampicillin were started on admission.
His cellulitis progressed over three days in the hospital despite intravenous antibiotics and he was taken to the operating room for exploration. Pus was seen throughout the muscles in his calf and, consequently, the planned above-ankle Guillotine amputation was extended to a below-the-knee amputation (BKA) which was left open to drain. Operating room cultures and multiple sets of blood cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
He seemed to improve post-operatively and his metabolic derangements resolved quickly. However, he had persistent fevers, despite negative blood cultures, and developed pain and swelling at his left sternoclavicular joint.

He had hypertension, morbid obesity, and Type II diabetes mellitus.

e lived in the northeast United States, and had a sedentary occupation. He did not smoke and reported no history of alcohol abuse, intravenous drug abuse, pets, other animal exposure or recent travel. There was a positive family history for type II diabetes mellitus.

Medications included nafcillin, gentamicin, heparin (subcutaneously), ranitidine and insulin.
exam_studies:
He appeared toxic and tachypneic. The temperature was 102.2°F (39°C), blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg, pulse 115/minute, oxygen saturation 92% on oxygen (5 liters). There was mild tenderness and swelling at his left sternoclavicular joint. The surgical wound looked relatively benign, although there was evidence of necrosis at the distal edges.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 20,100 cells/mm³ (85% neutrophils, 8% bands), hematocrit 41% and platelets 307,000/mm³. The serum level of urea nitrogen (BUN) 48 mg/dL and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. The urinalysis revealed 3+ glucose and 2+ protein. A chest radiograph revealed trace bilateral pleural effusions.

Computed tomography (CT) was performed (Figures 1 through 4).
Figure 1. Sagittal chest CT scan.
Figure 2. Sagittal chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Hematogenous osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Sternoclavicular osteomyelitis was seen on the CT scan (Figure 1). The lung windows of the chest CT scan revealed small, peripheral nodular infiltrates consistent with septic emboli (Figure 4).

A transthoracic echocardiogram was non-diagnostic, but a transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrated a vegetation on his tricuspid valve. His below-the-knee amputation was revised and closed, and he was transferred to a rehabilitation center to complete a six-week course of nafcillin for osteomyelitis and endocarditis. His sternoclavicular osteomyelitis responded slowly to medical therapy and over six months of follow-up, he continued to do well.

Primary hematogenous osteomyelitis is more common in children, but can occur in adults as a consequence of high-grade bacteremia including endocarditis. While vertebral osteomyelitis is a well-known complication of endocarditis, especially in intravenous drug users, seeding of the sternoclavicular joint or the clavicular head has also been described.
Surgical debridement is frequently required. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism implicated.
This case illustrates both the high frequency of acute bacterial endocarditis with S. aureus bacteremia, as well as the high incidence of severe metastatic foci of disease. Patients who have persistent fever or signs of sepsis despite clearance of S. aureus bacteremia with appropriate antibiotics should be thoroughly evaluated for foci of infection.

title:
Summary: A man with fever and bullae on his skin.
A man in his fifties was admit
history:
Summary: A man with fever and bullae on his skin.
A man in his fifties was admitted with nephrolithiasis and urosepsis from Escherichia coli. In the hospital, he developed acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), requiring prolonged ventilatory support and a tracheostomy.
Four weeks into his hospitalization, he developed fevers, respiratory distress, and left lower lobe pneumonia by chest radiograph, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus grew on sputum culture. He was treated with vancomycin, with gradual improvement. Nine days into his course of vancomycin, fever recurred, with no clear source. The next day, he developed a rash.

Medications included vancomycin.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 103.2°F (39.6°C) and the heart rate 84 beats/minute. The skin examination revealed erythematous areas primarily in both axillae, the middle of the back, and the left thigh. On the erythematous base, there were tight bullae, which expressed yellow, serous, nonpurulent fluid when opened. The remainder of the examination was normal. (See Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white cell count (WBC) was 15,700 cells/mm³ (84% neutrophils, 9% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, and 3% eosinophils), and the hematocrit 28.6%. Cultures, including for gonorrhea, of the bullous fluid were negative.
diagnosis:
Linear IgA bullous dermatosis from vancomycin.

The diagnosis was established by a skin biopsy. The hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain showed an inflammatory rich infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction with numerous neutrophils (Figure 3). Immuno-fluorescent stain for immunoglobulin (Ig) A showed IgA deposition on the basement membrane at the dermal-epidermal junction (Figure 4).
Figure 3. Biopsy results.
Figure 4. Immunofluorescent stain.

The vancomycin was discontinued, and the bullae gradually resolved after one week. As this was immunologically mediated, the patient should be considered allergic to vancomycin.

The histology demonstrates necrolysis at the dermal-epidermal junction with IgA deposition seen on immunofluorescence staining. This is diagnostic of bullous dermatosis from vancomycin.
Dermatitis herpetiformis typically presents with grouped vesicles. Bullous pemphigoid, though possible, typically occurs later in life, involves mucosal surfaces and is not triggered by medication. Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and erythema multiforme should be considered; however, the lack of mucosal involvement (for TEN) and the histopathologic tissue reaction exclude these diagnoses.

title: Summary: A man with fever, cough and dyspnea one year after a bone marrow transp
history:
Summary: A man with fever, cough and dyspnea one year after a bone marrow transplant.
A man in his thirties developed weakness, fatigue, dry cough, and progressive exertional dyspnea of 2 days' duration, one year after an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for aplastic anemia. He presented for evaluation.

He had had an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for aplastic anemia, which was complicated by skin and liver graft versus host disease (GVHD), and myasthenia gravis, and was status post thymectomy.

Medications included prednisone (30 mg per day), cyclosporine, mycophenolic acid, and dapsone.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 96.5°F (35.8°C). Oxygen saturation was 89% while breating room air. Skin examination revealed a desquamating rash consistent with his known GVHD. The lung examination revealed diffuse crackles.

The white blood cell count was 9,900 cells/mm³.

Unfortunately, within 3 hours of presentation the patient expired. An autopsy was performed. Pathological examination of tissues obtained at autopsy are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Mucicarmine stain.
Figure 2. Hematoxylin and eosin stain.
diagnosis:
Disseminated cryptococcal infection in a patient status post bone marrow transplantation.

The pathologic appearance of the tissues shown (Figure 2) is consistent with cryptococcosis.

The large capsule seen around each organism on histopathologic evaluation is diagnostic of Cryptococcus. Often, a mucicarmine stain is useful for demonstrating the organism. Cryptococcosis can cause disseminated disease months to years after transplantation.

title:
Summary: A middle-aged man with AML, fevers and a skin eruption.
A middle-aged m
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with AML, fevers and a skin eruption.
A middle-aged man with a history of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and status post an allogeneic bone marrow transplant (BMT), presented with fevers and a skin eruption, which progressed to confluent blisters and necrosis.

As above, there was a history of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and bone marrow transplantation.

The patient had recently received vancomycin and meropenem.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable, with temperatures to 101°F (38.3°C). There was a diffuse blistering skin eruption, which involved the mucous membranes of his mouth and genital region, and conjunctival injection was present. Figure 1. Physical finding. Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The patient’s skin lesions progressed to involve approximately 80% of his body surface area (Figures 1 and 2).
diagnosis:
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

Skin biopsy revealed full thickness epidermal necrosis and subepidermal vesicle formation consistent with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

The patient received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and was treated supportively with aggressive local skin care and intravenous fluids. Unfortunately, he expired due to sepsis.

Erythema multiforme typically presents with target-like macular skin lesions without mucosal involvement. Pemphigus vulgaris is predominantly a bullous skin disorder. The presence of mucosal lesions argues against staphylococcal skin syndrome. A biopsy is the only way to exclude an IgA-associated vancomycin reaction.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is characterized by full thickness epidermal necrosis and is considered part of the spectrum of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Cases with involvement of >30% of the body surface area are labeled as TEN, and mortality rates can be higher than 40%. The majority of cases of TEN are drug-induced. Treatment is largely supportive, although small case series have suggested that IVIg may be beneficial in shortening the duration of symptoms.

title:
Summary: A teenager with osteosarcoma and a question of an "insect bite."
A teen
history:
Summary: A teenager with osteosarcoma and a question of an "insect bite."
A teenaged patient with a history of osteosarcoma of left humerus, 4 months status post resection and bone grafting. The most recent course of chemotherapy was 1 week prior to admission and included methotrexate, doxorubicin and cisplatin. One day before presentation, an “insect bite” on left forearm appeared. The night before, the patient awakened because of sweats and a fever to 102°F (38.9°C), and noted that the insect bite was larger and darker in the center. The patient was seen in an orthopedic clinic, noted to have temperature of 101.2°F (38.4°C, and admitted to the hospital.

There was a history of osteosarcoma of left humerus.

There was no history of alcohol, tobacco or illicit drug use. The patient lived with parents and a younger sibling.

The patient was allergic to amoxicillin (reaction unknown).

Current medications included tetracycline and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF).
exam_studies:
The temperature was 101.2°F (38.4°C), blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 96 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. There was alopecia, a supple neck, and clear lungs; the cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm with 2/6 systolic ejection murmur. The abdomen was soft, without masses or tenderness, and there was no lymphadenopathy. The left upper arm was in a brace, without erythema, swelling or tenderness. The left forearm revealed an area of erythema (6 cm by 4 cm) with necrosis (1 cm area) in the center (Figure 1), and was slightly tender.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 400 cells/mm³, hematocrit 30%, and platelet count 16,000/mm³.
diagnosis:
Ecthyma gangrenosum secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

A punch biopsy of the lesion was performed, and the specimen was sent for culture and Gram’s stain.The gram stain showed numerous gram-negative rods (Figure 2) and the culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Figure 2. Gram stain of skin biopsy.

The patient was empirically started on ticarcillin-clavulinic acid and gentamicin, and defervesced within 48 hours.

Ecthyma gangrenosum is characteristically a round, indurated area with a black eschar and surrounding erythema, as seen in this case. The lesion is usually painless. Although ecthyma gangrenosum is classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis, similar lesions may be seen in sepsis associated with other bacteria, as well as with fungi (such as Candida, Mucor, and Aspergillus). Thus, a stain and culture of a biopsy of the lesion may be helpful in evaluating the underlying etiology.

title:
Summary: A woman in her forties with fever and right hand weakness.
A woman in h
history:
Summary: A woman in her forties with fever and right hand weakness.
A woman in her forties, with a history of sarcoidosis and chronic steroid dependence, was in her usual state of active health until five days before admission when she began to experience fever and symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI).
Two days later, she noted weakness and numbness of the right hand and her right leg also felt weak. On the day of admission, she had difficulty walking and was brought by her family to the emergency room.

She had a history of sarcoidosis with pulmonary, cardiac, hepatic and dermatologic involvement; pulmonary hypertension and a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (AVM). She was on 4 liters of oxygen chronically.

She was originally from West Africa and had immigrated to the United States more than a decade before. She had several children, worked at home, and reported no risk factors for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), recent travel, pet exposure, or sick contacts. She had undergone a dental procedure one month prior to admission.

She had no known drug allergies.

Medications included prednisone 15 mg orally, daily.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 97.6°F (36.4°C), heart rate 90 beats/minute, blood pressure 137/51 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on 4 liters O2. The patient did not appear toxic. Chest examination revealed diffuse dry rales, and the cardiac examination revealed a II/VI systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border. Otherwise, her exam was notable for 4/5 strength of the right upper and lower extremities. Sensation and reflexes were intact.

The white blood cell count (WBC) 5,920/mm³. A chest radiograph showed diffuse interstitial markings, unchanged when compared with a previous film. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed no evidence of bleeding but three hypodense lesions, the largest of which was 3.4 cm by 1.9 cm. No calcification or hemorrhage were noted and there was no mass effect. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed these ring-enhancing lesions with mild vasogenic edema (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Brain MRI scan.

The patient was admitted and meropenem and vancomycin were administered intravenously after initial blood cultures were taken. Blood cultures remained negative and the patient continued to have fevers and worsening lethargy and right-sided weakness. A screening test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
diagnosis:
Streptococcus intermedius brain abscess.

The patient was taken to the operating room for stereotactic biopsy of a brain lesion. The brain biopsy revealed gram-positive cocci in pairs (Figure 2). Brain biopsy grew Streptococcus intermedius (formerly identified as Streptococcus milleri group), in addition to other oral flora.
Echocardiogram demonstrated a right-to-left shunt.
Figure 2. Gram stain of brain biopsy.

The surgery was complicated by right-sided neglect which improved over the following week. Brain biopsy grew Streptococcus intermedius (formerly identified as Streptococcus milleri group), in addition to other oral flora; the patient’s antibiotics were changed to penicillin G 4 million units intravenously every 4 hours, as well as metronidazole 500 mg orally three times daily.
She improved over a month-long hospitalization. Upon discontinuation of her antibiotics, the strength in her right arm had nearly returned to normal.

Bacterial brain abscesses may occur as a result of direct spread or hematogenous seeding. In this situation, the patient’s underlying immunocompromise as well as her right-to-left shunt and recent dental work may have contributed to her condition.
Brain abscesses are often polymicrobial with a common pathogen being among the Streptococcus milleri group. The S. milleri group has a propensity for abscess formation due to its production of proteolytic enzymes. Neurocystercycosis typically presents with cystic brain lesions rather than as abscesses. Actinomyces typically spreads locally. Nocardia and M. tuberculosis may present with this type of radiographic pattern, however the rapid progression over five days would be unusual for these organisms.

title:
Summary: An African woman with weight loss, early satiety and night sweats.
An E
history:
Summary: An African woman with weight loss, early satiety and night sweats.
An East African woman in her thirties presented to the local hospital in western Kenya with an eight-month history of fatigue, weight loss, and early satiety. She reported episodic non-bloody diarrhea, occasional night sweats and weight loss of 10 kilograms (22 pounds).

She had no known chronic illnesses; human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) status was unknown. She has had malaria several times as child, and had given birth to five children, one of whom had died as infant.

She lived in small village in western Kenya, and worked in a family plot growing corn and tea. She reported no alcohol or tobacco use. Her husband occasionally traveled to Nairobi for business. Several family members had tuberculosis, and one sibling had died from AIDS.
exam_studies:
She appeared thin and malnourished. The temperature was 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg. There was shotty lymphadenopathy in the neck, supraclavicular and axillary regions. The abdominal exam revealed massive hepatosplenomegaly with the spleen occupying the entire left hemi-abdomen and extending well below the pelvic brim. (See Figure 1 for area of liver and spleen enlargement.) The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 5,400/mm³, hematocrit 25%, and platelets 60,000/mm³. The levels of plasma electrolytes were sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, chloride 97 mmol/L, and carbon dioxide (HCO3) 22 mmol/L; the aspartate aminotransferase (AST, SGOT) was 40 U/L and total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL.
diagnosis:
Chronic malaria.

Amastigotes were not seen on Giemsa stain of the blood. The stool studies were negative for any ova or parasites. Testing for HIV (ELISA) was negative. Rare Plasmodium were seen in erythrocytes, identified as P. falciparum based on morphology. She was treated with seven days of quinine and doxycycline and her hepatosplenomegaly regressed over several weeks.

Massive tropical splenomegaly may be caused by hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly, schistosomiasis, visceral leishmaniasis, thalassemia major, and malignancies (including lymphoproliferative disorders). In a study from West Africa, hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly (HMS) and B cell lymphoproliferative disorders were the most common cause of massive splenomegaly [Bedu-Addo and Bates]. In this study, HMS was more associated with younger (less than 40 years) age, female gender and lower absolute lymphocyte count as compared to lymphoproliferative disorders.

title: Summary: An elderly man with anorexia, weight loss and cough, nine months after
history:
Summary: An elderly man with anorexia, weight loss and cough, nine months after vascular surgery.
A man in his seventies with a history of steroid-dependent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presented for a right femoral-popliteal bypass surgery. A routine pre-operative chest radiograph revealed a cavitary lesion in the left lung apex, measuring approximately 9.2 cm by 4.4 cm (Figures 1 and 2). His surgery was uneventful, and he was discharged to home.
Nine months later, he appeared cachectic at a follow-up visit. He reported a 50-pound weight loss over the preceding year-and-a-half, anorexia, chronic cough productive of purulent sputum, and progressive shortness of breath. He denied fevers, chills, night sweats or hemoptysis.
Figure 1. Pre-operative chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Pre-operative chest radiograph.

There was a history of long-standing COPD on 2L home oxygen supplementation and prednisone daily, as well as peripheral vascular disease with a chronic non-healing right lower extremity (RLE) stasis ulcer, status post a RLE deep venous thrombosis (DVT), gout, osteoporosis, and hypothyroidism.

He was born and raised in New England. He had worked for decades as a manager of a factory where he was exposed to employees who were recent immigrants, and to significant fumes. He had smoked 2 packs per day for thirty years, but quit thirty years before. There was no history of pet exposure, significant travel, alcohol or drug use.

Medications included prednisone (10 mg daily for at least ten years), albuterol (2 puffs four times daily), aerosol triamcinolone (2 puffs four times daily), aerosol ipratropium bromide (2 puffs four times daily), theophylline slow release tablets (125 mg orally three times daily), and levoxyl (100 mg orally per day).
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic but in no distress. He was afebrile with stable vital signs and an oxygen saturation of 88% while breathing room air, which increased to 94% with 2L oxgen supplementation by nasal cannula. He had no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Examination of the lungs revealed distant breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase. He had inspiratory crackles at the left apex. The rest of his examination was normal except for a chronic 2 cm ulcer on the right lower extremity.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,500/mm³ (86% polys, 8% lymphs, 5% monos, 1%eosinophils), hematocrit 32%, and platelets 338,000/mm³. The level of albumin was 2.4 g/dL; other test results of electrolytes, liver function tests and extended chemistries were normal. His chest radiograph showed enlargement of the left-sided cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level; the right lung was clear (Figure 3).
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a large thick-walled cavity in the left upper lobe with an air fluid level and associated collapse of the left upper lobe. Centrilobular emphysema was noted throughout the lung parenchyma and a “tree and bud” pattern of inflammation was seen scattered throughout both lungs. Pleural plaques were noted on the right. There was no lymphadenopathy and the mediastinal structures were normal (Figure 4).
Figure 3. Admission chest radiograph.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan. Link to Highest Resolution Image Available
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex pulmonary infection.

The patient underwent bronchoscopy. Gram stain showed abundant polys and rare gram-negative rods. Culture grew several strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one of which was resistant to ceftazidime, ticarcillin and aminoglycosides. Anaerobic culture grew one colony of Propionibacterium acnes. Acid-fast smear revealed 3+ acid-fast bacilli and culture grew Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex after 7 days. Cytology was negative for malignant cells. He underwent CT-guided biopsy, which was negative for malignancy, and showed chronic inflammatory changes.

The patient was started on meropenem, ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, ethambutol and rifabutin. He developed Clostridium difficile colitis, and oral metronidazole was added. Surgical resection was considered because of the large size of the cavity, but the patient was deemed not to be an operative candidate. After six weeks, he had gained 5 pounds and was no longer oxygen-dependent.
The original mycobacterial isolate was found to be susceptible to clarithromycin and ethambutol, but had intermediate sensitivity to rifabutin and ciprofloxacin. The meropenem, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were stopped, and he was continued on clarithromycin and rifabutin.
After six months of therapy, a repeat chest x-ray showed disappearance of the air fluid level, slight shrinkage of the left upper lobe cavity and subtle improvement in the peripheral opacities in the right lung. (See Figure 5.) He will most likely require life-long therapy.
Figure 5. Chest radiograph at six month follow-up.

Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex (MAC) is the most common cause of pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Individuals with underlying lung disease are particularly at risk. According to American Thoracic Society guidelines, chemotherapy of the non-HIV infected patient includes clarithromycin or azithromycin, rifabutin or rifampin, ethambutol and amikacin or streptomycin (for the first 2 months as tolerated). Treatment should be continued until monthly sputum cultures are negative.
Surgery should be considered for patients with cavitary disease, those who fail medical treatment after six months despite susceptible organisms, or patients who can not tolerate the medications due to side effects.
