title:
Summary: An elderly man with bacteremia and recurrent left arm abscesses.
A man
history:
Summary: An elderly man with bacteremia and recurrent left arm abscesses.
A man in his eighties with nephrotic syndrome, transiently requiring hemodialysis, was found to have coagulase-negative Staphylococcus bacteremia. His dialysis catheter was removed. Because he had a permanent pacemaker in place, he received a six-week course of vancomycin and rifampin.
One week after completing the antibiotics, surveillance cultures were drawn and again were positive for coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. As there were some differences in the antibiotic susceptibility patterns of the blood isolates, there was concern that he was seeding his blood from another source. On further review, the patient mentioned that he had been having recurrent skin abscesses on his left forearm during the previous several months. The abscesses tended to be along the ulnar aspect of his forearm, started as a papule and progressed to a draining abscess over several weeks, then slowly resolved. He could recall no trauma to the area.

He had a history of nephrotic syndrome due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (transiently requiring hemodialysis), complete heart block treated by permanent pacemaker placement two years prior, pneumococcal pneumonia five months prior, Type II diabetes mellitus, and peptic ulcer disease.

He was a retired office worker who divided his time between New England and Florida. He denied having pets, including fish or aquariums.

Daily medications included prednisone 10mg, cyclophosphamide 50 mg, glipizide 2.5 mg, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 single-strength tablet. Vancomycin had also been restarted.
exam_studies:
He appeared well, in no acute distress while breathing room air. The temperature was 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse 102 beats/minute, blood pressure 148/72 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The pacemaker pocket was not tender, and there was no fluctuance, induration, or erythema noted. Six tender abscesses were noted on the ulnar aspect of his left forearm (Figures 1 and 2), which measured between 1-2 cm. He had 1+ pedal edema; the examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 8,900 cells/mm³ (75% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes) and hematocrit 30%; the serum level of urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Results of electrolytes and tests of liver function were normal. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 6.

His pacemaker wire was evaluated as a nidus of infection with serial echocardiograms, which did not demonstrate vegetations either on the pacemaker wire or on his native heart valves. A tagged WBC scan was also unrevealing. Superficial wound cultures of the forearm abscesses were negative.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium abscessus skin infection with recurrent Staphylococcus bacteremia and pacemaker wire infection.

After superficial cultures were unrevealing, a biopsy and deep cultures were taken of a dominant lesion. The pathology demonstrated granulomas with very rare acid-fast bacilli. Within one week of culture a rapid-growing mycobacterial species was presumptively identified by the lab as either Mycobacterium chelonae or Mycobacterium abscessus and the isolate was referred to a reference lab for final identification. The organism was identified as M. abscessus.

It was thought that his skin lesions may have predisposed him to a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus bacteremia. It was also felt that his pacemaker wire was likely infected and would probably need to be removed. As he was traveling immediately following discharge, he refused vancomycin therapy for his bacteremia; instead he was treated with a six-week course of oral linezolid. His cutaneous mycobacterial abscesses were treated with gatifloxacin and clarithromycin and plans were made for an extended course based on clinical improvement. However, the patient experienced severe nausea and anorexia due to the clarithromycin and stopped it after two weeks. After four weeks, his skin lesions had completely healed and his gatifloxacin was stopped as well. The organism was identified as M. abscessus.
After he finished the course of linezolid, his bacteremia promptly returned. His pacemaker wire was removed surgically and the wire grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. After completing another course of intravenous antibiotics, his bacteremia did not recur.

Mycobacterium abscessus is similar to M. chelonae and M. fortuitum in that it is a rapid-growing mycobacterium. They are all hardy environmental saprophytes found widely in nature and able to withstand extremes of temperature and nutrient deprivation. They can be isolated from soil, dust, water, a variety of animals, and hospital environments. M. fortuitum is the most common rapid-growing mycobacteria isolated in the United States. Culture is essential for diagnosis and identification of the isolate is critical in selecting the appropriate antibiotic regimen. Drugs considered traditional anti-tuberculosis medications are generally ineffective against rapid-growing mycobacteria. Clarithromycin is generally considered the drug of choice for M. chelonae or M. abscessus infections, and 6 to 12 months of therapy may be required. In vitro susceptibility testing suggests that fluoroquinolones are unlikely to be successful in treating M. chelonae or M. abscessus, but may have a role in treating M. fortuitum. Linezolid may prove to have a role in treating certain atypical mycobacterial infections in the future, but preliminary data suggest the MICs are quite high. Isolates can be referred to a reference laboratory for antibiotic susceptibility testing.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with fever, chills and abdominal pain.
A man in his eigh
history:
Summary: An elderly man with fever, chills and abdominal pain.
A man in his eighties presented with four days of fever, shaking chills and crampy abdominal pain, without diarrhea.

There was a history of hypertension and benign prostatic hypertrophy.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill; the temperature was 102°F (38.9°C). The abdomen was not tender and the pulses in the lower extremities were full.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 11,000 cells/mm³. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed extensive soft tissue stranding around the abdominal aorta with a focal aneurysmal dilatation below the right renal artery, consistent with a mycotic aneurysm (Figure 1). Blood cultures were positive.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
diagnosis:
Salmonella enteritidis aortitis.

The patient was taken emergently to the operating room, where a mycotic aneurysm of the infrarenal aorta was found. The area was debrided and the patient underwent right axillobifemoral bypass grafting. Operative specimens and blood cultures were positive for Salmonella enteritidis (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Gram stain from aortic aneurysm.

The patient was treated with antibiotics, did well and was discharged home.

A mycotic aneurysm is a localized dilatation of an artery due to infection in the vessel wall. Mycotic aneurysms arise following bacterial infection of a previously normal arterial wall or through secondary infection of a pre-existing aneurysm. In some series, Salmonella species are the second most common cause of mycotic aneurysms, after Staphylococcus aureus. Salmonella enteritidis is one of the non-typhoidal salmonellae and is commonly associated with foodborne outbreaks of diarrheal disease.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with intermittent fevers.
Three years before this presen
history:
Summary: An elderly man with intermittent fevers.
Three years before this presentation, a man in his seventies underwent an extensive abdominal surgery for an intraductal papillary mucinous tumor, including Whipple’s procedure with near-total pancreatectomy, duodenectomy, partial gastrectomy with Bilroth reconstruction, cholecystectomy and splenectomy. He had done very well in the intervening three years, although he had developed insulin-dependent diabetes and pancreatic insufficiency.
During the month prior to this presentation, intermittent fevers had developed; the fevers occurred daily, peaking between 100.4°F (38°C) and 100.9°F (38.3°C), and were associated with night sweats, anorexia, and fatigue. He denied any change in exercise tolerance, change in weight, or any localizing symptoms. He had had no recent trauma, dental work, or invasive procedures. His primary care physician obtained two blood cultures which were sterile and ordered computed tomography (CT) scan (Figures 1, 2, and 3). He was subsequently admitted for further management.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 2. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 3. Abdominal CT scan.

He had had abdominal surgery as detailed above, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and pancreatic insufficiency.

He was born and worked in Venezuela for much of his adult life, and moved to New England more than a decade earlier. He was retired and lived with his wife. He had no pets and had not traveled recently outside of the Northeastern United States.

Medications included insulin and pancrease.
exam_studies:
He was an elderly man who appeared well. The temperature was 100.2°F (37.9°C), pulse 50-60/minute and blood pressure 90-110 mm Hg systolic and 50-50 mm Hg diastolic. There was shotty inguinal adenopathy; the remainder of the examination was otherwise benign and without focal findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 18,200 cells/mm³ (70% neutrophils, 4% bands, 20% lymphocytes) and hematocrit 30.0%. The level of serum urea nitrogen (BUN) was 18 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL; electrolytes and tests of liver function were normal. Review of the computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen reportedly showed several large cystic fluid collections in the former pancreatic bed and under the liver (Figure 3). A routine admission electrocardiogram (EKG) was obtained (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Electrocardiogram.

He was started on ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole.
As there was a suspicion for pulmonary nodules on the superior cuts of the abdominal CT scan, a dedicated contrast-enhanced chest CT was performed. The chest CT scan demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules less than 3 mm in diameter, as well as pulmonary emboli in the right upper lobe and right middle lobe pulmonary arteries (Figure 5). He was also noted to have EKG changes consistent with right heart strain and suggestive of pulmonary embolus (S1 Q3 T3).
Interventional radiologists placed a drainage catheter into the largest peri-hepatic collection and drained 250 cc of frank pus. Immediately following the procedure, he developed rigors and then the temperature rose to 101.0°F (38.3°C). The next day, his white cell count was 84,800/mm³ (74% neutrophils and 23% bands).
Figure 5. Contrast-enhanced chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Abdominal abscess from Actinomyces naeslundii.

Gram stain of the purulent fluid removed from his drainage catheter at the time of insertion (Figures 6 and 7) revealed fine filamentous branching Gram positive rods. Three days later, the microbiology lab reported that cultures were growing Actinomyces species, with a presumptive identification as A. naeslundii.
Figure 6. Gram stain of peri-hepatic drainage.
Figure 7. Gram stain of peri-hepatic drainage.

He required three further percutaneous drainage catheters to drain his abdominal abscesses. His leukemoid reaction was noted to quickly improve following drainage and although transient bacteremia during the procedure was suspected, blood cultures drawn while he was having rigors were negative. He received treatment with ampicillin and anticoagulation.

Actinomyces species are commonly found as oral flora and in the GI tract; A. israelii is the most common clinical isolate with A. naeslundii, A. viscosus, and A. odontolyticus accounting for a minority of other cases. They are uncommon pathogens and usually cause abdominal abscesses after recent intestinal surgery, a perforated abdominal viscous, colonic neoplasia, or trauma. There has been an association with actinomycosis and pelvic inflammatory disease and intrauterine contraceptive devices.
Over half of cases of actinomycosis begin in the oropharynx and are characterized by granulomatous inflammation, extensive and progressive necrosis, and sinus tracts which may drain sulfur granules. The organism can spread locally across tissue planes when mucosal membranes are breached either by foreign objects or other local disease. Either penicillin or ampicillin is the preferred treatment; a prolonged course is generally necessary to achieve cure.

title:
Summary: An elderly man, on total parenteral nutrition, with fever and chills.
A
history:
Summary: An elderly man, on total parenteral nutrition, with fever and chills.
A man in his eighties with a history of severe Crohn’s disease was maintained on total parenteral nutrition via a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line. He presented with fever and chills.

He had a history of Crohn's disease.
exam_studies:
The patient was thin and chronically ill-appearing. The vital signs were normal. The PICC line site was not tender or erythematous. The remainder of his general physical examination was normal.

Gram stain of a blood culture specimen revealed the forms shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Gram stain.
diagnosis:
Malassezia furfur line infection.

The gram stain of the blood culture demonstrates oval broad-based budding cells that are suggestive of Malassezia furfur and inconsistent with the other organisms in the differential diagnosis. Plating of the culture samples on Sabouraud dextrose agar supplemented with sterile olive oil yielded Malassezia furfur (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Culture plate.

The patient’s central line was removed and he was treated with a course of systemic amphotericin B.

Malassezia furfur is a lipophilic yeast which commonly causes cutaneous infections such as pityriasis versicolor. M. furfur sepsis is most likely a result of contamination from the colonized skin of the patient. It is particularly associated with total parenteral nutrition (TPN) infusions, which are supplemented with intralipid and provide a necessary source of fatty acids for growth of the organisms. M. furfur does not routinely grow in usual cultures. Because the organisms cannot synthesize long-chain fatty acids, the culture needs to be plated on a substrate that is supplemented with a source of free fatty acids, such as sterile olive oil. Optimal treatment of M. furfur sepsis is unclear, but removal of the line and treatment with amphotericin B is commonly utilized.

title:
Summary: A man in his fifties with rapidly progressive fever and leg swelling.
A
history:
Summary: A man in his fifties with rapidly progressive fever and leg swelling.
A man in his fifties with a history of type II diabetes and morbid obesity underwent a vein stripping on both lower extremities at a tertiary care medical center. The procedure was complicated by cellulitis, necessitating two weeks in hospital for intravenous antibiotics and two more weeks of outpatient oral antibiotics. He noted that an ulcer had never completely healed at his surgical site on his right lower extremity. The ulcer initially drained purulent material, but with the extended course of antibiotics, it had developed an eschar and closed over. He was able to return to work.
In early summer, two weeks before this presentation, he went on a vacation to Virginia Beach and submerged his ulcer in seawater. On the day of presentation, he went swimming in his backyard pool and noted some right lower extremity pain. He then went to work, but over the next several hours, the right leg pain dramatically worsened and he developed swelling of his leg, with fever, malaise and rigors.

He had type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea and gout.

He lived and worked in suburban New England. A scratch on his leg by his cat had healed over several days before his acute illness. He had a history of previous tobacco abuse, and reported no alcohol abuse, illicit drugs use or foreign travel.

Medications included atenolol, enteric-coated acetylsalicylic acid, furosemide, lisinopril and insulin (NPH and lispro).
exam_studies:
He appeared uncomfortable and toxic. The temperature was 102.2°F (39°C), pulse 73 beats/minute, blood pressure 144/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/minute and oxygen saturation 98% on supplemental oxygen (3L). There were dry mucous membranes, chronic venous stasis changes on both legs, a very edematous right lower extremity, with purple discoloration notable over the shin, a crusted shallow ulcer (1 cm diameter) medially and exquisite tenderness below his right knee. (See Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 13,200 cells/mm³ (84% neutrophils, 5% bands, 6% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes). The serum level of urea nitrogen (BUN) was 51 mg/dL, creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (baseline 1.5 mg/dL). Electrolytes and tests of liver function were normal. Urinalysis and a chest radiograph were negative. A radiograph of his right leg was reported to show pronounced distal soft-tissue swelling and mid-tibial periosteal reaction; the radiologist noted that one “cannot exclude osteomyelitis”.

He was felt to have cellulitis and ampicillin-sulbactam was administered given concern for polymicrobial involvement. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity was negative for a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). However, he remained febrile. By the 3rd hospital day, his leg had not yet responded to intravenous antibiotics.
diagnosis:
Vibrio parahaemolyticus wound infection with bacteremia.

Blood cultures drawn on admission grew Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Gram stain of blood culture. (Photo by Lynn Bry, M.D.)

After the patient’s blood cultures grew V. parahaemolyticus, the antibiotic regimen was changed to levofloxacin and clindamycin to cover for possible Gram-positive superinfection. Bone and gallium scans were negative for osteomyelitis. After the isolate was found to be sensitive to tetracyclines, he was discharged on a two-week course of doxycycline.

Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a relatively common cause of food-borne gastrointestinal illness worldwide. As the organism grows relatively poorly in a colder environment, the incidence of disease increases in the summer. This species, like most Vibrio species, grows best in the presence of salt. Vibrio species generally grow well on laboratory media but automated systems may have difficulty correctly identifying isolates. Filter-feeding organisms, particularly shellfish and mollusks, can accumulate large numbers of Vibrio species in the process of eating; this, in turn, exposes humans who eat raw shellfish to a large inoculum. The gastrointestinal illness caused by V. parahaemolyticus is relatively benign and self-limited; antibiotics are generally not indicated. Primary septicemia is much less common than with V. vulnificus, but presents with fulminant shock after oral ingestion of contaminated food. Most cases occur in patients with underlying liver disease or alcohol abuse, and mortality approaches 30%. Wound infection with V. parahaemolyticus (as in our patient) is also uncommon and usually follows an injury on a submerged body part or exposing an existing wound to seawater. Mortality is less than 5%, but most cases occur in patients with diabetes, liver disease or alcohol abuse.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with a painful red eye.
A man in his seventies presented
history:
Summary: An elderly man with a painful red eye.
A man in his seventies presented with decreased vision and a painful, red right eye. One month prior to admission, while trimming pine trees, he had suffered a penetrating injury to his right eye. He required keratoplasty, and foreign material was removed from the cornea.

There was a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and renal failure, and he was status post cataract extraction and penetrating keratoplasty.

Medications included insulin and antihypertensives.
exam_studies:
The visual acuity of the right eye was significantly diminished, with the patient perceiving hand motion only. Conjunctival injection and a hypopyon were present (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.

Cultures were obtained. (See Figures 2 and 3.)
Figure 2. Culture plate.
Figure 3. Culture results.
diagnosis:
Fusarium endophthalmitis.

Corneal, aqueous, and vitreous cultures grew Fusarium, a septate filamentous fungus, as seen in Figure 3. Numerous organisms are seen in Figure 4 with a corneal silver stain. Blood cultures were negative.
Figure 4. Silver stain of cornea.

The patient underwent a vitrectomy and received intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and amphotericin B. He was also given systemic itraconazole, and topical amphotericin B and vancomycin. In addition, he underwent a repeat penetrating keratoplasty.

Fungal endophthalmitis generally presents more indolently than bacterial endophthalmitis. As in this case, there may be several weeks between the traumatic event and the development of symptoms.
Candidal endophthalmitis usually occurs in the setting of candidemia. Aspergillus endophthalmitis generally occurs in immunosuppressed hosts, although it may occur in injection drug users. Mucormycosis involves the eye generally after direct extension from a sinus infection. Fusarium endophthalmitis may follow traumatic inoculation, as seen here.

title:
Summary: A man with fever and rash.
A man in his sixties with a history of M1 ac
history:
Summary: A man with fever and rash.
A man in his sixties with a history of M1 acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) received induction chemotherapy that included cytarabine (ara-C), daunorubicin, and gemtuzumab ozogamicin, and consolidation treatment with high dose cytarabine. Following a relapse three months later, he received cytarabine and topotecan. This was complicated by fever and neutropenia, and the development of a generalized papular rash.

The patient had AML, as per the history of the present illness.

Medications included cytarabine and topotecan; previous medications listed above.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared toxic. The temperature was 106.5° F (41.4° C), with rigors and hypotension. There was a generalized erythematous, non-blanching papular rash. The rash on his right thigh is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 100 cells/mm³, with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 0 cells/mm³.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Candida lusitaniae.

Cultures of the blood and a specimen from a punch biopsy of a lesion on his right thigh grew Candida lusitaniae. Pathological examination of the tissue was consistent with invasive fungal disease.

This patient developed disseminated candidiasis following chemotherapy for relapsed AML. He was treated with fluconazole and caspofungin with sterilization of his blood cultures and resolution of the skin lesions.

The patient’s profound neutropenia predisposed him to disseminated candidiasis. Biopsy of the skin lesion allowed early diagnosis. Candida lusitaniae is intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B. Consequently, he received azole therapy and caspofungin.

title:
Summary: A man with headache, fever and confusion.
A man in his sixties develope
history:
Summary: A man with headache, fever and confusion.
A man in his sixties developed a frontal headache, fever to 104°F (40°C), lethargy, and rapidly progressive extremity weakness (right greater than left) over 24 hours in late August.

There was a history of hypertension and prostate cancer, for which he had had a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), with a negative metastatic evaluation, a few years earlier.

He lived in Massachusetts, and had traveled to Cape Cod 3 weeks before admission. He had no animal exposures and enjoyed gardening as a hobby.

Medications included atenolol and aspirin.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was 101°F (38.3°C), and there was marked lethargy, confusion, and spastic quadriparesis with sensory sparing.

The peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count was 9900 cells/mm³ with a normal differential. The level of plasma sodium was 134 mmol/liter; the glucose level was normal. The lumbar puncture revealed a white cell count of 1196 cells/mm³ (80% neutrophils, 2% lymphocytes, and 18% monocytes); the red cell count was 12 cells/mm³; protein measured 140 mg/dL and glucose 74 mg/dL. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Head MRI scan.
Figure 2. Diffusion-weighted MRI scan.
diagnosis:
Eastern Equine Encephalitis

Serum and CSF were positive for Eastern Equine Encephalitis indirect fluorescent antibody and IgM capture by enzyme immunoassay (EIA). A tenfold rise in the titer of the serum IgM capture EIA occurred over 5 days.
His MRI findings were notable for upper pons, tectal plate, left temporal lobe, left occipital lobe, bilateral internal capsule and left postero-lateral fourth ventricle hyperintensities in T2 and FLAIR images (Figure 1) with a bright signal in the diffusion-weighted images in these areas (Figure 2).

The presentation with fever, headache, confusion, and basal ganglia changes on MRI in August all strongly suggest an arboviral infection, particularly Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Herpes encephalitis typically involves the temporal lobes. Pneumococcus, Listeria, and Cryptococcus can all cause meningitis, but typically these abscesses are associated with enhancement on imaging.

title: Summary: A man with a history of renal transplantation in the past presented wit
history:
Summary: A man with a history of renal transplantation in the past presented with a swollen foot.
A man in his fifties, five years after renal allograft for probable diabetic nephropathy, presented with progressive right foot swelling of approximately five days' duration. His symptoms had started with a small ulcer medial to his first metatarsal-phalangeal (MTP) joint, which had drained copious white liquid. The foot was not painful and he denied trauma to his foot. He felt systemically well and reported no subjective fever or rigors.

He had type II diabetes with nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and was status post renal allograft five years previously.

He denied smoking, alcohol abuse, travel or exposure to pets.

He was taking prednisone 20 mg daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, insulin, atenolol and atorvastatin.
exam_studies:
He was in no acute distress. The temperature was 101.5°F (38.6°C) and other vital signs were stable. The right foot was a swollen, erythematous and warm (Figures 1 and 2). The foot was not tender and the white material draining from the medial aspect of the first metatarsal head was of cottage-cheese consistency.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 14,300 cells/mm³ (88% neutrophils); the serum level of urea nitrogen was 39 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL; other laboratory studies were normal. A chest radiograph and urinalysis were negative.

The patient was started on vancomycin, clindamycin, and levofloxacin after two sets of blood cultures and a urine culture were obtained. Surgery was consulted.
diagnosis:
Gout (podagra) with soft tissue superinfection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

A gram stain of a specimen of the white exudate (Figure 3) demonstrated very rare gram-positive cocci. The material was also examined under polarizing light (Figure 4) which revealed negatively bi-refringent crystals, which were diagnostic of gout.
Figure 3. Gram stain of discharge.
Figure 4. Joint discharge under polarizing light.

Colchicine was begun and the dose of steroids was temporarily increased. Culture of the exudate grew rare methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and the vancomycin was continued for soft tissue superinfection.
He did quite well and was discharged home on the fifth hospital day.

Many noninfectious inflammatory processes can be confused for infectious diseases. Gout can be a late complication of renal transplant and typically occurs 18-24 months post-transplant. Hyperuricemia is quite common in renal allograft recipients, particularly those on cyclosporine, which may lower tubular secretion and glomerular filtration rate. Perhaps 10-20% of solid-organ allograft recipients suffer one or more episodes of acute gouty arthritis.
Colchicine is the preferred treatment, but increased doses of corticosteroids may be quite helpful. Patients treated with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be monitored closely for nephrotoxicity, particularly if they are also on cyclosporine.

title: Summary: A middle-aged man with chronic myelogenous leukemia, cavitary lung dise
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with chronic myelogenous leukemia, cavitary lung disease and brain lesions.
A man in his forties had a history of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and was status post allogenic bone marrow transplant (BMT) two years before admission. His post-transplant course had been complicated by graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) thirteen months before, for which he was treated with FK506 and dexamethasone, and a right leg ulcer seven months previously. The ulcer had persisted with gradual increase in size, and a biopsy, done at an outside hospital, was thought consistent with venous stasis. In the two months before admission, he had further GVHD, which was treated with extracorporeal photophoresis, and a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia treated with ribavirin and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg). He returned to the hospital with increasing dyspnea and was admitted.

There was a history of CML (see above); cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia, renal insufficiency (baseline creatinine 2.0), and peptic ulcer disease.

He lived in a metropolitan area of Massachusetts, and denied travel or pet exposure.

Medications included dexamethasone, FK506, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and valganciclovir.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 96.3°F (35.7°C) and the blood pressure 140/68 mm Hg. The examination of the chest revealed diffuse expiratory wheezes, and a few diffuse crackles. The right leg had a large ulcerative lesion (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white cell count (WBC) was 2,500 cells/mm³ (86% neutrophils, 3% bands, 11% lymphocytes), the hematocrit 28%, and the creatinine 1.9 mg/dL. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed multiple cavitating nodules (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan.

Three days after admission, left arm weakness developed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed one left frontal and two right parietal lesions (Figure 5). A methenamine silver stain of the right leg skin biopsy is shown (Figure 6).
Figure 5. Head MRI scan.
Figure 6. Methenamine silver stain of right leg skin biopsy.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Alternaria.

The methenamine silver stain shown in Figure 6 (above) demonstrated an invasive mycosis. The culture grew Alternaria (Figures 7 and 8).
Figure 7. Lactophenol blue stain (40x), photo by Lynn Bry, M.D.
Figure 8. Lactophenol blue stain (80x), photo by Lynn Bry, M.D.

The patient was treated empirically with liposomal amphotericin B, at a dose of 10mg/kg/day. Caspofungin was added when the neurological lesions developed. Unfortunately, progressive neurological and respiratory decline occurred, and he died from respiratory failure.

The combination of a necrotic cutaneous lesion and focal lung and brain abscesses in an immunocompromised host strongly suggests an invasive mold infection. Thus aspergillosis and Alternaria infection should be strongly considered. The findings on the biopsy and in culture diagnosed disseminated Alternaria. Ecthyma gangrenosum, pyoderma gangrenosum and disseminated candidiasis can all produce a necrotic skin lesion; however, the other features in this case would be atypical for these processes.

A man in his fifties w
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with fever and abdominal pain.
A man in his fifties was three years status post cadaveric renal transplant when he was admitted to a hospital for fever and abdominal pain. He had also noted an erythematous maculopapular rash on his face, trunk, and extremities.

He was status post cadaveric renal transplant, and had a history of cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, and hypertension.

Medications included prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and azathioprine.
exam_studies:
He was toxic in appearance, and the temperature was 103°F (39.4°C). The abdomen was tender, and a maculopapular rash was noted across his face, trunk (Figure 1), and extremities (Figure 2). Some lesions appeared fluid-filled.
Figure 1. Skin findings.
Figure 2. Skin findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 12,000 cells/mm³, platelets 12,000/mm³, lipase 84 U/L, amylase 700 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (ASP, SGOT) 7700 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT, SGPT) 2424 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 5552 U/L, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a distended gallbladder; the renal allograft was without apparent abnormality.
diagnosis:
Disseminated varicella zoster virus (VZV).

Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) of a specimen obtained from a papule was strongly positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV). Testing for cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigen was negative, as were blood cultures.

Ganciclovir was administered intravenously, with resolution of his abdominal pain, liver function tests, and rash.

Disseminated varicella zoster infection occurs more frequently in immunocompromised hosts. Visceral involvement, including pneumonitis, hepatitis, and meningoencephalitis, may occur. Despite widespread involvement, disseminated herpes zoster is rarely fatal.

title:
Summary: A middle-aged man with headache and left-handed clumsiness.
A right-han
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with headache and left-handed clumsiness.
A right-handed male in his forties presented with two weeks of a severe headache that had originated on the right but had become bifrontal, and two days of left-handed clumsiness.

There was a history of migraines for many years and Hepatitis C virus infection.

He lived on the United States Northeast coast with his female partner, and traveled yearly to Asia. There was a remote history of intravenous drug use several decades earlier, but none since. He denied smoking or alcohol use, pets, unusual hobbies, recent dental work or oral infections.

Medications included ibuprofen and acetaminophen-oxycodone had been given for his headaches, without relief.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared acutely ill. The temperature was 100.2°F (37.9°C), heart rate 108 beats/minute, blood pressure 110/88 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 14/minute. His pupils were equal and reactive to light; fundoscopic examination revealed sharp discs bilaterally, and the tympanic membranes were clear bilaterally. There was no sinus tenderness, tooth tenderness or gingivitis noted. His neck was supple and there was no lymphadenopathy. The S1, S2 heart sounds were normal, with no murmur. Examination of the lungs, abdomen and skin were normal. He was fully oriented with fluent speech, but had diminished attention and impaired immediate recall (1/3 objects). Cranial nerves were intact and symmetric, and there were no motor or sensory deficits. He declined a more detailed neurological examination.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,300 cells/mm³, with 85% polys, 13% lymphs, 1% monos, and 1% eosinophils. The level of aspartate aminotransferase (AST/SGOT) was 44 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT/SGPT) 69 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 44 U/L. The remainder of his laboratory test results were normal. His chest radiograph was clear. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed a, heterogeneous, rim-enhancing lesion (4 centimeter (cm) by 5 cm by 5 cm) with surrounding edema within the right parietal lobe (Figures 1 and 2). There was mass effect on the lateral ventricle with early entrapment of the frontal horn.
Figure 1. Head MRI scan.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan.
diagnosis:
Polymicrobial brain abscess in a patient with hepatitis C virus infection.

The patient was taken to the operating room where a right-sided craniotomy was performed. At least 15cc of pus were evacuated from a fluctuant lesion in the right temporo-parietal region. The cavity was irrigated copiously and empiric ceftriaxone and metronidazole were begun based on a gram stain of the fluid, which revealed moderate polys, few gram-positive cocci in pairs, few gram-negative rods, and few short gram-positive rods (Figures 3 and 4). The aerobic culture grew abundant Haemophilus aphrophilus and Actinomyces odontolyticus. The anaerobic culture grew abundant Peptostreptococcus micros.
Figure 3. Gram stain of the aspirate.
Figure 4. Gram stain of the aspirate.

The patient’s headache improved dramatically, and he felt neurologically back to baseline the day following surgery. His complete neurological exam at that time was normal. He underwent a thorough otolaryngological and oral surgery evaluation, which showed no sinus or odontogenic infection. He had a transesophageal echocardiogram that revealed a patent foramen ovale without evidence for endocarditis.
The aerobic culture grew abundant Haemophilus aphrophilus and Actinomyces odontolyticus. The anaerobic culture grew abundant Peptostreptococcus micros. He completed eight weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone (1gm every 12 hours) and penicillin G (4MU every four hours), followed by penicillin 500mg and probenicid 500mg orally four times daily in order to complete a yearlong course. A follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain performed 3 months after initial presentation revealed near complete resolution of the brain abscess with only minimal enhancement (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Follow-up head CT scan at three months.

Brain abscesses can be caused by organisms reaching the brain by either the hematogenous route, direct spread from a contiguous site, or trauma or post-surgical circumstances. The bacterial species found in this patient’s brain abscess suggest an odontogenic source despite the fact he could not recall any dental infection or even recent teeth cleaning. Approximately 30% of brain abscesses occur without an obvious source or underlying condition. The clinical manifestations of brain abscesses are nonspecific such that the average duration of symptoms is 14 days prior to the diagnosis being made. Headache is the most common symptom whereas fever and/or neurological deficits are only present in 50% of patients. Diagnosis is made by CT or MRI scan in the appropriate clinical setting. Treatment consists of empiric therapy based on the probable pathogens and, usually, surgical drainage. Antibiotics are continued for 6-8 weeks with close follow-up after their discontinuation. The decision to treat this patient for one year with oral penicillin following his intravenous course was based on the isolation of Actinomyces, a particularly slow-growing bacteria, which typically requires months of therapy to fully eradicate.

title:
Summary: A middle-aged woman with leg ulcers.
A woman in her fifties developed a
history:
Summary: A middle-aged woman with leg ulcers.
A woman in her fifties developed a pruritic rash four months before admission. The rash became excoriated and developed into expanding non-healing ulcers with necrotic eschars.

There was a history of alcoholism. There was no history of diabetes or other known immunosuppressive conditions.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared disheveled and chronically ill. The temperature was normal, and the othervital signs were stable. There were multiple deep 2-10 centimeter ulcers with eschars on both legs (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous mucormycosis secondary to Rhizopus.

Surgical debridement was performed. Fungal wet prep revealed large non-septate hyphae with right angle branches (Figures 3 and 4). Cultures grew Rhizopus (Figure 5). Pathological examination confirmed invasive mucormycosis.
Figure 3. Calcofluor stain.
Figure 4. Calcofluor stain.
Figure 5. Fungal stain.

This patient underwent multiple debridements, aggressive local wound care, and ambisome (10 mg/kg/day) resulting in slow improvement of her ulcers. Her caregivers suspected that this patient had an unrelated pruritic eruption four months before admission that became excoriated and then locally inoculated with Rhizopus. Her only clear immunosuppressive conditions were alcoholism and malnutrition.

Treatment of cutaneous mucormycosis typically involves wide surgical debridement with aggressive antifungal therapy.
An outbreak of primary cutaneous mucormycosis occurred in the 1970s due to contaminated elastic bandages. Cutaneous mucormycosis may also occur after trauma or burns. Dissemination from the skin site can also occur.

title:
Summary: A woman in her sixties with an infestation.
A woman in her sixties had
history:
Summary: A woman in her sixties with an infestation.
A woman in her sixties had a history of metastatic melanoma with innumerable in-transit metastases affecting her right leg. Several months prior to admission, and after receiving multiple cycles of experimental chemotherapy, she chose to initiate comfort care measures. She was bedbound at home, when she was admitted with a question of an infestation.

As above.
exam_studies:
She appeared cachectic and ill, with multiple cutaneous nodules over her trunk, back, and legs. The largest in-transit metastases essentially covered her right lower extremity. The large nodules were necrotic and bleeding, and measured up to the size of grapefruits. The biggest necrotic melanoma nodule was on the inner aspect of her right thigh, with innumerable highly mobile forms (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Myiasis in a necrotic melanoma nodule.

Speciation of the highly mobile, larval forms revealed common fruit fly larvae.

Multiple methods of local control were attempted. The leg was covered with a thick layer of petroleum jelly twice daily, which resulted in rapid elimination of all live larvae.

Myiasis refers to infestation by the larval forms of dipterous (two-winged) flies. Some species lay eggs directly on compromised tissue causing the entity of wound myiasis. Secondary bacterial infection may complicate wound myiasis. Although this problem occurs most often in the tropics, myiasis may occur in patients who have not left the United States.

history:
Summary: A woman with a non-healing wound, fever, and knee pain.
A woman in her sixties underwent right mastectomy for breast cancer, complicated by non-healing of the wound with chronic discharge. She presented with two days of fever and one day of acute left knee pain.

There was a history of rheumatoid arthritis and a seizure disorder.

She had traveled in the previous month to Florida, and had no animal exposures.
exam_studies:
She was an obese woman with a temperature of 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 70/30 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats/minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. The skin was erythematous over the right chest wall, with no drainage from the wound (Figures 1 and 2). There was no adenopathy. The neck was supple, without jugular venous distention, and she had a clear chest. Cardiac examination revealed a I/VI systolic murmur at the left sternal border, without rub or gallop. The abdomen was obese, soft and nontender, without hepatosplenomegaly or masses. The left knee was swollen and tender, with a decreased range of motion to 60 degrees.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 13,000 cells/mm³ (with 35% band forms) and the platelet count 112,000/mm³. There was a mild transaminitis, and the prothrombin time was 14.0 seconds; the plasma level of creatinine was elevated at 3.6 mg/dL.

The patient had persistent hypotension for which pressors were required.
diagnosis:
Group G streptococcal cellulitis and septic arthritis, with toxic shock syndrome.

All blood culture bottles, knee aspirate cultures, and a swab from open area of wound were grew Group G Streptococcus.

The hypotension, liver function abnormalities, and renal dysfunction normalized after forty-eight hours with supportive therapy and antibiotics. She was treated for six weeks with penicillin G, and improved.

Group G Streptococcus colonizes the skin, nasopharynx and genital tract, and can cause skin and soft tissue infection, septic arthritis and bacteremia. The rate of underlying malignancy is high (20-65%) in series of patients with serious group G streptococcal infection. Toxic shock syndrome may occur after Group G streptococcal infection, although this organism is not known to secrete any exotoxin.

history:
Summary: A woman with AIDS, fever, and abdominal symptoms.
A woman was reportedly infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) by her husband approximately one decade before admission.
Five years before admission, after immigrating to the United States Midwest from Uganda, a skin test for tuberculosis PPD was positive, with a negative chest radiograph, and she completed 6 months of isoniazid (INH) treatment. She then started on zidovudine (AZT) and lamivudine (3TC), and later switched to stavudine (D4T)-3TC-nevirapine, with intermittent adherence.
One year before admission, she moved to urban New England, and stopped all medications. Five months later, she was admitted to the hospital with Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia. Three induced sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and mycobacterial culture were negative, and she was treated with steroids and pentamidine. At the end of treatment, her CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 4 cells/mm³ (0.5%) and the HIV nucleic acid viral load was 210,000 copies/mL. Her HIV genotype revealed the following mutations: K70R, K103N, Y181C, M184V, and G190A. Her course was complicated by diabetes and pancreatitis. The patient was started on antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, abacavir, 3TC and lopinavir-ritonavir. Five days later, she presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, general malaise and fever. She denied cough, shortness of breath, rash or myalgias.

See above.

She had immigrated from Uganda to the United States approximately five years before admission, and had not returned to Africa. She had worked in the healthcare industry until shortly before admission, and denied tobacco or alcohol use, or pet exposures.

Her HIV medications included tenofovir 300 mg daily and abacavir 300 mg, 3TC 150 mg, and lopinavir-ritonavir 400/100 mg twice daily. Other medications included daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength), metformin 1gm, rosiglitazone 8 mg; NPH insulin (40U) subcutaneously each evening, iron sulfate, and azithromycin 1250 mg orally once per week.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable. The temperature was 101°F (38.3° C), blood pressure 110/86 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/minute, and respiratory rate 18/minute. The lungs were clear, the heart was tachycardic with a flow murmur, and the abdomen was mildly tender throughout, with more marked epigastric tenderness to deep palpation. There was no abdominal rebound or guarding, rash or other skin lesions.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 7,600 cells/mm³, CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count 53 cells/mm³ (17%), and hematocrit 32%. The level of lactate was 1.8 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 416 U/L, amylase 34 U/L, and lipase 3 U/L; electrolytes and results of liver function tests were normal.

After admission, her antiretroviral medications were stopped and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed (Figure 1), which revealed several peri-pancreatic lesions consistent with pseudocysts or lymphadenopathy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) indicated the peri-pancreatic lesions were enlarged lymph nodes; retrocrural lymphadenopathy was also appreciated (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 2. Abdominal MRI scan.
diagnosis:
Immune reconstitution syndrome with intra-abdominal tuberculous lymphadenitis in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

An endoscopic, ultrasound-guided biopsy of the peri-pancreatic lymph nodes was performed. The gram stain was negative, but acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain revealed sheets of acid-fast bacilli. Pathology showed sheets of inflammatory cells, but no granulomas. Culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis after 12 days.

The patient spiked fevers daily to 103-104°F (39.4-40°C) until three days after the discontinuation of her antiretroviral medications, after which her temperature curve trended back to normal and her abdominal pain began to resolve. She was initially started on treatment for both Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and M. tuberculosis (MTB) with isoniazid (INH), rifabutin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, pyrazinamide (PZA), and pyridoxine. Three induced sputum samples were negative for AFB. Once the culture results were available, clarithromycin was stopped.
After one month, the organism proved to be susceptible to all of the drugs used, and ethambutol was stopped. She developed a pruritic rash that resolved after stopping PZA. She was later started on thrice weekly directly observed therapy (DOT) with INH and rifabutin. Her repeat CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count, off of antiretrovirals, was 10 cells/mm³ (2%). Follow-up MRI of the abdomen was done 6 weeks after starting treatment and showed no significant change in the size of the intra-abdominal lymph nodes (Figure 3). Antiretroviral therapy was restarted at this point with the plan of adding systemic steroids if fevers and abdominal pain recurred.
Figure 3. Abdominal MRI scan.

The development of symptomatic MAC or tuberculosis infection within the first two months of starting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has been well described. This clinical presentation is referred to as immune reconstitution syndrome. Patients improve with either the withdrawal of antiretrovirals, the addition of systemic steroids, or both. These reactions are thought to represent a new inflammatory response to pre-existing infection that is unmasked due to restoration of CD4+ and/or CD8+ T-lymphocyte cells by HAART.

history:
Summary: A woman with fever, hemoptysis and respiratory distress.
A woman in her forties, recently diagnosed with stage IIIA non-small cell lung cancer, underwent neoadjuvant non-myeloablative chemotherapy and radiation therapy prior to having a right upper lobectomy. She was discharged on the sixth post-operative day to complete a ten-day course of levofloxacin for pneumonia. One week later, she presented to clinic complaining of fevers, chills, sweats and cough productive of yellow to red-brown sputum; she was prescribed levofloxacin for presumed pneumonia. She returned to the emergency room three days later with progressive dyspnea on exertion, persistent fevers, and cough productive of red-brown sputum.

She had a history of extensive tobacco use (60 pack-year exposure). Her family history included coronary disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). She had no pets and had never traveled outside of New England.

She was taking levofloxacin (day #17).
exam_studies:
She appeared uncomfortable, dyspneic, and toxic. The temperature was 104.7°F (40.4°C), pulse 110 beats/minute, blood pressure 65/50 mm Hg to 120/70 mm Hg after fluid resuscitation, respiratory rate 22/minute, and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing supplemental oxygen (on 3L). Her mucous membranes were dry and decreased air entry was noted throughout the right chest, with egophony at the right base.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 13,700 cells/mm³ (75% neutrophils, 13% bands, 9% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes). Serum levels of electrolytes and tests of renal and liver function were normal. Urinalysis was negative.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest on admission showed findings consistent with a patchy consolidation in the right lower lobe distal to a large pulmonary embolus (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Admission chest CT scan.

Intravenous heparin and ceftriaxone were started, but she remained febrile and hypoxic during the next three days. Blood and sputum cultures were unrevealing.
A chest CT was repeated and demonstrated extension of consolidation and the development of necrosis (Figure 2). The antibiotics were changed to vancomycin, ceftazidime, and gentamicin. Bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage werenon-diagnostic. When she developed frank hemoptysis by hospital day #5, another chest CT scan was done, which showed further progression of the necrosis and the development of a cavity that extended superiorly to the level of the carina (Figure 3).
Figure 2. Second chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Third chest CT scan showing progression.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary zygomycosis (sometimes known as mucormycosis) caused by Rhizopus.

Given the extent of parenchymal destruction, she was scheduled for completion of the right pneumonectomy. Two days later, lung tissue sent for culture was noted to be growing the organism seen in Figure 4. Lactophenol cotton blue stain (seen in Figure 5) demonstrated the fungal elements, including nonseptate hyphae, sporangia, and rhizoids of Rhizopus species.
Pathologic specimens included a Gomori methenamine silver stain (Figure 6) and demonstrated broad non-septate hyphae invading necrotic pulmonary tissue, diagnostic of pulmonary zygomycosis.
Figure 4. Aerial mycelium on fungal media plate.
Figure 5. Lactophenol cotton blue stain.
Figure 6. Gomori methenamine silver stain.

Amphotericin B was started, and was changed to liposomal amphotericin B when renal insufficiency developed. She subsequently developed empyema with Aspergillus terreus and Neisseria elongata and a chest tube was placed for drainage and ceftriaxone was added. The empyema was refractory to drainage, and a window thoracotomy was performed. Post-operatively, aerial mycelium of A. terreus was visible to the naked eye on her medial chest wall. Aggressive debridement was continued yet cultures repeatedly grew Rhizopus spp. and A. terreus, and therefore caspofungin was added. Eight weeks of amphotericin B and four weeks of caspofungin were completed before achieving microbiologic cure. Closure of the window thoracotomy was performed and she did well in follow-up.

Invasive fungal disease caused by members of the class Zygomycetes is often called mucormycosis, however, taxonomists prefer the term zygomycosis. Zygomycetes grow as molds both in the environment and in tissue and appear as nonseptated broad hyphae that branch at nearly right angles. Rhizopus species in particular grow so well that they are nicknamed "lid-lifters" due to the abundant cotton candy-like mycelium that fills the petri dish. While the most common manifestation of zygomycetes infection is rhinocerebral mucormycosis, pulmonary zygomycosis is increasingly recognized. As the hyphae are quite vasculotropic, hemoptysis occurs in about 25% of patients and massive pulmonary hemorrhage can result in death. Distal metastatic disease may result from vascular involvement and the fungus may directly invade other organs in the chest, including the chest wall and mediastinal structures. In some reported cases, many organs are involved, including the lung, and although the exact origin of the mold is not clear, it is presumed that the fungal process started in the lung and subsequently disseminated.
The role of host immunity in preventing zygomycosis is incompletely understood; however, macrophages of diabetic and glucocorticoid-treated mice are unable to attach to Rhizopus spores and prevent germination. In contrast with rhinocerebral mucormycosis, where diabetes is the most common predisposing factor, pulmonary zygomycosis seems to occur more frequently in patients with hematologic malignancies, neutropenia, and solid-organ transplants. Treatment of invasive zygomycosis requires both aggressive surgical debridement and antifungal drugs, but despite combination therapy, mortality can be as high as 80%. Amphotericin B or its lipid formulations are considered the only effective antifungals and high doses may be required.

title:
Summary: A woman with fever, neutropenia and a rash.
A woman in her fifties with
history:
Summary: A woman with fever, neutropenia and a rash.
A woman in her fifties with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) and persistent neutropenia presented with fever. She had no localizing symptoms or signs.
The patient had been on prophylactic oral levofloxacin as an outpatient; the medication was changed to ceftazidime and vancomycin on admission. After two days in the hospital, fevers persisted and she developed hypotension refractory to intravenous fluid administration. She was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) for vasopressor therapy.

She had acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), morbid obesity, and type II diabetes mellitus.

She lived in the northeast United States. She did not smoke, and reported no history of alcohol abuse, intravenous drug use (IVDU), foreign travel, or exposures to pets or other animals.

Medications included ceftazidime, vancomycin, dopamine, insulin, and acetominophen.
exam_studies:
She appeared toxic and tachypneic, and could speak only short sentences. The temperature was 103.2°F (39.6°C), blood pressure 100/50 mm Hg on dopamine, and pulse 115/minute. There was mild tenderness and erythema around the site of a subcutaneous reservoir and intravenous catheter and a new skin eruption on her lower extremities that did not blanch (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 200 cells/mm³ (5% neutrophils, 40% blasts, 50% lymphocytes), hematocrit 25%, and platelets 20,000/mm³. The serum level of urea nitrogen (BUN) was 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase (ALT, SGPT) 75 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST, SGOT) 90 U/L, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL. The urinalysis was negative. A chest radiograph revealed clear lung fields.

A diagnostic procedure was performed; the patient’s antibiotic regimen was broadened to vancomycin, imipenem, and amphotericin B.
diagnosis:
Disseminated candidiasis in a patient with acute myelogenous leukemia and neutropenia.

Multiple sets of blood cultures, drawn over several days and despite the administration of amphotericin B, grew Candida pseudotropicalis.

The indwelling reservoir and intravenous catheter were removed and the tip grew abundant C. pseudotropicalis. Despite removing the apparent focus, candidemia persisted. Caspofungin was added three days after the catheter was removed.
A transthoracic echocardiogram was negative but a vascular ultrasound discovered an extensive deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in her right subclavian vein where a central line had been placed. The central line was removed and 5-fluorocytosine (5-FC) was added. The patient and her family declined further aggressive interventions, and she died after three weeks of persistent candidemia.

Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines regarding the management of fever and neutropenia clearly stratify level of risk for invasive fungal infection amongst patients based on the duration of neutropenia.
In our patient, her neutropenia predated the diagnosis of AML and persisted as a result of her underlying leukemia. The catheter and reservoir likely served as the immediate portal of entry, but once the yeast gained access to her bloodstream she quickly developed metastatic foci. The persistent candidemia initially led us to believe she had fungal endocarditis, but the discovery of a DVT provided another intravascular focus to explain failure of appropriate antifungal therapy. Although we were concerned about the high risk of bone marrow suppression with 5-FC, her situation was grave.
Skin lesions of disseminated candidiasis can have many different appearances including bullae, macronodular lesions, and purpura fulminans; satellite lesions can also be seen as in our patient.

title:

A woman with
history:
Summary: A woman with perirectal ulcers and acute hepatic failure.
A woman with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and advanced AIDS was admitted with progressive perirectal ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding. Acute hepatic failure was diagnosed, and she developed acute adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute renal failure, and hypotension.

There was a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS, cryptococcal meningitis, Cryptosporidium gastroenteritis, and herpes simplex virus (HSV) ulcers.

Medications included dapsone, azithromycin, fluconazole, paromomycin, and acyclovir.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared chronically ill and in respiratory distress. She was icteric and tachycardic, with bilateral crackles, tender hepatomegaly, 3+ edema, and confluent erosive perirectal ulcers (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 7,000 cells/mm³, CD4 T-lymphocyte count 9 cells/mm³, total bilirubin 6.7 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST, SGOT) 499 U/L, prothrombin time (PT) 20 seconds, and HIV nucleic acid 34,000 copies/mL.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdominal showed bilateral air space disease, a markedly enlarged liver and moderate ascites.

She was admitted to the Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU) and required intubation for respiratory failure, pressors for hemodynamic support, continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVH) for anuric renal failure, and multiple transfusions of packed red blood cells (pRBCs) and fresh frozen plasma (FFP) for coagulopathy and blood loss.
diagnosis:
Herpes simplex virus, type 2 (HSV-2) ulcers, and acute hepatic failure in a patient with HIV and AIDS.

A swab of the perirectal ulcers was positive for Herpes simplex virus, type 2 (HSV-2).

The patient's erosive HSV-2 lesions were treated with foscarnet because of a concern of acyclovir-resistance, since she had been on acyclovir chronically. Unfortunately, this patient with advanced AIDS died of hepatic failure and multi-organ system dysfunction. The etiology of her hepatic failure and multiple organ system failure was not determined. Disseminated HSV disease was thought possible but was not proven. All blood cultures were negative.

HSV-2 is a common cause of perirectal ulcers. Patients with HIV may have more severe HSV-2 disease, and it may be difficult to treat. CMV also can cause ulcerative disease, in either the gastrointestinal (GI) or genito-urinary (GU) tract. Drugs used in HIV that can cause genital ulcers include foscarnet and ddC.

A man in his twenties presented with a
history:
Summary: A young man with fever and rash.
A man in his twenties presented with a three day history of fever to 104°F (40° C), oral lesions, sore throat, and rash that began on his palms and soles and spread to his entire body.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 103°F (39.4° C). Numerous vesicular and erythematous oral lesions and exudative tonsillopharyngitis were present. There were numerous maculopapular lesions on the palms (Figure 1), soles, extremities, torso (Figure 2), back, and face.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Rash on torso.
diagnosis:
Erythema multiforme due to primary Herpes Simplex Virus, type 1 (HSV-1) infection.

Testing for syphilis, antibodies to HIV and HIV nucleic acid were negative. A culture of the oral lesions grew Herpes Simplex Virus, type 1 (HSV-1). HSV-1 immunoglobulin G (IgG) serology was negative. Figure 1. Physical findings. Figure 2. Rash on torso.

The patient improved with complete recovery of his oral and skin lesions after treatment with acyclovir.

The acral distribution of the rash suggests Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, syphilis, atypical measles or erythema multiforme. Acute HIV-1 may present with a maculopapular rash. The target-shaped rash of erythema multiforme may follow HSV-1 infection or mycoplasma infection, or may be due to a drug reaction.

title:
Summary: A young man with fever and rash.
A previously healthy male in his twent
history:
Summary: A young man with fever and rash.
A previously healthy male in his twenties presented with 2 days of fever and rash. He denied any other symptoms.

The patient lived in New England and was sexually active with one female partner. He denied any recent travel or animal exposures.
exam_studies:
Oral and hand lesions were present (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Erythema multiforme associated with herpes simplex virus infection.

The culture of one of the ulcers was positive for herpes simplex virus, type-1 (HSV-1).
A more detailed past medical history revealed that he had developed his first episode one year earlier, at which time he had had an oral ulcer.

He was treated with acyclovir with complete resolution of his symptoms. Subsequently, he has had multiple further episodes of fever and rash.

Erythema multiforme is most commonly due to HSV infection. The rash of erythema multiforme is typically target-shaped, as seen in this case. The rash associated with the other conditions noted in the differential diagnosis do not have this target-like pattern: syphilis typically has a papulosquamous eruption; acute HIV-1, a diffuse macular exanthem; RMSF, an acrally distributed petechiae; and erythema migrans, an expanding circular eruption.

Summary: A woman with abdominal distension, pleural effusion and ascites.
A woma
history:
Summary: A woman with abdominal distension, pleural effusion and ascites.
A woman in her forties presented with three weeks of abdominal distension, fever to 103°F (39.4°C), nausea and diarrhea. She also reported 2 weeks of a dry cough and dyspnea on exertion.

There was a history of sarcoidosis with uveitis and pulmonary nodules, which had never been treated, and a positive skin test for tuberculosis (PPD) at age 20 years for which she had received nine months of isoniazid (INH).

She lived in urban Maryland, and reported no tobacco, alcohol or drug use, or travel or animal exposures.

None
exam_studies:
The temperature was 101.6°F (38.7°C). Examination of the lungs revealed decreased breath sounds on the right. The abdomen was soft and distended with shifting dullness.

A chest radiograph showed a right pleural effusion. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed ascites. The ascitic fluid was tapped and had a white blood cell count 1800 cells/mm³ with 3% polys and 97% lymphs, glucose 76 mg/dL, protein 5.6 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 300 U/L.

At laparoscopy, there was diffuse nodularity of the uterine serosa, fallopian tubes, ovaries and studding of the large and small bowel and peritoneal surfaces. Similar findings were seen throughout the peritoneum (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Findings on laparoscopy.
diagnosis:
Peritonitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Laparoscopic biopsies showed caseating granulomas. Intra-operative cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The patient was tested for human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) and was found to be negative. She received treatment for tuberculosis and her symptoms resolved.

The clinical presentation of tuberculous peritonitis is divided into the serous or plastic type. The serous type is characterized by ascites, as in this case. The plastic type is notable for abdominal masses and a "doughy" abdomen.

Summary: A woman with abdominal pain and a liver lesion.
A woman in her sixties
history:
Summary: A woman with abdominal pain and a liver lesion.
A woman in her sixties developed anorexia and nausea of 4 weeks' duration, followed by 1 week of fever and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She presented for evaluation, and denied any change in bowel habits.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus and an endoscopic procedure with biopsy of a gastric ulcer had been performed 2 months before.

She had traveled to India 6 months before the onset of her illness. She had also spent time on Cape Cod and worked in the healthcare industry.

Medications included omeprazole.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C). There was right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness, and the liver edge was palpable 1 centimeter below the right costal margin.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 12,000 cells/mm³, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 195 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT, SGPT) 50 U/L.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen (Figure 1) and aspiration of the liver lesion were performed. Gram stain of the liver aspirate is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 2. Gram stain.
diagnosis:
Hepatic actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces israelii.

Direct fluorescent antibody stain and culture of the liver aspirate were positive for Actinomyces israelii. (See Figure 3.)
Figure 3. Fluorescent stain.

The patient was treated with a prolonged course of penicillin and fully recovered.

The most common sites of involvement with actinomycosis are the jaw, the lung and intra-abdominal disease. Hepatic actinomycosis represents about 5% of cases of actinomycosis. The infection may result either from direct extension from a contiguous focus or from hematogenous spread. It is usually related to a breach in the gastrointestinal mucosa, although extension from pleuro-pulmonary infection is sometimes seen. Other companion organisms may be present.

history:
Summary: A man from Brazil with a rash of several years' duration.
A Brazilian man in his sixties was urged by a relative to have his rash of several years' duration evaluated. The lesions were mildly dysesthetic. He reported no fevers, chills, weight loss or other symptoms.

Non-contributory.

The patient had recently immigrated to the United States from Brazil to live with his relatives.
exam_studies:
He appeared well and was afebrile. The examination revealed a rash (shown in Figures 1 and 2). An area in the center of the rash had mildly decreased sensation.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Borderline tuberculoid leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

A skin biopsy was performed and revealed a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with multinucleated giant cells (Figure 3) consistent with borderline tuberculoid leprosy. Special stains, including acid-fast staining, were all negative.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy results.

He was successfully treated with dapsone and rifampin.

The physical findings are consistent with Tinea, however the duration of symptoms and biopsy results are not. Cutaneous leishmaniasis typically presents as a papule that subsequently ulcerates. Psoriasis typically occurs on extensor surfaces and has more scales. The rash of secondary syphilis does not last years. The history and biopsy results are diagnostic of borderline tuberculoid leprosy.

title:
Summary: A man with AIDS and pain on defecation.
A man in his forties with human
history:
Summary: A man with AIDS and pain on defecation.
A man in his forties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS presented with four weeks of pain on defecation. Evaluations revealed pyuria, and he received multiple courses of antibiotics. Urine cultures were sterile.

He had HIV-1 infection; the most recent CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 43 cells/mm³, and level of HIV-1 RNA was 225,000 copies/mL.

His only medication was trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 100.5°F (38.1°C). Examination revealed a tender, boggy prostate.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 2,500 cells/mm³. Urinalysis revealed 5-10 white cells per high powered field. Urine culture was sterile. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the pelvis was performed and revealed a prostatic abscess (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Pelvic CT scan.

The patient underwent aspiration of the abscess, and stains of the prostatic aspirate are shown (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Silver stain of prostatic aspirate.
Figure 3. Hematoxylin and eosin stain.
diagnosis:
Prostate abscess caused by Cryptococcus neoformans in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

The silver stain and hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain revealed yeast forms (Figures 2 and 3). Culture of the prostatic aspirate grew Cryptococcus neoformans.

Cryptococcus neoformans enters the body via the respiratory route. The organism has a tropism for the central nervous system, and cryptococcal meningitis is a common site of disseminated disease in patients with advanced HIV-1 infections. Other focal sites of cryptococcal involvement include the skin, bone and prostate, as seen in this case.

Summary: A man with fever and rash after travel to Africa.
A man in his fifties, approximately 2.5 weeks before evaluation, had spent time in the grasslands of South Africa, including lying on the ground observing animals. Ten days later, he developed a "black spot" on his right upper thigh and, three days later, developed acute fever, shaking chills, night sweats, and myalgias.

He had a history of cataracts and duodenal ulcer disease.

He had recently traveled, as above.
exam_studies:
There was a necrotic lesion (2 centimeters in diameter) on the right upper thigh, with tender right inguinal adenopathy and several scattered papulovesicular lesions over the back, arms and legs (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count and differential were normal.

South African Tick Bite Fever, due to the spotted fever group of Rickettsia.

Acute and convalescent serology demonstrated a rise in titer to the spotted fever group of Rickettsia, from less than 1:16 to positive at 1:512 dilution.

title:
Summary: A man with pneumonia.
A man in his sixties was admitted because of feve
history:
Summary: A man with pneumonia.
A man in his sixties was admitted because of fevers and chills for four days, and cough (without sputum) for two days. He was disabled due to long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and was on prednisone (10 mg every other day).

He had rheumatoid arthritis and was status post gastrectomy for peptic ulcer disease. There was no other significant past medical history or epidemiologic exposure.

He took prednisone, as above.
exam_studies:
His temperature was 105°F (40.6°C), and his lungs were clear.

The white blood cell count was 9,200 cells/mm³ with 79% polymorphonuclear leukocytes and 3% band forms.
The initial chest radiograph revealed a nodular infiltrate in the left upper lobe (Figure 1). Sputum gram stain revealed polymorphonuclear leukocytes with mixed oral flora. Bronchoscopy and cultures were unrevealing.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

A chest radiograph five days later showed a worsening infiltrate (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Chest radiograph five days later.
diagnosis:
Legionella micdadei atypical pneumonia.

Following empiric antibiotic treatment, a diagnosis of Legionella micdadei infection was made retrospectively by testing acute and convalescent sera for causes of atypical pneumonia.

The patient improved on empiric therapy that included erythromycin.

The commensal organisms that promote the growth of Legionella pneumophila do not support L. micdadei, perhaps accounting for the lower frequency of the latter in the water supply. Legionella micdadei usually affects individuals who are immunosuppressed or have undergone prolonged hospitalization. At the time of this publication, treatment of L. micdadei pneumonia should include a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone. In immunosuppressed individuals, a longer course of therapy (up to 21 days) may help prevent relapse.
