title: A five-week-old infant with a fever and fussiness.
history: A five-week-old infant presented to the pediatric office with a history of fussiness for a few nights. The baby was eating and urinating well. A sibling was reported to have had a rhinorrhea but no fever. The mother had a history of pre-eclampsia and genital warts, and denied a history of vaginal or oral herpes simplex virus (HSV) or any active genital lesions at delivery.
exam_studies:
The patient was very irritable, especially when moved, and occasionally moaned in her mother’s arms. The temperature was 101.9°F (38.8°C). A tachycardia was present, and thought to be consistent with the fever. The anterior fontanelle was flat and the skin was clear. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 9,550/mm³ with 47% segmented neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes and 1% basophils, and the platelet count was 507,000/mm³. The urinalysis was normal. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen was bloody with 8990 red blood cells, 230 white blood cells (12% segmented neutrophils, 67% lymphocytes and 21% monocytes), glucose 49 g/dl and protein 198 g/dl. All cultures remained sterile.

Ampicillin and cefotaxime were initiated at admission. Seizures developed on the third hospital day. The patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit and anti-seizure medications and intravenous acyclovir were begun.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head with contrast (Figure 1) showed an increased density to the right of the midline near the apex of the tentorium, which was thought to represent calcium or blood. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head with gadolinium (Figures 2 and 3) showed a ‘tiny’ amount of hemorrhage as noted on the CT scan, with normal parenchyma.
Ophthalmology and neurology evaluations were obtained. An electroencephalogram (EEG) was abnormal with excessive number of sharp waves but no focal slowing and no evidence of electrographic seizures. Herpes simplex virus IgG was reactive. The cultures remained negative. All herpes cultures were sterile and the herpes polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the CSF was negative.
An Infectious Diseases consultation was obtained; on further questioning, the mother reported that shortly before delivery she had fallen ill with vomiting and felt feverish.
Figure 1. Head CT scan.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan.
Figure 3. Head MRI scan.
diagnosis:
Enteroviral meningoencephalitis.

A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen for enterovirus was positive by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

The patient was treated with anticonvulsants and discharged home on phenobarbital.

Non-polio enteroviruses are responsible for significant and frequent illnesses in infants and children and result in protean clinical manifestations. The most common presentation is nonspecific febrile illness, which in young infants may lead to evaluation for bacterial sepsis. Neonates who acquire infection without maternal antibody are at risk of severe disease with a high mortality rate. Neurologic manifestations include aseptic meningitis, encephalitis and paralysis.
The non-polio enteroviruses are RNA viruses. Enterovirus infections are common and are spread by fecal-oral and respiratory routes and from mother to infant in the peripartum period. This seems of particular significance in reference to this case, given the history obtained from the mother of vomiting and fever close to the time of delivery.
Specimens providing the highest rates of viral isolation are those obtained from the throat, stool and rectal swabs. Specimens should also be obtained from any sites of clinical involvement, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). In patients with serious illnesses, viral isolation as a means of diagnosis is particularly important. Viral isolation from any specimen except feces usually can be considered causally related to the patient’s illness.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for the presence of enterovirus RNA in CSF is more sensitive than viral isolation. At the time of this publication, no specific therapy is available although an antiviral agent, pleconaril, is undergoing clinical evaluation in infants with aseptic meningitis. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) also has been used in life-threatening neonatal infections, although there is no convincing evidence of efficacy for this use. Contact precautions are indicated for infants and young children for the duration of hospitalization.
Neonatal herpes simplex virus and enteroviral meningoencephalitis have very similar presentations and a work-up for HSV should always be undertaken in such clinical situation and acyclovir therapy immediately initiated until either HSV is excluded or a diagnosis of enteroviral infection or another diagnosis is made.

title: A man in his twenties with weight loss, pulmonary infiltrate, respiratory failure and skin lesions.
history:
A previously healthy man in his twenties was diagnosed as having community-acquired pneumonia by his primary care physician three months before his presentation. At that time he had complained of dyspnea on exertion, a non-productive cough and a low-grade fever. He was prescribed a course of oral antibiotics without clinical response. His symptoms persisted and a presumptive diagnosis of sarcoidosis with pulmonary involvement was made. He was started on high dose systemic steroids (oral prednisone 70 mg/day reduced by 10 mg every week) that resulted in temporary relief of symptoms.
On this admission, the patient complained of 25-pound weight loss over three months, night sweats, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. He denied cough, hemoptysis and sputum production. He noticed small papular lesions, primarily on the face, neck, upper chest and upper back, that had appeared over the past few weeks. There was no discharge from the lesions and they were not pruritic or painful. The surrounding skin appeared normal.

As above.

The patient lived in Texas and had not traveled outside of the region. He worked in the construction industry and denied exposure to animals. He drank alcohol occasionally, and reported no tobacco or injection drug use.

He had been taking prednisone, which was started at 70 mg/day, tapered over a period of 8 weeks, and stopped 2 weeks before his presentation.
exam_studies:
He was awake, alert and oriented, and appeared to be in moderate respiratory distress. The maximum temperature was 39.7°C (103.5°F), pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/73 mm Hg, respirations 24 breaths per minute, with a pulse oximetry 87% on room air and 95% on 2 liters of oxygen via nasal cannula.
There were multiple cervical lymph nodes 1-2 cm in size, firm, mobile and non-tender. The lungs had coarse ronchi with bilateral expiratory wheezes. The liver was palpable 2 centimeters below the costal margin, firm, and non-tender. The spleen was not palpable. There were multiple papular lesions (varying in size from 4-6 mm in diameter) involving the face, neck, upper chest and back, some of which were hyperpigmented. (See Figures 1 and 2.) The lesions were extra-follicular and some had central umbilication. The rest of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 2,800/mL (granulocytes 80.7%, lymphocytes 14.6%, monocytes 1.8%, eosinophils 2.2%, bands 0.7%), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 66 mm after one hour. Electrolytes were sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 106 mmol/L, CO2 20 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 31mg/ dL, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL. The total bilirubin was 1 mg/dL, albumin 1.7 g/ dL, alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 58 U/ L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 156 U/L, gamma glutamyl-transpeptidase (GGT) 936 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 4558 U/L.
A chest radiograph (CXR) showed diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates, and a mildly enlarged heart. Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen showed extensive diffuse ground glass alveolar opacities with some thickening along the bronchoalveolar bundles, mild mediastinal, bi-hilar and upper abdominal lymphadenopathy. There was also mild hepatosplenomegaly. Urine Legionella antigen and antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative. A blood culture showed no growth at 72 hours. There were rare mononuclear cells and rare neutrophils but no organisms on the sputum gram stain. The sputum culture showed 1+ respiratory flora.
An electrocardiogram (ECG) had diffuse ST segment and T wave changes compatible with pericarditis.

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed. During the procedure the patient developed respiratory distress and required intubation and ventilator support.
Specimens were sent for cell count, cytology and culture (routine, fungal and mycobacterial). Skin biopsy was done of the papular lesions on the face, neck and upper trunk. The ECG indicated pericarditis but an echocardiogram did not reveal any evidence of pericardial effusion or tamponade. A chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral infiltrates, hilar lymphadenopathy and a small right-sided pleural effusion. A presumptive diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia was made, pending results of the evaluation, and intravenous cefotaxime and azithromycin were begun.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.

There were 2 nucleated red blood cells (RBCs) per 100 white cells. Serum Histoplasma antibody was positive. The bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed rare budding yeast with moderate mononuclear cells and moderate leukocytes. Cytopathology also showed budding yeast (mostly intrahistiocytic) on Wright-Giemsa stain (Figure 3) and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) (Figure 4) stains. Hematoxylin and eosin (Figures 5 and 6) and GMS stains (Figure 7) of the skin biopsy of the papillary dermis showed mixed inflammation with leukocytoclasia associated with budding yeasts. Fungal blood culture, sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage specimen cultures all grew Histoplasma capsulatum.
Figure 3. Wright-Giemsa stain of BAL specimen.
Figure 4. GMS stain of BAL specimen.
Figure 5. H and E stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 6. H and E stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 7. GMS stain of skin biopsy.

Intravenous amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) was administered for 3 weeks, with dramatic improvement and significant resolution of the skin lesions. Oral itraconazole (200mg twice daily) was started with the intention of completing a 6-month course.

Histoplasma capsulatum is a ubiquitous dimorphic fungus that causes opportunistic infection in patients with an impaired immune system. In the United States, it is endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. The initial infection is acquired by inhaling mycelial fragments and conidia from the soil. Construction workers and spelunkers are at increased risk. The mycelia settle in the alveoli, are engulfed by neutrophils and macrophages and are transported to the lymph nodes, liver and spleen.
A majority of the cases are asymptomatic and go unrecognized. Some patients develop cavitary pulmonary disease, which is similar in clinical and radiographic presentation to pulmonary tuberculosis. Few patients develop progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH). Major risk factors for disseminated disease are age (>54 years or <2 years of age) and immunosuppression (HIV with a CD4+ count <200, Hodgkin’s or non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, patients on immunosuppressive drugs). Patients usually present with fever, night sweats, headache, non-productive cough and chest pain. Physical findings include hepatosplenomegaly, cervical lymphadenopathy, rales, jaundice and oropharyngeal lesions. Cutaneous lesions may present as a maculopapular rash, petechiae or ecchymosis. Laboratory abnormalities may include anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and alanine aminotransferase. Chest radiographs may reveal patchy pneumonitis with mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Acute pericarditis is seen in up to 6% of cases and is usually detected on ECG. Progressive mediastinal fibrosis, a rare presentation of histoplasmosis, can be fatal and untreatable.
The diagnosis is made by the isolation of H. capsulatum from tissue samples that include sputum, BAL specimen, blood and tissue. Tissue specimens can be stained with Gomori methenamine silver stain or Wright-Giemsa stain. The organism may take up to three weeks to grow in culture. The antigen can be detected in the serum and urine by radioimmunoassay or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Serologic tests are available for the detection of H. capsulatum antibodies and may help in a rapid diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis of a patient with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis can be difficult to distinguish from influenza, community-acquired pneumonia and sarcoidosis as illustrated by this case. The patient was initially diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and treated with oral antibiotics without any improvement. A presumptive diagnosis of sarcoidosis was then made and the patient was put on high dose systemic steroids. It can be a challenge to differentiate between the two clinically. Serum angiotensin converting enzyme levels may be elevated in both diseases and they can both present with hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. In a patient from an endemic area who presents with these symptoms and a hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, a diagnosis of histoplasmosis should be considered. Also, if present, skin lesions may provide an opportunity for rapid tissue diagnosis.

title: A man had lower extremity pain, fever and malaise after cardiac surgery. An elderly man, seven months after aortic valve replacement with a bovine allograft for aortic stenosis, was admitted with complaints of fevers, chills, bilateral intermittent lower extremity and back pain, and weight loss of 30 pounds (13.6 kg) during the preceding two months. The patient's aortic valve replacement surgery had been complicated by atrial fibrillation. He had received beta-blocker therapy and converted to normal sinus rhythm.
history:
Five months before admission, he had an episode of sudden right calf pain while riding his bicycle. He was seen in the Emergency Department where an evaluation for deep venous thrombosis, including a venous Doppler study, was negative. Two months later, he had an episode of abrupt onset thigh and calf pain in the left leg, with edema and erythema over the dorsum of the left foot. A venous Doppler examination of the left limb was negative for deep venous thrombosis. Cellulitis was diagnosed and he was treated as an outpatient with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and oral cephalexin for fourteen days. His lower extremity symptoms increased over the next two weeks. Both legs were tender to palpation, but no longer edematous or warm.
Two months before admission, he had a non-invasive ultrasound duplex scan of the arteries of both lower extremities, which showed a reduced systolic pressure and monophasic waveform in the left posterior tibialis artery. At the time of admission, he reported generalized weakness and malaise that had increased over the previous two months. His leg pains were not improving with either antibiotics or the NSAIDs therapy, and backaches had begun, which were worse with movement and at night. Fevers and chills occurred mostly in the evenings. A loss of appetite had resulted in a 30 lb (13.6 kg) weight loss.
He had a chronic mildly productive cough with clear mucoid sputum, which had not changed in character or severity since the time of surgery. Two months before admission, he had had a recurrence of genital herpes, one of many recurrences over the last thirty years, which had resolved spontaneously after 5 days. He denied chest pain, shortness of breath, headache, photophobia, abdominal pain, dysuria, hematuria, dental procedures or injections of any sort (intravenous drug use or acupuncture) after surgery, or other invasive procedures.

There was a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, depression, hypothyroidism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and syncope twice before valve replacement.

He was monogamous with his wife. He had traveled across the country more than 30 years before. He reported moderate remote tobacco and alcohol use.

He was retired and lived with his wife.

Medications included furosemide (40 mg daily), lisinopril (5 mg daily), metoprolol (100 mg twice daily), lovastatin (20 mg each night), multi-vitamin supplement, and ibuprofen (800 mg three times daily as needed for back pain).
exam_studies:
The patient was alert and oriented to time, place and person. He appeared wasted and fatigued but was not in acute distress. The temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), pulse 75 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/50 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 97% on 2 liters of supplemental oxygen. He had fair dentition and moderate periodontal disease. There was a new 2/6 systolic murmur over the left 2nd intercostal space, and diffuse non-focal weakness (4 of 5) was noted in proximal muscle groups in both upper and lower extremities.

The complete blood count (CBC) included white blood count of 12,600/mm³ (85% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, and 1% basophils), hematocrit 30%, and hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL; the remainder was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 87 mm/hour. The level of C-reactive protein was 10.9, INR 1.4, sodium was 131 mmol/L, and glucose 128 mg/dL. Other chemistry tests, liver function tests, B12, folate, haptoglobin, anti-globulin (Coomb’s) tests and the urinalysis were normal. Stool occult blood was negative. Iron, transferrin and total iron binding (TIBC) were all decreased; ferritin was elevated. Lactic dehydrogenase was elevated at 333 U/L. Testing for antibodies to human immunodefiency virus (HIV) and serology tests for hepatitis A, B and C viruses were negative; the RPR was non-reactive.
A chest radiograph had no acute infiltrates.

Blood and urine cultures drawn on admission were negative. Isolator tubes for fungal and mycobacterial organisms were sterile. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a mobile density (3.0 centimeters by1.2 cm) on the aortic root side of the aortic valve that was continuous with an abscess in the posterior aspect of the aortic ring. There were less well-defined fibrinous strands attached to the aortic leaflet tips. These findings were confirmed on a subsequent trans-esophageal echocardiogram.
Vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampin were administered. The patient continued to have daily fevers to 101-103°F (38.3-39.4°C) and his constitutional symptoms increased. Metronidazole and ceftriaxone were added to the antibiotic regimen on fourth and sixth hospital days, respectively.
On the eighth hospital day, he complained of blurry vision bilaterally. Fundoscopic examination was consistent with vitritis and endophthalmitis. A vitreal tap was done and fluid was sent for culture. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed scattered small areas of hyperintensity, involving multiple areas and consistent with scattered small infarcts. On the FLAIR images, there was loss of the normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal at small areas of the central sulcus bilaterally, that was thought to represent small amounts of blood or pus in the subarachnoid space. MR angiography of the great vessels of the neck and the circle of Willis was normal.
On the ninth hospital day, the patient became lethargic. He suffered a cardiac arrest and expired.
A limited autopsy of the chest revealed pulmonary congestion and cardiomegaly. There was a large (4.3cm by 3.5 cm) vegetation of the bio-prosthetic aortic valve and an abscess of the aortic annulus. Figure 1 shows the large aortic vegetation, and Figure 2, after the removal of the vegetation, shows a divided suture on the bovine aortic valve allograft (see arrows).
Figure 1. Aortic valve vegetation.
Figure 2. Divided suture on allograft.
diagnosis:
Aspergillus fumigatus prosthetic valve endocarditis.

The abscess fluid and valve tissue were cultured, with heavy growth of Aspergillus fumigatus in all specimens. Histopathology showed tissue invasion by fungal hyphae on Wright stain (Figure 3) and Gomori methenamine silver stain (Figures 4 and 5).
Figure 3. Valve tissue, septate hyphae on Wright’s stain.
Figure 4. Valve tissue with hyphal invasion (silver stain).
Figure 5. Valve tissue with hyphal elements (silver stain).

Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) occurring sixty days to twelve months after valve replacement is most commonly due to coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus, and Streptococcus species. Fungi cause between 10-15% of PVE during this time period. Aspergillus may infect a prosthetic heart valve. Diagnosis may be difficult since blood cultures are usually negative, as in this case. Surgery is generally necessary for cure.

title: A man in his seventies presented with increasing dyspnea.
history:
A man in his seventies presented with increasing dyspnea of four months' duration. The patient had chronic shortness of breath of unclear etiology, which had progressed from occurring only upon exertion to dyspnea at rest. Steroids and diuretics had been administered during the preceding three months, without improvement.
He also reported a productive cough with yellow sputum for one week, and a 20-pound weight loss over the previous two months. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, chest pain, gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms.

He had a history of metastatic thymoma (diagnosed 2 years before, status post chemotherapy and radiation therapy, with known mediastinal and right upper lobe mass), myasthenia gravis, congestive heart failure (ejection fraction 35%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1): 1.58 liters, forced vital capacity (FVC): 2.02 liters), alcoholic cirrhosis complicated by ascites, atrial fibrillation, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and diabetes mellitus type II. He had also had a basal cell carcinoma, and was allergic to cephradine.

The patient lived in Minnesota and was retired. He had stopped drinking alcohol five years before and, a former heavy smoker, had stopped smoking 10-15 years before. He denied illicit drug abuse and had no animal exposures. He had traveled to Las Vegas in the previous year.

Medications included prednisone, glipizide, insulin, ipratropium, albuterol, salmeterol, aspirin, spironolactone, furosemide, finasteride, and insulin.
exam_studies:
On admission, the patient was in mild respiratory distress and appeared cachectic. The temperature was 98.7°F (37.1°C), pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 83/52 mm Hg, respirations 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 93%. The mucous membranes were dry, and a jugular venous pressure of 5 centimeters was noted. The cardiac rhythm was irregularly irregular; there were diffuse expiratory wheezes, mild bibasilar crackles, and decreased breath sounds in the right upper lung field. The liver edge was palpated two centimeters below the right costal margin, and the spleen tip was palpable. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 35%, white blood cell count 5,600 cells/microliter, and platelet count 52,000/microliter. The creatinine was 2.2 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 84 mg/dL, D-dimer 886 (normal range 0-95).
Chest radiography revealed bibasilar infiltrates on the left more than right, a left pleural effusion and a right apical soft tissue density that was stable compared to previous findings.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, without the admnistration of intravenous contrast (Figure 1), revealed a large left pleural effusion, new sub pleural nodules in the left base, and lymph nodes in the pre-vascular space that were suspicious for metastatic disease. There was also a paramediastinal consolidation of right upper lobe that was unchanged from an earlier scan.
Figure 1. Chest CT scan without contrast.

The patient's shortness of breath increased. Oxygen requirements also increased, despite treatment with antibiotics for possible community acquired pneumonia and thoracentesis.
Progressive pancytopenia developed (hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, white blood cells 3,400/mm³, platelets 16,000/mm³), and blood transfusions were administered. Pre-renal azotemia resolved with hydration.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.

A thoracentesis was performed. Examination of the aspirate with potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation did not reveal any fungal elements, but pleural fluid cytology showed yeast forms in macrophages (Figure 2). No malignant cells were identified. Culture of the pleural fluid culture grew Histoplasma capsulatum.
Pathologic examination of a bone marrow biopsy showed normocellular bone marrow. Gomori methenamine silver stains performed on the bone marrow sections were strongly positive for fungal organisms (Figure 3). An increased number of histiocytes were seen, several of which contained multiple small intra-cytoplasmic organelles surrounded by a halo consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum (Figure 4).
The bone marrow biopsy culture grew Histoplasma capsulatum. Urine Histoplasma antigen was positive.
Figure 2. Pleural fluid cytology.
Figure 3. Gomori methenamine silver stain of bone marrow.
Figure 4. Bone marrow biopsy with histiocytes and intra-cytoplasmic organelles.

Disseminated histoplasmosis was diagnosed and the patient was treated with amphotericin B lipid complex. Shortly after initiation of therapy, cardiogenic shock and respiratory failure developed. He was intubated and ventilated, and pressors were administered; however, a sustained ventricular tachycardia occurred, followed by cardiopulmonary arrest.

title: A man in his sixties with fever, pulmonary infiltrates, abnormal liver function tests and anemia.
history:
A man in his sixties was admitted to the hospital with a two-week history of fevers, chills, abdominal pain and non-productive cough.

He had diabetes mellitus, which was well-controlled, and hypertension.

The patient was born and raised in the Philippines, and had lived in an urban area on the west coast of California for 30 years. He worked in an office, and did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He took frequent automobile trips to Las Vegas, and had traveled to the Philippines three years before this evaluation. He had no pets but regularly visited his neighbor who owned parakeets. His mother was deceased and may have had tuberculosis.

He lived with his family.

Medications included nifedipine, losartan, glipizide and metformin.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill but not toxic. The temperature was 103.5°F (39.7°C), blood pressure 150/82 mm Hg, pulse 92 beats per minute, and respirations 18 breaths per minute. There were rales at the right lung base. There were no heart murmurs. His abdomen was soft and without masses or organomegaly, and there was no rash or palpable lymphadenopathy.

A peripheral blood count showed white blood cells 4,900/mL, hemoglobin 11.0 gm/dL and platelets of 97,000/mL. The serum levels of alanine and aspartate aminotransferases were elevated at 177 and 118 mg/dL, respectively, and the level of creatinine, total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase were normal. Cultures of the blood were sterile. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral stranding infiltrates.
An abdominal ultrasound showed non-obstructing gallstones. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis yielded no additional findings.
A tuberculosis skin test (PPD) was positive, with 11 millimeters of induration. Legionella antigen was not detected in urine. A qualitative screening test for infection with Coccidioides immitis was positive for immunoglobulin (Ig) M and negative for IgG antibodies.

On admission, the patient received piperacillin-tazobactam empirically for possible biliary sepsis. The patient’s clinical condition worsened over the next 5 days, and he became more dyspneic and hypoxemic.
A follow-up chest radioraph showed prominent infiltrates in the right upper and left lower lung fields (Figure 1). CT scan of the chest showed infiltrates and bibasilar effusions (Figures 2 and 3).
The patient’s hemoglobin decreased to 7.5 gm/dL, and packed red blood cells (3 units) were transfused. A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy was performed (Figure 4).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, after clinical deterioration.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
Figure 4. H and E stain of bone marrow (80x).
diagnosis:
Acute Q fever in urban California, caused by Coxiella burnetii.

The bone marrow aspirate had normal cell lines with increased numbers of well-differentiated plasma cells. Flow cytometry was negative for monoclonal cells. Special stains were negative for microorganisms.
Histopathological exam of the biopsy (Figures 4 and 5) revealed numerous granulomatous lesions composed of dense rings of fibrin and epithelioid histiocytes surrounding clear, lipid-filled vacuoles. These lesions, so called “doughnut” granulomas, most often represent an immune inflammatory response to infection with Coxiella burnetii (the cause of Q fever). Figure 5 shows a typical “doughnut” granuloma with dense fibrin ring (arrowhead) and central lipid vacuole (arrow) (original magnification x 200).
Figure 5. H and E stain of bone marrow (200x).

Treatment for Q fever was instituted with doxycycline 100 mg by mouth twice daily. Within 48 hours the patient showed dramatic improvement. His chest radiograph cleared and liver function tests normalized. A transesophageal echocardiogram showed no evidence of endocarditis. He was discharged to complete a 21-day course of therapy.
The results of Coxiella antibody tests were consistent with the diagnosis of acute Q fever. The titer of phase I IgM antibody was elevated at 1:128; titers of phase II IgM and IgG antibodies were normal. After three months, the phase II IgG antibody titer rose to greater than 1:1024.
Before the patient was discharged, he was queried thoroughly about possible zoonotic exposures. He reported that five weeks before he became ill, he visited a neighboring cousin who kept goats in his backyard. On that occasion, a goat was slaughtered and the patient used the goat meat to prepare “birrias”, a goat meat stew. Other than the patient, no one else who ate the stew or handled the slaughtered goat became ill.

Q fever is a zoonosis caused by the strictly intracellular bacterium Coxiella burnetii. Clinical syndromes range from self-limited febrile illness to pneumonia, hepatitis, and endocarditis. Infection develops after inhalation of highly infectious C. burnetii spores. Cattle, sheep, and goats are the most common animal reservoirs. As a result, the majority of human infection occurs in rural settings. Of note, fifty years before this presentation, the disease was considered to be endemic in California. In the decade before, two cases of Q fever were reported to the Los Angeles City Health Department.
This case demonstrates that human contact with Coxiella -infected animals can still occur in urban areas of California. Thus, residence in metropolitan areas should not preclude a diagnosis of Q fever in patients who have a compatible clinical illness and substantive exposure to potentially infected animals.

title: A man in his sixties with pulmonary infiltrates.
history:
A man in his sixties presented with the acute onset of fever, hemoptysis, and dyspnea.

He had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), coronary artery disease, sick sinus syndrome requiring a pacemaker, micronodular cirrhosis (Child’s Class B) and a history of alcohol abuse.

He lived in Tennessee, and denied travel to the southwestern United States, South America, Europe, Asia, or Australia. He had a history of alcohol abuse and 30 pack-year history of smoking, with no use of illicit substances or injection drug use. He denied exposures to tuberculosis, other ill contacts, animals or arthropods.

Medications included ramipril, albuterol metered dose inhaler, and ipratropium metered dose inhaler.
exam_studies:
The patient was in severe respiratory distress. The temperature was 96°F (35.6°C), blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats per minute, respirations 30 breaths per minute. He appeared jaundiced and had scleral icterus. There were increased bronchial breath sounds in the right middle and upper lung fields, and 1+ bilateral pitting edema of the legs. The remainder of his examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 28,700/mm³, 91% polymorphonuclear neutrophils, platelet count 114,000/mm³, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, albumin 1.8 g/dL, total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, and INR 1.4. An arterial blood gas, while breathing 40% inspired oxygen, revealed pH 7.34, partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) of 54 mm Hg, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) of 46 mm Hg.
A chest radiograph revealed a new right upper lobe infiltrate (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.

The patient was intubated and placed on a mechanical ventilator. Bronchoscopic examination was performed. The gram stain of the bronchial washings of the right upper lobe is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Gram stain (100x magnification).
diagnosis:
Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia.

The bronchoscopy did not reveal any endobronchial lesions. In Figure 3 (Gram stain of right upper lobe bronchial washing), the arrows point to gram negative rods, a neutrophil, and (on the bottom of the image) a respiratory epithelial cell. Cytology of the right upper lobe brushings (Figure 4) revealed reactive atypical bronchial epithelial cells with degenerative changes, reactive atypical bronchial epithelial cells, neutrophils, and normal typical bronchial epithelial cells.
Routine culture of the bronchial brushings and washings grew Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant only to ampicillin and ticarcillin. Other cultures of the bronchial specimens and blood cultures were sterile; acid-fast and silver stains of the brushings and washings were negative. Tests for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and urinary Legionella antigens were also negative.
Figure 4. Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology, Papanicolaou stain (40x magnification).

The patient was diagnosed with Klebsiella pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia. He was treated with two weeks of pipercillin-tazobactam and levofloxacin. He was eventually transferred to a skilled-nursing facility, where he unfortunately acquired and ultimately succumbed to a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus nosocomial pneumonia.

Klebsiella has been a known human pathogen since it was first isolated in the late nineteenth century by Edwin Klebs. It is often referred to as Friedlander’s bacillus in honor of Carl Friedlander who identified it as a significant respiratory pathogen in 1882. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, non-motile, aerobic rod. There is a prominent polysaccharide capsule with more than 80,000 antigen serotypes. No unique virulence factors have been identified save for the capsule that inhibits phagocytosis and endotoxin. Humans are the primary reservoir for Klebsiella although these organisms can also be found in soil and water. Nasopharyngeal colonization in the general population has been estimated to be about 5%. However, certain risk factors such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, and alcoholism increase the rate of colonization and infection.
Klebsiella has been estimated to cause about 5% of community-acquired pneumonia and along with Enterobacter about 10% of nosocomial pneumonia. Klebsiella pneumoniae has a tendency for abscess formation, cavitation, and empyema. Rarely, there are metastatic complications such as pericarditis, arthritis, meningitis, or pulmonary gangrene.
The disease is typically acute with the sudden onset of cough, pleurisy, dyspnea, and fever. It is a very inflammatory process with necrosis that can culminate in the classic thick, bloody, “currant jelly” sputum. Fever, tachypnea, and lung consolidation are usually features on physical examination. Leukocytosis and hypoxemia are typical laboratory features. The radiographic appearance is typically dense lobar consolidation with a predilection for the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Bowing of the fissure downward due to intense consolidation give rise to the bulging fissure sign.
The diagnosis is suggested by the findings of many polymorphonuclear neutrophils and plump gram-negative rods on a sputum gram stain. Definitive diagnosis is made by recovery of Klebsiella from lower respiratory tract secretions or from blood cultures. Bacteremia is common and seen in about 75% of cases.
The mainstay of therapy has traditionally been comprised of combination therapy with a cephalosporin and aminoglycoside. However, due to the acquisition of various genetic elements such as R plasmids, resistance of Klebsiella to cephalosporins and aminoglycosides has been increasing. Newer agents such as carbapenems, and fluoroquinolones have thus been used either as monotherapy or in combination with good results. Recently, multi-drug resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae outbreaks have been described, especially in intensive care units with strains that elaborate an extended-spectrum Beta-lactamase. The antibiotic treatment of nosocomial Klebsiella infections requires susceptibility determination for optimal results. Empirical antibiotic coverage should be tailored to the drug resistance pattern seen in the local hospital setting.
The mortality rate from Klebsiella pneumoniae is quite significant. In the pre-antibiotic era, classic Klebsiella pneumoniae was considered almost universally fatal. The use of antibiotic therapy has markedly decreased the mortality rate. A poor prognosis is usually associated with severe underlying medical diseases or inadequate therapy.

title: A man in his thirties with vertigo and nausea.
history:
A man in his thirties began experiencing dizzy “spells” acutely one morning. Over subsequent days, the dizziness increased and he developed an unsteady gait. He went to an emergency room, where benign positional vertigo was diagnosed and meclizine was prescribed. However, his symptoms increased and became persistent. He developed nausea and vomiting and returned to the emergency room. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed an area of hypoattenuation in the medial left cerebellum.
He was transferred to another hospital for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). He reported no history of headache, photophobia, fever, chills, stiff neck or change in sensorium.

He was monogamous with his wife. He reported eating raw oysters and uncooked fish. He had visiting a petting zoo eight months earlier, and had traveled to Kenya five years before. In Africa, he had swum in Lake Victoria and gone on safari. He had had mild diarrhea for two days during his return from Kenya. He had no recollection of subsequent fevers or rashes. He had no pets, drank alcohol rarely and did not smoke.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable. The temperature was 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, and respirations 12 breaths per minute. Neurological examination showed bilateral horizontal nystagmus and terminal dysmetria on finger-nose-finger testing, especially on the left. The gait was wide-based and unsteady. There was no meningismus. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites, and his skin had no lesions. The remainder of his examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 8,000/mm³ (70% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes, monocytes 6.3%, eosinophils 1.4%). The remainder of the complete blood cell count (CBC) and levels of electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose and liver function tests were normal. A test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed normal levels of protein and glucose, 1550 red cells and 110 white cells per cubic millimeter, with 4% neutrophils, 86% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils, with no other cells noted. Examination of a stool specimen by trichrome stain showed no ova and parasites.
The MRI scan, performed with gadolinium, demonstrated a T-2 abnormality (Figure 1), which included a frond-like enhancement in the inferior cerebellar vermis and nodulus, the left superior cerebellar peduncle, medial cerebellum (the left more than right) and the medial aspect of the right brachium pontis. A T-1 abnormality was also seen (Figure 2).
Figure 1. MRI scan with gadolinium.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan T1.

The patient’s nausea and dizziness increased. He did not developed a headache, change in sensorium, fevers or systemic signs.
diagnosis:
Neuroschistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma mansoni leading to cerebellar tumoral lesion.

Because the differential diagnosis included malignancy, a brain biopsy via a suboccipital approach was performed. The frozen section was consistent with “parasite”. Approximately 25% of the lesion was resected.
On pathologic examination, sections of the cerebellum reveal scattered large necrotizing granulomas composed of eosinophils, histiocytes, lymphocytes and giant cells (Figure 3). Figure 4 demonstrates Schistosoma mansoni ova within the granulomata, some with prominent lateral spines. The eggs measure approximately 120 by 50 microns. They were widely spaced, with one to three eggs present per granuloma. Figure 5 demonstrates an ovum within a granuloma. Figures 6 (low power) and Figure 7 (high power) demonstrate the Splendore-Hoeppli reaction, composed of antigen-antibody complexes surrounding the ovum. Figure 8 demonstrates an ovum with a prominent lateral spine. Most eggs show maturing miracidium larvae within, although occasional eggs appear as empty shells. None were calcified, and no adult parasites were identified.
Figure 3. Brain biopsy of cerebellum.
Figure 4. Brain biopsy results.
Figure 5. Brain biopsy.
Figure 6. Splendore-Hoeppli reaction on low power.
Figure 7. Splendore-Hoeppli reaction.
Figure 8. An ovum with lateral spine.

After neurosurgery, the patient was placed on high-dose dexamethasone. Nonetheless, he had an acute deterioration of his mental status. By CT scan he was noted to have developed hydrocephalus and cerebellar herniation. He had a ventriculostomy placed. He was treated with 5 days of praziquantel (45 mg/kg/day) and high dose steroids. Post-operatively while on therapy he had severe nausea, vomiting, photophobia and meningismus which began to resolve by post-operative day 6. Ten days post-operatively his ventriculostomy was removed, his mental status had improved and his cerebellar signs and symptoms had begun to resolve. He continued to improve to baseline, with some residual nausea.
Testing for antibodies to Schistosoma was positive at 5.71 (negative=<1.00) using the microsomal fraction of adult S. mansoni worms as antigen (Focus Technologies). No ova were identified in his stool.

Schistosomiasis is common worldwide, with an estimated 200 million people infected. The infection is acquired in fresh water when the cercarial form of the fluke penetrates human skin, then changes form into the schistosomulum, which migrates through the pulmonary and then systemic circulation and eventually to the portal veins. In the portal system the organisms mature into adult flukes. The male and female forms pair and then, for S. mansoni, they typically migrate to the mesenteric venules to mate. The female migrates further against venous flow and lays eggs. Some eggs embed into the venule wall and arrive eventually in the intestinal lumen, and then are shed in stool. Other eggs are carried into the hepatic microvasculature, where they lodge and instigate a granulomatous inflammatory response. Eventually, this process can lead to portal tract fibrosis and portal hypertension. Eggs are passed in stool and hatch in freshwater.
The hatched miracidiae penetrate snails (Biomphalaria). Within the snails, sporocysts form and metamorphose into cercariae, which are released into freshwater. There are two potential ways in which Schistosomiasis can involve the central nervous system: aberrant migration of flukes or, more commonly, systemic embolization of eggs (typically in the setting of portal hypertension and collateral circulation). It is thought that S. mansoni is a less common cause of brain disease than S. japonicum because the larger size of S. mansoni eggs and the presence of their lateral spine makes egg migration through the vertebral venous plexus to the brain less likely. However, in this patient, it was likely ectopic migration of the fluke pair to the cerebellar venous system, followed by attachment and subsequent prolific egg deposition that led to the large area of eosinophilic granulomata and mass effect. This area of inflammation with multiple eggs present can be many times larger than single egg granulomas and is a rare manifestation within the brain - the so-called “tumoral” form of neuroschistosomiasis. The presentation reflects the anatomic location of the granulomatous lesion and mass effect. The cerebellum is the most common site reported in the literature. A high stool egg burden need not be evident.
Our patient most likely acquired his disease during his swim in Lake Victoria five years earlier. S. mansoni flukes can survive up to 30 years in a host, though average life span is estimated 5-10 years. His presentation is relatively late in comparison to other reports of tumoral neuroschistosomiasis in the literature. Typical treatment for central nervous system (CNS) schistosomiasis involves praziquantel directed towards the fluke and steroids to lessen the granulomatous inflammatory response provoked by the eggs. Although steroids can significantly decrease CNS levels of praziquantel, generally the venules in which the flukes reside are outside the brain tissue itself. In cases found in the literature, treatment was successful in some after two doses of praziquantel, while others described patients with CNS disease requiring additional doses. Though the literature is divergent, most experts favor 5 days of therapy along with a very slow steroid taper. Reemergence of symptoms can be associated with too rapid a steroid taper.

title: A man in his twenties with prolonged fever and cutaneous papules.
history:
A man in his twenties presented with a history of fevers of 3 weeks' duration. Two weeks before presentation, cutaneous lesions had developed on his arms and, 3 days before, on his face. He also reported weight loss of 4-kilograms and poor appetite. He denied chill, myalgias, cough, or diarrhea.

He had had urethritis five years before, and was otherwise well.

He lived in an urban area of Thailand. He denied travel in the previous three months.

He was single and lived alone.
exam_studies:
He was alert, and appeared weak and thin. He was not pale and there was no jaundice. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F) and pulse 84 beats per minute. There was bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, 0.5-1 cm in diameter. Numerous skin-color cutaneous papules, some with umbilication, were present on his face and both arms (Figures 1 and 2). The examination of the lungs and heart was normal. The liver was enlarged and extended 2 cm below right costal margin, without tenderness. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical findings on arm.

The hematocrit was 33%, white blood cell count 2,200 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 78%, lymphocytes 20%, monocytes 2%) and platelets 185,000/mm³. The level of alkaline phosphatase was 85 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 50 U/L, and bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. A test for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive.
A chest radiograph was normal.
Cutaneous lesions on his face and the right arm were scraped; examination of the tissues with Wright staining (Figure 3 and 4) showed numerous intracellular yeasts with binary fission.
Figure 3. Wright stain of arm lesion.
Figure 4. Wright stain of face lesion.
diagnosis:
Disseminated penicilliosis, caused by Penicillium marneffei, in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

The level of CD4 T-lymphocytes was 78 cells/mm³. A bone marrow study was performed and showed hypocellular marrow with numerous yeasts. Cultures of the blood and bone marrow grew Penicillium marneffei.

The patient was treated for disseminated penicilliosis after the result of bedside cutaneous-lesion scraping and Wright stain was known. Amphotericin B was administered for 2 weeks, and then was stopped and oral itraconazole was begun. The fevers and skin lesions resolved. Two months after starting anti-fungal therapy, the patient was started on anti-retroviral medications.

Penicilliosis is a common opportunistic infection in Southeast Asia. The patients usually present with fever, anemia, weight loss, skin lesions, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatomegaly. The skin lesions are most commonly papules with central umbilication (molluscum-like lesions). Most of the patients have CD4 T-lymphocyte cell counts less than 100 cells/mm³. The characteristic finding of Penicillium marneffei is binary fission of the yeast. The fungus is susceptible to amphotericin B and itraconazole.

title: A man with a skin rash.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with a painless, non-pruritic vesicular eruption over his right flank, bilateral inguinal and lower buttock areas, left subclavicular region and infra-mammary areas. The lesions appeared gradually over 2 weeks. All lesions had crusted over at presentation, leaving areas of hyper-pigmentation and mild silvery scaling.

He had received a cadaveric renal transplant for chronic glomerulonephritis three months before presentation. He was treated with isoniazid (INH) and pyridoxine for a positive tuberculosis skin test (PPD) 12 months before.

He had no known allergies.

Medications included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone, and valganciclovir.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, and was afebrile with normal vital signs. The skin lesions were flat erythematous areas (1-2 cm in diameter) with scaling (Figures 1 and 2). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 12,700/mm³ with a normal differential. Other hematologic and chemistry parameters were normal. Tzank preparation and direct fluorescent antibody staining for herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 and 2 were negative.

Acyclovir was started empirically for presumed Herpes zoster. A skin biopsy was performed.
diagnosis:
Trichophyton rubrum skin infection.

The skin biopsy revealed septate hyphae of a dermatophyte (Trichophyton rubrum) in the keratinous layer of skin (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. PAS stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 4. GMS stain of skin biopsy.

The patient was treated with a single dose of ketoconazole while his immunosuppressive medications were held, followed by topical terbenafine, with resolution of the rash over a month.

Dermatophytoses are superficial infections caused by fungi capable of colonizing keratinized tissues such as stratum corneum of the epidermis, nails and hair. The three fungal genera that are most commonly involved are: Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. In areas of skin trauma, maceration or occlusion with non-porous material, these fungi may invade and cause skin rashes.
Dermatophyte infections routinely affect individuals who are otherwise healthy, but people with compromised immune systems are particularly susceptible. Extensive disease and failure to respond to treatment should alert providers to the possibility of an underlying immunologic problem.
Clinical syndromes caused by theses fungi are described by the site affected. (For example, Tinea capitis: affecting the scalp, Tinea barbae: affecting the beard area, Tinea corporis: affecting glabrous skin, Tinea cruris: affecting groin and pelvic area, Tinea pedis: affecting feet, Tinea manuum: affecting hands, Tinea unguium: affecting the nail plate, etc.) Trichophyton rubrum is named for the red pigmented colonies produce on Sabouraud’s agar. It is most commonly associated with tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis and tinea unguium.
A presumptive diagnosis of dermatophyte infection should be supported by microscopic examination of clinical material and culture. In a 10% KOH preparation they appear as septate branching hyphal elements. Sabouraud’s dextrose agar is the most commonly used medium for growth of these organisms.

title: A man with fever, fatigue, and abdominal pain.
history:
A man in his thirties was seen in the Emergency Room with fatigue, fever, new-onset jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. The patient reported fatigue for the previous six weeks. Two weeks before admission, fevers, chills, and night sweats developed. He was evaluated at a health services clinic. Blood tests revealed elevated liver transaminases. A monospot test was negative; a presumptive diagnosis of mononucleosis was made. The patient was advised to take antipyretics for symptomatic relief.
He continued to experience fatigue and fever. The patient medicated himself with oral tetracycline during the week before admission. He was seen in an Emergency Department with persistent fever, two days of intermittent epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, and one day of scleral icterus. He denied rash, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

He had a history of depression. Testing for hepatitis B virus surface antigen and antibodies to hepatitis A and C viruses and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) had been negative within the preceding two years.

The patient was originally from southern Europe. He had most recently traveled there seven months earlier, without illness at that time. He denied other travel, as well as alcohol, tobacco, or intravenous drug use. He was bisexual.

Medications included fluoxetine, ibuprofen and naproxen.
exam_studies:
In the emergency room, he was an ill-appearing, diaphoretic male, lying in bed. The temperature was 38.7°C (101.7°F) orally, pulse 119 beats per minute, respirations 29 breaths per minute, blood pressure 93/56 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 95% while breathing ambient air. He had scleral icterus, clear lungs, and normal heart sounds with tachycardia. There was mild tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastric region and right upper quadrant, without rebound or guarding. The liver was enlarged; the edge was palpable below the costal margin. The rectal exam was guaiac-negative. There was no peripheral edema, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 17,000/mm³ with increased bands, hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, and platelets 69,000/mm³. The level of serum urea nitrogen (BUN) was 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, the anion gap 10, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 76 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 121 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 419 U/L, total bilirubin 7.1 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL.
The arterial blood gas had a pH of 7.41, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 42 mm Hg, and partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) 77 mm Hg on ambient air.
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed moderate gallbladder wall thickening, measuring 6.7 mm, with pericholecystic edema. There was no evidence of cholecystitis or ductal dilatation, and mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted.

The systolic blood pressures ranged from 80 to 100 mm Hg, and intravenous fluids were administered. The patient was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for presumed ascending cholangitis and septic shock. He was empirically treated with ampicillin-sulbactam. During the following eight hours, the patient became increasingly hypotensive, tachypneic and hypoxic. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral patchy infiltrates and the patient was subsequently intubated.
On the second hospital day, computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous and oral contrast revealed marked hepatosplenomegaly with possible splenic infarcts, moderate upper abdominal, retroperitoneal, and pelvic adenopathy and a dilated heart. There was no evidence for cholangitis. A bronchoscopy was performed to evaluate the possibility of infection and alveolar hemorrhage after the appearance of bloody mucus in endotracheal secretions.
On the third hospital day, blood cultures that were drawn on admission grew gram-variable coccobacilli from both the aerobic and anaerobic cultures. The carbol fuchsin stain from a culture is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Carbol fuchsin stain of blood culture.
diagnosis:
Haemophilus parainfluenzae endocarditis.

A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular function with mild chamber enlargement. The study also showed an abnormality consistent with either a flail aortic valve cusp or aortic valve vegetation with severe aortic insufficiency. Two large vegetations (measuring roughly 1.5 cm by 1.7cm and 0.7 cm by 0.7cm) were on the mitral valve, and two regurgitant jets of mitral regurgitation were evident.
Two sets of blood cultures from admission grew Haemophilus parainfluenzae on the fifth hospital day.

The patient rapidly developed cardiogenic shock requiring vasopressor and inotropic support. Antibiotic therapy was changed to imipenem and dialysis was initiated for worsening acidosis. CT scanning of the head showed multiple focal hypodensities within the right frontal lobe.
Emergent aortic and mitral valve replacements with St. Jude’s mechanical valves were performed on the fourth hospital day. Intraoperative findings included perforated anterior and posterior leaflets of the mitral valve and vegetations on the aortic valve. (See Figure 2 below.)
Therapy was changed to ceftriaxone following the identification of the pathogen as Haemophilus species. The post-operative course was complicated by congestive heart failure, which was managed medically, and the development of a pericardial effusion that required drainage.
Following a six-week hospitalization, the patient had a complete recovery of his renal function and a mild residual left upper and lower extremity weakness.
Other laboratory tests included a positive Hepatitis B surface antigen, negative Hepatitis B surface antibody, positive Hepatitis B core antibody, and the presence of HIV-1 antibodies with CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of 408 cells/mm³.
Figure 2. Mitral and aortic valves following resection.
Figure 3. Haemophilus speciation plate (see Discussion).

This is a case of subacute endocarditis that presented as right upper quadrant pain. The patient’s abdominal complaints and the absence of other peripheral signs of endocarditis led to increased difficulty in making the diagnosis of endocarditis for several days. Prior to diagnosis, the patient underwent multiple studies including abdominal ultrasound, CT scanning, and bronchoscopy. The patient did eventually develop evidence of septic embolization to multiple organs including spleen, brain, kidney, as well as (presumably) the liver and gastrointestinal tract emboli that had resulted in his abdominal pain.
The pathogen Haemophilus parainfluenzae belongs to the group of pleomorphic, fastidious gram-negative rods collectively referred to as the HACEK organisms (Mandell, Douglas and Bennett 2000). The microbiological growth characteristics of this group are notable for slow growth and a preference for carbon dioxide for growth on solid medium. Haemophilus species are usually coccobacillary to rod-shaped (see Figure 1 above), and most are normal oral and pharyngeal flora (Mandell, Douglas and Bennett 2000).
Classification among Haemophilus species is based on requirements of X (hemin) and V (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) growth factors, carbon dioxide, and biochemical testing (King 1983). The initial identification of this patient isolate as Haemophilus species was expedited with the use of 16S ribosomal sequence analysis.
The species specific identification of our patient’s isolate is based on requirement of V but not X growth factor, lack of hemolysis, and additional biochemical tests. Figure 3 (above) shows these growth characteristics in a plate divided in quadrants. In counterclockwise direction from the top, lack of hemolysis on horse blood, no growth in presence of X factor, growth in presence of V factor, and growth in presence of both X and V factor is seen.
This case illustrates many features classically seen with Haemophilus endocarditis. Haemophilus parainfluenzae is the most common cause of Haemophilus endocarditis (Darras-Jolly et al 1997). The typical clinical syndrome consists of the insidious onset of an unexplained, prolonged febrile illness and nonspecific signs and symptoms (Ellner et al 1979). In a review of 42 cases of Haemophilus endocarditis from France, the mean duration of disease before diagnosis was 34 days, with a range from two days to one year.
H. parainfluenzae endocarditis is frequently associated with a high incidence of systemic embolization (Darras-Jolly et al 1997, Ellner et al 1979, Lynn et al 1977). Despite bacteriologic response to antibiotics, significant morbidity and mortality usually results from the development of systemic embolization and congestive heart failure both during and following the course of antibiotic therapy (Ellner et al 1979). This case illustrates the challenge of diagnosing endocarditis and the importance of a high index of clinical suspicion.
