title: A middle-aged man with hemorrhagic bullous lesions.
history:
A man in his fifties with alcoholic cirrhosis presented to the hospital with a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, chills, pedal edema, dyspnea, and a painful rash with blisters. The rash on his feet started as erythematous papules, which had evolved into hemorrhagic bullae.

There was a history of alcohol-induced liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension and hepatic encephalopathy, and he was status post upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding caused by esophageal varices.

He consumed one pint of alcohol every 4-5 days; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs. He had had dinner at a seafood restaurant with his family the day before his illness and ate raw oysters. He had a cat at home and denied recent travel, recent trauma or exposure to fresh or salt water.

Medications included propranolol, rabeprazole, spironolactone, olanzapine, lactulose, fexofenadine, and multivitamins.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and malnourished. The temperature was normal; the blood pressure was 99/74 mm/Hg and pulse 75 beats per minute. There was conjunctival icterus and the abdomen was distended with hepatosplenomegaly. There were spider angiomas on his chest. He had bilateral palmar erythema, and purpuric and hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the arms and legs, with +2 bilateral leg edema (Figures 1, 2, and 3).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding on leg.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,500/mm³, hematocrit 29%, platelets 59,000/mm³, and INR 1.87. The level of sodium was 127 mmol/L, potassium 3.3 mmol/L, carbon dioxide (CO2) 18 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 38 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 27 U/L.
diagnosis:
Vibrio vulnificus cellulitis in a patient with cirrhotic liver disease.

Aspirations of bullae showed numerous white blood cells (WBC) and rare gram negative rods on the gram stain. A culture of the aspirate grew Vibrio vulnificus. Blood cultures were negative.

The patient was started on intravenous doxycycline and cefepime on admission. After his culture results were available, the antibiotic therapy was narrowed to doxycycline alone, with improvement. The patient remained hemodynamically stable. He was discharged home after two weeks of treatment.

Vibrio vulnificus is a motile gram negative bacillus, part of the normal marine flora. Approximately 50% of oysters and 10% of crabs are culture-positive in the summer. More then 90% of patients report consuming raw oysters. It accounts for 90% of all seafood related deaths in the United States.
Vibrio vulnificus is associated with a severe, distinctive soft tissue infection. It invades the bloodstream of cirrhotic and other susceptible hosts such as patients with iron overload, hemolytic anemia, renal failure, and AIDS. Progression to sepsis is rapid. It causes metastatic cutaneous lesions that start as erythematous lesions evolving to hemorrhagic bullae and necrotic ulcers. Approximately 90% of skin lesions appear on legs.
Patients at risk should avoid uncooked oysters, contact with seawater during warm months, and they should use protective gloves when handling shellfish.

title: A man with a persistent right upper lobe lung cavity.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with a productive cough, progressive shortness of breath, lethargy and weight loss for eighteen months. He was diagnosed with a right upper lobe infection and was treated with piperacillin-tazobactam for two months, without improvement. Six months later, he was treated with ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for a total of 6 months. He was admitted to the hospital for an elective right thoracotomy.

He had a history of hemochromatosis, cirrhosis, esophageal varices, emphysema, and diabetes mellitus. He was awaiting a liver transplant.

He had recently traveled to Florida. He was a former smoker, denied alcohol use and had no pets.

He was retired and lived in the state of New York.

Medications included a fentanyl patch, insulin, fluoxetine, ciprofloxacin, and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.
exam_studies:
He was alert and cooperative, and appeared cachectic and in mild respiratory distress. The blood pressure was 100/50 mm Hg, temperature 98.8°F (37.1°C), pulse 90 beats per minute, and respirations 20 per minute. There was no cyanosis, clubbing, or icterus. Chest examination showed dullness to percussion and reduced air entry in the right upper lung zones. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium and splenomegaly. The remainder of his examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 4,900 cells/mm³, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, and platelet count 153,000/mm³; the level of creatinine was 0.7 mg/dL, and liver function tests were normal.
The chest radiograph revealed a right upper lobe opacification and bilateral emphysematous changes. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed cavitary lesions in the right upper lobe, with a fluid level, and left lower lobe (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.

The patient underwent a right thoracotomy with drainage of purulent material from the right upper lobe. A biopsy was performed (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of biopsy.
Figure 3. Cytopathology (Gomori silver stain) of the biopsy.
diagnosis:
Chronic necrotizing aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus.

In the operating room, a large empyema cavity of right upper lobe was found. Microscopically, the biopsy sections demonstrated mild acute inflammation, fibrinous exudates, neutrophils, and cell debris. There were numerous septated hyphal forms with acute 45° branching consistent with Aspergillus species (Figure 2). The cytopathology (Figure 3) showed acute inflammation admixed with abundant hyphal forms consistent with Aspergillus species.
Fungal culture was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. Acid-fast bacillus (AFB) smears and culture were negative.

The patient was treated initially with voriconazole and changed to liposomal amphotericin B after two days because of possible hepatotoxic effect. On liposomal amphotericin B, the level of creatinine increased to 2.5 mg/dl. Therapy was changed to caspofungin.

Aspergillus is a mold with septate hyphae. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common cause of aspergillosis. Pulmonary aspergillosis presents with a variety of clinical syndromes. Aspergillomas occur in patients with pre-existing lung cavities. Invasive aspergillosis is a severe and often fatal disease that is seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those who are neutropenic and on prolonged courses of antibiotics. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus antigen that mainly affects patients with asthma. Chronic necrotizing aspergillosis occurs in those who are mildly immunosuppressed or have chronic lung disease.

title: A man with fever and acute right upper extremity erythema and edema.
history:
A man in his fifties with mantle cell lymphoma was in his usual state of health until four days before admission when he was admitted to another institution with nausea and small bowel ileus, which was attributed to chemotherapy. He was treated with bowel rest and received intravenous hydration via a peripheral line placed in the antecubital fossa. His symptoms resolved and he was discharged from the hospital.
One day before admission, he developed right upper arm pain and swelling, which progressed rapidly over 24 hours. These symptoms were accompanied by fever to 39ºC (102.2ºF).

There was a history of mantle cell lymphoma; 3 weeks before admission, he had received vincristine, cyclophosphamide, prednisone and doxorubicin.

He was allergic to fluoroquinolones.
exam_studies:
The patient was alert and in extreme discomfort secondary to pain. The temperature was 38.1ºC (100.6ºF), blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, pulse 108 beats per minute and respirations 18 breaths per minute. The right upper arm was circumferentially edematous with bluish-purple discoloration, which extended during the course of his evaluation. Crepitus was evident from his right shoulder to his elbow; distal pulses were absent. Mild erythema was noted along the lateral aspect of right hip and thigh, as well. The abdominal examination was normal, without tenderness or masses on palpation. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 6,700 cells/mm³ (85% neutrophils); the levels of electrolytes, including serum calcium, and tests of renal and liver function were normal. Radiographs of the right upper extremity and right hip (Figures 1 and 2) showed gas within the soft tissue planes.
Figure 1. Radiograph of the arm.
Figure 2. Radiograph of hip.

Based on the clinical presentation, blood cultures were drawn and empiric antibiotic therapy was instituted with intravenous penicillin G, vancomycin and clindamycin. Prompt surgical evaluation resulted in right upper extremity amputation with shoulder disarticulation. Debridement and fasciotomy of the right lateral thigh were also performed. Operative tissue was sent for gram stain (Figures 3 and 4), cultures and histopathologic examination with hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figure 5).
Figure 3. Brown and Hopps tissue gram stain, without oil. (40x magnification)
Figure 4. Brown and Hopps tissue stain, with oil. (100x magnification)
Figure 5. H and E stain of muscle specimen. (40x magnification)
diagnosis:
Clostridium septicum bacteremia and myonecrosis secondary to perforated viscus due to underlying adenocarcinoma of the colon.

Samples of tissue from the right upper extremity revealed extensive necrosis of soft tissue with involvement of muscle. Brown and Hopps gram staining of a wound specimen revealed gram-positive organisms (Figure 4). Sheets of large bacilli in association with minimal inflammatory response were seen in the tissues on the histopathologic stains (Figure 5.) One set of blood cultures taken before antibiotic therapy grew anaerobic gram-positive rods, later identified as Clostridium septicum.

The patient received antimicrobial coverage in the intensive care setting. Activated protein C was instituted for persistent hemodynamic instability.
Fifteen days after amputation, the patient developed fever and abdominal distension with passage of grossly bloody stool. Computed tomographic examination of the abdomen revealed the presence of free air and an emergent exploratory laparotomy was performed. A perforation in the ascending colon was identified with an associated mass lesion. Histologic examination revealed full transmural infiltration due to adenocarcinoma with necrotizing inflammation. An evaluation for metastatic lesions was unrevealing and patient underwent colectomy with subsequent chemotherapy for colon cancer.

Clostridial infections are typically associated with surgical and traumatic wounds. However a subset of these soft-tissue infections, in particular those caused by Clostridium septicum, have been described in the absence of trauma and are referred to as atraumatic or spontaneous myonecrosis.
C. septicum is a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic bacillus, which causes fulminant muscle necrosis due to the production of a potent alpha toxin (lecithinase). This aerotolerant organism has been associated with atraumatic myonecrosis in the setting of both obvious and occult gastrointestinal and hematologic malignancies, as well as in persons with diabetes mellitus and cyclic neutropenia. In one retrospective review, 92% of the 38 cases of atraumatic myonecrosis had underlying malignancy; 50% had occult tumor at the time of clostridial infection. Unlike other clostridial species, C. septicum is not a common isolate of stool but has high carriage rates in the appendix. Breach of mucosal integrity at the site of a colonic malignancy may serve as a portal of entry for these organisms resulting in subsequent seeding at distant sites. In patients with leukemia, it has been suggested that associated necrotizing colitis favors translocation of organisms into the blood stream. Despite aggressive management with antibiotics and surgery, case fatality rates of 79% have been reported.
Atraumatic myonecrosis secondary to infection with C. septicum is a rare, but recognized clinical presentation of occult gastrointestinal malignancy. Our case reinforces this association and underscores the need to evaluate patients with atraumatic myonecrosis for an underlying malignancy.

title: A man with fever and wasting.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with a two-week history of fevers, which were initially intermittent but progressed to daily fevers with chills. He reported a weight loss of more than 40 pounds (18 kilograms) over six months, with gradually worsening fatigue and malaise, but no night sweats. There was no headache, confusion or difficulty with coordination. His appetite was very poor but there was no nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, myalgias, arthralgias or rash.

He had had malaria twice (as an adolescent and approximately 20 years before this presentation).

The patient had grown up in Eastern Africa and had traveled to Southeast Asia. About 20 years before this presentation, he moved to an urban area in the Midwestern United States. He had a remote history of tobacco use, and reported no alcohol or illicit drug use. He had no known tuberculosis exposures, had not eaten undercooked meats or unpasteurized milk products, and reported no recent animal exposures or insect bites.

He lived alone and had had heterosexual sexual exposures intermittently during the previous few years.

He had healthy children living in Eastern Africa.

He had no known drug allergies.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 38.9°C (102.0°F), blood pressure 117/81 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats per minute, and weight 54 kg. The patient was very thin with cachexia and temporal wasting. There were no oropharyngeal lesions or cervical adenopathy. The lungs were clear bilaterally; the heart rhythm was regular, and there was no cardiac murmur or gallop. The abdomen was moderately tender to palpation in the left upper quadrant. The spleen was firm and palpable to 6 centimeters (cm) below the costal margin and the liver was palpable to 3 cm below the costal margin. There was no peripheral edema or skin rash. The neurologic examination showed mild generalized weakness, without focal deficits.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 1200 cells/mm³ (50% leukocytes, 40% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 0% eosinophils), hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, hematocrit 25.7%, platelet count 63,000/mm³. The serum level of creatinine was 1.7 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 79 u/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 41 u/L, alkaline phosphatase 115 u/L, total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, total protein 9.7 g/dL, and albumin 3.0 g/dL. Coagulation parameters and electrolytes were normal.
A chest radiograph was normal. Blood cultures were sterile. A test for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) was positive. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 54/mm³ and the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) RNA level was 500,000 copies/mL.
During the next week, the results of multiple tests were negative, including peripheral blood smears for parasites, serologic tests for syphilis, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus (CMV), antibodies to hepatitis B and C viruses, and cryptococcal antigen; blood polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests for Epstein Barr Virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV) and parvovirus, urine Histoplasma antigen and a tuberculosis skin test (PPD).
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with the administration of contrast, revealed massive splenomegaly, moderate hepatomegaly, and mild perihilar and axillary lymphadenopathy.
Pathological examination of a bone marrow biopsy, performed on the seventh hospital day, showed normal trilineage hematopoeisis with nonspecific plasmacytosis. A lymph node biopsy of a small right axillary node showed normal architecture and reactive changes. Routine, fungal and acid-fast stains and cultures were negative for both the bone marrow and lymph node biopsy.

The patient had high spiking fevers during the first few days, which then subsided into persistent low-grade fevers. On the 19th hospital day, antiretroviral therapy with lamivudine, efavirenz and stavudine was started. On the 36th day, the patient was transferred to another hospital for further evaluation.
He had low-grade fevers, marked hiccupping and increasing dull epigastric and left upper abdominal pain. At that time, the white blood cell count was 1700/mm³ (78% leukocytes, 20% monocytes, 0% eosinophils), the hemoglobin was 7.8 g/dL, the hematocrit 21.8% and the platelet count was 60,000/mm³.
A second bone marrow biopsy was performed on the 40th hospital day (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Bone marrow aspirate.
Figure 2. Bone marrow aspirate.
diagnosis:
Reactivated visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) due to Leishmania donovani, three decades after exposure; precipitated by CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count decline secondary to more recently acquired HIV infection.

Staining of the aspirate and core biopsy revealed many tiny oval organisms with clear cytoplasm and multiple blue organelles. They measured approximately 4 micrometers in length and were mostly intracellular, within monocytes, but occasionally appeared free or within granulocytes.
Serology for Leishmania species at the Center for Disease Control (CDC) was strongly positive, to a dilution of 1:512. The bone marrow aspirate was cultured in NNN media and grew Leishmania donovani. (See Figures 3 and 4.)
Figure 3. Culture results day 10.
Figure 4. Culture results day 10.

The patient received a 21-day course of the liposomal formulation of amphotericin B (5 mg/kg daily dosing), which he tolerated well. The treatment plan was to continue once or twice weekly therapy for a prolonged period and then change to maintenance therapy of intermittent liposomal amphotericin indefinitely.
HIV-antiviral therapy was continued and, at eight weeks, the patient's CD4 T-cell count had increased to 112 cells/mm³.

This case illustrates the potential for reactivation of Leishmania donovani in the setting of HIV-induced impairment of cell-mediated immunity. The presentation was dominated by the classic findings of massive splenomegaly and a severe wasting syndrome. Pancytopenia is highly characteristic and the absence of eosinophilia is typical. Also notable was the hypergammaglobulinemia.
The initial gastrointestinal symptoms that this patient experienced by this patient is unusual in classic visceral leishmaniasis but has been described in cases associated with HIV. The reason for the negative initial bone marrow biopsy may have been due to improper staining technique or simply early timing. Classically, splenic aspirates are used to confirm the diagnosis and are still used widely.

title: A man with psoriatic arthritis who presented with hypoxia after transit via an area affected by severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS).
history:
A man in his fifties with psoriatic arthritis traveled from the United States to India at the end of February 2003. In March 2003, he traveled to Singapore, where he stayed for only one day. (See Figure 1.) He continued that evening on a flight back to his home in the Southeastern United States.
Approximately 2 weeks after his visit to Singapore, he developed a low-grade fever with malaise. He was evaluated at a walk-in clinic and diagnosed with a probable viral illness and sent home with symptomatic therapy.
Six days later, he returned and reported daily high fevers with occasional cough. In the emergency room, he was found to have a temperature to 103.3°F (39.6°C) and oxygen saturation 96%. The lungs were clear and a chest radiograph was normal. He was discharged and given empiric treatment for malaria (quinine sulfate and doxycycline), without improvement.
A few days later, he was admitted for evaluation because of persistent symptoms.
Figure 1. Graph of SARS cases in Singapore.

He had psoriatic arthritis with scleritis and diabetes mellitus.

He was a native of India, and had immigrated to the United States many years before. He did not drink alcohol and smoked cigarettes rarely. He denied animal exposures and he noted some “mosquito-bites” while abroad.

Medications included glipizide, celecoxib, methotrexate for several years, and infliximab for approximately six months. He had not taken malaria prophylaxis during his trip to India.
exam_studies:
He was an obese and appeared slightly dyspneic. The temperature was 103.0°F (39.4°C) and oxygen saturation was 89% on room air. The oropharynx was normal, the lungs were clear and there was no hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal tenderness or rash.

Arterial blood gases (ABG) revealed a pH 7.55, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30.0 mm Hg and partial pressure of oxygen 50.0 mm Hg. The hematocrit was 35.6%, white blood cell count (WBC) 9,400/mm³ (including 29% band forms, 41% neutrophils, and 21% lymphocytes), platelets 326,000/mm³, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 313 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 729 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dl.
Blood cultures, drawn five days apart, and malaria smears were negative. A chest radiograph revealed no infiltrates or effusion.

The patient was placed in respiratory isolation (not SARS-isolation) and empiric therapy (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and steroids) for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PCP, formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) was initiated. Bronchoscopy was performed on the third hospital day. He became hypoxic after the procedure and required intubation and mechanical ventilation. He was transferred to the intensive care unit where SARS-isolation procedures were instituted.
diagnosis:
Tuberculosis, caused by pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Induced sputum was negative for PCP, and three sputum samples showed no acid fast bacilli (AFB). Bronchoscopy revealed 142 cells (6% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 57% macrophages, 25% pneumocytes); staining of bronchoscopic specimens were negative for PCP and AFB. An in-house SARS PCR assay, based on published sequence data, was negative and the patient gradually improved on PCP therapy and was extubated on hospital day#10. He had been transferred to a rehabilitation facility when the laboratory identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis growing from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid (Figure 2). The three sputum samples subsequently grew M. tuberculosis as well.
Figure 2. TB cording in culture.

The patient improved on rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and vitamin B6. The culture subsequently grew a pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He had received Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) as a child in India and prior to initiating infliximab, had had a 10 mm reaction to a PPD test. His chest radiograph was previously normal and he was not treated for latent tuberculosis.

This case highlights two important points. First, little has been reported about the clinical presentation of SARS coronavirus infection in immune-compromised patients. If the pathogenesis of SARS coronavirus infection is at least in part mediated through immune dysregulation, epidemiologic (incubation period) and clinical clues may be misleading.
Secondly, although it is unknown to what extent we will see new, emerging infections in years to come, it is certainly the case that we will see more patients with immunosuppression using new and more potent immune-modifying agents. As such, our more “traditional” infections will increasingly emerge as a larger percentage of the population joins the ranks of the immunocompromised.

title: A patient status post renal transplantation with chronic diarrhea.
history:
A man in his thirties, who was two years post-cadaveric renal transplant, reported intermittent diarrhea for eight months, with marked increase in symptoms during the preceding three weeks. He noted an average of seven watery, non-bloody stools per day. He denied cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, or chills. He had not lost weight and was not experiencing postural symptoms. He had experienced similar symptoms of diarrhea starting approximately six months after his transplant, which had resolved after being given an antibiotic.

There was a history of congenital renal dysplasia, hypertension, an elevated hematocrit, seizure disorder and a positive tuberculin skin test three years before transplantation, for which he had completed 12 months of isoniazid therapy. As above, he had had a cadaveric renal transplantation two years earlier, with delayed graft function.

He had no history of smoking, use of recreational drugs or alcohol. He had a pet dog, but reported no other animal exposures. He was originally from Mexico, and resided in United States Northwest. He had not returned to Mexico in more than a decade.

He was married and had children.

Medications include sirolimus and tacrolimus.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 100/70 mm Hg, pulse 64 beats per minute, and temperature 35.2°C (95.4°F). The remainder of the examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 53%, and other standard laboratory tests were normal. Testing for fecal leukocytes, Clostridium difficile toxin A, Giardia antigen in stool, and cytomegalovirus pp65 antigen in polymorphonuclear leukocytes was negative.

Fresh and preserved stool was submitted for bacterial culture and parasitological examination. Samples were examined directly in saline, as well as following concentration by modified trichrome, calcofluor, auramine and modified acid-fast stains. (See Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Modified acid fast stain of stool specimen.
Figure 2. Modified acid fast stain of stool.
diagnosis:
Isosporiasis caused by Isospora belli in a patient following renal transplantation.

Modified acid-fast (Figures 1 and 2) and auramine stains were positive for oocysts of Isospora belli.

The patient was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 160/800mg three times daily for three weeks with resolution of his diarrhea. On reducing his dose to one tablet twice daily, his symptoms recurred but responded to increasing back to a higher dose of the antibiotics.

Isospora belli is a coccidian parasite, with worldwide distribution. Infections are more common in tropical and subtropical regions. Humans are definitive hosts, and no clear evidence for an animal reservoir has been reported (Lindsay et al 1997). The mode of infection is through ingestion of infectious sporulated oocysts.
Symptomatic infection results in profuse diarrhea, which is self-limited within 2-3 weeks in the immunocompetent person. The illness is similar in presentation to other coccidia (Marshall et al 1997). Protracted illness, even fatal cases, among immune competent persons have been reported but are rare (Lindsay et al 1997, Shaffer and Moore 1989, Jongwutiwes et al 2002, Bialek et al 2001). Infants may have a more severe clinical course than adults. Clinical experience with Isospora is most extensive among immunocompromised patients, particularly those infected with HIV. Infection with Isospora in this setting frequently is protracted. Chronic intestinal isosporiasis is included in the 1993 AIDS surveillance case definition of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (MMWR 1992). Other forms of immune compromise that have been associated with chronic isosporiasis include malignancy (Lindsay et al, 1997), treatment with antineoplastic chemotherapy (Hammouda et al 1996), and chronic renal insufficiency (Ali et al 2000).
Treatment with combinations of protozoal dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors with sulfonamides (e.g. TMP-SMX) is most effective (Pape et al 1989, Verdier et al 2000), although other agents have been used (Zulu et al 2002). In patients with HIV/AIDS, prolonged treatment followed by suppressive therapy is required, while for immunocompetent persons treatment is advocated only in persons who do not undergo spontaneous resolution of symptoms. In the transplant setting, intestinal infection with other coccidian parasites may not require ongoing suppressive therapy (Ok et al 1997). In this case, the patient had at least two recurrences of symptoms, spanning at least one year of follow-up, suggesting that chronic suppressive therapy is indeed indicated in this case.
The issue of how the patient acquired the infection bears consideration. In prior studies among HIV-infected patients, birth outside the United States was an independent risk factor for isosporiasis (Sorvillo et al 1995, Hu et al 1995). The patient had not traveled back to Mexico in over 11 years. It is interesting to consider that he may have been latently infected with Isospora for that length of time, given the low likelihood of infection within the United States. The possibility of infection by exposure to possible paratenic animal hosts appears remote.

title: A man with a rash after receiving a smallpox vaccine.
history:
A young adult presented with a fever and rash thirteen days after receiving a primary smallpox vaccination in right deltoid. He had been well until ten days post-vaccination when a low-grade fever and slight headache developed, and he noted a progressive rash involving his trunk, back and arms. He was referred for further evaluation.

He had a history of chickenpox as a child.

He was sexually active with one female partner for the preceding six months, and testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative one year earlier. He occasionally drank alcohol, and denied smoking or recent blood transfusions.
exam_studies:
He appeared well. The blood pressure was 137/74 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, temperature 36.9°C (98.4°F), respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. There were numerous small erythematous papulo-macular lesions and a few vesicles on the back, trunk and buttock, with sparing of the mouth and palms. The right deltoid vaccine site had evidence of a good take and no vesicles were present. The skin lesions are shown in Figures 1 and 2. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Vaccine site on right deltoid.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,900/mm³, hemoglobin 16 gm/L and platelet count 153,000/mm³. The chest radiograph was normal and testing for antibodies to HIV was negative.

The skin lesion was swabbed, and direct fluorescence antibody assays for herpes simplex and varicella virus, and for vaccinia PCR and culture were performed. The patient was sent home without treatment but with close observation and daily follow-up in the first 48 hours.
The skin lesions were photographed again 24 hours after his initial presentation (Figure 3). There were numerous small erythematous maculopapular lesions and a few vesicular lesions on the back, trunk, and buttocks. The rash spared the mouth and palms.
Figure 3. Twenty-four hour follow-up.
diagnosis:
Generalized vaccinia following a smallpox vaccine.

Skin lesion swabs for direct fluorescence antibody assay for herpes simplex virus and varicella virus were negative. Skin lesion swabs for vaccinia polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and culture were negative.

The patient did well; the skin lesions did not progress, and resolved in several weeks.

On December 13, 2002, President Bush announced that smallpox vaccination was required for military personnel as a national program for preparedness against biological weapons. From December 13, 2002 through May 28, 2003, 450,293 military personnel were vaccinated (70.5 % primary vaccinees and 29.5% re-vaccinees). Smallpox vaccine is made from live vaccinia virus and is administered by using the multiple-puncture technique with a bifurcated needle. By days 6-8 post-vaccination, formation of a papule, vesicle, ulcer or crusted lesion surrounded by an area of induration signifies a response to vaccination and is referred to as a major reaction or a take.
The evolution of the normal local reaction to primary smallpox vaccination includes development of papule on days 3-4, vesicle on days 5-6, pustule on days 8-9, crusted forms after day 12 and scab-detached scar on days 17-21.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that response to vaccination be evaluated on post-vaccination day 6, 7, or 8. During the 14 days post-vaccination, the normal reaction includes fatigue, headache, myalgia, pruritus, fever, lymphadenopathy and edema at the vaccination site.
Generalized vaccinia is characterized by a disseminated macular or vesicular rash on an erythematous base, which occurs 6-9 days after first-time vaccination and might be preceded by fever. It is self-limited in immunocompetent hosts. Vaccine immune globulin (VIG) might be beneficial in the systemically ill vaccinee.

title: A teenager with a cerebellar mass.
history:
A teenager presented with moderately severe occipital headache of one-year's duration. She also reported nausea, vomiting, intermittent diplopia and photophobia for four months. She denied fever, loss of consciousness, seizures, bladder or bowel disturbances, abnormalities in ambulation or any other neurological complaints.

She had emigrated from West Africa and arrived in the United States Northeast three weeks before admission. The patient reported no other travel history and no animal exposures. She denied smoking, alcohol or illicit drug use, sexual activity or close contact with people suffering from tuberculosis.

Her medications were ibuprofen and acetaminophen.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well nourished. The temperature was 98.9°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 107/64 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. She had bilateral papilledema and bilateral sixth nerve palsy. The rest of the examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 35% and white blood cell count (WBC) and differential were normal. Results of serum chemistries, liver function tests, urinalysis and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis were normal. An enzyme-linked immunoassay (EIA) for antibody to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1 and HIV-2) was non-reactive. The number of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells was within the normal range. Serum levels of immunoglobulin (Ig) and its subsets (IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, IgM) were within normal limits. Purified Protein Derivative (PPD) test was negative (0 mm) with concomitant positive skin test reactions for Candida and diphtheria and tetanus (dT) showing measurements of 10 mm and 24 mm, respectively.
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head without contrast showed a large posterior fossa mass closely related to the right cerebellar hemisphere with marked vasogenic edema (Figure 1). Contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed a 55 mm by 43 mm ring-enhancing mass with central liquefaction in the right cerebellar hemisphere (Figure 2). Chest radiograph and computed tomography (CT) with contrast of the thorax and abdomen were normal.
Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.
Figure 1. Head CT scan without contrast.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan with contrast.

A craniotomy for removal of a possible cerebellar neoplasm was performed. Histopathology of the mass is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Histopathology of cerebellar mass.
diagnosis:
Cerebellar abscess caused by both Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in an immunocompetent individual.

The cerebellar mass upon gross inspection was described as firm, gritty and poorly vascularized. Histopathologic examination of the tissue revealed epithelioid granulomas with caseous necrosis (Figure 3).
Acid-fast staining of the specimen was positive, suggesting mycobacterial infection. Subsequently, cultures grew both Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), which were confirmed by DNA probes.

Postoperatively, she received presumptive treatment for tuberculoma with isoniazid (INH), rifampin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB). She subsequently had complete resolution of her presenting symptoms and cranial nerve palsies.
Four months later, a repeat MRI scan of the head (Figure 4) showed resolution of the cerebellar lesion with no new abnormalities. After treatment for 6 months, her regimen was modified to rifabutin (RFB), EMB and clarithromycin, which she was to receive for another 12 months for the treatment of Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection.
At nine months follow-up, the patient was doing well without any signs or symptoms of relapse of the disease.
Figure 4. Follow-up MRI scan at four months.

While central nervous system (CNS) infections with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) are not uncommon, neurological disease caused by other mycobacteria is much less frequent. Mycobacteria other than MTB and Mycobacterium leprae are generally free-living organisms that are ubiquitous in the environment. They have been recovered from surface water, tap water, soil, domestic and wild animals, milk and food products (Cegielski and Wallace 1997, Gruft et all 1981, Chapman 1971). These organisms may inhabit body surfaces or secretions without causing disease. Consequently, when recovered from a clinical specimen, nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are sometimes considered environmental contaminants (Cegielski and Wallace 1997,Debrunner et al 1992).
The incidence of disease due to NTM has increased substantially in the past 15 years, in large part due to the pandemic of HIV infection. One of the most common species is Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), which commonly causes disseminated disease in patients with the Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) (Cegielski and Wallace 1997). In one report, evidence of disseminated MAC was found in 60% of AIDS patients at autopsy (Chin et al 1990). In patients with AIDS, the typical setting of MAC infection is late in the course of the disease when CD4 cell counts are <50 cells/mL. Thus, the AIDS epidemic has been accompanied by an epidemic of disseminated NTM disease as severely immunocompromised patients are exposed to these ubiquitous but relatively less virulent organisms (Cegielski and Wallace 1997).
In non-immunocompromised patients, the most common site of localized NTM infection is the lung. Other manifestations reported in literature include recurrent granulomatous tenosynovitis (Lefevre et al 2000), peritonitis (Miailhes et al 2000), osteomyelitis (Raszka et al 1994), soft tissue infection (Leautez et al 2000) and lumbar spinal infection (Suttner et al 2001). In non-immunosuppressed patients, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and inherited connective disorders are the most common predisposing factors for the development of NTM disease, especially MAC (Florakis et al 2002).
In our patient none of these predisposing factors were identified. We investigated other factors that might have predisposed our patient to this particular infection, but there was no other evidence of impairment of host defense mechanisms such as neutropenia, poor nutrition, debility, cancer, or HIV infection.
Central nervous system (CNS) infections with MAC can occur secondary to trauma, surgery, hematogenous dissemination and contiguous spread of long standing disease like otitis media and mastoiditis (Cegielski and Wallace 1997). Such infections have been reported in patients with and without identifiable immunologic deficits (Klein et al 1985, Gentry et al 1977, Uldry et al 1992, Horsburgh et al.1985). The reported neurological manifestations of CNS disease due to MAC are variable and include meningitis, encephalitis, organic brain syndrome, cranial nerve palsy, progressive neurological deterioration, hydrocephalus, subdural empyema and ventriculitis (Gyure et al 1995).
Co-infection with pathogens like Cytomegalovirus, Cryptococcus neoformans and Toxoplasma gondii has been reported in some cases of NTM central nervous system (CNS) disease (Gyure et al 1995). Such cases can cause diagnostic dilemma. Only two cases of CNS infection with both MTB and NTM have been described in literature. Both patients had meningitis with the co-infecting NTM being Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI) in one (Klein et al 1985), and Mycobacterium kansasii in the other patient (Herman et al 1966). No HIV test or other tests evaluating the immune status of the patients involved were reported in these cases.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case report of a brain abscess caused by both MTB and MAC in an immunocompetent individual. In the setting of the current worldwide HIV epidemic and with the increasing use of immunosuppressive treatment modalities for various medical conditions, dual mycobacterial infections may be seen more frequently in the future. An awareness of and an increased index of suspicion for the possibility of such co-infections could potentially expedite the diagnosis, and decrease morbidity and mortality in such patients.

title: A teenager with a chronic suppurative lesion on the forehead.
history:
A teenager presented with a 2-year history of a suppurative lesion on the forehead. The lesion started as a red papule on the surface of a traumatic scar. The papule began to suppurate and drain a yellowish material through multiple sinus tracts. Two years before this evaluation, a surgical resection was performed, followed by a course of oral dicloxacillin, with only partial remission.
On this presentation, the patient reported a frontal headache and drainage of granular material.

The patient suffered a motor vehicle accident many years earlier that had resulted in an extensive scar on the right forehead.

The patient was born and living in the high jungle of Peru.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile. A lesion extending from the right forehead to the upper eyelid was observed. The lesion was painless with a granular aspect. Spontaneous drainage of a yellowish material through multiple sinus tracts was observed. (See Figure 1.) The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The hematocrit, white blood cell count, and liver function tests were normal. The chest radiograph was normal. Serologic tests for human immunodeficiency virus, type 1 (HIV-1) and HTLV-1 were negative. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed osteomyelitis of the frontal bone, subdural effusion and cerebritis (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Brain CT scan.

A skin biopsy was performed. Purulent material was obtained for culture in aerobic and anaerobic media.
diagnosis:
Botryomycosis, caused by Staphylococus aureus.

Pathology of the skin biopsy shows a large granule surrounded by eosinophilic material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon), micro abscesses and sinuses are also seen (Figure 3). A closer view of the granule shows that it is composed of aggregates of cocci-form bacteria (Figure 4). Staphylococus aureus was isolated.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy.
Figure 4. Granule with cocci-form bacteria.

An extensive surgical resection of the frontal bone and drainage of the subdural collection was performed. Intravenous oxacillin was started and maintained for 1 month, then oral clindamycin was given for 6 months, with complete remission of the skin lesion. Six months after finishing the course of antibiotics, the patient returned with a relapse. At that time Staphylococus aureus resistant to oxacillin was isolated. Vancomycin was started, but was changed to clindamycin because the patient became pregnant.

Botryomycosis is a chronic bacterial infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Less commonly, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella spp. and other bacteria have been implicated.
The disease is rare - at the time of this publication, no more than 200 cases have been published - and is globally distributed. The skin and subcutaneous tissues are the most frequent locations. While the disease may remain localized to the skin for a long time, disseminated infection has been reported in debilitated patients. Chronic pulmonary infection has been reported in immunocompetent and in patients with AIDS. The pathogenesis is unclear. S. aureus may be seeded into the skin after trauma, as appears to have happened in this case, and after a silent period varying from months to years, a suppurative lesion may ensue. Host and bacterial factors may play a role in determining who will develop a chronic infection. Interestingly, neither humoral nor cellular immune deficiencies tend to markedly predispose patients to this infection.
The differential diagnosis includes other chronic and suppurative infections, particularly those where drainage of grains is a salient feature. Actinomycosis and fungal mycetoma are the main diagnoses to rule out. In actinomycosis, the pathological specimen will show a grain composed of filamentous bacteria, and the anaerobic culture will grow Actinomyces. In fungal mycetoma, the grain is composed of hyphae, with Madurella mycetomatis as the main causative agent. Other conditions such as leishmaniasis, tuberculosis, and endemic fungal infections are less frequently associated with this clinical picture. The treatment consists of both surgical resection and prolonged antibiotic treatment. Relapses and failure to eradicate the bacterium have been reported. This case depicts all classical features of this disease. It is not clear whether the infection will be eradicated in this patient despite prolonged courses of antibiotics and extensive surgical procedures.

title: A teenager with an occipitoparietal brain lesion on the right side.
history:
A teenager presented with a two-month history of a headache and a two-week history of gait disturbance, dizziness, and nausea. The headache was diffuse and occurred mostly nocturnally. There was no history of emesis. The patient denied visual changes but his teachers had noted his handwriting was less legible during the previous month of school. There was no history of fever, night sweats or weight loss.

He was born in a rural area of Mexico and had moved to the Southeastern United States several years before this presentation. There was no history of exposure to tuberculosis. The patient was not sexually active.

He lived with his family and attended high school.

He had no known allergies.
exam_studies:
He was cooperative with slow speech. The temperature was 98°F (36.6°C), respirations 20 breaths per minute, pulse 92 beats per minute, and blood pressure 124/74 mm Hg. The oropharynx and dentition were normal, and the pupils were equal, round and reactive to light. There was no cervical adenopathy or meningismus.
On neurologic examination, he had left exotropia and a left-sided visual field cut. The tone decreased in left upper and lower extremities. His strength was slightly decreased on the left compared with the right, and sensation was decreased in the left arm and leg. His gait was guarded due to the visual deficit and left-sided weakness.

A complete blood count was normal, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 6 mm/hour. Serologic testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was negative. The chest radiograph was normal, and a tuberculosis skin test (PPD) was nonreactive. Computed tomography (CT) showed a large right-sided brain lesion involving the occipital, parietal, and temporal lobes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.
Figure 1. Brain MRI scan.
Figure 2. Brain MRI scan.
Figure 3. Brain MRI scan.

Corticosteroids were administered and a biopsy of the brain lesion was obtained.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium bovis tuberculoma.

Pathologic examination of the brain tissue demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation (Figure 4). Special stains showed an acid-fast bacillus (Figures 5 and 6). Culture of the tissue grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which was subsequently identified as M. bovis.
Figure 4. Results of needle biopsy.
Figure 5. Stain of brain biopsy.
Figure 6. Detail of Figure 5.

Antituberculosis chemotherapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) was initiated and corticosteroids were continued. After four weeks of treatment, MRI scanning showed significant decrease in edema and mass effect. After 6 weeks of daily therapy, isoniazid and rifampin alone were continued based on susceptibilities. Corticosteroids were continued for 8 weeks. Because of lower back pain, a radiograph of the spine was obtained which showed dystrophic calcification of a retroperitoneal node (Figure 7), probably representing primary abdominal tuberculosis caused by M. bovis.
After 12 weeks of therapy (four weeks after completion of corticosteroids), the patient developed worsening headaches and nausea. MRI scanning showed edema and mass effect similar to that at presentation. The patient underwent surgical decompression after failing to respond to medical management with mannitol and corticosteroids. A biopsy of brain tissue revealed necrotizing granulomas. Special stains and culture for acid-fast bacilli were negative. The patient continued on isoniazid and rifampin. Corticosteroids were continued for several months.
His headaches resolved but the visual deficit persisted. Sequential MRI scans of the brain demonstrated a significant decrease in the size of the lesion (Figures 8 and 9).
Figure 7. Lumbar spine radiograph.
Figure 8. MRI scan at 12 months.
Figure 9. MRI scan at 12 months.

Mycobacterium bovis, the causative agent of bovine tuberculosis, is a member of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which also includes M. tuberculosis, M. africanum, M. microti, and M. cannettii. Transmission of this pathogen to humans occurs primarily by ingestion of contaminated unpasteurized dairy products. With the elimination of bovine tuberculosis and pasteurization of dairy products, M. bovis has been largely eradicated in developed countries.
In this case, a teenaged Hispanic male with a central nervous system tuberculoma due to M. bovis is described. Although sporadic cases of meningitis due to M. bovis have been reported, M. bovis tuberculoma has not been previously described in the English literature at the time of this publication.
In the United States, M. bovis accounts for 0.1% of all tuberculosis isolates. In areas with large populations of immigrants from countries without universal pasteurization, M. bovis is more prevalent. In San Diego County, for example, M. bovis accounts for 5.1% of all reported tuberculosis cases and 6.6% of all culture-proven cases. The impact of the disease is greatest in the pediatric population in which M. bovis accounts for 10.8% of tuberculosis cases and 33.9% of culture-proven cases. M. bovis tuberculosis in San Diego is almost exclusively confined to the Hispanic population and is largely attributed to cross-border exposure to unpasteurized dairy products in Mexico. Clinical and radiological features of tuberculosis due to M. bovis are indistinguishable from those of M. tuberculosis. Given the route of infection, M. bovis is more likely to cause extrapulmonary disease. In children, common sites involved are the cervical lymph nodes and the abdomen. In adults, M. bovis disease most often represents reactivation. Extrapulmonary sites of infection include the genitourinary tract and bones and joints. The patient we describe likely acquired primary abdominal infection during childhood, as suggested by the calcified retroperitoneal node, with reactivation of central nervous system disease during adolescence.
The initial treatment of intracranial tuberculomas is medical. Surgical intervention reserved for those with clinical deterioration despite adequate medical management. Chemotherapy regimens for the treatment of M. bovis disease are based on those used for M. tuberculosis, but the innate resistance of M. bovis to pyrazinamide should be considered when using short-course regimens that rely on the rapid sterilization provided by this drug. The adjunctive use of corticosteroids is recommended to diminish neurological symptoms and improve outcome. Response to medical management is usually noted in 6 to 12 weeks.
Radiological improvement occurred in our patient 4 weeks after initiation of therapy, but subsequent clinical and radiological relapse necessitated surgical intervention. Multiple case reports describe paradoxical enlargement of a tuberculoma during the first 2-3 months of treatment. Typically the enlargement occurs coincident with the tapering or discontinuation of steroids. The increase in size is thought not to be a consequence of failure of treatment but rather an interaction between the host immune response and direct effects of the mycobacterium. Human M. bovis tuberculosis is uncommon in the United States. Given the trends in immigration, especially from countries where bovine tuberculosis has not been eradicated, continued surveillance for this pathogen is warranted.

title: A woman in her seventies with chyluria.
history:
A woman in her seventies presented to the emergency room with progressive weakness, fainting spells, and myalgia. She had also noticed a milky color to her urine, which had begun more than three months before this evaluation. She reported no fever, chills or diarrhea.

She had had a carcinoma in the left breast, treated with lumpectomy and radiation therapy, and also had had a subtotal thyroidectomy.

She was born in Guyana, and had immigrated to the United States 50 years before. She traveled to Guyana frequently for extended periods of time, most recently nine months before admission when she stayed for one month. She did not smoke or drink alcohol, and had no pets.

She was taking thyroxine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared weak. The blood pressure was 113/63 mm/Hg, temperature 99.7°F (37.6°C), pulse 70 beats per minute and regular, and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The chest was dull to percussion, and there was reduced air entry at both lung bases posteriorly. Extremities showed bilateral leg pitting edema. The foley catheter drained white-colored urine. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 6,900/mm³, hemoglobin 15.7 gm/dl, and platelet count 264,000/mm³. The sodium was 122 mmol/l, and tests of liver and renal function were normal. Urinalysis revealed a turbid and whitish color and was positive for blood and protein. (See Figure 1, with the patient's urine on the right, and normal urine on the left.) Urine microscopy showed 5-10 white cells per high-power field (HPF) and red blood cells were too numerous to count per HPF. The total 24-hour urine protein was 8.6 gm. She had evidence of chyluria.
A chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed extensive bilateral retroperitoneal low attenuation density and a right simple renal cyst (Figure 2). A transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.
Figure 1. Patient's urine on the right.
Figure 2. Abdominal CT scan.

During the hospitalization, the blood pressure was borderline low. The level of potassium was mildly elevated; the level of serum cortisol was normal.
diagnosis:
Filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti.

Examination of a blood smear obtained during the night was positive for Wuchereria bancrofti (Figure 3). Filarial serology revealed a high IgG titer.
Figure 3. Blood smear.

The patient was treated with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for 14 days, with partial resolution of chyluria. She was readmitted with chyluria and hyponatremia, and was treated with DEC again. She also received intrarenal pelvic instillation of silver nitrate. Her condition improved with resolution of her chyluria at three months follow-up.

Lymphatic filariasis results from infection with vector-borne tissue-dwelling nematodes called filariae. Adult filariae may live in the lymphatic, blood vessels, connective tissue or serous membranes.
There are three species: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori.
Chyluria, the presence of chyle in the urine, follows the rupture of dilated lymphatics into the urinary excretory system. Hematochyluria or chyluria mainly develops as a late complication of filarial infection. Diagnosis is based on finding microfilaria on blood smears. Specimens obtained during the night (between 2100 and 0300 hours) are most likely to show the parasite. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for circulating filarial antigen and polymerase chain reaction assay are useful tests as well.
Treatment of filariasis aims to prevent and/or reverse the progression of disease. Antiparasitic drugs used include diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and ivermectin. Clinically, the most effective treatment of chyluria is renal pedicle lymphatic disconnection. An alternative treatment is intrarenal pelvic instillation of silver nitrate.

title: A woman in her sixties with shortness of breath.
history:
A woman in her sixties was admitted with rapidly progressive shortness of breath over the course of one week. On admission, she was short of breath at rest. She denied chest pain, cough, sputum or hemoptysis.

She had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma three months earlier and had received three cycles of chemotherapy.

She lived in urban Texas. She denied travel and did not own a pet.

She was a homemaker.

She had no allergies.

She had received pulse chemotherapy with vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone.
exam_studies:
She was obese and short of breath while talking. The temperature was 97.8°F (36.6°C), respirations 22 breaths per minute. There were fine inspiratory crackles heard over all lung fields bilaterally. The remainder of her examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 28.2%. The white blood cell (WBC) count, differential, and other hematological and serologic chemical test results were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest with contrast showed a general pulmonary mosaic pattern associated with foci of ground glass opacity (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.

The patient was treated with gatifloxacin for a community-acquired pneumonia, and then underwent bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy. Pathological examination of the transbronchial biopsy showed a mild interstitial thickening with ill-defined collections of epithelioid cells (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of transbronchial biopsy (20x).
diagnosis:
Pulmonary cryptococcosis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans.

Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain of the transbronchial biopsy specimen showed budding yeast forms with surrounding transparent capsule (Figures 3 and 4). Bronchial biopsy washings and brushings grew Cryptococcus neoformans on culture. The serum cryptococcal antigen titer was 1:8.
Figure 3. GMS stain of transbronchial biopsy (100x).
Figure 4. GMS stain of transbronchial biopsy (100x).

The patient had no evidence of dissemination of cryptococcosis to the central nervous system (CNS) on lumbar puncture. She was started on fluconazole 800 mg orally daily for eight weeks, which was followed by 400 mg daily for 12 weeks, then 200 mg daily, to be continued for a year.

Cryptococcosis is a worldwide infection that only rarely causes dissemination in healthy individuals. The life cycle of Cryptococcus neoformans involves asexual and sexual forms. The asexual form exists as yeast and reproduces by budding. These haploid, unicellular yeasts are the only forms of C. neoformans that have been recovered from human infections. Cryptococcus neoformans has been recovered from soil samples from around the world in areas frequented by birds, and in association with rotting vegetation and river red gum trees (Eucalyptus camaldulensis) and forest red gum trees (Eucalyptus tereticornis) in Australia.
The lungs are thought to be the initial site of almost all infections due to Cryptococcus neoformans. Following inhalation, C. neoformans causes a small focal pneumonitis. The immune status of the affected individual then determines whether the infection disseminates or resolves.
Pulmonary cryptococcosis may present with cough, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, pleuritic chest pain, and night sweats. Chest radiographic features of pulmonary cryptococcosis vary widely. Most common are solitary or few well-defined, non-calcified nodules. Cavitation in cryptococcal nodules is rare. Lobar infiltrates, hilar and mediastinal adenopathy, and pleural effusions may be seen.
Diagnosis is based on culture and histology. Expectorated sputum samples can be positive, but higher yields are obtained using bronchoscopic sampling. Cryptococcus neoformans produces white, mucoid colonies on a variety of agars that usually become visible to the naked eye within 48 hours.
The yeast form of cryptococci can be identified in histopathologic specimens using methenamine silver stain. Mucicarmine stain shows both the yeast form and the capsule. The serum cryptococcal antigen is positive in virtually all patients with HIV infection, and in most patients with other underlying immunocompromising conditions. Therefore, the serum antigen assay serves as an excellent screening test in immunocompromised patients with atypical presentations of respiratory disease. Because many immunocompromised patients with pulmonary cryptococcosis may also harbor extrapulmonary disease, it is prudent to rule out CNS involvement.

title: A woman with a non-healing cat scratch wound.
history:
A woman was scratched by a cat at a veterinarian’s office four weeks before admission. A single small puncture wound from a claw was noted, without other complications. There were no other recollections about the cat noted.
One week later, the lesion became raised and erythematous, and the following week it was the size of a dime (1.5-2.0 cm) and pustular. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was administered.
One week before admission, the lesion had increased to the size of a quarter (2.0-2.5 cm), with expanding erythema and red streaking up her arm. Ciprofloxacin was added to the amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. The patient presented to the emergency room because of the increasing wound, and reported recent low-grade fevers.

She had a history of endometriosis.

The patient had children and worked with animals. She had traveled to Australia two years before, with no additional travel since.

Medications included amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, ciprofloxacin, and oral contraceptives.
exam_studies:
She was well-developed and in no apparent distress. The temperature was 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/50 mm Hg, and respirations 12 breaths per minute. The right wrist had an moderately tender, ulcerated lesion (2 by 2 cm) with no purulence; scant clear discharge was noted. There was patchy red streaking extending up the arm and an antecubital node was palpated. The right axilla was mildly tender, with a small palpable nodule (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 4,600/mm³ (67% leukocytes, 24% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes), hematocrit 38%, and platelet count 293,000/mm³. The levels of electrolytes, glucose, urea nitrogen, creatinine, and tests of liver function were normal.

The antibiotics were discontinued. The wound was cultured, and Bartonella serologies were sent. Azithromycin was started empirically while awaiting culture results, with some improvement.
diagnosis:
Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii and acquired from feline claws.

The wound culture of the right wrist exhibited slow growth of colonies that were small and white. Pigment was seen developing in the center of colonies, with possible rosettes (Figures 3 and 4). The organism was identified as Sporothrix schenckii.
Figure 3. Culture plate of wound.
Figure 4. Wound culture plate under microscope.

The patient was initially treated with itraconazole orally. However, within 24 hours, she developed a severe full body rash (Figure 5), and the drug was discontinued.
Subsequently, amphotericin B was administered, which was changed to liposomal amphotericin because of the development of acute renal insufficiency. She received liposomal amphotericin for 3 weeks, with excellent resolution of the ulcer and decrease in the size of the right arm nodules (Figure 6). She then received a course of ketoconazole for 4 weeks, until the ulcer had completely resolved. Following completion of anti-fungal therapy, she had no evidence of recurrent disease.
Figure 5. Reaction to treatment.
Figure 6. Two months after treatment.

title: A woman with increasing abdominal girth and discomfort.
history:
A woman in her forties presented with slowly increasing abdominal girth and occasional abdominal discomfort over two months. During this time, the patient experienced several episodes of fever and night sweats. The patient also complained of ribbon-like stools and irregular menses. On review of systems, the patient reported no neurological, pulmonary, urinary, skin, or musculoskeletal symptoms.

She was status post left oophorectomy for benign disease in the remote past.

The patient was of Hispanic descent and lived in a city in Texas. She had not traveled recently.
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The temperature was 99.7°F (37.6°C). The abdomen was distended, with normal bowel sounds and an evident fluid wave. It was not tender to palpation, and there were no palpable masses. The remainder of the examination, including the pelvic exam, was normal.

A complete blood count (CBC) revealed a hematocrit of 35%, a total white blood cell count (WBC) of 6,000/mm³, with 10.1% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count of 606/mm³). The CA-125 was 365 U/ml (normal range 0.6-35.0) and testing for antibodies to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. The urinalysis was normal.
The pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a normal appearing uterus, ascites, and a right ovarian complex hypoechogenic mass. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast enhancement showed massive ascites, a right ovarian complex mass (3-centimeters in diameter, shown in Figure 1), and an irregular anterior abdominal peritoneum suggestive of peritoneal studding (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Pre-op contrast pelvic CT scan.
Figure 2. Pre-op contrast abdominal CT scan.

A laparotomy, with total abdominal hysterectomy/right salpingo-oophorectomy/omentectomy, was peformed for debulking and staging. The peritoneum was studded with malignant-appearing nodules on all serosal surfaces, including the uterus, fallopian tube, and ovary. Frozen sections, however, demonstrated non-caseating granulomatous inflammation (Figure 3).
Figure 3. H and E stain of peritoneal serosa biopsy.
diagnosis:
Peritoneal coccidioidomycosis, caused by Coccidioides immitis.

Histopathology (Figure 3) revealed spherules with endospores within non-caseating granulomas, diagnostic of infection with Coccidioides immitis. Calcofluor white examination of centrifuged peritoneal fluid (Figure 4) and urine (Figure 5) also revealed spherules with endospores. Growth of this fungus occurred out of tissue biopsies, peritoneal fluid, and urine.
Figure 4. Calcofluor stain of spun peritoneal fluid (400x).
Figure 5. Calcofluor stain of spun urine (400x).

On the first post-operative day, the patient developed fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and decreased urine output. The patient was treated with fluid resuscitation, liposomal amphotericin B (LAmB), and empiric piperacillin-tazobactam for sepsis. After two days of therapy, the patient improved, and she completed a nine-day total course of LAmB. The antibiotics were changed to oral fluconazole 800 mg daily, which she tolerated well. She was discharged to home with Infectious Diseases follow-up. Prior to discharge, results of a lumbar puncture and bone scan were normal and showed no evidence of further disseminated disease. The serum complement fixation titer was low at 1:2, and the cerebrospinal (CSF) complement fixation titer was negative.

Coccidioides immitis is a fungus endemic to the Lower Sonoran life zone of the southwestern United States. Human infection occurs by inhalation of airborne fungal arthoconidia; less than one percent of those so infected will develop extrapulmonary disease. Risk factors for disseminated disease include: black race, Filipino race, pregnancy, HIV infection, and immune suppression. The most common sites of dissemination are skin, bones, joints, and meninges.
At the time of this presentation, no prior description of coccidioidomycosis mimicking ovarian cancer had been reported in the literature. Peritoneal coccidioidomycosis has been described, with 26 cases having been reviewed [Phillips and Ford, 2000]. Mortality occured but perhaps less commonly than expected, with 4 of the 26 (15%) previous cases having died, although two of these did not receive antifungal therapy at all. Only three patients had previously been treated with azoles; one (with ketoconazole) failed, two (one with fluconazole, and one with ketoconazole, then itraconazole) were treated successfully (although these successes were preceded by amphotericin B courses).
The visualization of spherules of C. immitis on microscopy of the pertinent body fluids in this case was a reflection of the heavy load of the organism in her tissues despite the apparent absence of other, more usual sites of infection. The presence of culture-positive C. immitis in urine has been reported in pulmonary (presumed non-disseminated) disease, and the ease of culturing the fungus out of the urine has been suggested as an opportune way to help diagnose coccidioidomycosis. This case demonstrates the protean ability of coccidioidomycosis to present in an uncommon manner, in this case mimicking a more ominous intra-abdominal process.
