title: A woman with leukemia and joint pain.
history:
A woman in her fifties with relapsed acute myelocytic leukemia (AML) was admitted for Pseudomonas bacteremia. She was started on piperacillin-tazobactam and amphotericin B lipid complex (ABLC) for a presumed fungal pneumonia on computed tomography (CT) of the chest. She initially defervesced, however she began to have new fevers and vancomycin was added. Two weeks into the admission, she acutely developed severe right hip pain.

There was a history of breast cancer, status post mastectomy and chemotherapy, secondary AML (M-5) due to adriamycin, with relapse after induction and consolidation, and cardiomyopathy believed to be due to mitoxantrone.

Medications included vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and amphotericin lipid complex.
exam_studies:
A thin woman in mild distress with the right hip in flexion. The temperature was 100.6°F (38.1°C) and pulse 121 beats per minute. The right hip was exquisitely tender to palpation and she would not allow any extension. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

She was neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count 15 cells/mcL, hematocrit 32.7%, and platelet count of 3300/mm³. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated nodular densities in the apices. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis demonstrated narrowing of the right hip joint space with erosions of the femoral head and acetabular surfaces, and the iliacus and gluteal muscles adjacent to the joint demonstrated edematous changes (Figure 1). A juxta-articular fluid collection (6 cm by 3 cm) communicated with the joint (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Pelvic MRI scan.
Figure 2. Pelvic MRI scan.

The patient underwent CT-guided needle aspiration and drainage of the fluid. The fluid analysis demonstrated 87,000 white blood cells/mcL (WBCs) (89% leukocytes, 7% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes) and 15,708 red blood cells/mcL (RBCs). The cytopathology did not reveal malignant cells but showed rare fungal hyphae. The fungal culture identified the pathogen (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Culture of joint aspiration.
Figure 4. Culture of joint aspiration.
diagnosis:
Scedosporium apiospermum (the asexual form of Pseudallescheria boydii) joint infection in a patient with acute myelocytic leukemia (AML).

Fungal cultures grew Scedosporium apiospermum, the asexual form of Pseudallescheria boydii. Figures 3 and 4 show the hyphae and terminal annelloconidia of S. apiospermum.

Because of clinical progression while the patient was on liposomal amphotericin, the antibiotic was changed to voriconazole. She became afebrile and her hip pain resolved.

Invasive fungal infections are the leading cause of death due to infectious agents in neutropenic patients. The majority of these fungal infections are presumed due to Aspergillus species, however rare molds are emerging as major pathogens in neutropenia. Despite the implementation of early empiric amphotericin B therapy, mortality is still high (>50%).
Scedosporium apiospermum is a ubiquitous mold found in soil and water, and rarely causes disease in humans. It morphologically can resemble other fungi, like Aspergillus species, which highlights the importance of culturing biopsy material for proper identification and appropriate treatment. Therapy is difficult due to resistance of this organism to amphotericin B. Voriconazole may be effective against Scedosporium apiospermum infections, but close monitoring is essential.

title: A woman with right lower quadrant pain.
history:
A woman in her seventies presented with a two-day history of right lower quadrant pain and back pain. Her symptoms began after she had taken ciprofloxacin for an ear infection. She denied fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, or cough.

There was a history of type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, seizure disorder, gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD) and hypercholesterolemia.

She denied use of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs.

Oral medications included glimepiride (4mg twice daily), and atenolol (100mg daily), valsartan (80mg daily), amlodipine (10mg daily), furosemide (40mg daily), phenytoin (300mg daily), lansoprazole (30mg daily), and atorvastatin (20mg daily).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared to be in severe distress. The oral temperature was 99.9°F (37.7°C), blood pressure 232/107 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats per minute and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild right lower quadrant tenderness and no rebound or guarding. There was also mild tenderness in the lumbar portion of her back. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The level of the white blood cell count (WBC) was 14,800/mm³ and hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL. Blood cultures were sterile. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed an infra-renal periaortic soft tissue density (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.

The patient’s vital signs stabilized after treatment with her usual medications. Vascular surgery consultants decided no surgical intervention was indicated at that time. The patient was discharged home and she returned three days later with increasing abdominal pain. A repeat abdominal CT scan showed an increase in the size of the periaortic soft tissue density (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Abdominal CT scan three days later.
diagnosis:
Mycotic aneurysm of the abdominal aorta caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The aneurysm was surgically repaired with placement of a dacron stent graft. Histologic examination of the aorta revealed heavy inflammatory infiltration (Figure 3), and gram positive cocci in pairs were found (Figure 4). Subsequently, the cocci were identified as Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Figure 3. Histopathology of the aorta.
Figure 4. Stain of the aorta.

The patient’s antibiotics were changed to a six-week course of penicillin G and she was discharged to an extended care facility for full recovery.

Sir William Osler introduced the term mycotic aneurysm in 1885 when he described an aortic arch aneurysm resembling “fresh fungal vegetations”. Presently, the term is used to describe aneurysms associated with a variety of arterial wall infectious processes. The exact incidence of mycotic aneurysms is unknown. In one surgical series, twenty-two out of several thousand cases (0.9%) were mycotic. In the pre-antibiotic era, infected aneurysms were most commonly reported in endocarditis related to Streptococcus viridans and other “virulent” organisms including Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Today, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella spp, and Treponema pallidum are the common pathogens.
Streptococcus pneumoniae has only very rarely been reported as a cause of mycotic aneurysms in the last 25 years. The mechanism of infection is thought to be from hematogenous “seeding” of damaged endothelium during bacteremia. Atherosclerotic disease with subsequent endothelial damage can predispose to infection. Other causes of endothelial damage include cardiac valve vegetations, cardiac catheterization, needle trauma (especially in intravenous drug users) and trauma from gun shot wounds.
The source of this patient's infection was probably a sub-optimally treated ear infection. There have been recent reports of S. pneumoniae, including penicillin-resistant strains, reemerging as a cause of mycotic aneurysms. While the most common source of infection by S. pneumoniae has been the lower respiratory tract, this patient had no respiratory symptoms. Blood cultures were negative and no appreciable heart murmur or other signs of endocarditis were found. Endocarditis may cause mycotic aneurysms by microemboli traveling through the heart and embedding in the vasa vasorum, infecting the arterial wall.
Other potential sources of mycotic embolism were also considered. One mechanism is the possibility of contiguous infection as occurs in Mycobacterium tuberculosis as well as Salmonella spp. In rare instances, caseous, tuberculous lymph nodes cause contiguous infection of the aorta; similarly, pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis can be caused by Salmonella. In addition, Salmonella is also reported to cause mycotic aneurysms by hematogenous spread, especially to abnormal tissue (hematoma, altered endothelium, aortic aneurysm, tumors).
Fungal infections, including Aspergillus spp, Candida spp., and Bipolaris spp., are also associated with mycotic aneurysms from either fungemia or from direct contamination during intracranial vascular surgery. They are most often associated with intracranial mycotic aneurysms and, consequently, were not thought to be likely in this patient.
The presenting signs and symptoms of patients with infectious mycotic aneurysms differ substantially from those with non-infectious abdominal aortic aneurysms. Those with mycotic aneurysms are less likely to present with a pulsatile mass or a dilated aorta on CT scan. Therefore, a high clinical suspicion for mycotic aneurysms is needed for elderly patients who present with fever, abdominal pain or back pain shortly after bacterial infections.
Surgical resection comprises the most important treatment for mycotic aneurysms. Without surgical resection, most patients will die because of rupture and bleeding. Treatment must also include at least 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. The survival rate is 4% with antibiotics alone and 60% with both surgery and antibiotics.

title: A young adult with a facial lesion.
history:
A young adult woman developed a facial lesion. She was in her usual state of health when, four months before her presentation, she traveled to Costa Rica and stayed for 33 days. She visited a rural village in the forest during the first half of her trip and spent the rest of the time on the coast.
One week after her arrival, she developed a rash that started on both her legs, spared her feet, and came to involve up to her mid-thighs. This rash also involved both her forearms, sparing her palms, shoulders, upper chest, and face. She described this rash as red, with small “bumps”, itchy, and associated with swelling. She reported shaking chills, but denied nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The local physician she saw in Costa Rica diagnosed an allergic reaction to foliage and administered two injections of unknown medications. He described them as medications to help her pruritus and to decrease the inflammation. The rash lasted one-and-one-half weeks before completely resolving.
One week after returning home, she noticed a red papule on her right cheek. At first, it appeared to be a small acne lesion, but it did not improve. It grew in size and lost its smooth surface, becoming “bumpy”. She recalled no discharge or vesicular formation, but the lesion was slightly pruritic. She also noted some sensation of swelling at right lower eyelid. There were no associated fevers or chills with this rash.
About three weeks before presentation, she visited her primary physician. She was given mupirocin cream for one week as well as an unknown antibiotic, without improvement. Oral fluconazole (100 mg daily) was added for ten days, without change. She was then treated with itraconazole and minocycline for another 4-5 days. She stopped the minocycline when she developed a fine rash over her peripheral extremities on the second day of that medication. The day before presentation, erythromycin was begun.
She also noted swollen right axillary lymph nodes two weeks before her presentation; these resolved without treatment after four days. She reported no abdominal pain, dysuria, change in vision, headaches, change in hearing, or dysphagia.
Before her presentation, she had had two biopsies of the lesion, which had revealed a granulomatous dermatitis; no infectious organisms were seen.

She had received immunizations for hepatitis A and B viruses before travel.

She was a student living in an apartment. She engaged in occasional alcohol use, and denied tobacco or illicit drug use.

As above, minocycline caused a rash.

She was currently taking erythromycin. She had taken three “malaria pills” before travel to Costa Rica and the same medicine for one week in Costa Rica. While there, she was advised not to continue the medications.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 97.9°F (36.6°C), blood pressure 104/60 mm Hg, pulse 68 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute. She was a well-developed, well-nourished young woman in no distress, who was alert and oriented. There was a red lesion (5.5 cm in diameter) on the right cheek, with an overlying scab (2-cm diameter). (See Figure 1.) The surface of the lesion had several bumps, and was not smooth. A fine blanching light pink rash covered both aspects of bilateral lower arms and lower legs. There was a non-tender soft, motile right preauricular node (1.5 cm diameter), and no axillary lymphadenopathy. The neck was supple with full range of motion. The rest of her examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The results of a third punch biopsy of the right cheek (performed one week before presentation) are shown in Figures 2, 3 and 4.
Figure 2. Figure 2: Hematoxylin and eosin stain of facial punch biopsy.
Figure 2: Hematoxylin and eosin stain of facial punch biopsy.
Figure 3. Punch biopsy of cheek.
Figure 4. Giemsa stain of punch biopsy.
diagnosis:
Facial cutaneous leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania spp.

The third punch biopsy of the right cheek demonstrated pan-dermal non-necrotic granuloma formation with surrounding lymphocytic inflammation. There was striking lymphocytic interface reaction with overlying parakeratosis. (See Figures 2 and 3.) Giemsa stain (Figure 4) demonstrated the presence of small intracellular organisms consistent with Leishman-Donovan bodies.
Acid-fast bacilli (AFB)/Fite stains and methenamine silver/PAS stains were negative for acid fast bacilli and fungi respectively.
Figure 2: Hematoxylin and eosin stain of facial punch biopsy.

With the biopsy results and patient history, the diagnosis is most likely leishmaniasis. She received 21 days of pentavalent antimony by daily intravenous infusion. Her only symptoms were generalized myalgias, which resolved when the medication was completed. She also had an elevation of liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 227 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 208 U/L) during therapy. The pentostam was continued, and the liver enzymes decreased on their own to AST 75 U/L and ALT 111 U/L. She never developed abdominal complaints or hepatomegaly, jaundice, or liver tenderness on physical examination.
During therapy, the lesion decreased in size, as did the right-sided preauricular lymph node. When the pentavalent antimony was completed, the lesion was not yet completely healed, but did progressively improve. Near-complete healing to a flat, brown discoloration on her right check was accomplished 31 days after the treatment was completed.

New world cutaneous leishmaniasis has several possible causative species: Leishmania braziliensis, L. mexicana, L. panamensis, and possibly L. chagasi. It is a zoonosis endemic to South and Central America, from Texas to Northern Argentina, but is most prevalent in Brazil and Peru. Small forest rodents are the major natural reservoirs of these organisms, and the vectors for human disease are Lutzomyia sandflies. Pets may serve as secondary reservoirs, and for L. peruviana, the major reservoir is dogs. The sandflies are most abundant in the forest. Thus, rural settlers and people working at the edge of the forest are most susceptible to disease, as was this young lady the first two weeks that she was in Costa Rica.
L. braziliensis was considered the most probable infectious species because she acquired this in Costa Rica. Among the new-world cutaneous leishmaniasis, L. braziliensis is the only form of these that carries a significant mortality. Old world leishmaniasis was considered less likely.
There are three different forms of leishmanial disease—cutaneous, mucosal, and visceral. Absence of mucosal involvement or physical findings other than the above cheek lesion localized lymphadenopathy suggested cutaneous disease. There was no detectable hepatosplenomegaly, and her arms and legs had no rash. The first rash she developed while in Costa Rica was probably a cutaneous reaction to the local flora.
A decision was made to treat this young lady as quickly as possible with pentostam partly to prevent dissemination, but also because of the infection’s location on the face, which can be disfiguring.

title: A young adult with a swollen left knee.
history: A young adult man was admitted with a three-year history of swelling and induration of the left knee. Multiple nodules on the knee revealed draining sinuses.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 36.5ºC (97.7ºF). Swelling of the left knee extended to the distal third of the thigh. There were numerous woody hard nodules and sinus tracts with drainage (Figure 1). There was no regional lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Left knee.

The level of hemoglobin was 14.8 g/dL, white blood cell count (WBC) 9,000/mm³ (leukocytes 70.5%). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 82 mm per hour. A radiograph of the left knee (Figure 2) showed soft tissue swelling and lytic lesions at the medial cortex of the femur, with cortical thinning and osteoporosis.
Figure 2. Radiograph of knee.

Computed tomography (CT) of the leg showed exostosis and multiple small lytic lesions with ill-defined margins in the internal femoral condyle. (See Figure 3.)
Figure 3. CT scan.
diagnosis: Actinomycosis of the left knee, with bone involvement. Biopsies from deep tissue and bone revealed the presence of sulfur granules (Figures 4 and 5). A gram stain of the specimens demonstrated the presence of beaded, branched, gram-positive filamentous rods, consistent with Actinomyces. Cultures were negative. Figure 4. Stain of biopsy. Figure 5. Stain of biopsy. Based on the histology, the patient was diagnosed with actinomycosis. Incision and drainage of the abscesses was performed and penicillin (300,000 UI/Kg/day) was administered for six weeks. Subsequently, he received a 6-month course of oral amoxicillin. Treatment images are shown in Figures 6 and 7. Figure 6. Radiograph of left leg. Figure 7. Follow-up.

title: A young adult with fever and lymphadenopathy.
history:
A young adult man was well until two weeks before admission when he developed fever and myalgias. He was treated with cephradine empirically at a private clinic for five days. However, his fever persisted and a headache developed.

He had no history of smoking, heavy alcohol use or intravenous drug use. He had no history of blood transfusion or prior surgery. The patient also reported no recent travel, animal exposures, or known exposure to tuberculosis.
exam_studies:
On admission, he appeared acutely ill. The temperature was 38.6°C (101.5°F), blood pressure 100/50 mm Hg, pulse 100/minute, and respirations 20/minute. There were several tender enlarged lymph nodes (measuring approximately 0.8cm by 0.8cm by 0.5 cm) in the left supraclavicular area and posterior neck triangle. The liver edge descended 1 cm below right costal margin. The remainder of examination was normal.

On admission, the white blood cell count was 18,000/mm³ (neutrophils 80% and lymphocyte 11%), hemoglobin level 13.9 g/dL and platelet count 427,000/mm³. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 60 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 86 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 357 IU/L, gamma glutamyl-transpeptidase (g-GTP) 144 IU/L, total protein 6.5 g/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 357 IU/L. Laboratory analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were normal. An initial chest radiograph was normal.

On the 4th hospital day, the patient continued to be febrile and the leukocytosis persisted (26,300/mm³ with neutrophils 71%). He also reported epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness. There was increased left cervical lymph node swelling and tenderness.
On the 6th day, several erythematous papules appeared over his back and extremities (Figures 1 and 2). Cultures of the blood and urine were sterile. A computed tomography (CT) of the neck revealed lymphadenopathy in the left posterior triangle and supraclavicular area with some central necrosis.
The results of the cervical lymph node biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining are shown in Figures 3 and 4.
A chest radiograph revealed the presence of new nodular pulmonary infiltrates and findings suggestive of mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A chest CT scan is shown in Figure 5. Bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial lesion.
Testing of the bronchial washing fluid and brushing were negative by cytological examination, gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction (PCR). An abdominal CT scan showed mild hepatomegaly with intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy in the porta hepatis, portocaval space and near the hepatoduodenal ligament. The hepatic artery and vein were encased by enlarged lymph nodes.
On the 8th hospital day, the patient developed slurred speech without focal neurologic deficit. A MRI scan of brain was normal. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study showed opening pressure of 14.5 cm of water, white cells of 32/mm³ (lymphocyte 98%), protein 34 mg/dL, and sugar 75 mg/dL. No organisms were seen on gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain or India ink preparation of the CSF. PCR for M. tuberculosis and a latex agglutination test for cryptococcal antigen in the CSF were negative.
Figure 1. Skin findings on the sixth hospital day.
Figure 2. Skin findings on the eighth day.
Figure 3. Cervical lymph node, H and E stain (x 100 magnification).
Figure 4. Cervical lymph node, H and E stain (x 400 magnification).
Figure 5. Chest CT scan on the sixth day.
diagnosis:
Disseminated cryptococcosis (involving lymph nodes, skin, lung and probably central nervous system) in an immunocompetent host.

Microscopic examination revealed granuloma with giant cells and multiple fungal yeast in cervical lymph node and skin (Figures 4 and 6). The bronchoscopy specimen grew Cryptococcus.
Figure 6. Cervical lymph node PAS stain x 1000.

A 14-day course of systemic amphotericin B with flucytosine was administered, with two months of oral fluconazole. He has had no evidence of recurrent disease.
The ELISA for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody was negative on two successive tests (interval of 6 weeks). The level of immunoglobulin E was 1,030 IU/mL (reference value < 100 IU/mL), and serum immunoglobulin G, A and M levels were normal. The total peripheral blood lymphocyte count was 1,478/mm³ and the CD4 T-cell to CD8 T-cell count ratio was normal.

Cryptococcus is an ubiquitous yeast with a worldwide distribution. Defects in cell-mediated immunity and HIV infection constitute the major predisposing conditions for disseminated cryptococcal infection. Other risk factors for cryptococcal disease include: lympho-reticular malignancy, corticosteroid treatment, sarcoidosis, diabetes mellitus and hepatic cirrhosis. Although the attack rate is many times higher among immunocompromised persons, cryptococcal disease does occur in persons without any apparent predisposing condition.
Meningoencephalitis is the most common manifestation of cryptococcal infection. Other sites of cryptococcal infection include blood, bone marrow, lungs, skin, and genito-urinary tract. Although most pulmonary infections are “clinically silent”, symptomatic disease can occur. Dissemination of cryptococcal infection to the CNS also occurs even in the immunocompetent hosts.

title: A young adult with leg ulcers for several months.
history:
A young adult woman from a rural village in the Republic of Guinea presented to the outpatient clinic of a regional hospital complaining of painless ulcers on her right leg that had progressed for several months. Before the onset of the ulcers, she had sustained a laceration to the lateral aspect of her right ankle in a farming accident.
Several weeks after this occurrence, she noted a subcutaneous nodule, the size of her thumbnail, at the site of the laceration. The lesion was painless and pruritic, and had gradually broken down and developed into an enlarging cutaneous ulcer that expanded over her right ankle and foot. She denied fever, chills or any other constitutional symptoms.

She was from a rural village along a river in a southern province of the Republic of Guinea.
exam_studies:
She was appearing well and looked her stated age. The temperature was 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 110/82 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats per minute, and respirations 16 breaths per minute. On her right ankle and on the dorsal surface of her foot, there were two large full-thickness ulcers consisting of necrotic eschar with a clear line of demarcation between affected and unaffected tissue (7 centimeters by 14 cm and 6 cm by 6 cm, respectively; Figure 1). There was a small amount of edema around the lesion; however, there was no edema of her leg. The ulcers were painless and not malodorous. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 1. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 10,200 cells/mm³, hemoglobin 12.1 gm/dL and platelets 393,000/mm³.
diagnosis:
Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans infection).

Buruli ulcer was diagnosed clinically, by means of the World Health Organization (WHO) standard case definition. Buruli ulcer is an infectious disease involving the skin, which begins with a painless nodule, papule, plaque or edema and evolves into a painless ulcer with undermined edges. This skin lesion is characterized by necrotic center, undermined edges and edematous skin. In the absence of superinfection, ulcers are painless or minimally painful, and not significantly malodorous.

Given the advanced nature of her presentation, she was immediately admitted and had the wound surgically debrided the following morning. She remained in the hospital for three months for observation, daily soaks, and wound care. In an effort to make the wound inhospitable to common skin organisms, the attending physician wrapped the wound twice daily with sugar-laden bandages. It is hypothesized that the sugar absorbs fluid from the wound while altering the pH. Figure 2 demonstrates a good response to debridement and local wound treatment, with a continued clear area of demarcation but healthy confluent granulation tissue.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

Buruli ulcer is a disease of the skin caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans; its etiological factors and transmission are not known. Clues to transmission, however, can be found in environmental factors. The endemic foci of disease tend to occur in the wetlands of tropical and subtropical countries implying that an essential feature in the survival of the causative agent is probably environmental. Indeed focal outbreaks have followed alterations to the environment such as flooding, human migrations, and man-made topographic modifications such as dams and resorts. Destruction of forest and increase of agricultural activities in countries in West Africa have more than likely contributed to the rapid emergence and increased incidence rates of the disease.
Children under the age of 15 years have the highest rate of disease prevalence. Nevertheless, individuals of all ages are affected and both genders are equally affected. West and Central Africa have the highest burden of this disease.
The pathophysiology of Buruli ulcer has not been well established. Trauma from the slight (e.g. hypodermic needle) to the sizeable (e.g. land-mine explosion) is thought to precede infection. Once inoculated, M. ulcerans proliferates and produces a toxin that causes necrosis of the dermis, panniculus, and deep fascia. As the necrosis develops, it extends to the overlying dermis and epidermis, which at this point is closed. The necrosis promotes an ulceration of the overlying tissue with undermined edges and a necrotic slough in the base of the ulcer. At this time in the course of the disease, clusters of extracellular acid-fast bacilli are frequently limited to the base of the ulcer and adjacent necrotic subcutaneous tissue. There are few inflammatory cells in active lesions, possibly due to immunosuppressive activity of the toxin. With healing, there is a granulomatous response and a depressed scar eventually replaces the ulcerated area.
The clinical presentation of Buruli ulcers varies. The lesion may initially present as a pruritic nodule, which then ulcerates. An ulcer may remain small and heal without treatment, or may spread rapidly and undermine the skin over large areas, possibly including an entire leg, thigh, or arm. Involvement of eyes, breasts and genitalia has been described and, reportedly, these organs may be severely damaged or completely necrosed. Involvement of the bone, osteomyelitis, has led to amputation. Deformity and extensive scarring are likely to occur without appropriate treatment, yet most lesions will heal spontaneously.
The diagnosis of Buruli ulcer can be made accurately in highly endemic areas based on the history and physical examination. Laboratory investigations, if available, can also be utilized to increase diagnostic yield. Smears from the base of ulcers may reveal acid-fast bacilli. Growth of M. ulcerans can be accomplished from cultures from lesions; growth of the organism may take months. Biopsy of necrotic tissue can also be diagnostic. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a useful tool for diagnosis when the culture or histopathologic analyses fails to reveal a causative organism.
Debridement and good wound management remain the mainstay of management of Buruli ulcer. Unfortunately, there are no effective prophylactic measures.

title: A young boy with a fever and rash.
history:
A young boy presented to an emergency department with fever, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. He was diagnosed with a viral syndrome.
When seen in follow-up the next day, he was afebrile and asymptomatic, but he had a new non-pruritic, blanching, morbilliform rash on his proximal extremities and trunk. He was referred to a clinic for follow-up. When seen in clinic less than twenty-four hours later, he felt well except for a new left heel pain, which caused him to limp. His parents noted that the rash was no longer itchy, and had a different appearance than on the first day.

He had previously been healthy.

The patient had traveled to rural Colorado six days before the onset of fever, where he played in native scrub. He had also had contact with lizards, a hermit crab and a parakeet on the trip. He had not traveled out of the United States recently, but had been to Mexico several years before.
He had a pet rat and “love birds” at home. There had been no ingestion of unpasteurized cheese or milk, and no known tick, flea or other insect bites.

He had taken ibuprofen for fever.
exam_studies:
In general, he appeared well. The temperature was 97°F (36.1°C), blood pressure 135/69 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats per minute and respirations 24 breaths per minute. A petechial rash (Figures 1 through 4) involved the distal extremities, including palms and soles, and became slightly purpuric on feet and ankles. Both feet and ankles were mildly puffy. There was mild tenderness to firm palpation of the left heel with no overlying ecchymosis. The patient walked favoring the left heel. The rest of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.
Figure 4. Physical findings.

In the emergency department, the white blood cell count (WBC) was 23,900/mm³ (86% neutrophils, 8% bands), platelet count 284,000/mm³, and hemoglobin 14 g/dL. The level of urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose and electrolytes were normal. Urinalysis revealed trace blood, and a normal microscopic exam; an abdominal ultrasound did not show an appendix, and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen with contrast was normal.
In the clinic at follow-up, the WBC was 11,700/mm³ (92% neutrophils on automated differential), platelet count 151,000/mm³, and hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL. The urinalysis had a small amount of blood, protein >300 mg/dl, and urobilinogen 1; the microscopic examination was normal. Plain radiographs of the foot were normal.
diagnosis:
Rat bite fever and calcaneal osteomyelitis caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis.

The blood culture grew Streptobacillus moniliformis, which was confirmed in a reference laboratory.
A few days later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the foot demonstrated changes consistent with osteomyelitis of the calcaneus (Figures 5 and 6). There was abnormal hyperintensity on T2 sequences within the posterior os calcis, at the metaphysis-growth plate margin. Hyperintense signal was also noted within the adjacent os calcis, which was compatible with bone edema. There was also adjacent soft tissue edema noted, but the ankle and subtalar joints appeared normal.
Figure 5. MRI scan of feet.
Figure 6. MRI scan of the left foot.

The patient denied any history of rat bites, but reported that he occasionally kissed the rat. He was initially treated with cefotaxime intravenously, and defervesced rapidly.
After final identification of the organism, he was switched to oral amoxicillin (at 80-90 mg/kg/day) to complete a six-week course. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, which had been elevated, normalized in the first week. Nine months later, at follow-up, he was clinically well and walking normally.

Rat Bite Fever is usually due to Streptobacillus moniliformis, and less commonly due to Spirillum minor (also known as S. minus). These two agents can often be distinguished clinically.
Infection with Spirillum minor usually develops approximately 10 days after a rat bite. The bite wound may become painful and swollen. Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache and a macular or urticarial rash. Unlike streptobacillary rat bite fever, infections with S. minus generally do not present with arthritis.
Streptobacillus moniliformis is part of the normal oral flora of rodents and is also shed in the urine and stool. A bite is not necessary for infection and, if present, has frequently healed at presentation. Incubation period is usually 2-10 days. Haverhill fever is caused by ingestion of S. moniliformis contaminated material and is associated with sore throat, vomiting and fever. S. moniliformis is sensitive to penicillin (the drug of choice at the time of this publication) and (at least in vitro) to cephalosporins. It has not previously been associated with osteomyelitis, but is commonly associated with fever, vomiting, rash, arthralgias, myalgias, and septic arthritis. Occasional cases of abscesses, endocarditis, meningitis and sepsis have been described.

title: A young man with a neck mass.
history:
A young adult male presented with a mildly tender swelling over the left side of the neck, associated with ten-pound weight loss over three months. He denied fever, chills, loss of appetite, shortness of breath or cough.

The patient had immigrated to the United States from Vietnam four years before.
exam_studies:
He was a slender and had normal vital signs. There were multiple, mildly tender, fluctuant lymph nodes in the anterior and posterior cervical chains and in the supra-clavicular area on the left side. Most nodes measured 1-2 centimeters; the largest was 4 centimeters in diameter. The remainder of examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) count and differential were normal. Other hematological and chemical parameters in the blood were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck and chest are shown in Figures 1 and 2 respectively.
Figure 1. Neck CT scan.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.

An excisional biopsy of an enlarged lymph node was performed. Following appropriate treatment, the lesions recurred six months later as shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Physical findings.
Figure 4. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Scrofuloderma with underlying pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Excisional biopsy showed necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Acid-fast bacillus (AFB) stain of the biopsy was positive. Culture of biopsy was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

He was treated with rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and isoniazid (INH) for 6 months, with recurrence 12 months later. He was re-treated with the same four drugs for an additional 6 months.

Scrofuloderma results from contiguous extension from an underlying tuberculous focus due to infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium bovis. The overlying tissue starts as a red-brown nodule and then becomes indurated and breaks down. The resulting ulcers and sinuses may drain watery, purulent or caseous material. It is often associated with pulmonary tuberculosis.
Mycobacterium bovis from unpasteurized milk may cause scrofuloderma involving the cervical lymph nodes in developing nations. Biopsy of the lesions shows necrosis with abscess formation with numerous acid-fast bacilli. The patient is often PPD positive. The lesions may heal spontaneously over the course of years.

title: An elderly man with a rash and peripheral neuropathy.
history:
An elderly man presented with a five-month history of non-pruritic macular rash. He noted diminished sensation over the skin lesions and in the feet. He had received several topical treatments, without improvement, and denied fever or other systemic symptoms.

He had hypertension. There were no known allergies.

The patient was born in Spain, and lived in a rural area of Venezuela for the previous 20 years. He was a smoker, but did not use illicit drugs or alcohol. He had several domestic animals at his home.

There were no known allergies.

His medications included enalapril.
exam_studies:
He appeared in good health. The temperature was 95.2°F (35.1°C) and respirations 14 breaths per minute. There were several macular lesions present on his body, up to eight centimeters in diameter (Figures 1 and 2). Pain and temperature sensation were diminished over the skin lesions, the ulnar area of left hand, the right thumb, and the right foot. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The level of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 43 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 84 IU/L and lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) 463 IU/L; all other test results were normal. Results of serology testing, a chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and abdominal ultrasound were also normal. The electromyogram showed a predominantly sensory asymmetric peripheral polyneuropathy.
diagnosis:
Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

A skin lesion was biopsied. Pathological examination of the skin biopsy showed a granulomatous infiltrate with numerous acid-fast bacilli, often found in large clumps, i.e. "globi". A diagnosis of leprosy was made.

The patient received dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Improvement occurred in the skin lesions over the following months.

Leprosy, a well-known illness since the sixth century B.C., is a chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, peripheral nervous system, upper respiratory tract, and eyes, and in men may involve the testicles. The disease may be transmitted from one person to another, and if left untreated may cause characteristic deformities that historically have resulted in a profound social stigma in sufferers. In the present day, leprosy can be diagnosed in early stages, and can be treated effectively, resulting in successful prevention of deformities and cure of the infection.

title: An elderly woman with cyanosis of the fingers.
history:
An elderly woman presented with a one-week history of increasing weakness and malaise. Three days before admission, she was scratched by a turtle on the index finger of her left hand. She reported nausea, vomiting, and loose bowel movements for one day, associated with lightheadedness and subjective chills at home. After admission, her fingers became cyanotic with increasing pain and numbness.

She had hypertension and hyponatremia, and was status post thyroidectomy.

She lived in a rural area of Texas and owned several dogs. She did not smoke, reported no illicit drug or heavy alcohol use, and had not traveled outside of the state.

She had no known allergies.

She was taking enalapril.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/60 mm Hg, and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The head and neck examination was normal. There were firm mobile non-tender masses in each breast. The lungs were clear. The heart rhythm was regular and there were no murmurs. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. There was acrocyanosis on the distal tips of all fingers (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 2,300/mm³, hemoglobin 12.3 gm/dL, and platelet count 33,000/mm³. The sodium was 123 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 95 mmol/L, CO2 19 mmol/L, glucose 73 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 54 mg/dL, creatinine 2.9 mg/dL. The prothrombin time (PT) was 12.3 seconds and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 31 seconds; the level of C3 was 74 and C4 14.5. Urinalysis and liver function tests were normal.
The chest radiograph was normal. Blood cultures (6 out of 6) grew gram-negative bacilli.

The patient developed acute renal failure, but did not require hemodialysis. The cyanosis gradually improved. The thrombocytopenia initially worsened and then gradually improved.
diagnosis:
Capnocytophaga bacteremia with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

Capnocytophaga was identified growing in six blood cultures obtained over 3 days.

The patient did not develop endocarditis. The thrombocytopenia and acute renal failure resolved. She was treated with ampicillin-sulbactam for 14 days.
A presumptive diagnosis of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) secondary to Capnocytophaga bacteremia was made on the basis of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, acute renal failure and thrombocytopenia, with normal clotting times. The patient never underwent plasmapheresis.

Capnocytophaga is a fastidious, slow-growing, gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium that belongs to the normal flora of dogs and cats. Alcohol abuse is an important associated risk factor for the development of septicemic Capnocytophaga infection. Bacteremia rarely manifests with disseminated intravascular consumption coagulopathy or purpura.
Most of the cases of Capnocytophaga bacteremia occur in patients with hematologic malignancy and neutropenia. Infection may be associated with severe oropharyngeal mucositis or periodontal disease. Capnocytophaga bacteremia is usually an uncomplicated infection without serious organ involvement and has a good outcome after antibiotic therapy. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) has been rarely described with Capnocytophaga infection. To our knowledge, at the time of this publication, acrocyanosis secondary to vasculitis with HUS and Capnocytophaga has not been reported. The patient was thought to have contracted the bacteremia after her dog licked the injury caused by the turtle.

title: An HIV-positive man with fever, weight loss, and nonproductive cough.
history:
A man presented with a one-month history of fever, chills, sweats at various times of day, poor appetite, nausea, arthralgias, eighteen-pound (8.2 kilograms) weight loss, and a nonproductive cough without hemoptysis. The patient also complained of dysuria and chronic back pain. He denied headaches, visual changes, sore throat, neck pain, diarrhea and abdominal pain. He had been diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection two decades earlier and had no history of opportunistic infections or treatment with antiretroviral medications.

He had HIV infection with recent CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of 505 cells/microliter, viral load 88,000 RNA copies/milliliter, anti-phospolipid antibody (APLA) syndrome with multiple deep venous thromboses, and hepatitis C virus infection. He had had an inferior vena cava filter placed six years before admission.

He lived in Texas, had several tattoos, and was bisexual with no partners within the last month. He owned dogs that appeared to be healthy. He denied intravenous drug use and had stopped smoking several years before.

Medications included acetaminophen for pain, quinapril, amlodipine for hypertension, and warfarin for APLA syndrome, none of which had been recently changed or added.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure 150/100 mm Hg, and the oxygen saturation was normal while breathing ambient air. There was trace pitting edema in his legs, prominent palmar erythema and multiple non-pruritic lesions with peripheral erythema distributed only on the upper back. The skin lesions are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The level of hemoglobin was 12.3 g/dL, platelets 98,000/mm³, and white blood cell count (WBC) 3,400 cells/mm³, with a normal differential. The INR ws 2.4 on warfarin, and the levels of electrolytes, liver function tests, and lactate dehydrogenase were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed splenomegaly. The chest radiograph is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Chest radiograph.

Broncho-alveolar lavage was performed and the skin and bone marrow were biopsied.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis (including cutaneous, bone marrow, and pulmonary involvement) caused by Histoplasma capsulatum in an HIV-positive patient with no prior history of opportunistic infections and a CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of 505 cells/mm³.

Pathological examination of the bone marrow biopsy showed one small, non-caseating granuloma, and that of the skin biopsy showed yeast forms. Culture of a broncho-alveolar lavage specimen grew Histoplasma capsulatum.

The patient was treated with two weeks of amphotericin B after which he was started on oral itraconazole. He experienced fever and rigors when amphotericin B was administered, despite pretreatment with diphenhydramine and meperidine, but agreed to continue treatment. After discharge, his fevers, rash, arthralgias, and cough continued to improve slowly. Additionally, given his first opportunistic infection, the patient was started on antiretrovirals despite his CD4 T-lymphocyte count.

Histoplasmosis is common in the central and south central United States and occurs in approximately 5% of HIV-positive patients in endemic areas. At diagnosis, most cases in HIV-positive patients are disseminated. Clinical presentation most commonly includes fever and weight loss. Pulmonary complaints are seen in over 50% of patients, but a variety of other organs can be affected, with manifestations including retinitis, prostatitis, pancreatitis, colitis, and, rarely, skin lesions. The median CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count in HIV-positive patients with histoplasmosis is 50 cells/mm³; there are few reports of histoplasmosis in HIV-positive patients with CD4 cell counts >500/mm³. The skin lesions in this patient are a rare occurrence in any HIV-positive patient, but particularly one who has a CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count over 500 cells/mm³ and no previous history of opportunistic infections.
The diagnosis is made by blood and bone marrow cultures, which have 90% sensitivity. Polysaccharide antigen tests have sensitivity of 90% in urine and 75% in blood from HIV-positive patients. At the time of this publication, treatment is with amphotericin B initially until clinical improvement occurs (typically 7-14 days), then with itraconazole. Lifetime therapy is typically used to prevent relapse although no studies have been done in HIV-positive patients with CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count over 500 cells/mm³.

title: An HIV-seropositive woman with blurred vision.
history:
A middle-aged African woman presented with a three-week history of headaches and decreased visual acuity. She described seeing blurred and distorted images and reported several instances of walking into objects such as street signs. Three months before admission, she had been diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection; the CD4 T-cell count was 40 cells/mm³ and the level of HIV-1 RNA was 114,000 copies/ml. She was also found to have a cavitary lung lesion, for which she underwent bronchoscopy. Pathological examination of the bronchial biopsy revealed fungal organisms, and cultures grew Cryptococcus neoformans.
Approximately seven weeks before admission, antiretroviral therapy with efavirenz, zidovudine and lamivudine was begun. The antiretroviral therapy resulted in an excellent virologic control (the HIV-1 RNA decreased to less than 400 copies/ml) and immunologic response, with the CD4+ T-cell count increasing to 135 cells/mm³. However, there was a delay in starting the patient on antifungal therapy. She remained well and free of physical complaints until three weeks before this presentation, when headaches and visual disturbances developed.

She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, for which she was treated approximately 2 years earlier.

She had immigrated to the United States nine months earlier from Northwestern Africa. There was no history of smoking, illicit drug or heavy alcohol use. She was not sexually active and reported no animal exposures.

She had no known allergies.

Medications included efavirenz, lamivudine, zidovudine, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and in no acute distress. The temperature was 99.9°F (37.7°C), blood pressure 132/68 mm Hg, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and pulse 72 beats per minute. There was left homonymous hemianopsia, and the remainder of the general medical and neurological examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 4,300/mm³, hematocrit 35.6%, and the levels of serum electrolytes, glucose, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and liver function tests were normal. A lumbar puncture was performed. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 3 white cells and 2 red cells per cubic millimeter, glucose 64 mg/dL and total protein 47 mg/dL. The CSF gram stain, bacterial and fungal cultures, and cryptococcal antigen were all negative. Serologic testing for Toxoplasma gondii was negative, and serum cryptococcal antigen was positive at 1:4.
A chest radiograph was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head demonstrated an enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe and a mildly enhancing subcortical lesion with edema in the right occipital region along the occipital horn (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Brain MRI scan showing occipital lesion.

Amphotericin B was started for the treatment of presumed cryptococcal central nervous system infection. She initially described some improvement in her clinical symptoms, without any objective changes in her visual defects.
Two weeks into her hospital course, nausea, headaches and blurred vision increased. An MRI scan revealed no change in the right frontal lesion but worsening of the right occipital lesion, with greater enhancement. Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and systemic corticosteroids were initiated for presumptive Toxoplasma encephalitis, and neurosurgeons were consulted to consider a diagnostic brain biopsy.
diagnosis:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) as sequelae of immune reconstitution syndrome in an African patient with polyomavirus JC virus and HIV infection and AIDS.

The brain biopsy revealed focal demyelination (Figure 2, with myelin stained blue-green) and extensive perivascular and intraparenchymal infiltration by mononuclear inflammatory cells including macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.
Rare cells with large nuclei and ill-defined amphophilic inclusions were observed, representing oligodendrocytes of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (Figure 3). The stains for bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were all negative. However, immunostaining for JC virus antigens was positive (Figure 4).
Figure 2. Brain biopsy with myelin stain.
Figure 3. Brain biopsy with oligodendrocytic inclusions.
Figure 4. Brain biopsy immunostain for JC viral antigens.

The patient was continued on the anti-retroviral regimen and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Amphotericin, pyrimethamine, and sulfadiazine were discontinued. She was discharged with the steroids to be tapered slowly. She described stabilization of her symptoms after her discharge. She was lost to follow-up after she returned to Africa.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in the setting of advanced AIDS has been associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Highly-active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has demonstrated efficacy in stabilizing disease and improving survival in AIDS patients with PML.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy has also been described as presenting as an immune reconstitution syndrome, after initiation of HAART. This is typically seen in patients with a good immunologic and virologic response to retroviral therapy as demonstrated by an increase in CD4+ T-cell counts and decrease in HIV-1 RNA level. This patient developed neurologic symptoms four weeks after the introduction of antiretroviral therapy. At six weeks, her CD4+ count had increased from 40 to 135 cells/mm³, and her HIV-1 viral load had decreased from 114,000 to less than 400 copies/mL.
PML as an immune reconstitution event characteristically presents 3 to 8 weeks after the initiation of HAART. A subset of patients progress rapidly to death despite continuing HAART. A definitive diagnosis of PML requires the demonstration of the characteristic pathologic changes on brain biopsy. Numerous foci of demyelination can be seen in the cerebral white matter. Cerebral PML lesions typically reveal minimal inflammatory changes.
However, in the subset of patients with immune reconstitution-related PML there may be marked mononuclear infiltration in the brain, as seen in this patient. This inflammatory response correlates with the radiologic findings in such patients. Whereas CT scans of patients with PML characteristically reveal hypodense, non-enhancing lesions of the cerebral white matter, the CT scans of patients with immune reconstitution-related PML exhibit contrast enhancement, especially at the leading edge of the lesion. Biopsy of this area demonstrates marked inflammation. Treatment involves continuing antiretrovirals. A possible role for cidofovir and corticosteroids has not been clearly defined.

title: An immunocompetent woman with bilateral infiltrates.
history:
A woman was admitted to the hospital because of fever, chills, sore throat, myalgias, periumbilical pain and vomiting, which had begun two days before admission.
One month before admission she was evaluated in an emergency room with diffuse myalgias and dizziness while on diet pills. The pills were stopped and she was discharged home on cyclobenzaprine. Two weeks later, she returned to the emergency room and again reported myalgias, which were not responding to cyclobenzaprine. She was discharged on naproxen and reported symptomatic improvement until two days before admission.
On admission, she reported no cough or shortness of breath. There was no history of fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

She had no significant past medical history.

She was from an island in the Caribbean. She had no history of drug or alcohol use. There was no recent travel, exposure to ill persons or known animal exposures.

Medications included naproxen as needed.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 104.3°F (40.2°C), blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg, pulse 140 beats per minute, and respirations 20 breaths per minute. There was mild erythema of the conjunctiva. The tonsils were enlarged and a white exudate was noted. There was tender adenopathy in the anterior cervical and submandibular regions, and mild tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium and peirumbilical areas, without guarding or rebound tenderness. The legs were tender to palpation, and the remainder of the exam was normal.

The hemoglobin was 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 43.8%, white blood cell count (WBC) 3,400/mm³ (with 63% neutrophils, 26% band forms, 6% lymphocytes, and 2% monocytes), platelets 200,000/mm³, prothrombin time (PT) 17.2 seconds, partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 37 seconds, INR 1.6, sodium 134 mmol/l, potassium 3.8 mmol/l, chloride 98 mmol/l, bicarbonate 20 mmol/l, urea nitrogen 18, creatinine 1.2, glucose 103 mg/dl, bilirubin 4.9 mg/dl (direct 3.1 mg/dl), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 339 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 376 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 164 U/L, amylase 65 U/L, lipase 34 U/L, creatine phosphokinase (CPK) 3193 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1572 U/L.
The chest radiograph showed bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

The patient was treated with clindamycin and cefotaxime initially. On the third hospital day she became afebrile. Her sore throat and abdominal pain resolved. However, the myalgias continued. A tuberculosis skin test (PPD) was positive, with 30 mm induration. Three sputum samples for acid fast bacilli (AFB) were negative.
On the sixth hospital day, she became more hypoxic and required intubation. A bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed and smears were negative for AFB, fungus and Pneumocystis carinii (PCP). Electromyography did not reveal any evidence of acute denervation. Serologic tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies and viral load were negative.
The liver function tests increased: AST 985 U/L, ALT 601 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 635 U/L, and direct bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL. The platelet count decreased to 124,000/mm³. The patient had recurrent fevers and a bone marrow biopsy was performed.
diagnosis:
Disseminated tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A transbronchial biopsy was not performed due to marked desaturation. The bone morrow biopsy showed multiple non-caseating granulomas but no acid fast bacilli (AFB). The sputum and BAL grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis on culture.

Blood, urine and throat cultures were negative for bacteria and fungi. Sputum, urine and throat cultures were negative for virus. The cefotaxime and clindamycin were changed to piperacillin-tazobactam, azithromycin and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol). The patient’s condition worsened despite this therapy. She became profoundly acidotic and severely hypoxic with cardiac tachyarrhythmias. She expired on the fourteenth day of the hospitalization.
An autopsy revealed adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and pathologic changes consistent with disseminated tuberculosis involving multiple organs. (Figures 2 through 7).
Figure 2. Heart histopathology.
Figure 3. Lung histopathology.
Figure 4. Liver histopathology.
Figure 5. Ovarian histopathology.
Figure 6. Adrenal histopathology.
Figure 7. Bone marrow.

This case describes a very atypical presentation of a fatal case of disseminated tuberculosis. The literature does describe cases of septic shock or sepsis syndrome associated with tuberculosis, termed "sepsis tuberculosis gravissima". These cases have generally occurred in elderly patient or those with AIDS and other chronic illnesses such as lupus. Another unusual presentation of tuberculosis is adult respiratory distress syndrome in association with miliary tuberculosis. The case reports in the literature describing this entity all involve patients with histories of alcohol abuse who were ill for weeks to months prior to diagnosis.
This patient was a young woman with no history of immunocompromise and no medical complaints except for myalgias. Her initial presentation was most consistent with a severe acute viral illness with pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, myositis, hepatitis and pneumonitis. Given the unusual presentation, tuberculosis was not considered likely especially when the sputum and a bronchoalveolar lavage were negative on smear for AFB. It has been noted that the diagnosis of miliary tuberculosis maybe difficult since smears of sputum for acid-fast bacilli may be positive in only 20-40% of patients and the PPD maybe negative in 30-60% of cases. Had her clinical condition permitted a transbronchial biopsy, it is expected that the yield from this procedure would have been higher than from the BAL.
This patient died on her third day of anti-tuberculous therapy and the autopsy was consistent with tuberculosis infection of multiple organs. The literature indicates a very poor survival rate for cases of disseminated tuberculosis associated with septic shock or ARDS. It remains an unproven possibility that a severe viral illness predisposed this patient to fatal disseminated tuberculosis.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A middle-aged man with fever, cough and
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A middle-aged man with fever, cough and diarrhea.
A middle-aged man, status post heart transplantation, presented with fever, cough, and diarrhea.
Six years earlier, the patient had required heart transplantation for dilated cardiomyopathy. Five months before admission, mild rejection occurred. Azathioprine was stopped and mycophenolate and prednisone were begun.
One month before admission, shortly after consuming bottled spring water and barbequed beef, he developed nausea, vomiting, and severe, non-bloody diarrhea. Two weeks later, sore throat, sinus congestion, cough with white sputum and fever developed. One week before admission, he had increasing dyspnea and fever to 104°F (40°C).

There was a history of chronic renal insufficiency and dilated cardiomyopathy that had necessitated heart transplantation. The donor and recipient had negative serologies for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and toxoplasmosis. The recipient was varicella zoster virus (VZV) and Epstein Barr virus (EBV) antibody positive.

The patient lived with his wife and owned dogs and birds. He worked in the construction industry and denied recent travel.

Medications included mycophenolate (1500 mg twice daily), prednisone (10 mg daily) and cyclosporine.
exam_studies:
The patient was diaphoretic and dyspneic, using accessory muscles of respiration while receiving 6 liters of supplemental oxygen. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure 126/68 mm/Hg and pulse 102 beats/minute. Examination of the head, ear, eye, nose and throat was normal and without lymphadenopathy. Jugulovenous distension (JVD) was 10-12 centimeters. The lungs had diffuse upper airway wheezes and rhonchi. There were coarse rales at the left base with egophony and dullness to percussion. Heart sounds were distant and the abdomen was distended, tympanitic, soft without rebound, guarding, or hepatomegaly. There was 2+ edema of the extremities.

The white blood cells count was 6700/mm³, serum urea nitrogen 66 mg/dL, creatinine 4.7 mg/dL, carbon dioxide 15 mmol/L, anion gap 15 and alkaline phosphatase 61 U/L. Other liver function tests were normal.
The chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1 and computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.

The patient's respiratory status declined quickly and mechanical ventilation was initiated. Empiric treatment with vancomycin, ceftazidime, levofloxacin, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and ganciclovir was administered. Hemodialysis was begun after renal function declined further. The patient required intermittent pressor support.
diagnosis:
Adenoviral (serotype 7) pneumonia in an immunocompromised patient.

The chest radiograph (Figure 1) demonstrated a dense left upper and patchy left lower lobe consolidation and small left pleural effusion. The non-contrast, high-resolution CT scan of the chest (Figure 2) demonstrated extensive, severe consolidation involving both the left upper and left lower lobes, accompanied by a small left pleural effusion. Cardiomegaly, mild hilar adenopathy and a slight mediastinal shift to the right were present.
Cultures of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimens were negative for bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and Legionella growth. Staining for Pneumocystis was negative, as were cultures for cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), and varicella zoster virus (VZV). Stool specimens, sent for bacterial pathogens, ova and parasites, Cryptosporidium, microsporidia, Clostridium difficile, and mycobacteria were negative. Cryptococcal serum antigen and urine Legionella and Histoplasma antigens were negative. Serologic testing for CMV and coccidioidomycosis were negative. On the fifth hospital day, adenovirus cultures were positive from bronchoalveolar lavage and stool specimens, and subsequently identified as adenovirus serotype 7.

Given the limited therapeutic options to treat adenovirus, cidofovir was begun on the sixth hospital day. The hospital course was complicated by pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum. The patient became neutropenic, presumably secondary to cidofovir.
Candida krusei line infection, upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding, and seizures followed. The patient expired on the twenty-eighth hospital day. No pathogen other than adenovirus was isolated.

The differential diagnosis of pneumonia in this immunocompromised, heart-transplant patient is broad. This patient's illness is consistent with severe adenovirus infection (serotype 7). Adenoviruses, a family of DNA viruses, infect the epithelial cells of the respiratory, GI, and GU tracts. There have been over 50 serotypes identified and these cause a variety of clinical syndromes. Adenoviruses are ubiquitous and primary infection usually occurs within the first year of life, resulting in serotype-specific immunity.
In immunocompetent hosts, adenoviruses generally cause self-limited or asymptomatic infection, most often involving the respiratory tract and conjunctiva. Adenovirus accounts for 2-7% of childhood respiratory infections and 5-10% of acute diarrheal illnesses. Serotype 7, in particular, is associated with acute upper and lower respiratory tract infections, especially in military recruits and can cause fulminant bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants.
In immunocompetent patients, adenoviruses can also cause acute hemorrhagic cystitis, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, and tonsillopharyngitis. Although the infection is generally self-limited in immunocompetent patients, adenovirus can cause a disseminated, fatal infection in immunocompromised individuals.
Adenoviruses cause lytic infection, but are also capable of establishing latency. Disease in immunocompromised hosts can occur either due to primary infection or reactivation. In transplant patients, the transplanted organ is often the site of infection, perhaps due to reactivation of latent virus in the transplanted organ or limited host immune surveillance in the allograft recipient. Infection in transplant patients is associated with case fatality rates of approximately 50%. There have been case reports of disseminated adenovirus infections years after transplantation.
Since viral shedding is reasonably common, attributing symptomatic disease to adenoviral infection can be difficult given the variety of other possible etiologies. Exclusion of other causes is often used to establish probable disease, but definitive disease requires histopathology, which is often not available. There is no established therapy for adenovirus infections. Anti-viral therapies have been attempted, in particular with ribaviran, ganciclovir, and cidofovir, but the data regarding their efficacy remain anecdotal. There are no randomized trials, and therefore the treatment of choice, if any, is not certain. Cidofovir may have significant toxicities associated, most notably renal failure and myelosuppression, both of which complicated the care of this particular patient.

title:
Summary: An African man in his twenties with papules.
A man in his twenties pres
history:
Summary: An African man in his twenties with papules.
A man in his twenties presented with a 3-week history of fevers and papules on his face and body.

The patient was heterosexual and incarcerated in South Africa at the time of his presentation. He denied a history of exposure to animals, and had never traveled outside of the country.
exam_studies:
The patient looked ill. His temperature was 38.5°C (101.3°F). Papules were present diffusely, involving the face (Figure 1), limbs (Figure 2) and trunk.
Figure 1. Physical findings on the face.
Figure 2. Upper extremity physical findings.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 4,500 cells/mm³ (lymphocytes 600/mm³), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 507,000/mm³. The plasma levels of urea and electrolytes were normal; the level of alkaline phosphatase was 168 U/L, gamma glutamyl-transpeptidase (GGT) 236 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT, or glutamic pyruvate transaminase (SGPT)) 65 U/L.
A chest radiograph and ultrasonography of the abdomen were normal.
diagnosis:
Bacillary angiomatosis due to Bartonella infection in an African patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Screening and confirmation tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were positive. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 10 cells/mm³. Pathological examination of a skin biopsy showed vascular proliferation with a neutrophilic infiltrate. Warthin starry stain of the tissue revealed clumps of organisms consistent with Bartonella.

The patient improved after treatment with erythromycin (500 mg every six hours for two weeks). Follow-up examination is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Appearance after treatment.

This patient with HIV infection and AIDS had bacillary angiomatosis (BA). This disease is caused by Bartonella quintana and Bartonella henselae. BA occurs in immunocompromised patients, such as individuals with AIDS, and is characterized by proliferation of endothelial cells. BA generally involves the skin and lymph nodes, but may occasionally affect the liver or spleen (bacillary peliosis) or other internal organs. The cutaneous lesions of BA often have a vascular appearance and may bleed when incised. The appearance of the cutaneous lesions is similar to that of verruga peruana, but the latter is restricted to South America.

title:
Summary: An African woman in her twenties with a rash.
An African woman in her t
history:
Summary: An African woman in her twenties with a rash.
An African woman in her twenties reported a 3-month history of a rash.

The patient was heterosexual and lived in South Africa.
exam_studies:
The patient was well-appearing and afebrile. There were shotty cervical and inguinal lymph nodes. There was an annular plaque involving the muzzle area of the face, a plaque on one thigh and an ulcerating lesion on the other thigh (Figures 1 through 3). She also had pigmented lesions on the palms and soles (Figures 4 and 5). There were no mucosal lesions. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Facial findings.
Figure 2. Left thigh findings.
Figure 3. Thigh findings.
Figure 4. Findings on palm.
Figure 5. Findings on soles.

Results of routine laboratory testing and a chest radiograph were normal. Screening and confirmation testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive.
diagnosis:
Secondary syphilis in an African patient with HIV infection.

Resutls of a Wassermann reaction test for syphilis was positive with a titer greater than 1:32.

Intramuscular benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units weekly was administered for 3 weeks.

Secondary syphilis is important to consider when macular lesions on the palm and sole lesions are detected. In the setting of HIV infection many different syphilitic rashes may present simultaneously. Tinea typically presents as an annular rash with scale. The rash associated with acute HIV is typically a viral exanthem and does not have significant dermal infiltration. The skin lesions of leprosy and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are important to consider, however these processes are not usually associated with macular lesions on the palms and soles.

title:
Summary: An African woman with a rash.
A woman in her thirties complained of a r
history:
Summary: An African woman with a rash.
A woman in her thirties complained of a rash for one month. She reported no other symptoms; in particular, she denied fever, chills or sweats.

The patient lived in South Africa.
exam_studies:
The patient was well-appearing and afebrile. There was generalized lymphadenopathy. She had an eruption of papules involving the extensors of the arms and pinna of the ears, sparing the rest of the face (Figures 1 and 2). The lesions on the legs and shins were necrotic (Figure 3). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Lesions on pinna.
Figure 3. Necrotic leg lesions.

An antibody test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive. Routine laboratory tests were normal, as was a chest radiograph. A Mantoux skin test revealed induration that measured 15mm by 15mm, with blistering (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Mantoux test result.
diagnosis:
Papulonecrotic tuberculid in an African patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

Pathologic examination of a skin biopsy showed a crust with a granulomatous infiltrate that was perifollicular. There was also evidence of vasculitis. Special stains for fungi and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were negative.

Full anti-tuberculosis therapy was administered for 6 months.

Papulonecrotic tuberculid is a symmetric eruption of necrotizing papules, generally on the extensor surfaces of the extremities. The crops of papules may develop central necrosis, forming an ulcer. Most patients with papulonecrotic tuberculids have a positive Mantoux test. About one-third has a deep-sited focus of tuberculosis. In others, tuberculids may represent a hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacteria. A granulomatous vasculitis with thrombosis of blood vessels is a characteristic finding. The obliteration of the vasculature leads to a wedged-shaped area of necrosis of the dermis and epidermis.
This condition is more common in areas where tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is highly prevalent, such as South Africa. Generally, there is a prompt response of the rash to anti-tuberculous therapy.

title:
Summary: An African woman with skin ulcers.
A woman in her thirties presented wi
history:
Summary: An African woman with skin ulcers.
A woman in her thirties presented with ulcerative skin lesions of two months' duration.

The patient lived in a suburb of a South African city and had not recently traveled.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no apparent distress. Her temperature was 37.5°C (99.5°F), and she had generalized lymphadenopathy. The skin lesions included ulcers and plaques involving the face (Figure 1), trunk (Figure 2), palms and genitalia. The rest of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Facial lesions.
Figure 2. Skin lesions on back.

There was a normocytic normochromic anemia. An antibody test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive. The chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary nodules.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis due to Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

A Wassermann reaction test for syphilis was negative. Pathological examination of a skin biopsy showed numerous 2-4 micron organisms in the dermis that stained with PAS stain. Fungal cultures of the skin grew Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum.

The patient received itraconazole 400 mg daily for 1 month and thereafter was placed on maintenance therapy with itraconazole 200 mg daily. Her appearance after treatment is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Appearance after treatment.

Histoplasmosis is present in North and South America, Asia, Africa and Europe. There are two varieties, H. capsulatum var. capsulatum and H. capsulatum var. duboisii, both of which may cause disease in Africa. African histoplasmosis is characterized by skin, subcutaneous and bone disease. The cutaneous lesions of African histoplasmosis may include chronic ulcers and tender subcutaneous nodules.

title:
Summary: A young woman with buttock and leg complaints.
A young adult African-Am
history:
Summary: A young woman with buttock and leg complaints.
A young adult African-American female presented with buttock pain and left thigh swelling of 2-3 weeks duration.

Vertebral coccidioidomycosis had been diagnosed eight years earlier, and was treated with surgical debridement, amphotericin B and fluconazole suppression. Fluconazole suppression was stopped after six years.

She had lived most of her life in the United States Southwest.
exam_studies:
The patient was well appearing, afebrile, and in no distress. There was a mass (5 centimeter by 7 cm) in the left groin and swelling of the left thigh. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory testing including the white blood cell count was within normal limits.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis was performed (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Abdominal-pelvic CT scan.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Coccidioides immitis.

A CT-guided aspiration of the abscess was performed. Cytopathological examination of the aspirate showed fungal forms consistent with Coccidioides immitis. A spherule of Coccidioides immitis is seen in Figure 2. Cultures ultimately grew C. immitis.
Figure 2. Aspirate results.

Interventional radiology placed a drainage catheter in the iliopsoas muscle abscess. The patient was treated with liposomal amphotericin for one month, followed by itraconazole for approximately six months. She was followed closely with serial imaging studies and maintained on long-term fluconazole therapy.

The patient presented with a cold abscess many years after her initial presentation, having stopped chronic suppressive therapy. The disease at presentation was quite extensive, despite minimal symptoms. She continues to be followed closely on suppressive itraconazole therapy.
Coccidioides immitis generally enters the body via inhalation. Extrapulmonary dissemination is rare. The risk of dissemination is greater in immunosuppressed individuals, men, pregnant women or persons of African or Filipino ancestry. Sites of dissemination include the skin, lymph nodes, bones or joints and the meninges. Vertebral osteomyelitis due to Coccidioides immitis may involve multiple vertebral bodies, and may spread to parasinous structures, as in this case.
Treatment of Coccidioides vertebral osteomyelitis is difficult and there is a life-long risk of relapse. Following control of infection, chronic suppressive antifungal treatment may be necessary.
