title:
Summary: A middle-aged adult with altered mental status.
A middle-aged adult pre
history:
Summary: A middle-aged adult with altered mental status.
A middle-aged adult presented with altered mental status. According to family members, the patient appeared to have difficulty hearing for several days before presentation. Two days before admission, the patient seemed to have difficulty walking, fell down, and thereafter was not acting normally. Increasing lethargy developed, and the patient was taken to a hospital emergency room. Computed tomography (CT) of the head and a toxicology screen were negative.
Upon transfer to a tertiary care hospital, the patient was minimally responsive and had nuchal rigidity. A lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure of greater than 550 mm of water. After the lumbar puncture, the patient became more responsive. Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, ampicillin and acyclovir were administered in the emergency room.

The patient had emigrated from sub-Saharan Africa several years earlier.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), pulse 72 beats per minute, and the blood pressure 141/81 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation was 100% while breathing ambient air. Nuchal rigidity and thrush were present; there were no conjunctival lesions or adenopathy. The pulmonary, cardiac and abdominal examinations were normal. An ulcerated lesion was noted on the genitalia; the remainder of the skin was normal.
The patient was resting comfortably, able to track visual stimuli, but unable to hear. Questions were answered if they were written, but not if they were spoken. Responses were in full sentences, and the question, “How do you stop this noise?” was asked. The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 9,000/mm³ with 93% leukocytes, 5% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes, hematocrit 32%, platelet count 347,000/mm³, and sodium 123 mmol/L. Chest radiography and head CT scanning, without the administration of contrast, were normal.
The level of glucose in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was 36 mg/dL, protein 34 mg/dL, with 17 white blood cells/mm³ (predominantly lymphocytes with a few mononuclear cells) and 64 red blood cells/mm³. An organism, shown in Figure 1, was seen.
Figure 1. Cerebrospinal fluid.
diagnosis:
Meningitis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Gram stain and fungal stain of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed abundant round budding yeast. An India ink was also positive. The CSF cryptococcal antigen was 1:8192; CSF cultures grew Cryptococcus neoformans.

Amphotericin B and flucytosine were administered. The patient had a waxing and waning course, requiring repeated lumbar punctures to reduce the opening pressure; a lumbar drain was placed. Despite therapy for the cryptococcal infection, permanent neurologic deficits of blindness and deafness developed. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was positive; the CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 19 cells/mm³ and the level of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) RNA was 18,300 copies/mL.

This patient presented with a subacute meningoencephalitis. The presence of thrush suggested severe immunocompromise.
Having lived in sub-Saharan Africa, the patient was at increased risk for HIV and tuberculosis. Arguing against an acute bacterial meningitis (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Hemophilus influenza) was the rather subacute course, the low number of white blood cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the lymphocytic predominance.
The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis was quickly made based upon results of the lumbar puncture. The very elevated opening pressure and a clinical improvement after lumbar puncture is common in cryptococcal meningitis. There was a significant burden of infection with a low number of white blood cells in the CSF, characteristic of AIDS patients with cryptococcal meningitis, in contrast to immunocompetent patients who develop cryptococcal disease.

history:
Summary: A man with fever and chills.
A man in his seventies presented with a one-week history of fevers and chills. He denied any other systemic complaints. There was no history of nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, or rash.

He had undergone a prostatectomy for localized prostate cancer.

He was sexually active with a single female partner. He denied any recent travel or any history of international travel, animal bites, or tick bites. He resided in a suburban community of northeastern Massachusetts in a home with a large garden. He also enjoyed golf.
exam_studies:
He was well appearing, with a temperature 102°F (38.9°C). The rest of the examination was normal, with no rash, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.

The hematocrit was 35%, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 70 IU/L, and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 55 IU/L. Other routine laboratory testing was normal. Urinalysis was negative. A chest radiograph was normal.

While in the hospital, the patient continued to have intermittent fevers. Cultures of the blood and urine were negative. A blood smear is shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear findings.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Babesia microti infection.

The blood smear revealed intraerythrocytic parasites consistent with Babesia microti.

The patient was treated with azithromycin and atovaquone for 10 days with an excellent clinical response. Serologic testing for Ehrlichia and Lyme disease was negative.

Given his geographic history, Babesia infection is much more likely than malaria or typhoid. The identification of the intra-erythrocytic maltese cross form is pathognomonic of Babesia infection. The development of fever without localizing symptoms in an endemic area for Babesia requires a careful examination for this organism. The absence of an identified tick bite is common.

title:
Summary: A man with headaches and mental status changes.
A male in his thirties
history:
Summary: A man with headaches and mental status changes.
A male in his thirties presented with severe headaches and decreased mental status over two weeks.

He had a history of hepatitis C virus infection, which had previously failed to respond to a six-month course of interferon therapy.

He was raised in the Caribbean, had moved to the United States 10 years before presentation and lived in the Northeast. His last trip overseas was two years previously. He denied other international travel and had no pets.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile. There was temporal wasting and findings consistent with oral thrush was noted in the posterior pharynx. Examination of the heart and lung was normal. There were no skin abnormalities, and no evidence of septic embolic phenomena. His mental status was greatly reduced, and he was unable to answer questions. There was a left facial droop and mild left hand weakness. Gait could not be assessed.

The white blood cell count was 8,000 cells/mm³ (4.6% lymphocytes, 1.1% monocytes, and 94% neutrophils). Computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed multiple ring enhancing lesions. Blood cultures were unrevealing.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple ring enhancing lesions (Figures 1 and 2) and entrapment of the right temporal horn.
A lumbar puncture was performed; analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed total protein 162 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, and 5 white blood cells/mm³.
Figure 1. MRI scan of the head.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the head.
diagnosis:
Cerebral toxoplasmosis in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS, and a history of hepatitis C virus infection.

Serological testing for human immunodeficiency virus antibody was positive, with HIV-RNA level of greater than 500,000 copies/ml and CD4 T-lymphocyte count level of 16 cells/mm³. Testing for serum Toxoplasma IgG was positive.

The patient was treated empirically with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine for presumed toxoplasmosis. Later cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies confirmed Toxoplasma with a positive polymerase chain reaction test (PCR). The patient was treated for this and clinically improved, before the initiation of antiretroviral therapy.

The patient presented with neurologic complaints and lesions on CT scan, but without a previous diagnosis of HIV infection. Although the MRI scan confirmed the presence of lesions, it was not specific enough to determine the etiology of disease. Based on his clinical presentation, he was thought to have a moderate likelihood of being HIV-positive (e.g., hepatitis C infection and the presence of oral thrush) and was treated empirically for toxoplasmosis while further studies were pending. Ultimately studies confirmed this diagnosis.

Summary: A man with right forearm and hand ulcerating lesions.
Three months earl
history:
Summary: A man with right forearm and hand ulcerating lesions.
Three months earlier, a male in his thirties from the southern highlands of Peru had developed a firm nodule on his right hand that ulcerated. He recalled having an insect bite at the location of the lesion. Two weeks before, he developed a second lesion on his right forearm. He denied any fever, chills or sweats.
He had no response to topical or systemic antibiotics, and had used a salve of crushed plants with no improvement.

He smoked one-half pack cigarettes per day, occasionally drank alcohol, worked in construction and occasionally harvested crops. He owned a dog, cats and chickens.

He was married and had children.

He had no known allergies.
exam_studies:
His temperature was 37.2°C (99°F), pulse 68 beats per minute, respirations 14 per minute, blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg. He was a well-appearing, robust male. His examination was normal except for the skin of his right extremity. (See Figure 1.)
Figure 1. Right arm and hand lesions.

Complete blood count (CBC) and electrolytes were within normal limits. A Gram stain of the exudate was non-diagnostic. The exudative fluid was sent for bacterial culture, fungal culture and Giemsa staining.
diagnosis:
Giemsa staining was negative for evidence of Leishmania and acid-fast and modified acid-fast stains were also negative. Bacterial and mycobacterium cultures were negative. Fungal culture grew filamentous colonies with a dark brown appearance. Microscopy of the colonies demonstrated hyphal forms consistent with Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporotrichosis classically presents with an erythematous nodule that or ulcer, followed by development of multiple subcutaneous nodules that spread along the course of regional lymphatics. This pattern of nodular lymphangitis may also be seen with non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections (particularly Mycobacterium marinum), nocardiosis and cutaneous leishmaniasis. Rarely, botryomycosis, staphylococcal lymphangitis and tularemia present as a nodular lymphangitis. A skin biopsy and culture is critical in distinguishing among these different etiologies of nodular lymphangitis.

Cutaneous sporotrichosis, with cultures consistent with Sporothrix schenckii.

A middle-aged woman noted a
history:
Summary: A middle-aged woman with a fever and rash.
A middle-aged woman noted a “bite” on her left thigh seven days before her presentation. The lesion enlarged over the next several days. Four days before her admission, she had the acute onset of fatigue, arthralgias, myalgias, a severe headache and a fever to 103.4°F (39.7°C). On the day of her presentation, she developed a rash on her extremities, trunk and back.

She lived in a city in the Northeast, and had been in Georgia six months before. She owned a dog, and had noted one mouse in her basement.
exam_studies:
Her temperature was 100.5°F (38.1°C), pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, respirations 16 breaths per minute. She was in no apparent distress, and there was no lymphadenopathy. There was a blanching papular erythematous rash on her extremities, back, and chest (Figures 1 and 2). A lesion was present on her left thigh (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 1. Rash on back.
Figure 2. Rash on leg.
Figure 3. Lesion on leg.
Figure 4. Detail of leg lesion.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 3,200 cells/mm³, hematocrit 34.6% and platelet count 180,000/mm³. The level of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 64 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 57 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 95 U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 454 U/L; the bilirubin level and chest radiograph were normal. Blood cultures were sterile.
diagnosis:
Rickettsialpox.

Serologic testing at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) showed a titer of 1:256 against Rickettsia rickettsii and other members of the spotted fever group of rickettsiae, including Rickettsia akari.

The patient was treated with doxycycline, with rapid improvement in her fever and rash.

Rickettsialpox is caused by Rickettsia akari, a member of the spotted fever group of rickettsiae. The organism is transmitted to humans by a mouse mite. After the bite of an infected mite, Rickettsia akari proliferates locally resulting in a papule, which ulcerates to form an eschar. Three to seven days later, patients develop high fever, chills and headache. Two to three days after the onset of fever, many patients develop a generalized papulovesicular rash.
Diagnosis of rickettsialpox is generally by serologic testing. At the time of this publication, treatment usually includes a tetracycline for 3-5 days, and clinical response is typically rapid.
One of the main possibilities in the differential diagnosis in a patient with suspected rickettsialpox is chickenpox, which, of course, is much more common. The following features may help distinguish rickettsialpox from chickenpox: in rickettsialpox, an eschar is typically present, whereas this does not occur in patients with chickenpox; the lesions of chickenpox often occur in crops, whereas this does not generally happen with rickettsialpox; patients with rickettsialpox usually have relatively few skin lesions (20-40), whereas individuals with chickenpox may have many more and, lastly, the skin lesion in rickettsialpox is usually a papulovesicle, whereas vesicles characterize the rash of chickenpox.

history:
Summary: A middle-aged women with abdominal pain.
A woman in her forties had a history of endometriosis, for which she had undergone multiple surgical procedures. Her most recent procedure, prompted by abdominal pain, included removal of the right ovary and fallopian tube, ligation of the left tube, and extensive fulguration of areas of endometriosis requiring conversion from laparoscopic to an open procedure via a Pfannenstiel incision.
Five weeks post-operatively, she developed yellow-green drainage around the periumbilical surgical wound. Culture of the drainage grew Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, and enterococci. Oral levofloxacin was administered.
She then developed a painful red nodule in the right periumbilical laparotomy site and a series of similar nodules along the right side of the Pfannenstiel incision. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen did not show a fistula. Resection of nodules in operating room yielded tissue with “foreign body giant cell” reaction. There was no evidence of endometrioma.
Two weeks later, nodules and green drainage from the wounds recurred.

Figure 2. Acid fast stain.
Figure 3. Detail of Figure 2.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium fortuitum wound infection.

Pathological examination of the tissue showed necrotizing granulomas (Figure 1). Staining was positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) (Figures 2 and 3). Cultures grew Mycobacterium fortuitum.
An extensive epidemiologic evaluation revealed no other recent cases of mycobacterial infection in the institution and no contamination of any surgical instruments or other wound care materials.

Based on the susceptibility patterns of the isolate, a course of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and levofloxacin was administered. After four months of therapy, she developed migratory joint pains that were thought to be possibly related to antibiotic intolerance. The sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and levofloxacin were discontinued, and clarithromycin monotherapy was administered to complete a 6-month total treatment course. She remained asymptomatic twelve months after finishing this therapy.

Wound infections that develop within a few days of an operation are most commonly due to streptococci, clostridia and Staphylococcus aureus. Infections that present several weeks after the operation, as in this case, may be due to more indolent organisms, such as non-tuberculous mycobacteria. This case illustrates the importance of surgical debridement and appropriate cultures in the setting of delayed wound infections.

history:
Summary: A woman in her fifties with a fever and skin lesions.
A woman in her fifties noted a fever and generalized myalgias for ten days. A high fever, chills, and non-pruritic skin rash developed five days before her visit to her doctor.

She lived in a city in Korea and had visited a farm two weeks before her illness. She did not recall any insect bites.
exam_studies:
Her blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, pulse 90 per minute, respiratory rate 20 per minute, and temperature 38.5°C (101.3°F). She had a faint, maculopapular rash on her trunk and extremities, and a dark scab in the pubic area (Figure 1). There was tender lymphadenopathy in the left inguinal region.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The hemoglobin was 12.1 g/dL, the white blood cell count (WBC) 11,000/mm³ (neutrophils 62%, lymphocytes 25%, monocytes 12%, eosinophils 1%), and the platelet count 115,000/mm³. The serum level of aspartate aminotransferase (AST or SGOT) was 455 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT or SGPT) 718 IU/L, urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. The urinalysis had 4-9 red blood cells and 4-9 white blood cells per high-power field. The chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal.
diagnosis:
Scrub typhus caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi.

An immunofluorescence test for Orientia tsutsugamushi (the etiologic agent of scrub typhus) was positive at a 1:1280 dilution.

She was treated with doxycycline (200 mg daily) for 7 days. Her fever resolved three days after the initiation of therapy.

Scrub typhus is caused by a rickettsial organism, Orientia tsutsugamushi. This disease occurs in eastern Asia and the Western Pacific, including Korea, Japan, Australia and the Indian subcontinent. The organism is transmitted to humans by the bite of the larval stage (chigger) of the tromiculid mite.
Following inoculation, a papule forms at the site of the bite. This papule subsequently ulcerates and forms an eschar. There is frequently regional adenopathy, as was seen in this individual. Approximately 6-18 days after the bite, the patient develops fever, headache and myalgias. Five day after the onset of these symptoms, a maculopapular rash and generalized lymphadenopathy may occur.
Diagnosis of scrub typhus is generally made by serologic testing, as in this case. Treatment with doxycycline may shorten the duration of symptoms.
The main clue that this patient had the rickettsial illness scrub typhus was the presence of the eschar. Although typhoid fever, dengue and brucellosis present with systemic symptoms, they are not associated with an eschar. Tularemia may cause lymphadenopathy and an ulcer at the site of inoculation. However, the ulcer of tularemia is typically tender with raised borders, and the lymphadenopathy is often suppurative.

title: Summary: A woman in her fifties with acute myeloid leukemia and a new skin lesio
history:
Summary: A woman in her fifties with acute myeloid leukemia and a new skin lesion.
A woman in her fifties had been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) three months before presentation. She had been treated with daunorubacin, etoposide, and araC, and initially achieved a remission. One month before, she developed recurrent disease manifested as thrombocytopenia and recurrent left cervical adenopathy. She was treated with high dose araC.
Two weeks later, she was admitted with fever and neutropenia. She was treated empirically with vancomycin and ceftazidime. Approximately one week into her hospitalization, she developed a lesion on her left breast. She recalled itching in that area at the tape around her Hickman catheter three weeks earlier, which she had scratched. The area had then become red and developed a central black eschar.
She also noted several lesions on her back, which had been present since admission at a site where she had received a moxibustion, a traditional Chinese therapy in which mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) is placed over acupuncture sites and burned.

She also had a history of hepatitis C virus infection.

She worked in the healthcare industry. She had a distant history of intravenous drug use and smoking. She smoked marijuana occasionally and had used it for nausea after chemotherapy. She denied gardening, and had traveled years ago to Mexico and the Southwest United States.

As above, she had received vancomycin and ceftazidime.
exam_studies:
She was in no acute distress. The temperature was 101.3°F (38.5°C), pulse 86/minute, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. There was poor dentition and left cervical adenopathy. The cardiac, pulmonary, and neurologic examinations were normal. There was mild right upper quadrant pain, and the rest of the abdominal examination was normal. The skin had a necrotic left breast lesion surrounded by erythema (Figure 1), and three similar lesions on her back in a linear array (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 280 cells/mm³, hematocrit 28%, and platelets 10,000/mm³, and results of serum chemistries were normal. The aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 113 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 112 U/L, with normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin. The level of hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA by PCR was >850,000 copies/mL. Blood cultures and urine cultures were sterile.
diagnosis:
Invasive Aspergillus infection in a patient with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Pathological examination of a skin biopsy with fungal staining showed widespread dermal hemorrhage associated with septate hyphae showing dichotomous branching and an arboreal growth pattern consistent with Aspergillus species. Vascular involvement was noted. Subsequently, fungal culture grew Aspergillus.

She was treated with amphotericin and voriconazole.
Shortly after her skin biopsy, she developed pleuritic chest pain. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a nodule in her left upper lobe and a small area of focal consolidation in the right base with surrounding ground-glass opacity that were consistent with fungal infection. CT scan of the head was unrevealing.
Her fungal disease remained relatively stable on antifungal therapy despite her prolonged neutropenia. She did not achieve a remission and ultimately underwent an allogenic bone marrow transplantation (allo-BMT). She still failed to achieve a hematologic remission and was discharged with hospice services.

The profound neutropenia in this patient put her at risk for invasive fungal infection and impaired the success of potential anti-fungal therapy. In this case, the necrotic nature of the lesion is quite suggestive of an angio-invasive fungus. Most commonly this would be caused by Aspergillus, but Fusarium, Pseudoallescheria boydii or Scedosporium prolificans could cause similar appearing lesions.
The pulmonary nodules suggest that she had disseminated disease, as opposed to inoculation confined to her skin. The lesions on her back had a similar appearance, but were apparently caused by burns and never evolved over time to suggest an infectious etiology.

title:
Summary: A woman returned from Costa Rica with skin lesions.
Ten days before her
history:
Summary: A woman returned from Costa Rica with skin lesions.
Ten days before her presentation, a woman returned from a two-week vacation in Costa Rica. While there, she had traveled in a rainforest and jungle and had sustained multiple mosquito bites. After her return to the United States, two bites on her right leg and one on her left anterior chest had become enlarged and painful. She was seen by her primary care physician, who had prescribed doxycycline.

She was previously in good health.

See HPI.

She had no known allergies.

Doxycycline.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. She was afebrile. A furuncular lesion on her left infraclavicular chest was draining serous fluid from a central opening. There was surrounding erythema, edema and a few small bullae. One enlarged, painful node was palpated in her left axilla. On the right anterior calf, there were two additional draining furuncular lesions with central openings, with minimal surrounding erythema. All three lesions had central pores and observation through the openings disclosed movement within the lesions.

The patient was given one dose of oral cephalexin and levofloxacin prior to manipulation of the lesions. The three lesions were covered with occlusive lubricant and suction was applied with a snakebite kit suction syringe, with no result.
The patient was sent home with dicloxacillin and told to apply petroleum jelly to the lesions and cover with plastic wrap overnight. She returned the next morning. (See Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Physical finding on thigh.
Figure 2. Physical finding on chest.
diagnosis:
New World cutaneous myiasis (Botfly; Dermatobia hominis).

A small white larva was visible protruding from her chest lesion. Suction was again applied to all three lesions, and motile white larvae, 1 cm long and 1/4 cm wide at largest, were extracted from all. (See Figures 2, 3, and 4.)
Figure 3. Botfly larvae after suctioning.
Figure 4. Botfly larvae.

In Central and South America, myiasis is caused by the botfly, Dermatobia hominis. The female fly lays her eggs on the underside of a female mosquito; with a blood meal, a newly hatched larva penetrates the skin of the human or animal host, where it feeds and matures for 4-10 weeks before exiting to pupate in soil.
The larvae pictured in this case are in the second stage of larval development. The cutaneous lesions are notable for the presence of a central breathing pore, and sometimes movement within the lesions can be felt by the host. Treatment is by extraction, best accomplished after the larva has been coaxed to the surface of the lesion by occlusion of the breathing pore. Asphyxiation of the larvae often facilitates extraction; sometimes surgical excision is required. Larvae should be extracted whole. Bacterial supra-infection is common. Antibiotics are often used to prevent or treat super-infection, as in this case.

history:
Summary: A young adult man with a tonic-clonic seizure.
A young adult man was brought to an emergency room after his first tonic-clonic seizure.

The patient had lived in Haiti until early adolescence and had returned most recently two years before his presentation for an eight-day visit. He ate meat, but had no known ingestion of pork while in Haiti. He lived with relatives in the Northeast United States, and no other members were known to have seizures or diarrheal illnesses. He had no known risk factors for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

He had no known allergies.
exam_studies:
He appeared well, with a muscular physique, and was in no apparent distress. The physical examination, including ophthalmic and neurological exams, was normal.

The complete blood cell count (CBC) revealed mild neutrophilia and no eosinophils. A lumbar puncture revealed a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Testing for HIV and tuberculosis (PPD) was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was performed (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Head MRI scan, FLAIR image.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan, FSE image.

The patient was briefly post-ictal but returned to his baseline within hours.
diagnosis:
Neurocysticercosis, caused by the tapeworm Taenia solium.

The MRI scan of the head demonstrated a cystic lesion in the right frontal lobe with an apparent scolex. (Figures 1 and 2). No retinal pathology was noted. CSF cysticercosis antibody (immunoblot assay) and serum cysticercosis antibody (immunoblot assay) were positive.

Dexamethasone, prednisone and albendazole were administered, without complications. A follow-up MRI scan of the brain was performed the following month, which showed decreased size of frontal cyst with decreased surrounding edema (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. MRI at six-week follow-up, FLAIR image.
Figure 4. MRI at six-week follow-up, T1 image.

Given the radiological identification of a scolex within a cyst, history of residence in an endemic area and presentation with a new onset seizure, the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis can be made. Treatment with antihelminthics and steroids should be considered before confirmatory serologic tests yield results.
In treating this disease, special considerations should include:
1. An ophthalmic exam to make sure no retinal lesions exist, which may cause destructive reaction during antihelminthic treatment and
2. Consideration of co-infection with Strongyloides and treatment with ivermectin prior to initiation of corticosteroids.

Summary: A young adult woman with fever, joint pain and a vaginal discharge.

history:
Summary: A young adult woman with fever, joint pain and a vaginal discharge.
A young adult woman presented to her primary care clinic with fever, chills, pain in multiple joints and a purulent vaginal discharge. One week earlier, she had noted a yellow-greenish vaginal discharge. The day before presentation, she developed right elbow pain. Over the next several hours, she also developed pain in her right wrist and right fingers.
On the morning of presentation, she awakened with increased pain in the involved joints, and new pain in her right knee and bilateral shoulders. She also began to feel feverish and chilled, and noticed a rash on her left fourth finger and left shin. Her most recent menstrual period had been three weeks before this presentation. She was referred to the emergency department.

She had a previous history of Chlamydia and gonorrhea, and had had varicella virus (chickenpox) during childhood.

She had lived in a city in the United States Northeast her entire life and worked in an office. She had one current sexual partner and multiple previous partners.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared moderately uncomfortable. Her temperature was 99.8°F (37.7°C), pulse 96 beats per minute and blood pressure 136/84 mm Hg. She had severe pain on passive motion of her shoulders, right elbow, right wrist and right knee. There was a pustule (3 mm by 3 mm) on her left 4th finger (Figure 1) and three vesiculopustules (1 mm by 1 mm) with erythematous bases on her left shin. A vaginal examination using a speculum revealed purulent discharge from the cervical os and the cervix appeared inflamed. The neurological exam was normal.
Figure 1. Left hand with fourth finger pustule.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 10,700/mm³ (neutrophils 70%, lymphocytes 15%, monocytes 5%, eosinophils 1%).
diagnosis:
Disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection (gonorrhea) associated with acute cervical discharge, right elbow arthritis, and skin pustules with concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis.

A cervical swab was taken for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcus) and Chlamydia trachomatis amplification. Both results were positive. A throat swab and fluid from a pustule were obtained following the initiation of antibiotics, both of which returned negative. Two sets of blood cultures drawn prior to the initiation of antibiotics showed no growth.
Attempts were made to aspirate the right elbow, which was the most severely affected joint, but no fluid was recovered.

The patient received ceftriaxone one gram intravenously daily for 7 days and a single dose of azithromycin one gram orally to treat disseminated gonococcus and Chlamydia, respectively. She was sent home on the fifth hospital day after her joint pain had subsided significantly. She also underwent screening for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and syphilis (RPR), both of which were negative.

This patient had the typical features of disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), including the triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgias without purulent arthritis. Another presentation of DGI is purulent arthritis in the absence of skin lesions. It should be noted that these two syndromes often overlap.
This patient had a history of prior sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), highlighting the importance of counseling patients about safe sex and of testing for HIV and syphilis in any patient who presents with an STD. Patients with gonococcal infection should also be treated concurrently for Chlamydia.
It is difficult to culture Neisseria gonorrhoeae from joint fluid (<50%), blood (<1/3) and pustular skin lesions. When gonococcal septic arthritis is suspected, culture material should be collected on chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin medium. Additional cultures of the cervix, urethra, rectum and throat may lead to a higher rate of recovery of the organism.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with fatigue and fever.
An elderly man with stage IV non
history:
Summary: An elderly man with fatigue and fever.
An elderly man with stage IV non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) had recently received chemotherapy. He complained of fatigue for two days and a fever to 102°F (38.9°C) and chills on the day of admission. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest 2 weeks earlier had revealed pulmonary nodules for which he was started on voriconazole while awaiting tissue diagnosis. He reported having had temporary peripheral intravenous lines for chemotherapy, but denied having had any central lines.

He had stage IV large cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) and diabetes mellitus.

Medications included chemotherapy (most recent course 2 weeks earlier) with cyclophosphamide, etoposide, vincristine, prednisone and rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody). He was also taking voriconazole.
exam_studies:
He appeared chronically ill with a temperature of 102.5°F (39.2°C), pulse 130/minute, and blood pressure 78/52 mm/Hg. Examination of the lungs revealed decreased breath sounds at the right base. The rest of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 5,300 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 63%, bands 22%, lymphocytes 0%, monocytes 15%).
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed two nodules in the right lower lobe: 1.7 centimeters (cm) by 1.9cm and 1.4cm by 2 cm. There was also a small right-sided pleural effusion (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.

A CT-guided fine needle aspirate was done on a pulmonary nodule, but an insufficient amount of tissue was obtained. A gram stain of the positive blood culture revealed the findings seen in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Gram stain of blood culture.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary nocardiosis (Nocardia asteroides) with bacteremia.

The gram stain of the positive blood culture revealed branching gram-positive rods (Figure 2). A modified acid-fast stain performed on the blood culture also showed branching rods (Figure 3) that were identified as Nocardia asteroides.
Figure 3. Modified acid-fast stain.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) was started, and the patient became afebrile within 24 hours. He was sent home on oral TMP-SMX, and did well clinically.

This case illustrates the importance of obtaining a definitive diagnosis in an immunocompromised host with pulmonary nodules, since the differential diagnosis is very broad. For example, it is not possible to differentiate fungal disease from nocardiosis on the basis of imaging. An accurate diagnosis is essential in providing appropriate therapy.
A broad range of immunocompromised patients is at increased risk of infection with Nocardia. Risk factors include hematological malignancies, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, steroids and chemotherapy.
Nocardia bacteremia is unusual. In a recent study from the Massachusetts General Hospital, positive blood cultures accounted for 8.1% of the total Nocardia isolates seen between 1990-1997. Pulmonary involvement occurs in about 2/3 of patients with Nocardia bacteremia. The incubation times for the positive blood cultures ranged from 2-14 days, with a median time to growth of 4 days. Of note, 30% of patients with Nocardia bacteremia had concomitant bacteremia with other organisms, usually gram negative bacilli. This was probably due to the fact that many of the patients were predisposed to such infections by virtue of their immunocompromised state. Finally, patients with bacteremic nocardiosis appear to have similar presentation, risk factors, clinical course and therapeutic outcome as non-bacteremic patients with nocardiosis.

history:
Summary: A female teenager with fatigue, headache and fever.
A teen-aged girl from the Ivory Coast presented fatigue and intermittent headache, with progressive symptoms, of three weeks' duration and high fever for one day.

A tuberculosis skin test (PPD) had been positive in the past.

The patient had been born in Western Europe and had moved to Ivory Coast at age 1 year. Four years before this presentation, she moved to the United States. She had returned to the Ivory Coast several times, most recently four weeks earlier for a 2-week trip. The patient reported multiple mosquito bites while there.

She had taken chloroquine for one week 3 weeks earlier.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no apparent distress. The temperature was 105.8°F (41°C), pulse 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 90/53 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% on ambient air. There was no scleral icterus or hepatosplenomegaly. The rest of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 5,800 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 55%, bands 1%, lymphocytes 34%, monocytes 10%), hematocrit 39%, and platelet count 189,000/mm³, and tests of liver function were normal. Images of peripheral blood smears are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear.
Figure 2. Peripheral blood smear.

Thin and thick smears of the peripheral blood were positive for intraerythrocytic forms consistent with Plasmodium falciparum, with 0.5% parasitemia (Figures 3 and 4).
diagnosis:
Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

The patient was treated with quinine sulfate and doxycycline. She defervesced soon after starting anti-malarial medications, and was discharged from the hospital on the second hospital day. Figure 3. Figure 2, with arrow. Figure 4. Peripheral blood smear, higher magnification.
Figure 3. Figure 2, with arrow.
Figure 4. Peripheral blood smear, higher magnification.

Malaria should be considered in anyone presenting with fever who has recently traveled to an endemic region. In this patient, the presence of multiply infected erythrocytes and appliqué forms were suggested of P. falciparum as the causative organism.
The choice of malaria prophylaxis should reflect the organism resistance of the destination region; for instance, in this case mefloquine should have been utilized because chloroquine is not appropriate for a patient who has been in an area with chloroquine-resistant malaria. Treatment options should be determined by consulting current recommendations at the time of diagnosis, using reputable sources such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or World Health Organization (WHO), and taking into consideration the region of the likely exposure and the medications available.

title: Summary: A man in his twenties with leukemia and ulcers on the lip and hard pala
history:
Summary: A man in his twenties with leukemia and ulcers on the lip and hard palate.
A man in his twenties with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) presented with a painful ulcer on his hard palate and a painless ulcer above his right upper lip. He had received induction chemotherapy for AML three months earlier, but had not achieved clinical remission. He therefore underwent re-induction chemotherapy several weeks after the initial cycle, and subsequently had marrow aplasia. The patient had been neutropenic for three months at the time the oral lesions developed. He was on broad-spectrum antibacterial and anti-fungal therapies. Because of the oral lesions, he received intravenous acyclovir, but the ulcers did not resolve.

He had acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), M4 sub-type.

The medications are noted above.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no acute distress. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C). There was a macular lesion above right upper lip and an ulcerated lesion with a white base on his hard palate (Figure 1). The gums were markedly hypertrophied, which was thought to be due to tissue infiltration from his underlying M4-AML. The examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings on hard palate.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 90 cells/mm³ with 85% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes and 12% atypical cells.
diagnosis:
Herpes simplex virus Type 1 (HSV-1) lesion of the lip and hard palate in a neutropenic patient with M4-AML.

Cultures of the lip and hard palate were positive for herpes simplex virus, type 1 (HSV-1).

Because the oral lesions persisted while the patient received acyclovir, there was concern that the virus may be resistant to this medicine. Acyclovir was stopped and intravenous foscarnet begun, and the lesions slowly improved. The patient subsequently underwent a non-myeloablative matched related donor allogeneic stem cell transplant for his failure of marrow recovery following chemotherapy.

Acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex virus (HSV) should be considered in patients whose HSV lesions do not improve with therapy, especially if cultures remain positive despite treatment doses of acyclovir or related antivirals. Candidiasis generally causes whitish plaques in the oropharynx, although erythematous lesions and angular cheilitis may also occur. Histoplasmosis can cause deep and painless oral ulcers, usually as part of the syndrome of chronic progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. Both cytomegalovirus (CMV) and aspergillosis can cause oral ulcers in patients with prolonged neutropenia; a biopsy is often necessary to exclude these diagnoses.

history:
Summary: A man with chest pain and dysphagia.
A man in his fifties presented to the emergency room with a history of chest pain and dysphagia.

The patient was from El Salvador, and had recently arrived in the United States. He had a history of smoking 20 cigarettes per day.
exam_studies:
Results of a complete blood count (CBC), blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and liver function tests were normal, and a test for syphilis (RPR) was non-reactive.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Chest CT scan.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.

A barium swallow is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Barium swallow.
diagnosis:
Chagas mega-esophagus, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi.

The chest CT scans and barium swallow revealed mega-esophagus. Serologic testing for Chagas disease was positive.

Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, is present only in the Western hemisphere. Most cases occur in Central and South America. Chronic Chagas Disease may cause cardiomyopathy or gastrointestinal tract dysfunction (megadisease). In South America, both cardiomyopathy and megadisease are seen, whereas in Central America megadisease seems to be less common; the reason for this difference in presentation is not clear.
The most common clinical manifestation of chagasic gastrointestinal disease is mega-esophagus, which typically presents with dysphagia. Other common sites of chagasic gastrointestinal disease are the colon, the parotid glands, and the stomach.

Summary: A man with facial pain and diplopia.
A man in his fifties with a histor
history:
Summary: A man with facial pain and diplopia.
A man in his fifties with a history of non-Hodgkins lymphoma presented with facial pain and diplopia of three days' duration.

He had non-Hodgkins lymphoma, for which chemotherapy was administered two weeks before presentation.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.5°F (37.5°C). There was left sided proptosis (Figure 1) with pain and diplopia on upward gaze.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The level of white blood cells (WBC) was 2,100 cells/mm³ and neutrophils 800 cells/mm³. Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and liver function tests were normal.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head and the sinuses was performed. (See Figure 2.)
Figure 2. Head CT scan.
diagnosis:
Aspergillus fumigatus sinusitis in a patient with non-Hodgkins lymphoma.

The CT scan shows complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus. There was erosion of the inferior orbital plate with the mass extending into the orbit below the inferior rectus muscle (arrow). (See Figure 3.)
A surgical debridement procedure was performed. Histologic examination of the resected specimen is shown. (See Figure 4.) Histopathology showed fungal elements, which were identified as Aspergillus fumigatus, with extension into bone.
Figure 3. Head CT scan.
Figure 4. Silver stain of debridement specimen.

Following extensive surgical debridement, the patients was treated with systemic amphotericin B.

Aspergillus may cause severe sinusitis, particularly in patients with neutropenia. Anaerobic infections generally develop in patients who have a history of chronic sinusitis. Given the broad differential diagnosis of the causes of sinusitis in a neutropenic host, debridement, histologic examination and appropriate microbiologic culture are key to management.

title:
Summary: A man with headaches and hallucinations.
A man in his fifties presented
history:
Summary: A man with headaches and hallucinations.
A man in his fifties presented with a five-day history of headaches, diffuse myalgias, chills, and anorexia. He had discontinued alcohol intake three days prior to admission. On the evening of admission, he became disoriented with visual hallucinations.
In the emergency room, he was hypertensive and tachycardic. The patient was treated with a benzodiazepine and intubated for airway protection. Computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast showed no acute abnormality. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
A lumbar puncture demonstrated 267 white blood cells per cubic millimeter (82% lymphocytes), 56 red blood cells per cubic millimeter, protein 333 mg/dL, and glucose 83 mg/dL. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results revealed negative gram stain, bacterial, fungal and viral cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and testing for syphilis (VDRL). He was treated with intravenous vancomycin (2 g/d), ceftriaxone (4g/d), and acyclovir (30 mg/kg/d). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with gadolinium was normal. An electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrated diffuse slowing without epileptiform discharge or localization.

There was a history of alcohol abuse, and two episodes of aseptic meningitis that had occurred a decade earlier.
exam_studies:
He was lethargic. His blood pressure was 160/90 mm Hg, heart rate 100 beats/minute, and temperature 100.6°F (38.1°C). There was minimal nuchal rigidity. There was no rash, and no oral or genital ulcers were seen. The remainder of his examination was normal.

Two days later, a repeat lumbar puncture revealed 313 white blood cells (WBCs) per cubic millimeter, with 95% lymphocytes, protein 305 mg/dL, and glucose 75 mg/dL. The gram stain was negative. All cultures for microorganisms were negative.

Eleven days after the first lumbar puncture, a third lumbar puncture was performed and showed 538 white blood cells per cubic millimeter, with 91% lymphocytes, total protein 111 mg/dL, and glucose 83 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures remained negative. Cytology of the cerebrospinal fluid showed large, atypical cells with abundant pale blue cytoplasm and large, footprint nuclei (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Laboratory finding.
diagnosis:
Herpes Simplex Virus Type-2 meningitis with Mollaret's cells.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) was detected in the cerebrospinal fluid by PCR amplification (See Figure 2.) Type-specific ELISA of serum showed no evidence of prior HSV-1 infection but was strongly positive for HSV-2 IgG.
Figure 2. Laboratory finding.

The patient received 3 weeks of acyclovir (30 mg/kg/d). He improved clinically, but his headache persisted and fevers occurred intermittently. He discontinued alcohol use, according to family, but continued to have headaches. A subsequent lumbar puncture showed 30 WBCs per cubic millimeter (98% lymphocytes), 0 RBCs, total protein 58 mg/dL, and glucose 70 mg/dL. The repeat HSV PCR was negative.

A syndrome of recurrent episodes of aseptic meningitis was first described by Mollaret. Patients present with acute onset of fever, headache and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination reveals a mixed pleocytosis with lymphocytes and polymorphonuclear leukocytes. In addition, there are large atypical cells with abundant pale blue cytoplasm and irregular footprint shaped nuclei (Mollaret cells). Initially thought to represent endothelial cells, recent evidence suggests Mollaret cells are actually derived from the monocytic lineage. The unusual features of this case are (1) the long duration of symptoms and CSF pleocytosis (typically the clinical and CSF findings resolve after 2-5 days) and (2) the high CSF protein (generally the CSF protein is <100 mg/ml in cases of Mollaret's meningitis). The discovery that some cases of Mollaret's meningitis are linked to HSV infection has resulted in the use of acyclovir to prevent recurrences. Although both HSV-1 and HSV-2 have been associated with Mollaret's meningitis, the latter is more common in this syndrome.

Summary: A middle-aged man with headache and hallucinations.

history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with headache and hallucinations.
A middle-aged man presented with headache, dizziness, somnolence and hallucinations, which had begun three weeks earlier.

The patient had been diagnosed nine years earlier with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. The level of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells was 560 cells/microliter (17%) and the HIV-RNA level was 3700 copies/mL. Other medical problems included diabetes mellitus, hepatitis C virus infection, and a history of Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid valve endocarditis 7 years earlier.

Medications included stavudine (d4T) and lamivudine (3TC).
exam_studies:
The patient was somnolent and did not appear toxic. The temperature was 100.4°F (38°C). His neck was supple and the neurological examination had no focal findings.

The white cell count in the blood was 6,000 cells/mm³. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a glucose level of 218 (serum >600 mg/dL) and protein 58 mg/dL. The CSF white cell count was 275 cells/mm³ (leukocytes 81%, lymphocytes 6%, and monocytes 13%) and red cell count was 25 cells/mm³ in tube #4. Magentic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed a lesion in the right cerebellum (3.6 centimeter (cm) by 3.6 cm), a lesion in the right posterior temporal lobe (3 cm by 3.9 cm) and a small left frontal lesion, all of which were ring-enhancing (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain.
diagnosis:
Aspergillus fumigatus brain abscesses in a patient with HIV infection and diabetes mellitus, and a history of hepatitis C virus infection.

A brain biopsy with abscess drainage was performed; examination of the aspirate revealed branching septate hyphae. This was speciated as Aspergillus fumigatus (Figures 3 and 4, provided by Alex Babic, M.D.).
Figure 3. Gram stain of abscess aspirate.
Figure 4. Fungal stain of abscess aspirate.

The patient was started on amphotericin, voriconazole and caspofungin. Despite drainage and aggressive antifungal therapy, he developed adult respiratory distress syndrome and renal failure, and unfortunately died from cardiopulmonary arrest on the 15th hospital day.

This patient had a normal CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count, and was therefore not at high risk of having the typical causes of focal central nervous system disease associated with AIDS, which include toxoplasmosis, lymphoma, Cryptococcus and tuberculosis. His history of endocarditis should raise concern for recurrent endocarditis causing septic emboli. Pyogenic abscess due to contiguous spread from the teeth, sinuses or ears should also be considered in any patient with imaging suggestive of abscesses. Although this patient had diabetes mellitus and HIV infection, Aspergillus brain abscess generally occurs as part of disseminated infection in severely immunocompromised individuals, such as patients with prolonged neutropenia.

title:
Summary: A middle-aged woman with tingling and numbness in her hand.
A woman in
history:
Summary: A middle-aged woman with tingling and numbness in her hand.
A woman in her forties, originally from India, presented to her primary care doctor complaining of right hand tingling and numbness for several years.
In India, she had been diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome and underwent a release procedure. This had no effect on her symptoms, which slowly progressed. She stopped using her arm altogether due to decreased sensation. She was seen by a neurologist who noted a polyneuropathy on physical examination.

She was status post carpal tunnel release.

She was born and raised in India.
exam_studies:
Examination of the skin revealed two very large hypopigmented and anesthetic lesions on her back and left deltoid area (Figures 1 and 2), and a polyneuropathy noted earlier.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Lepromatous leprosy due to Mycobacterium leprae infection.

A sural nerve biopsy was performed. Gram stain revealed few polymorphonuclear cells and no organisims. The bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear was positive (Figure 3). AFB culture was negative.
The pathologic specimens of the sural nerve sheath were diagnostic of lepromatous leprosy.
Figure 3. Acid-fast stain of biopsy.

The patient was treated with dapsone and rifampin. The lesions resolved completely, although she had persistent anesthesia with minimal improvement. The duration of treatment was planned for more than twelve months.

Mycobacterium leprae is the causative agent of leprosy, also known as Hansen’s Disease. Leprosy is a disease of the peripheral nervous system; the central nervous system is spared. The dysesthesia induced by the peripheral nervous system involvement and the indolent nature of the infection are hallmarks of the clinical presentation. It grows best at cooler temperatures, cannot be cultured from artificial media, and likely is transmitted via the nasorespiratory route and not from close contact as previously thought.
There are two classification systems used:
1. World Health Organization (WHO): Paucibacillary -> Multibacillary
2. Ridley-Jopling: Tuberculoid -> Lepromatous
In this case, the presence of large numbers of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on the smear of the skin biopsy demonstrated multibacillary or lepromatous form of the disease.

Summary: A teenager with pneumonia.
A girl in her mid-teens developed a cough fi
history:
Summary: A teenager with pneumonia.
A girl in her mid-teens developed a cough five days before admission. She was seen by her primary provider as an outpatient and sent home.
One day before admission, fever, vomiting, fatigue, and increased productive cough occurred. She was seen at a community hospital; on examination, the respiratory rate was 40-60 breaths per minute, temperature 104.5°F (40.3°C), and a chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates consistent with pneumonia. She was treated with ceftriaxone and azithromycin.
Her medical condition rapidly deteriorated, however, and she developed increasing respiratory distress, tachypnea, hypotension to 70/50 mm Hg and decreasing oxygen saturation. She was intubated, treated with intravenous fluids and dopamine, and transferred to a tertiary care facility.

There was a history of mild asthma, recent extremity fracture in an accident, occasional headaches, and a history of smoking 2 packs per day.

She had taken acetaminophen as needed for headaches. At the community hospital, ceftriaxone, azithromycin and dopamine were initiated.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 100.6°F (38.1°C), pulse 123 beats/minute, respirations 20 per minute (intubated), and blood pressure 91/39 mm/Hg. Coarse breath sounds were heard.

The hematocrit was 31.3%, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white blood cell count 2,200 cells/mm³ (44% neutrophils, 13% bands, and 29% lymphocytes), platelets 98,000/mm³; sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, chloride 112 mmol/L, carbon dioxide 21.5 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, urea nitrogen 9 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.6 mg/dL.
A chest radiograph revealed pneumonia (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was performed later in her course and revealed extensive pneumatoceles, abscesses and loculated hydropneumothoraces (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Severe necrotizing pneumonia due to methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).

Staphylococcus aureus was present on gram stain and grew from her sputum. It was sensitive to methicillin.

The patient's course was complicated by septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and the development of pneumatoceles and hydropneumothorax. She required a right thoracotomy with pulmonary debridement and decortication, chest tube placement, tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placement. She gradually improved.

Staphylococcal pneumonia is a virulent, rapidly progressive, necrotizing pneumonia. It typically occurs in the elderly on the heels of a respiratory viral infection, such as influenza. Due to the necrosis, multiple mechanical complications are common, as seen in this case. Legionella, RSV, and EBV do not cause necrosis. Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia (PCP) would be an important consideration if this patient were immunosuppressed, such as with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) or corticosteroid use.

title:
Summary: A woman from Ethiopia with a neck mass.
An Ethiopian woman in her twent
history:
Summary: A woman from Ethiopia with a neck mass.
An Ethiopian woman in her twenties was referred to the Infectious Disease clinic for evaluation of a neck mass. She had noted a gradually enlarging painless swelling in her right neck for the previous four months. One month before, she had begun to note similar symptoms on the left side. She denied fevers, chills, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, malaise, or cough.

There was a history of excessive sweating and bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccination as a child. There was no known tuberculosis exposures and no history of a prior tuberculosis skin test.

She had immigrated to the United States from Ethiopia six years before, and had not traveled since. She was married; her husband was her only sexual partner and was reportedly monogamous. She had no children or pets, worked in an office, and denied any history of tobacco, alcohol or drug use.

Medications included glycopyrrolate (doubled dose over previous six months) and oral contraceptives.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 97.9°F (36.6°), pulse 60 beats per minute, and blood pressure 100/68 mm Hg. She was well-nourished and appeared well. There were no oral lesions, and she had excellent dentition. There was a non-tender, rubbery, non-fixed lymph node (4-centimeters in diameter) in the right anterior cervical chain midway up the sternocleidomastoid (Figure 1), and a non-tender, rubbery, non-fixed lymph node (two-centimeters in diameter) just lateral to the left margin of the thyroid. There was no supraclavicular, axillary, inguinal or other lymphadenopathy. Lungs were clear bilaterally, and the liver and spleen were non-tender and not enlarged. There was no clubbing, edema or rash noted in extremities.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed no air space disease, granulomas or lymphadenopathy. A test for human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) was negative.
diagnosis:
Lymphadenitis due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A Mantoux (PPD) test was placed and resulted in a positive reaction that measured 30 millimeters.
The fine needle aspiration produced five milliliters (ml) of cloudy material that was sent for gram stain, culture, fungal stain, fungal culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain and mycobacterial culture, as well as cytopathology. Rapid cytology showed necrosis, and the AFB stain was positive. The final pathology revealed granulomas with a few giant cells and necrosis (Figures 2 and 3).
The culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Figure 2. Pathology of aspiration specimen.
Figure 3. Pathology of aspiration specimen.

She was started on 4-drug therapy with isoniazid (INH), rifampin, pyrazinamide (PZA) and ethambutol. After one month, the organism was found to be susceptible to all of the above drugs and the ethambutol was stopped. Her lymph nodes decreased in size without suppuration.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis is the most common cause of lymphadenopathy in developing countries (30-64%), and cervical nodes are most frequently affected (75%). Most adult cases are thought to represent a reactivation of the initial lymphatic spread of primary pulmonary infection, although this assumption has not been confirmed using newer molecular epidemiological tools.
The differentiation between cervical lymphadenitis due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis versus atypical Mycobacterium is critical because the treatment strategy differs (medical vs. surgical, respectively). Epidemiology is particularly helpful: ~97% of mycobacterial lymphadenitis in U.S. adults is due to M. tuberculosis, whereas ~90% in U.S. children is due to atypical mycobacterium such as M. avium-intracellulare and M. scrofulaceum. The size of the PPD reaction is not a reliable way to differentiate because nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis in healthy children has been associated, in one study, with a mean PPD of 15.5 millimeters.
Where available, fine needle aspiration (FNA) is the initial diagnostic test of choice based on its low morbidity and high clinical yield (~80%). Specimens should be evaluated for cytopathology as well as AFB smear and mycobacterial culture.
As with all forms of TB, therapy needs to be individually guided based on the site(s) of infection, the organism burden and the underlying immunocompetence of the host. Although a six-month course of therapy is generally recommended, some experts suggest that a longer duration may be helpful in preventing relapse. In up to one third of cases, node enlargement with pain, suppuration and even sinus formation can occur during chemotherapy. This paradoxical worsening is thought to represent an immune reaction to tuberculous antigens rather than failure of drug treatment, and improvement ultimately ensues. Short courses of corticosteroids and surgical excision have been reported to help in extreme circumstances. Affected lymph nodes may not disappear despite successful treatment: up to 20% of patients will have residual small (<1cm) lymph nodes.

Summary: A woman with a headache and dizziness.
A middle-aged woman presented wi
history:
Summary: A woman with a headache and dizziness.
A middle-aged woman presented with headache and dizziness.

She had hypertension and diabetes mellitus type II, and was status post partial hysterectomy.

The patient had been raised in a rural area, and lived in a city in a mid-Atlantic state. She denied tobacco, alcohol or drug use. She had a dog, but denied exposure to farm animals. She had traveled to Texas and Mexico two decades earlier.

Her mother had a history of a benign brain tumor.

Medications included conjugated estrogen, enalapril, and glyburide.
exam_studies:
Her temperature was 37°C (98.6°F), pulse 90 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 150/95 mm/Hg, and respiratory rate 18 per minute. She had no lymphadenopathy. The lungs were clear. There were no cardiac murmurs. The abdomen was soft and there was mild right upper quadrant tenderness, but no enlargement of liver or spleen. On neurologic exam, she was alert and oriented and cranial nerves were intact. There was mild ataxia on tandem gait. The remainder of her examination was normal.

The results of a complete blood count (CBC), electrolytes and tests of renal function were normal. The level of glucose was 211 mg/dL, and aspartate aminotransferase (AST, SGOT) 39 U/L; other liver function tests were normal. A chest radiograph showed a normal heart size and no infiltrates.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed multiple ring-enhancing lesions scattered throughout the white matter of both hemispheres (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Brain MRI scan.
Figure 2. Brain MRI scan.

The patient underwent a brain biopsy of a right frontal lesion. Pathologic examination of the tissue is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Brain biopsy.
Figure 4. Brain biopsy with necrosis and inflammation.
diagnosis:
Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

The pathology of the brain biopsy showed trophozoites of Toxoplasma gondii (Figures 5 and 6). A test for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive. The HIV RNA level was 510,000 copies/mL; CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 69 cells/mm³.
Figure 5. Biopsy showing a tissue cyst.
Figure 6. Tissue cyst of Toxoplasma.

The patient received treatment with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms. She subsequently was also treated for HIV infection.

This case illustrates the importance of considering underlying HIV disease in any patient that presents with focal brain lesions. If the patient had been diagnosed with HIV infection prior to the brain biopsy, then empiric therapy for toxoplasmosis would have been considered.
Toxoplasma encephalitis in patients with HIV generally presents with subacute onset of focal neurologic abnormalities. Imaging of the brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions, often involving the basal ganglia. In a patient with AIDS and focal brain lesions, alternative diagnoses must be sought if empiric therapy for toxoplasmosis does not result in clinical improvement within 10-14 days or if the patient clinically worsens.

Summary: A woman with nodules on her arm.
A woman in her sixties, admitted to th
history:
Summary: A woman with nodules on her arm.
A woman in her sixties, admitted to the hospital for cardiac bypass surgery, was found incidentally to have several erythematous, non-tender nodules on her right arm. The patient reported that the first nodule developed slowly at the site of a glucose fingerstick done during an earlier hospitalization. Over the next 3 months, thenodules had spread up her arm. During that time, she had not noted any fevers, chills, or other constitutional symptoms.

There was a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, Type II diabetes mellitus, sleep apnea, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma (10 years prior).

She denied recent travel within or outside the United States. She also denied recent exposures to pets, fish tanks, marine-life, insect bites, gardening or other horticulture exposure.
exam_studies:
She was afebrile and the blood pressure was 158/76 mm/Hg. Oxygen saturation was 94% on while breathing 2 liters of supplemental oxygen. She was an elderly, chronically-ill-appearing woman who did not look toxic. There were scattered wheezes and bibasilar crackles. The skin over her right extremity revealed multiple erythematous, violaceous, non-tender nodules. There was no lymphangiitic streaking. The lesions were confined to right upper extremity only. Figure 1. Physical finding. Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium chelonae soft tissue infection.

Biopsy of one of the nodules was performed, and examination of the tissue revealed a gram stain with a few Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The culture was positive for coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and the fungal wet preparation and culture were negative. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining was positive; modified AFB testing was negative.
Culture from the biopsy of one of the nodules subsequently grew Mycobacterium chelonae.

The patient was treated with clarithromycin and gatifloxacin. The nodules were improving slowly when she expired from her cardiac disease.

The pattern of nodular lesions starting on the hand and slowly spreading up the extremity suggests a sporotrichoid pattern. The infectious pathogens causing these types of lesions include mycobacteria (especially M. chelonae and M. marinum), fungi (especially Sporothrix), and bacteria (especially Nocardia). In this case the exposure history is not specifically provocative thus M. chelonae should be strongly considered given its ubiquitous nature. Biopsy is absolutely required to identify the causitive pathogen, which was M chelonae in this case.
Mycobacterium chelonae falls under the group of non-tuberculous mycobacteria known as the “rapid growers.” Other rapid growers include Mycobacterium abscessus and Mycobacterium fortuitum. These three are probably the most common non-tuberculous mycobacteria involved in cases of community and nosocomial acquired skin and soft tissue infections. The organisms are ubiquitous in the environment; in the hospital they have been isolated from hospital water supplies, topical skin solutions, injectable medicines, and other sources.

title:
Summary: A young man with a fever and facial rash.
A Vietnamese man in his twent
history:
Summary: A young man with a fever and facial rash.
A Vietnamese man in his twenties with a history of injection drug use presented with a ten-day history of fever and a non-pruritic rash on the face.

There was a history of injection drug use.

He lived in Vietnam.
exam_studies:
There were papules and pustules on the face (Figure 1), lips, and inside his mouth, where lesions were present on the buccal mucosa and soft and hard palates. Some pustules had a black center. The rest of the body was spared.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Penicillium marneffei in an HIV-positive patient from Vietnam.

Penicillium marneffei was cultured from a pustule. A test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive. On a complete blood count (CBC), there were 1% lymphocytes. A CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was not performed.

He was treated with itraconazole, and his fever and rash resolved.

Penicillium marneffei is a common opportunistic infection in HIV-positive persons in Southeast Asia, generally occurring when the CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count is below 200/mm³. Patients may present with fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and cutaneous lesions. In HIV-positive individuals, the skin lesions of penicilliosis are often papular with central necrosis or umbilication. Although the skin lesions of penicilliosis resemble those of molluscum contagiosum, the latter condition is distinguished by the absence of systemic symptoms.

history:
Summary: A man with ear pain and confusion.
A man in his seventies presented to the emergency department with altered mental status. He had been in his usual state of excellent health until the evening prior to admission when he experienced some right ear pain and discharge. He instilled topical ciprofloxacin eardrops (recently prescribed to a family member for an otitis externa). The next morning he felt tired and was noted to have slurred speech by his family. After a nap, he was noted to be confused and aphasic. He was brought to the emergency room.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 103°F (39.4°C) and blood pressure 95/77 mm Hg. He was obtunded, and sanguineous fluid drained from his right ear.

The peripheral leukocyte count was 8600/mm³ with 74% polymorphonuclear cells and 24% band forms. His evaluation included a head/maxillofacial computed tomography (CT), which demonstrated fluid in the external ear canal and opacification of the right mastoid air cells, but no temporal bone fracture. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 27 cm H20, glucose of 91 mg/dL (serum concentration 202 mg/dL), and total protein of 322 mg/dL. Cell count showed 371 leukocytes/mm³, with a differential of 58% polymorphonuclear cells, 36% band forms, and 2% lymphocytes.

Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is shown in Figure 1. He rapidly developed progressive shock and obtundation, requiring multiple pressors and intubation. A head MRI scan was performed, as seen in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Gram stain of spun CSF.
Figure 2. Head MRI scan, coronal view.
diagnosis:
Otitic meningitis due to Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).

The CSF gram stain and subsequent culture revealed Group A Streptococcus, M type 1, NADase positive.

Despite the treatment noted above, and broad spectrum antibiotics, the patient unfortunately died within 19 hours of presentation secondary to refractory hypotension, renal failure, with possible toxic shock syndrome.

In the antibiotic era, otitic meningitis due to Streptococcus pyogenes is rare. Extension of infection via the mastoid bone may result in meningitis. Other complications of mastoiditis include temporal lobe brain abscess and septic thrombosis of the lateral sinus.

title:
Summary: A 6-year-old with fever and a scalp lesion.
A 6-year-old boy, who had p
history:
Summary: A 6-year-old with fever and a scalp lesion.
A 6-year-old boy, who had played in grassy areas outdoors on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, developed a fever and a sore spot on his head one day in July. The family's physician prescribed dicloxacillin for a cellulitis. Three days later, the sore spot persisted and fever increased to 105°F (40.6°C). He was admitted to a hospital.

He had had outdoor exposure on Cape Cod, Massachusetts.

He was taking dicloxacillin.
exam_studies:
There was a lesion on his scalp (Figure 1) that was associated with a tender post-auricular lymph node.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Tularemia due to Francisella tularensis.

Upon specific questioning, the patient's family reported having found a tick on the patient's scalp recently. Serologic testing for Francisella tularensis, the causative agent of tularemia, was positive.

The systemic symptoms in this case ruled out the diagnosis of tinea capitis. The ulcerative lesion on his scalp did not suggest cellulitis or Lyme disease. Cutaneous anthrax generally presents with a pruritic papule that enlarges into an ulcer with a black necrotic central eschar and significant edema. This patient had the ulceroglandular form of tularemia, caused by Francisella tularensis, most likely transmitted by a tick bite.
