title: A man with fatigue, fever, aches and photophobia.
history:
A man in his fifties presented with increasing fatigue of three-to-four weeks' duration. Five days before presentation, photophobia, fevers (which occurred throughout the day and improved with ibuprofen), shaking chills and diaphoresis that soaked the sheets occurred. He reported diffuse aches, particularly in the head, neck, chest, and calves; a dry mouth; dry cough and mild dysuria. The urine appeared dark orange.
There was no weight loss, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. The patient increased his oral intake of water.

He had hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and a recent left axillary cyst, which had been treated with antibiotics ten days before presentation. He had had coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) several years earlier; a recent echocardiogram had not shown decreased ejection fraction.

The patient had had no recent sick contacts. He was married and had traveled extensively, most recently to the Middle East three-to-six months earlier. He had gone camping for one week in the Sierra Nevada mountains and had noted the onset of fever and myalgias on the last day of that trip.
He did not smoke tobacco or abuse alcohol.

Daily medications included thyroxine, atorvastatin, pantoprazole, lisinopril, and aspirin. Ibuprofen was taken as needed for fevers. Previous therapies had included malarial prophylaxis while the patient was abroad 3-6 months before and a course of antibiotics ten days earlier.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well-nourished, tired and uncomfortable. The temperature was 38.1°C (100.6°F) on admission, and rose to 40°C (104°F) within six hours. On admission, the blood pressure was 86/50 mm Hg, pulse 94 beats per minute, respirations 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing ambient air. The sclerae were injected and the oral mucosa was dry. There were oral lesions in the right upper and lower labial fold. The neck was supple without lymphadenopathy. There were crackles at the lung bases and a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur was present. The midepigastrium and right upper quadran were tender with deep palpation. The calves were tender; Homan's sign was negative. There was no clubbing, cyanosis, rash, petechiae or edema.

The white blood cell count was 6,590 cells/uL (polymorphonuclear leukocytes 39%, bands 42%, lymphocytes 5%, monocytes 13%), hematocrit 34.5%, and platelets 15,000/mm³. The peripheral blood smear is shown (Figures 1 and 2). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 91 mm per hour. Prothrombin time was 14.9 seconds, partial thromboplastin time 32 seconds, and INR 1.2.
The level of plasma sodium was 135 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, glucose 96 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 174 U/L, bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 36 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 27U/L, total protein 6.1 g/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 531 U/L, amylase < 30 U/L, and lipase 61 U/L. The level of vitamin B12 was 401 pg/ml and folate 13.8 ng/ml. The urinalysis contained trace protein.
Figure 1. Blood smear.
Figure 2. Blood smear.
diagnosis:
Relapsing fever caused by Borreliosis.

Spirochetes of Borrelia are seen in Figures 1 and 2.

title: A man with HIV presented with productive cough and fever.
history:
A man in his fifties had been infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) for twenty years. Ten days before presentation, he was admitted to another hospital with a productive cough and fever. Community-acquired pneumonia was diagnosed and ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered.

The patient was HIV-positive and had acquired immunodefiency syndrome (AIDS). Three weeks before admission, his CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 35 cells/mm³, and the level of HIV-RNA 250,000 copies per milliliter. The patient had failed highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) several times, possibly due to non-adherence. He had had Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in the past but was not on prophylaxis therapy at the time of admission.

The patient lived in the Southwestern United States.
exam_studies:
He was a mildly cachectic man in no apparent distress. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute and respirations 26 breaths per minute. There was non-tender adenopathy in the cervical, axillary and inguinal regions. No thrush was seen. Dry rales were heard in the left upper posterior lung fields. No murmurs, abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions or focal neurological findings were noted.

The hematocrit was 38%, white blood cells 7,600/mm³, with 12% lymphocytes, 1% eosinophils and no bands.
Chest radiography revealed a streaky infiltrate in the left upper lobe (Figures 1 and 2). Gram staining of a sputum specimen revealed scattered polymorphonuclear leukocytes, without significant organisms. Blood and sputum cultures were obtained.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Lateral chest radiograph.

The patient declined bronchoscopy, lymph node biopsy or further evaluation. His condition markedly deteriorated and vital signs became unstable. He was diagnosed with severe sepsis syndrome and died in the Intensive Care Unit.
Five days after admission, blood and sputum cultures drawn on admission grew the same organism.
diagnosis:
Coccidioidomycosis caused by Coccidioides immitis in a patient with HIV and AIDS.

The blood and sputum cultures grew Coccidioides immitis.

title:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with weight loss and cough.
Fou
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with weight loss and cough.
Four months before this presentation, a woman in her thirties was seen at an outside medical facility with a one-week history of nonproductive cough (The presence or absence of purulent sputum can be a useful diagnostic clue. "Typical" bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae tend to cause productive cough, whereas viral or atypical pathogens more often do not.) and night sweats (Night sweats are a relatively non-specific symptom but are not a typcial feature of most common respiratory infections. Consideration of uncommon symptoms can help guide the differential diagnosis. A number of infections can cause night sweats, but the combination of cough and night sweats raises the possibility of tuberculosis.). Chest radiography and computed tomography (CT) showed left upper lobe consolidation and scattered bilateral pulmonary nodules. The patient was treated with levofloxacin and the symptoms abated.
In the following two months, she noted a poor appetite and a 20-pound weight loss (Significant weight-loss is an important "red flag" symptom, and is very unusual without serious underlying illness. Two months of weight loss suggests a persistent catabolic state, which would be quite uncommon in most common pulmonary infections seen in the US.). Three weeks before this presentation, left pleuritic chest pain and cough productive of yellow sputum occurred. There was no recurrence of fever, chills or night sweats.

She had a history of anemia.

The patient was originally from India (Travel history, including distant history is critical to infectious disease diagnosis since a number of important pathogens can establish persistent latent infection that can reactivate years after exposure.) and had last visited more than five years earlier. There was no known exposure to tuberculosis and no animal exposure.

Medications included iron sulfate.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared tired, with a normal temperature and vital signs. 0xygen saturation was 100% while breathing ambient air. Examination of the lungs revealed fine crackles over the left upper lung field; no wheezes were heard. There was no hepatosplenomegaly or rash, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 9,900 cells/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000); with a normal differential (The differential - that is, the relative numbers of different white blood cell types - can provide diagnostic information. Typical serious acute bacterial infections tend to cause a "Left Shift", with elevated polymorphonuclear leukocytes, also called "polys" or neutrophils, and bands - immature neutrophils - and decreased lymphocytes and eosinophils. The absence of a left shift here is a sign that this may not be a typical acute bacterial infection.) (59% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 2% bands, 30% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 3% eosinophils), hematocrit 32.3% (reference range 36.0-46.0 in women), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 68 fL (This is a microcytic anemia. Most typically associated with iron deficiency, it can also be seen in other conditions, such as chronic inflammatory states or hereditary diseases.) (reference range 80-100), and platelets 350,000/mm³. Results of electrolytes and liver function testing were normal. Radiography of the chest is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, lateral view.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Chest radiography revealed a large left upper lobe mass with cavitation (Only a limited number of pathogens will cause cavities to form in the lung, narrowing the differential diagnosis.) and CT scanning showed a left upper lobe mass with cavitation and bilateral pulmonary nodules (Figures 1 through 4 above).
A purified protein derivative (PPD) Mantoux test (In this test, a partially purified extract of Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria is injected intradermally. If the person has been exposed to TB, T-lymphocyte cells will migrate to the injection site, causing an area of induration, or skin hardening.) was administered and a reaction of 15 centimeters induration recorded. Induced sputum revealed 4+ acid-fast bacilli (Mycobacteria have an outer layer containing mycophenolic acid making them difficult to stain and visualize by microscopy. Auramine O can stain mycobacteria and the stain does not come off with an acid wash, giving them the name acid-fast.) by Auramine O staining. After three weeks (Mycobacteria grow much more slowly than most typical bacteria. This can make diagnosis challenging and often treatment decisions must be made before culture and sensitivity data are known.), sputum cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Figure 5), which was sensitive to all antibiotics tested.
Figure 5. Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelson) stain from culture.

Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol were administered initially; the ethambutol was discontinued after the sensitivity results were known. Pyrazinamide was administered for the first two months and isoniazid and rifampin for 6 months. Follow-up sputum obtained at 2 months revealed no acid-fast bacilli on staining and culture.

The classic presentation for pulmonary tuberculosis includes upper lobe consolidation, weight loss and night sweats. Those features were present in this case, however the diagnosis may have been delayed by the empiric therapy for pneumonia with levofloxacin, which has activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
In a study of patients with culture-confirmed tuberculosis, initial empiric therapy with a fluoroquinolone was associated with a delay in initiation of antituberculous therapy [Dooley et al 2002]. Thus, clinicians should consider the diagnosis of tuberculosis in patients with upper lobe cavitation or infiltrates, especially if they have epidemiologic risk factors for acquisition or reactivation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A young adult with headache and fever.
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A young adult with headache and fever.
A young adult (A patient's age is often a critical factor in infectious disease diagnosis, affecting both the spectrum of illness and type of organisms involved.) male student presented with fever and headache (While many infections can produce fever, often with secondary symptoms such as headache, the combination of fever with prominent headache should always raise the possibility of central nervous system infection.). One week before his presentation, the patient was seen at an outside clinic with a sore throat. An upper respiratory viral syndrome was diagnosed and supportive care, including fluids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and decongestants, advised.
Sore throat and low-grade fevers continued.
On the day of presentation, headache developed. His friends reported that the patient was not behaving normally. He was brought back to the clinic and, after he became more confused (The combination of fever, headache and changes in mental status in a previously healthy young person strongly suggests central nervous system infection and should be considered a medical emergency.) and combative, transferred to a hospital.

The patient had received the meningococcal vaccine (The meningococcal vaccine is recommended for people who will be living in close quarters, such as dormitories. Of note, one common type of meningococcus, group B, is not covered by this vaccine, since the polysaccharides of this type are very similar to a human antigen. Therefore, even vaccinated people are still at risk for group B infection.).

He lived in a dormitory (Dormitories, military barracks, prisons, and other settings where individuals live in close contact increase the rate of spread of organisms transmitted by contact or droplets.) and was sexually active (The sexual history is a critical part of the infectious diseases work-up [Terminology: The work-up refers to the entire process of diagnosis, including history, physical examination, laboratory studies, cultures, and imaging], both because the organisms involved may be sexually transmitted and because it influences that the patient may have HIV infection and be immunocompromised. [Terminology: A patient whose immune system is not functioning normally is said to be 'immunocompromised'.] Knowing the immune status of the patient is one of the most critical parts of the infectious diseases work-up, since it has a major influence on the type of organisms involved and upon the risk of severe infection.), with men (Although being sexually active with men is not in and of itself a risk factor, among men who have sex with men (MSM), there are higher rates of high risk behaviors such as unprotected anal intercourse, so it is important to elicit the patient's sexual history, in order to better assess HIV risks.). He denied any sick contacts (Exposure to a person with similar symptoms is often an important diagnostic clue.) or drug use (Patients with a history of injection drug use should be asked about sharing of needles, to assess the risk of blood-borne infections.).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared confused and combative. The temperature (Normal: approximately 97-99°F.) was 100.3°F (37.9°C), pulse (Normal heart rates can vary widely, but in general a heart rate over 100 beats per minute would be considered tachycardia.) 117 beats per minute, blood pressure (Normal value 100-120 systolic and 60-80 diastolic.) 120/82 mm Hg, respirations (Normal value 12-20 breaths per minute.) 20 per minute, and oxygen saturation (Normal value 95-100 % while breathing ambient air.) 99%. There were no exudates (Exudate in this context refers to visible and typically whitish pus, which consists of white blood cells and often indicates acute bacterial infection.) on his tonsils; the neck was stiff (The lining around the central nervous system, the meninges, is extremely sensitive to inflammation of any kind, including infection. Patients experience inflammation of the meninges as an inability to flex the neck, since this action stretches the meninges. The combination of fever, headache and stiff neck strongly suggests the patient has clinical meningitis. Many illnesses can give sore muscles including neck muscles, but a fever and a stiff neck is a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation.); the lungs were clear (Jargon: clear lungs refers to the presence of normal breath sounds.) and there was a II/VI holosystolic (Terminology: a holosystolic heart murmur, constant all the way from the first heart sound (S1) to the second (S2), may be due to increased blood flow when the heart is beating forcefully and fast, or it could indicate dysfunction of particular valves, such as the sound heard in mitral regurgitation.) murmur. The skin and joints were normal. On neurological examination, he alternated between confused and somnolent; Kernig’s (Terminology: pain and resistance on extension of the knee when the leg is flexed at the hip, indicating meningeal inflammation.) and Brudinski’s (Terminology: involuntary lifting of the leg when the patient is lying supine and the neck is flexed, indicating meningeal inflammation.) signs were negative (Concept: most medical tests are not 100% sensitive, that is, there are some false negatives.).

Computed tomography (CT is often performed before lumbar puncture since the latter can be risky if intracranial pressure is too high.) (CT) of the head was negative. The white blood cell (The normal reference range at the hospital was 5,000-11,000 cells per cubic millimeter.) count was 18,000/mm³ with 25% band forms (Terminology: Newly created neutrophils have a band-like nucleus visible under the microscope. The presence of many bands suggest the immune system is making a large number of new white blood cells, indicating severe infection.). Tests of liver function were normal.

The patient was started emergently (The disease process in meningitis progresses very rapidly and may be life-threatening, so antibiotics and antivirals must be given empirically as quickly as possible, without waiting for culture data.) on steroids (Much of the tissue injury in meningitis is caused by inflammation, so rapid institution of powerful anti-inflammatory medicines are used to block this. At the time of this publication, exactly which patients should receive steroids is still somewhat controversial and is a matter of active research.), ceftriaxone (A long-acting beta-lactam antibiotic that would be effective against Neisseria, Haemophilus influenzae, and most Streptococcus pneumoniae, also referred to as pneumococci.), vancomycin (An antibiotic with very broad activity against Gram positive organisms, including pneumococci resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.), and acyclovir (An antiviral drug effective against Herpes Simplex Viruses.). A lumbar puncture was performed after the above treatment was administered. A gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid (Normal cerebrospinal fluid has no cells in it. The presence of white blood cells suggests inflammation and the presence of large numbers of neutrophils is highly suggestive of bacterial infection.) is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Gram stain of spun cerebrospinal fluid.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Meningococcal meningitis.

The gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid was positive for gram-negative diplococci consistent with Neisseria meningitidis. The gram stain is shown under high power (The size, shape, color and uniformity of the objects visible in the cytoplasm of some of the neutrophils suggest bacterial infection, and in particular, the kidney-bean shaped diplococci suggest Neisseria, of which Neisseria meningiditis would be by far the most likely.) in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid, high power.

Steroids were administered for three days and the antibiotic therapy changed to intravenous penicillin 24 million units daily. The patient's mental status improved within 36 hours, and he was discharged home to complete ten days of penicillin.
The culture of the cerebrospinal fluid did not grow the organism, most likely due to the treatment with antibiotics prior to his lumbar puncture. Blood cultures remained negative.

In cases such as this one, it is important to treat for bacterial meningitis expeditiously even though several more benign diagnoses may be in the differential.
Epidemiologically, the patient is at risk for meningococcal meningitis given his group-living situation in a dormitory. The risk of invasive meningococcal infection appears to be higher during the first year than in subsequent years of college attendance. Pneumococcal meningitis also remains a significant possibility, and therefore both should be covered. Lack of exposure to areas endemic for the vectors responsible for the spread of rickettsial disease and the absence of rash make Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever less likely.
Viral causes of meningitis/encephalitis should also be entertained, including HIV and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Bacteremic seeding of the meninges from endocarditis or other sources is possible, though less likely than the previously mentioned causes of meningitis.
Given the patient’s altered mental status, CT scanning of the head is a reasonable first step in evaluation, but antibiotics should not be withheld while awaiting data.

title:
Summary: A man with a fever and a headache.
A man in his thirties presented with
history:
Summary: A man with a fever and a headache.
A man in his thirties presented with five days of fever and headache. He had had minimal photophobia and significant neck stiffness. He denied having any rash, respiratory symptoms, myalgias, abdominal pain, focal neurological symptoms or seizures.

Two-and-one-half months before presentation, the patient had traveled by automobile from Central America to an urban area in the Northeast United States via California. In Central America, he had eaten raw seafood and unpasteurized cheeses, lived on a farm with livestock including pigs and cows and had some minimal contact with wild animals.
He had worked in a factory in the Northeast United States since his arrival.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and was in no acute distress. The temperature was 96.2°F (35.7°C), pulse 56 per minute, respirations 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air, and blood pressure 110/68 mm Hg. There was mild meningismus, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 8,000/mm³ with 66% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes, and 7% eosinophils. A lumbar puncture showed 418 white blood cells per high-powered field with 0% neutrophils, 59% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, 29% eosinophils, and 7% large atypical mononuclear cells with marked basophilic cytoplasm and irregularly shaped prominent neucleoli. (See Figures 1 and 2.) PPD testing was negative.
Figure 1. Cerebrospinal fluid.
Figure 2. Cerebrospinal fluid.

Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the head showed no obvious lesions or calcifications, and chest and abdominal CT scans were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a left temporal extraaxial cystic lesion (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Brain MRI scan.
diagnosis:
Eosinophilic meningitis due to neurocysticercosis, consistent with infection by the tapeworm Taenia solium.

Cysticercosis immunoblot testing of the serum was positive.

Neurosurgical and ophthalmologic evaluations were obtained. A tapering course of steroids was started two days before the treatment for cysticercosis began. The patient then received eight days of albendazole. In addition, ivermectin was administered for two days to prevent dissemination of Strongyloides since co-infection with this helminth could not be excluded in a timely manner. (Serology is the most sensitive test for Strongyloides, but this was expected to take several weeks to return).
The PPD was negative and therefore the patient did not need to receive prophylactic isoniazid (INH) therapy.

Eosinophilic meningitis is defined by the presence of ten or more eosinophils per microliter in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or eosinophilia of at least 10% of the total CSF leukocyte count. Parasites account for a large percentage of eosinophilic meningitis from the developing world, and the prevalence of neurocysticercosis, caused by the tapeworm Taenia solium, is very high in this population.
Other possible infectious causes of eosinophilic meningitis include Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, which is the most common cause of eosinophilic meningitis worldwide. It is found primarily in Southeast Asia and the Pacific Basin; however, ship-borne migration of rats has led to the spread of this disease outside of this area. In 2002, a report of an outbreak which occurred among U.S. travelers returning from Jamaica appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine. The larvae are obtained by consuming raw snails that have fed upon the excrement of rats. The hallmark neurological features of angiostrongyliasis are facial and ophthalmologic palsies and truncal and extremity paresthesias.
Gnathostomiasis is another condition that can lead to eosinophilic meningitis. It is caused by the tissue nematode Gnathostoma spingerum. This parasite is endemic in southeast Asia and southern China but has also been identified in parts of Latin America. Humans acquire the disease by consuming raw or inadequately cooked freshwater fish, poultry or pork that harbor the larvae. Unlike Angiostrongylus, G. spingerum does not migrate to neural tissue as part of its life cycle but becomes trapped there on an accidental route. This parasite is much larger and therefore has a more destructive course. Intraparenchymal hemorrhage is more common as well as permanent neurological deficits.
Baylisascariasis has also been associated with fatal cases of meningoencephalitis. The parasite Baylisascaris procyonis is a raccoon ascarid, and is found in humans who have consumed soil material in areas close to raccoon habitats. The severity of the disease depends upon the number of eggs ingested. Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis include infection with other helminths (such as neurotrichinosis, paragonimiasis, cerebral toxicariasis, and cerebral and spinal schistosomiasis) and fungal meningitis due to Coccidioides immitis.

title:
Summary: A man with a rash after travel to India and Europe.

history:
Summary: A man with a rash after travel to India and Europe.
A man in his thirties presented with a rash after returning from a recent trip to India and Western Europe. Two days before presentation, he had developed vesicular skin lesions that were followed by malaise and fever. The rash had started on his head and spread to involve the trunk, all extremities, and genitalia. He denied cough or shortness of breath.

There was a history of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) and no known history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination.

The patient had immigrated to the United States from India more than ten years earlier. One week before presentation, he had returned from a three-week trip to India and Western Europe. He had stayed with family members while traveling; no one was ill during his stay. He denied sexual contact with anyone other than his wife and had had no exposure to animals.
exam_studies:
He appeared ill, but not toxic. The conjunctiva were injected; a vesicular rash had a preponderance of lesions on his face, back, and chest (Figures 1 and 2). There were also ulcerated oral and genital lesions.
Figure 1. Skin lesions.
Figure 2. Skin lesions.

The white blood cell count was 6,300/mm³, hematocrit 44% and platelets 197,000/mm³. The level of serum chemistries, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin were normal. The aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 61 U/L and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 58 U/L.
diagnosis:
Varicella (chickenpox) caused by varicella zoster virus (human herpes virus 3) infection.

A direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test was positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV). Figure 2. Skin lesions.

The patient was treated with oral acyclovir.

This patient had a disseminated vesicular rash. The differential diagnosis includes chickenpox (primary varicella zoster virus or VZV) as well as other pox viruses such as monkeypox and smallpox. Several aspects of his history suggest chickenpox as the most likely diagnosis. First, he appeared ill, but non-toxic. Secondly, the constitutional symptoms followed the appearance of the rash, whereas in smallpox, a febrile prodrome precedes the rash. Thirdly, he had lesions in multiple stages of evolution in a given body area. In smallpox, the lesions will be in the same stage of evolution in a given body area. Smallpox lesions also tend to be greatest centrifugally, e.g. on the face and extremities, whereas his lesions were maximal on his back and chest. The lesions had evolved rapidly and did not involve the palms or soles, which also is more characteristic of chickenpox than smallpox. Finally, he had no known history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination.
Although the patient presented shortly after an outbreak of monkeypox in the United States, he had no known exposure to animals. The constitutional symptoms of monkeypox precede the rash and lymphadenopathy, which he lacked, is often present.
The diagnosis was quickly confirmed to be varicella zoster virus (VZV) by direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing of a lesion. It is unclear whether his penile lesions were due to chickenpox or reactivation of HSV as the lesions were not tested by DFA.

title:
Summary: A woman with a rash and fever following chemotherapy.
A middle-aged wom
history:
Summary: A woman with a rash and fever following chemotherapy.
A middle-aged woman had a history of Hodgkin's disease that was diagnosed several decades earlier and breast cancer diagnosed one year before this presentation. A mastectomy had been performed and chemotherapy administered. There was metastatic spread to the chest wall, liver and kidneys.
Six months before this presentation, she began a clinical trial of oral vinorelbine and capecitabine. She had tolerated seven cycles well, without complications of neutropenia or fever.
Four weeks before her presentation, her pre-teen child had an acute illness with fevers and mouth sores that was thought to be Coxsackie virus. There was no skin exanthem.
The eighth cycle of chemotherapy began approximately two weeks before this admission and lasted eight days. On the fifth day of chemotherapy, she presented to a local emergency room with a temperature of 102°F (38.9°C) and general malaise. The white blood cell count (WBC) was 3,300 cells/mm³ with 81% polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Chest radiography and urinalysis were negative.
On the eighth day of the cycle, she was evaluated at a cancer center for intermittent fevers, mouth sores, and two vesicular lesions on the left forearm that were neither painful nor pruritic. Blood cultures and chest radiography were negative. The possibility of Coxsackie viral infection was considered and her dose of capecitabine was reduced.
The patient continued to have temperatures to 103.3°F (39.6°C), chills, and malaise. The rash gradually involved hands, trunks, arms and legs, and she also reported increasing oral and genital discomfort. She was re-evaluated by an oncologist on the fourteenth day, at which time she was found to have a white blood cell count of 500 cells/mm³ with 88% polymorphonuclear lymphocytes.
She was admitted to a community hospital, and the hospital course was complicated by persistent neutropenia, Streptococcus viridans bacteremia, elevated transaminases (aspartate aminotransferase 2692 U/L and alanine aminotransferase 329 U/L), encephalopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC). Intravenous acyclovir was administered for possible disseminated varicella zoster virus (VZV); fluconazole 200 milligrams intravenous daily and meropenem one gram every eight hours were also administered. She was transferred to a tertiary hospital on the seventeenth day for further management.

There was a history of breast cancer with metastatic disease and Hodgkin's lymphoma. The vaccination history was not known.

There was no history of tobacco or alcohol use. She lived in the northeastern United States and had previously resided in the northwestern United States.

She was married, had children and lived with her family.

See above.
exam_studies:
The patient was disoriented and delirious. The temperature was 96.6°F (35.9°C), blood pressure 106/64 mm Hg, pulse 109 beats per minute, and the oxygen saturation was 97% on three liters of oxygen per nasal cannula.
There was conjunctival injection with a mild whitish exudate. A severe oral mucositis was present, with a white exudate in soft palate consistent with thrush, and a few vesicular lesions visualized. The examination was limited due to pain. The neck was supple and there was no lymphadenopathy. There were bilateral rhonchi and decreased breath sounds at the left base. There were no cardiac murmurs, and the abdomen was soft with some voluntary guarding, and positive bowel sounds. There was no hepatomegaly or peripheral edema. The patient moved all four extremities, and had no meningismus or gaze preference.
There was a diffuse papulo-vesicular rash (Figures 1 through 3). Individual lesions had erythematous well-circumscribed ring-like borders, with a dark center, and involved the trunk, extremities, back, and face. All lesions appeared similar; there was no crusting, no erythematous base, and some lesions were coalescing. Palms and soles had a marked erythroderm, edema and exfoliation. Discrete bullae were present on the soles and were very tender to touch.
Figure 1. Skin lesions.
Figure 2. Skin lesions.
Figure 3. Skin lesions.

Chest radiographs showed left-sided air-space disease, with bronchograms suggestive of pneumonia, and pulmonary edema throughout the right lung. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the head was normal.
Laboratory testing revealed a white blood count of 200 cells/mm³ (84% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes), platelets 133,000/mm³, hematocrit 27.9%, prothrombin time 44 seconds, INR 2.2, fibrinogen 332 mg/dL, partial thromboplastin time 52 seconds, and D-dimer >5000 mg/L. The urea nitrogen (BUN) was 28 mg/dL and the creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 4818 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 455 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 688 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2mg/dL, creatine kinase 9385 U/L. The urinalysis had 40 red blood cells, no white blood cells, and some granular casts.
diagnosis:
Disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) in the setting of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia in a patient with Hodgkin's disease.

The direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) from a skin biopsy was positive for herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Intravenous acyclovir was administered. The patient improved clinically and the neutropenia resolved.

Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) and HSV-2 are distributed worldwide and the seroprevalence in adults reaches approximately 80–95% for HSV-1 and 20–25% for HSV-2. Disseminated Herpes simplex virus has been well described in immunocompromised patients, especially in those with defects in cell- mediated immunity: patients undergoing chemotherapy and organ transplant patients among others. Without preventive antiviral drug treatment, HSV reactivation occurs in about 65–80% of seropositive patients receiving induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia or an allogeneic stem cell transplant.
The most common manifestation of HSV infection is mucocutaneous disease. The characteristic skin lesions are papules and grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. Patients may also develop localized pain, tingling, burning and paresthesias before the formation of skin lesions. Systemic symptoms such as fever, headache, anorexia and malaise may occur, especially during primary infection.
In addition to extensive mucocutaneous infections, HSV may disseminate to visceral organs and cause hepatitis, pneumonitis, adenitis and encephalitis. Intravenous acyclovir is the therapy of choice for severe mucocutaneous or visceral HSV disease in immunocompromised hosts. If initiated early in the disease course, it may significantly shorten the duration of virus shedding and pain, and induce more rapid healing of the lesion.

title:
Summary: A woman with HIV and asthma presented with shortness of breath.
A middl
history:
Summary: A woman with HIV and asthma presented with shortness of breath.
A middle-aged woman presented in the winter with increasing shortness of breath and wheezing for three days. She also reported a non-productive cough. A child with whom she lived had had a respiratory illness ten days earlier.
She had a history of infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), asthma and a malignancy that had metastasized to the lung.

Medical problems included:
1. HIV infection, with a recent CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of 150 cells/mm³, CD4 T-lymphocyte percentage 26%, and HIV RNA 4,100 copies/ml.
2. Asthma with 2-3 exacerbations per year that required treatment with an oral prednisone taper. She had never been intubated and was not on chronic steroids.
3. A malignancy that had metastasized to the lung; a left lower lobe nodule was present.
4. Hepatitis C virus infection.
5. Hypersplenism with chronic leukopenia (white blood cell count 1,500-2,000 cells/mm³) and thrombocytopenia.

She lived in an urban setting in the United States Northeast. She denied recent travel and animal exposures.
exam_studies:
The patient was a well-developed woman in severe respiratory distress, leaning forward and using her accessory muscles of respiration. The blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, the pulse 110 beats per minute, temperature 99.6°F (37.6°C), and respirations 28 breaths per minute. The oxygen saturation was 93% on 2 liters of supplemental oxygen. There were bilateral expiratory wheezes with poor air movement. Her peak flow was 100. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 1,000 cells/mm³ (75% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 10% lymphocytes, 10% monocytes, and 5% eosinophils.) A chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1 and computed tomography (CT) of the chest in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.

Bronchodilators, intravenous steroids and oral levofloxacin were administered. A diagnostic test result was received on the second hospital day.
diagnosis:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonia and asthma in a patient with HIV infection.

CT scanning (Figure 2) showed a "tree in bud" appearance. A nasal washing was positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
In Figure 3, columnar respiratory epithelial cells with a fluorescent respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) antibody tag are shown using a tetramethyl rhodamine isothiocyanate (TRITC) filter. RSV cells are yellow-orange and negative cells are red. In Figure 4, a different filter (fluorescein isothiocyanate or FITC) is used to view the same slide and the RSV appears a duller yellow than in the previous slide. Figure 5 shows RSV-infected columnar cells staining green using the fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) tag. RSV has an apple green fluorescence and is seen at 20 x magnification. Figure 6 is the same slide shown at 40x magnification. (Influenza A infected cells would stain red in this preparation.)
Figure 3. RSV staining red (TRITC), pool antibodies in green.
Figure 4. RSV slide seen in Figure 3, using FITC filter.
Figure 5. RSV with FITC tag, apple-green fluorescence.
Figure 6. Detail of Figure 5.

The patient improved with treatment for an asthma exacerbation, a steroid taper and bronchodilators. She did not receive ribavirin therapy. She recovered completely.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common cause of upper respiratory infection, but may also involve the lower respiratory tract. In immunocompromised hosts, RSV pneumonia can be severe. For example, in bone marrow transplant recipients, RSV may be a cause of fatal pneumonitis. RSV pneumonia has been reported in patients with HIV infection; such individuals may have prolonged shedding of the virus.
In this patient, the chest CT scan showed a "tree in bud" pattern, often seen in mycobacterial infection. However, this radiographic pattern is not specific for mycobacterial infection and can also be seen with other disease processes, such as RSV pneumonia.
Addendum:
Since publication of this case in 2004, RSV vaccines have been FDA approved for adults who are over the age of 60 years. The CDC also recommends two approaches to protect babies from RSV: 1) an RSV vaccine given during pregnancy; 2) an antibody called nirsevimab that is FDA approved to prevent RSV in babies and toddlers.

history:
Summary: A woman with right-sided chest pain and abdominal symptoms.
A woman in her sixties, who had a history of extensive colonic diverticuli, presented with vague right-sided chest and abdominal pain of six-months duration. Initially, the pain was intermittent, radiated to the right neck, and was not related to eating. Laboratory testing had included complete blood count, liver function testing, electrocardiography and chest radiography that were normal.
She presented for further evaluation of the chest and abdominal symptoms after nausea, vomiting, fevers, and chills developed and the right upper quadrant pain worsened.
The patient denied headache, diarrhea, melena, or dysuria.

Colonic diverticuli had been noted on a colonoscopy four months before the onset of symptoms. The patient had dental work performed eight months before her admission.

There was a 45-pack-year smoking history and no history of recent travel.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared toxic. The temperature was 101.6°F (38.7°C), blood pressure was stable and oxygen saturation was 99% on ambient air. Examination of the oropharynx showed good dentition. There was no gingivitis, tooth abscess, or thrush. The lungs were clear, and there was no cardiac murmur. The abdomen was distended and mildly tender with hepatomegaly. No splenomegaly was palpated and no skin lesions were seen.

The white blood count was 20,300 cells/mm³ with 47% neutrophils and 38% bands. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 67 U/liter, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 173 U/liter, alkaline phosphatase 201 U/liter, and total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL.

Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant showed multiple hypoechoic masses in the liver with no ductal dilatation, and a normal gallbladder. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed multiple cystic lesions with thick enhancing septa and rims in the right lobe of liver (Figures 1 and 2); a small right pleural effusion was also seen.
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Pyogenic liver abscess and bacteremia due to Fusobacterium nucleatum.

Aspiration and drainage of the liver masses were performed by interventional radiological techniques. Gram stain of the aspirate revealed thin gram negative rods (Figure 3) and blood cultures grew gram negative rods in the anaerobic bottles (Figure 4). Final speciation of the organism that was cultured from the blood and aspirate identified Fusobacterium nucleatum.
Figure 3. Gram stain of the liver aspirate.
Figure 4. Gram stain of the blood culture.

Metronidazole, penicillin and levofloxacin were administered and multiple drainage procedures of the abscesses performed. CT scanning of the head and neck did not reveal an obvious source of bacteremia.

Liver abscesses are generally amebic or pyogenic. Pyogenic liver abscesses are usually due to the spread of bacteria from another source, such as biliary tract disease, portal system infection, hematogenous spread or trauma.
The bacteriology of pyogenic liver abscesses is usually mixed and may include Enterobacteriaceae, streptococci (aerobic, microaerophilic and anaerobic) and anaerobic gram negative rods (e.g. Fusobacterium and Bacteroides). Fusobacterium nucleatum is an anaerobic bacterium that is part of the normal oral flora. It is characteristically spindle-shaped and often appears in pairs arranged end-to-end.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with aspiration pneumonia and epistaxis.
An elderly man
history:
Summary: An elderly man with aspiration pneumonia and epistaxis.
An elderly man with a history of ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement and multiple admissions for aspiration pneumonia presented to an outside hospital with recurrent aspiration pneumonia. The pneumonia was found to be due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and vancomycin was administered.
After treatment, he required readmission for epistaxis and aspiration, and was intubated. Broad spectrum antibiotics were administered, but the patient became increasingly obtunded. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed increased ventricular size, and the patient was transferred for additional care.

There was a history of hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, deep venous thrombosis with implantation of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter and an open reduction internal fixation procedure of the right hip. He had had an anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture four years before admission and required placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt at that time.
The patient was a chronic carrier of Hepatitis B virus (Hepatitis B surface antigen positive and surface antibody negative); testing for hepatitis C virus and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was known to be negative the year before.

The patient had been monogamous for ten years and had traveled to Europe in the past. There was modest alcohol use and no exposure to pets, tobacco, or intravenous drug use. The tuberculosis skin test (PPD) status was unknown.
exam_studies:
The patient was intubated and sedated. The temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 120/68 mm Hg, and pulse 88 beats per minute. The chest examination revealed coarse breath sounds bilaterally. The head, heart, abdomen and extremity examinations were normal. The site of the ventriculoperitoneal shunt was clean, dry and intact. Plantar reflexes were down-going.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed large ventricles and periventricular low absorption consistent with ventriculitis.

A lumbar puncture revealed 113 white blood cells per cubic millimeter in the first tube, of which 93% were leukocytes, 3% lymphocytes and 3% monocytes. There were 82 cells per cubic millimeter (95% leukocytes) in the fourth tube. The level of glucose in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was 27 mg/dL and that of total protein was 158 g/dL. A gram stain of the CSF is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Gram stain of CSF.
diagnosis:
Ventriculitis caused by Candida dubliniensis infection.

The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) gram stain (Figure 1) showed multiple budding yeast. The culture grew Candida dubliniensis (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Culture plate of CSF.

The ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) was removed. The patient was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (at 7 milligrams per kilogram) and 5-flucytosine.
Fungal staining of the CSF showed successful clearance of yeast within two days. Unfortunately, progressive respiratory failure developed and the patient expired.

This is a case of fungal ventriculitis with an unusual Candida species, Candida dubliniensis, in a patient with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. In a patient with an external ventricular drain in place, the risk of ventriculitis is high and correlated with the length of time the device is in place. Bacteria, usually skin flora such as Staphylococcus species are the most common causes of ventriculitis in the setting of an in-dwelling device. In this case, the individual had also received a long course of broad-spectrum antibiotics during prolonged hospitalization. Both circumstances would be expected to increase his risk of fungal disease.
Candidal species such as Candida albicans, C. glabrata, and C. parapsilosis are the most common fungal causes of ventriculitis. To our knowledge, this is the first published report of C. dubliensis causing ventriculitis. It is possible that the infection may have been acquired nosocomially. Candida dubliniensis has most frequently been described in HIV-infected individuals on fungal prophylaxis with fluconazole, which reduces the presence of other Candidal species. This patient’s last known HIV test was negative one year before admission.
Other non- Candida fungi such as Aspergillus species, have also been reported as causes of ventriculitis, but usually occur after a longer period following placement of a drain, and more often in the setting of steroid use or other immunosuppression. Tuberculous ventriculitis is a less common diagnosis and would be less likely to be associated with a drain.

history:
Summary: A child with fever and vomiting after a trip to Africa.
A pre-adolescent African-American child returned from a one-month visit to West Africa. On the airplane ride home, the child developed fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting. The patient went emergently to the hospital upon arrival in the United States.

The patient was diagnosed with dactylitis and sickle cell disease as an infant and had received three blood transfusions in the past in West Africa. There was an allergy to chloroquine.

The child had lived in the United States for the previous three years, and had visited extended family in West Africa for one month before admission. No antimalarial prophylaxis had been taken during the trip.

Medications included penicillin and folic acid.
exam_studies:
The patient was febrile and tachycardic, alert and in no distress. Mild scleral icterus and a soft systolic heart murmur were present. The liver edge was three centimeters below the costal margin. There was no splenomegaly or rash.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 23,000 cells/mm³, with a left shift in the differential. The hematocrit was 21%, and platelets 351,000/mm³. The bilirubin was 5.1 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 55 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 32 U/L. Images of the peripheral blood smear are shown (Figures 1 through 3). Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear. Figure 2. Peripheral blood smear. Figure 3. Peripheral blood smear.
Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear.
Figure 2. Peripheral blood smear.
Figure 3. Peripheral blood smear.
diagnosis:
Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a child with sickle cell disease.

The blood smear was positive for Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites. The parasitemia was estimated to be 10%.

Doxycycline and a quinidine infusion were administered. The parasite load fell from 10% at presentation to 4% on the second hospital day; no parasites were seen on the day of discharge. The quinidine infusion was discontinued. No dysrhythmias developed. The child was discharged on oral doxycycline and quinine for five days.

Malaria is one of the most important causes of fever in the returning traveler. The differential diagnosis depends on exposure history and how soon after the trip the traveler presents with fever.
About 90% of Plasmodium falciparum cases are acquired in sub-Saharan Africa; 90% of infected travelers become ill within one month of their return. Chloroquine-resistance is common in much of Africa. The high frequency of the sickle-cell hemoglobin gene in malaria endemic regions is believed to be due to a heterozygote advantage against fatal malaria. However, malaria still occurs in those with sickle cell trait and disease and is associated with crises in the latter; therefore, prophylaxis should be considered.

Summary: A man presented with confusion and ataxia.
A middle-aged man with a pas
history:
Summary: A man presented with confusion and ataxia.
A middle-aged man with a past history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and Hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-infection presented with confusion and ataxia.
One month before his presentation, he developed a severe headache without neurological signs. While riding a bicycle on a trip to the Southeastern United States, he noted a loss of balance. After his return home and during the two weeks preceding his presentation, a rapid deterioration with increasing confusion occurred. He developed repetitive automatic and stereotypic actions, and emotional lability. During the two days before admission, he had difficulty with fine motor skills and coordination. The patient reported chills, without fever or neck stiffness.

HIV-infection had been diagnosed a decade earlier, and recent laboratory testing included an HIV-RNA level of 77,000 copies/mL and CD4 T-lymphocyte count of 34 cells/mm³. There was also a history of chronic active hepatitis C virus infection and, in the past, intravenous drug use. Thrush, leukopenia, and neuropathy had been documented previously.

There was a history of intravenous heroin use in the past.

Medications included didanosine (ddI), stavudine (D4T), and delavirdine.
exam_studies:
The patient was resting in bed comfortably. The temperature was 97°F (36.1°C), pulse 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 136/92 mm Hg, respirations 24 per minute, and oximetry 97% on ambient air. He was awake and oriented to self with a paucity of speech and movements. He had a severely ataxic gait, rising up on his toes in order to walk forward. Strength and sensation were normal, cranial nerves intact, and reflexes symmetrical. The plantar reflexes were flexor. He was confused with poor short-term memory. No asterixis was present and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 2,000/mm³ with a normal differential. A lumbar puncture had a normal opening pressure, with 2 white blood cells and 71 red blood cells per cubic millimeter. The levels of glucose and protein in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were normal and the gram stain was negative. Toxoplasma serologies were negative.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed bilateral white matter signal abnormality primarily involving the frontal lobes. (See Figures 1 through 6.)
Figure 1. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 4. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 5. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 6. MRI scan of the brain.

Ceftriaxone, metronidazole and voriconazole were administered empirically to cover bacterial and fungal brain infections. Despite this therapy, his mental status deteriorated significantly.
diagnosis:
Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy secondary to JC virus infection in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

A brain biopsy was performed and showed extensive macrophage infiltrates, bizarre astrocytic cells and scattered glial nuclei with enlarged amphophilic cytoplasm, consistent with virally infected cells (Figures 7 through 9). Immunohistochemistry was positive for JC virus. JC virus was also detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Figure 7. Brain biopsy viewed under low power magnification.
Figure 8. Brain biopsy.
Figure 9. Brain biopsy.

Zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), ritonavir and lopinavir were initiated and the patient had some minimal response to this. Seizures developed that were initially controlled with antiepileptics, however his mentation never returned to baseline. He subsequently expired from an aspiration event.

Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a demyelinating disease of the central nervous system caused by the polyoma virus JC. It is primarily found in the setting of profoundly immunosuppression such as that seen in advanced AIDS or bone marrow transplanted individuals.
The hallmark of PML is patchy or confluent areas of low attenuation on CT scanning or hyperintensity of T2 weighted images on MRI scanning. These lesions are not usually contrast-enhancing and are not surrounded by edema. As a result, substantial mass effect on surrounding structures is absent. The lesions are usually bilateral, asymmetric and localized in the periventriular areas and subcortical white matter.
Patients with PML present with acute or subacute onset of neurological symptoms, often with focal deficits. The CSF typically does not show inflammatory cells. A CSF PCR test for JC virus is usually positive.
Therapy of HIV-associated PML centers on the use of antiretroviral therapy to achieve immune reconstitution. The prognosis is poor. The use of cidofovir has had mixed results.

Summary: An elderly man with fatigue, fever, and sweats.
A man in his seventies
history:
Summary: An elderly man with fatigue, fever, and sweats.
A man in his seventies presented with a one-month history of progressive fatigue. He noted diffuse arthralgias and had had a poor appetite with a 7-pound weight loss over the preceding three weeks. During the prior week, he had developed low-grade fevers with chills and drenching sweats.

He had a history of prostate cancer for which a radical prostatectomy had been performed. He also had gastroesophageal reflux, diverticular disease with gastrointestinal bleeding in the past, and a history of bilateral total knee replacements.

The patient lived in an urban area of New England. He had traveled to Western Europe three months before becoming ill. He denied recent sick contacts, but did report playing with his grandchildren, including one from Central America. He consumed 1-2 alcoholic beverages per day, never smoked, and had no pets.

The patient was married and retired.

There were no allergies.

Medications included proton pump inhibitor and aspirin.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no distress and the temperature was normal. There were non-tender mobile nodes (1cm by 1cm) present in the posterior cervical chain and left inguinal region. There was no icterus, rash, ecchymoses, or petechiae. The remainder of the dental, pulmonary, cardiac, and abdominal examinations was normal.

The white blood cell count was 23,300 cells/mm³ (13% segmented cells, 1% bands, 60% lymphocytes, 16% atypical cells, 9% monocytes, and 1% prolymphocytes); hematocrit 42.5%; platelets 247,000/mm³ with clumps, prothrombin time 12.5 seconds, and partial thromboplastin time 30.3 seconds. The creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 455 U/liter, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 447 U/liter, alkaline phosphatase 687 U/liter, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 526 U/liter.

Serologic tests were sent and flow cytometry was performed on peripheral blood. Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen were performed (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Acute mononucleosis due to Epstein Barr virus (EBV) infection in an elderly adult.

Testing for cytomegalovirus (CMV) Immunoglobulin G was positive, consistent with prior infection. Testing for Hepatitis B surface antigen, antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody was negative. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood showed T-cell lymphocytosis with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio. The serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) was normal.
Ultrasonography of the liver showed cholelithiasis, without cholecystitis, and a fatty liver. CT scanning of the abdomen demonstrated mesenteric adenopathy and colonic wall thickening with multiple low attenuation foci within the spleen, as well as cholelithiasis, diverticulosis and evidence of past radical prostatectomy (Figures 1 and 2).
The heterophile test was positive. Epstein Barr virus (EBV) serology was consistent with acute Epstein Barr virus (EBV) infection: Anti-VCA IgG 640, anti-VCA IgM 20, early antigen > 640, and antinuclear antigen <10.

The patient recovered uneventfully without additional treatment.

Epstein Barr virus (EBV) is a pathogen found throughout the world with great geographical variation in its pattern of disease. In much of the world, where poor hygiene and crowding are common, virtually all people are seropositive by age 4 years. Less is known about infection in middle and late adulthood, since less than 10% of persons over age 60 years lack Epstein-Barr virus-specific antibodies and are therefore at risk.
Older adults infrequently present with sore throat, peripheral lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly and are more likely to present with enigmatic fever, jaundice, hepatitis, or neurologic disorders. Elderly hosts typically have fewer atypical lymphocytes and less prominent leukocytosis and lymphocytosis. Heterophile-negative acute EBV infection is also more common in the elderly and young children. Older individuals therefore are more likely to undergo unnecessary tests, such as biopsies of lymph nodes, bone marrow, liver, temporal arteries. Thus clinicians must be alert to the diagnosis.
EBV syndromes are generally self-limited, and there is no role for acyclovir in this situation.

history:
Summary: A man with chest wall pain and induration after a dog bite.
A man in his forties presented with one week of chest wall pain, redness, swelling and induration. The pain had started in the right axilla and then moved into the chest wall and abdomen.
Three weeks before his presentation, he had suffered a dog bite that had punctured the skin of his right hand. He did not seek medical care or notice any signs of infection at the time.

He had a history of childhood polio.

He was originally from Puerto Rico, and had lived in United States for the previous ten years.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C), pulse 124 beats per minute; the other vital signs were normal. There was a soft tissue abscess in the right chest wall that extended into the right axilla and mid abdominal wall. (See Figure 1 for appearance after incision and drainage procedure.) The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings after initial incision and drainage.

The white blood cell count was 15,300 cells/mm³ with 71% polymorphonuclear leukocytes and 16% band formss. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the chest showed a soft tissue mass consistent with an abscess in the subpectoralis area (Figure 2).
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.

The patient was started on vancomycin and ampicillin-sulbactam intravenously. The soft tissue mass was incised and revealed a purulent discharge that was sent for stains and cultures. The gram stain is shown in Figure 3. A biopsy of the fascia showed no evidence of necrotizing fasciitis.
Figure 3. Gram stain of purulent discharge.
diagnosis:
Soft tissue abscess secondary to Pasteurella multocida infection, following a dog bite.

Culture of the purulent discharge grew Pasteurella multocida (Figure 3).

The patient went to the operating room where the surgeons found 600 cubic centimeters of purulent material. Intravenous penicillin was administered for two weeks and was followed by oral amoxicillin. On follow-up, the patient was doing very well.

Pasteurella multocida is a gram-negative aerobic rod that is frequently isolated from infected dog or cat bite wounds. Characteristically, infections by Pasteurella species become symptomatic during the first 24 hours after the injury. Symptoms include erythema, swelling, tenderness and drainage at the site of the bite.
Infections due to Pasteurella most often remain localized to the inoculated wound with cellulitis and abscesses. Direct extension to surrounding tissues may lead to lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy. Bacteremia may occur with metastatic foci including osteomyelitis, arthritis, tenosynovitis, sepsis, meningitis, brain abscess, pneumonia and endocarditis. Pasteurella multocida bacteremia is associated with cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, hematologic malignancies, neoplasms and immunosuppression.
Penicillin is the drug of choice for P. multocida infections. Ampicillin and amoxicillin-clavulanate also offer adequate activity. Cefuroxime and cefpodoxime have better in vitro activity against Pasteurella species than other cephalosporins. Nafcillin, dicloxacillin, cefazolin, cefaclor, cefadroxil, and cephalexin have inadequate activity against most strains of Pasteurella species. Clindamycin and the aminoglycosides have poor activity against Pasteurella spp.

history:
Summary: A man with congenital heart disease and skin lesions.
A man in his forties with a history of congenital cyanotic heart disease and polyarteritis nodosum presented with nodular skin lesions.
One year before admission, the patient developed fevers, rash and testicular pain and swelling. A biopsy of the skin and testicles showed vasculitis, and a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosum was made. Prednisone (60 mg daily) was administered.
Approximately six months before admission, he was diagnosed with an occlusion of the basilar artery. Angiography showed irregularity of the intracerebral vessels that was consistent with, although not diagnostic of, vasculitis of the central nervous system. At that time, low-grade fevers were documented and, because additional immunosuppressive therapy was being considered for his vasculitis, an evaluation for an infectious etiology was performed.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a cavitary lesion (2.5-centimeters in diameter) in the right lower lobe and a left lower lobe nodule (1cm in diameter). It was thought that these might be due to infarct, septic emboli, or vasculitis. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and trans-thoracic echocardiography were negative.
Approximately three months before admission, cyclophosphamide treatment was begun. One month before admission, he developed a lesion on his right forearm. In the following weeks, lesions appeared on all four extremities. A skin biopsy showed a neutrophilic panniculitis; bacterial and fungal stains and cultures were negative. The patient also noted several weeks of a non-productive cough.
On the day of admission, the temperature rose to 101.5°F (38.6°C) and the patient noted fatigue.

He had a history of congenital cyanotic heart disease, polyarteritis nodosum, diabetes mellitus, reactive airway disease, gout and osteoarthritis.
Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tuberculosis (Mantoux skin test) were negative.

There were no exposures to sick contacts or recent travel. The patient had lived in California and Arizona in the past, and had moved to the United States Northeast. He was heterosexual.

He lived with his wife and children.

Medications included prednisone 25 mg daily, cyclophosphamide monthly and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily.
exam_studies:
The patient was cyanotic, with a chronically ill and cushingoid appearance. The temperature was 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure 90/56 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respirations 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 70% on 3 liters of oxygen. Breath sounds were decreased at the bases, and there was no lymphadenopathy. The cardiac examination was unchanged from baseline.
There were approximately 20 nodular skin lesions on his upper and lower extremities (Figures 1 through 4). Skin lesions were also present around the rectum.
Figure 1. Physical findings on the thigh.
Figure 2. Physical findings on the thigh.
Figure 3. Physical findings on the ankle.
Figure 4. Physical findings.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 15,700/mm³ (93% neutrophils and 2% lymphocytes), hematocrit 53% (his baseline level) and platelets 331,000/mm³. The serum level of urea nitrogen (BUN) was 25 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 50 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 65 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L and total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL.
CT scanning of the chest showed cavitary lesions in the left lower lobe and right lower lobe (Figures 5 and 6). CT scanning of the abdomen showed a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the peri-rectal fat with a sinus tract extending into a phlegmonous collection in his inferior right buttocks.
Figure 5. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 6. CT scan of the chest.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Mycobacterium abscessus in a patient with congenital cyanotic heart disease, polyarteritis nodosum, and diabetes mellitus.

Cultures of the blood, sputum and skin (by biopsy) were sent. The skin biopsy showed necrosis with abscess formation and was positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB).
The skin biopsy, sputum, and blood cultures all grew acid-fast bacilli within several days. The patient was diagnosed with disseminated rapidly growing mycobacterial infection, subsequently identified as Mycobacterium abscessus.
Figure 7. Abscesses in the left and right lungs.
Figure 8. Lung pathology with abscesses.
Figure 9. Acid-fast stain of a lung abscess.
Figure 10. AFB staining of a lung abscess.

He was treated with cefoxitin, amikacin, and clarithromycin, but was readmitted one week later with acute renal failure.
At the time, his antibiotics were changed to linezolid, gatifloxacin, clarithromycin, and cefoxitin. Unfortunately, the patient expired on the fifth hospital day. A limited autopsy was performed. His lungs showed an abscess cavity, and acid-fast bacilli were identified (Figures 7 through 10). There were microabscesses in his kidneys that were AFB-smear negative.

Mycobacterium abscessus is one of the rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). Mycobacterium fortuitum, Mycobacterium chelonae, and M. abscessus account for more than 90% of infections caused by rapidly growing NTM. Rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) cause pulmonary disease, skin and soft tissue infections, bone and joint infection, catheter-related infections, and disseminated disease. In over 80% of cases of pulmonary disease caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria, M. abscessus is the pathogen.
This patient's case is unusual in that presumably he initially had a pulmonary infection with M. abscessus that later disseminated after he received immunosuppressive therapy.
In most reported cases of disseminated rapidly growing mycobacterial infections, the primary site of infection is not clear. Disease caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria can occur in immunocompetent patients as well, but in that setting is most often post-traumatic or a surgical wound infection. Disseminated disease generally occurs in patients who are immunocompromised, often those on steroid therapy or with a history of end-stage renal disease. Multiple skin lesions, usually involving extremities, characterize disseminated disease.
The treatment of rapidly growing mycobacteria depends upon the antibiotic sensitivity of the isolate. Rapidly growing mycobacteria are not sensitive to agents used for tuberculosis and have different antibiotic sensitivities from each other. M. abscessus isolates are resistant to most oral agents. They are generally susceptible to amikacin, cefoxitin, and imipenem. Clarithromycin is one of the few oral antibiotics with activity against M. abscessus. Based upon in vitro data, linezolid also appears to have activity against some RGM. Extensive infection or disseminated disease should be treated with combination therapy. Pulmonary disease due to M. abscessus has generally not been successfully treated with antibiotic therapy. Courses of clarithromycin, cefoxitin, and amikacin may result in clinical improvement but not microbiologic cure.

history:
Summary: A man with fatigue, jaundice and dark urine.
A man in his forties with a history of an aortic valve replacement and pacemaker placement presented to his primary care physician with fatigue, abdominal pain, jaundice and dark urine. Hepatitis serologies revealed that the patient had acquired hepatitis A. Blood cultures drawn in clinic grew a gram-positive bacillus, and the patient was admitted to an outside hospital.
At the outside hospital, a transesophageal echocardiogram was positive for an aortic vegetation (1.3 centimeter by 1.5 centimeter) that was new when compared to a study one year earlier. The patient was transferred to a tertiary medical center.

The patient had previously used intravenous drugs, and six years earlier had developed native valve enterococcal endocarditis. A homograft aortic valve replacement and one-vessel coronary artery bypass graft were performed. A dual chamber pacemaker was inserted for treatment of complete heart block in the setting of an embolic coronary event. He also had Hepatitis C virus infection and hypertension, and had had a cerebrovascular stroke and a splenic infarct in the past.

The patient resided in the southern United States. He denied intravenous drug use for the preceding three years, and also denied other recent drug use, tobacco or alcohol use. He was employed and lived with a relative.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.2°F (36.8°C), pulse 67 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, respirations 12 per minute, and oxygen saturation 97%. A systolic ejection murmur was present, unchanged from earlier examinations.

The patient was transferred to the tertiary medical center, and was not receiving antibiotics. Additional blood cultures were obtained and were positive for the same organism found growing in the blood cultures that had been drawn at the outside hospital (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Stain of growth from blood culture.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Prosthetic valve endocarditis due to a rapidly growing mycobacterium, Mycobacterium chelonae.

All blood cultures eventually grew out a gram-positive bacillus in the aerobic bottles. This was initially identified at the outside hospital as modified acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain positive, and later shown to be AFB-stain positive, shown in Figures 1 and 2, as well. Probes were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC).
Blood cultures drawn at the tertiary hospital were positive after five days, and the organism was classified as a rapidly growing mycobacterium. Subsequent biochemical tests identified the organism as Mycobacterium chelonae.

After cultures were obtained, vancomycin, cefotaxime, and doxycycline were administered to treat common gram-positive rods as well as atypical causes of endocarditis. Soon after the patient's admission, an embolic lesion on his left fifth digit appeared.
When the organism was found to exhibit modified acid-fast-bacilli (AFB) staining, cefotaxime was discontinued and imipenem was administered. The doxycycline was changed to minocycline for increased activity against possible Nocardia infection.
The following day, when the laboratory of the initial hospital determined that the isolate was also AFB-stain positive and probes were negative for M. tuberculosis and M. avium complex (MAC), clarithromycin and levofloxacin were added for their activity against the rapidly growing mycobacteria. The patient received imipenem, clarithromycin, amikacin and levofloxacin while the M. chelonae susceptibilities were being determined.
Fourteen days after the patient's admission to the tertiary center, with negative blood cultures documented, an ascending aortic resection was performed with St. Jude's aortic valve replacement and partial homograft endarterectomy.
Life-long suppression with oral antibiotics based on susceptibility testing was planned.

There are few reported cases of rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) causing endocarditis. The majority of cases were reported in patients with prosthetic valves and occurred soon after valve replacement raising the possibility of hospital acquisition. Only one other “late occurrence” is reported.
Surgery is critical in managing these patients with close to 100% mortality resulting if the valve is not removed. Antimicrobials should be selected based on susceptibilities of the known RGM. Mycobacterium fortuitum is usually susceptible to amikacin, cefoxitin, amikacin, and quinolones. Mycobacterium abscessus and Mycobacterium chelonae are more resistant but these mycobacteria are generally susceptible to clarithromycin. These organisms are also usually susceptible to amikacin.

history:
Summary: A man with lymphoma and a fever.
A male in his sixties, with a history of relapsed non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that included central nervous system involvement, presented with temperature to 102°F (38.9°C), chills, rigors, and erythema and tenderness at the site of a long-term intravenous catheter at the subcutaneous tunneling site.
The patient was receiving cyclophosphamide via the catheter for stem cell mobilization in preparation for a bone marrow transplant. A course of chemotherapy had been completed eight months earlier and included CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone), rituximab and intrathecal cytarabine.
Two days before his presentation, a painful pustule had been noted on the left side of his neck. The pustule had become necrotic over the previous 24 hours. On the day of admission, he was noted to have a new left forearm pustule that was painful and erythematous.

There was a history of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and varicella zoster.

He was taking cyclophosphamide.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared toxic. The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C), pulse 128 beats per minute, respirations 16 per minute, and the oxygen saturation was 96% on ambient air. The sclera were anicteric, and there were no conjunctival hemorrhages or petechiae. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. The lungs were clear; there were no cardiac murmurs, and the abdomen was benign. Examination of the skin revealed a 0.5-centimeter punctate lesion with central necrosis and surrounding erythema on the left forearm and a necrotic, painful lesion (2-centimeter by 2-centimeter) with surrounding erythema and tenderness on the left neck (Figures 1 and 2). No exudates were seen. The hands and nails were free of rash or lesions.
Figure 1. Physical finding on arm.
Figure 2. Physical finding of neck.

The white blood cell count was 10 cells/mm³, hematocrit 21%, platelets 27,000/mm³, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Tests of liver function and urinalysis were normal, and the urine culture was negative. A chest radiograph did not show an infiltrate, and an echocardiogram did not reveal a vegetation.

Treatment with vancomycin, ceftazidime, and amphotericin was begun empirically for febrile neutropenia and the possibility of disseminated fungemia. Cultures and a skin biopsy of the neck lesion were obtained (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. H and E stain of neck biopsy.
Figure 4. Gram stain of neck biopsy.
diagnosis:
Ecthyma gangrenosum secondary to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia in a neutropenic patient.

Blood cultures (four of four) were positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. A skin biopsy of the neck lesion was obtained and showed dermal and subcutaneous bacterial infection with abundant gram-positive cocci. There was no accompanying inflammatory or necrotic response in vessels. Silver stains for fungal organisms were negative.

The intravenous catheter was removed and vancomycin was administered for six weeks.

In a neutropenic patient, fever and necrotic skin lesions may reflect systemic blood-borne infection. The differential diagnosis in such cases is broad and includes disseminated fungal infection (fusariosis or candidiasis, for example), ecthyma gangrenosum and (occasionally) anaerobic infection or anaerobic-and-gram-negative mixed infections. Given the breadth of the differential diagnosis, early skin biopsy is important for successful management.
Although ecthyma gangrenosum is classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other gram-negative rods, similar lesions may be seen in sepsis due to other organisms, including Staphylococcus aureus.
