title:
Summary: A middle-aged man with a headache and fevers.
A middle-aged man present
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with a headache and fevers.
A middle-aged man presented with a right posterolateral headache and fevers up to 101.4°F (38.6°C) for three days. He had no nausea, vomiting, visual symptoms, dysarthria, aphasia or weakness. There had been no recent trauma or dental work.

He had a history of Osler Weber Rendu Syndrome and pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). He had a right temporal brain abscess seven years previously, which had been treated with surgical resection and antibiotics.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable and drowsy. He was afebrile with normal vital signs; the oxygen saturation was 88% on ambient air. His speech was slow and labored, and some word finding difficulty was noted. The motor and sensory examinations were normal. There was mild clubbing and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical findings.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (Figures 2 and 3) revealed a round, 2-centimeter by 2-centimeter ring-enhancing lesion in the anterior portion of the right temporal lobe and a 4-millimeter left frontal lobe lesion. There was also right occipital lobe encephalomalacia at the site of the resection of his previous brain abscess.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain.
diagnosis:
Bacterial brain abscess in a patient with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler Weber Rendu) and pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

The patient underwent a craniotomy, and cultures from resected brain mass grew a mixture of organisms, including alpha-hemolytic Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group), Prevotella intermedia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Peptostreptococcus species and Bacteroides ureolyticus.

The patient was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole for a prolonged course and recovered completely.

There are several underlying conditions that are associated with bacterial brain abscesses. Extension of infection from the paranasal sinuses, middle ear or teeth may lead to brain abscess. Brain abscess also sometimes develops following penetrating head trauma or after neurosurgery. Cerebral emboli in the setting of endocarditis can result in multiple brain abscesses. Finally, metastatic seeding from distant sites of infection or from transient bacteremia may rarely lead to brain abscess. The likelihood of this is increased by conditions in which there is shunting of blood from the right to the left side of the circulation. These conditions include certain types of congenital heart disease and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), including pulmonary AVMs as in this case.
Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are common in patients with Osler Weber Rendu (OWR) disease (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia) who have neurologic involvement. In a case series of patients with pulmonary AVMs, more than half had OWR and 37% of all patients had neurological complications, including bacterial brain abscess.

title:
Summary: A patient with leg swelling.
A middle-aged patient presented with lower
history:
Summary: A patient with leg swelling.
A middle-aged patient presented with lower extremity swelling.

The patient lived in a shelter.

Naproxen.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The vital signs were normal. The lower extremities had several ulcers with surrounding erythema and superficial exudates; some had central eschar. The neurologic and vascular examinations were normal. Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The complete blood count (CBC) including the white blood cell differential was within normal limits. Liver function tests were normal. Tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Hepatitis B virus or Hepatitis C virus infections were negative, and testing for autoimmune diseases was normal.
diagnosis:
Pyoderma gangrenosum.

A biopsy showed extensive neutrophilic abscess formation with focal vasculitis consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum. Superficial cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

Azathioprine and broad spectrum antibiotics were administered and the patient had a good clinical response.

Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is one of a group of disorders known as neutrophilic dermatoses. The lesions are characterized histologically by an epidermal and/or dermal inflammatory infiltrate that is predominantly composed of neutrophils without evidence of vasculitis or infection. The lesions in PG can be single or multiple, chronic and recurrent. Lesions are most commonly found on the extremities and particularly in the pretibial area, as in this case.
A lesion begins as a follicular erythematous papule or pustule or a hemorrhagic bulla on an erythematous base, which then breaks down to form an ulcer with a ragged, violaceous gunmetal colored border. Lesions enlarge at sites of trauma and heal with an atrophic cribiform scar.
The lesions are usually associated with an underlying systemic disease such as arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease or a lymphoproliferative disorder. Diagnostic testing should include a skin biopsy involving the inflamed border and cultures for bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal organisms. A complete blood count, sedimentation rate, liver function tests, creatinine, coagulation studies, serum protein electrophoresis, cryoglobulins and testing for anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA) should be performed.

title:
Summary: A teenager presented with a skin ulcer after a trip to South America.
A
history:
Summary: A teenager presented with a skin ulcer after a trip to South America.
A teenager presented with a non-healing skin ulcer after returning from South America.
Two weeks after returning to the United States, the patient noted a swollen lymph node in the right groin. This was followed by the development of three papular skin lesions located below the right knee. A primary care physician evaluated the patient and administered antibiotics. The lesions did not improve and evolved into a single, non-painful, intermittently weeping ulcer.
Two months after the appearance of the swollen lymph node, the patient presented for further evaluation. There was no history of fevers or trauma to the affected area, and the patient felt well.

Six months before presentation, the patient had traveled to South America. The first three months of the trip were spent working with children in Peru and traveling to highland areas and Titicaca. During the fourth month, the patient traveled to Bolivia and the jungle area in Rurrenabaque before returning to the United States in the late spring.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. There was a single 4 x 5 centimeter ulcerated lesion with heaped-up margins and violaceous base immediately below the right patella (Figures 1 and 2). There was no surrounding erythema, lymphangitis or sporotrichoid manifestations noted. A lymph node (two-centimeters in diameter) was palpable in the right groin. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 7,600/mm³, with 63% leukocytes, 30% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 2% eosinophils. Other laboratory tests, including hemoglobin, hematocrit, electrolytes, and testing for renal and liver function, were normal.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous New World Leishmaniasis, due to Leishmania braziliensis.

A skin biopsy was positive for Leishmania braziliensis.

Intravenous antimony was administered for twenty-one days, and the lesion resolved completely.

The subacute development, in a returned traveler, of papules that coalesce into an ulcer without associated systemic symptomatology is characteristic of Leishmania infection. New World (braziliensis, mexicana) and Old World (major, aethiopica, tropica, donovani) Leishmania should be distinguished from one another. When Leishmania braziliensis is the causative agent, treatment may prevent remote recurrences in nasopharynx (bundia). The primary lesions heal spontaneously over many months and treatment is not indicated in most cases. The gold standard of treatment is 20mg/kg antimony intravenously per day for 20-28 days; proposed alternatives pentamadine, amphotericin, and ketoconazole have not been fully evaluated.

title: Summary: A woman on chemotherapy for a malignancy with back pain and urinary ret
history:
Summary: A woman on chemotherapy for a malignancy with back pain and urinary retention.
A middle-aged woman presented with back pain, suprapubic pain, urinary retention and constipation. She denied fevers, chills and nausea.

The patient had recently been diagnosed with a malignancy. Multiple cycles of chemotherapy had been administered, the most recent ending the week prior to presentation.

She had been receiving doxorubicin, vincristine, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, and ifosfamide.
exam_studies:
The patient was unable to sit due to discomfort. The temperature was 97°F (36.1°C), pulse 140 beats per minute, and the blood pressure 128/57 mm Hg. The abdomen was soft, with mild suprapubic tenderness, and decreased bowel sounds. There was no rebound or guarding. A reducible vaginal prolapse and mild perirectal inflammation were present, but no other significant skin changes were seen in the perineum or perirectal area and no spinal tenderness was noted.

The white blood cell count was 110 cells/mm³ with 3% neutrophils. A chest radiograph was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine did not reveal any cord compression. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen demonstrated fat stranding surrounding the anorectal tissues and edema to the level of the sigmoid colon, as well as free fluid in the pelvic cavity (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. CT scan of the pelvis.
Figure 2. CT scan of the pelvis.

Within hours of presentation, the temperature increased to 101.3°F (38.5°C) and the blood pressure became unstable. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and the trachea was intubated due to respiratory distress. The abdomen became distended and tense; the perineum and perirectal region became erythematous and then progressed to an ashen appearance.
diagnosis:
Spontaneous, nontraumatic gas gangrene (Clostridium septicum myonecrosis) in a neutropenic patient.

Blood cultures grew Clostridium septicum.

Vancomycin, gentamicin, imipenem, clindamycin, intravenous immunoglobulin and activated protein C were administered. Surgical consultation was obtained soon after presentation to the emergency department and felt the patient was not a surgical condidate. Unfortunately, the patient died within 48 hours of admission.

The rapid clinical progression to critical illness and positive blood cultures for Clostridium septicum are consistent with spontaneous, nontraumatic gas gangrene. Typically, there is a predisposing, underlying intestinal tract abnormality such as colon cancer, diverticulitis or bowel infarction. Mucosal ulceration or perforation may lead to intra-abdominal infection or, less frequently, to bacteremic spread. Leukemia, diabetes mellitus and neutropenia (as in this case) are also risk factors.
Spontaneous Clostridium septicum gas gangrene often presents fulminantly and the mortality may be as high as 67-100%. Most patients succumb in the first 24 hours of presentation. At the time of surgical inspection, the involved muscle groups fail to contract on stimulation and do not bleed from a cut surface. These areas later become discolored and friable.

title:
Summary: A woman with a history of colon cancer and a pulmonary nodule.
A woman
history:
Summary: A woman with a history of colon cancer and a pulmonary nodule.
A woman in her sixties had a pulmonary nodule (1-centimeter in diameter) found incidentally on computed tomography (CT) scanning of the chest, without parenchymal disease. The study (Figure 1 below) had been performed for a routine follow-up of colon cancer. The patient reported no respiratory symptoms, fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss. Previous CT scanning from three months before admission was negative.
A positron emission tomographic (PET) scan was obtained and showed increased metabolic activity in the area of the nodule. She was admitted and underwent surgical resection of the nodule.

Stage II colon cancer had been diagnosed two years before admission. A sigmoid colectomy was performed and adjuvant chemotherapy, comprised of 5-fluorouracil and leucovorin, was administered. There had been no evidence of relapse on prior studies.

She was born and raised in New England, lived in a suburb, and had no pets. She had traveled to Europe many years ago, and spent a few days in the United States Southwest four months before admission. There was no other history of travel to other states or countries. She was retired, and had worked in a medical facility in the past. She had no known exposure to tuberculosis; a PPD test had been negative years ago.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile with stable vital signs. The examination was normal except for a healing surgical scar.

The complete blood count and metabolic profile were normal. A tuberculin skin test (PPD) was negative. Sputum cultures were also negative.
CT scanning of the chest (Figure 1) showed a one-centimeter soft tissue, nodular opacity deep to the right margin of the sternum, at the level of the top of the right mainstem bronchus.
Figure 1. CT scan of the chest.

The patient did well following the surgical resection of the nodule. Pathologic examination of the tissue is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Stain of resected lung nodule.
Figure 3. Stain of resected lung nodule.
diagnosis:
Histoplasmosis.

Pathologic examination of the excised nodule showed necrotizing granulomas with organisms consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum. Hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figure 2) showed necrotizing caseating granulomas, and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining of the organisms revealed budding forms (Figure 3). Cultures taken during the surgical procedure were negative.

The patient was started on itraconazole (200 mg oral solution twice daily) with the plan of continuing therapy for three months.

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that causes a wide spectrum of disease in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. It is found in temperate zones around the world.
In the United States, H. capsulatum is endemic within the Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys. A few cases of histoplasmosis in the New England area without travel to the histoplasmosis “belt” have been described. The natural habitat of H. capsulatum is soil, especially soil with high organic content such as that enriched with bird, chicken, or bat excrement. Many types of occupational and recreational activities (e.g. cave exploring, excavation) have resulted in outbreaks of histoplasmosis.
The vast majority of infections caused by H. capsulatum are acquired by inhalation and deposition of mycelial fragments into the alveoli. The organism converts into its pathogenic yeast form and is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages. The yeast forms multiply within the macrophages, eventually causing the destruction of these macrophages. The released yeasts spread to the regional lymph nodes and other organs via the lymphatics and blood. Specific T cell-mediated immunity develops in 2-4 weeks and inhibits the growth of the organisms. Resolution occurs with production of a granulomatous inflammatory reaction, which may be caseating but usually becomes calcified. The yeasts persist for prolonged periods within these caseating granulomas.
The severity of illness after inhalation exposure to H. capsulatum varies, depending on the intensity of exposure and the immunity of the host. Asymptomatic infection or mild pulmonary disease follows low-intensity exposures in healthy individuals, whereas heavy exposure may cause severe diffuse pulmonary infection. Progressive dissemination occurs primarily in those with underlying immunosuppressive disorders or those at the extremes of age. Progressive pulmonary infection is common in patients with underlying centrilobular emphysema. A variety of acute and chronic manifestations of histoplasmosis appear to result from unusual inflammatory or fibrotic responses to the infection, including rheumatologic syndromes and pericarditis during the first year after exposure, and chronic mediastinal inflammation or fibrosis, broncholithiasis, and enlarging parenchymal granulomas occurring later.
The indications for treatment in patients with histoplasmosis vary. In this case, because the patient showed active inflammation and necrotizing granulomas, and because there was a risk of immunosuppression in the future due to her history of colon cancer, itraconazole was administered for three months.

title:
Summary: A woman with rectal bleeding.

history:
Summary: A woman with rectal bleeding.
A young adult woman presented with bright red blood per rectum.
She had a history of a congenital clotting factor deficiency that had been discovered in her teenaged years when she had symptoms of menorrhagia, bleeding gums and episodic hematochezia. Several hospitalizations for gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding had occurred, including an admission one month earlier that was treated conservatively with packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and epsilon aminocaproic acid. Between bleeding episodes, bowel movements were normal.
She was admitted to the intensive care unit after 4-5 episodes of hematochezia. There were no systemic symptoms such as weight loss, fevers, chills, night sweats, cough, or abdominal pain.

There was a history of a congenital clotting factor deficiency.

Three months before admission, she had emigrated from an urban community on the Indian sub-continent. She reported no exposures to animals or sick contacts.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well-developed and in mild distress. The temperature was 99.4°F (37.4°C), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 103/57 mm Hg and 100% oxygen saturation on 2-liters oxygen by nasal cannula. There was no scleral icterus, oral lesion, or lymphadenopathy. The lungs were rhonchorous bilaterally, and no cardiac murmurs were present. The abdomen was soft and there was no organomegaly. Skin and joint examinations were normal.

The hematocrit was 17% and the remainder of the laboratory tests was normal. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Chest radiography showed patchy airspace disease in the perihilar region. An upper endoscopic examination was negative. Colonoscopy revealed ileal ulcers and pseudopolyps (Figures 1 through 4).
Figure 1. Findings on colonoscopy.
Figure 2. Findings on colonoscopy.
Figure 3. Findings on colonoscopy.
Figure 4. Findings on colonoscopy.

A biopsy of the terminal ileum was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stains of the biopsy are shown in Figures 5 and 6.
Figure 5. H and E stain of biopsy.
Figure 6. H and E stain of biopsy (detail).
diagnosis:
Gastrointestinal tuberculosis (clinical diagnosis).

The biopsy of the terminal ileum showed ulcerative granulomatous colitis (Figures 5 and 6). Warthin starry and Brown Hopps stains were negative. Ziehl Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli was positive (Figures 7 and 8).
Purified protein derivative (PPD) skin testing was positive at 14 millimeters induration. Sputum was induced three times and the results were negative. Stool ova and parasites and cultures were negative. Culture of the ileal biopsy was negative.
Chest radiography cleared rapidly; the abnormal chest radiography at admission was thought to be the result of pulmonary hemorrhage due to her underlying coagulopathy.
Figure 7. Ziehl Neelsen stain of biopsy.
Figure 8. Detail of Figure 7.

The patient was started on antituberculous therapy with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, as well as Vitamin B6 supplementation. She had no further bleeding and did well.

Extrapulmonary tuberculosis constitutes an increasing proportion of tuberculosis (TB) cases reported in the United States (16% in 1991 vs. 20% in 2001). Risk factors for extrapulmonary TB include younger age, HIV infection and female gender.
The most frequently reported extrapulmonary sites of the disease are the lymph nodes, pleura, and bones or joints. However, central nervous system (CNS) disease, genitourinary disease, and abdominal/intestinal disease (as in this case) have been described. The negative stool cultures and ova and parasites ruled out entamoeba and Yersinia in this case. The biopsy of this patient was not consistent with lymphoma or adenocarcinoma.
Granulomatous disease in a young woman with episodic hematochezia placed inflammatory bowel disease quite high on the differential. Gastrointestinal tuberculosis, however, has the characteristic colonoscopic features noted in this case: ileal ulceration and pseudopolyp formation. The diagnosis of gastrointestinal tuberculosis is supported by the patient's exposure to an area endemic for tuberculosis, the positive mantoux (PPD) skin test, and the acid-fast bacilli visible on colonic biopsy.

title:
Summary: A woman with suprapubic and left flank pain.
A woman in her thirties pr
history:
Summary: A woman with suprapubic and left flank pain.
A woman in her thirties presented to the hospital with a three-month history of suprapubic and left flank pain. She was initially evaluated in the Caribbean, diagnosed with a kidney stone and a urinary tract infection, and treated with ciprofloxacin. She had persistent symptoms and presented for further evaluation.

The patient was originally from an island in the Caribbean.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 97.9°F (36.6°C), vital signs were normal. There was tenderness in the left costo-vertebral and suprapubic regions. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the abdomen and pelvis showed a ureteral stone (4-millimeter in diameter) with hydroureter, a low-attenuation rounded lesion (2.3cm by 3.4cm) in the left kidney that enhanced and had thickened walls (Figure 1), and an irregularly thickened bladder wall (Figure 2).
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Renal tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A mantoux test (PPD) was placed and was positive with 17 millimeters induration. Aspiration of the renal mass revealed 3+ acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis that was sensitive to all drugs tested. M. tuberculosis from renal aspirate is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Mycobacterium tuberculosis from renal aspirate, acid-fast stain.

The patient was treated with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. A stent was placed and she was discharged home. After two months, the medications were changed to isoniazid and rifampin to complete a six-month course of therapy.

Renal tuberculosis begins with hematogenous seeding, usually at the time of primary pulmonary infection. Disease may occur in the immediate post-primary period or, more commonly, due to reactivation of a renal focus. Less often, late reactivation at another site may lead to miliary disease and hematogenous seeding of the kidney, followed by clinical disease. The majority of patients develop granulomatous lesions in the glomeruli that, in most cases, heal without producing any significant renal disease. An autopsy study of pulmonary tuberculosis revealed unsuspected renal foci in 73% of patients.
Occasionally the granulomas may caseate and rupture into the tubular lumen, with passage of bacilli into the medullary interstitium, eventually leading to granuloma formation and progressive medullary injury. The onset is usually insidious. Dysuria and gross hematuria are the most common symptoms. Renal colic, respiratory complaints and systemic symptoms are uncommon, since rupture of the glomerular granulomas is independent of disease elsewhere. Some patients are asymptomatic and are incidentally found to have pyuria or microscopic hematuria.
Radiologic studies are often helpful. Intravenous pyelogram (IVP) may be normal in early disease, however, moderate to marked urinary tract abnormalities are usually present by the time the patient becomes symptomatic. Changes on IVP include erosion of the tips of the calyces, blunting of the calyces, papillary necrosis and parenchymal scarring and calcification. Computed tomography may show similar findings. Occasionally patients can present with mass-like lesions or tuberculomas.
Signs of extrarenal disease include ureteral strictures and a contracted bladder. In males, calcification of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles or prostate may be seen.
The finding of acid-fast organisms in the urine is not pathognomonic for tuberculosis, since nonpathogenic mycobacteria may rarely be present. Although sterile pyuria is typical of renal tuberculosis, positive urine cultures for routine bacterial pathogens may lead to misdiagnosis. Urine culture for mycobacteria is the gold standard for establishing the diagnosis. Three large volume specimens should be sent to maximize sensitivity. Appropriate treatment with antituberculous agents is usually successful.

history:
Summary: A young child with a fever, rash and mouth ulcers.
A young child with a history of eczema was admitted with a 6-day history of temperatures to 103°F (39.4°C), diffuse tender lymphadenopathy, increasing eczema with scabbing, rhinorrhea, and mouth ulcers.
Two days before admission, a pediatrician prescribed clarithromycin to treat a bacterial superinfection of the eczema. The skin condition worsened and the patient developed diffuse lesions, described as “small blisters”, on the hands, feet and legs. The child was brought to the hospital for further evaluation. The mother reported that the patient had been eating poorly because of a sore mouth, and had lost two pounds in one week.

The patient's past history included:
1. Eczema, with episodes of cellulitis multiple times each year
2. Streptococcal pharyngitis
3. Aphthous ulcers
4. Surgical repair of an atrial septal defect

The child lived in an urban area of the United States Northeast. There was no history of recent travel, ill contacts, or insect bites.

The patient was allergic to penicillin, cephalosporins, and multiple foods.

Clarithromycin.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile and in no distress. There was a normal oropharynx without oral or perioral ulcers. There was shotty cervical and groin adenopathy; no organomegaly was palpated. Sparse small vesicles were present on an erythematous base overlying erythematous, largely scabbed plaques on the anterior thighs, shins, ankles, and feet. There were intact periungual vesicles near the 2nd and 3rd digits of the right hand and over the ankle. Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Eczema herpeticum (herpes simplex virus-1 infection) with impetigo due to Staphylococcus aureus.

An intact vesicle was unroofed and sent for immunofluorescent assay (IFA) and viral culture. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) was detected by the IFA and HSV-1 grew on viral culture. A swab obtained from a weeping area of lower leg grew Staphylococcus aureus on bacterial culture.

After one week of therapy with acyclovir and clindamycin, there was near total resolution of the lesions.

Eczema herpeticum has also been called “Kaposi’s varicelliform eruption due to herpes simplex virus.” It frequently occurs in atopic individuals, such as this patient, or in persons with other skin conditions which compromise the epidermis. The stomatitis described by the mother might have represented primary herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Mouth-hand contact may have lead to herpetic whitlow with subsequent spread of the viral infection to the legs.
Varicella could be considered given the appearance of vesicles of different ages but the limited distribution to areas of atopic dermatitis suggests HSV. While eczema herpeticum is usually limited to the skin, systemic dissemination can occur.
Mortality prior to the availability of antiviral therapy was as high as 9%. The coalescence of vesicles leads to plaques that look impetigenous; superinfection with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes may also occur.

history:
Summary: A young woman with fever, rash and joint pains for one day.
A young adult female, who was in the second trimester of pregnancy, presented to the obstetrician with fever, rash, and joint pains for one day.
The patient awoke from sleep the night before her presentation with a temperature to 100.3°F (37.9°C). She went back to bed but remained uncomfortable due to diffuse muscle aches. She awakened in the morning and felt as if she had “jammed her left thumb,” a feeling she attributed to tossing and turning in bed. She called her obstetrician and arranged for an evaluation.
Her child had recently had a febrile illness with a rash that had been attributed to a virus by the child’s pediatrician. No antibiotics had been administered and the child had improved over the preceding three days.
The patient developed a rash while in the triage unit and was transferred to the emergency department.
exam_studies:
The temperature and blood pressure were normal. The neck was supple. Left thumb swelling (Figure 1) and a non-blanching rash were present (Figures 2 and 3). There was no photophobia.
Figure 1. Physical findings on hands.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 22,000 cells/mm³ with 15% bands. Other laboratory testing was normal. A lumbar puncture was performed; analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed no cells and normal chemistry results.

The patient was admitted and vancomycin, ampicillin, and ceftriaxone were administered. Droplet precautions were instituted.
diagnosis:
Meningococcemia due to Neisseria meningitidis, without evidence of meningitis.

Two of four aerobic blood cultures were positive for Neisseria meningitidis.

The vancomycin and ampicillin were discontinued. She improved significantly and was discharged to complete a ten-day course of ceftriaxone.
Her child was reevaluated and had blood cultures drawn, which remained negative. The child was treated with intramuscular ceftriaxone by the pediatrician. Ciprofloxacin was administered orally to close household contacts for prophylaxis.

This case illustrates the clinical spectrum of Neisserial disease.
During the initial evaluation, Neisseria gonorrhoeae was a significant concern given the “dermatitis/arthritis" presentation. Neisseria meningitidis can also cause a similar syndrome and should be included in the differential diagnosis. Parvovirus may cause fever and small joint arthralgias, symptoms that are more common in women than in men. The rash of parvovirus has classically a "slapped cheek" appearance when occurring in children, whereas in adults a lacy evanescent rash may be present. Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever often presents with fever, headache and a rash involving the palms and soles. Acute HIV infection should be considered in any sexually active patient with fever and rash; typically the rash is maculopapular and the presence of arthritis would be less likely.
Despite the presence of negative findings and studies initially, one must rely on clinical suspicions and institute appropriate precautions and therapy. When a case of meningococcemia is documented, tracking contacts and administering appropriate prophylaxis is of great importance.

title:
Summary: An elderly man with a headache, confusion and history of falling.
An el
history:
Summary: An elderly man with a headache, confusion and history of falling.
An elderly man presented with headache, increasing confusion, diaphoresis and multiple falling episodes during the previous day. There was no history of witnessed head trauma, seizure activity, incontinence, fever, chills, or sinus or ear pain.

He had a history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and lower extremity ulcers.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared disoriented and lethargic, was moving all extremities and having rigors. The blood pressure 93/49 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats per minute and respirations 26 per minute. The temperature was initially normal, but subsequently rose to 103.1°F (39.5°C) soon after admission. There were equally reactive pupils, a dry oropharynx, and moderate neck stiffness. The lungs were clear and there was a 2/6 systolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. The abdomen was normal. The right hand was erythematous and warm. There was erythema in a bilateral pre-tibial distribution, and a shallow right foot ulcer (2 cm by 3 cm) was present. On neurologic examination, he was lethargic and nonverbal, with intact reflexes. The Babinski reflex was equivocal.

The white blood cell count was 8,800 cells/mm³ (39% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 46% bands, 5% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, and 2 metamyelocytes.) Toxic granulations and Dohle bodies were seen on the peripheral smear. The hematocrit was 34.6% and the platelets were 64,000/mm³. The sodium was 132 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 64 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.3 mg/dL.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head was performed without contrast and showed small vessel ischemic changes, and a right subdural collection consistent with a hygroma (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Head CT scan without contrast.

A lumbar puncture was performed and the cerebrospinal fluid revealed 129 white blood cells/mm³ (89% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 3% bands), 3420 red cells/mm³, protein 298 mg/dL, and glucose 72 mg/dL. The gram stain showed few white blood cells and no organisms.
diagnosis:
Cranial subdural empyema, with evidence of methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and group G Streptococcus infection.

Within twelve hours, blood cultures that had been sent from the Emergency Room grew gram-positive cocci in pairs, chains, and clusters. These were identified as methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and group G Streptococcus.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head with gadolinium was performed and revealed a right subdural collection with enhancement that was suggestive of a subdural empyema. A right parietofrontal infarct was also identified. (See Figures 2 and 3.)
Figure 2. Head MRI scan.
Figure 3. Head MRI scan with gadolinium.

The patient's course was complicated by hypotension, atrial arrhythmias, myocardial infarction and seizure activity. Intravenous nafcillin was administered and, when his condition continued to deteriorate, ceftriaxone and metronidazole were added. Neurosurgical evacuation of the right subdural collection was performed, and fifteen cubic centimeters of purulent material was drained. Intra-operative gram stain showed gram-positive cocci in clusters. Cultures were sterile. (Of note, the patient had been on antibiotics for several days prior to surgery). Transesophageal echocardiography did not reveal vegetations.
The patient's course was notable for development of a diffuse erythematous rash. Phenytoin, ceftriaxone, nafcillin and metronidazole were stopped and valproic acid, vancomycin and chloramphenicol were administered. He initally improved, but subsequently his clinical condition worsened with development of recurrent fever and hypotension. Despite all efforts, the patient died one month after initial presentation.

The dura mater and arachnoid membrane enclose a potential subdural space, traversed by numerous small veins. Infection may spread to this space by direct extension (e.g. from sinus or middle ear disease) or, less commonly, by metastatic infection. In adults, cranial subdural empyemas most commonly follow neurosurgery. Septic thrombosis of veins within the empyema may cause venous infarction.
The diagnosis of cranial subdural empyema should be suspected in a patient with meningeal signs and focal neurologic deficit.

title:
Summary: A child with leg pain and a fever.
A pre-teen child presented with left
history:
Summary: A child with leg pain and a fever.
A pre-teen child presented with left lower leg pain and a fever. Eleven days earlier, the child had fallen while running to catch a baseball. A radiograph was read as negative and a pediatrician prescribed antipyretics/analgesics and rest. Three days before admission, the patient developed a fever and pounding pain in the medial aspect of the left lower leg. The child was brought to the hospital.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no apparent distress; the temperature was 38.4ºC (101.1ºF). The cardiovascular examination was normal, and there was no lymphadenopathy. There was mild erythema and swelling over medial lower left calf; the range of motion was full at the hip, knee, and ankle and occurred without pain.

The white blood cell count was 10,300 cells/mm³ and the differential was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 56 millimeters per hour and the C-reactive protein was elevated at 6.7 mg/dL.

Blood cultures were drawn.
Radiography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left lower leg were obtained (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Radiograph of the left lower leg.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the lower legs.
diagnosis:
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with an intramedullary abscess of the tibia.

Radiography of the lower leg (Figure 1) revealed a linear sclerotic band in midshaft of the left tibia that was worrisome for a nondisplaced fracture.
MRI scanning with the administration of contrast (Figure 2) revealed a diffuse signal abnormality involving the mid and distal left tibia with almost complete replacement of normal marrow signal (low on T1 weighted and high on T2 weighted images). Enhancement was heterogeneous circumferentially and absent centrally, which raised the concern for abscesses. The serpiginous area of high T2 signal distally, which did not enhance, suggested infarction. This appearance was suggestive of osteomyelitis, but a diffuse infiltrative process involving the bone marrow could not be excluded.
The blood culture was positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.

Intravenous cefazolin was administered empirically at presentation. Because of concern for an intramedullary abscess with involvement of the distal growth plate, the patient was taken to the operating room for a surgical procedure. Purulent material was found to be under pressure when the tibia was opened; pulse lavage was used to debride the entire metaphysis.
The patient was treated with intravenous cefazolin for six weeks.

Osteomyelitis in children is usually of hematogenous origin. Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis occurs especially in young children, presumably because of the rich vascular supply of their rapidly growing bones. The femur and tibia are the most frequent sites; growth plate involvement occurs infrequently. Osteomyelitis in children is frequently treated with oral antibiotics alone.
In this case, the dramatic MRI scanning prompted concern primarily for an intramedullary abscess, although a concomitant neoplasm was also considered. Under these circumstances, surgical intervention to establish the diagnosis is important.

title:
Summary: A child with vomiting and a skin rash.
A 3-year-old boy presented with
history:
Summary: A child with vomiting and a skin rash.
A 3-year-old boy presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy and skin rash. The patient was in good health until nine days before admission. He developed vomiting and lethargy, which resolved spontaneously after three days. Five days before admission, he again became lethargic, appeared glassy-eyed, and was admitted to an outside hospital. Intravenous fluids and supportive care were administered for two days for a presumed diagnosis of gastroenteritis. At the time of his discharge, his family noted bilateral foot swelling with pain on ambulation.
One day before this admission, a rash on his lower extremities was noted. During the night, the patient began complaining of abdominal pain and started vomiting brown material. His rash was noted to have spread to his arms. He was admitted to the hospital.

Six weeks before this admission, he had had Streptococcal pharyngitis and had received a course of amoxicillin.

He had no siblings or pets, and there had been no day care exposures. A grandparent had been ill with an upper respiratory infection.

He lived with his parents.

There was no family history of blood dyscrasias or malignancies.

The patient had multiple food allergies (including corn, wheat, rice, milk, eggs and soy) that led to vomiting. He also had multiple environmental allergies for which he took an antihistamine.
exam_studies:
The patient was a lethargic, minimally interactive young boy in mild distress. He was afebrile but tachycardic with otherwise normal vital signs. His eyes were glassy with clear conjunctivae. He would not open his mouth for examination. His neck was supple without lymphadenopathy or meningismus. The lungs were clear to auscultation, and the cardiac examination did not reveal any murmurs. The abdomen was mildly tender diffusely without rebound or guarding. The liver edge was palpable and nontender. The feet and ankles were diffusely swollen and mildly tender to passive range of motion. There was a left-sided greater than right-sided non-blanching pinpoint rash on the top of his feet, legs, buttocks, and in his left antecubital fossa. (See Figures 1 and 2.) The rash spared the trunk. His stool was guaiac positive.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 13,400/mm³ with 57% polymorphonuclear cells, 17% bands, and 19% lymphocytes. Coagulation studies, renal function and liver function tests were normal. The urinalysis had no protein or blood.
diagnosis:
Henoch-Schonlein Purpura.

Blood and urine cultures were negative. A rectal swab for enterovirus and a respiratory viral panel were negative. A test for anti-DNase B was negative. A skin biopsy of his petechial lesions was performed and revealed a leukocytoclastic vasculitis with immunoglobulin (Ig) A immunofluorescent staining consistent with Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Ceftriaxone was administered for the first 72 hours until blood cultures were negative. He was monitored for renal involvement of vasculitis but there was none. He was managed conservatively with hydration and anti-inflammatory medications and recovered fully.

Henoch-Schonlein Purpura is a multi-organ vasculitis involving skin, gastrointestinal tract, kidney and joints. It typically affects children ages 4 to 7 with a male predominance, but adult cases have also been reported. Although the etiology remains unknown, a preceding upper respiratory illness or vaccination has been reported in some cases.
This is an immune-mediated disease whose hallmark is immunoglobulin (Ig) A staining in the vascular walls of effected organs and elevated IgA serum levels. Clinical manifestations may occur all at once or in stages. Characteristic features include a maculopapular and then purpuric rash in dependent areas, as was the case here, as well as arthralgias and non-pitting edema of the extremities. Gastrointestinal involvement may manifest as colicky abdominal pain with or without guaiac positive stools or gross bleeding. Renal involvement with microscopic hematuria, nephritic or nephrotic syndrome is the dreaded complication occurring in 20-60% cases because it can have long term sequelae in an illness for which there is otherwise an excellent prognosis.
In this case, the absence of fever, evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or positive blood cultures, as well as the negative serologic studies, made a vasculitis the leading diagnosis. This was confirmed by the typical biopsy appearance.

title:
Summary: A woman in her fifties presented with wrist pain and swelling.
A woman
history:
Summary: A woman in her fifties presented with wrist pain and swelling.
A woman in her fifties presented to the Infectious Disease outpatient clinic for evaluation of pain and swelling in her right wrist.
One year before her presentation, the patient had been diagnosed with DeQuervain’s tenosynovitis. An injection of corticosteroids was administered without improvement. Two months later, tenolysis was performed that was complicated by a local wound infection, which required incision, drainage and a tenosynovectomy.
After the surgical procedure, she had persistent erythema and swelling. Cephalexin was administered, without improvement. At the time, wound purulence with soft tissue thickening and edema was noted.

She had a history of degenerative joint disease and asthma.

She was employed in the meat industry and owned a cat. She denied any history of travel outside of the United States.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and was afebrile. There was a positive Finkelstein test in the right wrist. An erythematous area (approximately 1.5-centimeter in diameter) was present on the base of the right thumb and on the previous incision area (Figure 1). No purulence or drainage was seen. The remainder of her examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

Laboratory test results of the complete blood count and chemistries were normal.

The patient underwent an incision and drainage procedure. Pathological examination of the tissue from the procedure is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Surgical pathology.
Figure 3. Surgical pathology.
diagnosis:
Prototheca tenosynovitis.

The pathology showed acute tenosynovitis with non-caseating granulomatous inflammation (Figure 2 above). Figure 3 shows giant cells that are surrounding organisms consistent with Prototheca. Figure 4 shows septated endosporulating organisms also consistent with Prototheca. Fungal cultures grew Prototheca.
Figure 4. Surgical pathology with septated endosporulating organisms.

The patient was started on oral itraconazole (200 mg twice daily). Her pain and swelling improved over the following four weeks.
Somnolence developed and the itraconazole was stopped for two weeks, during which the somnolence resolved. The medication was restarted at a dose of 200 mg daily.
Subsequently, her wrist symptoms increased and another surgical debridement was performed. The surgical pathology showed the presence of Prototheca organisms, but the cultures were negative. Her symptoms improved after the second procedure.
The course of itraconazole was continued until generalized edema developed after two months of therapy. The edema was thought to be secondary to the itraconazole and the medication was discontinued. Oral fluconazole 200 mg daily was administered.

Prototheca are unicellular achloric algae that reproduce by endosporulation. The organisms are found in a wide range of environmental sites, including tree slime, sewage, fresh or marine water, soil, and foodstuffs. The geographic distribution of the reported cases is wide.
The most common presentation of protothecosis is a single lesion of the skin or subcutaneous tissue. The typical skin lesion is a painless, slowly progressive, well-circumscribed plaque or papulonodular lesion that may ulcerate. Soft tissue lesions favor the olecranon bursa, sites of minor trauma or corticosteroid injection, or surgical wounds exposed to soil or water, such as hand tendon repair. Gradual enlargement of the lesion over weeks or months is commonly seen.
Other reported sites of infection include nasopharyngeal ulcerations following prolonged endotracheal intubation, peritoneal dialysis catheters, and viscera in immunosuppressed patients.
Protothecosis is best diagnosed by biopsy for histologic study and culture. The inflammatory response shows both microabscesses and granulomas with multinucleated giant cells. Prototheca cells usually range from 8 to 20 micrometers in diameter, stain well with Gomori methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff stains, and often contain two to eight packed endospores in each cell or sporangium, giving the appearance of morulae.
Protothecosis generally does not resolve unless treated. Surgical excision of lesions is a key component of therapy. Intravenous amphotericin B, sometimes combined with tetracycline, has been used successfully. Ketoconazole, fluconazole and itraconazole have also been used with some success.

title:
Summary: A woman with a fever and swollen right upper arm.
A woman in her sixtie
history:
Summary: A woman with a fever and swollen right upper arm.
A woman in her sixties presented with a red, tender, swollen right upper arm and fevers to 104°F (40°C). Two weeks earlier, the fourth cycle of adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer had been administered. Fourteen hours before her presentation, she had been scratched and nipped by her pet cat at the site of her current symptoms.

She had a history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, treated with lumpectomy, with no positive lymph nodes. Adjuvant chemotherapy was being administered.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no acute distress. The temperature was 103.5°F (39.7°C), pulse 110 per minute, and blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg. The right upper arm is shown in Figure 1. Scratch marks were faintly visible. There was full range of motion at the elbow, without crepitus or fluctuance. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 400 cells/mm³, absolute neutrophil count 100 cells/mm³, hematocrit 29%, and platelets 98,000/mm³. The remainder of the laboratory testing was normal.

Forty-eight hours after admission, 4 out of 4 blood culture bottles were positive. A gram stain from one of the aerobic bottles is shown in Figure 2.
The patient received intravenous antibiotics and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). Although the fever subsided after 48 hours, the arm lesion progressed despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy with increased erythema, bullae formation and an eschar at the site of the cat bite. No extension to deep tissue, bone or joint space was detected.
The patient's white blood cell count was reconstituted by the fifth hospital day, and she slowly improved over the subsequent two weeks.
Figure 2. Gram stain from an aerobic bottle.
diagnosis:
Pasteurella multocida infection, following a cat-bite, in a patient receiving adjuvant chemotherapy.

Blood cultures, drawn before antibiotics were administered, grew gram-negative rods in four out of four bottles. The organism was identified as Pasteurella multocida (Figure 2).

Progression of the skin findings is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Physical findings (Day 3).
Figure 4. Physical findings (Day 7).

Up to 80% of cat bites become infected, and Pasteurella multocida is the most common organism responsible. Intense local inflammation and rapid progression are typical. Abscesses, tenosynovitis, septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, particularly of the hands are the most common complications. Bacteremia is rare.
Penicillin G remains the drug of choice against Pasteurella multocida. When treating animal bite infections before culture data is available, it is important to cover broadly with an agent such as oral amoxicillin-clavulanate or intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam. Doxycycline and clindamycin can be used for the penicillin-allergic patient.
The duration of therapy should be determined by the severity of the infection and the response to treatment. It is not unusual to treat P. multocida soft tissue infections with a three-to-four-week course of antibiotics.

title:
Summary: A woman with a headache, fever and neck stiffness.
A young adult woman
history:
Summary: A woman with a headache, fever and neck stiffness.
A young adult woman with a history of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia presented to the emergency department with a frontal headache, photophobia, fever and neck stiffness for two days.

She had a history of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (AVM), a lower lobectomy of the right lung, renal cell carcinoma status post a curative resection, and a cerebellar stroke related to an AVM.

The patient had recently traveled to a Caribbean island for vacation.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 100.6°F (38.1°C). There was neck stiffness and positive Kernig and Brudzinsky signs present. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 12,200/mm³ (74% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), hematocrit 39%, and the platelet count was normal. A lumbar puncture was done after antibiotics had been administered. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 6650 white blood cells (84% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes), 11 red blood cells, protein 213 mg/dL and glucose 16 mg/dL. The chest radiograph showed no changes from previous studies after the lobectomy.

The patient was admitted to the neurology service with a presumed diagnosis of meningitis. Antibiotics were administered intravenously and included vancomycin (1 gram) and ceftriaxone (2 grams) every twelve hours, and metronidazole (500 mg) every six hours. Cultures from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the blood remained negative for bacterial pathogens.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head with and without contrast was performed (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT scan of the head.
diagnosis:
Brain abscess in a patient with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome).

CT scanning of the head with contrast showed a 1.5 cm ring enhancing lesion with thin rim (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning could not be obtained because of the history of coils in her lungs.
Due to the proximity of the abscess to the ventricles, an aspiration of the lesion was considered to be dangerous and was not performed. Cultures remained negative, capsular antigens in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were also negative.

The patient improved slowly during the following two weeks. She completed six weeks of vancomycin, ceftriaxone and metronidazole therapy, followed by 4 weeks of oral amoxicillin and metronidazole. Her symptoms resolved except for a mild deficit in her left leg. Follow-up CT scanning was performed on day 60 and is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Follow up CT scanning, day 60.

Brain abscess is a focal collection within the brain parenchyma that can arise as a complication of a variety of infections, trauma or surgery. Bacteria can invade the brain either by direct spread or through hematogenous seeding. Primary infections that can directly spread to the cerebral cortex include otitis media and mastoiditis, sinusitis and dental infections.
Brain abscesses associated with bacteremia usually result in multiple abscesses that are most commonly located in the distribution of the middle cerebral artery. Episodes of bacteremia can lead to brain abscesses in patients with cyanotic congenital heart disease or arteriovenous malformations.
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by abnormalities of the vasculature structure in the nose, skin, lung, brain and gastrointestinal tract. Studies of prevalence show that the disease is more prevalent than previously thought. Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations are seen in 5 to 15% of patients with HHT. Brain abscesses occur in patient with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations who have right-to-left shunting, which facilitates the passage of septic and bland emboli into the cerebral circulation.
Case reports implicate a wide variety of organisms as the cause of brain abscess. Anaerobic organisms are commonly found, particularly in patients with brain abscesses originating from otorhinolaryngeal infections. Aerobic Gram positive cocci are also frequently encountered. Aerobic Gram negative rods are not commonly recovered except following neurosurgery or head trauma. In immunocompromised patients the range of organisms is broader and includes Toxoplasma, Listeria, Nocardia, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus.
The most common symptom of a brain abscess is headache. Neck stiffness occurs in 15% of the patients and is associated with a leak into the ventricles. Changes in mental status can be seen together with focal neurological signs. Fever is seen in half of the patients. The diagnosis of brain abscess is usually suggested by findings on imaging studies. Blood cultures are positive in 15% of the cases. Lumbar puncture can be dangerous if the patient has signs of increased intracraneal hypertension.
CT scanning is not as sensitive as MRI scanning for the diagnosis of brain abscess but may be easier to obtain on an emergent basis. Early cerebritis appears as an irregular area of low density that does not enhance following contrast injection. As cerebritis evolves the lesion enlarges with thick and diffuse ring enhancement following contrast injection. The lesion later becomes encapsulated.
Successful management of a brain abscess requires a combination of antibiotics and surgical drainage for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The duration of antibiotics should be prolonged, usually six to eight weeks. Options for empiric therapy include the use of penicillin with metronidazole or a third generation cephalosporin and metronidazole.

title:
Summary: A woman with an expressive aphasia and right-sided weakness.
A middle-a
history:
Summary: A woman with an expressive aphasia and right-sided weakness.
A middle-aged woman presented with word-finding difficulties, expressive aphasia and right upper extremity weakness that had developed gradually over the preceding four weeks.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed T2 intensity in a left frontoparietal subcortical white matter lesion, without edema or enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal without oligoclonal bands; and serologic testing for syphilis and Lyme were negative. Magnetic-resonance angiography (MRA) was negative for stroke.
The patient was treated empirically with steroids for presumed multiple sclerosis with mild improvement initially. However, she presented again a few days later with worsening aphasia and weakness. MRI scanning was repeated and showed a larger left frontoparietal lesion with additional lesions in the pons. She denied headaches, eye pain, visual changes, vertigo, dizziness, fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

The patient was healthy until four weeks before her presentation.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared thin and cachectic. She was afebrile and the vital signs were normal. Thrush was present on the tongue and hard palate. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Examinations of the fundi, lungs, heart and abdomen were normal. There was no rash on the skin. The patient was alert and oriented. She was able to follow simple commands but was not able to speak in long sentences or execute complex tasks. She had echolalia and could not name objects. Her strength was 5- out of 5 in right upper and lower extremities and 5 out of 5 in left extremities. Cranial nerves were intact, reflexes were brisk and symmetrical, and the toes were downgoing.

The white blood cell count (WBC) was 2,200/mm³ with 44% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes, platelets were 188,000/mm³. The total protein was 7.3 g/dL and globulin 3.7 g/dL; the level of creatinine and liver function tests were normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple foci of abnormal T2 signal involving the white matter in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, with the largest abnormality seen in the left frontal lobe (Figures 1 and 2). There was minimal enhancement after contrast and no mass effect was seen. There was no evidence of a tissue mass in the left frontal lobe.
Figure 1. MRI scan of the brain, axial T2-weighted image.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain, axial T2-weighted image (higher cut).

Her speech and strength did not improve. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed abnormal brain activity in the left frontal area.
diagnosis:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Subsequent evaluation revealed a positive antibody test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 20 cells/mm³ and the level of HIV RNA was 182,000 copies/mL. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed no pleocytosis and a positive JC virus PCR test was consistent with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The CSF HIV RNA was 21,000 copies/mL.
MRI scanning T2 images, shown in Figures 1 and 2, reveal subcortical white matter disease in the left frontoparietal lobe. (Figure 1 is a lower cut than Figure 2.)

The patient was started on combination therapy that included zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), and lopinavir-ritonavir with a decrease in the HIV RNA level and increase in the CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count. The neurologic examination improved over the subsequent three months.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by JC virus (JCV). The infection reactivates and invades glial cells in patients who are immunosuppressed. The diagnosis is made by either histology or establishing the presence of JCV in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by PCR.
The classic appearance of PML on MRI scanning is that of multiple foci of T2 intensity involving only the white matter, without mass effect and with no or minimal enhancement. All patients who have the typical radiologic findings should be tested for HIV infection. Most patient who have PML as a result of HIV are usually very immunosuppressed with CD4 cell counts of less than 50 cells/mm³. Other risk factors for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in addition to HIV infection include hematologic malignancy, and immunomodulatory medications (such as natalizumab or rituxamab). Patients often present with rapidly progressive focal neurologic deficits, usually due to cerebral white matter disease.
The treatment for this disease is directed at reversing the underlying immunosuppression. In cases of HIV-related PML, antiretroviral therapy may result in improvement of the neurologic disease.
This patient was unlikely to have an arboviral infection, such as West Nile Virus encephalitis, because of the absence of features such as confusion, headache, meningeal signs or symptoms, or paralysis. Herpes simplex virus infection typically involves the temporal lobe, and septic cerebral emboli would have been associated with more radiological enhancement.

title:
Summary: A young adult with a fever and neck pain.
A young adult college student
history:
Summary: A young adult with a fever and neck pain.
A young adult college student presented with fever, sore throat and left sided neck pain and stiffness. She had been in her usual state of good health until two weeks earlier when she developed low-grade temperatures and a mild sore throat. She presented to her university health clinic where a streptococcal throat culture was negative. The patient was treated with clarithromycin for possible bronchitis and felt somewhat better.
Three days before admission, she began to have shaking chills with temperatures to 104°F (40°C), focal left neck soreness and stiffness. On the day of admission, she began to experience left-sided pleuritic chest pain.

She had a history of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis as a child.

She lived in a college dorm and had no known sick contacts. She denied drug or alcohol use.
exam_studies:
She was a mildly toxic-appearing young woman, who was alert, oriented and appropriate. The temperature was 102.5°F (39.2°C), pulse was 110 beats per minute, and the respirations and blood pressure were normal. Her conjunctivae were clear; the cranial nerves were normal, without proptosis. There was no trismus, and mucous membranes were moist without lesions. Focal left neck tenderness was present with palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. There was no overlying erythema. A II/VI systolic ejection murmur was heard.

The white blood cell count was 20,300 cells/mm³ with 46% polymorphonuclear cells, 37% bands, and 3% lymphocytes. Coagulation studies and liver function tests were normal. A chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1. Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the neck is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. CT scan of the neck with contrast, sagittal view
Figure 3. CT scan of the neck with contrast, axial view.
diagnosis:
Lemierre’s Syndrome (septic internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis), caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum.

The chest radiograph revealed multiple peripheral nodules consistent with septic embolic lesions (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the head and neck with contrast enhancement revealed left internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis with surrounding inflammation and lymphadenopathy (Figures 2 and 3). Blood cultures obtained on admission grew Fusobacterium necrophorum.

The patient was treated with one month of ampicillin-sulbactam and quickly became afebrile. Follow-up CT scanning of the chest at the end of intravenous therapy showed resolving cavitating lung nodules. The patient was treated with a tail of oral amoxicillin therapy and recovered completely.

Lemierre’s syndrome is a primary head and neck infection in a young, previously healthy person that goes on to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. The main pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic gram-negative rod, but the infection can also be polymicrobial. The presentation seen in this case is classic: an initial pharyngotonsillitis in a young person that was followed by swelling and tenderness along the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and sepsis due to a septic thrombus of the ipsilateral internal jugular vein. The illness is biphasic, such that within a week or so of the initial symptoms, patients develop high fevers and rigors signifying intravascular infection and embolic phenomena.
Fusobacterium necrophorum is part of the normal flora and it is not known why it penetrates the mucosa in some patients, but it is thought that reduced host defenses in the pharyngeal mucosa due to an unrelated pharyngitis may play a role. High-dose penicillin with metronidazole or clindamycin is often used; anticoagulation is typically not advised because of the risk of extension of the infection, except in cases of cavernous sinus involvement.
