title: A man with a lung nodule after treatment for a germ cell tumor.
history:
A man in his thirties presented with a lung nodule two years after receiving treatment for an extragonadal germ cell tumor. Two years earlier, he had presented with a retroperitoneal mass, and the germ cell tumor was diagnosed. A retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy had also been performed at the time for hydronephrosis, and four cycles of chemotherapy were administered. Two years after his treatment, surveillance chest radiography revealed a new lung nodule. Two months later, computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed the nodule was increasing in size.
There was no history of night sweats, loss of weight, chest pain, shortness of breath, cough or hemoptysis.

He also had chronic arthritis of the back, ankles, and hips.

The patient was single and lived in Alaska. He smoked tobacco and drank alcohol on weekends.
exam_studies:
The patient was well appearing, with a blood pressure was 117/28 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats per minute, temperature 98.7°F (37.1°C). The physical examination was normal with a well healed midline surgical scar. There were no oral lesions, no lymphadenopathy or testicular masses; the lungs were clear and the abdomen had no organomegaly or masses.

Laboratory test results were normal, including levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 16 U/liter, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 13 U/liter, lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) 200 U/liter, human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) < 2.0 and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 1.2 ng/ml. Testing for tuberculosis (PPD skin testing) and antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
Chest radiograph and computed tomography of the chest are shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.

Bronchoscopic examination revealed normal airways and bronchial washings showed no acid fast bacilli (AFB).
diagnosis:
Tuberculoma of the left upper lung due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A wedge resection of the lung nodule was performed without complications and revealed caseating granulomatous disease (see Figure 3.) Pathological staining was negative for malignancy. Initial sputum and bronchial washings were negative for acid fast bacilli, but a single bacillus was found on AFB staining of the biopsy (Figures 4 and 5). After 6 weeks, cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Figure 3. Biopsy of lung nodule.
Figure 4. AFB staining of lung nodule.
Figure 5. Detail of Figure 4.

A four-drug regimen was administered for eight weeks, followed by isoniazid (INH) and rifampin for an additional sixteen weeks, for a total of six months of therapy.

title: A man with increasing weakness and difficulty breathing.
history:
A man in his eighties, native to Alaska, presented with progressive weakness and difficulty breathing at rest. One day before presentation, diarrhea and vomiting began abruptly. There was a mild headache, dry mouth, and the patient was unable to eat or drink. There were no fevers or chills.

His past medical history included hypertension, degenerative arthritis, pneumonia and bladder carcinoma for which he had received chemotherapy years before.

The patient lived on the coast of the Bering Sea (Figure 1). There was no history of recent travel, alcohol or tobacco use. He owned dogs. The patient presented during the summer season, when many mosquitoes were in the environment.

Medications included atenolol, ibuprofen, quinine and aspirin.
exam_studies:
He was alert and oriented to person, place and time, with moderate respiratory distress. The temperature was normal; the pulse 56 beats per minute, and blood pressure 120/74 mm Hg supine and 96/42 mm Hg standing. There was ptosis of both eyelids, absent bowel sounds and symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis; deep tendon reflexes were normal.

The forced vital capacity was markedly decreased.

The patient was intubated shortly after presentation. A diagnostic test was performed. Figure 1. View in Alaska.
Figure 1. View in Alaska.
diagnosis:
Botulism, Type E, caused by Clostridium botulinum.

Additional history became available: two days before the patient’s illness, members of the village had found a whale on the shore. According to local customs; it was shared among all people in the village with elders receiving the best part: Maktaaq, (the thick skin and thin layer of blubber of whales), a traditional delicacy in the arctic (Figures 2 and 3). Shortly after this patient became ill, several other elders presented with nausea, vomiting and weakness, some with blurred vision and diplopia. The whale was thought to have been dead for several days before it found on the shore.
Botulism was suspected, and botulism testing performed by the Center for Disease Control later returned positive for Type E.
Figure 2. View in Alaska.
Figure 3. Maktaaq (thick whale skin and blubber).

Empiric therapy with botulism antitoxin and supportive care in intensive care unit was initiated. The patient was intubated for five days; the ileus resolved in two weeks and he was discharged to home in good health.

title: A man with myelodysplasia and new ulcerating nodules.
history:
A man in his sixties with a history of myelodysplastic syndrome complained of the development of small pruritic pustules on his lower extremities. These pustules progressed to nodular, ulcerating lesions. He received two short courses of oral cefazolin with transient improvement, which was not sustained.

There was a history of myelodysplasia.

He had recently traveled to Spain.

He was retired and enjoyed sports.
exam_studies:
The vital signs were normal. There were scattered nodular erythematous lesions with superficial ulceration on the lower extremities, as shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 15,000 cells/mm³ with 12% blasts.

A skin biopsy was performed (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Biopsy result.
Figure 3. Biopsy result.
diagnosis:
Botryomycosis secondary to Staphylococcus aureus infection.

A skin biopsy revealed a neutrophilic infiltrate and granules consistent with basophilic cocci surrounded by an eosinophilic coat, typical of the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon (Figures 2 and 3). Culture grew Staphylococcus aureus.

The patient was treated for six weeks with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, and the lesions resolved. He then underwent a bone marrow transplant as treatment for his myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) associated acute myelogenous leukemia (AML).

Pyoderma gangrenosum and Sweet's syndrome are non-infectious dermatoses. Thus, the presence of gram positive cocci excludes these diagnoses. Myiasis and Leishmaniasis are associated with epidemiologic exposures that are absent in this case.
Botryomycosis, a chronic suppurative bacterial infection, may present with recurring scattered papular and nodular skin or soft tissue lesions. It often occurs in immunosuppressed patients and is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Successful treatment requires a prolonged course of antibiotics. The Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon is the characteristic finding on biopsy and superficially resembles a sulfur granule of actinomycosis. Rarely, botryomycosis may present with visceral disease, such as in the lung.

title: A woman from Alaska with lower extremity weakness and unsteady gait.
history:
A woman in her sixties presented with weakness of lower extremities and unsteady gait. The symptoms had begun two years earlier and progressed to a total inability to ambulate for several weeks before her presentation. Weight loss had occurred. There was no history of back pain, bowel or bladder incontinence, fever, headache, and no sensory deficits or complaints. She was admitted to the hospital, where magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine had revealed a mass at the T9 vertebra, associated with cord compression. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) showed no malignant cells. An open biopsy and decompression procedure was performed; pathological examinations of the specimens revealed necrosis and inflammation. A wide excision of the mass was performed and symptomatic pain relief was achieved. The patient slowly recovered and eventually was able to ambulate with a cane. She was discharged to home.
Three months before this presentation, the weakness increased and she noted sensory loss with bowel and bladder incontinence. She began to fall frequently while ambulating with a cane and was re-admitted for further evaluation. There was no history of night sweats or fevers. She reported decreased appetite and her family thought that weight loss had occurred.

Medical problems included hypertension, glaucoma, degenerative joint disease, chronic Hepatitis B virus carrier state, and recurrent urinary tract infections. There was no known exposure to tuberculosis.

The patient was a married homemaker in Alaska. There was a history of dog sledding when she was younger; she did not drink alcohol, smoke tobacco or travel.

Medications included ibuprofen, atenolol and aspirin.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 132/55 mm Hg, pulse 65 beats per minute and the temperature was normal. The fundoscopic examination was normal, motor strength was diminished 4/5 in both legs, and sensation was diminished to pain, temperature and light touch. The plantar response was extensor bilaterally; there was no clonus. The gait was very unsteady.

Laboratory testing was normal. A chest radiograph showed no pulmonary infiltrates and tuberculosis skin testing was negative. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was also negative. Repeat MRI scanning of the spine revealed a compressive lesion at the 7th and 8th thoracic vertebrae (T7-T8), which was destructive to bone and extrinsic to the cord (Figures 1, 2 and 3).
Figure 1. MRI scan of the spine.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the spine.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the spine.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed a new ring-enhancing lesion of temporal lobe (Figure 4).
Figure 4. MRI scan of the brain.
diagnosis:
Echinococcal disease, with osteomyelitis of the thoracic spine and involving the brain, most likely caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

A second surgical procedure included extensive removal of the recurrent spinal mass. Pathological and microbiology studies were sent for analysis and culture. The vertebral bodies at T7-8 revealed chronic osteomyelitis, with cystic necrotic structures and adjacent foreign body granulomatous inflammation including lymphocytes and plasma cells. The cysts had a complex layered structure with distinct membranes, consistent with echinococcal cyst (Figures 5 and 6).
Figure 5. Biopsy of the 7th thoracic vertebra (T7).
Figure 6. Biopsy of the 7th thoracic vertebra (T7).

The patient received albendazole and was doing well, ambulating with a walker, at follow-up three months later. The central nervous system lesion had essentially resolved. No other organs were involved.

title:
Summary: A man in his forties with a swollen foot.
A man in his forties had a hi
history:
Summary: A man in his forties with a swollen foot.
A man in his forties had a history of painless swelling around the right malleolus bilaterally and dorsal foot papules, which had begun several years earlier. One year after the onset of symptoms, he noted discharge of clear particles of less than one millimeter in diameter from the papules. There was no history of fever, sweats, anorexia, weight loss or other systemic symptoms. There was no history of trauma.
The patient had received antimicrobial therapy intermittently, without improvement.

None. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) had been negative in the recent past.

The patient had immigrated more than a decade before to the northeastern United States from an island off the western coast of Africa, where he had spent significant time out-of-doors. He lived with his wife and children and worked in an industrial setting. He denied tobacco, alcohol or injection drug use.
exam_studies:
The examination revealed edema, multiple papules, and sinus tracts in the right lower pretibial region (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Plantar surface of foot.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning of the foot is shown in Figures 2 and 3. An incisional biopsy was performed and sent for staining and cultures.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the distal lower extremity.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the distal lower extremity.
diagnosis:
Eumycetoma (Madura foot) due to Acremonium falciforme.

Histopathological examination of the biopsy demonstrated a non-pigmented fungal form with septated hyphae that was consistent with eumycetoma (Madura foot). Based on the appearance of the fungal forms, the possible pathogens included Acremonium spp., Fusarium spp., and Pseudallescheria boydii.
Initial cultures were negative. A sample was sent to the mycology branch of the Center for Disease Control, which grew Acremonium falciforme.

Initially, oral itraconazole (200 mg) was administered twice daily, but was changed to voriconazole (200 mg) twice daily due to persistent swelling of the right lower extremity and intermittent discharge. The symptoms gradually improved. Six weeks after initiating voriconazole, the affected lower extremity demonstrated decreased swelling and no active discharge, with crusting of many of the papules. (See Figure 4.)
Figure 4. Physical findings after therapy.

Mycetoma is a chronic, localized, and progressive infection that most commonly occurs on the foot. It begins in the subcutaneous tissue, often spreading to adjacent structures including the bone. Multiple sinus tracts may develop and discharge purulent material that is embedded with grains of either aerobic actinomycetes (actinomycetoma) or fungi (eumycetoma). The agents causing Madura foot are usually present in the soil. In the initial phase of the infection and after a breach in the skin has lead to the inoculation of the offending microbe, a small, painless papule may appear. Swelling occurs slowly and progressively; infection by actinomycetes generally causes more rapid swelling than that seen with fungal infection. After several months, sinus tracts may appear and discharge suppurative grains. The grains may be black, white, yellow, red, or clear depending on causative organism. Cycles of swelling, suppuration, and scarring may then begin.
Infections occur in nearly a 4:1 ratio of male-to-female patients. Those with mycetoma are most commonly between the ages of 20-40 years, but the infection can occur at any age. The diagnosis of mycetoma and Madura foot should be considered when the triad of lower extremity swelling, sinus tracts, and discharge composed of grains is seen in a patient from a mycetoma endemic region. Choice of medical therapy will depend on whether the lesion is a eumycetoma or actinomycetoma. Newer broad spectrum triazoles should be considered for the eumycetoma group.

title:
Summary: A man in his thirties with sinusitis and confusion.
A right-handed man
history:
Summary: A man in his thirties with sinusitis and confusion.
A right-handed man in his thirties had been well until two weeks before admission when he developed symptoms of sinusitis. During the days immediately preceding his presentation, fatigue, somnolence, decreased appetite and oral intake had occurred. On the day of admission, the patient was confused and unable to speak. There was no history of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, neck pain, headache, or trauma to his face or his head. He had not had head surgery or sinus surgery.
He was brought to another hospital where computed tomography (CT) revealed pneumocephalus. He was then transferred to a tertiary care hospital.

There was a history of hypertension and bipolar disorder.

There was no history of alcohol or illicit drug use and no epidemiologic exposures.

He had no allergies to medications.

The patient had been on antihypertensive medications until a few weeks before admission.
exam_studies:
The patient was mildly diaphoretic. The temperature was 101.6°F (38.7°C). He was aphasic and a right-sided hemiplegia was present.

The white blood cell count was 15,600 cells/mm³ (74% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 15% bands and 3% lymphocytes). The potassium was 2.6 mmol/liter, aspartate aminotransferase 165 U/liter, and alanine aminotransferase 145 U/liter.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed a left subdural lesion consistent with an empyema and meningeal enhancement with left frontal and parietal lobe cerebritis (Figures 1 through 3). There was a 9-millimeter rightward midline shift with early uncal and subfalcine herniation and paranasal sinus mucosal thickening, with possible acute sinusitis.
Figure 1. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain with contrast.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain with contrast.
diagnosis:
Intracranial subdural empyema, with mixed flora (including anaerobic organisms, Fusobacterium necrophorum and Peptostreptococcus, and aerobic organisms consistent with Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group)), following sinusitis.

Craniectomy was performed with drainage of a subdural fluid collection. The gram stain of the aspirate showed mixed flora, including gram positive cocci in pairs and short chains and gram negative rods of mixed morphology (Figures 4 and 5).
Culture of the aspirate later grew multiple organisms including anaerobic organisms, Fusobacterium necrophorum and Peptostreptococcus, and aerobic organisms consistent with Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group). In addition, three out of four blood cultures drawn at initial presentation were positive for Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group). Two of four bottles were positive for Fusobacterium necrophorum and Peptostreptococcus species.
Figure 4. Gram stain of an aspirate from a subdural collection.
Figure 5. Detail of Figure 4.

The patient was initially treated with broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy (vancomycin, ceftriaxone and metronidazole). The blood cultures cleared the following day. He required repeat drainage because of reaccumulation of the subdural collection.
Antimicrobial therapy was changed to penicillin and metronidazole, which were continued for approximately 6 weeks. He was seen in follow-up on several occasions and made slow improvement with rehabilitation. Cranioplasty was performed one year after his initial presentation.

Subdural empyema (abscess) is an intracranial focal collection of purulent material located between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater. A single abscess focus in the brain is most likely from contiguous spread. Mastoiditis, otitis, sinus infection, or dental infections can lead to contiguous spread. Thorough examination of the sinuses, mouth and ears should be done at the time of an initial examination.
If multiple abscess foci are found, hematogenous spread should be suspected. Bacterial endocarditis is one possible source of hematogenous spread.
Brain abscesses usually possess mixed flora and often include anaerobic pathogens. Fusobacterium and Peptostreptococcus are both common pathogens isolated; Bacteroides species (including B. fragilis), Prevotella melaninogenica, Propionibacterium, Eubacterium, Veillonella, and Actinomyces may also be isolated. Of the aerobic bacteria, Streptococcus (milleri group) is particularly common because it predisposes to necrosis and abscess formation. If the patient has had sinus or intracranial surgery, then Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa should be suspected.
Treatment with broad spectrum antibiotics is appropriate for empiric coverage. Once the etiology is known a more selective choice of antibiotics is appropriate.

title: Summary: A man was admitted to the hospital with a severe headache and choreoath
history:
Summary: A man was admitted to the hospital with a severe headache and choreoathetotic movements.
A man in his thirties was transferred from another hospital with severe headache and choreoathetotic movements.
He had been well until four months earlier, when he developed fevers, rigor, cough, and night sweats. Chest radiography revealed a cavitary right upper lobe lesion. He was seen at an outside hospital where tuberculosis skin testing and a sputum stain were negative for tuberculosis. He did not return for a lung biopsy and was lost to follow-up for three months.
The patient was admitted to another hospital with severe headache, cough and choreoathetotic movements. Fever was present and computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a right upper lobe mass that was stable and less than 1 centimeter in diameter. Multiple attempts to perform lumbar puncture at the other hospital were unsuccessful, and he was treated with multiple psychotropic medications to ameliorate his movement disorder. The patient was transferred to a tertiary hospital for further evaluation and treatment.

Results of tuberculosis skin testing (PPD) and testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies were negative, by history.

The patient had immigrated to the United States from western Africa a few years earlier. He had lived in the American Southwest but moved to the Northeast six months before his presentation.
exam_studies:
The examination at his initial presentation revealed an axillary temperature of 102.2°F (39.0°C), pulse 73 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, respirations 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. The patient was difficult to rouse and once awake, appeared in distress and unable to control his movements. The heart rhythm was regular and there was a 2/6 systolic murmur, heard loudest at left upper sternal border. The breath sounds were clear and the abdomen was normal. Extremities had 1+ edema bilaterally, and pulses were normal with quick capillary refill. The patient was oriented to person, place and time, and had normal muscle tone and muscle strength in all extremities. He was able to follow commands, but had coarse control of movements. Reflexes were normal. There was increased sensitivity to pain. No focal deficits were present. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory testing from the lumbar puncture revealed a glucose of less than 20 mg/dL and a total protein of 197 mg/dL. The white count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) ranged from 120-174 cells/mm³ with a lymphocytic predominance. Cryptococcal antigen and a test for syphilis (RPR) were negative.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Cultures of the cerebrospinal fluid were negative with the exception of a single colony of Candida albicans and Enterococcus species, which were thought to represent contamination due to difficulty performing the procedure.
Figure 1. MRI scan of the brain (axial T1 with gadolinium).
Figure 2. MRI scan of the brain (axial T1 with gadolinium).

The patient was initially treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin, ceftriaxone, acyclovir and fluconazole.
He improved clinically. Due to concern about tuberculosis, anti-tuberculosis medications were added and the patient was discharged. Cultures and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the cerebrospinal fluid were negative for tuberculosis, as were multiple induced samples of sputum and a specimen from a bronchoalveolar lavage.
diagnosis:
Coccidioidomycosis meningitis.

MRI scanning of the brain, axial T1 with gadolinium images, showed pontine enhancement that extended to the pre-sylvian fissures (Figures 3 and 4).
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) complement fixation (CF) antibodies for coccidioidomycosis returned with a positive titer to 1:64 dilution. A coccidioidomycosis agar gel test was positive for F precipitant. Serum coccidioidomycosis complement fixation was positive at greater than 1:256 dilution. Histoplasmosis and blastomycosis agar gel tests were negative. A histoplasmosis CF test was positive at 1:8 dilution and blastomycosis CF test result was negative. Testing for HIV infection was also negative.
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain (axial T1 with gadolinium).
Figure 4. MRI scan of the brain (axial T1 with gadolinium).

Fluconazole was to be administered indefinitely, anticipating a multi-year course, and tuberculosis medications were discontinued. The patient was stable on multiple follow-up visits over next 6 months, and then transferred care to another state.

The etiologic agent of basilar meningitis is often difficult to discern initially. The differential diagnosis and empiric therapies are based largely on the patient’s possible exposure to endemic mycoses, tuberculosis, or Lyme disease, known or suspected immunosuppression due to HIV or other immunosuppressive medications, and history of sexually transmitted diseases such as syphilis.
This case presented particular challenges due to the patient’s recent immigration from western Africa, where there is a high prevalence of tuberculosis and HIV, as well as his recent stay in the American Southwest where exposure to Coccidioides was possible. The CSF revealed results consistent with chronic meningitis, including an elevated white blood cell count with a lymphocytic predominance that would have been consistent with tuberculosis, Coccidioides and multiple other infections. Given his possible exposures, and negative serum and CSF studies for syphilis and cryptococcal meningitis, the decision to start therapy both for tuberculosis and Coccidioides meningitis was made. His rapid improvement, and subsequent positive CSF complement fixation for Coccidioides lent further support for this diagnosis, and tuberculosis therapy was discontinued after one month of negative cultures for Mycobacterium.

history:
The patient reported occasionally passing stools with mucus and blood during the preceding six months. He otherwise felt well during that time; his symptoms had resolved without any intervention.

The patient lived in an urban area and was sexually active with men. He reported one sexual partner during the preceding four years and denied alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use.
exam_studies:
In the emergency ward, the temperature rose to 104°F (40°C). There was mild tachycardia; blood pressure and respirations were normal. The examination revealed some abdominal tenderness with mild rebound in the left lower quadrant and a palpable spleen tip. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, rash or abnormal joint findings. Rectal exam revealed hemoccult positive stool.

The white blood cell count was 15,600 cells/µL, with 32% neutrophils, 40% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes, and 18% atypical lymphocytes. The hematocrit was 33.8% with microcytosis. Levels of serum alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin were normal. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 58 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 42 U/L.
Computed tomography (CT) scanning of his abdomen and pelvis revealed splenomegaly with a normal appearing liver, marked inflammatory thickening of the colonic wall extending from the distal transverse colon to the anus with pericolonic fat stranding and lymphadenopathy in the pericolonic and retroperitoneal regions.

Intravenous fluids and empiric antimicrobial therapy with ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole were administered. Blood, urine and stool cultures were sent and the stool was examined for parasites. Serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, and a heterophile antibody were also ordered.
A colonoscopic examination revealed ulcerated mucosa extending from the rectum to the distal transverse colon that was most consistent with ulcerative colitis. Pathological examination of a colonic biopsy is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Biopsy of the colon.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Primary cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection with colitis in a patient with ulcerative colitis.

Biopsies confirmed the findings of ulcerative colitis (Figure 1), though the specimens were also noted to contain a multitude of cells with intranuclear inclusions (Figure 2), findings characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. Viral cytopathic effect was also seen. Serologic testing confirmed the presence of both IgG and IgM antibodies to the virus, and blood testing with the CMV antigenemia assay revealed 10 positive cells per two slides. Serological testing for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (including antibody serology and viral nucleic acid copies), and a heterophile antibody were negative.

Intravenous ganciclovir was begun at a dose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) twice daily with improvement. The patient defervesced quickly on this regimen and was discharged home shortly thereafter.
Two weeks later, the patient remained asymptomatic with a normal physical examination. Intravenous ganciclovir was discontinued and oral valganciclovir begun.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection has been described as a complication of ulcerative colitis. Though the association between the use of immunosuppressant medications such as prednisone and CMV infection is widely documented, the association between CMV colitis and patients with ulcerative colitis not on immunosuppressants is less clearly understood.
In this case, a man with newly diagnosed ulcerative colitis developed primary infection with CMV leading to worsening colitis and a systemic illness. His symptoms improved with therapy that included intravenous ganciclovir followed by oral valganciclovir.
Colitis caused by CMV is uncommon in a normal host but is well-documented in the immunocompromised host. Infection with CMV in patients with ulcerative colitis is more likely to lead to colitis even in the absence of immunosuppressant therapy compared to otherwise normal hosts. Primary CMV infection as opposed to reactivation seems likely to cause a more severe course. CMV colitis is generally treated with intravenous ganciclovir. Valganciclovir may be a reasonable alternative therapy in some patients, although randomized clinical trials to demonstrate its benefit in this setting have not been done to date.

history:
Summary: A man with shortness of breath after stem cell transplantation.
A man in his fifties, with a history of recurrent non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, autologous transplant and mini allograft unmatched stem cell transplant, and graft-versus-host disease, presented with progressive shortness of breath of seven weeks' duration. Graft-versus-host disease had worsened six months before and affected 35% of the skin; immunosuppressive medications were increased.
Three weeks before admission, the patient presented with shortness of breath of four weeks' duration that was associated with weight loss of fifteen pounds. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figure 1. Cultures of the sputum and blood were negative. The patient was treated empirically with levofloxacin and imipenem without improvement.
Three weeks later, he developed hemoptysis and increasing weakness.
Figure 1. Chest CT scan three weeks before current admission.

There was a history of recurrent non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma for which an autologous transplant and mini allograft unmatched stem cell transplantation had been performed. He also had a history of graft-versus-host disease and coronary artery disease.

The patient was born in Europe and had lived in the Middle East as a child. He had moved to the United States decades before. There was a history of minimal alcohol ingestion; there was no history of smoking or exposure to pets.

Medications included tacrolimus, sirolimus and prednisone (20 mg) daily.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared tired and cachectic. The temperature was 98.3ºF (36.8ºC), pulse 112 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on 2 liters inspired oxygen. The skin revealed extensive breakdown and peeling. Examination of the lungs revealed crackles bilaterally, which were most prominent in the left mid-lung field. There were no cardiac murmurs; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 15,060 cells/mm³, sodium 128 mmol/L, and C-reactive protein 195.0 mg/liter. A sputum sample revealed 2+ polymorphonuclear cells and 4+ epithelial cells. Chest radiographs are shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph.
Figure 3. Chest radiograph, lateral view.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest is shown in Figure 4. Bronchoscopy revealed purulent material.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan, post hemoptysis.
diagnosis:
Lung abscess due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a patient with graft-versus-host disease.

Cultures of the sputum and bronchoscopic aspirate grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Tobramycin and ceftazidime, to which the organism was sensitive, were administered. However, the infection progressed; inhaled tobramycin and colistin were added.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a non-fermentative gram-negative aerobic rod. One of the most common causes of gram negative nosocomial pneumonia, it is notoriously difficult to treat. Part of the challenge is that the bacteria have barrier properties in the outer membrane. To enter through the outer membrane porins, a compound must have a low molecular weight and zwitterionic properties.
In addition, P. aeruginosa has developed a wide variety of resistance to anti-pseudomonal antibiotics. Data regarding monotherapy versus combination therapy is limited. Studies which compare combination therapy with monotherapy in patients with cystic fibrosis have shown no difference in outcome, but the density of bacteria was lower in the sputum and time to next pulmonary infection requiring hospitalization was prolonged in those patients with combination therapy. Eradication of P. aeruginosa from bronchial secretions is difficult; the potential risk for emergence of resistance is high, as is mortality in patients with pneumonia due to P. aeruginosa. Due to these factors and despite the absence of data, treatment with at least two agents is often recommended.

title: Summary: A woman presented many years after lung transplantation with fever, mal
history:
Summary: A woman presented many years after lung transplantation with fever, malaise and cough.
A woman in her sixties presented with fever, malaise, and cough.
The patient had a history of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, for which a single lung transplant had been performed more than a decade earlier. Progressive renal failure had developed and was thought to be related to calcineurin toxicity.
During the week before presentation, she developed fevers to 102°F (38.9°C) associated with occasional chills and generalized malaise. There was a slightly productive cough without dyspnea. Two wounds on her lower extremities, which she had received during home gardening activity, were healing poorly.

She had congenital alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and had had a single lung transplantation more than a decade before presentation. There was also a history of progressive chronic renal failure and hypertension.

She lived in the suburbs and worked in an office. There were no unusual activities, travel or exposures.

The patient was married.

Medications included tacrolimus, azathioprine, prednisone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) combination (single strength) three times weekly, acyclovir, atenolol, aspirin, ranitidine, pravastatin, alpha1-proteinase inhibitor, potassium chloride, furosemide, salmeterol, alendronate, calcitriol, enalapril, epoetin alfa, and multiple vitamins.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, the temperature, pulse and respirations on room air were normal. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds, without rales or wheezes. The extremities showed trace pedal edema and a poorly-healed ulcer on her right shin. Cardiovascular, abdominal and lymphoreticular examinations were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed a hematocrit of 26.8% with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. The creatinine was slightly elevated from her baseline to 4.6 mg/dL with a serum urea nitrogen of 76 mg/dL.
A chest radiograph revealed a pleural-based lesion in her right mid-thorax (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) scan of the lungs confirmed a wedge-shaped focal area of consolidation.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

The patient was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. Sputum samples were obtained for staining and culture (Figures 2 through 4).
Figure 2. Gram stain of sputum sample.
Figure 3. Gram stain of sputum sample.
Figure 4. Modified acid fast stain of sputum.
diagnosis:
Pneumonia secondary to Nocardia nova infection in a patient with congenital alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, after lung transplantation.

Initial gram stain examination of the primary sputum sample showed Candida albicans. Specimens obtained during bronchoscopy revealed branching gram-positive rods.
The sputum was planted on modified Thayer Martin plate. Stains of the growth on that plate are shown in Figures 5 and 6. The organisms were identified as Nocardia nova complex.
Figure 5. Modified acid fast stain of growth from modified Thayer Martin plate.
Figure 6. Gram stain of growth from Thayer Martin plate.

Intravenous meropenem and vancomycin were administered empirically. After the diagnosis of Nocardia was made and no other pathogens were identified, the vancomycin was discontinued. Susceptibility testing of the isolate showed it was sensitive to amikacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). Aminoglycoside use was withheld due to the patient’s renal failure.
The patient completed a six-month course of meropenem intravenously and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) orally with complete resolution of her symptoms. Chest radiography and CT scan abnormalities also improved. TMP-SMX therapy was then changed to single strength once daily for chronic suppression and prophylaxis.

Nocardia are filamentous gram-positive branching rods that can mimic Actinomyces species. Nocardia can be differentiated from Actinomyces by modified acid fast staining because of the mycolic acid content of their cell wall.
Nocardia infection is typically regarded as an opportunistic infection and T-cell immunity plays a critical role in its control. Two-thirds of patients will have an underlying immunodeficiency, such as pharmacological immunosuppression after a solid organ transplant seen in the patient presented. Pneumonia is the primary syndrome associated with Nocardia infection, and the presentation can vary from acute to chronic. Occasionally, dissemination and other forms of infection can be seen, such as cutaneous, lymphatic or central nervous system disease.
Sulfonamides are the mainstay of therapy, though some in vitro susceptibilities and animal models have demonstrated that amikacin, imipenem, third generation cephalosporins, and minocycline can have activity. The duration of therapy is not clear with treatment regimens generally lasting 6-12 months.

title: 2005 December Featured Case Summary: An elderly man presented with leg numbness
history:
2005 December Featured Case Summary: An elderly man presented with leg numbness and difficulty with walking and swallowing.
An elderly man presented with left leg numbness and progressive difficulty ambulating for the preceding two weeks. Two days before his presentation, he developed drooling and difficulty swallowing. He denied any fever, chills, headache or other constitutional symptoms.
He had a history of ulcerative colitis for which he had been on chronic prednisone therapy. During the preceding six months, there had been a 30-pound weight loss. He reported intermittent diarrhea; there had been no incontinence of stool or urine. There had been no fevers, chills, night sweats, chest pain, palpitations, respiratory symptoms, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, rectal bleeding, or melena. He had no other neurologic symptoms, and no muscle, bone, or urinary complaints.

Ulcerative colitis had been diagnosed several years earlier, and bullous pemphigoid more recently. He also had glaucoma and hypertension. One month before, ampicillin had been administered for an upper respiratory infection.

He lived in the United States and had traveled extensively throughout the country. He had also spent time in South America and Africa.He had smoked cigarettes for many years, and did not drink alcohol or use recreational drugs. He had owned pets in the remote past, denied known exposure to tuberculosis and did not know his PPD status.

He was married and lived with his wife.

The patient was on prednisone, usually at a dose of 40 milligrams daily but the dose had recently been tapered to 20 mg per day before the patient's admission. The dose of prednisone had varied during the preceding 5 years; the highest had been 80 mg day several months earlier. The patient also received balsalazide 2.25 grams three times daily, and alendronate sodium 70 mg weekly.
exam_studies:
He appeared comfortable. The temperature was 95.6°F (35.3°C), blood pressure 152/90 mm Hg, pulse 92 beats per minute, and respirations 18 per minute. Pulse oximetry was measured at 92% on ambient air. The pupils were reactive and extraocular movements were intact. There were no conjunctival lesions. A lesion on the soft palate was indurated, and thrush was noted under the dentures. The neck was supple and there was a left supraclavicular fullness. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. The examination of the lung, heart and abdomen was normal, and the extremities had no edema. There were multiple areas of healing blisters and hyperpigmented violaceous lesions, and findings consistent with onychomycosis were present. There was a left seventh (VII) nerve palsy, and the muscle strength of the left leg was 4 out of 5. The sense of light touch was intact, but temperature sensation was impaired on the left.

The white blood cell count was 12,800/mm³ (97% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 4% lymphocytes and 2% monocytes), hematocrit 37%, and platelets 285,000/mm³. The liver function tests were normal, the urea nitrogen was 20 mg/dL and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Two blood cultures were sterile.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning of the head showed a cluster of ring enhancing lesions, the largest measuring 1.9 x 1.9 x 2.1 cm, within the right basal ganglia and corona radiata. There was extensive surrounding edema and mild mass effect but no evidence of midline shift or herniation. Fluid was present within multiple left mastoid air cells. In addition, small air fluid levels were seen within the left sphenoid sinus. (See Figures 1 through 3.)
Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the chest showed bilateral lower lobe atelectasis and two small ground glass nodes in the right lower lobe. CT scanning of the abdomen and pelvis did not show any lesions.
Figure 1. MRI scan of brain.
Figure 2. MRI scan of brain.
Figure 3. MRI scan of brain.

A stereotactic brain biopsy was performed in the operating room. Approximately twenty cubic centimeters of purulent white debris were aspirated from the largest lesion. Staining of the brain biopsy is shown in Figures 4 and 5.
Figure 4. Gram stain of brain biopsy.
Figure 5. Gram stain of brain biopsy.
diagnosis:
Invasive infection of the central nervous system infection by Scedosporium apiospermum.

A gram stain of the tissue revealed moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes and rare septated hyphae. (See Figures 4 and 5 above.) Necrotic tissue and rare fungal hyphae were present on pathologic examination (hematoxylin and eosin staining and gomori methenamine silver staining) of the brain biopsy. (See Figures 6through 9.) Fungal culture grew Scedosporium apiospermum.
Figure 6. H and E stain of brain biopsy.
Figure 7. Detail of Figure 6.
Figure 8. GMS stain of brain biopsy.
Figure 9. GMS stain of brain biopsy.

The patient was treated with the antifungal agents voriconazole and caspofungin. The steroid dose was tapered, and the patient is being followed closely.

Scedosporium apiospermum is the asexual form of Pseudallescheria boydii, a saprophytic fungus frequently isolated from soil, manure, decaying vegetation and polluted streams.
The fungi that most commonly cause central nervous system (CNS) infections are Candida species and Cryptococcus neoformans. S. apiospermum has traditionally been known as a cause for cutaneous and soft tissue infection (Madura foot). More recently with the increasing prevalence of immunosuppression due to organ transplantation, AIDS and potent drugs, opportunistic fungi and specifically S. apiospermum have become relatively rare but well-documented potential CNS pathogens.
Review of the literature suggests that the most common clinical and radiographic presentation of CNS involvement is either multiple or solitary parenchymal brain abscesses. In addition, other presentations described include meningitis, ventriculitis or ependymitis, sagittal sinus infection and spinal dural or epidural abscess.
The most common risk factor described is medical immunosuppression due to cytotoxic chemotherapy, solid and bone marrow transplantation or the use of immunosuppressive drugs including prednisone. Other risk factors include direct inoculation, motor vehicle accidents, near-drowning episodes and diabetes mellitus.
The prognosis for patients with CNS infections is poor, even when early and aggressive therapeutic interventions are undertaken, with the mortality as high as approximately 70% (Nesky et al. 2000). In order to establish early appropriate therapy, microbiologic diagnosis is essential. The histopathological examination reveals hyphae that morphologically resemble Aspergillus species.
The treatment of choice remains surgical resection with adjuvant antifungal therapy. Scedosporium and Pseudallescheria are generally resistant to amphotericin B. Available data do not support the use of it or its liposomal preparations for treatment of brain abscesses due to infection with these organisms. The azoles (miconazole, ketoconazole, and itraconazole) generally have been ineffective except for a few cases that were amenable to complete neurosurgical drainage. Successful treatment with newer azoles (voriconazole and posaconazole) has been reported but surgical drainage, when possible, is clearly the key therapeutic intervention.
The choice of antifungal therapy poses a challenging dilemma. Obtaining a definitive fungal culture and standardized antifungal drug susceptibility testing is of great importance for immunosuppressed patients with suspected fungal infection.

title:
Summary: A woman presented with a fever and sore throat.
A woman in her sixties
history:
Summary: A woman presented with a fever and sore throat.
A woman in her sixties presented with a sore throat, fever and headache of two days duration. Pain occurred with swallowing, but she was able to tolerate oral intake. She also noted chills, sweats and general body aches. There was no change in her voice.

The patient was from Haiti.
exam_studies:
The patient was ill-appearing with a temperature of 103.0°F (39.4°C), pulse 87 beats per minute, and blood pressure 146/84 mm Hg. Respirations were 18 per minute and oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air. The oropharynx was erythematous and the tonsils were enlarged and covered with a white exudate. There was no trismus. The lungs were clear, and the heart and abdomen were normal.

The white blood cell count was 7,600 cells/mm³ (79% polymorphonuclear leukocytes and 15% lymphocytes), the hematocrit 38.0%, and platelets 184,000/mm³. The level of serum sodium was 133 mmol/liter, potassium 3.3 mmol/liter, chloride 102 mmol/liter and carbon dioxide 124.3 mmol/liter, with a serum glucose of 113 mg/dL.

A rapid group A streptococcal antigen test was positive. Intravenous fluids and intramuscular benzathine penicillin were administered.
A culture of the throat showed growth the following day; a gram stain of the culture is shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Gram stain of throat culture.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Corynebacterium diphtheriae pharyngitis.

The throat culture was planted on a Loeffler slant and tellurite plates. It was positive for abundant Corynebacterium diphtheriae, toxinogenic strain. A blood culture was negative.
Figure 3. Tellurite plate.
Figure 4. Loeffler slant.
Figure 5. Growth on blood agar.

Penicillin G benzathine (1.2 million units) had been given intramuscularly, and the patient's symptoms and physical findings improved. The culture was reported to the state's Department of Public Health as required by law. Follow-up occurred and all family members were cultured. No one else became ill. The following month, the patient received immunization with diphtheria and tetanus toxoid.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a gram positive rod with an irregular or ‘club-shaped’ appearance for which it is named (Coryne = club in ancient Greek). Both toxigenic and non-toxigenic forms are associated with pharyngitis. Diphtheria throat infection from the toxigenic strain is potentially life-threatening, especially in the pediatric population with smaller airways. Toxigenic sub-species are also seen in cutaneous infections and may be associated with clinical syndromes that include fever and inflammation and pseudomembrane formation at the site of the lesions. Asymptomatic carrier states are also seen. Infections more commonly associated with non-toxigenic forms include endocarditis and foreign-body infections.
The incidence of throat infection caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae, or diphtheria, has decreased in the United States since the availability of vaccination with diphtheria toxoid. However, the disease is still present in many other countries with less access to vaccination, and cases do occur in the United States, most commonly associated with immigrant populations. Diphtheria has been documented to be endemic in Haiti in the past.

title: A woman in her twenties presented with a productive, persistent cough of three w
history:
A woman in her twenties presented with a productive, persistent cough of three weeks duration.
She was in good health until aged eight years, when jaundice and hepatitis A were diagnosed. Subsequently, persistent right upper quadrant pain developed. An echinococcal cyst was diagnosed.
Five years before this presentation, a partial hepatic resection was performed. The patient was not certain if albendazole was administered. A residual cyst was found and annual ultrasounds advised. She was unsure of the date of the last ultrasound.
Three weeks before admission, persistent and productive cough developed. There was also a history of headaches.

There was a history of echinococcal disease.

The patient was originally from Eastern Europe and owned dogs.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared anxious. The vital signs were normal. There was mild right upper quadrant tenderness to palpation; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood count was 8,000 cells/mm³ with 11.8% eosinophils; all other laboratory testing was normal. A chest radiograph revealed collapse of the right middle lobe (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest and upper abdomen is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 3. CT scan of the upper abdomen.
diagnosis:
Echinococcal (hydatid) cyst.

The CT scan of the chest (Figures 2 and 3) revealed a mass that measured 7.1 centimeters by 5.8 centimeters. There was a well-defined capsule and internal septations with wall calcification that extended from the dome of the liver through the diaphragm and resulted in right middle lobe collapse.
Bronchoscopy revealed a thick mucus plug that occluded the right middle lobe bronchus and emanated from the medial segment. It could not be cleared despite attempts at aspiration.
The echinococcal serology was positive at 2.9 (normal 0-1.1).

The patient was referred for surgical excision through a combined thoracic and abdominal approach. Pre-treatment medications included albendazole and praziquantel.

Hydatid cysts of the liver are most commonly caused by the larval form of Echinococcus granulosis, commonly acquired from dogs. Lesions grow indolently and often do not present until they are quite large, impinging on local structures or until the contents leak and the patient presents with symptoms of hypersensitivity. Diagnosis rests on classic radiographic findings and serology.
Treatment modalities include surgery, percutaneous aspiration, introduction of a protoscolicidal agent and re-aspiration (PAIR) and antiparasitic chemotherapy (albendazole or praziquantel).

title: Summary: A woman with fever and abdominal pain.A woman in her forties presented
history:
Summary: A woman with fever and abdominal pain.A woman in her forties presented with right upper quadrant pain and fever.

The patient was from South America and had immigrated to the United States more than five years earlier. She had not returned in the intervening years. She did not smoke and denied alcohol or illicit drug use.
exam_studies:
The patient did not appear to be in any acute distress. The temperature was 100.9°F (38.3°C). On examination, there was right upper and lower quadrant tenderness, without rebound or guarding.

The white blood cell count was 11,690 cells/mm³ (81% polymorphonuclear leukocytes). The hematocrit was 32%, and platelets 506,000/mm³. Alkaline phosphatase was 123 U/liter, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 31 U/liter and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 58 U/liter.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Pyogenic liver abscess, caused by Streptococcus intermedius.

CT scanning of the abdomen revealed a liver abscess measuring 9.6 centimeters in diameter in the posterior segment of the right lobe of the liver. Scattered bubbles of peritoneal gas were noted and suggested a perforated viscus. Multiple diverticula were also noted in the sigmoid colon.
CT-guided drainage of the liver lesion produced 175 cubic centimeters of purulent fluid, which grew Streptococcus intermedius. Blood cultures were negative. Serology for Entameoba histolytica was negative.

Ampicillin, levofloxacin, and metronidazole were administered for broad spectrum coverage prior to drainage. She was discharged with plans to continue broad spectrum coverage with levofloxacin, metronidazole, and cefuroxime for a six-week course of antimicrobial therapy. Follow up CT scanning revealed decreased size of the abscess.

The most common cause of pyogenic liver abscess is from local spread due from intra-abdominal infection (such as the biliary tree or peritoneal cavity). This patient had evidence of diverticula on scanning and possibly had had diverticulitis that perforated and seeded the liver.
Amebic abscess was also high on the differential in this case because the patient was originally from an endemic area. However, amebic liver abscess usually occurs within months of return from the endemic region (though longer lag times have been reported). In this case, the aspirated fluid did not have the “anchovy paste” appearance typical of amebic abscess and serology was negative.
Pyogenic abscesses are usually of mixed morphology (typically involving anaerobic pathogens). When a single organism is isolated, as in this case, it may be due to hematogenous seeding of the organ. Blood cultures were negative in this case.

title:
Summary: A woman with a swollen and painful finger.
A woman in her forties prese
history:
Summary: A woman with a swollen and painful finger.
A woman in her forties presented with a red, swollen and painful left third finger distal phalanx of two days duration. There was no history of trauma or fever and she had never had a similar problem in the past. There was no history of herpes simplex infection.
The patient had punctured the lesion with a needle the day before presentation; no purulent drainage was obtained. The patient presented due to increasing discomfort.

Past medical history included asthma and hypothyroidism.

The patient cared for a relative with Alzheimer's disease who had recently had lesions described as "cold sores".
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The temperature was 100°F (37.8°C), other vital signs were normal. There was redness, swelling, tenderness and slight "bubbly" appearance of the entire left middle finger nail fold, without fluctuance. A small amount of purulent material extruded from the lesion the patient had pricked. See Figures 1 and 2. A small amount of subcutaneous blood was also present. There was no lymphangitis or proximal lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
diagnosis:
Herpetic whitlow of the left third finger with possible Staphylococcus aureus superinfection.

An intact vesicle was incised and cultured. Standard bacterial and herpes virus cultures were sent; the standard culture grew pan-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and the viral culture was positive for Herpes simplex virus.

At the time of the first visit, the patient was started on dicloxacillin.
Two days later, the culture results were available and the patient was notified. She reported that the finger felt worse, and acyclovir 400 milligrams, three times daily, for primary herpes infection was added to the dicloxacillin. Her symptoms increased during the following day and were much improved by five days later.

Apparent infections of the distal finger are not always bacterial infections. The small areas of loculated fluid (Figure 2) have a flatter appearance than the vesicles usually seen in Herpes simplex infections due to the thicker epithelium of the finger. This appearance should suggest the possibility of a viral etiology.
The social history - such as an occupation of dental or health care worker, or exposure to oral or genital herpes - may suggest a source. Attempts to drain all collections of fluid or pus may result in more severe symptoms for the patient with herpetic whitlow.

title:
Summary: A woman with fevers, fatigue and headache.
A woman in her forties devel
history:
Summary: A woman with fevers, fatigue and headache.
A woman in her forties developed fatigue, headache, decreased appetite and fevers of six days' duration. Chills and sweats later occurred, and she presented for evaluation.

The patient had hiked in late summer in New Hampshire with her dog. There was no history of tick bites.

She was taking acetaminophen.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 103.5°F (39.7°C), blood pressure 104/50 mm Hg, pulse 113-122 beats per minute, respirations 18 per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing ambient air. The remainder of the examination was normal. There was no pallor, icterus, meningismus, abdominal tenderness, organomegaly or rash.

The white blood cell count was 2,300/mm³ (51% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 29% band forms, 14% lymphocytes, and 4% atypical lymphocytes). The hematocrit was 39% and platelets were 24,000/mm³. The peripheral blood smear is shown in Figure 1. Serum chemistries values were normal and blood cultures were negative.
Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear.
diagnosis:
Human granulocytic anaplasmosis (also known as human granulocytic ehrlichiosis), caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum and transmitted by the tick Ixodes scapularis.

The peripheral blood smear (Figure 1) showed morulae inside white blood cells, consistent with human granulocytic anaplasmosis. The diagnosis was confirmed with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.

Oral doxycycline (100 milligrams) was administered twice daily for seven days.

Human granulocytic anaplasmosis is a tick-borne illness, caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum and transmitted by the tick Ixodes scapularis. The incubation period is one to two weeks and patients present with non-specific symptoms including fevers, chills, malaise and headache. Rash is exceedingly rare.
Fifty to ninety percent of patients are leukopenic and most have associated thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. The diagnosis is made through visualization of intraleucocytic morulae on the blood smear, by serology or by serum PCR testing.
At the time of this publication, treatment is with doxycycline for one week; mortality approaches 4.9%.

title:
Summary: A woman with hemoptysis.
A woman in her forties was well until approxim
history:
Summary: A woman with hemoptysis.
A woman in her forties was well until approximately twenty years earlier when, while breast-feeding, she had the sudden onset of hemoptysis, described as "cups and cups" of blood. She was admitted to a hospital and a left lower lobectomy was performed. Histoplasma was seen on pathological examination of the resected lung. Intravenous amphotericin was administered for three months without complication. Follow-up computer tomography (CT) scans of the chest remained abnormal but she did not require further intervention.
Three years before admission, she developed recurrent pneumonias and pulmonary hypertension. She was found to have possible pulmonary artery stenosis and was referred to a tertiary care medical center for dilatation.

There was a history of histoplasmosis, as indicated above.

The patient lived in rural Kentucky.

Medications included fluconazole (200 milligrams) and colchicine (0.6 milligrams) daily; both of which were started three weeks before referral to the tertiary care hospital.
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The temperature was 97°F (36.1°C), blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. There was no clinical evidence of pulmonary hypertension, cyanosis or clubbing. The jugular venous pressure was normal.

Laboratory test results were normal, including a negative urinary Histoplasma antigen. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed calcifications in the mediastinum, proximal pulmonary artery stenosis and superior vena cava obstruction (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT scan of chest.
diagnosis:
Fibrosing mediastinitis in a patient with a history of prior pulmonary Histoplasmosis.

The diagnosis of fibrosing mediastinitis was made on the basis of the clinical history and the findings on CT scan of the chest, including the presence of mediastinal calcifications. No biopsy or other invasive confirmatory test was performed.

The patient underwent successful pulmonary artery dilatation. Fluconazole (200 mg) was administered daily for three months.

Mediastinal fibrosis caused by prior histoplasmosis is rare but can be devastating.
Yeast are not seen in the mediastinum, which is effaced by massive fibrosis. The pathophysiology remains unclear. The fibrosis encroaches on all mediastinal structures including the pulmonary arteries, superior vena cava (SVC), airways and esophagus. Patients present with recurrent pneumonias, dysphagia, pulmonary hypertension and superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome.
There are no data in support of antifungal therapy at the time of diagnosis; intervention is palliative and involves stenting of the occluded structures.

title:
Summary: An elderly woman with finger swelling.
An elderly woman presented with
history:
Summary: An elderly woman with finger swelling.
An elderly woman presented with pain, redness, and swelling of her left fifth finger that had gradually worsened during the next five days. There was no history of trauma or similar problems in the past. There were no other joint symptoms or fever.

The patient had osteoarthritis and hypothyroidism, and had recently had an urinary tract infection.

There was a family history of gout.

Medications included furosemide, ciprofloxacin, acetaminophen, atenelol and levothyroxine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, and younger than her stated age. The temperature was 100°F (37.8°C) and other vital signs were normal. There was redness and swelling of the entire left fifth finger, most marked on the dorsal surface of the distal phalanx. Fluctuance and maximal tenderness were present there as well. There was no lymphangitis or proximal lymphadenopathy. There was a decreased range of motion of both joints of the distal small finger, especially in the distal interphalangeal joint. There were chronic arthritic deformities of both hands. See Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 13,810/mm³ (segmented cells 81.8%, lymphocytes 8.95, monocytes 7.4%, eosinophils 1.8%, basophils 0.1%), hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, hematocrit 40.6%, platelet count 174,000/mm³ and the serum uric acid 9.4 mg/dL. Radiographs of the fifth finger showed degenerative joint changes consistent for age.
diagnosis:
Crystal arthropathy, consistent with gout, of the left fifth finger.

Aspiration of the fluctuant area on the dorsum of the distal interphalangeal joint yielded 0.1 milliliters of thick white material, which was almost entirely composed of needlelike crystals, consistent with gout. There were rare polymorphonuclear leukocytes present. Figure 1. Physical finding. Figure 2. Physical finding.

Prednisone (40 milligrams daily for five days) was administered. Several days later, the symptoms were almost entirely resolved.

Not all red, painful swelling of the distal finger is infectious. Non-infectious causes include acute inflammatory processes, such as crystal arthropathies. Aspiration of fluctuant areas can often yield data invaluable for appropriate treatment. The first clinical episode of gout may appear late in life.

title:
Summary: A man presented with scrotal discomfort.
A man in his fifties presented
history:
Summary: A man presented with scrotal discomfort.
A man in his fifties presented with scrotal discomfort. Approximately twenty-five years earlier, a lesion on his buttocks had developed. The lesion was associated with inguinal lymphadenopathy and swelling of the scrotum. Over the ensuing years, the swelling and pain in his scrotum and buttocks became so severe that the patient reported difficulty sitting. Frequent discharge occurred from these lesions. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics for bacterial infections.
The patient presented with fevers, chills and increased pain and discharge, and was admitted to the hospital for evaluation and treatment.

There was a history of hypertension and anemia.

The patient was born and raised in the Caribbean, where he lived in a city but regularly visited relatives living in rural environments. He had immigrated to the United States more than a decade before admission, and lived in the Northeast with his family. He was monogamous with one sexual partner for more than two decades. He was unable to work because of groin swelling.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 100.3ºF (37.9ºC). There was inguinal lymphadenopathy, scrotal swelling and thickening of scrotal skin, thickening of skin on buttocks, and trace edema at ankles bilaterally (Figures 1 through 4).
Figure 1. Physical findings: Groin.
Figure 2. Scrotum.
Figure 3. Inguinal lymph node.
Figure 4. Buttocks.

Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count 13,200 cells/mm³ (86% neutrophils, 6% lymphocytes, and 6% eosinophils) and hematocrit 28%. Blood cultures were negative.
diagnosis:
Lymphatic filariasis.

An antifilarial antibody was 19.2 ug/ml (positive >14.0 ug/ml). Scrotal ultrasound was negative for “filarial dance sign” and a blood sample drawn at midnight was negative for microfilariae.

The patient was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate with improvement in symptoms, followed by isotretinoin therapy. Diethylcarbamazine therapy is also a possible therapy.

Lymphatic filariasis is caused by infection with one of three nematodes: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori. W. bancrofti occurs in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, Pacific islands and focal areas in Latin America and the Caribbean, and is the cause of 90% of cases of lymphatic filariasis.
Several mosquito species including Anopheles, Culex, Aedes and Mansonia can serve as vectors for transmission. The quantity of accumulating adult worm antigen, duration and level of exposure to infective mosquitoes, number of secondary bacterial and fungal infections, and host immune responses all influence the pathogenesis and clinical progression of filarial disease. In general, symptoms are related to dead or dying worms in the lymphatics resulting in obstruction of lymph flow.
Lymphedema is most common in individuals without detectable microfilaria in their blood as they tend to be highly immunoresponsive and clear antigens from the blood stream. They often have the most severe clinical symptoms due to immune responses to adult parasite antigens resulting in inflammation and fibrosis.
The diagnosis is made by analysis of the following:
1. Blood smear. Both Bancroftian and Brugian filariasis show a nocturnal periodicity. Blood should be drawn between 10 PM and 2 AM because the greatest number of microfilariae is present during this peak biting time of the mosquito vector. The microfilariae stain with Wright’s or Giemsa stains.
2. Serology.
A. Antibody tests: Tests for filarial antibodies which detect elevated levels of IgG and IgE are available. They are reported to be 100% sensitive; however, they have poor specificity as they also cross react with other helminths such as Strongyloides. They cannot distinguish between active and past infections. Newer serodiagnostic tests are being developed that use either excretory-secretory antigens or reagents to detect antibody isotypes or subclasses with sensitivities of 80% and specificities of 100%.
B. Antigen Tests: Monoclonal antibodies have been used to detect the presence of filarial adult worms and may be positive in people who are amicrofilaremic. These tests reflect adult worm burdens rather than microfilariae. Circulating filarial antigen tests are now the gold standard for diagnosing W. bancrofti infections. Two commercial tests are available: enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay (ELISA) yielding quantitative results and immunochromatographic technique (ICT) yielding qualitative results.
3. Radiology: Ultrasound may localize worms within lymphatics, especially the epididymal lymphatics. If the worms are in continuous motion and detected by ultrasound, this is called the “filarial dance sign”.

title:
Summary: A man with an abnormal finding after defecation.
A man in his thirties
history:
Summary: A man with an abnormal finding after defecation.
A man in his thirties presented after finding an abnormality in the toilet bowl after a bowel movement. He denied abdominal pain, fevers, chills, obstipation, constipation or diarrhea.

The patient had lived in Africa for several years during his childhood, departing over ten years earlier. While in Africa, he lived in major cities and occasionally visited remote areas.
exam_studies:
The physical examination was normal.

Images of the findings are shown in Figures 1 and 2. The finding measured 12 inches in length.
Figure 1. Finding after defecation.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Ascariasis.

Examination revealed a gravid female nematode, Ascaris.

After the identification of the nematode, the patient was treated with one dose of albendazole. He was advised to return to his primary care physician in 1-2 weeks for repeat stool evaluation for ova and parasites to confirm clearance. If ova are found, one additional treatment would be considered.

Ascariasis is the most common helminthic infection in the world. More than one billion people are estimated to be infected with this helminth. The most common route of transmission is through contamination of food and water by ova contained in the soil. Once ingested, the eggs hatch and small larvae penetrate the small intestine and travel to the lung where they are coughed up and re-ingested. The adult worms establish themselves in the jejunum where they can live for over a decade. Eosinophilia is not a feature of chronic infection with ascariasis, yet can sometimes be found in early infection, during the the tissue-migratory phase.
Most infections with Ascaris are asymptomatic, but may be complicated by intestinal obstruction, cholangitis, and pancreatitis. A single dose of albendazole is the preferred agent for therapy. It is important to remember that individuals may be infected with multiple parasites, and ova and parasite tests should be sent to rule out concurrent infections.

title:
Summary: A woman in her twenties with diabetic ketoacidosis.
A woman in her twen
history:
Summary: A woman in her twenties with diabetic ketoacidosis.
A woman in her twenties presented in diabetic ketoacidosis. She had recently had poor control of glucose levels. During the preceding two months, nausea, fatigue, anorexia and a 20-pound weight loss had been noted.

Type 1 insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus had been diagnosed in her early teens. There had been poor adherence to insulin and monitoring regimen during recent years and the HgB A1C level was 10.6%. She had a history of lower leg abscess and furunculosis.

The patient lived alone. She denied sexual activity or the use of alcohol, tobacco or illicit drugs. She had traveled to the islands in the mid-Atlantic in the past.

Medications included insulin.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 102.9°F (39.4°C), pulse 130 beats per minute, and the blood pressure was hypotensive. Retinopathy was present. There was no abdominal tenderness.

The hematocrit was 30.7% and glucose 179 mg/dL. The electrolytes and anion gap were consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis, and normalized after treatment. The alkaline phosphatase was 138 U/liter. Computed tomography (CT) of abdomen (Figures 1 and 2) showed multiloculated cystic structures in the liver that were consistent with abscesses.
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of the abdomen.

Blood cultures were obtained and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy was started. Severe abdominal pain developed after a diagnostic interventional radiology procedure. Low-grade fevers continued. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
diagnosis:
Liver abscess due to Candida albicans in a patient with diabetes mellitus.

Percutaneous aspiration of the largest cystic lesion by interventional radiologists yielded fluid that grew Candida albicans in culture. Percutaneous drainage was limited by loculations.

Caspofungin therapy was started. The patient did not defervesce in first few days of treatment, and fluconazole was added. The Candida isolate was sent for susceptibility testing, which showed good sensitivity to fluconazole. After two weeks, she was discharged home on high-dose oral fluconazole (600mg daily). Repeat CT scanning showed no change in her loculated abscesses.
At home, the patient's abdominal pain and nausea worsened progressively and, two weeks later, she became febrile again. CT scanning was repeated and showed partial rupture of one of the abscesses into the liver capsule (Figure 3). Percutaneous drainage was attempted but again limited due to loculations. She was taken to the operating room for open debridement which she tolerated well and a surgical drain was left in place.
Intravenous (IV) liposomal amphoteracin was administered briefly and followed by a four-month course of intravenous caspofungin and high-dose oral fluconazole (800 mg daily). The larger lesions drained fully and resolved after evacuation (Figure 4), but one smaller lesion remained stable on follow-up imaging (Figure 5). The patient remained on lower-dose fluconazole (200-400mg) for a prolonged treatment course.
Figure 3. Abdominal CT scan with rupture into capsule.
Figure 4. Post-operative CT scan.
Figure 5. CT scan one year later with right lobe lesion.

Liver abscesses may be bacterial, parasitic or fungal in etiology. The Candida species may account for as many as 22% of pyogenic liver abscesses, as found in a large series of cases spanning 42 years. Diabetes mellitus may predispose to Candida albicans infection in particular.
Susceptibility testing may be useful in selecting antifungal therapy for Candida, as it is for bacterial pathogens. Liver abscesses that are not fully drained may rupture into the hepatic capsule. When complete percutaneous drainage is not possible, surgical intervention may be required.

title:
Summary: A young adult woman with abdominal discomfort.
A woman in her twenties
history:
Summary: A young adult woman with abdominal discomfort.
A woman in her twenties presented with abdominal discomfort of 3-4 months' duration and weight loss of eight pounds.

The patient had emigrated from rural Cambodia to the United States several years earlier.
exam_studies:
The physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 8,000/mm³ with 5% eosinophils. Other routine laboratory testing, including results of liver function tests, were normal. The level of CA-125 was elevated at 1445 U/ml.

Computed tomography (CT) revealed paraaortic lymphadenopathy, omental and diffuse peritoneal thickening and a large pelvic mass (Figures 1 through 3).
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.
Figure 2. Pelvic CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
diagnosis:
Tuberculous peritonitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Laparotomy revealed diffuse peritoneal studding with nodules (Figures 4 and 5). Pathologic sections showed granulomata. Three weeks later, cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Figure 4. Laparotomy findings.
Figure 5. Laparotomy findings.

Antituberculous therapy was administered and the patient improved clinically.

A high index of suspicion, secondary to this patient’s epidemiological history and unusual age for pelvic neoplasm, was critical in this case. The diagnosis of peritoneal tuberculosis was considered despite the apparent pelvic mass (which was eventually determined to be loculated fluid related to inflammation), peritoneal studding and very high CA-125 test result.
