title: 2006 January Featured Case Summary: A man from the Middle East presented with fe
history:
2006 January Featured Case Summary: A man from the Middle East presented with fever, chills and low back pain.
A man in his sixties had undergone diskectomy of the 4th-5th lumbar disc (L4-L5) for disc herniation with radiculopathy more than fifteen years earlier. He did well until approximately ten years later, when his symptoms recurred. Disc repair of the L5-S1 disc was performed (without placement of hardware or prosthetic material) and his symptoms resolved.
Approximately six months before presentation, he developed fevers to 102-104°F (38.9-40.0°C), chills and headache of two weeks duration. No source of infection was identified; amoxicillin-clavulanate was administered and the fevers and chills resolved. The patient never returned fully to his normal state, however, and over the following months lost five kilograms due to anorexia and aesthenia.
Approximately two months prior to his presentation, intermittent lower back pain recurred. The pain slowly progressed and became chronic and unrelenting. One month after the pain had returned, the patient was seen as an out-patient, where examination revealed a stiff lumbar spine with normal neurological function. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were administered and the symptoms improved but did not resolve.
Four days later, the patient was awakened at night due to the pain. During the following week, fever to 102°F (38.9°C) and daily rigors developed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine, though difficult to interpret due to his previous surgeries, suggested abnormal enhancement of the L4-L5 disc, L4 and L5 vertebral bodies and a soft tissue mass anterior to the vertebrae at this level. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 53 millimeters per hour; tuberculosis skin testing and blood cultures were negative. Computed tomography (CT) guided needle aspiration showed polymorphonuclear cells and gram-negative rods by gram stain; the culture was negative. Pathological staining for acid fast bacilli and fungi were negative, as were cultures for these organisms.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin and doxycycline were given for two weeks and the patient defervesced. At the completion of the course of antibiotics, he was found to have persistent back pain with new sciatic symptoms and absent patellar and ankle reflexes on the left. A repeat MRI scan showed increased size of the paravertebral collection at the level of the L5 vertebra. The patient traveled to the United States for further evaluation and treatment.

The past medical history included the lumbar-sacral surgery as noted above, benign prostatic hypertrophy and hyperlipidemia.

The patient was from the Middle East, where he lived in an urban area. He had eaten cheeses while in Europe several months earlier. He had no animal or chemical exposure, no known exposure to tuberculosis, and no one in his family or other contacts was ill.

See the history above for recent antimicrobial treatment.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, pulse 64 beats per minute, respirations 12 breaths per minute and the temperature was normal. The neurologic examination revealed normal cognition and mood, full sensation and motor strength. There was point tenderness over the lumbar spine with associated paravertebral muscle spasm. The left patellar tendon and ankle reflexes were absent; the toes were down-going bilaterally. Straight leg raising and rectal tone were normal; there was no clonus. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 5,100 cells/mm³ (53% leukocytes, 39% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 1% eosinophils and 1% basophils). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 80 millimeters per hour. Serum chemistry tests were normal. Blood cultures, drawn when the patient was off antibiotics, were negative. An MRI scan of the spine (Figure 1) showed a high signal intensity at the fifth lumbar (L5) vertebra with extension into the L4-5 disk space and the lower half of the L4 vertebra. There were signal changes involving the soft tissue anterior to the L4-5 and the upper part of first sacral (S1) vertebrae as well as over the posterior longitudinal ligament area with no significant pressure on the dura or on the nerve roots. These areas enhanced with gadolinium.
Figure 1. MRI scan of the spine.

A laminectomy (posterior approach) at the level of the L4 vertebra with decompression and aspiration of the epidural abscess produced free-flowing malodorous purulent material. Gram stain of the aspirate is shown in Figure 2. Pathological samples from an open biopsy of the L5 vertebra are shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 2. Primary gram stain of aspirate.
Figure 3. Biopsy of L5 vertebra.
Figure 4. Detail of Figure 3.
diagnosis:
Osteomyelitis, discitis and paravertebral abscess due to Brucella melitensis biovar 3.

MRI scans with gadolinium, which showed T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of the L4-L5 disc, the anterior inferior endplate of the L4 vertebral body and the entire L5 vertebral body, were consistent with osteomyelitis and discitis. There was also a round enhancing lesion consistent with phlegmon in the left anterior epidural space extending from L4—S1 with thecal compression and encasement of the L4 and L5 nerve roots (Figure 1).
A laminectomy (posterior approach) at L4 and decompression and aspiration of the epidural abscess produced free-flowing malodorous purulent material. On gram stain, surgical specimens had rare polymorphonuclear leukocytes; no organisms were seen (Figure 2). Gross pathology confirmed acute and chronic osteomyelitis and acute discitis. Pathological examination with Brown-Hopps and Giemsa stains of material from an open biopsy of the L5 vertebra showed focal epithelioid histiocytes with intracellular coccobacilli consistent with Brucella species (shown in Figure 5).
All operative cultures, including the abscess collection, disk and bone grew small gram negative coccobacilli, which were identified as Brucella melitensis biovar 3 by the Center for Disease Control (CDC). (See Figures 6 and 7.) These organisms were grown on a Brucella agar plate with horse blood (Figure 8). A urease slant, treated with Brucella, was positive, and is shown in Figure 9 on the right (negative control on the left).
The Brucella standard agglutination test, performed by the state laboratory, was positive with a titer of 1:320. Testing for Brucella antibodies was also positive (titers of the IgM component 1:320 and IgG 1:640). Tuberculosis skin testing was negative.
Figure 5. Detail of L5 biopsy.
Figure 6. Gram stain of culture.
Figure 7. Detail of Figure 6.
Figure 8. Brucella colonies on horse blood agar plate.
Figure 9. Urease slants, Brucella inoculate on right.

As noted above, surgical decompression and drainage of the epidural abscess, an L4 laminectomy for epidural abscess and an open biopsy of the L5 vertebrae were performed.
Vancomycin and gentamicin were given initially and then the vancomycin was discontinued and rifampin and doxycycline were added. He was discharged to complete a three-week course of intravenous gentamicin and a three-month course of doxycycline and rifampin. The patient improved, with increased strength and decreased pain.

The constellation of fever and back pain should immediately alert the physician to the possibility of vertebral osteomyelitis. Infection of the vertebrae usually begins by hematogenous seeding of the poorly vascularized bone with contiguous spread to the discs and surrounding tissues, which can include the psoas muscles and aorta anteriorly, and the epidural space with spinal cord compression posteriorly. Tissue that has been compromised by injury or previous surgery is more likely to become a site for potential infection, as was illustrated in this case.
In the United States, the most common causes of vertebral osteomyelitis include routine bacterial and fungal pathogens which can be introduced into the bloodstream by intravenous drug use, a chronic in-dwelling line, or systemic infection such as endocarditis. Staphylococcal species are the most common pathogen in this setting, and Streptococcal species, gram-negative pathogens and Candida species are also quite common. Worldwide, pyogenic vertebral abscess must be differentiated from tuberculosis and brucellosis. While all of these can infect any part of the spine, thoracic involvement is more commonly associated with Pott’s disease while Brucella and pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis are most commonly seen in the lumbar spine. Brucellosis, also called undulant, Mediterranean, or Malta fever, is a zoonotic disease that remains endemic worldwide and is an important source of morbidity primarily in the Mediterranean basin, Arabian peninsula, India, Central and South America. Brucella species are aerobic, non-encapsulated facultative gram-negative coccobacilli.
As a zoonosis, infection is acquired through exposure to animals and their products with goat and sheep herders, veterinarians, abattoir workers, farmers and laboratory personnel at highest risk. It can be acquired through aerosol or ingestion and consumption of unpasteurized cheeses—this was the likely mode of transmission in the case above. Once exposed, the bacteria localize within the reticulo-endothelial system and evade the immune system.
Brucellosis is a systemic infection and can manifest in numerous ways which includes a non-specific prolonged febrile illness (it is a well-established cause of fever of unknown origin), neurobrucellosis, epididymo-orchitis, endocarditis, splenomegaly, pneumonitis, prosthetic hardware infection, and pyogenic abscess formation of various organs. The most common localization is in the osteoarticular system, described in 10-30% of patients, and includes sacroiliitis, septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, spondylitis, bursitis and osteomyelitis.
Diagnosis is made by serologic testing with the standard agglutination test (SAT), which is a tube agglutination assay. This is the standard test in the United States. Blood, synovial tissue, bone, or abscess drainage can be cultured for Brucella, although the cultures require special media. Treatment includes combination therapy utilizing fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfa, rifampin, aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.

title: 2006 February Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man w
history:
2006 February Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with shortness of breath and respiratory failure.
A man in his thirties (Age and gender are often a critical factor in ID diagnosis affecting both the spectrum of illness and type of organisms involved.) presented during the winter season (Certain infections are very common during a particular season of the year.) with progressive shortness of breath and fever (The combination of breathing difficulty and fever should arouse suspicion for lung infection.).
Four days before admission (It is important to elicit the onset, duration and progression of symptoms as some infections progress rapidly and can be fatal if not diagnosed and managed in time.), the patient stayed home from work (Taking time off from work may be an indication of the severity of symptoms.) due to fevers and flu-like symptoms, which included nausea, generalized malaise and fatigue. He traveled out of town the following two days (The timeline relating the onset of illness to the travel history is very important, as some infections have early and late stages of symptoms. In addition, it is important to know the destination and details of activities and the eating and drinking habits during travel - for example, drinking unfiltered tap water. Eliciting a history of exposure to air conditioning units and water sources during travel and learning if any travel companions are suffering from a similar illness that suggests a common exposure or source of infection are also important considerations. All these factors will influence the differential diagnoses) and continued to feel unwell.
One day before admission, he presented to the emergency room of an outside hospital with fever to 101°F (38.3°C), vomiting and diarrhea. Five liters of intravenous fluid were infused and a prescription for ciprofloxacin (Whenever possible the exact details of previous therapy should be sought, as previous treatment may influence future choice of antibiotics since an organism already exposed to an antibiotic may have developed resistance to it.) was given for presumed infectious gastroenteritis (Not all patients presenting with vomiting and diarrhea have gastroenteritis. Other infections - including, at times, pneumonia - may present with a preponderance of GI symptoms). The patient returned the following day with worsening shortness of breath and the sensation that his lungs were filling with fluid. There was no history of (Thoroughly eliciting the absence of some symptoms may be as, and sometimes even more, important than the presence of other symptoms.) rashes, arthralgias, chest pain, neck stiffness, rectal bleeding, hematemesis, headache, sinus pressure, cough or hemoptysis.
On presentation to the outside hospital, the patient was able to speak in full sentences (Whenever a patient presents with breathing difficulty, the ability to speak in full sentences can be a good early and objective measure of the severity. If one is not able to speak in full sentences then breathing may be severely compromised.) and appeared diaphoretic (It is very important to determine if the patient looks unwell or toxic, as that may indicate the need for aggressive and broad-spectrum therapy, often with supportive measures.). The temperature (A normal temperture is generally considered to be 97.0-99.9 degree Fahrenheit.) was 97.9°F (36.6°C), pulse (Normal: 60-100 beats per minute.) 118 beats per minute, blood pressure (A normal systolic blood pressure usually ranges between 90-139 mm Hg and normal diastolic between 60-85 mm Hg.) 133/73 mm Hg and the oxygen saturation (Normal: 95-100% while breathing ambient air.) ranged between 90-95% on 100% inspired oxygen (This patient has tachycardia and hypoxia even while breathing a high concentration of oxygen. This may suggest significant lung involvement, but systemic infection or anemia can cause this picture even in the absence of lung involvement. The respiratory rate has not been mentioned but can safely be predicted to be raised to compensate for the low oxygen saturation.). An echocardiogram did not show any evidence of left ventricular dysfunction or valvular pathology (The presence of a vegetation or new valvular regurgitation by echocardiography are major criteria for diagnosing infective endocarditis.). Results of arterial blood gases included pH 7.25, partial pressure of oxygen 54 mm Hg (Normal: 80-100 mm Hg), and partial pressure of carbon dioxide 44 mm Hg (Normal: 35-45 mmHg) while breathing 70% inspired oxygen by face mask. Cultures and sputum samples drawn. Chest radiography showed dense bilateral alveolar infiltrates (The radiograph reveals prominent involvement of the lungs. Examples of infections that can progress rapidly include primary influenza pneumonia and Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.).
The patient's respiratory status declined, and he required intubation. Prednisone (40 milligrams) and broad spectrum antibiotics, including doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole, were administered. The patient was admitted to the intensive case unit of the outside hospital and gatifloxacin and rifampin were added. He was then transferred to a tertiary care hospital.

The patient had previously been in good health (Previously damaged lungs can harbor a different set of organisms than healthy lungs. Similarly, previous co-morbidities such as diabetes mellitus may predispose a patient to develop certain infections.).

The patient lived in an urban area. He was employed in the scientific sector, and his laboratory space had recently been moved to a temporary structure (A patient's living situation, and type and setting of work are important factors to be considered in determining one's potential exposure to infectious diseases.). He did not work with biological agents (Exposure to biological agents can predispose one to specific organisms, possibly including bioterrorism agents.). Two weeks earlier, he had traveled to the Midwestern United States. He smoked cigarettes, occasionally drank alcohol and denied illicit drug use (Cigarette smokers, illicit drug users and people who consume excessive alcohol are at risk of developing certain infections. For example, intravenous drug users are at higher risk for developing right-sided heart valve infective endocarditis.). He owned a dog and had no other recent exposures to animals (Exposure to animals influences the differential diagnosis, such as the possibility of Cat scratch disease in people who own cats. Similarly, a history of insect or animal bites is important.). A friend had recently returned from Asia with pneumonia (Exposure to someone with a similar illness should be considered, as a significant number of infections are contagious.).

None (Some medications can influence the diagnosis, including those that suppress the immune system, such as corticosteroids.).
exam_studies:
On examination (See the annotation above for normal ranges for the vital signs.) at the tertiary care hospital, the temperature was 99.1°F (37.3°C), pulse 98-120 beats per minute, blood pressure 73-104/41-63 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20-24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% on 100% inspired oxygen. The patient was intubated, sedated, and paralyzed. He appeared his stated age and well-nourished (Malnourishment increases the risk of acquiring certain infections by suppressing immunity.). There were coarse breath sounds present bilaterally; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 10,800 cells/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000); (differential of 77% neutrophils, 12% bands, 7% lymphocytes and 3% monocytes), hematocrit 41.2% and hemoglobin 14.7 grams/dL. The level of alanine aminotransferase (Of note, the levels of ALT and AST are elevated and the albumin level is low. Abnormal liver function tests can be seen in infections, including those not specifically targeting the liver, such as Legionnaires’ disease.) was 93 U/L (reference range 10-55), aspartate aminotransferase 109 U/L (reference range 10-40) and albumin 2.4 grams/dL (reference range 3.3-5.0); other routine laboratory tests were normal.
A chest radiograph showed diffuse dense infiltrates bilaterally.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph

A sputum specimen (Obtaining a sputum specimen for gram stain may elucidate the cause of illness early in the course and is a relatively inexpensive test.) was obtained and cultured. A gram stain of the sputum is shown in Figure 2, and gram stain of the culture plate is shown in Figure 3 below.
Figure 2. Gram stain of sputum sample.
Figure 3. Gram stain of culture growth from a sputum specimen.
diagnosis:
Legionella pneumophila, serogroup 1, pneumonia.

The urine was positive for Legionella pneumophila antigen (Some pathogens such as Legionella can be difficult or slow to grow in culture, and may require specialized growth media. For Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae, diagnosis can often be made more rapidly by checking a urine sample for the presence of pathogen-specific cell-surface antigens.), serogroup 1. The primary sputum gram stain showed a few polymorphonuclear leukocytes but no organisms. The sputum was then cultured on several types of media including a buffered charcoal yeast extract (CYE) plate, which grew Legionella pneumophila, serogroup 1. (See Figure 4.) PCR testing for Mycoplasma, an examination for Pneumocystis and fungal culture were negative. Testing for HIV infection was negative.

Azithromycin (Many antibiotics that show effective in vitro killing of Legionella are clinically ineffective, in part due to Legionella's growth within intracellular endosomes, where most antibiotics do not reach levels sufficient to be effective. Azithromycin is notable for excellent uptake into cells, making it useful for intracellular pathogens such as Legionella.) was administered daily for 21 days. The patient gradually improved and was discharged.
Figure 4. Detail of Figure 3.

This patient had Legionnaires’ disease, an acute consolidating pneumonia. There is usually a prodrome of fever and generalized malaise, often with gastrointestinal complaints including nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. This can delay diagnosis in the early phase, as illustrated by this patient. Legionnaires’ disease is caused by Legionella pneumophila, a gram negative bacillus with fastidious growth requirements. While there are at least 16 different serogroups, L. pneumophila, serogroup 1, causes 70-90% of human infections and is the only serotype identified by the urinary antigen test. Legionella pneumonia is initiated by aerosolization, generally by an infected water source. It is often indistinguishable from other causes of acute community acquired pneumonia, particularly pneumococcal pneumonia; however, Legionella tends to cause multi-lobar, diffuse consolidation and there may be significant gastrointestinal symptoms with abnormalities of the liver function tests.
In any previously healthy person with an acute serious pulmonary process, other considerations, including emerging infections such as SARS and community-acquired necrotizing MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) pneumonia, agents of bioterrorism, such as plague and tularemia, and an undiagnosed immunodeficiency, such as HIV infection or malignancy, with an opportunistic infection must be considered.

title: 2006 March Featured Case Summary: A man from Morocco with epigastric pain, obstr
history:
2006 March Featured Case Summary: A man from Morocco with epigastric pain, obstructive jaundice and eosinophilia.
A man in his thirties presented to a community hospital with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain that had begun acutely. The pain was colicky and severe and associated with mild nausea. There was no fever, chills or other constitutional symptoms. The eyes appeared slightly yellow. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the abdomen showed a 5 centimeter by 6 centimeter lesion in the right lobe of the liver. He was transferred to a tertiary medical center for further evaluation and treatment. Three months earlier, he had presented to the same hospital complaining of mild pain and “heaviness” over the epigastric region. A proton pump inhibitor had been administered with little relief.

The patient had lived in Morocco until immigrating to the United States one year before presentation. In Morocco, he had visited rural areas multiple times, having contact with farm animals including sheep, cattle and goats, and with domesticated animals including cats and dogs.

The patient was not taking any medications at the time of admission. A proton pump inhibitor prescribed earlier had been discontinued.
exam_studies:
The patient was awake, alert and in mild discomfort. The temperature was 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure 126/64 mm Hg and pulse 95 beats per minute. The oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. The sclera were icteric; the oral mucosa moist. There were no oropharyngeal lesions. The neck was supple and there was no lymphadenopathy. He had slightly decreased breath sounds at the right base with normal percussion. Cardiac sounds were regular and rhythmic without murmurs heard. There The abdomen was soft and not distended; bowel sounds were present. There was voluntary guarding and tenderness to superficial and deep palpation in the epigastric and right upper quadrant areas, without rebound tenderness. The skin was jaundiced without lesions. There was no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly or peripheral edema and the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory testing revealed a white blood count of 7000 cells/mm³ (60% neutrophils, 17% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, 18% eosinophils), platelets 203,000/mm³, and hematocrit 45.8%. The urea nitrogen was 11 mg/dL and the creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 109 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 252 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 142 U/L, total bilirubin 6.7 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 3.4 mg/dl.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a lesion (5.5 centimeters by 6.4 centimeters) with multiple cysts in segment four of the liver. The lesion had a central matrix around which cysts were arranged peripherally. (See Figure 1.) In some views, the lesion bulged out from the contour of the liver, but there was no evidence of diffuse peritoneal spread. A cluster of lesions approximately 1-centimeter in diameter was seen within the liver near the fundus of the gallbladder. There was diffuse intrahepatic biliary dilatation.
Blood cultures were negative. Stool examination showed no evidence of protozoa or helminths.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT scan.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) revealed two large amorphous, mobile filling defects in the common bile duct and common hepatic duct. (See Figures 2 and 3.) A biliary sphincterotomy was performed and two clear gelatinous cysts were extracted. There was some internal debris within the cysts. (See Figures 4 and 5 and video stream of ERCP.)
Video 1. ERCP findings.
Figure 2. ERCP scanning.
Figure 3. ERCP scanning.
Figure 4. ERCP findings.
Figure 5. ERCP findings.
diagnosis:
Echinococcus granulosus infection of the liver and biliary tree, with hydatid cyst of the right lobe of the liver complicated by obstruction and biliary rupture.

Cannulation of the bile duct and administration of contrast during ERCP showed multiple filling defects. (See Figures 6 and 7.) Gelatinous and cystic material, subsequently discharged into the duodenum via the common bile duct, was consistent with Echinococcus. Fluid aspirated during the ERCP and serologic testing were positive for Echinococcus granulosus was.
Figure 6. Biliary tree filling defects seen in Figure 4.
Figure 7. Biliary tree filling defects seen in Figure 5.

The ERCP and sphincterotomy were diagnostic and therapeutic. Combination anti-parasitic therapy with albendazole and praziquantel was initiated during the procedure followed by significant symptomatic improvement. Biliary dilatation decreased, associated with decreasing cholestasis, resolving jaundice and improvement on CT scanning. Three weeks after initiation of therapy, the patient underwent surgical resection of hydatid cysts. (See Figures 8 and 9.) The post-operative course was uneventful. He completed a seven-day course of praziquantel peri-operatively and three months of albendazole treatment. Imaging was repeated 10 months after surgery and showed a healing cyst bed with no evidence of relapse.
Figure 8. H and E stain of liver and cyst, magnified x 4.
Figure 9. H and E stain of cyst wall, magnified x 20.

Human Hydatid Disease is caused by infection with larval stages of cestodes (tapeworms), of the genus Echinococcus, which belongs to the family Taeniidae. Four species of Echinococcus produce infection in humans; E. granulosus and E. multilocularis are the most common, causing cystic echinococcosis (CE) and alveolar echinococcosis (AE), respectively.
Epidemiologically, E. granulosus represents a public health problem in rural grazing areas in the Middle East, Mediterranean countries, Russia, China, Northern Africa and South America. Up to 30-60% of hydatid cysts cases are asymptomatic. Symptoms usually occur in the setting of an allergic or immunological phenomenon to the parasite after cyst rupture or as a result of mechanical factors associated with the cysts in the affected organs. The incubation period is months to years and signs and symptoms vary depending on the location of the cysts. The most common affected organs are: liver 70%, lung 20%, bone 1%, central nervous system 1%, cardiac 1%, spleen 1%, retroperitoneum 1%, and renal disease 1%.
The clinical features of hepatic hydatid cysts typically include symptoms of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting and jaundice. Complications include biliary obstruction resulting in cholestasis and/or obstructive jaundice and cholangitis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, cyst rupture and secondary bacterial infection. Until recently, surgery was the only option for the treatment of echinococcal cysts, and to date it is still considered the treatment of choice. However other potential treatment modalities are available including chemotherapy and the PAIR (Percutaneous Aspiration, Introduction of a protoscolicidal agent and Reaspiration) procedure.

title: 2006 April Featured Case Summary: A woman on immunosuppressive therapy presented
history:
2006 April Featured Case Summary: A woman on immunosuppressive therapy presented with fever and respiratory symptoms.
A middle-aged woman presented with cough, dyspnea, low-grade fever, and malaise for approximately two weeks. There was a history of psoriatic arthritis for which prednisone, methotrexate, and infliximab had been administered for at least ten months.

She had a history of psoriatic arthritis.

She lived in the Eastern United States and had traveled to the Midwest in the past. There was no history of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substance use.

The patient was a homemaker.

Medications included prednisone, methotrexate, and infliximab. (She was not receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.)
exam_studies:
The patient appeared tired and short of breath. The respiratory rate was 32 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation ranging from 96-100% while breathing 100% supplemental oxygen; other vital signs were normal. The lungs had coarse rales bilaterally with decreased breath sounds at each base. There was no murmur, rubs or gallops on cardiovascular exam. The abdomen was obese and the extremities had trace edema. The remainder of the examination was normal.

A chest radiograph revealed extensive bilateral interstitial infiltrates. (See Figure 1.)
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered empirically at an outside hospital and bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed. Sputum and culture results were initially negative. The patient's condition worsened and she was transferred to a tertiary care hospital.
Stains of the bronchoalveolar lavage are shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Bronchoalveolar lavage.
Figure 3. Bronchoalveolar lavage.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis due to Histoplasma capsulatum in an immunocompromised patient.

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed small, narrow-budding yeast (Figures 2 and 3) in both lung fields that were initially thought to be Pneumocystis jirovecii. High-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was administered but the patient did not improve.
Blood isolator cultures taken on admission eventually grew Histoplasma capsulatum. Retrospective analysis of the bronchoalveolar lavage samples was thought to be consistent with this. Cultures from the lavage sample at the outside hospital eventually grew H.capsulatum as well.

The patient required intubation and mechanical ventilatory support in the intensive care unit within 24 hours of her admission to the tertiary care hospital. The antimicrobial regimen was changed to intravenous amphotericin B (liposomal) and the patient gradually improved. Mechanical ventilatory support was weaned and the patient was extubated after she defervesced. She was discharged to a rehabilitation facility for a prolonged course of therapy of oral itraconazole.

The patient had been on several different immunosuppressive medications for psoriatic arthritis. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis had not been initiated and she was thus at high risk for this disease. The presence of yeast in her lavage and the clinical picture was suggestive (but not conclusive) of PCP. This diagnosis ultimately was found to be incorrect.
The blood cultures and lavage cultures eventually grew Histoplasma capsulatum. The patient had a history of travel to endemic areas in the past, and with a history of the use of immunomodulatory drugs, she was at higher risk of reactivation of infection with histoplasmosis. The small size of the yeast and the narrow-budding seen in the figures are characteristic of this dimorphic fungus.

title: 2006 May Featured Case Summary: A woman with skin lesions several years after a
history:
2006 May Featured Case Summary: A woman with skin lesions several years after a lung transplantation.
A woman in her fifties with a history of lung transplantation was well until approximately three weeks before admission when the medial malleolus of her left ankle bumped against a portable oxygen tank. A few days later, she noticed redness, warmth, tenderness, and swelling over the ankle that progressed up her leg to the level of the knee. She was admitted to a community hospital, cellulitis was diagnosed, and cefazolin and metronidazole were administered. When she failed to improve, the regimen was changed to vancomycin and imipenem but the redness and tenderness continued to advance. The patient was transferred to a tertiary medical center for further evaluation and treatment.

The patient had a long history of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis for which transplantation of the right lung had been performed several years before. Diabetes mellitus had developed following steroid administration. Several months before admission, cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia had been diagnosed.

She resided in the northeastern United States and denied recent travel, animal contact, natural water exposure or gardening.

The medications included prednisone (20 mg) daily, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared chronically unwell. Her face was cushingoid and breathing was moderately labored with pursed lips. The temperature was 98.1°F (36.7°C), pulse 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respirations 20 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on 50% oxygen via mask. There were decreased breath sounds and fine crackles throughout the left chest. The left leg was swollen, red, and warm from the ankle to immediately below the knee. The redness was confluent in the central part of the shin but at the edges had more of a nodular character (Figures 1 and 2).
Erythematous nodules (one-centimeter in diameter) were also noted on the deltoid of the left shoulder and distal clavicle of the right shoulder (Figure 3). The rest of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Skin findings.
Figure 2. Left leg lesions.
Figure 3. Right shoulder lesion.

The white blood cells count was 14,400 cells/mm³ (93% neutrophils and 7% lymphocytes) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 115 mm per minute. Glucose was 121 mg/dL and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 409 U/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 176 mg/L and tacrolimus 49.4 ng/ml. Tests of liver function were normal.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Aspergillus fumigatus infection in an immunocompromised patient.

A skin biopsy of the shoulder nodule and leading edge of leg rash was performed and revealed invasive fungal forms (Figure 4). The culture of the biopsy tissue grew abundant Aspergillus fumigatus.
Figure 4. Biopsy results.

The patient was treated with high dose voriconazole and caspofungin and the advance of her leg rash was arrested. However, her respiratory status deteriorated. Mechanical ventilation was initiated after intubation, however these efforts were not successful and the patient eventually died.

The nodular appearance of the leg rash with satellite lesions and the emergence of nodules elsewhere on the body raise concern for a disseminated process as opposed to a simple bacterial cellulitis. Risk factors for disseminated Aspergillus fumigatus infection include sustained high dose immunosuppression and a recent episode of cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis. CMV disease appears to increase the susceptibility to subsequent severe infections in transplant recipients.
The morphology of the fungus seen on initial skin biopsy appeared more globular than is characteristically seen with Aspergillus, leading clinicians to initially suspect disseminated Fusarium. The diagnosis was revealed, though, when tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus. Invasive fungal disease cannot be reliably speciated by histologic morphology alone and tissue culture is needed to make a final diagnosis. Of note, tacrolimus is an agent with some antifungal properties. The patient's supratherapeutic level of tacrolimus might have altered the morphology of the fungus in tissue.

A man in
history:
2006 June Featured Case Summary: A man with fever, nausea and vomiting.
A man in his forties presented with fever, nausea, and vomiting of four days duration. His symptoms began after eating food that had been left unrefrigerated overnight. Fever and chills occurred and were followed first by an episode of diarrhea and then severe nausea and vomiting. Headache occurred intermittently.
After four days of persistent fever and vomiting, he presented for medical evaluation. The patient denied sore throat, upper respiratory symptoms, rash and joint pains. The diarrhea had resolved after a single episode.

The patient resided in the northeastern United States and was in a stable monogamous relationship with a female partner. He denied recent travel, hiking or camping. He had been in wooded areas prior to this illness and owned dogs that had scratched him in the past. He denied other animal exposures. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) had been negative several years before admission.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared anxious and tired but did not appear toxic. The temperature was 101.4°F (38.6°C), pulse 120 beats per minute, and blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg. There was physical evidence of volume depletion, diffuse small lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen tip. There was no rash and no inflamed joints; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The sodium was 120 mmol/liter with a normal creatinine. The white blood cell count was 3,700 cells/mm³, hematocrit 34%, and platelet count 40,000/mm³.
Liver function studies revealed a total protein of 8.4 g/dL, albumin of 3.3 g/dL, globulin 5.1 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 97 U/liter, alanine aminotransferase 77 U/liter, total bilirubin 4.0 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Peripheral blood smear.
Figure 2. Blood smear, 100x magnification.
diagnosis:
Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis (also known as Human Granulocytic Ehrlichiosis) caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

The peripheral blood smear showed blue cytoplasmic inclusions that were suspect for morulae of Ehrlichia. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of a blood specimen confirmed the presence of Anaplasma phagocytophilum (formerly known as Ehrlichia equi), the causative agent of human granulocytic ehrlichiosis. In addition, a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) ELISA test and confirmatory western blot test were positive.

Treatment with doxycycline was initiated. The patient’s nausea and vomiting resolved and he rapidly defervesced. Liver function tests improved, the white blood cell count remained decreased and the platelet count rose to about 100,000/mm³. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 312 cells/mm³ and the level of HIV RNA was 110,000 copies/ml. Antiretroviral therapy was planned to begin after the ehrlichiosis has resolved.

The initial suspicion was that of a foodborne illness in light of the patient’s history of eating unrefrigerated meat, prominent vomiting, and increased liver function tests. Foodborne illness failed to account, however, for the patient’s marked leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. The most likely foodborne illness to cause hepatitis, hepatitis A virus, has an incubation period of about two weeks.
The combination of fever, headache, hepatitis, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia is, however, consistent with a rickettsial illness. The species endemic to the patient's northeastern state is Anaplasma phagocytophilum (formerly Ehrlichia equi). PCR confirmed the diagnosis. The absence of a known history of a tick bite is not unusual, however, since this patient’s exposure to wooded areas and for close play with his dogs put him at risk of tick bites.
Patients with Anaplasma can also be co-infected with Borrelia burgdorferi and Babesia microti, organisms carried by the same species of tick that transmits Anaplasma. Lyme serology and multiple thin smears looking for parasites were negative in this case.
Several clues were present leading clinicians to suspect a second disorder in addition to Anaplasma, including the diffuse lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and the degree of thrombocytopenia and leukopenia that seemed more pronounced than normally seen with ehrlichiosis. The diagnosis of HIV infection likely accounts for these additional findings.
Anaplasma has been reported to cause more severe disease in patients with HIV; fortunately this gentleman responded well to prompt therapy with doxycycline.

title: 2006 July Featured Case Summary: A woman in the third trimester of her pregnancy
history:
2006 July Featured Case Summary: A woman in the third trimester of her pregnancy presented with cough, edema and fever.
A woman in her thirties presented during the third trimester of pregnancy with a dry cough, general malaise and fatigue for fourteen days. During the five days preceding her presentation, lower extremity edema and orthopnea developed. She had also noted dyspnea with minimal exertion, chills, and intermittent chest tightness. One day before admission, the patient had subjective symptoms associated with fever.
The pregnancy had been complicated by:
1. Hyperemesis gravidarum requiring a two-week hospitalization six months earlier. A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC line) placement had occurred for total parenteral nutrition and had been removed shortly before this presentation.
2. A urine culture had grown coagulase-negative Staphylococcus three weeks before this presentation.

There was a history of a heart murmur since childhood and marfanoid habitus for which an echocardiogram was performed annually. The most recent echocardiogram had been without abnormalities.

There was no history of tobacco, alcohol or illicit drug use.

The patient lived with her husband in a suburban community in the United States.

There were no allergies to medications.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 110/85 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, temperature 97.9°F (36.6°C), respirations 25 per minute and oxygen saturation 97% on 2 liters of oxygen delivered by nasal cannula. The patient appeared fatigued, pale, and in mild distress. There was generalized pallor; the conjuctiva were clear. Breath sounds were decreased at the bases greater on the right than the left, the jugulovenous pressure was elevated, and the point of maximal cardiac impulse (PMI) was located in the 5th intercostal space of the mid-clavicular line. The heart sounds were normal, and there was a holosystolic murmur at the apex, and a 2/4 diastolic murmur in the right sternal border. The abdomen was gravid, and no hepatosplenomegaly was noted. The extremities had 2 + pitting edema and no clubbing. The skin was clear.

The white blood cell count was 10,300 cells/mm³, hematocrit 26% and platelets 282,000/mm³. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with poor R-wave progression and a P-R interval of 122 milliseconds. Chest radiography revealed vascular cephalization and bilateral bronchial opacities. Lower extremity non-invasive studies were negative for deep venous thrombosis.

Diuretics were administered and blood cultures drawn. Vancomycin and gentamicin were administered empirically. On the second hospital day, a cesarean section was performed and the infant delivered without complications.
On the fourth hospital day, an echocardiogram performed. (See Figures 1, 2, and 3.)
Video 1. Echocardiography of aortic valve.
Figure 1. Echocardiography of aortic valve.
Figure 2. Doppler flow study across aortic valve.
Figure 3. Echocardiography.
diagnosis:
Endocarditis caused by coagulase-negative Staphylococcus epidermidis infection.

Four sets of blood cultures grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus epidermidis. The organism was resistant to penicillin, erythromycin and ampicillin, and sensitive to the other agents routinely tested including oxacillin, gentamicin, vancomycin and rifampin. Echocardiography revealed the following: Figures 1 and 4 show a view of the aortic valve with a prominent elongated mobile echo density consistent with a vegetation prolapsing into the left ventricular outflow tract. This appears to be attached to the noncoronary leaflet and measures 1.9 x 0.4 centimeters in orthogonal dimensions.
Figures 2 and 5 show a Doppler image showing moderate aortic insufficiency with an eccentric anteroseptally directed jet (no systolic flow reversal is documented in the descending aorta).
Figures 3 and 6 reveal the trileaflet aortic valve with an echo density consistent with a vegetation measuring 0.5 cm at the leaflet base in the cross-sectional diameter.
Figure 4. Aortic valve lesion by echocardiography.
Figure 5. Aortic valve lesion by echocardiography.
Figure 6. Aortic valve lesion by echocardiography.

After diuresis and transfusion with packed red blood cells, the patient noted slight improvement of her dyspnea on exertion. On the fifth hospital day, there was a symptomatic episode of ventricular tachycardia that was not sustained.
On the sixth hospital day, an aortic valve replacement with a St. Jude's valve was performed. The gram stain and culture of the excised valve were negative. Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stains of the valve are shown in Figures 7 and 8 and revealed active endocarditis with valve destruction, mural thrombus and abundant coccal organisms. The outflow surface of the cusp had a thick fibrous appearance.
Nafcillin was administered for six weeks, and gentamicin and rifampin for 2 weeks post-operatively.
Figure 7. Valve pathology (H and E stain).
Figure 8. Valve pathology (H and E stain).

Historically, coagulase negative Staphylococci (CoNS) were regarded as culture contaminants or non-pathogenic skin colonizers. In recent years, the importance of these organisms as a human pathogen has been recognized. As the utilization of artificial devices becomes more widespread, the role of CoNS as nosocomial pathogens is on the rise. Resistance to multiple antibiotics makes the treatment an increasing challenge.
The presenting symptoms of coagulase-negative Staphylococcus endocarditis are similar to those found in infective endocarditis by other organisms: fever, malaise and unexplained weight loss. CoNS native valve endocarditis remains uncommon. A striking feature is the frequency of complications leading to surgery, caused by an organism that is often disregarded as a blood culture contaminant.
Community-acquired infections are associated with underlying valvular disease, with a significant number of patients having chronic indwelling catheters as the identifiable risk factor.
Medical therapy for coagulase-negative Staphylococcus endocarditis remains challenging, as multiple drug resistance and heterotypic phenotypes are commonly seen. Typically, a bactericidal antibiotic or a combination that is bactericidal is used.

title: 2006 August Featured Case Summary: An elderly man with coffee-ground hematemesis
history:
2006 August Featured Case Summary: An elderly man with coffee-ground hematemesis and ascites.
An elderly man was admitted with confusion, nausea and hematemesis.
The patient had been in poor health with a history of alcohol abuse, guaiac positive stools and transaminase elevation. Approximately six weeks before this presentation, he was struck by a motor vehicle and sustained several lacerations, abrasions and contusions, and chest trauma. He was hospitalized for ten days when he was found to have a left hemothorax that required thoracotomy.
After discharge, he stayed in Florida for a few more days and then returned to his home in the northeastern United States. Approximately five days before his presentation, he developed abdominal pain and melenotic diarrhea. He was brought to the hospital by family members and presented to the hospital with confusion, nausea and dark emesis.

There was a history of elevated bilirubin and liver function tests, alcohol abuse and gastritis. As above, he had been in an accident several weeks earlier during which he sustained chest trauma. Two weeks before admission, laboratory testing to evaluate liver abnormalities and to rule out the possibility of hemachromatosis revealed a serum iron of 166 mcg/dL, total iron binding capacity (TIBC) of 168 mcg/dL, and ferritin 753 ng/ml. He was heterozygote for the HFE gene mutation. There was also a history of renal calculi.

He had recently traveled to Florida, where he had waded in the ocean and eaten oysters. He had no other travel history. He did not own pets or have any contact with animals. He had a history of alcohol abuse; he did not smoke.

The patient lived with his wife in suburban New England.

He had no known drug allergies.

He had recently been on furosemide, potassium, and iron but had run out of medications shortly before admission.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared somnolent and the skin appeared tanned. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C); the pulse 88-120 beats per minute, the blood pressure normal and the oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. The conjunctiva were mildly icteric. The jugular veins were flat. There were inspiratory crackles greater on the right base than the left. The left thoracotomy site was well healed. The abdomen was modestly distended and diffusely tender; a fluid wave was present. Excoriations were present over the extremities. In the emergency room, he appeared to have hallucinations intermittently. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Upon admission, the white blood cell count was 13,600 cells/mm³, with 86% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 11% lymphocytes and 3% monocytes, hematocrit 40%, platelets 124,000/mm³, prothrombin time was 16 seconds and partial thromboplastin time 35.5 seconds. Bilirubin was 2.7 mg/dL; direct bilirubin was 1.0 mg/dL, total protein 8.0 grams/dL and albumin level was 3.1 grams/dL. The ammonia level was 71 mcmol/L (normal 12-48 mcmol/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 115 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 40 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 182 U/L.
The ascitic fluid was aspirated and revealed yellow, slightly turbid fluid with 644 white blood cells/mm³ (78% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 2% eosinophils and 3% non-hematologic cells), total protein of 1.1 grams/dL and albumin 0.6 g/dL. A gram stain of the ascitic fluid cytospin is shown in Figure 1. CT scanning of the abdomen revealed a large volume of ascites. There was no evidence of a focal hepatic mass or biliary obstruction.
Figure 1. Gram stain of ascitic fluid (primary cytospin).

The ascitic fluid was cultured; gram stains of the growth in the blood bottles are shown in Figures 2 and 3. Blood cultures were negative. Ceftriaxone was started empirically for bacterial peritonitis.
Figure 2. Gram stain of culture of aspirate, from blood bottle.
Figure 3. Gram stain of culture of aspirate, from blood bottle.
diagnosis:
Subacute bacterial peritonitis secondary to non-01 Vibrio cholerae, non-cholera toxin producing.

Gram stain of the ascitic fluid cytospin (Figure 1 above) shows neutrophils but no organisms. Figures 2 and 3 above show gram stains from the primary blood-bottle cultures of the ascitic fluid and reveal curved gram negative rods that proved to be oxidase positive. Figure 4 shows the gram stain of the growth on the blood agar plate. The organism was identified as Vibrio cholerae non-cholera toxin producing, serotypes non-O1, non-O139 by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) of the United States.
Figure 4. Gram stain of growth from blood agar plate.

Ceftriaxone, lactulose, furosemide, albumin and aldactone were administered with improvement in the patient's clinical condition. Blood cultures were negative. The patient's antimicrobial therapy was changed to levofloxacin, and a 14-day course was administered.

Vibrio cholerae is an organism known for causing epidemics of severe diarrhea with high rates of mortality (secondary to dehydration). There are almost 200 serotypes of V. cholerae; only the O1 and O139 serogroups are associated with epidemics. This patient had a non-O1 and non-O139 isolate. Infection with non-O1 and non-O139 isolates is sporadic. These isolates can also cause extra-intestinal infections, especially in those who are immunocompromised. Patients with liver disease appear to be particularly susceptible to serious infection with Vibrio spp.
Infection with non-O1 and non-O139 V. cholerae can occur after ingestion of contaminated food. In temperate regions, seafood, particularly raw or undercooked, is the most likely source. Contact with contaminated water can also lead to infection. In a series from Taiwan [Ko et al 1998], thirty cases of culture-positive non-O1 and non-O139 V. cholerae were identified in a nine-year period. Of these, fifteen isolates were recovered from the blood and all of these patients had cirrhosis: 14 of 15 were men. Of these fifteen cases, five also had spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). The mortality rate for patients with cirrhosis and bacteremia was 47%. Eight of the thirty isolates were recovered from the stool of patients with acute gastroenteritis: symptoms included fever, chills, abdominal pain, diarrhea – occasionally bloody – and sometimes nausea and vomiting. Four isolates were from soft tissue (three of four had necrotizing fasciitis); all four of the patients had had pre-existing minor trauma that could have provided a portal of entry.
Patients who have liver disease should be cautioned against ingesting raw or undercooked seafood and also against contact with seawater or freshwater.

title: 2006 September Featured Case Summary: A woman with fever, headache, and a new ra
history:
2006 September Featured Case Summary: A woman with fever, headache, and a new rash.
A woman in her fifties presented with fever, headache, myalgias and a new rash on her left flank that had begun seven days earlier.

She had recently (Timeline is very important in relation to the travel history as some infections have early and late stages of symptomatology.) returned from opening her summer home on an island off the northeastern coast of the United States (Certain infections are very common during a particular season of the year and are endemic in some areas so the time of the year and geographical location/travel history is very important to elicit in ID. Also exposure to animals, pets and insect-bites can provide a key to diagnosis. Infections seen in the warm months of the year in temperate climates raise the possibility of arthropod-borne pathogens.).
exam_studies:
The patient was uncomfortable but did not appear toxic (It is very important to determine if the patient looks unwell or toxic as that may indicate the need for aggressive and broad-spectrum therapy, usually with supportive measures.). The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C) (The degree of temperature elevation does not necessarily correspond to the severity of the illness.) and there was a large annular rash on her left flank (It is very important to differentiate a generalized rash from an isolated rash as that may be a manifestation of systemic response to the infecting organism. The appearance of the rash may be pathognomonic for a particular infection.), which measured approximately 20 centimeters in diameter. (See Figure 1.)
Figure 1. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Erythema chronicum migrans and Lyme Disease, caused by infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and Western Blot tests for Lyme disease were positive.

The patient was treated with doxycycline.

Lyme disease is a multi-organ disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, and is spread by the bite of an infected Ixodes tick. This patient’s annular rash (called erythema chronicum migrans) is the hallmark of early localized disease and occurs in 90% of infected patients. An expanding annular rash in a patient from an area endemic for Lyme disease is considered diagnostic of primary Lyme disease. Approximately 10-20% of the time, there may be multiple erythematous patches. Serologic studies may be negative if testing is performed early in the course of the illness.

title: 2006 October Featured Case Summary: A man from northern Brazil with respiratory
history:
2006 October Featured Case Summary: A man from northern Brazil with respiratory symptoms and a facial lesion.
A man in his fifties developed sore throat, dry cough, difficulty swallowing and change in his voice. Swelling around the mouth occurred, followed by the development of a lesion between the upper lip and nares. The lesion increased in size to involve the peri-oral skin and mucosa. Five years after the onset of symptoms, he presented for evaluation. He also reported fevers, night sweats and anorexia.

The patient was born and lived in Brazil, and had worked for many years as an agricultural laborer in a rural area in the northeastern section of the country. He was in frequent contact with numerous types of domesticated animals, livestock and fresh water sources. He smoked tobacco regularly until his throat began to bother him and had previously consumed several alcoholic beverages per night.
exam_studies:
The patient's facial lesion is shown in Figure 1. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Facial findings.

There were no laboratory tests available.
diagnosis:
Paracoccidioidomycosis caused by the fungus Paracoccidioides spp in a man from Brazil.

The diagnosis of paracoccidioidomycosis was made by pathological examination of a wet mount swab from the lesion. The identifying features of Paracoccidioides spp. include the appearance of large fungal cells with translucent walls and multiple buddings.

Amphotericin B was administered intravenously for four weeks and sulfamethoxazole was given orally. A treatment course of sulfamethoxazole for three to five years duration was planned.

Paracoccidioidomycosis is an endemic dimorphic fungus of South America (from Mexico to Argentina). It is also known as South American Blastomycosis. Infection is most common in Brazil, with lower rates in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Argentina, and still lower in the rest of the continent. The habitat of the fungus in nature is not known. It has rarely been isolated from soil, and has been found occasionally to infect armadillos and dogs. Endemicity appears to be centered in coffee- and tobacco-growing regions, as well as in areas with high humidity and heavy precipitation.
Most patients affected are over 30 years of age. Whereas the prevalence of infection, as determined by skin testing, suggests rates in men and women are approximately equal, the ratio of clinical disease in men to women is 15:1. Occupations related to agriculture appear to be a risk factor for disease. It does not spread from one person to another.
Paracoccidioidomycosis may remain latent for decades. Reactivation occurs in the setting of immunosuppression or malnourishment and is also associated with chronic alcohol and tobacco use. The fungus is thought to be acquired through inhalation (> 90% of those infected have lung lesions), with subsequent dissemination possible. Patients may present with a range of findings from dry cough and dyspnea to hemoptysis. The most common site of extra-pulmonary disease is the mucosa (60%), and can be seen in the mouth (lips, gingival, tongue, palate), naso- and oropharynx, and larynx. As a result, dysphonia and dysphagia are common findings. The gastrointestinal tract, from the mouth to the anus, can be affected and patients may suffer from diarrhea and emaciation. The adrenal glands, skin and reticuloendothelial system can also be sites of active infection. Constitutional symptoms such as fever, malaise and weight loss are common.
Diagnosis is often made with wet mount from sputum or purulent material arising from a lesion. Histological examination may show granulomas around yeast cells. Cultures should be incubated for six weeks.
At the time of this publication, treatment is with itraconazole or ketoconazole, with amphotericin given in severe cases. Sulfonamides are sometimes used and may have some efficacy. Investigation is ongoing into the use of posaconazole and terbinafine. Attention should also be paid to address immunosuppression, malnourishment, and the use of alcohol and tobacco.

title: 2006 November Featured Case Summary: A woman with a sore throat, neck fullness a
history:
2006 November Featured Case Summary: A woman with a sore throat, neck fullness and respiratory symptoms.
A woman in her thirties was in good health, in mid-winter, until eight days before admission when she developed sore throat, neck fullness and felt feverish. She was seen in urgent care the following day. The pharynx was injected and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. A throat culture was negative and viral pharyngitis was diagnosed. She was discharged to home, with rest, gargles and lozenges advised.
During the next six days, her throat soreness improved but dry cough, nausea, intermittent vomiting and lightheadedness developed. Contacted at home by phone, she was advised to continue with conservative management including over-the-counter analgesics and anti-tussive medication.
One week after the onset of symptoms, dyspnea on exertion and wheezing developed; she presented to the emergency room for further evaluation.

She had previously been in good health.

The patient lived alone, worked in an office, and did not have contact with animals. She did not smoke, and occasionally drank alcohol. There was no history of recent travel.

She was on no medications prior to this illness.
exam_studies:
In the emergency department, the patient appeared fatigued. The temperature was initially 97.6°F (36.4°C), blood pressure was 120/74 mm/Hg, pulse 124 beats per minute, and respirations 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and decreased to 91% with ambulation. The neck revealed bilateral tender lymphadenopathy and swelling; there was no trismus. The base of the right lung was dull to percussion with decreased fremitus; breath sounds were decreased in both bases, and inspiratory crackles were heard in the right base. The remainder of the examination was normal

The white blood cell count was 15,400 cells/mm³ (67% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 18% bands, 3% immature forms, 7% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes) and the hematocrit was 44.3%. Plasma creatinine was 0.7 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.5 mg/dL) albumin 2.6 grams/dL (normal 3.3-5.0 grams/dL), globulin 3.4 grams/dL (normal 2.6-4.1 grams/dL), total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL (normal 0.0-1.0 mg/dL), direct bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL (normal 0-0.4 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 280 U/liter (normal 30-100 U/liter), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 180 U/liter (normal 7-30 U/liter), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 123 U/liter (normal 9-32 U/liter). Carbon dioxide was 18.3 mEq/liter (normal 23-32 mEq/liter). A rapid enzyme immunoassay (EIA) test of a nasal swab was negative for Influenzavirus A and B antigens.
A chest radiograph, shown in Figure 1, revealed patchy opacities involving the right upper lobe, left lower lobe, and right middle lobe, which were thought to represent multilobar bronchopneumonia.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.

In the emergency department, azithromycin, albuterol nebulizers and two liters of intravenous normal saline were administered. An evaluation by otorhinolaryngology did not show any airway deviation or obstruction. Blood and sputum cultures were sent. The patient was admitted to the hospital. Within hours, the temperature rose to 101.5°F (38.6°C), supine blood pressure was 120/65 mm Hg with pulse 114 beats, standing 110/50 mm Hg with pulse 147 beats per minute.
On the first hospital day, combination therapy with ampicillin-sulbactam was initiated. On the second hospital day, a repeat chest radiograph showed the pulmonary infiltrates and a right-sided pleural effusion (Figure 2). Two anaerobic blood culture bottles, of four total blood culture bottles, were positive. A gram stain of the positive culture is shown in Figure 3. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed patchy air space disease in the lung bases, a right pleural effusion, and a spleen with a span of 15-centimeters.
During the next three days, the patient began to feel better, with diminishing fevers. The white blood cell count fell to 10,300 cells/mm³ (78% neutrophils and 15% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes). The following day, the temperature increased and was associated with neck discomfort, swelling and a white blood cell count of 13,400 cells/mm³ (92% neutrophils, 5% lymphocytes and 3% monocytes).
Figure 2. Chest x-ray, hospital day 2.
Figure 3. Gram stain of blood culture.
diagnosis:
Influenzavirus B infection complicated by Lemierre's syndrome caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum.

On the fourth hospital day, a direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test of a sputum sample was positive for Influenzavirus B antigen. On re-examination, a left neck mass measuring 4-centimeters in diameter had developed. CT scanning of the neck revealed an abscess of the left neck deep to the sternocleidomastoid and extending into the retropharyngeal space with occlusion of the left jugular vein. A necrotic lymph node was also seen on the left. (See Figure 4.) Ultrasonography of the neck showed a large abscess in the sternocleidomastoid muscle and an occluded left internal jugular vein.
The laboratory identified the organism grown in the blood culture bottles as fusiform bacteria. Intravenous penicillin G and clindamycin were administered. The neck abscess was incised and drained without complications; thirty cubic centimeters of purulent material was aspirated. Two day later, the organism was speciated as Fusobacterium necrophorum.
Results of laboratory tests for Influenzavirus A, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza, Legionella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and other respiratory bacterial pathogens were negative.
Figure 4. CT scan of neck.

The patient clinically improved after the surgical drainage procedure. Intravenous penicillin was continued and oral metronidazole was begun, and she completed a six-week course. The patient recovered completely.

This patient initially presented with a syndrome suggestive of a viral illness, and later shown to be due to Influenzavirus B. The rapid enzyme immunoassay (EIA) test of a nasal swab was performed in the emergency department and was negative for influenzavirus. However, this test has a lower sensitivity than that of the direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, which was performed after her admission to the hospital. This initial illness was complicated by the development of Lemierre's syndrome.
Lemierre's syndrome is also known as jugular vein suppurative thrombophlebitis. One published review [Chirinos et al 2002] calculated that most cases of Lemierre's syndrome (73%) occurred in patients aged 16–25 years, most of whom had been previously healthy. This entity usually begins with pharyngitis. A characteristic of this syndrome is that infection from the oropharynx extends into the carotid sheath vessels, classically causing thrombosis in the jugular vein. The delay between onset of pharyngitis and clinical thrombophlebitis was usually less than one week. Of those patients with jugular vein infection, nearly all are observed to have septic pulmonary emboli. Bacteremia is common and septic emboli to other sites are also reported, with most patients having evidence of emboli by the time of diagnosis.
The most common causative organism is the anaerobe Fusobacterium necrophorum, although several other oropharyngeal organisms have been associated with this clinical entity. In the above-mentioned review, authors found that in 70% of the cases reviewed, Fusobacterium necrophorum in the blood was the first clue to the diagnosis, as it was in this case. Lemierre, however, who originally described this clinical syndrome, warned that fever developing several days after sore throat, especially with evidence of embolic phenomena, should raise suspicion for this disease.
