title: 2006 December Featured Case Summary: A woman with a cough and pulmonary nodule.
history:
2006 December Featured Case Summary: A woman with a cough and pulmonary nodule.
A woman in her sixties presented with a three month history of a non-productive cough and night sweats. During this time, a ten-pound loss of weight occurred. Clarithromycin was administered, without resolution of the symptoms. She denied chest pain, fever, or chills.

There was a history of hypertension.

There was no history of smoking, illicit drug or alcohol abuse. She had no exposure to animals. She had traveled in the preceding year to South America, Europe, and Arizona.

Medications included nifedipine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 98.6°F (37°C) and her respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute. The remainder of her examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 35%; other laboratory test results, including the white blood cell count and differential, were normal. A chest radiograph showed a left upper lobe infiltrate. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, shown in Figure 1, revealed a pulmonary nodule.
Figure 1. CT scan of the chest.

A biopsy of the lung mass was performed. Results of pathological examination of the biopsy are shown in Figure 2 (hematoxylin and eosin stain) and Figure 3 (Gomori methenamine silver stain.)
Figure 2. H and E stain of lung biopsy
Figure 3. GMS stain of lung biopsy.
diagnosis:
Coccidioidomycosis, caused by Coccidioides immitis.

Pathological examination of the lung biopsy revealed multiple caseating and non-caseating granulomas, with fungal yeast forms present. Figures 2 and 3 show spherules with endospores, consistent with coccidioidomycosis. Culture revealed a filamentous organism, and a gene probe was positive for Coccidioides immitis.

Coccidioides immitis is endemic to the Southwestern United States, as well as parts of Central and South America. After entering by inhalation, C. immitis can cause pneumonia and pulmonary nodules. C. immitis may also disseminate systemically and cause meningitis, occasionally with an eosinophilic pleocytosis. This patient most likely contracted C. immitis pulmonary infection while hiking in Arizona.
The pathology in this case exhibits the classic spherules of Coccidioides immitis. Following inhalation, the spores of C. immitis swell and develop a thick wall. The resulting large spherule contains hundreds of endospores. This pathologic picture is not seen with the other organisms in the differential diagnosis. The yeast form of Histoplasma capsulatum exhibits narrow-based budding. Cryptococcus neoformans has a characteristic capsule, and a mucicarmine stain would be positive. Pneumocystis jirovecii, although now classified as a fungus, would not create a spherule; a silver stain may show helmet shaped organisms. Paracoccidioidomycosis occurs in Latin America, from Mexico to Argentina. In tissue biopsies, the yeast-like cells of this organism exhibit multiple, narrow-based oval "daughter" cells budding from a "mother" cell in a so-called "Mickey Mouse" pattern.

title: A man from Southeast Asia with HIV and AIDS, fever and a rash.
history:
A man in his forties, with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS, presented with fever, weakness, malaise, cough, occasional hemoptysis, and a rash. His symptoms had developed during the preceding week.

The patient had HIV and AIDS. The most recent CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 13 cells per microliter and the level of HIV RNA was 177,000 copies per milliliter. He had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and had been taking directly observed therapy for seven months.

He was born and raised in Southeast Asia, and had been living in the Southwest United States for approximately five years. He was divorced and worked as a laborer. He denied alcohol or drug abuse, recent travel or exposure to pets.

Medications included lopinavir-ritonavir, abacavir-lamivudine, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, azithromycin, isoniazid and rifampin.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic and lethargic, but arousable. The temperature was 101.3°F (38.5°C), respirations 20 breaths per minute, pulse 118 beats per minute, and blood pressure 98/56 mm Hg. The oral mucosa revealed white patchy areas consistent with thrush. Rales were heard in the right basal area of the chest. The abdomen was soft and the spleen tip was palpable. There were multiple ecchymoses and bleeding from puncture sites including in the area where a lumbar puncture had been performed. A maculopapular rash, with an erythematous base, was scattered on the face, torso and arms (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The hemoglobin was 10.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 9,800 cells/uL, platelets 78,000/uL. Partial thromboplastin time was 64.2 seconds, prothrombin time 16 seconds, and INR 1.6. The plasma level of urea nitrogen was 35 mg/mL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 148 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 894 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 651 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 5805 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL. The D-dimer was positive. An image of the blood smear is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Blood smear.

The patient developed melena and bleeding from puncture sites soon after admission and was transferred to the intensive care unit. An Infectious Diseases consult was obtained.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

A diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis was made upon examination of the blood smear. A specimen of urine revealed a positive Histoplasma antigen at a titer of 55.93 EIA units and a culture of the blood grew H. capsulatum.

Liposomal amphotericin B was administered with excellent response. At the time of discharge, the antifungal therapy was changed to oral itraconazole.

The natural reservoir of Histoplasma capsulatum is in the soil, including bat and avian habitats in the mid- and southwest regions of the United States. Disseminated disease is associated with AIDS, steroid use, renal allografts, hematologic malignancies and use of tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. The urinary Histoplasma antigen test is highly sensitive in AIDS patients and can be followed to monitor response to therapy. Itraconazole can be discontinued in patients who are treated and have a sustained response to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with a CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of greater than 150 cells/ul for at least 6 months.

title: A woman in her fifties presented with a lesion on her neck.
history:
A woman in her fifties was well until one month before presentation, when a painful left neck swelling developed, associated with arthralgias, myalgias, fevers, and chills. Tenderness and swelling of the left shin occurred episodically, less severe in the morning and worse later in the day. The swelling in left neck dissipated after 3-5 days, and a new circular, painless area of erythema and induration (3 centimeters (cm) by 4 cm) developed on the anterior neck. Two weeks before presentation, fevers, chills, arthralgias, and myalgias resolved. However, the lesion increased in size and became more indurated, beefy, heaped-up and, later in the course, more friable. Two days before presentation, scleral injection of the left eye developed. There was no history of headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, cough, sputum production, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, joint pains, or other skin lesions or rash. On the day of admission, the patient was evaluated in an otolaryngology outpatient clinic.
On examination, there was left ear fullness and tinnitus, and injection of the sclera of the left eye. The neck lesion was present and the left shin was tender. A fine needle aspirate was performed in the clinic, and the patient was then admitted to the hospital.

Two months earlier, a skin test for tuberculosis was negative. Twelve months before, she had had an influenza-like illness, with cough, myalgias, and arthralgias, for which she had not taken antibiotics.

She was born in China, spoke Cantonese and immigrated to the United States more than five years earlier. She lived with relatives in a predominantly Asian community on the West Coast. She had not traveled out of the country in recent years, had no exposures to pets, farms, birds, fish tanks, freshwater ponds or salt water, and had not seen visitors from East Asia. She did not smoke tobacco, drink alcohol or use intravenous drugs. There was no family history of cancer, diabetes or cardiovascular disease.

She had no allergies.
exam_studies:
On examination, she appeared anxious. The temperature was 37.0°C (98.6°F), the blood pressure 160/90 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on ambient air. The left sclera was injected; the neck was supple, with a round, indurated, beefy-looking lesion (4 cm by 5 cm) on the anterior neck (Figures 1 and 2). The tissue appeared friable and was not tender. The left shin had subtle soft tissue swelling and was tender to palpation. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 12,100 cells/mm³ (76% neutrophils and 20% lymphocytes), hematocrit 40.2%, and platelet count 435,000/mm³. Serum levels of electrolytes, glucose, liver enzymes and tests of renal function were normal.

A fine needle aspirate of the lesion was performed in the clinic. Pathological examination of the biopsy specimen with hematoxylin and eosin staining is shown in Figure 3.
Cultures of the biopsy specimens were sent.
Figure 3. H and E stain of biopsy.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous coccidioidomycosis, caused by Coccidioides immitis.

Cultures of fluid obtained by fine needle aspirate grew Coccidioides immitis. Figure 4 shows the growth on Sabouraud dextrose agar, and Figure 5 reveals the fungus stained with lacto-phenol-cotton blue stain. Coccidioides complement fixation titer was 1:16.
Figure 4. Cultures of biopsy specimen.
Figure 5. Culture growth with lacto-phenol-cotton blue stain.

Initially, amphotericin B was administered intravenously, until a lumbar puncture was performed and central nervous system involvement was ruled out. The patient was then treated with itraconazole for six months, during which time the Coccidioides complement fixation titer decreased from 1:16 to 1:4, and the lesion resolved.

Coccidioides is a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Central Valley region of California, the desert of the Southwest United States, Mexico, and Central and South America. The mycelial (or mold) form grows in the soil in endemic areas, and the branching, septate hyphae produce arthroconidia, which become airborne. In tissues, a characteristic spherule is formed.
Coccidioides immitis was first identified in the 1890s in an Argentinian soldier, who developed a lesion resembling mycosis fungoides. It was initially thought to be due to a protozoan. Emmet Rixford, a surgeon from Stanford University, identified two additional cases in the 1890s. In 1905, it was speciated as a fungus (Ophuls, 1905). Surges in the number of cases are related to cycles of drought and rain. In 1992-1993, a 10-fold increase in cases was seen in California. Person-to-person transmission is not possible but caution with secretions is advised. Approximately 60% of people infected with C. immitis are asymptomatic while the other 40% of those infected develop upper respiratory symptoms (including fevers, diaphoresis, arthralgias, cough sputum, chest pain). Erythema nodosum or erythema multiforme may also develop.
Symptomatic extrapulmonary symptoms develop in 0.5-1% of those infected, usually within the first year, but possibly later if the host is or becomes immunocompromised. Common sites of involvement are the meninges, bone, joints, skin, and soft tissues. The frequency of dissemination is higher in pregnant individuals, and immunocompromised hosts, and in individuals of specific ethnicities. Those of Filipino ancestry are affected more often than African Americans, and then, in descending frequency of infection, are native Americans, Hispanics, other Asians and Caucasians.
Symptoms, especially central nervous systems and musculoskeletal complaints, should prompt further investigation, including a lumbar puncture and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), imaging, and bone scans. A definitive diagnosis requires biopsy and culture of lesions and/or the CSF.
Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii, the two recognized etiologies of coccidioidomycosis, may be detected by direct microscopy, culture, and serologic documentation. C. immitis grows rapidly, and if the organism is suspected, the microbiology laboratory staff should be notified in advance. Stains that are used include the Grocott methenamine silver and the calcofluor white. Other useful stains used in histopathology include hematoxylin and eosin stain and periodic acid schiff. Nucleic acid amplification tests to detect Coccidioides spp. are being developed in research settings. Isolates may be confirmed as Coccidioides spp. by molecular probes. Speciation of C. immitis and C. posadasii is achieved by specialized molecular techniques, and is not normally available in routine clinical laboratories. Humoral antibodies are used for the diagnosis and prognosis of coccidioidomycosis. Although positive serologies are specific for coccidioidomycosis, negative serologies cannot be used to rule out the disease. Enzyme immunoassays (EIA) and immunodiffusion methods are commonly used for detection of both immunoglobulin (Ig) M and IgG antibody groups. Sequential complement fixation (CF) studies for the IgG antibody class are also useful. Serologic testing plays a role in diagnosis and management. CF antigen test results correlate with the degree of dissemination. Antibodies to Coccidioides can also be assessed in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by complement fixation and may be helpful since the culture of the CSF is negative in 5% of patients with meningeal infection. Other testing includes skin testing to Coccidioides antigen, which may be positive in 83% during the 1st week of infection, and 99% after the 4th week (Saubolle, 2007).

title: A man with dyspnea and cough.
history:
A man in his forties presented with a nonproductive cough, dyspnea and decreased oral intake of three months' duration. The symptoms had worsened during the preceding week. There was subjective fever, chills and weight loss of an unspecified amount.

There was a history of mental illness and a positive tuberculosis skin test (PPD), which had not been treated in the past.

He was born in Haiti and immigrated to the northeastern United States more than two decades before. He lived in an urban area and had not traveled recently. While in Haiti, he had owned a cat; he had no pets in the United States. He smoked marijuana, but denied intravenous drug use. He denied any sexual contacts; however, witnesses had seen him in the presence of sex workers.

Medications included haloperidol, valproic acid and olanzapine.
exam_studies:
On examination, he was an ill-appearing, lethargic male with mild tachypnea. The temperature was 39.1°C (102.4°F), respirations 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air. The lungs revealed slight crackles anteriorly. The mucous membranes were dry. There were no oral lesions or lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 6,600 cells/mm³. Arterial blood gases revealed a partial pressure of oxygen of 69 mm Hg on ambient air; the alveolar and arterial oxygen gradient was 44 mm Hg. The level of lactate dehydrogenase was 2,706 IU/L (elevated).
A chest radiograph from three years earlier is shown in Figure 1, and one from this admission in Figure 2. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, three years before admission.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest on admission.

Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive (ELISA) and confirmed by Western Blot analysis. The CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 10 cells/mm³, CD4 percentage 1%, and the HIV-RNA level was >750,000 copies/ml. A bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy of right middle lobe was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the biopsy specimen is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 4. H and E stain of lung biopsy.
diagnosis:
Toxoplasma pneumonitis caused by Toxoplasma gondii in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

The biopsy specimen revealed Toxoplasma. The arrows in Figures 5 and 6 indicate the location of encysted forms of the organism.
Figure 5. H and E stain of lung biopsy.
Figure 6. Immunohistochemical stain of biopsy.

Initial therapy on admission included sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and prednisone (due to a concern for Pneumocystis) and azithromycin (for possible atypical bacterial pneumonia). However, on this regimen, the patient remained tachypneic, tachycardic, and became increasingly hypoxic. Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine were administered when the pathological examination of tissue obtained via bronchoscopy revealed Toxoplasma encysted forms. Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and azithromycin were discontinued, and prednisone was tapered. His respiratory status improved significantly with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine therapy. Repeat chest radiographs showed resolution of the pulmonary infiltrates.
The patient then began to spike fevers. Sulfadiazine was discontinued, and clindamycin begun, due to the possibility of sulfa-related drug fevers; the patient improved and defervesced. Clindamycin and pyramethamine (with leucovorin) were administered.
The fundoscopic exam was normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed scattered cerebral calcifications. There was no other evidence suggestive of extrapulmonary toxoplasmosis.

Most cases of Toxoplasma pneumonitis in patients with HIV infection and AIDS are related to reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii infection. The most common symptoms are nonproductive cough and dyspnea. Definitive diagnosis requires either histological demonstration of the organism or isolation by culture. Direct visualization with Giemsa or hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining may show crescent-shaped tachyzoites. Stains may show encysted forms, as in this case. Standard therapy at the time of this publication is pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.

title: A man with fever and pain in the leg and foot.
history:
A man presented with severe left leg and foot pain of five days' duration. After the third day of symptoms, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and numerous skin lesions developed. He presented for evaluation.

He had been in good health.

The patient spent time fishing in the Chesapeake Bay, drank 2-3 beers per day, and did not smoke or use intravenous drugs.

There were no allergies to medications.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared toxic and lethargic. The temperature was 104°F (40°C), blood pressure 60/40 mm Hg, pulse 126 beats per minute, respirations 30 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 90% while breathing room air. There were multiple hemorrhagic bullae, predominantly on the extremities. See Figure 1.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 3300 cells/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear cells, 23% bands), hemoglobin 12 grams/dL, and platelets 122,000/mm³. The prothrombin time was 18 seconds, INR 2, and the partial thromboplastin time was 49 seconds. The level of plasma creatinine was 3.5 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, creatine kinase 23,500 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 465 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 145 U/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL and D-dimer 658 ng/mL.
diagnosis:
Septicemia, due to Vibrio vulnificus infection.

Multiple blood and wound cultures grew Vibrio vulnificus.

Despite the administration of cefepime and doxycycline, aggressive surgical debridement and intensive care support, the patient unfortunately died.

Vibrio vulnificus is a common, naturally-occurring bacterium present in marine or estuarine environments. Infections from this organism are typically seen in summer months since the bacteria grows best at temperatures greater than 20°C. Exposures most often occur from contaminated seafood (such as raw oysters) or from contact with estuarine water. Those at high risk for infection include patients who abuse alcohol, or those with liver disease, chronic renal failure, iron overload states (e.g. hemochromatosis), hematopoietic disorders or immunosuppression (e.g. HIV, malignancy, diabetes) or those on immunosuppressive medications, such as steroids.
Symptoms seen most often in V. vulnificus septicemia include fever (94%), chills (91%), skin lesions (70%), nausea (59%), vomiting (54%), and diarrhea (58%).
The skin lesions are often preceded by severe localized prodromal pain and typically occur within 1-3 days after ingestion of raw oysters or contact with estuarine water. The lesions are most commonly found on the extremities, but can be widespread, and often begin as erythematous plaques, which then rapidly evolve into bullae and later into necrotic ulcers. The bullae typically appear on an edematous and/or erythematous base and are classically hemorrhagic. Frequently, an underlying necrotizing cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis is present.
Multimodal treatment is usually needed. Antibiotic options include tetracyclines, cephalosporins (3rd or 4th generation), aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones (newer generation). Antibiotics should be used in combination with surgical debridement of devitalized tissue in patients with concomitant necrotizing fasciitis.

title: A man with HIV and AIDS and a skin rash.
history:
A man in his twenties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) presented with a rash of three weeks' duration. The rash started between his fingers and spread to his head, neck, back, chest and extremities. The skin lesions initially appeared as brown spots, which later turned grey. The rash was painful. On his hands, the skin was cracked and bleeding. He had fatigue and ow-grade fevers of one week's duration. There was no pruritus. The patient denied any sick contacts with a rash.

There was a history of HIV infection and AIDS, with CD4 T-lymphocytes level of 4 cells/mm³ and HIV-RNA level of 92,000 copies/ml. Disseminated histoplasmosis had been diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy four months before. He also had anemia, poor adherence to medical therapy, and thrush. Several years earlier, he had had a deep venous thrombosis in the left leg.

The patient lived with his family in the United States and had pet dogs at home. He had been sexually active with men in the past, but not for several years, and had also used cocaine by inhalation in the past.

Medications included itraconazole, dapsone, iron sulfate, azithromycin, ritonavir-lopinavir combination therapy, lamivudine and enfuvirtide.
exam_studies:
The patient was a lethargic, thin male. The temperature was 99.8°F (37.7°C), blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse 148 beats per minute, and respirations 18 breaths per minute. The S1 and S2 heart sounds were rapid and in a regular rhythm, with a II/VI systolic ejection murmur at the apex. The neck was tender, with decreased range of motion secondary to rash, and there was a superficial ulcer on the left shin. Dry, raised white-grey thick plaque-like lesions were present and became confluent on the dorsum of hands, sides of face, neck, scalp, and back. The rash also affected the arms, legs, palms, soles, shaft and glans of the penis and was tender to palpation. Cracks were present on hands, with minimal erythema. (Figures 1 through 4.)
Figure 1. Physical findings, on admission.
Figure 2. Physical findings, on admission.
Figure 3. Physical findings
Figure 4. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 2500 cells/mm³ (27% neutrophils, 2% bands, 18% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 48% eosinophils), hematocrit 21.0%, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume 78 fl and platelets 63,000/mm³.

The patient was placed in contact isolation and started on amphotericin B. The temperature rose to 103ºF (39.4°C). Blood cultures were drawn and a culture of the skin ulcer on the lower leg was obtained.
diagnosis:
Crusted scabies caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Skin biopsy revealed scabies, Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, shown in Figure 5.
Figure 5. Skin biopsy.

He was treated with 5% permethrin cream and ivermectin 200 ug/kg. Petrolatum jelly with 6% sulfur was applied daily. The rash sloughed off in large sheets. Images taken in follow-up are shown in Figures 6 and 7.
The culture obtained from the shin ulcer grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and the blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.
He was treated with vancomycin, with sterilization of his blood cultures and resolution of his fevers. Appropriate infection control measures were taken.
Figure 6. Follow up, day 7.
Figure 7. Follow up, day 7.

Crusted scabies is also known as Norwegian scabies, and is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. It was first described in 1848 in Norwegian patients with Hansen’s disease (leprosy). Risk factors include HIV infection, Hansen's disease, Down’s syndrome, leukemia, lymphoma, topical corticosteroid use, organ transplantation, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus or vasculitis.
The infection often represents the presence of thousands to millions of mites. Complications include secondary skin infections and bacteremia. It is very contagious and infection control issues must be considered.

title: A man with HIV infection and AIDS and small bowel obstruction.
history:
A man in his forties, recently diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), presented with recurrent symptoms of night sweats, cough, severe nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, associated with weight loss of 40-pounds (18.2 kilograms. He denied dysphagia. He had been admitted three times in the previous three months with similar symptoms. Recurrent small bowel obstructions were diagnosed and his symptoms improved with medical management. Three sputum samples had been positive by fluorescent staining for acid fast bacilli. He was admitted to a tuberculosis unit and started on anti-tuberculosis therapy, while sputum specimens were being cultured. A skin test for tuberculosis was negative.

The patient had a history of HIV infection, AIDS (CD4 T-lymphocyte count of 27 cells/mm³ and HIV-RNA level of 2750 copies/ml). He also had Hepatitis C virus infection (diagnosed ten years earlier) for which no treatment had been given.

The patient was born in Puerto Rico, immigrated to the United States as a teenager and had last visited twenty years earlier. He lived in the northeastern United States with his wife and children. He had a pet dog and reported travel to Florida. He had smoked cigarettes in the past, and stopped drinking alcohol and using intravenous drugs approximately 6 months earlier.

Highly active anti-retroviral therapy had been initiated approximately four months earlier (three to six weeks before his first admission). His medications included ritonavir-lopinavir and tenofovir-emtricitabine combination therapy, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, rifabutin, isoniazid (INH), pyrazinamide, ethambutol, levofloxacin, clindamycin, and vitamin B6. He reported having difficulty taking his medications consistently.
exam_studies:
On admission, he appeared cachectic. The temperature was 96.9°F (36.1°C). There was mild thrush, severe gingivitis with dental caries and missing dentition, and bilateral sub-mandibular lymphadenopathy. The lungs were clear, the abdomen was soft and moderately distended with scant bowel sounds and severe left lower quadrant abdominal pain. There were no skin lesions or genital ulcers.

The white blood cell count was 1800 cells/mm³ (59% neutrophils, 28% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 2% eosinophils). Sputum specimens were positive for acid-fast bacilli by fluorescent staining.
The chest radiograph revealed diffuse reticulonodular densities (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.

An abdominal radiograph and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed findings consistent with a high grade small bowel obstruction and mass-like thickening in right lower quadrant (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Abdominal radiograph.
Figure 4. Abdominal CT scan.
diagnosis:
Intestinal histoplasmosis and pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection, in a patient with HIV and AIDS, in the setting of immune reconstitution syndrome.

Resection of the mid and distal small bowel was performed. Pathological examination of tissue from the resected intestinal wall showed caseating granulomas and ulcerated bowel wall on hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) staining (Figures 5 and 6). Silver staining of the intestinal wall showed yeast-like organisms consistent with histoplasmosis (Figure 7). Urinary Histoplasma antigen was positive at 9.60 units. Sputum cultures grew Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC).
Figure 5. H and E stain of caseating granuloma.
Figure 6. H and E stain of mucosal ulceration.
Figure 7. Silver stain of biopsy.

After surgical resection of ulcerated and strictured segments, the pathologic diagnosis of histoplasmosis was made and itraconazole was administered. Rifabutin, ethambutol, and azithromycin were given for the treatment of pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection.

Histoplasma is identified in gastrointestinal tract of 70-90% patients with disseminated histoplasmosis, but causes clinical symptoms only in 3-12% patients. Histoplasma microconidia are inhaled and hematogenously spread to organs of the reticuloendothelial system. The yeast form is responsible for disease production.
Pathologic findings include caseating granulomas and calcifications. Intestinal disease may include gastrointestinal hemorrhage, bowel perforation, or obstruction.
Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is uncommon in patients with AIDS, but may occur in the setting of immune reconstitution syndrome (as in this case).

title: A young girl with a rash of two days' duration.
history:
A pre-teenaged girl presented with a rash on her arms and ankles that had developed over the preceding 48 hours.
Two weeks before, while camping, she had scraped her wrist on a branch in a creek. The scrape had turned red while healing. Six days before admission, she had been bitten in the face by the family's dog. Three days later, symptoms of a “flu-like” illness occurred including fatigue, low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting. Other family members were also ill. The day before admission, a goat jumped on her arm. The arm appeared purple and bruised, and a small red rash appeared on her ankle.
On the day of admission, the rash on her arms and ankles increased in size and the coloration turned from pink to purple. The scars on her wrist (from the branch) and face (from the dog bite) turned black. Other symptoms included headache and diffuse myalgias. She was brought for evaluation and admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit.

She was born with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Shortly after her birth, during surgical repair of the hernia, the spleen was nicked and a splenectomy was performed. At age 14 months, she was hospitalized with pneumococcal sepsis. She had not taken amoxicillin prophylaxis during the five years preceding this admission. Childhood immunizations were up to date, and she had received pneumococcal vaccines, a meningococcal vaccine, and a full Haemophilus influenzae type B series. There were no allergies to medications.

She lived in the northwestern United States, in a rural area with no running water. She had pet hamsters, and had contact with horses, rabbits, dogs and cats. She had received multiple mosquito bites, had possibly been exposed to mice, and was not aware of any tick bites.

She lived with her family.
exam_studies:
The patient was lethargic but arousable. The maximal temperature was 38.3°C (100.9°F),blood pressure 113/69 mm Hg, pulse 98 beats per minute, respirations 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation, as measured by oximetry, was normal. There was dried blood in the nares, dry mucus membranes and poor dentition. Breath sounds were decreased. The chest was hyperdynamic, with no cardiac murmur. There were multiple purpuric lesions on the face, extremities and torso. Several of the lesions appeared necrotic, including a lesion on the right wrist (1 centimeters (cm) by 2 cm); right posterior upper arm (1 cm in diameter); a purpuric lesion on the right buttock (2 cm by 4 cm); purpuric lesion with necrotic center on right cheek (1 cm by 0.5 cm); a less dark area on left cheek, and three lesions on the right malar ridge (2-3 millimeters in diameter). There was circumferential purpura around both ankles, an area of darkening necrosis (2 cm in diameter) on the right foot and petechiae on the soles; the palms were clear. See Figures 1 through 5. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.
Figure 4. Physical findings.
Figure 5. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 11,100/mm³ (69% neutrophils, 16% bands), hematocrit 31% and platelets 31,000/mm³. The prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times were norma; the level of fibrinogen was 727 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 108 units/L, alanine aminotransferase 79 units/L and the D-Dimer >20 micrograms/mL. Serum test results for total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), urea nitrogen, and creatinine were normal.
There were no infiltrates seen on chest radiography. Blood cultures were obtained.
diagnosis:
Postsplenectomy sepsis caused by Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection.

The microbiology laboratory initially identified a long, thin gram-negative rod growing in the anaerobic bottle. The organism did not look like Enterobacteriaceae, and appeared to resemble Fusobacterium, but was less pointed. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and 16S-v3 ribosomal DNA partial sequencing identified the organism as Capnocytophaga canimorsus.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus is a facultative anaerobe that is fastidious, and difficult to subculture from blood bottles. Of 141 cases reported in the literature through 1995, animal exposures were noted in 86%, and of those, 94% were secondary to contact with dogs (Rosenman et al 2003). In 26% of the cases, the contact was non-traumatic, and 8% were due to scratches (Rosenman et al 2003). Rapid severe disease may occur in patients with asplenia, alcoholism, or corticosteroid therapy (Gill 2004). The case fatality rate is approximately 30%, even in patients with an intact spleen (Rosenman et al 2003, Gill 2004). C. canimorsus is sensitive to numerous antibiotics including beta-lactams, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, vancomycin, chloramphenicol, rifampicin, fusidic acid, and clindamycin (Gill 2004, Gottwein et al 2006). Resistance against aztreonam, methicillin, aminoglycosides, polymyxin, metronidazole, fosfomycin, and trimethoprim has been reported (Gill 2004, Gottwein et al 2006). Beta-lactamase production is becoming increasingly common in Capnocytophaga species (Roscoe et al 1992, Jolivet-Gougeon et al 2000).
Other organisms that may cause postsplenectomy sepsis (PSS) include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis, Salmonella species, alpha–hemolytic streptococci, staphylococci, Bacteroides, and Enterobacteriaceae (Lutwick 2004).

title: Summary of IDSA 2006 Case Submission: A man in his fifties with recurrent skin a
history:
Summary of IDSA 2006 Case Submission: A man in his fifties with recurrent skin abscesses.
A man in his fifties presented for evaluation because of recurrent abscesses over the abdomen and groin. Eight months before, painless pustules had developed. Each lesion began as a small pustule, growing in size before yielding a grainy, yellow discharge. Initially, the wounds healed, each leaving behind a 1-2 inch (2.5 - 5.1 cm) scar. Two weeks before admission, increasing scrotal and abdominal wall edema developed. Ten days before presentation, he was evaluated at a local clinic and metronidazole and cephalexin were administered, without improvement.

The patient reported a similar (but much milder) skin infection that had affected his right calf and resolved without intervention, which occurred when he lived in Mexico more than ten years earlier. There was a history of diabetes mellitus that was diet-controlled, and an inguinal hernia repair on the left, six years before.

The patient had been born in Mexico, and immigrated to United States a decade earlier. He was heterosexual and monogamous, and had been a field worker in Mexico and a maintainance worker in the United States.

Medications included metronidazole and cephalexin, for ten days.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.1°F (37.3°C). The right lower abdomen had multiple, well-healed scars with surrounding induration. The left lower abdomen had multiple wounds draining a small amount of yellow discharge. The overlying skin was indurated, but not erythematous. The right calf had multiple pitted, well-healed scars (Figures 1 and 2). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white cell count was 8,100 cells/µL, with 76% neutrophils. The serum level of glucose was 120 g/dL and albumin was 2.8 g/dL.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis is shown in Figure 3. A gram stain of a swab of one of the lesions is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 3. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.
Figure 4. Gram stain of specimen.
diagnosis:
Actinomycetoma caused by Nocardia brasiliensis.

A modified acid fast stain of the growth from the culture is shown in Figure 5, and the culture plate of a sample from the lesion is shown in Figure 6.
Nocardia brasiliensis was identified.
Figure 5. Modified acid fast stain of specimen.
Figure 6. Culture of specimen.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (2 double-strength tablets three times daily) was administered for nine months. Once on therapy, no new lesions arose. After therapy, residual scar tissue remained, but symptoms of induration, pain, and discharge resolved completely.

Mycetomas are chronic, granulomatous infections of the subcutaneous tissue leading to necrotic abscess, sinus tract, and fistula formation. Untreated, lesions may expand to include adjacent muscle and bone. Mycetomas are caused by true fungi (eumycetomas) or aerobic bacteria (actinomycetomas) and typically occur in tropical and semitropical climates. Mycetomas in the United States are most commonly due to Pseudoallescheria boydii, however, in Mexico, Nocardia brasiliensis is responsible for 86% of cases [Welsh 1993].
The initial infection usually results from trauma, leading to subcutaneous inoculation. Affected patients are often herdsmen, farmers, or other field workers in direct contact with the environment [McGinnis 1996]. This patient reports that he frequently worked outdoors in Mexico, and as a result, likely sustained the initial injury to his right leg (Figure 2). While cases of mycetoma typically affect the feet and hands, in highly endemic areas, infection may include the thighs and perineum, less commonly involving the chest and abdominal walls [Ahmed et al 2004].
Mycetomas progress over months to years, and periods of latency or regression are not uncommon [Lederman and Crum 2004]. Agents of infection spread locally or via the lymphatic system. Secondary nodules subsequently arise and progress to sinus tract formation. Subcutaneous masses consist of grains, or aggregates of bacterial elements, embedded in tough, fibrinous tissue.
Cutaneous infection due to Nocardia spp. may also manifest as a cellulitis, isolated subcutaneous abscess, or lymphonodular process clinically indistinguishable from sporotrichosis (sporotrichoid nocardiosis) [Lerner 1996]. In 10% of cases, cutaneous involvement may be indicative of disseminated Nocardia infection [Kalb et al 1985].
While any pathogenic Nocardia species may cause cutaneous or subcutaneous disease, invasive and locally progressive infection leading to actinomycetoma formation is most commonly due to Nocardia brasiliensis. While systemic Nocardia infection suggests underlying host immunodeficiency, cutaneous infection often occurs in healthy patients with an antecedent superficial injury [Georghiou and Blacklock 1992]. An animal model study suggests that cutaneous inoculation leading to mycetoma formation may be hastened by an impaired cell-mediated immune system [Folb et al 1977].
Mycetoma diagnosis, once suspected, is usually confirmed by culture of purulent drainage or punch biopsy. Nocardia spp. will grow on standard blood agar, however, plating on an enriched media such as Lowenstein Jensen or Sabourand-dextrose agar allows for optimal detection. Gram-positive, variably acid-fast, and filamentous, Nocardia spp. are slow-growing, often requiring 2-5 days for identification. Delayed growth may lead to the premature disposal of cultures and therefore the microbiology lab should be alerted in suspected cases [Lerner 1996]. On occasion, close evaluation of grain morphology may allow preliminary organism identification. Grains due to N. brasiliensis are invisible to the naked eye, but by microscopy they are characterized as white-yellow [McElroy et al 1992].
Actinomycetoma can be treated with medical therapy alone; however, adjuvant surgical excision or drainage may be warranted in complicated cases [Georghiou and Blacklock 1992]. Sulfonamides are the drug of choice for actinomycetoma due to N. brasiliensis; in patients intolerant of sulfa-containing drugs, minocycline may be considered [Lerner 1996]. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is commonly administered. Linezolid also has activity against Nocardia [Gomez-Flores et al 2004], although clincial experience with this agent is limited. Actinomycetoma therapy is lengthy, requiring several months to two years for symptom resolution.

history:
Summary of IDSA 2006 Case Submission: A man in his twenties with headaches of two months' duration.
A man in his twenties presented with a two-month history of severe headaches. The pain was in the occipital and temporal regions, bilaterally, and was rated 9 on a scale of 0 to 10 (where 10 is the most severe). Fevers, non-productive cough, vomiting, blurred vision, neck stiffness, and photophobia were also present. He felt chills in the morning and diaphoretic in the afternoon.
One month earlier, he was admitted to a local hospital. A skin test for tuberculosis was negative. Viral meningitis was diagnosed and the patient was discharged.

There was no significant past medical or surgical history.

The patient was of Hispanic ethnicity, and lived in the Southern United States. There was no history of smoking, drug use, or alcohol, and no exposures to animals. He worked in the construction industry and had traveled in the past to Indiana, Florida, and California.

Medications included hydrocodone and acetaminophen combination, and an over-the-counter preparation of acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine.
exam_studies:
On examination, he was pale and ill-appearing. The temperature was 35.4°C (95.7°F), blood pressure 128/85 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats/minute and respirations 16 breaths/minute. He was alert and oriented to person, place and time. Kernig and Bruzinski signs were positive, and there was no focal neurological abnormality. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 16,900 cells/µL (95% segmented neutrophils and 5% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 13.5 g/dl, hematocrit 40.1%, and platelets 363,000 cells/µL. Serologic levels of electrolytes and glucose, tests of renal and liver function and a chest radiograph were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in Figure 1.
Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained by lumbar puncture revealed 5 red cells/µL and 336 white cells/µL (26% neutrophils, 64% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 2% other cells). The protein level was 266 mg/dl and glucose 24 mg/dl.
Figure 1. MRI of the brain, day 5.

A skin test for tuberculosis measured 16 millimeters of induration. Tuberculous meningitis was diagnosed presumptively, and anti-tuberculosis therapy with four drugs was administered.
Analysis of the CSF for cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus (HSV) by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), acid-fast bacilli (AFB) by smear, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test, cysticercosis immunoglobulin G antibody, Mycobacterium tuberculosis by PCR, and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) were negative. Cultures of the CSF for bacteria and fungi were sterile. Serologic tests for Varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal antigen, and antibodies to Leptospira, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Bartonella and Rickettsia were negative. Analysis of the urine for Histoplasma antigen was negative.
The patient developed increasing hydrocephalus. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed, however, the patient continued to deteriorate and expired.
diagnosis:
Coccidioidomycosis of the lung, meninges and brain.

A post-mortem examination was performed. Pathological examination of the lungs revealed a granuloma in the left lower lobe, in which a spherule was identified (Figures 2 through 4). Pathological examination of the brain (shown in Figures 5 through 8) revealed severe basilar involvement and a multi-nucleated giant cell engulfing two spherules in brain tissue. The findings are consistent with coccidioidomycosis of the lungs, meninges and brain.
Figure 2. Post-mortem examination, left lung.
Figure 3. Post-mortem examination, left lung.
Figure 4. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of lung tissue.
Figure 5. Post-mortem examination of the brain.
Figure 6. Post-mortem examination of the brain.
Figure 7. H and E stain of the brain.
Figure 8. H and E stain of the brain.

Coccidioidomycosis is endemic in desert regions of the southwestern United States, and Central and South America. Primary infection involves the lungs, and clinical evidence of dissemination occurs in the minority of patients. Of those patients with disseminated coccidioidomycosis, meningitis occurs in approximately half [Johnson and Einstein 2006]. Although most cases of coccidioidal meningitis occur weeks to months after primary infection, this feared complication can develop years after primary exposure. Diagnosis can be made by identifying spherules in infected tissue specimens; samples should also be sent for culture since in some cases direct visualization is negative but the organism will grow. When Coccidioides infection is suspected, laboratory personnel should be notified so that appropriate precautions to decrease exposure to this infectious agent can be implemented.

history:
Summary of IDSA 2006 Case Submission: A woman with cough and chest pain following kidney transplantation.
A woman in her fifties presented with a two-week history of pleuritic chest pain and a cough that was not productive. The symptoms had developed four months after kidney transplantation. There was no history of fevers, chills, rigors, or weight loss.

She had undergone kidney transplantation from a related donor four months earlier. There was also a history of cerebral vascular accident that had affected the mid-brain and pons, and from which she had minimal residual deficits.

The patient was of African-American ethnicity. There was no history of illicit drug use, or alcohol and tobacco use. She tended numerous potted plants inside of the home, and had no travel history outside her home region in a mid-Atlantic state. She did not live near the coast.

Medications included prednisone (10 mg daily), tacrolimus (2 mg in the morning and 1 mg in evening), and mycophenolate (500 mg every 12 hours).
exam_studies:
The temperature was normal. There were crackles upon inspiration noted in the upper lobe of the right lung. The remainder of the examination was otherwise normal.

The white cell count was 8,700/µl, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dl, serum urea nitrogen 16 mg/dl, and creatinine 1.2 mg/dl.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) revealed a wedge-shaped opacity seen in the periphery. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) showed a mass-like consolidation that measured 4.3 centimeters (cm) by 4.0 cm.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.

Bronchoscopy was performed and specimens were sent for culture, acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains, but results were not diagnostic. A right upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection was performed. Pathological examination of surgical specimens are shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.
Figure 3. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of the lung, 40 x magnification.
Figure 4. Gomori-methenamine stain of the lung, 40 x magnification.
Figure 5. GMS stain of the lung, 100x magnification.
diagnosis:
Brain abscess caused by Cladophialophora bantiana, in a patient following renal transplantation.

Cultures of specimens from the brain and lung grew Cladophialophora bantiana.

Following recovery from the thoracotomy, the patient was discharged from the hospital on voriconazole (200 mg orally every 12 hours) and caspofungin (50 mg intravenously daily), and the same immunosuppressive medications as on admission.
Six weeks after discharge, mild headache developed, associated with vertigo, decreased manual dexterity, and loss of balance to the left. Two weeks later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (Figures 6 and 7) revealed findings consistent with a brain abscess.
The patient was re-admitted and aspiration of the brain lesion performed, followed by complete resection of the lesion. A gram stain of the aspirate is shown in Figure 8. Due to the patient’s development of central nervous system (CNS) disease while on a combination of voriconazole and caspofungin therapy, amphotericin B lipid complex (5mg/kg/day), flucytosine (5-FC) (12.5 mg/kg every 6 hours), and itraconazole oral solution (300 mg every 12 hours) were administered.
Micafungin was also initiated at a dose of 150mg intravenously, daily. Aggressive surgical excision of the lesion was performed with minimal neurologic sequela. At follow-up three months after discharge, the patient had improved clinically and tolerated the antifungal medications without adverse renal or hematological toxicities. A follow-up MRI scan, after resection of the brain abscess, is shown in Figure 9.
Figure 6. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 7. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 8. Gram stain of the aspirate, 100 x magnification.
Figure 9. Follow-up MRI scan of the brain.

Cladophialophora bantiana is a dematiaceous, or “black mold” fungus, which contains melanin pigments in the cell walls. These organisms appear to have a neurotropism for causing CNS infections. Treatment of CNS lesions requires both surgical excision and combination antifungal therapy with amphotericin B, azoles (itraconazole or voriconazole), and flucytocine. Echinocandins have activity against some dematiaceous fungi, although clinical experience is limited. Despite aggressive therapy, mortality rates approach 75% [Revankar et al 2004].

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with a biphasic (Some kinds of
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with a biphasic (Some kinds of infections can have different symptoms at different points in the illness. This can be due either to intrinsic properties of a pathogen - for example, one that begins as a local infection that later becomes systemic - or because one pathogen can increase the risk of a secondary infection with another organism.) respiratory illness.
A woman in her thirties (A patient's age is often a critical factor in infectious disease diagnosis, affecting both the spectrum of illness and type of organisms involved. Relatively few common infectious diseases make a previously healthy young adult severely ill, which can narrow the differential diagnosis of likely causes.) presented in February (Many infectious illnesses show at least some seasonality, so the time of year an illness occurs can help suggest which pathogens are more likely. Influenza has one of the most striking seasonal patterns of any common infectious disease, with high rates in the cold winter months in Northern and Southern hemispheres, while being present at low levels year-round in the tropics.) with a history of fever, and temperatures ranging between 100-101°F (37.8-38.3°C), headache, myalgias (Terminology: diffuse muscle aches.) and cough. There was no sputum production. She was breathing comfortably and the examination was normal. Laboratory testing included a normal white cell count (The total white blood cell count is often a clue to the diagnosis. Most common bacterial infections severe enough to provoke fever will usually cause an elevated white blood cell count, whereas many viral infections will not.). A chest radiograph was taken and is shown in Figure 1 (This chest radiograph shows symmetrical interstitial changes characteristic of viral or atypical infection.). She was discharged home with a diagnosis of probable influenza (For common illnesses, a diagnosis can often be made presumptively, without requiring specific testing (though currently, most people would be tested for influenza antigens, if testing is available).).
Several days later, she returned to the emergency room due to worsening symptoms, including cough productive of purulent sputum (The pattern of initial improvement from a viral infection followed days later by worsening symptoms and the development of a productive cough with purulent sputum is suggestive of secondary bacterial infection, and important complication of several viral infections, notably influenza. Terminology: Purulent means pus-producing.).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on initial presentation.

The patient had been in good health (Serious pre-existing medical illnesses such as diabetes mellitus or emphysema increase the risk and spectrum of infections and, in contrast, the differential diagnosis is narrower in a previously healthy patient.).

The patient was from Western Europe. She resided in an urban area in New England where other residents had symptoms of a flu-like illness (Identifying clusters of cases of people with same illness is one of the key tools of infectious disease epidemiology.).

She had not been on medications (Medication and vaccination history is important in infectious diseases diagnosis. Recent antibiotic use and use of immunosuppressive drugs will alter the risks of certain infections.) before this illness.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared to be in moderate respiratory distress (Trouble breathing is an extremely distressing symptom, often immediately visible when a patient is being examined. Young, healthy people have a large amount of pulmonary reserve, so any process severe enough to actually produce respiratory distress in a young person is very worrisome.). The temperature was 103°F (39.4°C). The lungs revealed diminished breath sounds and rhonchi, most notably on the right, and inspiratory rales in the left posterior lung field.

A chest radiograph obtained on her return visit, when she was admitted to the hospital, and is shown in Figure 2 (The grossly asymmetrical appearance, and dense white-out of pulmonary lobes reflect the filling of alveolar space with fluid -in this case, pus- and are highly suggestive of acute bacterial infection.).
Figure 2. Chest radiograph upon return visit.

A gram stain of the sputum specimen is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Gram stain of sputum specimen.
diagnosis:
Viral illness, consistent with influenza, complicated by secondary Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.

A gram stain of the sputum sample showed mononuclear white cells (suggestive of an underlying viral etiology), leukocytes, and gram positive cocci in clusters (Figure 3). Culture of the sputum grew abundant Staphylococcus aureus, sensitive to oxacillin (Oxacillin is a semi-synthetic beta-lactam antibiotic with good activity against many Gram-positive aerobic bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus. At the time this case occurred, oxacillin was a reasonable empiric therapy for S. aureus. Unfortunately, with the emergence of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) - this antibiotic would no longer be used in a life-threatening infection until antibiotic sensitivity results were known.).

The patient was treated with oxacillin and recovered fully.

Fever, malaise, headache, myalgia and cough are the most common presenting symptoms of influenza. The physical examination is often normal except for fever, with the temperature peaking between 100°F (37.8°C) and 104°F (40.0°C), on average. The most frequent pulmonary complications of influenza are primary influenza viral pneumonia, which has a high mortality rate, and secondary bacterial infection, most commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. The appearance of pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus (Streptococcus pneumoniae, an organism specifically adapted to the respiratory tract, is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and the most common cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia. In contrast, Staphylococcus aureus, an organism adapted to the nasal spaces and skin, is a very uncommon cause of pneumonia except when the lungs defenses are impaired, as can happen after influenza infection.) in otherwise healthy individuals may be an early indicator of an emerging Influenza A outbreak. In addition, secondary infection with community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) has been reported after influenza; in the setting of a suspected post-influenza bacterial pneumonia, empiric therapy for MRSA should be strongly considered.
Influenza is also notable for its high mortality rate, especially in the elderly and very young children, and epidemic nature. Other groups at high-risk include those with cardiovascular (especially valvular) disease, pulmonary complications (such as asthma), chronic metabolic disease, renal dysfunction, pregnancy, or immunodeficiency, including HIV infection. More recently, the 2009 H1N1 influenza A outbreak has also shown a significant rate of severe infection in previously healthy young adults. Of note, the majority of patients who contract influenza have been active and ambulatory up until the onset of illness. Early treatment of influenza may reduce the duration and severity of illness.
Additional resources for students:
1. Barry, J. 2005. The Great Influenza: The Epic Story of the Deadliest Plague in History, Penguin, October. [Excellent, non-fiction accounts of the Spanish Flu]
2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza website: http://www.cdc.gov/ncidod/diseases/flu/fluvirus.htm [clinical summaries]
3. Kolata, G. November 1999. Flu: The Story of the Great Influenza Pandemic of 1918 and the Search for the Virus That Caused It. Farrar Straus & Giroux.
4. Willis, C. August 1993. Doomsday Book, Spectra [Science fiction account of what the "next" Spanish Flu could look like, and comparison with the Plague]
5. World Health Organization (WHO) influenza website: http://www.who.int/csr/disease/influenza/en/ [outbreak tracking and vaccine status]

history:
Summary: A young man presented with fevers and a liver abnormality.
A man in his twenties presented to the outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic with fevers of approximately three weeks duration.
The patient was well until fevers, associated with intermittent chills, malaise and low backache, developed as he returned from a visit to a wooded area of New England. There was no history of arthralgias, rash, sore throat, nasal congestion, cough, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or diarrhea.
One week later, the patient was seen in an outpatient walk-in clinic; he appeared well. The temperature was 102.4°F (39.1°C), pulse 95 beats per minute, and blood pressure 127/75 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination was normal. Initial screening tests revealed a white blood cell count of 13,100 cells/mm³ with 75% polymorphonuclear cells, 15% lymphocytes and 9% monocytes. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 53 mm per hour. Other testing, including Lyme and heterophile antibodies, chest radiograph, and blood cultures, were negative.
The following week, he was reevaluated and the temperature was 100.5°F (38.1°C). A referral to an infectious disease specialist was made, and additional testing was ordered.
On evaluation, he reported temperatures up to 103°F (39.4°C), night sweats, occasional mild low back discomfort when lying flat at night, loss of appetite and a 10-15 pound loss of weight. He denied lymphadenopathy, sore throat, headache, visual changes, cough, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Laboratory testing was similar to previous values, except the ESR had increased to 93 mm per hour. One week later, he was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation of persistent fevers.

He had no allergies and had been in good health except for a brief bout of diarrhea that followed a trip to an island in the Pacific two years earlier, and for which he took antibiotics upon his return. Serologic testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection had been negative approximately two years earlier.

He lived in an urban area in New England, and was monogamous. He drank alcohol moderately, and did not smoke tobacco or use illicit drugs. He had had no sick contacts or exposure to tuberculosis. Recent travel included trips to communities by the ocean in the Northeastern United States and to wooded areas of New England. Two years earlier, he had traveled to an island in the Pacific Ocean, and had visited a travel clinic before his trip.

Medications included acetaminophen up to four times daily as needed for fever.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 99.8°F (37.7°C), blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute, and weight was 198 pounds. The examination was normal.

On admission, the white blood cell count was 12,400 cells/mm³ with 81% leukocytes, 12% lymphocytes, and 7% monocytes. Hemoglobin was 11.9 gm/dL, hematocrit 34.3% and platelet count 388,000/mm³. The mean corpuscular volume was normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 millimeters per hour. Tests of liver function were normal. Cultures of the urine and blood were negative, including cultures for Bartonella and Brucella. A chest radiograph was normal. Testing for heterophile antibody, Lyme antibody, thick and thin smears for Babesia, and serologic testing for syphilis (RPR) and HIV infection were negative. Rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibodies were also negative.

Results of computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Liver abscess secondary to methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, with an underlying appendiceal mucinous neoplasm.

CT scanning of the abdomen revealed a large-attenuating abnormality in the right lobe of the liver that measured 10.2 centimeters (cm) by 6.6 cm. The abnormality was surrounded by a hypodense rim and had a multiloculated appearance, which was strongly suggestive of a pyogenic hepatic abscess. In addition, there was a dilated tubular structure emanating from the base of the cecum, separate from the terminal ileum, with a calcified rim strongly suspicious for a mucocele of the appendix.
The liver abscess was aspirated and cytological examination of the aspirate showed abundant necrotic debris and neutrophils consistent with pyogenic abscess. Pathological examination showed no evidence of other organisms besides bacteria and no malignant cells were identified. A gram stain of the aspirate is shown in Figure 3. Culture of the material grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Testing for Entamoeba histolytica and Echinococcus was negative.
Figure 3. Gram stain of liver abscess aspirate.

The patient was treated with a two-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole, followed by oral dicloxacillin for an additional two weeks. The patient did well with resolution of the fevers, increasing energy levels, and weight gain.
Follow up CT scanning of the abdomen, shown in Figure 4, revealed evidence of a resolving liver infarct in the posterior aspect of the right hepatic lobe associated with thrombosis of the branch of right portal vein. Four months after his presentation, laparoscopic appendectomy revealed a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the resected appendix is shown in Figure 5.
Figure 4. Follow-up CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 5. H and E stain of mucocele of the appendix.

Pyogenic liver abscess is most commonly due to Enterobacteriaceae and anaerobes, and is often a polymicrobial infection. Staphylococcus aureus is an uncommon cause of pyogenic liver abscess, accounting for less than 10% of cases. Cases of S. aureus liver abscess tend to be monomicrobial.

title: Summary: A woman presented with a rash, one year after cardiac transplantation s
history:
Summary: A woman presented with a rash, one year after cardiac transplantation surgery.
A woman in her sixties experienced epigastric pain, and several days later developed a diffuse rash. One year before presentation, she had received a heart transplant.

She had had a heart transplant one year earlier. In the intervening year, she had had several episodes of rejection that were treated with short courses of steroids.

Medications included mycophenolate (500 mg twice daily), tacrolimus (1 gram twice daily), and prednisone (7.5 mg daily).
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile and the vital signs were normal. There was right upper quadrant tenderness. The oral mucosa showed several white plaques and there was a diffuse vesicular eruption of the skin (Figures 1 through 4). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Findings on the oropharynx.
Figure 2. Detail of the palate.
Figure 3. Skin lesions.
Figure 4. Skin lesions on the abdomen.

The levels of aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase were twice the upper limits of the normal reference ranges; other routine laboratory test results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. Serum testing for cytomegalovirus antigen was negative. A chest radiograph did not show an acute cardiopulmonary process. An abdominal ultrasound revealed mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed raised lesions with underlying ulcers that had clean bases (Figure 5). Colonoscopic evaluation revealed scattered superficial ulcers (Figures 6 and 7).
Figure 5. Findings on esophagoscopy.
Figure 6. Findings on colonoscopy.
Figure 7. Findings on colonoscopy.
diagnosis:
Disseminated varicella zoster virus (VZV) disease, one year after cardiac transplantation.

Testing of a skin biopsy sample for varicella zoster virus (VZV) direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) was positive. A viral culture of an esophageal biopsy was also positive for VZV, and immunohistochemical staining for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus-1 and -2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2) were negative. Examination of the patient's previous laboratory testing for VZV antibody revealed a borderline immunoglobulin G result.

Intravenous acyclovir was administered and the skin lesions crusted over during the following two weeks.

The skin lesions shown above are typical for varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection, and are often described as a ‘dew drop on a rose petal’. Immunosuppression is known to be a predisposing factor to disseminated VZV infection. The elevated levels of aminotransferases are characteristic of hepatic involvement in the setting of disseminated VZV infection, and may be seen in immunosuppressed hosts (Fehr et al 2002). The observed esophageal and colonic involvement are less common manifestations of disseminated VZV infection, and while esophageal involvement has been described with VZV infection (Johnson 1940; Miliauskas and Webber 1984; Smith et al 2002; Laun and Venkatesan 2002), colonic involvement is more rarely seen (Okimura et al 1996).
The diagnosis of disseminated VZV infection was important to have made expeditiously both for this patient and for any persons involved in her care who were not immune to VZV.

title:
2007 January Featured Case Summary: An elderly man with a left wrist ulcer.
An e
history:
2007 January Featured Case Summary: An elderly man with a left wrist ulcer.
An elderly man presented with an ulcerated lesion over the dorsum of the left wrist.
He had been gardening ten days earlier. The lesion had grown in size with surrounding erythema, and he noted that two small nodules had developed proximal to the lesion on the forearm.
Cephalexin was started. He was seen two days later with an expanding, increasingly painful lesion associated with swelling that extended above the elbow.

There was a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease (CAD), coronary artery by-pass grafting (CABG) had been performed ten years earlier.

The patient was visiting New England from his home in Florida, where he gardened frequently. He may have recently scraped his hand on some metal in an area of overgrown weeds under his house. There were no rose bushes in the area, and although he had seen rabbits occasionally, he had not seen evidence of them under the house. He reported no fresh- or salt-water exposures, history of recurrent infections, or risk factors for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

He had been taking cephalexin (500 mg four times per day, orally) for 2 days.
exam_studies:
He was a well-appearing elderly man in no acute distress. The temperature was 99.2°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 140/71 mm/Hg, and pulse 70 beats/minute. The conjunctivae and oropharynx were clear. The neck was supple without lymphadenopathy in the cervical or supraclavicular chains. The lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally; cardiac and abdominal examinations were normal.
The left arm had an ulceration measuring 1-2 centimeter (cm) in diameter over the dorsum of the wrist, with multiple subcutaneous nodules proximally and surrounding erythema. The nodules were painful and extended in a chain to the epitrochlear region where a warm, tender mass (2 cm by 3 cm) was palpated. There were 2-3 shotty, non-tender axillary nodes present, and no sub-pectoral nodes. (See Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Physical Finding.
Figure 2. Physical Finding.

The white blood cell count revealed 18,000/mm³ (59% leukocytes, 36% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, 1% eosinophils). A radiograph of the forearm did not reveal a foreign body.
diagnosis:
Lymphocutaneous nocardiosis (due to Nocardia brasiliensis).

The center of the lesion was biopsied and the tissue was cultured. A modified acid fast stain of the culture is shown in Figure 3. Culture of the biopsy material grew Nocardia brasiliensis.
Figure 3. Modified acid fast stain of tissue culture.

Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim therapy was administered, with significant improvement over one week.
He returned to Florida and it was noted that his white blood cell count did not decline with resolution of the infection. He was subsequently found to have chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Stage 0.

Nocardia is a ubiquitous saprophyte, and is classified as one of the aerobic Actinomycetes, a phylogenetically heterogeneous group of bacteria that share the morphology of filamentous branching cells.
Once considered fungi because of their branching quality and ability to produce aerial hyphae, they were confirmed as bacteria when found to have peptidoglycan and lipid cell walls, without chitin present. Nocardia asteroides is the most commonly diagnosed worldwide, and has a substantial predilection for immunocompromised hosts. Nocardia brasiliensis is commonly diagnosed in immunocompetent hosts.
There are four types of cutaneous nocardiosis:
1. Primary cutaneous nocardiosis resulting from direct inoculation;
2. Lymphocutaneous infection as an extension of untreated primary cutaneous disease or as an initial presentation;
3. Mycetoma, a chronic suppurative granulomatous reaction that can be secondary to Nocardia or a host of other pathogens;
4. Cutaneous involvement from disseminated nocardial infection.
The differential for lymphocutaneous infection includes:
-Sporothrix schenckii: found in similar geographic environs as Nocardia, and has a similar incubation period of up to 2 weeks.
- Mycobacterium marinum: usually follows exposure to the organism growing in a pool, ocean or aquarium.
-Leishmaniasis: requires inoculation by the bite of a sandfly, usually in Central or South America, although occasional cases have occurred in Texas.
- Francisella tularensis: the ulcer of this infection is often particularly painful, and more associated with fever and systemic symptoms.

history:
2007 March Featured Case Summary: A man with fever and a splenic lesion.
A man in his thirties was well until 5 months before presentation, when he developed a non-specific febrile illness. A course of clarithromycin was administered, and the fever resolved over 10 days. A diagnosis of viral syndrome was made, presumptively. Two months before presentation, the patient developed low-grade fevers, diffuse myalgias, and progressive night sweats. Weight loss of fifteen pounds (6.8 kilograms) occurred.

The patient worked in Pennsylvania, and took frequent trips throughout much of the Midwest and Southwest of the United States. He had no known animal exposures.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was 99.4°F (37.4°C). Mild tenderness in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen and splenomegaly were present.

Serum test results for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and a skin test for tuberculosis were negative. Blood cultures were sterile. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed splenic lesions (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.

Aspiration of the splenic lesions was performed. Cytologic examination of the splenic aspirate and a wet prep of the culture growth are seen in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.
Figure 2. Cytologic examination of splenic aspirate.
Figure 3. Wet prep of culture.
diagnosis:
Splenic abscess due to Blastomyces dermatitidis.

Cultures from splenic aspiration grew Blastomyces dermatitidis. Figure 2. Cytologic examination of splenic aspirate. Figure 3. Wet prep of culture.

In retrospect, the patient reported having been caught in a "dust storm" in Wisconsin, six weeks before his initial febrile presentation. The patient had no evidence of pulmonary disease at the time of diagnosis. He was treated intravenous amphotericin B for two weeks, followed by six months of oral itraconazole, and made a complete recovery.

The broad based budding of the organism is characteristic of Blastomyces and is not seen with the other organisms mentioned. Blastomycosis is acquired by inhalation, but then may disseminate throughout the body. Focal lesions may occur in the skin or bones. Splenic abscess is a rare complication of blastomycosis.
