title: 2007 April Featured Case Summary: A man with HIV infection, shortness of breath
history:
2007 April Featured Case Summary: A man with HIV infection, shortness of breath and anemia.
A man in his thirties, with a history of untreated human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for greater than ten years, presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 33 cells/mm³, the hematocrit 14.4%, mean corpuscular volume of 84.4 um³, reticulocyte count of 0.3%, and red cell distribution width of 13.4. Packed red blood cells were transfused. He was admitted to the hospital.

His past medical history included HIV infection, recurrent giardiasis, oral thrush, cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia, Hepatitis B virus and Hepatitis C virus infections, and herpes zoster. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) had been grown from his sputum and stool. He was not allergic to medications and had normal levels of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) at baseline.

He lived in New England and traveled occasionally to New York. He had sex with both men and women, smoked cigarettes, drank alcohol and used intravenous drugs occasionally.

The patient did not have a fixed residence.

He was not allergic to medications.

He did not take any medications on a regular basis.
exam_studies:
The physical examination was normal. Rectal exam was refused.

The hematocrit was 14.4%, mean corpuscular volume of 84.4 um³, reticulocyte count of 0.3%, and red cell distribution width of 13.4. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 33 cells/mm³. The white cell count was 2,190 cells/mm³ (64% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 4% bands, 14% lymphocytes, 4% atypical lymphocytes, 10% monocytes, and 4% eosinophils), and platelets 439,000/mm³. The iron level was 160 ug/dL (reference range 40-159 ug/dL), increased from 11 ug/dL one year before; transferrin 135 ug/dL (150-450 ug/dL) and ferritin 531 ug/dL (10-345 ug/dL). The serum levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), folate and vitamin B-12 were normal, and haptoglobin was elevated. Erythropoietin was 2,185 mU/mL (4.1 – 19.5 mU/mL). Urine histoplasma antigen was negative.

The patient was transfused and later left the hospital against medical advice, without completion of his evaluation. He was lost to follow-up for approximately 18 months, when he presented again to the emergency room with shortness of breath. The hematocrit was 10.8%. He was re-admitted and blood was transfused. A bone marrow biopsy was performed; hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of the biopsy is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. H and E stain of a bone marrow biopsy.
diagnosis:
Chronic parvovirus B19 infection in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

A bone marrow biopsy revealed numerous immature erythroid forms with viral nuclear inclusions (Figure 2). Maturing erythroid elements were moderately to markedly decreased. Myeloid elements, including interstitial and perivascular plasma cells and megakaryocytes were increased. Multiple non-paratrabecular lymphoplasmacytic aggregates comprised approximately 20% of the marrow cellularity and about 15% of the intertrabecular space. Hemosiderin was present. Erythroid elements and bare nuclei with intranuclear inclusions were present, consistent with parvovirus infection. No micro-organisms were seen on pathological examination of the specimens with special stains, including acid fast and silver stains.
Serum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for parvovirus B19 DNA was positive, and parvovirus immunoglobulin (Ig) M and IgG antibodies were negative.
Figure 2. H and E stain of marrow, showing viral inclusion bodies (arrows).

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was administered. Over the next year, serum repeatedly tested positive for parvovirus DNA. The patient was non-adherent to his HIV treatment and died the following year of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

In immunocompetent persons, parvovirus infection is largely asymptomatic, with its major manifestation in healthy children being rash that starts on the face and then moves to the trunk and extremities. In healthy adults, the major recognized clinical manifestation is inflammatory arthritis. Joints of the hands, ankles, knees and wrists can become symmetrically inflamed. This usually resolves within a few weeks to months and there is no joint destruction. In pregnant women, however, acute infection can result in abortion or in hydrops fetalis.
Experimental parvovirus infection of adults revealed that viremia was detectable about one week after inoculation and lasted up to seven days. Viremia was associated with low-grade fever, chills, myalgias and headache; parvovirus B19 was detectable in the upper respiratory tract during the same time span, suggesting a route of transmission. Reticulocyte count dropped precipitously to undetectable levels in peripheral blood, and mature erythrocytes, lymphocytes, granulocytes and platelets all showed a downward trend. Parvovirus B19 IgM developed about 8-12 days after inoculation. This study showed that persons with low pre-existing IgG titers can develop transient viremia with re-inoculation. After the clearance of viremia, new symptoms developed including rash, arthralgias and arthritis lasting several days, that are thought to be immune-mediated [Anderson et al 1985].
In persons who are immunosuppressed and cannot mount an effective IgG response, parvovirus can become a chronic infection causing anemia and sometimes affecting other cell lines. It has been described in patients with advanced HIV-disease, those with hematologic malignancies, as well as in persons on immune suppression following organ transplantation. Lack of immunoglobulin permits the chronicity of the infection: patients treated with IVIG can achieve remission in their anemia (and notably can also develop the symptoms thought to be immune-related, rash, arthralgias and arthritis). It is essential to recognize that IVIG does not always eliminate viremia. Retreatment on a monthly basis has been recommended in these cases along with the reversal of immune suppression when possible. Erythropoietin has not been useful in the treatment of chronic Parvovirus infection in HIV-infected patients, and has even been reported to exacerbate the clinical manifestations of parvovirus infection in one HIV positive patient [Borkowski et al 2000].
Diagnosis is usually clinical, but can be confirmed with serology. Those who are immunosuppressed and have chronic parvovirus infection may not have antibodies against the virus. In these cases, diagnosis is by serum PCR for viral DNA or by bone marrow biopsy.
In this patient, the findings on the bone marrow are characteristic of immunosuppressed patients with chronic parvovirus B19 infection [Crook et al 2000]. This cohort of patients had bone marrow biopsy findings identical to those seen in the current specimen, consisting of numerous erythroblasts with viral inclusions and a persistent population of maturing erythroid precursors. These findings differ from those seen in immunocompetent patients, in whom acute parvovirus infection is typically associated with transient red cell aplasia. As a result, erythroblasts with viral inclusions are rarely seen in immunocompetent patients.
Although the patient was given intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), the recommended treatment for chronic parvovirus B19 infection, this can be little more than a temporizing measure. Cure is sometimes only achieved with some measure of immune restoration.

history:
2007 May Featured Case Summary: A seven-month-old boy presented in autumn with constipation, lethargy and hypotonia.
Two weeks before admission, a seven-month-old boy developed constipation, which resolved after the addition of prune juice to his diet. Seven days before admission, he appeared more subdued, tired and lethargic, and had longer periods of sleeping and less spontaneous activity. Three days before admission, he was evaluated as an outpatient by his pediatrician and was then observed in the emergency department. He appeared well, was afebrile with a normal physical examination. The hematocrit was 31.1% and reticulocytes 0.9%, serum carbon dioxide 20.7 mmol/L, and globulin 1.9 g/dl (reference range 2.6-4.1 g/dl); other laboratory test results including other electrolytes, liver function tests, and creatine kinase were normal. A radiograph of the chest and abdomen, shown in Figure 1, revealed fecal loading. A blood culture was sterile and an abdominal ultrasound was normal.
The following day, his oral intake and his activity level improved. However symptoms recurred over the next two days. On the morning of admission, he was as floppy "as a rag doll" when his mother picked him up. Emergency medical services were called and he was brought to the emergency department by ambulance for reevaluation, and admitted to the hospital.
[Figure 1. Radiograph of the chest and abdomen.]
Figure 1. Radiograph of the chest and abdomen.

He was born at 41 weeks gestation by cesarean section, and had previously been well. Developmental milestones were met early or on time, including sitting at 5 months and crawling at 6 months. In the weeks preceding admission, he was pulling to stand and cruising. His diet consisted of breast milk and solids. There was no history of honey ingestion.

Several months earlier, in summer, he had traveled to Cape Cod, Massachusetts.

He had had routine childhood immunizations, and had received the second dose of influenza vaccine two days before the onset of symptoms.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared sleepy and moved gently to light touch. The pulse was 112 beats per minute, temperature 98.9°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 77/33 mm Hg, and respirations 26 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 100% while breathing ambient air. The weight was 7.54 kg (10-25th percentile) and length 74 centimeters (cm) (97th percentile). The head circumference was 45 cm (50th percentile). The neurologic exam revealed diffuse low tone with head lag. The pupils were reactive and the remainder of the physical examination was normal.

Laboratory test results revealed a white count of 8100 cells/mm³ (20% neutrophils, 73% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 1% basophils), hematocrit of 31.2%, and platelet count 340,000/mm³. Serum carbon dioxide was 19.2 mmol/L, with an anion gap of 15.8. Serum glucose was 49 mg/dl (reference range 70-100 mg/dl). Urinalysis revealed 2+ ketones, and was otherwise normal.
Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the head and an electroencephalogram were normal.

A lumbar puncture revealed two red cells and two white cells per cubic millimeter, with normal glucose and protein levels. Intravenous fluids were administered, including glucose and normal saline. Hydrocortisone (stress dose) was also given intravenously on admission, but was stopped after a cortisol level drawn before treatment and a cosyntropin stimulation test, performed off hydrocortisone for 24 hours, were normal. Cultures of specimens of blood, stool and cerebrospinal fluid were sterile. Tests for serum Lyme antibody, and cerebrospinal fluid and nasal washings for adenovirus, influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus were negative. A toxic screen and lead screen were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis and amino acid levels were normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast enhancement was normal. On the third hospital day, a barium swallow was performed and revealed tertiary esophageal contractions, slow movement of barium and transient stasis of barium in the esophagus. There was no evidence of aspiration (Figures 2 and 3). The patient's condition gradually deteriorated with the development of ptosis bilaterally, hyporeflexia, decreasing suck and oral intake. On the fifth hospital day, a nasogastric feeding tube was placed because of increasing pooled secretions, absent gag reflex and an inability to protect the airway. The patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. By the seventh hospital day, the patient was using his diaphragm with abdominal breathing and was not using chest wall muscles, and the trachea was intubated.
[Figure 2. Barium swallow.] [Figure 3. Barium swallow.]
Figure 2. Barium swallow.
Figure 3. Barium swallow.
diagnosis:
Infant botulism, due to Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin type B.

Nerve conduction studies revealed motor responses with low amplitude in the ulnar nerves bilaterally, and borderline low amplitude of left median and left tibial nerves. High frequency repetitive nerve stimulation revealed incremental response of the right ulnar nerve (98% increase in amplitude), left ulnar nerve (74%), left median nerve (52%), and left tibial nerve (37%). Median and sural nerve sensory potentials on the left were normal.
The results of high frequency repetitive nerve stimulation were consistent with a pre-synaptic neuromuscular junction disorder (infantile botulism). A stool sample was sent to the state laboratory for testing for botulinum toxin and was positive for Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin type B.

Anti-botulism immune globulin was administered. The patient improved and the trachea was extubated within five days of receiving the treatment. The gag reflex and ability to suck and swallow improved gradually, and he was discharged three weeks after admission, with outpatient physical therapy. Follow-up in the outpatient neurology clinic at age nine months revealed a delightful infant with normal neurologic function and meeting all developmental milestones.

The key clinical features of this case include the progressive onset of cranial nerve findings (ptosis; swallowing difficulty; weakening cry; loss of gag reflex); autonomic dysfunction (constipation); and marked hypotonia in a child of seven months, whose gross-motor milestones had previously been on time.
Intracerebral bleeding and masses were excluded by negative imaging studies. Multiple non-infectious causes of hypotonia were considered. These included spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) Types 1 and 2, which affect anterior horn cells. The onset of SMA-1 (Werdnig-Hoffman disease) is seen in the first 3 months, making it unlikely. SMA-2 (infantile types A and B) typically has a later age of onset, in the middle of the first year. Pompe disease, the glycogen storage disease most likely to present in infancy, is diagnosed at a mean age of roughly four months. Congenital myasthenia gravis (MG), is not necessarily present at birth, unlike neonatal MG, which is secondary to mother's illness. Porphyria can cause hypotonia and muscle weakness that often begins proximally in legs with loss of reflexes, and then associated with cranial nerve and autonomic dysfunction. Fatty-acid oxidation and organic acid disorders, and mitochondrial diseases were also considered, but would have been more likely to occur in the setting of antecedent metabolic stress. Acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre syndrome), in the setting of recent vaccinations, was also of concern.
Infectious etiologies of the neurological clinical findings included infant botulism and tick paralysis. His vital signs did not suggest acute infection and results of laboratory testing, including cultures of blood and cerebrospinal fluid, and Lyme serology, were negative. Physical examination did not reveal the presence of a tick, excluding tick paralysis. The results of the high frequency repetitive nerve stimulation supported the diagnosis of pre-synaptic neuromuscular junction disorder consistent with infant botulism. Identification of Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin type B in the stool confirmed the diagnosis.
In infant botulism (as with a similar but very rare illness described in adults), spores of C. botulinum are ingested and then germinate in the intestine, producing toxin that is subsequently absorbed systemically to cause irreversible disruption of acetylcholine release by presynaptic nerve terminals. Other forms of botulism include food-borne botulism in which pre-formed toxin is consumed, and wound botulism in which the toxin is produced in vivo in a wound that infected with C. botulinum. Inhalation botulism is a syndrome that could be seen as part of a bioterrorism event.
Treatment of infant botulism consists of supportive care, meticulous monitoring for respiratory failure, and treatment with antitoxin. If administered sufficiently early, treatment of babies who have infant botulism with human anti-botulism immune globulin (BIG-IV or babyBIG) has been shown to markedly decrease time to recovery by a period of weeks [Arnon et al 2006]. Antibiotics should be avoided to avoid increased release and adsorption of toxin.

title: 2007 June Featured Case Summary: A college student with fever and headache, appr
history:
2007 June Featured Case Summary: A college student with fever and headache, approximately six months after a trip to East Africa.
A man in his twenties (Age, gender and race provide important clues to the diagnosis.) presented in the late fall (Certain infections are very common during a particular season of the year.) with fever, myalgias, and headache for one week. Earlier in the year, he had spent the four months of his spring semester in East Africa, returning in June (Timeline is very important in relation to the travel history as some infections have early and late stages of symptomatology. Infections may also reactivate or recur. Concept: In reactivation, a pathogen that has been latent - that is, present but not growing or causing symptoms - begins to replicate and become clinically apparent. Reactivation is sometimes triggered by physiologic stress on the host. In contrast, the term recurrence is used to indicate that a person who had cleared an infection has become re-infected.). He took mefloquine weekly while in Africa, but had stopped the medication immediately upon his return (The administration of drugs aimed at preventing malaria infection, or suppressive chemoprophylaxis, should be continued until 4 weeks after leaving endemic areas in order to be effective against hypnozoites, dormant liver stages of non-falciparum plasmodia.). Approximately four weeks later, he developed temperatures to 103°F (39.4°C), myalgias and headache. Malaria, caused by Plasmodium falciparum, was diagnosed and atovaquone-proguanil and quinine (Note that these medications only act on the blood stage of the parasitic life cycle.) were administered, with improvement.
Approximately four months later, temperatures to 101.7°F (38.7°C), myalgias and headache developed again. The symptoms were similar to those several months before (Recurrence of similar symptoms may suggest the presence of a pathogen that has remained present but dormant and then reactivated.), and followed a temporal pattern, with the most intense symptom occurring every 48 hours (Fever pattern can be an important clue in diagnosis. The replication of plasmodia within red cells is often synchronized, producing a burst of red cell lysis and fever every two or three days. Although seen less often now, this is the classic fever pattern of malaria. In older literature, fever that occurs every 48 hours is referred to as tertian; that occurring every 72 hours is called quartan.). He presented the following week for evaluation.

The patient had been in good health until his trip to Africa (Prior health and detailed travel itinerary are very important since the differential diagnosis may be different based on where the disease was acquired.). While in Kenya, during his second month in Africa, he was hospitalized for a few days because of temperatures to 103°F (39.4°C), of unknown origin; testing at that time was negative for malaria.

He had been born in the Midwestern United States and attended a university in the Northeast. He had studied in several locations throughout East Africa, including prolonged periods in Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda. While there, he had received several bites from mosquitoes, particularly while sleeping uncovered in Northern Uganda. Since returning to the U.S., he had gone camping in Wisconsin and on Cape Cod (Camping in these areas would raise the issue of tick-borne infections such as Lyme disease. Frequently the tick bites are not noticed.), but did not notice any tick bites.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared fatigued and was sensitive to light, preferring a darkened room. The blood pressure (Normal range is 100-120 mm Hg systolic and 60-80 mm Hg diastolic.) was 120/58 mm Hg, pulse (Normal range is 60-100 beats per minute) 76 beats per minute, and the temperature (Normal range is 97-99 degrees fahrenheit.) 97.8°F (36.6°C). The remainder of the examination was normal (Normal examinations can be seen in malaria on the days between fevers.) and there was no meningismus, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, or notable skin rashes.

The white blood (This patient’s white blood cell differential reveals more neutrophils and band forms, and fewer lymphocytes, than normal, a finding referred to as a left shift.) cell count was 6,100 cells per cubic millimeter, with 63% neutrophils, 10% band forms, 16% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, and 3% eosinophils; the hematocrit was 40%, platelet count 94,000 per cubic millimeter (Decreased platelets, known as thrombocytopenia, may be seen in malaria, as well as some other infections.), and serum transaminase levels were normal. The total bilirubin was 1.4 mg per deciliter and direct bilirubin 0.5 mg per deciliter (His indirect bilirubin is elevated, suggesting that red blood cells are breaking down or hemolysing, and releasing hemoglobin into the bloodstream. This is often observed in malaria since the parasites lyse red blood cells during their replication cycle.), with reference ranges of up to 1.0 and 0.4 mg/dl respectively. Stains of peripheral blood smears are shown in Figures 1 through 4.
Figure 1. Stain of whole blood specimen.
Figure 2. Thin smear of whole blood specimen.
Figure 3. Thin smear.
Figure 4. Thin smear.
diagnosis:
Malaria, most consistent with Plasmodium vivax infection.

Thin preparations of blood smears reveal intracellular forms with morphology most consistent with Plasmodium vivax (Figures 3 and 4). Parasitemia was estimated at 0.5%.

Chloroquine was administered for three days with complete resolution of symptoms. The serum level of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) was normal, and the patient subsequently received primaquine (Primaquine is used to treat the liver forms of non-falciparum plasmodia. G6PD levels are checked before administration of the drug because people with G6PD deficiency may experience severe hemolysis if given primaquine.) for 14 days.

Malaria is a serious concern for patients who travel to and from endemic regions. Malaria is a serious concern for patients who travel to and from endemic regions. Unfortunately, recommended chemoprophylaxis with blood schizontidicides has been shown to fail, particularly with Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale, which can form dormant hepatic hypnozoites. When this patient presented four weeks after returning from Africa, malaria was rapidly diagnosed at another facility, attributed to Plasmodium falciparum, and treatment was administered. Based on that species diagnosis, no therapy targeting hepatic hypnozoites was administered. Four months later, the patient represented with malaria.
Differentiation between Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale can be difficult on morphology alone. The round gametocyte seen in this case (Figure 5) is most consistent with P. vivax. The trophozoite has an amoeboid form (Figure 6). Between 50-70% of malaria cases in United States are caused by P. falciparum, 20-40% by P. vivax; P. ovale and P. malariae account for lesser percentages. (See references.) P. vivax has a substantial presence in Ethiopia (up to 30% in literature, compared with 60% malarial cases caused by P. falciparum) and other Horn of Africa countries, where the presence of the duffy blood group is higher than that found in sub-Saharan Africa. However, P. vivax has been reported in cases originating in Kenya, and in patients with negative duffy blood group typing.

title: 2007 July Featured Case and IDSA 2006 Case Submission Summary: A man from the Ca
history:
2007 July Featured Case and IDSA 2006 Case Submission Summary: A man from the Caribbean with diarrhea, nausea and vomiting.
A man in his fifties presented with diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting of three days' duration. He had recently been discharged from another hospital where he had received a one-week course of steroids intravenously for chronic back pain.

He had a history of spinal stenosis, hypertension, and a cerebrovascular accident.

The patient had immigrated to the United States two decades earlier from an island in the Caribbean, and had returned to visit one year before presentation.

Medications included atenolol, clopidogrel, naproxen, and prednisone.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 115/87 mm Hg, pulse 87 beats per minute, and respirations 17 breaths per minute. There was mild epigastric pain, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 12,000 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 43%, bands 38%, lymphocytes 10%). The serum creatinine was 1.8 mg/dl.

Dehydration, azotemia and hypokalemia were diagnosed, and thought to be secondary to acute gastroenteritis. Intravenous fluids, potassium supplementation, metoclopramide and famotidine were administered.
On the third hospital day, the patient became lethargic and the temperature rose to 39.1°C (102.4°F). Shortly thereafter, respiratory failure developed and he was transferred to an intensive care unit and an infectious disease consult was obtained. Gram-negative rods were isolated from cultures of the blood. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is shown in Figure 1 and a gram stain of the sputum in Figure 2.
[Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.] [Figure 2. Gram stain of a sputum specimen.]
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 2. Gram stain of a sputum specimen.
diagnosis:
Hyperinfection syndrome with Strongyloides stercoralis, associated with Klebsiella sepsis and meningitis, presenting as enterocolitis.

A gram stain of a sputum specimen and an iodine stain of a stool specimen revealed Strongyloides stercoralis (Figures 2 and 3, respectively). In addition, Klebsiella pneumoniae was identified growing in 4 out of 4 blood culture bottles, resistant only to ampicillin. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed mild colonic wall inflammation, with minimal ascites and cholelithiasis, without evidence of cholecystitis.
Figure 3. Iodine stain of a stool specimen.

Meropenem and vancomycin were administered intravenously and empirically. Metronidazole was added because of persistent diarrhea and possible Clostridium difficile colitis. Ivermectin (200 mcg/kg/day) was administered after the identification of Strongyloides. The patient was not able to take oral medications and, consequently, neither albendazole nor thiabendazole was administered.
Meningitis and sepsis developed, and culture of the cerebrospinal fluid grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. Meropenem was changed to ceftriaxone after the diagnosis of meningitis was made. Despite treatment, renal failure, hydrocephalus, and a sub-acute infarct of the internal capsule developed, the latter two requiring ventriculostomy. On the twelfth hospital day, testing revealed loss of brain function, and in consultation with the family, respiratory support was withdrawn and the patient expired.

Strongyloides stercoralis is an intestinal nematode of humans that infects tens of millions of people worldwide [Keiser and Nutman 2004]. Strongyloidiasis is endemic in parts of Asia, South America, Europe, the Southeastern United States and the islands of the Caribbean [Genta 1989].
S. stercoralis is unique among intestinal nematodes in its ability to complete its life cycle within the host through an asexual autoinfective cycle, allowing the infection to persist in the host indefinitely [Keiser and Nutman 2004].
Infection is usually asymptomatic and confined to the intestinal tract. After penetrating the skin, the filariform larva enters the blood stream and is transported to the lungs. The life cycle of the filariform larva involves migration up the respiratory tract; the larva is then swallowed into the gastrointestinal tract. Maturation and reproduction in the small intestine result in the formation of rhabditiform larvae that pass in stool. Rhabditiform larvae then mature to infectious filariform larvae. This maturation usually occurs outside of humans in the environment. This maturation can also occur in the perirectal area (or less commonly in the intestinal lumen) and infectious filariform larvae are then able penetrate the intestinal wall or perianal skin causing autoinfection [Gupta et al 2006].
The Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome may occur when there is increased generation of filariform larvae, which may occur in the setting of corticosteroid treatment, use of other immunosuppressive medications, hematologic malignancies or infection with human T cell lymphotropic virus-1. The filariform larvae then penetrate the intestinal mucosa and enter the blood stream. During penetration of the intestinal epithelium, enteric bacteria (usually gram-negative coliforms) disseminate systemically. This can lead to gram-negative sepsis and meningitis, a common and potentially serious complication of Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome. Pulmonary complications include lung abscess and adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) [Igra-Siegman et al 1981].
Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome may occur years after exposure as a result of the unique ability of Strongyloides to autoinfect the host without an obligatory external portion of the life cycle [Newberry et al 2005]. This condition has a mortality exceeding 80% [Lim et al 2004]. Patients who are at risk for strongyloidiasis should be screened for this condition prior to the initiation of immunosuppressive medications.

title: 2007 August Featured Case Summary: A man with HIV infection, fevers and abdomina
history:
2007 August Featured Case Summary: A man with HIV infection, fevers and abdominal symptoms.
A man in his forties presented with fevers to 104°F (40.0°C) of one month's duration. He also reported chills, abdominal bloating and nausea. There was a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection; recent CD4 T-lymphocytes measured 14 cells per cubic millimeter and HIV-RNA was 83,000 copies per microliter.
A positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was performed in a city in Asia and revealed diffuse lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. The patient came to the United States for a second opinion.

As above, a history of HIV infection, acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) and herpetic zoster.

The patient was from a large city in southeastern China. There was no history of travel to rural Southeast Asia and no intravenous drug use.

The patient worked in the service industry.

The patient took azithromycin weekly and was also on ritonavir, indinavir, delavirdine, fosamprenavir, valgancyclovir, enfuvirtide, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and tenofovir.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared unwell and fatigued. The temperature was 96.7°F (35.9°C), blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats per minute and oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air. Mild scleral icterus was present without hepatosplenomegaly. One small umbilicated papule was seen on his left hand. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy.

The white blood cell count was 5,900 cells/mm³, hematocrit 29.5% and platelets 94,000/mm³. Serum sodium was 126 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 29 mg/dL, creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 95 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 288 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 771 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 434 U/L and total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL.

Specimens of blood were cultured; a gram stain of the culture is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Gram stain of blood culture.
diagnosis:
Penicillium marneffei in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS from a large city in southeastern China.

Culture of the blood grew Penicillium marneffei, shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Gram stain of blood culture.
Figure 3. Plate of blood culture growth.

The patient received intravenous amphotericin B (liposomal) for two weeks followed by a course of oral itraconazole. The fevers resolved and the blood cultures cleared on therapy.
At follow-up, highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) was re-instated with lamivudine, zidovudine, tenofovir, ritonavir, and tipranavir. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and azithromycin prophylaxis medications were also administered.

Penicillium marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes disseminated infection in patients with AIDS. It is the third most common opportunistic infection seen in AIDS patients in Northern Thailand and has been described throughout Southeast Asia as well as southern China and Hong Kong. Patients present with a subacute illness characterized by fever, weight loss and skin lesions; these lesions tend to be papular with central umbilication reminiscent of molluscum. Fifty percent of patients present with fungemia, lymphadenopathy and cough. Diagnosis of Penicillium marneffei infection is made when a smear of blood or tissue reveals yeast forms extracellularly and within phagocytes. The extracellular forms may have a transverse septum. Culture at 30°C reveals a mold that produces a characteristic soluble red pigment (Figure 3). As of this writing, patients are often treated with amphotericin for two weeks, followed by ten weeks of itraconazole. Secondary prophylaxis with daily itraconazole is standard.

history:
2007 September Featured Case Summary: A teenager with headache, vomiting and a new rash.
A teenager presented to the emergency room with headache, vomiting and a rash. The patient had been in good health until approximately thirty-six hours before admission when she developed generalized malaise, myalgias and fever. Headache and shortness of breath followed, and her family brought her to another hospital. Pneumonia was diagnosed; azithromycin was prescribed and she was discharged.
At home, she was lethargic and slept several hours. Later that evening, she complained of having the worst headache of her life. She developed nausea, vomiting and photophobia; speech became incomprehensible with muttering. Her eyes were observed to be rolled back; an ambulance was called emergently and she was transported to a tertiary care hospital.
On arrival in the triage area, vomiting occurred again, after which a rash was noted on her torso and legs.

The patient had a history of asthma with intermittent symptoms.

A friend had been ill during the preceding week.

She lived with her family and attended high school.

The patient had taken one dose of azithromycin (500 milligrams) following the evaluation at the other hospital. She had previously been prescribed an albuterol inhaler, which she used infrequently. Childhood immunizations were up-to-date.
exam_studies:
On examination, the patient was obtunded. She was responsive to pain and vomiting intermittently, once with coffee-ground emesis. She opened her eyes spontaneously and moved all extremities. The blood pressure was 94/66 mm Hg, pulse 113 beats per minute, respirations 20 breaths per minute, and temperature 99.0°F (37.2°C). The lungs were clear, heart sounds rapid and otherwise normal, and the abdomen soft and non-tender. There was a diffuse petechial rash on the torso and leg. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory results included a white blood cell count of 33,800 cells/mm³ (68% leukocytes, 15% bands, 11% monocytes, and 6% lymphocytes), hematocrit 33.7%, hemoglobin 12.0 gram per deciliter, and platelet count 319,000/mm³. Prothrombin time was 15.1 seconds and partial thromboplastin time 30.3 seconds.
Serologic test results included sodium 133 mmol/liter, potassium 3.7 mmol/liter, chloride 101 mmol/liter, carbon dioxide 21.0 mmol/liter, urea nitrogen 8 mg/dl, creatinine 0.6 mg/dl, glucose 192 mg/dl, calcium 8.8 mg/dl, phosphorus 2.6 mg/dl, magnesium 1.3 mmol/liter, and protein 7.1 g/dl. A pregnancy test was negative.
Other testing included fibrinogen 519 mg/dl (reference range 150-400 mg/dl) and D-Dimer 3026 ng/ml (reference range <500 ng/ml).

Ceftriaxone and vancomycin were administered emergently, followed by a lumbar puncture and computed tomography (CT) of the head, shown in Figure 1.
The fourth tube of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was cloudy white. There were 29 red cells per cubic millimeter and 1156 white cells per cubic millimeter (neutrophils 80%, monocytes 6% and lymphocytes 14%.) Additional testing of the CSF revealed glucose level of 83 mg/dl and total protein 85 mg/dl. A gram stain of the CSF is shown in Figure 2.
[Figure 1. Scan of the brain.] [Figure 2. Gram stain of spun CSF.]
Figure 1. CT scan of the brain.
Figure 2. Gram stain of spun CSF.
diagnosis:
Meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis infection.

Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the brain showed diffuse swelling, without evidence of an acute infarction or mass lesion (Figure 1). There was debris within the suprasellar and interpeduncular cisterns and the sylvian fissures, which was thought to be purulent material. The chest radiograph showed mild peribronchial cuffing, which could be seen with reactive airways disease and bronchitis; no focal pneumonia was identified.
The gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes and moderate numbers of gram-negative diplococci. (See Figure 3, with arrows showing bacteria.) Latex agglutination was positive for meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis). The CSF culture grew abundant N. meningitidis; the chocolate agar plate is shown in Figure 4 and reveals the smooth, moist colonies, with a glistening surface, characteristic of that organism
Figure 3. Gram stain of CSF, with gram negative diplococci (arrows).
Figure 4. Chocolate agar plate with N. meningitidis colonies.

Ceftriaxone and vancomycin were administered in the emergency room before the lumbar puncture and CT scanning were performed. Promethazine, ranitidine, ondansetron, and dexamethasone were also administered in the emergency room, and one dose of acyclovir and gentamicin were administered pending the identification of the gram-negative rods on gram stain. With the identification of meningococcus, ceftriaxone alone was continued. Transient hypotension in the emergency room resolved with intravenous isotonic fluid boluses. The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and droplet precautions were instituted for the first twenty-four hours.
Her mental status improved markedly during the first ten hours of her admission and she was felt to be back to baseline within two days. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, performed on the sixth hospital day, was normal. Testing for hepatitis B and C viruses, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and complement deficiency were negative. Audiology and ophthalmology evaluations were normal. Ceftriaxone was administered for seven days.

Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and the timeliness of treatment can make a crucial difference in patient outcome. It is appropriate to begin antibiotics when the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis is suspected and prior to lumbar puncture or cranial computed tomography (CT). The organism can frequently be isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) after the initiation of antibiotics or occasionally can be identified through the use of antigen tests.
This particular patient's presentation in the emergency room waiting area included the development of a petechial rash, a sign suggestive of meningococcal infection and, fortunately, treatment was initiated urgently. Although the characteristic petechial rash is helpful in the diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis, patients may instead manifest a non-specific maculopapular rash or no rash at all.
At the Massachusetts General Hospital, the historic case fatality rate from meningococcal meningitis is 10% [Durand et al 1993]. This is lower than the historical case fatality rate associated with pneumococcal meningitis (28%) and gram-negative bacilli meningitis (36%). Further, compared with the other common causes of meningitis, the risk of neurological sequelae among survivors of meningococcal meningitis is lower. Although adjunctive corticosteroids are commonly administered in meningococcal meningitis, there is not a large body of evidence to support their use. Prophylaxis to household or other close contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis consists of either ciprofloxacin or rifampicin.
In 2005 and 2007, the United States Centers for Disease Control Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), recommended routine vaccination with a tetravalent meningococcal polysaccharide-protein (Groups A/C/Y and W-135) conjugate vaccine (MCV4 or Menactra®) of all unvaccinated children 11 to 18 years of age, as well as individuals 19-55 years with increased risk of infection with meningococcus including "college freshmen living in dormitories, microbiologists routinely exposed to isolates of Neisseria meningitidis, military recruits, travelers to or residents of countries in which N. meningitidis meningitis is hyperendemic or epidemic, persons with terminal complement component deficiencies, and persons with anatomic or functional asplenia" [Bilukha et al. CDC 2005, CDC 2007].

title: 2007 October Featured Case and IDSA 2007 Fellows Day Case Presentation Summary:
history:
2007 October Featured Case and IDSA 2007 Fellows Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with dyspnea, weight loss, back pain and weakness.
A man in his sixties presented to the Pulmonary Clinic for evaluation of a possible lung primary carcinoma. Three days before admission, he developed fatigue, exertional dyspnea, decreased oral intake with constipation, low back pain, lower extremity weakness and difficulty ambulating. During the preceding 2 months, anorexia developed and his weight decreased 10-pounds. There were no fevers, chills, nausea, or abdominal pain.

The past medical history included an orthotopic heart transplantation and excision of a cerebellar tumor, which had been positive for metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary site. Other past medical history included coronary artery disease, hypertension, deep venous thrombosis, diverticulosis, internal hemorrhoids, and basal cell carcinoma of the occipital scalp.

The patient had a 96 pack-year smoking history.

There were no allergies to medications.

Medications included mycophenolate 500 mg twice a day, cyclosporine 75 mg every morning and 100 mg every evening, dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 hours, ranitidine, warfarin, and oxycodone 5 mg as needed every 6 hours. All medications were taken orally.
exam_studies:
He appeared well. The blood pressure was 120/81 mm Hg, pulse 111 beats per minute, respirations 24 breaths per minute, and temperature 98.1°F (36.7°C). Edema and proximal muscle weakness of legs were present bilaterally. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 5,600 cells/mm³ (48% bands, 40% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes). Laboratory test results of a metabolic panel revealed a bicarbonate level of 20 mmol/L, and were otherwise normal. A radiograph of the chest revealed clear lungs (Figure 1). An abdominal radiograph (upright) revealed free air in the peritoneum beneath the diaphragms (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 2. Radiograph of the abdomen, with free air beneath the diaphragms.

Ticarcillin-clavulanate was administered intravenously, and a laparotomy was performed emergently, which revealed a perforation of the colon with stool in the left lower quadrant. Resection of the sigmoid colon with an end-colostomy and Hartmann’s pouch was performed. The resected colon was sent for pathological examination, shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. H and E stain of resected sigmoid colon.
Figure 4. H and E stain of resected sigmoid colon.
diagnosis:
Cytomegalovirus colitis and diverticulitis with perforation in a patient status post solid organ transplantation.

The diagnosis was obtained by histological and immunohistochemical staining of the resected colon and cytomegalovirus (CMV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) performed on the plasma. Pathological examination by hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figure 3) shows a ruptured diverticulum with inflammation and perforation into mesenteric adipose tissue. No muscularis mucosa was identified in this section, with the mucosa directly adjacent to mesenteric adipose tissue, confirming diverticular disease. Figures 4 and 5 show mixed inflammatory cells in the background, with lymphocytes and neutrophils seen. In the center, there is a large CMV inclusion cell (Figure 5, see arrows), with nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. The cytoplasm is distended with eosinophilic inclusions and the nucleus is enlarged with a single basophilic inclusion. There is a clear halo surrounding the nucleus, and no multinucleations are seen.
Figure 6 shows immunohistochemical staining with antibody specific to CMV antigen. The patient’s plasma CMV DNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was 106,655 copies/ml.
Figure 5. H and E stain of colon, showing giant cell (arrows).
Figure 6. Immunohistochemical staining of colon specimen for CMV.

Ticarcillin-clavulanate was administered intravenously for 7 days, followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for an additional 7 days. The patient also received intravenous ganciclovir at a dose of 5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 3 weeks until the CMV DNA PCR was undetectable; then oral valganciclovir was given. The patient did well and was discharged to a temporary rehabilitation facility, and follow up as an outpatient was scheduled with the Infectious Diseases Clinic.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is the viral infection that occurs most frequently after solid organ transplantation, and an increased level of immunosuppression escalates the risk of reactivation disease.
Patients may present with constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, and anorexia, as well as symptoms localizing to the involved organ, such as those of pneumonitis or colitis.
In those who develop CMV disease after solid organ transplantation, the gastrointestinal tract is involved in 10% to 30% of cases. CMV infection of the gastrointestinal tract usually presents as bleeding due to ulceration and diffuse mucosal irritation, but only rarely presents as a perforation of the viscera.
The increased risk of colonic perforation in patients with diverticulitis who are taking steroids has been recognized since 1950. Steroids mask clinical signs of peritonitis in cases of colonic perforation, and the patients may present with a normal abdominal examination. Delay in diagnosis by more than 24 hours doubles the already high mortality from 30% to 60%, even in current series. A high index of suspicion is necessary to diagnose perforation of the viscera in patients on immunosuppressive therapy.

title: 2007 November Featured Case Summary: A woman with headache and periorbital swell
history:
2007 November Featured Case Summary: A woman with headache and periorbital swelling on the right side.
A woman in her thirties was well until eleven days earlier, when dizziness and headache over the temporal region on the right developed. The pain improved transiently, but headaches in the right temporal region recurred, and were worse with noise. Three days before admission, the severity of the pain increased significantly, and the next day, emesis and pleuritic chest pain on the left side occurred. Later that day, she called her primary care provider and then went to the emergency department of another hospital in the evening. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, performed according to a pulmonary embolus protocol, revealed two pulmonary nodules on the right and a left lower lobe abnormality that was thought to be consistent with either an inflammatory process or infarct. The D-dimer level in the serum was elevated at 1029 ng/ml (reference range <500 ng/ml).
While in the emergency department, the patient noted that both eyes felt “weird”, but there was no diplopia or changes in vision. Prochlorperazine and diphenhydramine were administered, and the symptoms partially improved. She was discharged home on azithromycin.
Early the next morning, she awoke with nausea and vomiting. Later that day, she saw her primary care provider; trimethobenzamide and intravenous fluids were administered, and she returned home. That evening, bilateral eye pain developed and during the next 3 hours, periorbital swelling and proptosis of the right eye occurred. She returned to the emergency department. Five hours after the onset of eye pain, diplopia was noted. The patient was transferred to a tertiary care hospital for further evaluation.

There was a history of temporomandibular joint disorder.

Both of her children had recently had staphylococcal skin infections. She had traveled recently to Northern New England with her family, and reported no trauma, tick exposure, or insect bites. She did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

She lived with her husband, two young children and two dogs.

There were no allergies to medications; amoxicillin had caused vomiting.

Medications included oral contraceptive pills.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable, lying in bed with her eyes closed. She was easily roused, was oriented, and answered questions appropriately. The temperature was 101.9°F (38.8°C), the pulse 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 133/66 mm Hg, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing ambient air. Pupils were 4.5 millimeters in diameter bilaterally, and decreased to 3 mm with illumination. There was mild facial swelling of the right cheek, mild periorbital edema, and erythema and 3-4 millimeters proptosis of the right eye when compared to the left eye. Chemosis and ptosis were present on the right. Extraocular movements of the left eye were normal; the right eye had limited medial adduction, and no lateral, superior or inferior motion. (See Figures 1 and 2.) There was mild tenderness periorbitally on the right, and a small crusted papule on forehead between the eyebrows. The fundoscopic examination and tympanic membranes were normal. There was neck stiffness, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 18,600 per cubic millimeter (93% neutrophils, 3% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes), hematocrit 33.6%, and platelets 216,000 per cubic millimeter. Laboratory test results of serum chemistries and liver function were normal. A pregnancy test was negative.

Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained by lumbar puncture revealed a glucose level of 69 mg/dL and protein of 180 mg/dL. Tube #1 had 1575 red cells per cubic millimeter, 1130 white cells per cubic millimeter (83% neutrophils, 17% monocytes); Tube #4 had 195 red cells per cubic millimeter and 3000 white cells per cubic millimeter (82% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes). A gram stain of a cytospin of the CSF revealed abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and no organisms. (See Figure 3).
Figure 3. Gram stain of CSF.
diagnosis:
Multiple septic venous thromboses (including bilateral cavernous sinus thrombosis, ophthalmic vein thrombosis, right sigmoid sinus, right internal jugular thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary septic emboli), bacteremia and meningitis caused by methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was suggestive of thromboses, and also showed evidence of dural enhancement suggestive of meningitis (Figures 4 and 5). CT angiography of the head revealed thrombosis of both cavernous sinuses, both superior ophthalmic veins (complete on the right, partial on the left), the dorsal clival venous plexus, right sigmoid sinus, right internal jugular vein, and likely bilateral sphenoparietal sinuses. Cultures of the blood and CSF from the day of admission grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) (Figure 6).
Figure 4. MRI scan of the head.
Figure 5. MRI scan with dural enhancement.
Figure 6. Gram stain of aerobic blood culture.

Vancomycin, ceftriaxone and metronidazole were started empirically, and the patient was anticoagulated. When the culture results were known, the antibiotics were changed to nafcillin and rifampin and continued for four weeks.
During the admission, right-sided facial pain persisted, moving to the lateral jaw and neck on the right side, and was associated with trismus. CT scanning of the neck showed some soft tissue swelling but no evidence of abscess. CT of the chest showed a left upper lobe cavitary lesion as well as small other scattered lesions, consistent with septic pulmonary emboli. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of vegetations.
The fevers resolved and she had slow but significant improvement in ptosis, proptosis and eye movement. Approximately three months after completing treatment, her symptoms had improved markedly, and were resolved except for intermittent headaches at approximately nine months. Ten months after admission, CT angiography revealed non-significant opacification in the bilateral cavernous sinuses with normal caliber superior ophthalmic veins bilaterally, and stable persistent thrombosis of the right sigmoid sinus, jugular sinus and internal jugular veins. The ophthalmic veins were normal in caliber and the transverse sinus enhanced normally. She remained anticoagulated on coumadin pending further evaluation to rule out coagulopathies.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a relatively rare disease. The facial veins and pterygoid plexus via the inferior and superior ophthalmic veins drain into the cavernous sinus and therefore infections on the face, especially from nose and eyes as well as sphenoid and ethmoid sinus infections can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis. Dental infectious, otitis media and mastoiditis can rarely lead to this complication as well. This patient may have had a pustule on her forehead that was infected with Staphylococcus aureus, which she squeezed or drained prior to the initial onset of symptoms.
Patients with cavernous sinus thrombosis typically present with headache, usually unilateral in a frontal or retro-orbital distribution. They subsequently may develop unilateral eye swelling or proptosis, which may become bilateral in 1-2 days as the cavernous thrombosis spreads to contralateral side. Other symptoms include diplopia (due to ophthalmoplegia), ptosis and photophobia. Some patients will develop altered mental status with confusion and obtundation. Physical findings correlate with the anatomic location of the cavernous sinus, which encompasses the third and fourth cranial nerves as well as the 1st two branches of the fifth cranial nerve.
Staphylococcus aureus accounts for up to 70% of infectious that cause cavernous sinus thrombosis; other potential pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, and rarely gram-negatives, anaerobes or fungi.
Treatment is with antibiotics directed at the causative organism, as well as surgical drainage of abscess if present. The role of anticoagulation is controversial, and the decision to treat should be individualized.

title: 2007 December Featured Case Summary: A boy with fever, lip lesions, conjunctivit
history:
2007 December Featured Case Summary: A boy with fever, lip lesions, conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, rash and pneumonia.
A 7-year-old boy with a history of glomerulonephritis was well until 4 days before admission when mild upper respiratory tract symptoms, rhinorrhea and cough developed. The next day (in mid-summer), he went to the beach and waded in the ocean water. Two days before admission, the temperature rose to 104.0°F (40.0°C). The next day, pharyngitis, swollen lips associated with mouth sores, swollen eyelids, conjunctivitis and a rash on his back and trunk developed; urine output decreased, and the urine became tea-colored. He had poor oral intake and vomited non-bloody emesis. He was admitted to the hospital.

Approximately four months before admission, cellulitis behind the left knee occurred. Streptococcus was cultured, and cefoxitin and hydrocortisone administered. Two weeks later, gastroenteritis caused by rotavirus occurred, after which his urine became tea-colored, and hematuria was noted. Fluids and ceftriaxone were administered. The evaluation revealed normal test results for anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer and immunoglobulin (Ig) A level, but borderline deoxyribonuclease (DNase) 1:170 titer, where the normal reference range is less than 1:170. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis was presumptively diagnosed. He was followed by a nephrologist and did well, with decreasing microscopic hematuria, until this illness. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) was positive at 1:40 and 1:160 in a speckled pattern. Growth and development were normal for age.

There was no exposure to standing water (ponds or lakes) and he had swum in a chlorinated pool and waded in the ocean. There was no known exposure to anyone with herpes simplex virus, or to insect bites or wild animals.

He lived with his mother and attended school.

There was a family history of hypertension, stroke and diabetes. One cousin had growth problems. There was no known history of renal disease.

He was allergic to amoxicillin, which had caused hives, and had tolerated cephalosporins.

He had received routine childhood immunizations, including Varicella vaccination.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared fatigued but not toxic, with moderate lip pain. The temperature was 101.1°F (38.4°C), pulse 131 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/61 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation while breathing ambient air was 95%. There was palpebral conjunctival injection; the bulbar conjunctivae were only minimally injected. The lips were swollen with a hemorrhagic crust. The anterior gingiva was relatively spared. The hard palatal roof had myriad tiny superficial ulcerations and the posterior pharynx was poorly visualized due to a sensitive gag reflex. There was tender cervical lymphadenopathy. The tongue was normal; there was no rhinorrhea or sinus tenderness, and the neck was supple. Decreased basilar breath sounds were heard, with no rhonchi. There were numerous crimson oval-round lesions on the back, with a few more on the anterior chest and abdomen. Several had central punctate ulcers, and a few had larger areas of central superficial sloughs. A pustule occupied most of an erythematous lesion in the right scapular area; there were no lesions on the hands or feet. (See Figures 1 through 4.) The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Rash on back.
Figure 2. Lip lesions and rash.
Figure 3. Detail of rash on back.
Figure 4. Eye findings.

The white cell count was 13,500 cells per microliter (66% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 1% basophils, and 14% bands), hematocrit 36.7%, platelets 380,000 per microliter, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 millimeters per hour. Serum electrolytes and tests of renal function were normal. Analysis of the urine revealed red, cloudy urine with 3+ blood (25-50 red cells per high-powered field) and 3+ protein, with 1+ leukocytes, and 0-2 hyaline casts. A rapid strep test was positive.

A chest radiograph was interpreted as showing a left lower lobe pneumonia. Acyclovir and cefazolin (600 mg intravenously three times daily) were administered for possible herpetic syndrome and pneumonia. On the 2nd hospital day, an episode of diarrhea and emesis occurred. The patient was transferred to a tertiary care hospital.
On examination, there was a low-grade fever, and multiple skin lesions with sharp borders, some of which had a punctate central vesicle. The lesions measured less than 2 centimeters, and were present on the back, chest, abdomen, and extremities. A repeat chest radiograph (Figure 5) revealed a partial obscuration of the left hemidiaphragm, which was thought to represent a left lower lobe pneumonia. The heterophile antibody was negative.
Figure 5. Chest radiograph.
diagnosis:
Pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, with skin and mucosal membrane lesions consistent with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of a specimen from the throat was positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae nucleic acid. Pathological examination of a skin biopsy of lesion on the chest revealed impetiginized vesicular dermatitis with epidermal necrosis, dyskeratotic cells, ulceration, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate, which were thought to be compatible with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Cytopathic changes diagnostic of a viral etiology such as herpes or coxsackie virus were not seen and immunohistochemistry stains for varicella zoster virus and herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 were negative.
Indirect immunofluorescence testing for anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA) and ELISAs for antibodies to p29 (proteinase 3) and myeloperoxidase were negative. The following were negative: ASO, rheumatoid factor (RF), ANA, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-Sm, anti-RNP, lupus anticoagulant, and anticardiolipin IgG; anticardiolipin IgM was 29.4 (reference range 0-15 mpl). Total urine protein over 24 hours measured 520 mg (reference range 0-165 mg per 24 hours). Immunoglobulin A was 279 mg/dl (reference range 33-199 mg/dl), and smooth muscle antibody was positive at 1:40 dilution (reference range, negative at 1:20).

On the 2nd hospital day, azithromycin was added. After the results of the PCR test were known, the other antibiotics were stopped and azithromycin alone continued. During the 5 months after discharge, hematuria and proteinuria persisted, and hypertension developed. Pathological examination of a renal biopsy revealed IgA deposition, and IgA nephropathy was diagnosed.

A unifying diagnosis of this child’s multiple acute findings is a primary infection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae, with pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and skin lesions, some of which were vesicular and some present at the mucocutaneous junction, consistent with erythema multiforme major or Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Of note, the pneumonia of Mycoplasma pneumoniae is more typically thought of as a non-lobar or interstitial process, however does not always present as such, as seen in this case. Children less than 3 years of age primarily exhibit upper respiratory symptoms, and those 5 and above are more likely to have bronchitis or pneumonia. The association of the skin lesions of erythema multiforme major, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, described as erythematous vesicles, plaques and bullae, have occurred in up to 7% of patients with Mycoplasma pneumonia, particularly in younger, male patients. The distribution of infection is worldwide, and most studies have shown no seasonal preference. Cases of IgA nephropathy have been associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, although in this patient, with pre-existing renal disease, a clear association is more difficult to make.
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis was unlikely, given all the findings including pneumonia. His illness was not suggestive of leptospirosis despite his conjunctival findings. The rash of Kawasaki’s disease is usually acral and the lesions are not typically vesicular; the lips are more likely to appear chapped rather than with a hemorrhagic crust. There were no hand or foot lesions to suggest hand, foot and mouth disease due to Coxsackie virus infection.

title: A man with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in remission and headache, confusion and fever.
history:
A man in his forties, who had received consolidation chemotherapy while in remission from B-cell acute lymphocytic leukemia, presented with a 2-day history of malaise, headache and fever to 38.3°C (100.9°F). He was seen in the emergency room, and results of computed tomography (CT) of the sinuses were consistent with sinusitis. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was begun.
Later that day, the patient was found by one of his neighbors confused in his front yard; he was brought back to the emergency department.
His wife reported that two days earlier mental status changes had developed, which included flight of ideas and tangential thought. Headache and fever had remained the same.

There was a history of B-cell acute lymphocytic leukemia in remission on chemotherapy; chronic sinusitis for which bilateral antrectomies and ethmoidectomy had been performed 1 year earlier; cytomegalovirus infection; and depression. Laboratory test results for antibody to herpes simplex virus-1 were positive.

He did not have pets and had not traveled recently. Two weeks earlier, after a torrential downpour, he had cleaned debris out of the gutters of his home.

He was married, had children, and worked in an office.

He was allergic to amphotericin B (liposomal), which had caused dyspnea.

Medications included amoxicillin-clavulanate, valacyclovir, sertraline, esomeprazole, ondansetron, and lorazepam. The patient had completed consolidation chemotherapy according to a protocol, which had included cyclophosphamide, daunorubicin, vincristine, L-asparaginase and dexamethasone; followed by methotrexate (intrathecally), cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, and L-asparaginase; followed by methotrexate (intrathecal and orally) with leucovorin rescue and vincristine. Two months earlier, he had also received alemtuzumab.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 38.9°C (102.0°F), blood pressure 164/95 mm Hg, pulse 107 beats, respirations 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95%, while breathing ambient air. He appeared ill, but was alert and not in respiratory distress. There was lymphadenopathy in the cervical and periauricular regions, and no nuchal rigidity. The maxillary sinus was tender on the right side. The fundoscopic examination was normal; there was no photophobia. On neurological examination, the patient was oriented to person only. There was confusion as to the order of events that had occurred earlier in the day, with confabulation. Cranial nerves II-XII were intact. Strength and sensation were normal bilaterally. There was urinary incontinence, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory test results included serum sodium 125 mmol/L. The hematocrit, white cells and differential were normal. Analysis of cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) revealed an opening pressure of 33 mm H2O, white cell count 43 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 56%, lymphocytes 40%, and monocytes 4%), total protein 53 g/dl, glucose 59 mg/dl. A gram stain of the CSF did not show any organisms, and cultures of the CSF for fungi, bacteria, and acid-fast bacilli were sterile. Computed tomography of the head revealed sphenoid sinusitis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a small arachnoid cyst; the remainder of the brain parenchyma was normal.

Cefepime, vancomycin, ampicillin, voriconazole, and ganciclovir were begun. The mental status declined, and the trachea was intubated for airway protection. Electroencephalography showed slow diffuse left parietotemporal spikes consistent with encephalitis. Hypotension developed associated with supraventricular tachycardia, and cardioversion with amiodarone was performed. The pupils became fixed and dilated, and a repeat MRI scan was obtained (Figure 1). Neurosurgeons placed an intraventricular drain, with no improvement in mental status.
The patient expired and an autopsy was performed.
Pathological examination of the brain tissue is shown in Figure 2, which shows necrotizing vasculitis and extensive acute parenchymal necrosis and hemorrhage, and in Figure 3.
Figure 1. Brain MRI scan.
Figure 2. Brain tissue at autopsy.
Figure 3. Brain tissue at autopsy.
diagnosis:
Granulomatous amebic encephalitis, in a patient with a history of acute lymphocytic leukemia in remission.

Pathological examination of the brain tissue obtained at autopsy revealed amebic cysts, shown in Figure 4 with arrows and in Figure 5 with gomori methenamine silver stain.
Figure 4. Brain tissue with arrows showing amebic cysts.
Figure 5. GMS stain showing amebic cysts.

Free-living amebas survive and replicate in the environment without requiring a host, and are ubiquitous in soil and water. There are four relevant genera: Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba species, Balamuthia mandrillaris, and Sappinia diploidea. More than 50% of the population has antibodies to Acanthamoeba.
Granulomatous amebic encephalitis afflicts immunocompromised hosts and presents subacutely with focal neurologic deficits with progression to a diffuse meningoencephalitis. There is no definitive treatment for amebic encephalitis. Multidrug therapy has been reported with ketoconazole-rifampin-trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole-sulfadiazine, and pentamadine-amphotericin-flucytosine-rifampin-itraconazole-chlorhexidine.
Opportunistic infections have been reported after the use of alemtuzumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against CD52 that depletes lymphocytes. These infections include, most notably, cytomegalovirus infection, invasive fungal infections (e.g. cryptococcosis), toxoplasmosis, nocardiosis and mycobacterial infections. Amebic infections have also been reported after the use of alemtuzumab, and must be considered in the differential diagnosis in a patient with altered mental status who has received this drug.

title: A man with hypertension, hepatitis and hemoptysis.
history:
A man in his fifties with a history of hypertension and hepatitis of unknown etiology presented to an emergency department with hemoptysis of 2-months' duration. Cough, productive of red blood mixed with yellow sputum, was present; the patient was not able to quantify the amount of blood. There was dyspnea on exertion after walking 1 block and diffuse pleuritic chest pain. Night sweats, decreased appetite, and a 10-pound weight loss over 2 months had occurred. There were no fevers, chills or other sites of bleeding. He did not know of anyone who was ill, including anyone with tuberculosis.

There was a history of hypertension and hepatitis of unknown etiology.

He was born in Honduras and had immigrated to the United States 26 months earlier. He lived in Florida until moving to the Ohio River valley basin 8 months before presentation. He lived with two relatives who were not ill, and worked in a factory. There were no pets and no exposures to animals. The patient was a former smoker and denied alcohol or drug use.

There were no allergies to medications.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic and in no acute respiratory distress. The temperature was 99.8°F (37.7°C), blood pressure 120/52 mm Hg, pulse 62 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90% while breathing 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula. There were crackles at the bases of both lungs, bilaterally. There were no wheezes or rhonchi. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 14,600 cells/mm³ with 80% neutrophils. The other laboratory tests, including serum chemistries and liver function tests, were normal. A chest radiograph (Figures 1 and 2) showed multiple pulmonary nodules diffusely and some areas of cavitation.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figures 3 and 4) showed multiple scattered nodular opacities with numerous cavitary lesions. Irregular foci of airspace disease, especially in the lower lobes bilaterally, and extensive mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy were seen. A gram stain of the sputum showed many polymorphonuclear cells and mononuclear cells, and no organisms. Three specimens of sputum were negative for acid-fast staining organisms. Serological testing (ELISA) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, lateral.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.
Figure 4. Chest CT scan.

A bronchoscopy with bronchial washings, bronchoalveolar lavage, and biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of the tissue was examined with Gomori methenamine silver stain (Figure 5) and hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figure 6).
Figure 5. GMS stain of lung biopsy.
Figure 6. H and E stain of lung biopsy.
diagnosis:
Paracoccidioidomycosis of the lung caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.

Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain of the lung biopsy is shown in Figure 5. Fungal microorganisms that were morphologically consistent with Paracoccidioides were seen. Pathological examination of the biopsy (Figure 6) showed mixed acute and chronic inflammation and poorly formed granulomas, and no malignant cells. There were no acid-fast organisms.
Six weeks later, cultures of specimens obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage and bronchial washing cultures grew a moderate amount of mold, which was identified as Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.

The patient was discharged on itraconazole 100 mg twice a day, orally. At follow-up six weeks later, the hemoptysis and shortness of breath had resolved and his appetite was improved. He has returned to work.

Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is a dimorphic fungus. Microscopically, it is characterized by multiple sporulations of small buddings covering the whole surface of the mother cell. This steering wheel appearance is pathognomonic. Paracoccidioidomycosis is endemic in Latin America, between Mexico 20ºN and Argentina 35ºS. Most published cases are from Brazil, Venezuela, and Colombia. It has not been described in the Caribbean or Chile [Bethlem et al 1999]. The adult chronic progressive form is characterized by reactivation of quiescent lung lesions. Symptoms include weight loss, malaise, productive cough, and eventually hemoptysis. Fever is rare. It can often be misdiagnosed as tuberculosis, although tuberculosis can coexist in 10-25% of cases [Manns et al 1996]. The adult disseminated form is characterized by multifocal dissemination to the skin, oral mucosa, tongue, palate, and vocal cords. It is often accompanied by cervical, axillary, and/or mediastinal lymphadenopathy [Bethlem et al 1999]. Subacute or overt adrenal insufficiency occurs in 15% of cases [Manns et al 1996]. It can also involve the spleen, liver, male genitourinary tract, and vascular system [Sugar 1988].

title: A man with weakness and cognitive changes.
history:
A man in his forties presented to the emergency department with progressive weakness in his legs and unstable gait. He had recently fallen several times at home. A cough had developed several weeks before, which was productive of brownish sputum and associated with dyspnea on exertion.
The patient’s family reported that the patient had undergone personality and cognitive changes over the preceding six months, becoming isolated from family members and exhibiting lapses in memory and judgment. There was a history of weight loss of 40 pounds (18.2 kilograms) during the previous year.

There was a history of depression.

He had had sexual intercourse with men, including 6 partners in the last five years, but none in the past year. There was a 30 pack-year tobacco history, and no use of illicit drugs. In the previous year, he had traveled to Southern California. He had no pets. A member of his household had been treated decades earlier for pulmonary tuberculosis; he did not recall being tested for tuberculosis and had never received anti-tuberculosis treatment.

He was not allergic to medications.
exam_studies:
The patient was gaunt, and appeared chronically ill. He coughed frequently, but was not in acute respiratory distress. The temperature was 100.1°F (37.8°C); other vital signs were normal. The affect was flat, and he was inattentive during the interview. There were raised white plaques on the palate and tongue, and rales were heard throughout the right lung, with no percussive dullness or egophony. Neurological examination revealed a paucity of conversation; inability to name any of 3 objects at 5 minutes; an ataxic, wide-based gait; and diminished strength and deep tendon reflexes in the legs, which were more prominent on the right than left.

The hematocrit was 26%, platelets 563,000 per cubic millimeter and a white cell count of 12,500 per cubic millimeter. Serological testing for antibody to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay or ELISA test) was positive. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 26 cells per cubic millimeter, with HIV-RNA level of 30,018 copies per milliliter. Tests of renal and liver function were normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, shown in Figures 1, 2 and 3, revealed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe, and T2 signal changes in the periventricular white matter and pontine region.
Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a white cell count of 1 cell per cubic millimeter; red cell count 1 cell per cubic millimeter; glucose 57 mg/dL; protein 50 mg/dL; and an HIV-RNA level of 30,000 copies/mL. Results of other CSF studies (gram stain, fungal stain, cryptococcal antigen, cultures, testing for JC virus, and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) testing) were negative.
Figure 1. MRI of the brain, T1 post-gadolinium.
Figure 2. MRI of the brain, T2 FLAIR.
Figure 3. MRI of the brain, T2 FLAIR.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 4) showed mediastinal lymphadenopathy, a bulky mediastinal homogeneous mass (5 centimeters (cm) by 7.6 cm in maximum diameter) on the right and multiple right-sided lung masses. A drainage procedure of the mediastinum was performed by thoracic surgeons, and the aspirate was cultured. A gram stain of the culture growth is shown in Figure 5.
Figure 4. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 5. Gram stain of culture of aspirate.
diagnosis:
Mediastinal empyema and brain abscess, caused by Nocardia asteroides infection, in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

The gram stain reveals beaded, thin, filamentous gram-positive rods (Figure 5). The culture of the aspirate grew Nocardia asteroides.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was administered intravenously at first and then the patient was placed on an oral regimen. Anti-retroviral therapy with tenofovir-emtricitabine and lopinavir-ritonavir was begun. After six months on therapy, he had an excellent response with virtual resolution of the pulmonary and brain abscesses, an undetectable HIV-RNA viral load, 30-pound weight gain, and nearly full recovery of his gait.

Although nocardiosis is not a common opportunistic infection in patients with HIV infection and AIDS, it should be suspected in any patient presenting with simultaneous pulmonary and intracranial disease evolving over an extended time course. The portal of entry for Nocardia is the respiratory tract and the skin. Pulmonary manifestations are the most common and include nodules, often cavitating, as well as pneumonia and empyema. The differential for similar indolent pulmonary processes includes mycobacteria, Cryptococcus and Aspergillus. Central nervous system involvement occurs in up to 40% of patients with systemic nocardiosis, and includes abscess and granuloma formation. The infectious differential for such a ring-enhancing lesion might include toxoplasmosis, lymphoma, or less likely amoebic, pyogenic or fungal abscess. Definitive diagnosis relies on obtaining aspirates of suspected lesions for culture. Growth of Nocardia may take 48 hours to several weeks in standard media, and isolation can be facilitated by usage of special media, such as buffered charcoal-yeast extract.
