title: A newborn with a rash and hepatosplenomegaly.
history:
A male infant was delivered by emergency cesarean section because of suspected maternal genital herpes infection. The neonate was the product of a full-term pregnancy. The mother was in her thirties, gravida 2 para 1, and had a history of cocaine addiction. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by gonorrhea and syphilis, for which she had been treated one year earlier. The last known rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer was 1:32. Serological test results for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) had been negative. Amniotic membranes were ruptured at home; the period of elapsed time to presentation at the hospital was not known.

There had not been any maternal prenatal care and prenatal laboratory test results were not known.
exam_studies:
The weight was 2.5 kilograms; weight and head circumference were at the 50th percentile. Apgar scores were 3, 6 and 8 at 1, 5 and 10 minutes, respectively. There was poor respiratory effort, and the patient was intubated emergently and placed under a radiant warmer. The temperature was 97.8°F (36.5°C); other vital signs were normal. Examination of the skin revealed multiple petechiae (mostly on the torso), and rounded cutaneous lesions that measured 0.3 centimeters (cm) to 1 cm on the palms and soles (Figures 1 through 4, the feet are shown after ink was applied for footprinting). The heart sounds were normal. There were bilateral rales in the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy and hypotonia. He was poorly responsive to the examination.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
Figure 3. Physical finding (with ink applied)
Figure 4. Physical finding (with ink applied)

The white cell count was 25,000 cells/mm³ (neutrophils 21%, lymphocytes 47%, monocytes 22%, metamyelocytes 2%), hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelet count 9,000/mm³, aspartate aminotransferase 1,219 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 219 U/L; prothrombin time 28.7 seconds and partial thromboplastin time 48.1 seconds. Other laboratory test results were normal.

A chest radiograph revealed an increased cardiac silhouette and no radiographic evidence of pneumonia. A computed brain tomography scan and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
diagnosis:
Congenital syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum infection, with hepatitis and central nervous system involvement.

Maternal rapid plasma reagin (RPR) testing at the time of delivery was positive at 1:256, and the infant’s RPR at 1:16. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 350 white cells per cubic millimeter (14% segmented polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 423 mg/dL, and a reactive Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test, with a titer of 4. Radiographs of the long bones showed metaphyseal osteochondritis and periostitis (Figure 5), commonly found in congenital syphilis. The findings were consistent with the diagnosis of congenital syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum infection.
Laboratory test results of the mother's serum did not show evidence of infection with hepatitis B virus or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and immunity to rubella was documented. Cultures of the infant's blood at birth were negative. Cytomegalovirus was not detected in the urine by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or culture. Bacterial cultures of the CSF and testing for herpes simplex virus PCR were negative. Viral cultures of the skin, eyes, rectum, and nasopharynx were negative, and cultures of the cutaneous lesions did not reveal bacterial pathogens. Newborn laboratory screening tests for metabolic diseases and hemoglobinopathies were normal.
Figure 5. Radiographs of long bones.

The infant was treated with intravenous penicillin G crystalline (150,000 U/kg/day) for 14 days. Follow-up laboratory test results are shown in Figure 6, and measurement of the RPR at 2 months was positive at 1:4, reflecting a four-fold decrease.
Figure 6. Laboratory test results.

The constellation of findings at birth in this case indicated the need to consider the TORCH group of infections, as well as other unusual disorders. (The TORCH acronym represents the following infections: toxoplasmosis; other infections including hepatitis B, syphilis, and herpes zoster; rubella; cytomegalovirus; and herpes simplex virus.)
Serious involvement of the central nervous system, intrauterine growth retardation, and petechiae and purpura (i.e., blueberry muffin baby) are characteristic of symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection. Infants with staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome are usually very ill and have diffuse skin involvement. Kawasaki disease is an extremely rare diagnosis in a neonate and presents with rather atypical features.
Congenital syphilis continues to be diagnosed in the United States, particularly in infants of mothers with no or inadequate prenatal care. Pregnant women with syphilis should receive adequate treatment and follow up to document cure.
Cutaneous lesions of the palms and soles are classic manifestations of Treponema pallidum infection and are highly contagious until 24 hours after institution of penicillin therapy. Significant hepatitis can occur, and may resolve slowly after institution of therapy. Serious neurologic sequelae may occur as a result of congenital syphilis; audiology testing, ophthalmologic exam and early neurodevelopment intervention are necessary to improve the outcome of affected infants.

title: An elderly woman with rheumatoid arthritis and a painful, swollen right elbow.
history:
A woman in her seventies, with a history of rheumatoid arthritis that was treated chronically with prednisone and methotrexate, was seen in an outpatient clinic because of a painful right elbow. There was a history of recurrent synovitis of the right shoulder, which had been treated with arthroplasty. Four months before admission, left elbow bursitis developed. Fluid obtained by arthrocentesis grew Candida albicans and coagulase negative Staphylococcus. A course of oral fluconazole and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was administered with resolution of her symptoms.
Approximately six weeks before presentation, a rheumatoid arthritis flare developed, with joint pain and stiffness associated with swelling of her knees, wrists and elbows. Infliximab was added. Two weeks later, swelling and erthema developed over the right elbow, associated with tenderness on movement. She denied fever, chills, sweats or any systemic symptoms. She was seen in the outpatient clinic for further evaluation.

There was a history of rheumatoid arthritis.

The patient was born in the Middle East. She had immigrated to the United States 25 years earlier, but returned to the Middle East regularly, most recently five months earlier. She did not drink alcohol or smoke, and had no unusual eating habits.

Medications included prednisone 10 mg each morning and 5 mg each evening, metrothexate 15 mg weekly, and infliximab weekly.
exam_studies:
She appeared well; the vitals signs were normal. The right elbow was edematous, erythematous, warm and tender to the touch. Pain occurred with movement of the elbow and the range of motion was limited to 100 degrees of extension.

The white blood cell count was 11,400 with 73% neutrophils.

Arthrocentesis of the right elbow was performed and the aspirate was cultured. Culture results are shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Culture growth from aspirate.
Figure 2. Papanicolaou stain of aspirate growth.
diagnosis:
Olecranon bursitis caused by Prototheca wickerhamii.

The culture grew Prototheca wickerhamii. Figure 1 shows the organism growing on Sabouraud's medium. Papanicolaou stain of the organism is shown in Figure 2.

Voriconazole was administered for 8 weeks. Aspiration of the joint was repeated after 4 weeks of therapy, and cultures were still positive for Prototheca wickerhamii. After 8 weeks, cultures of the joint fluid were sterile. The patient improved and did well.

Protothecosis is an unusual infection caused by achlorophyllous algae of the genus Prototheca. Prototheca are ubiquitous in nature and can be isolated from soil, pond scum, grass and water. The two main species that cause infection in humans are Prototheca wickerhamii and P. zopfii. Three major infection syndromes have been observed: cutaneous involvement, olecranon bursitis and disseminated infection. The majority of these infections occur in patients who are on immunosuppressive therapy, or who have AIDS, malnutrition, renal or hepatic disease, cancer or autoimmune disorders. Treatment traditionally has been with amphoterecin B but now there is microbiologic data and clinical experience with voriconazole. Olecranon bursitis generally requires bursectomy but in this case the patient responded to voriconazole with resolution of the infection.

title: A man in his seventies with low back pain, weakness and fatigue.
history:
A man in his seventies presented with lower back pain, generalized weakness, fatigue, and exercise intolerance of six weeks’ duration. There was no fever, chills, night sweats, headache, mental status change, or neck stiffness. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed as an outpatient and showed abnormal marrow signal intensity of L5 and S1 vertebral bodies and in the intervertebral disc spaces. Abnormal signal was also detected in S2 and S3 (Figure 1). He was admitted for evaluation.
Figure 1. MRI of the spine.

There was a history of heart disease, cancer of the thyroid and bladder (status post bladder resection and treatment with Bacille Calmette-Guérin or BCG), abdominal aortic aneurysm, Barrett’s esophagus, duodenal ulcer, and right total hip arthroplasty.

He was retired and lived in homes in the Northeastern United States and Western Europe. He ate goat cheese, but was not aware of eating unpasteurized products.

Medications included zoledronic acid for hypercalcemia. He was not taking any antibiotics or immunosuppressants.
exam_studies:
He appeared pale, but otherwise well. The temperature was 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 132/60 mm Hg and pulse 72 beats per minute; oxygen saturation was 96% while breathing ambient air. There was tenderness of the lower spine to palpation and ankle edema bilaterally. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The hemoglobin was 9.9 grams/dL, and other test results, including white cell count, electrolytes, and liver function, were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 106 millimeters per hour and C-reactive protein was 39.7 mg/L.

Aspiration of the abnormal discs was performed under fluoroscopic guidance. Gram stain of the culture of the aspirate is shown in Figure 2. Blood cultures were also positive.
Figure 2. Gram stain of the culture of the aspirate.
diagnosis:
Listeria monocytogenes osteomyelitis.

Grams stain of the aspirate of the L5-S1 intervertebral disc space was positive for gram-positive rods (Figures 2 and 3), and negative for acid-fast bacilli. The organism Listeria monocytogenes was identified, and grew from the blood cultures, as well. Evaluation for malignant cells by cytological examination of the aspirate was negative.
Figure 3. Detail of Figure 2.

Ampicillin and gentamicin were administered intravenously initially, and after the blood cultures became sterile, ampicillin intravenously alone was continued for 6 weeks. His clinical symptoms improved and inflammatory markers returned to normal.

Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod that most commonly affects immunocompromised individuals, including those who are pregnant or at extremes of age; it can also affect the normal host. The principal clinical syndrome includes diseases of the central nervous system, such as meningitis, meningoencephalitis, and rhomboencephalitis. Development of osteomyelitis is uncommon. In this patient, his consumption of goat cheese and other endemic cheeses of Europe is the most likely risk factor for Listeria infection.

title: A man with draining abscesses on his buttock.
history:
A man in his fifties was admitted to the hospital with two abscesses on his right buttock.
Approximately three weeks before admission, a firm nodule developed on the patient's right buttock. Within one week, the nodule rapidly increased in size, became indurated, painful, and drained a purulent discharge. He was seen in Dermatology clinic two weeks before admission and had no constitutional symptoms or fever. Physical examination revealed two nodular lesions on the right buttock. One nodule was firm, tender and measured 10 centimeter (cm) by 5 cm. Just inferior to this was a second nodule that was 3 cm in diameter and draining purulent fluid. The larger nodule was incised and drained, and a sample of the discharge was sent for gram stain and culture. Oral clindamycin was administered, but discontinued by the patient after one dose because of nausea and vomiting.
Seven days later, he returned to the Dermatology clinic because of persistent drainage and enlargement of the second nodule. The second nodule was then incised and drained, and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole begun. One week later, the evening before admission, he developed a tactile temperature. He returned to the clinic the next day because of increasing pain and fever, and was admitted to the hospital. An infectious disease consult was obtained.

There was a history of pustular psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, diabetes, hypertension, glaucoma, osteoporosis, and gastric reflux. He had pulmonary tuberculosis, which was fully treated several years earlier.

The patient was from eastern Africa, and had immigrated to the Northwestern United States approximately eight weeks before the onset of this illness. He had worked in an office in a large city.

For many years, while living in Africa, the patient intermittently applied topical steroids and frequently took tapering courses of steroids orally for treatment of his psoriatic disease. He also occasionally received intramuscular injections of steroids, his last dose having been administered in his right buttock approximately 2.5 months before this illness while he resided in a refugee facility in Africa.
The most recent intensive psoriasis therapy was administered four weeks before admission when he was hospitalized for a severe flare. At that time, he was treated with cyclosporine and topical triamcinolone with a sauna suit.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well nourished. Vital signs were normal. There was a scaling and pustular rash on his skin, and two large draining nodules on the right buttock (Figure 1). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 13,100 cells per microliter. Two sets of blood cultures were sterile and results of testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative. Gram's stain of the swab from the first incision and drainage procedure is shown in Figure 2 and modified acid-fast stain is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 2. Gram stain of swab of lesion.
Figure 3. Modified acid-fast stain of swab of lesion.
diagnosis:
Nocardia cyriacigeorgica mycetoma.

Nocardia cyriacigeorgica (Figure 3) was identified by molecular analysis.

High dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) was administered intravenously. Computed tomography (CT) of the right buttock revealed enhancement of soft tissue in the right buttock with extension into the gluteus maximus, and a fluid collection that measured 6.8 centimeter (cm) by 6.1 cm, consistent with abscess. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was normal. CT scanning of the lung showed patchy tree-in-bud formation in the right lower lobes that was consistent with an endobronchial infectious process. (It was unclear if this was related to the Nocardia skin infection.)
A deep incision and drainage procedure of the abscesses was performed in the operating room.
He was discharged from the hospital on intravenous TMP-SMX. Two weeks later, he was re-admitted because of continued pain and local drainage. Another incision and drainage procedure was performed and he was continued on high-dose TMP-SMX. Upon discharge after this admission, he was sent to a skilled nursing facility for intravenous antibiotics and wound care.
At last follow-up in the Infectious Diseases clinic, he had completed a 6-month course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and was feeling well. Physical examination revealed two well-healed buttock incisions and no evidence of residual abscess.

The skin is the second most common site of Nocardia infection, after the lung. There are four clinical forms of Nocardia skin infection – 1) superficial, 2) lymphocutaneous, resembling sporotrichosis, 3) disseminated, and 4) actinomycetoma (an indurated mass with draining sinuses, as seen in this patient). Organisms that cause actinomycetoma include Actinomadura pelletieri, Actinomadura madurae, Streptomyces somaliensis, and Nocardia species (mostly N. brasiliensis). Among these organisms, only Nocardia species are weakly acid fast or modified acid fast staining positive (as seen in the image above).
Nocardia brasiliensis causes the majority of Nocardia cutaneous infections and is found mainly in the tropics. N. asteroides group skin infections are rarely reported. N. cyriacigeorgica is a unique Nocardia species, previously grouped with N. asteroides, which was identified in 2001 based upon 16S rRNA gene sequence data and biochemical characteristics. One study from Japan and Thailand found approximately 25% of past N. asteroides isolates were actually N. cyriacigeorgica. At this writing, there are five cases of N. cyriacigeorgica specific infections reported in the literature; all were in immunocompromised patients and infection sites included the lung, brain and blood stream. There have been no reported cases of N. cyriacigeorgica causing skin/soft tissue infections.

title: A man with fever and skin lesions.
history:
A man in his thirties developed fever, chills and a non-pruritic eruption 2-3 weeks before admission. The lesions initially appeared on his face, spreading to his back, groin, scalp, and extremities over 1-2 days. During the previous six months, he noted malaise, anorexia, and weight loss of 40 pounds (18 kilograms).

There was no significant medical history.

The patient was from the Midwestern United States. There was no recent travel, animal bites, or tick exposure. He had a remote history of sex with men. At the time of presentation, he reported being monogamous with a female partner of two years.

There were no allergies.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic. The temperature was 39°C (102.2°F). White plaques were present on the oral mucosa. There was a diffuse, crusted, papular and nodular eruption on the skin. Individual lesions ranged between 0.5-3.0 centimeters in size and were located over the back, chest, arms, legs, groin, face (including lips), and scalp, notably sparing of the palms and soles (Figures 1 through 4). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.
Figure 4. Physical findings.

Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 5,500 cells/mm³ (69% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes, 10% monocytes), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, and platelet count 199,000 cells/mm³. Serum chemistries and liver function tests were within normal limits. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) EIA and Western blot were positive. An absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 109 cells/mm³; HIV-1 RNA was 520,000 copies/ml.

A biopsy of a representative papule was performed. The hematoxylin and eosin stain of the specimen demonstrated lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction (Figures 5 and 6).
Figure 5. H and E stain of biopsy.
Figure 6. H and E stain of biopsy.
diagnosis:
Lues maligna (secondary syphilis) caused by Treponema pallidum in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

A silver stain of the biopsy material revealed treponemes (Figure 7 with arrows). A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was positive at 1:8 dilutions, and a fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA-Abs) was reactive.
Figure 7. Silver stain of biopsy.

Benzathine penicillin, 2.4 million units, was administered intramuscularly once weekly for three weeks. Antiretroviral therapy was also initiated. The patient's symptoms resolved within 3 weeks.

When an initial syphilitic chancre is left untreated, treponemes proliferate and disseminate hematogenously, leading to a secondary eruption. Such lesions generally appear 4 to 10 weeks after the primary infection, presenting as generalized macules, papules, pustules, or rarely, vesicles. Secondary syphilitic eruptions are often accompanied by malaise, fever, and diffuse lymphadenopathy [Baughn and Musher 2005].
Lues maligna (malignant, or rupioid syphilis) is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis. Initially described in 1864, lues maligna is characterized by multiple, pleomorphic, noduloulcerative lesions [Dubac 1864]. Patients present after an incubation period of 6 weeks to 1 year with a subacute prodrome of fevers, arthralgias, headache, and photophobia.
On examination, the lesions initially appear as papules, and evolve into pustules within a few days. Central necrosis, clean, well-demarcated ulcers, and a surrounding halo of erythema characterize lesions as they progress. Terminal ulcers are covered with layers of crust. Classically, the trunk, mucosal membranes, palms and soles are spared.
Histopathologic findings in lues maligna resemble those of other lesions of secondary syphilis. A band-like, lichenoid infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells appears at the dermal-epidermal junction (Figures 5 and 6). There may be hyperkeratosis or necrosis in the epidermis [3]. On occasion, treponemes are visible on silver stain, as in Figure 7.
While the pathogenesis of lues maligna is still unclear, host factors likely play an important role; patients are characteristically malnourished, cachectic and, increasingly, HIV-positive [Kumar and Muralidhar 1998, Don et al 1995]. Untreated or incompletely treated patients may have a recurrence of constitutional symptoms and severe, scarring ulcers, leading to the description of such lesions as “malignant”.
In this case, the patient’s RPR was positive at 1:8 dilutions and FTA-Abs was reactive. He received benzathine penicillin (2.4 million units) intramuscularly weekly for three weeks, and had complete resolution of his symptoms immediately after treatment. His HIV viral load became undetectable on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). He was transiently lost to follow-up. Ten months after treatment, the RPR was non-reactive.

title: A man with fevers, weight loss, abdominal pain and diarrhea.
history:
A man in his fifties developed intermittent fevers four months before admission. Approximately 3 months later, abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea developed. Weight loss of 30 pounds (approximately 14 kilograms) occurred during the 4 months preceding admission.

There was a history of a seizure disorder.

He was born in Puerto Rico, and immigrated to the Unites States more than 15 years earlier. He lived in a large urban area in the northeastern United States, and worked as a driver. He reported no risk factors for exposure to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). His mother had had tuberculosis more than thirty years before.

He was taking phenytoin for the seizure disorder.
exam_studies:
He appeared ill. The blood pressure was 116/61 mmHg, pulse 129 beats per minute, and temperature 102.4°F (39.1°C). The lungs were clear. Pain in the right lower abdomen was noted on palpation, and no abdominal masses were felt. There was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 14,100 cells/mm³, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, and results of liver function testing were normal. A screening test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), urinalysis and staining of a sputum specimen for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT), shown in Figures 1 and 2, demonstrated circumferential wall thickening of the terminal ileum, and the ascending colon, hepatic flexure and transverse colon. There was no lymphadenopathy and no ascites.
Figure 1. CT scan of abdomen.
Figure 2. CT scan of abdomen.

Colonoscopic examination revealed diverticulosis with inflamed and ulcerated mucosal lesions, colonic polyps, and an incompetent ileocecal valve (Figures 3 through 5). Pathological examination of biopsy specimens from the terminal ileum showed moderate acute and chronic inflammation and acute cryptitis. There were no granulomas identified. Specimens from the ascending colon showed marked acute and chronic colitis with acute cryptitis, and granulomatous inflammation. The findings were thought to be consistent with chronic inflammatory bowel disease. Staining for acid-fast bacilli and fungi were negative.
Figure 3. Colonoscopy findings.
Figure 4. Colonoscopy findings.
Figure 5. Colonoscopy findings.
diagnosis:
Gastrointestinal tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A skin test for tuberculosis was positive at 22 millimeters induration. Two weeks later, sputum and stool cultures grew acid-fast bacilli, identified as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Figure 6).
Figure 6. AFB growth from culture.

A diagnosis of Crohn’s disease was initially made and high dose steroids, plus isoniazid for tuberculosis prophylaxis, were begun. After the cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, rifampin and isoniazid were administered and steroids were stopped.

An increase in the number of tuberculosis cases has been seen in the United States, because of the incidence of AIDS, drug abuse and an influx of immigrants from areas of high TB endemicity. Within the gastrointestinal tract, the ileocecal valve is the most common site of involvement. Symptoms are vague and non-specific, and may be acute, acute-on-chronic, or chronic in presentation. A positive purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test for tuberculosis is found in 70-86% of patients. Colonoscopy is the most valuable diagnostic tool and the diagnostic yield is increased by performing histology, smear and culture on all specimens.

title: A man with HIV infection, weakness and confusion.
history:
A man in his sixties, with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, developed changes in mental status, decreased oral intake, and generalized weakness.
One month earlier, he had been admitted to the hospital with pneumonia. Antibiotics were administered, with no improvement. Bronchoscopy was performed and Pneumocystis pneumonia diagnosed. Subsequent test results revealed antibody to human immunodeficiency virus, the CD4 cell count was 12 cells per microliter (6%) and HIV-RNA level was 389,000 copies/mL. Additional laboratory test results were negative, including testing for syphilis, hepatitis B and C antibodies, blood cultures for acid-fast bacilli, serum cryptococcal antigen, and toxoplasma antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, performed with gadolinium, showed no abnormalities. He was transferred to a skilled nursing facility for assistance with activities of daily living.
One month later, worsening mental status and increased fatigue developed, and he was no longer ingesting his medications. He was re-admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. On admission, a relative reported he had had weight loss of 50 pounds (approximately 23 kilograms) over three months.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and, as noted above, HIV infection. Four months before admission, colonoscopy had been normal.

He had no known risk factors for HIV infection. He had smoked cigarettes in the past; there was no history of alcohol or intravenous drug abuse. He had no pets, hobbies, or recent travel.

He was retired and married.

The patient was allergic to sulfa drugs, which had caused leukopenia.

Medications included dapsone and azithromycin.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic, and appeared comfortable. He was awake, alert, but not oriented. The blood pressure was 136/72 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats per minute, respirations 21 per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 97% while breathing ambient air. The temperature was 97.1ºF (36.2ºC). Examination of the oropharynx revealed white plaques on the tongue and palate. The patient was unable to cooperate with a complete neurologic examination, however cranial nerves were grossly intact, and motor strength was 4/5 in general. Gait was not tested. There was no lymphadenopathy or skin lesions, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 4,400 cells/microliter (neutrophils 69%, lymphocytes 19%, monocytes 11%, and eosinophils 1%), hemoglobin 9.4 grams per deciliter, and platelets 77,000/microliter. No schistocytes were present on blood smear. The plasma level of urea nitrogen was 92 mg/dL, creatinine 3.0 mg/dL, and glucose 471 mg/dL. Repeat CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 58 cells/microliter (8%) and the level of HIV-RNA was 388,000 copies/mL.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed age-related atrophy and some periventricular changes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed one white cell, which was a lymphocyte, protein 123 mg/dL, and glucose of 154 mg/dl. Testing of the CSF for syphilis (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test), cryptococcal antigen, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes simplex virus was negative. MRI of the head, compared with the study done one month earlier, revealed age-related atrophy and small vessel disease; there was no evidence of acute infection or mass effect. Three sets of blood cultures were negative. The blood cultures for acid-fast bacilli (drawn during the previous admission) remained negative.

The metabolic laboratory abnormalities corrected with intravenous fluid hydration. His mental status improved; he became more alert but remained disoriented. A diagnosis of AIDS dementia was suspected, and initiation of antiretroviral medication was planned after resolution of his acute issues. Dapsone and azithromycin were continued for Pneumocystis and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) prophylaxis, respectively, and pyrimethamine with leucovorin added for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis. On the 5th hospital day, oxygen saturation by pulse oximeter decreased to 86% on ambient air. A sonogram of the lower extremities revealed an acute deep venous thrombosis of the right leg. CT of the chest revealed multiple pulmonary emboli. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed an annular constricting mass of the ascending colon with marked narrowing of the lumen, which was thought to be consistent with carcinoma. The liver was normal. (See Figure 1, with arrow pointing to the annular mass.) Laboratory testing of carcinoembryonic antigen was normal (1.1 ng/mL). Colonoscopy was performed to the terminal ileum without difficulty. There was erythema and ulceration noted in the cecum near the ileocecal valve. The region of the ileocecal valve was edematous with erythema and ulceration on the mucosal surface; a biopsy was taken at this site (see Figure 2).
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen, with annular mass.
Figure 2. H and E stain of the ileocecal valve biopsy.
diagnosis:
Cytomegalovirus-associated pseudotumor of the colon, in a patient with HIV and AIDS.

Pathological examination of the biopsy revealed enlarged cells with nuclei containing structures suspicious for inclusion bodies (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytomegalovirus (Figure 3). Sections of cecum also showed an ulcerated focus with features suggestive of ischemia, surface erosion, and crypt atrophy; these findings were thought to be consistent with cytomegalovirus-induced vascular injury. Cytomegalovirus-associated pseudotumor of the colon was diagnosed.
Figure 3. Immunohistochemical stain of the biopsy.

Intravenous ganciclovir (5mg/kg twice daily) was administered. Ophthalmology was consulted; there was no evidence of retinitis. The patient underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube placement; no esophageal lesions were seen. On the 12th day of ganciclovir therapy, the patient experienced vomiting and a sudden decrease in his hemoglobin. Later that evening. the patient was found without pulse or respirations, and expired. No postmortem examination was performed.

Mass lesions in the gastrointestinal tract of immunocompromised patients can be caused by Kaposi’s sarcoma (60%), non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (35%), squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, or other sarcomas, but are rarely due to infectious pathogens such as cytomegalovirus (CMV). Cytomegalovirus intestinal disease is an erosive or ulcerative process in the wall of the gut in which the presence of CMV is shown by routine histologic exam, culture, antigen, or DNA staining, in a person in whom other explanations have been excluded. There are few case reports of pseudotumors of the gastrointestinal tract secondary to CMV. They have been reported as lesions of the right colon and ileocecal region, and less commonly as involving the esophagus, fundus, and pylorus. A mass lesion forms as result of CMV-induced stromal reactivity, vasculitic changes, inflammatory cell infiltration, and eventual fibrous replacement of the muscularis mucosa, leading to an exophytic luminal mass. Clinical presentation is often nonspecific, but patients may report abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea. Less commonly, patients can present with obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract or a palpable mass. Pathological examination of the lesions reveals classic cytomegalic cells with inclusion bodies, fibrosis, necrosis, and a positive immunoperoxidase stain. At the time of this writing, treatment is with ganciclovir induction therapy for two to three weeks followed by a maintenance dose. Foscarnet is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate ganciclovir. Surgery is reserved for patients presenting with evidence of intestinal obstruction.

title: A man with HIV infection and AIDS and fever, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy.
history:
A male in his forties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS, on highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART), presented with a 3-month history of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, progressive weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes in the neck, axilla, and groin.

There was a history of HIV-1 infection, cryptococcal meningitis, herpes zoster, hypertension, chronic renal insufficiency, and transfusion-dependent anemia. The most recent CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 152 cells/mm³ and the HIV-1 RNA level was less than 50 copies/mL.

He worked in an office setting, was sexually active with men only and was currently in a monogamous relationship. He smoked cigarettes and occasionally marijuana. There was no history of alcohol abuse, injection drug use, pet exposures, or recent travel.

Medications included abacavir/lamivudine, efavirenz, fluconazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and diltiazem.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic and appeared ill. The temperature was 100.5°F (38.1°C). The other vital signs were normal. There was tender, fixed bilateral lymphadenopathy in the preauricular, submandibular, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions. Edema was present at both ankles. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 5,900 cells/mm³ with a normal differential, hematocrit 23.4%, and platelets 221,000/mm³. The creatinine was 2.8 mg/dL with a glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL per minute. Albumin was 1.6 g/dL. Other routine laboratory test results were normal.
Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis (with the administration of oral contrast) revealed innumerable pathologically enlarged lymph nodes, within the supraclavicular, subpectoral, and axillary regions bilaterally. The largest node measured 3.3 cm in diameter (see Figure 1). Within the abdomen, the liver and spleen were diffusely enlarged, and the gastrohepatic and gastrosplenic lymph nodes were also enlarged (see Figure 2). In addition, numerous lymph nodes were enlarged within the retroperitoneal region, extending along both iliac chain, throughout the pelvis, and into the inguinal regions (Figure 3).
Figure 1. CT scan of chest.
Figure 2. CT scan of abdomen.
Figure 3. CT scan of pelvis.

An excisional biopsy of five inguinal lymph nodes was performed. Figures 4 and 5 reveal hematoxylin and eosin staining and immunohistochemical staining, respectively.
Figure 4. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of lymph node.
Figure 5. Immunohistochemical stain of lymph node.
diagnosis:
Castleman’s disease in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Five enlarged lymph nodes in the right axillary region were excised. Pathological examination of the axillary lymph node tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining (Figures 4 and 6) revealed regressively transformed germinal centers rimmed by lymphocytes (A), hyperplastic vessels with hyaline changes (B) and interfollicular areas with dense infiltrates of plasmacytes (C). Immunohistochemical stain demonstrated mantle zone positivity, characteristic of Castleman's disease (see Figure 5).
Figure 6. H and E stain of lymph node biopsy.

The patient was discharged, referred to oncology as an outpatient and started on chemotherapy. Several weeks later, he presented to the emergency room in acute respiratory distress with severe hypotension. He was intubated and started on pressors. Chest radiography showed infiltrates in the right middle lobe and left lower lobe.
Maximal amounts of pressors were administered, however, he remained hypotensive and developed pulseless electrical activity. Despite attempts at resuscitation, he expired.

Multicentric Castleman's disease (CD) is a rare clinicopathological entity that presents with fever, widespread lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and peripheral edema. There is also a localized, or unicentric, form of the disease.
Many HIV-positive patients with multicentric CD also have Kaposi’s sarcoma. Human herpes virus 8 (HHV8) has been detected in all cases studied. At this writing, no standardized treatment is available. However options include chemotherapy, anti-virals against HHV8, anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, and interferon alpha. The role of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in the treatment of CD is uncertain.

title: A man with right upper quadrant abdominal pain for six months.
history:
A man in his thirties was admitted to the hospital with intractable abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant, of six months’ duration. At the time of the onset of the abdominal pain, dyspnea and a productive cough had occurred, and resolved with no antibiotic therapy. He described the pain as “gnawing” and “pushing” in quality, gradually increasing over time and focused in the right upper quadrant. Lying on his right side exacerbated the pain.
During the previous 2-3 months, some swelling of the skin had developed over the area where he experienced the pain. He had had an occasional cough over the previous several weeks that was recently productive of purulent sputum. There was no hemoptysis, dyspnea, fevers, chills, or night sweats. He reported a normal appetite without early satiety or weight loss.

He was previously healthy with no known medical illnesses, no history of surgery, but had a history of a traumatic stab wound to the left scapular region.

The patient was incarcerated at the time of the onset of symptoms, and had previously lived in the Southwestern United States. Within the previous year, he had been in an automobile accident and had also suffered an assault with trauma. There was no travel outside the area, known tuberculosis exposure, animal exposure, recent stab wounds, bites, injections, other breaks in the skin at the site of his pain or intravenous drug use. He reported a ten pack-year smoking history, occasional alcohol consumption, and occasional marijuana use. A tuberculosis skin test had been negative within the year.
exam_studies:
On examination, he appeared well, and was fully alert and oriented. The temperature was 36.8°C (98.2°F), and other vital signs were normal. There was gingivitis and several teeth were chipped. The pulmonary exam did not reveal any adventitial breath sounds. Soft tissue swelling near the right lower costal border, roughly 3-4 centimeters in diameter, was present. There was no evidence of a break in the skin or sinus tract at the surface. He had moderate right upper quadrant tenderness in the region, without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds were present throughout. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 20,500 cells per mm³, with 80% granulocytes, 11% lymphocytes, and 9 % monocytes. The hemoglobin was 10.3 grams/deciliter and platelet count was 513,000 per mm³. The aspartate aminotransferase was 14 units per liter, alanine aminotransferase 30 units per liter, alkaline phosphatase 204 units per liter, and albumin was 3.5 grams/deciliter, urea nitrogen 13 milligrams/deciliter and creatinine of 0.6 milligrams/deciliter. The electrolytes were normal.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the lower thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a large subphrenic abscess, measuring 11.8 centimeters (cm) by 6.1 cm by 15.0 cm, with a multiseptated, peripherally enhancing, fluid collection. There was a second 3.7 cm by 6.2 cm collection just below the right ribcage in the subcutaneous tissues (Figure 1). Also noted was a small layering right pleural effusion with parenchymal airspace opacification that was suggestive of atelectasis or pneumonia (Figure 2).
Interventional radiologists placed a drain, and 500 cubic centimeters of thick, foul-smelling, purulent fluid was removed.
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT of the lower thorax.
diagnosis:
Subphrenic abscess due to Actinomyces israelii, and other anaerobic bacteria.

Gram stain of the aspirated fluid, shown in Figure 3, revealed numerous gram-positive, beaded filamentous rods. Actinomyces israelii grew in culture. The anaerobic cultures also grew Capnocytophaga and Fusobacterium species.
Figure 3. Gram stain of aspirate.

The patient was treated with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam. Within one week of therapy, a repeat CT scan revealed a marked decrease in size of the subphrenic abscess, as well as complete resolution of the thoracic disease. The drain was successfully removed, and he was discharged from the inpatient facility.

Actinomyces israelii is an anaerobic gram-positive beaded, filamentous rod typically found in the mouth. The organism is known to cause oral disease, such as “lumpy jaw,” as well as gastrointestinal disease and lung abscesses. In this particular patient, aspiration of a food particle or chipped tooth may have initiated the infection, which then crossed the diaphragm from the lung. Pelvic actinomycosis has also been associated with intra-uterine devices. Actinomyces tends to be a slow-growing organism that can cross normal tissue planes and create abscesses. As the infection progresses, the organism often forms sinus tracts, which may leak pus, as well as characteristic sulfur granules. At this writing, Actinomyces is susceptible to penicillin, which is the drug of choice for treatment.

title: A woman with acute myelogenous leukemia, neutropenia and fevers.
history:
A woman in her fifties with acute myelogenous leukemia became neutropenic after receiving the first cycle of chemotherapy (idarubicin and cytarabine). Fevers to 38.8°C (101.8°F) and chills occurred, associated with rhinorrhea and a mild headache. An infectious disease consult was obtained.

There was a history of acute myelogenous leukemia, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and seasonal allergies with chronic sinusitis.

The patient lived in the Southern United States with her husband, worked in an office and did not use tobacco, alcohol, or drugs. She had not traveled recently and had no pets.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 38.7°C (101.7°F), blood pressure 155/80 mm Hg, pulse 98 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. The patient appeared comfortable. There was clear nasal discharge but no sinus tenderness. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 500 cells/mm³, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dl, and platelet count 4000 cells/mm³. Results of a serum chemistry panel were normal. Cultures of the blood and urine were sterile. A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed moderate mucosal thickening of the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses on the left (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT of the head.

Sinusitis was diagnosed, and surgical debridement of the affected sinuses performed. Intraoperatively, specimens were sent for culture and pathological examination. Pathological evaluation of the sinus tissues revealed tissue necrosis and fungal hyphae with invasion of the lamina propria of the respiratory mucosa. (See Figures 2 through 5.) Amphotericin B was initiated pending the results of the cultures.
Figure 2. H and E stain, magnified x 200.
Figure 3. H and E stain, magnified x 400.
Figure 4. H and E stain, magnified x 400.
Figure 5. H and E stain magnified x 400.
diagnosis:
Invasive fungal sinusitis caused by Curvularia, a dematiaceous filamentous fungus, in an immunocompromised, neutropenic patient.

Fungal tissue cultures of the sinuses obtained intraoperatively showed Curvularia, a dematiaceous filamentous fungus (see Figures 6 and 7).
Figure 6. Fungal culture of biopsy specimen.
Figure 7. Fungal culture.

Amphotericin B was administered for 14 days, followed by therapy with voriconazole. The fevers resolved and her symptoms of headache and rhinorrhea improved. On follow-up endoscopic evaluation by the Otolaryngology service, there was no evidence of recurrence of infection. The neutropenia resolved, and she was discharged from the hospital in good condition. Another cycle of chemotherapy was administered, without evidence of recurrence of fungal sinusitis. She remained on suppressive therapy with voriconazole.

Invasive fungal sinusitis is usually seen in immunosuppressed patients, including those with hematologic malignancies, bone marrow transplants, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, solid organ transplants, advanced HIV disease, and diabetes mellitus. It may be due to invasion of fungi, which have chronically colonized the sinuses in patients with a history of chronic sinusitis or anatomic abnormalities of the sinuses. The fungi establish local infection and then invade tissues. The disease may be rapidly progressive depending on the degree of immunosuppression. Spread is by direct extension but fungemia with metastatic spread can occur.
Some of the fungi implicated in invasive fungal sinusitis in immunosuppressed patients are listed in the differential diagnosis section above. Clinical presentation may include fever, facial pain, nasal congestion, epistaxis, or visual disturbances. A non-specific diagnosis of sinusitis may be made by imaging studies (such as computed tomography) but prompt surgical evaluation is necessary to establish the diagnosis of fungal sinusitis as well as to obtain culture data. Treatment is urgent surgical debridement.
Amphotericin B is often used for initial therapy, followed by continued therapy with an agent appropriate for the organism. Intravenous therapy is generally continued until clinical response or reversal of immunocompromising conditions in achieved. Chronic suppressive therapy may be employed thereafter. Curvularia is a dematiaceous filamentous fungus with a dark cell wall. It can cause sinusitis, brain abscesses, and cutaneous disease in both humans and animals. Limited data is available on management of this organism and there is no standard method for in-vitro susceptibility testing of
Curvularia species. In-vitro data showed that Amphotericin B, ketoconazole, miconazole, itraconazole, and voriconazole have low minimum inhibitory concentrations for Curvularia, so these agents are usually employed for treatment of this organism.

title: A woman with fevers and a swollen neck.
history:
A woman in her thirties presented with neck swelling and intermittent fevers up to 102.5°F (39.2°C) of three weeks’ duration. Rapid strep testing and a heterophile antibody test were negative. An empiric course of amoxicillin was given with no improvement. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck showed extensive cervical lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). After three weeks of persistent symptoms, she was referred to Otolaryngology for a lymph node biopsy.
Figure 1. CT scan of the neck.

There was a history of a positive tuberculosis skin test as a child and cervical dysplasia. It was not known if she had received prophylactic isoniazid treatment.

She was born in Korea, and had lived in Germany, the Southern United States, before living in the Northeastern United States with her boyfriend and child. There was no recent travel outside the Northeast. She had no pets and no recent new sexual exposures.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure was 112/94 mm Hg and pulse 80 beats per minute. There was extensive adenopathy in the left anterior and posterior neck, and smaller nodes in the scalene and submandibular regions were palpated on the left. No thrush or oral lesions were noted. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 2,900 cells per cubic millimeter with 53% segmented cells, 30% lymphocytes, 8% bands, 8% monocytes and one atypical lymphocyte. The hematocrit was 42% and platelets were 329,000 per cubic millimeter. Results of routine chemistries and liver function tests were normal, and HIV screening was negative.

A lymph node biopsy was performed(Figure 2). Figure 2. Biopsy results.
Figure 2. Biopsy results.
diagnosis:
Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.

Lymph node biopsy revealed necrotizing lymphadenitis consistent with Kukuchi- Fujimoto disease (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 3. Biopsy with cresentic shaped nuclei.

Kukuchi-Fujimoto disease is a form of necrotizing lymphadenitis. It was originally identified in Japan in 1972, but has now been described in Europe, the United States and the Middle East. Patients may present over a broad age range but the majority of patients present before thirty with a female predominance.
The pathogenesis is unknown, however efforts have been made to implicate a post-viral exposure reaction to Epstein-Barr virus, parainfluenza, and human herpes virus six. Reaction to environmental stimuli has also been proposed. It is typically self-limited though it may take several months to resolve.
Lymph node pathology shows patchy necrosis with marked nuclear fragmentations (karyorrhexis). Distinctive “crescentic-shaped” histiocytes are thought to be pathognomonic. The pathological differential diagnosis includes other types of necrotizing lymphadenitis, such as herpes simplex virus and lymphoma. It is often mistaken for lymphoma: a review of 108 cases [Dorfman and Berry 1988] revealed that up to 30% of cases were initially mistaken for lymphoma.

title: An African woman with breast cancer and anorexia. A woman in her sixties, with locally advanced adenocarcinoma of the breast, developed anorexia.
history:
An evaluation for metastatic disease revealed dilatation of the common bile duct, associated with a filling defect.

Breast cancer had been diagnosed and a lumpectomy and axillary node dissection performed. There was also a history of asthma and a positive tuberculin skin test. She had not received isoniazid prophylaxis.

The patient was raised on a farm in East Africa and then moved to an urban area. She had traveled to the northern Lakes region of the United States within the previous year to visit relatives. She was exposed to sheep many years earlier, and had ingested fresh water and raw vegetables in Africa. She did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.
exam_studies:
The weight was 47.3 kilograms (104 pounds) and the temperature was normal. No cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymph nodes were palpable. The thyroid gland was enlarged, non-tender with a 2-centimeter nodule in the left lobe, which was a chronic and stable finding. The abdomen was not tender and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. There was a healed surgical scar on the inferior, outer quadrant of left breast, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 4500 cells/mm³, with 4% eosinophils. Serum levels of liver enzymes and bilirubin were normal. Thyroid studies were within normal limits. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus, types 1 and 2 (HIV-1 and -2, by ELISA) was negative. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen is shown in Figure 1, with arrows, and revealed subcapsular enhancement of the liver (A) and a dilated common bile duct (B).
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen.

Finding on endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) are shown (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. ERCP findings.
Figure 3. ERCP findings.
diagnosis:
Fasciola hepatica.

ERCP showed a live liver fluke of Fasciola hepatica. The examination of stool did not reveal Fasciola eggs.

Nitazoxanide (500 mg) was administered twice daily for seven days. The patient’s symptoms resolved and there was no evidence of eggs on follow-up stool microscopy.

Fasciola hepatica is a trematode flatworm, and the hermaphroditic adult fluke is brown, leaf-shaped, and measures approximately 3 x 1.5 centimeters. Transmission is usually through ingestion of fresh water plants (such as water cress) containing infectious metacercariae. Following ingestion, immature stages of the parasite penetrate the intestinal wall, migrate through the peritoneal cavity, and penetrate through the hepatic capsule. The immature parasites then migrate through hepatic parenchyma until they reach the biliary tracts where they mature and begin to lay eggs that are passed through the bile into the feces to be expelled from the body. The parasite then completes its lifecycle in specific snail intermediate hosts. During the hepatic migratory phase, patients are often symptomatic with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia, and peripheral eosinophilia may be prominent. Imaging studies often disclose migratory "tracts" within hepatic parenchyma. Once the parasites reach the biliary tracts, symptoms usually resolve, and patients may be relatively asymptomatic for years. Fascioliasis is global in distribution.
At the time of this publication, standard treatment is with triclabendazole or bithionol, neither of which is commercially available in the United States. In a single study, administration of nitazoxanide was also associated with clearance of eggs from stool in 40% of children and 60% of adults with fascioliasis.

title: Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with HIV infection and cough, d
history:
Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with HIV infection and cough, dyspnea on exertion and fevers.
A woman in her forties, with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (Background medical information such as HIV status is important to include early in the history, since it greatly changes the differential diagnosis. An HIV person with cough and fever is at high risk for ordinary infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, but compared to the general population is at much more increased risk of opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis or tuberculosis.) (HIV) infection, was admitted to the hospital with fevers and dyspnea. She had been well until approximately 6 weeks (The tempo of symptoms provides important diagnostic clues. All common bacterial and viral infections of the lungs would earlier have resolved or become obvious within a couple of weeks. This prolonged course suggests fungal or mycobacterial infection, or non-infectious causes.) earlier when she noted fatigue. During the following month, fevers, dry cough (Typical bacterial pneumonia will often cause cough productive of purulent sputum. A dry cough suggests viral, fungal, or atypical bacteria.), and dyspnea on exertion developed gradually. Two weeks before admission, she was seen in an emergency department. A chest radiograph (Cough and fever with a normal chest radiograph would suggest bronchitis in a normal host, and should be treated symptomatically, rather than with antibiotics. With HIV, this pattern should always raise concern for Pneumocystic jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) or TB and a microbiological diagnosis must be sought, rather than the institution of empiric therapy.) (Figure 1) was normal. Levofloxacin (A quinolone antibiotic with good activity against most respiratory pathogens. It has some activity against TB and may thus confuse or delay the diagnosis.) was prescribed for a 10-day course, however she only took a 5-day course of the medication.
Thirteen days after her initial visit, and 6 days after the antibiotic was taken, she was seen in an outpatient infectious disease clinic because of increasing shortness of breath and cough, associated with dyspnea on exertion, fevers, headaches, and chills. She had paroxysms of cough (Fits of coughing are seen more commonly with certain pathogens, such as Bordatella pertussis.) intermittently and diarrhea (Extra-pulmonary signs can be a clue since certain pathogens such as Legionella or Mycoplasma can have prominent symptoms outside the lungs.) once or twice daily. There was no photophobia or stiff neck.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph 13 days before admission.

More than 10 years earlier, HIV infection had been diagnosed. One year before her presentation, the CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 81 cells per microliter and the plasma level of HIV RNA was 273,000 copies per milliliter. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) that included tenofovir, emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir (TDF/FTC/ATV/RTV) was begun. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count increased to 690 cells per microliter and the level of HIV RNA became undetectable. Approximately 2.5 months before admission, scleral icterus occurred and she discontinued the medications. Ten days before admission, the CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 203 cells per microliter (Risk of opportunistic infections begins to rise rapidly once CD4 counts go below 200 cells per microliter.) (23%).
One year earlier, anemia of uncertain etiology had been noted, with a normal level of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase. There was a history of aphthous ulcers.

She worked in a medically related field. She did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs, and denied recent travel or exposures to animals.

She was allergic to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole would be the main drug used for PJP prophylaxis, but HIV patients have a higher rate of sulfa allergy.), which had caused a rash, and possibly to dapsone. Erythromycin had caused gastrointestinal distress.
exam_studies:
She appeared ill and tremulous, with frequent coughing. The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C) and rose to 103.9°F (39.9°C), blood pressure 116/60 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respirations 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92%-96% (An oxygen saturation level this low in a young person breathing this fast suggests a substantial A-a gradient.) while breathing ambient air. There was conjunctival icterus; the left tympanic membrane revealed a fluid level and the right ear canal was impacted with cerumen. Crackles were heard in the lungs bilaterally, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

A chest radiograph (Cough and fever with a normal chest radiograph would suggest bronchitis in a normal host, and should be treated symptomatically, rather than with antibiotics. With HIV, this pattern should always raise concern for Pneumocystic jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) or TB and a microbiological diagnosis must be sought, rather than the institution of empiric therapy.) was normal (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Chest radiograph on admission.

High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is shown in Figure 3. The same CT image is depicted in Figure 4, with a portion magnified.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest, high resolution.
Figure 4. CT scan of the chest, with portion magnified.
diagnosis:
Pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii, formerly called Pneumocystis carinii, in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Sputum was induced and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing for Pneumocystis jirovecii (previously known as Pneumocystis carinii) was positive (Figure 5). The plasma level of (1, 3)-beta-D-glucan ((1, 3)-beta-D-glucan is a component of fungal cell walls, and its presence in serum denotes invasive fungal disease. P. jirovecii is a fungus, albeit a somewhat unusual one that was previously thought to be a protozoan. The presence of an elevated 1,3 -beta-D-glucan level with a normal galactomannan level may help distinguish Pneumocystis infection from invasive aspergillosis, a condition in which both tests are more likely to be elevated.) was greater than 500 pg/ml (reference range: greater than 80 pg/ml is positive).
Figure 5. DFA of an induced sputum specimen.

Steroids, clindamycin and primaquine (A second line therapy that can be used in trimethoprim-sulfa allergy.) were administered. The latter two were initially started because of possible allergies to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and dapsone. After further discussion and review of her history, the medications were changed to dapsone and trimethoprim (Most allergies are to the sulfa component.). A hemolytic anemia developed, however, which was thought to be due to dapsone; treatment with clindamycin and primaquine were resumed. A trial of atovaquone was stopped secondary to dysgeusia (A distortion in the sense of taste.).
The hospital course was also complicated by gram-negative bacteremia caused by Enterobacter cloacae, which occurred following placement of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Additional antibiotic therapy directed against this organism was given (initially with cefepime empirically, followed by ceftriaxone and, finally, ciprofloxacin orally). No other source for this infection was documented. A new regimen of antiretroviral therapy, which included lopinavir-ritonavir and emtricitabine-tenofovir, was begun.
At the time of discharge, she had improved: breathing ambient air for approximately one week, able to ambulate up and down the stairs while maintaining an oxygen saturation of 90% or greater, and afebrile for 48 hours. Her cough had nearly resolved and laboratory tests of liver function were normal.

Pneumocystis jirovecii, formerly called Pneumocystis carinii, is known to cause pneumonia in immunosuppressed individuals, and was one of the first infections associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) in the 1980's. It was initially thought to be protozoal; however, genetic analysis has led to its identification as a fungus.
This case illustrates the subacute course that can be seen in patients with HIV infection and AIDS who develop Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). Also of note is how patients with PCP can have a normal chest radiograph (a finding which occurs in about 10% of HIV-infected patients with PCP). Computed tomography of the chest is more sensitive than the chest radiograph for demonstrating PCP-related findings.

title: Summary: An African man in his twenties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
history:
Summary: An African man in his twenties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and cough, fever and shortness of breath.
A South African man in his twenties presented to a hospital in Kwa-Zulu Natal province because of cough, fever and acute shortness of breath, which was not related to exertion or position. He had not felt well for the previous two months, and reported symptoms of cough with white sputum, fever, poor appetite and loss of weight. At a clinic visit three weeks earlier, a chest radiograph was normal and the sputum was negative for acid-fast bacilli. He had recently completed a short course of antibiotics, without improvement. There was no pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis or leg pain or swelling.

He was HIV positive; the level of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells was not known. There was no history of asthma.

He lived with a sibling, who had been hospitalized for one month with tuberculosis two years earlier. He had smoked cigarettes briefly in the past.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared cachectic and in mild respiratory distress. The temperature was 99.5°F (37.5°C) orally, pulse 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 95/53 mm Hg, and respirations 26 breaths per minute. There was oral thrush and no lymphadenopathy. The jugular venous pressure was normal. The trachea was midline. The chest was clear to auscultation on the right side and there were absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion on the left side. Extremities were symmetrical without swelling, tenderness, or erythema.

The white blood count was 6,400/uL, hematocrit 18%, and platelet count 418,000/uL. Serum testing for sodium was 133 mEq/L, potassium 5.2 mEq/L, chloride 107 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 14 mEq/L. An arterial blood gas revealed a pH of 7.47, partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 26.5 mm Hg, and partial pressure of oxygen of 161 mm Hg, on supplemental oxygen. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 78 cells/uL.
A chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
diagnosis:
Pneumothorax secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis, in an African patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

A chest radiograph revealed a large left-sided pneumothorax (Figure 1). The patient was continued on supplemental oxygen, and a chest tube was placed. Upon re-expansion of the lung, a parenchymal cavity became evident (Figure 2).
On the 3rd hospital day, a stain of a sputum specimen revealed acid-fast bacilli, consistent with Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, after chest tube placement.

Four-drug tuberculosis therapy was initiated. The chest tube was clamped five days after placement. There was no evidence of recurrence of the pneumothorax by chest radiograph 24 hours later. The patient’s dyspnea and fever curve improved on therapy. He was discharged to a step-down facility and referred for outpatient HIV care.

Patients with HIV infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) are at increased risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. Most reported cases in patients with HIV have been related to Pneumocystis jiroveci (PCP) infection and, in patients with PCP, pneumothorax is an independent risk factor for poor outcome. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) also can cause pneumothorax among patients with or without HIV infection through rupture of a cavitary lesion into the pleural space. Any pneumothorax in a patient with HIV infection is an indication to rule out concurrent infection with PCP or TB. Other less common causes of pneumothorax in patients with HIV infection include pulmonary cryptococcosis, cavitary bacterial or fungal pneumonia, and pulmonary Kaposi’s sarcoma [Floris et al 1989; Martinez-Vazquez et al 2001;Torre et al 1995].
Small pneumothoraces (<1 cm rim) can often be managed conservatively with oxygen therapy and followed to resolution with serial imaging. However for large or symptomatic pneumothoraces, tube thoracostomy is normally indicated. Bronchopleural fistula is a feared complication and in such cases surgical or medical pleurodesis may be effective. Patients with Pneumocystis jiroveci tend to have large subpleural cysts and parenchymal necrosis, and are more likely to have a persistent air leak requiring aggressive management.

title: 2008 January Featured Case Summary: A man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV
history:
2008 January Featured Case Summary: A man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and increasing dyspnea for one week.
A man in his fifties with a history of HIV infection, who had been lost to follow-up for 13 months, presented to the outpatient infectious disease clinic because of progressive dyspnea on exertion. Seven days earlier, he had first noticed significant shortness of breath after a long bicycle ride, associated with minimal cough productive of clear sputum. During the following week, his symptoms increased in severity to dyspnea at rest.
He had lost weight during the preceding 3-4 months, though he was unsure of the amount. Two months before presentation, blurred vision had developed, and during the preceding 2 weeks, he had noted some "floaters" in his left eye. During the month before presentation, white material in his mouth developed that he attempted to clear with mouthwash. He experienced worsening chest discomfort, which he attributed to gastric reflux symptoms, that progressed to odynophagia over the 1-2 weeks preceding his visit. Approximately 3 days before presentation, intermittent headaches developed, which he attributed to frustration at being unable to eat. There was no fever and he did not have a headache at presentation.

There was a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Thirteen months earlier, the CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 215 cells/mm³ (17.4%) and the plasma HIV RNA level was 177,000 copies per milliliter. He had subsequently been lost to follow-up until the current presentation. He had never taken antiretroviral medications.
There was also a history of hypertension, eczema, recurrent herpes simplex virus on the buttocks, latent tuberculosis (treated with at least 6 months of isoniazid 5 years earlier), latent syphilis and possible neurosyphilis (treated five years earlier).

He drank alcohol, had used intranasal cocaine in the recent past, and smoked cigarettes. He did not own pets. He had had sexual activity with men, but was not currently sexually active.

He lived with a roommate and worked sporadically.

His only medication was hydrochlorothiazide (25 mg daily).
exam_studies:
He was thin and appeared in moderate respiratory distress. The blood pressure was 110/71 mm Hg, pulse 97 beats per minute, respirations 24-40 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 93% while breathing 60% oxygen administered by face mask. The temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C). There was angular cheilitis and the oropharynx revealed patchy hyperpigmentation. There were fine scattered inspiratory crackles in both lungs, extending from the bases to 2/3 up the lung fields posteriorly. There was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 6,500 cells/mm³ (reference range 4,500-11,000) with 78% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes and 1% basophils, hematocrit 36.1% (reference range 41.0-53.0), and hemoglobin 12.1 gm/dl (13.5-17.5). Lactic dehydrogenase was 505 U/L (reference range 110-210). Results of plasma electrolytes, and tests of renal and liver function were normal. Test results for cardiac isoenzymes and troponin T were negative. An electrocardiogram revealed a normal sinus rhythm with left atrial enlargement, and non-specific ST segment and T wave changes.
Chest radiographs are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 2. Lateral view of chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest is shown in Figures 3, 4 and 5.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 4. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 5. CT scan of the chest.
diagnosis:
Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia, in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS, with Cytomegalovirus and Herpes Simplex virus co-infections.

The chest radiographs revealed diffuse alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, with some bullous disease in the apices. The CT scan of the chest demonstrated paraseptal and centrilobular emphysema, diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities, with increasing confluence of consolidation in the bases, and sparing of the bases more inferiorly. There was also a 7-millimeter nodule at the right apex.
Immunofluorescent staining of an induced sputum specimen for Pneumocystis jirovecii was positive, (Figure 6), and revealed the ovoid organisms in clusters. Testing for respiratory viruses and cultures of the sputum for tuberculosis were negative.
Figure 6. Immunofluorescent stain for Pneumocystis.

High dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone 40 mg twice daily, orally, were begun immediately upon admission, for a presumptive diagnosis of Pneumocystis pneumonia. His pulmonary status gradually improved over the course of his admission. At the time of discharge, he was comfortable at rest while breathing ambient air, and was able to perform activities of daily living without significant difficulty.
Fluconazole was administered empirically for his odynophagia, with little improvement. Subsequently, an endoscopic examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract was performed and revealed diffuse grade IV esophagitis with ulceration. Immunohistochemistry was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV), types 1 and 2. Viral cultures of specimens obtained during the endoscopy grew CMV and HSV, type 1. Immunofluorescent stain of HSV is shown in Figure 7. Ganciclovir was administered intravenously; his odynophagia and oral intake of solids and liquids improved. Ganciclovir was changed to oral valganciclovir.
Examination by an ophthalmologist revealed no evidence of CMV retinitis, although a cotton wool spot and a partial vitreous detachment on the left were noted. At discharge, medications included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength, 2 tablets three times daily for 8 days and followed by 1 tablet daily indefinitely; prednisone 20 mg for 8 days, valganciclovir, atenolol, clotrimazole troches, azithromycin, protonix and mupirocin 2% cream as needed to areas on his face. Two days after discharge, he returned to clinic and highly-active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was prescribed.
Figure 7. Immunofluorescent stain of HSV from culture.

Pneumocystis, an organism known to cause infections in immunocompromised hosts, was one of the pathogens diagnosed in the first reports of the disease that became known as acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) [CDC 1981 (1) and CDC 1981 (2)]. Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) was named one of the first AIDS-defining illnesses.
It was initially thought to be protozoal; however, genetic analysis of Pneumocystis has led to its identification as a fungus. Subsequent research indicated that Pneumocystis is host-specific; that is, a strain that infects rats does not appear to be the same as that which infects humans. Consequently, the name of the human pathogen was changed from Pneumocystis carinii, which was isolated from rats, to Pneumocystis jiroveci, and then to Pneumocystis jirovecii [Walzer and Smulian 2005].
Pneumocystis infection is acquired and communicable, and its distribution is worldwide. Specific seasonal variation has not been clearly established. The most common presenting symptoms include fever, dyspnea, and cough, which is often non-productive. Infection in patients with HIV may develop sub-acutely (especially in comparison to immunocompromised individuals not infected with HIV), with symptoms occurring gradually over a period of weeks to months. Chest radiographs typically reveal diffuse interstitial changes in the perihilar regions, though significant radiographic variability occurs, ranging from clear lung fields to focal infiltrates and cavities. High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) that demonstrates ground glass opacities may be helpful in suggesting a diagnosis of PCP, particularly in the setting of a normal chest radiograph. Culture of the organism remains difficult; diagnosis is often made by pathological examination of secretions or tissue, with the use of immunofluorescent or other staining, or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing [Walzer and Smulian 2005].
In this patient, who was known to be infected with HIV and presented with severe dyspnea and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest radiography, the diagnosis of PCP was immediately considered, and appropriate treatment begun. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) infection was also considered given the high-rate of M. tb co-infection with HIV, his previous history of infection and recent weight loss. Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Legionella pneumophila might also present with bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Although Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can cause a similar radiographic picture, it is an uncommon cause of pneumonia in patients with AIDS. Streptococcus pneumoniae infection would more commonly present as a focal lobar consolidation. The presence of Pneumocystis co-infection with cytomegalovirus has been reported previously [Lemert et al 1996, Drut el al 1997]. Of interest is the documentation of a third co-infection, herpes simplex virus, in this patient.
