title: 2008 February Featured Case Summary: An elderly woman with pain in the right sho
history:
2008 February Featured Case Summary: An elderly woman with pain in the right shoulder and skin changes of the left forearm five weeks after surgery on the left arm.
A woman in her seventies with diabetes mellitus and chronic renal failure was admitted to the hospital because of severe right shoulder pain and skin changes over an arteriovenous (A-V) fistula on the left forearm. Five weeks before admission, the A-V fistula had been surgically created, and the immediate post-operative period had been without complication.
One week before presentation, left arm pain and swelling developed, associated with blistering at the surgical site. Two days later, on awakening, the patient noted pain in the right shoulder, and limitation of movement developed. There was no history of trauma to the joint, fevers, chills, diaphoresis, headache, neck stiffness, chest or back pain, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or other joint pain. The next day, four days before admission, she was seen in the emergency room of another hospital, and given pain medications. The pain increased in intensity, and she was brought to the hospital for evaluation.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus, end stage renal disease, coronary artery and peripheral vascular disease, hyperlipidemia and hypertension.

She lived in a wooded area. There were several pets in the home (two small dogs and a cat), with which she played and that licked her hands. She had smoked cigarettes, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She denied travel to other countries or known exposure to tuberculosis.

She lived with her daughter.

She was allergic to hydralazine, which had caused hives.

Medications on admission that were taken daily included aspirin 81 mg, amlodipine, metoprolol, atorvastatin, NPH insulin, pantoprazole, and polysaccharide-iron complex. Calcium acetate was administered three times daily, furosemide twice daily, calcitriol every other day, and epoetin alfa subcutaneously twice weekly..
exam_studies:
The patient appeared frail. The temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C), pulse 65 beats per minute, blood pressure 150/67 mm Hg, respirations 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula. Auscultation of the heart revealed a normal S1 and S2 heart sounds with a 3 of 6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. Palpation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) revealed no tenderness or overlying erythema. There were rare basilar crackles heard in the lungs. The left arm was swollen and large blisters were noted over the arteriovenous graft site; a thrill was present. Clear discharge emanated from the blisters; there was no erythema or increased warmth. Multiple ecchymoses were seen on the right arm and the right shoulder was tender to palpation anteriorly and posteriorly. Severe pain in the shoulder with motion and fluctuance of the soft tissue, consistent with an anterior shoulder effusion, were noted; there was no increased warmth. The legs demonstrated trace edema and hyperpigmentation consistent with venous stasis changes.

The white cell count of the blood was 11,900 cells per cubic millimeters, hematocrit 29.6%, mean corpuscular volume 98 cubic microliters, and platelets 201,000 per cubic millimeters. The prothrombin time was 13.8 seconds, INR 1.2, and partial thromboplastin time 33.4 seconds. The level of plasma sodium was 130 mmol/l, potassium 4.1 mmol/l, chloride 93 mmol/l and carbon dioxide 93 mEq/l; urea nitrogen was 114 mg/dl and creatinine 6.8 mg/dl, glucose 184 mg/dl, calcium 9.0 mg/dl and phosphorus 6.3 mg/dl.
A radiograph of the right shoulder revealed progressive erosion and degenerative changes of the humeral joint. Computed tomography (CT) of the right shoulder, shown in Figures 1 and 2, revealed a fluid collection around the shoulder joint that extended down into the triceps.
Figure 1. CT of right shoulder.
Figure 2. CT of right shoulder.

Cultures of the blood were sent, after which vancomycin and gentamicin were administered empirically. On the 2nd hospital day, a right internal jugular dialysis catheter was placed. Two days later, the blood cultures remained sterile. The right shoulder joint was aspirated; examination of the aspirate revealed 200,000 white cells per cubic millimeter with 94% polymorphonuclear cells. A gram stain of the aspirate is shown in Figure 3.
Irrigation and debridement of the shoulder joint was performed intraoperatively. Pathological examination of the tissue demonstrated inflammatory tissue without frank purulence. On the 4th hospital day, ultrasonography of the left forearm revealed an abscess, which was drained, and 10 cubic centimeters of purulent fluid was evacuated.
Figure 3. Gram stain of aspirate.
diagnosis:
Septic arthritis of the right shoulder and soft tissue infection of the left forearm caused by Pasteurella multocida.

The gram stain of the aspirate revealed numerous leukocytes and one cluster of gram-negative bacilli (Figure 4, with arrow). Culture of the organism grew Pasteurella multocida, shown in Figures 5 and 6.
Figure 4. Gram stain of aspirate with organisms (arrows).
Figure 5. Culture plate of aspirate.
Figure 6. Gram stain of culture growth.

Antimicrobial therapy was changed to intravenous ceftazidime. Several days after the initiation of therapy, erythema and fluctuance developed in the left hand. Incision and drainage of the site yielded clear fluid, which contained no detectable leukocytes. There were no organisms seen on gram stain and aerobic culture remained sterile. Subsequently, she demonstrated steady clinical improvement, with resolution of pain in the right shoulder. She completed a total of six weeks of antimicrobial therapy and has remained well since.

Pasteurella multocida is a facultatively anaerobic, gram-negative coccobacillus that is known to cause skin and soft tissue infections following cat and dog bites. The genus was first characterized by Pasteur in 1880. Pasteurella grows readily on sheep blood and chocolate agar media. The colonies appear watery and mucoid with a smooth, iridescent blue character [Zurlo 2005].
The organism inhabits the oral cavity and gastrointestinal tract of a wide variety of animals, with particularly high levels of colonization in cats. Pasteurella may also colonize the respiratory tract of humans. Its distribution is worldwide [Zurlo 2005].
Human infection with Pasteurella commonly manifests as cellulitis or soft tissue abscess following an animal bite or other animal contact [Zurlo 2005, Octavio et al 2001], including the licking of open wounds. Localized signs of infection typically develop within 24 hours, and may be associated with regional lymphadenopathy. Fever is present in only 20% of cases [Zurlo 2005].
Though rare, other reported manifestations of P. multocida infection include septic arthritis and osteomyelitis; bacteremia and endocarditis; upper and lower respiratory tract infections; and intra-abdominal infections. In a literature review of 14 cases of Pasteurella septic arthritis, half were associated with animal bites, approximately one-third involved animal exposure without known bites or scratches, and in two cases there was no animal exposure. Infection commonly involved joints affected by rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or joint prosthesis [Ewing et al 1980].
As of this writing, penicillin remains the drug of choice for the treatment of Pasteurella infection. Ampicillin and amoxicillin are also effective, whereas the antistaphylococcal penicillins (oxacillin, dicloxacillin) have less in vitro activity and should be avoided. Second and third generation cephalosporins have excellent activity. Of note, beta-lactamase producing strains have been reported.
For penicillin-allergic individuals, treatment with fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and tetracyclines may be considered. Aminoglycosides are not recommended for treatment of P. multocida infections [Zurlo 2005].

title: 2008 March Featured Case and IDSA 2007 Fellows Day Case Presentation Summary: A
history:
2008 March Featured Case and IDSA 2007 Fellows Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with fevers and skin lesions after surgery.
A woman in her fifties suffered an intraparenchymal hemorrhage of the brain, for which hemi-craniotomy and clot evacuation were performed. The four-week post-operative course was complicated by a ventilator-associated pneumonia that was treated with vancomycin and cefepime. Fevers persisted while she was receiving these antibiotics, despite resolution of the pneumonia by radiography. Cultures of blood, urine and cerebral spinal fluid were sterile. Vancomycin and cefepime were discontinued after fourteen days, and the temperatures returned to normal.
The patient remained afebrile for six days off all antibiotics, and then returned to the operating room for placement of ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt, followed by revision of the right craniotomy flap. Immediately post-operatively, fever to 38.9°C developed and the blood pressure transiently dropped to 80s/40s mm Hg. Specimens of blood and urine were cultured, and vancomycin and cefepime administered. Over the next twelve hours, the temperature rose to 40.6°C (105.1°F) and a rash developed.

There was a past medical history of hypercholesterolemia.

She was allergic to penicillin, but the reaction to this medication was unknown.

Other medications included levetiracetam, lansoprazole, lisinopril and metoprolol.
exam_studies:
The patient was sedated and mechanically ventilated with minimal oxygen requirements. The maximum temperature was 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse 108 beats per minute and blood pressure 112/52 mm Hg. A tracheostomy tube, gastric tube and subclavian triple lumen catheter were in place. There was a non-blanching erythematous eruption with tense bullae on the skin (Figures 1 through 3). Nikolsky sign was negative.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 11,900 cells/microliter with a normal differential and no eosinophils. The creatinine was 0.7 milligrams/deciliter and urinalysis revealed trace protein, but was otherwise normal. A gram stain of the culture sent from the operative site during the craniotomy revision revealed gram-positive cocci.

A punch biopsy of the skin was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the sample showed a sub-epidermal blister with numerous neutrophils (Figure 4).
Figure 4. H and E stain of biopsy.
diagnosis:
Antibiotic-induced linear IgA bullous dermatosis, caused by vancomycin.

A portion of the punch biopsy of the skin was sent for direct immunofluorescence, which revealed linear deposits of immunoglobulin (Ig) A along the dermal-epidermal junction (Figure 5).
Figure 5. IgA immunofluorescent stain of biopsy.

Cultures from the operative site grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Cefepime was discontinued, but fevers persisted and new bullous lesions extended proximally up the patient’s extremities. Vancomycin was then discontinued and linezolid was begun; the fever resolved and the bullous rash improved. The patient completed a course of linezolid and rifampin for treatment of post-operative MRSA meningitis and ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt infection. Several weeks later, after the patient had recovered, she recalled that she had had a similar skin reaction (described as a “blistering sunburn”) several years earlier, possibly after receiving vancomycin.

Linear immunoglobulin (Ig) A bullous dermatosis (LABD) is an autoantibody-mediated subepidermal blistering disease that is often idiopathic or, less commonly, drug-induced. Drug-induced LABD usually develops within one to 15 days after the first dose of the offending medication and resolves within two weeks of its discontinuation. Clinically, this disorder is characterized by tense blisters in linear or annular groups that cluster preferentially on the trunk, extremities, palms, soles, and spare the head and neck. On histological examination, the blisters are sub-epidermal and filled with neutrophils, as seen in this case. Direct immunofluorescence reveals linear deposition of IgA at the dermal-epidermal junction; the antigenic targets of the autoantibodies are located in the basement membrane zone. Drug-induced LABD is most frequently reported with vancomycin, but has also been reported with penicillins, cephalosporins, lithium, furosemide, amiodarone and phenytoin. The development of vancomycin-induced LABD is not dose dependent and the severity of the eruption does not correlate with serum trough levels.

title: 2008 April Featured Case Summary: A man in his seventies with shaking chills and
history:
2008 April Featured Case Summary: A man in his seventies with shaking chills and back pain.
A man in his seventies was well until approximately 9 days before admission, when an episode of shaking chills and diaphoresis developed, associated with bilateral lower back pain and anorexia. During the next 5 days, two additional episodes of rigors occurred. There was no dysuria, nausea, vomiting, headache, upper respiratory symptoms, cough, pain in the chest or abdomen, arthralgias, myalgias or fevers.
He was seen in the urgent care department. He appeared well, and the examination was normal. Laboratory test results included a white blood cell (WBC) count of 16,000 cells per cubic millimeter. Analysis of the urine revealed positive nitrites, 5-10 white cells per high-powered field (HPF), and no bacteria. The urine was cultured. Possible urinary tract infection was diagnosed and levofloxacin administered.
The following day, he was seen in the emergency department because of persistent symptoms and flank pain. The white cell count was 18,900 cells/mm³ (84% leukocytes, 10% lymphocytes and 6% monocytes) and urinalysis revealed 3-5 WBCs per high-powered field. A chest radiograph demonstrated left basal pleural thickening, which was unchanged from previous studies. Pyelonephritis was diagnosed, and narcotic analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications were prescribed. He was discharged, advised to follow-up with his physician the next day and to return sooner if rigors or fever recurred. Cultures of the urine grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus.
Three days later, he returned to the emergency department because of increasing back pain and chills.

There was a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, colonic polyps and a lung nodule.

He lived in the northeastern United States. He smoked cigarettes and drank alcohol occasionally. He had not traveled recently and there was no history of exposure to tuberculosis.

He was married.

Medications included atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and levofloxacin (500 mg daily).
exam_studies:
On examination, the blood pressure was 180/94 mm Hg, and the other vital signs were normal. The lungs were clear, the heart sounds normal. There was mild tenderness to deep palpation in the suprapubic area. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 16,200 cells/mm³, platelet count 480,000/mm³, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 29 mm per hour. The level of alkaline phosphatase was 130 U/L (reference range 45-115 U/L), levels of aminotransferases, amylase and lipase were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen with arteriography, shown in Figures 1 and 2, demonstrated an infrarenal aortic aneurysm.
Figure 1. CT scan with angiogram.
Figure 2. CT angiogram.

Vancomycin and meropenem were administered empirically and surgical repair of the abdominal aneurysm was performed emergently. A gram stain of the resected material is shown in Figure 3. Pathological examination of the resected specimen, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E), is shown in Figures 4 and 5. Blood cultures were sterile.
Figure 3. Gram stain of specimen.
Figure 4. H and E stain of aneurysm.
Figure 5. H and E stain of wall of vessel, under higher power.
diagnosis:
Mycotic aneurysm caused by Salmonella, group B.

The gram stain of tissue from the resected aorta revealed white cells with no organisms. Pathological examination by hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain demonstrated calcifications from atherosclerosis, disruption of the structure of the blood vessel (Figure 4) and dense acute inflammation involving the blood vessel and surrounding tissue (Figure 5).
Cultures of the excised aneurysm grew Salmonella, group B, shown in Figures 6 through 8, which was sensitive to all antibiotics tested, including nalidixic acid. A Steiner stain of the resected tissue, shown in Figure 9, revealed abundant intracellular and extracellular bacilli consistent with Salmonella species.
Figure 6. Culture growth on blood agar.
Figure 7. Culture growth on MacConkey agar.
Figure 8. Gram stain from culture.
Figure 9. Steiner stain of resected tissue.

The patient was initially treated with vancomycin and meropenem, and then received ceftriaxone intravenously for two weeks, followed by levofloxacin for 4 weeks. Lifelong oral suppression therapy with levofloxacin is planned.

Many pathogens can cause mycotic aneurysms. Infections of the abdominal aorta may be due to secondary infection of an atherosclerotic lesion. Staphylococci cause 40% of cases, of which two-thirds are Staphylococcus aureus. Gram-negative organisms represent 35% of cases. Non-typhoidal Salmonella is the gram-negative most frequently identified, and is ranked second only to Staphylococcus as the causative infectious agent of aortic mycotic aneurysms.
In cases where blood cultures are positive for Salmonella and a definitive source of the infection is not apparent, an endovascular lesion and secondary mycotic aneurysm should be strongly considered, and the appropriate evaluation undertaken, as that is a far more likely source than gram-negative endocarditis [Mandell et al 2005]. In cases of gram-negative mycotic aneurysm, the source is believed to be the gastrointestinal tract. Salmonella may be introduced by oral intake via undercooked ground beef or poultry exposure, or exposure to pets such as reptiles or amphibians. In this patient, given the lack of known immunosuppression or epidemiologic risk factors, etiologies such as tuberculosis or fungi are unlikely. Syphilitic aortitis more commonly involves the ascending aorta than the descending abdominal aorta.
This patient presented with chills, rigors and non-specific back pain, and later developed flank pain, suggestive of pyelonephritis. Other patients who have later been diagnosed with mycotic aneurysm of the abdominal aorta have reported pain radiating into the groin or scrotum, and their pain may suggest that caused by nephrolithiasis.
Retrospective analysis of patient outcomes revealed a 43% mortality rate in patients with endovascular infection caused by Salmonella [Nielson et al 2006]. Patients with mycotic aneurysm do poorly when treated with medications alone: in another retrospective study, 100% mortality was documented in patients who did not have surgery, whereas 70% (9 of 13 patients) survived who were treated with surgical resection of the aneurysm and antibiotics [Wang et al 1996]. Many expert consultants elect to keep these individuals on longterm suppressive antibiotics, especially if prosthetic grafts are placed primarily into the aortic bed, as is frequently done.
Testing of Salmonella for nalidixic-acid susceptibility may be helpful in guiding therapy, as some patients, whose organism is resistant to this drug, may fail treatment with fluoroquinolones [Stevenson et al 2007]. Organisms which are resistant to nalidixic acid are relatively resistant to the usual fluoroquinolones, yet still formally test sensitive to these drugs by the current National Committee on Clinical Laboratory Standards (NCCLS) breakpoints. Although still relatively uncommon in nontyphoidal strains, the incidence of nalidixic acid resistance is increasing.

title: 2008 May Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: An elderly w
history:
2008 May Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: An elderly woman with diabetes and lung disease developed fever and confusion.
A woman in her seventies (Patient age is often an important diagnostic clue, both due to different sorts of exposures as well as age-related changes in immune function. Even the the absence of concomitant illness, host immune responses to a variety of pathogens typically begins to decline slowly beyond fifty years of age. This puts patients at elevated risk for some pathogens less often seen in younger patients. It also increases the risk of reactivation disease, such as tuberculosis or herpes zoster, and decreases the immune response to vaccinations, including to influenza or pneumococcal vaccines.) was generally well until 3 days before admission when she reported to a family member that she felt stiffness between her clavicles. The following day, she spoke again with her family, and her conversation and behavior were thought to be normal. On the day before admission, she participated in social activities with residents at the senior housing complex in which she lived. The next afternoon, she was found in bed, confused, and was taken to another hospital by emergency medical services.
On examination, she was lethargic, confused, and somnolent. The temperature (Fever and mental status changes raise the issue of central nervous system infection, which needs to be addressed immediately. However, fever itself can cause some degree of altered mental status, particularly in the elderly, so this presentation should not preclude a thorough search for other sources of fever.) was 103.9°F (39.9°C). Results of tests for white blood cells and plasma levels of cardiac enzymes, including troponin, were reportedly elevated. Ceftriaxone (1 gram), moxifloxacin (In possible bacterial meningitis, rapid institution of antibiotics targeted at the most likely pathogens is essential, and failure to do so is associated with poor outcome. The regimen of ceftriaxone and moxifloxacin would not have adequately covered the possible pathogens in this case.) (400 mg), methylprednisolone (A corticosteroid anti-inflammatory agent. Since the pathophysiology of bacterial meningitis involves tissue injury due to the host inflammatory response, there is a biological rationale for giving steroids in suspected bacterial meningitis. The data are complex but currently support the use of steroids in adults for possible or proven pneumococcal meningitis. In order for them to be effective, however, they must be given very early, ideally with or before initial antibiotics.) and aspirin were administered. Computed tomography (Given the extreme rapidity of disease progression, once the issue of suspected bacterial meningitis has been raised, lumbar puncture and institution of therapy should occur immediately. There are a limited number of indications for initial CT scanning, but judging by the physical exam reported below, this patient did not meet them. Obtaining a CT scan when not indicated has been associated with delay of therapy and poorer outcomes in meningitis.) (CT) reportedly showed no evidence of acute infarction or hemorrhage. She was transferred to a tertiary care hospital.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus (Co-morbid conditions are an important consideration in the infectious diseases work-up. Diabetes mellitus, in particular, increases the risk of infection, the spectrum of likely pathogens, and the likelihood of fulminant disease.), hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

She lived in a senior living facility. She had smoked 4 packs of cigarettes per day for many years (A very high pack-year smoking history such as this would cause concern for smoking-related illness, such as cancer with metastasis to the brain, in a patient presenting with mental status changes.), but had stopped more than 5 years earlier, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.
Four days before admission, she had attended a house party where she ate a variety of foods, and had taken some leftovers home with her. No other guest had reportedly become ill. There was no history of travel, animal exposures, or ingestion of unpasteurized (Before the advent of pasteurization, dairy products were a significant cause of food-borne illness, such as botulism. Currently, some people deliberately consume such items for perceived health benefits but, by doing so, put themselves at risk for a number of serious infections, in particular Listeriosis.) milk or cheese, or raw or uncooked meat or fish.

She had no allergies.

Daily medications included hydrochlorothiazide, glimepiride, risedronate, pioglitazone, atorvastatin, and omeprazole (The patient's medication list is a useful cross-check on the medical history. Here, the patient's hypertension and diabetes medications correspond to the history, but the presence of a statin suggests hypercholesterolemia. Omeprazole, a gastric proton-pump inhibitor, is taken by many patients for a variety of GI complaints such as ulcer disease or reflux.).
exam_studies:
On examination, the patient was responsive, oriented and appeared mildly agitated. The temperature was 100.7°F (38.2°C) initially, and rose to 101.9°F (38.8°C). The blood pressure was 149/72 mm Hg, pulse 117 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 100% while breathing supplemental oxygen from a non-rebreather mask. There was pain on passive flexion and extension of the neck (This finding indicates "meningismus". In combination with fever and agitation, it is highly suggestive of meningitis.), and the neck was supple with rotation. The jugulovenous pressure was 6 cm. The lungs revealed mild crackles at the left base, and breath sounds were otherwise clear. A 2/6 systolic murmur (It is important to know whether this murmur is new. Some systolic murmurs can be heard with tachycardias on occasion, but in this patient, if the murmur was new, a possible diagnosis of endocarditis with emboli to the brain should be considered. This finding emphasizes the importance of complete documentation in medical records.) was heard loudest at the base. The patient was able to follow simple commands, but speech was not fluent. Testing for cranial nerves III-XII, strength and sensation was normal, as was the remainder of the examination.

The level of D-dimer, drawn at the other hospital, was reportedly elevated. The white blood cells measured 17,700 cells per cubic millimeter (94% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 4% lymphocytes, and 2% monocytes (Although not a "hard" sign, monocytes typically fall to very low levels during severe acute bacterial infection. Their presence may suggest certain particular pathogens such as M. Tb or Listeria.)) and levels of hemoglobin and platelets were normal. An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia, a prolonged QT interval for the rate, and diffuse ST segment and T wave abnormalities (An elderly patient with pre-existing cardiovascular disease and an acute infection will have an elevated risk of an acute cardiac event, due to the tachycardia as well as the inflammatory response.).

Initial medications included atrovent and albuterol nebulizers, methylprednisolone (125 mg intravenously), crystalloid intravenous fluid 1.5 liters, and nitroglycerin by continuous intravenous drip. Computed tomography, performed according to a pulmonary embolism protocol, was negative.
A lumbar puncture was performed, and analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed yellow, moderately turbid fluid with 1823 white cells (Very large numbers of neutrophils in the CSF strongly support the diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis.) (77% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes, and 2% monocytes) and 433 red cells per cubic millimeter in the 1st tube, and 1188 white cells and 175 red cells (The presence of red cells may suggest a necrotizing process in the CSF - as is seen with HSV encephalitis - or may simply be due to trauma from the lumbar puncture. The decrease in RBC's from tube 1 to tube 4 is suggestive of the latter in this case. Sometimes these can be distinguished if the CSF shows xanthochromia, a change in color that only occurs if blood has actually entered the CSF.) per cubic millimeter in the 4th tube. The level of glucose was 124 mg/dl (The slightly elevated glucose is likely due to her diabetes, but such high levels would argue against most common bacterial pathogens such as pneumococcus, where CSF glucose levels would be very low.) (reference range 50-75 mg/dl) and protein 505 mg/dl (ref. range 5-55 mg/dl). Stain of the cytospin of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Additional ceftriaxone (2 grams) was administered, and acyclovir (To cover the possibility of HSV encephalitis, where therapy must be instituted very early for maximum efficacy.) (600 mg), vancomycin (For the possibility of antibiotic-resistant pneumococcus. For meningitis, initial therapy must cover all the reasonable possibilities. One cannot wait for antibiotic sensitivity testing to guide therapy.) (1 g), and ampicillin (For Listeria coverage. This pathogen rises in incidence as a cause of meningitis after age fifty.) (2 g) were added.
Figure 1. Stain of CSF cytospin.
Figure 2. Stain of CSF cytospin.
diagnosis:
Meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes, and acute myocardial infarction in an elderly patient.

Cultures of the CSF and blood grew Listeria monocytogenes. A gram stain of the blood culture growth is shown in Figure 3, and a subculture of the organism of a blood agar plate is shown in Figure 4. Results of polymerase chain reaction testing of the CSF were negative for Herpes simplex virus.
Figure 3. Gram stain of aerobic blood culture.
Figure 4. Culture of organism on blood agar plate.

Broad spectrum antibiotics were administered pending the results of the CSF and blood cultures, when gentamicin (Rapid killing of bacteria with high concentrations of bactericidal antibiotics that penetrate into the CSF is the key to successful therapy of bacterial meningitis. Because ampicillin shows delayed killing of Listeria at levels achievable in the CSF, gentamicin, an aminoglycoside is often added for synergy.) was added. The patient's temperature decreased to below 100°F (37.8°C); her mental status improved; and the acyclovir, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin were stopped. The patient declined to have a repeat lumbar puncture despite continued complaints of mild headache. The ampicillin and gentamicin were continued, with a plan to treat for 2.5-3 weeks intravenously. She developed increased cardiac enzymes and associated ST elevations, which were thought to be caused by increased myocardial demand in the setting of tachycardia and infection. A beta-blocker was added to her medications. She gradually improved, and was discharged on the 15th hospital day to a rehabilitation facility to complete her course of antibiotic therapy. At follow-up in Infectious Disease clinic one month after discharge, she had returned to her baseline health and felt well.

Listeria monocytogenes, a gram-positive bacillus and facultative anaerobe, is one of the leading causes of community-acquired meningitis in adults older than 60 years of age, infants younger than 1 month, pregnant women and immunocompromised hosts, with the highest incidence of L. monocytogenes infection occurring in the first two groups. L. monocytogenes is ubiquitous in nature, and has been isolated from many foods including, but not limited to, soft cheeses, processed delicatessen meats, and raw vegetables. Consumption of contaminated food is thought to represent the mode of transmission in most patients; vertical transmission from mother to child during or after childbirth is also thought to be responsible for neonatal infections. Incubation periods are long and may range from 11 to 70 days [Lorber 2005, Tunkel and Scheld 2005]; therefore, in isolated cases it may be difficult to identify the exact source of the bacteria.
L. monocytogenes is the only species of Listeria that is pathogenic in humans. Presenting symptoms of L. monocytogenes meningitis may include fever, altered mental status and/or headache. In one review, all patients with documented L. monocytogenes meningitis had at least one of the symptoms described above, and 28% had all three [Mylonakis et al 1998]. Listerial infection of the central nervous system may also present as an abscess and be mistaken for primary or metatstatic malignancy. Rarely a rhombencephalitis of the brainstem occurs. In these cases, CSF may be very bland, and even culture-negative.
In this patient, gram-positive bacilli were seen on the stain of cerebrospinal fluid, and the diagnosis of L. monocytogenes meningitis confirmed by culture results. However, in other clinical specimens, the organism may have a coccoid, diplococcoid or diphtheroid appearance with variable colorization on gram staining [Lorber 2005] and, consequently, identifying the causative agent may be more difficult until specific culture results are known.
Although L. monocytogenes is only the 5th leading cause of community acquired meningitis, it has the highest mortality rate [Lorber 2005, Tunkel and Scheld 2005]. The organism’s pattern of resistance to cephalosporins, a common empiric therapy for meningitis, may contribute to its high mortality rate. Consequently, it is important to consider this entity and administer appropriate antibiotics, which may include penicillin or ampicillin as well as the addition of gentamicin, in relevant patients.

history:
2008 June Featured Case Summary: A teenager with cervical lymphadenopathy.
A 17-year old boy was seen by an otolaryngologist because of cervical lymphadenopathy on the left side
Approximately 2.5 months earlier, a lymph node in the left cervical chain developed, which was followed by a smaller satellite lesion inferiorly two weeks later. He also reported a history of headache and sinus congestion. He saw his physician and a chest radiograph and skin test for tuberculosis were reportedly negative. Empiric therapy with cefaclor was administered for presumed chronic sinusitis with an associated headache, followed by a course of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, without improvement in the lymphadenopathy.
Weight loss of 10 pounds (4.5 kilograms) occurred, attributed by the patient to anorexia associated with the antibiotics. During the month before his presentation, the patient felt feverish (but did not record his temperature) and noted an intermittent cough, body pain and fatigue. There was no history of sweats or chills. He was referred to an otolaryngologist.

There was a history of migraine headaches, for which computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including vascular studies, were performed in the past and which were reportedly normal. Skin tests for tuberculosis were reportedly negative 2.5 years and 2 months before presentation. He had had a small occipital cyst and shin splints, and 2 years earlier, left knee arthroscopy was performed for cartilage injury.

The patient had emigrated from India to the United States 2.5 years before, lived in the Northeast and had traveled to the Southeast. There was no recent history of air travel and his only exposure to pets was indirect, in his friends’ homes, with no cat scratches or contact with animal litter or cages. He was a vegetarian and did not smoke cigarettes or abuse alcohol. There were no known exposures to individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis. A sibling was healthy.

He had no allergies.

Valproic acid (1000 mg daily) had been administered for the migraine headaches.
exam_studies:
He appeared well. Multiple well-defined, ballotable, soft lesions, up to 2 cm in diameter, were present in the left cervical region and consistent with lymph nodes. The remainder of the otolaryngologic examination, including voice, ears, nose and anterior nasal mucosa, oral cavity and oropharynx, buccal membranes, floor of mouth, and lips, were normal. Flexible fiberoptic examination was performed, under local anesthesia because of gagging, and the nasal cavity and nasopharyngeal mucosa, base of tongue, vallecula, and epiglottis were clear. The larynx demonstrated normal laryngeal anatomy and mobility. A remnant adenoid was present and noted to be within normal limits for his age. The parotid and thyroid beds were clear bilaterally and his cranial nerves were completely intact.

Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated extensive lymphadenopathy of the left posterior cervical chain with 2 additional enlarged nodes superficially. There was central cavitation of the nodes, asymmetrical prominence of the left tonsil, and no calcification or soft tissue stranding (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT scan of the neck.

A fine needle aspiration of one of the lymph nodes was obtained. Pathological examination of the lymph node tissue demonstrated necrotic cellular tissue fragments, which were thought to be consistent with an origin from granulomatous lymphadenopathy. No fungus, yeast, or acid-fast bacilli were observed. Chest radiographs, shown in Figures 2 and 3, revealed a linear density (2 mm) in the right mid lung (possibly a minute granuloma) and a patchy opacity (17 mm) overlying the right lower lung, which was thought to possibly represent overlap of a rib and vessel or mild atelectasis. There was no well-defined consolidation or pleural effusion.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph.
Figure 3. Chest radiograph, lateral view.
diagnosis:
Cervical lymphadenopathy (scrofula) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A skin test for tuberculosis was repeated and demonstrated 40 millimeters (mm) by 60 mm induration, with greater than 10 mm central vesiculation and ulceration.
The enlarged necrotic lymph nodes located superiorly were excised. Pathological examination of the tissue (Figure 4) revealed necrotizing granulomas and multinucleated giant cells (see arrow), and genetic probe testing confirmed the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Culture of the lymph node tissue obtained by fine needle aspiration eventually grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, shown in Figure 5, which was sensitive to all antituberculous drugs tested.
Figure 4. H and E stain of excised lymph node.
Figure 5. Acid-fast stain of growth from fine needle aspiration.

The patient was referred to a Pediatric Infectious Disease specialist. On further questioning, after the diagnosis was known, it was learned that six years earlier, his mother was treated in India for Pott's disease of the lumbar spine (L3-4), for 18 months with multiple drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide).
After Mycobacterium tuberculosis was identified, isoniazid (300 mg), rifampin (600 mg), ethambutol (1000 mg) and pyrazinamide (1500 mg) were initially administered daily with pyridoxine (50 mg), and topical steroid cream was applied to the skin test site. Abstinence from alcohol during the course of his therapy was advised. Results of tests of liver function were normal while on anti-tuberculous therapy.
When the results of sensitivity testing were known after 5 weeks, ethambutol was discontinued, and pyrazinamide was stopped after 2 months. After 6 months of therapy, CT scanning demonstrated diminution in the size of all residual cervical nodes, and minimal and mostly punctate calcified caseous material in the center of one of the nodes. Rifampin and isoniazid were stopped after 9 months of treatment.

The subacute development of cervical lymphadenopathy (scrofula), appearing unilaterally in this recent immigrant from Asia, strongly suggested a clinical diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis lymphadenitis. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is the most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, and the cervical nodes are those most often affected.
Mononucleosis and streptococcal pharyngitis are more likely to present as acute illnesses with bilateral lymphadenopathy, although asymmetrical involvement can be seen. The presence of necrosis on pathological examination of the lymph node tissue made the diagnosis of lymphoma, in the absence of previous chemotherapy, unlikely. Other infectious agents, such as Bartonella henselae, atypical Mycobacteria and Toxoplasma, can also cause lymphadenitis. In this patient, there was not a history of significant pet exposure to strongly support the diagnosis of Bartonella infection. In the United States, mycobacterial lymphadenitis is more often caused by atypical mycobacteria than by M. tuberculosis (M.tb.), though selected populations, such as Latinos, Native Americans and immigrants from Asia and Haiti, experience higher rates of M.tb.than that seen in the general population. A tissue diagnosis, with culture and sensitivities, was needed to identify the causative agent and, in this time of increasing multi-drug resistant organisms, the appropriate therapy.
The “cording” morphology of the organisms grown in liquid media, such as that seen in Figure 5, is more typical of M. tuberculosis than other types of mycobacteria. Although other mycobacteria, such as M. kansasii and some of the rapid growers, may also cord, they tend toward a looser, less-organized pattern referred to as "pseudo-cording". The presence of the cording morphology may help guide subsequent genetic probe testing for speciation of the organism.
It is not certain why the initial screening Mantoux skin test for tuberculosis exposure was reportedly negative in this patient. Difficulties with this test may arise from the quality of the purified protein derivative (PPD) solution itself and whether it has been stored properly, the correct placement of the PPD solution intradermally, the timing and procedure for reading the area of induration, and the correct interpretation of the significance of the physical findings, which vary depending on the exposure risk of the individual being tested. In elderly or immunocompromised individuals, who may be anergic, false negatives may occur. When exposure to tuberculosis is highly suspect, repeating the test in 1- 3 weeks may be helpful. The development of additional options to determine exposure to tuberculosis, such as an in-vitro interferon-gamma release assay, may provide benefit when questions arise.

history:
2008 July Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man presented in mid-summer with abdominal discomfort and fever.
A man in his sixties was well until one month earlier, when intermittent generalized abdominal discomfort developed, predominantly located in the left lower quadrant and associated with abdominal fullness and decreased appetite. There was no nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. His weight increased 15 pounds (7 kilograms) and he reported his clothing no longer fit him.
One week before admission, he felt flushed and his temperature rose to 103°F (39.4°C). During the next week, fevers recurred daily. He saw his physician and ciprofloxacin was begun for possible diverticulitis. Several days before his evaluation, melena developed. A chest radiograph performed at another hospital was reportedly normal, and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen, performed without contrast, demonstrated an enlarged prostate and mild diverticulosis with possible diverticulitis. He was admitted to the hospital.
On admission, moxifloxacin and metronidazole were begun. However, his fevers persisted. An infectious disease specialist was consulted and doxycycline added. A blood test for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever was reportedly negative. During the admission, dyspnea developed, and the platelet count decreased to 50,000 per cubic millimeter, associated with a normocytic anemia and mild elevation of serum transaminases. Cultures of specimens of blood and urine were sterile, and the stool culture was negative for pathogens. On the 4th hospital day, he was transferred to another hospital.
At the second hospital, he reported a cough, occasionally productive of blood-streaked sputum, which he associated with the initiation of lisinopril 2 weeks earlier. The medication had been stopped, and the cough was improving. He also reported headaches and fatigue, with no orthopnea, chest pain, dizziness, photophobia, confusion, neck pain, difficulty speaking, joint pain or swelling, back pain, nausea, vomiting, rash, or urinary symptoms.

There was a history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, hematuria and prostatic hypertrophy. Colonic polyps had been noted on a screening colonoscopy several years earlier. He had never been tested for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

He lived in a forested area near a large metropolitan center in the United States Northeast. Approximately 2-3 weeks earlier, he had traveled to Cape Cod, Massachusetts. He had traveled to Asia over 30 years earlier, had no recent international travel, and had no exposures to tuberculosis. He denied recent tick exposures or mosquito bites, and was not currently sexually active. He had smoked cigarettes for many years, and drank 2-3 alcoholic beverages several days each week.

He was retired.

There was history of heart disease in his second-degree relatives.

Penicillin had caused a rash in the remote past.

Medications on admission included levofloxacin 500 mg (orally) daily, metronidazole 500 mg (intravenously) three times daily, atorvastatin, and aspirin.
exam_studies:
He appeared mildly dyspneic when conversing. The maximum temperature on the day of admission was 103.7°F (39.8°C); the pulse was 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/64 mm Hg, and respirations 18 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation was 95% while breathing ambient air initially, and decreased intermittently to 83%. There were slightly diminished breath sounds throughout, and no wheezes, rales or dullness to percussion. There was a systolic murmur, loudest (2 on a scale from 0 to 6) at the left lower sternal border, and no extra heart sounds. The abdomen was soft, with no tenderness, hepatic or splenic enlargement or shifting dullness. There was trace pedal edema, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 6700 cells per cubic millimeter (69% neutrophils, 7% bands, 14% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes and 1% eosinophils), hematocrit 29.7%, hemoglobin 10.7 gm/dL, and platelet count 64,000 per cubic millimeter; the mean corpuscular volume was normal. The peripheral blood smear is shown in Figures 1 and 2. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm per hour. The level of plasma carbon dioxide level measured 19.7 mmol/l (reference range 23.0-31.9); calcium, phosphorus and magnesium were slightly decreased, and other electrolytes were normal. Direct bilirubin measured 1.3 (reference range 0-0.4), total bilirubin 3 mg/dl (ref. range 0.0-1.0), alanine aminotransferase 85 U/L (ref. range 10-55), aspartate aminotransferase 79 U/L (ref. range 10-40), and lactate dehydrogenase 886 U/L (ref. range 110-210); alkaline phosphatase and tests of renal function were normal.
A chest radiograph revealed hazy airspace opacities in the upper lobes bilaterally, mild emphysema, and small bilateral pleural effusions (Figure 3).
Figure 1. Blood smear, Giemsa stain.
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.
Figure 3. Chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated diverticulosis, with no evidence for diverticulitis. There were bilateral perinephric fluid collections, with no nephrolithiasis, and an enlarged prostate; the scan was otherwise normal.
diagnosis:
Babesiosis, most likely caused by Babesia microti (based on geographical distribution).

The findings on Giemsa staining of the peripheral blood smear (thin smear) (Figures 1 and 2, and Figures 4 and 5) revealed Babesia, an intracellular parasite, with an estimated parasitemia of 7%. The upper lobar hazy airspace opacities seen on the chest radiograph were thought to represent non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, or possibly pulmonary hemorrhage in the setting of thrombocytopenia, although atypical infection, caused by viral infection, Pneumocystis, Mycoplasma, or Legionella, were also considered. Test results for syphilis, viral hepatitis, human immunodeficiency virus, and Ehrlichia were negative. Cultures of the blood were sterile, and tests of the stool were negative for pathogens and Clostridium difficile toxin. Induced sputum specimens showed no Pneumocystis; cultures and stain were negative for Mycobacterium.
Figure 4. Blood smear, Giemsa stain.
Figure 5. Detail of Figure 4, with arrow.

Atovaquone, azithromycin and doxycycline were administered for ten days. On the 3rd day, the patient experienced transient confusion, which subsequently resolved. Omeprazole was added after gastroscopy revealed a peptic ulcer. His fever and abdominal pain improved. His thrombocytopenia resolved by day 5; the hematocrit gradually fell to 21.0% on day 6, and he was transfused 3 units of packed red cells. A follow-up blood smear on the 9th hospital day showed no parasites.

Babesiosis is a tick-borne febrile illness that may clinically resemble malaria, and is caused by a genus of intra-erythrocytic protozoan parasites, Babesia. B. microti is the species most commonly found on Cape Cod and in the Northeastern United States. In humans, Babesia infection is transmitted by nymph or adult forms of the Ixodes tick, which are present in the Northeastern United States. Less commonly, it can be transmitted by blood transfusions.
Like malaria, the pathophysiologic manifestations of babesiosis result from infection of erythrocytes with subsequent hemolysis and splenic sequestration. Clinically, babesiosis presents as an acute or subacute illness with fevers, chills, and fatigue. Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and hemoglobinuria are common; jaundice and splenomegaly may be present. In severe cases, microvascular obstruction may cause central nervous system, renal, or hepatic involvement. Pulmonary manifestations, while rare, are frequently due to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
The clinical course of babesiosis is more severe in asplenic individuals and persons over the age of 60 years. At the time of this publication, current standard of care for treatment is combination therapy with azithromycin and atovaquone for 10 days; alternatively, clindamycin plus quinine may be given. Individuals who are immunocompromised, e.g. due to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), may require longer or repeated treatment courses.
The laboratory findings and morphologic appearance of the Plasmodium and Babesia species may be quite similar. Consequently, the diagnoses may be difficult to distinguish in patients who may have been in areas endemic for both organisms. Ring forms in erythrocytes (shown in the center of Figure 2) may be seen in both Plasmodium and Babesia infections. Banana gametocytes, schizonts and hemozoins (golden brown pigment clumps within infected erythrocytes that represent hemoglobin degradation by-products) are seen in P. falciparum infection and are not seen in Babesia infection. A rare but characteristic finding in Babesia infection is an intra-erythrocytic tetrad of merozoites, appearing in a ‘Maltese cross’ configuration. (Infected cells with four chromatin clumps can be seen in the lower left of Figure 2 and the center of Figure 5. An arrow in Figure 5 highlights a cell in which the intracellular chromatin is suggestive of a Maltese cross.) Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is available and may detect low levels of parasitemia.
As this patient had been in an area endemic for B. microti, and had not traveled to an area endemic for malaria, and because of the parasitic morphology, malaria was thought to be unlikely. Of note, Lyme borreliosis and human granulocytic ehrlichiosis share a common vector (the Ixodes tick) and geographic distribution with Babesia, and concurrent infection should be considered.

title:
2008 August Featured Case Summary: A woman in her seventies with lung nodules.
A
history:
2008 August Featured Case Summary: A woman in her seventies with lung nodules.
A woman in her seventies was in her usual state of health until 8 weeks before admission when sinus and respiratory symptoms developed. Sinusitis was diagnosed and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was administered. Diffuse wheezing and cough persisted, and albuterol and fluticasone and salmeterol inhalers were added. A chest radiograph (shown in Figure 1) revealed a nodular opacity in the left lung, which measured 1.8 cm in diameter and was new compared with studies 5 years earlier. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) demonstrated two nodules, one of which was calcified, that appeared to be contiguous with one another. Her sinus and respiratory symptoms improved shortly after completion of the antibiotic course.
One week later, a follow-up study combined with positron emission tomography (PET) demonstrated two confluent calcified nodules measuring 14 and 7 mm in diameter, in the left lower lobe, with mildly increased FDG uptake. The pulmonary arteries were enlarged. The appearance of the lung nodules was thought to be atypical for primary lung malignancy.
Seven weeks later, she was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation of the lung nodules.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.

There was a history of osteoarthritis, and obesity. She had had a multiple surgical procedures, including excision of a basal cell carcinoma, tonsillectomy, and bilateral hip replacements. There was no history of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), and skin testing for TB had been negative 10 years earlier.

She had traveled extensively, including trips to the Caribbean, North Africa (more than a decade earlier), and the American Southwest (5 years earlier). She had no contacts with tuberculosis, and had not been incarcerated or homeless. She drank alcohol moderately, and did not smoke tobacco.

She was married.

There was a family history of lymphoma; her children were well.

As above, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, albuterol, fluticasone and salmeterol inhalers had been administered. Other medications included estrace (vaginally, as needed), glucosamine chondroitin, and multivitamins.
exam_studies:
The lungs were clear, with no wheezing or ronchi, and the remainder of the physical examination was normal.

Laboratory test results, including a complete blood count, serum levels of electrolytes and glucose and tests of liver and renal function, were normal. Results of pulmonary function tests were also normal.

Flexible bronchoscopy, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), and wedge resection of the pulmonary nodules in the left lower lobe were performed. Pathological examination of a frozen section of the resected tissue revealed necrotizing granulomas. Specimens of the resected tissue with trichrome and reticulin staining are shown in Figures 3 and 4, respectively.
Figure 3. Lung nodule, trichrome stain.
Figure 4. Detail of nodule, reticulin stain.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary infarction with granulomatous inflammation and dystrophic calcification, caused by zoonotic filariasis, consistent with Dirofilaria immitis infection.

Pathological examination of the biopsy revealed a coiled, degenerated nematode that was occluding a muscular pulmonary artery, with associated pulmonary infarction, granulomatous inflammation and dystrophic calcification. The morphology of the nematode, with cuticle and prominent muscular lateral cords, was consistent with Dirofilaria immitis. Remnants of the nematode, and internal structures of the organism, are seen in Figures 5 and 6. Multiple stains, including hematoxylin and eosin, acid-fast, GMS, and Steiner stains, were performed and no other pathogen or evidence of malignancy was identified.
Figure 5. Detail of nodule, reticulin stain, with nematode fragments.
Figure 6. Nematode in cross-section, reticulin stain.

No additional therapy other than the excisional biopsy was needed to treat the dirofilarial infection.

Filariae are long thin round worms. Humans are the definitive host for a number of filarial infections including Onchocerca volvulus (the cause of river blindness), and Wuchereria bancrofti (a cause of lymphatic filariasis). Humans can also be dead-end hosts for many zoonotic filarial infections. All filarial infections are transmitted by the bite of an arthropod vector. Most zoonotic filarial infections are transmitted by the bite of an infective mosquito. Following the bite of an infective arthropod, injected zoonotic microfilariae migrate through human tissues and develop into immature or young adult nematodes, but are unable to complete their life cycle in humans. The worms die and degenerate and are eventually walled off, giving rise to a granulomatous reaction and nodule. Zoonotic filarial infections of humans are usually asymptomatic, but they can present as a subcutaneous nodule, a migratory worm (especialy in and around the eye: "eyeworm"), or as a symptomatic pulmonary or lymphatic nodule.
Most pulmonary zoonotoc filarial infections of humans are ascribed to Dirofilaria immitis, the dog heart worm. The definitive host for these infections is the dog and other canines, and human infections have been reported from all areas of the world. In the dog, the adult worms reside in a coil in the right ventricle where the females produce microfilariae that circulate in the dog's blood; these microfilariae are then ingested during a subsequent blood meal by a mosquito. Humans are infected by the bite of a mosquito that has previously fed on an infected dog. In humans, the worms are unable to complete their development and are flushed from the right ventricle into the pulmonary circulation where they give rise to a pulmonary nodule.
D. immitis infection in humans is asymptomatic in more than half of the cases, and often presents incidentally as a coin lesion on a chest radiograph. [Orihel and Eberhard 1998, Cifferi 1982] Occasionally, patients with pulmonary dirofilariasis develop cough, chest pain or hemoptysis, which is most likely a sequela of pulmonary infarction [Kochar 1985]. Peripheral eosinophilia may or may not be present.
A definitive diagnosis can be made only by biopsy as the available serologic tests are inadequate to rule out other potentially life-threatening diagnoses, such as lung cancer.

title: 2008 September Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woma
history:
2008 September Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman in her thirties with fevers and a pruritic rash.
A woman in her thirties was well until approximately 3 days before presentation in mid-autumn, when fevers up to 103°F (39.4°C) developed, associated with a sore throat and malaise. She took ibuprofen for her symptoms. On the day of presentation, she awoke with a rash over her face, scalp, trunk, and proximal extremities. The lesions were pruritic and tender, and associated with headache and nausea. There was no cough, dysuria, vaginal discharge, or chest, abdomen, or joint pain. She was seen in a walk-in clinic, and referred to an emergency department for evaluation by an infectious disease consultant.

She reported having had chickenpox as a child and was up-to-date on her immunizations.

She worked in a healthcare setting, and had no pets or known sick contacts. She traveled intermittently to a wooded area in Northern New England to visit relatives. There was no history of any unusual skin contacts, or tick or other insect bites. She did not smoke tobacco, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. Her last sexual contact was 5 months earlier, and she reported using condoms, without exception, whenever sexually active.

She had taken ibuprofen for her symptoms.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared fatigued and uncomfortable. The temperature was 96.6°F (35.9°C), blood pressure 133/77 mm Hg, pulse 96 beats per minute, and respirations 20 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 97% while breathing ambient air. There were numerous discrete, tender, erythematous macules, less than 1 centimeter in diameter with a 1-to-3 millimeter pustular center, on the face, scalp, chest, back, inner thighs, and arms, and one lesion on her palm. The physical examination was otherwise normal.

The white blood cell count was 6,300 cells/mm³, with 35% neutrophils, 35% lymphocytes, 21% atypical lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 1% basophils. A Wright stain of the blood smear is shown in Figures 1 and 2. The remainder of the complete blood count analysis, and levels of electrolytes and renal function, were normal. Additional tests were pending.
Figure 1. Blood smear, on admission. (Image courtesy of Bernard Khor, MD, used with permission.)
Figure 2. Blood smear. (Image courtesy of Bernard Khor, MD, used with permission.)

The patient was discharged to home to await the remaining test results, with further close follow-up.
She felt worse the following day, with increasing headache and skin lesions. On examination, the temperature was normal; the neck was supple, and examination of the skin revealed approximately 30 pustules on an erythematous base. The remainder of the examination was unchanged from the previous day. She was admitted to the hospital.
Additional test results included an alkaline phosphatase of 154 U/L (reference range 30-100 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L (reference range 9-32 U/L), alanine aminotransferase 47 U/L (reference range 7-30 U/L), and total bilirubin 0.3 mg/dl.
A lumbar puncture was performed, and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid showed no white blood cells and normal levels of glucose and protein. A chest radiograph and computed tomography of the brain were also normal. An ultrasound of the abdomen showed diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver and the spleen size was normal. The patient was seen by the dermatology service and a skin biopsy was performed.
Acyclovir was administered empirically. Over the next two days, some lesions evolved to become crusted with a central eschar (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Physical findings on day 3.
Figure 4. Physical findings on day 3.
diagnosis:
Primary varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox) in an adult.

After the initial history of chickenpox in childhood was elicited, the patient’s mother was contacted and reported that the patient had not had the disease. The varicella immunoglobulin (Ig) G antibody test was negative. Bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral cultures of the skin biopsy were negative. A direct fluorescent antibody stain of the tissue showed the presence of varicella zoster virus (VZV) antigens (Figure 5).
Additional testing for heterophile antibodies, blood cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigenemia and immunoglobin G antibodies, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) for syphilis, Lyme antibodies, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody and ribonucleic acid (RNA) was negative. Epstein Barr virus (EBV) antibody titers were positive, and consistent with past infection, and IgG antibodies to rubella and measles were also positive. Cultures of the blood, urine, throat, and cerebrospinal fluid were sterile, and VZV was not detected in the CSF by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.
Figure 5. Fluorescent stain of skin specimen for VZV antigen.

The patient was initially treated with acyclovir until it was confirmed that she had no evidence of pneumonia, central nervous system involvement, or immunosuppression. The levels of liver function tests rose to approximately double their normal values during the first days of her admission, then declined, and the atypical lymphocytosis resolved. She improved clinically and was discharged on the 5th hospital day.

The typical presentation of chickenpox, or primary varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection, includes a prodrome of fever, malaise and, frequently, pharyngitis. The rash usually occurs within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms and is classically described as vesicular lesions on an erythematous base. These lesions are present in a variety of stages from maculopapular to vesicular to crusted.
This patient's presentation was atypical in several ways, and led to the broad differential diagnosis. First, fewer than 10% of chickenpox cases occur in those over the age of 14 years. Secondly, while a pustular-appearing rash can occur in chickenpox (as in this case), the classic findings are of vesicles. Finally, the patient reported that she had had chickenpox as a child. After further inquiry, her mother corrected this history and indicated that the patient had not had the disease. A negative varicella immunoglobulin (Ig) G antibody confirmed that the patient had not been exposed in the past.
Atypical lymphocytes can have several features including increased nuclear granularity, elongated nucleus, vacuolated cytoplasm, and an irregular border that tends to flow around surrounding red blood cells (Figures 1 and 2, above). They are found in various acute viral infections including those resulting from VZV, EBV, CMV, HIV, and hepatitis viruses. They may also be found in other infections such as acute toxoplasmosis, as well as in certain drug reactions, e.g., those secondary to phenytoin.
Adults make up a small percentage of chickenpox cases, but have a high rate of complications and account for more than half of varicella-related deaths. Complications may include bacterial superinfection, encephalitis, pneumonia, and hepatitis. As no baseline liver function tests were available, the patient’s transaminase elevations may well have been a result of the varicella. Subclinical transaminase elevations are common in normal hosts, but hepatitis may be life-threatening in immunosuppressed hosts.
A far more common manifestation of VZV infection seen in adults is the development of herpes zoster, caused by the reactivation of the virus. This is in part due to the waning of cell-mediated immunity to VZV over time. The Shingles Prevention Study, published in 2005, showed that a live attenuated VZV vaccine was able to reduce the incidence of herpes zoster by 51% and postherpetic neuralgia by 67%. The zoster vaccine is now recommended for all individuals aged 60 years and older with the exception of those who are immunocompromised.

title: 2008 October Featured Case Summary: A woman with migraine developed increasing h
history:
2008 October Featured Case Summary: A woman with migraine developed increasing headache, blurred vision and nausea.
A woman in her twenties was well until one week earlier, when a persistent headache developed. The headache pain was similar to, but more intense than, her usual migraine, and associated with blurred vision, nausea, and photophobia. Three days before presentation, her family noted her speech was not clear, and she sounded “confused”. A transient episode of numbness on the dorsum of her right foot developed, and resolved spontaneously 2 hours later. She presented to the Emergency Department of a local hospital, where computed tomography (CT) of the head was reportedly normal. Butalbitol-acetaminophen-caffeine, and prochlorperazine were prescribed, and she was discharged home.
The following day, the pain persisted, and an episode of vomiting occurred. She felt subjectively febrile; however, her temperature was not measured. She returned to the Emergency Department; a lumbar puncture was discussed, which she declined, and she returned home.
Two days later, episodes of vomiting recurred. Family members noted she had increasing difficulty with word-finding and naming. She returned to the hospital, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reportedly demonstrated a lesion in the left fronto-parietal lobe (approximately 2 cm in diameter) with ring enhancement and surrounding edema. Dexamethasone (10 mg) was administered intravenously, and she was transferred to a tertiary care hospital for further care.
At the 2nd hospital, she reported mild nasal congestion but no recent sinus pain, earache, tooth pain, dyspnea, anorexia, or back pain. Approximately one month earlier, she had had her lip pierced; she had no recent dental cleanings or procedures.

She had had migraines since adolescence (1-2 episodes per month), and a history of sinusitis.

She worked in a healthcare setting. She smoked cigarettes, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. There was no history of exposure to tuberculosis.

She lived with a relative.

She had no allergies, but had felt itchy after recent gadolinium administration.

Medications on transfer included dexamethasone.
exam_studies:
On examination, she was somnolent but arousable. The temperature was 102.1°F (38.9°C), blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, respirations 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. The right tympanic membrane was perforated, with no evidence of infection on either side and no sinus or mastoid tenderness. There was no gingival or dental tenderness. She was oriented to person, place, and year, and appropriately interactive. Her affect was normal, and there were multiple non-fluent paraphasic errors. Naming was poor, with very poor repetition and reading. She was able to comprehend normally and followed all commands. Cranial nerves 2 -12 were intact; 1 was not tested. Mild updrift of the right arm was noted, with minimal pronation. The tongue and lip were pierced. The remainder of the examination was normal, with clear lungs, and no rash, petechiae, or murmurs.

The hematocrit measured 35.4%, and white blood cell count of 15,200 cells per cubic millimeter (95% leukocytes, 4% lymphocytes and 1% monocytes). A portable chest radiograph was normal.
Lumbar puncture was performed, and specimens of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood were cultured. There were 49 and 47 white cells in tubes 1 and 4, respectively, and 4 and 3 red cells per cubic millimeter in Tubes 1 and 4, respectively. The white cell differential included 53% leukocytes, 31% lymphocytes, and 16% monocytes. The level of glucose in the CSF was 89 mg/dl, and the total protein was 45 mg/dl. A gram stain of the CSF revealed few white cells and mononuclear cells, and no organisms (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Gram stain of CSF cytospin.

Neurology and neurosurgery consultations were obtained, and ceftriaxone, metronidazole and vancomycin administered empirically, as well as phenytoin.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was repeated, and demonstrated a T2/FLAIR heterogeneous lesion (4.2 cm maximally) within the left posterior and inferior frontal lobe, with large Sylvian vessels directly adjacent to the lesion both anteriorly and inferiorly, and extensive T2 hyperintensity surrounding this lesion (representing vasogenic edema), and evidence of a mass effect with a midline shift (Figures 2 and 3). Low-lying cerebellar tonsils and a prominent right cerebellar hemisphere dural venous anomaly were also seen.
Figure 2. MRI of the brain, T2 axial FLAIR.
Figure 3. MRI of the brain, T1 FLAIR post contrast.
diagnosis:
Brain abscess caused by mixed flora, including Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group) and Peptostreptococcus species, possibly related to lip and tongue piercings, dental abscess, or pneumonia in a patient with a patent foramen ovale.

Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody was negative, and subsequently, test results for Toxoplasma gondii DNA in the CSF (by polymerase chain reaction) also were negative.
Neurosurgical drainage of a brain abscess was performed, and 11 cc of purulent material aspirated. A gram stain of the aspirate, shown in Figure 4, demonstrated abundant gram-positive cocci (GPC) in pairs and short chains, and few GPC in clusters, and abundant short gram-positive rods. Culture of the aspirate grew abundant alpha-hemolytic Streptococcus anginosus (milleri group) and, in the anaerobic culture, few colonies of Peptostreptococcus species.
Cardiac echocardiography demonstrated evidence of left-to-right shunting by color Doppler, and a right-to-left shunt by agitated saline contrast study at rest (moderate to large amount of bubbles, 1 beat after appearance of contrast in the right heart), consistent with a patent foramen ovale. The day after her surgical procedure, CT of the lung demonstrated septal thickening, bronchiolar mucoid impaction, and peribronchial opacities in the right lower lobe, consistent with bronchopneumonia, with a small right-sided pleural effusion.
Figure 4. Gram stain of abscess aspirate.

After the culture results and sensitivities of the brain aspirate were known, ceftriaxone was stopped and penicillin G started. Eight days after the first procedure, and after studies indicated an increase in the size of the abscess, an additional 11 cc of purulent material was aspirated. Follow-up chest radiographs were clear, and she was discharged on the 16th day to a rehabilitation facility on antibiotics.
Recovery was complicated by increased headache and fever, and she was readmitted to the hospital. Cultures of the blood were sterile, and brain imaging revealed the abscess had decreased in size. Dental radiographs revealed an abscessed tooth (#30, 1st right mandibular molar) and, while still on antibiotics, a root canal was performed. Rash and hepatitis developed, which were thought to be related to one or more of her medications. Consequently, the medications were changed to levetiracetam, linezolid, metronidazole and dexamethasone; levofloxacin was added because of evidence of recurrent pneumonia on chest radiographs.
Four months after her initial admission, while on metronidazole and levofloxacin and after she agreed to remove the tongue piercing, the patent foramen ovale was repaired with an occlusion device. An MRI scan performed one year later is shown in Figure 5. Fourteen months after the onset of her illness, she was doing well, with some residual foot pain and occasional mild speech delays.
Figure 5. MRI of the brain, 1 year later.

Brain abscess, a focal intracerebral infection, begins as a discrete area of cerebritis, which expands and develops central necrosis and a surrounding capsule that is well-vascularized and ring-enhancing (Mathisen GE and Johnson JP 1997; Tunkel 2004). The microbial source of brain abscesses may be from infected sites within the cranium by indirect or direct extension (the most common etiology), by hematogenous spread from distant sites, by disruption of the integrity of the central nervous system from penetrating trauma or neurosurgery, or from a “cryptic” or unknown source. Men appear to be affected more often than women (Mathisen GE and Johnson JP 1997; Carpenter J, Stapleton S, and Holliman R. 2007).
Brain abscess may develop by direct extension from infection of the sinuses, teeth or inner ear. Lesions from the inner ear are more likely to cause abscesses in the temporal lobe or cerebellum; infections in the sinuses, the frontal or temporal lobes; and those from the teeth are more likely to affect the frontal lobe (Tunkel, 2004). Infections from the sinuses occur with greater frequency in patients 10-30 years of age, and extension from the middle ear are the primary causes of brain abscesses in patients less than 20 years or older than 40 years (Tunkel 2004); of note, the latter are on the decline with the advent of more aggressive antibacterial treatment of chronic otitis media (Mathisen and Johnson 1997). Bacterial infections are the most common cause of brain abscess, and Streptococcus species are the most common organism (with milleri group the most frequent sub-species), although staphylococcal infections are seen most often in neurosurgical patients (Carpenter J, Stapleton S, and Holliman R. 2007).
Brain abscess may also develop after hematogenous spread of organisms from another site of infection, such as pyogenic lung infection, endocarditis or intraabdominal infection. (Tunkel 2004). Cyanotic congenital heart disease and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia are also risk factors for brain abscess. In the latter, pulmonary arteriovenous malformations may allow bacteria to traverse the pulmonary circulation without removal by capillary filtration or may permit sterile paradoxical emboli of the brain, which then become superinfected (Tunkel, 2004). In immunocompromised individuals (such as those with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), malignancy with use of immunosuppressives, or steroid use), fungal infections are of increased concern.
The clinical outcomes associated with brain abscesses, which were once nearly uniformly fatal, have markedly improved since the advent of computed tomography in the 1970s, along with refinements in surgical drainage technique and improvement in the antimicrobial options (Mathisen and Johnson 1997). The most common presenting complaints are headache and neurologic symptoms (Carpenter J, Stapleton S, and Holliman R. 2007; Tunkel, A. 2004). The neurological symptoms may include confusion or decreased level of consciousness; one or the other was seen in 50% of patients in one review (Carpenter J, Stapleton S, and Holliman R. 2007). There may also be focal neurological symptoms, dysphasia, poor balance, photophobia, impaired memory and seizures; these specific symptoms appear related to the location and size of the abscess. Of note, the classic triad of headache, focal neurologic findings, and fever is present in less than half of patients presenting with brain abscess (Carpenter J, Stapleton S, and Holliman R. 2007; Tunkel 2004).
In this patient, who appeared on initial examinations to have healthy dentition, hematogenous exposure to bacteria by tongue-piercing (Martinello RA and Cooney EL. 2003) was strongly considered, especially with the added risk of a patent foramen ovale. Subsequently, when headache and fever did not resolve, a molar abscess was diagnosed and, in retrospect, this common source of brain abscesses could also have been involved, although given the location of the tooth abscess on the right mandibular side, a direct contiguous spread seems less likely. Lastly, the source of her brain abscess may have been pneumonia.
