title: 2008 November Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation S
history:
2008 November Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with dyspnea, pharyngitis and dysphagia, while incarcerated.
A man in his forties, who was incarcerated, developed progressive dyspnea, sore throat, and dysphagia with solids and liquids, over the previous 6 months. There was bilateral otalgia, and liquids were excreted from his nares after drinking. He reported having a non-productive cough. There was no fever, night sweats, chills, weight loss, or gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints.

He was born in Mexico and had immigrated to the United States more than five years earlier. He had been incarcerated for most of the time he had been in the U.S. He had no ill contacts, smoked tobacco but did not use illicit drugs or alcohol.
exam_studies:
He appeared to be in mild respiratory distress, with stridor present. The temperature was 99.3°F (37.4°C), blood pressure 111/70 mm Hg, pulse 89 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. External inspection of the head was normal. The oropharynx was clear without lesions or thrush. Masses were seen obstructing both nares. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed partial laryngeal obstruction. The neck was supple without lymphadenopathy. There were no rales or rhonchi, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The complete blood count with differential and results of a basic metabolic panel were normal. Testing for anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, and rapid plasma reagin were negative. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate measured 7 mm per hour. Computed tomography (CT) scans of chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal. A purified protein derivative skin test was negative.

Rigid laryngoscopy was performed with biopsy. Pathological examination of the tissue is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Biopsy of the epiglottis, PAS stain, high magnification.
diagnosis:
Rhinoscleroma caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae ssp. rhinoscleromatis.

Pathological examination of the biopsy revealed short, plump bacilli within foamy macrophages (or Mikulicz cells) in the epiglottis submucosa, consistent with Klebsiella rhinoscleromatosis infection. (Figure 2, see arrow). Tissue culture grew gram-negative Klebsiella pneumoniae ssp. rhinoscleromatis. (See Figures 3 and 4.) Special stains, including acid-fast bacilli (AFB), silver stains, and stains for fungal pathogens, were negative.
Figure 2. Bacilli on biopsy specimen (see arrow), PAS stain.
Figure 3. Growth from biopsy specimen on sheep blood agar.
Figure 4. Gram stain of culture growth.

The patient underwent a tracheostomy because of airway obstruction. He received ciprofloxacin orally, with stabilization of his condition. A course of ciprofloxacin for at least 12 weeks was planned but, based on the severity of his obstruction, was extended to 1 year. Six months after initial diagnosis, the tracheostomy remained in place and he was being evaluated for more extensive surgical intervention.

Rhinoscleroma is a granulomatous disease of the respiratory tract caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatosis. It can be mistaken for other diseases such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the endemic mycoses, and non-infectious etiologies such as Wegener’s granulomatosis. Rhinoscleroma can progress to severe nasal and airway obstruction. The diagnosis is made on histopathology of involved tissue, which reveals characteristic vacuolated macrophages with gram-negative coccobacilli [Stone et al. 2007; Andraca et al. 1993] Cultures may be positive for the organism 50-60% of the time [Andraca, ibid] Long-term antibiotic treatment with tetracyclines have been the mainstay of therapy, however, more recent information indicates that use of fluoroquinolones may be effective [Badia et al. 1993; Andraca et al. 1993]

title: 2008 December Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation S
history:
2008 December Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with leg weakness and urinary incontinence.
A woman in her twenties, from Honduras, was well until 6 months earlier when pain in her right buttock, which radiated down her leg posteriorly, developed. She saw her primary care physician (PCP) who diagnosed sciatica. Over-the-counter analgesics and narcotics were administered, with no improvement. Two weeks before admission, she returned to her PCP because of bilateral groin numbness, which was new. Sciatica was diagnosed, and a 10-day course of steroids was prescribed. She developed progressive lower leg weakness. Three days after completing the steroids, urinary incontinence and difficulty initiating urination developed. She presented to the Emergency Department for evaluation.
There was no history of back pain or trauma, fever, chills, night sweats, headache, diplopia or other visual disturbance, or weight loss.

She had a history of migraine headaches, and no allergies.

She was born in Honduras and had immigrated to the United States 6 years earlier. She worked as a housekeeper, and did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. One year earlier, she had returned to Honduras for a visit. She had no sick contacts or pets.

She had recently taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen as needed for pain.
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The temperature was 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure 110/66 mm Hg, pulse 73 beats per minute and respirations 16 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 96% while breathing room air. There was no deformity of the spine or tenderness on palpation. Straight leg raising did not elicit pain. Strength was diminished in the legs, with measurements on a scale of 0 to 5 (where 5 is normal strength) of 4/5 in the muscles of the right and left legs. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ in the right and left legs and 2+ in the arms. The plantar reflexes were flexor. There was decreased sensation to light touch bilaterally across the hips, and sphincter tone was normal. Proprioceptive sensation and coordination was intact. Sensation to light touch was decreased in both legs. The examination was otherwise normal.

The white blood cell count was 9,200 cells/mm³ (including neutrophils 79%, lymphocytes 14%, monocytes 5%, and eosinophils 2%). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine revealed multiple intradural cysts, which did not enhance, extending from T12 to L5 vertebrae, with the largest at the L5 level measuring 2.2 by 1 cm, and displacing the cauda equina anteriorly. The MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine also revealed multiple subarachnoid cysts without any cord compression. The MRI of the brain and computed tomography (CT) of the head were normal.
Figure 1. MRI of the lumbar spine.
Figure 2. MRI of the lumbar spine, transverse cut.
diagnosis:
Spinal subarachnoid neurocysticercosis caused by Taenia solium.

High dose dexamethasone was administered. On the 2nd day, decompression laminectomy with evacuation of the thecal cysts was performed. On gross examination, multiple thin-walled cystic structures filled with serous fluid (0.2 to 1.1 cm in diameter) were seen, with single and clustered cysts. The pathological examination of resected tissue (Figure 3) demonstrated multiple fluid-filled thin-walled structures consistent with larval cysts ('A' arrow points to the cyst wall) containing mineralized calcareous bodies ('B' arrows). Serology for cysticercosis was positive by western blot.
Figure 3. Surgical pathology of the resected tissue.

Post-operatively, her neurologic dysfunction completely resolved. Repeat imaging showed residual cysts without any cord compression. Albendazole (7-day course) was added to the steroid therapy, and she was discharged with outpatient follow-up.

Cysticercosis is a tissue infection with the cystic larval form of the tapeworm Taenia solium. Humans serve as intermediate hosts for the adult tapeworm after ingestion of raw or undercooked pork containing cystic larvae, and human cysticercosis is acquired through consumption of T. solium eggs. Infection of the central nervous system (CNS), also known as neurocysticercosis (NCC), is the most common parasitic CNS infection in humans. It has become an increasingly important emerging infection in the United States, largely due to the influx of immigrants from endemic regions.
Spinal cord involvement in NCC is a very uncommon presentation. Its incidence is estimated to be 0.7 to 3% of all cases of NCC [Sotelo et al. 1985; Amaral et al. 2003; Bandres et al. 1992]. It may be intramedullary (20%) or subarachnoid (80%) [Colli et al. 2002; Alsina et al. 2002; Leite et al. 1997]. Very few cases of extradural spinal NCC have also been reported [Amaral et al. 2003]. The intramedullary form is thought to occur by hematogenous dissemination, while the subarachnoid type, which our patient had, is thought to occur by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dissemination from a source in the cerebrum. It usually affects patients with a history of cerebral NCC but can be found without cerebral NCC in about 25% of cases [Colli et al. 2002; Goodear et al. 1997; Carydakis et al. 1984; Leite et al. 1997]. The thoracic and lumbar spine are the most commonly involved spinal segments [Leite et al. 1997]. A favorable outcome can be expected with prompt recognition and appropriate surgical management [Colli et al. 2002; Garcia et al. 2002]. The prognosis is worse if there is significant arachnoiditis [Colli et al. 2002; Canas et al. 2005].

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his sixties wit
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his sixties with fever, fatigue and cough with occasional sputum of 3 weeks' duration.
A man in his sixties was well until three weeks (Duration of symptoms is an important diagnostic clue. Most acute infections resolve or become obvious within two weeks.) before presentation when, in late spring (Seasonality can be a useful clue. Illnesses occurring in the Spring may suggest environmental exposure to plants or soil.), he developed fever, fatigue, and cough, with occasional sputum production.

There was a history of psoriasis (Psoriasis is thought to be a disorder of dysregulation of the cellular immune system. Severe cases may be treated with immunosuppressive drugs, which may increase the risk of infection.) and prostate cancer, for which radiotherapy had been administered several years earlier.

He lived in New England. He had stopped smoking (Smoking impairs host defenses against respiratory infection. Although infection risks begin to fall quickly after smoking cessation, there is still detectable increased risk for several years.) one year earlier after smoking for decades. He did not drink alcohol and had no pets. Six weeks before, he had driven through the American South and Midwest (Geographical exposures are a critical part of the infectious diseases history. In particular, even brief stay in areas with specific soil fungi such as Histoplasma or Coccidiodes can result in infection.), staying in urban areas; he had traveled to the Caribbean and Mediterranean in the remote past.

Methotrexate (Methotrexate is an inhibitor of DNA synthesis and can cause immunosuppression by blocking the growth of rapidly growing cells of the host immune system.) (10mg weekly) had been administered for many years for psoriasis.
exam_studies:
He appeared well. The temperature was 100.2°F (37.9°C), blood pressure 100/55 mm Hg, pulse 69 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% while breathing ambient air. There were fine inspiratory crackles at the bases of both lungs, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The hemoglobin (13.2 gm/dl) and white cell count (9100 cells/mm³) were normal, and the platelet count was low, at 55,000/mm³. Serum levels of electrolytes and tests of renal function were normal; the level of bilirubin was 2.1 mg/dL (reference range 0.2 -1.1 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 142 IU/L (reference range 40-130 IU/L) and alanine aminotransferase 67 IU/L (reference range 5-40 IU/L). The serum level of angiotensin converting enzyme (Elevated angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) levels would suggest the diagnosis of sarcoidosis but false positives can occur.) was 107 U/L (reference range 13-60 U/L.)
A chest radiograph is shown in Figure 1. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) showed bilateral diffuse micronodular opacities (This pattern is different from the usual patchy infiltrates of localized disease and suggests either large exposure or disseminated disease.) and mild mediastinal lymphadenopathy (Mediastinal lymphadenopathy is not typically seen in ordinary pneumonia and is suggestive of certain particular conditions such as sarcoidosis or histoplasmosis.).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.

Ceftriaxone, levofloxacin (This broad-spectrum antibiotic combination would be adequate for most community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.) and steroids (Steroids may be administered for many inflammatory conditions. Presumably in this case they were given for the possibility of sarcoidosis. The immune-suppressive effects of steroids can, however, make some infections such as fungal infections much worse.) were administered intravenously, with initial improvement (The anti-inflammatory effects of steroids can often mask symptoms and give apparent initial improvement even if the underlying disease is progressing.). Seven days later, abdominal pain, hypotension, respiratory failure and renal failure developed. A Wright stain of the blood is shown (Figure 3).
The patient was intubated and transferred to a tertiary medical center. A laparotomy was performed emergently, and revealed a dusky congested stomach, dusky distal small bowel and edematous colon.
Figure 3. Wright stain of blood.
diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum in a patient taking methotrexate.

Yeast forms consistent with Histoplasma were seen in neutrophils on the blood smear (Figure 3, above), and the serum Histoplasma antibody was positive at greater than 1:1024 dilution. Specimens obtained by bronchoalveolar lavage were positive for Histoplasma capsulatum by DNA probe. Blood cultures also grew H. capsulatum (Figures 4 and 5). At the time of laparotomy, the liver was mildly nodular in appearance. A biopsy of the liver showed numerous yeast forms on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining (Figure 6).
Figure 4. Growth of blood isolate showing filamentous mold stage.
Figure 5. Growth from blood culture.
Figure 6. GMS stain of liver biopsy, magnified x 40.

Resection of the stomach and bowel was not performed, as the risk of surgical resection was thought to be too great. Despite maximal supportive care and intravenous amphotericin B lipid complex (This antifungal medication is the current drug of choice for severe disseminated histoplasmosis but even with appropriate therapy, the mortality rate is substantial.), the patient died 2 days later.

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that is endemic in the Southeastern United States, in states bordering the Ohio and southern Mississippi Rivers. Clinical presentation depends on the immune state of host and burden of exposure to the fungus. Immunosuppressed patients can present with overwhelming infection and multi-organ failure, including shock, respiratory, renal and hepatic failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Mortality can be up to 50% despite optimal care. [Kaufmann 2007]
The most commonly involved organs are the gastrointestinal system (which is involved in approximately 70% of patients but clinically evident less than 10% of the time), the skin, adrenals and meninges. Less commonly, other organs such as liver, spleen, heart or peripheral white blood cells can reveal yeast forms in acute disseminated disease. [Deepe 2005; Kahi et al. 2005]
Teaching points:
1) Travel history is a key part of the Infectious Diseases work-up. Even distant history of travel and brief exposure can sometimes be significant if the acute illness results from reactivation of a latent infection. This principle is important for a number of infections, notably histoplasmosis and tuberculosis.
2) Immunosuppression is critical to consider in the diagnosis of infectious diseases. Histoplasma usually causes only mild or asymptomatic infection in the immunocompetent host but can cause severe disseminated infection in the immunocompromized host.
3) The diagnosis of histoplasmosis should be considered in any immunosuppressed person with disseminated febrile illness and appropriate exposure history. It can be confirmed by direct identification of the organism from involved tissues on morphological grounds, as well as by culture from blood, tissue or urine.
4) Drugs, which affect the immune system, can put patients at elevated risk of severe infection and so must be used cautiously. In this case, both the methotrexate and the steroids may have contributed to the patient’s severe infection.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his eighties wi
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his eighties with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease developed increased cough and dyspnea.
A man in his eighties, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) developed recurrent fevers, cough and dyspnea. Approximately 3 weeks earlier, in the autumn, respiratory symptoms, including productive cough and dyspnea had developed, associated with fevers. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and he was admitted to the hospital. Urinary Legionella antigen testing was positive. Moxifloxacin was administered for 14 days. He did not require intubation, and was transferred to a skilled nursing facility upon discharge.
One week before this presentation, the initial symptoms had resolved and the antibiotics were completed. Two days before admission, increasing dyspnea and cough, with minimal sputum production, developed. The night before admission, his temperature rose to 102.0°F (38.9°C). He was re-admitted to the hospital.

Before his recent illness, he had not had any exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or required steroids, during the previous year. There was also a history of transitional cell bladder cancer, with resection and creation of an ileal conduit more than a decade earlier, and chronic kidney disease. He had no allergies to medications.

The patient had smoked tobacco for more than 60 years. There was no significant alcohol use, and he did not use illicit drugs. After his recent discharge, he had lived in skilled nursing facility. There was no recent travel, or exposure to tuberculosis. He had a pet cat at home.

He had lived with his wife in the community until his admission 3 weeks earlier.

He had no allergies to medications.

Medications on admission included albuterol and tiotropium inhalers, aspirin (81 mg daily), and esomeprazole (20 mg daily).
exam_studies:
He was alert and oriented, and appeared in mild to moderate distress, with accessory muscle use. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse 79 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/55 mm Hg, respirations 31 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% while breathing 50% inspired oxygen by ventilation mask. The tongue was dry, with several vesicular ulcerations. There was also a large vesicle on his posterior pharynx, and an ulcerated area of skin (4 cm in length) extending inferiorly from the corner of his mouth. Auscultation of the lungs revealed decreased breath sounds in all lung fields and bibasilar crackles. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 11,600 cells per cubic millimeter, with 60% polymorphonuclear cells, 22% band forms, 5% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 5% eosinophils, 1% basophils, and 1% atypical lymphocytes. The creatinine was 1.4 mg/dL (reference range 0.7-1.5 mg/dL), and the potassium was 2.9 mmol/L (reference range 3.3-5.3 mmol/L). The other initial laboratory results were normal, including levels of the remaining electrolytes, glucose and tests of liver function. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figures 1 and 2) revealed diffuse lymphadenopathy in the mediastinal and hilar areas, marked emphysematous changes, and pleural effusions with adjacent compressive atelectasis and infiltrates within the hemithoraces. The upper lobes demonstrated a more interstitial pattern than the lower lobes.
Figure 1. CT of the chest.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.

Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and piperacillin-tazobactam were administered empirically for treatment of a possible hospital-acquired pneumonia. Hypoxia and respiratory distress increased, and he was transferred to a step-down unit for closer observation; he did not require intubation. On the 3rd day, fevers and hypoxia persisted, and chest radiographs revealed increasing infiltrates despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. Piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped, and meropenem and acyclovir were added empirically.
Bronchoscopy with alveolar lavage (BAL) did not reveal any abnormalities on gross examination. Examination of the aspirate with gram stain showed few polymorphonuclear cells and no organisms. Cytopathological examination of the BAL specimen is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. BAL cytopathology.
diagnosis:
Herpes simplex virus, type 1, (HSV-1) pneumonia.

Direct fluorescent antigen of the oral ulcer was positive for herpes simplex virus (HSV), type-1. Bacterial cultures from the aspirate were sterile, but cytopathologic examination of a specimen from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed evidence of HSV invasion with multinucleated giant cells (Figure 3). Viral culture from the BAL was positive for HSV, type 1.

The fevers resolved, and the respiratory symptoms and hypoxia slowly improved. A two-week course of acyclovir and meropenem were administered. He was discharged back to the skilled nursing facility on minimal supplemental oxygen. Two months later, a chest CT scan showed minimal residual bilateral infiltrates and reduction of the mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) virus. The clinical presentation of HSV pneumonia or pneumonitis is uncommon in immunocompetent hosts, unless the patient is intubated. HSV pneumonia more typically occurs in transplant recipients, burn victims, and other immunosuppressed patients. HSV infections in the lower respiratory tract have also been associated with adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mechanical ventilation. It is difficult to determine the incidence of HSV-1, lower respiratory tract infections given the occurrence of colonization in some individuals. HSV-1 was present in 2.7% of lower respiratory specimens of critically ill patients in one study [Camps et al 2002] and was associated with higher mortality in patients with ARDS in another study (60% mortality when HSV-1 was isolated versus 45% when HSV-1 was not isolated) [Tuxen et al 1982]. Clinical features of HSV pneumonia include fever, bronchospasm, cough, leukocytosis and persistent unexplained hypoxemia. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the pathogenesis of HSV pneumonia, including aspiration, contiguous spread (which may be supported by the presence of oral lesions and/or a history of tracheal intubation), hematogenous transmission, and possible direct tracheobronchial spread of reactivated virus originally present in vagal ganglia. Bronchoscopy may show edema, erythema, secretions, ulcers, exudative membrane, or can be completely normal. Chest radiographs most commonly show scattered areas of consolidation and ground glass opacities, but there is no characteristic pattern. Isolation of the virus in tissue culture or by direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing is rapid, but does not distinguish between infection and colonization. Cytological examination, with characteristic multinucleated cells and ground-glass intra-nuclear inclusion bodies, is the most specific test, but is not very sensitive. At the time of this publication, there are no guidelines or randomized controlled studies for the treatment of HSV pneumonia. In immunocompromised hosts with evidence of parenchymal invasion or clinical deterioration, acyclovir treatment is generally recommended. In normal hosts, or critically ill patients without the factors noted above, treatment guidelines are not as clearly established.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his twenties wi
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his twenties with headache, neck stiffness and cognitive decline of 4 months' duration.
A man in his twenties was well until 4 months before presentation, when headache and neck stiffness developed. The headache was a moderately painful, dull ache that was worse with coughing or lying down. During the three weeks before admission, his family members noted a gradual slowing of his speech. Marked word-finding difficulties developed, and he was seen in an emergency department for evaluation. He also reported intermittent fevers (with no night sweats) and weight loss of 10-pounds.

He was born in the Southern United States. He smoked cigarettes daily, drank beer weekly, and smoked marijuana frequently. He had no history of sick contacts or foreign travel.

He was unemployed and lived with his parents.
exam_studies:
The patient was cachectic and not in acute distress. The temperature was 101.4°F (38.6°C), blood pressure 110/75 mm Hg, pulse 112 beats per minute, and respirations 18 breaths per minute. There was bilateral papilledema, massive splenomegaly into the left lower quadrant, with no lymphadenopathy. The neurologic exam demonstrated psychomotor slowing and hyperreflexia. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 5,800 cells/mm³ (89% neutrophils, 6% lymphocytes), hematocrit 27%, and platelets 29,000 cells/mm³. There was mild hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dl), and other tests, including a metabolic panel and liver function tests, were normal. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed an opening pressure of 39 cm of water, white cells <1 cells/mm³, red cells 0 cells/mm³, glucose 34 mg/dl, and total protein 122 mg/dl. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for antibody to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was positive, and confirmed by a positive Western blot. The CD4+ T-lymphocyte cell count was 12 cells/mm³ and the level of HIV ribonucleic acid (RNA) measured 83,557 copies/ml.

During the first week of hospitalization, the spleen enlarged further, with increasing abdominal tenderness. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis showed hepatic enlargement and massive splenomegaly (Figure 1). On the 9th day, due to concern for spontaneous splenic rupture, the spleen was surgically removed. On pathological examination, the spleen weighed 2.7 kilograms.
Figure 1. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Massive splenomegaly due to disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans in a patient with newly-diagnosed HIV and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Cryptococcus neoformans was cultured from specimens of blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Pathologic examination of the excised spleen showed marked infiltration of the spleen with numerous budding yeasts, consistent with C. neoformans (Figure 2 through 4).
Figure 2. Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain of spleen specimen, low magnification.
Figure 3. H and E stain of specimen, higher (40x) magnification.
Figure 4. Mucicarmine stain of spleen specimen, 40x magnification.

The patient was treated with amphotericin-B and 5-flucytosine (5FC) and had gradual neurologic improvement. He required repeat lumbar punctures to control symptomatic elevation of intracranial pressure. Cultures of the blood and cerebrospinal fluid remained positive until the 10th hospital day (one day after splenectomy.) After he completed three weeks of amphotericin and 5FC therapy, he was discharged on oral fluconazole, and planned to initiate antiretroviral therapy as an outpatient.

The differential diagnosis of massive splenomegaly in the HIV-infected individual includes both non-infectious and infectious etiologies. The non-infectious causes include sarcoidosis, Gaucher’s disease and hematologic or neoplastic disorders, such as chronic leukemias, myelofibrosis and hairy-cell leukemia. Of the infectious causes, Histoplasma capsulatum, Mycobacterium avium complex, and M. tuberculosis would be most likely in a patient from the Southern United States without significant travel history. This patient had no known exposure to tropical diseases, such as malaria, leishmaniasis, or schistosomiasis, all of which are associated with tropical massive splenomegaly [Bedu-Addo and Bates 2002].
Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic pathogen that can lead to significant mortality in the immunocompromised host [Chuck and Sande 1989]. It is a rapidly growing, encapsulated yeast found in soil, often in association with pigeon droppings. Involvement of the central nervous system (CNS) is the most frequent non-pulmonary manifestation [Chuck and Sande 1989; Mitchell et al. 2003]. Disseminated infection to multiple organ sites can occur (Lewis and Rabinnovich 1972). Previous studies have described C. neoformans splenitis [Lewis and Rabinnovich 1972; Manner et al. 1992; Coskun et al. 2007] and one case report has described massive splenomegaly with lymphadenitis [Coskun et al. 2007].
The standard of care (at the time of this publication) for disseminated cryptococcosis with central nervous system involvement in HIV-infected patients is at least 2 weeks of induction therapy with amphotericin B and flucytosine, followed by fluconazole until the patient achieves immune reconstitution after initiation of potent antiretroviral therapy [Saag et al. 1999; Dismukes 1993; van der Horst et al. 1997]. Patients should then receive chronic maintenance therapy with fluconazole 200 mg/day until the CD4 count is consistently equal to or greater than 200 cells/mm³ for 6 months after initiation of potent antiretroviral therapy [Saag et al. 1999; Dismukes 1993; van der Horst et al. 1997]. Some experts recommend that patients have a lumbar puncture to determine whether the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is sterile and antigen-negative before stopping maintenance therapy. At least one other report [Manner C et al. 1992], and the experience with this patient, suggest that splenectomy may be an important adjunctive step in the management of massive splenomegaly due to C. neoformans.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with fevers, cough
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with fevers, cough, chest pain and axillary swelling after traveling to Hawaii for a competitive canoe race.
A man in his fifties was well until 2 days before presentation, when cough, fevers, sweats, pleuritic chest pain, malaise, and swelling under his left arm developed. Twenty-four hours earlier, he had returned from a trip to Hawaii, during which he had participated in an outrigger canoe race. He was seen in the Emergency Department of a community hospital 12 hours after the onset of his symptoms. A chest radiograph was normal, and community-acquired pneumonia was presumptively diagnosed. He was prescribed levofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and discharged.
At 72 hours after his return from Hawaii, right anterior chest wall swelling and left eye injection developed. He presented to another hospital for further evaluation.

There was a history of an appendectomy and shoulder surgery in the past, and episodic rashes.

He worked in a biomedical field, with no laboratory or patient care activities.

He was married with adult children.

He had no drug allergies.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and diaphoretic, with frequent coughing. The blood pressure was 100/56 mm Hg, pulse 116 beats per minute, temperature 39°C (102.2°F), and respirations 24 breaths per minute. The left eye was injected (Figure 1) and painful; vision was intact. A left axillary nodule was tender, warm and measured 1 inch in diameter. There were rhonchi in multiple lung fields and decreased breath sounds especially at the left base, without any dullness. A warm, firm erythematous mass, which was not fluctuant or tender, protruded below the right clavicle along the pectoral muscle (Figure 2). Cardiovascular examination revealed tachycardia with hyperdynamic state and no murmur. The rest of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The white blood cell count was 16,160 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range: 4500-11,000), with 84% polymorphonuclear cells, 2% band forms, 7% lymphocytes and 7% monocytes. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate measured 81 millimeters per hour (reference range 0-15) and C-reactive protein 14.1 milligrams per deciliter (0-0.5 mg/dl).
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed multiple abnormalities. There was a mass-like infiltrate, which measured 3.3 by 3.4 centimeters, in the medial right upper lobe with central hypodensity and air. There was extension of soft tissue density into the superior mediastinum and anterior chest wall with thickening of intercostal muscles and right pectoral muscle. Soft tissue stranding was noted in the subcutaneous fat of the anterior chest wall with skin thickening. There were enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes in the right paratracheal and subcarinal regions as well as right axillary lymphadenopathy. The left medial upper lung demonstrated a small nodule with central hyperdensity. A trace pericardial effusion, small loculated complex right pleural effusion with adjacent pleural thickening and enhancement, and an adjacent ill-defined infiltrate in the posterior right lower lobe were noted, as well as multiple small nodules in both lungs. (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. CT of the chest, chest wall and mediastinal view.
Figure 4. CT scan (lung view).

The patient was evaluated in the Emergency Department of the 2nd hospital 72 hours after returning from Hawaii. After multiple blood cultures were drawn, antibiotics were administered intravenously. He was admitted to the Medicine Service, and Infectious Diseases, ophthalmology, and thoracic surgery consultations were requested. A trans-thoracic echocardiogram was performed.
Ninety-six hours after returning from Hawaii, because of the rapidly progressive nature of the infection, he was taken urgently for thoracic surgery. A right thoracotomy, with mediastinal debridement, decortication of right upper, middle, and lower lobes, and incision and drainage of a chest wall abscess were performed. The postoperative diagnosis was metastatic infection with empyema necessitans involving the right hemithorax, mediastinum, and anterior chest wall.
diagnosis:
Rapidly progressive necrotizing Panton Valentine Leukocidin positive disseminated Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection, with nodular scleritis, cutaneous abscesses, mediastinal abscess requiring debridement, empyema requiring decortication, and multiple cavitary pulmonary lesions.

Cultures of specimens of blood, operative specimens and swabs of the eye grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing was positive for Panton Valentine Leukocidin. The organism was resistant to clindamycin, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, and tetracycline and had intermediate susceptibility to levofloxacin and gatifloxacin. It was susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), gentamicin, linezolid, vancomycin and rifampin.

Echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis. Vancomycin (1.75g) every 12 hours was administered intravenously for 6 weeks. He was also diagnosed with nodular scleritis and was treated with vancomycin ophthalmic drops. He was treated then with oral TMP-SMX therapy for 2 weeks thereafter. The patient did well, with full recovery. Upon further questioning, his previous rashes had been multiple episodes of furunculosis caused by culture-positive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, which had also affected other canoe-racing teammates.

Panton-Valentine Leukocidin positive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (PVL-MRSA) is an increasing cause of community-acquired infections. It is usually USA300 pulsed-field type [Francis et al. 2005] and in some cases it moves across tissue planes and invades anatomic structures via contiguous spread [de Bentzmann et al. 2004]. It has an aggressive phenotype, and can cause pulmonary disease, soft tissue infection, and multiple sites of infection, often with rapid progression.
Optimal antimicrobial therapy for this infection is debated, and the role of exotoxin-blocking antimicrobials (linezolid and clindamycin, if susceptible) is under investigation [Morgan 2007]. There is also debate about the role of Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) in these infections. PVL can be produced by methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) strains as well as methicillin-resistant S. aureus strains (MRSA); both are associated with severe pneumonias in young, healthy people [Gillet et al. 2008]. Some investigators have characterized PVL as a potent pore-forming leukotoxin which is sufficient to cause pneumonia and to induce transcription of staphylococcal proteins including lung inflammatory factors [Labandeira-Rey et al. 2007]. Other investigators, however, have shown that in mice infected with S. aureus, PVL is not a major virulence determinant [Voyich et al. 2006] or pathogenic factor [Wardenburg et al. 2008], although it is an epidemiologic marker of severe CA-MRSA infections. These are ongoing areas of investigation including in rabbits, whose leukocytes, like human leukocytes, are more PVL-sensitive than are those of mice [Diep et al. 2008].
Empyema necessitans results from the spontaneous dissection of infected pleural fluid into chest wall. It usually occurs after chronic untreated necrotizing pneumonia [Hockensmith et al. 1999] although in this case the process was very rapid, and required urgent surgery. Many organisms have been reported to cause empyema necessitans, including S. aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, anaerobes, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Actinomyces [Ahmed et al. 2007].
This patient had previously been healthy and active, with no apparent immunodeficiency, but a history of MRSA skin disease. The progression of disease in this case was fulminant, and rapid mobilization of surgical intervention was most likely critical to the favorable outcome. The patient’s water exposure was most likely less important than his sports-related exposure. Other members of the patient’s competitive canoeing team had had MRSA soft tissue infections in the past. MRSA transmission has been documented on sports teams [Kazakova et al. 2005].

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with HIV infection
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with HIV infection and AIDS and progressive weakness in his legs.
A man in his thirties with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) developed generalized myalgias and progressive leg weakness during the previous 6 months. The weakness was greater on the right than the left, associated with a sharp pain in the left flank and mid-lower back that radiated into his thighs, and had resulted in several falls. There was also a burning sensation on the anterior aspect of the right thigh that was exacerbated by touch. He had no bowel or bladder dysfunction and no visual deficits.
During the previous year, he reported an estimated weight loss of 10-20 lbs. There was no history of fevers, chills, night sweats, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dysuria or rash. Pneumocystis pneumonia had been diagnosed 3 months earlier, and fatigue and a mild cough had persisted since that time.

There was a history of HIV and AIDS, diagnosed more than 15 years earlier, with a recent CD4 T-lymphocyte count of 67 cells per cubic millimeter and HIV RNA level of 40,000 copies per milliliter. AIDS-defining illnesses included Pneumocystis pneumonia recently and recurrent cryptococcal meningitis several years earlier. Antiretroviral therapy had been started 9 months before admission, but non-adherence to medication had been documented. There was also a history of substance abuse in the past, including injection drug use.

He had emigrated from Mexico to the Southwestern United States more than 15 years earlier, and worked in construction and landscaping. He had last traveled internationally 6 years before to Mexico for a visit. Five years earlier, he had been incarcerated for several weeks. He had stopped alcohol and tobacco 4 years earlier, and crack cocaine and marijuana more than 5 years before.

Medications included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength three times weekly), azithromycin (1200 mg weekly), fluconazole (200 mg daily), acetaminophen with codeine (as needed for pain), gabapentin (300 mg daily), atazanavir (300 mg daily), ritonavir (100 mg daily), and a fixed dose combination of tenofovir and emtricitabine (300 and 200 mg daily, respectively.)
exam_studies:
He was thin and appeared ill. The temperature was 99°F (37.2°C), the blood pressure 100/53 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute. The calves of the lower legs were tender to touch. Strength measured 4 on a scale up to 5 in the left leg and right hip, and 3 of 5 in the lower leg on the right. Specifically, the strength in the right quadriceps and hamstring measured 4/5; right extension and flexion of lower leg, and the dorsal and plantar foot muscles, 3/5; and in the left quadriceps, hamstring, extension and flexion of lower leg, dorsal and plantar foot muscles, 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes were 1+ bilaterally, and the Babinski plantar reflex was flexor. Hyperesthesia was present over the right anterior thigh, and there was decreased sensation to vibration in the left leg.

Laboratory values included a white blood cell count of 12,200/mm³ (83% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes, 1% eosinophils), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL and hematocrit 32.3%. The basic metabolic panel was normal. The aspartate aminotransferase was 61 U/L (elevated) and albumin of 2.4 g/dL (low). Other metabolic test results and coagulation tests were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 109 mm/Hr. The CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 127 cells/mm³, with an HIV RNA level of 34,955 copies/ml. Testing for Toxoplasma immunoglobulin (Ig) G was negative at 0.5 IU/mL (less than 6.4 IU/mL is negative). Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid was normal, except for slightly elevated protein of 48.8 mg/dL. Testing of the cerebrospinal fluid for syphilis (venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test), cryptococcal antigen, and nucleic acid by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for cytomegalovirus, Epstein Barr virus, and varicella zoster virus were all negative.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine revealed expansile intramedullary enhancing lesions at the level of the T11-T12 disc space (Figures 1 and 2). MRI of head was normal.
Figure 1. MRI of the lumbosacral spine, T-1 weighted.
Figure 2. MRI of the spine, T-1 weighted, transverse view.

On admission, a T11/12 laminectomy was performed. After the dura was opened, a thick arachnoid membrane and large tangle of blood vessels including dilated arteries and veins were observed. An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) was suspected; the wound was closed and a thoracic spinal angiogram performed, however no AVM was seen. Two weeks later, a second surgical resection was performed and hypervascularity was noted over the dorsum of the spinal cord. There was a firm, tan, avascular intramedullary mass in the spinal cord. Frozen section showed inflammation. Pathological examination of the spinal tissue is shown in Figure 3.
Figure 3. Biopsy of the spinal cord lesion.
diagnosis:
Disseminated toxoplasmosis caused by Toxoplasma gondii in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Pathological examination of the spinal cord tissue, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stain, revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites of Toxoplasma gondii (Figure 3).

Therapy was begun, including sulfadiazine 1000 mg every 6 hours, pyrimethamine 75 mg daily, leucovorin 20 mg daily and dexamethasone taper, as well as tenofovir-emtricitabine, atazanavir and ritonavir. He transferred to a rehabilitation facility. Ten days later, he returned to the hospital with pneumonia and complaints of progressive weakness, which involved his arms as well. Electromyelography (EMG) showed abnormal activity. A muscle biopsy was performed; hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stain of the muscle tissue revealed necrotic skeletal muscle with lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate (Figures 4 and 5). Within the necrotic inflamed areas were abundant bradyzoites and tachyzoites of T. gondii.
The patient was unable to take oral medication secondary to difficulty swallowing pills. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy was given intravenously. Several days later, cardiac arrest occurred. Resuscitation efforts were not successful, and the patient died.
Figure 4. H and E stain of the muscle biopsy.
Figure 5. Muscle biopsy with necrotic tissue surrounding tachyzoites.

Extracerebral toxoplasmosis is a relatively rare manifestation of reactivation and primary disease in AIDS patients. This intracellular parasite can cause disease in almost any organ. The most common extracerebral sites include eyes, lungs, spine, heart and muscle. Dissemination is defined by two or more extracerebral sites. In areas of high seroprevalence, such as France (70%) or the United States (45%), there should be a high index of suspicion for this diagnosis. Extracerebral diagnosis is definitively made with histological evidence of tachyzoites, an indicator of active disease. Treatment consists of sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid for 6 weeks after resolution of all signs and symptoms, followed by maintenance therapy until immunodeficiency resolves.
An unusual feature of this case was the negative Toxoplasma IgG antibody test. This serologic test is positive in almost all cases of cerebral toxoplasmosis, and a negative test result usually suggests that a biopsy should be pursued, as occurred in this case.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with HIV infecti
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with HIV infection and AIDS developed nausea, vomiting and a rash.
A woman with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), developed nausea, vomiting, and a diffuse rash 2 weeks before admission. The rash was mildly pruritic and involved her face, chest, back and extremities, while sparing the palms and soles. She reported abdominal bloating, with no diarrhea, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
Five years earlier, she had been diagnosed with HIV infection. Within the previous year, toxoplasmosis involving the central nervous system had been diagnosed and treated, responding well to therapy. Highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) had been started three months earlier. Her pretreatment HIV-RNA level was greater than 750,000 copies/mL; one month after starting HAART, the HIV-RNA level was less than 400 copies/mL. Focal weakness developed, which was attributed to immune-reconstitution syndrome. One month before admission, prednisone (40 mg daily) was begun and the neurological symptoms resolved.
Two weeks later, nausea with vomiting occurred, and increased in severity during the following weeks. By the day of admission, she could not tolerate any oral intake, and complained of a pruritic rash.

One year before starting HAART, a nadir of 8 CD4 T-lymphocyte cells per cubic millimeter had been documented; a recent CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 16 cells/mm³. There was also a history of genital herpes and histoplasmosis.

She was born in Central America, immigrated to the United States a decade earlier, and lived in California. She denied any recent travel, animal exposure, sick contacts and did not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs.

She was a single mother and a homemaker, in a monogamous relationship with her boyfriend.

She had no drug allergies.

Medications included prednisone (40mg daily), tenofovir-emtricitabine, atazanavir-ritonavir, sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and leukovorin, voriconazole (200 mg daily), acyclovir (400mg twice daily), and azithromycin for Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis.

The pulse was 114 beats per minute, and other vital signs were normal. There was a lacey, serpiginous rash over the face, neck, back, chest, abdomen, and extremities, with sparing of her palms and soles. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The pulse was 114 beats per minute, and other vital signs were normal. There was a lacey, serpiginous rash over the face, neck, back, chest, abdomen, and extremities, with sparing of her palms and soles. The remainder of the examination was normal.

On admission, all medications were held except for prednisone. On the 4th day, dyspnea with tachycardia developed. A chest radiograph (Figure 1) revealed diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) demonstrated diffuse, bilateral fine nodular opacities with densely confluent ground glass opacities.
Respiratory droplet precautions were instituted. The next day, her respiratory status deteriorated, and the trachea was intubated emergently. A bedside flexible bronchoscopy showed severe diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.
diagnosis:
Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Cultures of specimens of blood for bacteria, fungi, viruses, and acid-fast organisms were sterile. Examination of a tracheal aspirate wet mount (Figures 3 and 4 and Video 1) revealed multiple, mobile larvae consistent with Strongyloides stercoralis. Subsequent stool and nasogastric aspirates also contained Strongyloides ova, larvae, and adult nematodes. Eosinophilia rose to 13% during the hospitalization. Culture of a sputum specimen (Figure 5) revealed serpiginous tracts.
Video 1. Wet mount of sputum specimen.
Figure 3. Wet mount of tracheal aspirate sputum specimen (also see Video 1).
Figure 4. Wet mount of tracheal aspirate.
Figure 5. Culture of sputum specimen, with serpiginous tracts.

Ivermectin and albendazole were initially administered by nasogastric tube. However, an ileus developed with high tube feed residuals. Ivermectin was then given by rectal administration, but after 3 weeks of treatment, repeat analysis of the gastric aspirates continued to show a high burden of parasites. Subsequently, a veterinary formulation of ivermectin was given subcutaneously as salvage therapy.
Four days after starting parenteral ivermectin, the patient was transferred out of the intensive care unit. Her mental status gradually improved, though her ileus persisted. Repeated nasogastric and sputum isolates showed a subjective decline in nematode number and activity. Unfortunately, acute respiratory distress developed, which did not respond to therapy. The patient subsequently died. An autopsy was not obtained.

Strongyloides stercoralis is an intestinal nematode (roundworm) endemic to the tropical/subtropical regions, as well as the southeastern United States. Its estimated prevalence in the United States is 0.4-4.0%, but it affects 50 million people worldwide [Siddiqui and Berk 2001]. The unique ability of Strongyloides to auto-infect its host can lead to persistent infection for decades.
Strongyloides hyperinfection is rare and is caused by increased larval burden and migration. This is usually precipitated by corticosteroids used anywhere from 3 weeks to several years prior [Keiser and Nutman 2004]. Solid organ transplants, malnutrition, and HTLV-1 infection are also predisposing factors, though HIV alone is not associated with hyperinfection [Segarra-Newnham 2007]. Symptoms may include cough, abdominal pain, ileus, protein-loosing enteropathy, and rash which may be urticarial or petechial. Eosinophilia is often, but not always, present. Migrating nematodes may also carry enteric bacteria into the bloodstream leading to gram-negative sepsis. Alveolar hemorrhage is an infrequent complication of Strongyloides hyperinfection [Gupta et al. 2006; Kinjo et al. 1998].
Diagnosis is often made from visualization of the nematode in stool, duodenal aspirates, or sputum. However, specimens of stool analyzed for ova and parasites are only ~30% sensitive, and multiple samples may be needed [Siddiqui and Berk 2001]. Organisms have been isolated from specimens of cerebrospinal fluid, pleural fluid, urine, ascites, and blood [Keiser and Nutman 2004]. Serology is highly sensitive, but cannot distinguish acute disease from previous exposure, and may be falsely negative in the severely immunocompromised [Segarra-Newnham 2007].
Treatment options for strongyloidiasis include thiabendazole, albendazole, and ivermectin, which are only available orally. Ivermectin is the preferred agent and is well tolerated and highly effective. Unfortunately, severe Strongyloides infection can cause intestinal ileus, making oral agents less effective. A veterinary formulation of ivermectin is available in the US but not approved for human use. There are six published case reports of veterinary subcutaneous ivermectin given to patients with Strongyloides hyperinfection, and one report of successful treatment following rectal administration [Segarra-Newnham 2007]. It appears well tolerated when given by these routes.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A child with f
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A child with fever and emesis.
A child, under 10 years of age, was admitted because of fever and emesis. She had been well until 2 weeks before admission, when sore throat, cough, chest discomfort, emesis and abdominal distension had developed, associated with subjective fevers. She was evaluated as an outpatient at three visits to healthcare facilities; pharyngitis was initially diagnosed, followed by pneumonia and finally urinary tract infection. Treatment had included trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. On the day of admission, increasing discomfort in the right side of her abdomen also occurred, and she went to the emergency department.

She had been well, and her immunizations were up-to-date.

She had moved with her family from Mexico to the United States approximately 15 months earlier. While in Mexico, she lived on a small farm, drank bottled water and ate unpasteurized home-made cheeses. Food was cooked with tap water, not well-water, and she did have contact with farm animals. No family members were ill.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 39.7°C (103.5°F). The blood pressure was 80/60 mm Hg, pulse 113 beats per minute, and respirations 40 breaths per minute. Respirations were shallow with mild splinting. She took deep breaths on command but reported discomfort over the right flank; clear breath sounds were auscultated over the anterior and posterior left lung fields, but air entry was decreased in lower 1/3-1/4 right posterior and lateral lung fields. No dullness to percussion was elicited, and no adventitious sounds were heard. There was moderate distension of the abdomen, and tenderness to superficial palpation in right upper and lower quadrants with involuntary guarding; no rebound tenderness was elicited. The liver spanned approximately 14 cm in right mid-clavicular line.

The white blood cell count was 32,700 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-14,500/cmm) with 83.2% granulocytes and a left shift. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) measured 109 mm/hr (ref. range 0-20 mm/hr) and C- reactive protein (CRP) 34.4 mg/dl (ref. range 0.0-0.8 mg/dl). Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) was 153 U/L (ref. range 14-36 U/L). Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels were within normal. Urinalysis revealed positive leukocyte esterase (250/ul), proteinuria (100 mg/dl), and 14 white cells per high power field but negative nitrite test.
A radiograph of the chest and abdomen (Figure 1) showed under-aerated lungs and prominence of the liver. Ultrasonography of the abdomen (Figure 2) demonstrated a well circumscribed focal liver lesion (7.3 cm by 7.0 cm by 7.3 cm) with heterogeneous echogenicity seen in the right lobe.
Figure 1. Radiograph of the chest and abdomen.
Figure 2. Ultrasonogram of abdomen.

Computed tomography (CT) scan (shown in Figures 3 through 5) revealed lesions that appeared cystic, and which were thought to be consistent with a large liver abscess and satellite lesions.
Cefotaxime (intravenously) was begun empirically on admission for treatment of possible pyelonephritis, pending the results of laboratory tests, and Pediatric Infectious Disease consultation was obtained following the imaging studies.
Figure 3. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 4. CT scan of the abdomen.
Figure 5. CT scan of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Amebic liver abscess, consistent with Entamoeba histolytica infection.

Antibody studies for Entamoeba histolytica were highly positive; immunoglobulin (Ig) G measured 16.3 (where greater than 1.2 is suggestive of a current or past infection). Culture of the liver aspirate was sterile, with no growth of aerobic or anaerobic organisms. Stains for ova and parasites, performed on abscess fluid specimens, were negative; numerous leukocytes and numerous red blood cells were seen. An antigen test was not performed. Stool studies were negative for ova or parasites. The clinical picture was thought to be most consistent with an amebic liver abscess.

She received empiric cefotaxime, vancomycin and metronidazole pending the results of the serologic studies. Percutaneous abscess drainage was performed and reddish-brown (‘anchovy paste’) fluid was aspirated, and a hepatic drain placed. Amebic liver abscess was diagnosed based on the serologic test results, and supported by the epidemiologic and clinical findings. Vancomycin and cefotaxime were discontinued, and oral metronidazole (10-day course), followed by paromomycin (1-week course) were given. She was followed in the outpatient clinic after discharge, and made a complete clinical recovery.

Entamoeba histolytica is the parasitic organism responsible for invasive amebiasis. Amebiasis occurs in 10% of the world’s population [Chung and Friedman 2006], and is found mostly in tropical or sub-tropical regions. Amebic liver abscess is the most common manifestation of extra-intestinal amebiasis, and is a rare disease in children [Haque et al. 2003, Hotez and Strickland 2004]. Among adults, amebic liver abscesses are most common in men (male:female ratio may be as high as 9:1); among children, amebic abscesses affect males and females equivalently.
Presentation of amebic liver abscess may be indolent, sub-acute or acute. There may be a latency period of years between intestinal and liver infection [Chung and Friedman 2006]. It is thought that this patient most likely acquired the disease in Mexico, and had a latency period of more than one year before development of liver abscess.
Symptoms and signs include fever, right upper quadrant pain, malaise and myalgias, cough and right sided chest pain, and jaundice. [Chung and Friedman 2006, Hotez and Strickland 2004] The toxic appearance of this patient was atypical for a localized amebic liver process, and may reflect thoracic or parapneumonic extension. A moderate sized pleural effusion was evident on the right side of the chest, although no radiographic evidence of rupture of the abscess on ultrasound or CT scan was seen. The pleural fluid was not sampled. The septated nature of this patient's abscess is also atypical since amebae actively lyse tissues without respecting borders.
In this case, the diagnosis was based on a combination of a high index of clinical suspicion, targeted imaging and serology. Serologic testing has a sensitivity of 95% [Chung and Friedman 2006], but must be interpreted in the context of the presentation. Serologic testing modalities include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), indirect immunofluorescent test, indirect hemagglutination, countercurrent immunoelectrophoresis, latex fixation, complement fixation, and gel diffusion [Chung and Friedman 2006, Hotez and Strickland 2004]. Aspiration of the abscess is recommended for those patients for which the diagnosis is uncertain (microscopic yield is low) or for impending rupture into pericardium, pleural or peritoneal space [Chung and Friedman 2006]. In patients with amebic liver abscess, E. histolytica antigen is found in almost 100% of serum samples and 40% of stool samples [Johannsen and Madoff 2005]. In cases of amebic invasive liver disease, the organism is isolated from the stool in only 50% of cases [Chung and Friedman 2006]. An antigen assay would have established a definitive diagnosis, but was not performed in this case.
At the time of this publication, therapy for liver amebiasis includes metronidazole (intravenously or orally, for 5-10 days) [Chung and Friedman 2006, Haque et al. 2003, Hotez and Strickland 2004, Stanley 2003], or alternatively, tinidazole [Haque et al. 2003]. Chloroquine may also be used adjunctively with metronidazole [Hughes and Petri 2000], but its use is rarely indicated. Adjunctive therapeutic modalities include luminal therapy to clear intestinal colonization, iodoquinol (three times daily) for 20 days [Stanley 2003], diloxanide furoate (three times daily) for 10 days [Haque et al. 2003] or paromomycin (three times daily) for 7 days [Haque et al. 2003].

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A pre-teen boy
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A pre-teen boy with left hip pain.
A pre-teen boy presented with a 5-week history of left hip pain and limping.
During the previous 2 months, he had had several minor injuries during football practice. Five weeks before, a throbbing pain, which radiated from the left hip to the ankle, developed. The pain was constant, improved with rest, but increased with activity and at night. There was no fever, weight loss, headache, or cough.

At 6 months of age, he presented with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and subsequently was diagnosed with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency. Three months later, he underwent a T-cell depleted haploidentical allogeneic hematopoetic stem cell transplant from his mother with no pre-transplant chemotherapy or post-transplant graft-versus-host-disease (GVHD) prophylaxis. He developed excellent T-cell engraftment, but B-cell function remained poor, requiring monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions. During the past 8 years, there had been no serious or opportunistic infections, or graft versus host disease.

The patient lived with his parents, had no siblings and no sick contacts and was an avid athlete, who participated in contact sports. There were numerous goose droppings on the field where he was practiced.

Medications included monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions via a peripheral venous catheter.
exam_studies:
The patient was overweight, and otherwise appeared well. Vital signs, including temperature, were normal. There was tenderness on flexion and internal rotation of the left hip but no erythema, swelling, or warmth was present. He ambulated with a limp. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 11,000/mm³ (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 21%, monocytes 11%, and eosinophils 4%) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 67 mm/hour. The hemoglobin concentration and platelet count were normal.
Analysis of lymphocytes by flow cytometry demonstrated 15.8% CD4 T-cell lymphocytes (reference range 33-41%) with an absolute number of 420 cells/ml (reference range 700-1100 cells/ml). The levels of CD3 and CD8 T-cell lymphocytes were normal, and the percentages were slightly low. The ratio of CD4 to CD8 lymphocytes was normal. The percentage and absolute number of CD19 B-cell lymphocytes were elevated. The T-cell proliferative responses to mitogens and antigens were normal. Quantitative immunoglobulin (Ig) levels, while the patient was receiving immunoglobulins intravenously, were IgG 1230 mg/dl (reference range 698-1560 mg/dl), 2 weeks after his monthly immunoglobulin infusion; IgM 112 mg/dl (reference range 31-179 mg/dl); and IgA less than 50 mg/dl (reference range 53-204 mg/dl).
A radiograph of the left proximal femur showed a lytic lesion and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a lytic lesion in the left femoral head with disruption of the cortex. (Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Radiograph of the left hip.
Figure 2. MRI of the left hip.

The patient was admitted for biopsy of the lesion, and an open, fluoroscopic-guided biopsy and curettage of the proximal, medial left femur was performed. His pain improved post-operatively.
diagnosis:
Cryptococcus neoformans osteomyelitis of the femoral head in a patient with severe combined immunodeficiency status post remote stem cell transplant.

Pathological examination of the biopsy using hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figure 3) revealed foci of necrotizing granulomata and histiocytes with numerous yeast forms, many with identifiable surrounding non-staining capsules (see arrows). Gomori methenamine silver stain (Figures 4 and 5) showed budding yeast with a narrow base, morphologically suggestive of Cryptococcus species.
A gram stain of the aspirate was negative for organisms; only few white cells were seen. Routine bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial culture of the surgical specimen were negative. The blood culture of the bone aspirate grew yeast, subsequently identified as Cryptococcus neoformans.
Additional studies included a chest radiograph that was normal, and examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which had normal cell counts, and levels of glucose and protein. CSF bacterial and fungal cultures were negative, and the level of cryptococcal antigen in the CSF was negative by latex agglutination. Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive to a dilution of greater than 1:4096 (normal, negative).
Figure 3. Biopsy of lesion (H and E stain)
Figure 4. Biopsy of lesion (GMS stain).
Figure 5. Biopsy of lesion (GMS stain), higher magnification.

Fluconazole, 400 mg daily, was administered orally. After two months of treatment, he remained asymptomatic and serum cryptococcal antigen had decreased to positive at 1:16 dilution. After 5 months of treatment, his serum cryptococcal antigen was negative. Fluconazole therapy (400 mg daily) for 1 year was planned.

Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast which grows at 37°C and in the environment. It is isolated from soil - especially soil contaminated with pigeon droppings - and it is acquired by inhalation.
Most patients with dissemination have defects in cell-mediated immunity caused by chemotherapy, congenital immune deficiency, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, or transplantation and immunosuppression to prevent rejection. However, cryptococcosis can also occur in healthy individuals.
The clinical presentation varies from asymptomatic or symptomatic pulmonary involvement to hematogenous dissemination to any organ. The immunosuppressed patient may present with multiple organ involvement.
The two most common sites of infection involve the central nervous system (CNS) and the lungs. Meningitis is the most common infection caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. The course is usually indolent, with headache, fever, cranial nerve palsies, and altered mental status, and the presentation may be subtle with personality changes only. Cryptococcus can also cause a pneumonitis syndrome with cough, chest pain, and constitutional symptoms. The chest radiograph may show diffuse or focal infiltrates, a solitary nodule, or hilar lymphadenopathy. In each case, careful assessment of the CNS is required to rule out occult meningitis.
The first case of cryptococcal infection described, by Busse and Buschke in 1894, was osteomyelitis of the tibia. Nevertheless, cryptococcal osteomyelitis is a relatively rare manifestation of cryptococcal disease: and only 39 case descriptions of cryptococcal osteomyelitis have been published in a review over 30 years [Behrman 1990]. Bone infection occurs in about 5% to 10% of patients with disseminated cryptococcosis. Pain and swelling can be present but bone lesions are often found incidentally. Radiographs typically reveal well-defined osteolytic lesions without marginal sclerosis or periosteal change. Joint involvement is rare [Long et al. 2008].
Once a cryptococcal infection is suspected, the diagnosis of cryptococcosis is established by isolation of Cryptococcus neoformans in culture from body fluids or tissue, or detection of cryptococcal capsular antigen in blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or urine [Long et al. 2008]. The serologic tests for detection of cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen in serum and CSF are extremely accurate for the diagnosis of invasive disease. Both latex agglutination and enzyme immunoassay tests are greater than 90% specific, and in HIV-infected patients more than 90% sensitive, for invasive infection [Perfect 2005]. In HIV-negative patients, however, serum cryptococcal antigen is positive only in 56% and 86% of those with pulmonary and CNS disease, respectively, and thus less reliable [Pappas et al. 2001].
At the time of this publication, patients with severe cryptococcosis and/or meningitis are treated with combination therapy, which includes amphotericin B and flucytosine for 2 weeks followed by a longer course (minimum of 10 weeks) of fluconazole. For children with mild-to-moderate cryptococcosis that does not involve the central nervous system, fluconazole alone can be considered for primary therapy [Long et al 2008]. Following treatment, suppressive doses of fluconazole may be needed as long as immunosuppression persists.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy with fever and a petechial rash.
The patient had been well until the day before admission, when fever and petechial rash developed. He was brought to the hospital for evaluation and admitted.

The patient was otherwise healthy. His immunizations were complete for his age.

There were no pets at home, and no history of recent travel.
Ten days earlier, a younger teenaged brother had developed a febrile illness and sore throat. Amoxicillin therapy was begun; three days later, a diffuse rash erupted and he was admitted to the hospital. An extensive evaluation for infectious etiologies was negative. Ceftriaxone was administered for 7 days, and he recovered completely. A second brother developed fever and a petechial rash on the same day as the patient. The other members of the family were well.

The patient lived with his parents and four siblings.

He had no known drug allergies.
exam_studies:
On examination, he appeared ill, but was awake and oriented. The temperature was 39.2°C (102.6°F), blood pressure of 88/35 mm Hg, pulse 87 beats per minute, and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The pharynx was erythematous, with ulcers and a few petechiae on the soft palate, which appeared similar to those seen on his brother's examination. A maculopapular petechial rash was distributed predominately on the distal extremities, and his hands and feet were erythematous and swollen. (See Figures 1 and 2.) There were no meningeal signs, conjunctival injection, or swollen joints. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 1,800/mm³ (reference range: 4,100-10,100/mm³) with 40% neutrophils, 40% lymphocytes, 10% eosinophils, and 10% monocytes. The hemoglobin was 12 g/dl, and the platelet count was 108,000/mm³.
diagnosis:
Parvovirus B19 infection, mimicking familial outbreak of meningococcemia.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for parvovirus B19 nucleic acid was positive for both the patient and the brother admitted at the same time as he, and confirmed viremia with parvovirus. On the second day of admission, parvovirus IgG antibodies and parvovirus IgM antibodies remained undetected in this patient, whereas the brother admitted with him had parvovirus serum IgG antibodies at a level of 5.33 units (reference range 0 to 0.89) and positive parvovirus IgM antibodies.
The other brother, who had first become ill, was discharged and parvovirus testing was not performed.

Ceftriaxone was administered for 5 days until PCR results became available, and was then stopped. The patient did not return for convalescent serologic testing.

Parvovirus B19 is the etiologic agent of the common childhood exanthem erythema infectiosum. It is a small, non-enveloped, single stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (ssDNA) virus. Humans are the only known host for parvovirus B19. [Kaufmann et al. 2004] Viremia occurs seven to 10 days after exposure and usually lasts approximately five days, with virus titers peaking on the first few days of infection. [Young and Brown 2004] Approximately 25 percent of infected individuals will be completely asymptomatic during their infection, while 50 percent will have only non-specific flu-like symptoms. The remaining 25 percent of infected individuals will present with the classic symptoms of B19 infection including rash and/or arthralgia. [Chorba et al. 1986, Hayakawa et al. 2002, Woolf et al. 1989]
Parvovirus B19 infection is responsible for a wide range of clinical manifestations depending on the underlying host. Erythema infectiosum is commonly seen among children infected with parvovirus B19 infection. In sickle cell disease, parvovirus B 19 infection could result in transient aplastic crisis. [Serjeant et al. 2001] Furthermore, parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy can result in fetal complications including miscarriage, intrauterine fetal death and/or non-immune hydrops fetalis. Some other rare disease associations are arthritis, vasculitis, myocarditis, nephritis, lymphadenitis, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and hemophagocytic syndrome, Papular-purpuric “gloves & socks” syndrome, encephalopathy, and fulminant liver disease. [Bakhshi et al. 2002, Brown 2007, Harms et al. 1990]
