title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy with headache of 3 months’ duration, associated with diplopia and emesis.
A teenaged boy was well until 3 months before admission when severe headaches developed. One month later, diplopia and emesis occurred. Computed tomography (CT) of the head, ordered by his primary care physician, was reportedly normal. During the next 2 months, weight loss of approximately 10 kilograms occurred, and generalized weakness developed. He was admitted to a community hospital.
On admission, CT scan of the head, with the administration of contrast, showed mild ventriculomegaly and mild hydrocephalus. A ventriculo-peritoneal (VP) shunt was placed to control intracranial pressure. On the 5th hospital day, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed abnormal flair signal in the right thalamus. Lumbar puncture was performed twice, and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyzed. (Results are shown in Figure 1.) Generalized tonic-clonic seizures developed, and fever occurred during the hospitalization. Vancomycin, cefotaxime and doxycycline were administered, as well as antiepileptic medications and dexamethasone. The temperature returned to normal, the headache decreased, and the episodes of vomiting resolved.
He was discharged home on the 26th day, with residual lower extremity weakness, on antiepileptics and dexamethasone. Four days later, status epilepticus developed, and the patient was readmitted to the hospital. On examination, he was febrile, and altered mental status was present. Two days later, lumbar puncture was repeated (see Figure 1). He was transferred to a tertiary care hospital for further evaluation.
Figure 1. Results of CSF analysis

He was born after a full-term gestation, with no neonatal complications. Growth and development had also been normal, and he had had no serious illnesses, hospitalizations, or surgical procedures. He reported knee pain chronically for 1 year or longer, which he attributed to playing sports.

He traveled monthly from the American Southwest to Mexico to visit family. He had not been exposed to pets.

There were no known contacts with tuberculosis, autoimmune disease or neurologic disease in the family.

There were no allergies to medications.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure 119/70 mm Hg, pulse 94 beats per minute, and respirations 25 breaths per minute with oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing ambient air. His weight was 45.2 kg. The patient was confused and disoriented as to time, place and person. He did not follow simple commands and spoke in incoherent phrases. He was unable to ambulate without assistance. Cranial nerves 2 through 12 were intact (CN 1 not tested). Strength was decreased (3 out of 5, where 5 is normal) with reduced muscle bulk and clonus in both legs; examination of the arms was normal.

On admission to the 2nd hospital, the white blood cell count measured 3,600/mm³ (66% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 1% band forms, 17% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, and 2% atypical lymphocytes). Hemoglobin measured 10.4 g/dL, hematocrit 30%, and the platelet count 118,000/mm3. The level of plasma sodium was 131 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 97 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL and creatinine 0.4 mg/dL. A chest radiograph was normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, with the administration of contrast, revealed diffuse leptomeningeal disease with enhancement that was thought to be suggestive of neoplastic disease - sarcoid or granulomatous disease could not be excluded - and a focal lesion in the right thalamus (Figure 2). The ventricular shunt was noted to be in place. A lumbar puncture was performed; analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is shown in Figure 1; see "2nd admission” columns.
Figure 2. MRI of the brain.
diagnosis:
Leptomeningitis and cerebritis, with findings consistent with Central Nervous System Whipple's Disease, caused by Tropheryma whipplei.

A surgical procedure was performed and areas of dura, leptomeningeal and cerebral cortex, and subcortical white matter biopsied. Pathological examination of the dural specimens showed no evidence of vasculitis. The leptomeninges showed fibrosis, and macrophage infiltration, with no atypical or malignant cells seen. (See Figure 3 stained for HLA-DR class II MHC.) Examination of the brain specimens showed focal well-circumscribed lesions, consisting of sheets of foamy macrophages. The macrophages were PAS positive, and some cells revealed distinct PAS+ granules (Figure 4). Figures 5 and 6 demonstrate foamy macrophages, seen by Wright stain of a CSF specimen and in a brain specimen examined by electron microscopy, respectively. Stains for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms were negative, including on the electron microscopy preparations. No well-defined granulomata, or multinucleated giant cells were present.
After the patient had received doxycycline, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for Tropheryma whipplei was performed, and was negative.
Figure 3. HLA DR stain of biopsy.
Figure 4. PAS stain of brain biopsy.
Figure 5. CSF with foamy macrophages, Wright stain.
Figure 6. Electron microscopy of brain biopsy.

The patient received cefotaxime (2 grams intravenously every 8 hours) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160 mg/800 mg orally every 8 hours) for 2 weeks, followed by monotherapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. His mental status and motor strength gradually improved. One month after his discharge, he was able to converse appropriately, was alert and oriented to time, place and person, and could walk unassisted. However, he tired easily, had persistent lower extremity weakness and stiff gait, and difficulty processing questions that required recall of information.

The presence of PAS (+) inclusions in the brain biopsy in the setting of suggestive clinical signs and symptoms is consistent with a diagnosis of Whipple's Disease of the central nervous system [Louis et al. 1996). A positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for Tropheryma whipplei deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) would confirm the diagnosis [Schneider et al. 2008]; in this case, however, the result was negative, possibly related to the prior antibiotic therapy.
Whipple's Disease can present as three different clinical entities: Classic Whipple's disease, endocarditis with negative cultures and isolated neurologic infection [Fenollar et al. 2007]. Neurologic Whipple's disease has three variants: classic Whipple's disease with neurologic involvement, isolated neurologic disease and neurologic relapse of previously treated Whipple's disease [Fenollar et al. 2007]. The most common manifestations of neurologic Whipple's disease are cognitive dysfunction, decreasing level of consciousness and memory impairment [Schneider et al. 2008]. Oculomasticatory (OMM) and oculofacial-skeletal myorhythmia (OFSM) are pathognomonic findings of neurological Whipple's disease. [Louis et al. 1996]. The diagnosis of Neurologic Whipple's disease requires one of the following: (1) OMM or OFSM; (2) positive tissue biopsy (PAS positive inclusions in macrophages or evidence of microorganisms on electron microscopy) or (3) positive PCR for Tropheryma whipplei in the setting of high clinical suspicion [Louis et al. 1996]. At the time of this publication, the recommended treatment for Whipple's disease includes an initial 2 weeks of ceftriaxone, followed by long term therapy of 1 year or more of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [Fenollar et al. 2007, Schneider et al. 2008]. This patient’s presentation highlights the importance of vigilance for evolving physical findings and of histopathologic examination of biopsied tissues in establishing the diagnosis of CNS Whipple’s disease.

title: 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A toddler with
history:
2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A toddler with muscle aches and clumsiness.
A toddler was well until 10 days prior to presentation when an upper respiratory infection, associated with a persistent cough, developed. Seven days before presentation, he began to stumble. Two days later, myalgias and weakness in his left leg occurred, which progressed to involve the right leg. One day before presentation, he complained of weakness in his arms, neck and head, and refused to get out of bed. He was brought to a pediatric urgent care facility.
He reported dizziness for several days, and denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and headache.

There was a history of asthma and environmental allergies. His immunizations were reportedly up-to-date.

He lived with his family in Southeast Asia, and had been vacationing in the United States for the previous month at the time of his illness. All other family members were healthy. They had flown into a city in the American Southeast, took a cruise in the Caribbean for 1 week, visited family in Northwest, and then went to a city in the Mid-Atlantic region. He had no pets or animal contacts. While on the cruise, he may have spent some time in the ocean swimming, and his diet had included the fare provided on the ship.

He lived with his parents and an older sibling.
exam_studies:
He was reportedly unable to walk, and was carried into the office by his parents; he otherwise appeared well. There was occipital lymphadenopathy on the left. There was wheezing in the lungs bilaterally, with no retractions. A skin lesion was present. Cranial nerves were intact. With assistance, he attempted ambulation with a very ataxic gait. He was unable to raise his arms to midline and deep tendon reflexes were reported as 1 to 2 throughout. The sensory exam was normal. The rest of his examination was normal.

Complete blood count revealed 9,300 white cells per cubic millimeter with a differential of 37% polymorphonuclear cells, 51% lymphocytes. Hemoglobin and hematocrit were 12.9 g/dL and 37.5%, respectively. Platelet count was 326,000 per cubic millimeter. The basic metabolic panel was normal limits. Creatine kinase was also normal at 114 units/L.

The skin lesion was removed (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Figure 1.
diagnosis:
Tick paralysis.

On further examination, the skin lesion, which was first thought to be a skin tag when noted by his mother 10 days earlier, was an engorged tick, which was removed (See Figure 1). The tick was not identified further.

Within 2 hours of the removal of the tick, he had significant improvement in his ability to ambulate. Within 8 hours, his neurological abnormalities had resolved. A post-inflammatory nodule at the site of the tick bite developed that did not resolve with steroid treatment. He underwent a local incision and biopsy of the nodule without further sequelae. Five months after tick removal, his mother reported that he was still doing well.

Tick paralysis is a neurologic syndrome that is frequently confused with other acute disorders. It causes an ascending paralysis due to a potent neurotoxin produced by attached, engorged ticks.
Both Ixodes and Dermacentor ticks can cause tick paralysis. The Ixodes holocyclus tick, mostly found in Australia, causes a more severe neurologic impairment than does the toxin from Dermacentor sp. of North America. The incubation, or onset of symptoms, most often occur 4-7 days after female tick attachment. The tick is most commonly found in the Rocky Mountain region, western Canada, and Northeast US. In this case, the tick was most likely acquired during the family's stay in the Northwest United States.
The proposed mechanism of the holocylotoxin is paralysis due to failure to release acetylcholine from nerve terminals at the neuromuscular junction. This results in abnormalities of excitation-secretion mechanism possibly due to reduced calcium availability. The toxin is noted to be temperature-dependent in its action.
Treatment includes identification and removal of the tick. This typically leads to prompt recovery. In the North American Dermacentor sp. ticks, patients typically show improvement within 1 hour, and all symptoms generally resolve within 24 hours. Dog serum antitoxin is used for animals with tick paralysis. Rarely, antitoxin has been used in humans for severely ill patients. The occurrence of adverse events including acute reactions and serum sickness, and variable efficacy due to different toxins secreted by different ticks, limits its use.
After removal of the ticks, the prognosis is very good. However, the disease is potentially fatal if undiagnosed, with a reported mortality rate of up to 11% [Rose, 1954]. Rare complications of myocarditis, myositis, and myoglobinuria have been reported in humans. Possible autonomic, cranial nerve, and central nervous system involvement have also been reported.

title: 2008 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Case Submission Summary: A toddler with fever and a
history:
2008 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Case Submission Summary: A toddler with fever and an abdominal mass.
A previously healthy toddler developed fever of three weeks duration, associated with cough and congestion. He saw his pediatrician and azithromycin was administered. The cough and congestion improved, but fever persisted, and temperatures rose to 103-104°F (39.4-40.0°C) daily. Ten days before presentation, a stiff and shuffling gait developed. He was seen by another pediatrician, who palpated an abdominal mass on the left side. The patient was referred to a pediatric hospital for further care.
Review of systems revealed a history of fever, left-sided stiffness and hip pain, decreased activity, fatigue, decreased appetite and oral intake, and weight loss of one to two pounds.

He was born at full-term, with an uncomplicated gestation and delivery, followed by a normal neonatal period. He had had several episodes of otitis media and occasional wheezing. Immunizations were up-to-date, excluding the second dose of Hepatitis A vaccine.

The boy lived in a wooded residential area in the American Southwest. He had no siblings, and attended daycare. There was a dog and a cat in the home, and he had visited petting zoos in the previous month. He had not traveled outside of his home state and had no sick contacts.

The boy lived with his parents.

There was no family history of chronic diseases or cancer.

There were no known drug allergies.

Medications included azithromycin and ibuprofen as needed for pain.
exam_studies:
The child appeared calm, comfortable, and well-developed for his age. The temperature was 104.6°F (40.3°C), the blood pressure 100/64 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats per minute, respirations 30 breaths per minute and the weight 10 kg. The neck was supple, with shotty cervical lymphadenopathy. There were normal bowel sounds, and a soft, tender mass was palpated in the left flank 2-3 cm below the costal margin. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. He would not bear weight on his left leg, and held his left thigh in flexion and abduction when reclining. Pain in his left flank was elicited with straight leg-raising. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell (WBC) count was 20,720 cells/µL (53% neutrophils, 8% bands, 27% lymphocytes, 11 % monocytes, 1% eosinophils), hematocrit 25.4% and platelets 790,000/µL. Routine serum chemistries, urinalysis and tests of liver and renal function were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate measured 104 mm per hour (normal 0-20 mm/hr), and the C-reactive protein level was 28.7 mg/dL (normal <1.0mg/dL). Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed enlargement of the left kidney with abnormal echotexture (Figure 1). Computerized tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a large mass-like density emanating from the mid and lower pole of the left kidney extending inferiorly to the left pararenal space, and close to the left iliopsoas muscle (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Ultrasonography of the abdomen.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen, with contrast.

In the Emergency Department, aspiration of the left hip was performed, but little fluid was obtained. He was admitted and intravenous clindamycin and cefotaxime were begun.
diagnosis:
Perinephric abscess in a toddler, caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

The CT of the abdomen (Figure 3) revealed a mass consistent with a large perinephric abscess. Percutaneous drainage of the mass, guided by ultrasonography, was performed and purulent material aspirated. Cultures of the aspirate grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which was susceptible to clindamycin. Blood and urine cultures were sterile.
Figure 3. CT of the abdomen, with left renal mass (arrows).

After the procedure, intravenous clindamycin was administered for 2 weeks, with complete resolution of symptoms and signs. A follow-up CT scan is shown in Figure 4.
Figure 4. Follow-up CT of the abdomen.

Renal and perinephric abscesses are uncommon in children and clinical manifestations are variable [Practice Parameter. Pediatrics 1991]. All age groups are affected and there is no gender predominance. Staphylococcus aureus continues to be an important cause of hematogenously-acquired disease. Enterobacteriaceae also can cause infection, especially if the abscess is precipitated by a urinary tract infection [Steele et al. 1990]. Anaerobic bacteria are isolated rarely, usually in association with recent urologic or abdominal surgery, renal anomalies or abdominal trauma [Brook 1994, Casullo et al. 2001].
Non-specific symptoms, such as malaise, lethargy, decreased appetite, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting, are common and typically associated with fever and pain in the flank or abdomen [Steele et al. 1990]. The clinical picture can mimic retrocecal appendicitis with or without rupture. When a palpable mass is present, evaluation for pediatric neoplasms such as Wilm’s tumor or neuroblastoma is warranted [Angel et al 2003]. The possibility of renal abscesses should be investigated in patients with persistent fever, flank pain or mass, and abdominal pain with elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and leukocytosis [Practice Parameter. Pediatrics 1991].
Renal ultrasonography and computerized tomography (CT) are the current imaging modalities of choice for diagnosis. CT scans are very accurate and have the added advantage of distinguishing between renal and perinephric abscesses. The mainstay of treatment is broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics with agents effective against Staphylococcus aureus and Enterobacteriaceae as well as percutaneous or open surgical drainage of the abscess. Anaerobic coverage in patients with predisposing factors should be considered [Angel et al 2003].

title: A man with chronic sinusitis developed rhinorrhea, cough and periorbital pain.
history:
Two weeks before presentation, a man in his thirties with a history of chronic sinusitis developed rhinorrhea associated with a mild non-productive cough, fatigue and frontal and bilateral periorbital pain. He also noted a tender right submandibular lymph node.
Three days before, fevers to 102°F (38.9°C) and night sweats occurred. Periorbital pain localized around the right eye, and blurred vision in the right eye developed, which evolved into a blind spot in the center of the visual field.

He had chronic sinusitis and an anxiety disorder.

He was born in western Europe and had immigrated to the United States several decades earlier. He drank alcohol in moderate amounts and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. He owned a cat, and had not traveled recently or had any sick contacts.

He was married, and monogamous.

There were no known drug allergies.

Medications included clorazepate, amitriptyline and desipramine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 128/86 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats per minute, respirations 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. The head was normocephalic, without sinus tenderness. The conjunctivae and eyelids were normal. Fundoscopic examination of right eye is shown in Figures 1 and 2. There were no neck masses or lymphadenopathy. A 2/6 systolic ejection murmur was heard, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Fundoscopic examination.
Figure 2. Fundoscopic examination.

The white blood cell count was 9,700/mm³ (reference range 4,000-11,000), with a normal differential. The hematocrit was 42.5% (ref 40-54%), platelet count 501,000/mm³ (ref 150,000-400,000) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 44 mm per hour (ref 0-15). The level of plasma glucose was 134 mg/dl (ref 70-110). Tests of liver function were normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with angiography (MRI/MRA) showed no acute intracranial abnormality. There were nonspecific scattered subcortical hyperintensities on FLAIR/T2 imaging, bilaterally.

A demyelinating disease was diagnosed presumptively, and the patient was started on high dose steroids, with mild visual improvement.
diagnosis:
Neuroretinitis, as a manifestation of cat-scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae.

The ophthalmologic examination of the right eye, shown in Figure 1, revealed a normal-appearing macula and optic disc edema with a peripapillary retinal hemorrhage at the temporal border. Figure 2 shows a more magnified view of the optic disc with associated edema and hemorrhage.
Serological testing for Bartonella henselae was positive; the acute serum IgM titer was 1:16 (reference range: 1:16 or greater is positive) and the titer of IgG, 1:64 (less than 1:64, negative; 1:64–1:128, equivocal; and 1:256 or greater, positive). The IgM convalescent titer was less than 1:16 (negative) and that of IgG 1:256 (positive), which represented a fourfold increase in the IgG titer of the convalescent serum. Blood cultures were sterile and polymerase chain reaction testing of the serum was negative.

Doxycycline and rifampin were administered. Two weeks later, follow-up fundoscopic examination showed the typical “macular star” of neuroretinitis (Figure 3, with arrows, 10 weeks after admission). At that time, visual acuity had improved but had not returned to baseline. The patient was treated for a total of 8 weeks and was able to return to his normal daily activities.
Figure 3. Fundoscopic exam, 10 weeks after admission, with macular star.

The clinical manifestations of cat-scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae result from either local infection with lymphadenopathy, or from bloodborne disseminated infection, such as occurs with neuroretinitis or visceral organ involvement.
Ocular manifestations include Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome (conjunctivitis, conjunctival granuloma, and preauricular lymphadenopathy), neuroretinitis, chorioretinitis and optic neuritis [Cunningham and Koehler 2000, Ormerod and Dailey 1999].
The prevalence of neuroretinitis in patients with systemic B. henselae infection is unknown, but appears to be uncommon, occurring in 1% to 2% of patients. Simultaneous or subsequent retinitis in patients with Parinaud’s oculoglandular syndrome is uncommon but has been reported [Wong et al 1995].
Neuroretinitis primarily presents unilaterally, although patients with bilateral optic disc swelling and macular star formation have been reported [Wade et al 1999]. Optic disc edema, often accompanied by a peripapillary subretinal fluid, usually precedes the formation of the typical macular star (a stellate macular exudate) by 2 to 4 weeks [Wade et al 2000]. Some patients never form a macular star. Others develop massive disc edema with widespread subretinal and intraretinal exudates. Macular exudates may take months to resolve and patients may be left with residual disease (mild to moderate optic disc pallor, subnormal contrast sensitivity, abnormal color vision, and abnormal evoked potentials).
Before the identification of the etiologic agent, virtually all immunocompetent patients with cat scratch disease improved without antimicrobial therapy. As Bartonella is an intracellular organism, it is reasonable to use antibiotic agents which achieve high intra-erythrocytic concentrations, such as the macrolides, quinolones, the tetracyclines, and rifampin [Reed et al 1998]. Rifampin has good penetration into the central nervous system, an advantage in treating neuroretinitis.
Immunocompetent patients develop long-lasting immunity and are therefore at relatively low risk for repeat infection by B. henselae. For prevention of disease, any wounds caused after a cat scratch or bite should be immediately washed and disinfected.

title: 2009 January Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Prese
history:
2009 January Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenager with an ulcer on the hand and lymphadenopathy.
A boy in his mid-teens was well until 3 weeks earlier when a small papule developed on the dorsum of his right hand. The lesion gradually increased in size and became more painful during the following weeks, associated with painful “red knots” around the right elbow and axilla. Fevers, up to 102°F (38.9°C), had occurred intermittently during the previous 5-6 days.
He presented to his primary care provider’s office for evaluation. Incision of the lesion was performed, but there was no drainage noted and no improvement in symptoms following the procedure. Clindamycin was administered orally for 5 days without improvement. He was admitted to a hospital near his home, and vancomycin was given intravenously for 3 days, again with no improvement. He was transferred to a pediatric hospital for further care.

He had several pets at home, including 3 cats, several dogs and pet deer. He went hunting regularly, and had handled both deer and rabbit carcasses during the previous month. He had also scratched his hands on hay, briars in the woods, and inside beaver dams.

Family history was negative.

Recent medications included clindamycin and vancomycin, as per the history.
exam_studies:
The patient was an adolescent male who appeared well. The temperature was 100.0°F (37.8°C); other vital signs were normal. There was an ulceration (2 centimeters (cm) by 3 cm) on the dorsum of his right hand, which was granulated in the center, red at the edges (Figures 1 and 2), and painful. Range of motion of the fingers was full. Tender lymphadenopathy was palpated in a chain along the dorsal aspect of his forearm, up to and including his epitrochlear nodes, and in the lower right axilla.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 16,600 cells per cubic millimeter, with 47% neutrophils and 13% bands, 3% monocytes and 37% lymphocytes. The levels of hemoglobin, platelets, and electrolytes were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 33 mm per hour (reference range 0-10 mm per hour) and C-reactive protein (CRP) 47 mg/L (reference range 0-10 mg/L). Radiographs of the right arm and hand were normal.
diagnosis:
Ulceroglandular tularemia caused by Francisella tularensis.

The microagglutination titer for antibody to Francisella tularensis was positive at 1:256 dilution. Culture of the wounds grew a few colonies of Francisella tularensis. Serological test results for Bartonella henselae immunoglobulin (Ig) G and IgM and Sporothrix schenckii IgG were negative.

Gentamicin was administered intravenously for 14 days; after 2 days, his fevers resolved. After 1 week of therapy, the epitrochlear nodes were aspirated for comfort, with good response. During the following week, the lymph nodes increased in size again, with less pain. After completion of the gentamicin therapy, there was near-complete resolution of the ulcer and improvement in the lymphadenopathy. He recovered completely, without relapse.

Tularemia is caused by Francisella tularensis, a highly infectious gram-negative zoonotic infection [Cross et al. 1995]. It can present as multiple clinical syndromes, the most common of which are ulceroglandular and glandular tularemia, in which a patient develops an ulceration at the site of the initial inoculation of bacteria into the skin and regional lymphadenopathy. Other presentations include oculoglandular, pharyngeal, typhoidal and pneumonic tularemia. Animal reservoirs include over 100 species of wild mammals. The most commonly reported animal reservoirs are rabbits, hares, prairie dogs, muskrats and other rodents. In the United States, ticks and biting flies can serve as vectors to spread disease from infected mammals to humans. Posterior cervical or occipital adenopathy following a tick bite on the scalp is the most common presentation of tularemia in the pediatric patient. Transmission of F. tularensis via contaminated water or soil is uncommon in the United States [Ellis et al. 2002].
The diagnosis of tularemia is usually established with serologic testing. A single serum antibody titer of greater than 1:128 dilution (microagglutination) or greater than 1:160 dilution (tube agglutination) is consistent with recent infection. Confirmation of infection requires a four-fold greater change in titers over at least two weeks, with at least one specimen positive at greater than 1:128 dilution [Tarnvik and Chu 2007]. Definitive diagnosis of tularemia is complicated by its poor growth on routine laboratory culture. The organism can be cultured from specimens of lymph node tissues, sputum, blood, pharyngeal washings and fasting gastric aspirates [Ellis et al. 2002].
Laboratory personnel should be notified whenever tularemia is suspected so that they may optimize recovery of this organism, as culturing it is technically difficult. In addition, the organism is highly infectious and cultures must be handled with care to prevent accidental inhalation [Dennis et al. 2001]. Cultures should be held for a minimum of ten days to allow adequate time for colonies to appear on routine microbiology agars [Ellis et al. 2002].
Gentamicin and streptomycin are bactericidal against F. tularensis and remain the drugs of choice for tularemia treatment. For less severe infections, oral ciprofloxacin or doxycycline may be considered, but these drugs are associated with a high rate of relapse [Ellis et al. 2002]. Other etiologies considered in this case included sporotrichosis, given his known hay exposure and chain of nodular lesions, and blastomycosis, with his physical exam findings and exposure to beaver dams. Cat scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae was also considered because of the degree of lymphadenopathy and fever. His prompt response to treatment with gentamicin, as well as the severity of his ulceration with no underlying bone involvement, made these other etiologies less likely.

title: 2009 February Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation S
history:
2009 February Featured Case and 2008 ICAAC/IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his eighties with chest wall purulence for one month.
A man in his eighties presented with a 1-month history of purulent chest wall drainage. There was no history of trauma to the chest wall, fevers, or chills. Two years earlier, a pacemaker in the left chest wall and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen were upgraded to a biventricular system on the right chest wall. The generator of the old devices was removed, but the old leads on the left side remained in place.
A course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was administered, but the drainage persisted.

There was a history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass grafting, and herniorrhaphy.

He lived alone in a city in a mid-Atlantic state in the United States. He did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. There was no history of travel and he had no pets.

Medications included digoxin, carvedilol, simvastatin, glipizide, and furosemide.
exam_studies:
The patient was pleasant and in no acute distress. His temperature was 97.7°F (36.5°C), blood pressure 139/57 mm Hg, and pulse 65 beats per minute. There was a healed surgical scar (3 cm) on the left chest wall, with an opening (1 mm in diameter), which was draining purulent discharge. A maculopapular rash (few lesions, 5 mm in diameter) was also present on the chest wall. The chest wall on the right side was intact, with a biventricular cardiac device present. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 9,000 cells/mm³ (with 90% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13 gm/dl, and the platelet count was 127,000/mm³. Blood cultures were sterile. The lesion on the chest was swabbed, and a Gram stain showed many white cells with no organisms.

The lesion of the chest was cultured (Figures 1 and 2.)
Figure 1. Sabouraud dextrose agar.
Figure 2. Growth on cornmeal agar (high magnification)
diagnosis:
Cardiac device infection caused by Trichosporon beigelii.

Culture of the swab of the lesion on the chest grew Trichosporon beigelii (Figure 2). The organism was sensitive to amphotericin (mean inhibitory concentration (MIC) =1 microgram/mL), fluconazole (MIC=8 microgram/mL), and voriconazole (MIC=1 microgram/mL). It was borderline sensitive to caspofungin (MIC=16 microgram/mL).

The old leads, which were noted to be capped with purulent discharge, were surgically extracted. Cultures of the blood were repeated and remained negative. Transesophageal echocardiogram showed no evidence of cardiac vegetation. Oral fluconazole was administered for 4 weeks, with resolution of the wound infection.

Trichosporon beigelii is a yeast which is found in soil and water. In humans, it colonizes the skin, and the urinary and gastrointestinal tracts [Walsh et al. 1993]. Trichosporon can cause superficial skin infections, such as white piedra. In immunocompromised hosts, it can cause deep invasive infections, including fungemia, endocarditis and chronic meningitis [Haupt et al. 1983; Keay et al. 1991; Mathews and Prabhakar 1995]. To our knowledge, this is the first case of pacemaker infection with Trichosporon beigelii. Trichosporon species grow easily on routine fungal plates and appear creamy. Microscopic features include pseudohyphae, hyphae, blastoconidia (which differentiate it from Geotrichum spp.) and arthroconidia (which differentiate it from Candida spp. and can resemble the arthroconidia of Coccidioides spp.) [Kwon-Chung and Bennett 1992]. Of note, this organism can cause a false positive latex agglutination test for Cryptococcus neoformans [Melcher et al. 1991] when infection is disseminated. Trichosporon spp. have variable susceptibility to azoles and amphotericin B, but consistently demonstrate high minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to echinocandins, such as caspofungin. Recently, some taxonomists have favored dropping the species name T. beigelii (also known as T. beigelli) in favor of other species designations but, at the time of this publication, this is not yet settled [Chagas-Neto et al. 2008, www.doctorfungus.com].

history:
2009 March Featured Case Summary: A man in his fifties with epigastric pain.
A man in his fifties was admitted to the hospital with epigastric pain. He was well until the day before his presentation, when a sharp upper abdominal pain developed suddenly after eating a spicy meal. The pain was most severe in the epigastrium and rated 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, where 10 is the most severe. His temperature reportedly rose to 102.0°F (38.9°C). The pain decreased slightly, and then increased in severity 17 hours later. On the day of his admission, he felt chilled, became nauseated and vomited undigested food, with no blood. He took ibuprofen, and went to an urgent care clinic.
On evaluation, the pain rated 10 in intensity. The temperature was 99.2°F (37.3°C), and he appeared uncomfortable, flushed, and was shaking. There was tenderness in the epigastrium and right lower quadrant, with guarding in the right lower quadrant. An inguinal hernia was present on the right. There was no rebound or costovertebral angle tenderness. He was transferred to the emergency department of a hospital for evaluation.
On arrival, he reported that the pain had decreased to a level 3 in intensity and was not altered by sitting or standing. There was no history of diarrhea, blood per rectum, or urinary symptoms.

He was otherwise well, with a past history of intermittent musculoskeletal strain related to lifting activities, bilateral simple renal cysts, and anemia (hematocrit 36.0%) noted 10 years earlier.

He was of Hispanic ancestry. He drank alcohol socially, and did not smoke or use illicit drugs.

He was married, and performed physical labor in a service industry.

His mother had had hypertension, and maternal relatives had diabetes mellitus.

He had no allergies.

He had taken ibuprofen, and was on no other medications.
exam_studies:
On examination, he was thin and anicteric. The temperature was 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 85/58 mm Hg, pulse 117 beats per minute, and respirations 20 breaths per minute with oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing ambient air. The abdomen was soft, with mild epigastric pain, and no distension, rebound or guarding. Obturator, psoas, and Rovsing’s signs were absent, and there was no blood in the stool. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 5,500 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000 cells, with 75% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 16% band forms, 6% lymphocytes and 1% monocytes), the hematocrit 30.9% (ref 41.0-53.0%), hemoglobin 10.7 gm/dl (ref 13.5-17.5) with a mean corpuscular volume of 59 fl (ref 80-100), with 3+ microcytes and 1+ teardrops. The level of total bilirubin was 1.6 mg/dl (ref 0-1.0), direct bilirubin 0.5 mg/dl (ref 0-0.4), and the levels of amylase, lipase, cardiac enzymes and tests of liver function (alkaline phosphatase and transaminases) were normal. An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia and right bundle branch block.

During the next 8 hours, the pain level ranged from 0 to 5. Six hours after his arrival in the emergency department, an abdominal radiograph and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis were performed (shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3).
Figure 1. Abdominal radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
Figure 3. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (coronal view).
diagnosis:
Acute appendicitis, with bacteremia caused by Eikenella corrodens and Citrobacter freundii, and post-operative wound infection by Eikenella.

The CT scan revealed an enlarged inflamed tubular structure in the right lower quadrant (Figures 4 and 5, with arrows, and Figure 6), with surrounding inflammatory changes and fat stranding, a small amount of free fluid in the right paracolic gutter, a distended gallbladder and no free air or evidence of an abscess collection. There were also small renal cysts in the left kidney and degenerative changes of the bilateral iliac joints and lower lumbar spine. The findings were thought to be suggestive of acute appendicitis. A follow-up study, with contrast in the large bowel, did not show evidence of a patent appendix. An open appendectomy revealed acute suppurative appendicitis and periappendicitis, see Treatment/Follow-up section for more details.
Figure 4. CT with tubular abnormality (see arrows).
Figure 5. CT (coronal view) with tubular abnormality (arrows).
Figure 6. Detail of Figure 3, right lower quadrant magnified.

Approximately 10 hours after his presentation, his temperature rose to 103°F (39.4°C), associated with rigors, tachycardia and nausea. Repeat examination revealed focal right lower quadrant tenderness and guarding. A follow-up white count was 14,700 cells/mm³. Cefoxitin was administered intravenously, and an open appendectomy was performed, revealing an inflamed appendix without perforation. Pathological examination of the resected tissue revealed an appendix (5.7 cm by 1.2 cm by 0.7 cm) and attached mesoappendix (4.2 cm by 0.6 cm by 0.2 cm), with pink-red, dull and hemorrhagic serosa and tan-yellow exudate, diagnostic of acute suppurative appendicitis and periappendicitis. No fecoliths were identified.
Post-operatively, the patient did well, and defervesced. He increased his activity and oral intake, and was discharged 25 hours after presentation, and advised to follow-up in Surgery Clinic for post-operative evaluation and with his primary care provider regarding the anemia.
Four days after discharge, blood cultures drawn on admission were reported as growing Eikenella corrodens (Figures 7 and 8) in the anaerobic bottle and Citrobacter freundii in the aerobic bottle, the latter of which was resistant to ampicillin and cefazolin. Attempts to reach the patient by telephone were unsuccessful.
Sixteen days post-operatively, the patient was seen in Surgery Clinic. Earlier that day, he had noted cloudy drainage from the wound. On examination, the incision was indurated; 3-5 cc. purulent discharge was expressed from the site, and a wick inserted. The remainder of the examination was normal.
A culture of the purulent discharge grew few Eikenella corrodens and few gram-negative rods which could not be speciated further. Metronidazole and levofloxacin were administered for 8 days; a follow-up examination revealed resolution of the incisional induration and purulent discharge. The results of evaluation of the patient’s anemia were not known.
Figure 7. Growth from anaerobic bottle on blood agar plate.
Figure 8. Gram stain of Eikenella, isolated from anaerobic bottle.

On initial presentation, the diagnosis of appendicitis was not obvious. The patient had post-prandial epigastric pain; there was no fever on initial examinations, and he did not have pain with obturator, psoas, or Rovsing’s maneuvers. Eventually he developed more typical symptoms and signs of appendicitis: abdominal pain that varied in intensity and location; evolved over a 24-hour period; was associated with intermittent fever, anorexia, nausea and vomiting; and eventually became localized to the right lower quadrant with guarding. This case highlights the importance of considering the diagnosis of appendicitis, even in patients who initially have an atypical presentation.
The diagnosis of acute appendicitis was suggested by CT scan imaging and confirmed by the operative and pathologic findings. Although luminal obstructions and fecoliths appear responsible for some occurrences of appendicitis, they are not documented in many others, as in this case.
Acute appendicitis usually presents in young people, with less than 25% of cases seen in patients older than 45 years [Sifri and Madoff]. Cultures of inflamed appendiceal tissue most often yield mixed flora from the bowel, and cultures from surrounding tissue, including peritoneal fluid, have most often grown Escherichia coli from aerobic bottles and Bacteroides species from anaerobic bottles [Carr]. Bacteremia in appendicitis is not commonly identified: a study of 89 children with perforated appendices revealed only 5 cases of bacteremia (anaerobes were identified in all 5 cases) [Marchildon and Dudgeon], and bacteremia in cases of appendicitis without perforation is rare.
Eikenella, a facultative gram negative anaerobe and one of the HACEK organisms, is part of the normal flora of the oral cavity, and is more commonly identified as a pathogen in head and neck infections, such as those resulting from human bites. However, it is also found normally in the respiratory, gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts [Steinberg and DelRio]. In a series of 19 intraabdominal infections caused by Eikenella, appendicitis occurred in 7 of the cases, and was the most common diagnosis [Danziger]. Citrobacter is found in the genitourinary tract, the respiratory tract, and has been identified in intraabdominal, soft tissue and bone infections [Donnenberg].
The other diagnostic possibilities listed in the differential were far less likely given the clinical course and CT findings. Pancreatitis may cause epigastric or diffuse abdominal pain; however, with normal levels of amylase and lipase as seen in this case, this diagnosis was unlikely. Distension of the gallbladder, seen on the CT scan, may occur after periods of anorexia and decreased oral intake and can be a normal finding; no gallstones or other specific findings of cholecystitis were seen. The examination made no mention of pain with the inguinal hernia, and the CT scan did not show dilated loops of bowel suggestive of an obstruction, and therefore incarceration of the bowel was also unlikely.

title: 2009 April Featured Case Summary: A woman in her thirties with fever and diarrhe
history:
2009 April Featured Case Summary: A woman in her thirties with fever and diarrhea after traveling to Africa.
A woman in her thirties was admitted to the hospital after developing fever and diarrhea after traveling to Africa.
In mid-summer, five weeks before her departure for Kenya and Tanzania, the patient was seen in a travel clinic. Immunizations for tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis and yellow fever were administered parenterally, and oral typhoid vaccine given. Malarial prophylaxis with atovaquone and proguanil, and azithromycin as needed for diarrhea, were prescribed.
In Africa, she traveled to rural areas and went camping in the plains and mountainous regions. She ate local fare, drank boiled water and used iodine tablets. During the first week, she noted 2 mosquito bites, and none thereafter. One week after her arrival in Africa, episodes of diarrhea developed, for which she took loperamide, with improvement but not complete resolution of her symptoms. On the return flight home, 16 days after her arrival, she felt feverish and developed shaking chills, myalgias, and arthralgias, of 4 hours’ duration, and generalized malaise, associated with a mild cough and post-nasal drip.
During the following 4 days, malaise and fatigue gradually improved. On the 5th day, fever to 100.3°F (37.9°C) developed, associated with headache, chills, myalgias, and nausea. The next day, the temperature rose to 102°F (38.9°C), and mild abdominal pain developed. She vomited once and had multiple episodes of watery diarrhea, without blood. She also reported a frontal headache, stiff neck, and photophobia. She was not aware of any travel companions’ illnesses, and was not sexually active during the trip.

She had a history of eosinophilic esophagitis. She had received the complete vaccination series for Hepatitis A virus, Hepatitis B virus, rabies, measles, mumps and rubella, tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis, polio (with a booster dose as an adult) and had had chickenpox in the past. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus had been negative a decade earlier.

She was born on the west coast of the United States. She had recently traveled to Kenya and Tanzania, and to Europe, India, Southeast Asia and Istanbul within the previous 4 years. She was monogamous with one male partner, and had always had protected intercourse. She occasionally drank alcohol and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. Paternal relatives had eosinophilic esophagitis.

She was allergic to sulfa drugs.

Medications included atovaquone-proguanil, and ibuprofen and acetaminophen as needed for fever and pain.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 103.0°F (39.4°C), blood pressure 89/61 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, respirations 12 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing ambient air. The mucous membranes were dry, the cheeks were flushed, and there was tenderness with percussion over the right maxillary sinus and flexion of the neck. The abdomen was soft, with normal bowel sounds and minimal tenderness to deep palpation in the lower abdomen. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 11,500 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000) with 81% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, 2% eosinophils and 1% basophils, hemoglobin 14.6 gm/dl (ref 12.0-16.0) and platelets 484,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-400,000). The level of potassium was 3.2 mmol/liter (ref 3.4-4.8), chloride 97 mmol/liter (ref 100-108), and glucose 136 mg/dl (non-fasting); the levels of other electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, amylase, lipase, bilirubin, total protein, albumin, globulin, and tests of coagulation, renal and liver function were normal. Urine analysis showed yellow clear urine with pH 6.0, 1+ bilirubin, 2+ ketones, and 3-5 white cells, few squamous cells and few bacteria per high-powered field. An electrocardiogram was normal.

In the emergency department, vancomycin (1 gram), ceftriaxone (1 gram), ciprofloxacin (500 mg), atovaquone and proguanil were administered, as well as normal saline (4 liters over 24 hours, intravenously). The blood pressure rose to 114/74 mm Hg.
Computed tomography of the brain showed bilateral maxillary sinus thickening, and was otherwise normal. A lumbar puncture revealed 1 white cell per cubic millimeter (cmm)(47% neutrophils and 53% lymphocytes) and 1805 red cells/cmm in Tube 1 and 1 white cell/cmm (20% neutrophils and 70% lymphocytes) and 49 red cells/cmm in tube 4, with a glucose level of 63 mg/dl and total protein of 22 mg/dl. A chest radiograph was normal. Gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated moderate mononuclear cells and few red cells, with no neutrophils or organisms. A blood smear for malaria was negative.
Stool specimens were obtained for gram stain and culture for enteric pathogens and ova and parasite analysis. Gram stain of a primary stool specimen is shown in Figure 1; a subculture of a stool specimen and gram stain of the culture growth are shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 1. Gram stain of stool specimen.
Figure 2. Growth of stool pathogen at 42°F, low oxygen.
Figure 3. Gram stain of stool subculture.
diagnosis:
Gastroenteritis caused by Campylobacter jejuni and Cryptosporidium parvum infection in a traveler returning from Africa.

Culture of a stool specimen grew Campylobacter jejuni (Figure 3). A positive tube test for Campylobacter is shown in the tube on the far left in Figure 4, with the negative control shown on the far right and the positive control in the middle. Before the culture results were known, testing for stool ova and parasites by direct immunofluorescent antibody staining demonstrated Cryptosporidium parvum oocytes (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Tube test for Campylobacter.
Figure 5. Cryptosporidium oocytes by direct immunofluorescence.

After results implicating Cryptosporidium parvum were received, nitazoxanide was administered for 3 days, with marked improvement but without total resolution of her symptoms. One day later, stool cultures grew Campylobacter jejuni; no additional antibiotic treatment was administered. She returned to the Infectious Disease clinic 2.5 weeks later because of persistent intermittent soft stools and abdominal cramping. Follow-up stool cultures and ova and parasites were negative. She was advised to abstain from dairy consumption for 1 week, and then gradually increase her dietary intake, with improvement. Testing for antibodies to Strongyloides was negative one month later; test results for evidence of human immunodeficiency virus were also negative.

Fever and diarrhea in a returning traveler may be caused by multiple infectious agents, most of which are self-limited, but some of which are potentially life-threatening. Information should be sought regarding the diseases endemic to the areas visited, and the patient’s risk factors and potential exposures. In febrile patients who have traveled to a malaria-endemic area, specimens of blood should be examined for Plasmodium species. Infectious gastroenteritides caused by bacteria (including enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, Salmonella (such as S. enteritidis, S. typhi, the cause of typhoid fever, or S. paratyphi), Shigella, Campylobacter, and Vibrio cholerae) or parasitic agents (such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium) should also be strongly considered. Viral gastroenteritides (such as rotovirus or Norwalk virus) have been implicated in significant outbreaks in traveler’s diarrhea, and may be associated with low-grade fevers, but are not usually as prolonged as in this case. Dengue fever is relatively uncommon in Africa, and usually presents with fever, myalgias, and thrombocytopenia. Other illnesses, such as leptospirosis, rickettsial diseases, and acute human immunodeficiency virus infection, should also be considered, particularly in patients with potential exposure histories.
This case illustrates how travelers may be exposed to multiple infectious agents. Cryptosporidium parvum, an intracellular protozoan pathogen found worldwide, causes about 2% of traveler’s diarrhea, and is a common cause of childhood diarrhea in developing countries. It can be transmitted by animal contact, person-to-person and environmental (waterborne) exposure. Oocysts can be found in lakes, rivers, swimming pools (usually due to fecal accidents), vegetables, unpasteurized milk and contaminated apple, and are highly resistant to chlorination. The largest outbreak related to contaminated drinking water occurred in Milwaukee in 1993, with an estimated 403,000 people stricken with a diarrheal illness [Kramer et al., 1996]. Clinical manifestations of infection usually begin within 5-7 days of ingestion, and include watery diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps and, less commonly, symptoms related to the biliary tract (acalculous cholecystitis, sclerosing cholangitis) and respiratory tract (bilateral respiratory infiltrates). A prodrome of fever, mylagia and headache may occur around the time of onset of diarrhea. The median duration of illness is between 5 to 10 days. It is usually self-limited, but anti-parasitic agents nitazoxanide and paromomycin have also been used in the setting of severe illness and/or immunocompromised state. Infection in immunocompetent patients is generally localized to distal small bowel and proximal colon. However, in immunocompromised patients, parasites have been found throughout the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, hepatobiliary system and respiratory tract. Chronic intestinal cryptosporidiosis is an AIDS-defining illness.
Campylobacter jejuni is a comma-shaped gram-negative rod found in the GI tract of cattle, goats, sheep and poultry, and may cause both enteric and extraintestinal illness. It may be transmitted via consumption of contaminated water and food, including poultry, raw clams, undercooked beef and unpasteurized cheeses. Other modes of transmission include direct contact with animals, person-to-person transmission, or fecal-oral contact. The incubation period after exposure ranges between 1 and 7 days and most commonly a prodrome of fever, headache and malaise develops before the onset of acute enteritis, with crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhea (which may be bloody). The clinical course is usually a self-limited, typically lasting between 1 to 7 days. Treatment includes fluid and electrolyte replacement, with antibiotic treatment generally reserved for patients with high fever, bloody diarrhea, symptoms lasting more than 1 week, or those with eight or more bowel movements a day. Other manifestations include colitis, pseudoappendicitis, and bacteremia. The choice of antibiotics may include macrolides or fluoroquinolones, depending on resistance patterns in the area. Complications arising from C. jejuni infections include reactive arthritis which may be especially severe and prolonged in patients with HLA-B27 antigens, interstitial nephritis, hemolytic uremic syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). Reports suggest that 20-40% of GBS cases occur after C. jejuni infections, usually 2-3 weeks after diarrheal illness. Of note, a significant percentage of Campylobacter isolates, especially from Southeast Asia, are now resistant to fluoroquinolone antibiotics.
Supportive care is often all that is needed for traveler’s diarrhea, as many episodes are self-limited. Travel clinics may prescribe antibiotics for self-administration by travelers going to remote areas. In some circumstances, however, antibiotics have been shown to prolong symptoms and shedding of the infectious agents, especially when combined with other anti-diarrheal agents such as loperamide. In this patient, because of the duration and increasing symptoms, hypotension, and possible meningeal signs, broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered until test results, including blood and stool cultures, were available.

history:
2009 June Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman presented with a painful foot lesion after a trip to Africa.
A woman in her forties had returned four days earlier from a six-week trip to Tanzania. She was well until the day before presentation when she felt a sharp twinge of pain in her left foot while descending stairs. The pain was located between the first and second toes and, upon examination, she noted a new lesion in that location.
While in Tanzania, she had worked at an orphanage located at approximately 6,000 feet elevation. She had noticed that some of the children in the orphanage had lesions on their feet, which were similar to her lesion.

She had visited a travel clinic prior to her departure, and received malaria prophylaxis medications. She had had diarrhea for one day during her trip, and had otherwise been well.

As noted above, she had recently returned from a trip to Africa. While there, she had swum in a salt water pool, but not in fresh water lakes or rivers. She had worn socks and shoes, and had not had any trauma, insect or animal bites to her feet. She denied recent sexual contact.

Malarone had been taken for malaria prophylaxis. A tetanus toxoid booster had been administered three months earlier.

A lesion on the left foot was present, shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.
diagnosis:
Tungiasis, caused by the flea Tunga penetrans.

The local area was sterilized and anesthetized, and then aspirated with a syringe and a 14-gauge needle. Forceps were also used to extract foreign material. The contents of the aspiration and extraction were consistent with a diagnosis of tungiasis, caused by infestation by the flea Tunga penetrans. Figures 3 and 4 show the body contents of the flea magnified times four, and Figures 5 and 6, magnified times 10, show additional features of the flea and eggs, respectively.
Figure 3. Aspirate of lesion, magnification x 4.
Figure 4. Aspirate of lesion, magnification x 4.
Figure 5. Aspirate of lesion, magnification x 10.
Figure 6. Aspirate of lesion, magnification x 10.

In addition to the physical extraction under sterile conditions of the flea, eggs and foreign contents, the patient received ceftriaxone (one gram) intramuscularly, followed by a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate of seven days duration.

Tungiasis is caused by infestation by the burrowing flea Tunga penetrans. The flea was first identified in the Caribbean and Central and South America, and subsequently spread to Africa and Central Asia, including Pakistan and India. Other names by which it is known include jiggers, chigoe fleas or pigue.
The flea invades upon contact with unprotected skin, usually of feet (interdigitally or subungually). The impregnated female flea feeds on dermal blood vessels, and eggs are extruded through the surface orifice. Lesions usually appear papular or nodular, with a dark central opening, but some may be wart-like, pustular, bullous or ulcerative. Lesions may grow up to approximately one centimeter in diameter, and can be painful or pruritic. Patients usually have one or two lesions, although on occasion multiple lesions--dozens to even hundreds--may be seen. Most lesions resolve spontaneously, but ulceration and fibrosis may occur. There is a high rate of secondary infection, and occasionally development of lymphangitis, gangrene or tetanus.
As noted above, the definitive therapy is the physical extraction of the flea, eggs and foreign contents with forceps or needle, under sterile conditions. Topical ivermectin, metrifonate and thiabendazole kill the flea, but do not remove the organism. Petroleum jelly over the breathing hole suffocates the flea. Anti-bacterial prophylaxis and immunization against tetanus are essential to prevent the morbidity associated with the infestation.

title: 2009 July Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A 16-month-
history:
2009 July Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A 16-month-old toddler developed acute respiratory distress.
A 16-month-old toddler had been well until approximately 2 days before admission when clear rhinorrhea developed, and occurred intermittently thereafter, without fevers or other symptoms. On the morning of admission, ibuprofen was administered for presumed teething pain. During the late morning, the patient's mother noted increasing irritability and work of breathing, mild drowsiness, and a hoarse cry, without fever, drooling, or inability to drink.
In the afternoon, the child was brought to the pediatrician's office. On examination, there was respiratory distress, with stridorous breath sounds, and no meningismus. Dexamethasone, 0.6 milligrams per kilogram weight, was administered intramuscularly, emergently. The patient was transferred to the emergency department of a nearby hospital, and vomited once en route.

The patient was the product of a full-term gestation, and an uncomplicated delivery. Episodes of ear infections requiring antibiotic treatment had occurred four times in the previous 5 months, and ear tubes were scheduled to be inserted in the upcoming weeks. There was no history of suppurative complications, sinopulmonary infections, headaches, visual or hearing deficits, chest or abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, myalgias, arthralgia, or skin rashes.

The patient lived with an older sibling and parents, and did not attend daycare. Diet included breast milk and table foods.

There was no family history of immunodeficiency.

There were no known allergies.

All recommended childhood immunizations had been administered through age 14 months; doses of Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine had been given at ages 2, 4, and 6 months on schedule; however the fourth dose had been withheld due to the national shortage and prevailing guidelines at that time. As noted above, ibuprofen for teething discomfort was given the morning of admission.
exam_studies:
At the hospital, the temperature was 101.3°F (38.5°C), with stridorous breathing. The weight was 8.9 kg. The pharynx was not exudative, and no foreign body was seen.

The white cell count was 13,100 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 6,000-17,500), with 87% polymorphonuclear leukocytes (ref. range 25-49%), lymphocytes 9% (ref. range 60-67%), and monocytes 4% (ref. range 4-11%). The hematocrit was 30.7% (ref. range 33.0-39.0%) and hemoglobin 10.3 gm/dl (ref. range 10.5-13.5).

Racemic epinephrine by nebulizer was administered. A specimen of the blood was cultured, followed by the administration of ampicillin-sulbactam (500 mg), and normal saline intravenously. Radiographs of the chest and neck were obtained (Figures 1 through 4). Humidified oxygen and additional racemic epinephrine treatments were administered by nebulizer.
Contact with the child was minimized while otolaryngology and pediatric anesthesia consultants were called emergently. The toddler demonstrated severe inspiratory stridor with labored breathing, head bobbing, supraclavicular retractions, increased work of breathing and possible tiring. The cry was hoarse. The patient was taken urgently to the operating room for airway management.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Lateral chest radiograph.
Figure 3. Neck radiograph.
Figure 4. Lateral neck radiograph.
diagnosis:
Acute epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b infection in a toddler.

The lateral neck radiograph revealed swelling of the epiglottis in the upper airway (Figure 5, arrows), also known as the "thumb sign," diagnostic of epiglottitis. There was also some narrowing of the trachea, possibly suggestive of tracheitis; there were no foreign objects visible in the radiographs.
The patient was examined in the operating room. Examination by rigid bronchoscopy demonstrated a thickened and obstructing, cherry-red epiglottis, consistent with epiglottitis. There were increased secretions, which were cultured. The glottis and subglottic regions were not well visualized. The anesthesiologist was able to obtain a grade 1 view during intubation. Initially, the airway was intubated with a 3-0 uncuffed tube, which was replaced with a 3-0 cuffed tube because of an air leak. There were also findings consistent with acute otitis media in the right ear, and ear tubes were inserted bilaterally.
Gram stain of the secretions demonstrated very rare polymorphonuclear leukocytes, very rare squamous epithelial cells, few gram-positive cocci in pairs, and few gram-negative rods of mixed morphologies.
Within 24 hours, the blood culture grew organisms that were initially interpreted as gram-positive coccobacilli. The following day, the gram stain was reviewed, and gram-negative coccobacilli reported; the organism was identified as Haemophilus influenzae type b, shown in culture on chocolate agar (Figure 6) and on gram stain (Figure 7). Cultures of the secretions taken in the operating room grew mixed flora.
Figure 5. Lateral neck radiograph, with thumb sign (arrow).
Figure 6. Sub-culture growing H. influenzae, type b.
Figure 7. Gram stain of culture growth, showing H. influenzae type b.

Ceftriaxone and vancomycin were administered, and dexamethasone continued in a tapering dose. The patient was paralyzed and sedated, and the trachea remained intubated for 4 days while the inflammation in the epiglottis resolved. After the initial culture results were known, vancomycin was stopped, and ceftriaxone alone was continued. On the 5th day, amoxicillin alone was administered for a total antibiotic course of 10 days. Ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone otic drops were also given.
One month after discharge, the patient returned for follow-up with the infectious disease consultant. Levels of T-cell lymphocyte subsets and immunoglobulin were normal. The level of immunoglobulin G antibody to H. influenzae type b (Hib) was 1.95 mg per liter (reference range greater than or equal to 0.15); other tests of immunity to vaccine antigens were also consistent with a normal immune response. Additional Hib vaccination was administered as recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (The Red Book) for children younger than 2 years of age with invasive Hib disease.

The causes of acute respiratory distress in a child may include non-infectious and infectious etiologies, as indicated by the differential listed above. Clues to the diagnosis are provided by the history, with an acute time course over several hours leading to respiratory distress and a hoarse voice suggestive of obstruction or swelling around the level of the larynx, without the barking cough more typical of croup. Physical examination should be performed in a manner that minimizes distress because children can decompensate and obstruct their airways rapidly. If epiglottitis is strongly suspected, examination of the mouth and pharynx should be avoided. Exudative pharyngitis caused by Epstein Barr virus (EBV) or Group A Streptococcus does not typically cause a hoarse voice, and is usually less pronounced in a child of this age. In this case, a foreign object was not seen in the mouth, posterior pharynx or on radiographs. The lateral neck radiograph demonstrated swelling at the level of the epiglottis, also known as the “thumb sign”, which is diagnostic of epiglottitis; the findings were confirmed by bronchoscopic examination. Although the radiographs were diagnostic in this case, they are often not performed when epiglottitis is suspected because of a concern of rapid clinical deterioration and, particularly in children, efforts instead are directed to immediate visualization of the upper airway, with intubation and establishment of a secure airway. The time course of croup is generally over several days, and radiographic findings may show gradual subglottic swelling, also called the “steeple sign”. The causes of life-threatening upper airway infections in pediatric populations in the United States have changed markedly since the late 1980s, when the Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine became widely available. According to one study at a pediatric hospital, the rate of epiglottitis fell from 3.5 cases per 10,000 admissions (57 cases total, with a mean age of 4.1 years), of which 84% (48 cases) were caused by H. influenzae type b during 1969-1977, to 0.3 cases per 10,000 (2 cases, both 18-years-old), which were caused by Streptococcus species, during 1995-2003 [Faden 2006]. In a second study, admissions to a pediatric intensive care unit for respiratory distress between 1997-2006 were caused by bacterial tracheitis 48% of the time (17 cases, of which 83% progressed to respiratory failure), compared with 46% due to croup (16 cases, 19% with respiratory failure), and 6% due to epiglottitis (2 cases, both with respiratory failure). Culture results were positive for Staphylococcus species 60% of the time, and other bacterial organisms identified included Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus group A; influenza viruses, were also identified as co-infectious agents in several cases. One additional patient died before arrival at the hospital; autopsy results revealed bacterial tracheitis and cultures grew H. influenzae and S. pneumoniae [Hopkins et al 2006]. Haemophilus influenzae type b is a small gram-negative pleiomorphic coccobacillus (1 µm by 0.3 µm). It is responsible for causing severe morbidity and mortality throughout the world, particularly in children less than 5 years of age. H. influenzae type b may cause septicemia, as well as infections of the meninges, epiglottis, lungs, joints, and bones. Before the introduction of the Hib vaccine, it was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children less than 5 years in the United States. An analysis of reports of Hib meningitis has shown a case-fatality rate of 3.2% in industrialized countries compared to a rate of 17.3% in resource-poor countries (up to 27.6% in Africa) [Bennett et al, WHO report 2002]. Following the introduction of the Hib vaccine in the United States, the incidence of Hib disease in children less than 5 years, reported to be previously up to 20,000 cases per year, decreased by 71%, and that of H. influenzae type b meningitis by 82% [Adams 1993]. Distribution of the Hib vaccine to resource-poor countries remains a top priority of the World Health Organization [Danovaro-Holliday et al 2008]. This case illustrates that, although the incidence of serious H. influenzae type b infections has markedly decreased since the advent of the Hib vaccine because of the benefits of individual and herd immunity, the risk has not disappeared.

title: 2009 August Featured Case, Case Presentation from the 2008 Annual Workshop on Ad
history:
2009 August Featured Case, Case Presentation from the 2008 Annual Workshop on Advanced Clinical Care - AIDS in Durban, South Africa and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman receiving therapy for HIV and TB with malaise and acute chest pain.
A woman in her thirties with a history of tuberculosis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) presented to a hospital in South Africa with increasing malaise and acute chest pain.
Two years earlier, she had felt well, when she tested positive for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was begun prophylactically. During the following 24 months, weight loss (greater than 10% of her usual weight) developed, associated with white plaques on her oral mucosa, which were consistent with oral thrush. Abdominal pain developed, and she was evaluated by medical personnel. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin of 3.4 g/dL, and a chest radiograph demonstrated multiple densities in a miliary pattern, with minimal blunting of the left costophrenic angle (Figure 1). Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed extensive intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy, multiple splenic hypodensities, and fluid in the pelvis. Tuberculosis was presumptively diagnosed. Two units of red cells were transfused, and antituberculosis medications, including a 4-drug combination pill (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) and pyridoxine, were administered; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was continued. Her abdominal pain improved, and she became asymptomatic. The CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 45 cells per cubic millimeter.
Stavudine (D4T), lamivudine (3TC), and efavirenz (EFV) were begun.
Two weeks after the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), malaise, night sweats, and loss of appetite developed and weight loss recurred; she continued her medications. During the next 2 weeks, the severity of the symptoms increased, and pleuritic chest pain developed, followed by dyspnea on exertion. A chest radiograph was repeated (Figure 2). Six weeks after initiation of ART, she was admitted to the hospital.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, on initial presentation.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, 4 weeks after initiation of ART.

She had had 2 cesarean sections.

She lived in an urban area of the Kwa-Zulu Natal province in South Africa.

She had no allergies.

Medications included stavudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, pyridoxine, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
She appeared pale, without respiratory distress or jaundice. The respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute. There was shotty lymphadenopathy and crackles in the bases of the lung, bilaterally. The liver spanned 18 centimeters, and was tender, with a smooth edge and firm consistency. There was no splenomegaly or ascites. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Results of laboratory tests included hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL (reference range 11.5-13.5 g/dl), white blood cells 8600 per cubic millimeter, platelets 360,000, total protein 9.3 g/dL (ref 6.0-8.0 g/dL), albumin 3.0 g/dL (ref 3.2-5.0 g/dL), alkaline phosphatase 176 U/liter (ref 42-121 U/L), and gamma glutamyl transpeptidase 161 U/L (ref 10-60 U/L). The levels of total bilirubin and alanine aminotransferase were normal.
An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated multiple lesions in the spleen (Figure 3), liver, and pancreas, a solitary lesion in the right kidney, and findings consistent with para-aortic lymph nodes.
Figure 3. Splenic ultrasound.

Biopsies of the liver and bone marrow were performed, and pathological examination with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain of the tissue are shown in Figures 4 and 5, respectively.
Figure 4. H and E stain of hepatic tissue.
Figure 5. H and E stain of bone marrow.
diagnosis:
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and tuberculosis (TB).

The abdominal ultrasound findings in the liver, spleen and pancreas were thought to be consistent with granulomas. Pathological examination of tissue from the hepatic biopsy revealed granulomas in the portal tracts and lobules, with no evidence of cirrhosis, hepatitis or signs of portal hypertension (Figure 4, above). Pathological examination of tissue from the bone marrow demonstrated all three cell lines, with a normal appearance, and reduced iron stores. There was one granuloma seen (Figure 5). On examination of the marrow with Ziehl-Neelson staining (Figure 6), one clump of possible acid-fast bacilli was present.
Figure 6. Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelson) stain of marrow, with cluster of possible acid-fast bacilli.

The patient's treatment with ART and anti-tuberculosis medications was continued. Ten days after discharge, she felt well, and had no further symptoms. Chest radiographs, repeated 2 months and 7 months after the initiation of HAART, are shown in Figures 7 and 8, respectively.
Figure 7. Follow-up after 2 months of ART.
Figure 8. Follow-up after 7 months of ART.

The microbiologic diagnosis of tuberculosis in advanced HIV disease is a particular challenge. In resource-limited settings, empiric treatment when TB is suspected is common, and clinical response to a trial of anti-TB treatment is often the only means to confirm the diagnosis. This approach may be confounded by diseases that mimic tuberculosis - such as fungal opportunistic infections, multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), malignancies and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). This case illustrates the diagnostic and therapeutic dilemma faced when a patient, on empiric treatment for TB, deteriorates following commencement of anti-retroviral treatment. IRIS has, over the last few years, emerged as an important complication of ART, particularly in resource-limited settings. IRIS is believed to be an exaggerated response to foreign antigens by a reconstituting immune system. Two types of IRIS are described: (a) Unmasking IRIS: When an opportunistic infection manifests for the first time after commencing ART. The presumption is that the infecting agent was present, in a clinically silent form, prior to commencement of ART. (b) Paradoxical IRIS: When an individual on appropriate treatment for a recently diagnosed opportunistic infection deteriorates clinically after commencing effective ART. Recently the International Network for the Study of HIV-associated IRIS (INSHI) published a case definition for IRIS. Diagnosis of paradoxical TB IRIS requires the following: 1. Diagnosis of TB prior to starting ART. 2. Evidence of response to anti-TB treatment prior to commencing ART. 3. Onset of IRIS phenomenon within 3 months of ART. 4. New and/or worsening symptoms and/or signs consistent with TB. 5. Absence of an alternative explanation for the clinical deterioration, such as another opportunistic infection, malignancy or drug toxicity. IRIS was considered high on the differential diagnosis since the first 4 criteria were adequately met. The challenge was meeting the fifth criteria. The differential diagnosis included conditions that mimic TB, such as chronic fungal infections and malignancies associated with AIDS. The choice of organs to sample for tissue diagnosis was based on clinical suspicion of involvement and ease of access. The presence of granulomas on liver biopsy and the fortuitous finding of a clump of acid fast bacilli on the bone marrow biopsy was consistent with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The unusual morphology of the organism on Ziehl-Neelson staining was felt to be the result of antibiotic effect. The failure to grow the organism and subsequent course of the patient’s illness effectively excluded the diagnosis of MDR-TB and mycobacterium other than TB (MOTT). This case clearly underscores the demands placed on the clinician to make a definitive diagnosis of IRIS by the current case definition. This diagnosis poses a significant challenge in under-resourced areas where many prevalent diseases can mimic TB and the incidence of IRIS is likely to be high. The need for a diagnostic test is urgent.
