title: 2009 September Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man
history:
2009 September Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man in his sixties with fever and dyspnea following smoke inhalation, 5 months after heart-kidney transplantation.
A man in his sixties, seen for routine follow-up 5 months after heart and kidney transplantation, reported fever and increasing dyspnea of approximately 6 days’ duration. Six days earlier, his temperature had risen to 100.0°F (37.8°C). The following day, he had mild smoke exposure due to a neighborhood fire; mild shortness of breath developed, with cough, productive of scant blood-tinged sputum. He had reduced exercise tolerance and increasing dyspnea on exertion. He was seen for routine follow-up in the cardiac transplantation clinic.

There was a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy, heart failure and chronic renal failure, for which he had undergone heart and kidney transplantation 5 months before. There was no evidence of rejection on follow-up endomyocardial biopsies. He also had chronic anemia, diabetes mellitus (on insulin), and had had Clostridium difficile colitis 5 months before, which was treated with oral vancomycin. A Mantoux skin test for tuberculosis had been negative the previous year before the transplant.

He lived in an urban area, and had not traveled recently. He was without known asbestos exposure, but had previously worked in a field in which asbestos exposure may have occurred. He owned a dog, which was healthy. He had smoked cigarettes in the past, and stopped more than 20 years earlier.

The patient was married and retired.

He was allergic to penicillins (rash).

Medications included azathioprine (100 mg daily), tacrolimus (0.5 mg at night), prednisone 7.5 mg daily, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, valganciclovir prophylaxis (450 mg daily), insulin, levothyroxine, amlodipine, omeprazole, metoprolol, latanoprost, multivitamins, and calcium citrate.
exam_studies:
He was alert and comfortable. The vital signs were normal. There was good excursion of the diaphragm, with no dullness to percussion or increased fremitus. The breath sounds were slightly increased over the right upper lung field and there were minimal crackles in both bases, without wheezes. A systolic murmur was heard in the aortic and pulmonary regions. The sternal incision was closed, without tenderness, and the abdominal incision was well-healed. There was mild leg edema and chronic skin changes in both malleolar regions. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory test results included hematocrit 26.5% (reference range, 41.0-53.0 in men), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm per hour (ref, 0-11 in men), potassium 5.5 mmol/L (ref 3.5-4.8), urea nitrogen 46 mg/dl (ref 8-25), creatinine 2.03 mg/dl (0.60-1.50), glucose 359 mg/dl (ref 70-110); the levels of white cells, platelets, other electrolytes, total protein, albumin, creatine kinase and tests of liver function were normal.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) revealed a new large (8 cm by 6 cm) pleural based mass overlying the right upper chest. Gram stain of a sputum specimen revealed moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes, rare squamous epithelial cells, and few mixed gram positive and gram negative organisms.
Pathological examination of a routine endomyocardial biopsy showed no evidence of rejection. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, (Figures 2 and 3), showed a large focus of airspace opacity in the right upper lobe, which was thought to most likely to represent necrotic pneumonia, with multiple new pulmonary nodules and enlarged right hilar lymph node. There was interstitial pulmonary edema, and bilateral pleural effusions with pleural thickening and rounded atelectasis in the left lower lobe were stable.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest.

Culture of a sputum specimen revealed normal respiratory flora, and cultures of the blood were sterile.
Two days after admission, a percutaneous needle aspiration of the mass was performed (Figure 4). Cytological examination of the aspirate is shown in Figure 5.
Figure 4. Needle aspiration of mass.
Figure 5. Cytology of aspirate.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary zygomycosis caused by Rhizopus species, in an immunocompromised patient with diabetes mellitus, 5 months after heart-kidney transplantation.

The cytology of the aspirate demonstrated a non-septate fungus, which was consistent with zygomycosis. Four days later, a right upper lobectomy, with apparent clean margins, was performed. An image of the gross pathology of the lesion is shown in Figure 6; a wet prep of the lung tissue with calcofluor white stain under a fluorescent microscope is shown in Figure 7 and pathological stains of the mass are shown in Figures 8 through 10. The culture of the right lung tissue grew Rhizopus species (Figure 11).
Figure 6. Right upper lung.
Figure 7. Wet prep, with calcofluor white stain, under fluorescent microscope.
Figure 8. GMS stain, 40x magnification.
Figure 9. H and E stain, 10x magnification.
Figure 10. H and E stain, 40x magnification.
Figure 11. Lactophenol cotton blue stain of culture growth.

As soon as the cytology results from the aspirate were known, amphotericin B (liposomal) (5 mg per kilogram, intravenously) and posaconazole (400 mg orally, twice daily) were administered, and amphotericin B was given by nebulizer. Postoperative recovery was complicated by pancytopenia and acute renal failure, which improved with decreasing doses of amphotericin B (liposomal). The patient also developed an Escherichia coli urinary tract infection and C. difficile colitis, which were treated. Follow-up CT of the chest showed evidence of lymphadenopathy, which was thought to be reactive, and no evidence of recurrence of pulmonary zygomycosis.
One year later, his shortness of breath was stable. He remained on posaconazole and prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and immunosuppressive agents. The doses of immunosuppressive agents were reduced: azathioprine was decreased to 25 mg daily and prednisone to 5 mg daily, and tacrolimus was adjusted to keep levels between 7-9 ng/ml.

Invasive fungal infections are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality following solid organ transplantation. In this patient, the immunosuppressive regimen (which included steroids) and his underlying diabetes mellitus were likely contributing factors in the development of his post-transplant fungal infection. Although Candida and Aspergillus infections account for most of the fungal infections following organ transplantation, other fungi, including dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) fungi, hyaline molds (such as Fusarium, Pseudallescheria and Scedosporium), zygomycetes (ubiquitous fungi found in the soil, including Rhizopus, Rhizomucor, Mucor and Absidia), and dimorphic fungi related to geographic exposures (such as Histoplasma and Coccidioides) may also rarely be involved. The incidence of zygomycoses infection in organ transplant recipients has been shown to be less than 1% [Almyroudis et al 2006, Singh 2003].
There are no specific clinical characteristics to distinguish pulmonary zygomycosis from invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. In this case, the cytological evidence of a non-septated, wide, ribbon-like, branching organism suggested a zygomycete, and was not consistent with Aspergillus, Scedosporium, or Fusarium.
Rhizopus is a pathogen in the phylum Zygomycota, class Zygomycetes, order Mucorales and family Mucoraceae, which also includes Absidia, Mucor and Rhizomucor species. This order (Mucorales) and family (Mucoraceae) includes opportunistic fungi that can cause angioinvasive disease in immunocompromised hosts, thus the disease name of ‘mucormycosis’.
In a review [Almyroudis et al 2006] which included 116 patients with post-transplantation zygomycotic infections, Rhizopus was responsible for 73% of the infections. Of zygomycotic infections, rhino-sino-orbital or rhino-cerebral infections occurred most commonly post-transplantation; the former had the best prognosis, and the latter accounted for most of the mortality in patients with localized disease. Pulmonary zygomycosis was seen in 28 patients (24.1%). Improved clinical outcomes have occurred with early diagnosis of invasive fungal infections combined with decreasing the level of immunosuppression, surgical excision of localized disease when possible, and appropriate antifungal medications [Singh 2003, Tobon et al 2006].

title: 2009 October Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman
history:
2009 October Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman in her twenties with pre-auricular pain, erythema and swelling on the left side of the face.
A woman in her twenties was well until 9 days before presentation, and 2 weeks after she had returned from the Caribbean, when pre-auricular swelling developed on the left side of the face, followed by pain and erythema. She saw her primary care provider who reportedly performed blood tests; no antibiotics were given.
Five days later, she returned because of increasing symptoms, associated with anterior ear swelling and temporomandibular joint pain. There was no history of fevers, chills, headaches, trauma, rash, oral or ear pain, or visual or hearing symptoms. On examination, there was reportedly prominent local swelling, without trismus. Cefadroxil was administered. Four days later, she went to an emergency department because of increasing symptoms, including left pre-auricular pain and swelling, temporomandibular joint tenderness and increased pain with jaw motion.

She had had a tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as a child. She was otherwise well. Skin tests for tuberculosis had been negative in the past.

Two weeks before the onset of symptoms, she had returned from the Caribbean, where she had swum in fresh- and salt-water, and walked in a rainforest. Two months before, she had performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation on a person with a history of intravenous drug abuse. There were 2 pet cats in the house in which she lived. She was in a monogamous relationship, and did not use barrier methods during sexual activity. She drank alcohol socially on weekends and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. There was no known exposure to tuberculosis or insect bites.

She lived in an urban area with roommates and worked in an office.

Her grandmother, who smoked, had bronchitis.

She had no allergies.

Medications included cefadroxil.
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The temperature was 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure 141/77 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing ambient air. There was an edematous, tender region (0.5 cm by 1 cm) from the tragus anteriorly on the left side, with mild fluctuance, and moderate lymphadenopathy in the anterior cervical chain, without surrounding erythema or warmth. The oropharynx was normal, and there was no trismus. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 10,200/mm³; (reference range 4500-11,000) with neutrophils 70%, lymphocytes 21%, monocytes 7%, and eosinophils 2%; the remainder of the complete blood count, and levels of electrolytes and glucose, and tests of renal function were normal.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head with the administration of intravenous contrast (Figures 1 and 2) demonstrated enhancement of the soft tissues anterior to and surrounding the left external auditory canal, with findings suggestive of a phlegmon, including surrounding rim-like enhancement of the soft tissues and possible early abscess, with a thick proteinaceous fluid collection (1.6 cm by 1.4 cm).
Figure 1. CT of the head, axial view.
Figure 2. CT of the head, coronal view.

Clindamycin (300 mg four times daily, orally for 10 days) was begun and warm soaks were advised; she was discharged home to return for follow-up.
Three days later, she returned to the emergency department because of increasing swelling and persistent tenderness, and was also seen in the oral maxillofacial clinic. The swelling on the left appeared larger and more fluctuant than on previous examination. The left side of the neck was tender to palpation. Ultrasonography, performed at the bedside, showed a collection (1 cm in diameter). An abscess was diagnosed and incision of the lesion performed, with drainage of a small amount of white fluid. The fluid was sent for culture, which was sterile. Narcotic analgesia was prescribed in addition to the clindamycin, and she was discharged.
Two days later, she returned for follow-up because of increasing discomfort: incision, drainage of thick purulent discharge (less than 2 cc) and a fine needle aspiration of the pre-auricular lesion were performed. Gram stain of the discharge showed polymorphonuclear leukocytes and no organisms, and thioglycollate broth tube grew Propionibacterium species; cytological examination of the aspirate revealed evidence of neutrophils and histiocytes with degeneration, consistent with an abscess.
Three days after the procedure, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with the administration of gadolinium (Figures 3 and 4) demonstrated increased soft tissue swelling and enhancement of the left periauricular, facial, and temporal soft tissues with extension into the left external auditory canal. There was enhancement of the left parotid gland, post-styloid space, and temporomandibular joint, and multiple enhancing lesions within the left posterior cervical triangle consistent with lymph nodes (up to 1.7 cm in diameter), with no evidence of a drainable fluid collection.
She returned 4 days later because of increasing swelling and spontaneous yellow-pink drainage from the incision site. On examination, there was a mass (3 cm in diameter) extending from mid-anterior preauricular region to the edge of the jaw. There was a small amount of sero-sanguinous discharge present. Fine-needle aspiration was repeated, and yellow fluid (approximately 5 cc) was collected from the 5 mm incisional site. Amoxicillin-clavulanate, narcotic analgesics and ibuprofen were prescribed.
Gram stain of the new specimen revealed moderate leukocytes and few mononuclear cells, and no organisms; culture of the tissue grew (in the thioglycollate broth tube only) coagulase negative Staphylococcus of two types, and very rare Propionibacterium species grew in the anaerobic culture. The fine needle aspirate specimen was paucicellular; staining for Nocardia and acid-fast bacteria, Warthin-Starry staining, amplification testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis nucleic acid and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi were negative. Cytological examination of the aspirate showed a cluster of epithelioid histiocytes consistent with granulomatous inflammation (Figure 5, courtesy of Richard L. Kradin, MD), and there were no organisms or evidence of malignancy seen.
Four days later, she was seen in the Infectious Diseases clinic. There was a soft mass (3 cm in diameter) in the left preauricular area extending from the parotid to the edge of the tragus, with induration and seropurulent discharge. The white cell count was 6900 cells per cubic millimeter with a normal differential; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 38 mm per hour (reference range less than 17); the level of C-reactive protein was 2.2 mg/L (ref less than 8.0), alanine aminotransferase 88 U/L (ref 7-30) and aspartate aminotransferase 64 U/L (ref 9-32), and Hepatitis B virus surface antibody was reactive. Tests for Hepatitis B surface antigen, Hepatitis C virus, human immunodeficiency virus antibody, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA) were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.
Figure 3. MRI of the face (T2 axial).
Figure 4. MRI of the face (T1 post gadolinium, fat-saturated).
Figure 5. Cytological exam of aspirate (Papanicolaou stain, x 250).
diagnosis:
Cat-scratch disease, with parotiditis and lymphadenitis, caused by Bartonella henselae.

Serologic testing for immunoglobulins (Ig) to Bartonella henselae were positive; the titer of IgM was 1:20 (reference range less than 1:64) and of IgG was greater than or equal to 1:1024 (reference range less than 1:20).
Test results for antibodies to B. quintana and Brucella, cryptococcal antigen, tularemia agglutination, urine Histoplasma antigen, and a skin test for tuberculosis were negative. All abscess and wound cultures for fungal and mycobacterial organisms were negative.

At follow-up 3 weeks later, when the positive results were received, the patient felt markedly improved and there was minimal left preauricular swelling abutting the tragus and tests of liver function were normal. At that time, serological testing demonstrated negative IgM titers and a positive IgG titer at 1:512. Azithromycin (500 mg loading dose and 250 mg daily) and rifampin 300 mg twice daily, orally, were administered for a 2-week course. In follow-up, she reported resolution of her swelling without significant sequelae.

Bartonella henselae is a small, pleomorphic gram-negative rod, of the Alphaproteobacteria class, which is fastidious, aerobic and oxidase-negative, and found intracellularly in vivo. It is distributed world-wide and has been shown to be the primary causative agent of cat-scratch disease; up to 51% of domestic cats in the United States are reported to have antibodies to B. henselae, with the mode of vector transmission between cats attributed to the cat flea, Ctenocephalides felis. B. henselae has also been implicated in multiple other clinical entities, including fever of unknown origin, neuroretinitis, endocarditis, encephalopathy, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenic purpura and cases of oculoglandular syndrome, bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis hepatis (the latter two more commonly seen in immunodeficient patients) [Florin et al 2008, Slater and Welch 2005]. Clinical presentations mimicking malignancies such as lymphoma can occur; unilateral parotid enlargement, caused by B. henselae and thought to be a parotid malignancy, has also been reported [Kempf et al 2001, Ridder et al 2000].
Cat scratch disease typically presents with the development of an erythematous lesion 3-10 days after inoculation (which may resolve in 1-3 weeks) and is commonly associated with fever (which occurs in up to 60% of patients) and localized lymphadenopathy (in more than 90%)]. The nodal regions most often affected include the axillary and epitrochlear, head and neck, and groin. Suppurative lymphadenopathy may occur and require aspiration for pain relief; concern for possible tract formation after incision and drainage has been raised. The disease may remain localized and be self-limited, with a duration between 2-6 months [Florin et al 2008, Slater and Welch 2005]. Antibiotic therapy may be beneficial [Slater and Welch 2005]; azithromycin in particular has been shown to reduce the duration of lymphadenopathy in typical cat-scratch disease in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial [Bass et al 2000].
Because of the difficulty identifying the organism in pathological specimens or growing it in culture, the diagnosis of B. henselae infection is more commonly made by serologic testing for species-specific immunoglobulins, and/or by identification of B. henselae nucleic acid by polymerase chain reaction analysis. In this case, Warthin-Starry staining, a silver stain originally developed to detect for spirochetal infection and used to identify B. henselae, was performed on a paucicellular specimen and was negative. The granulomatous inflammation, identified on cytological examination of the fine needle aspirate (Figure 5), may be seen with Bartonella infection but it is not specific for it.
In presentations of facial swelling such as seen in this patient, other causes of unilateral acute cervical lymphadenitis and sialoadenitis should be considered, including M. tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria (including M. marinum when after recent water exposure), other bacterial infections (such as Francisella tularensis and syphilis), fungal infections (less common in immunocompetent individuals), and viral infections (including mumps, infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus and HIV); many of these however would more commonly present with bilateral lymphadenopathy.

title: 2009 November Featured Case and 2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentati
history:
2009 November Featured Case and 2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenager with constipation and weight loss.
A teenaged male was well until 3 months before presentation, when constipation and anorexia developed. Multiple courses of laxatives were prescribed, without improvement, and weight loss of 30 pounds (13.6 kilograms) occurred. He also noted the development of fecal incontinence. There was no history of fever, chills, night-sweats, abdominal pain or diarrhea.

The patient had previously been well.

The patient was born and lived in the northeastern United States. He did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages or use recreational drugs. He had been sexually active with one female partner and had used condoms. Several months before his presentation, he had traveled to Florida.

He was a student.

The patient had no allergies.

The patient was not taking any medications at the time of presentation. He had reportedly received all childhood immunizations.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared thin. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 109/60 mm Hg and respirations 17 breaths per minute. The abdominal examination was normal; the rectal examination revealed slightly decreased anal tone and was otherwise normal, without bleeding or masses. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The leukocyte count was 12,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,000-10,500) with neutrophils 34% (ref 40-74), band forms 14% (ref 0-10), lymphocytes 50% (ref 19-48) and monocytes 2% (ref 3-11), hemoglobin 10 grams per deciliter (ref 12.5 - 16.1), hematocrit 32% (ref 36-47), platelet count 738,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 130,000-400,000) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 124 mm per hour (ref 0-15). The level of total protein was 8.6 grams per deciliter (ref 6.0-8.5), and albumin 3.2 grams per deciliter (ref 3.3-6.1). The C-reactive protein level was 3.5 mg per deciliter (ref less than or equal to 0.4). Other routine laboratory test results were normal.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis after the administration of oral and intravenous contrast revealed findings suggestive of an enhancing lesion in the rectum (Figures 1 and 2, arrows), which was not homogeneous. A large amount of stool was present in the colon, and multiple small inguinal lymph nodes (Figure 2, 'LN') were also noted.
Figure 1. CT of the pelvis.
Figure 2. CT of the pelvis.

A test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test was positive, and the level of CD4 T-lymphocytes was 739 cells per cubic millimeter. The plasma level of HIV ribonucleic acid was 24,000 copies per milliliter.
After receiving these test results, the patient reported having had receptive anal intercourse in the past, with a male partner that he met via the internet.
diagnosis:
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) proctocolitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis in an adolescent with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Colonoscopic examination to 75 centimeters from the anus revealed very edematous and friable rectal mucosa with nodularity. White plaque-like lesions were noted at approximately 5 to 7 cm, and an ulceration was visible at about 10-15 cm from the anus. Multiple samples were obtained for biopsy and microbiologic studies, including microscopic analysis of rectal, sigmoid and colonic tissue. Pathological examination with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain (Figure 3), revealed granulation tissue, with granulocytic, lymphocytic and plasmacytoid infiltration, and evidence of acute and chronic inflammation and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) hyperplasia. Gram’s, periodic acid-Schiff and acid-fast stains did not reveal any organisms. Routine bacterial and viral cultures were negative. Culture of tissue from the rectal biopsy for Chlamydia (done in cycloheximide-treated McCoy cells with culture confirmation with fluorescein-conjugated Chlamydia trachomatis species-specific monoclonal antibody) was positive. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) of the urine for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis were negative.
Figure 3. H and E stain of biopsy.

After the colonoscopic results were available, doxycycline (100 mg orally twice daily for three weeks) was administered, the currently recommended treatment [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2006, Mclean et al. 2007]. The patient’s symptoms improved within 48 hours of starting doxycycline and completely resolved within a week. The patient was followed in an adolescent HIV clinic. He was initially monitored off antiretroviral therapy, but subsequently started antiretroviral therapy after a decrease in his CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) was relatively rare in the United States and other industrialized countries until recently, and seen almost exclusively in cases imported from areas where LGV is still endemic, such as West and East Africa, India, Southeast Asia, South and Central America, and some Caribbean islands. In 2003, a cluster of LGV was reported in men who have sex with men (MSM) in the Netherlands [Nieuwenhuis et al. 2004]. This report was followed by several reports of similar cases throughout Europe, Canada and the United States (US) [Kropp et al. 2005, Meyer et al. 2005, Ward et al. 2007, NYC DOHMH BSTDC 2005].
Common characteristics of these outbreaks included the patient population affected, who were predominantly Caucasian men who had sex with men (MSM), the presentation as proctocolitis (without inguinal syndrome) and very high HIV co-infection rate (approximately 70%). Patients often reported multiple sexual contacts met at casual sex gatherings: 71% met partners at sex-on-premises venues or sex parties, and 23% had met partners via the internet. While LGV can be caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1, L2, L3, most of the cases from the recent clusters in Europe and the US were due to L2 [Nieuwenhuis et al. 2004].
To our knowledge, cases in the pediatric population have not been reported since the emergence of the new clusters of cases in 2003. The diagnosis of LGV, in particular when it presents with proctocolitis, relies on a high index of suspicion that would lead to emphasizing certain aspects of the history and ordering the pertinent diagnostic tests. The diagnosis can be made by C. trachomatis testing: culturing the organism - such as in our case – or, more commonly by nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT). NAATs for C. trachomatis are not currently FDA-approved for testing rectal specimens. The role of serology in establishing the diagnosis of LGV is limited. A complement fixation (CF) titer of greater than 1:64 in the appropriate clinical setting can be supportive of the diagnosis. The diagnostic utility of other serologic tests commercially available has not been well established. Screening for other sexually-transmitted co-infections, including syphilis, gonorrhea and herpes simplex virus, should also be performed.
Complications of LGV proctocolitis, including rectal stricture, may occur if the diagnosis is not made and effective treatment is not given in a timely manner.

title: 2009 December Featured Case and 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary
history:
2009 December Featured Case and 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his sixties with fever, dysuria and dark urine.
A man in his sixties was admitted to a hospital because of fevers, dysuria and dark urine. One week earlier, temperatures up to 103-104°F (39.4-40.0°C) had developed, associated with dysuria, urinary frequency and dark urine.
On the 7th day, he saw his primary care provider; prostatitis was diagnosed and ciprofloxacin (250 mg twice daily) administered. The next day, pleuritic chest pain developed on the right side, associated with mild dyspnea. He was admitted to the hospital. There was no history of cough, sputum production, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or rash.

He had benign prostate hypertrophy. The level of prostate specific antigen (PSA) had been normal during the previous 4 years, most recently 3 months earlier.

He had traveled extensively to South America, South Asia, Asia, Mexico, the Pacific Islands, and Australia.

He was married.

He had no known drug allergies. He had no known drug allergies.

Medications included doxazosin and ciprofloxacin.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The temperature was 102.4°F (39.1°C), pulse 85 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/82 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. The mucous membranes were dry. The abdomen was soft, mildly tender in the right upper quadrant, with suprapubic discomfort to palpation. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. The rectal exam revealed an enlarged and boggy prostate, which was soft and non-tender. The remainder of his examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 17,700 per cubic millimeter (neutrophils 75%, lymphocytes 17% and monocytes 8%) and the hematocrit 34% (reference range 40.7-50.3% in men). The level of serum glucose was 134 mg/dL (ref 65-199), alkaline phosphatase 393 IU/L (ref 38-126 IU/L) and albumin of 3.1 g/dL (ref 3.6-5.0 g/dL). The levels of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, creatinine and other tests of liver function were normal.
The urinalysis revealed pH 6.0, leukocyte esterase 3+, red cells 3 cells per high-powered field, white cells greater than 50 cells per high-powered field, bacteria 1+, and no nitrites.
A radiograph of the chest showed multifocal irregular nodular opacities bilaterally (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin and cefepime were administered, however, fevers persisted. On the 4th day, tests revealed a persistent leukocytosis, alkaline phosphatase 487 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 83 IU/L (ref 11-47 IU/L), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 113 IU/L (ref 7-53 IU/L). Cultures of the blood demonstrated polymicrobial oral flora, which were thought to be contaminants, and culture of a urine specimen was sterile.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed multiple cavitary pulmonary nodules (Figure 2), an enlarged prostate with surrounding fat stranding (Figure 3), and an irregular hypodense lesion on right liver lobe, associated with a thrombosed right hepatic vein tributary (Figure 4).
Figure 2. CT of the chest.
Figure 3. CT of the pelvis.
Figure 4. CT of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Liver abscess caused by hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae, associated with prostatitis and pulmonary septic emboli.

The patient underwent an ultrasound-guided aspiration of the liver abscess. Gram stain of the aspirate revealed a gram negative rod (Figure 5), and the specimen grew heavily mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey agar (Figures 6 and 7), which were identified as hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistant only to ampicillin. A urine culture that had previously been obtained by the primary care provider’s office also grew Klebsiella pneumoniae with the same susceptibility pattern.
The "string test", which demonstrates the hyperviscosity of K. pneumoniae, is shown in Figure 8.
Figure 5. Gram stain of liver aspirate.
Figure 6. Growth of liver aspirate on MacConkey agar.
Figure 7. Hypermucoviscous colonies on MacConkey agar.
Figure 8. String test.

Antibiotics were changed to ciprofloxacin (750 mg orally twice a day) and ertapenem (1 gram intravenously, daily) with a duration of 6 weeks planned, or until radiographic evidence of resolution of abscess. The patient became afebrile within 24 hours after the procedure and gradually improved.

Klebsiella pneumoniae, a gram-negative rod-shaped encapsulated bacillus and facultative anaerobe, has emerged in the last 20 years as the most common cause of primary liver abscess in Southeast Asia. It is now also identified as the most frequent cause of primary liver abscess in the United States, and according to a recent series [Lederman et al, 2005], the organism has been identified in up to 30% of reported cases. This case, of a patient with liver abscess as well as thrombosis of the hepatic venous system, acute prostatitis, and pulmonary septic emboli, illustrates a clinical presentation of infection with the hypermucoviscous phenotype of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
The hypermucoviscous strain typically forms very mucoid colonies and may be diagnosed by forming a 5-millimeter or longer strand from a colony with a loop (Figure 8), also known as the “string test” [Fang et al, 2004]. The hypermucoviscous strain of Klebsiella pneumoniae is associated with metastatic lesions, including the brain, lungs, bone, spleen, joints and soft tissue. In Taiwan, the strain has been reported to cause endophthalmitis and meningitis. Liver lesions are usually solitary in the right lobe.
There is evidence that hypermucoviscosity provides resistance to phagocytosis [Fang et al, 2004]. The hypermucoviscous strain of K. pneumoniae is usually associated with the K1 serotype, which has been identified as a risk factor for endophthalmitis or central nervous system disease. The specific virulence factors of this organism are not well characterized and are the topic of ongoing study. The most important identified to date is the mucoviscosity-associated gene A (mag A), which is essential for the formation of the capsule exopolysaccharide. This gene was present in most strains found in patients in Taiwan with liver abscess [Fang et al, 2004]. Another gene, rmpA (rmp = regulator of the mucoid phenotype) has also been implicated in the pathogenesis of these liver strains [Yu et al, 2006].
Hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae is typically acquired from environmental sources in the community, and a history of prior hospitalization is not a risk factor for developing disease with this organism. No anatomic predisposing factors have been described, although there is an increased incidence of the infection in patients with diabetes mellitus.
The bacterium is usually susceptible to most antibiotics including cephalosporins, carbapenems and fluroquinolones [Fang et al, 2007]. Therefore, choice of antimicrobial therapy is based on the antimicrobial susceptibility profile of the isolate, drug penetration into the affected tissue and patient factors.

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Case Submission Summary: A woman with fever, chills, myalgias
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Case Submission Summary: A woman with fever, chills, myalgias, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
A woman in her sixties, developed fevers to 102°F (38.9°C) approximately 5 days before admission, associated with shaking chills, myalgias, arthralgias, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Three days before admission, she took ibuprofen and acetaminophen with codeine, and noted some improvement during the next 2 days. The following day, however, nausea and vomiting recurred, associated with mild fevers. She went to an emergency department.

There was a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia and sarcoidosis, which had been diagnosed on lung biopsy, was not active and had not been treated.

She worked in a professional occupation in an office, and had traveled to Lake Tahoe and the Mammoth Lake region of the Sierra Nevada mountains of California during the month before her illness, returning home approximately 10 days before admission. She drank 1-2 glasses of wine per day, and did not smoke or use illicit drugs.

She lived with her husband and was monogamous, and had 2 healthy children.

There were no known drug allergies.

Medications included triamterene, low-dose acetylsalicylic acid, atorvastatin and amlodipine besylate.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C), blood pressure of 100/40 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, respirations 12 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on 2 liters of oxygen via nasal cannula. She appeared tired, but alert and oriented and in no acute distress. The mucous membranes were dry and jugular veins were flat. Her abdomen was diffusely tender to palpation, more in the right upper quadrant; she had a palpable spleen. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 4300 cells per microliter (reference range (ref) 4000-11,000), with neutrophils 70%, band forms 15% (ref less than 11), lymphocytes 7%, monocytes 7%, and eosinophils 1%. The platelet count was 18,000 per microliter (ref 150,000-400,000). A specimen of blood is shown in Figure 1. The level of serum sodium was 129 mmol/L (ref 135-145 mmol/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 401 U/L (ref less than 46), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 259 U/L (ref less than 53), total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL (ref 0.1-1.2), direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL (ref less than 0.3), and alkaline phosphatase 364 U/L (ref less than 125); the remainder of the chemistry panel was normal. The urinalysis showed 2+ hemoglobin, trace leukocyte esterase, trace ketones, 1-5 white blood cells per high-powered field (HPF), 5-10 red blood cells per HPF and 1+ bacteria.
The chest radiograph demonstrated a cardiac size at the upper limits of normal, and increased markings at both lung bases with no consolidation, effusion, atelectasis or pneumothorax.
Figure 1. Wright stain of the peripheral blood.

The abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly, borderline hepatomegaly and a thick-walled tender gallbladder with trace adjacent fluid, and no obvious calculi. A hepatobiliary imino-diacetic acid (HIDA) scan showed no evidence for cholecystitis or obstruction of the common duct, and mild enlargement of the liver with no filling defects.
diagnosis:
Tick-borne relapsing fever, caused by Borrelia species.

While reviewing the stain for the manual platelet count, the laboratory technician identified a parasite-like organism, which was referred for review by pathologist. The morphology of the organism was consistent with Borrelia, and tick-borne relapsing fever was diagnosed (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Detail of Figure 1.

The patient was admitted to a telemetry bed, and doxycycline and cefotaxime were administered. On the second day, fevers and rigors increased after the doxycycline was given. Intermittent third degree atrioventricular block developed. A cardiology consultant, requested for evaluation for pacemaker placement, felt that the episodes of heart block were vagally induced because of fevers (with more effect on the atrioventricular (AV) node than the sinus node). During her hospitalization, the level of platelets returned to normal and the liver enzymes improved. She was discharged to follow-up with an out-patient Holter monitor to evaluate her cardiac rhythm.

Tick-borne Relapsing Fever is usually caused by Borrelia hermsii (in higher elevations) and Borrelia turicata (in drier climates, lower elevations). Louse-borne Relapsing Fever is caused by Borrelia recurrentis, and the distribution of the disease is primarily in western United States and central Mexico, as well as in Central Asia and throughout Africa [Dworkin et al 2002].
The host is usually the soft tick Ornithodoros hermsii and O. turicata. These ticks usually feed at night and usually in cabins that have been infested with rodents and Ornithodoros ticks. When the rodents leave, humans are the only host for the ticks to feed on. Feeding takes less than one hour and usually occurs while the human is asleep. Borrelia species are actively motile spirochetes that appear as loose coils [Roscoe and Epperly 2005].
Tick-borne Relapsing Fever is characterized by headache, myalgias, arthralgias, shaking chills, and abdominal pain. Fevers are sudden and high (up to 102.5°F (39.2°C)) and, after about 30 minutes, are associated with chills, rigors, and hypotension [Uhlmann et al 2007]. The relapsing phenomenon is caused by antigenic variation. Immunoglobulin (Ig) M forms against one serotype, but the organism replicates and expresses new outer surface proteins. The diagnosis is usually clinical. Abnormal laboratory tests include a mild leukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated bilirubin, elevated transaminases, proteinuria, and hematuria. Electrocardiographic (EKG) findings may include a prolonged QT interval if myocarditis has developed. Occasionally, spirochetes can be found on thick and thin smears (Wright or Giemsa stains) or culture isolations. However, in order to increase the yield of the peripheral smear, blood needs to be collected during a febrile episode [Roscoe and Epperly 2005]. There is a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test, but it is not widely available at the time of this publication [Uhlmann et al 2007].
The treatment of Tick-borne Relapsing Fever at present is doxycycline or tetracycline. In children or pregnant women, macrolides are recommended (e.g., erythromycin). If there is central nervous system involvement, then intravenous penicillin is the treatment of choice. With all treatment options, the clinician must be mindful that a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur within 1-4 hours of the first treatment (occurs in 54%). The reaction is usually less than 4 hours in duration, but patients should be observed for 12-24 hours. Mortality for patients appropriately treated is about 5% in Louse-borne relapsing fever, and less for Tick-borne Relapsing Fever [Roscoe and Epperly 2005]. Prevention is key and is different from most tick-borne illnesses. Normal preventive measures are usually unhelpful because Ornithodoros is a soft tick, the feedings are relatively quick, and most tick bites occur at night while the patient is asleep [Dworkin et al 2002]. It is prudent to avoid contact with potential animal hosts (even dead ones), have rodent-infested areas treated by pest control specialists, and report the disease when it is found so that public health officials can disseminate warnings.

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with fevers, four years
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with fevers, four years after liver transplantation.
A man in his fifties, status post liver transplantation 4 years earlier, presented to an emergency department in late summer after a two-week history of fevers, with temperatures ranging up to 101-104°CF (38.3-40.0°C). During the previous 2 months, night sweats and weight loss of 20 pounds (9.1 kilograms) had occurred, with minimal dyspnea on exertion. He had also had mild nausea, right upper quadrant pain (which he rated 4 on a scale of 1 to 10, where 10 is the most severe) and intermittent diarrhea. There was no history of cough, chest pain or vomiting.

He had a history of hepatitis C virus infection, and liver transplantation had occurred 4 years earlier. He had had one episode of acute rejection, immediately post-transplantation. Results of laboratory tests had shown normal levels of neutrophils for the preceding 8 months. He also had hypertension, coronary artery disease, and a history of small bowel obstruction.

He worked in the construction industry in the mid-Atlantic region of the United States. There was no recent travel or exposure to sick contacts.

He had no drug allergies.

Medications included tacrolimus, filgrastim every other week and pegylated interferon injection every week.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 36.0°C (96.8°F), which rose to a maximal temperature of 40.0°C (104.0°F), blood pressure 118/67 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats per minute, respirations 17 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. There were healed surgical scars on the abdomen, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 3100 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4800-10,800), with neutrophils 60.8% (ref 53-79), lymphocytes 25.5% (ref 13-46), monocytes 12.8% (ref 3-9), eosinophils 0.5% (ref 0-4) and basophils 0.2% (ref 0-2). The sodium was 134 mmol/L (ref 135-145), glucose 111 mg/dL (ref 70-105), protein 6.9 g/dL (ref 6.0-8.3), albumin 3.0 g/dL (ref 3.5-5.0), total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL (ref 0.1-1.0); aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 58 IU/L (ref 10-37), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 44 IU/L (ref 10-40), alkaline phosphatase 181 IU/L (ref 39-117), calcium 8.1 mg/dL (ref 8.4-10.2) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 millimeters per hour (ref 0-20). The level of tacrolimus was 6.9 ng/mL. Results for other electrolytes and routine screening tests were normal. Six hours after presentation, the white cell count was 2600/mm³, with 55.8% neutrophils, and the absolute neutrophil count was 1450 cells per cubic millimeter (ref 1800-7800).
The chest radiograph, shown in Figure 1, demonstrated scattered pulmonary nodules, less than 1-centimeter in diameter. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 2) and abdomen revealed numerous new pulmonary nodules. Findings also included mild apical pleural thickening, small bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, mild abdominal lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly; the splenomegaly, when compared to findings on CT done one year earlier, was stable and exerted a mass effect on the left kidney.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.

Results of tests of the urine for Histoplasma antigen and of the serum for cryptococcal antigen and antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV, by ELISA) were negative. A specimen obtained from a bronchial washing grew a few colonies of Staphylococcus aureus, which was methicillin sensitive.
Video-assisted thorascopic surgery (VATS) was performed. Pathological examination of the specimens is shown in Figures 3 through 5.
Figure 3. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of lung tissue.
Figure 4. Gomori methenamine silver stain of lung tissue.
Figure 5. Modified Giemsa stain of lung tissue.
diagnosis:
Histoplasma capsulatum infection of the lung in a liver transplant recipient.

Pathological examination of the specimen obtained from the VATS revealed organisms consistent with Histoplasma (Figures 4 and 5). Results of cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage initially grew Staphylococcus aureus and later, 3 weeks after admission, were positive for Histoplasma capsulatum.

The patient was initially treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) for twelve days, followed by oral itraconazole. The level of creatinine increased slightly while on amphotericin, and corrected once the medication was discontinued. Approximately one month after starting treatment, follow-up chest CT showed an overall improvement with decrease in the size of many of the pulmonary nodules.
At follow-up after eleven months of treatment, the patient had done well clinically, however significant increases in the level of bilirubin and aminotransferases had occurred. These elevations were thought to be caused by either the azole therapy or the hepatitis C virus infection, as the level of hepatitis C viral nucleic acid had remained elevated. However, after voriconazole was stopped, there was no improvement in the liver enzyme abnormalities, suggesting the HCV infection was responsible for the elevated liver enzymes.

Histoplasmosis is not common in solid organ transplant recipients, and particularly is not common in liver transplant recipients. Most case series have focused on renal transplant recipients, and even then in larger case series an infection rate of <1% has been found [Freifeld 2005]. In one case series, of nine patients with histoplasmosis after receiving a liver transplant, all presented with fever, fatigue, and dry cough. All of the patients had abnormal imaging (either diffuse military pattern, mediastinal adenopathy, or lung nodules) and all nine patients had a positive histoplasma antigen. The average time of onset was eleven months post-transplant and in seven patients, onset was within 18 months [Freifeld 2005].
Antigen testing may provide a relatively rapid non-invasive means of establishing a diagnosis, although the sensitivity may not be as high as it is among patients with HIV infection. Treatment in this transplant patient likely requires prolonged therapy and also may require a decrease in the immunosuppression regimen, although it is difficult to make any firm conclusions given the relatively small number of case reports.

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman in her forties with na
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman in her forties with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain.
A woman in her forties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) was admitted to a hospital because of nausea, vomiting, watery and non-bloody diarrhea and diffuse abdominal pain of two weeks’ duration. The abdominal pain increased with eating and was relieved by vomiting. There was no history of fever, chills or dyspnea.

The patient had been diagnosed with HIV infection more than a decade earlier, and had AIDS. She was not taking antiretroviral medications because of gastrointestinal symptoms caused by the medicines, and was on no prophylactic medications. An ovarian cystectomy had been performed several months earlier.

There was no history of travel, exposure to sick contacts or pets.

She had no known allergies.

She was not taking any medications at the time of admission.
exam_studies:
She appeared comfortable, in no acute distress. The temperature was 97.7°F (36.5°C), blood pressure 109/78 mm Hg, pulse 94 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. The abdomen was soft, with bowel sounds. There was mild tenderness around the cystectomy surgical site, without guarding or rigidity. The remainder of the physical exam was normal.

The white cell count was 3,400 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-11,000), with neutrophils 84.9%, lymphocytes 8%, and monocytes 7.1%; the hemoglobin and hematocrit were normal. The serum level of sodium was 134 mmol/l (ref 135-141), potassium 2.4 mmol/l (ref 3.3-4.6), chloride 96 mmol/l (ref 101-110), and bicarbonate 27 mmol/l (ref 21-29), urea nitrogen 10 mg/dl (ref 6-22), creatinine 0.6 mg/dl (ref 0.5-1.1). Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 142 U/L (ref 14-33), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 56 U/L (ref 10-42), alkaline phosphatase 59 U/L (ref 35-104), and total bilirubin 0.2 U/L (ref 0.2-1.0). The levels of amylase and lipase were normal. The level of CD4 T-cell lymphocytes was 27 cells per cubic millimeter and the level of HIV ribonucleic acid was 10,000 copies per milliliter by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Cultures of the blood for bacteria, including acid fast bacilli, were sterile.
Testing of stool samples for Clostridium difficile toxin, fecal leukocytes and acid fast bacilli (AFB) stain were negative, and stool cultures did not grow any bacterial pathogens.

The abdominal pain increased in severity and localized to the right upper quadrant. An ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse increased echogenicity and a distended gallbladder, without a thickened gall bladder wall or pericholecystic fluid, which was suggestive of acalculous cholecystitis. A hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan did not visualize the gallbladder; the findings were thought to be suggestive of acute cholecystitis. A cholecystectomy was performed laparoscopically. Pathological examination of the specimen with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain is shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Histopathological examination of the gallbladder with H and E stain.
Figure 2. Histopathological examination of the gallbladder with H and E stain.
diagnosis:
Disseminated cryptosporidiosis caused by Cryptosporidium parvum, presenting as cryptosporidial acalculous cholecystitis, in a patient with with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

A cholecystectomy was performed laparoscopically. Pathological examination of the specimen with hematoxylin and eosin stain revealed numerous organisms consistent with Cryptosporidium parvum (Figures 3 and 4, arrows). Examination of a stool specimen for ova and parasites was also positive for Cryptosporidium parvum.
Figure 3. Cryptosporidium on H and E stain of gallbladder (arrows).
Figure 4. Cryptosporidium on H and E stain of gallbladder (arrows).

Following surgery, her abdominal pain and tests of liver function improved. Nitazoxanide was administered, with minimal improvement in diarrhea. She declined initiation of antiretroviral therapy, and was discharged to a skilled nursing facility for intravenous fluids and total parenteral nutrition.

Cryptosporidiosis is a defining illness of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), if accompanied by diarrhea of more than one month’s duration [Fahey 2003, Schneider et al 2008]. It can lead to a severe, debilitating illness in severely immunocompromised patients with HIV/AIDS and CD4 T-cell lymphocyte counts of less than 100 cells/mm³. Biliary tract involvement is more common in advanced HIV disease with CD4 T-cell lymphocytes of less than or equal to 50 cells/mm³ [Vakil et al 1996]. Symptoms of cholangiopathy may include constant or intermittent right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. Abnormalities in the values of liver chemistries are commonly found. Infections commonly occur in warm moist months, transmitted by ingestion of contaminated drinking water or swimming in public swimming pools. Oocysts are resistant to killing by chlorination, but killed by heat.
Common radiologic findings of cryptosporidial biliary tract disease include acalculous cholecystitis and intrahepatic sclerosing cholangitis with papillary stenosis [Chen and LaRusso, 1999]. The increased mortality observed in patients with AIDS who have biliary disease has not been attributed to the disease itself, but to the degree of the underlying immunosuppression [Vakil et al 1996].
In the older literature, cryptosporidial biliary disease has only been described in immunosuppressed patients and occurred in 20-65% of HIV patients with AIDS cholangiopathy [Chen et al 1999].
The differential diagnosis includes disseminated Mycobacterium avium intercellulare complex, disseminated Cytomegalovirus infection, disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis, bacterial acalculous cholecystitis, Candidal cholecystitis and other causes of diarrheal diseases in HIV/AIDS such as Isospora, Cyclospora, and Microsporidium. Therapeutic options are limited. Drugs such as nitazoxanide may achieve symptomatic relief and parasitological cure in some immunocompetent individuals.
In patients with HIV who have CD4 counts greater than 50 cells/mm³, rates of parasitological cure are 63% as compared to 25% in the patients treated with placebo [Fox et al 2005]. In patients with CD4 T-lymphocytes levels less than or equal to 50 cells/mm³, no difference has been noted between treatment and placebo groups. Other therapeutic options such as paromomycin or spiramycin have had disappointing treatment results [Abubakar et al 2007]. Sphincterotomy has not been associated with relief of pain, but cholecystectomy is indicated in patients with cholecystitis [Vakil et al 1996]. Highly active antiretroviral treatment (HAART), with restoration of the CD4 count, is the most effective treatment. HIV-infected patients should avoid drinking tap water and contact with persons with diarrhea, farm animals and domestic pets [CDC 2009].

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: An elderly woman with fevers,
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: An elderly woman with fevers, chest pain and dyspnea.
A woman in her seventies was admitted in the spring to a hospital because of fevers, chest pain and shortness of breath. She had been well until 6 days before admission, when subjective fevers, severe myalgias, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, dry cough and frontal headache developed. She self-administered ibuprofen, without relief. She presented to an emergency department.

There was a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism.

She lived in a city in Minnesota, and spent most weekends in a cabin in a rural area where she gardened, but did not hike or camp. She owned a dog, and had no sick contacts, or recent tick bites, and had not traveled recently. She did not smoke or drink alcohol.

Medications included atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide, simvastatin, acetylsalicylic acid and levothyroxine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and lethargic. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats per minute, respirations 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% while breathing ambient air. There were diffuse crackles and decreased breath sounds at the bases of the lungs bilaterally and tachycardia; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 21,000/mm³ (reference range 4,000-11,000) with polymorphonuclear leukocytes 96%, lymphocytes 3%, and monocytes 1%, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL (ref 13.3-17.7) and platelets 205,000/mm³ (ref 150,000-450,000). The level of creatinine was 2.6 mg/dL (ref 0.66-1.25 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 343 IU/L (ref 0-55 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 288 IU/L (ref 0-70 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase 151 IU/L (ref 40-150 IU/L), and total bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL (ref 0.2-1.3 mg/dL). INR and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) were 2.87 and 129 seconds respectively, (ref 0.86-1.14 and 22-37 seconds, respectively), fibrinogen 129 mg/L (ref 200-420 mg/dL), D-dimer was greater than 20 µg/mL (ref <0.5 µg/mL) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 9150 IU/L (ref 325-750 IU/L).
A radiograph of the chest demonstrated a pleural effusion on the left and bilateral perihilar infiltrates (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Specimens of blood, sputum and urine were cultured. Imipenem, vancomycin and intravenous fluids were administered for presumed bacterial sepsis. Bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP) was initiated, however, the patient's hemodynamic and respiratory status deteriorated. The trachea was intubated and pressors administered. She was transferred by helicopter to a tertiary care center. A Wright stain of a peripheral blood smear is shown (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Peripheral blood smear, 10x magnification.
Figure 3. Peripheral blood smear, 40x magnification.
diagnosis:
Human granulocytic anaplasmosis caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum.

Peripheral blood smears (Figures 2 and 3) demonstrated numerous neutrophils with morulae consistent with human granulocytic anaplasmosis.

Pulseless electrical activity developed. In consultation with the family, comfort measures only were administered, and the patient died shortly thereafter.
Results of the peripheral blood smear demonstrated numerous neutrophils with morulae consistent with human granulocytic anaplasmosis. Cultures of the blood, urine, and sputum remained sterile.

Human granulocytic anaplasmosis is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, an obligate intracellular bacterium that grows within membrane bound vacuoles in neutrophils. Ixodes ticks are the primary vectors, and white footed mice and deer serve as animal reservoirs. Incidence has been increasing in the United States over the past decade; the highest rates are seen in Minnesota, Connecticut, Wisconsin, New Jersey and New York (CDC).
Clinical presentation is variable, ranging from asymptomatic infection to fatal disease. The most common symptoms are fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise (Bakken et al. 1996; Bakken et al. 2006). Severe complications may develop including a sepsis-like picture, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and acute renal failure. Laboratory studies often reveal thrombocytopenia, elevated liver function tests, and leukopenia, although roughly 50% of patients will not have depressed white blood cell count (Dumler et al. 2005). Diagnosis can be made by detection of intracellular morulae on Wright or Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear during the early stage of infection, although sensitivity ranges from only 20% to 80% (Bakken et al. 2006; Dumler et al. 2007). Demonstration of a four-fold increase in antibody titers from acute-to-convalescent serum or documentation of seroconversion is highly sensitive, but less useful in the acute setting (Aguero-Rosenfeld 2002; Bakken et al. 2002). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is increasingly being used.
Treatment is with doxycycline, 100 milligrams twice daily, generally for 7 to 10 days. Rifampin can be used in patients with tetracycline allergy. Response to therapy is usually very rapid, with resolution of fever occurring within 24 to 48 hours.

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Submission Summary: A man with fevers, sweats, decre
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Submission Summary: A man with fevers, sweats, decreased appetite, sore throat, aches and weakness for 2 weeks.
A man in his twenties was well until two weeks before presentation when fevers developed, and occurred intermittently thereafter, associated with diaphoresis, decreased appetite, mild sore throat, generalized weakness and diffuse body aches. One week before admission, he went to an urgent care clinic. A rapid test for streptococcal pharyngitis was negative, and he was sent home without antibiotic therapy. He took over-the-counter medications, without improvement. The following week, increasing weakness developed, associated with the sensation of loss of balance when walking. He presented for evaluation.

He reported a history of a heart murmur since childhood. He reported no history of sexually transmitted diseases, and his human immunodeficiency (HIV) status was not known.

He was sexually active with men, without condom use, and reported 5 total lifetime partners. He did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. There were no sick contacts, pets or recent travel.

He was single and worked in an office.

Medications included acetaminophen, diphenhydramine and phenylephrine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 121/68 mm Hg, pulse 102 beats per minute, temperature 38.7°C (101.7°F), and respirations 18 breaths per minute. Dentition was poor. A grade 3/6 systolic ejection crescendo-decrescendo murmur was heard loudest at the upper right sternal border and radiated to the carotid arteries bilaterally. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 20,000 cells/mm³ (reference range 4,400 -11,300), with polymorphonuclear leukocytes 85%, lymphocytes 9%, monocytes 6%, and basophils 0.1%). Hemoglobin was 9.4 g/dL, hematocrit 28.2 % and platelet count was 404,000/mm³. The levels of electrolytes and tests of renal and liver function were normal. A chest radiograph, including heart size, was normal, without evidence of pulmonary infiltrates.

The patient was admitted to the hospital and remained febrile for 11 days with a maximal temperature of 39.1°C (102.4°F). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed thickening of the aortic valve, consistent with a vegetation (Figure 1). Blood cultures were obtained; gram stain of the blood culture is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Echocardiogram.
Figure 2. Gram stain of blood culture growth.
diagnosis:
Infective endocarditis and aortic valvular abscess caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Blood cultures grew Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which was sensitive to ceftriaxone [0.12 S] and meropenem [0.03 S], showed intermediate response to penicillin [0.50I], and was resistant to ciprofloxacin [>=32 R]. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative and HIV nucleic acid was not detected.
A transesophageal echocardiogram also demonstrated a vegetation on the aortic valve. An aortic valve replacement was performed, and an extensive aortic root abscess was noted. Pathological examination of the resected valve showed a perforation of the aortic valve specimen and an acquired fusion of the valve leaflets, with rough edges due to vegetations (Figure 3). Figures 4 and 5 show histopathologic changes of inflammation.
Figure 3. Gross pathology of the valve.
Figure 4. Histopathology of the surgical specimen.
Figure 5. Histopathology of the surgical specimen.

The post-operative course was uncomplicated; the administration of intravenous ceftriaxone was begun 9 days before surgery and continued for 4 weeks following surgery.

Gonorrhea was described by Hippocrates as early as the 4th to 5th B.C., as “strangury”, meaning obtained from the “pleasures of Venus”. In 130 A.D., the term “gonorrhea” (or “flow of seeds”) was coined by Galen. The association between carditis and gonorrhea was described in 1838, and the causative agent,Neisseria gonorrhoeae, was discovered in 1879. The incidence has decreased with the advent of antibiotics in the 1930s [Edwards and Apicella 2004]. In 2004, the incidence of gonorrhea was estimated to be 113.5 per 100,000 persons [CDC]. In the preantibiotic era, an estimated 11 to 20% of bacterial endocarditis was caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. There was a predilection for males, and the organism affected primarily the left-sided heart valves [Jackman and Glamann 1991]. Clinical manifestations of gonococcal endocarditis include fever (described as double quotidian) in 74%, arthralgia (44%), and rash (12%); affected patients may have had no antecedent history of urethral discharge. The organism has a tendency to be aggressive, which may lead to valvular destruction [Jurica and Bomzer 1987]. Studies in the post-antibiotic era report mortality of up to 19% despite medical and surgical treatment. Surgical intervention may be necessary in more than half of cases [Jackman and Glamann 1991]. In this case, persistent pyrexia despite antibiotic therapy and evidence of a valvular abscess prompted surgical intervention. Due to increasing antimicrobial resistance, fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended for the treatment of gonorrhea in the United States. Third generation cephalosporins are considered first-line therapy. In summary, endocarditis was once a common and often fatal complication of N. gonorrhoeae infection. Now, with the advent of antimicrobial treatment of gonococcal infection, it is far more rare, but may still occur, with potentially life-threatening consequences.

title: 2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Submission Summary: A woman with fever and abdominal
history:
2009 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Submission Summary: A woman with fever and abdominal pain.
A woman in her forties developed fever, epigastric pain, and nausea one week before admission. She took ibuprofen, without improvement, and then saw her primary care physician, who diagnosed possible gastritis.
Seven days later, she was brought to the emergency room with confusion, fever, and hypotension. She reported no neck stiffness, photophobia, cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms.

There was a history of cervical cancer, status post hysterectomy, ten years earlier.

She had immigrated to the United States from Asia more than 5 years earlier, lived in a mid-Atlantic state on the East Coast, and had not traveled in the previous year. She had no sick contacts or pets.

She was married and had children.

She had taken ibuprofen for this illness, and was on no other medications.
exam_studies:
She was not in acute distress but appeared to have generalized edema. The temperature was 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, pulse 96 beats per minute, respirations 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing 2-liters oxygen by nasal cannula. The skin was slightly pale and anicteric. The lungs were clear, with decreased breath sounds at the lung bases, and the right upper quadrant of the abdomen was tender to palpation. The remainder of her examination was normal.

The white cell count was 14,500 cells per cubic millimeter with 85% neutrophils, 7% bands, 7% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes; hemoglobin level was 11 g/dl; and the platelet count was 57,000 per cubic millimeter. The level of aspartate aminotransferase was 44 IU/L (reference range 15-46), alanine aminotransferase 70 IU/L (ref 9-41), alkaline phosphatase level of 230 IU/L (ref 54-217) and albumin level of 2.0 g/dl (ref 3.3-4.7). A chest radiograph revealed bilateral pleural effusions; both abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography of the abdomen (Figure 1) showed a liver mass, 10-centimeters in diameter. Urinalysis revealed 0-5 white cells per high-powered field.
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen.

The hepatic mass was aspirated by the interventional radiology staff, and a culture of the aspirate is shown (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Culture growth of aspirate.
Figure 3. Culture growth of aspirate.
diagnosis:
Invasive Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess.

Culture of the aspirated fluid revealed a mucoid colony growth (Figure 2), which was later identified as Klebsiella pneumoniae, of the hyperviscous phenotype. Results of a string test were positive (Figure 3). The isolate was resistant to ampicillin, and susceptible to the other antibiotics tested.

The patient did not improve with aspiration of the mass and the administration of levofloxacin and metronidazole. Resection of the liver abscess was performed, and she improved and was discharged.

Klebsiella pneumoniae is a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. A distinct clinical syndrome has emerged in the past 20 years in Southeast Asia that includes invasive liver abscess, bacteremia, and metastatic infection. Clinical manifestations include endophthalmitis, meningitis, brain abscess, pneumonia, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, osteomyelitis, soft tissue abscess, necrotizing fasciitis, and septic arthritis.
Most cases are community-acquired and affect immunocompetent hosts. Diabetes mellitus and Asian ancestry have been identified as important risk factors. The source of the infection is usually unknown; fecal-oral transmission is considered likely and most patients do not have an identifiable gastrointestinal or hepatobiliary anomaly. The outcome is generally good.
The colonies exhibit extreme “stickiness” on agar plates, termed the “hypermucoviscosity phenotype” [Lee et al 2006]. The result of the string test is positive if a “string” of more than 5 millimeters is made when one touches the colony. Two genes associated with this phenotype are the mucoviscosity-associated gene A (magA), seen with serotype K1 type [Fang et al 2004], and the regulator of mucoid phenotype A (rmpA), which is a plasmid-mediated regulator of extracapsular polysaccharide synthesis [Nassif et al 1989].

title: 2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy with
history:
2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged boy with fever, headache, and suprapubic and left clavicular pain.
A teenaged boy had been well until 2 weeks before admission, when fever developed, associated with chills, intermittent frontotemporal headache, myalgias, and suprapubic and left clavicular pain. He also reported a transient diffuse, non-pruritic, erythematous macular rash that had spared his palms, and resolved. Initial screening tests, including cultures of the blood and urine, and plain radiographs of the abdomen and left shoulder were normal.

He lived with his parents and siblings in the midwestern United States. He did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs, and was not sexually active. Household pets included dogs, a rabbit, and rats. A pet cockatiel had died one month before admission.

He had no known drug allergies.

Medications included ibuprofen as needed for fevers or headache.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared mildly ill and fatigued. The temperature was 40°C (104.0°F), blood pressure 99/45 mm Hg, pulse 140 beats per minute, and respirations 16 times per minute. The lips were dry, without oral lesions. There was a harsh 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border, a 2/6 vibratory systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and a 2/4 diastolic decrescendo murmur. There was no evidence of peripheral embolic phenomena or rash. The suprapubic region of the abdomen was mildly tender, without guarding or rebound tenderness.

The white blood cell count was 20,300 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-13,500), with segmented neutrophils 80% (ref 39-75), band forms 12% (ref 5-11), lymphocytes 4% (ref 28-48), monocytes 3% (ref 2-8) and eosinophils 1% (1-4).
A transesophageal echocardiogram revealed a large aortic valve vegetation and severe aortic regurgitation, as well as an apparent right atrial mass (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Echocardiography.
Figure 2. Echocardiography.

Gram stains of growth from an anaerobic blood culture, with sodium polyanethol sulfonate (SPS) activity inhibited by addition of gelatin to the media, are shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Results of a bone scan were negative. Ampicillin-sulbactam and gentamicin were administered, and the temperatures returned to normal. Shortly thereafter, the ampicillin-sulbactam was changed to penicillin.
Despite antibiotic therapy, his clinical condition worsened. He developed respiratory distress, severe hypotension and severe aortic regurgitation, which required emergent operative intervention.
Figure 3. Gram stain of growth from anaerobic bottle, 100x magnification.
Figure 4. Gram stain of growth from anaerobic bottle, 100x magnification.
diagnosis:
Aortic valve endocarditis caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis infection.

Multiple anaerobic blood cultures with media that did not contain sodium polyanethol sulfonate (SPS) activity, which inhibits Streptobacillus moniliformis growth, revealed growth consistent with Streptobacillus moniliformis, (Figure 4). The identification of the organism was confirmed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). A bone scan did not reveal evidence of osteomyelitis. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), types 1 and 2, and Bartonella were negative and testing for parvovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus titers were consistent with past infections.
A transesophageal echocardiogram performed at the beginning of the hospitalization and the intraoperative echocardiogram done 2 weeks later revealed an enlarging aortic valve vegetation, as well as severe and increasing aortic regurgitation, moderate to severe mitral regurgitation, and an intraventricular abscess.

Two weeks after admission, aortic root replacement, debridement of an intraventricular abscess that involved the right coronary artery, and repair of the mitral and tricuspid valves were performed. The patient continued to have intermittent fevers post-operatively. Rifampin was added to the treatment regimen, with plans to continue the gentamicin for the first two weeks of therapy, and the other antibiotics for six weeks. The patient improved significantly, but aortic insufficiency persisted and an aneurysmal eruption occurred at the site of his aortic root patch. He continued to be followed closely by cardiology.

Streptobacillus moniliformis is a fastidious gram-negative anaerobic bacillus, which is known to cause rat-bite fever and erythema arthriticum epidemicum (also known as Haverhill fever). Its natural habitat is the upper respiratory tract of rodents. Human infection is usually caused by rat bites or rat contact with a break in the skin. Clinical findings occur anywhere from two to twenty-one days after inoculation, with an abrupt onset of fever, headache, vomiting, myalgias and a rash that routinely involves the palms and soles. Reported complications of S. moniliformis infection include endocarditis, meningitis, hepatitis and nephritis. Growth of the bacteria on blood culture media requires media that does not contain sodium polyanethol sulfonate, an anticoagulant known to inhibit S. moniliformis growth. Penicillin is the drug of choice for patients with rat-bite fever.
