title: 2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged girl, rec
history:
2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged girl, receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, presented with nodules on her extremities.
A teenaged girl was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia three weeks before this presentation. Induction chemotherapy, which included vincristine, daunorubicin, prednisone, pegylated-asparaginase, intrathecal methotrexate and Ara-C, was administered.
Two weeks before admission, neutropenia developed. On the last day of induction chemotherapy, she was seen in the Hematology Oncology Clinic because of “painful red bumps” on her left shoulder and right knee, of one day's duration. The nodules had initially appeared like a “bug bite”, and later became more hyperpigmented with an erythematous base. One day after the clinic visit, the temperature rose to 100°F (37.8°C). She reported pain in the back, bilateral elbows and legs, for which she was taking multiple pain medications, as well as generalized malaise and mild nasal congestion. There was no history of cough, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, night sweats, chills or extremity weakness. The number of lesions had progressively increased, and involved her back and all extremities.
She was admitted to the hospital and broad-spectrum antibiotics, including vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam and gentamicin, were administered.

A left ovarian cyst, which was asymptomatic, had been diagnosed incidentally by computed tomography (CT) of her abdomen during evaluation for leukemia.

Recent chemotherapy is noted above. She was also on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, and had received vancomycin, gentamicin and piperacillin-tazobactam while in the hospital.
exam_studies:
She appeared tired. The temperature was 97.2°F (36.2°C), blood pressure 115/65 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute and respirations 15 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 100% while breathing ambient air. The mucous membranes were moist, with no evidence of mucositis. The nares revealed clear nasal drainage with blackish necrotic areas on the nasal septum and turbinates. There was an erythematous painful papule (2 mm in diameter) on the scalp. There were multiple small erythematous papular lesions over the right knee, left thigh, right shoulder, right arm and back, most measuring approximately 5-6 mm in diameter, some with hyperpigmented centers, erythematous bases, or early ulcerations (Figure 1). All lesions were tender to palpation. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Skin lesion.

The white blood cell count was 1900 cells/mm³ (reference range (ref) 4500-13,500), with neutrophils 2.5% and lymphocytes 97%), hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL (ref 13.0-16.0) and platelets 34,000 cells/mm³ (ref 150,000-450,000). Tests of liver function, including aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase, and gamma glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), and of renal function were normal.

A lesion on the left thigh was biopsied, and the tissue cultured; micropathological examination of the tissue is shown in Figure 2. Cultures of the blood, obtained from a peripherally-inserted central catheter, and urine were sterile.
Computed tomography (CT) of her sinuses, chest (Figure 3), abdomen (Figure 4) and pelvis, with and without contrast, revealed pansinusitis, pulmonary and renal nodules. An ophthalmological examination revealed endophthalmitis and a vitreal lesion in the left eye (Figure 5).
Figure 2. Skin biopsy, Giemsa stain.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest.
Figure 4. CT of the abdomen.
Figure 5. Ophthalmic examination.
diagnosis:
Disseminated fusariosis in an immunocompromised patient.

Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy demonstrated angioinvasive filamentous fungi, which were subsequently identified as Fusarium spp (Figure 2). Computed tomography (CT) revealed nodules consistent with disseminated fusariosis (Figures 3 and 4) and ophthalmological examination revealed a vitreal fungal lesion (Figure 5) in the left eye.

Amphotericin B was initially started, and voriconazole added to the regimen. The fungal isolate was sent for antifungal susceptibility testing and found to be sensitive only to amphotericin B with mean inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 0.5 to 1. There were necrotic lesions on the inferior turbinates including the right and left anterior nasal septum (Figure 6), and four debridement procedures of the sinuses were performed. Two intravitreal injections of amphotericin B and voriconazole were followed by vitrectomy. The clinical symptoms and cutaneous, sinus, renal, and pulmonary lesions improved.
Figure 6. Nasal examination.

Fusarium is a common soil saprophyte and plant pathogen. It is present ubiquitously in the environment, especially in soil and water. Its tissue form is hyaline in nature and is similar to other filamentous fungi (Aspergillus, Scedosporium, Scopulariopsis, Acremonium spp.) in that it has septate hyphal forms [Ammari et al. 1993]. However it may also have unpigmented toruloid forms [Anaissie et al. 2001].
Many species of Fusarium exist. Most infections in humans are associated with the Fusarium solani species complex (FSSC) and the F. oxysporum species complex [Boutati and Anaissie 1997]. In immunocompetent patients, it may cause keratitis, especially in contact lens wearers. It is also known to cause onychomycosis, peritonitis and cellulitis in the immunocompetent host [Dignani and Anaissie 2004]. In the immunocompromised patients, particularly in patients with hematological malignancies and hematopoetic stem cell transplant recipients, Fusarium causes disseminated disease [Boutati and Anaissie 1997, Dignani and Anaissie 2004, Nucci and Anaissie 2002, Nucci and Anaissie 2007].
The mortality rate from disseminated fusariosis in the immunocompromised host ranges between 50-80% [Dignani and Anaissie 2004, Nucci and Anaissie 2002, Nucci and Anaissie 2007]. The clinical spectrum most commonly includes refractory fever, followed by cutaneous manifestations, sinusitis and pulmonary involvement [Dignani and Anaissie 2004, Nucci et al. 2003]. Cutaneous manifestations range from painful erythematous papules with or without central necrosis to target lesions and those mimicking ecthyma gangrenosum [Nucci et al. 2003]. In contrast to disseminated aspergillosis, in which blood cultures are rarely positive, fusariosis can be diagnosed by blood culture in 40% of these patients [Dignani and Anaissie 2004]. Endophthalmitis and endocarditis are some of the other complications. Diagnosis is based on histopathology and blood cultures. If suspicious of fungal disease, CT scan of the sinuses, chest, abdomen and pelvis, ophthalmological examination and echocardiogram should be considered.
Management of disseminated fusariosis includes debridement of the affected tissues, appropriate antifungal therapy, granulocyte or granulocyte-monocyte stimulating factor for persistently neutropenic patients and removal of infected catheters [Boutati and Anaissie 1997, Dignani and Anaissie 2004, Nucci et al. 2003]. Fusarium spp. have varied susceptibility to antifungal agents. Depending on the species, Fusarium may have low in-vitro susceptibility to 5-flucytosine, fluconazole and amphotericin B and variable susceptibility to the newer azoles [Dignani and Anaissie 2004]. Thus combination therapy may be required for a successful outcome. Poor prognostic factors are persistent neutropenia and corticosteroid therapy [Boutati and Anaissie 1997, Dignani and Anaissie 2004, Nucci and Anaissie 2002, Nucci et al. 2003].

title: 2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged male with
history:
2009 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teenaged male with back pain and leg weakness.
A teenaged male developed back pain and leg weakness approximately 2 weeks before presentation. He was seen at a hospital one week after the onset of pain, and a herniated disc at L5-S1 vertebral disc space was diagnosed. He was referred to physical therapy and given naproxen for pain relief. During the next week, weakness increased, involving both legs, and was associated with numbness in his feet, bilateral hand tingling, and urinary hesitancy. He was seen at another hospital for evaluation. There was no history of fevers, constitutional symptoms, and bowel or bladder incontinence.

Three weeks before this presentation, he had had an upper respiratory tract infection. He had no prior hospitalizations or surgeries.

He lived in a city in the northeastern United States, and had no pets. He had traveled to East Africa several years before, and while there, he swam in a lake. He smoked tobacco and marijuana, did not consume alcohol or use other illicit drugs, and reported no history of sexual activity.

He lived with his parents and sibling.

He had no known drug allergies.

His only medication was naproxen for 2 weeks.
exam_studies:
He appeared comfortable and was talkative. The temperature was 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 129/63 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats per minute, and respirations 14 breaths per minute. On neurologic examination, the cranial nerves were intact. Bilateral hip flexion, knee flexion, and dorsal and plantar flexion strength was 4 out of 5. Sensation was mildly decreased in both feet below the ankles. His gait was mildly wide-based. All reflexes were intact; coordination and the remainder of the examination were normal.

The white blood cell count was 9100 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4000-10,500) with neutrophils 68%, lymphocytes 18%, monocytes 8%, and eosinophils 6%. The hematocrit was 49% (ref 36-47) and platelet count 273,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-400,000). Test results of routine chemistries and tests of liver function were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 2 millimeters per hour (ref 0-10); C-reactive protein (CRP) was less than 7 mg/L (ref <10), and creatine kinase was 115 U/L (ref 30-170).

A lumbar puncture was performed; examination of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed a total protein of 119 mg/dL (ref 12-60), glucose 60 mg/dL (ref 40-70), 1 red blood cell per cubic millimeter (ref 0), 110 white blood cells per cubic millimeter (ref 0-5) with 86% lymphocytes and 10% monocytes. The gram stain and bacterial culture of the CSF, and a viral encephalitis panel, were negative. Tests for Lyme disease, syphilis, Epstein Barr virus, ova and parasite of the stool and urine, and a tuberculin skin test were negative. A serum test for antibodies to cytomegalovirus (CMV) was immunoglobulin (Ig) M positive and IgG negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine showed a conus medullaris that was mildly enlarged (Figure 1, A, before gadolinium) with patchy enhancement (Figure 2, B, after gadolinium), with thickened and enhancing ventral nerve roots from the T12 to L1 vertebrae, and increased signal at the level of the T8 to T10 vertebrae (Figure 3, C).
Figure 1. MRI of spine, before gadolinium.
Figure 2. MRI of the spine, T1-weighted, after gadolinium.
Figure 3. MRI of the spine, T2-weighted.
diagnosis:
Spinal neuroschistosomiasis, caused by Schistosoma mansoni.

A sample of peripheral blood and cerebral spinal fluid were sent to the Centers for Disease Control for Schistosoma antibody testing. Both were positive for S. mansoni.

The patient was treated with praziquantel for 3 days, which was repeated after 4 weeks, and corticosteroids for six months, with complete resolution of his symptoms. A follow-up MRI at 4 months was normal.

Spinal neuroschistosomiasis should be considered in any patient with myelopathy and a history of travel to an endemic area. Schistosomiasis infects 200 million people worldwide, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa [Gryseels et al 2006]. Neuroschistosomiasis is a rare and threatening complication of chronic infection. Although this patient had complete resolution of his symptoms, up to 25% of patients may have functional limitations after appropriate therapy [Silva et al 2004]. Such sequelae may be prevented with testing for peripheral eosinophilia and stool ova and parasites in patients after travel to endemic areas. This patient’s symptoms are inconsistent with transverse myelitis since his deep tendon reflexes were normal. Although this patient did have an upper respiratory infection 3 weeks before presentation, neurologic complications of Mycoplasma pneumoniae are extremely rare, whereas neuroschistosomiasis is more common in a patient with a consistent travel history. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) myeloradiculitis has been reported in AIDS patients. This patient denied sexual activity and had no other risk factors for HIV infection, making this diagnosis as well as the diagnosis of neurosyphilis unlikely. Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott’s disease) generally involves vertebral bodies rather than the spinal cord itself. It may present with myeloradiculopathy, but this is usually secondary to spinal cord compression from either bony deformity (skeletal destruction or kyphosis) or from extension of a cold abscess. Tuberculosis is unlikely to produce the enhancement in the spinal cord on MRI seen in this patient. There was no history of tick bites, travel to wooded areas, or erythema migrans to suggest Lyme disease.

title: Summary: A middle-aged man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection dev
history:
Summary: A middle-aged man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection developed fever, a productive cough and pleuritic chest pain.
A man in his fifties (A patient’s age is often a critical factor in the diagnosis of infectious diseases, affecting both the spectrum of illness and type of organisms involved.) with human immunodeficiency virus (Patients who are immunosuppressed are susceptible to infections with both common and uncommon organisms, with the risk and spectrum of illness related to the extent of CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count depression.) (HIV) infection presented to an emergency department because of fever, a productive cough and pleuritic chest pain (Terminology: Pleuritic pain refers to sharp pain on inhalation and/or coughing. Learning point: The combination of fever, a productive cough and pleuritic chest pain should always raise the possibility of a lower respiratory tract infection, specifically pneumonia. Pleuritic chest pain is often indicative of an underlying pulmonary process, particularly when there is inflammation of the lung pleura.).
The patient had been well until four days before presentation, when malaise occurred, followed by fever to 104°F (40°C), chills (The combination of fever with chills is suggestive of possible bacteremia.) and a cough productive of yellow-green sputum. Intense chest pain developed and he went to a local emergency department. He had stopped his antiretroviral medications (efavirenz, emtricitabine and tenofovir) because of unpleasant side-effects and had run out of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an antibiotic prescribed for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, which was previously referred to as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP). PCP prophylaxis is advised in patients whose level of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells is less than 200 cells per cubic millimeter; lack of this prophylaxis puts such individuals at high risk of developing PCP infection.) a few weeks before presentation.
One week before presentation, he had visited southern California (A history of travel is extremely important in determining the differential diagnoses of an infection, as some infections are more prevalent in certain geographic areas.) with his family. At the time, two other family members were sick with respiratory symptoms (Exposure to a person with similar symptoms is often an important diagnostic clue.). There was no history of headache, confusion, diarrhea or abdominal pain.

The patient had been diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection more than 15 years earlier. Eight months before admission, the level of CD4 T-cell lymphocytes was 80 cells per cubic millimeter and the level of HIV-RNA was 75,000 copies/ml. Over the course of the preceding year, he had been seen in emergency departments twice and admitted to the hospital once for pneumococcal pneumonia, which had been confirmed by sputum culture.
Four months after admission, testing of the urine for pneumococcal antigen was positive. He had been immunized with the pneumococcal vaccine (The pneumococcal vaccine PPV23 is a polyvalent vaccine against 23 serotypes of pneumococcus and is recommended for adults over the age of 65 and for younger individuals at increased risk of invasive pneumococcal infection due to chronic cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus or immunocompromised status.) in the period between both episodes. Other medical problems included asthma, hypertension, and Hepatitis C virus infection. There were no known allergies.

He had 2 cats in his home, and smoked (Long-standing smokers are not only more susceptible to pulmonary infections but are also at increased risk of malignancies. The occurrence of recurrent pneumonias in the same anatomical location in such individuals is highly suspicious for an obstructive lesion caused by a malignancy. Active smokers are also at increased risk of pneumococcal bacteremia and Legionella infection.) 20 cigarettes per day, with a 40 pack-year history.

He lived with his family.

Medications included lisinopril daily and albuterol-metered dose inhaler intermittently. He had stopped antiretroviral medications and had recently run out of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared comfortable. The temperature was 99.5°F (37.5°C), pulse (The normal range for heart rates can vary widely depending on the individual, but in general a heart rate over 100 would be considered tachycardia.) 118 beats per minute, blood pressure (The normal blood pressure range is generally 90-139 systolic and 60-85 diastolic.) 151/88 mm Hg, respirations (The normal respiratory rate ranges between 12-20 breaths per minute.) 16 per minute and oxygen saturation (The normal range of oxygen saturation while breathing ambient air is 95-100%.) 93% while breathing ambient air. There was no evidence of tonsillar exudates (Terminology: Exudate in this context refers to typically whitish pus, consisting of white blood cells, which is visible on the tonsils and often indicates acute bacterial infection.), oral thrush or generalized lymphadenopathy. Auscultation of the lungs revealed crackles and bronchial breath sounds (Terminology: Bronchial breath sounds are loud, harsh breath sounds that are normally heard over the trachea, the presence of these on auscultation of the lungs often indicates underlying consolidation, as in pneumonia, or atelectasis.) on the anterior aspect of the right lung. Egophony (Terminology: Egophony is said to occur when a patient says the letter “e” and the examiner hears the letter “a” on auscultation. It is heard in any condition that results in pulmonary consolidation, such as pneumonia.) and bronchophony (Terminology: Bronchophony is clear transmission of the patient\'s spoken voice through the chest wall. It results from alveolar consolidation, such as in pneumonia.) were also present over the same area. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 26,000/mm³ (reference range 5,000-11,000) with 7% band forms (Terminology: Newly-created neutrophils have a band-like nucleus visible under the microscope. The presence of many bands suggest the immune system is making a large number of new white blood cells, possibly in response to a severe infection.). The serum sodium level was 133 mmol/L (It is not uncommon to have slightly low sodium levels in the context of pulmonary infections; this may be due to the syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) hypersecretion. Extremely low sodium levels should alert the clinician to the possibility of Legionella infection.). Tests of liver function were normal.
Chest radiographs (Figures 1 and 2) revealed an opacity in the upper zone of the right lung, most consistent with a right upper lobe pneumonia, as well as possible opacification in the left lower lobe, with no evidence of a pleural effusion.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, lateral view, on admission.

Specimens of blood and sputum were sent for culture, followed by the administration of ceftriaxone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. A gram stain of the sputum (A sputum sample with minimal epithelial cells is best for analysis of lower respiratory infections. A large number of epithelial cells should alert the clinician to the possibility of contamination with oral flora possibly rendering the results of the gram stain invalid. The presence of white blood cells suggests inflammation and the presence of large numbers of neutrophils is suggestive of bacterial infection.) is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Gram stain of sputum.
Figure 4. Gram stain of sputum.
diagnosis:
Community-acquired pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus) in a patient with HIV infection.

The gram stain showed some cocci in chains and a predominance of gram-positive encapsulated lancet-shaped diplococci, which were highly suggestive of Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus). Cultures of the blood and sputum grew S. pneumoniae.
Figure 5. Sputum culture on blood agar plate.

After blood cultures grew gram-positive cocci and before sensitivities were known, vancomycin (Vancomycin is an antibiotic with very broad activity against gram-positive organisms, including pneumococci resistant to other antibiotics.) was added. The dose of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was adjusted from that suitable for treatment of Pneumocystis jiroveci infection to Pneumocystis prophylaxis.
Antibiotic sensitivities revealed the organism was sensitive to ceftriaxone (Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that, at the time of this publication, is effective against most organisms commonly causing community-acquired pneumonia; however atypical organisms would not be covered by this antibiotic.), and the vancomycin was discontinued (Once the identity of the organism and the range of antibiotic sensitivities are known, antibiotics can be more precisely targeted against the relevant pathogen.). Ceftriaxone was continued intravenously for 7 days, with improvement. Upon discharge, oral cefpodoxime (Cefpodoxime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin that can be taken orally.) was prescribed for 1-week, for a total duration of antibiotic therapy of 14 days (An adult who requires hospitalization for community-acquired pneumonia should be treated with antibiotics for a minimum of 5 days; however the duration of therapy should be individualized based on the comorbidities and the clinical response to treatment.). Follow-up for a post-treatment chest radiograph was arranged, in order to document complete resolution of the infiltrate.

This patient's presentation with history of exposure to sick contacts, symptoms of less than one week’s duration, fever and cough with mucopurulent sputum, in combination with leukocytosis, bandemia and lobar consolidation on chest radiograph, was most consistent with acute community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. The presence of gram-positive diplococci on the sputum gram stain was highly suggestive of Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) infection.
The radiographic appearance of a lobar pneumonia is less suggestive of infections by atypical bacteria or viral infections, which more commonly cause diffuse, patchy infiltrates on chest radiographs. The acute 4-day time course was neither suggestive of the biphasic illness seen with influenza complicated by bacterial superinfection, nor of tuberculosis, a serious co-infection in patients with HIV infection in many parts of the world, which has a typically more gradual onset. Lastly, once the results of the sputum gram stain were known, other possible pathogens were thought to be less likely: the gram-positive cocci of Staphylococcus aureus would more commonly be found in clusters; Mycoplasma pneumoniae are more typically pleomorphic and stain poorly with gram stain; Legionella and Chlamydophila pneumoniae (formerly Chlamydia pneumoniae) are both pleomorphic and poorly gram-staining or gram-negative bacilli and Haemophilus influenzae are small gram-negative coccobacilli. Pneumocystis jiroveci, a fungus, would also not appear as lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci.
In most series, pneumococcal pneumonia is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia [Donowitz 2009]. Individuals who are HIV-positive, even those on highly active anti-retroviral therapy and with normal levels of CD4 T-lymphocytes, are at increased risk compared with the general population of developing pneumococcal disease, including pneumonia requiring hospitalization [Sogaard et al 2008]. In this patient, with a low CD4 T-lymphocyte count and lacking both anti-retroviral therapy and PCP prophylaxis, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy for PCP infection was administered until the results of the gram stain were available, given the potentially grave consequences of missing this diagnosis, and the amount was converted to prophylactic dosing once the bacterial infection was diagnosed.
At the time of this publication, a beta-lactam antibiotic, with or without a macrolide (Macrolides are antibiotics which generally are effective against atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma and Chlamydia.), is a good choice for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, especially when the suspicion for pneumococcal infection is high. Given the high incidence of penicillin-resistant pneumococci, third or fourth generation cephalosporins are usually preferred over penicillin for severe pneumococcal infections. Mismatch between the antibiotic spectrum and the susceptibility of a common causative organism, infection with a pathogen not covered by the usual empirical regimen, and nosocomial superinfection are major causes of apparent antibiotic failure. As per current recommendations, [WHO 2009] this immunocompromised patient had received the pneumococcal vaccine after recovery from a previous pneumococcal infection because infection with one serotype does not necessarily provide protection against the others. There is evidence that vaccination helps to protect against invasive pneumococcal disease; however, it remains controversial whether vaccination has significant protective effect against pneumonia [Huss et al 2009; Moberley et al 2008]. Additionally, it is not clear if the vaccine is effective if administered to an HIV-positive individual with a viral load greater than 100,000 copies/ml [Teshale et al 2008].

title:
2010 January Featured Case: An elderly woman with right arm and shoulder pain.

history:
2010 January Featured Case: An elderly woman with right arm and shoulder pain.
A woman in her eighties presented to the emergency department because of acute, rapidly progressive severe right upper arm and shoulder pain. She had been well, without fevers or chills, until approximately 6 hours earlier when, upon awakening from a nap, she noted severe sudden right arm and shoulder pain, associated with swelling and redness. She applied an over-the-counter emollient to the area. During the following 6 hours, nausea and vomiting developed, and the pain progressively increased in severity. She came to the emergency department for evaluation.
She reported lifting furniture in the days before this presentation, but there was no history of trauma to the area.

She had osteoporosis, anemia, and had also recently had a fungal skin infection on her foot, which had been treated with topical creams. She had had a parathyroidectomy because of hypercalcemia and, years earlier, cellulitis of the left foot caused by Proteus and Pseudomonas. There was no history of allergies.

She had not had any unusual exposures or travel, and did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

There was no history of allergies.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 120/54 mm Hg, pulse 89 beats per minute, temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. There was a bluish discoloration covering the entire right shoulder, with surrounding erythema and edema extending to right scapula (Figures 1 and 2). The right upper extremely and surrounding shoulder girdle were tender to light touch, and there was crepitus around the right shoulder extending anteriorly along the clavicle, superiorly to the neck, posteriorly almost to the midline spine, and inferiorly to just above the iliac crest. She was unwilling to move the arm because of pain, but was able to squeeze the right hand, with 4 out of 5 strength. The radial and ulnar pulses were 2+, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 34,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000), with 67% neutrophils, 22% band forms, 5% lymphocytes and 6% monocytes, and the hematocrit was 34% (ref 36.0-46.0). The level of potassium was 3.3 mmol per liter (ref 3.4-4.8), carbon dioxide 19.8 mmol per liter (ref 23.0-31.9), creatinine 1.35 mg/dL (ref 0.60-1.50), non-fasting glucose 193 mg/dL, and lactic acid 5.9 mmol per liter (ref 0.5-2.2). The levels of serum sodium, chloride, urea nitrogen and calcium were normal.

Narcotic analgesia for pain, intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, including clindamycin, penicillin G, vancomycin, and cefepime were administered. She was taken to the operating room emergently. Upon exploration of the upper arm, shoulder and chest wall, there was diffuse crepitus within the muscle, foul-smelling odor and dishwater-type fluid present within the tissues, and nonviable muscle. A gram stain of a specimen obtained from the right shoulder surgical field is shown (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Gram stain of superficial swab of operative site.
diagnosis:
Spontaneous gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) caused by Clostridium septicum.

Gram stains of specimens obtained in the operating room from the right shoulder wound showed abundant rods, with variable gram-colorization, some of which revealed sub-terminal spores (see Figure 4, with arrows). Anaerobic cultures on blood agar dishes grew a film or 'swarm' (Figure 5) within 24 hours; the bacteria were speciated as Clostridium septicum. Gram stain of the cultured organisms is shown in Figure 6.
Pathological examination of the resected muscle tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain is shown in Figures 7 and 8, at low- and high-magnification, respectively. Air cysts, seen in Figure 7 and Figure 8, demonstrate organisms in the tissue; both images show loss of muscle striation associated with myonecrosis.
Figure 4. Figure 3, with arrows showing spores.
Figure 5. Culture of surgical specimen, with an uninoculated plate on right.
Figure 6. Gram stain of culture growth.
Figure 7. H and E stain of muscle (low magnification)
Figure 8. H and E stain of muscle (high magnification)

A right upper extremity forequarter amputation of the right arm and scapula, with debridement of the surrounding musculature, was performed, and a vacuum dressing was placed. Specimens of tissue were sent to the microbiology laboratory from the operating room, and broad spectrum antibiotics (penicillin, clindamycin, vancomycin, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole) were administered.
The patient returned to the operating room on the 2nd and 5th hospital days; no evidence of ongoing tissue necrosis was seen. After identification of the organism, penicillin and clindamycin were continued for three weeks. The patient received skin grafting to the chest wall site. Additional evaluation later revealed invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon.

This patient was diagnosed with spontaneous gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis), caused by Clostridium septicum. In this case, the organisms seen in the primary gram stain appeared bacillary, suggesting that the cause was not a staphylococcal, streptococcal or mixed infection. There was no history of liver disease, water or raw oyster exposure, as is commonly seen in Vibrio vulnificus infections. Clostridial infections of the skeletal muscle may cause myonecrosis and are frequently rapidly progressive and life-threatening. Clostridium perfringens accounts for 80%-95% of cases of myonecrosis and is usually associated with an open wound. In contrast, C. septicum, a less common cause of myonecrosis (5-20%), is almost always spontaneous or nontraumatic [Pasternack and Swartz 2009], as seen in this case.
C. septicum is a gram-positive motile pathogen resulting in “swarming” on blood agar plates, and in comparison to C. perfringens, is more aerotolerant. C. septicum produces 4 different toxins (alpha, beta, gamma and delta), each of which inhibits leukocyte migration and function, and are thought to explain the rapid progression of disease with relatively little immune response.
The alpha toxin produced by C. septicum, which is unrelated to the alpha toxin in C. perfringens, is secreted as a pro-toxin and cleaved by host cell proteases before binding to cell surfaces via glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins. It assembles into hexameric complexes and inserts into the cell membrane, leading to cell lysis. In a mouse model of infection, strains of C. septicum constructed to have a mutation in the gene encoding the alpha toxin were unable to lyse red cells, demonstrating that the toxin is essential for C. septicum virulence and inhibition of leukocyte migration [Kennedy et al 2005].
The clinical presentation of gas gangrene can be difficult to discern from anaerobic cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis caused by streptococcal or staphylococcal infections. The onset of gas gangrene is usually acute, and pain may be out of proportion to the initial findings on examination. Overlying skin is usually discolored and purplish in color, with associated edema, and hemorrhagic bullae may develop. Crepitus is usually, but not always, present. Patients quickly become systemically ill and often develop fever, hypotension, and tachycardia. Leukocytosis is common; hemolysis is caused by toxin production [Pasternack and Swartz 2009].
Gas gangrene caused by C. septicum is associated with a very high mortality rate, estimated to be 60%, and most patients die within 24 hours of presentation. Immediate treatment is imperative and includes emergent surgical exploration to confirm the diagnosis and definitively debride the affected area. Amputation is usually required in limbs. Penicillin has been the traditional antibiotic of choice, at the time of this publication, and clindamycin is often added due to a theoretical benefit because it halts bacterial toxin synthesis [Pasternack and Swartz 2009].
In cases of spontaneous gas gangrene, it is thought that C. septicum is spread hematogenously from the gastrointestinal tract, with entry into the blood stream via an ulceration or perforation of the bowel. Many case reports and literature reviews link spontaneous gas gangrene with malignancy. In a series of 32 patients with C. septicum infection, 50% of patients had a malignancy (compared to 11% with other Clostridial infections). Seventy percent (70%) of those with malignancy had colorectal cancer; 24% had a hematological malignancy. Other associated conditions include immunosuppression, in particular, neutropenia and diabetes [Larson et al 1995].

history:
2010 February Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A man with a cough, fevers and hypotension.
A man in his fifties had been well until 2 weeks before presentation, when upper respiratory symptoms, including nasal congestion and sore throat, developed transiently. Approximately four days before admission, fevers occurred, which rose during the next few days to 102.5°F (39.2°C), associated with diaphoresis. Three days before, he went to work but left early because of fatigue. Subjective fevers persisted, and he slept through the afternoon and night. He had self-administered acetylsalicylic acid for his symptoms.
The day before admission, at a medical out-patient clinic, he reported fatigue and diffuse myalgias, without cough; the upper respiratory symptoms had resolved. He looked tired and pale; the temperature was 102.3°F (39.1°C) and blood pressure 118/88 mm Hg, with no other abnormalities noted. A rapid test for influenza viruses was negative, and blood tests were sent. Acetaminophen was administered and he returned home. In the evening, a nurse contacted him after the results of the blood tests, including a white cell count of 15,600 cells per cubic millimeter (neutrophils 87%, lymphocytes 6%, monocytes 6% and eosinophils 1%) were known. His symptoms reportedly were unchanged; he was drinking fluids and had a friend staying overnight. He was advised to seek follow-up for change in symptoms and be in contact the next morning.
That night, chest and shoulder pain developed on the right side, which was relieved by sitting up and forward; he later fell asleep. At 5 AM on the day of admission, he called his friend because of difficulty breathing. His friend noted he could barely speak and called emergency medical services (EMS). Upon arrival, the patient was diaphoretic with a systolic blood pressure of 70-79 mm Hg. He was brought to an emergency department, where he reported cough productive of reddish sputum.

He had a history of hypertension.

A friend had recently been ill with upper respiratory symptoms.

He worked in an office, lived alone and was physically active.

His father had had lung cancer.

He had no allergies.

Medications included hydrochlorothiazide.
exam_studies:
On examination, he appeared toxic, diaphoretic, and coughing up rust-tinged sputum. The temperature was normal; the systolic blood pressure was 70-80 mm Hg with tachycardia and labored breathing. There were decreased breath sounds on the right. The distal extremities were cyanotic and cold, and the skin was diffusely mottled, without rash, petechiae, purpura, or stigmata of embolic disease. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Arterial blood gases showed pH 7.30, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 29 mm Hg and partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) 97 mm Hg while breathing 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask. The white blood cell count was 3,000/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000) with neutrophils 46%, band forms 40% and lymphocytes 14%; the serum level of urea nitrogen was 30 mg/dl (ref 8-25), creatinine 3.0 mg/dl (ref 0.6-1.5), lactic acid 4.8 mmol/L (ref 0.5-2.2), total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dl (ref 0-1.0) and direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl (ref 0-0.4), and there were mildly decreased levels of potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium. The hematocrit, platelet count, and levels of alkaline phosphatase, transaminases, amylase, lipase, total protein (6.7 g/dL), creatine kinase, and troponin T were normal.
A chest radiograph showed opacities in the right lower lobe suggestive of pneumonia (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed opacities in the middle and lower lobes, with a large pleural effusion on the right side (Figure 2). A spiculated nodule (1.3 cm in diameter) was also noted in the right upper lobe (Figure 3), with multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan.
Figure 3. Chest CT scan.

Shortly after arrival in the emergency department, the trachea was intubated emergently for respiratory distress, mechanical ventilation was begun and a central line was placed. Pressors, intravenous fluids (5 liters normal saline) and broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin, levofloxacin, and vancomycin) were administered, and metronidazole, clindamycin and cefepime were added. He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
Ninety minutes after arrival, arterial blood gases, while ventilated on 100% oxygen, showed pH of 7.10, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 71 mm Hg and partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) 164 mm Hg. Additional studies included transthoracic echocardiography, which showed severe global hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 17%.
A sputum specimen was obtained; gram stain is shown in Figure 4. Pleurocentesis was performed; gram stain of the pleural fluid is shown in Figure 5. The level of protein in the pleural fluid was 4.0 g/dL, cholesterol 53 mg/dL and lactate dehydrogenase was 3950 U/L. Culture of a blood specimen from the day before admission was sterile.
By the 3rd day, he was oliguric; the level of urea nitrogen was 74 mg/dL and creatinine 7.3 mg/dL; coagulation tests had increased; tests of liver function had doubled, and the level of creatine kinase was 2242 U/L (ref 60-400 in men) and creatine kinase isoenzymes 15.7 ng/ml (ref 0.0-6.9).
Figure 4. Gram stain of sputum.
Figure 5. Gram stain of pleural fluid.
diagnosis:
Toxic shock syndrome, pneumonia, and empyema caused by group A Streptococcus.

The gram stains of the sputum and pleural fluid showed abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes and gram positive cocci in pairs and a few short chains. The culture of the sputum and the pleural fluid grew moderate group A Streptococcus, which was susceptible to all antibiotics tested.
Testing of a nasal specimen for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a urine specimen for Legionella pneumophil a antigen and a stool specimen for Clostridium difficile toxin was negative. Other tests for respiratory viruses, mycobacteria and Pneumocystis were also negative.

Steroids, drotrecogin alfa and intravenous immunoglobulin were administered, in addition to broad spectrum antibiotics, pressors, and intravenous fluids. Oliguric renal failure required initiation of renal-replacement therapy by means of continuous venovenous hemofiltration and, later, hemodialysis. During the first 10 days, the level of creatine kinase rose to 14,000 U/L (ref 60-400 in men), which was thought to be due to rhabdomyolysis, and the aspartate aminotransferase level peaked at 10 times normal. He gradually improved and was discharge from the hospital 3 weeks after admission. Coagulation parameters had returned to normal within 10 days of admission, hepatic function within 1 month, and renal function within 2 months. Four months after admission, a follow-up echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 60%, with normal ventricular function.
Follow-up CT of the chest, performed 2 months after admission, revealed a persistent spiculated lesion in the right lung (Figure 6) and resolving pneumonia. The next month, fine needle aspiration of the lesion was performed, and pathological examination of the tissue showed non-small cell carcinoma, which was later confirmed by pathological examination of tissue after lobectomy to be moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.
Figure 6. Follow up chest CT scan.

This patient developed group A streptococcal pneumonia complicated by streptococcal toxic-shock syndrome (STSS). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2010 case definition for STSS [CDC 2010] includes the following criteria: hypotension with systolic blood pressure less than or equal to 90 mm Hg plus at least 2 criteria indicating multi-organ involvement (renal, hepatic, coagulopathy, respiratory with hypoxia, macular rash and/or soft-tissue necrosis), and laboratory isolation of group A Streptococcus. This patient met the case definition for STSS based on fulfilling the following criteria: hypotension, renal failure, elevated transaminases, prolonged coagulation parameters and confirmation of the diagnosis with growth of group A Streptococcus from a normally sterile space (the pleural fluid), as well as from a non-sterile site, the sputum. In addition, he demonstrated evidence of cardiomyopathy.
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) has been associated with streptococcal infection, usually group A streptococci, and Staphylococcus aureus infection. The disorder is thought to be mediated by bacterial superantigen production. In contrast to conventional antigens which bind 0.01 to 0.1% of T-cell receptors (TCR), superantigens interact directly with the V-beta region of the TCR and can activate 5-30% of T-cells. This excessive T-cell activation is thought to lead to a "cytokine storm", which causes hypotension and multi-organ failure. Streptococcal TSS has been associated with mortality rates between 13% (from any source) and 80% (with myositis) [Lappin and Ferguson 2009]. Staphylococcus aureus TSS, which has a lower mortality rate than streptococcal TSS, has been seen in association with a superficial burn, a surgical wound or menses. Staphylococcal TSS may also occur in the absence of a known source of infection, possibly because of colonization with a toxin-producing species and disruption of skin or mucosa. Both streptococcal and staphylococcal TSS may present with rash and can proceed to desquamation.
In this patient, the sputum and pleural fluid gram stains, with gram-positive cocci in pairs or short chains, are more suggestive of streptococci than staphylococci. While Legionella could cause sepsis, the gram stains in this case are not consistent with this pathogen.
The biphasic nature of this patient’s illness suggests that this episode of streptococcal TSS may have been a post-viral complication. Analysis of multiple influenza pandemics from the 20th century has suggested that secondary infection by common respiratory tract bacteria, including non-pneumococcal Streptococcus, has been responsible for the majority of associated deaths [Morens et al 2008].

title: 2010 March Featured Case Summary: A man in his seventies with fevers and confusi
history:
2010 March Featured Case Summary: A man in his seventies with fevers and confusion.
A man in his seventies (Patient age helps guide differential diagnosis. For example, a patient over 70 with fever and central nervous system symptoms would have a higher prior odds of having HSV encephalitis, West Nile Virus Encephalitis, or Listeria Meningitis than a younger patient.]) presented in autumn (Several important infections show pronounced seasonality, with insect-borne pathogens in particular common in late Summer and early Autumn, when insect bites are more common.) with fevers to 101°F (38.3°C), chills, sweats, fatigue, malaise, rigors and headache. The headache was severe, and located predominantly in the frontal and temporal regions on the left side. He remained in bed for several days (The tempo of progression of symptoms has great diagnostic value. Most typical bacterial central nervous system infections progress over hours whereas viral, fungal, and atypical bacterial pathogens provoke illness more slowly.) because of his symptoms. On the fourth day, he was unable to recall the name of a close friend and the content of his speech was incoherent, without slurred speech. His wife brought him to a hospital because of increased confusion (The combination of fever, headache, and changes in mental status would satisfy the clinical criteria for encephalitis - that is, inflammation of the brain itself - in comparison to meningitis, where there is typically a stiff neck but intact mental status early in infection. Fever itself can cause some degree of confusion but usually only at much higher temperatures.). He reportedly denied dizziness, diplopia, blurry vision, cough, sore throat, runny nose, dyspnea, sputum production, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain or urinary symptoms.
On evaluation, the temperature was 97.4°F (36.3°C), pulse 65 beats per minute and blood pressure 125/84 mm Hg. He was awake and oriented, without focal neurologic findings. The white cell count was 8100 cells per cubic millimeter (90% leukocytes, 5% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes), hematocrit 41.7%, and platelets 164,000 per cubic millimeters; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 7 mm per hour and the level of sodium was 131 mmol/L. Tests of liver and renal function were reportedly normal. Chest radiography and computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast administration were reportedly normal. He was admitted to the hospital and vancomycin, ceftriaxone and doxycycline (In a patient with fever and mental status changes, antibiotics are often given initially even if the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis is unlikely, because even brief delays in treatment can greatly increase mortality. The antibiotics are stopped once cultures are negative and-or another diagnosis is made. Vancomycin and ceftriaxone would be empiric therapy for typical bacterial meningitis, whereas doxycycline would treat a number of atypical infections such a Lyme meningitis.) were administered. A lumbar puncture was attempted but was not successful. The next day, his symptoms had improved and he appeared less confused.
On the 3rd day, the headache returned gradually in the morning, followed by an abrupt increase in confusion and disorientation, associated with stable vital signs and transient weakness on the right side. CT of the head reportedly revealed a possible aneurysm (11 mm) in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery. A rapid test of a nasal swab for influenza and blood tests for Ehrlichia and Babesia were negative. Cultures of the blood from admission were sterile. Acyclovir (Acyclovir is a drug that inhibits the DNA polymerase of Herpes Viruses. Early empiric administration of acyclovir when there is suspicion for HSV CNS infection is critical, since without it rates of death or long-term neurological deficits are greatly increased.) and levetiracetam (an anti-convulsant) were added. While awaiting transfer to a tertiary hospital, he became obtunded, arousable to painful stimuli only, with intermittent bradycardia. The trachea was intubated electively and the patient was sedated; labetolol was administered in transport for transient elevations of systolic blood pressure up to 200 mm Hg.

There was a history of coronary artery disease and hyperlipidemia. He had had prostate cancer (status post radiation), skin cancer, and surgery for spinal stenosis.

He moved seasonally between New England and the southern United States, and had recently returned from a cross-country motor vehicle trip between the Midwest and California (Travel history is an important and too-often overlooked part of the infectious disease work-up. Fever and headache in a person with recent travel to California would raise the question of coccidiomycosis.). He had stopped smoking and drinking alcohol years earlier, and had not used illicit drugs.

He lived with his wife.

A sibling had had a stroke, and there was otherwise no other family history of neurological disease.

He had no allergies.

Medications at the other hospital included vancomycin, ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and acyclovir, intravenously, and levetiracetam. Medications taken before admission included clopidogrel bisulfate, simvastatin, trazodone, ropinirole, meloxicam, acetylsalicylic acid, nitroglycerin tablets and multivitamins. He had received an influenza vaccine within the month, and a pneumococcal vaccine (Vaccine history is important to obtain in all patients with suspected infection. In this case the pneumococcal vaccine was given to decrease the risk of future infection, but it would not have had time to affect the course of the current illness if the patient had an ongoing infection with this organism.) had been given at the other hospital.
exam_studies:
The patient was sedated and intubated. The temperature was 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure 164/68 mm Hg, pulse 56 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% while ventilated with 100% oxygen. The skin had multiple puncture marks on the back consistent with lumbar puncture attempts and was otherwise normal. After 1 hour off sedation, the patient did not open his eyes to voice or painful stimuli; he did withdraw his limbs to painful stimuli. He intermittently moved his mouth and bit down on the endotracheal tube, and did not follow commands. The eyes were roving and did have some movement across midline when held open for examination. Plantar reflexes were extensor.

The white count was 9600 (The normal white blood cell count would argue against acute bacterial infection, although it would be important to check the white cell differential, since there can be low or normal total counts in the setting of peripheral destruction of white cells.) /mm³ (ref 4500-11,000) and hematocrit 34.6% (ref 41.0-53.0). The serum sodium was 126 mmol/L (ref 135-145), chloride 94 mmol/L (ref 100-108), glucose 140 mg/dL (ref 70-110); levels of other electrolytes, troponin-T, C-reactive protein, tests of coagulation, renal and liver function and urinalysis were normal.
A chest radiograph demonstrated left lower lobe atelectasis or consolidation consistent with a left perihilar aspiration or pneumonia (Patients will often have findings unrelated to the principal acute illness, which can sometimes confuse the work-up. In this patient with profound mental status changes and minor chest radiographic findings, it is quite unlikely that he has a significant pneumonia, although people with depressed consciousness may aspirate and develop secondary infection. A useful general principal is that immunocompetent people usually present with one significant infection at a time, and one should be suspicious of multiple diagnoses) (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) and CT angiogram of the head revealed a hyperdense lesion in the left anteromedial temporal lobe (1.2 cm by 1 cm) that was thought to be suspicious for a hematoma (Figures 2 and 3, see arrows), without vasogenic edema, evidence of an aneurysm or vascular malformation.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 2. CT of the head.
Figure 3. CT of the head, reformatted.

He was admitted to the Neurology intensive care unit. An electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, which were more prominent on the right side, without electrographic seizure activity. Doxycycline was stopped and ampicillin (Ampicillin was added to cover the possibility of Listeria meningitis, which could present this way in a patient of his age.) and phenytoin were added.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with the administration of gadolinium-based contrast was performed; fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), T2-weighted, and T1-post contrast enhancement images are shown in Figures 4 through 6.
A lumbar puncture was performed by interventional radiologists under fluoroscopy. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear and colorless, and revealed 292 red cells (Red blood cells in a CSF sample may simply indicate small trauma during the procedure, but also raise the possibility of a necrotic process, such as HSV infection. One can sometimes distinguish between a traumatic tap and true bleeding into the CSF by whether xanthochromia is present, a color change which occurs only after the red cells have been present for some time in the CSF.) and 104 white cells per cubic millimeter (Normal CSF should have 0-5 WBCs. Most bacterial meningitis would show over a thousand WBCs, nearly all neutrophils. In this patient, a hundred WBCs that are predominantly lymphocytes - a lymphocytic pleocytosis - would suggest viral infection.) (83% lymphocytes and 17% monocytes) in tube 1, with similar results in tube 4. The level of glucose was 78 mg/dl (ref 50-75) and protein 67 mg/dl (ref 5-55). Gram stain of the CSF (Gram stain of the CSF is the key initial step in ruling out bacterial meningitis. Culture and other specialized data will not be available until the next day, but the Gram stain can be done in minutes. Gram stain data are very important in guiding the initial therapy for many serious bacterial infections.) showed rare polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and moderate mononuclear cells and red blood cells.
Figure 4. MRI of the head, FLAIR.
Figure 5. MRI of the head, T2-weighted.
Figure 6. MRI of the head, T1 post contrast enhancement.
diagnosis:
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 encephalitis.

MRI of the brain revealed medial temporal lobe (Unilateral temporal lobe inflammation with hemorrhage are common findings with HSV1 encephalitis, since these viruses reactivate from latent sites in the nearby Trigeminal ganglia.) T2 hyperintense signal and enhancement, left greater than right, with evidence of hemorrhage (Figures 4, 5 and 6). Testing of the CSF by DNA melting curve analysis (HSV diagnosis is most often made by PCR of CSF, but some centers use Real-Time PCR techniques such as melting curve analysis, which can give results more quickly and with less sample manipulation.) was positive for herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and negative for HSV type 2 (Figure 7, where 'A' and 'B' represent control samples with both HSV-1 and HSV-2 DNA, and 'C' represents the patient's CSF specimen. The HSV-1 peak is on the left of the graph and HSV-2 on the right).
No organisms were seen on gram stain of the CSF, and bacterial cultures of the CSF and blood were sterile. Testing of the CSF and serum for antibodies (immunoglobulin M) to West Nile and Eastern Equine Encephalitis viruses was negative. Testing of the serum for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and for nucleic acid of varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) were also negative.
Figure 7. Graph of DNA melting curve analysis. The 'A' and 'B' curves represent control samples with both HSV-1 and HSV-2 DNA present, and the 'C' curve represents the patient's CSF specimen, demonstrating that only HSV-1 DNA is present.

After the results of the CSF analysis were known, vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin were discontinued and acyclovir continued. The trachea was extubated on the 5th day. Complications during his recovery included mild syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH), with a sodium level that decreased to 133 mmol/L; this responded to administration of 3% hypertonic saline and fluid restriction. He was discharged on the 12th hospital day to a rehabilitation facility.
At follow-up 5 weeks later, he had some residual short-term memory and word-finding difficulties, but was reported by his wife to be continuing to improve.

Encephalitis is a potentially fatal illness, for which the etiology is never identified in up to two-thirds of patients [Beckham and Tyler 2009]. When a causative agent of sporadic encephalitis in adults has been determined, viruses were the most frequently identified, occurring in approximately 38-69% of cases [Beckham and Tyler 2009]; among these cases, herpes simplex virus (HSV), is among the most often identified, occurring in up to 32% [Beckham and Tyler 2009]. HSV encephalitis occurs in approximately 1 in 250,000 individuals per year in the United States [Schiffer and Corey 2009]. HSV-1 is responsible for approximately 95% of all cases of HSV encephalitis, but among newborns, HSV-2 is more common, caused by vertical transmission from the mother. The age distribution of HSV-1 encephalitis is bi-modal, with about one third of all cases in patients younger than 20 years of age, and fifty percent in those greater than 50 years [Kimberlin 2007].
Transmission of herpes simplex virus occurs through close contact with a person shedding the virus from a lesion, leading to inoculation at a mucosal site such as the oropharynx or genital tract, with most primary episodes occurring after incubation periods of 5 days or less. [Schiffer and Corey 2009] Once infection is established, the virus travels to the nerve root ganglia and replication, which is a characteristic of primary infection, generally ceases. Viral DNA, however, can still be recovered from the nerve root ganglia [Schiffer and Corey 2009]. The precise mechanism of reactivation is not fully understood. Studies have shown that CD8+ T-lymphocytes can block reactivation [Decman et al 2005]. Patients with defects in cell-mediated immunity, such as those with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, are at risk for disseminated disease.
The reactivation process is now known to be much more common than had been thought previously. Once reactivation occurs, it can be subclinical, produce a local lesion, or be associated with disseminated disease, such as occurs in the case of HSV encephalitis. In patients with HSV encephalitis, reactivation is often in the trigeminal ganglion and spreads along the orbitofrontal and temporal meningeal branches of the 5th cranial nerve to the anterior and middle cranial fossa [Patel et al 2009].
The majority (97-100%) of patients presenting with HSV encephalitis have altered mental status and depressed consciousness, which makes it difficult to obtain an accurate history. Other signs and symptoms include headaches (70-81%) and fever (90-100%) along with cranial nerve deficits, seizures, dysphasia and aphasia [Beckham and Tyler 2009]. Behavioral findings, such as hypomania, have been described [Fisher 1996]. Kluver-Bucy Syndrome (KBS) - characterized by inappropriate behavior, memory loss, seizures and dementia and thought to be secondary to damage to both anterior temporal lobes of the brain - has been associated with herpes encephalitis, as well as to trauma to these regions.
Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with HSV encephalitis has demonstrated a pleocytosis in 96%, with a lymphocytic predominance. Red blood cells may be present in the CSF if the encephalitis has caused necrosis; if red cells are present, it is not necessary to search for another cause. This finding is not specific for HSV encephalitis however; other, much more rare, causes of hemorrhaghic encephalitis include anthrax and amebic infection. The level of protein may be abnormal, as seen in this case, while the glucose is normal in about 95% of cases [Beckham and Tyler 2009]. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the CSF for HSV DNA is highly sensitive (98%) and specific (94%), though false negatives can rarely occur.
Classic imaging findings include inflammation and necrosis of the medial temporal lobes, as demonstrated in this case, and orbital surfaces of the frontal lobes. Bilateral involvement is common [Patel 2009]. The classic EEG pattern includes periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLED’s), as in this case.
Altered mental status and fever, though common presenting features of HSV encephalitis, are also non-specific, and thus clinicians should consider a broad differential in a patient for whom HSV encephalitis is a leading diagnosis. Encephalitis caused by other viruses - including enterovirus, influenza, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), Epstein Barr virus (EBV), West Nile virus and Eastern Equine encephalitis virus - often needs to be considered. Among non-viral infectious etiologies, neurosyphilis and brain abscesses may present with fever and confusion. Among non-infectious etiologies, autoimmune disorder, paraneoplastic disease and collagen vascular disorders should be considered [Beckham and Tyler 2009].
Early treatment with acyclovir is essential to improve clinical outcomes, and should be initiated in individuals with a suspicion of HSV encephalitis until confirmatory data is obtained. Of note, acyclovir-resistant HSV has been described in a small percentage (about 0.1-0.7%) of immunocompetent hosts, and is more commonly seen in immunocompromised hosts, where the prevalence is 4-14% [Aoki et al 2009]. Mortality associated with HSV encephalitis remains high and is associated with older age. Those who survive often have residual memory deficits and seizure disorder.

title: 2010 April Featured Case Summary: A woman with right upper quadrant pain, radiat
history:
2010 April Featured Case Summary: A woman with right upper quadrant pain, radiating to the right shoulder, and a cystic mass in the right upper quadrant.
A woman in her fifties had been well until approximately 3 months before, when right upper quadrant and flank pain developed, which increased with respirations and radiated to the right shoulder. She was seen at another hospital, where abdominal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a large complex cystic lesion, with septa and calcifications, adjacent to the liver and possibly extending above the diaphragm. A biopsy of the lesion was attempted, but was not successful. She was otherwise well.
She was admitted electively to the hospital for further evaluation and management.

There was a history of hypercholesterolemia and hypothyroidism. She was known to have a right lower lobe pulmonary nodule, discovered incidentally on chest radiography during evaluation for anaphylaxis five years earlier. She had had a root canal three years before admission and an appendectomy complicated by perforation more than a decade earlier, as well as several gynecologic procedures and a tonsillectomy in the remote past.

She worked in a healthcare field. She had lived in the Middle East and Africa as a child, and had also traveled to Mexico. She drank alcohol in moderation and did not smoke.

She was married and had children.

She was allergic to naproxen (anaphylaxis), penicillin and erythromycin, which had caused hives.

Medications included rosuvastatin (weekly), omega-3-fatty acids and levothyroxine. She had stopped acetylsalicylic acid 2 months before.
exam_studies:
The vital signs were normal. Breath sounds in the right base were markedly diminished, and the lungs were otherwise clear bilaterally. The abdomen was soft, without tenderness, distension, masses, bruits or organomegaly. The examination was otherwise normal.

Pre-operative laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, plasma levels of electrolytes and tests of renal and liver function, were performed 9 days before admission and were normal. An electrocardiogram demonstrated counterclockwise rotation and non-specific ST-segment and T-wave changes.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) demonstrated blunting of the right costophrenic angle. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed a complex mass, 7-centimeters in diameter, associated with the right lower lung, liver, adjacent chest wall and diaphragm (Figures 2 and 3, showing lung and abdominal views, respectively), as well as numerous bilateral calcified and noncalcified pulmonary nodules (2 to 8 mm), atelectasis in the right lower lobe, minimal nodularity at the apices that suggested possible prior granulomatous disease and a thyroid nodule.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest, lung view.
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest, abdominal view.

Flexible bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage, with right video-assisted thoracoscopy (VATS) and thoracotomy, revealed a complex cystic lesion involving the intrathoracic and intraabdominal cavities, including the lower margin of the right lower lobe of the lung, crossing the diaphragm and confluent with the superior portion of the right lobe of the liver, retroperitoneum and right adrenal gland. A wedge resection of the right lung, diaphragm resection and resection of a hepatic cyst was performed, and the cyst oversewn. Gram stain of the cyst aspirate is shown in Figures 4 and 5, and pathological examination of the resected tissue in Figures 6 and 7 (courtesy of Richard L. Kradin, MD), shown with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) and Steiner stains.
Figure 4. Gram stain of cyst aspirate.
Figure 5. Gram stain of cyst aspirate.
Figure 6. Biopsy of tissue, H and E stain.
Figure 7. Biopsy of tissue, Steiner stain.
diagnosis:
Intrathoracic and intraabdominal abscess caused by Actinomyces israelii and Bacteroides fragilis infection.

Gram stain of the cyst demonstrated abundant leukocytes and gram negative rods, and rare long thin gram positive rods. Pathological examination of the resected tissue revealed granulohistiocytic inflammation with foamy macrophages in a necrotic complex inflammatory cystic mass that was beneath the diaphragmatic leaflet adjacent to the dome of the liver. A large 'sulfur granule' was seen (Figures 6 and 7), composed of gram-positive GMS-positive filamentous bacteria, (Figure 8, Brown-Hopps (gram) stain, courtesy of Richard L. Kradin, MD) and Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon. Cultures of the specimen grew few Actinomyces israelii and, in the thioglycollate broth tube only, Bacteroides fragilis.
Figure 8. Biopsy of excised tissue, Brown-Hopps (gram) stain.

The patient was initially treated with parenteral vancomycin, cefepime, levofloxacin and metronidazole; after pathological and culture results were available, those antibiotics were stopped and clindamycin and ciprofloxacin were begun. She underwent penicillin desensitization in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit and was transitioned to penicillin, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for 4 weeks, followed by a 12-month course of penicillin and probenecid.

This patient's clinical presentation included a complex cystic mass that crossed tissue planes and involved the liver, diaphragm, and lung; pathological examination of resected tissue demonstrated 'sulfur granules' and filamentous gram-positive rods. 'Sulfur granules', yellow granules which occasionally are identified extruding from abscesses, may be seen in infections caused by Nocardia, Actinomyces, and Staphylococcus aureus (as seen in botryomycosis), Streptomycetes and other eumycetes associated with maduromycoses.
In this case, the large 'sulfur granule' was composed of gram-positive GMS-positive filamentous bacteria, which was most suggestive of Actinomyces infection. Intraoperative cultures eventually grew Actinomyces israelii, confirming the diagnosis. Actinomycetes spp. are filamentous, gram-positive, fastidious anaerobes. Culture of the organism is the diagnostic gold standard, but is rarely positive. Strict anaerobic processing and obtaining cultures before the institution of antibiotic therapy may improve the yield of a positive identification.
Actinomyces, when isolated, is frequently found with companion organisms in polymicrobial cultures. Specifically, cervicofacial co-infections have involved Actinobacillus, Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus infections [Pulverer et al 2003]. Actinomyces are considered normal flora of the human oropharynx, gastrointestinal tract, and female genital tract. Actinomycosis infections occur most commonly in the cervicofacial (50-60%), the abdominopelvic (20%) and pulmonary (15%) regions and, much less commonly, in the central nervous system (2%). Rarely, infections of the skin, cardiac, or genitourinary tract, or disseminated infections occur [Mabeza and Macfarlane 2003]. Infections are slowly progressive, often crossing tissue planes. They mimic malignancy and often are diagnosed through invasive sampling of tissue as part of presumed oncologic management.
In the case described, the primary focus of infection is difficult to ascertain given transdiaphragmatic involvement. Poor dentition, compounded by aspiration, had been proposed as one mechanism of basilar pulmonary infection. In cases of hepatic infection, involvement of adjacent tissues occurs in one third of cases [Sharma et al 2002]. A similar presentation with involvement of the liver, diaphragm and lung, has been previously reported [Kasano et al 1996]. Intraabdominal infections are often thought to result from a breach in the gastro-intestinal mucosa with subsequent introduction of Actinomyces. Growth occurs in an indolent fashion, often lying clinically silent for years. In this regard, the remote history of a perforated appendix may be relevant in this case.
