history:
2010 May Featured Case Summary: A boy with fevers after traveling to Nigeria in summer.
A 5-year-old boy was well until 2 days before admission when, while visiting relatives during a one-month trip to Nigeria in summer, headache developed bilaterally. He felt warm to the touch and his mother administered ibuprofen. The next day, before returning to the United States, he saw a family physician because of a high fever, and amoxicillin (one dose), paracetomol (acetaminophen) and a vitamin supplement were reportedly administered.
During the plane flight to the United States, fevers reportedly recurred intermittently and nausea developed, with one episode of vomiting non-bloody emesis. At approximately 5 AM, jerking of the arms occurred, with shaking of 2 minutes’ duration, associated with hypersalivation, transient loss of consciousness and urinary incontinence; tongue-biting did not occur. The flight crew administered oxygen via mask. After the shaking resolved, he was placed on the floor and was somnolent. He was later transferred to business class for the remaining 45 minutes of the flight. When the plane landed, he was reportedly acting himself, crying, moving all four extremities spontaneously. He did not appear confused, and was able to identify his mother.
He was taken by ambulance to the emergency department of the nearest hospital.

He had previously been well, with no history of sickle cell disease, previous hospitalizations or surgery.

The patient was born in the United States of Nigerian parents, and lived in the Southeastern United States. The family frequently returned to Africa to visit relatives.

The mother reported that her family could not take ‘quin’ medications, but did not know if any relatives had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

He had no allergies.

He had recently taken ibuprofen, amoxicillin (one dose), paracetomol (acetaminophen) and a vitamin supplement.
exam_studies:
The patient was awake and conversant. The temperature was 104.8°F (40.4°C), pulse 140 beats per minute, and respirations 28 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. The weight was 19.5 kilograms. The abdomen was soft, and the liver was palpated 2 cm below the costal margin. There were multiple small excoriated lesions on the arms and legs, and 5-6 facial nonerythematous papules (1-2 mm diameter) on the face and neck. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 14,200 per cubic millimeter (reference range 5500-15,500) with 50% leukocytes, 34% band forms, 11% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes and 4% metamyelocytes; the hematocrit was 32.8% (ref. 34.0-40.0), hemoglobin 11.8 gm/dl (ref. 11.5-13.5) and platelets 197,000 per cubic millimeter, with 1+ polychromasia and 1+ microcytosis, and possible intracellular abnormalities. The serum sodium was 131 mmol/liter (ref 135-145), chloride 95 mmol/liter (ref 100-108), carbon dioxide 21.3 mmol/liter (ref 23.0-31.9), glucose 120 mg/dl (ref 70-110), total bilirubin level 4.8 mg/dl (ref 0-1.0), direct bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl (ref 0-0.4), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (ref 10-40) and alanine aminotransferase 97 U/L (ref 10-55). The levels of potassium, protein, albumin and alkaline phosphatase and tests of renal function were normal.
Urinalysis revealed 1+ bilirubin, 2+ ketones, and 1+ occult blood and there were 5-10 white cells and 3-5 red cells per high-power field and 0-2 hyaline casts per low-power field.

Thick and thin smears of the peripheral blood with Giemsa staining are shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Peripheral blood, thick smear, with Giemsa staining.
Figure 2. Peripheral blood, thin smear, with Giemsa staining.
diagnosis:
Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum in a young child, after a visit to family in Africa.

The hematology laboratory personnel suspected intracellular organisms on examination of the peripheral blood smear. The parasitology laboratory staff examined thick and thin peripheral blood smears with Giemsa staining, and identified intracellular organisms within the erythrocytes, including cells with ring forms with double chromatin dots (“headphone’ formations) and multiple ring forms (Figure 3, with arrows showing some of the intracellular trophozoite ring forms). The organisms were identified to be consistent with Plasmodium falciparum. The parasitemia level was estimated to be 10%. A blood culture was sterile.
Figure 3. Detail of Figure 2, thin smear, Giemsa stain, with trophozoite ring forms (arrows).

In the emergency department, normal saline was administered intravenously and acetaminophen was given; the child’s headache improved and the temperature decreased. Once the results of the laboratory tests were known and after discussion with physicians at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) regarding the family history and possible risk of an adverse reaction, quinidine gluconate (10 mg/kg of salt) was administered intravenously over 2 hours, followed by continuous infusion of 0.02 mg salt/kg/minute under close monitoring. Clindamycin (10 mg/kg loading dose, then 5 mg/kg every 8 hours) was also given and oral intake was encouraged. The parasitemia decreased to 8% on the afternoon of admission, to 3.5% the next day and less than 0.5% the 3rd day. At discharge on the 4th day, no parasites were seen. The hematocrit decreased to 29.1% on the 3rd day; tests of liver function test returned to normal and the bilirubin levels improved. The electrocardiogram was closely monitored while the patient was on quinidine therapy. Within 24 hours on therapy, the QTc interval increased from an admission measurement of 0.499 to a peak of 0.585; 3 hours later, it had improved 0.515.
The patient improved and was discharged on the 4th day. He returned to his home in the Southeastern United States, to follow up with his pediatrician and complete the therapy. After discharge, results of stool examination returned positive for Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts.

Fevers in a traveler returning from Africa may be due to infectious illnesses that can rapidly cause severe morbidity and mortality, and consequently urgent evaluations are required to administer appropriate treatment quickly. Very young and/or malnourished children are especially vulnerable to adverse outcomes related to high fevers, sepsis, dehydration and other sequelae, such as seizures and anemia. Regardless of age, diagnosis of P. falciparum, especially with central nervous system involvement, is a medical emergency in which prompt diagnosis and treatment can be lifesaving.
In this case, clues to the diagnosis included the history of recent travel to an area endemic for P. falciparum (and its vector, the female Anopheles mosquito), the high fever on examination, the absence of eschar lesions (more suggestive of Rickettsial diseases) or other focal findings, and the laboratory findings. Of note, intraerythrocytic parasites in Babesiosis, caused by Babesia microti and other subspecies, may be similar in appearance to P. falciparum. When present, the ‘Maltese cross’ configuration seen in Babesiosis may help differentiate the two. In this case, the travel history is far more suggestive of P. falciparum. Serologic and molecular testing may be used to make the diagnosis definitively, if needed. The dimorphic fungus Histoplasma, though present in Africa, is seen inside white blood cells, not red blood cells, on peripheral smear.
Travel-related illnesses, such as malaria, can often be prevented with appropriate measures. Vaccinations should be delivered and antimalarial medications (chosen based on regional resistance patterns) begun before the planned journey, followed by avoidance measures, such as insect repellant and insecticide-treated mosquito netting, while traveling. This patient had not received prophylactic antimalarial treatment. Expatriates, who may have waning or absent immunologic protection, and individual travelers visiting relatives in endemic areas are among those travelers with the highest rates of malaria infection [Ladhani et al 2007].
In the hospital, the patient's initial treatment was directed towards decreasing the temperature (lowering the risk of febrile seizures) and rehydration. After the diagnosis of P. falciparum was made, the organism was presumed to be resistant to chloroquine based on the geographical region visited [CDC references 2 and 3]. Because of the concern for cerebral malaria and the high parasitemia level, the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit and treated with intravenous quinidine and clindamycin, with close cardiac and glucose monitoring. More recently, intravenous artesunate has become available for the treatment of individuals with severe or complicated malaria in the U.S. through an investigational new drug (IND) protocol maintained by the U.S. CDC. Information on indications and logistics of receiving artesunate are available at the CDC web site (http://www.cdc.gov/malaria/diagnosis_treatment/artesunate.html) [CDC reference 1].
In recent years, new efforts are being made to eradicate malaria worldwide. Approximately 850,000 deaths per year occur worldwide from malaria, of which approximately 90% are caused by P. falciparum and, in sub-Saharan Africa, greater than 80% of malaria-related deaths occur in children under the age of 5 years [Crawley et al 2010]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has revised guidelines for treatment to include recently developed artemisinin combination therapies (ACTs) and suggested removing artemisinin monotherapy from availability to avoid the development of resistance [WHO 2010]. In April, 2009, the first artemisinin-based combination drug (artemether-lumefantrine) was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the oral treatment of individuals with uncomplicated malarial infections caused by P. falciparum. This medication is considered to be a front-line therapy for individuals with uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum malaria in the U.S. Other oral agents include 1) therapeutic dose atovaquone-proguanil; 2) quinine plus either doxycycline, tetracycline or clindamycin; or 3) mefloquine, although, because of drug resistance, this agent is not recommended in persons who have acquired malaria in Southeast Asia.

title:
2010 June Featured Case Summary: A man with vomiting and mid-epigastric pain.
A
history:
2010 June Featured Case Summary: A man with vomiting and mid-epigastric pain.
A man in his thirties was in his usual health until 6 days before when, in late summer, vomiting with non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and mid epigastric pain developed after eating. Three days later, he saw his physician. On examination, the blood pressure was 115/72 mm Hg, pulse 139 beats per minute and temperature 99°F (37.2°C), with mild epigastric tenderness. Gastroesophageal reflux disease was diagnosed and ranitidine with esomeprazole was administered. During the next 2 days, fevers and fatigue occurred. One day before admission, he returned to the out-patient clinic because of persistent nausea and abdominal discomfort. He reported no chest pain, dyspnea, cough, headache, lightheadedness, diarrhea, constipation or night sweats, and no exposures to sick contacts. The blood pressure was 98/65 mm Hg, pulse was 135 beats per minute and the temperature 100.5°F (38.1°C). Urinalysis showed 2+ bilirubin and urobilinogen. An abdominal ultrasound was scheduled. The next day, he went to an emergency department for further evaluation.
He reported no weight loss, anorexia, or cardiac or gastrointestinal symptoms.

Eighteen months earlier, he had been admitted to the hospital because of cough, with occasional blood-streaked sputum and calcifications on chest radiograph. On computed tomography (CT), there were calcified nodules in the right middle lobe and lymphadenopathy in the right hilum and subcarinal space. Three sputum specimens had been stained and cultured, and were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. After discharge, and while he was asymptomatic, a tuberculosis skin test was positive at greater than 10 cm diameter induration. Isoniazid was administered for 9 months. A screening test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was reportedly negative 5-7 years before; the patient declined repeat testing. He had had abdominal pain in the past with Helicobacter pylori infection, which had been treated.

He had emigrated from East Africa to the United States more than 5 years before. He had been homeless for several months in the past, drank alcohol and did not use illicit drugs or smoke. He was currently monogamous with his girlfriend.

He was employed and lived with his girlfriend. He had one child who lived with the child's mother in Africa.

He was taking esomeprazole.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure 106/76 mm Hg and pulse 119 beats per minute; respirations and oxygen saturation were normal. Neck veins were distended and heart sounds were distant. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The hematocrit was 31.1% (reference range 41.0-53.0), white blood cells 6500/mm³ (ref 4500-11,000) with neutrophils 84%, lymphocytes 12% and monocytes 4%. The sodium was 125 mmol/L (ref 135-145), chloride 94 mmol/L (ref 100-108), albumin 2.6 gm/dl (ref 3.3-5.0), globulin 5.1 gm/dl (ref 2.6-4.1), aspartate aminotransferase 121 U/L (ref 10-40), alanine aminotransferase 119 U/L (ref 10-55) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 275 U/L (ref 110-210); other tests, including alkaline phosphatase, amylase, lipase and cardiac enzymes, were normal.
A chest radiograph, shown in Figure 1, demonstrated an enlarged cardiac silhouette and an electrocardiogram (Figure 2) revealed tachycardia and diffuse ST-segment elevations and P-R depressions. A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a large circumferential pericardial effusion, with evidence of tamponade physiology and fibrin stranding.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, on admission.
Figure 2. EKG on admission.

The patient was taken emergently to the cardiac catheterization lab for pericardiocentesis, and 1300 cc of fluorescent green-yellow, clear, free-flowing fluid was aspirated. The pericardial fluid revealed 130 white cells/mm³ (ref 0-1000), with neutrophils 84%, lymphocytes 6%, and monocytes 10%, glucose 27 mg/dl, total protein 9.3 gm/dl, and LDH 1216 U/L. There were no organisms seen on staining of the fluid and cytological examination showed no malignant cells.
During the next 6 days, the pericardial fluid re-accumulated, requiring additional aspirations approximately every 6 hours. On the 3rd day, the chest radiograph revealed a persistently enlarged cardiac silhouette and computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figure 3 and 4, lung and mediastinal views, respectively) showed a large pericardial effusion.
On the 7th day, a left anterior lateral thoracotomy was performed with pericardial stripping of the anterior and left pericardium, drainage of a large loculated pericardial effusion and placement of pericardial and left pleural drains.
Pathological examination of the pericardial tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining is shown in Figures 5 and 6. (Pathology images courtesy of Richard Kradin, M.D.)
Figure 3. CT scan of the chest, lung view.
Figure 4. CT scan of the chest, mediastinal view.
Figure 5. Pericardial tissue, H and E stain.
Figure 6. Pericardial tissue, H and E stain.
diagnosis:
Tuberculous pericarditis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Pathological examination of the pericardial tissue revealed granulomas (Figures 5 and 6, above). A pericardial biopsy specimen demonstrated acid-fast organisms (Figure 7). Cultures of the pericardial fluid obtained by pericardiocentesis during the first 3 days of admission and the pericardial biopsy tissue grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which was resistant to isoniazid, ethambutol, streptomycin and pyrazinamide. A sputum specimen grew Staphylococcus aureus. Testing for HIV was positive, the level of CD4 T-lymphocytes was 9 cells per cubic millimeter and the level of HIV RNA was 25,900 copies per milliliter.
Figure 7. Pericardial tissue, acid-fast stain.

The patient was placed in respiratory isolation and, after surgery, antituberculous therapy was begun with 5 drugs: rifabutin, ethambutol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin, with pyridoxine and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, and a tapering course of prednisone. After 10 days, tests of liver function had increased 5 times admission levels, and the 5-drug therapy was stopped. The liver function tests improved. During the next month, additional drug sensitivity testing was performed, which revealed the isolate was susceptible to moxifloxacin (MIC <= 0.5), cycloserine (60 mcg/ml), PAS (8 mcg/ml), and amikacin (<= 2.0 mcg/ml). A new regimen with rifabutin, amikacin, moxifloxacin, cycloserine and PAS was introduced in a step-wise manner.
Between 6 to 8 weeks after admission, signs of constrictive pericarditis developed including anasarca, ascites, tachycardia and restrictive physiology by echocardiography. A total pericardectomy was performed. Histopathological examination of the tissue showed 3+ to 4+ acid fast bacilli.
After 6 months, amikacin was stopped, and the other medications were continued for a total course of 24-months. One month after initiation of antituberculus treatment, antiretroviral medications were begun.
The patient's initial hospital course was complicated by a deep venous thrombosis with decreased protein S level and increased anticardiolipin IgG; he received coumadin for 3 months, with improvement.

This patient from Africa presented with vomiting and epigastric pain, tachycardia, distended neck veins and distant heart sounds, and exhibited electrocardiographic abnormalities of diffuse ST-segment elevations and PR depressions with an enlarged heart on chest radiography, which was confirmed by echocardiography and computed tomography studies. This presentation is consistent with a diagnosis of pericardial disease. The severity and course of pericarditis can range from a sub-clinical condition to a life-threatening illness depending on the underlying etiology, which may include idiopathic causes (representing up to 40-86% of patients hospitalized with acute pericarditis and thought to be caused by as yet unidentified viruses [Knowlton et al 2009]) and the etiologies listed in the differential above. Large pericardial effusions are more likely to be caused by M. tuberculosis in patients in resource-poor countries (approximately 70%) than in patients in the industrialized world (4%) [Syed and Mayosi 2007]. In patients with HIV who live in regions endemic for tuberculosis (TB), TB causes more than 90 percent of pericardial effusions [Syed and Mayosi 2007]. In this patient from Africa, TB pericarditis was statistically the most likely etiology. Because of the implications for treatment and with a potential mortality rate ranging between 17%- 40% [Syed and Mayosi 2007], the diagnosis of TB pericarditis should be established expeditiously. A range of symptoms, signs and echocardiographic findings may occur. Symptoms may be nonspecific and not limited to the cardiovascular system, and a significant proportion may eventually be noted to have concomitant pulmonary TB as well. Multiple physical findings may be present, including tachycardia, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds, hypotension and, if tamponade is present, pulsus paradoxus. If TB is suspected in cases of pericarditis with effusion, pericardiocentesis should be performed. The pericardial fluid is most often exudative [Mayosi et al. 2005]. Histopathological and microbiological evaluation of pericardial tissue significantly aids in the diagnosis of TB pericarditis. Treatment includes close follow-up, with repetitive aspiration of pericardial effusion and, if constrictive pericarditis occurs, pericardectomy. Treatment with combination antituberculous therapy has been shown to dramatically reduce mortality, from 80-90% to 7-40% [Syed et al 2007, Wiysonge et al 2006]. Drug susceptibility testing is important given the high prevalence of multi-drug-resistant TB in some settings where TB is endemic. The role of corticosteroids in the treatment of TB pericarditis remains controversial [Ntsekhe et al 2003]. Although some studies have suggested a benefit to the use of steroids in TB pericardititis, many of the studies were performed in the pre-HIV era and are not large enough to draw definitive conclusions. The most recent TB treatment guidelines recommend treating TB pericarditis with corticosteroids unless drug resistance is suspected [WHO 2009]. Patients with HIV infection and TB pericarditis merit special consideration. There is conflicting data concerning whether or not patients with HIV infection have higher mortality rates from TB pericarditis, although many studies suggest that outcomes are comparable [Syed et al 2007]. HIV-infected patients with TB pericarditis may have higher relapse rates and drug interactions are an important consideration, especially with rifampin. The management of this patient posed additional challenges given his extensive underlying poly-drug resistance, which led to a significant extension of therapy as noted above.

history:
2010 July-August Featured Case and Medical Student Curriculum Case Summary: A woman with recurrent fevers after visiting Bangladesh.
A woman in her early twenties was well until one week before presentation, when she reportedly developed fevers up to 104°F (Fever is the most common symptom in severe systemic infection, and high fevers with rigors suggest -but do not prove- bloodstream infection.) (40°C), associated with chills and occasional rigors. She took acetaminophen (Acetaminophen, which acts as an antipyretic and analgesic, may be taken by patients with febrile illnesses for comfort, but may also sometimes be taken under the mistaken impression that the fever itself is harmful. It is important to ask about antipyretic use, since this can mask a fever or make a constant fever appear sporadic.), with transient improvement; however, fevers recurred daily. Three days before admission (The timing and tempo of symptoms provide important diagnostic clues. In this case, the patient had high fever beginning two weeks after travel, then diarrhea several days after that, which would be uncommon for most ordinary gastroenteritis.), she had non-bloody diarrhea (The absence of blood is evidence against enterohemorrhagic infections such as Shigellosis, classic bacillary dysentery.). The next day, she developed occasional cough (Localizing symptoms such as cough may occur even when the infection is primarily acting elsewhere in the body. For example, malaria, typhoid fever, and dengue -the top three serious causes of fever in the returning traveller- can all be associated with coughing in a significant minority of patients, even though none are primarily lung infections.) productive of clear sputum and infrequent nausea, without vomiting. She reported no hematochezia, melena, hemoptysis, hematuria, dark urine, bone pain, myalgias, arthralgias or rash. She had had an intermittent headache and fatigue.
Three weeks before presentation (An incubation period is often a useful clue. Appearance of symptoms more than two weeks after exposure argues against most ordinary infections and in particular against most viral infections other than hepatitis, Epstein Barr virus, and HIV.), she had returned to the United States from a month-long visit to her family's home in Bangladesh (People returning to visit friends and relatives are a major source of travel-related illness, since they may mistakenly feel that they do not require precautions such as malaria prophylaxis, vaccines, and avoidance of unsafe water.). She had had no ill contacts during the trip, and had not taken malaria prophylaxis. Her roommate had recently recovered from a mild upper respiratory illness.

She was previously well.

She was from Bangladesh and attended college in the United States. During her month-long trip home, she had lived in an apartment complex and only visited urban areas. She reported some mosquito bites during the trip and did not exclusively drink bottled water (Exposure to unsafe water is a major risk for gastrointestinal infections, notably enteric bacteria and Hepatitis A.). She reported no exposures to animals (including pets), had not gone swimming (History of water exposure is important to elicit, since fever in a traveller with fresh water exposure raises several possibilities, notably Schistosomiasis.) in fresh or salt water, and was not sexually active (Sexual history is an important part of the travel-related fever work-up, especially since both HIV and hepatitis B virus can present as non-specific fever.).

She was a student.

She had no known allergies.

As above, she had taken acetaminophen for fevers. She had not taken malaria prophylaxis, did not know her hepatitis vaccination history, and had not received typhoid, H1N1 or seasonal influenza vaccinations.
exam_studies:
The temperature (Normal temperatures occurring between high fevers might be a sign of an infection with this alternating pattern, such as malaria, or might be due to acetaminophen use. The distinction is important since absence of fever can mislead attempts at diagnosis.) was 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure 101/61 mm Hg, pulse 53 beats per minute, and respirations 14 breaths per minute with oxygen saturation with 99% while breathing ambient air. The heart and lung sounds were normal. Bowel sounds were present, and there was no abdominal tenderness or organomegaly. The remainder of the examination was normal. While in the emergency department, the temperature rose to 104°F (40.0°C), and she experienced rigors.

The white cell count (The absolute white cell count provides useful diagnostic information. A normal white blood cell count would be uncommon in serious bacterial infection with the important exception that in severe infection white blood cells may be being consumed as quickly as they are produced. For this reason, it is important to have a manually-read count of the types of white cells, known as the "differential". A large number of immature neutrophils, known as "bands", would be worrisome in the context of a normal white cell count.) was 5700 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000) with 64% neutrophils, 29% lymphocytes, and 7% monocytes; the hematocrit was 39.0% and the platelets 149,000 per cubic millimeter. The level of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 90 U/L (ref 7-30) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 123 U/L (ref 9-32). Other tests, including levels of electrolytes, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, globulin, total and direct bilirubin and tests of renal function, were normal. A chest radiograph (Figure 1) showed clear, well-inflated lungs with mild elevation of the left hemidiaphragm, and was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

During the first day, the temperature rose to 106.7°F (41.5°C), associated with rigors, and an episode of non-bloody diarrhea occurred. Ceftriaxone (Information about local antibiotic resistance patterns is critical. In this case, ceftriaxone, a third generation cephalosporin, would have been used because of the high rates of resistance to quinolone antibiotics on the Indian sub-continent.) was administered empirically (For patients with severe symptoms - particularly the combination of high fever and low blood pressure - it is critical to quickly obtain relevant cultures and then start antibiotics empirically while waiting for culture data to come back. A delay in therapy may lead to increased risk of mortality.).
A rapid malaria test (Malaria is the most common cause of death from infection in travelers, so it is essential to rule this out promptly in anyone returning from a malarial area with fever. Classically, this was done by direct examination of the blood smear for parasites, but recently rapid antigen detection tests have become available, requiring less operator expertise.) was negative. Within 24 hours, both anaerobic and aerobic bottles of a blood culture specimen were positive; gram stain is shown in Figure 2 (photograph courtesy of Ji Yeon Kim, MD). On the second day, the level of lactate dehydrogenase was 737 U/L (ref 110-210). The level of ALT rose to 644 U/L and AST U/L 1044 by the 3rd day.
Figure 2. Gram stain of blood culture.
diagnosis:
Cultures of the blood grew Gram-negative rods (Figure 3, photograph courtesy of Ji Yeon Kim, MD) in both aerobic and anaerobic bottles, which were later identified as Salmonella typhi. Cultures showing growth of S. typhi on MacConkey and blood agar plates are shown in Figures 4 and 5 respectively. Serologic tests for antibodies to Salmonella flagellar (H) and somatic (O) antigens were positive.
Thick and thin smears of the blood showed no intra- or extracellular organisms by Giemsa staining. Dientamoeba fragilis trophozoites (Figures 6) and abundant Blastocystis hominis (Figures 7) were found upon examination of a stool specimen (D. fragilis and B. hominis are unlikely to be pathogens in a normal host. Their presence here is a sign, however, of exposure to unsafe water, their main mode of transmission. This finding should alert the clinician to look for other sanitation-related infections.). Serologic testing for Epstein Barr virus (EBV) was consistent with past infection; results for heterophile antibody (The mono-spot test for mononucleosis, called heterophile, takes advantage of the fact that serum from people with acute EBV infection will cause horse red blood cells to clump.) and hepatitis B surface antigen were negative and hepatitis B surface antibody was equivocal. Testing for other infections, including Leptospira, Dengue fever, schistosomiasis, Legionella, Ehrlichia, hepatitis A virus, hepatitis C virus, human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalovirus, influenza A and B viruses, parainfluenza, adenovirus and respiratory syncytial virus, was negative.
Figure 3. Gram stain of blood culture.
Figure 4. Subculture on MacConkey agar.
Figure 5. Subculture on blood agar.
Figure 6. Chlorazol black staining of stool specimen, with Dientamoeba fragilis trophozoites.
Figure 7. Chlorazol black staining of stool specimen, with Blastocystis hominis.

Ceftriaxone (2 gm daily, intravenously) was administered on admission. After she improved clinically, the temperatures returned to normal and susceptibility testing was available, ceftriaxone was stopped and oral ciprofloxacin (At the time of this patient's presentation, oral ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice for antibiotic-susceptible strains of S. typhi. In practice, what is actually measured is sensitivity to nalidixic acid, the prototype quinolone, since this can best detect low-level resistance to ciprofloxacin.) (500 mg twice daily) and metronidazole (500 mg three times daily) were begun. Upon discharge on the seventh day, the levels of transaminases were gradually improving; antibiotics were continued as an outpatient, for a total course of 14-days.

Fever in the returning traveler must be considered carefully and urgently, as prompt diagnosis and rapid treatment may be necessary. In this patient’s presentation, with fevers, rigors, and fatigue, the differential diagnosis remained broad and included malaria, enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid (The symptoms described in this case were highly suggestive of enteric fever, but one cannot distinguish on clinical grounds between S. typhi and S. paratyphi. S. paratyphi is not covered by the typhoid vaccine, and therefore should be a diagnostic consideration in vaccinated travelers.)), dengue, and Chikungunya fever. Malaria must always be considered as a common cause of fever in the returning traveler requiring hospitalization and the leading cause of death in this patient population [Speil et al 2007]. A rapid malaria test was negative, which reduced the concern for malaria, and subsequent examination of the peripheral smear showed no parasites. Another common cause of fevers in all returning travelers is dengue. However, particularly in south-central Asia to which our patient traveled, enteric fever also occurs frequently [Speil et al 2007] and must be considered promptly, given the differences in therapy. Paratyphoid and typhoid fever can be distinguished only when identified by culture. Chikungunya fever has also been reported in this region, although there was no concurrent epidemic, and our patient did not have the classic severe joint pains typically associated with infection.
In the evaluation of a returning traveler, important aspects of the history include details of the location visited (e.g. rural or urban, altitude), type of accommodation, activities, sexual exposures, food, vector and animal exposures. Pre-travel preparation, including prophylaxis and vaccination history, will inform pre-test probabilities of different diseases. Duration of travel and time until symptom onset will influence the differential diagnosis because of different pathogen’s incubation times. Other causes of illnesses, unrelated to recent travel, must also be considered [Speil et al 2007].
A specific subset of these patients who merit special consideration are those who are returning to their home region after a period of time away, also known as “travelers visiting friends and relatives” or “VFR.” Such travelers are at increased risk for illness from infectious diseases. They often stay for longer visits, in under-developed regions, and may be exposed to untreated water and local food. Additionally, these travelers are less likely to obtain pre-travel medical care with consideration of vaccinations and prophylaxis [Angell et al 2005].
This patient’s clinical presentation was typical for enteric fever. The incubation period is commonly 7-14 days (range of 3-60 days), and the onset of illness is associated with fevers and flu-like symptoms, including cough. Either constipation or diarrhea can be reported, as well as abdominal pain, nausea and headache. A rash is sometimes reported and described as subtle “rose spots” or pink, blanching macules on the trunk. Other physical findings are rare, although hepatosplenomegaly can be noted and paradoxical bradycardia is suggestive. Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and mild transaminase elevations are common but not diagnostic. Blood culture is the most frequent method of making the diagnosis; serology is often not dependable. Culture of the bone marrow is the most sensitive method of diagnosis [Speil et al 2007], but rarely performed in clinical practice. Complications are most common in patients who are not diagnosed within two weeks of illness and include intestinal perforation, bleeding, and encephalopathy.
Antibiotic resistance of Salmonella typhi is of increasing concern. First noted in 1989, multi-drug resistant salmonella (resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) prompted reliance on quinolones, but increasing rates of fluoroquinolone resistance are now evident [Thaver et al 2009; Effa et al 2008]. This patient was initially treated with a third-generation cephalosporin out of concern for quinolone-resistance based upon epidemiologic factors. However, after fluoroquinolone susceptibility testing was performed, her antimicrobial was changed to ciprofloxacin on hospital day 5 to complete a total of 14 days of antibiotic therapy.
Of note, typhoid fever is particularly prevalent among VFR. In studies of typhoid in the United States, 50-80% of cases occurred in returning VFR, especially from south-central Asia [Ackers et al 2000; Steinberg et al 2004]. Other areas of high risk include Mexico, Caribbean, Central and South America and regions in Africa. Vaccination rates among VFR are especially low. Vaccines, either the one-time capsular polysaccharide injectable (Vi) or five-dose oral live attenuated (Ty21a), provides 50-80% protection that lasts 2 or 5 years, respectively. The most important method of reducing infection rates is improved food and water safety [Crump et al 2010].
Additionally, this patient presented with parasitic intestinal infection with both Blastocystis homini s and Dientamoeba fragilis. The ability of both of these organisms to cause symptomatic disease is controversial, but many clinicians would treat symptomatic individuals in whom these agents are identified. Individuals with dientamoebiasis may be treated with metronidazole. A 10-day course may be only 70-80% effective and re-treatment is often employed. Iodoquinol and paromomycin may be more effective [Stark et al 2010], but are less readily available. The pathogenicity of Blastocystis has also been a subject of much debate. A randomized clinical trial demonstrated that treatment with metronidazole resulted in significant clearance of the parasite at one month. However, either recurrence or reinfection rates were high at six months post-treatment; up to 48% of patients at six month follow-up were now asymptomatic but with Blastocystis still isolated from stool culture [Nigro et al 2003].

title: 2010 September-October Featured Case Summary: A woman with ulcerations of the ri
history:
2010 September-October Featured Case Summary: A woman with ulcerations of the right hand and left leg.
A woman in her sixties developed ulcerations on the right hand and left leg.
Approximately one week before admission, she sustained a friction injury when a dog leash wrapped around her left leg. Four days before admission, she burned the second finger of her right hand on a hot oven; a blister formed over the site of the burn. The next day, the blister opened and she noted purulent discharge. She administered hydrogen peroxide and an over-the-counter triple antibiotic ointment locally, and applied gauze to the lesions. Later, while at a beach on the Atlantic Ocean, the bandages over her wounds became wet.
One day before admission, she was seen at a health center because of progressive enlargement of the wounds. Clindamycin was administered intravenously and then orally, for a total of 4 doses, without improvement. Pain radiated from the right hand to her wrist, with local paresthesias around the finger lesion. She reported chills, but denied fevers, erythematous streaking, chest pain, or respiratory, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. She was referred to the burn unit of a hospital.

She had a history of chronic obstructive lung disease, hyperlipidemia and vitamin B12 deficiency. She had been obese in the past, and had had Roux-en-y gastric bypass surgery 2 years before, after which she had lost weight. Laboratory testing prior to surgery had revealed anti-cardiolipin immunoglobulin G antibodies (26.4 gpl with reference range 1-15), and a heterozygous mutation for the prothrombin gene mutation G20210A. Routine screening evaluations for malignancy, including mammogram, gynecologic examination and colonoscopy, had been negative within the previous year.

She was right-handed. She lived alone in coastal New England and worked in healthcare with patients. She had stopped smoking several years earlier, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She had no pets and had not traveled recently. Her mother had died of a stroke and her father had had a pulmonary embolus after a fall.

She was right-handed. She lived alone in coastal New England and worked in healthcare with patients. She had stopped smoking several years earlier, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She had no pets and had not traveled recently. Her mother had died of a stroke and her father had had a pulmonary embolus after a fall.

Clindamycin had been administered, as above. Her tetanus immunization was up-to-date.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 132/68 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, temperature 96.6°F (35.9°C) and respirations 18 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturation 100% while breathing room air. The right index finger was swollen, with wounds consistent with second degree burns over the dorsal aspect of the proximal phalanx (3 cm in length), associated with purulent discharge, and a tender blister over the lateral middle phalanx (1 cm in diameter). The compartments were soft, with intact neurovascular function, and no tendons were visible. Limitation of flexion of the right finger was thought to be secondary to swelling; range-of-motion was otherwise normal. There were two lesions on the left lateral leg (3 cm diameter and 2 cm diameter), without purulent discharge. The leg lesions were tender to palpation with trace foot edema. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 15,400 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000) with 81% leukocytes, 13% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils. The level of serum carbon dioxide was 19.2 mmol/L (ref. 23.0-31.9) and C-reactive protein was 148.2 mg/L (ref. less than 8.0, for inflammation). Other screening test results, including electrolytes and tests of renal function and coagulation, were normal.
A radiograph of the right hand (Figure 1) showed diffuse soft tissue thickening of the second digit, without evidence of a lucent lesion to suggest osteomyelitis or an acute osseous injury.
Figure 1. Radiograph of the right hand, on admission.

Vancomycin was administered in the emergency department; however, pain developed acutely and the infusion was stopped. Ampicillin-sulbactam was then administered, without improvement. During the next 2 days, new blistering lesions developed on the left index finger and hand.
On the 3rd day, debridement of the lesions was performed in the operating room, and infectious disease specialists were consulted. On examination, the lesions were well-demarcated (Figures 2 and 3, images provided by Raj M. Vyas, MD). There was swollen and inflamed tissue associated with granulation and scant purulence in the wounds, without evidence of eschar. Specimens from of the wounds, examined by gram stains, showed abundant leukocytes and mononuclear cells (Figure 4, image provided by John Branda MD). Rare gram positive cocci in pairs were seen on gram stain of a specimen from the left index finger; other specimens showed no organisms and a fungal wet prep was negative.
Figure 2. Physical findings on right hand, intra-operative.
Figure 3. Physical findings on left ankle, intra-operative.
Figure 4. Gram stain of specimen.
diagnosis:
Pyoderma gangrenosum of the hands and left leg.

Cultures of the lesion on the left leg and right hand, obtained on admission, grew rare methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus colonies; the culture of the leg also grew Enterococcus in the thioglycollate broth tube, which was thought to be a contaminant. Cultures of the leg and right hand obtained in the operating room were sterile; the culture of the left index finger grew rare methicillin-susceptible S. aureus and methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. All other wound cultures, including for fungi and mycobacteria, were sterile, as were blood cultures. Testing for 1, 3 beta D glucan was negative. Indirect immunofluorescence testing for anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA), serum protein electrophoresis and testing for lupus anticoagulant and syphilis were also negative. The level of anticardiolipin IgG was 21.1 gpl (ref 1-15).
Histopathological examination of the biopsied specimens with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stains are shown in Figures 5 through 8 (images provided by Lyn Duncan MD and Madelyn Lew MD), and revealed normal tissue, as well as an intraepidermal blister, a dense dermal acute inflammatory infiltrate and tissue necrosis. The findings were thought to be consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum, in the appropriate clinical setting.
Figure 5. H and E stain of biopsy, showing normal skin.
Figure 6. H and E stain of skin, with a dense acute inflammatory infiltrate and dermal necrosis.
Figure 7. H and E stain of skin, with epidermal necrosis and an intraepidermal blister.
Figure 8. H and E stain, with necrosis and acute inflammation.

The patient initially received broad spectrum antibiotics, including vancomycin, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, pending the culture results. Prednisone (70 mg daily) was administered, with topical antimicrobial ointment and local wound care. On the 2nd post-operative day, the parenteral antibiotics were stopped. Physical findings of the lesions are shown (Figures 9 and 10, images provided by Michael Calderwood, MD). The patient was discharged, on the 3rd post-operative day.
Two weeks later, at follow-up, the lesions on the hands and the left leg had markedly improved. Continued Dermatology follow-up, with a slow taper of prednisone and possible administration of a steroid-sparing agent, was planned.
Figure 9. Physical findings, post-operatively.
Figure 10. Physical findings, post-operatively.

Pyoderma gangrenosum is an idiopathic inflammatory disease that is often mistaken for an infectious process. Diagnosis of this condition is based upon clinical history, pathology, and exclusion of other diseases that cause erosive or ulcerative skin lesions. While an underlying systemic disease such as inflammatory bowel disease, myeloproliferative disorder, or inflammatory arthritis is found in approximately 50% of cases of pyoderma gangrenosum, this disease has also been associated with trauma (including burns) and surgery [Callen and Jackson 2007, Ouzzani et al. 2007, Kalu and Williams 2007]. It is important to consider this disease in patients with non-healing wounds and obtain early dermatologic consultation whenever possible, because surgical intervention, including debridement, may exacerbate pyoderma gangrenosum and lead to worsening ulceration.
In this patient, a broad differential was considered, including several possible infections. The rare gram positive cocci seen on the gram stain of the specimen from the left index finger raised the possibility of an aggressive skin and soft tissue infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus; however, only rare S. aureus were isolated. The patient’s possible exposure to brackish ocean water and the severity of the skin and soft tissue lesions in the setting of prior tissue injury raised the possibility of more atypical infections caused by Aeromonas, Vibrio vulnificus and Mycobacterium marinum. However, results of gram staining and cultures did not suggest either Aeromonas or V. vulnificus. Similarly, infection by M. marinum, with an incubation period typically of 2-4 weeks, was also thought unlikely. Finally, the possibility of a deep fungal infection or ecthyma gangrensum secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa were considered, but were not supported by microbiologic staining or culture data. Other non-infectious causes, including vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa, vasculitis associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and mixed cryoglobulinemia) as well as thrombophilic states (antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and Factor V Leiden mutation) should be considered [Callen and Jackson 2007].
In this case, a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum was made after exclusion of other conditions; this diagnosis was also supported by the development of new ulcerations on the left hand at the site of a peripheral intravenous line. The patient's elevated anticardiolipin IgG and heterozygous mutation for the prothrombin gene mutation G20210A may have been contributing factors.
While there is no published algorithm for the treatment of pyoderma gangrenosum, the literature suggests the use of prolonged systemic glucocorticoid therapy; the ulcers often require months to years to resolve. A subset of patients requires the use of other immunomodulators (e.g. cyclosporine, thalidomide, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha blockers such as infliximab) [Miller et al. 2010]. One analysis that reviewed time to remission found that patients with pyoderma gangrenosum typically required a mean of 11.5 months of treatment to achieve remission [Bennett et al. 2000]. Presently, the goal of treatment is to obtain initial rapid control with corticosteroids, and administer a concomitant steroid-sparing agent in prolonged or recurrent cases to allow for steroid taper.

2010 November-December Featured Case and 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with congestive heart failure and cough, decades after heart transplantation.
A woman in her thirties, more than 2 decades after heart transplantation, was admitted to a hospital in mid-winter because of respiratory symptoms and signs of congestive heart failure. One week before admission, upper respiratory symptoms, including rhinorrhea, sinus fullness and sore throat, developed. She also had cough productive of white sputum, which was more severe than that associated with previous heart failure exacerbations. She reported no fever, chills or night sweats and knew of no specific sick contacts.

She had a history of familial dilated cardiomyopathy; heart transplantation had occurred more than 2 decades before, and had been complicated by restrictive cardiomyopathy. She reported adherence with her immunosuppressive regimen. She also had chronic renal insufficiency caused by calcineurin inhibitor toxicity.

She did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs, and had no recent foreign travel.

She lived with her husband in a Mid-Atlantic state, and worked in the medical profession.

Medications on admission included prednisone (2 mg twice daily), cyclosporine (75 mg twice daily), aspirin (81 mg daily), captopril (7.5 mg, divided doses), and furosemide.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 96.5°F (35.8°C), blood pressure 133/79 mg Hg, pulse 95 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. There were scattered crackles in the lung fields and decreased breath sounds at the bases. Trace edema was present at the ankles, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The level of white cells was 8,900/mm³ (reference range 4,000 - 11,000), hematocrit 35.5% (ref. 36–45, in women), and platelets 183,000/mm³ (ref. 150,000 - 450,000). The serum level of creatinine was 2.5 mg/dL (ref. 0.4–1.3). Other routine screening testing was normal.
Chest radiographs on admission are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Lateral view of chest.

Intravenous furosemide (160 mg twice daily) for congestive heart failure and ceftriaxone (1 gm daily) and oral azithromycin (500 mg daily) were administered empirically for presumptive community-acquired pneumonia. Diuresis occurred; however, the cough persisted.
Testing of a nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viruses was negative, and cultures of the blood and sputum, obtained on admission, demonstrated no growth on the 3rd hospital day.
diagnosis:
Whooping cough caused by Bordetella pertussis infection in an immune-compromised host, status post heart transplantation.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of a nasopharyngeal swab specimen was positive for Bordetella pertussis; culture was negative.

Azithromycin (500 mg once, followed by 250 mg daily for 4 days) was administered, with minimal improvement in cough, and prophylaxis treatment with azithromycin was provided to her asymptomatic contacts.

Bordetella pertussis is a highly contagious gram-negative coccobacillus responsible for the respiratory illness known as whooping cough. Bordetella has an unusually long incubation period of 1-3 weeks; most respiratory viruses such as influenza have incubation periods of 24-72 hours [Hewlett 2005]. This organism is fastidious in culture, and has proven difficult to recover in cultures from immunized hosts. Vaccination has markedly decreased the morbidity of this illness, however it continues to be a significant and often overlooked pathogen, particularly in adults [Dworkin 2005].
The classic clinical syndrome of whooping cough consists of three symptomatic periods. The catarrhal phase lasts 7-10 days and consists of upper respiratory symptoms indistinguishable from the common cold. The paroxysmal phase lasts 1-10 weeks and is defined by paroxysms of coughing that can be quite severe. Post-tussive vomiting is not uncommon during this period and should always warrant evaluation for Bordetella infection [Cornia 2010]. This is followed by the convalescent phase, which lasts weeks to months and is characterized by persistent cough that gradually decreases in severity. Immunocompetent hosts are thought to be contagious three weeks after onset of cough or four weeks after the onset of any symptoms [Crowcroft 2006].
The introduction of a vaccine to Bordetella in the 1940s dramatically changed the epidemiology of this pathogen. In the pre-vaccine era, young children with waning maternal antibodies were at risk of acute infection. Adults maintained immunity after childhood infection and received natural boosting of this immunity through recurrent exposure in the population. In the vaccine era (1940s to present), children are no longer at risk due to serial immunization in the first months of life. Adolescents and adults are increasingly at risk as their vaccine immunity wanes, as are infants who do not receive maternal antibodies [Hewlett 2005]. Mortality is highest in infants and young children, which likely explains the mortality benefit of vaccination. This also is likely the reason that most clinicians perceive Bordetella to be a pathogen of childhood, and often overlook this diagnosis in adults [Dworkin 2005].
In regard to diagnosis, culture and PCR are both commercially available. Culture is considered the gold standard, however PCR from a naso-pharyngeal swab can detect fewer than 10 organisms including non-viable organisms, and can distinguishes between B. pertussis, B. parapertussis and B. bronchiseptica [Cornia 2010]. B. parapertussis can cause a pertussis-like syndrome, and B. bronchiseptica can cause respiratory disease in immune compromised patients.
At the time of this publication, macrolides or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are recommended antibiotics for patients diagnosed with whooping cough. While antibiotics serve to clear the organism and prevent transmission, it is unclear that they shorten the duration or severity of illness after the first week of infection. Asymptomatic contacts are treated with same regimen [Cornia 2010]. Primary vaccination is recommended in infants with the diphtheria-pertussis (DTaP) vaccine at months 2, 4, 6 and 18, followed by booster doses at years 6 and 12. A single adult booster vaccine (Tdap) is recommended between the ages of 19-64 [MMWR 2010].

title: 2011 January-February Featured Case and 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation
history:
2011 January-February Featured Case and 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with an ulcerated lesion on her left thumb.
A woman in her fifties developed a large ulcerated lesion on her left thumb (The anatomical site of a lesion is often of both diagnostic and prognostic value. Lesions on exposed areas like the hand can suggest contact with something in the environment. In addition, infections involving functionally important and anatomically complex anatomy like the hand can increase the urgency of appropriate diagnosis and treatment.), which increased in size despite the administration of multiple antibiotics (Failure to respond to multiple antibiotics raises the issue of non-bacterial or non-infectious etiologies.) (see image below). The lesion was initially painless, but became painful (Most acute bacterial soft-tissue infections are painful. Large, painless lesions suggest indolent or atypical pathogens. An initially painless lesion that becomes painful may indicate a secondary process, for example secondary infection of a open lesion.) after swelling increased. Gram stain of a specimen obtained by scraping the skin showed no cells or organisms (Gram stain of an acutely-infected area would typically show neutrophils. Failure to visualize an organism may suggest either a non-infectious process, or a pathogen not visible with Gram stain, which specifically stains bacterial cell walls.), and wet mount revealed no fungal elements. Cultures of tissue (Open wounds offer moisture and nutrients to environmental organisms and may become colonized with a variety of bacteria and fungi. Recovery of a non-pathogen organism from an open wound in an immunocompetent host may indicate colonization rather than deep infection.) grew Rhodotorula minuta. Radiographs of the hand and results of a three-phase bone scan showed soft tissue swelling, with no evidence of osteomyelitis. Empiric antibiotics, tried in successive order over a 3-month period (Chronic progressive lesions unresponsive to this very wide array of antimicrobials would be unusual for common bacterial or fungal infections. On an area such as the hand, with the risk of functional loss, failure of initial therapy should prompt more aggressive attempts at definitive diagnosis.), included amoxicillin-clavulanate, fluconazole, clindamycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, linezolid, levofloxacin, clarithromycin and voriconazole.
She also noted irritation of the left nostril, with brief episodes of epistaxis. She reported no sore throat, fever, chills, dyspnea or cough.

She had been in good health before this illness.

Three months before presentation, she traveled to Ecuador (Prevalence of organisms varies widely by geography; consequently, travel history (including location and duration of stay and any specific exposures) is an important part of an infectious diseases evaluation.) for one month, staying in an ecotourism hotel in the region of the Napo River. She reported no direct water exposure, and did not take malaria prophylaxis or use insect repellent. She reported seeing several different kinds of insects and receiving several bites (Arthropod vectors are responsible for many travel-related infections, so exposure history is important.).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The vital signs (The vital signs listed here are normal, providing some evidence against a systemic infection.) included blood pressure 135/82 mm Hg, pulse 66 beats per minute, temperature 36.7°C (98.1°F), and respirations 18 breaths per minute. There was a large (4 cm in diameter) raised ulcerated lesion with a violaceous border on the thumb (Figure 1), which was painful to the touch. There was no discharge, bleeding, tracking or other lesion seen. Nasal endoscopy revealed a flesh-colored mass in left middle meatus (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Physical findings on left thumb.
Figure 2. Nasal examination.

Results of routine laboratory testing were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is a century-old test that provides a rough measure of systemic inflammation. A normal ESR is generally around 0-11 mm/hr; the normal value in this case does not suggest systemic inflammation.) measured 11 millimeters per hour.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania guyanensis, after traveling to Ecuador.

A skin biopsy (For cases in which the condition does not resolve and cultures are uninformative, histopathological examination of affected tissue is often the diagnostic maneuver with the highest yield, particularly for organisms that are difficult to culture. Increasingly, PCR-based molecular detection is also being used on biopsy specimens.) (3 mm deep) was performed. Histopathological examination of the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain revealed an amastigote (Amastigote refers to the trypanosomal organisms at the stage of the life-cycle where they do not have flagella.), with kinetoplast in a vacuole (Figure 3). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the tissue identified Leishmania guyanensis; PCR of the blood and nasal washings was negative for the organism. Culture of tissue from the skin biopsy in Schneider’s Media revealed promastigotes, seen in Figure 4 and in the Video.
Video 1. Culture of skin biopsy tissue in Schneider’s medium.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy, H and E stain.
Figure 4. Culture of skin biopsy tissue in Schneider’s medium.

Liposomal amphotericin B (Amphotericin is a broad-spectrum anti-fungal that binds to ergosterol in fungal cell membranes. The lipid formulation has lower nephrotoxicity. It is also used for some parasitic infections, including leishmaniasis, when the standard therapies of pentavalent antimony or pentamidine are contra-indicated or unavailable.) (3 mg/kg daily for 7 consecutive days, and 1 additional dose one week later) was administered. Upon follow-up one week after treatment, the skin was improving (Figure 5). After three months, there was no recurrence of the lesion (Figure 6). No further treatment was administered.
Figure 5. Follow-up, one week after treatment.
Figure 6. Follow-up at 3 months.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) has historically been divided into Old and New World, the latter referring to the Americas. This patient was diagnosed with Leishmania guyanensis by PCR and culture. Biopsy is key to the diagnosis; tissue stained with H and E or Giemsa may show rounded amastigotes with kinetoplast (as seen in Figure 3).
This patient's exposure and infection most likely occurred during her recent trip to the jungle regions of Ecuador and Napo River. L. guyanensis is found in Guyana, Suriname, Ecuador and northern Amazon basin. L. guyanensis has several mammalian reservoirs [Banuls et al 2007].
The vector is a female sand fly (Lutzomyia spp) that may infect the host during a blood meal. Promastigotes (seen in Figure 4) are injected and then phagocytosed by macrophages and are transformed into amastigotes (Figure 3). Amastigotes rupture out of the cells and are phagocytosed by other reticuloendothelial cells. The cycle is complete when another sand fly ingests the amastigotes by biting non-human mammals; humans are generally accidental hosts and are not bitten with enough frequency to be a major part of the life cycle [Banuls et al 2007]. Clinical symptoms are generally painless, indolent, raised and ulcerating lesions [Magill et al 2005]. Secondary infections and swelling can cause significant pain as in the case of our patient. Mucosal leishmaniasis is limited to certain species with L. guyanensis having a small risk of mucosal involvement. In this patient, the nasal symptoms had resolved before treatment, and nasal endoscopy was thought to be not consistent with leishmaniasis. When there is mucocutaneous involvement, it is one of recrudescence after resolution of primary skin lesions, often a few years later. This patient’s presentation and findings were not consistent with mucocutaneous disease.
Treatment for CL is dependent on the species, geographic origin, evolution of the lesion, and presence or probability of mucosal involvement. Most CL is self-resolving and does not cause systemic disease, but can leave disfiguring scars. The current main treatment is pentavalent antimony, but because of significant side effects and the long duration of treatment, treatment with other drug agents has been investigated [Minodier et al 2007]. Depending on the species, other possible therapies include miltefosine, azoles, and pentamidine [Lai et al 2002]. Currently the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) has approved liposomal amphotericin B for visceral leishmaniasis. While more studies are needed on the use of liposomal amphotericin B for CL, it appears promising [Solomon et al 2007].

title: 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his forties with HIV
history:
2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man in his forties with HIV developed shortness of breath.
A man in his forties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection developed shortness of breath with exertion, in mid-summer. Dyspnea was associated with a dull chest pain, increasing fatigue, and difficulty performing activities of daily living. He also had chills and nasal congestion, without fevers or cough.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection 15 years before this presentation. The patient had previously been on antiretroviral therapy with an absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of 1000/µl and an undetectable viral load, after which he went on a drug holiday for two years. One year before this presentation, after the HIV ribonucleic acid (RNA) level increased to 42,000 RNA copies per milliliter and CD4 T-lymphocytes decreased to 500/µl, antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine and raltegravir was begun. One month before this presentation, the level of CD4 T-lymphocyte cells was 706 cells/µl and the level of HIV RNA was undetectable.
He also had hypertension, peripheral neuropathy and previous history of substance abuse. He had no history of pulmonary or cardiac disease.

The patient was a monogamous man who had sex with men. He had previously smoked and used illicit drugs, but reported no use of intravenous drugs. He had no sick contacts, pets or recent travel. There was no family history of heart disease.

Medications included tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir, lisinopril, gapabentin, atenolol, celecoxib, nortriptyline, testosterone gel, and aspirin.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable. The blood pressure was 106/74 mmHg, pulse 98 beats per minute, temperature 97.6°F (36.4°C) and respirations 18 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. There was facial lipoatrophy, without evidence of thrush. The jugular veins were distended and there was hepatojugular reflux. Breath sounds were decreased at the lung bases and heart sounds were distant, without murmurs or rubs. There was no adenopathy, lesions on the skin or edema, and the abdomen was non-tender. Neurological examination revealed decreased sensation to light touch, consistent with a peripheral neuropathy.

The white blood cell count was 7,400/µl (reference range 3,800-10,800/µl) with a normal differential, hemoglobin 11.6 gm/dl (ref. 13.2- 15.1) and platelet count of 200,000 µl (ref. 140,000-400,000/µl). The level of creatinine was 1.2 mg/dl (ref. 0.5-1.3) and triglycerides 642 mg/dl (normal less than 150). The levels of serum electrolytes, other lipids, cardiac enzymes and tests of liver and thyroid function were normal, and the antinuclear antibody was negative. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm, at 100 beats per minute, with low voltage in all leads (Figure 1). A chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly and a small right pleural effusion (Figure 2). The echocardiogram showed a large pericardial effusion (Figure 3), with features concerning for impending right ventricular collapse.
Figure 1. Electrocardiogram on admission.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph.
Figure 3. Echocardiogram.

A pericardial catheter was placed emergently, and one liter of bloody fluid was aspirated. The white cell count of the pericardial fluid was 9961/µl (24% neutrophils, 17% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes, 43% other cells) and erythrocytes 747,619/µl. Gram stain of the fluid revealed erythrocytes and leukocytes, with no organisms. The level of glucose was 10 mg/dl, protein 5.4 g/dl and the pH 7.14.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, performed after pericardial catheter placement, showed a large pericardial effusion and two small pleural effusions (Figure 4). CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed mild splenomegaly, and was otherwise normal. Pathological examination of a bone marrow biopsy was normal. Positron emission tomography (PET) scanning showed two small pericardial and phrenic lymph nodes with increased uptake.
Figure 4. CT of the chest.
diagnosis:
Primary effusion lymphoma and human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) infection in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Video-assisted thoroscopic surgery was performed, with biopsies of the pericardium and creation of a pericardial window. Pathological examination of the pericardium showed organizing pericarditis with extensive fibrosis; the biopsies of the 2 small lymph nodes revealed reactive changes, without evidence of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Cultures of the pericardial fluid for bacteria (including acid fast bacteria), viruses, and fungi were negative. Polymerase chain reaction tests for Coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus on pericardial fluid and the serum Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test were negative.
Papanicolaou stain (Figure 5) and Hematoxylin-Eosin stain (Figure 6) on the cell block of the pericardial fluid showed large atypical cells with prominent nucleoli. These cells were positive for CD45 and negative for CD20 by immunohistochemistry. Immunohistochemical stain was also positive for Human Herpesvirus-8 (Figure 7). In situ hybridization detected Epstein Barr Virus-encoded RNA (Figure 8). (Figures 5 through 8 images courtesy of Ninad Patil, MD, Dept. of Pathology, University of Cincinnati.)
Figure 5. Papanicolaou stain of pericardial fluid.
Figure 6. Hematoxylin-Eosin stain of pericardial fluid, cell-block.
Figure 7. Immunohistochemical stain for Human Herpesvirus-8.
Figure 8. In situ hybridization for Epstein Barr virus RNA.

Antiretroviral therapy was continued. Five cycles of chemotherapy were given (etoposide, cyclophosphomide, adriamycin, vincristine, prednisone and rituximab, with intrathecal methotrexate). Positron emission tomography done 5 months after diagnosis did not show any uptake. Repeat CT of the chest (Figure 9) performed one year later did not show any effusions or evidence of malignancy.
Figure 9. Follow-up CT of the chest.

Primary Effusion Lymphoma (PEL), previously called body cavity lymphoma, was first described in 1989 [Chen et al. 2007] It is a non-Hodgkin lymphoma of B cell origin with null lymphocyte phenotype that is associated with serosal surfaces, such as the pericardium, pleura and peritoneum [Boulanger et al. 2005, Chen et al. 2007]. PEL mainly occurs in HIV-infected patients and, less frequently, in the elderly and organ transplant recipients [Simonelli et al. 2003]. PEL comprises 4% of all HIV-associated Non-Hodgkin lymphomas [Chen et al. 2007]. It is caused by the Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpes virus, now called human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) [Boulanger et al. 2005, Chen et al. 2007, Simonelli et al. 2003].
Symptoms of PEL are due to the mass effects of the malignant effusion. There is growth of the malignant cells in the liquid phase without an infiltrative pattern [Simonelli et al. 2003].
The diagnosis of primary effusion lymphoma is based on pathology of a lymphomatous effusion and presence of HHV-8 in neoplastic cells. The virus may be demonstrated either by immunohistochemical stain or by molecular techniques (polymerase chain reaction or Southern blot analysis). The immunophenotype of the lymphoma cells is typically CD45 (Leukocyte common antigen) positive and CD20 (B-cell marker) negative. The mechanism by which HHV-8 contributes to oncogenesis of PEL is under investigation. Epstein-Barr virus is present in greater than 90% of HIV-infected individuals and plays an unclear role in PEL pathogenesis. By definition, PEL is stage IV [Chen et al. 2007].
There are no large prospective clinical trials to define optimal therapy. Antiretroviral therapy is recommended. Chemotherapy regimens using cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, and prednisone have been used [Boulanger et al. 2005, Simonelli et al. 2003]. The median survival is approximately six months [Simonelli et al. 2003].

title: 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man presented with fevers, c
history:
2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man presented with fevers, chills increasing headache and rash.
A man in his thirties from Brazil was well until 10 days before presentation, when fevers, chills, and increasing frontal headache developed. Three days later, arthritis and arthralgias developed and gradually increased. Five days before presentation, a rash began on his ankles, then spread to involve his legs, trunk and ears. He was admitted to another hospital, and ceftriaxone and doxycycline were begun. He was transferred to a tertiary care hospital.

As a child, he had had an episode of rash, fever and joint swelling that resolved spontaneously. Five years before this presentation, an episode of fever with rash occurred, which resolved after a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

He was born in Brazil and had spent time on a farm with cows, horses and chickens as a child. He immigrated to the United States as a teen, and lived in a coastal area of New England with his relatives. He worked in- and out-of-doors, and owned 2 cats. He visited Brazil frequently, and had returned for 3 months within the previous year. He was sexually active with women only, had had multiple lifetime partners and reported intermittent use of barrier protection. He did not report relations with sex workers, and did not smoke, drink alcohol or use injection drugs. He had had no sick contacts, and had played sports the previous week without difficulty.

Before this illness, he was not taking any medications.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable. The blood pressure was 120/72 mm Hg, pulse 93 per minute, temperature 102.9°F (39.4°C), respirations 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% while breathing ambient air. There was an enanthem, without exudates, in the oropharynx. There was no conjunctival injection. There were shotty right supraclavicular nodes, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (greater than 2 cm in diameter). Breath sounds were decreased at the right base and crackles were heard at the left base. There was a palpable splenic tip, and the remainder of the abdomen was normal. The ankles and knees were markedly edematous, and the wrists less so, without edema of non-joint areas. The skin was anicteric, with a raised “dermal” erythematous infiltrate over the eyebrows, nose, cheeks and ears (Figure 1). There were several similar lesions (2-5 cm in diameter) on the abdomen and back, and a diffuse blanching, erythematous and blotchy rash on both legs to the groin (Figures 2 and 3), and both arms to the shoulders, including soles, but not the palms.
Figure 1. Physical findings on forehead.
Figure 2. Physical findings on foot.
Figure 3. Physical findings on foot.

The white cell count was 4,400 cells/uL (reference range 4,000-11,000 cells/uL), with 85% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes, and hematocrit 32% (ref. 36-48). The level of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 107 IU/L (ref. 0-40), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 139 IU/L (ref. 0-40); the remainder of the comprehensive metabolic panel was normal.
A lumbar puncture was performed; analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 1 white cell/uL, protein 39 mg/dL and glucose of 79 mg/dL. A gram stain of the CSF showed no cells or organisms and a smear for parasites was negative.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest (Figures 4 and 5) revealed bilateral axillary and mediastinal lymphadenopathy (up to 2.6 cm by 1.7 cm), and bibasilar consolidation with associated effusions. CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed lymphadenopathy in the left paraaortic, right iliac chain and bilateral inguinal regions (up to 2.5 cm by 1.7 cm), and splenomegaly.
Figure 4. CT of the chest.
Figure 5. CT of the chest.

He was admitted to the medicine floor and ceftriaxone and doxycycline were continued. Increasing dyspnea with rapidly increasing oxygen requirement developed, and 100% supplemental oxygen by face mask was administered. He was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). Antibiotic coverage was broadened to include vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, streptomycin and doxycycline. Temperatures up to 103°F (39.4°C) were recorded nightly.
diagnosis:
Hansen's Disease, type 2 reaction (variant of erythema nodosum leprosum), caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

A skin biopsy was obtained; pathological examination of the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain showed scattered superficial to deep dermal perivascular, periappendageal and perineural granulomas (Figure 6), consistent with leprosy. Modified acid-fast bacilli and Fite stains revealed numerous bacilli in the granulomatous foci. (Fite stain is shown in Figure 7.)
A biopsy of an enlarged lymph node was also obtained, and hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figure 8) revealed multiple granulomas with focal areas of central necrosis and associated acute inflammation. Within these granulomas, there were many histiocytes with large cytoplasmic vacuoles filled with abundant, faintly staining beaded bacilli. The organisms were acid-fast by modified acid-fast staining and by Fite staining; the latter is shown in Figure 9.
All other testing, including for HIV, was negative.
Figure 6. H and E stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 7. Fite stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 8. H and E stain of lymph node.
Figure 9. Fite stain of lymph node.

The patient’s symptoms had fully resolved by the 5th hospital day and he was discharged home. He returned to the Infectious Disease clinic one month later to start a course of rifampin, dapsone and minocycline for multibacillary Hansen’s Disease. During first year of treatment, two episodes of rash occurred and resolved spontaneously. At follow-up after 18 months of therapy, he was doing well; 24 months of therapy was planned.

This previously-healthy man presented with fever, headache, rash, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, transaminase elevation and possibly pneumonitis. The differential diagnosis included acute viral infections, such as HIV, Epstein Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and parvovirus. Syphilis was another possibility. His exposure history and rapid respiratory decline raised concerns about tularemia, though the rash is atypical for this disease. His rash was thought to be inconsistent with a viral exanthem and a biopsy revealed Fite stain-positive organisms within granulomas, thus providing the clinical diagnosis of Hansen’s Disease.
The patient likely acquired Mycobacterium leprae infection as a child in Brazil, followed by many years of asymptomatic disease. A type 2 reaction, or erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), is a complication of lepromatous leprosy: it involves a cytokine storm that results from the release of large amounts of mycobacterial antigens, typically resulting in fever and other systemic symptoms such as malaise, iritis, neuritis, myositis, lymphadenitis, arthritis, dactylitis and orchitis. While this reaction generally occurs during antimycobacterial treatment, it occasionally occurs in untreated individuals, as in this case. The episodes of fever and rash in his medical history may have been unrecognized ENL-type reactions that resolved spontaneously. A variant of ENL with polymorphous lesions has been termed “erythema polymorphous-like reaction,” in which lesions may not be nodular [Cuevas et al. 2007].
Mycobacterium leprae is transmitted through aerosol spread of nasal secretions. The countries with the highest prevalence rates of Hansen’s Disease are India, Brazil, and Indonesia [WHO 2010]. Due to its highly variable incubation period of up to 30 years, and the increasing numbers of foreign-born individuals residing in developed countries, Hansen’s Disease should be considered in the differential diagnosis of rash in North America.
