title: 2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man presented with rash and
history:
2010 IDSA Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A man presented with rash and confusion.
A man in his sixties was well until the morning of admission when he awoke feeling lethargic. Over the course of the day, his hands and feet grew cold and numb; he had multiple dark bowel movements, and developed a rash that spread to his thighs, arms, nose, ears, and scalp. The rash was not pruritic or painful. His wife noticed that he became “incoherent” and his nose became dark red. She called emergency medical services, and he was transported to an emergency department.

He had had bacterial pericarditis as a teenager.

The patient lived with his wife in Northern California, in a rural community, and worked in a business occupation. He smoked cigarettes for 30 years. He drank alcohol, and had a history of occasionally “blacking out”. He reported no use of illicit drugs.
The day before admission, he had used a “weed-whacker” in his yard. He owned horses, which he often rode and fed, and several dogs. His dogs were in good health and were known to eat horse manure.
Three days before admission, he had been bitten on his right hand by one of the dogs while breaking up fight among the dogs. He reported no insect bites or mountain lion exposure. He regularly drank well water and, four days prior to admission, he had eaten grilled medium-rare hamburgers.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable. His temperature was 38.7°C (101.7°F), blood pressure 115/78 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats per minute, respirations 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while on supplemental oxygen (6 liters by nasal cannula). Patches of purpura were confluent on his scalp and bilateral upper pinnae, and were not palpable. Reticular lesions were present on the lower abdomen, back, penis, scrotum, and upper thighs (Figure 1). Three indurated puncture wounds (2-3 mm in diameter) were on the dorsal aspect of his right hand, without swelling, discharge, or surrounding erythema. The nose was markedly edematous and cyanotic (Figure 2), and skin lesions were diffusely present on the scalp (Figure 3). Mucous membranes were dry without mucosal lesions. The hands and feet were cyanotic (Figure 4) and cold, with decreased sensation. The strength was normal. The dorsal pedis pulses were normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings on back, buttocks and leg.
Figure 2. Physical findings on the nose.
Figure 3. Physical findings on the scalp.
Figure 4. Physical findings on the foot.

The white cell count was 21,800 cells per microliter (µl) (reference range 4100-10,900), with 94.9% neutrophils (ref 35-80), hematocrit 35.9% (ref 40-52), platelet count 34,000 per µl (ref 140,000-450,000), INR 1.5 (ref 0.9-1.2), and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 44.0 seconds (ref 18-28). The serum level of potassium was 5.2 mEq/L (ref 3.6-5.0), urea nitrogen 50 mg/dL (ref 7-21), creatinine 3.47 mg/dL (ref 0.5-1.4), alanine aminotransferase 356 U/L (ref 7-56), aspartate aminotransferase 959 U/L (ref 38-126), alkaline phosphatase 50 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL (ref 0.2-1.3), fibrinogen 283 mg/dL (ref 170-420 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 1883 U/L (ref 50-150), creatinine kinase 45,000 ng/ml (ref 38-120), and troponin I 1.18 ng/mL (ref <0.4). A troponin I level was repeated, and measured greater than 22 ng/ml. Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Urinalysis showed muddy brown casts, but no dysmorphic red blood cells or red cell casts.
The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, and left ventricular hypertrophy with repolarization abnormalities. A chest radiograph showed no evidence of infiltrate or volume overload.

The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit and intravenous fluids, ceftriaxone and vancomycin were administered. Continuous renal replacement therapy was begun. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed global hypokinesis and reduced left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 35%. There was no evidence of vegetations or thrombus. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal liver and spleen, and diffusely echogenic kidneys, without evidence of hydronephrosis. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain demonstrated a small subdural hemorrhage.
diagnosis:
Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection.

After 4 days incubation, cultures of the blood cultures grew anaerobic gram-negative rods, which were identified as Capnocytophaga canimorsus.

The patient slowly improved over the next 10 days, with gradual resolution of the purpuric rash and improvement of organ function. Peripheral cyanosis and dry necrosis of his upper and lower extremities were monitored for potential amputation.
The initial antibiotic regimen was narrowed to ceftriaxone after the gram-negative rod was isolated from blood cultures. The patient improved clinically and was discharged to a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation and wound care. He remained on hemodialysis at the time of discharge.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 4 million dog bites occur annually in the United States. Of these, 300,000 people seek care in the emergency room, and there are 13,000 hospitalizations and 20 deaths annually. A study of wound culture data from patients seeking care in the emergency room found that both dog and cat bites were often polymicrobial, with both aerobic and anaerobic organisms recovered from cultures. Pasteurella species are most commonly found in wound cultures, followed by streptococci, staphylococci, Moraxella, Corynebacterium and Neisseria species. The most frequently occurring anaerobic organisms cultured from these wounds include Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Porphyromonas, and Prevotella [Talan et al 1999].
Capnocytophaga canimorsus is a facultative, fastidious gram-negative bacillus found in the mouth flora of dogs, cats, and humans. Its name is derived from the Greek for carbon-dioxide loving (capnocytophaga) and dog bite (canimorsus).
C. canimorsus is often mistaken for other species of gram-negative bacilli. It may take days to identify this long, thin, slow-growing bacteria, and cultures may require at least 14 days incubation. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques are an option as well, though these are currently restricted to research laboratories.
Since this bacteria was first described in the literature more than 30 years ago, more than 100 cases of C. canimorsus infection have been described, with a mortality rate of about 30% [Lion et al 1996].
C. canimorsus infection occurs more frequently in males than females. Many patient are between age 50 to 70-years old. Risk factors include alcohol abuse, asplenia, immunosuppression, and corticosteroid treatment. However, in a case series of 56 patients in California, only 10% of patients with C. canimorsus sepsis were asplenic, and none had reported alcohol abuse in their medical charts [Janda et al. 2006]. In the same series, the median time from dog bite to onset of symptoms was 3 days. Eighty-five percent of patients presented with fever, while 32% had sepsis and 13% had disseminated intravascular coagulopathy or septic shock. C. canimorsus sepsis can present with rash, cellulitis, arthritis, gangrene, meningitis or endocarditis [Janda et al 2006].

title: 2010 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teen-aged girl pre
history:
2010 IDSA Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A teen-aged girl presented with anemia, fever and a rash.
A teen-aged Hispanic girl, with a 6-month history of anemia unresponsive to iron supplementation, developed intermittent fevers to 103°F (39.4°C) two months before presentation. Two weeks later, painful red lesions developed on her left arm and lateral thighs, associated with fatigue and weight loss of six pounds (2.7 kilograms).
She reported no history of cough, chest pain, night sweats, or abdominal symptoms.

She reported normal menses.

She had traveled to Mexico one year before presentation. She reported no previous hospitalizations or surgeries, no history of sexual activity and no alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use or exposure to sick contacts or animals.

The patient was taking oral iron supplementation.
exam_studies:
She appeared tired and slightly pale. The temperature was 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure 113/65 mm Hg, heart rate 137 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute. The lungs were clear, and there was a soft 1/6 systolic murmur. The spleen was palpable 3-centimeters below the left costal margin, without hepatomegaly. There were scattered petechiae on legs; painful, purpuric lesions on both upper thighs, and a fixed purpuric lesion on the left upper arm with a necrotic center. Skin findings are shown in Figures 1 through 3. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 4600/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000) with 36% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes and 2%basophils; hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (ref. 12.0 – 16.0); mean corpuscular volume 71.4 fl (ref. 78.0-100.0) and platelets 190,000/mm³ (ref. 150,000-450,000). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 109 mm/hr (ref 0-15) and C-reactive protein 3.4 mg/dL (ref. 0.0-1.0). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing (qualitative) for HIV nucleic acid was negative. C3 and C4 complement levels were normal. Testing for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-double stranded DNA antibodies were negative; results of rheumatoid factor and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic IgG antibodies (ANCA) were normal.
A punch biopsy of a skin lesion was performed. Pathological examination of the biopsy (Figures 4 and 5) demonstrated abundant thrombosed small and medium sized vessels with an infiltrate of neutrophils and minimal leukocytoclasis (karyorrhexis of leukocytes). The overlying epidermis showed ischemic changes with bulla formation. The findings were thought to show features of septic vasculitis.
Figure 4. Skin biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain.
Figure 5. Skin biopsy.

The patient was admitted for fever and presumptive cellulitis, and intravenous ceftriaxone and clindamycin were administered empirically. Blood cultures grew for gram-negative coccobacilli after eighty-one hours incubation; gram stain of the growth is shown in Figure 6. During the next two days, the patient continued to be febrile and additional blood cultures remained positive.
Figure 6. Gram stain of growth from blood culture.
diagnosis:
Brucellosis caused by Brucella melitensis, with vasculitic purpura.

Gram stain of the skin punch biopsy specimen (Figure 5) revealed rare gram-variable coccobacilli in the region of thrombosed vessels. The organism growing in the blood cultures was identified as Brucella melitensis (Figure 6). Testing for serum antibodies for Brucella revealed an IgM level of 4.92 and IgG 1.43 (reference range <0.8 negative, and greater than or equal to 1.10, antibody detected).

Upon further questioning, the patient revealed consumption of “queso blanco” (unpasteurized fresh cheese) as well as other locally prepared dairy and meat products while in Mexico. The patient received intravenous doxycycline and gentamicin for one week. After 72 hours on this therapy, the fevers resolved. At discharge, oral doxycycline and rifampin were begun, for a total of 6 weeks of antimicrobial therapy. At the completion of therapy, her symptoms, skin findings, and anemia had resolved.

The patient’s findings of fever, petechiae, purpura, and elevated inflammatory markers suggest a vasculitis, which was confirmed on histopathologic examination of the skin biopsy.
The clinical findings may be suggestive of infection with Rickettsia rickettsii, which causes a disseminated vasculitis. In cases of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever the petechial rash classically begins in the distal extremities, involves the palms and soles, spreads centrally, and can coalesce into purpura [Weber and Walker 1991]. Streptobacillis moniliformis which is the causative agent of rat-bite fever, may have clinical findings similar to Rickettsia rickettsii, including rash involving the palms and soles; arthralgia and arthritis are more prominent findings [Cunningham et al. 1998]. Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative rod that can cause extra-intestinal manifestations including a leukocytoclastic vasculitis as a complication in patients with iron-overload syndromes [Tak et al. 1992]. Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, is a fastidious gram negative rod, that can cause endocarditis, soft tissue infection, and central nervous system infection [Kaplan et al. 1989].
In the United States, Brucella is most commonly transmitted through the consumption of unpasteurized milk products [Wyatt 2005; Pappas et al. 2005]. Less than 100 cases per year are reported to the CDC [Cook et al. 2002]. The states with the highest incidence in the United States include Texas, California, and Florida. It is more prevalent in the Mediterranean basin, Arabian peninsula, Indian subcontinent, and Latin America [Doyle and Bryan 2000; Pappas et al. 2006; Hasanjani et al. 2004].
Patients present with fever, fatigue and malaise, weight loss, arthralgias, and splenomegaly. In children, a monoarticular arthritis is a common presentation, while in adults sacroiliitis or vertebral osteomyelitis are more frequently seen [al-Eissa et al. 1990]. Skin findings have been described rarely in brucellosis (6-12%) most commonly as either (1) disseminated papulonodular eruptions, (2) erythema nodosum-like lesions, (3) purpura, and (4) maculopapular eruptions. Other case reports of brucellosis have described a panniculitis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome [Ariza et al. 1989; Perez et al. 1999; Tanyel et al. 2008; Metin et al. 2001; Berger et al. 1981; Milionis et al. 2000]. Our patient’s findings likely represent hematogenous spread of the bacterium.

title: A pre-teen girl developed abdominal pain and vomiting.
history:
A pre-teen girl was well until 2 days before presentation when abdominal pain and vomiting developed. The pain was initially located in the left lower quadrant, and migrated to involve the entire lower abdomen, associated with nausea. On the day of presentation, more than twenty episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis occurred. She did not have fever or diarrhea.

Menarche had occurred one year before presentation; her last menstrual period was one month earlier. She had no history of previous recurrent abdominal pain or menstrual irregularities.

She was born in Mexico, and immigrated to the United States two years before. There was no history of animal exposure and she was not sexually active.
exam_studies:
The pulse was 100 beats per minute and blood pressure 110/64 mm Hg; the temperature was normal. The abdomen was tender to palpation, with rebound, in the right lower quadrant, and obturator and psoas signs were positive.

The white blood cell count was 19,000 per cubic millimeter with 90% neutrophils. The basic metabolic panel was normal. Urinalysis was negative for white cells, leukocyte esterase and nitrites. A urine pregnancy test was also negative. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed an enlarged appendix with hyperemic mucosa, with surrounding periappendiceal inflammatory stranding, that was thought to be consistent with acute appendicitis. A calcified mesenteric lymph node was also noted.

The patient was taken to the operating room for a laparoscopic appendectomy. Intra-operative findings included acute appendicitis, bilaterally enlarged fallopian tubes (left greater than right), adhesions from the omentum to the anterior abdominal wall, adhesions from the anterior surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and yellow plaques on the liver surface. The Gynecology service was consulted to perform an intra-operative examination, which revealed a dilated, hyperemic appearance of the fallopian tubes, with fluid within the tubes appearing slightly purulent. Pelvic examination revealed copious yellow vaginal discharge, a nulliparous cervix, and a fimbriated hymen with no evidence of trauma. Cervical specimens were sent for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and cultures.
An endometrial curettage and biopsy were performed. Pathological examination of the tissue is shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Endometrial biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain (600 x magnification).
Figure 2. Endometrial biopsy with acid-fast stain (1000 x magnification).
diagnosis:
Abdominal and pelvic infection caused by Mycobacterium bovis.

Pathological examination of endometrial tissue revealed a proliferative phase endometrium; Figure 1 shows granulomatous inflammation, H&E stain, at 600 x magnification and Figure 2, with acid fast stain, demonstrates rare acid-fast bacilli at 1000 x magnification.
Cultures of the endometrium grew acid-fast bacilli, identified as Mycobacterium bovis by multiplex, real-time PCR assay. Testing for N. gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia NAAT was negative.
Antibiotic susceptibility testing of the Mycobacterium bovis showed sensitivity to isoniazid, rifampin and ethambutol and resistance to pyrazinamide.
The patient improved following surgery and the abdominal pain and emesis resolved. A skin test for tuberculosis (PPD) was positive at greater than 25 mm induration at 40 hours. A Quantiferon-Gold test was also positive. A chest radiograph showed no evidence of past or active pulmonary tuberculosis.
Additional history, obtained from the patient and family, revealed that there was no significant exposure to persons with known Mycobacterium tuberculosis disease. In Mexico, the family had a history of consumption of fresh unpasteurized cheese (queso fresco).

The patient was started on isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. After susceptibilities were known, isoniazid and rifampin were continued to complete one year of treatment. Throughout follow-up visits, the patient continued to do well. Follow-up laparoscopy two months after the end of therapy showed normal fallopian tubes and ovaries with minimal adhesions seen in the pelvis. The intraabdominal adhesions had resolved, however, a few plaques on the liver persisted.

Mycobacterium bovis is one of the seven species in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (Ernst et al. 2007). Tuberculosis due to M. bovis is a zoonosis, as it primarily infects cattle, which can transmit the pathogen to humans through consumption of unpasteurized, contaminated dairy products (CDC 2005).
In industrialized nations like the United States, tuberculosis caused by M. bovis is rare because of pasteurization of milk and testing and culling of infected cattle (Hlavsa et al. 2008). M. bovis is a major public health issue in developing countries, however the true burden of disease is likely underestimated due to shortage of laboratory capabilities to isolate and differentiate members of the tuberculosis complex (Cosivi et al. 1998).
Tuberculosis caused by M. bovis and tuberculosis caused by M. tuberculosis cannot be distinguished clinically, radiographically or pathologically and thus further laboratory diagnosis is required for identification. Pyrazinamide susceptibility can be used to screen for M. bovis as it is inherently resistant; however, M. tuberculosis with resistance to pyrazinamide alone has also been described (Am. Thor. Society et al. 2003).
While abdominal tuberculosis caused by M. bovis is a well-described extrapulmonary manifestation of infection, cases of pelvic tuberculosis due to M. bovis may be missed because of lack of laboratory resources for speciation. Pelvic tuberculosis is an important cause of infertility in the developing world because it causes tubal blockage, peritubal, pelvic and abdominal adhesions and atrophy of the endometrium. The prognosis for fertility is reported to be poor in women with genital tuberculosis due to intrauterine adhesions and blockage of fallopian tubes (Sharma et al. 2009, Sharma et al. 2008, Varma 1991).
A careful exposure history, including inquiry about the consumption of unpasteurized milk products, eventually led to the ultimate diagnosis. Rapid identification of M. bovis was essential given its intrinsic resistance to pyrazinamide so that therapy could be tailored appropriately.

title: A teenager presented with increasing anorexia, weight loss, cough and headache.
history:
A teenaged boy was seen in an Emergency Department because of progressively increasing anorexia, fatigue and 43-pound weight loss (19.5 kilograms) during the previous 2 months. Two weeks before presentation, cough, post-tussive emesis, headache, and drenching night sweats developed, without documented fevers. He had occasionally taken acetaminophen for the symptoms.
During the previous week, discomfort occurred in the region of the lower ribs, posteriorly, on the left. His family noted that he was more pale and spent most of his time lying in bed. He had one episode of self-resolving epistaxis, and reported no dyspnea, phlegm production, or urinary or gastrointestinal complaints.

At age 2, a peri-rectal abscess occurred, which healed appropriately after drainage and antibiotics. He also had mild, intermittent asthma.

He was Asian-American, lived in a large, multi-generational household, and attended high school in California. He reported no sexual activity or intravenous drug use. Approximately five months before presentation, he traveled to urban and rural Vietnam for 3 weeks. His younger brother had anemia of unclear etiology for which he took iron supplements. Relatives with whom he lived had recently had respiratory illnesses.

Medications included acetaminophen every 1-2 days during this illness, and albuterol as needed.
exam_studies:
On examination, he appeared pale and fatigued, lying in bed. The weight was 57 kg (124.4 pounds), temperature 102.5°F (39.2°C), the blood pressure was 115/77 mm Hg, pulse 122 beats per minute, respirations 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing room-air. There were occasional end-expiratory wheezes, moderate tenderness in the abdomen with deep palpation on the left laterally, without hepatosplenomegaly, and mildly tender inferior, posterior ribs on the left; the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 12,500/mm³ (reference range 5,000-10,000) with 83% neutrophils, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, and platelets 505,000/mm³ (ref. 145,000-400,000). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 62 mm/hr (ref. 0-10), and the C–reactive protein (CRP) 8.4 mg/dl (ref. 0 - 0.9 mg/dl), total protein 10 gm/dL (ref. 6.0-8.0), and the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 1027 U/L (ref. 313-618). Other routine laboratory tests and a chest radiograph were normal.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen revealed a 6-7 cm heterogeneous mass in the upper pole of the left kidney, which did not appear calcified (Figure 1). The renal mass was associated with infiltrative changes in the surrounding fat and lymphadenopathy, and there was thickening of the diaphragm and spleen (Figure 2). A small, discrete lesion in the lower pole of the left kidney was also noted (Figure 3). Additionally, multiple pleural-based densities were detected.
Figure 1. CT of the chest and abdomen.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection.

A tuberculin-skin test, testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and cultures of the blood and urine were negative; results of a urinalysis were not available. A percutaneous, ultrasound-guided biopsy of the left kidney mass was performed. Pathological examination of the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of the specimens revealed inflammatory cells characteristic of acute and chronic pyelonephritis, including infiltration of lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages throughout the renal parenchyma, including the glomerulus (Figure 3) and renal tubule (Figure 4), consistent with a diagnosis of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Culture from renal tissue grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
Figure 3. Renal biopsy, H and E stain (x400 magnification).
Figure 4. Renal biopsy, H and E stain (x400 magnification).

After the pathology and culture results from the renal biopsy were known, vancomycin was started intravenously, with prompt defervescence and constitutional improvement. An inpatient voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) was unsuccessful as the introduction of the catheter was met with resistance and bleeding. After the fifth day of vancomycin therapy, ciprofloxacin, to which the organism was also sensitive, was administered for an additional 12 days intravenously. He was then discharged, and completed a total 6-week course of antibiotics with oral ciprofloxacin. Serial ultrasonographic examinations of the abdomen demonstrated gradual resolution of the pyelonephritis and decreasing size of his left kidney. At follow-up 1 month after completing his antibiotic course, he had regained 20 pounds (9.1 kilograms) and was asymptomatic.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XPN) is a rare and poorly understood progressive, inflammatory disease of the kidney. Mainly seen in adult females over the age of 40, the condition has been described in children as young as 21 days-old, and recently has been increasingly reported in the pediatric population; a review from 2009 stated that there had been about 240 childhood cases reported in the literature [Gupta et al 2009]. Considered to be a morphological and clinical variant of chronic pyelonephritis, the hallmark pathological feature of XPN is diffuse renal parenchymal destruction and replacement with lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells).
Genitourinary (GU) tract obstruction - particularly by urolithiasis - along with urinary tract infection, are the 2 most common predisposing factors associated with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Older pediatric reviews found 75% of XPN cases to be associated with calculi, but obstruction may also be due to congenital anomalies, tumors, and of a functional nature; in this case, though no obvious GU abnormalities or stones were detected, it may be noteworthy that the patient’s VCUG proved unsuccessful due to an inability to fully insert the catheter. Other risk factors for XPN, including diabetes, malnutrition, abnormal lipid metabolism, and immunologic disturbances, have been postulated but remain uncertain [Brown et al 1995]. The clinical features of XPN are inconsistent and generally non-specific, with two-thirds of cases having malaise, anorexia, fever, flank pain, or weight loss [Levy et al 1994]. Symptoms related to the urinary system, such as dysuria or hematuria, are infrequent. The duration of illness prior to diagnosis is often subacute to chronic, with 80% of patients being ill for greater than 1 month, and 40% for greater than 6 months. [Brown et al 1994]. Loin tenderness is a common physical exam finding, and occasionally a mass may be palpable. Anemia, leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and pyuria are common laboratory findings - but renal parameters are usually normal. Urine cultures may be positive in 50-70% of presentations; nevertheless, cases in which tissue culture is positive while the urine is found to be sterile are reported. Escherichia coli and Proteus species - often associated with staghorn calculi - form the bulk of recovered isolates, with other gram-negative pathogens and staphylococcal species also rarely being identified [Al-Hwiesh 2007]. Radiological imaging findings are variable, and may include an enlarged kidney with an expanding mass, raising concern for an oncologic etiology or tuberculosis. The diagnosis of XPN ultimately relies on renal biopsy: grossly the kidney is enlarged, with streaky, yellow granulomas and a thickened capsule, while microscopic histopathology demonstrates the defining dense infiltrate of foamy macrophages replacing normal parenchyma. Historically, XPN has been managed by total or partial nephrectomy, which is considered to be curative [Grainger et al 1982]. However, with the increasing availability of highly-sensitive radiologic techniques, and potential for percutaneous biopsy and non-operative diagnosis, some authors have advocated for attempts at medical management prior to approaching surgical resection in certain cases. For example, Brown et al. describe their experience with a 27-months-old boy, with focal upper pole XPN in an otherwise well-functioning kidney, who demonstrated excellent clinical and radiological response after 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotics [Brown et al. 1996]. Similarly, a number of other pediatric case reports support that a course of parenteral followed by oral antibiotics may be successful in cases of focal XPN [Gupta et al. 2009].

title: 2011 March-April Featured Case and IDSA 2010 Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Present
history:
2011 March-April Featured Case and IDSA 2010 Pediatric Fellows' Day Case Presentation Summary: A toddler presented with intermittent fevers and abdominal pain.
A toddler had been well until approximately 8 months before presentation, when episodes of abdominal pain developed. Initially, the abdominal pain was generalized and occurred two or three times per week, without exacerbating or alleviating factors, and unrelated to food intake. His appetite remained normal and there was no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Approximately two months after the onset of abdominal pain, gradually increasing abdominal distention developed, associated with fever to 40°C (104°F) daily. His weight decreased by 1.4 kg during the 2.5 months before admission. Shortly before admission, multiple temperature spikes occurred daily. There was no blood in stool, change in stool color, jaundice or icterus.

Approximately one year before presentation, an episode of cervical lymphadenitis (posterior and deep, bilaterally) occurred, which resolved completely after the administration of oral antibiotics.

The patient was born in the American Southwest and lived near a desert, with no history of travel outside of that area. The household included three pets: a dog, cat of unknown age, and bird. There was no history of bites or scratches. He had not consumed unpasteurized dairy products and had no known history of exposure to tuberculosis.

There was a possible but unconfirmed history of ulcerative colitis in the family, and no known history of celiac disease.
exam_studies:
He appeared well, except for diffuse pallor and abdominal distention. The blood pressure was 113/75 mm Hg, pulse 140 beats per minute, temperature 36.4°C (97.5°F), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. There was shotty lymphadenopathy in the anterior cervical and inguinal regions. The abdomen was distended with normal bowel sounds and shifting dullness, and without tympany or tenderness. The liver edge was palpated 2-3 cm below right costal margin, without other masses noted.

The total leukocyte count was 12,900/uL (reference range (ref.) 6000-17,000, adjusted for the patient's age), with 48% neutrophils, 31% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, and 12% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 1548/uL, ref. 0-700/uL), hematocrit 26% (ref. 34-40), platelet count 638,000/uL (ref. 150,000-400,000/ul), with a mean corpuscular volume of 61 fL (ref. 75-87), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/hour (ref. 0-9) and the C-reactive protein was 14.4 mg/dL (ref. <0.8). The serum level of protein was 7.5 g/dL (ref. 5.9-7.0). Serum levels of uric acid and lactate dehydrogenase, and the remainder of a comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. The serum level of iron was 11 ug/dL (ref. 50-120), iron binding (IBC) 244 ug/dL (ref. 261-462); iron saturation 5% (ref. 20-50), and ferritin 206 ng/mL (ref. 7-140). The level of immunoglobulin (Ig) E was 66 IU/ml (ref. 0-12), IgG 2463 IU/ml (ref. 423-1090), IgA at 616 IU/ml (ref. 56-343), and IgM 144 mg/dL (ref range 43-163).
Urinalysis revealed 1+ protein, and was negative for nitrites, leukocyte esterase, with one white cell per high-power field, and no bacteria. The stool was negative for occult blood, ova and parasites, and Clostridium difficile toxin.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis showed marked ascites; all intraabdominal organs appeared normal (Figure 1). Doppler ultrasonography of the liver was normal.
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen.

During the hospitalization, the patient continued to appear well, but spiked fevers daily. Multiple cultures of the blood were sterile.
A repeat CT scan demonstrated worsening ascites; endoscopy of the upper GI tract was normal. Paracentesis was performed; analysis of the peritoneal fluid revealed a white blood cell count of 4175/ul. Romanowsky staining (Diff-Quik type) of the peritoneal fluid is shown in Figure 2. Peritoneal fluid culture grew Burkholderia species.
The degree of distention on examination decreased after paracentesis, and then gradually increased with reaccumulation of fluid, without tenderness.
Figure 2. Peritoneal fluid, Romanowsky stain.
diagnosis:
Burkholderia sp. peritonitis as the initial presentation of classic X-linked chronic granulomatous disease.

A neutrophil oxidative burst assay showed no detectable increase in stimulated granulocyte dihydrorhodamine fluorescence; the findings most closely resembled the “Classic X-linked” histogram shown in Bender et al. 2009. Light microscopy examination of the peritoneal fluid (Figure 2) showed marked chronic lymphocytic inflammation and moderate acute (neutrophilic) inflammation. Cytopathologic examination of the peritoneal fluid also showed marked chronic lymphocytic inflammation and moderate acute (neutrophilic) inflammation, with no evidence of erythrophagocytosis.
Genetic testing revealed a homozygous mutation in exon 7 of the gp91-phox gene, at position c.703_704delAG, p.S235fsX239. This mutation, noted 3 times in the cytochrome b-245, beta polypeptide (CYBB) database, causes a premature stop codon in the amino-terminal domain of the gp91-phox beta polypeptide subunit of cytochrome b-245 (also known as cytochrome b-558), a component of the membrane-bound phagocytic NADPH oxidase (phox) enzyme complex [Heyworth et al 2010, Piirilä et al. 2006].

A neutrophil oxidative burst assay performed on the patient’s mother in the outpatient immunology clinic confirmed the diagnosis of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (CGD).
Meropenem (intravenously, for three weeks) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were administered (mostly orally) for 3 weeks for Burkholderia sp. peritonitis. In addition, recombinant interferon gamma therapy was administered three times weekly, and continued indefinitely. After completion of treatment for Burkholderia, he continued to receive prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole.

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare inherited disorder of phagocytes. Due to a defect in the generation of microbial oxygen metabolites, neutrophils and monocytes are able to ingest but unable to effectively kill some organisms. Affected patients usually present early in life with recurrent and/or unusual infections, often involving catalase-positive organisms, such as Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Burkholderia cepacia, Aspergillus, and Nocardia.
Burkholderia species are gram-negative bacilli, catalase-producing and non-glucose fermenting organisms. They are commonly found in the soil and water. The genus Burkholderia was proposed in 1992 for 7 species which were previously in Pseudomonas homology group II [Burns 2008].
Burkholderia cepacia rarely causes disease in immunocompetent hosts, but organisms in the B. cepacia complex and B. gladioli can cause severe pulmonary disease in cystic fibrosis patients and fatal bacteremia in CGD patients. 16s sequencing-based identification of the organism from our patient identified it as very closely related to B. gladioli. The unexpected isolation of Burkholderia sp. led to testing for CGD. Infection due to Burkholderia spp. (in addition to other atypical infections) should prompt an evaluation for underlying immunodeficiency, including a neutrophil oxidative burst assay.
The majority (65%) of patients with CGD are males who demonstrate X-linked inheritance of large mutations in the gp91-phox gene [Vowells et al. 1996, Dinauer et al. 1987, Segal 1987, Teahan et al. 1987]. The next most common pattern is due to autosomal recessive inheritance of mutations in the gp22-phox gene. Both result in a severe phenotype. More recently, patients with a milder phenotype of CGD with partial oxidative burst activity have been recognized. These are inherited by autosomal recessive and variant X-linked mechanisms. These patients may present at an older age [Nunoi et al. 1988, Dinauer et al. 1990, Volpp et al. 1998, Bender et al. 2009].
Historically, the diagnostic test for CGD was the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye test; however, it has been replaced with the flow cytometry test using dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) because of superior sensitivity and specificity. DHR fluoresces when it is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide; therefore, in the absence of an oxidative burst, as in X-linked CGD, no increased fluorescence will be detected. Patients with partial oxidative burst activity (more commonly associated with autosomal recessive CGD) may have stimulation index values that are intermediate between normal and abnormal values and careful review of the flow cytometry histograms is needed to interpret the findings accurately. Newer molecular diagnostics looking specifically at the most common gene mutations are also now available [Bender et al. 2009, Hill et al. 2010].

history:
2011 May-June Featured Case Summary: A man with pain in the right leg.
A man in his forties was admitted to the hospital because of pain and swelling in the right leg.
Approximately 2 months before admission, a sharp pain developed in his right leg, which he initially attributed to a muscle strain. During the next 2-3 weeks, the pain increased in severity, followed by swelling of the right lower leg and ankle. The pain was localized, non-radiating, and eventually disturbed his sleep and gait.
Approximately four weeks before admission, he went to the emergency department of another hospital; a radiograph of the right lower leg was performed, which was thought to show a lytic lesion of the distal tibia. He was referred to an orthopedist, and two weeks later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed with the administration of gadolinium, showed a tibial lesion with no changes in the cortex or evidence of fracture; the study was thought to be possibly consistent with a cyst. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen-oxycodone were administered as needed for pain, without improvement. He was referred to another orthopedist at a tertiary medical center for further evaluation, and seen 12 days later.
He reported weight loss of 5 pounds (2.2 kg) during the previous 5 months, without history of trauma, fevers, chills, gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, or other systemic symptoms.

He had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. Five months before presentation, approximately 3 months before the onset of pain, he had had dental surgery, including treatment of dental caries and a root canal. He did not take any antibiotics and had not noted any complications. Several years before, he had had a partial nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma and had been disease-free thereafter. Ten years before, cervical spine surgery for disc herniation was performed.
He had no drug allergies.

He worked in a medical facility. He had traveled to California 4 years before and Mexico decades earlier. He owned a pet cockatiel.

He was married, lived with his wife and children. He drank alcohol in moderation, had smoked cigarettes until several months before admission, and did not use illicit drugs.

His paternal grandfather and mother had diabetes mellitus.

Medications included simvastatin and metoprolol, as well as ibuprofen and acetaminophen-oxycodone as needed for pain.
exam_studies:
On examination, the body mass index was 30.1 kg/m²; the right leg was swollen below the knee, with firm and slightly erythematous skin, and warm, pitting edema locally. The distal portion of the right tibia was tender to deep palpation. Passive rotation of the hips, hip flexor and quadriceps muscle strength, sensation and neurovascular tone, as well as the remainder of the examination, were normal.

The white cell count was 9300 cells/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000), with 67% neutrophils, 25% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 1% eosinophils and 1% basophils. The hematocrit was 38.6% (ref. 41.0-53.0, in men), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 25 mm per hour (ref 0-11). The serum level of glucose was 297 mg/dl (ref. 70-110) and C-reactive protein (CRP) 19.8 mg/L (ref. less than 8.0); other tests including electrolytes, total protein, albumin, and globulin and tests of renal and liver function, were normal.
Radiographs of the right lower leg, shown in Figures 1 and 2, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the tibia (Figure 3) were reviewed.
Figure 1. Radiograph of lower leg.
Figure 2. Radiograph of the lower leg.
Figure 3. MRI of the tibia, T2-weighted.

Two days later, the patient was admitted to the hospital. The blood pressure was 152/92 mm Hg; other vital signs were normal and the examination was unchanged. An open distal tibia biopsy with irrigation and drainage was performed. Purulent material (approximately 30cc) was aspirated after entering the bone; gram stain of the specimen is shown in Figure 4 (image courtesy of JiYeon Kim, MD). Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen demonstrated features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis.
Figure 4. Gram stain of the specimen.
diagnosis:
Osteomyelitis of the tibia caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Heidelberg in a patient with newly-diagnosed diabetes mellitus.

Gram stain of the specimen demonstrated abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and rare gram-negative rods (Figure 4). Culture of the specimen grew moderate-to-abundant gray, glistening colonies on blood agar and translucent, lactose-negative colonies on MacConkey agar (Figures 5 and 6 respectively), which were identified as Salmonella group B that was susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. No other organisms (including mycobacteria, fungi, or other bacteria) were isolated by stain or culture. The organism was later determined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to be serotype S. Heidelberg.
Urinalysis demonstrated 2+ glucose and was otherwise normal. The organism was not recovered from cultures of the blood, urine or stool. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus was negative.
Figure 5. Culture of the specimen on blood agar plate.
Figure 6. Culture of the specimen on MacConkey agar plate.

The Salmonella organism isolated was susceptible to quinolones and nalidixic acid. The patient was initially treated with broad spectrum antimicrobials; when the organism was identified, ceftriaxone was administered intravenously, followed by oral ciprofloxacin on discharge.
The source of the Salmonella infection was not determined.
While hospitalized, a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus was made. The level of hemoglobin A1c was 10.50% (ref 3.80-6.40). Insulin was administered, followed by metformin, in addition to an American Diabetes Association (ADA) diet.
One month later, he was pain-free, and able to bear weight while wearing a bivalve cast when walking. The ESR was 11 mm/hr and CRP 2.1 mg/L. A course of ciprofloxacin of least 3 months' duration was planned.

A diagnosis of osteomyelitis of the distal tibia was strongly considered in this patient with a sub-acute clinical presentation that included localized pain and swelling of the distal leg, laboratory testing with elevation of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (suggestive of inflammation), and plain radiographs and MRI with gadolinium that revealed a localized lesion with T2-weighted enhancement. The diagnosis was confirmed, and metastatic carcinoma excluded, by pathological and microbiological examination of tissue obtained by surgical aspiration and debridement of the tibia; the bone culture grew Salmonella enterica serotype Heidelberg. Following the identification, antimicrobial treatment was guided by results of susceptibility testing of the organism.
Staphylococcus species, particularly S. aureus and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, cause greater than 50% of cases of osteomyelitis. However, the gram stain of this patient's aspirate did not demonstrate gram-positive cocci but, rather, showed gram-negative bacilli. Gram-negative causes of osteomyelitis include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, and Serratia, and acid-fast bacilli such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis (which may be gram-variable). Salmonella subspecies, also gram-negative bacilli, are identified in less than 5% of osteomyelitis cases [Berbari et al. 2009], except in the subset of patients with sickle cell disease, in whom Salmonella, with Staphylococcus, is one of the two most frequent causes of osteomyelitis [Burnett et al. 1998].
The clinical presentation of osteomyelitis and mechanism of infection may vary significantly among patients. This patient’s history did not implicate local penetrating trauma and there was no hardware in the affected bone to serve as a nidus for bacteria, nor was the patient’s sub-acute course and examination (with deep symptomatic discomfort preceding the appearance of superficial erythema) suggestive of contiguous spread of infection. The most likely mechanism of infection was thought to be hematogenous seeding; however, the exact source of this patient’s organism, Salmonella Heidelberg, remained unclear. Exposures to contaminated food, an unrecognized gastrointestinal illness or exposure to an infected bird are possible source considerations. At the time of his infection, contamination of peanut butter with Salmonella had recently been identified, but S. Heidelberg was not the subspecies implicated. S. Heidelberg has been cultured from multiple food sources including chickens and turkeys [Hoelzer et al. 2011] and swine [Han et al 2011] and these could have been potential sources of the infection. Several bird populations, including pet birds such as parakeets and cockatoos, have been shown to harbor Salmonella (infected birds may be asymptomatic or may have lethal disease) [Hoelzer et al. 2011]. Of the Salmonella subspecies, S. Heidelberg has been shown to cause more invasive disease than some of the others [Jones et al. 2008].
Osteomyelitis occurs more commonly in patients who are immunocompromised. The contributing or predisposing illnesses that cause osteomyelitis may be systemic - including (but not limited to) malignancy, renal or hepatic failure, pediatric or geriatric ages or diabetes mellitus - or factors that lead to decreased local immunity such as radiation fibrosis, scarring, lymphedema, hypoxia or vascular compromise. Most cases of diabetes-related osteomyelitis affect the foot, and are associated with small vessel disease and diabetic neuropathy. Salmonella osteomyelitis of a long bone has been reported as the presenting illness of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus [Gondusky et al. 2009], as seen in this case.

history:
2011 July-August Featured Case Summary: A pregnant woman with HIV infection and new onset of fever, decreased hearing and painful lesions in the left ear.
An HIV-positive woman in her forties, at 29 weeks' gestation, developed fever and malaise. Two days later, approximately 5 days before presentation, tinnitus and decreased hearing occurred, associated with a sense of ear fullness, and painful pustular lesions in her left ear developed. One week after the onset, she saw a physician because of increasing symptoms. She reported diarrhea, headache, rhinorrhea and cough, and a burning sensation on her left cheek and ear of two-days' duration.

She was HIV-positive; 41 days earlier, the CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 478 cells per cubic millimeter, with an undetectable level of HIV RNA. She had received pre-natal care during this pregnancy. She was multigravida, and had had postpartum hemorrhage, for which she had received blood transfusions. She also had peptic ulcer disease, sickle cell trait, anemia and a history of depression. She had received treatment for tuberculosis 10 years before and had had chickenpox in childhood.

The patient was from sub-Saharan Africa, but had not returned in many years. She did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

She was allergic to aspirin and latex.

Medications included lopinavir-ritonavir combination, lamivudine-zidovudine combination, iron, and calcium.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.5°F (36.9°C), blood pressure 103/75 mm Hg and pulse 108 beats per minute. Physical findings involving the left ear are shown in Figures 1 and 2. The tympanic membrane (TM) was intact, with fluid noted behind the TM. Weber lateralized to the left; Rinne testing was normal. Hearing was slightly decreased in the left ear subjectively; facial function and sensation was normal and other cranial nerves II through XII were normal; taste was not tested. There was dried blood on the anterior septum on the left side, moderate bilateral mucosal congestion, and crust on the posterior pharyngeal wall. There was tender lymphadenopathy in the cervical and submandibular areas on the left (less than 1 cm in diameter). Faint basilar crackles were present on the right, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The hematocrit was 31.1% (reference range 36.0-46.0 in non-pregnant women) and the total white cell count was 3600 per cubic millimeter (ref 4500-11,000) with 51% neutrophils, 1% band forms, 34% lymphocytes, 2% atypical lymphocytes, and 12% monocytes. The level of serum sodium was 131 mmol/L (ref 135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (ref 3.4-4.8), glucose 134 mg/dl (ref 70-110), total protein 8.5 gm/dl (ref 6.0-8.3), globulin 5.1 g/dl (ref 2.6-4.1), and urinalysis revealed 10-20 white cells per high-power field with squamous cells suggestive of a contaminated specimen; the remainder of the routine serologic laboratory test results was normal.

A chest radiograph showed no infiltrates. She was admitted to the hospital, cefepime was administered and antiretroviral medications continued.
diagnosis:
Herpes zoster oticus, with decreased hearing, also known as Ramsay-Hunt syndrome, caused by varicella zoster virus.

Examination of the left ear (Figure 1) revealed multiple raised vesicular lesions (approximately 3 mm in diameter) in the conchal bowl surrounding the external auditory canal meatus and extending into the lateral third of the canal, with a surrounding erythematous base that was tender, and multiple areas (1-2 mm diameter) of black colored debris. An audiogram demonstrated conductive and high frequency sensorineural hearing loss on the left.
Testing of a swab of a lesion with fluorescent antibodies to varicella zoster virus (VZV) was positive (Figure 3). Wound cultures of the ear grew few coagulase negative staphylococcus of 2 types; heterophile antibody screening, testing for syphilis, and cultures of the blood were negative.
Figure 3. VZV fluorescent antibody testing.

Acyclovir was administered intravenously, followed by oral valacyclovir at discharge, for a total course of 14 days; a 10-day tapering course of prednisone was also administered. Cefepime was stopped after cultures of the blood were sterile. A follow-up audiogram one week later was improved. At full-term 2 months later, the patient delivered a healthy infant. At follow-up 9 months after this ear infection, she reported diminished and sometimes unpleasant sense of smell, as well as an unpleasant taste on the left side of her tongue.

Patients who have varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection of the head and neck involving the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (VIIth cranial nerve), also known as Ramsay Hunt syndrome, may present with a vesicular rash affecting the external auditory canal and auricle, a facial nerve palsy and ear pain. In addition, other cranial nerves (CNs) may also be involved, including the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII, which runs in proximity to CN VII in the internal auditory canal), as well as the V, VI, IX, and X nerves [Goldani et al. 2009]. This patient developed painful vesicular lesions in her ear (herpes zoster oticus) in the region enervated by CN VII, with tinnitus and decreased hearing (enervated by CN VIII). During follow-up, she reported an altered sense of smell and taste; her persistent taste abnormalities were thought to be related to involvement of the facial nerve chorda tympani branch, which extends to the anterior tongue.
Varicella zoster virus, also known as herpes zoster virus (HZV) or human herpes virus type 3 (HHV-3), is known to recur in patients with decreased immune responses. This patient was immunocompromised by her pregnancy and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. In HIV-infected patients, severe complications of herpes zoster infection, such as ocular complications (including herpes zoster ophthalmicus and herpes retinitis) and infections of the central nervous system (myelitis) are more likely to occur in patients with less than 200 CD4 T-lymphocyte cells per cubic millimeter [Glesby et al. 1995]. However, in a review of 8 patients with HIV infection who specifically developed Ramsay Hunt syndrome, 4 of the 5 patients for whom the levels were available had CD4 T-lymphocyte levels that ranged between 336 to 560 cells per cubic millimeter, and all 5 patients had levels higher than 200 per cubic millimeter [Goldani et al. 2009].
Other entities, including organisms responsible for bacterial cellulitis, otitis externa and otitis media, should also be considered in patients presenting with erythema and swelling of the pinna, and an exudative or purulent discharge from the auditory canal. Similarly, a contact dermatitis can result in swollen and inflamed tissue with a weeping exudate. However, the vesicular lesions seen in this case were more suggestive of a herpetic cause, and the specific location within the concha of the ear, and concomitant tinnitus and hearing deficits, strongly suggested varicella zoster virus affecting the seventh and eighth cranial nerves. Cranial nerve palsies in the absence of the vesicular rash may be caused by other infections by Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, and Treponema pallidum, the cause of syphilis, but were not considered as likely in this case.

title: 2011 September-October Featured Case Summary: An HIV-positive man with a painful
history:
2011 September-October Featured Case Summary: An HIV-positive man with a painful rash of three weeks’ duration.
A man with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (In Infectious Diseases, some conditions, such as HIV, have such a profound influence on the differential diagnosis that they are generally included in the Chief Complaint in addition to the Past Medical History.) (HIV) infection developed a painful rash.
The patient had been in his usual state of health until three weeks (The duration of symptoms is often an important clue. For example, although many viral infections can cause rashes, it would be very unusual for them to persist for weeks.) before admission when an erythematous painful (Most rashes are not painful and this information limits the differential. Painful skin lesions are most classically associated with herpes viruses such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV), but these infections do not persist for weeks unless the patient is deeply immunosuppressed.) lesion developed on his arm. During the following weeks, skin lesions developed on his face, trunk, extremities, back and genitalia. He also developed headache, neck pain and photophobia (This combination of symptoms is descriptive of "meningismus", suggesting central nervous system involvement with inflammation of the meninges.). One week before presentation, lightheadedness and nausea (Nausea and meningismus could be a worrisome sign of increased intracranial pressure.) occurred.
He was brought to the emergency department for evaluation. He reported some joint discomfort, without focal joint swelling or erythema. He reported no diplopia, focal weakness, numbness, dysuria, urethral discharge, chest pain, dyspnea, cough, upper respiratory symptoms, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

He was diagnosed with HIV several years earlier. Two years before admission, the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (The CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is the most important variable in framing the differential diagnosis in the HIV-infected patient. Serious opportunistic infections are unusual until CD4+ cell counts drop below 200 per cubic millimeter, but more subtle signs, such as increased herpes lesions can be seen when the CD4+ count is higher.) was approximately 400 cells/mm³. He had never had a history of opportunistic infections or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) defining illnesses, and had never taken antiretroviral medications (For more than twenty years, the administration of antiretroviral drugs was only recommended for when CD4+ counts dropped below a set threshold - initially 200, and more recently 350 per cubic millimeter - in order to balance benefit with toxicity, but in 2012, the US Dept. of Health & Human Services amended its guidelines to suggest offering antiretrovirals to all HIV-infected people ready to commit to take medication regardless of CD4+ count. (http://aidsinfo.nih.gov/guidelines) This reflects decreasing toxicity of the drugs, increasing evidence for benefit of early therapy and accumulation of data showing the value of treatment in preventing transmission.).

He had not traveled outside of the country. He was sexually active with men and did not always practice safe sex (The details of the sexual history are important in assessing a patient's HIV risks, since there exist several orders of magnitude difference between very low HIV risk acts such as oral sex and very high risk acts like unprotected receptive anal intercourse.). He denied exposure to any animals or tick bites (Animal and insect exposure are essential elements of the history illnesses associated with a rash. The skin lesion depicted in this case would be consistent with an insect-borne rickettsial infection, but this patient has not had the relevant exposure.). He reported that he had not had any sick contacts.

He had no allergies.

Medications included an over-the-counter non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 140/88 mm Hg, pulse 109 per minute, respirations 18 per minute and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing ambient air. He appeared uncomfortable, lying flat in bed. There was evidence of white plaques on the oral mucosa, suggestive of thrush (Thrush is a candidal infection in the oral cavity that is often seen in people on steroid therapy, but may also be an early sign of immunodeficiency, such as in HIV disease.). There was neck pain with flexion (This is the physical finding to go along with his symptoms of meningismus.). The abdomen was tender in the right upper quadrant (Raising the question of liver or gallbladder inflammation.). Numerous infiltrated papules with variable amounts of scale were scattered over the face, arms, legs, and trunk (Figures 1 and 2). Many of the lesions had a central scale-crust, suggestive of prior pustular or vesicular appearance, or drainage, and several infiltrated papules on the palms (Although a large number of illnesses can cause rashes, only a handful typically involve the palms and soles, and this is a major diagnostic clue. Among bacterial infections, involvement of the palms and soles is classically associated with secondary syphilis, meningococcemia, disseminated gonorrhea, and Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever.) had a central hemorrhagic crust. A few lesions appeared acneiform (The varied character of the lesions is unusual for most rashes associated with infections but is common in secondary syphilis.). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding.
Figure 2. Physical finding.

The hematocrit was 34.2% (reference range 41.0-53.0 for men), white cell count 4500 cells/mm³ (ref 4500-11,000), with a normal differential (The differential provides the percentage and/or absolute cell counts for the components of the total white cell count - that is, the number of neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, etc. It often provides valuable clues to the diagnosis. Here the normal differential argues against severe acute bacterial infection, in which a higher neutrophil count or a higher percentage of band forms might be seen.), and the level of CD4+ T-lymphocytes was 247 (This is moderate immunosuppression, enough to increase risks of infection overall but not enough to be at high risk for severe opportunistic infection.) /mm³ (ref 348-1456). The serum sodium was 131 mmol/L (ref 135-145), alkaline phosphatase (Elevation of the alkaline phosphatase suggests cholestasis or an infiltrative process of the liver) 1030 U/L (ref 45-115), alanine aminotransferase 76 U/L (ref 10-55) and aspartate aminotransferase 75 U/L (ref 10-40). Levels of other electrolytes and calcium and tests of renal function and coagulation were normal.
A chest radiograph revealed slightly under-inflated lungs, and was otherwise normal, with no evidence of pneumonia. An electrocardiogram was normal.

During the first day, the temperature rose to 102.2°F (39.0°C). Acyclovir, morphine and intravenous fluids were administered. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head demonstrated mucosal thickening throughout the paranasal sinuses, symmetric prominence of the nasopharyngeal soft tissues and partial opacification of the mastoid air cells bilaterally, with prominent cervical lymph nodes. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed splenomegaly.
The level of HIV RNA by PCR was 245,000 copies per milliliter (This level of HIV RNA falls within a common range found in HIV-infected individuals not taking antiretrovirals. In acute HIV infection, a newly-infected person will typically have negative antibody tests, and the diagnosis needs to be made by testing directly for viral RNA.), and testing for viral hepatitis (types B and C) was negative.
A biopsy of a lesion was performed. Pathological examination of the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) staining, shown in Figures 3 and 4, revealed superficial and deep plasmacytic infiltrate. (Pathology images provided by Devon C. Gimbel, MD.)
Figure 3. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of skin biopsy.
Figure 4. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of skin biopsy.
diagnosis:
Secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum in a patient with HIV infection.

The serum rapid plasma reagin (The common screening tests for syphilis, the RPR and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test or VDRL, rely on the observation early in the 20th Century that people with syphilis developed antibodies against a component of beef heart extracts, eventually shown to be cardiolipin. The tests are still in wide use today since they are very sensitive, inexpensive, and well-validated.) (RPR) test was positive at a dilution of 1:256, and testing for anti-treponemal antibody (Positive RPR screening tests are usually confirmed by more specific testing for antibodies against the syphilis organism itself.) was also positive. Treponema pallidum immunohistochemical staining of a skin biopsy revealed spirochetes between keratinocytes within the epidermis (Figure 5). (Pathology image provided by Devon C. Gimbel, MD.)
Serum tests for Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1 and -2 were negative. Serologic testing was consistent with past VZV infection. Skin cultures (Superficial cultures of the skin will usually grow normal skin flora, which are often unrelated to the underlying infection.) also grew two types of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, in rare to moderate amounts. Blood cultures were sterile.
Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (This patient's CSF showed a slightly elevated number of lymphocytes: a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Most commonly seen in viral infections, it can also be seen in more subacute to chronic CNS infections such as syphilis and Lyme disease.) (CSF) obtained by lumbar puncture revealed 11 white cells/cubic millimeter (ref 0-5 cells), with 4% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes and 6% monocytes and 2 red cells per cubic millimeter in the 4th tube, with protein 26 mg/dl (ref 5-55) and glucose 49 mg/dl (ref 50-75). There were no organisms visible on gram stain. The CSF venereal disease research laboratory (A positive CSF VDRL test confirms the diagnosis of neurosyphilis since the test is very specific, but a negative test does not rule it out, since it has more limited sensitivity.) (VDRL) test was negative. Tests of the CSF for VZV, Cryptococcus, Borrelia burgdorferi and enterovirus were negative. Cultures of the CSF were negative, as was DNA amplification tests for HSV. Culture of a skin lesion for HSV and VZV was also negative.
Figure 5. Immunostain of biopsy, showing spirochetes.

Acyclovir (Acyclovir is an antiviral drug with activity against Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella Zoster Virus. Therapy is often instituted empirically when the question of central nervous system herpesvirus infection is raised, since early therapy can be life-saving.) was stopped after testing for HSV was negative. Intravenous penicillin G was administered for possible neurosyphilis. There was no evidence of retinal involvement by ophthalmological examination. Urine tests for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae nucleic acids were negative.
Elevation of the level of alkaline phosphatase was thought to be consistent with syphilitic hepatitis. The liver tests improved after treatment for syphilis.
Repeat clinical evaluation and serologic testing by RPR at months 1, 3, 6, and 12 post-treatment were planned, with a goal of a four-fold decrease in titers.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (Prophylactic antibiotics to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia, the most common AIDS-associated infection in the U.S., would usually be started when the CD4+ cell count fell below 200. With highly-active antiretroviral therapy, there is usually a sustained increase to normal levels of the CD4+ cell count, after which the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can be stopped.) and treatment with fluconazole (An antifungal of the azole class, inhibiting the synthesis of egosterol, an essential component of fungal, but not animal, cell membranes.) for thrush were begun. Follow-up for initiation of anti-retroviral medications was scheduled.

This case illustrates distinctive aspects of the presentation of secondary syphilis, including the protean nature of its rash. Though a maculopapular eruption is common in syphilis, macular, papular, psoriasiform, and pustular lesions, as in our case, are also reported [Chapel TA 1980]. The rash can involve any area of the body and most commonly begins with development of discrete macular lesions, evolving into red papules, sometimes progressing to pustules, known as pustular syphilids [Tramont 2010].
The patient also had headache and meningismus. Meningeal signs, including headache and neck stiffness, are seen in 8-40% of patients with secondary syphilis and can signal dissemination of spirochetes into the central nervous system [Merritt 1940]. Alternate manifestations of early neurosyphilis include ocular and auditory abnormalities, dysfunction of other cranial nerves, and stroke [CDC 2007]. Any of these findings in a patient with syphilis warrants a lumbar puncture for evaluation. The diagnosis of neurosyphilis can be challenging, especially in patients with HIV due to baseline CSF abnormalities [Ghanem, Moore et al. 2008], but can be divided into 'definitive' by positive CSF Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL), and 'probable' by elevated white blood cell count (greater or equal to 10 cells/mm³) or protein (greater or equal to 50 mg/dL) in the absence of a positive VDRL and an alternate diagnosis [Marra 2009]. In those with a negative CSF VDRL, a treponemal antibody test can be performed; this test has increased sensitivity (approaching 100%) but less specificity (approximately 40%) [Marra et al. 2004]. In this case, there was not enough CSF available to perform a specific treponemal test. Because of the severity of the patient's meningeal symptoms and signs, a decision was made to treat him with intravenous penicillin for possible neurosyphilis.
Finally, the patient's elevated liver function tests suggested the possibility of syphilitic hepatitis.
As noted above, repeat clinical evaluation and serologic testing by RPR extending through 12 months post-treatment were planned, with a goal of a four-fold decrease in titers to confirm successful treatment [Workowski and Berman 2006]. Failure to achieve a serologic response, which might be more common in HIV-positive patients [Ghanem et al. 2007], warrants repeat evaluation and possible re-treatment.
The presenting triad of fever, headache, and rash as seen in this case warrants rapid evaluation and empiric antibiotics while diagnostic evaluation is performed. The most worrisome causes are meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, and Toxic Shock Syndrome. In this case, lack of petechiae or diffuse erythematous macules, lack of a neutrophilic pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid, and relatively prolonged duration of symptoms made these diagnoses unlikely. Other infectious etiologies, including disseminated herpesvirus infections (HSV, VZV), Coxsackie virus infection, and disseminated cryptococcal disease were considered, and ruled out. Non-infectious etiologies, including adverse drug reaction and pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, remained in the differential until the diagnosis of secondary syphilis was confirmed.

history:
2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with HIV infection and new fever and hypoxia, after recent Pneumocystis infection.
A man in his fifties with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, and admission for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) four weeks before, developed fever and acute respiratory distress with hypoxia.
During the previous admission for PCP, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and a tapering course of corticosteroids were administered, with clinical improvement. He was then transferred to another facility.
Antiretroviral therapy was begun two weeks after the initiation of treatment for PCP and included raltegravir, etravirine, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir, which were chosen based on a genotype obtained several years earlier that revealed high-level nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) resistance. Eight days after the initiation of antiretrovirals, altered mental status and hypoxemia developed.
He was transferred to an intensive care unit (ICU), and methylprednisolone (one dose of 120 mg, intravenously) was administered; hypoxia and mental status improved. A diagnosis of immune reconstitution syndrome (IRIS) was made.
A second course of tapering corticosteroids was administered; however, respiratory distress and hypoxia recurred, for which the patient was intubated. Methylprednisolone (60 mg daily) was administered intravenously. The clinical course was complicated by pulmonary embolus and an ileus. Vancomycin and imipenem were administered for possible ventilator-associated pneumonia. During two weeks in the ICU, respiratory support was weaned to a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 40% and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to 5 cm H20. However, acute respiratory decompensation recurred, associated with temperatures to 38.5°C (101.3°F). Ventilatory support was increased (FiO2 70% and PEEP 10 cm H20).

A diagnosis of HIV infection had been made more than 15 years earlier. Antiretroviral therapy was administered intermittently thereafter, and high level resistance to NRTIs was documented (genotypic mutations included M184V, M41L, L210W, T215Y, M46L, L10F, L33F, A71V and T74P). Opportunistic infections included Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and oral candidiasis.
He also had a chronic psychiatric illness, hyperlipidemia and a history of alcohol abuse.

The patient was born in a city in the Pacific Northwest and lived alone, with an older cat. He had never traveled outside of the United States. He drank alcohol, had a 30 pack-year smoking history, and occasionally smoked marijuana. He had never used injection drugs.

He had no known drug allergies.

Medications included raltegravir, etravirine, ritonavir-boosted darunavir, TMP-SMX, corticosteroids, azithromycin, and risperdone.
exam_studies:
He appeared chronically ill, thin, and was markedly diaphoretic. He was intubated and sedated, on a respirator. The temperature was 38.5°C (101.3°F), blood pressure 90/63 mm Hg, and pulse 144 beats per minute. The oxygen saturation was 98% on FiO2 70% and PEEP 10 cm H20. Breath sounds were mechanical, and slightly coarse on the right. The pulse rate was regular, and heart sounds were without any murmurs, rubs or gallops. The legs were edematous, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

On admission, the CD4+ T-lymphocyte cell count was 22 cells/cubic millimeter and the level of HIV nucleic acid by PCR was 2.3 million copies/mL.

Bronchoscopic examination revealed white-tan plaques throughout the tracheal and bronchial tree, with some ulcerations (Figures 1 and 2, images courtesy of Dr. Sharon Peach). Endobronchial biopsies were obtained and bronchial alveolar lavage (BAL) performed. Specimens were sent for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast staining, as well as viral studies and galactomannan. Serologic specimens for viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus were obtained.
Acyclovir was administered intravenously for presumptive viral tracheobronchitis, and high level ventilatory support continued.
Figure 1. Bronchoscopic findings.
Figure 2. Bronchoscopic findings.
diagnosis:
Tracheobronchitis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Pathological examination of specimens from the endobronchial biopsy revealed mycetomas (Figures 3 and 4, images courtesy of Dr. Rodney Schmidt) and necrotic tissue with eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions (Figure 5, image courtesy of Dr. Rodney Schmidt), consistent with a necrotizing viral infection.
Cultures of both the endobronchial biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage grew Aspergillus fumigatus (Figure 6, image courtesy of Dr. Lindley Barbee). A galactomannan level obtained from the lavage fluid was 7.49 (normal < 0.499) The CMV shell vial culture was positive on day one, and the level of serum CMV nucleic acid was 14,000,000 copies/mL. Testing of the serum and BAL aspirate for VZV and HSV was negative, as were tests of the BAL aspirate for influenza and other respiratory viruses.
Figure 3. Histopathology of endobronchial biopsy showing mycetoma.
Figure 4. Histopathology showing hyphal elements.
Figure 5. Histopathology with cytoplasmic inclusions.
Figure 6. Fungal culture.

Ganciclovir and voriconazole were administered intravenously, and the acyclovir was stopped.
During the following two weeks, the patient’s fevers resolved and his respiratory status improved, as marked by a decrease in the ventilatory support requirement. Unfortunately, he developed cutaneous Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS), a pneumothorax complicated by cardiac arrest that required resuscitation, and lastly, gastrointestinal bleeding thought to be due to either KS or cytomegalovirus infection. In consultation with the family, he was transitioned to comfort measures and, nearly four months after his original admission, he expired.

Aspergillus tracheobronchitis occurs in less than 5% of all cases of invasive aspergillosis [Wu et al 2010]. It can manifest as either a bronchial obstruction from a pseuomembrane consisting of necrotic tissue, exudates and hyphal elements, or as discrete plaques in the trachea and bronchi [Clarke et al 1991, Denning et al 1991, Wu et al 2010], as seen in this patient. The lung parenchyma can also be involved [Clarke et al 1991, Denning et al 1991]. It is most often associated with severe immunosuppression, such as in the case of advanced HIV, stem cell transplant or lung transplant.
Among HIV patients, invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is rarely a cause of pulmonary infections (~1.4%) [Kemper et al 1993], and Aspergillus tracheobronchitis is even less common (3/35 cases) [Lortholary et al 1993]. When diagnosed in patients with HIV, Aspergillus tracheobronchitis is more commonly found in advanced cases (<100 CD4+ T-lymphocytes per cubic millimeter) and in those patients who have concomitant steroids or neutropenia [Kemper et al 1993, Klapholz et al 1991].
Treatment for Aspergillus tracheobronchitis is the same as for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, with voriconazole being the antifungal agent of choice [Walsh et al 2008]. Amphotericin B is also an option if voriconazole is not tolerated [Walsh et al 2008]. Voriconazole dosing can be problematic among patients on ARVs as both are metabolized by the CYP450 enzymes. Voriconazole is both metabolized by and inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C19 and CYP2C9. Ritonavir is also an important inhibitor of CYP3A as well as an inducer of CYP2C19. Thus when prescribing both voriconazole and ritonavir, higher levels of voriconazole are expected at first, as inhibition has a faster onset of action than induction. However, in steady state, decreased levels of voriconazole are expected. For this reason, it is recommended to avoid the concomitant administration of voriconazole and ritonavir. Another important ARV interaction with voriconazole is with efavirenz. Efavirenz both induces and inhibits CYP3A4. In studies, co-administration was shown to decrease voriconazole levels by 77% and raise efavirenz levels by 44%. When dosing voriconazole with efavirenz, it is recommended that one double the daily dose of voriconazole and halve the daily dose of efavirenz [Yakiwchu et al 2008]. When planning to co-administer voriconzole and anti-retrovirals, consultation with a pharmacist is recommended.
