title: 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with sarcoidosis and n
history:
2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A woman with sarcoidosis and new cough and dyspnea.
A woman in her forties with pulmonary sarcoidosis developed a new cough and dyspnea. Amoxicillin and a short tapering course of corticosteroids were administered, with symptomatic improvement.
One month later, slurred speech, lightheadedness, loss of balance, and a posterior headache developed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figures 1 and 2) revealed hyperintense white matter lesions in the cerebellum (Fig. 1 see arrows) and brain stem on fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences.
A diagnosis of possible neurosarcoidosis was made, and prednisone was administered (60 mg daily, decreasing to 40 mg daily). Ataxia and dysarthria increased, and she was referred to another hospital. Neurology and Infectious Diseases consultations were obtained.
Figure 1. MRI of the brainstem and cerebellum.
Figure 2. MRI scan.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis was diagnosed 6 years earlier by mediastinoscopy. The most recent symptomatic flare had occurred 3 years before admission, when corticosteroids were administered. Three months before the onset of the current symptoms, shingles involving the right chest and flank had occurred.
She had also been exposed to tuberculosis in the past; subsequent tuberculin skin testing was negative.

She worked in a medical facility. The patient had lived in the Midwest United States before moving to the Southeast more than 5 years before admission. Three months before admission, she received a tick bite near her home.

Medications included prednisone (40mg orally, daily).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 37.1°C (98.8°F), blood pressure 191/107 mm Hg, pulse 65 beats per minute, and respirations 18 per minute. There were scattered crackles in the lung fields. Her speech was dysarthric. Horizontal nystagmus was present bilaterally. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes were normal, and Babinski reflexes were plantar. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin examination revealed dysmetria bilaterally, which was worse on the left compared to the right. Gait was ataxic, requiring assistance.

The white blood cell count was 15,000 cells/µL (reference range (ref.) 3,500-10,500) with 87% segmented neutrophils (ref. 44.4-70.9). Results of testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody testing, rapid plasma reagin, immunoglobulin subclasses, Histoplasma and Lyme serological tests, anti-neutrophil antibody, rheumatoid factor and blood interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis were negative. Other results, including the erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal.

Lumbar puncture examination for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed no white blood cells/µL (ref. 0-5), 2 red blood cells/µL (ref. 0), glucose 59 mg/dL (45-80mg/dL) and protein 20 mg/dL (ref. 15-45).
diagnosis:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus in a patient with sarcoidosis.

Polymerase chain reaction amplification (PCR) of the CSF for herpes simplex virus (HSV), Epstein Barr virus (EBV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Tropheryma whipplei were negative. Testing of the CSF for cryptococcus antigen, arbovirus and West Nile virus antibody panels and Histoplasma antibodies was negative. Aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, acid fast bacilli and viral cultures of the CSF were all negative.
JC virus was identified in the CSF by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. Subsequent quantitative testing revealed a JC virus nucleic acid level of 25,205 copies per mL (ref: <500).

Mefloquine (500mg, orally biweekly for 1 week, followed by 250mg orally, weekly) and mirtazipine (30mg orally, daily) were administered, based on prior studies and case reports of PML in patients with sarcoidosis [Gofton et al. 2010, Owczarczyk et al. 2007]. Prednisone was tapered and discontinued. However, at follow-up 1 month later, her clinical course had worsened. Repeat MRI of the brain revealed progression of the lesions (Figures 3 and 4). A repeat JC viral level of the CSF was 31,102 copies per mL.
A stereotactic brain biopsy was performed, and showed the presence of demyelination, and oligodendritic viral inclusions in the cerebellar white matter, confirming the diagnosis of JC virus-associated PML (see Figures 5 through 7. Pathological images courtesy of Dennis Dickson, M.D.)
Cytarabine (2mg/kg daily) intravenous infusion was administered for 5 consecutive days, with stabilization but without improvement in ataxia, dysarthria or dysphagia.
Figure 3. MRI scan, 1 months later.
Figure 4. MRI scan, 1 months later.
Figure 5. Brain biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain.
Figure 6. Brain biopsy, Luxol fast blue stain.
Figure 7. Brain biopsy, SV-40 T-antigen staining (in which JC viral nuclei stain brown).

JC virus is a small, enveloped polyomavirus named after the first patient in which it was isolated. The virus is ubiquitous in nature, causing an asymptomatic primary infection; seropositivity occurs in approximately 86% of adults. It lays dormant in the kidneys, tonsils, bone marrow lymphocytes and other lymphoid tissue, reactivating during immunosuppressed states when it enters the peripheral blood with tropism for the brain [Berger 2007].
JC virus-associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) was initially described in 1958 in patients with hematologic cancers [Berger 2007]. In the 1980s, prevalence increased with the advent of HIV and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). The virus infects oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, causing white matter disease by destruction of the myelin sheath. Spinal cord involvement is rare, but has been described [Tan et al. 2010].
PML is a neurologic disease of the immunocompromised host, specifically in relation to defects in cell-mediated immunity. More recently, it has been recognized in patients receiving monoclonal antibodies, such as natalizumab for multiple sclerosis and rituximab for lymphoma, rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. At the time of this report, 26 cases of PML in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis have been described, in whom five were not on any immunosuppression for active disease [Goften et al. 2010, Volker et al. 2007, Goldbecker et al. 2010]. Our patient received only a brief steroid taper 1 month prior to onset of her neurological symptoms, which suggests her sarcoidosis, a T-lymphocyte mediated disorder, may be an underlying cause of her immunosuppressed state.
Clinical symptoms vary by the area of brain involvement. Our patient demonstrated significant dysarthria, dysmetria and ataxia, consistent with her cerebellar involvement. In classic PML, MRI of the brain shows asymmetric, subcortical white matter lesions that are hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences.
Brain biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. A less invasive alternative is PCR testing for JC virus in the CSF. In HIV-infected patients, sensitivity of this test in the era of highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) ranges from 58-75%, with a specificity of 96-100% [Fong et al.1995, Marzocchetti et al. 2005]. Viral load testing in CSF is also now available, which may be helpful in assessing response to therapy [Bossolasco et al. 2005].
Current treatments for PML show poor efficacy. The first goal is to reduce immunosuppression. In AIDS patients, HAART must be initiated. Medications that inhibit JC viral replication in vitro include cytarabine (cytosine arabinoside), cidofovir and mefloquine. Most of the experience with using cidofovir has been in AIDS patients; in this patient population, several studies showed no significant difference in 1-year survival compared to HAART alone [Gasnault et al. 2009, Kraemer et al. 2008, De Luca et al. 2008]. An open-label study demonstrated clinical stabilization and even improvement in 7 of 19 non-AIDS PML patients after treatment with cytarabine [Aksamit 2001]. A clinical trial is currently underway examining the effectiveness of mefloquine, a drug traditionally used for malaria [clinicaltrials.gov/ NCT00746941]. Serotonin receptor blockers, specifically mirtazipine, are now being studied because it has been found that the JC virus enters cultured cells via the serotonin (5-HT2a) receptor [Tan et al. 2010].
Unfortunately, non-AIDS PML has a poor prognosis; one-year survival is estimated between 36-50% [Aksamit 2001]. Realistic goals of treatment are for stabilization, not complete reversal, of neurological symptoms.

title: 2011 IDSA Case Presentation Summary: A woman with hyperesthesia, weakness and un
history:
2011 IDSA Case Presentation Summary: A woman with hyperesthesia, weakness and unsteady gait.
A woman in her forties with ulcerative colitis developed hyperesthesia over her left posterior forearm, which spread to her entire left arm and shoulder, chest, and back over a two-week period, associated with weakness of her left arm and unsteady gait.
She saw her primary care physician, who sent her to the emergency department; she was admitted for further evaluation. She reported no fever, chills, headache, neck pain, and denied any respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms before the onset of her neurologic symptoms.

She had a history of ulcerative colitis.

She had not traveled recently, and denied intake of unpasteurized dairy or deli meats.

She had no allergies.

Medications included infliximab and prednisone (20 mg daily), which she had been taking for the previous 7 months.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, alert and fully oriented. The blood pressure was 125/73 mm Hg, pulse 54 beats per minute, temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), respirations 12 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% while breathing ambient air. The neurological examination revealed poor coordination during fast, alternating movements; left upper extremity motor weakness and hyperesthesia of the left arm, shoulder, chest and back. There were no meningeal signs, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 9100 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range 4000-12,000); other routine laboratory test results were normal. Blood cultures were sterile. An interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cervical spine, performed with the administration of gadolinium, showed an abnormal signal in the medulla predominant on T2 and FLAIR images, with small amount of gadolinium enhancement that extended to the entire cervical cord down to the level of the first thoracic vertebra (T1) (see Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. MRI of the brain and brainstem, with gadolinium.
Figure 2. MRI of the cervical spine, with gadolinium.

The patient initially declined lumbar puncture. Because of a concern for a rapid demyelinating condition, the patient was immediately started on methylprednisolone (60 mg every 6 hrs, intravenously), with slight improvement in her weakness.
On the fifth hospital day, double vision and a peripheral facial palsy on the left side developed. The next day, difficulty in swallowing and speaking occurred, without shortness of breath. Her mental status remained intact. Dysphagia progressed and the trachea was subsequently intubated for airway protection.
A repeat MRI of the brain showed increased T2/FLAIR signal with enhancement in the brainstem and a new region of increased uptake in the posterior left pons (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Follow-up MRI of the brain and brainstem, with gadolinium.
Figure 4. Follow-up MRI, with gadolinium.
diagnosis:
Brainstem encephalitis and cervical myelitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes in an immunocompromised woman with ulcerative colitis.

A lumbar puncture was performed and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 269 leukocytes per cubic millimeter (55% neutrophils and 45% monocytes), protein 92 mg/dL (reference range 14-45 mg/dL)), and glucose 54 mg/dL (ref 40-80 mg/dL).
Gram stain of the CSF showed no organisms, but culture of the CSF grew gram positive rods with tumbling motility characteristic of Listeria monocytogenes (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Gram stain of CSF culture growth.

The patient was started on high dose ampicillin and gentamicin intravenously and steroids were tapered. Within forty-eight hours of starting antibiotics, the patient noted improvement of the hyperesthesia. By day 6 of antibiotics, she noted 50% improvement of the hyperesthesia and by day 7, she was extubated. A repeat brain and cervical MRI after 2 weeks of antibiotics still showed abnormal signal in the pons and medulla which was stable but the enhancement seen previously on cervical cord had decreased.
Ampicillin was administered intravenously throughout her admission and, at discharge, penicillin G was administered to complete an eight weeks' course of therapy.
Her overall function improved, but her neuropathy, diplopia and left-sided facial palsy persisted.

Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne facultative anaerobic gram-positive bacterium which, when ingested by susceptible individuals, typically causes infection in the blood and central nervous system (CNS). It grows at refrigeration temperatures bwtween 4°C to 10°C. Several food-borne Listeria outbreaks have occurred in the past 20 years. Foods most classically associated with this infection are Mexican-style cheeses, turkey deli meats and frankfurters.
Recently, Listeria has been linked to cantaloupe consumption. This latest outbreak started in summer of 2011 with all illnesses starting on or after July 31, 2011. The initial 7 cases were reported from Colorado and all seven patients had eaten cantaloupes within a month prior to onset of their symptoms. These contaminated cantaloupes were traced back to Jensen Farms in Colorado. Four strains with widely differing PFGE pattern combinations and 2 serotypes (1/2a and 1/2b) were identified (CDC, 2011). All the 4 outbreak strains were isolated from whole and cut cantaloupe samples from patients’ homes, grocery stores and the farm. Jensen Farms recalled all their cantaloupes on September 14, 2011. As of November 1, 2011, there were 139 cases in 28 states with 29 deaths including one pregnant woman who miscarried at the time of illness (CDC Listeria outbreak website). More cases are still being reported at the time this case was written due to the lag time between diagnosis and laboratory confirmation as well as the incubation period which may take up to 2 months.
Immunocompromised patients and pregnant women are at particularly high risk for Listeria infection. Infection with Listeria has also been reported as an infectious complication of anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) treatment, but the majority of reported cases are septicemia and meningitis [Slifman et al. 2003, Wallis et al. 2004].
By contrast, Listeria brainstem encephalitis, one of its rare CNS manifestations, has been reported predominantly in healthy adults with only about 8% seen in immunocompromised patients [Armstrong and Fung 1993]. It is typically a biphasic illness, usually beginning with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting, followed by cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, weakness, decreased consciousness and occasionally, seizures. Myelitis and spinal cord abscesses are even rarer manifestations of neurolisteriosis and have been reported in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients [Bartt 2000, Josephson et al. 2000].
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination is the most useful diagnostic test for both Listeria brainstem encephalitis and cervical myelitis. In a review of CSF findings in reported cases of brainstem encephalitis, CSF leukocytes ranged from 100 to 499 cells, which may either be neutrophilic or lymphocytic predominant cells [Armstrong and Fung 1993]. CSF protein is high and CSF glucose is often normal. Blood cultures are positive in half of the cases. In general, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more useful than CT scan in visualizing the posterior fossa which often shows increased intensity of the lesions on T2-weighted images which may or may not enhance with contrast [Alper et al. 1995].
Demyelinating conditions, with intense lesions on MRI T2-weighted images, as seen in our patient, have been reported in a case series of 20 patients during and following treatment with TNF-alpha antagonists [Mohan et al. 2001]. However, patients typically improved with discontinuation of the offending drug and the start of alternative therapies such as glucocorticoids, interferon (IFN)-beta or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Our patient’s symptoms worsened on steroids, which raised suspicion for an infectious etiology.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae can also cause an acute transverse myelitis or disseminated encephalomyelitis condition [Daxboeck 2006]. It is more common in children and is usually preceded by respiratory symptoms. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM can also persist for an extended period of time, sometimes up to 12 months after an initial infection, in some patients. In this case, Mycoplasma infection was less likely because of the absence of preceding respiratory symptoms and the patient’s improvement on ampicillin, a drug that does not target Mycoplasma.
There is an increased risk of reactivation of tuberculosis (TB) in patients on anti-TNF-alpha treatment with the majority presenting as extrapulmonary disease [Keane et al. 2001]. Tuberculosis may potentially have atypical presentations as well. However, the majority of TB CNS infections presents with basilar arachnoiditis or meningeal enhancement associated with some degree of hydrocephalus on neuroimaging. In addition to the lack of compatible clinical and radiologic findings, our patient had negative interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis.
Listeria monocytogenes infection should be considered in an immunocompromised patient presenting with acute craniopathies, hemiparesis or any focal neurological deficits, even with lack of systemic signs and symptoms of infection. Examination of the CSF is a crucial tool in the evaluation of acute neurologic symptoms prior to giving empiric high-dose corticosteroids or other treatment modalities which would potentially worsen an underlying infection.

title: 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with rapidly progressive
history:
2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with rapidly progressive generalized weakness, myalgias and respiratory distress.
A man in his thirties presented in mid-winter with rapidly progressive generalized weakness, myalgias and respiratory distress. The patient was well until approximately three weeks before admission, when diffuse weakness and myalgias developed, followed by increasing rapidly progressive respiratory distress. He went to a hospital and a diagnosis of a viral illness was made. Supportive treatment was advised, and he returned home.
Two days later, increasing weakness developed, associated with diarrhea, non-productive cough, fevers and chills. One week after the onset of symptoms, he went to the emergency room of another hospital. He reported weight loss of 4.5 kilograms since the onset of symptoms.
On examination, there was hypotension, fever and acute respiratory distress with oxygen saturation of 80%. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed bilateral minimal pleural effusion, right middle lobe and lingular lobe consolidation. CT of the abdomen revealed splenomegaly. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54% and a large pericardial effusion, with features of cardiac tamponade.
He was admitted to the intensive care unit and his clinical condition rapidly deteriorated. The trachea was intubated because of respiratory failure and vasopressors were administered for blood pressure support.
A pericardial window procedure and biopsy were performed, and 700 cc pericardial fluid aspirated. Analysis of the pericardial fluid revealed lactate dehydrogenase 1533 IU/L, protein 3250 g/dL, glucose 86 mg/dL, and white cells 31,000 /cumm with a lymphocytic predominance; the results were thought to be consistent with an exudative process. Pathological examination showed reactive changes and fibrin deposition consistent with acute and chronic inflammation. No evidence of malignancy was seen, and culture of the pericardial fluid was sterile. Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative. Diagnoses of idiopathic myopericarditis, hospital acquired pneumonia and septic shock were made. Intravenous vancomycin, aztreonem and high-dose methylprednisolone were administered.
The patient's clinical condition continued to worsen and he was transferred, approximately three weeks after the onset of his symptoms, to another hospital for further evaluation and treatment.

He had previously been healthy.

He may have had exposures to cleaning solvents and other chemicals. His wife had had viral symptoms one week before admission. He had no exposure to pets, and no recent travel.

He lived with his wife and worked in industry.

He was allergic to penicillin.
exam_studies:
The patient was sedated, on mechanical ventilation. The blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg (on vasopressors), pulse 130 beats per minute, temperature 38.3°C (100.9°F), and respirations 20 per minute. He was obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 34.1 SI units (weight in kilograms divided by the height in meters squared).
The sclera were icteric. There was crepitus in the lower lung fields bilaterally and anasarca was present. The abdomen was mildly distended, with normal bowel sounds, and was soft, without organomegaly.

The hematocrit was 35.0% (reference range 41.0-53.0 in men), white blood count 7700/cubic millimeter (reference range 3800 - 9800), and platelets 49,000/cubic millimeter (reference range 140,000 - 440,000). The serum level of total bilirubin was 3.0 mg/dl (reference range 0.3 - 1.1), direct bilirubin 2.1 mg/dl (reference range 0.0 - 0.3), aspartate aminotransferase 352 U/L (reference range 11 - 47), alanine aminotransferase 265 U/L (reference range 7 - 53), and creatinine 3.08 mg/dl (reference range 0.70 - 1.30).
Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Cultures of the blood culture, urine and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were sterile. A chest radiograph revealed multiple areas of airspace consolidation throughout all lobes of both lungs, which were thought to represent multifocal pneumonia (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Cultures of the pericardial fluid for bacteria, fungus and acid-fast bacilli remained sterile. Fevers persisted, and the antibiotics were changed to vancomycin, cefepime, and metronidazole. Continuous veno-venous hemodialysis and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation were begun because of renal failure and respiratory distress syndrome.
diagnosis:
Influenza A (H1N1) 2009 virus infection with myopericarditis, respiratory failure and hemophagocytic syndrome.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of a nasopharyngeal specimen and a tracheal aspirate detected influenza A virus (H1N1) 2009 RNA. PCR testing of the pericardial fluid was negative for enterovirus. Analysis of the stool was negative for enterovirus shredding. The level of serum ferritin was 9000 ng/ml (reference range 22 – 322).
By the tenth hospital day, the white cell count had decreased to 600 cells per cubic millimeter, and thrombocytopenia persisted. A bone marrow biopsy was performed. Pathological examination of a bone marrow biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain and CD25 staining for histiocytes and macrophages revealed hypocellular marrow with evidence of hemophagocytosis (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Bone marrow biopsy specimen, hematoxylin and eosin stain.
Figure 3. Bone marrow biopsy specimen, CD25 stain showing histiocytes and macrophages.

Oseltamivir (75 mg twice a day) was administered per nasogastric tube for 10 days.
Cultures remained negative for bacterial infection, and vancomycin,cefepime, metronidazole and micafungin were stopped. Viral cultures of nasal and tracheal specimens were repeated, and were negative for influenza.
After hematology-oncology consultation, infliximab and granulocyte-colony stimulating factor were administered for hemophagocytic syndrome. On the 16th day, pressors and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation were discontinued, however, mechanical ventilation was temporarily continued due to respiratory failure. The patient did eventually recover, and was discharged home after 3 months in the hospital.

The patient developed severe complications after infection with influenza A (H1N1) 2009, including myopericarditis, respiratory failure and hemophagocytic syndrome. Independent factors contributing to a high risk for severe H1N1 influenza infection include the extremes of age (either the elderly or neonates), pregnancy, immunocompromised states (e.g. HIV, solid organ transplantation), and obesity. This patient was obese, with BMI of 34.1 SI units. Severe influenza A H1N1 2009 infection can also develop in young healthy individuals, underlining the importance of promoting annual influenza vaccination.
Influenza A (H1N1)-associated reactive hemophagocytic syndrome has been reported rarely in the literatures [Puzzelli et al. 2010, Zheng et al. 2010]. The most common viral infection that is reported to have association with hemophagocytic syndrome is Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) [Letsas et al. 2007]. The diagnosis of hemophagocytic syndrome should be considered in a patient who develops persistent fever, organomegaly and cytopenias in the setting of an infectious process.
Hemophagocytic syndrome may be considered a contributing factor to fatal outcomes in patients with influenza A H1N1 2009 infection, despite treatment [Beutel et al. 2011]. It is a rare disease, first described in 1939, and is caused by dysregulation of natural killer T cells, resulting in activation and proliferation of lymphocytes or histiocytes with uncontrolled hemophogocytosis and cytokine overproduction or “cytokine storm”. This process leads to cellular damage and multiorgan dusfunction [Fisman 2000]. The diagnosis is established by molecular or clinical criteria, and this patient fulfilled 5 out of 8 clinical criteria for the diagnosis [Rouphael et al. 2007] including fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, evidence of hemophagocytic syndrome in bone marrow biopsy and hyperferritinemia. Natural killer (NK) cell analysis and soluble CD25 tests, which are considered part of the diagnostic criteria, were not obtained.

title: 2012 January-February Featured Case and 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation
history:
2012 January-February Featured Case and 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: An elderly man with fever, abdominal pain, myalgias, arthralgias, and headache.
A man in his seventies presented to the hospital during the summer with fever, abdominal pain, myalgias, arthralgias, and headache. He also reported malaise, dyspnea, loss of appetite secondary to early satiety, mild diarrhea, and scrotal pain. His symptoms had begun four days before presentation.

He had a history of gout and hyperlipidemia.

Three days before admission, he had worked on a horse ranch in mountains of the Western United States, where he received multiple mosquito bites. One week before presentation, he slept in an old, musty cabin near a lake in a neighboring state, and he had recently attended a livestock fair. He owned a dog that slept in his bed with him at night.

Medications included simvastatin and allopurinol.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared apprehensive. The temperature was 102.3°F (39.1°C), pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/78 mm Hg, and respirations 20-25 per minute. The abdomen and scrotum were diffusely tender, and there was lower extremity edema, and a petechial rash on his lower extremities.

The level of serum sodium was 130 mmol/L (reference range 133-145), creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (reference range 0.4-1.2), aspartate aminotransferase 101 U/L (reference range 0-47), alanine aminotransferase 70 U/L (reference range 0-47), alkaline phosphatase 77 U/L (reference range 3-117), total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL (reference range 0.0-1.3), direct bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL (reference range 0.0-0.4), platelets 105,000/cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-400,000), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/hr (reference range 0-38), and C-reactive protein 171 mg/L (reference range 0-10). Other routine laboratory tests were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed gallstones and was otherwise normal. A chest radiograph was normal.

Doxycycline was administered empirically. He initially defervesced, but fever recurred on the fourth day of therapy, and persisted through the tenth hospital day; doxycycline was discontinued. Anemia developed, and serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) revealed a monoclonal IgG kappa spike.
A bone marrow biopsy was performed and shown in Figure 1. The clinical data were not consistent with multiple myeloma, and a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) was made.
A hepatobiliary imino-diacetic acid (HIDA) scan revealed abnormal uptake with a reduced ejection fraction of approximately 24% (normal greater than 35%). A tagged white blood cell scan was non-diagnostic.
The patient was discharged on moxifloxacin for presumed cholecystitis. Four days after discharge, he returned to the hospital because of tachycardia, fever, and hypotension. A repeat CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed periportal edema, lymphadenopathy along the celiac axis, gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fat stranding.
Figure 1. Bone marrow biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain (100x magnification).
diagnosis:
Acute Q Fever cholecystitis, caused by Coxiella burnetii.

Pathological examination of bone marrow biopsy specimens with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain revealed granuloma with fibrin rings and lipid-filled vacuoles (Figures 2 and 3).
Coxiella burnetii IgG phase I antibodies were present at 1:128 dilution and IgG phase II antibodies were detected at 1:512 dilution.
Anti-Parvovirus IgM and IgG antibodies were positive at titers of 1:1.3 and 1:1.8, respectively. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for Parvovirus was negative. Coccidiodes IgG EIA was slightly positive. A transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.
Figure 2. Bone marrow biopsy.
Figure 3. Bone marrow biopsy.

The options for therapy, including doxycycline with either hydroxychloroquine or rifampin, were discussed with the patient, who chose the doxycycline and rifampin because he preferred the side effect profile of rifampin to hydroxychloroquine. He improved clinically on therapy, and within a month felt well enough to resume his active lifestyle. Coxiella titers initially increased, and a longer course of treatment for acute Q fever was recommended. He took doxycycline and rifampin for one year.

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an intracellular gram negative coccobacillus that contains a chromosome and plasmid. There are four different plasmid types which vary in virulence characteristics. The usual host cell in mammals is the macrophage. The bacteria exhibit antigenic alteration, called phase variation. Phase I antigen is associated with expression of full-length lipopolysaccharide and infection. Phase II antigen expression is associated with the noninfectious phase and involves a chromosomal deletion resulting in an irreversible modification of lipopolysaccharide molecules [Fournier et al. 1998; Raoult et al. 2005].
Q fever occurs worldwide, with the most reported cases coming from France and Australia [Hartzell et al. 2008]. It often occurs in outbreaks; 808 cases were reported in the Netherlands from January – August 2008 [Delsing and Kullberg 2008]. More than 30 cases have been reported in military personnel returning from Iraq and Afghanistan [Hartzell et al. 2007]. An outbreak involving seroconversion of 137 people at the University of Colorado Medical School in 1981 occurred in association with exposure to pregnant sheep which were used for perinatal research. 70% of the people who seroconverted had no direct contact with the sheep but were located along routes followed by sheep carts [Meiklejohn et al. 1981].
Natural reservoirs for C. burnetii include mammals, birds, reptiles, and arthropods. Infected animals shed the bacteria in urine, feces, milk, and birth products, particularly the placenta. The dessicated bacteria become aerosolized and may remain virulent for months. Humans can become infected by inhalation, or less commonly by ingestion or skin penetration [Hartzell et al. 2008]. The bacterium is highly contagious, and only a few organisms can cause disease. One gram of infected placenta may contain enough bacteria to infect 100,000,000 guinea pigs [Parker et al. 2006].
Primary infection is commonly asymptomatic [Tissot-Dupont and Raoult 2008]. The incubation period is about 20 days, and the illness has acute and chronic forms, with chronic infection defined as infection for more than 6 months. The most common clinical presentations include flu-like illness, pneumonia, or hepatitis. Pneumonia is usually mild with a nonproductive cough and nonspecific chest radiograph findings. Hepatitis is granulomatous on histologic assessment and is typically asymptomatic except for fever. Chronic infection (<5% of cases) usually involves the heart, bones, arteries, or liver. Q fever endocarditis is the most serious form of chronic Q fever and usually develops in patients with previous valvular disease or in immunocompromised patients [Hartzell et al. 2008; Parker et al. 2006; Tissot-Dupont and Raoult 2008].
Q fever cholecystitis has been previously described in 15 patients. This diagnosis has been based on the presence of radiographic evidence of cholecystitis, positive phase I and II serologies, demonstration of C. burnetii in the gallbladder using PCR, or liver biopsy showing a “doughnut granuloma,” (a granuloma surrounded by a fibrin ring and containing a lipid-filled vacuole). This histologic finding in the liver or bone marrow is suggestive of Q fever in the correct clinical setting, though it can also be present in other infections (such as Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus or ehrlichiosis) or in Hodgkin’s Disease. The first case series, published in 2003, described seven new cases of Q fever cholecystitis from France, and reviewed the two cases previously reported [Rolain et al. 2003]. Subsequently, 6 additional cases have been reported from Spain, France, Israel, Australia, and Iraq [Hartzell et al. 2007; Reina-Serrano et al. 2005; Gonzalez Delgado et al. 2005;Ergas et al. 2008; Figtree et al. 2010]. Following an outbreak of 30 cases of Q fever in soldiers in Iraq and Afghanistan, empiric treatment of Q fever cholecystitis was administered to two patients who demonstrated clinical improvement within 48 hours [Hartzell et al. 2007]. Over half of reported cases of Q fever cholecystitis resolved on medical therapy alone, and did not require cholecystectomy.
Laboratory findings for Q fever are nonspecific but may include leukocyte elevation or depression, high erythrocyte sedimentation rate, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia, thrombocytopenia (in 25% of cases), or elevated liver enzymes (85%). The diagnosis is usually made by serologic testing for IgM, IgA, and IgG to the phase I and phase II antigens. A titer of greater than 1:200 for IgG or1:50 for IgM against Phase II signifies acute infection. Phase I IgG titer above 1:800 is associated with chronic infection [Fournier et al. 1998]. It is recommended that all patients with chronic Q fever have an echocardiogram to assess for endocarditis or underlying valvular disease, a condition which predisposes Q-fever-infected individuals to endocarditis [Raoult et al. 2000].

title: 2011 November-December Featured Case and 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentatio
history:
2011 November-December Featured Case and 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with fevers, vomiting, and cyanosis of the feet.
A man in his fifties was well until one week before admission when nausea, vomiting, malaise, and headaches developed after eating a hamburger. The symptoms were associated with polydipsia, polyuria, and decreased oral intake. Approximately three days before admission, fevers and chills occurred, and his feet became mottled. His weight reportedly decreased by 10 pounds (4.5 kilograms).
On the day of admission, a friend noted changes in his mental status and slurred speech.

He had a history of hypertension, colonic diverticulosis, osteoarthritis and a remote history of alcohol dependence. He had no history of peripheral vascular disease or claudication.

He lived in California and owned cats. He was monogamous. He did not smoke or use illicit drugs, had not traveled recently and had had no known sick contacts. His yard was visited by opossums, coyotes and deer.

He lived with his girlfriend and was retired.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared drowsy, with slightly slurred speech. The blood pressure was 132/61 mm Hg, pulse 146 beats per minute irregular, temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), and respirations 35 per minute. Breath sounds were coarse. The pulse was rapid and irregularly irregular, without cardiac murmurs. The scrotum was erythematous and mildly edematous. There was violaceous to dusky-gray, non-blanching, non-palpable purpura involving all the toes, with overlying hemorrhagic bullae, and necrosis just proximal to the tips of toes. Distal pedal pulses were 1 to 2+, and there was 1+ pitting edema, one hemorrhagic bulla on the left shin, and reticulate erythema of the palms. He was able to follow simple commands.

The hematocrit was 56% (reference range 39-54), white count 17,400 cells per cubic millimeter (ref 4,100 -10,800) with 90% neutrophils (ref 35-80), and the platelet count 16,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-450,000). The peripheral smear showed 1-2 schistocytes or fragmented red cells per high power field. The partial thromboplastin time (PTT) was 44.5 seconds (ref 25.2- 36.8) and fibrinogen 86 mg/dl (ref 269-589) and INR 1.4 (ref 0.9-1.2). The serum level of sodium was 125 mEq/L(ref 133-146), potassium 3.8 mEq/L (ref 3.6-5.0), urea nitrogen 65 mg/dL (ref 7-21), creatinine 2.2 mg/dL (ref 0.5-1.4), alanine aminotransferase 40 U/L (ref 7-56), aspartate aminotransferase 112 U/L (ref 38-126), alkaline phosphatase 128 U/L (ref 44-147), total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL (ref 0.2-1.3), lactate dehydrogenase 403 U/L (ref 50-150), D- Dimer >6000 ng/ml (ref < or = 250 ng/mL), and creatine kinase 1324 ng/ml (ref 38-120).
Serologic testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tests for hepatitis B and C viruses were negative. Urinalysis screening revealed a large quantity of blood but was negative for leukocyte esterase and ketones; microscopic examination showed 15 red cells per high power field and hyaline casts were present. Results of stool analysis, including testing for Escherichia coli 0:157, were negative.
A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT), without contrast enhancement, of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, showed bilateral paraseptal emphysematous changes and dependent bilateral groundglass opacities in all lung fields. CT of the head was normal. Echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% and no evidence of vegetations, and there was no evidence of thrombosis by non-invasive testing (Doppler) of the legs.

Ceftriaxone, azithromycin, intravenous fluids, and high dose corticosteroids were administered and cryoprecipitate was infused for possible pulmonary infection, acute kidney injury cryoglobulinemia and vasculitis. After one dose, azithromycin was stopped and acyclovir and vancomycin were added for possible meningitis. Lumbar puncture was not performed because of thrombocytopenia.
During the next two days, dyspnea increased, scrotal edema and pain worsened and the mottled appearance of the feet evolved into frank necrosis. Physical findings are shown in Figures 1 and 2. CT of the chest demonstrated bilateral opacities.
A punch skin biopsy of the proximal first toe was performed; pathological examination of the biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Ultrasonography demonstrated evidence of epididymo-orchitis on the right.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings, with reticulate erythema on the palms.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain.
Figure 4. Skin biopsy, H and E stain.
diagnosis:
Murine typhus caused by Rickettsia typhi.

Pathological examination of the biopsy, shown in Figure 3 at 20 x magnification, revealed epidermis with full thickness necrosis and focal detachment. The papillary dermis was edematous, with separation of collagen bundles. Figure 4, shown at 600 x magnification, demonstrates the reticular dermis with small blood vessels involved by a leukocytoclastic vasculitis surrounding eccrine ducts. Trans mural fibrinoid necrosis (solid arrow), characteristic of a leukocytoclastic vasculitis, is seen, with nuclear dust (open arrow) from degenerating neutrophils. There were also swollen vascular endothelial cells (solid arrow with notched tail) and intraluminal fibrin thrombi (open arrow with notched tail), as well as white cells in the vessel wall, and reactive endothelial cells.
Testing for antibodies to Rickettsia typhi was positive: IgG Rickettsia typhi >1:1024 (reference range <1:64 = Negative, 1:64-1:28 = Equivocal, >1: 256 = Positive) and IgM Rickettsia typhi >1:1024 (ref <1:64 = Negative and >1:64 = Positive).

Doxycycline was administered empirically, before the results of the diagnostic tests were available, with improvement in mentation, fevers, and shortness of breath. The platelet count improved and acute renal failure resolved. Necrotic toes required amputation.

Rickettsia typhi is the etiologic agent of murine typhus, which is often referred to as “endemic typhus” or “fleaborne typhus.” R. typhi is a small (0.4×1.3 µm), gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium that depends on hematophagous arthropods (e.g., fleas and ticks) and mammals to maintain its life cycle [Civen and Ngo 2008]. In the United States, many of the cases of murine typhus are reported in Texas, California and Hawaii [Civen and Ngo 2008], and there has been a recent documented outbreak in a community of coastal California [Green et al. 2011]. Given these geographic considerations, a diagnosis of murine typhus merited consideration in this patient.
Murine typhus is commonly a mild illness associated with a rash with an incubation period of 8 to 16 days. However, as in this case, it can cause an illness with significant morbidity, and deaths can occur if appropriate treatment is not administered. The primary pathological lesion of R. typhi infection is an inflammatory vasculitis characterized by perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma, and mast cells. In rare cases, the vasculitis may be accompanied by mural or intimal thrombi in small vessels of the heart, lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system or, as in our case, small vessels of the feet. The pathophysiology of the rickettsial diseases could well explain the formation of clots within blood vessels. Rickettsiae are known to invade the endothelium of blood vessels - arterial, capillary, as well as venous. The damage to the integrity of the endothlial lining may thus begin the clotting cascade and cases of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolus have been reported in the literature as well [Potasman and Bassan 1986]. The clinical and lab findings in murine typhus are frequently non-specific; because patients respond well to treatment, prompt consideration of the diagnosis and empiric therapy are essential [Potasman and Bassan 1986]. The drug of choice in adults is doxycycline. Doxycycline should be continued for 48 hours after the patient becomes afebrile or for a minimum of five days

title: 2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with pain in the lumbar
history:
2011 IDSA Fellows’ Day Case Presentation Summary: A man with pain in the lumbar back and legs.
A man in his seventies developed progressive pain in the lumbar region extending to the both legs. He was in good health until approximately two years earlier, when intermittent fevers, chills, and malaise developed. Unintentional weight loss of 50 pounds (22.7 kilograms) occurred; the weight was regained over the next four months as his symptoms spontaneously resolved.
During the year before admission, pain developed throughout his body, particularly in the lower back, the buttocks, the joints, and both legs; the pain was eventually refractory to analgesics. During that period, he was evaluated by his primary care physician, and consultants in rheumatology, neurology, and infectious diseases; however, no definitive diagnosis or etiology for his symptoms was made.
His back pain became intolerable, and he was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. There was no history of trauma to his back or bowel or urinary incontinence.

He had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus. Transitional cell bladder cancer (stage 0) was diagnosed 7 years before and treated with partial tumor resection and Bacille Calmette Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy; a recurrence occurred the following year, with subsequent resection and immunotherapy. He had also had bilateral knee replacements because of osteoarthritis.

The patient was born in the Midwest, and as a young adult lived in Europe for several years. He had worked as a firefighter and moved to the Southeast upon retirement. His hobbies included gardening and fishing. He had smoked cigarettes in the remote past, after smoking one pack of cigarettes per day for 20 years. He drank alcohol in moderation, and did not use illicit drugs or own pets.

He had no allergies to medications.

Medications included gabapentin, cyclobenzaprine, methylprednisolone, amlodipine, lisinopril, omeprazole, fenofibrate and acetylsalicylic acid. He had also received three injections of epidural steroids.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared clinically stable. The blood pressure was 133/62 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature was 96.9°F (36.1°C), and respirations 16 breaths per minute. Examination of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine revealed no visible abnormalities or tenderness to palpation. He did not have pain with straight leg raise in the sitting and supine position. Mild decrease in range of motion was noted at the hips and bilateral knees. Mild sacroiliac joint tenderness was noted on palpation. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The level of C-reactive protein was 2.4 mg/dl (reference range 0.0-1.0). Other initial laboratory results, including serum electrolytes, glucose, and tests of liver function, were normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine (Figures 1 and 2) revealed spondylosis and abnormal signal intensity in the lumbar disk between the 4th and 5th lumbar vertebrae (L4 and L5), the adjacent endplates, bilateral facet joints, and the left sacroiliac (SI) joint. A new large saccular infrarenal aortic aneurysm (52 mm in diameter) was also noted (Figures 3 and 4). Whole body bone scanning revealed focal increased uptake in the left inferior sacroiliac region, which localized to the SI joint. There was also focal increased uptake in the bilateral L4-L5 regions, right greater than left, which localized to the body and facet joints at L4-L5 bilaterally.
Figure 1. MRI of the lumbar spine.
Figure 2. MRI scan of sacroiliac joint.
Figure 3. MRI showing infrarenal aortic aneurysm.
Figure 4. Ultrasonography showing aortic aneursym.

Aspiration of the left SI joint under computed tomography (CT)-guidance was performed. Vancomycin and ceftriaxone were administered empirically for the treatment of spondylodiscitis.
diagnosis:
Sacroiliitis, vertebral osteomyelitis and mycotic aneurysm caused by Mycobacterium bovis secondary to Bacille Calmette Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy for bladder cancer.

Mantoux tuberculin skin test was positive at 20 mm induration. The result of a tuberculosis interferon gamma release assay was negative. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex PCR testing of periaortic tissue was negative; however, Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA was detected in tissue specimens from the aortic node. Cultures from the left SI joint aspirate were positive for Mycobacterium bovis.
Aortic resection with infrarenal periaortic tissue debridement and replacement with a rifampin-soaked tube graft was performed. Pathological examination of the tissue revealed necrotizing granulomas (Figure 5) by hematoxylin and eosin and Movat staining.
Figure 5. Pathology of resected aorta.

After initial identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA in the aortic node, vancomycin and ceftriaxone were discontinued, and isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol with pyridoxine were administered. The back pain improved significantly with medical therapy.
Follow up MRI of the lumbar region revealed interval improvement of the osteomyelitis. However, his bladder cancer recurred. BCG instillations were no longer part of his future immunotherapy plans.

The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex is composed of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis), Mycobacterium microti, Mycobacterium africanum, and Mycobacterium bovis (M. bovis) [Abu-Nader and Terrell, 2002]. Whereas M. tuberculosis remains the cause of most human tuberculosis, M. bovis is the causative agent of tuberculosis in certain animal species, affecting only a small percentage of humans. In the 1920s, Calmette and Guérin developed the Bacille Calmette Guérin (BCG) vaccine to prevent tuberculosis, using a live attenuated derivative of a virulent strain of M. bovis. BCG is genetically and phenotypically similar to other species of M. tuberculosis complex as well as to other strains of M. bovis. Intravesical form of BCG was first introduced in 1976 for treatment of superficial transitional cell bladder cancer [Vegt et al. 1997]. In the 1980’s studies reported complete remission in more than 70% of patients with superficial and stage 1 bladder cancer. In 1990, the US Food and Drug Administration approved intravesicular BCG for the treatment of superficial bladder carcinoma.
The exact mechanism of therapeutic benefit of BCG in bladder cancer remains unknown; however, BCG has been postulated to stimulate an immune response that leads to granulomatous inflammation and tumor cell destruction. Intravesicular BCG has generally been well-tolerated. The incidence of significant adverse effects has been minimal. Reports of associated complications have included high fever (>39°C (102.2°F)), hematuria, granulomatous prostatitis, pneumonitis, or hepatitis, arthralgias, epididymo-orchitis, BCG sepsis, urethral obstruction, bladder contracture, renal abscess, and cytopenia. Complications with disseminated M. bovis-BCG infection, such as the mycotic aneurysms and musculoskeletal lesions in this case, are rare [Witjes et al. 2003].
Risk factors for metastatic spread of M. bovis -BCG include immune deficiencies or direct trauma to the bladder epithelium, which may occur during catheterization or tumor resection, or urethral injury during cystoscopy or instillation [Abu-Nader and Terrell, 2002]. Patients who undergo procedures such as transurethral resection of the prostate or biopsy within a few weeks of BCG instillation may also facilitate hematogenous spread. The discovery of viable BCG bacilli in biopsy specimens and morning urine cultures up to a year following intravesicular therapy might explain disseminated infection years after BCG instillation [Siatelis et al. 2011; Bowyer et a. 1995; Lamm et al. 1992].
In this case, the detection of M. bovis in culture of aspirate taken from the SI joint was considered proof of BCG-induced infection [Seelig et al. 1999]. A presumptive diagnosis of BCG dissemination was justified by the presence of concurrent vertebral osteomyelitis and aneurysm, until subsequent aortic tissue samples could be surgically obtained. The relationship between infected aneurysm and vertebral osteomyelitis is known to occur with tuberculosis infection via local extension from an adjacent infected focus or hematogenous spread [Rozenblit et al. 1996; Seelig et al. 1999]. Presumably, BCG infection follows a similar pattern. Multiplex polymerase chain reaction can be used for rapid and specific detection of BCG, including representatives of M.bovis -BCG, non-BCG M. bovis, and other species of the M. tuberculosis complex [Talbot et al. 1997].
All strains of M. bovis are intrinsically resistant to pyrazinamide [Abu-Nader and Terrell, 2002]; combination antimycobacterial therapy with at least isoniazid and rifampin (with inclusion of additional drugs such as ethambutol and other agents including quinolones with activity) are the cornerstone of therapy for this infection. If complications arise with BCG immunotherapy, BCG should be stopped immediately and subsequent BCG instillations should be cancelled. Triple anti-mycobacterial therapy is warranted in cases involving disseminated infection or organ involvement. Corticosteroids may be added as adjunctive treatment. Surgical intervention may be necessary, as in this case. Prophylaxis with isoniazid has not been proven to reduce the frequency of adverse effects associated with BCG instillation.

title: 2012 March-April Featured Case: A woman in her twenties was admitted to the hosp
history:
2012 March-April Featured Case: A woman in her twenties was admitted to the hospital because of respiratory failure and supraventricular tachycardia.
The patient was well until 12 days before admission, when throat soreness developed. Two days later, at her doctor's office, testing for rapid streptococcal antigen was negative and a heterophile antibody test was positive. She was counseled regarding supportive care for infectious mononucleosis. One week before admission, she returned to the doctor's office because of increased throat pain and decreased oral intake. A 3-day course of prednisone was administered orally. Her throat pain improved, however, neck pain persisted and her appetite decreased.
Three days before admission, she reportedly returned to the doctor's office because of increased neck pain, chest tightness, and pain in the left upper quadrant. She was afebrile. A chest radiograph reportedly showed a right upper lobe infiltrate. An abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly. Azithromycin was begun.
On the day of admission, her parents noted shallow breathing and took her to the emergency department of a local hospital. She reported pleuritic chest pain on the left side, which improved with upright positioning. On evaluation, the blood pressure was 121/77 mm Hg, pulse 106 beats per minute, respirations 24 per minute and oxygen saturation 80% while breathing ambient air. Oxygen was administered via non-rebreather mask. An electrocardiogram showed diffuse ST-segment elevations. A chest radiograph (Figure 1) demonstrated findings that were thought to be consistent with congestive heart failure and large bilateral pleural effusions.
The pulse rose up to 160-169 beats per minute; and supraventricular tachycardia was diagnosed. A bolus of amiodarone was administered, followed by cardioversion. Ceftriaxone (1 gram), azithromycin (500 milligrams) and aspirin (321 mg) were also given. An echocardiogram performed at the bedside by a cardiologist reportedly showed depressed left ventricular function.
She was transferred from the emergency department to a tertiary care hospital for admission to the medical intensive care unit.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, other hospital.

She had been healthy before this illness.

She worked in a public service position. She drank alcohol in moderation and had never smoked tobacco or used illicit drugs. During the previous year, she traveled to Western Europe and the New England coast. She had recently cared for indoor, declawed cats. She had a new boyfriend. Her immediate family was healthy.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole caused a rash.

She had recently stopped taking oral contraceptives.
exam_studies:
On arrival in the medical intensive care unit, she appeared uncomfortable and in respiratory distress. The blood pressure was 109/64 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats per minute, temperature 99.0°F (37.2°C), respirations 36 per minute and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing oxygen via non–rebreather mask. There was a pericardial rub heard best at the upper and lower sternal border on the left side. Breath sounds were decreased at the lung bases. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 28,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-11,000) with 90% neutrophils and 4% band forms. The blood level of sodium was 119 mmol/L (ref 135-145), total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl (ref 0.0-1.0), direct bilirubin 1.4 mg/dl (ref 0.0-0.4), aspartate aminotransferase 53 U/L (ref 10-40), albumin 1.7 gm/dl (ref 3.3-5.0) and NT-proBNP 5444 pg/ml (ref 0-450); levels of the other electrolytes, glucose, globulin, alkaline phosphatase and alanine aminotransferase were normal.
Rapid direct fluorescent antibody testing for influenza A and B, parainfluenza 1, 2, and 3, adenovirus and respiratory syncytial viruses was negative. Gram stain of a sputum specimen showed mixed gram positive and negative flora. Cultures of the blood, urine and sputum, as well as urinary Legionella antigen, were obtained. A chest radiograph on admission (Figure 2) showed bilateral large pleural effusions, greater on the right, which appeared to be loculated.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, on admission.

The trachea was intubated for hypoxemia and increased work of breathing immediately after arrival, and norepinephrine and vasopressin were administered. Thoracenteses were performed bilaterally, and a liter of foul-smelling fluid removed from each side.
Specimens of pleural fluid had 8400 and 287,500 nucleated cells per cubic millimeter (ref 0-1000), many of which were disintegrated; differential cell counts could not be performed. The level of glucose in the pleural fluid from each side was less than 2 mg/dl. On the right side, the pH was 6.01, the level of lactate dehydrogenase was 18,810 U/L, and albumin 1.7 gm/dl. On the left side, the level of lactate dehydrogenase was 35,040 U/L, albumin 1.8 gm/dl, total protein 3.2 gm/dl, amylase 10 U/L and triglycerides 10 mg/dl.
Cefepime (2 gm intravenously (IV) every 8 hours), metronidazole (500mg IV every 8 hours), vancomycin (1gm IV every 12 hours), levofloxacin (750mg IV daily), and oseltamivir (100mg per nasogastric tube twice daily) were administered.
Computed tomography of the chest and neck (Figures 3 through 6) are shown.
Figure 3. CT of the head and neck, sagittal view.
Figure 4. CT of the neck.
Figure 5. CT of the chest, post thoracentesis, mediastinal window.
Figure 6. CT of the chest, lung window.
diagnosis:
Infectious mononucleosis caused by acute Epstein Barr virus infection, complicated by polymicrobial infections in the neck and chest, including pre-vertebral and retropharyngeal abscesses and bilateral pleural empyemas, and mediastinitis. Streptocococcus anginosus, alpha hemolytic Streptococcus, Prevotella melaninogenica, Fusobacterium necrophorum, Propionibacterium acnes, and Candida albicans were cultured.

Computed tomography of the chest, performed after thoracentesis, demonstrated gas in the pre-vertebral fascia (Figure 3 and, with arrows, Figure 7), gas around the thyroid gland (Figure 4), a mediastinal collection and small bilateral pleural effusions, right greater
than left, with fluid tracking into the right minor fissure (Figures 5 and 6). The jugular veins were patent.
Gram stain (Figure 8) of the pleural fluid showed short gram-positive rods, thin gram-positive rods, gram-positive coccobacilli, and gram-negative rods. The morning after admission, esophagoscopy, surgical exploration of the neck, and mediastinal washout were performed, with placement of four Jackson-Pratt drains. Gram stain of the aspirate from the neck showed short gram-positive rods, thin gram positive rods, gram positive coccobacilli, and gram negative rods (Figure 9).
Testing for IgM to Epstein Barr virus (EBV) viral capsid was positive and for IgG was negative; EBV nuclear antigen was negative. Testing for hepatitis A, B and C viruses, HIV antibody and RNA, and urine Legionella antigen was negative.
The cultures of the pleural fluid and neck aspirate grew Streptocococcus anginosus, alpha hemolytic Streptococcus, Prevotella melaninogenica of two types and Fusobacterium necrophorum. Cultures of the pleural fluid also grew Propionibacterium acnes, and the neck aspirate also grew rare Candida albicans. The antibiotics were changed to ampicillin-sulbactam and fluconazole after culture results were known.
Figure 7. CT of the head and neck, with arrows showing air in the prevertebral space.
Figure 8. Gram stain of pleural fluid.
Figure 9. Gram stain of neck aspirate.

Three days after admission, she underwent bronchoscopy, bilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery converted to open thoracotomy, drainage of mediastinal abscess, bilateral decortication and drainage of a serous pericardial effusion; four additional chest tubes were placed. The patient's hospital course was complicated by pancreatitis, hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm, thought to be secondary to necrotizing infection.
Ten days after admission, the trachea was extubated; however, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and associated hypotension developed, which resolved with cardioversion.
Eleven days after admission, tracheostomy was performed. The next day, pressors were discontinued. She was discharged on the 39th day to a rehabilitation facility, and one month later, to home, with some persistent vocal cord and swallowing dysfunction.

This patient had infectious mononucleosis caused by acute Epstein Barr virus infection, complicated by polymicrobial infection in the neck and chest, including pre-vertebral and retropharyngeal abscesses and bilateral pleural empyemas, and mediastinitis.
The majority of patients with infectious mononucleosis recover without apparent sequelae [Luzuriaga and Sullivan 2010]. The respiratory complications of infectious mononucleosis include upper airway obstruction from lymphoid hyperplasia, mucosal edema or pharyngeal abscess, bilateral hilar adenopathy, exudative pleural effusions, interstitial pneumonitis, superimposed bacterial pneumonia, and septic thrombophlebitis. Pleural empyema after infectious mononucleosis has been reported [Andrianakis et al., 2002; Kopec et al., 1997], but is rare.
Pleural empyema most often develops by direct extension from contiguous infections such as pneumonia, osteomyelitis, mediastinal infection or subdiaphragmatic abscess. Empyemas can also develop from direct implantation such as after trauma or surgery. Most empyemas are unilateral; bilateral empyemas most often result from hematogenous spread or from mediastinitis [Kopec et al., 1997]. Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Porphyromonas, and Fusobacterium nucleatum are the most common pathogens of anaerobic pulmonary and orodental infection [Bartlett 1993].
The role of steroids in infectious mononucleosis has been evaluated in multiple studies. In the 1950s, a small case series documented favorable effects of steroid administration on the clinical course of infectious mononucleosis, particularly in shortening symptoms. In the 1960s, the routine practice of administering steroids became controversial [Candy and Hotopf, 2006]and concerns were raised that the effect of steroids on T cell immunity may predispose to secondary infections [Hagelskjaer Kristensen and Prag, 2000; Matten and Grecu, 2006]. A Cochrane Review published in 2006 found insufficient evidence to support the use of steroids in patients with infectious mononucleosis [Candy and Hotopf, 2006]. This evaluation of seven studies was limited by the heterogeneity of the trials, including diagnostic criteria, corticosteroid regimens, and symptom assessment scales. Two of seven of the trials found a transient benefit that was not sustained at follow up. Some, but not all, studies found increased complications in the steroid recipients; one study reported a patient who developed peritonsillar abscess. The authors of a review in the New England Journal of Medicine, published in 2010, concluded that "Clinical experience suggests that corticosteroids may be helpful in the management of more severe complications of infectious mononucleosis, including upper-airway obstruction, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia, although randomized, clinical trials evaluating their efficacy are limited.” [Luziaraga and Sullivan 2010].
