title: 2012 May-June Featured Case: A man in his forties with a history of stem cell tr
history:
2012 May-June Featured Case: A man in his forties with a history of stem cell transplantation (The patient is immunocompromised. This is a key aspect of Infectious Diseases diagnosis, since such patients have a different and wider spectrum of possible pathogens and a greater likelihood of having multiple concurrent infections, and localizing inflammatory signs and symptoms may be less apparent.) was admitted with lightheadedness and renal failure, and developed headache after falling.
The patient had a history of constrictive pericarditis with peripheral edema and dyspnea, for which metolazone was recently added to his diuretic medications. Lightheadedness, muscle cramps and acute renal insufficiency developed. He was admitted to the hospital, the diuretics were stopped and fluids administered. His symptoms and renal function improved until the third hospital day, when he fell and hit his head. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head was normal. He complained of a headache afterwards, which was thought to be related to the fall.
On the fourth hospital day (The tempo of symptom evolution is an important clue. This relatively slow progression would be unusual for most bacterial infections of the central nervous system.), he rated the headache 10 out of 10 in severity (where 10 is the most severe) and reported photophobia (Not truly a phobia in the sense of causing fear but an aversion, since the light is perceived as painful. The combination of headache, photophobia and vomiting is strongly suggestive of increased intracranial pressure.). An episode of vomiting occurred. The following day, confusion developed, with unusual behavior such as urinating on the floor. On the sixth day he was somnolent and unable to follow commands. Repeat CT scan of the head was unchanged.

Five years before this admission, a diagnosis of anaplastic large T-cell lymphoma was made. He was initially treated with chemotherapy, but relapse occurred later that year, and an autologous stem cell transplant was performed. The following year, the lymphoma recurred and an allogeneic stem cell transplant was performed. The patient’s course was complicated by severe sclerodermatous graft-versus-host disease, for which phototherapy was administered weekly.
He also had constrictive pericarditis, congenital hearing loss, chronic lower extremity ulcers, chronic pulmonary nodules and, beginning approximately ten months prior to this admission, an elevated serum beta-D-glucan ((1->3) beta-D-Glucan is a component of the cell wall of most fungi. The presence of this compound in the blood suggests an invasive fungal infection. It is an important tool, since many of these infections are difficult to detect by conventional culture and because it can help distinguish between true infection and superficial colonization.) level. The patient had received two doses of micafungin intravenously over the two weeks preceding the admission because of the pulmonary nodules and elevated beta-D-glucan. He had also been receiving intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for hypogammaglobulinemia.

He lived in New England with a pet dog. He had worked in construction, but was not working at the time of this illness. He did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

He had had a rash caused by an azole antifungal drug.

Medications included prednisone (An anti-inflammatory steroid. This is a very common immunosuppressive agent that increases the risk of many infections.) (20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the evening), cyclosporine, gabapentin, omeprazole, metoprolol, methadone, oxycodone, acyclovir, penicillin VK, micafungin (An echinocandin antifungal agent that acts by inhibiting the synthesis of beta-D-glucan. In this case, it is being used preemptively, common strategy with immunocompromised patients, since infection can proceed too rapidly to wait for a proven diagnosis.) and monthly inhaled pentamidine (Originally developed as an anti-protozoan drug, inhaled pentamidine has been used since the early days of the AIDS epidemic as a prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia, even though this organism is now known to be a fungus. The use of prophylactic antimicrobials is an important part of disease prevention in immunocompromised patients.). He had been taking amlodipine, furosemide and metolazone, which had been stopped upon admission.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared uncomfortable, lying in bed with eyes closed. The temperature was 100.8°F (The combination of fever along with the patient's neurological signs is highly concerning for central nervous system infection, although stroke and intracranial bleeding can sometimes cause low-grade fever.) (38.2°C), blood pressure 161/121 mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The head, neck, chest, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were normal. The patient responded to painful stimuli but was unable to answer questions or follow commands. The cranial nerves were intact. The neck was stiff and extremities were rigid. Attempts to lift the patient by the back of the head led to elevation of the entire body (This patient has meningismus. When the meninges are inflamed as in meningitis, the neck and spine resist flexing, as flexion stretches the meninges. This symptom, along with the fever and mental status changes, indicate that the patient has meningoencephalitis: inflammation of both meninges and brain.), akin to lifting a rigid board. The skin texture was diffusely stiff and fibrotic, with scattered confluent patches of hypopigmentation.

The white blood cell count was 19,500 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-11,000). Blood levels of electrolytes and tests of hepatic and renal function were normal. The serum level of (1-3)-beta-D-glucan was 37 pg/mL (A normal beta-D-glucan argues against most fungal infections, but a few fungi, notably Xygomycetes and Cryptococcus usually do not cause elevated levels.) (reference range normal less than 60) and galactomannan (A component of the cell of the fungus, Aspergillus. Elevated serum galactomannan levels are used to diagnose invasive infection with this organism.) was less than 0.5 (reference range normal less than 0.5).

Vancomycin, ampicillin, meropenem, metronidazole, and acyclovir (In meningitis, infection proceeds so rapidly that broad antimicrobial coverage must be started immediately, without waiting for diagnostic culture. In this immunocompromised patient, the differential diagnosis is very broad, necessitating multiple antibiotics and an antiviral medication.) were administered intravenously. Prednisone was changed to hydrocortisone at stress doses.
A lumbar puncture was performed; the opening pressure was not recorded. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed clear fluid, with 175 red cells per cubic millimeter, 33 white cells per cubic millimeter (This is elevated, but much lower than would be seen in most cases of bacterial meningitis.) (27% polymorphonuclear cells, 49% lymphocytes (The predominance of lymphocytes also argues against bacterial infection.) and 3% eosinophils), protein 94 mg/dL and glucose 61 mg/dL (concurrent serum glucose 119 mg/dL). Gram staining of the CSF is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Gram stain of CSF.
diagnosis:
Cryptococcal meningitis in an immunocompromised patient after stem cell transplantation.

Gram staining (This stain is most often used to detect bacterial infections, but sometimes fungi are seen as deeply Gram-positive, but larger than Gram-positive bacteria. In cryptococcal meningitis, the organisms are usually not seen on Gram stain, but can often be seen with an India Ink stain. In an immunocompromised host with clinical data suggesting a non-bacterial process, it is important to know that cryptococcal infection is a possibility so that tests such as the India Ink stain and cryptococcal antigen measurement can be performed.) of the CSF showed gram-positive budding yeast cells of variable sizes, ranging from spherical to football-shaped, consistent with Cryptococcus (Figure 1). Their thin cell wall differentiates them from Blastomyces, while budding and lack of endospores distinguish them from Coccidioides immitis.
Fungal culture (Culture confirms the diagnosis but, in meningitis, therapy must be started before culture results data are available.) of the CSF grew Cryptococcus, and the CSF cryptococcal antigen (In communities with the necessary resources, this is the most common way this infection is diagnosed. The test is highly sensitive and specific and the data are available much more rapidly than culture.) was positive at a titer of 1:512.

The patient was started on induction therapy (For some serious infections, therapy starts with high-dose intravenous induction to contain the infection, followed by a longer course of usually oral therapy to consolidate the cure of the illness.) with liposomal amphotericin B (Amphotericin is an anti-fungal that acts by binding ergosterol, a components of fungal cell membranes, but not those of animal cells. When formulated in liposomes, much higher doses can be given with less renal toxicity.) (5 mg/kg every 24 hours, intravenously) and flucytosine (25 mg/kg every 6 hours by nasogastric tube). His mental status and meningismus rapidly improved. Two additional lumbar punctures were performed for management of increased intracranial pressure; on the fourth hospital day the opening pressure was 37 cm H2O and on the sixth hospital day the opening pressure was 12 cm H2O. By the sixth day of treatment, the CSF cryptococcal antigen had decreased to 1:8 and fungal stain and culture were negative.
Fluconazole desensitization (Through mechanisms that are not well-understood, many patients with severe allergies to a drug can receive it safely if the drug is given first in extremely low doses, then with escalating doses over several hours until therapeutic levels are reached. Desensitization is maintained as long as the drug is given but allergy returns when the drug is stopped.) was performed because of a history of rash with this class of antifungal medication. After two weeks of induction therapy, he successfully transitioned to oral fluconazole 800 mg daily for consolidation therapy for eight weeks, and then the dose was decreased to 200 mg daily for long-term maintenance therapy.

Cryptococcus (which is Latin for “hidden sphere”) is a genus of saprophytic fungus that is found throughout the world and primarily causes disease in immunocompromised hosts. The two species that are associated with human disease are Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gatii. Although the fungus is classically associated with bird droppings, most patients who develop disease report no history of close bird contact.
In HIV-negative patients, up to 20-60% of cryptococcal disease occurs in organ transplant recipients and consequently, it is important to consider the infection in this population [Vilchez et al. 2002]. In organ transplant recipients, symptoms can be severe and can progress rapidly, as in the case presented, and the mortality rate is high. One review found the overall rate of C. neoformans infection in transplant patients to be 2.8% with a death rate of 42% [Husain et al. 2001]. The immunosuppressive medications, in particular prednisone, are probably the most important risk factor for infection in this group of patients [Vilchez et al. 2002]. Other immunosuppressants, like cyclosporine and the calcineurin inhibitors, may have some antifungal properties, but their immunosuppressant effects are more powerful, and patients taking these drugs are still at high risk for developing cryptococcal infection. However, the type of immunosuppressant medication may influence clinical manifestations; according to one study, tacrolimus use made central nervous system manifestations less likely and skin, soft-tissue or osteoarticular involvement more likely [Husain et al. 2001]. A similar study suggested that an increasing rate of calcineurin inhibitors has led to a higher proportion of isolated pulmonary infection as opposed to disseminated or central nervous system disease [Sun et al. 2009]. Most infections occur more than six months after transplantation and can occur years later, as in the case presented, suggesting that the majority of infections occur by means of primary infection, though earlier infection and reactivation disease can occur.
Most data from this field comes from the solid organ transplant literature. In one series of solid organ transplant recipients, the incidence was higher after heart transplant and lower after kidney transplant [Vilchez et al. 2002]. Studies have also documented a risk of transmitted infection via solid organ transplant and have suggested evaluating donors for evidence of disease [Baddley et al. 2011]. Data from patients receiving stem cell transplants is scarce. In one of the few studies on this topic, it was shown that cryptococcosis is much more rare in hematopoetic stem cell transplant recipients than solid organ transplant recipients (only 9 cases worldwide in HSCT recipients documented) [Sun et al. 2009]. This report also showed that more cases occurred with autologous transplantation than allogeneic transplantation and that cases tend to occur earlier with autologous transplantation compared to allogeneic.
Diagnostic tests for cryptococcal meningitis include detection of the polysaccharide capsular antigen or detection of yeast by the India ink stain or routine fungal stain and culture [Vilchez et al. 2002]. The polysaccharide capsular antigen test can be done on serum, CSF or other samples like bronchoalveolar lavage and pleural fluid, though these are less standardized than the CSF and serum tests. There is a high rate of positivity of both CSF and serum cryptococcal antigen tests in disseminated and meningeal disease in transplant recipients, and a much lower rate in isolated pulmonary disease [Vilchez et al. 2002].
The treatment of cryptococcal meningitis involves decreasing immunosuppressant medication doses if possible, initiation of antifungal therapy, and management of elevated intracranial pressure. Antifungal therapy is divided into three states: induction, consolidation, and chronic maintenance therapy. For organ transplant recipients, the 2010 Infectious Disease Society of America Guidelines recommends liposomal amphotericin B or amphotericin B lipid complex (ABLC) plus flucytosine for 2 weeks of induction therapy (4-6 weeks if flucytosine not included) followed by fluconazole at 400-800 mg daily for 8 weeks of consolidation therapy and then 200-400 mg daily for chronic maintenance therapy for a minimum of 6-12 months [Perfect et al. 2010]. A key feature of this case is that the patient had been receiving micafungin as an outpatient because of an elevated serum beta-glucan test and pulmonary nodules, but micafungin does not treat Cryptococcus and did not protect him from this infection. It is difficult to know whether this patient’s elevated beta-glucan test was the result of cryptococcal infection, which rarely raises the beta-glucan level, or the result of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) administration, which may also elevate the beta-glucan level and cause false-positive results [Ostrosky-Zeichner et al. 2005].
It is important to note that initial worsening of cryptococcal meningitis symptoms may be caused by increased intracranial pressure rather than failure of treatment; elevated pressure should be managed with serial lumbar punctures and, if necessary, lumbar drains or ventriculoperitoneal shunts.

title: 2012 July-August Featured Case: A man with HIV infection and new onset ankle pai
history:
2012 July-August Featured Case: A man with HIV infection and new onset ankle pain, leg edema and erythema.
A man in his thirties, on antiretroviral therapy for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and with a history of previous treatment for tuberculous pleurisy and syphilis, was well until approximately 6 weeks before presentation when he had unprotected intercourse with another HIV-positive man. Shortly thereafter, sore throat, chills and subjective fevers developed, followed by a diffuse whole body erythematous rash. He was seen in a medical walk-in clinic. On examination, a morbilliform maculopapular, erythematous rash that blanched was present on his anterior torso, back, arms and thighs. A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was positive at 1:2 dilution, which was stable compared to routine testing performed one month before. A viral exanthem was diagnosed, and he was advised to return in 2 weeks for another RPR titer.
The symptoms and physical findings resolved in several days. Four weeks later, he contacted his medical providers because of intermittent bone pain of 2 weeks' duration, and skin irritation over the Achilles tendon region of the left ankle. He reported his skin was slightly red and warm, with a blister. He denied fever, chills, gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms. He was advised to return for examination and follow-up RPR testing.

HIV infection had been diagnosed 15 years before in the setting of weight loss, fevers, and fatigue. CD4 T-lymphocytes cell count at diagnosis was 330 cells per cubic millimeter, and the level of HIV nucleic acid was 1600 copies per milliliter. The patient began antiretroviral (ARV) therapy shortly after diagnosis, then stopped after 4 years because he felt well. The CD4 T-lymphocyte count decreased to less than 100 per cubic millimeter. He resumed ARV therapy four years before this evaluation. Two months before this evaluation, the CD4 count was 599 per cubic millimeter, and the level of HIV RNA was undetectable.
Eleven years before presentation, anal human papilloma virus had been diagnosed and local surgical excision performed.
Five years before presentation, pleurisy and pneumonia were diagnosed. A presumptive diagnosis of tuberculosis was made, and a 6-month course of antituberculous medications (4 drugs for 2-3 months, then 2 drugs for 4 months) was administered. Four years before presentation, a diagnosis of pneumonia was made, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) was administered for probable Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and, as noted above, the patient resumed ARV therapy.
Approximately 22 months before this presentation, he developed a rash on his arms, chest, palms, and soles; a diagnosis of syphilis was made. Benzyl penicillin was reportedly administered intramuscularly once weekly for 3 weeks. Eight months before this evaluation, he was noted to have a persistently positive RPR titer at 1:128 dilution. A CSF examination did not show evidence for neurosyphilis. He received another course of treatment for syphilis with benzathine penicillin intramuscularly once weekly for 3 weeks. After re-treatment, the RPR titer declined to 1:2 dilution when measured two months before this encounter.

He was born Mexico, had moved to Costa Rica 6 years before and to New England 18 months before this presentation. He was sexually active with men. He exercised regularly.

There was no family history of cancer, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease.

His medications included abacavir (300mg every 12 hours), lopinavir and ritonavir in combination (200mg/50mg, 2 tablets every 12 hours) and maraviroc (150mg twice daily. He also took ibuprofen (200mg 1-2 tablets every 8 hours as needed for pain).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, pulse 61 beats per minute, weight 194lb (88.2kg) and temperature 98.1°F (36.7C). There was mild retropharyngeal erythema, without exudates. Inguinal lymph nodes (sub-centimeter) were palpable and non-tender. There was erythema on both anterior shins (Figures 1 and 2), which was partially blanching; purpuric lesions were also present. The area of erythema was warm. There was 1+ anterior tibial edema bilaterally and trace to no pedal edema. The knees and ankles were tender to palpation and painful with active and passive range of motion, without joint effusion, warmth or erythema. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The complete blood count was normal (including the white blood cell count at 8100 cells per cubic millimeter, with 76% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes and 1% eosinophils), as were blood levels of electrolytes, glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, calcium, tests of renal and liver function and the urinalysis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 47 mm per hour (reference range 0-13).
diagnosis:
Disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea) infection with enthesopathy in a patient with HIV infection and prior syphilis.

An anal culture for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (also known as gonococcus or GC) was positive. Figure 3 shows growth on a JEMBEC agar plate and Figure 4 subculture growth on Thayer-Martin agar. Figure 5 demonstrates a gram stain of the cultured organism. Antibiotic susceptibility testing revealed that this gonococcus was resistant to penicillin G and tetracycline, intermediate to ciprofloxacin, and susceptible to ceftriaxone and spectinomycin. Pharyngeal culture for the organism was negative, as was urinary PCR testing for GC and Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid. Blood cultures were sterile. A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test was unchanged and reactive at 1:2 dilution. Testing for Lyme disease (antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi) and hepatitis B virus infection was negative.
Figure 3. Anal culture on JEMBEC agar plate.
Figure 4. Growth on a Thayer-Martin subculture plate.
Figure 5. Gram stain of organism, under oil at 100x magnification.

Azithromycin (250 mg 4 tablets (1gram) orally, once) and ceftriaxone injection (20 mg/ml solution, 1 gram injection every 24 hours for 48 hours) was administered, followed by oral cefixime 400mg orally, twice a day for an additional 6 days. At follow-up one month later, he reported some residual joint aches and fatigue but was otherwise improved, and a follow-up rectal culture on a JEMBEC plate was negative.

Of the possible diagnoses listed in the differential, recurrent secondary syphilis was a consideration based on the clinical history, but the absence of a rise in the RPR titer made this diagnosis less likely. Although the patient lived in an endemic area for Lyme disease, the initial rash was not typical for erythema migrans. Furthermore, Lyme disease more frequently causes a monoarthritis than the diffuse arthralgias and enthesopathy that this patient described. The clinical syndrome in this patient could correspond to an uncommon serum sickness-like presentation of acute hepatitis B virus (seen in fewer than 10% of cases). The unprotected sexual encounter is a plausible route of transmission, but the antecedent rash seen in this patient would be atypical. The serum sickness-like phase of hepatitis B virus infection can precede overt jaundice; however, this patient had no symptoms of nausea or vomiting and no elevation in transaminases that typify acute hepatitis B. Reactive arthritis was a reasonable consideration for his arthralgias; however, this patient did not have conjunctivitis, urethritis, or sacroiliitis, which are often seen with this condition. The exposure history, timing, and symptom complex all suggested the possibility of disseminated gonococcal infection; the positive rectal culture and clinical response to antibiotics confirmed this diagnosis [Rice PA, 2005].
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a common sexually transmitted pathogen that can cause asymptomatic infection (more common in women) as well as a multitude of clinical syndromes. The most common clinical presentation is urethritis; however, N. gonorrhoeae can also cause inflammation of other mucosal surfaces, including the cervix, the conjunctivae, the oropharynx, and the rectum. More serious complications include pelvic inflammatory disease in women, purulent arthritis, and a constellation of symptoms called disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI). DGI is characterized by tenosynovitis, dermatitis, arthralgias (typically of appendicular joints), and skin lesions [Rice PA, 2005]. Rare complications include perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome), and less commonly endocarditis or meningitis.
The type of clinical syndrome exhibited by a patient infected with gonococcus (asymptomatic, mucosal inflammation, septic arthritis, DGI) is thought to depend upon both microbial and host factors. For instance, certain strains of N. gonorrhoeae are thought more likely to cause DGI and minimal genital inflammation [Marrazzo JM et al., 2010; Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010; Tapsall JW et al., 1992]. Considering host factors, women are far more likely than men to exhibit asymptomatic infection and are three times as likely to exhibit DGI. Other host factors such as pregnancy, recent menses, and complement deficiency predispose to DGI [Marrazzo JM et al. 2010; Holmes KK et al., 1971; Wise CM et al., 1994; Ellison RT 3rd et al. 1987].
The diagnostic approach for gonorrhea depends on the clinical syndrome suspected. Symptomatic urethritis should be assessed by Gram stain of purulent exudate, which has excellent sensitivity and specificity in this context; however sensitivity is much reduced in asymptomatic infection [Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010]. Because of its improved performance characteristics in asymptomatic patients, nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) has replaced Gram stain and culture for first-line diagnostic testing of urine or vaginal swabs from asymptomatic individuals in much of the US [Marrazzo JM et al., 2010; Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010]. NAATs are not yet FDA approved for pharyngeal or rectal specimens, though preliminary data suggest that they may ultimately be useful [Marrazzo JM et al. 2010; Schachter J et al., 2008]. Culture is still important as well; in many cases (such as this one) it may be the only clue to disseminated infection. Additionally, it allows for susceptibility testing, which is of increasing importance given the rapid emergence of antibiotic resistance (see below). Cultures from non-sterile sites (e.g., oropharynx, rectum) should be inoculated shortly after collection onto appropriate pre-warmed media (usually selective Thayer-Martin media), then placed rapidly into a carbon dioxide containing environment. This can be accomplished either via a candle jar in a 35-to-37 degree celsius incubator, or (as for this case) by using a John E Martin Biological Environment Chamber (JEMBEC) plate, with a carbon dioxide generating tablet added at the time of inoculation, prior to incubation [Levi MH, 1997]. In all cases, patients with suspected gonococcal infection should also be screened for Chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis, given shared risk factors and rates of coinfection.
Treatment of DGI should include parenteral therapy. While few data are available to guide choice or duration of therapy, current recommendations include initial treatment with ceftriaxone (1g once daily). If a patient looks clinically well, or refuses admission, a single dose can be given in clinic via an intramuscular or intravenous route before switching to oral therapy. However, consideration should be given to either admitting the patient, or bringing him or her back to clinic the following day for a second dose of parenteral antibiotics and to confirm response to therapy (both for diagnostic clarity and in view of increasing antibiotic resistance). When clearly clinically improving, patients can be transitioned to oral therapy (as of this writing, typically cefixime 400mg twice daily), to complete 7 to 10 days of total therapy. [Editor's Note: As of August 10, 2012, and after publication of this case, CDC Guidelines for treatment of gonorrhea changed [reference CDC, MMWR 2012]. Before treatment, clinicians are advised to check for updated treatment guidelines.] Antibiotic resistance has emerged as a real threat in gonococcal infections. As such, antimicrobial susceptibility testing should be strongly considered in serious cases and should be pursued in all cases with poor initial response to empiric therapy [Marrazzo JM et al. 2010; Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010]. Fluoroquinolone resistance is sufficiently common that this class is no longer recommended for treatment in the US unless a patient’s isolate is cultured and shown to be susceptible [Marrazzo JM et al. 2010; CDC, 2007; Tapsall JW, 2008]. Even third generation cephalosporins, long the standard of care in the US, have begun to show resistance worldwide [Duncan S and Duncan CJ, 2012; Bolan GA et al.,2012; Martin I et al., 2012; Lo JY et al., 2012; Ross JD and Lewis DA, 2012].
Antibiotic resistance in the US is monitored by the CDC through state and local public health authorities, and the CDC’s Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP) routinely tests available samples to monitor trends. Gonorrhea is a reportable illness, allowing contact tracing and screening of sexual partners. All recent partners should be evaluated, and even those without symptoms of active infection should be considered for antibiotics for presumed asymptomatic gonorrhea and Chlamydia infection [Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010]. All involved parties should be told to abstain from sexual activity until treatment is completed and symptoms have fully resolved [Workowski KA and Berman S, 2010].

title:
A South African girl with dyspnea and cough productive of yellow sputum.
A pre-t
history:
A South African girl with dyspnea and cough productive of yellow sputum.
A pre-teen girl presented to a rural clinic in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa with a history of cough, productive of yellow sputum, shortness of breath, loss of appetite and weight loss, of 3 months' duration. The symptoms had not improved despite a course of amoxicillin.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) was thought to show findings suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis. She was admitted to a rural tuberculosis (TB) hospital and isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide were administered. Sputum specimens on admission were negative for acid-fast bacilli, and subsequent culture was negative.
After 2 months of intensive phase anti-TB therapy, her symptoms persisted. A repeat chest radiograph (Figure 2) was obtained. Two additional sputum specimens stained for acid fast bacilli and cultures were negative.
After 4 months in the hospital, testing for antibodies to HIV-1 was positive. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis was begun, and antituberculous medications continued. After completion of 6 months of intensive phase anti-TB therapy, she remained clinically unchanged. A chest radiograph (Figure 3) was unchanged and three sputum cultures were again negative for tuberculosis. She remained hospitalized on isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide for 11 months. Her clinical condition was unchanged. A pediatric specialist consultation was obtained.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, on presentation.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, after 2 months of anti-TB therapy.
Figure 3. Chest radiograph, after 6 months of anti-TB therapy.

She had been unwell for at least two years before this presentation, though details of her past medical history were limited.

She lived in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa with her aunt before her admission. Her aunt, who was her primary care giver, died while the patient was hospitalized.

The patient's parents were deceased; their HIV status was not known.

Medications included isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill and cachectic. The blood pressure was 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats per minute, temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), and respirations 54 breaths per minute. She weighed 20 kilograms (weight-for-age Z-score -3.9). There was soft mobile submandibular, submental, and cervical adenopathy. There were diffuse crackles throughout all lung fields, with scattered expiratory wheezes and occasional ronchi in the bilateral lower chest. There were no subcostal or abdominal retractions. A prominent second heart sound was heard, with no murmurs. The neck veins were flat and the point of maximal impulse was not displaced. The liver was palpated 3 centimeters below the costal margin. The spleen was not palpable. Her extremities revealed severe digital clubbing.

The level of CD4 T-Lymphocytes was 285 cells per cubic milliliter (11% of lymphocytes were CD4 T lymphocytes). Fifteen sputum specimens, obtained during a 12-month period, were tested for acid fast bacilli and were negative. Six sputum cultures for tuberculosis were negative during that time.
A chest radiograph was repeated (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Chest radiograph, after 12 months of anti-TB therapy.
diagnosis:
Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis (LIP), presumptive, in an Afrcian child with HIV infection.

Based on the history, physical examination, laboratory studies and clinical course, a diagnosis of presumptive lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis (LIP) was made.

Antiretroviral therapy, including efavirinez, lamivudine, and stavudine, was administered, in addition to inhaled bronchodilators and inhaled steroids. After 2 weeks of antiretroviral therapy she developed fever, purulent sputum, and increased work of breathing. She was treated with amoxacillin-clavanulate, with improvement. Tachypnea, dyspnea on exertion, and shortness of breath persisted.
After 2 months of antiretroviral therapy, inhaled bronchodilators and high dose systemic corticosteroids were administered. After 4 weeks of corticosteroids, the respiratory rate improved to 28 breaths per minute. She was able to play without resting, and her shortness of breath and cough improved. She began a slow taper off the steroids and resumed inhaled steroids. After 5 months of antiretroviral therapy her viral load was undetectable (less than 150 copies per milliliter and the absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count increased to 415 cells per cubic millimeter. A distant relative was identified, and she was discharged to that person's care after a 15-month hospital admission. At time of discharge, she had gained 5 kilograms, her cough had improved, and her shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion were improving.

Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis (LIP) is an interstitial lung disease that affects 25 to 40% of perinatally HIV infected children [Andiman WA and Shearer WT, 1998]. The overall etiology of LIP is unknown; however, it is thought to be related to the interaction of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and HIV [Andiman WA, Eastman R, et al. 1985; Montagnier L, et al. 1984; Joshi VV, et al. 1987; Katz BZ, Berkman AB, Shapiro ED. 1992; Bhoopat L, et al. 2010].
Children rarely present before the first year of life [Scott GB, et al. 1989]. Typically, they present with an insidious onset of cough, dyspnea and tachypnea. Auscultation of the chest can reveal wheezes, ronchi, or crackles but is often normal in early presentations. Associated physical findings include: digital clubbing, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and parotid enlargement. In HIV infected children the diagnosis is usually made clinically with the presentation of cough, dyspnea, hypoxia, chest radiographs with bilateral micronodular infiltrates [Marks MJ, et al. 1996; Pitcher RD, et al. 2010] and the exclusion of tuberculosis as an alternate diagnosis.
Treatment involves prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy for the underlying HIV infection. Severe cases often require systemic steroids [Desmarquest P, et al. 1998]. Mild to moderate cases can be controlled with ART, inhaled bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids. There are some reports of the use of intravenous gammaglobulin (IVIG) and hydroxychloroquine that have slowed or stopped the progression of LIP [Laraya-Cuasay LR. 1988; Waters KA, et al. 1991; Campos JM, Simonetti JP. 1993]. Delays in initial diagnosis often lead to bronchiectasis, cystic lung changes and right heart failure [Sheikh S, et al. 1997]. These children often have episodic worsening with recurrent bacterial pneumonias that respond to broad spectrum antibiotics [Sheikh S, et al. 1997]. With prompt diagnosis and early initiation of ART there is often resolution of symptoms [Innes AL, et al. 2004]. However, once there is pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure and evidence of end-organ damage the prognosis is poor despite ART.
Of note, in resource-limited settings, the diagnosis of many infectious diseases is often difficult and presumptive, taking into account the response (or lack thereof) to therapeutic trials. The other diagnosis listed in the differential would most likely have progressed in the absence of specific targeted therapy.

history:
2012 September-October Featured Case: A woman in her seventies was admitted to the hospital because of nausea, vomiting, weakness, diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue and chills.
The patient had been well, with a history of diabetes mellitus and vascular disease, until approximately 4 weeks before when, in mid-summer, she was scratched and bitten numerous times on the arms, legs, and trunk by a stray or feral cat she had taken in.
She was seen at another hospital where amoxicillin-clavulanate, a tetanus booster, and rabies vaccination were reportedly administered, followed by additional rabies immunizations on days 4, 7, and 14. She did not receive a fifth dose on day 21 because she was told it was not needed (she does not recall why). She reported no subsequent warmth, swelling, pain, or swollen glands in the arms, legs, axillae, or groin following the incident. The cat was taken in by an animal society, which intended to observe it; the results of the observation period were not known.
One week before this presentation, in late summer, nausea, vomiting (without hematemesis), abdominal pain, watery non-bloody diarrhea, anorexia, weakness and fatigue developed, associated with intermittent chills. She came to the emergency department. She reported no known fever, headache, numbness, tingling, dyspnea, chest pain or rash.

She had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (with average capillary glucose levels of 160 mg/dl), peripheral neuropathy, multinodular goiter, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, peripheral vascular disease with recent angioplasty in the left leg, esophageal reflux, anemia of chronic inflammation, and chronic knee and wrist pain.

She did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She had not traveled recently.

She lived alone in New England and was retired.

There was a family history of diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease.

She was allergic to sulfa, gemfibrozil, and erythromycin, which had caused rashes.

Medications included diltiazem, valsartan-hydrochlorothiazide, omeprazole, insulin, acetaminophen and acetylsalicylic acid (81 MG).
exam_studies:
She was fully oriented. The temperature was 101.4°F (38.6°C), blood pressure 178/80 mm Hg, pulse 79 beats per minute, respirations 18 per minute and oxygen saturation 98% while breathing ambient air. There was a grade 1-2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left lower sternal border, and heart sounds were otherwise normal. The abdomen was soft, minimally tender to palpation in left lower quadrant, without masses, and there were numerous scratches on her limbs and torso, without erythema or fluctuance. During the physical examination, she often repeated "I am tired" and "I can't remember". The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 12,500 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000; leukocytes 85%, lymphocytes 11%, monocytes 4%), hematocrit 32.9% (ref 36.0-46.0); hemoglobin 11.8gm/dl (ref 12.0-16.0), platelets 142,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150-400). Tests of coagulation were normal. The blood level of sodium was 133 mmol/L (ref 135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (ref 3.4-4.8), carbon dioxide 22.4 mmol/L (ref 23.0-31.9), glucose 166mg/dl (ref 70-110) and urea nitrogen 26mg/dl (ref 8-25); the estimated glomerular filtration rate was 57mL/min/1.73m2 (ref abnormal if <60 mL/min/1.73m2). Levels of chloride, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, lactic acid, creatinine, were normal. Testing for antibodies to platelet factor 4 was negative. Urinalysis revealed 2+ glucose and protein, with few bacteria and squamous cells.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with the administration of intravenous contrast was normal.
Culture of the stool grew normal enteric flora, without evidence of enteric pathogens. There was no evidence of Clostridium difficile toxin, protozoa, or helminth ova, and cultures of the blood and urine were sterile.

She was admitted to the hospital. Intravenous fluids were administered for rehydration, and her other medications continued, with gradual improvement in most symptoms. Fatigue persisted, and on physical therapy evaluation, tremulousness and loss of balance were noted. On the fourth day, a neurological consultant obtained additional history that increased tremor was present for one week, and she had recent mid-to-lower back pain that did not radiate, without bowel or bladder incontinence, headache, neck stiffness or photophobia.
On examination, she was anxious, alert, oriented in full, and with preserved language. She registered 3 of 3 words and recalled 2 of 3 words with word choice. She exhibited spinal tenderness to palpation in mid lumbar region, diminished vibratory sense at the toes bilaterally, 3+ symmetric reflexes except for absent Achilles, a mild fine postural tremor, a positive Romberg test, and diminished vibratory sense at the toes.
On the fifth day, computed tomography (CT) of the head without the administration of contrast (Figure 1) revealed central volume loss and chronic microvascular changes, without evidence of acute disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine with the administration of gadolinium showed focal T11-12 disc enhancement, thought to be related to degenerative joint disease, without abnormal enhancement. A lumbar puncture was performed; analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed a glucose level of 99 mg/dl and total protein level 26 mg/dl, with 20 white cells per cubic millimeter (96% lymphocytes and 4% monocytes) and 4 red cells per cubic millimeter in Tube 1. Gram stain of the CSF showed very few mononuclear cells and no organisms.
Infectious disease consultation was obtained. Her relatives reported that her speech was slower and word-finding difficulties more severe than at baseline, and that she had been relatively confused on admission, with partial improvement since admission.

diagnosis:
Meningoencephalitis caused by West Nile virus.

Testing of the CSF for West Nile virus (WNV) IgM and the West Nile virus plaque reduction neutralization test was positive, compatible with recent infection.
Testing for antibodies (IgM) to Eastern Equine encephalitis (EEE) was negative. Testing of the CSF for Herpes simplex virus (types 1 and 2) DNA and enterovirus RNA was negative, as was testing the blood for antibodies to Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana (IgG and IgM) and Treponema pallidum. Culture of the CSF was sterile. Stool specimens were negative for C. difficile toxin and viruses.

Before the results of the testing were known, doxycycline and rifampin (14-day course) were administered empirically for treatment of possible cat scratch disease. The patient's symptoms improved, and she was discharged on the 9th day, to a short-term rehabilitation facility for physical and occupational therapy to improve her gait, balance and activities of daily living.
Results of the positive diagnostic test results were received three weeks after discharge.

Among the possible diagnoses considered, Bartonella henselae meningoencephalitis was given strong consideration, as so-called “cat-scratch encephalopathy” was compatible with her exposure history, symptom time course, epidemiology, and laboratory findings. This entity is described as an encephalopathy of varying severity with paucicellular mononuclear pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid, with total WBC count generally less than 50 [Baylor P, et al. 2007; Pinto Jr VL, et al. 2008; Marra CM 1995]. Though rare, in patients with cat-scratch disease, encephalopathy is 6-fold more common in patients over 60 years of age than in younger patients, while lymphadenitis (which this patient did not have) is less common in elderly patients [Ronen B-A, et al. 2005]. However, her serological testing was negative for Bartonella exposure, which would be unusual given the duration of symptoms and time since the cat exposure.
While rabies is a consideration in a patient with encephalitis after this type of exposure to a wild animal, this is a rare entity in the US, and furthermore cats are an atypical vector. Additionally, she was appropriately vaccinated for this exposure, which decreases the likelihood of acquiring disease. Finally, her indolent course with improving encephalitis symptoms was incompatible with rabies encephalitis. Pasteurella multocida would be expected to cause a more fulminant illness. It is a gram-negative bacillus that can be transmitted by animal bites or scratches, typically causing localized inflammation with systemic toxicity and often high leukocytosis, and though disseminated infection can result in meningitis, this typically occurs in very sick patients, and more proximal to the animal exposure rather than the slow, indolent course this patient experienced [Oehler RL, et al. 2009; Green BT, et al. 2002]. While this patient lived in an endemic area for Lyme disease, she did not exhibit other signs of Lyme disease that typically precede neuroborreliosis. Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is clinically compatible with this patient’s presentation, and indeed there is extensive overlap between this flaviviral syndrome and that of the patient’s ultimate diagnosis, West Nile virus encephalitis. However, serologies for EEE were negative, while those for West Nile virus were positive. Listeria and herpes simplex virus infections were also considered; testing for these pathogens was negative.
West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne RNA virus of the Flavivirus genus, first described in the 1930s as a cause of an influenza-like febrile illness; by the 1950s, it was also recognized to cause meningoencephalitis in rare cases [Vaughn DW, et al. 2010]. It is one of the most widely distributed of the arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses), found in Africa, southern Europe, the Middle East, Australia, and (more recently) the Americas, particularly North America. The virus exhibits an enzootic life cycle in birds and mosquitoes. Humans are exposed by the bite of an infected mosquito and along with other mammals (notably horses) are thought to be dead-end hosts, incapable of transmitting the disease due to low-level viremia insufficient to re-infect mosquitoes [Vaughn DW, et al. 2010]. Cases of human transmission are only reported in the context of blood transfusions or transplanted organs [Pealer LN, et al.2003; Ravindra KV, et al. 2004]. Given the mosquito vector, the disease exhibits a classic seasonality, peaking in the late summer and early fall. The emergence of this illness in North America is relatively new, with the first reports occurring in 1999 with 62 confirmed human cases in New York [Nash D, et al. 2001]. Following its introduction to North America, it rapidly spread across the continent, reaching a peak of 10,000 clinical cases with 286 cases of neurologic disease in 2003. This year (2012) has to date the highest incidence of cases of West Nile virus infection reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) since that peak in 2003, and the second-highest on record [CDC 2012]. However, serological surveys of blood donor samples suggest that the incidence of antibodies to West Nile virus is considerably higher than previously recognized, leading to the recognition that only approximately 20% of infected people develop symptoms, and only 1 in 150 develops central nervous system disease [Pealer LN, et al.2003; Ravindra KV, et al. 2004]. However, whether due to reporting bias or a shifting epidemic, fully half of the reported cases to the CDC this year are neuroinvasive disease [CDC 2012].
Clinically, West Nile virus infection can present anywhere from asymptomatic infection (the majority of cases), to the classic symptoms of an influenza-like illness with fever, often with some combination of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, eye pain, and pharyngitis, as well as a rash in less than 50% of patients, to neuroinvasive disease such as meningitis and/or encephalitis [Zou S, et al. 2010]. It has an incubation period of between 2 and 14 days after exposure to an infected mosquito, though this may be longer in an immunocompromised host. Though the acute phase of illness is typically only 3-6 days, patients often report persistent symptoms, with up to half complaining of fatigue lasting more than a month [Petersen LR 2012]. Nervous system involvement may take the form of meningitis (more common in younger patients) or encephalitis (more common in the elderly). Risk factors for neuroinvasive disease include old age, alcohol use, and diabetes mellitus. Distinguishing features of West Nile encephalitis may include prominent extrapyramidal symptoms, or a poliomyelitis-like syndrome with acute flaccid paralysis that may occur before, during, or after the encephalitic phase of illness (Sejvar JJ, Leis AA, et al. 2003; Sejvar JJ, Haddad MB, et al. 2003]. Neuroinvasive disease often portends a protracted course of illness, with appreciable mortality (up to 15%) and, more strikingly, persistent neurological deficits reported in more than half of patients one year after symptom onset [Weiss D, et al. 2001; Loeb M, et al. 2008; Carson PJ, et al. 2006]. Fortunately, the patient described in this case report has enjoyed a full recovery, with no neurological complaints on follow-up with her primary care physician.
Diagnosis is most commonly achieved by serologic testing in a patient with an appropriate clinical syndrome in an endemic region at a plausible time of year. In addition to the clinical syndrome described above, laboratory studies can show normal or elevated total leukocyte counts. Cases of meningitis or meningoencephalitis typically show a lymphocytic pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid (though neutrophilia has been described as well), often with elevated total protein and normal glucose [Tyler KL, et al. 2006]. The most appropriate specific diagnostic test is serum and CSF antibodies, both IgM and IgG, often detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). These typically seroconvert quite early in illness, with IgM appearing by 4 days and IgG by 8 days of illness. IgM is positive in nearly all patients by 10 days and may remain positive for up to 6 months or more [Busch MP, et al.2008; Roehrig JT, et al. 2003], and CSF IgM may be the first detectable antibody in patients with neuroinvasive disease. Acute illness can also be detected by nucleic acid amplification testing, which may be a useful adjunct in endemic areas where an IgM may reflect prior infection [Tilley PA, et al. 2006]. The plaque reduction neutralization test, which was done for our patient, is a more specific test for flavivirus antibodies and can be used to rule out false-positive ELISAs.
Treatment of West Nile virus infection is largely supportive, including seizure control, intubation, and monitoring and management of cerebral edema as appropriate for neuroinvasive disease. Several immunomodulatory treatment modalities are being explored, but none is yet supported by clinical trials. Case reports suggest possible benefit to interferon alpha, though causality is in question [Sejvar JJ, Haddad MB, et al. 2003; Kalil AC, et al. 2005]. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) is thought to be possibly helpful in immunosuppressed hosts [Planitzer CB, et al. 2007; Agrawal AG, Petersen LR. 2003], and further investigations of this therapy are underway at the time of this publication. Ribavirin is to be avoided because of evidence of possible harm in uncontrolled studies [Chowers MY, et al. 2001]. While vaccines have been approved for use in horses and are under investigation for possible use in humans, the mainstay of prevention at present is mosquito avoidance, both by individual practices and by public health measures. In addition, the US and Canada have adopted blood donor screening because of concerns about transmission of illness from asymptomatic viremic donors [Busch MP, et al. 2005].

title: 2012 IDWeek Case presentation: A man with HIV infection and AIDS, and increasing
history:
2012 IDWeek Case presentation: A man with HIV infection and AIDS, and increasing dyspnea.
A man in his twenties with a history of HIV infection and AIDS was admitted to a hospital with a 1-month history of increasing dyspnea. A chest radiograph reportedly showed bilateral pneumonia. Azithromycin and ceftriaxone were administered intravenously, however, his symptoms worsened. Five days later, a repeat chest radiograph revealed bilateral pneumothoraces. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, performed with intravenous contrast, revealed large bilateral hydropneumothoraces with multifocal cystic spaces and diffuse infiltrates. Chest tubes were placed bilaterally, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and prednisone were administered empirically for treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia. Large air leaks were noted from each of the chest tubes, and the pneumothoraces persisted. No organisms were isolated despite multiple sputum cultures.
Thirteen days after presentation, he was transferred to a tertiary care facility for further evaluation and management. Upon transfer, treatment for Pneumocystis and bacterial pneumonia were continued. Symptoms upon transfer included cough, shortness of breath, and tachycardia.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection had been diagnosed 3 years before admission. Approximately 6 weeks before admission, the absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 15 cells per cubic millimeter and the level of HIV nucleic acid (viral load) was 364,639 copies per milliliter (mL). Emtricitabine-tenofovir in combination and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir were begun three weeks before this admission. Outpatient adherence to antiretroviral medications was uncertain.
A diagnosis of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia with associated pneumothorax was made approximately 7 months before admission. He also had a history of genital herpes simplex infection.

He smoked two packs daily for six years until three weeks before this presentation. He reported no alcohol or illicit drug use.

The patient had been incarcerated.

He had no allergies.

His prescribed outpatient medications included emtricitabine-tenofovir in combination (200/300mg daily), ritonavir (100mg daily), atazanavir (300mg daily), azithromycin (1200mg weekly) and trimethoprim(TMP)-sulfamethoxazole(SMX) (double-strength, daily), but his adherence was not confirmed. On transfer, his medications included emtricitabine-tenofovir in combination, ritonavir, atazanavir, prednisone (40 mg twice daily, orally), TMP-SMX (320 mg based on TMP dose, every 8 hours, intravenously), ceftriaxone (2 gm every 24 hours, intravenously) and azithromycin (500 mg every 24 hours, intravenously).
exam_studies:
On initial evaluation the patient was in minimal distress. The blood pressure was 127/110 mm Hg, pulse 108 to 139 beats per minute, temperature 98.1°F (36.7°C), respirations 18 to 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96-100% while breathing two liters supplemental oxygen through nasal cannula. The breath sounds were decreased bilaterally, and bilateral chest tubes were in place, with evidence of air leaks. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

On the day of admission, after approximately 3 weeks of antiretroviral therapy, the absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 23 cells per cubic millimeter and the level of HIV nucleic acid was 4729 copies per mL. A chest radiograph performed on admission is shown (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.

The patient was admitted to the medical intensive care unit in the tertiary care hospital. Five days after admission, bronchoscopy was performed, with balloon occlusion of identifiable air leaks and placement of endobronchial valves. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was not sent for Pneumocystis jiroveci testing. Empiric therapy for Pneumocystis pneumonia was continued and the patient was transferred to the medical floor one week later.
The patient completed three weeks of empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and a prednisone taper for Pneumocystis pneumonia. He remained clinically stable, but air leaks persisted from chest tubes despite endobronchial valve placement. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, performed with intravenous contrast one month after admission to the tertiary care hospital revealed interval worsening of bilateral hydropneumothoraces, with diffuse infiltrates and fluid levels suggestive of infection or inflammation (Figures 2 and 3) when compared to CT imaging done prior to transfer.
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with lung biopsy was performed on the right lung and demonstrated severe bullous disease in the upper lung lobe with two chronic fistula tracts into the upper lobe from chest tubes, and minor bullae in the middle and lower lobes. A right upper lobectomy was performed and lung tissue sent for pathology (Figure 4, hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain).
Four days later, VATS procedure was performed on the left lung, with wedge resection of the left upper lobe and mechanical pleurodesis.
Figure 2. CT of the chest. Arrows indicate chest tube placement.
Figure 3. CT of the chest.
Figure 4. H and E stain of lung tissue, 200x magnification.
diagnosis:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

Pathological examination of lung tissue obtained by VATS (Figures 3, 4 and 5) demonstrated chronic pneumonitis with abundant viral cytopathic changes morphologically consistent with infection. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figures 4 and 5) of the tissue revealed enlarged cells (cytomegaly), with large intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions and a surrounding halo. Pathological examination with cytomegalovirus (CMV) immunoperoxidase stain (Figure 6) stained enlarged nuclei. There was no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy.
Special stains for fungi, acid fast bacilli and Warthin-Starry stain were negative. Testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency was negative.
Figure 5. H and E stain of lung tissue, 400x magnification.
Figure 6. CMV immunoperoxidase stain of lung tissue, 400x magnification.

Ganciclovir was administered intravenously, with clinical improvement during the following three weeks.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis in HIV-infected patients is exceptionally rare. Although CMV is sometimes cultured from bronchoalveolar fluid in AIDS patients, it is rarely a cause of actual disease. Criteria for establishing diagnosis of CMV pneumonitis includes finding pulmonary infiltrates on a chest radiograph, presence of characteristic intracellular inclusions in lung tissue or bronchoalveolar macrophages, and absence of other pulmonary pathogens based on microbiologic studies or absence of response to empiric therapy [Rodriguez-Barradas et al. 1996]. A definitive diagnosis requires correlation of clinical findings with biopsy results demonstrating viral inclusions.
Pneumothorax in HIV patients is most commonly caused by Pneumocystis jiroveci. There are no reported cases of CMV pneumonitis with pneumothorax; a recent case report documented CMV pneumonitis causing pneumomediastinum [Katsidzira et al 2011]. Other possible causes of pneumothorax in AIDS patients include underlying lung diseases such as bullous emphysema, bacterial pneumonia with pneumatocele, and secondary pneumothorax. Except for tobacco abuse, there were no identifiable causes of bullous lung disease in our patient. Testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency was negative.
Pneumonia in a patient with AIDS warrants diagnostic testing for specific opportunistic pathogens. CMV pneumonitis, though rare in HIV/AIDS patients, should be considered in the differential diagnosis in patients with an absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count of less than 100 cells per cubic millimeter. Early diagnosis and treatment may be life-saving for the patient.

title: 2012 IDWeek Case presentation: A man in his thirties with neurosarcoidosis devel
history:
2012 IDWeek Case presentation: A man in his thirties with neurosarcoidosis developed stuttering and drooling.
The patient was well until approximately three days before admission when stuttering and drooling developed. On presentation to a local hospital, he reportedly had a seizure. Blood tests were obtained and a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis was made. He was stabilized and was transferred to another hospital.

Diagnoses of pulmonary and neurosarcoidosis had been made two years earlier, and he had been on glucocorticosteroid therapy chronically. He also had Type 2 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus, diabetic neuropathy, hypertension and chronic hearing loss in the right ear.

He smoked marijuana and tobacco (1 pack for 15 years) daily.

He was exposed to paint fumes at work, and had been incarcerated in the past. He owned a dog.

Medications included dexamethasone (6 mg twice daily, orally), metformin (1000 mg twice daily, orally), insulin (glargine and lispro) and gabapentin.
exam_studies:
The patient was alert, oriented, and appropriately interactive, and appeared well. The blood pressure was 124/69 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, temperature 98.9°F (37.2°C), and peripheral oxygen saturation 92% while breathing ambient air. There was mild flattening of the left nasolabial fold. The abdomen was protuberant, with abdominal striae. There was hearing loss in the right ear and a mild sensory loss in both feet. The remainder of the examination, including ophthalmologic and motor examinations, was normal.

The white cell count was 8400 cells per cubic millimeter (differential including neutrophils 77%, lymphocytes 16% and band forms 3%); hemoglobin 11.2 gm/dL and platelets 164,000 per cubic millimeter. The blood level of glucose was 418 mg/dl, sodium 123 mmol/L, anion gap 17 mmol/L; the remainder of the routine chemistry profile and tests of liver function were normal.
A radiograph of the chest (Figure 01) showed an opacity in the right base. CT of the chest (Figure 02) with the administration of contrast showed a small focal airspace opacity within the lateral aspect of the right lower lobe, which contained a small air fluid level associated with a small right pleural effusion and small mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast enhancement showed six ring-enhancing lesions: two in the right fronto-temporal region, two in the left frontal region, one in the right parasagittal frontal lobe and a left gyrus rectus multi-compartment ring-enhancing lesion (see Figures 03 and 04).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.
Figure 3. Sagittal T1-weighted MR image.
Figure 4. Axial T1-weighted MR image.

He was admitted to the intensive care unit.
The patient’s HIV serology, quantiferon-TB gold test and serum galactomannan were negative and blood cultures remained sterile. An echocardiogram showed no vegetations. Cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated 2 white cells per cubic millimeter, and normal levels of protein and glucose; Gram stain, India ink and cryptococcal antigen testing were negative; culture was sterile.
A bronchoalveolar lavage (without biopsy) was normal. An image-guided biopsy of a lesion (Figure 05) was performed. Histopathological examination of the tissue showed neutrophils, plasma cells, and lymphocytes, consistent with acute and chronic inflammation. Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stain (Figure 06), GMS stain (Figure 07) and Calcofluor stain (Figure 08) are shown.
Figure 5. Biopsy of lesion.
Figure 6. H and E stain of brain lesion.
Figure 7. GMS stain of brain aspirate.
Figure 8. Calcofluor stain of frontal abscess aspirate.
diagnosis:
Multifocal cerebral phaeohyphomycosis due to Curvularia.

GMS stain showed numerous fungal hyphal forms (Figure 07). Calcofluor stain showed narrow filamentous hyphal forms with acute branching angles (Figure 08). CNS Aspergillosis was suspected and the patient was started on voriconazole.
Two weeks later, his culture grew a pigmented fungi, which was identified as Curvularia sp. Figure 09 shows wet mount microscopy of Curvularia.
Figure 9. Wet mount microscopy with multicellular conidia of Curvularia.

An MRI scan performed 3 weeks later showed no change in the size of the lesions, but there was a mild increase in the surrounding vasogenic edema. He was readmitted to the hospital where he was continued on voriconazole and liposomal amphotericin was added.
To eradicate this infection, he underwent a two-staged surgical approach to remove the six lesions in both hemispheres through two separate craniotomies (Figures 10 and 11). All surgical specimens grew Curvularia sp. that were susceptible to voriconazole (MIC <= 0.06). Dual antifungal therapy was continued intravenously for 3 weeks; he was then discharged to home on oral voriconazole with the plan to treat for 6 to 12 months. A follow-up MRI 3 months later showed a stable post-surgical appearance of his brain with no new regions of enhancement.
Figure 10. Intra-operative digital photograph of the frontal cortex containing a posterior frontal fungal abscess.
Figure 11. Resected fungal abscess

Phaeohyphomycosis infections of the central nervous system (CNS) have been reported in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. Most of the immunocompromised patients with this type of infection had malignancy, solid organ transplant or neutropenia. Phaeohyphomycosis has rarely been reported in patients with suppressed immune system from steroids [Revankar et al. 2004]. This case illustrates the fact that patients with pharmacologic immunosuppression related to chronic steroid therapy may be at increased risk of developing CNS phaeohyphomycosis, and that this diagnosis should be included in the differential diagnosis of brain abscesses in such patients.
In CNS phaeohyphomycosis, the most frequent dematiaceous fungi species isolated is Cladophialophora bantiana [Revankar et al. 2004]. Only 6 cases of CNS phaeohyphomycosis due to a Curvularia spp. have been reported in the literature [Carter and Boudreaux 2004; de la Monte and Hutchins 1985; Ebright et al. 1999; Friedman et al. 1981; Lampert et al. 1977; Revankar et al. 2004; Singh et al. 2008].
The main postulated mechanism of disease is hematogenous spread from a possible subclinical pulmonary focus; direct extension from associated sinus disease is another possibility. In our case, hematogenous spread was the most likely route of dissemination to the brain given the pulmonary lesion, multifocal cerebral lesions and the absence of any history of sinus disease.
CNS phaeohyphomycosis is a severe disease with high mortality rates. Its management is difficult and involves a combination of surgical debridement and antifungal treatment, typically with amphotericin B or an azole antifungal therapy with good CNS penetration [Revankar et al. 2004].

title: 2013 January-February Featured Case and 2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: A man in
history:
2013 January-February Featured Case and 2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: A man in his fifties with nodules on his arm after a whale bite.
A man in his fifties developed two raised, red nodules on his right wrist and forearm, approximately 3 weeks after being bitten on the arm by a beluga whale. The patient also reported subjective fevers and malaise.

He was previously healthy.

The patient was a marine biologist. He was frequently bitten in the course of caring for marine animals but had never been ill as a result of these bites. The beluga whale was ill, and died shortly after the bite occurred.
Approximately one week after sustaining the bite, he had traveled to Taiwan for a conference. He stayed one week in a hotel in a large, urban area and reported no unusual activities or food exposures. During the previous decade, he had lived in French Polynesia, Japan, Mexico, United States and Canada.

None
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 99.4°F (37.4°C), blood pressure 159/105 mm Hg, pulse 98 beats per minute, respirations 18 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% while breathing room air. There were two raised tender violaceous and erythematous nodules on the dorsal surface of his right forearm (Figure 1), associated with erythematous tracking up the right forearm from the nodules. There was no drainage, warmth, fluctuance. or palpable axillary, supraclavicular, or cervical lymphadenopathy. His lungs were clear, without crackles or wheezes. The remainder of the examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.

Routine laboratory testing, including a complete blood count with differential, comprehensive chemistry panel, and electrolytes, was normal. Testing for HIV antibodies was negative, and blood and urine cultures were sterile. A chest radiograph was normal.

The patient was admitted to the hospital and clindamycin was administered for cellulitis with lymphangitis.
diagnosis:
Primary cutaneous histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, following a bite by a beluga whale.

Dermatology consultants performed a skin biopsy. On the third hospital day, histopathological examination of the tissue revealed oval yeast forms that stained positive with diastase periodic acid Schiff (DPAS) staining, consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum (Figure 2, with arrows); the organisms were also seen with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figure 3). Fungal culture of the skin biopsy specimen grew a fungus that was identified as Histoplasma capsulatum by 18s rRNA genetic sequencing at the Northwestern Memorial Hospital microbiology laboratory.
The patient’s urine Histoplasma antigen was 0.78 ng/mL (0.6 – 3.9 ng/ml considered low positive).
Histopatholgical examination of tissue from the lung of the beluga whale obtained at necropsy (performed by Dr. Michael Kinsel) also showed oval yeast forms that stained positive with Gomori’s methenamine silver stain, and were consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum (Figure 4, with arrow). This was also confirmed by genetic sequencing performed on the lung tissue at the University of Illinois veterinary pathology laboratory.
Figure 2. Skin biopsy, DPAS stain, with arrow showing organisms.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy, H&E stain.
Figure 4. Whale lung, GMS stain, with arrow showing organisms.

Clindamycin was discontinued and the patient was started on itraconazole. At follow-up one month later, his skin lesions and constitutional symptoms had completely resolved. He was treated for a total of three months with no signs of recurrent disease.

Zoonotic transmission of infection via marine mammal bite has been most commonly reported for Mycobacterium marinum, Mycoplasma spp., and Erysipelothrix spp. [Geraci JR and Ridway SH, 1991]. Fungal infections in marine mammals are reported occasionally [Higgins R, 2000; Dierauf LA and Gulland FMD, 2001], and may include cryptococcosis, coccidioidomycosis, aspergillosis, histoplasmosis and blastomycosis. One documented case of transmission of a fungal infection from a marine mammal to humans [Symmers WS, 1983] involved a case of Lobo's disease, also known as lobomycosis, which is now thought to be caused by Lacazia loboi [Paniz-Mondolfi et al. 2012].
Primary cutaneous skin lesions without systemic involvement are an uncommon presentation of histoplasmosis. They most often present as tender, erythematous nodules with associated lymphangitic streaking. Most cases in the literature are associated with accidental inoculations among patients with occupational exposure [Tesh RB and Schneidau JD. 1966; Saheki MN et al. 2008;Tosh FE et al. 1964; Krunic AL et al. 2002]. Diagnosis is usually made by histopathology or culture or a skin biopsy specimen. Need for treatment is unclear, but in reported cases, treatment with varying doses and durations of itraconazole produced clinical cure [Tesh RB and Schneidau JD. 1966; Saheki MN et al. 2008;Tosh FE et al. 1964; Krunic AL et al. 2002].
Primary cutaneous histoplasmosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of nodular skin lesions among patients with appropriate exposure history.
