A woman in her sev
history:
2012 IDWeek Case presentation: An elderly woman with a fever.
A woman in her seventies presented to the emergency department because of a febrile illness of one week's duration. She reported daily fevers up to 104°F (40°C), rigors and sweats. She also reported a dry cough, without shortness of breath, sinus congestion, headache, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria or urinary frequency.

She had hypertension and left bundle branch block, a previous history of invasive melanoma (status post excision in four years before) and, many years before, Lyme disease. She had never had a blood transfusion.

She lived in Illinois, and had vacation homes in the Pacific Northwest and coastal New England. She had traveled extensively, including to Africa, Europe and South America. Her most recent international trips were eight months earlier to South Africa where she visited Kruger National Park and participated in game drives and walking safaris and one year earlier to Kenya. She did not take anti-malarial prophylaxis. She did not report any recent sick contacts or insect bites.

She was retired, and had previously worked in an office.

She had no allergies.

She took verapamil daily.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared diaphoretic, but was not in any acute distress. The temperature was 104.7°F (40.4°C), blood pressure 122/69 mm Hg, pulse 68 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry 94% while breathing room air. There were fine crackles in the bases of both lungs, and the examination was otherwise normal.

The level of hemoglobin was 12.0g/dl, white blood count 4,400 cells per cubic millimeter (61% neutrophils, 32% lymphocytes, and 6% monocytes) and platelet count 52,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-450,000). The level of aspartate aminotransferase was 193 U/L (reference range 8-37 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase was 157 U/L (reference range 8-35 U/L). Results of other routine laboratory tests and urinalysis were normal.
A chest radiograph revealed small bilateral pleural effusions (Figure 1).
Cultures of the blood and urine were sterile.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph, on admission.

Thick and thin peripheral blood smears are shown (Figures 2 through 4). The intraerythrocytic parasites were thought to represent Plasmodium falciparum with 1.11% parasitemia. Atovaquone and proguanil hydrochloride (in combination, 4 tabs orally, daily) were administered.
On the evening of the first day, fevers persisted and the level of parasitemia was 0.83%.
On the second day, the maximum temperature was 104.2°F (40.1°C). The platelet count was 62,000 per cubic millimeter and the level of parasitemia 0.74%.
Figure 2. Peripheral smear, Wright-Giemsa stain, x1250 magnification.
Figure 3. Peripheral smear, Wright-Giemsa stain, x1250 magnification.
Figure 4. Peripheral smear, Wright-Giemsa stain, x1250 magnification.
diagnosis:
Babesiosis caused by Babesia microti.

Thick and thin peripheral blood smears revealed intraerythrocytic ring forms including multiple vacuolated forms (Figures 2 through 4). No schizonts or gametocytes were visualized. Because of the persistent fevers, the peripheral smears were reviewed and additional testing performed.
Malaria PCR was negative. Babesia PCR was positive for Babesia microti; Babesia microti IgG and IgM were elevated at greater than 1:1024 (reference range less than 1:64) and greater than 1:320 (reference range less than 1:20), respectively.

The patient was diagnosed with Babesiosis caused by Babesia microti, most likely acquired in coastal New England from the bite of an Ixodes scapularis tick. A 7-day course of atovaquone and azithromycin was administered, with subsequent resolution of the fevers, parasitemia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminase elevation.

Babesiosis is a tick-borne febrile illness caused by intracellular protozoa that invade erythrocytes and can clinically resemble malaria. Most human babesiosis in the U.S. is caused by Babesia microti which is transmitted by the nymphs of Ixodes scapularis, the deer tick. Less commonly, it can be transmitted by blood transfusions.
The incubation period for Babesia species usually ranges from one to six weeks after the tick bite. In contrast, the incubation period for Plasmodium species usually ranges from 8-25 days but may be much longer depending on the immune status of the infected person, the strain as well as the species of Plasmodium, the dose of sporozoites, and the possible effects of partially effective chemoprophylaxis.
The pathophysiologic manifestations of babesiosis result from infection of erythrocytes with subsequent hemolysis and splenic sequestration. Clinical manifestations of babesiosis range from asymptomatic to severe infection. Onset may be acute or subacute. Symptoms of mild illness typically include fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and anorexia. Severe illness may include manifestations of hemolysis (jaundice, hemoglobinuria) as well as multiorgan system failure (acute respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, congestive heart failure, and renal failure). Pulmonary manifestations are rare but, if present, usually secondary to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The clinical course of babesiosis is more severe in those who are asplenic, immunocomopromised and/or over the age of fifty.
The laboratory findings and morphologic appearance of Plasmodium and Babesia species are often very similar. As a result, the diagnoses may be difficult to distinguish in patients such as the one presented in this case who have been in areas endemic for both organisms. Ring forms in erythrocytes may be seen in both Plasmodium and Babesia infections. Banana-shaped gametocytes and schizonts, which may occasionally be seen on the peripheral blood smear in P. falciparum infection, are never seen in Babesia infection, but were not present in this case. A pathognomonic finding in Babesia infection is an intra-erythrocytic tetrad of merozoites, appearing in a “Maltese cross” configuration, but this is only seen in a minority of cases. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) testing are available and may detect low levels of parasitemia.
Because of fewer adverse effects, the combination of atovaquone and azithromycin is the treatment of choice for mild-to-moderate babesiosis. Patients with severe disease are often treated with clindamycin plus quinine, and sometimes with exchange transfusion.
In this patient with a summer house in coastal New England as well as frequent travel to malaria-endemic regions who presented with fevers, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, and intraerythrocytic ring forms (without tetrads, extracellular forms, schizonts, or mature trophozoites) on peripheral blood smear, the differential included babesiosis versus delayed onset Plasmodium falciparum malaria secondary to partial immunity, though the latter seemed less likely given the long delay between her travel to Africa and the development of symptoms. The lack of pathognomonic findings on peripheral blood smear together with the patient’s history of travel to areas endemic for both malaria and babesiosis did not allow us to clearly distinguish between Plasmodium and Babesia infection. In this case, adjunctive diagnostic tests including Babesia indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were essential to establishing the final diagnosis.

title: 2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: An elderly woman with fever, pleuritic pain, and
history:
2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: An elderly woman with fever, pleuritic pain, and left hip and leg pain after travel to India.
An Indian woman in her seventies, with a history of rheumatoid arthritis, was admitted because of fever, pleuritic pain, and left hip and leg pain after travel to India two months before.
Approximately 10 days before admission, sudden sharp pleuritic pain developed in the right upper quadrant, as well as severe left hip and thigh pain. Fevers to 103°F (39.4°C) occurred, associated with rigors and night sweats. Her daughter gave her homeopathic medications (including eucalyptus, an adrenal supplement derived from either animal or plants, echinacea and omatium) for a presumed urinary tract infection, without improvement. The patient became nearly immobile from pain, with altered mental status. Her daughter called emergency medical services, and she was brought to the hospital.
The patient also reported diarrhea of 2 days' duration and had been noted to drink an increased amount of water over this time period.
In the Emergency Department, intravenous normal saline, acetaminophen, vancomycin (1 g IV), levofloxacin (750 mg IV), and hydrocortisone (100 mg IV) were administered. She was admitted to the medical intensive care unit for 3 days, with improvement, and was transferred to the floor. Blood cultures grew oxacillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Urine culture grew E. coli and urinary tract infection was diagnosed. Her joint pains, myalgias, and immobility were attributed to uncontrolled rheumatoid arthritis.
Four days after admission, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis revealed a rim-enhancing fluid collection along the distal left iliopsoas muscle thought to be consistent with a left psoas abscess, and prominent soft tissue enhancement involving and surrounding the left hip joint, avascular necrosis of the hip and a right loculated pleural effusion. The same day, after resolution of her acute infectious symptoms, prednisone (20 mg orally, daily) was begun. Thrombocytopenia developed and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was subsequently diagnosed; subcutaneous heparin (given for prophylaxis against deep venous thrombosis) was stopped 8 days after admission. Diarrhea worsened. An abdominal radiograph performed 8 days after admission was normal, with gas seen in the rectum and no evidence of small bowel obstruction. Some calcifications, thought to be phleboliths, were seen in the right pelvis.
Twelve days after admission, anticoagulation was started with fondiparinux and warfarin. After administration of anticoagulation, diarrhea became frankly bloody. Stool specimens were obtained for Clostridium difficile PCR, ova and parasite screening, and cultures. Repeat abdominal radiography 13 days after admission showed dilated loops of bowel, particularly the colon. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen (Figure 1) revealed dilation of the cecum (8.3 cm), ascending colon (5.6 cm), and transverse colon (4.4 cm) with extensive wall thickening and pericolonic stranding and intraluminal air-fluid levels. No free air or pneumotosis coli was seen.
Surgery consultation was obtained, and she was taken to the operating room the same day for exploratory laparotomy, total abdominal colectomy, and end ileostomy. Intraoperative findings were notable for perforated colon and extensive intraperitoneal stool spillage. She was transferred to the surgical intensive care unit for recovery, and infectious disease consultation was obtained.
Figure 1. CT of the abdomen.

She had been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 7 years before admission, and was treated with methotrexate for four years, until recurrent multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli urinary tract infections and sepsis developed. Methotrexate was stopped two years before this presentation. Since then, her rheumatologic symptoms had worsened, and she had recurrent fever attributed to rheumatoid arthritis and her recurrent urinary tract infections.
She also had hypertension, gastro-esophageal reflux disease, a history of herpes zoster and mild dementia.

The patient was born in rural India and resided there until moving to the United States 4 years before admission. Since that time she had spent 6 months per year in each country. She had returned from her most recent trip to India approximately 2 months before admission. While in India, she had several episodes of fever and weakness that lasted for days to weeks. When she returned to the United States, she initially felt better and was more mobile. She did not drink alcohol, smoke, or use drugs. She denied any animal exposures.

She was a homemaker.

She had multiple allergies including penicillin (anaphylaxis), imipenem (anaphylaxis), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (itching), ciprofloxacin (unknown reaction), nitrofurantoin (itching).

She had previously received methotrexate, which she stopped approximately 2 years before this presentation. Medications during admission included metronidazole, micafungin, esomeprazole, metoprolol and prednisone (which was stopped a few days before surgery).
exam_studies:
The patient’s temperature was 97.7°F (36.5°C), pulse 110 beats per minutes, blood pressure 134/50 mm Hg, and respirations 20 breaths per minute. She was somnolent but could be aroused to answer questions. Breath sounds were coarse diffusely. There was a large abdominal midline incision covered with a clean bandage and a right-sided ileostomy with pink, healthy-appearing mucosa and brown stool in the ileostomy bag. There was 2+ bilateral pitting lower extremity edema to the knees. Neurological examination revealed global weakness without focal findings. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 23,700 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000), hemoglobin was 12.7 g/dL (reference range 12.0-16.0 g/dL), hematocrit 37.4% (reference range 36.0-46.0%), and platelets 51,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-440,000). Sodium was 132 mmol/L (reference range 135-145) and potassium was 2.9 mmol/L (reference range 3.5-5.0). Other routine laboratory tests were normal. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) antibody was positive. Cultures of the blood were sterile. Urine culture grew Candida glabrata. Stool examinations for ova and parasites and for Clostridium difficile were negative. Three separate sputum cultures were negative for acid-fast bacilli and her tuberculin skin test was nonreactive.

On gross examination, the excised tissue included a segment of terminal ileum (4.5 cm x 2.0 cm) contiguous with a segment of colon (73 cm x 8 cm). There were multiple areas along the serosa and mesenteric surface covered with tan-yellow creamy material and several areas with red/brown adhesions. There were three internal areas of ulceration. The first involved the ileocecal valve extending to the cecal mucosa (7.5 x 5.0 cm), the second was 9.0 cm distal to the first and measured 7.0 x 3.5 cm, and the third was 9 cm distal to the second and measured over 30 cm in length by up to 5 cm. All areas were characterized by tan/brown to yellow, slightly ulcerated, partially liquefied tissue. The edges were hyperemic and slightly raised. Surgical margins were viable. Micropathological examination of the excised tissue is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. Resected colon, hematolylin and eosin stain, low power.
Figure 3. Resected colon, H and E stain, high power.
diagnosis:
Toxic megacolon due to Entamoeba histolytica in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis.

Microscopic examination of the right hemicolectomy specimen revealed three confluent areas of colonic ulceration (Figure 2) associated with organisms consistent with Entamoeba histolytica (Figure 3). Findings included focal vasculitis of medium sized artery within pericolonic adipose tissue and serosal adhesions. Twelve lymph nodes were examined and nodal fibrosis was present. There were no granulomas, viral cytopathic effect, or dysplasia identified.

The patient’s amebic infection was treated with metronidazole for a 10-day course, followed by paromomycin for 7 days, and vancomycin was continued for treatment of her staphylococcal infection. Serological testing for E. histolytica was positive.
Recovery was complicated by the formation of intra-abdominal abscesses, which were drained and grew E. coli resistant to all antibiotics except carbapenems. She was desensitized to doripenem and this drug was added to her regimen. Two weeks later, the abscesses were re-cultured and the E. coli was found to be resistant to all drugs except for tigecycline. Vancomycin was discontinued and tigecycline was added to her regimen. Her hospital course was further complicated by Candida glabrata urinary tract infection, persistent intra-abdominal abscesses, adrenal insufficiency, healthcare-associated pneumonia (treated with a 10-day course of vancomycin) and Burkholderia cepacia line sepsis (requiring addition of ceftazidime to her antibiotic regimen). Four months after admission, she suffered a cardiac arrest and expired.

Diarrhea is a common problem in hospitalized patients and has a broad differential. This patient presented with non-bloody diarrhea that worsened during her hospitalization and became bloody after initiation of anticoagulation. Because she was on anticoagulants, it was difficult to determine if her diarrhea should be classified as dysentery. The differential diagnosis for infectious dysentery, particularly in an immigrant, includes Salmonella, Shigella, Escherichia coli (enteroinvasive and enterohemorrhagic forms), and Campylobacter. With the exception of Salmonella, most bacterial causes of dysentery can be eliminated because of their short incubation period. This patient had returned to the United States 6 months prior to hospitalization and had been in the hospital for almost 2 weeks, so infection with one of these pathogens was unlikely. Salmonella can chronically colonize the gall bladders of some patients, but recrudescence with this severity is uncommon. Findings were not consistent with tuberculosis (TB) on biopsy, and the patient had no other findings concerning for TB.
Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) was initially considered the most likely (though ultimately incorrect) diagnosis in this case, presuming that her bloody stools were caused by anticoagulants rather than the disease process itself. The patient was an elderly woman who had been on antibiotics for almost 2 weeks, so her risk of C. difficile colitis was relatively high. In fact, despite several negative tests for C. difficile in the stool, she had started treatment with metronidazole for presumed CDI. Ultimately the diagnosis of E. histolytica was made on biopsy, with later confirmation by positive serology.
Entamoeba histolytica is a single-celled protozoan parasite that can cause a range of clinical disease from asymptomatic infection to severe colitis or liver abscesses. Infection occurs when humans ingest the quadrinucleate cyst form, which releases trophozoites in the intestinal lumen (Haque 2003, CDC life cycle). These forms attach to mucins on the colon wall and can colonize the colon with minimal symptoms, or they can invade through the intestinal epithelium to cause colitis or spread to other parts of the body. E. histolytica is the third most common parasitic infection in the United States, with an incidence of 1.2/100,000 persons per year; the most frequently affected populations are travelers, immigrants, and institutionalized individuals.
The majority of infections are asymptomatic, but should still be treated to prevent later development of invasive disease and to decrease transmission of the parasite. Diarrhea is the most common presentation of clinical disease due to E. histolytica, with dysentery occurring in 15-33% of these cases (Mandell, Haque 2006, Haque 2009). Acute necrotizing colitis and toxic megacolon are both rare, occurring in about 0.5% of cases (Haque 2003, Ellyson 1986). Severe or fatal colitis and hepatic abscess due to E. histolytica associated with steroid use have been reported (Kobayashi 2011, Stuiver 1978), and steroids may increase the risk of toxic megacolon due to the pathogen (Haque 2003). Amebic colitis can acutely worsen if steroids or other immunosuppressive medications are given to a patient who is mistakenly thought to have inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Alternatively, in a patient with IBD who receives steroids, E. histolytica infection may worsen (Lysy 1991, Patel 1989, Mendonca 1977). Hepatic abscess is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of E. histolytica infection and usually occurs in adult men and affects the right lobe of the liver. Hepatic abscesses can extend into the thoracic cavity, but hematogenous dissemination is quite rare.
Diagnosis is usually made by identification of the organisms in stools samples in developing countries, but these tests are insensitive (10-60%) and cannot distinguish E. histolytica f rom nonpathogenic E. dispar and E. moshkovskii (Haque 2003). Stool antigen and PCR methods are more sensitive though not as widely available. Serological tests for antibodies to E. histolytica are 70-90% sensitive in symptomatic patients but can remain positive for years after infection (Haque 2003). Biopsy findings are variable; a flask-shaped ulcer is classic.
Many patients are asymptomatic but should still be treated to prevent later development of invasive disease. Isolated intestinal disease can be treated with paromomycin. Invasive infections such as hepatic abscess should be treated with metronidazole followed by a course of paromomycin because metronidazole does not reliably eliminate amoebas from the intestinal lumen. Percutaneous drainage is indicated for some hepatic abscesses. In cases of severe colitis, surgery is indicated for perforated bowel or toxic megacolon.

title: 2012 November-December Featured Case and 2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: A woman
history:
2012 November-December Featured Case and 2012 IDWeek Case Presentation: A woman with retro-orbital pain and "floaters" in the left eye.
A woman in her forties developed left retro-orbital discomfort three weeks before presentation. The following week, "floaters" developed in the left eye. She was seen by a local ophthalmologist who noted a temporal field deficit in her left eye on visual field testing. She was referred to specialty care.

She had a history of a pituitary adenoma eleven years before, and chronic lumbar and leg pain following a motor vehicle accident seven years before.

The patient lived in rural Pennsylvania, with her husband (with whom she was monogamous), son and a dog. She worked in a healthcare setting; one year before this presentation, a screening skin test for tuberculosis was negative. She smoked cigarettes (40 pack-years), drank 12 beers per week, and reported no illicit drug use.

She was married, and worked in a medical facility.

There was no family history of autoimmune diseases.

Tetracycline had caused swelling of the face and lips.

She took acetaminophen and celecoxib as needed for pain.
exam_studies:
She appeared well. The blood pressure was 138/88 mm Hg, pulse 94 beats per minute, temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F). Ophthalmologic funduscopic examination revealed hemorrhagic disc edema in the left eye (Figure 1). The examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Funduscopic examination.

Visual field testing (Humphrey Visual Field Test) revealed a temporal field deficit in the left eye (Figure 2). Nerve fiber layer average thickness assessment by optical coherence tomography demonstrated markedly increased optic nerve thickness of the left eye four times normal (416µm; normal average thickness = 100µm) (Figure 3).
Figure 2. Humphrey visual field test.
Figure 3. Nerve fiber layer thickness map.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a normal pituitary gland with a clear suprasellar cistern, normal optic chiasm and optic tracts (without mass or displacement), and prominent left optic cup (Figure 4).
Figure 4. MRI of the brain.
diagnosis:
Lyme optic neuritis, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi.

The Borrelia antibody index was positive by enzyme-linked immunosorbant assay (ELISA) (reference = negative). Western blot of the serum revealed 3 out of 3 Lyme reactive IgM bands (reference range = ≤1/3) and 3/10 IgG bands (reference range ≤4/10).
Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 15cm H2O. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 7 white blood cells per cubic millimeter, 18 red blood cells per cubic millimeter, glucose 60mg/dL, protein 35mg/dL, Western blot of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed 3/3 Lyme reactive IgG bands (reference = zero bands). Syphilis serology by semi-quantitative particle agglutination was negative, and testing for veneral disease research laboratory (VDRL) antibody in the cerebrospinal fluid was negative. Oligoclonal bands were not detected in the cerebrospinal fluid. Serological testing for antibodies against Bartonella henselae and Toxoplasma were negative.

Ceftriaxone (2g every 24 hours) was administered intravenously for 2 weeks, followed by oral amoxicillin (500mg three times daily) for 7 days. One week after completing antibiotics, she was seen in the ophthalmology clinic, where visual field testing revealed resolution of the left eye temporal field deficit (Figure 5). Optical coherence tomography revealed resolution of left optic nerve thickening (Figure 6).
Figure 5. Humphrey visual field test, 4 week follow-up.
Figure 6. Nerve fiber layer thickness map, 4 week follow-up.

The infectious differential diagnosis of unilateral optic disc edema includes Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella henselae, Toxoplasma gondii, Treponema pallidum, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, though each of these entities has a low incidence of ocular involvement (Durand, in Mandell et al. 2009; Ray and Gragoudas 2001). The presence or absence of systemic findings that accompany unilateral disc edema may assist in the diagnosis (Durand, in Mandell et al. 2009; Ray and Gragoudas 2001).
This patient had no known history of tick bite and no systemic symptoms to suggest Lyme disease, but the optic findings and residence in a rural, wooded area where Lyme disease is endemic increased the clinical suspicion for this cause. The definitive diagnosis of Lyme optic neuritis requires culture or histologic demonstration of Borrelia burgdorferi (Halperin 2008). Most often, however, the condition is diagnosed based on clinical, epidemiologic, and serologic evidence (Halperin 2008, Mikkila et al. 1999, Sibony et al. 2005). The epidemiologic context of this case, our patient’s confirmed optic neuritis along with the presence of Borrelia burgdorferi antibody in her serum and cerebrospinal fluid, and the exclusion of alternative diagnoses provide strong evidence for the diagnosis of Lyme optic neuritis (Sibony et al. 2005). Early diagnosis and treatment of optic neuritis due to Borrelia burgdorferi can restore vision; delay in therapy can result in devastating visual outcomes (Karma et al. 1996). This case highlights the criteria for diagnosis of Lyme optic neuritis and suggests that therapeutic response may be considered as additional evidence to support the diagnosis.

title: 2013 March-April Featured Case: An 18-year-old woman was admitted to a hospital
history:
2013 March-April Featured Case: An 18-year-old woman was admitted to a hospital because of hemoptysis and pulmonary cavities.
The patient had been well until 6 months earlier, when she intermittently felt the need to clear her throat, after which sputum with bright red blood was expectorated. Hemoptysis recurred intermittently during the following three months. There was transient weight loss of 2 kilograms, and no history of fevers, sweats, other constitutional symptoms, or cough other than that mentioned above. Azithromycin was administered, and she was well until one month before admission when the symptoms and sputum with blood recurred.
Computed tomography (CT) of the lungs performed at another hospital and revealed two cavities in the right upper lobe.
She was referred to a tertiary care hospital.

The past history included skin testing for tuberculosis at age 1 year that was negative. Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) vaccine was administered. Twelve years before admission, tuberculin skin testing was positive. Five years before admission, a chest radiograph was normal.

She was born in Southeast Asia and immigrated to the United States as a child. She lived in Arizona for several years before moving to New England. She was a student who lived with her parents. She did not smoke or drink alcohol, was not sexually active and had no sick contacts. She had traveled to Europe during the year before this presentation. She ate raw fish sushi.
Both parents had had negative chest radiographs 2 months before the patient's admission; her mother and a sibling had a slight cough. Her maternal grandmother had had tuberculosis many years before the patient was born.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The vital signs were normal; the temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C). There were mild egophony and rhonchi in the right upper lung field, posteriorly. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 7900 cells/mm³ (reference range 4500-11,000) and the hematocrit 36.5% (reference range 36.0-46.0). T-lymphocyte cell subsets were normal and testing for antibody to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
Radiographs of the chest revealed mild hyperinflation and two cavities in the right upper lobe, without evidence of surrounding consolidation or air fluid levels (Figures 1 and 2). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a right hilar lymph node measuring 1.5 centimeters (cm) by 1.2 cm and two cavitary lesions in the right upper lobe, with adjacent ground-glass and tree-in-bud opacities with bronchial wall thickening (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 1. Chest radiograph on admission.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph, lateral view.
Figure 3. CT of the chest, on admission.
Figure 4. CT of the chest, on admission.

The patient was placed on respiratory droplet precautions. Gram stain of sputum and bronchial washings revealed few polymorphonuclear leukocytes, rare ciliated respiratory cells and no organisms, and stains for acid-fast bacilli were also negative.
Rare Staphylococcus aureus colonies grew on culture of bronchial washings; two other colonies also grew (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Culture growth from bronchial washing.
diagnosis:
Chronic fibrocavitary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis.

Cultures of bronchial washings grew two colonies of Coccidioides species (Figure 5, shown on Sabouraud dextrose agar plate). A tape preparation with lactophenol cotton blue stain of the culture growth, shown in Figures 6 and 7, revealed the "box car" formation of Coccidioides. Identification performed by the Center of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed the presence of Coccidioides species. Two of five cultures of induced sputum also grew Coccidioides, and two other sputum cultures grew abundant methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Cultures for mycobacteria, Nocardia, Sporothrix, Rhodococcus and other routine bacteria (other than Staphylococcus aureus mentioned above) were negative.
Results of serum testing for antibodies Paragonimus and Cryptococcus, and urine testing for antibody to Histoplasma, were negative. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of induced sputum was negative for Mycoplasma.
Figure 6. Tape prep from culture growth, lactophenol cotton blue stain.
Figure 7. Tape prep of culture growth.

Itraconazole in a liquid preparation was administered and tolerated well. Surgical resection of the lesions was discussed with the patient and her parents, and declined. Before the diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis was known, she was treated with cephalexin.
Her symptoms improved. Follow-up CT scans showed decreased size of the larger cavity in the right upper lobe as well as improvement in the surrounding tree-in-bud patterned opacities in surrounding lung parenchyma (Figure 8). At eight months follow-up, a chest radiograph was normal.
Figure 8. Follow-up CT of the chest.

Coccidioides is a fungus endemic to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and northern Mexico, and is also present in other states in the American Southwest and countries of Central and South America with similar climate conditions [Parish and Blair, 2008]. The mycelial branching form, which grows in the arid soil, forms arthroconidia after exposure to rain. It is thought that infection occurs by inhalation of the arthroconidia by humans and other animals, which leads to transformation of the organism to its spherule form and eventual release of endospores and further reproduction [Gadkowski and Stout, 2008; Parish and Blair, 2008]. Studies of military recruits suggest that 60% of infections are asymptomatic [Hirschmann, 2007]. However, an acute pneumonia associated with fever, headache and fatigue may occur 1 to 3 weeks after exposure, and Coccidioides has been shown in endemic areas to account for up to 29% of community-acquired pneumonias [Valdivia et al., 2006].
Nodular or cavitary pulmonary disease, which this patient had, is a subsequent manifestation of coccidioidomycosis; other presentations or subsequent sequelae include chronic progressive pneumonia, extrapulmonary nonmeningeal disease (seen more often in pregnant women, immunocompromised hosts and those of Filipino or African ancestry) and coccidioidal meningitis [Parish and Blair, 2008]. In this case, diagnosis of coccidioidal infection was confirmed with the positive culture and identification from sputum and pulmonary aspirate. Diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis can also be made on pathological examination of tissue that reveals coccidioidal spherules, or with serologic identification of anti-coccidioidal antibodies [Valdivia et al., 2006].
Pulmonary tuberculosis was a strong consideration in this case given this patient's Asian birth history, positive Mantoux test (although in the setting of BCG vaccination as a child) and upper lobe cavitary disease. However, both sputum stains and cultures were negative for mycobacteria. Testing for Histoplasma and Paragonimus were also negative. Positive cultures for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus were possibly due to superinfection or colonization.
Addendum: Laboratory personnel should be notified whenever the possibility of Coccidioides infection is considered, in order to implement appropriate laboratory precautions and decrease the possibility of exposure to infectious aerosolized organisms.

title: 2013 May-June Featured Case: A woman in her thirties noted multiple (~10) prurit
history:
2013 May-June Featured Case: A woman in her thirties noted multiple (~10) pruritic raised, red lesions on the left arm and leg and the left side of her trunk during the second day of a trip to southwestern Uganda. During the next week, additional lesions appeared on the left side, and each lesion gradually increased to greater than 3-centimeters in diameter. She went to the dermatology clinic at the regional hospital for evaluation.
She reported no associated fevers, sweats, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or headache.

She had previously been healthy.

During her visit to Uganda, she resided at a residential facility at the local university. She slept underneath a bednet and wore sun-protective clothing. She had not used insect repellant. She went on a safari at a national park four days after the skin lesions appeared, but did not swim or hike during her stay. No other colleagues or contacts experienced similar symptoms. She had not used any new detergents or soaps. She drank alcohol in moderation and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. She was in a monogamous sexual relationship.

She had no known allergies to medicines.

Her only new medication was a sleep aid.
exam_studies:
There were approximately 20 erythematous lesions on the left side that were non-indurated, warm, and measured up to more than 3-centimeters in diameter. The lesions had a punctate pale central clearing (Figures 1 and 2). The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings on leg.
Figure 2. Skin lesion after lateral pressure applied.

The local dermatologist in Uganda made a clinical diagnosis based on presentation.
diagnosis:
African tumbu fly furuncular myiasis caused by Cordylobia anthropophaga larvae infection.

Lateral pressure was applied to a lesion as shown in Figure 2 and a single living larva consistent with the African tumbu fly (Cordylobia anthropophaga) emerged from the central pore. Another 10-15 larvae were removed manually in a similar fashion; however, due to significant pain and bleeding, the remaining 5 were left in place. The patient applied petrolatum jelly and occlusive dressings over the remaining lesions. After 24 hours, additional larvae were apparent in the center of those lesions (Figure 3). Lateral pressure was again applied to the remaining lesions and additional dead larvae (Figure 4 and Video 1) were produced with limited pressure, without pain or bleeding.
Figure 3. Physical findings, 24 hours after application of petrolatum jelly.
Figure 4. Extracted African tumbu fly Cordylobia anthropophaga larva, with breathing tube.

After extraction of all larvae, topical neomycin was applied to the lesions, which fully healed without further incident within one week.

The diagnosis in this case was made presumptively by typical clinical presentation of multiple furuncles without associated systemic symptoms or signs. Though each of the other listed diagnoses should be considered, most were excluded in this case by lack of fever or constitutional symptoms (as often seen in Rickettsialpox and African tick bite fever), lack of typical eschar formation (seen in Rickettsialpox, Bouttenouse fever and African tick bite fever) [Cook GC and Zumla 2009, Ch 49], lack of risk factors (syphilis), or an incorrect geographic distribution (Lyme disease has not been reported in Africa). Though Borrelia infections do occur in Africa, they tend to be relapsing fever-type infections. Lyme disease could not be entirely excluded because infection might have occurred prior to travel; however, the presence of multiple lesions would be most consistent with early disseminated disease, which is usually associated with systemic symptoms. Furunculosis by Staphylococcus aureus remained a likely possibility until extraction of the larvae established the diagnosis of Tumbu fly furuncular myiasis.
Myiasis refers to human infestation by the living larvae (maggots) of winged insects. Cutaneous forms of myiasis are divided into three clinical presentations: migratory (creeping), traumatic (wound), and furuncular [Robbins and Khachemoune 2010]. Furuncular myiasis is caused by one of four species of flies: Dermatobia hominis (human botfly), Wohlfahrtia vigil, Cuterebra spp. and Cordylobia anthropophaga (Tumbu fly). Of these, only the latter is found in tropical African regions. Adult flies are 7-15mm in length and yellow-brown in color. Adult females lay eggs in a variety of hosts, including rodents and dogs, and prefer shaded soil contaminated with urine or feces. Thus, incompletely washed clothes or linens serve as a target for deposited eggs. Hatched larvae penetrate the host when they come in contact with skin, a process that usually lasts less than 60 seconds and is typically painless. The larvae develop over a period of 8-12 days, forming a reactive, painful furuncle in humans. Rarely, hosts also experience localized lymphadenopathy, fevers, and/or malaise. Diagnosis can be made by noting the spiracles (breathing tube) which emanate from the skin as a 1-3mm dark line [Cook GC and Zumla 2009, Ch 88]. Primary control of Cordylobia anthropophaga myiasis is through prevention by thoroughly cleaning all fabrics, drying them indoors, and ironing them on both sides. Once infected, any identified boils should be covered with petroleum jelly or paraffin oil to suffocate larvae and promote simple, full extraction by digital pressure. Incomplete extraction can lead to granuloma or inflammatory response; surgical extraction serves as the definitive cure in these cases.

title: 2013 July-August Featured Case: A woman in her thirties developed a progressive
history:
2013 July-August Featured Case: A woman in her thirties developed a progressive bifrontal headache associated with a temperature to 100.0°F (37.8°C). She went to sleep in the late afternoon. Approximately 24 hours later, her husband found her difficult to arouse, nonverbal and non-interactive. She was unable to arise from bed, answer questions or follow commands, and appeared confused. She was brought to the emergency department for evaluation.

She had previously been well.

The patient was born and raised in Guatemala, and moved to the Southeastern United States nine years earlier. Two years before this evaluation, she moved to an urban area of New England. She lived with her husband and young daughter, and worked as a housekeeper. She did not drink alcohol, smoke tobacco, or use illicit drugs.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared somnolent, arousable to painful stimuli, and unable to follow commands consistently. The blood pressure was 143/60 mm Hg, pulse 59 beats per minute, temperature 38.3°C (101.0°F), respirations 20 beats per minute, and oxygenation 98% while breathing room air. On neurological examination, the pupils were symmetric and sluggishly reactive from 4mm to 3mm; extra-ocular movements were grossly intact. She was able to open her eyes and moved all four extremities spontaneously. Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ and symmetric bilaterally. The remainder of the examination was otherwise normal.

The white blood cell count was 17,900 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4,500-11,000) with an absolute neutrophil count of 14,770 cells per cubic millimeter (ref. 1800-7700). The hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. Other routine laboratory tests including blood levels of electrolytes, and tests of coagulation, renal function and liver function were normal. Serum toxicology panel was negative.
Urinalysis revealed a specific gravity of 1.030, trace ketones, trace urobilinogen, 2+ protein, and 10-20 red blood cells and 3-5 white blood cells per high power field. Culture of the urine and blood were obtained, and were sterile.
A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the head, performed without the administration of contrast (Figure 1) revealed enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles consistent with hydrocephalus, a fluid-filled vesicular structure in the frontal horn of the left lateral ventricle near the foramen of Monroe with a soft-tissue density inside the cyst, and calcified densities scattered throughout the supratentorial brain.
Figure 1. CT of the brain, sagittal view, without contrast.

The patient was intubated and bilateral external ventricular devices were placed emergently, with improvement in the severity of hydrocephalus on follow-up CT imaging. Dexamethasone (4mg every 6 hours), levetiracetam, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were administered. Analysis of cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) obtained from the external ventricular drains revealed a glucose level of 79 mg/dl (reference range 50-75), a normal total protein level; 1150 red blood cells per cubic millimeter, and 2 white blood cells per cubic millimeter.
On the second hospital day, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was performed with the administration of contrast (Figures 2, 3 and 4).
Figure 2. MRI of the brain, sagittal T1 view.
Figure 3. MRI of the brain, axial fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) view.
Figure 4. MRI of the brain, coronal view, reformatted.
diagnosis:
Intraventricular and intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis, caused by larval cysts of Taenia solium.

The soft-tissue density seen within the cyst on CT of the head (Figure 1) was consistent with a scolex, and the innumerable calcified densities scattered throughout the supratentorial brain were suggestive of neurocysticercosis. MRI of the brain (Figures 2, 3 and 4) revealed a nonenhancing multilobed cystic mass (28.4mm in its greatest dimension) within the left lateral ventricle and numerous calcified foci throughout the cerebral hemispheres, as were seen on CT. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine were negative. An ophthalmologic examination revealed no evidence of ocular involvement.
On the seventh hospital day, a left-sided mini-craniectomy with left frontal endoscopic removal of the intraventricular cyst (Figure 5) and fenestration of the septum pellucidum was performed. The left-sided external ventricular drain was also removed.
Histopathological examination of the resected tissue with hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed a cysticercus celluosac with the encysted larva (Figures 6 through 8). The scolex with suckers and hooklets were visible within the sac. Testing for cysticercus IgG antibodies was positive in the serum and negative in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Testing for serum HIV antibodies, interferon-gamma release assay, and mycobacterial DNA from the cerebrospinal fluid were negative. Cultures of the cerebrospinal fluid for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria were sterile.
Figure 5. Gross pathology of resected intraventricular cystic lesion.
Figure 6. H and E stain of resected cystic mass.
Figure 7. H and E stain of resected cystic mass showing suckers and hooklets.
Figure 8. H and E stain of T. solium with suckers and hooklets.

Ceftriaxone and acyclovir were stopped when cerebrospinal fluid studies returned. Vancomycin was continued while the external ventricular devices remained in place. Dexamethasone (4mg every 6 hours) was continued and ivermectin was administered for empiric treatment of strongyloidiasis.
On the first postoperative day, albendazole (400mg orally twice a day) was started for a two-week course in combination with dexamethasone at a reduced dose (4mg every 12 hours). Approximately two weeks after starting treatment, she was seen in follow up with near resolution of symptoms. The albendazole was stopped and a dexamethasone taper begun. Levetiracetam, which had been started at the time of diagnosis, was continued.

Cysticercosis is an infection caused by the larval stage of the pork tapeworm, Taenia solium [Del Brutto et al., 2001; Garcia et al., 2005; John and Petri, 2006; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Infection occurs through ingestion of Taenia eggs (typically fecal contamination) from an infected individual [Garcia et al., 2005;John and Petri, 2006]. Infections in the United States are largely from immigrant populations from Africa, Asia, and Latin America where prevalence rates are high [John and Petri, 2006;Nash and Garcia, 2011]]. This patient was from an endemic area which increased the clinical suspicion for this parasite as a cause of her symptoms.
Once ingested, the eggs travel through the blood stream to any part of the body where they settle and grow into larvae [Garcia et al., 2005; John and Petri, 2006; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. The most common location that leads to medical attention is the central nervous system, termed neurocysticercosis (NCC) [Garcia et al., 2005;John and Petri, 2006]. Initial infection is often asymptomatic as the parasites evoke mechanisms to avoid immune detection [John and Petri, 2006]. Over time, the cysticerci degenerate, often resulting in a profound inflammatory response leading to a multitude of symptoms dependent on the location of the parasites [Garcia et al., 2005;John and Petri, 2006]. In intraparenchymal NCC in which the cysticerci have lodged within the brain parenchyma, the most common clinical manifestations are headache and seizure due to cortical irritation from the inflammatory response [Garcia et al., 2005;John and Petri, 2006]. In extraparenchymal NCC, in which the cysticerci have lodged within the ventricular and/or subarachnoid spaces, hydrocephalus secondary to mechanical obstruction from the cysts or secondary inflammation is the common clinical presentation [Garcia et al., 2005;John and Petri, 2006], as it was in this patient. Dead cysticerci evoke little inflammatory response and remain as calcified lesions within the brain parenchyma, though patients with calcified lesions may still have periodic seizures [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011].
The diagnosis of NCC is often made clinically in combination with distinct radiographic findings and endemic exposure [Del Brutto et al., 2001; Garcia et al., 2005]. In this patient, the diagnosis was made with computed tomography (CT) of the head revealing hydrocephalus with identification of the cysticercus and its scolex within the lateral ventricle. Although not often seen on computed tomography due to the isodensity of the cyst and cerebrospinal fluid, the radiographic identification of the scolex within a cystic lesion is pathognomonic for NCC [Del Brutto et al., 2001]. The numerous hyperdense lesions also seen were consistent with calcified intraparenchymal NCC.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast confirmed the findings with calcified intraparenchymal lesions best seen with susceptibility sequence, and periventricular and intraventricular lesions best appreciated with a combination of T2/FLAIR and T1 sequences, especially FIESTA series [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. In general, magnetic resonance imaging is superior to computed tomography imaging in identifying key anatomy as well as the cysticerci at various stages of degeneration [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Serology for T. solium remains the gold standard for diagnosis and was positive in this patient. A positive serology alone, however, does not differentiate between active and past infection [Garcia et al., 2000]]. Newer monoclonal antibody T. solium antigen detection assays are also available and have been shown to be helpful in the differentiation of active versus inactive infection and response to treatment [Garcia et al., 2005; Garcia et al., 2002; Nash and Garcia, 2011; Rodriguez et al. 2009; Garcia et al., 2000]. As with this patient, basic serum hematology and chemistry tests are usually normal. Cerebrospinal fluid is often characterized by mild inflammation with a pleocytosis that can be eosinophilic with normal protein and glucose levels [Venna et al., 2012].
Primary treatment of NCC focuses on symptomatic management of the complications due to infection [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Antihelminthic treatment is deferred until the patient has stabilized as treatment may worsen symptoms [Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Antiepileptic medications and corticosteroids are administered to control seizures and reduce inflammation [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Urgent surgical treatment of intracranial hypertension, if present, is also required [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. Once medically stable, exoneration of intraocular and spinal infection should be performed [Venna et al., 2012]. This is best done with a direct fundoscopic exam, thorough neurological examination and in certain instances, spinal imaging. Once metastatic sites have been exonerated, further surgical and/or antihelminthic treatment can be considered depending on the location and extent of disease [Nash and Garcia, 2011]. In active intraparenchymal NCC, surgical treatment is often unnecessary. Medical treatment with albendazole (15mg/kg in two divided doses) with prednisone (1mg/kg/day) for 8 to 14 days is the recommended approach, as it reduces the probability of long-term epilepsy [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011; Venna et al., 2012]. Treatment of inactive/calcified parenchymal disease, however, is not indicated as it is of no known benefit [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. In extraventricular NCC, surgical removal of the obstructing cysts, if possible, remains the mainstay of treatment [Nash and Garcia, 2011; Venna et al., 2012]. Neuroendoscopic removal is the preferred method although open surgical procedures are also done [Venna et al., 2012]. With intraventricular disease alone, surgical treatment is the mainstay of management. Assessment for other sites of disease (including subarachnoid and spinal) is necessary as this may require additional management.
If surgery is not possible, combination treatment with corticosteroids and albendazole for 1 to 3 months can be considered [Nash and Garcia, 2011]. In cases of subarachnoid NCC, cure is difficult and longer courses of albendazole and corticosteroids are needed with repeated radiological and serum antigen assays to assess for recurrence [Garcia et al., 2005; Nash and Garcia, 2011]. In ocular and spinal cysticercosis, surgical treatment is often warranted [Venna et al., 2012]. In all cases which might require prolonged corticosteroid administration, screening for latent tuberculosis, hepatitis B and strongyloidiasis should also be performed given risk of co-infection [Venna et al., 2012].

title: 2013 September-October Featured Case: A man in his forties was seen in the emerg
history:
2013 September-October Featured Case: A man in his forties was seen in the emergency department of the hospital because of fever and pain and swelling of the right knee several days after nephrolithotripsy.
The patient was well until six weeks earlier, in early summer, when low back pain developed and persisted despite treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications. Approximately one month before this presentation, pain in the back and severe right flank pain that radiated down his right leg occurred, associated with hematuria. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with the administration of contrast revealed nephrolithiasis, including stones in the left renal pelvis (13mm by 7 mm), left lower pole (a cluster measuring together 10 mm by 5 mm), and in the right proximal ureter (4-to-6mm), with ureteral thickening surrounding the proximal right ureter and mild prominence of the collecting systems bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine showed disk extrusion on the right side at the 3rd and 4th lumbar level with moderate central canal stenosis and impingement on the right descending L4 nerve roots, central disk protrusion with an associated annular disk tear at the 4th and 5th lumbar level with impingement on the traversing right L5 nerve roots, and left paracentral disk extrusion at the 5th lumbar and first sacral level which contacted the descending left S1 nerve roots without evidence of impingement. Muscle relaxants and pain medications were administered.
Five days before this evaluation, retrograde cystoscopy and ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and stone retrieval on the right side and placement of a right ureteral stent were performed, with the administration of cefazolin (2 grams) preoperatively.
Three days after the surgical procedure, his temperature reportedly rose to 103.0°F (39.4°C). During the next two days, increasing pain and swelling of the right knee occurred. He contacted his physician and was referred to the emergency department for evaluation that day.

He had a history of bilateral nephrolithiasis, recent flank pain and lithotripsy. Stone analysis revealed calcium oxalate (70%) and calcium phosphate (carbonate-apatite) (30%). Urine cultures at the time of the procedure had grown mixed flora. A tuberculosis skin test had been negative the previous year.

He had not been sexually active in recent months. He smoked cigarettes, and did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He had visited a rural area in New England two weeks before admission, but had not gone camping or hiking, and did not recall any insect bites. He had not traveled internationally in several years.

He lived alone and worked in a service industry.

He had no allergies.
exam_studies:
On examination, the temperature was normal. The right knee was moderately swollen, without erythema, and there was tenderness with any range of motion. Knee flexion and extension were decreased. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 6400 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000) (68% neutrophils, 19% lymphocytes, 10% monocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 1% basophils), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 21 mm per hour (ref. range 0-11), blood level of C-reactive protein was 87.7 MG/L (reference range < or = to 8, for inflammation), and the level of uric acid was normal.
A radiograph of the right knee demonstrated mild degenerative changes and a moderate effusion (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Radiograph of the right knee with effusion.

Arthrocentesis was performed in the emergency department, and 50cc of serous fluid was aspirated.
Analysis of the joint fluid revealed 16,250 white cells per cubic millimeter, with 80% neutrophils, 2% lymphocytes, 16% monocytes, and 2% macrophages or lining cells; no crystals were seen. Gram stain of the joint fluid revealed moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes, few mononuclear cells and no organisms. Cultures of the joint fluid aspirate were obtained, and on the fourth day, one of two anaerobic bottles was positive. Culture of the organism is shown (Figures 2 and 3).
The patient was contacted and instructed to return to the emergency department. He reported persistent pain and swelling of his right knee.
Figure 2. Culture plate of growth in anaerobic bottle of joint fluid.
Figure 3. Culture growth from anaerobic bottle of joint fluid (4x magnification).
diagnosis:
Septic arthritis of the right knee caused by Mycoplasma species, after ureteral lithotripsy.

The anaerobic culture of the joint fluid grew Mycoplasma species (Figure 3).
Figure 4. Colonies of Mycoplasma species (10x magnification) on ureaplasma differential agar (A7).

The patient returned to the emergency department after culture of the initial joint fluid was positive and the organism identified as Mycoplasma species (thought to be Mycoplasma hominis). Arthrocentesis was repeated, and revealed brown fluid, with 66,250 white cells (98% neutrophils). The white blood cell count was 12,300 per cubic millimeter (71% neutrophils), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 69 mm per hour, and C-reactive protein 159.7 mg/L. Broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin, ceftriaxone and azithromycin were administered.
The next day, arthroscopy for pyoarthrosis was performed in the operating room, with irrigation (18 liters of solution) and debridement of pre-existing articular cartilage damage in the right knee.
An infectious diseases consultation was obtained. Azithromycin was stopped and doxycycline begun, and vancomycin and ceftriaxone were continued until cultures were confirmed to be negative for other organisms. Testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of the throat and urethra and Chlamydia infection of the urethra was negative.

This patient developed an acute monoarticular septic arthritis - a swollen painful knee with an effusion and a positive culture - shortly after a genitoureteral procedure, and despite the administration of cefazolin preoperatively. Analysis of the initial arthrocentesis aspirate revealed a leukocytosis, with no organisms on gram staining and no crystals seen, and without establishing either an infectious (bacterial, fungal or viral) or non-infectious (crystal-related or other reactive or inflammatory) etiology. On the fourth day, one of two anaerobic bottles grew Mycoplasma species, whose colonies had a characteristic “fried egg” appearance on agar [Meloni et al. 1980], as seen in Figures 3 and 4.
Mycoplasma, and specifically Mycoplasma hominis, in the family Mycoplasmataceae, is an uncommon cause of septic arthritis, but when present is more likely to occur in patients who are immunocompromised [Luttrell et al. 1994; Phuah et al. 2007]. Of cases of Mycoplasma septic arthritis, a review of the literature revealed 50% of cases (8 of 16) occurred after a structural abnormality or manipulation of the urogenital tract [Luttrell et al. 1994]. Delays in diagnosis were thought to be caused in part by the lack of staining by gram stain aniline dyes (which stain cell wall structures), the organism’s slow growth, and difficulties in detecting the organisms [Luttrell et al. 1994; Phuah et al. 2007] in culture bottles or the pinpoint and translucent colonies on agar (as seen in Figure 2 in this case). Mycoplasma’s lack of a rigid cell wall also contributes to its insensitivity to antibiotics that impair cell wall synthesis [Luttrell et al. 1994], a category that includes cefazolin, the antibiotic administered prophylactically before his urologic procedure.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Staphylococcus aureus are more common causes of acute septic arthritis and are organisms that have cell walls that stain with analine dyes; if present, either might have been more apparent in the gram stain of the knee aspirate. The prophylactic administration of cefazolin at the time of his procedure might have inhibited culture growth at the time of the first arthrocentesis; for that reason broad spectrum antibiotic coverage was administered on admission until repeat cultures were negative at 48 hours.
Haemophilus influenzae septic arthritis was historically seen more commonly in children and associated with H. influenzae type B in the pre-vaccination era, but its occurrence has diminished since the widespread use of vaccination. Though relatively uncommon in recent years, H. influenzae invasive disease is increasingly associated with noncapsulated or non-typeable isolates that are more antibiotic-resistant [Le Quellec et al. 2013; Dworkin et al. 2007].
Lastly, Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular gram-negative organism, is the most common cause of reactive arthritis [Carter and Inman 2011] and of sexually transmitted bacterial infections (with more than 91 million new cases of the annually) [http://www.who.int/docstore/hiv/GRSTI/003.htm], and can present in a triad associated with non-gonococcal urethritis and conjunctivitis (also known as Reiter's syndrome, among other eponyms) [Carter and Inman 2011]. Reactive arthritis related to Chlamydia infections is thought to be under-recognized, and the syndrome and mechanism of disease are poorly understood [Carter and Inman 2011].

title: 2013 November-December Featured Case and 2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in
history:
2013 November-December Featured Case and 2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in his twenties, living in Japan, developed fever and rash, followed by a generalized seizure.
The patient was well until 6 days before admission when, in winter, fever and mild headache developed. The next day, his physician prescribed a quinolone antibiotic (garenoxacin) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (loxoprofen) for presumed upper respiratory infection.
The following day, a faint rash appeared on his face, arms and trunk, and extremities. By the morning of the day of admission, the faint rash had changed to a deeper-colored, palpable rash. Later that day, a generalized seizure occurred.

He had been healthy, with no history of epilepsy, head injury, or travel. His vaccination history was not documented.

He lived with his wife in an urban area in Japan. He did not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He had had no recent sick contacts, exposure to forested areas or travel. There were no related family illnesses.

His medications included quinolone antibiotic (garenoxacin) and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (loxoprofen).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared in moderate distress and agitated, and unable to follow commands. The blood pressure was 120/60 mm Hg, pulse 63 beats per minute, temperature 97.9°F (36.6°C), and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The neck was supple. He had generalized maculopapules and palpable purpuric lesions (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Rash on torso.
Figure 2. Rash on legs.

The platelet count was 132,000/uL (reference range 150,000-350,000 in men), and the other routine laboratory test results were normal. The examination of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a pleocytosis with 38.4 cells per microliter, (reference range <5) including 6.7 polymorphonuclear cells and 31.7 mononuclear cells per microliter, and elevated protein level (130mg/dL, reference range 15-45).
An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed epileptic waves in the frontal lobes bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain performed with the administration of gadolinium revealed pia-arachnoid enhancement (Figures 3 and 4), which was thought to be consistent with meningitis or meningoencephalitis.
Figure 3. MRI of the brain, T1 gadolinium-enhanced view.
Figure 4. MRI of the brain, FLAIR view.

An anticonvulsant agent was administered for seizure activity, and after sedation was administered, the trachea was intubated for airway protection because of confusion. Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir were administered empirically.
diagnosis:
Rubella.

Results of serological tests for IgM and IgG antibodies against rubella obtained on his 4th day of illness were negative. On his 6th of day of illness, rubella virus was detected by PCR from a throat swab and testing for rubella IgM in the CSF was positive; rubella PCR of his CSF was negative. Serological testing for IgM against rubella was positive (9.15, ELISA index >=0.8) on his 10th day of illness.
The serological test for IgG antibodies against measles (rubeola) was positive at presentation, suggestive of previous infection or vaccination. Measles virus was not detected by PCR from a throat swab. Bacterial culture and herpes simplex virus PCR of the CSF, and HIV ELISA testing were negative.

On the 3rd hospital day, his mental status improved and the trachea was extubated. The purpura also changed and became non-palpable. Empiric antibiotics and antiviral agents were discontinued after bacterial cultures and herpes simplex virus PCR of the CSF were negative. The rash faded to faint pigmentation on the 5th hospital day, and resolved completely by the 10th hospital day.
He was discharged on the 11th hospital day, with no permanent sequelae. At discharge, he remained on anticonvulsant drugs for prophylaxis of seizures, was seizure-free at 1 month, and was followed by neurologist.

Rubella is a rare disease in the United States. From 2005 through 2011, a median of 11 rubella cases was reported each year (range: 4–18) [McLean et al., 2013]. Typical clinical manifestations of rubella are fever, lymphadenopathy (especially involving the posterior auricular, posterior cervical and sub-occipital lymph nodes), and generalized rash (which usually starts on the face and then moves downward). Prodromal catarrhal symptoms and conjunctivitis, findings also seen in measles, can occur, and are more commonly seen in adults than in children. Thrombocytopenia, pericarditis, myocarditis and encephalitis are reportedly rare complications [Maldonado et al., 2011].
The incidence of rubella encephalitis is approximately 1 in 6,000 patients [Figueiredo et al., 2011]. The causes are thought to be host immune responses and the direct invasion of the virus to the brain. Common clinical manifestations are headache and ataxia. Altered consciousness, coma, and seizure are relatively uncommon. The onset is usually within 1 to 8 days after the development of the typical rash. Most patients (80%) recovered without sequelae [Figueiredo et al., 2012], but in some patients, abnormal brain waves persist for a prolonged period [Pampiglione et al., 1963].
An outbreak of rubella has been occurring in Japan since 2012 in large cities such as Tokyo [National Institute of Infectious Disease, Japan web site - Infectious Diseases Weekly Report, Rubella, 2013 (week30)]; thousands of patients have been affected [CDC, MMWR 2013] and 18 patients of congenital rubella syndrome were reported during this outbreak [National Institute of Infectious Disease, Japan web site - Infectious Diseases Weekly Report, Congenital rubella syndrome, 2013 (week36)]. The number of cases of rubella in men aged twenty to forty-nine has been dramatically increasing in Japan since 2012, thought to be due to the adoption in Japan of a selective vaccination approach targeted on school-aged girls until 1995. Catch-up immunization was available between 1995 and 2003 for children born after April 1979; however, this coverage rate was very low [National Institute of Infectious Disease, Japan web site - Infectious Agents Surveillance Report 2013].

title: 2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in his sixties, with a history of chronic l
history:
2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in his sixties, with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and lymphoma developed fever, cough, shortness of breath, generalized weakness and fatigue.
The patient had a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and lymphoma, diagnosed seven years earlier. Therapy had included chlorambucil administered intermittently since his diagnosis; the most recent administration of chemotherapy was three years earlier. Three months before admission, pathological examination of a bone marrow biopsy showed interval progression of disease and possible relapse. Chlorambucil (8mg orally, daily) and prednisone (20mg oral daily) were administered.
Four weeks before admission, a productive cough developed and two weeks later, fever up to 102°F (38.9°C) occurred, associated with chills, night sweats, and weight loss of about 20 pounds, which he attributed to decreased appetite. Two courses of oral azithromycin were administered as an outpatient, without improvement.
He was admitted to the hospital. On admission, the temperature was 101°F (38.3°C). The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was 575 cells per cubic millimeter. A chest radiograph revealed a right middle lobe and right perihilar infiltrate (Figures 1 and 2). Computerized tomography (CT) of chest (Figure 3) showed extensive lymphadenopathy of mediastinal, cervical, axillary lymph nodes and consolidation of the right middle lobe. Sputum and blood culture grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54%, severe aortic stenosis without evidence of regurgitation or vegetation.
Nafcillin (2 grams every 4hours, intravenously) was administered, and his symptoms improved. Repeat blood cultures after 48 hours of treatment were sterile. He was discharged home on cefazolin (1 gram every 8 hours, intravenously) for a 3 weeks' treatment course. Upon discharge, the absolute neutrophil count was more than 1000 cells per cubic millimeter. Chemotherapy was held because of the presence of active infection.
One month after discharge, increasing weakness, recurrent fever, chills and productive cough developed. He had not received any chemotherapy since previous admission. The patient was re-evaluated and admitted to the hospital.
Figure 1. A chest radiograph.
Figure 2. Radiograph of the chest, lateral view.
Figure 3. CT of the chest

He had history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and lymphoma diagnosed seven years earlier. Therapy included intermittent chlorambucil since his diagnosis, and rituximab to which he had responded well in the past.

He was retired and lived in the region of the Central Valley of California for more than a decade. He did not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He had no known exposure to farm animals, tuberculosis, sick people or those who were homeless or incarcerated. He had traveled to Eastern Europe 3 years earlier.

Vancomycin caused urticaria and hives.

As noted, chlorambucil (8mg orally, daily) and prednisone (20mg orally, daily) had been restarted three months before, and multiple antibiotics had been administered.
exam_studies:
Laboratory test results revealed pancytopenia, including hemoglobin 8.5 gm/dl, hematocrit 26%, absolute neutrophil count 405 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range, above 1500), and platelet count 13,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 140,000-440,000).
A chest radiograph revealed a new cavitary lesion in the right middle lobe (Figure 4). Computerized tomography (CT) of chest demonstrated the new right middle lobe cavitary lesion (2.8cm by 2.9cm by 2.1cm) (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Radiograph of the chest, one month after first admission.
Figure 5. CT of the chest, one month after first admission.

Two doses of piperacillin-tazobactam were administered on admission, followed by the administration of cefepime, empirically for neutropenic fever. The patient remained febrile and voriconazole was later added empirically to cover invasive fungal infection.
Subsequent bronchoscopy and biopsy showed normal mucosa and no endobronchial lesions. Pathological examination of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid revealed numerous pulmonary histiocytes with background lymphocytes. There was no evidence of malignancy, and stains for fungus, acid fast bacilli (AFB), and Pneumocystis jirovecii (by direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)) from a bronchial fluid specimen and respiratory viral cultures were negative. Cultures of the fluid did not grow fungi or tuberculosis.
The Aspergillus galactomannan antigen index by enzyme immunoassay was 6.5 (normal index value equal to or greater than 0.5), which was thought to be a false-positive because of the administration of piperacillin-tazobactam on admission. A repeat galactomannan level was negative (0.13). Bronchoalveolar fluid bacterial cultures later grew Achromobactor xylosoxidans that was sensitive to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, ceftazidime, meropenem and piperacillin; cefepime was stopped and ceftazidime begun.
The patient's clinical condition rapidly deteriorated and he was admitted to the intensive care unit. He was intubated due to progressive respiratory distress and required vasopressors for blood pressure support. Antibiotics coverage was empirically broadened, and meropenem and tigecycline were administered to cover hospital acquired resistant bacteria.
The patient remained persistently febrile, pancytopenic and critically ill, requiring ventilator support and vasopressors.
The serum total bilirubin was 1.5 mg/dl (reference range 0.3 - 1.1), direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl (reference range 0.0 - 0.4), aspartate aminotransferase 10 U/L (reference range 11 - 47), alanine aminotransferase 11 U/L (reference range 7 - 53), and creatinine 1.8 mg/dl (reference range 0.70 - 1.30). Results of blood tests for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cytomegalovirus DNA by polymerase chain reaction, Mycoplasma antibody, TB gold quantiferon test, cryptococcal antigen, and beta-D-glucan were negative. Serological testing for Coccidioides, performed at the University of California Davis reference laboratory, was negative by both immunodiffusion and complement fixation on three separate occasions.
Urine tests for Legionella antigen, pneumococcal antigen and Histoplasma antigen were also negative. Sputum stain and culture for acid fast bacilli were negative. A repeat bone marrow biopsy revealed 95% lymphocytes and marked suppression of normal hematopoietic cells.
On the ninth hospital day, blood cultures drawn on the first day of admission were positive. Gram stain of the organism is shown in Figure 6.
Figure 6. Blood culture growth, gram stain (400x magnification).
diagnosis:
Disseminated coccidioidomycosis caused by Coccidioides immitis in a febrile neutropenic patient with underlying hematological malignancy.

Blood cultures showed thin filamentous hyphal elements (Figures 6 and 7); Coccidioides immitis was identified by gene probe. Hanks acid fast stain for Nocardia was negative.
Figure 7. Blood culture growth, Hanks Acid Fast Stain.

A diagnosis of septic shock secondary to disseminated coccidioidomycosis and fungemia in the setting of profound and prolonged neutropenia was made. He became hemodynamically unstable and responded poorly to vasopressors and fluid resuscitation. After blood culture result became available, voriconazole was changed to liposomal amphotericin B. Despite broad spectrum antibiotics and antifungal therapy, he died on the eleventh hospital day from septic shock and multiple organ failure.

The diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis can be challenging in immunocompromised patients. This patient had stage 4 chronic lymphocytic leukemia and lymphoma with signs and symptoms of disseminated fungal infection, radiologic findings of cavitary lesions on imaging studies of the lungs and positive blood cultures showing filamentous hyphae; however serum Coccidioides serology, both immunodiffusion and complement fixation tests, were repeatedly negative on three separate occasions performed at University of California-Davis Reference laboratory. Negative serologies were suspected to be caused by the patient's underlying malignancy and profound immunosuppression resulting in an inability to produce a humoral immune response to his disseminated fungal infection.
Disseminated coccidioidomycosis in patients with hematologic malignancies is associated with considerable morbidity and mortality [Blair, Smilack and Caples, 2005]. Rapid diagnosis and efficient therapeutic measures are essential. Treatments for coccidioidomycosis include azole antifungals, primarily fluconazole and itraconazole as initial therapy for most chronic pulmonary or disseminated infections. Amphotericin B is now usually reserved for patients with respiratory failure due to infection with Coccidioides species, those with rapidly progressive infections, or women during pregnancy (particularly the first trimester) [Galgiani et al, 2005].
Coccidioides fungemia is an uncommon manifestation of fulminant, disseminated coccidioidomycosis. Survival is significantly worse in immunocompromised patients [Keckich, et al., 2010]. A retrospective review of sixteen episodes of fungemia due to Coccidioides immitis in 15 patients over a 7-year period by Ampel and colleagues identified 13 patients who had underlying conditions, including malignancy in 6 and AIDS in 3. Ten of the patients were receiving corticosteroids at the time of fungemia. Eleven of the 16 episodes ended in death within 1 month of the positive blood culture [Ampel et al, 1986].
Physicians should be aware of the possibility of negative serology in immunocompromised patients and should start empiric antifungal therapy when clinical suspicion is high, particularly in patients from endemic regions. Development of new diagnostic studies and effective therapeutic and preventive antifungal therapy especially in patients with hematological malignancy and disseminated coccidioidomycosis may improve outcomes.
