title: 2014 January-February Featured Case and 2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in
history:
2014 January-February Featured Case and 2013 IDWEEK Case Presentation: A man in his fifties developed severe, sharp headaches one week before presentation. The pain started across his forehead and radiated to the back of his head, and was associated with diffuse myalgias, arthralgias, shaking chills and profuse sweating that awakened him at night. He reported no photophobia, visual disturbances, or fevers. The joint pain had begun in his left shoulder and improved after 2 days, followed by pain in his right ankle, without swelling at either site. A vesicle developed on the left thumb that became crusted and healed in the beginning of the week, followed by more vesicles on the left middle finger, left middle toe, and left first toe.

He did not smoke tobacco, use illicit drugs, or drink alcohol. He owned two dogs and worked in a pet store that sold exotic fish, reptiles, and amphibians including various species of snakes, lizards, turtles, and frogs. He had no known insect or tick bite exposures.

He had no known drug allergies.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure 140/88 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats per minute, respirations 12 per minute and oxygen saturation 95% while breathing room air. There was a dry healed scar on his left middle finger, a small vesicle with eschar formation on his left thumb (Figure 1), and a patch of erythema at the proximal left thigh (Figure 2) and a small hemorrhagic vesicle on his left big toe (Figure 3). There was pain in his mid-thoracic spine and tenderness on palpation over the distal interphalangeal joint of his left middle toe, which appeared inflamed. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Left hand lesion.
Figure 2. Left thigh lesion.
Figure 3. Left toe lesion.

The white blood cell count was 12,200 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref.) 4400 to 11,300 cells per cubic millimeter) with 97% neutrophils and the serum glucose was 144 mg/dl (ref. 70 to 100 mg/dl). The platelet count and levels of hemoglobin, routine chemistry tests and tests of liver function were normal. Testing for antibodies to HIV was negative.

In the emergency room, a lumbar puncture was performed and cultures of the cerebrospinal fluid and blood were obtained.
Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed 1215 red cells per cubic millimeter (ref. 0) in tube 1 and 1600 in tube 4. There were 17 white cells per cubic millimeter (including 93% neutrophils) in tube 1, and 25 white cells per cubic millimeter (93% neutrophils, 3% lymphocytes and 4% monocytes) in tube 4 (ref. <5 tubes 1 and 4). The level of protein in the cerebrospinal fluid was 70 mg/dl (ref. 15 to 45) and glucose was 70 mg/dl (ref. 40 to 75).
diagnosis:
Rat bite fever caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis.

Cerebrospinal fluid cultures were sterile. Blood cultures grew a fastidious gram negative rod, which was thought to be consistent with Streptobacillus moniliformis (Figures 4 and 5). Streptobacillus monoliformis was identified at the ARUP laboratories in Salt Lake City, Utah.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of a skin biopsy (performed at the University of Washington, Seattle) was also positive for Streptobacillus moniliformis.
Figure 4. Gram stain of blood culture, 100x magnification.
Figure 5. Gram stain of culture growth, 100x magnification.

Rat bite fever is caused by two different organisms, Spirillum minus, which is prevalent in Asia and Streptobacillus moniliformis, which is prevalent in North America and Europe. Streptobacillus moniliformis is a pleomorphic, filamentous, gram negative rod and part of the nasopharyngeal flora of rats, with 10% to 100% of domestic rats and 50% to 100% of wild rats a carrier.
The reported incidence of Streptobacillus infection is very low, with most reports coming from the United States. There are only about 200 cases documented but the true incidence of rat bite fever is unknown since it is not a reportable disease.
Historically, affected patients were those living in poverty or laboratory workers, but with the increasing popularity of rats as pets, children began to account for most cases, followed by laboratory workers and pet shop owners. There appears to be only a 10% infectivity rate after a rat bite, but not all cases involve bites. Transmission can also occur with handling, via scratches or exposure to excrement and saliva.
The incubation period ranges from 3 days to 3 weeks. Initial symptoms include fevers with temperatures ranging between 38° to 41°Celsius. Over 50% of patients develop migratory polyarthralgias, including both large and small joints. Rash may develop that is maculopapular, petechial, purpuric, or consist of hemorrhagic vesicles. Complications include endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis, meningitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, and nephritis.
Untreated, Streptobacillus infection carries a 7% to 10% case-fatality rate. The most described complication is endocarditis, which can carry up to 53% mortality. In 2003, two rapidly fatal cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from Florida and Washington State of previously healthy women who had 2 to 3 days of illness. The first was a 53-year-old woman who arrived in septic shock with multi-organ failure who died 12 hours after admission. The second case involved a 19-year-old woman who was dead on arrival. Histopathology revealed a systemic infectious process including disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, with involvement of the liver lung and heart.
Since rat bite fever is not a reportable disease, the incidence is difficult to determine. Also, because there are such few cases, the sensitivity of blood cultures in humans is unknown, but the organism is difficult to grow in culture and requires an enriched media. In this case, PCR testing, a newer diagnostic method only recently described for use in rat bite fever, was also positive on skin biopsy.

title: A woman in her seventies presented to the hospital with weight loss, abdominal p
history:
A woman in her seventies presented to the hospital with weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and rash for three months. She also reported shortness of breath, hemoptysis, and recent onset of a new painful sacral rash.
Two months before admission, glucocorticoids had been administered for an intensely pruritic rash on her arms, legs, and trunk. This rash initially improved but then intensified. She also developed thrush during this time, which was treated with a course of fluconazole.

She had a history of seasonal rhinitis and osteoarthritis.

She had had multiple sexual partners in her lifetime. She lived in a rural area in Louisiana and had one dog. She had no significant travel history, and had not been outside of the United States. She enjoyed gardening and frequently worked in her yard.

She was widow who lived with her boyfriend until a few weeks before admission, when she moved in with family for assistance with activities of daily living due to fatigue.

She had taken a course of glucocorticoids two months before this presentation.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared chronically ill. The blood pressure was 125/41 mm Hg, pulse 102 beats per minute, temperature 98.1ºF (36.1ºC), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The lungs were clear and there was tenderness to palpation in both right and left upper quadrants of her abdomen. Examination of the skin revealed a petechial rash with some linear features on her abdomen (Figure 1), a diffuse papular rash on both legs (Figure 2) and back, and several lesions on her sacrum that resembled denuded bullae had surrounding erythema and were exquisitely tender (Figure 3).
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.
Figure 3. Physical findings.

Laboratory values on admission revealed a white blood cell count of 5800 cells per cubic millimeter/L (with 8% eosinophils (reference range 0-7%)), hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL (reference range 12-16 g/dL) and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 79 fL. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody testing was positive and the absolute CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 6 cells per cubic millimeter. A chest radiograph was negative. Figure 4. Examination of a stool specimen.
Figure 4. Examination of a stool specimen.

The patient was admitted to the hospital and crystalloid and blood products were administered. Initial evaluation for weight loss, change in bowel habits, and anemia included esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), colonoscopy, and stool studies.
Examination of the stool is shown (Figure 4).
diagnosis:
Strongyloides stercolis hyperinfection syndrome in a patient with newly-diagnosed HIV infection and AIDS.

Pathologic review of the stool revealed Strongyloides stercolis. EGD revealed a small antral ulcer and colonoscopy was significant for pan-colitis.
With the patient’s respiratory symptoms and immunocompromised state, there was concern for dissemination of the S. stercolis and hyperinfection syndrome. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed alveolar infiltrates. Bronchoscopic examination with bronchial alveolar lavage revealed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and an abundance of S. stercolis on pathologic examination (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Examination of a sputum specimen.

The patient was initially treated with ivermectin alone but due to persistently positive stools, albendazole was added. Stool examination became negative on the ninth day of treatment. Antiretroviral therapy for her HIV was not started as an inpatient due to concerns of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
At discharge, the gastrointestinal symptoms had resolved and she reported feeling better. Ivermectin was administered again two weeks later. Her stool examinations at that time, and before initiation of antiretrovirals one month after discharge, were negative for organisms.

Strongyloides stercolis is an intestinal nematode which is endemic in tropical and subtropical climates, although there have been cases described in temperate climates such as southeastern United States. Infection in the United States is found in inhabitants of rural areas, institutionalized persons, immigrants, veterans, and those of low socioeconomic status. The prevalence of Strongyloides infection and associated deaths in the United States is likely underestimated. Immunocompetent hosts may have an asymptomatic or mild illness. Immune-compromised hosts have the potential for more severe infection.
Strongyloides is unique amongst helminths in its ability to complete its lifecycle within the human host, leading to autoinfection. Autoinfection results in an accelerated lifecycle, increasing parasitic burden and dissemination. This process, called the hyperinfection syndrome, carries a mortality rate as high as 85%. While Strongyloides stercolis may infect up to 100 million humans worldwide, hyperinfection is infrequent. The patient in this case displayed multiple characteristic findings of hyperinfection, including colon and lung involvement. This patient’s sacral rash and colitis may have represented sites of autoinfection after administration of systemic glucocorticoids. The diffuse rash was consistent with larva currens. Hyperinfection with S. stercolis is described in patients with AIDS but is rarely seen as the initial presentation of AIDS in the United States. As the AIDS epidemic reaches the elderly, clinicians should be more diligent in screening this vulnerable population.

title: A man in his thirties with morbid obesity and diabetes mellitus was transferred
history:
A man in his thirties with morbid obesity and diabetes mellitus was transferred to a tertiary care hospital in Pennsylvania because of shock, multi-organ failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
One week before admission, fatigue, myalgias, fever, chills, nausea and vomiting developed, for which the patient reportedly took acetaminophen as needed (no more than 2 grams daily). He saw his physician and erythromycin was prescribed for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis. Shortly afterwards, abdominal pain and diarrhea developed. Five days after the onset of symptoms, he presented to another hospital. He reported weight loss of 20 pounds (9.1kg) during the previous month.
At the other hospital, he was reportedly febrile and hypotensive. Laboratory test results reportedly included a white cell count of 1700 cells per cubic millimeter (including 13% band forms), platelet count 62,000 per cubic millimeter, alanine aminotransferase (ALT, SGPT) 1677 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST, SGOT) 5219 IU/L, and acetaminophen was reportedly present at a nontoxic level.
He was admitted to the hospital and vancomycin, levofloxacin, ceftriaxone and cefepime were administered, without improvement. The patient became obtunded and was transferred to a tertiary care hospital the next day.

The patient had diabetes mellitus type 2, morbid obesity, hypothyroidism and vitamin D deficiency. He had never received influenza vaccinations.

The patient lived in a rural area and had had a tick bite 5 months before this presentation. Three weeks before admission, one of his children was diagnosed with hand-foot-mouth disease. The next week, the patient had stripped the siding of an old house and scratched his wrist. He had been exposed to mud and fresh water 3 days before the onset of symptoms. He had no history of travel and did not drink alcohol, smoke or use intravenous drugs. He was monogamous with his wife. He had 2 pets at home.

He lived with his wife and children. He had been unemployed for several months before presentation.

Medications at home included metformin, testosterone, levothyroxine, calcium and vitamin D supplements.
exam_studies:
The patient was obese, and appeared in distress, disoriented and confused. The blood pressure was 80/61 mmHg, pulse 94 beats per minute, temperature 38.2°C (100.8°F), and oxygen saturation 94% while breathing oxygen at 6 liters per minute by nasal cannula. The mucous membranes were dry and there were petechiae on the palate. Rhonchi were heard in both lungs. The abdomen was soft, with hepatomegaly and exquisite tenderness in the right upper quadrant and diffuse tenderness in other regions. There were 1-to-2 beats of clonus, intact cranial nerves, and no nuchal rigidity; the patient was unable to cooperate with the remainder of the neurological exam. The remainder of the general examination was normal.

The white cell count was 3000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 3800-10,600) with a differential including neutrophils 52%, band forms 30%, lymphocytes 6%, hemoglobin 11.6 mg/dl (reference range 13.5-17.5), and platelets 27,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 156,000-369,000); the blood level of urea nitrogen was 44 mg/dl (reference range 8-26), creatinine 3.8 mg/dl (reference range 0.5-1.4), total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl (reference range 0.3-1.5), direct bilirubin 1.7mg/dl (reference range 0.1-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 2116 IU/L (reference range 17-63), aspartate aminotransferase 9208 IU/L (reference range 15-41), alkaline phosphatase 346 IU/L (reference range 38-126), GGTP 118 IU/L (reference range <66), and lactate 5.4 mMol/L (reference range 0.5-1.6). Blood gases revealed pH 7.23, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 33 mmHg (reference range 32-48), partial pressure of oxygen 104 mmHg (reference range 83-108), HCO3 13 mEq/L (reference range (22-26). Acetaminophen was not detected.
An ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated steatosis with no intra- or extrahepatic biliary dilatation, and the gallbladder was not distended. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis, performed without the administration of contrast, was negative.

The patient became somnolent and the trachea was intubated for airway protection. Shortly thereafter, hematemesis occurred; a Minnesota tube was placed to control bleeding and pressors were administered. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) did not reveal the source of bleeding. Piperacillin-tazobactam, doxycycline, metronidazole, fluconazole, vancomycin and acyclovir were administered. Blood, platelets and fresh frozen plasma were transfused.
Acidosis worsened, with pH decreasing to 7.07 and lactate rising to 17mMol/L. Continuous renal replacement therapy was started. Hypoxia occurred while being ventilated with 100% oxygen.
His condition deteriorated rapidly and he died, 36 hours after transfer. An autopsy was performed; pathological examination of the liver (Figures 1 and 2) and adrenal gland (Figure 3) is shown.
Figure 1. Pathological examination of the liver.
Figure 2. Pathological examination of the liver.
Figure 3. Pathological examination of the adrenal gland.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Herpes Simplex Virus-1 infection with fulminant HSV hepatitis.

Testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV) type-1 DNA in the blood by PCR revealed greater than 560,000 copies/ml. Other testing, including for nucleic acid of herpes simplex virus type-2, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus by PCR; hepatitis B core antigen and antibody; hepatitis B surface antibody; anti-hepatitis A antibodies; anti-hepatitis C antibodies; antibodies to leptospirosis and serum and urine Histoplasma antigen were negative.
On autopsy, there was hepatomegaly, with extensive coagulative necrosis, limited inflammatory infiltrate and hepatocyte nuclear inclusions (Figures 1, 2 and 4). Pathological examination of the adrenal gland (Figures 3 and 5) showed cortical necrosis with viral inclusions. Immune histochemical staining for HSV-1 was positive in the liver and adrenal gland (Figures 6 and 7, respectively). Other findings on autopsy included esophageal mucosal ulceration with necrosis and huge sloughed squamous epithelial cells with nuclear viral inclusions, congestive splenomegaly with acute immunoblastic proliferation suggestive of acute viral infection, and renal enlargement with acute tubular necrosis.
Figure 4. Pathological examination of the liver, viral inclusions shown with arrows.
Figure 5. Pathological examination of the adrenal gland, viral inclusions shown with arrows.
Figure 6. Immunohistochemical staining for HSV-1 in liver tissue.
Figure 7. Immunohistochemical staining for HSV-1 in adrenal tissue.

This young male patient presented with shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and multi-organ failure one week after the onset of prodromal symptoms of fever, fatigue, nausea and vomiting.
Regarding the diagnoses considered, if untreated, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF) can progress to multi-organ failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in 7-15 days. Spotless Rocky Mountain fever can be seen in black patients, which may delay diagnosis and treatment. However, RMSF is rare in Pennsylvania (0.1-1.0 per one million persons per year [Walker 2010]).
Weil’s disease can progress to acute renal and liver failure after the acute phase and is usually characterized by a high fever up to 40°C (104.0°F) and, unlike the findings in this patient, marked hyperbilirubinemia and a modest elevation of the transaminases [Levett 2001]. Reyes syndrome is most commonly seen in children but has been reported in adults. It is characterized by a prodromal viral illness followed by vomiting, worsening mental status in the absence of focal neurological deficits. The use of aspirin has been linked to the development of Reyes syndrome [Meythaler and Varma 1987].
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) fulminant liver failure can be seen in immunosuppressed patients, primarily in transplant recipients. HSV hepatitis accounts for less than 1% of all acute liver failure. Around 100 cases have been described in the literature. Fulminant HSV hepatitis may represent primary infection or reactivation. Clues to the diagnosis are mucocutaneous lesions, marked elevation in transaminases with normal or slightly elevated bilirubin and DIC [Wind et al. 2012]. Patients who are male, older age, immunocompromised, and/or presenting with significant liver dysfunction are more likely to progress to death [Norvell et al. 2007].
Herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1 typically causes orolabial infections and has an estimated seroprevalence of 62%. Hepatic involvement during infections with HSV-1 and HSV-2 is rare. Neonates, malnourished children, pregnant women, and patients receiving immunosuppressive medications are particularly at risk. Less than 10 cases of fulminate hepatitis described in immunocompetent patients [Talwani et al. 2011]
HSV hepatitis occurs as a so-called concomitant hepatitis in systemic HSV infection or HSV sepsis and is characterized by fulminant hepatic necrosis, with serum aminotransferase levels 100 to 1000 fold above normal [Riediger et al. 2009]. In one study, 24% were considered immunocompetent. The remaining patients were either pregnant (23%) or immunocompromised from a previous solid organ or hematopoietic cell transplantation (30%) or immunosuppressive agent (23%). The majority were first diagnosed after death on autopsy (57.6%) [Norvell et al. 2007].
In another study, at the time of hospitalization, HSV hepatitis patients had higher median HSV DNA load (6,000,000) compared to disease controls (171±2,854). Viral DNA load correlated with liver transaminase levels and disease severity. [Beersma et al. 2011].
Variables associated with death include age greater than 40 years, male gender, coagulopathy, immunocompromised state, encephalopathy, alanine aminotransferase greater than 5,000U/L, and platelet count less than 75,000 per cubic millimeter. Patients treated with acyclovir were less likely to progress to death or liver transplantation, 51% versus 88% (P value 0.001) [Norvell et al. 2007].
Empiric use of acyclovir, recommended by many authors, should be considered while the diagnostic evaluation of non-acetaminophen induced fulminant hepatitis is underway (Peters et al. 2000). In one study the percentage of treated patients who progressed to death or liver transplantation was 51% compared with 88.1% of those who were untreated [Riediger et al. 2009, Norvell et al. 2009].

title: A man in his eighties from Puerto Rico was admitted to the hospital because of a
history:
A man in his eighties from Puerto Rico was admitted to the hospital because of a productive cough, subjective fever, and dizziness. His family reported that one week before admission, he had slipped in the shower, hitting his face and chest. He was evaluated at a hospital in Puerto Rico where reportedly there was no evidence of a fracture.
Two days later, he was taken by a relative to another hospital because of pain in his chest, back, and left arm, and a non-productive cough. The evaluation included chest radiographs, computed tomography (CT) of the brain, an electrocardiogram, complete blood count, basic metabolic profile, and serial cardiac enzymes and was reportedly negative. His appetite was poor after the fall. His son noted his father was very warm to touch, and had a cough productive of yellow sputum, which progressively worsened over a week. The patient traveled to Florida and was brought to the hospital by relatives for evaluation.

The patient had Alzheimer’s disease, peripheral vascular disease (status post right below knee amputation with phantom limb syndrome), low back pain, and benign prostatic hypertrophy. He had had a cholecystectomy and appendectomy in the past.

He lived alone in Puerto Rico with family assistance until this illness, when he moved to Florida to live with relatives. His only previous travel was to Korea 60 years before. He had a dog and his activities included gardening.

He had no allergies.

Pneumococcal, tetanus, and influenza immunizations were current. Medications at home include aspirin (81mg daily), citalopram, donepezil, gemfibrozil, simvastatin, atenolol, omeprazole and pregabalin.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared tired, in no acute distress and able to engage in conversation. The blood pressure was 101/57 mm Hg, pulse 73 beats per minute, temperature 97.7°F (36.5°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. He had healing bruises around the right eye, and chest examination revealed bibasilar crackles. The scar of the below-the-knee amputation was well-healed, and the remainder of the general examination was normal.

On admission, the white count was 23,000 cells/mL (reference range 3,900-9,900), sodium 129 mEq/L (reference range 136 – 145), creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (from baseline of 1.1 mg/dL), and glucose at 219 mg/dL. Procalcitonin was 4.58 ng/mL (reference range 0.0-0.1). Tests of liver function were normal.
A nasal specimen screening for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) by PCR was negative. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained; he could not provide a sputum specimen.
Images of a chest radiograph (Figure 1) and CT scan of the thorax (Figure 2) are shown.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph with infiltrate in the left lung and a pleural-based density.
Figure 2. Chest CT, with areas of consolidation.
diagnosis:
Burkholderia pseudomallei pneumonia with bacteremia.

Both sets of blood cultures grew gram-negative rods from the aerobic bottles within 24 hours. The hospital microbiology laboratory was unable to identify the isolate definitively, but could not rule out Burkholderia species. The isolate was sent to the Florida State Laboratory, where a presumptive identification of Burkholderia pseudomallei was made, which was confirmed by the laboratories of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). MIC E-tests susceptibility revealed susceptibility to ceftazidime, meropenem, and minocycline.

The patient initiated treatment with levofloxacin, vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam for possible healthcare-associated pneumonia; follow-up blood cultures done 48 hours after admission remained negative.
On the sixth hospital day, the laboratory reported possible Burkholderia species, and the Infectious Disease service was consulted for management of the possible Burkholderia pseudomallei pneumonia and sepsis. The antibiotics were changed to oral doxycycline (150mg twice daily) and oral sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (1600/320mg twice daily) after completion of intravenous therapy (piperacillin/tazobactam and levofloxacin).
The patient was discharged with improved condition after thirteen days hospitalization. A skin reaction developed 2 days after discharge and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim was subsequently changed to amoxicillin-clavulanate. He completed 20 weeks of treatment with doxycycline and amoxicillin-clavulanate with clinical improvement. Follow-up CT scan of the chest (Figure 3) obtained 4 weeks after the first study was improved. He remained asymptomatic three years after his pneumonia.
Figure 3. Follow-up CT of the chest, 4 weeks later.

Melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei (a gram-negative, bipolar, aerobic, motile rod-shaped bacterium) occurs predominantly in Southeast Asia, Northern Australia, South Asia and China [Wiersinga et al. 2012]. Its known global distribution is expanding, a reflection of improvements in diagnostic microbiology and increasing numbers of cases in travelers. The Caribbean is not known to be endemic for the disease [Inglis et al. 2006], but cases originating from Puerto Rico have been described [CDC, MMWR 2006; Christenson et al. 2003; Dorman et al. 1998].
Common manifestations of infection include severe community-acquired pneumonia and sepsis. B. pseudomallei can cause abscesses, particularly of the skin and soft tissues. The greatest risk factor for B. pseudomallei infection is type 2 diabetes; other risk factors include thalassemia, renal disease, chronic alcoholism, and liver disease. Melioidosis should be an etiologic consideration for pneumonia in patients from Puerto Rico.

title: A man in his sixties was admitted to the hospital because of progressive shortne
history:
A man in his sixties was admitted to the hospital because of progressive shortness of breath and fatigue.
His symptoms had been increasing during the previous 2 years, and were associated with increasing fatigue and weight gain. He also reported chest pain, ankle swelling, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations and occasional diarrhea. An evaluation included cardiac catheterization, which demonstrated constrictive pericarditis.
He was admitted to the hospital. On the night of admission, a temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) developed.

He had had Hodgkin's disease for which radiation treatment had been administered. He also had congestive heart failure, sero-negative rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He had had a pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis, and 35 years earlier, an exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy.

He worked on a farm in the Great Lakes region of the United States, owned cats and dogs, and had traveled to the northeastern United States one year before this presentation.

Medications included prednisone (10 mg twice daily), torsemide, methotrexate (2.5 mg weekly), metolazone, carvedilol, and fondaparinux. He had received etanercept, which was stopped one month before this presentation.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared chronically ill. The blood pressure was 92/54 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats per minute, temperature 96.4°F (35.8°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were distant and there were dilated veins on the upper chest. The abdomen was slightly distended and the legs were edematous (2+). The remainder of the examination was negative.

The white blood cell count was 17,350 per cubic millimeter (reference range 3,700-11,000) on the day of admission, and rose to 25,420 on the third hospital day. The level of hemoglobin was 9.6 g/dl, platelets 151,000 per cubic millimeter. The creatinine level was 1.01 mg/dl and results of other blood chemistries and tests of liver function were normal. The urinalysis revealed cloudy urine, with trace protein, 1+ blood, 3+ leukocytes esterase, and 11-25 white cells per high-power field.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, performed without the administration of contrast, showed small pleural effusions and linear atelectasis and/or scar in the right lower lobe (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT of the chest, without contrast.

The blood culture showed no growth at 5 days. Culture of the urine grew 100,000 colony-forming units of Escherichia coli.
Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated moderate (2+) mitral valve (MV) regurgitation, with an attached mobile calcified echodensity on the anterior MV leaflet (Figure 2 and Video 1, in a video loop). Trans-esophageal echocardiogram (TEE) demonstrated a brightly echodense mobile lesion (1.8cm by 0.8cm) on the atrial surface of the anterior mitral valve leaflet (lateral side) and a linear highly mobile echodensity (at least 1.6cm in length) attached to the atrial side of the tricuspid valve.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the heart showed evidence of constrictive pericarditis.
Figure 2. Transthoracic echocardiogram, with a calcified mitral valve and mobile echodensity (arrows).
diagnosis:
Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis and pericarditis

Testing of the blood for nucleic acid of Tropheryma whipplei by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive.

Cardiac surgery was performed, including median sternotomy, pericardiectomy, mitral valve replacement and removal of tricuspid valve vegetation.
Surgical pathology is shown in Figures 3 through 6. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H & E) staining of the mitral valve revealed foamy macrophages (Figure 3), and Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining of the mitral valve (Figure 4) demonstrated PAS-positive organisms within the macrophages. H & E staining of the pericardium revealed a thick fibrotic pericardium (Figure 5), and PAS-positive organisms were identified in the pericardial tissue (Figure 6). Universal PCR testing of the mitral valve, the tricuspid valve vegetation and pericardium were positive for Tropheryma whipplei.
Ceftriaxone (intravenously for 6 weeks) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (oral, for a prolonged course) were administered. Prednisone was weaned and the methotrexate was stopped. The patient was doing well after 10 months of treatment.
Figure 3. H and E stain of the mitral valve.
Figure 4. PAS stain of the mitral valve.
Figure 5. H and E stain of pericardial tissue.
Figure 6. PAS stain of pericardial tissue.

Whipple’s disease, first described in 1907 by G.H Whipple, is a chronic multi-system infectious disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei. The most common symptoms of classic Whipple’s disease include weight loss, hypoalbuminemia, diarrhea, arthralgia and anemia [Moos and Schneider, 2011]. Patients with infective endocarditis due to T. whipplei may have no symptoms of classical Whipple’s disease [Geissdorfer, et al. 2012]. Tropheryma whipplei infective endocarditis (TWIE) often does not meet the clinical criteria for IE using the Duke’s Criteria [Geissdorfer, et al. 2012]. Diagnosis is usually by analysis of explanted heart valves using PCR, culture, and/or (immuno) histology [Lagier et al., 2010]. In a study of systemic T. whipplei in 142 patients in a reference center in Marseille, France, 80% of the patients had classical Whipple’s disease and 11% (16 patients) had endocarditis [Lagier et al., 2010].
Epidemiologic and clinical characteristics of patients with TWIE from the study by Lagier et al. were 100% male, with a mean age of 60.2 years, of whom 31% were on immunosuppressive therapy, 69% had arthralgias, and 81% had a cardiac vegetation [Lagier et al., 2010]. Evaluation of 1,135 cardiac valves in two Germany university centers from 2000 -2007 revealed T. whipplei as the 4th most common pathogen for endocarditis (16 cases, accounting for 6.3% of endocarditis cases)[Geissdorfer, et al., 2012].
Treatment recommendations have included intravenous ceftriaxone, meropenem, or penicillin G for 2 weeks, followed by oral sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for 12 months OR doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine orally for at least 18 months [Feurle, Junga and Marth, 2010; Schneider et al., 2008]. Clinicians should consider TWIE in males, age 50s to 60s with a history of arthralgia, new-onset heart failure and an echocardiogram showing valvular regurgitation and/or endocarditis [Love et al., 2012].

title: 2014 May-June Featured Case: A man in his thirties with a history of Hepatitis C
history:
2014 May-June Featured Case: A man in his thirties with a history of Hepatitis C virus infection and substance use disorder was seen in an emergency department after a fall from a bicycle; he reported recent illicit narcotic use. On examination, he initially appeared intoxicated, somnolent, and awoke intermittently to name and sternal rub. The temperature was 101.2°F (38.4°C) and rose to 104.2°F (40.1°C); other vital signs were normal. An acute laceration on the head and numerous abrasions were present, as well as injection marks on both arms. Breath sounds were shallow and coarse; heart sounds were regular, with a 1/6 systolic ejection murmur. He moved all extremities, and the remainder of the examination was normal. The white cell count was 5800 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4500-11,000), with 76.9% neutrophils, 11.6% lymphocytes, 10.5% monocytes, 0.3% eosinophils and 0.5% basophils; the hematocrit was 34.4% (ref 41.0-53.0). The blood level of the potassium was 3.0 mmol per liter (ref 3.4-4.8), alanine aminotransferase 95 U/L (ref 10-55) and aspartate aminotransferase 151 U/L (ref 10-40). Three sets of blood cultures were drawn. A chest radiograph showed no acute infiltrate. The mental status improved and the temperature returned to normal. Additional evaluation was planned, but was not completed as the patient requested discharge from the hospital.
Two days later, the patient was brought back to the emergency department by paramedical personnel after involvement in a motor vehicle accident; a cervical collar had been applied. On examination, numerous lacerations and a fractured fibula were noted. On review of the previously obtained blood cultures, two of three aerobic bottles were noted to be growing gram-positive bacilli.
The patient reported injecting narcotics with a needle and syringe someone had given him on the day before the blood cultures had been obtained. He reported using only clean needles, with tap water for injection, and noted he did not lick his needles. He was otherwise in his usual health, with no recent history of chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chest pain, shortness of breath, joint pain, back pain or rashes.

He had a history of alcohol use (6 beers per night) and substance use disorder, including heroin, cocaine, amphetamines and benzodiazepines. He reportedly had had seizures in the past that were thought to be caused by alcohol withdrawal. He had a history of hepatitis C virus infection; a viral nucleic acid level was undetectable approximately 8 months earlier. He also had depression, anxiety, and a neuropathy.

He reported no recent travel, sick contacts, or animal exposures.

He was homeless and had been incarcerated in the past.

He was on no other medications.
exam_studies:
The patient was somnolent and in no apparent distress; his drowsiness was thought to be caused by intoxication. The temperature was 100.5°F (38.1°C), blood pressure 103/63mm Hg, pulse 57 beats per minute, respirations 18 per minute and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing ambient air. There was a laceration over the left forehead and clotted blood scattered around the nose; a laceration across the chin had been sutured. There were missing teeth. No conjunctival hemorrhages were noted. The heart rate and rhythm were regular and the sounds were soft, with no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Breath sounds were diminished but clear. The abdomen was soft, non-distended and diffusely tender. The range of motion of the right leg was limited by pain. The extremities were warm and well-perfused. Abrasions over the dorsum of both hands were present, without Osler nodes or Janeway lesions. Neurological examination was limited by somnolence, but he was arousable, with no gross focal deficits.

The hematocrit was 31.2% and the white cell count was 4000 per cubic millimeter with 54% neutrophils, 26% lymphocytes, 14% monocytes, and 4% eosinophils. The blood level of alanine aminotransferase was 204 U/liter and aspartate aminotransferase 200 U/liter; the platelet count and blood levels of alkaline phosphatase, total and direct bilirubin, urea nitrogen and creatinine were normal. Toxicology screening of the urine and blood revealed methadone, diazepam, citalopram, cocaine, benzodiazepines, opioids, and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

Gram stain of the growth in a blood culture bottle is shown in Figure 1. Colony morphology on Brucella horse blood plate is shown in Figure 2, and gram stain of a colony at 24 hours is shown in Figure 3.
A chest radiograph showed no acute infiltrate and a radiograph of the right lower leg revealed a mildly displaced oblique fracture of the right proximal fibular diaphysis. An electrocardiogram showed no conduction abnormalities.
Figure 1. Gram stain of the growth in a blood culture bottle.
Figure 2. Colony morphology on Brucella horse blood plate.
Figure 3. Gram stain of the colony at 24 hours.
diagnosis:
Bacteremia caused by Rhodococcus equi in a patient with injection drug use.

Of the three sets of blood cultures drawn during the patient's first evaluation in the emergency department, two aerobic bottles grew gram-positive bacilli within 24 and 48 hours respectively. Figure 1, from the growth at 24-48 hours, reveals pleomorphic gram-positive bacilli. Colony growth on Brucella horse blood plate appeared pale pink, wet and mucoid on day 4 (Figure 2).
Morphology on gram stain varied from pleomorphic gram-positive bacilli at 24 hours (Figure 3) to gram-positive cocci at 48 hr (Figure 4, below). This appearance suggested the organism was Rhodococcus.
The organism was then identified by rapid API Coryne V3.0 (bioMerieux) as Rhodococcus spp at 94.1% probability. The Christie, Atkins, Munch-Peterson (CAMP) test, a phenotypic test to detect extracellular hemolytic protein or CAMP factor, yielded a positive result distinguishing Rhodococcus equi from other species. Additionally, the matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS, Vitek MS V2.0) identified the organism as Rhodococcus equi at 99.9% confidence value.
Figure 4. Gram stain of the colony at 48 hours.

A splint was applied to his leg and outpatient follow up with orthopedic surgery was scheduled. A transesophogeal echocardiogram revealed no vegetations. Antibiotics were administered and fevers resolved. Ciprofloxacin, orally, was prescribed for 2 weeks, and follow-up with his primary care provider scheduled.

Rhodococcus is a member of aerobic Actinomycetes, a large and diverse group of gram-positive bacilli, similar to clinically encountered genera Nocardia, Gordonia and Tsukamurella. These genera are aerobic, gram-positive, catalase-positive, partially acid-fast, branching, filamentous bacteria that can fragment into rods and cocci. Rhodococcus can appear coccoid or bacillary depending upon culture age, growth condition, and type of media (Figures 3 and 4). Colonies on solid media appear large, salmon-pink to red-colored, slimy or mucoid (Figure 2); however, these characteristics usually occur at days 4 to 7 of incubation [McNeil and Brown, 1994; Tille 2013].
Rhodococcus equi is the most important species of Rhodococcus species causing disease in humans. Greater than 80% of reported cases occurred in immunocompromised hosts particularly those with defects in cell-mediated immunity, e.g., patients with AIDS, chemotherapy recipients, those with leukemia or lymphoma, or stem cell or solid organ transplant recipients. R. equi has been found in soil, and is highly prevalent in some horse farms. Patients infected with R. equi frequently, but not always, have history of contact with farm animals, soil or both. Pneumonia accounts for about 80% of human cases of infection reported in the literature. Radiographically, pulmonary rhodococcal infection can present with nodules, infiltrates, cavitary lesions, effusion or abscesses which mimic tuberculosis, nocardiosis, fungal infections, or malignancy [Yamshchikov et al. 2010].
Extrapulmonary infection occurs in about 20% of cases, and may involve the central nervous system (CNS), subcutaneous tissue and internal organs causing abscesses. Bacteremia, catheter-associated infection, peritonitis, and osteomyelitis have also been described [Meyer and Reboli, 2009].
Owing to the small number of reported cases, there are no definitive guidelines for treatment. Similarly, there are no standardized methods for antimicrobial susceptibility testing. In vitro, Rhodococcus is generally susceptible to aminoglycosides, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, linezolid, macrolides, rifampin and vancomycin, whereas it is often resistant to penicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporins and clindamycin. Treatment of localized, non-CNS diseases in a normal host may be achieved with oral agents. In contrast, immunocompromised hosts, and those with serious infections, require treatment with 2-drug, and sometimes 3-drug, regimens that include intravenous antibiotics. It has been suggested that intravenous therapy be continued until clinical improvement occurs or for a minimum of 2 to 3 weeks, followed by oral agents until cultures are negative and signs and symptoms have resolved [Meyer and Reboli, 2009].
Of the other organisms in the differential, Staphylococcus aureus and Rothia mucilaginosa are gram-positive cocci that generally appear in clusters or tetrads, and would be unlikely to appear in the primary gram stain as a bacillary organism [Que and Moreillon 2010; Vaccher et al. 2007]. Rapidly growing Mycobacterium species are typically beaded gram-positive bacilli in clusters [El Helou et al. 2013]. Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a pleomorphic gram-positive rod that may appear as gram-negative rods at times because of rapid decolorization [Kichloo et al. 2013].

title: 2014 March-April Featured Case: A woman in her fifties with a history of human i
history:
2014 March-April Featured Case: A woman in her fifties with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was evaluated in an outpatient clinic because of recent abdominal cramping, diarrhea and a fecal abnormality.
The patient was in her usual state of health until three weeks before this presentation when abdominal cramping developed. Several days before this evaluation, diarrhea began, associated with nausea. One day before, while having a bowel movement, she noted a fecal abnormality described as a 'worm', about two feet in length. The next day, she went to the outpatient clinic, and brought in a portion and a stool specimen for examination. She reported feeling hungry for months, despite good food intake.

HIV infection and AIDS had been diagnosed 10 years earlier after a diagnosis of toxoplasmosis infection of the central nervous system was made. The CD4 T-lymphocyte count measured within months before this presentation was 722 per cubic millimeter (23.4%) and the HIV RNA level was undetectable. She also had had recurrent pneumonias, and a splenectomy following a motor vehicle accident as a teenager; an accessory spleen was present. A tuberculosis skin test had been negative the previous year.

She was born in a city and lived in a suburban area of the Northeast United States. She had traveled to the Caribbean 9 months earlier. She ate fish often, especially salmon which she did not always cook completely, and reported eating sushi within the previous week. She drank alcohol rarely, had stopped smoking many years earlier, and did not use illicit drugs.

She was married and worked in an office.

Medications included efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir fixed dose (600mg/200mg/300mg daily) and simvastatin.
exam_studies:
The patient was in no distress and thin. The weight was 134 pounds (61kg) and 3 pounds (1.4kg) less than previously recorded; the body mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) was 22. The vital signs and the remainder of the examination were normal.

Examination of the stool was performed.
Figure 1. Fecal product.
Figure 2. Fecal product.
diagnosis:
Diphyllobothriasis caused by infection consistent with Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) in a patient with HIV infection and AIDS.

The fecal abnormality (Figure 2) was identified as the cestode Diphyllobothrium (an adult fish tapeworm with numerous proglottid segments). Examination of the stool revealed numerous cysts or ova (Figure 3) consistent with D. latum.
Figure 3. Examination of the stool, 20x magnification.

Praziquantel (600 mg, orally) was administered daily for 2 days. A stool specimen obtained several months later showed no evidence of ova or parasites.

This patient with a history of HIV infection and AIDS developed diarrhea, followed by excretion per rectum of a worm (or helminth) segment, greater than 2 feet in length. Examination of the helminth revealed a multi-segmented flatworm (or cestode) consistent with Diphyllobothrium latum, of the genus Diphyllobothrium, a broad or fish tapeworm, in which each segment (proglottid) of the body (strobila) of the tapeworm contains both male and female productive organs [Scholz et al. 2009]. The stool specimen also revealed numerous ovoid cysts or eggs, which are released by the proglottids into the intestine. [Scholz et al. 2009].
Adult specimens of Diphyllobothrium species may grow up to 25 meters and 4000 segments in length; more often, D. latum grows up to 12 meters in length. Although many infections with D. latum can be asymptomatic, approximately 20% of patients may have diarrhea and/or abdominal discomfort [Scholz et al. 2009; Sampaio et a. 2005]; complications such as mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by the folded loops of the long worm, constipation, cholecystitis, and pernicious or megaloblastic anemia caused by factors related to vitamin B12 metabolism in the intestines and absorption of the vitamin by the worm can also occur [Scholz et al. 2009].
Diphyllobothrium species are found in freshwater nonsalmonid fish (such as perch, pike, burbot and walleye), salmonids that spawn in freshwater and live partly in the sea (including salmon, trout and whitefish), and possibly by brackish-water or marine fish. Infection with D. latum can be prevented by avoiding consumption of raw or uncooked fish or by prolonged and deep freezing of fish [Scholz et al. 2009].
Of the other organisms listed in the differential, Echinococcus granulosus and Taenia solium are also cestodes. Echinococcus, is generally in its larval form when found in human, and occurs after exposure to the eggs present in dog feces. Human illness may be caused by the body’s reaction to a growing or persistent cyst. Consumption of Taenia solium larval cysts in undercooked pork causes tapeworm infestation in the human intestine. The dimensions of the proglottids of T. solium are characteristically longer than they are wide, in contrast to those of D. latum in which the proglottids' width is greater than the length [Harada et al. 2006]. When a human ingests T. solium eggs shed in the stool of a person who is a tapeworm carrier, cysticercosis may result; in that instance, illness develops because of the presence of cysts in tissue, particularly the brain or central nervous system.
Ascaris, Trichuris trichiura and Strongyloides stercoralis are all roundworms and do not have the flat multi-segmented appearance shown in Figures 1 and 2 of this case.
Patients with HIV infection who are co-infected with helminths do not appear to have more rapid progression of their immunodeficiency [Brown et al. 2004] or more severe helminthic infestations that those not infected with HIV [Wiwanitkit 2006].

title: 2014 July-August Featured Case: A man in his eighties developed hematuria and dy
history:
2014 July-August Featured Case: A man in his eighties developed hematuria and dysuria, associated with nausea and vomiting.
The patient had been in his usual health until two weeks before admission when he noted a small amount of blood in his urine. One day before admission, urinary incontinence occurred. Approximately 11 hours before presentation, hematuria and dysuria developed, associated with nausea and, later that day, 4 episodes of vomiting. He came to the emergency department.
He reported some shivering and had had a normal bowel movement earlier that day. In the emergency department, he reported transient crampy abdominal pain, rated 5 out of 10 on a scale of 0 to 10, where 10 is most severe. He had no history of fevers, prostate problems, urinary retention, diarrhea, melena or hematochezia.

The patient had hypertension, coronary artery disease, osteoarthritis, hypothyroidism, dyslipidemia, and vitamin B12 deficiency. He had had angioplasty and stenting of left anterior descending and right coronary arteries 8 and 5 years earlier, a total hip replacement 5 years earlier, lymphocele repair, and back surgery.

The patient lived independently with his wife. He drank wine with meals, and had smoked in the remote past.

He reported no family history of genitourinary malignancy or nephrolithiasis.

Medications at home were enteric coated aspirin (81 mg every other day), atorvastatin, lisinopril, clopidogrel, L-thyroxine, and metoprolol succinate (extended-release). He received vitamin B12 parenterally every three months.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 99.4°F (37.4°C), blood pressure 127/59 mm Hg, pulse 114 beats per minute, respirations 20 per minute and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing ambient air. Dentition was poor. There was blood noted at the urethral meatus. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood cell count was 6800 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000), with 90.4% neutrophils (reference range 40-70%) and 8.5% lymphocytes (reference range 22-44%). The blood level of carbon dioxide was 21.4mmol/L (reference range 23.0-31.9), glucose 155mg/dl (reference range 70-110), urea nitrogen 28mg/dl (reference range 8-25), alkaline phosphatase 143 U/L (reference range 45-115); other initial laboratory test results including the creatinine level were normal.
Analysis of a urine specimen obtained by straight catheterization revealed grossly bloody urine that was positive for leukocyte esterase, with greater than 100 red blood cells (reference range 0-2), 20-50 white blood cells (reference range 0-2), and few bacteria and squamous cells per high power field; evaluation for nitrites could not be performed because of color interference. Cultures of blood and urine specimens were obtained.
In the emergency department, a 3-way indwelling urinary catheter was placed and bladder irrigation begun. Initially, the urine was burgundy in color, with some clots noted. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis performed with the administration of intravenous contrast revealed a layering hyperdensity in the bladder compatible with blood and mild-to-moderate right hydroureteronephrosis (Figures 1 and 2) to the level of the right ureterovesicular junction.
Figure 1. CT of the pelvis, showing layering hyperdensity in the bladder.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen and pelvis, with arrow showing hydroureteronephrosis of the right kidney.

Within 1 hour of presentation, the patient's blood pressure decreased to 98/52mmHg. Ciprofloxacin and normal saline were administered intravenously.
The patient was admitted to the hospital. After arrival on the inpatient floor, the temperature rose 100.8°F (38.2°C). Ciprofloxacin was stopped, and vancomycin and cefepime were administered intravenously.
On the second hospital day, the white blood cell count rose to 22,000 per cubic millimeter, with 87.2% neutrophils and 6.8% lymphocytes. A urine culture that had been obtained before the administration of antibiotics grew abundant (greater than 100,000) colonies per milliliter. After two days, preliminary blood culture results showed two of four blood cultures bottles (both anaerobic bottles) growing an organism similar to that in the urine; gram stain is shown in Figure 3.
On the third hospital day, colony growth was seen in the cultures plated from the anaerobic blood cultures and a urine specimen; subcultures are shown in Figure 4 and 5. (In Figure 5, detail of colonies is shown in upper right.)
Figure 3. Gram stain of growth in anaerobic blood culture bottle.
Figure 4. Colony growth on chocolate agar after 3 days, from blood culture specimen.
Figure 5. Colony growth after 3 days, from urine specimen subculture on blood agar TSA.
diagnosis:
Urosepsis caused by Actinobaculum schaalii infection.

The gram stain of the blood culture growth revealed gram-positive rods (Figures 3 and 6), and culture growth demonstrated a fastidious organism. Subsequent testing performed at the Mayo Clinic laboratories identified Actinobaculum schaalii.
Figure 6. Gram stain of growth from colony.

Infectious disease consultants saw the patient on the third hospital day and advised continuing the patient's intravenous antibiotic regimen. Fevers resolved on the third hospital day. The patient completed a 7-day course of vancomycin and a 14-day course of cefepime, with clearance of his infection.

This patient presented with signs, symptoms and findings of urosepsis, including dysuria, hematuria, and fever with positive cultures of the blood and urine, and abnormalities seen in the right kidney and bladder on radiographic imaging.
In this case, the organism isolated from blood and urine cultures was a fastidious, anaerobic gram-positive rod. Possible organisms that fit this description include Propionibacterium spp. (skin flora) and Actinobaculum schaalii. Clostridium species are spore-forming organisms that are commonly anaerobic gram-positive rods, though some may be gram-variable and others are able to grow aerobically. Eubacterium spp. (present in fecal flora) may also be considered in this case, though some may also be gram-negative. Peptostreptococcus anaerobius and Micromonas micros are fastidious anaerobic cocci, and Escherichia coli is a gram-negative rod.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are often thought to originate from organisms present in the external or distal genitourinary tract and may occur following genitourinary instrumentation [Brook, 2004; Nicolle 2013]. Bacteria on the genitalia and urethra and fecal flora, which include many anaerobic organisms, are thought to ascend the urinary tract to cause disease [Brook, 2004]. Although most UTIs are due to gram-negative aerobic or facultative anaerobic bacilli [Lipsky 1989, Nicolle 2013], anaerobic bacteria have been implicated in numerous infections of the urinary tract, including urethritis, cystitis, ureteritis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis and abscesses of the prostate, kidney or perinephric region [Brook, 2004]. Culture of fastidious organisms may be challenging, as suggested by a study of 10,760 urine specimens which found only 27 (0.8%) grew anaerobic bacteria [Hudác et al., 1991], and identification may require special growth conditions, media, and longer surveillance [Lipsky 1989; Brook, 2004; Beguelin et al 2010].
Multiple case reports since 1997 have identified a fastidious anaerobic gram-positive uropathogen, Actinobaculum schaalii, that appears to cause infection particularly in the elderly or patients with abnormalities of the urinary tract [Pajkrt et al 2003; Nielsen et al 2010; Salvado et al 2013, Cattoir 2012; Beguelin et al 2010]. A. schaalii is in the phylogenetic family Actinomycetaceae and closely related to Actinomyces and Mobiluncus spp; definitive identification is by gene sequencing, though other techniques are currently in development [Cattoir, 2012]. A. schaalii should be considered in the differential of UTI when urine analysis reveals significant pyuria and negative nitrite testing, and especially in cases with a negative aerobic culture and anaerobic gram-positive rod bacteriuria [Cattoir, 2012; Beguelin et al., 2011]. The organism’s resistance to ciprofloxacin and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim [Cattoir, 2012], which are commonly administered for urinary tract infections, heightens the importance of identifying this organism in order to guide appropriate therapy.

title: 2014 September-October Featured Case: A man in his forties with recent headache,
history:
2014 September-October Featured Case: A man in his forties with recent headache, cough, chills and diaphoresis, followed by a rash, was seen in a medical walk-in clinic.
The patient was well until 5 days before presentation when, in mid-spring (The time of year can be an important clue, since many infections show seasonal variation. For example, respiratory viruses - especially influenza - are more common during winter and early spring, and arthropod-borne infections such as Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever are more common in summer and early fall. Notably, these patterns are changing with global climate change.), headache associated with chills, diaphoresis (Chills, or the subjective sense of being cold in the absence of change in external temperature, is a sign that the body’s temperature regulation system is attempting to generate a fever, an adaptive response that aids in combating an infection. In constrast, diaphoresis, or sweating, results when that drive is removed and the body attempts to return to normal temperature. This pattern strongly suggests infection as opposed to other possible causes of the patient’s symptoms.) and sensitivity to sound (Hyperacusis, an increased sensitivity to sound, can be seen in a number of neurological conditions (including viral infections involving the inner ear) and is often accompanied by headache.) occurred. He took ibuprofen (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent with both pain-relieving (analgesic) and fever-suppressing (anti-pyretic) effects. Patients will often take these for pain, causing their fever to be masked and potentially obscuring the diagnosis of infection.) for his symptoms, with some improvement. Two days later, a non-productive cough (A cough without production of thick, yellow-to-green sputum is often seen in viral infection or infection with predominantly intracellular bacteria (“atypical bacteria”).) and a mildly itchy throat developed. The next day, his headache improved, and his eyes became watery and red (Findings commonly seen in conjunctivitis. Watery inflammation, without thick discharge, suggests viral or allergic etiologies rather than bacterial involvement.). The following day, he flew to New England from his home in the Midwest. On the morning of the 5th day after the onset of symptoms (Temporal patterns of symptoms are important clues, often reflecting the underlying pathophysiology. Here, for example, the pattern suggests an initial local respiratory infection followed by systemic dissemination several days later. Different pathogens may have characteristic timing of symptom progression.]), he awakened with a rash on his face (Where a rash appears first is often a useful clue. The rash of measles typically begins on the face and spreads down, whereas the rash of Rocky Mountain Fever usually begins peripherally on the wrists and elbows, then spreads to more central locations.) and upper torso, without pruritus or pain (Pruritus (itchiness) suggests allergic causes. Painful rashes suggest tissue destruction or nerve involvement, such as seen with herpes rashes. Many viral rashes (exantha) are neither.); his other symptoms had improved.
He came to a medical walk-in clinic for evaluation. He reported dark-colored urine (Dark urine usually suggests dehydration but if the patient is well-hydrated it may indicate bilirubin in the urine, either from hepatitis or hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells).) despite drinking 'lots of water'. The remainder of a review of systems was negative.

He had a history of asthma and seasonal allergies (People with seasonal allergies may develop watery eyes, rashes and, if there is sinus involvement, headaches. Chills and diaphoresis, as seen in this case, would be unusual with allergies alone.].).

He lived in an upper Midwestern state (Many infections are sharply limited by geography, greatly influencing the “prior odds” of a particular infection. For example, the upper Midwest and New England show a strong cluster of high prevalence pathogens transmitted by Ixodes ticks, including Lyme disease, Babesiosis, and Anaplasmosis. http://www.cdc.gov/lyme/resources/Tickbornediseases.pdf). He owned a dog, which occasionally had ticks (Several important tick-borne illnesses present with malaise and rash. These are more common in warmer months but ticks may over-winter in warm garages, barns, etc.). He had traveled in the preceding weeks through multiple airports (Travel even with exposure as brief as in airports can be an important risk. The confined space of an airplane, for example, can promote the spread of airborne pathogens such as measles.) throughout the United States for his job, including one day before his presentation, when he traveled by airplane to New England. He had also traveled internationally in the past, but not within the previous 3 months.

He lived with his wife (with whom he was monogamous (Sexual history is also important in illnesses presenting with rash, but often not obtained. Acute HIV infection, secondary syphilis, and disseminated gonococcal infection may all present with a rash.)), his children (Contact with small children, especially in school or daycare, is important to document as children are the principle reservoir for many infections, including parvovirus and influenza.) and a dog. His job required travel.

He drank 3 to 4 alcoholic beverages on weekend days, and had never smoked or used illicit drugs.

He had no allergies to medications.

He had taken medications for his acute symptoms, including ibuprofen, over-the-counter cold medications, antacids, and a cough suppressant. He reported having received all recommended childhood vaccinations (Vaccination history is critical in illnesses that involve rashes. Increasing numbers of parents are declining vaccination for their children, leading to outbreaks of vaccine-preventable infections. That said, no vaccine is 100% effective, and some cases may occur in vaccinated individuals.).
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C) and later rose to 100.1°F (37.8°C); the blood pressure was 137/86 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing room air. There was a diffuse erythematous, blanching (A blanching rash results from dilation of small vessels in the skin in the setting of inflammation. This is more typical of ordinary viral exantha. In contrast, petechial or purpuric rashes result from microscopic bleeding into the skin and these do not blanch with palpation. This is an important physical finding since some life-threatening infections like meningococcemia present most often with non-blanching rashes.) maculopapular rash on face (See above regarding anatomical patterns of rash.) and, less so, on the trunk and arms (Figures 1 and 2). The palms and legs were not involved. The conjunctiva (See above regarding conjunctivitis.) were slightly erythematous diffusely (right eye greater than left). An erythematous macule (approximately 5mm in diameter) was seen on the palate (Oral lesions may provide strong clues to the diagnosis since some viruses such as Herpes Simplex and Coxsackie produce characteristic oral lesions. In this case, if the lesion had a gray-white center, it could represent a Koplik spot and would be nearly diagnostic of measles.). There was mild diffuse lymphadenopathy (Diffuse lymphadenopathy is characteristic of viral infections, in contrast with the more regional lymphadenopathy seen in focal bacterial infections. In some cases, for example the posterior cervical predominance seen in mononucleosis, the distribution may provide additional clues.). The abdomen was obese and soft, with normal bowel sounds and without tenderness. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Rash on torso.
Figure 2. Rash on face and upper torso.

The white blood cell count (Leukopenia, or low white blood cell count, in the setting of infection is an important finding with a limited differential. Most infections will cause at least some elevation of at least some white blood cell types. Falling white blood cell counts happens with direct infection and destruction of the cells (as in Anaplasmosis), rapid consumption (as in severe sepsis), failure of white cell production (with bone marrow malignancy or cytotoxic chemotherapy), or indirect suppression via lack of help from infected T-cells and macrophages (as in measles).) was 3300 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000), with neutrophils 50.5%, band forms (Bands are newly derived neutrophils. Isolated changes in absolute numbers of white blood cells are often diagnostically unhelpful, since they can rapidly shift in and out of blood circulation for a variety of reasons. Elevated numbers of band forms, however, are usually significant, since it indicates an attempt by the immune system to ramp up neutrophil production.) 23.9%, lymphocytes 10.6% (This is a relative lymphopenia, a clue that this may be a pathogen that, like measles, infects and destroys lymphocytes.), atypical lymphocytes (Something of a misnomer, since the cells are not really “atypical”, just activated. High levels of atypicals lymphocytes are seen in some infections like mononucleosis. http://www.meded.uci.edu/macc/hematology-photos-with-descriptions/images/image077-Atypical-Lymphocyte-PB.jpg) 1.8%, monocytes 6.2%, eosinophils (Eosinophilia can be seen in allergy and some parasitic infections, neither of which is likely in this case. In contrast, normal eosinophil levels as seen here argue against serious bacterial infection, where there is usually marked eosinopenia.) 3.5%, basophils 0.9% and other cells (described as lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei, suspicious for plasma cells) 2.7%. Burr cells (Echinocytes. Can be seen in a number of types of altered blood chemistry but at least as often are simply sample preparation artifacts as a result of changes in osmotic strength.) were seen on review of the peripheral smear. Urinalysis revealed amber cloudy urine, with 1+ occult blood, 2+ albumin, 1+ urobilinogen (Possibly contributing to the dark-colored urine described in this case.]) by dipstick and 0 to 2 white and red cells, 1+ bacteria and mucin per high-power field. The blood level of alkaline phosphatase was 360 U/L (reference range 45-115), alanine aminotransferase (Low-level elevation of serum liver enzymes with a predominance of transaminase (ALT and AST) elevation indicates hepatocellular injury. This is a very non-specific finding, but would be consistent with viral infection where there is some liver involvement, such as cytomegalovirus or measles.) 218 U/L (reference range 10-55) and aspartate aminotransferase 121 U/L (reference range 10-40). The hematocrit, hemoglobin, platelet count and blood levels of electrolytes, calcium, glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, total bilirubin and tests of renal function were normal.
diagnosis:
Acute measles infection.

A nasal specimen was positive for measles virus by direct immunofluorescent antibody testing (Figures 3 and 4). On the second day, testing for Measles virus IgG antibodies was positive (At the time of the onset of the rash, the patient has usually been infected for more than a week, counting the period of incubation and subsequent non-specific systemic symptoms. Testing for IgG antibodies to measles may or may not be positive at this time point. When this test is negative, the diagnosis can be confirmed by documenting the appearance of specific antibodies in a “convalescent” serum sample obtained 2-4 weeks later. In this case, the diagnosis is made already by immunofluorescence. Increasingly, direct nucleic acid testing for viral RNA can provide a more sensitive screen.). The next day, testing for Measles virus IgM antibodies was positive, as reported by an outside laboratory.
Rapid test for influenza A and B and streptococcal pharyngitis were negative. Testing for hepatitis A was consistent with prior exposure or vaccination; testing for hepatitis B and C viruses was negative; testing for typhus IgG antibodies was 1:128 and was thought to be consistent with past disease. Testing for heterophile antibodies, antibodies to parvovirus B19, anti-treponemal antibodies, spotted fever IgM and IgG antibodies, rubella IgM and IgG antibodies, cytomegalovirus nucleic acids, Epstein Barr virus nucleic acids, and HIV nucleic acids and antibodies (HIV1 and HIV2) were negative. A sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae (H. influenzae would under ordinary circumstances be an unusual pathogen to recover from the sputum of an immunocompetent, non-smoking-adult with presumably normal lungs. Outside of the pediatric setting, this organism causes an infection of lungs with impaired defenses, since the organism lacks the virulence factors to commonly cause invasive disease in a healthy adult lung. However, if the lung’s defenses are impaired for any reason, it can get a foothold. Here, there is both direct injury through viral replication in respiratory epithelia and immune suppression of infected cells of the reticuloendothelial system. Although measles is usually a relatively mild, self-limited disease, secondary bacterial pneumonia is one of the most common serious complications.) and a sputum specimen was negative for respiratory viral antigens.
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated mild splenomegaly (Measles virus initially replicates mostly at respiratory mucosa where it is introduced upon infection, then spreads to the phagocyte and macrophage (reticuloendothelial) system, of which the spleen is by far the largest organ.), and was otherwise normal.
Figure 3. Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing of nasal specimen for measles virus (green = positive reaction).
Figure 4. DFA of nasal specimen for measles virus (1000x magnification).

Upon initial evaluation, the patient was immediately placed on airborne (respiratory) precautions (Different respiratory pathogens spread differently depending in part on the size of the exhaled water droplets to which the virions are associated. Large droplet pathogens such as rhinovirus, which causes colds, are spread mostly by direct contact with infected secretions. Infected patients need only contact precautions. Medium-sized droplet pathogens, such as influenza, can be spread a few feet through the air through coughing or sneezing, and these patients require droplet precautions. Small droplet pathogens like measles can float in air for significant distances and these patients need full respiratory isolation.) and, pending the results of diagnostic tests, placed in a negative pressure room upon transfer to the emergency department and when admitted to the hospital. The hospital infection control epidemiologist and local and state public health authorities were contacted regarding the suspicion of a diagnosis of measles, and contact exposure investigation was performed. Epidemiologic investigation eventually linked this patient to a person traveling from another country within the previous weeks (and before his travel to New England), who was at the same airport gate, but not on the same plane, and was diagnosed with measles. The measles genotype of both patients was the same (genotype D8).
Ibuprofen (Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, can be useful as analgesics, but are often given unnecessarily as antipyretics under the mistaken belief that fever is pathological. Rather, fever is usually an adaptive response and blocking it may results in a modest delay in clearance of a viral infection.) was administered as needed for headache. The patient was discharged on the sixth hospital day.

Measles is caused by a single-stranded enveloped RNA virus, a member of the Morbillivirus genus in the Paramyxoviridae family. The virus is highly contagious through respiratory secretions via coughing and sneezing. The period of contagiousness is up to five days before the appearance of rash and within four-to-five days afterwards. Classic measles has four clinical stages. First, the incubation period starts after measles enters the respiratory mucosa or conjunctivae, replicates, and spreads to reticuloendothelial sites. This period lasts 8-10 days. Secondly, the prodrome phase is characterized by fever and malaise, followed by cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. This period usually lasts 2-3 days. Patients may manifest Koplik’s spots (white spots on the buccal mucosa), which are pathognomonic. The third stage is the exanthema, which is a blanching maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading inferiorly to the trunk and extremities. Palms and soles are usually spared. Clinical improvement starts within 48 hours of the appearance of the rash. Complications include pneumonia, encephalitis, gingivostomatitis, gastroenteritis, hepatitis, and myocarditis. The fourth phase, recovery, is marked usually by lifelong immunity.
Measles remains a global public health problem with 120,000 deaths caused by the disease in 2012 [WHO, 2014]. Endemic measles in the United States was eliminated in 2000 [Katz et al, 2004]. However, during 2001-2008, there were 557 confirmed cases of measles and 38 outbreaks [Fiebelkorn et al, 2010]. Of these cases, 42% were directly imported from 44 countries, and the rest were US-acquired cases with either a link to an imported case or with unclear source (i.e. no established link to imported case or endemic transmission). Sixty-five percent of cases during this period were in unvaccinated patients, and vaccination status was unknown in 18% of cases. Two deaths were reported. The acute clinical syndrome may be very severe in adults without prior immunity.
Importation of measles cases from endemic areas of the world continues to occur, with a record number of measles cases reported in the US this year from January 1 to May 23, 2014. The Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) noted 228 confirmed cases during that period with fifteen outbreaks accounting for 79% of the cases [Gastañaduy et al, 2014]. Unvaccinated (69%) and those with unknown vaccination status (20%) again accounted for the majority of cases. Forty-five direct importations from abroad have been reported, and 49% of these importations were travelers returning from the Philippines, where a large outbreak has been occurring since October 2013.
Because of the limited experience that newer generations of US health care providers have had with measles, cases have been initially misdiagnosed as Kawasaki disease, dengue, and scarlet fever. There has also been a report of measles outbreak among persons with prior evidence of immunity [Rosen et al, 2014]. In cases of previously vaccinated patients who develop incomplete immunity, a “vaccine-modified measles” can occur, which is a milder form with a shorter prodromal period. The exanthem often does not progress to confluence, and Koplik’s spots may not appear [Cherry 1993; Choe et al, 2012]. These trends underscore the importance of maintaining high population immunity and vigilance for measles. Two doses of MMR vaccine is 95% effective in preventing measles [Marin et al, 2006].
Suspicion for measles requires immediate respiratory isolation of the patient, including potential hospitalization, as well as notification of relevant public health authorities. While these precautions are necessary for minimizing the risk of an outbreak, they create a considerable amount of work for clinical staff and inconvenience for the patient. Nevertheless, given the highly contagious nature of measles and the potential for significant morbidity and mortality in individuals without adequate immunization, clinicians should be vigilant in considering the diagnosis of measles in at-risk patients who present with suggestive signs and symptoms and should isolate such patients while diagnostic testing is undertaken.
Of the other pathogens on the differential, the rash of secondary syphilis is highly varied, but classically is a macular lesion on the palms and/or soles [Cohen et al, 2013]. Scarlet fever produces a diffuse erythematous rash with “sandpaper” quality to the skin due to small 1-2mm papular elevations. Classically, there is circumoral pallor [Cherry 1993]. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, leads to a macular blanching erythematous rash that becomes petechial over time, beginning on the ankles and wrists, spreading to the trunk [Woods 2013]. The rash of rubella is similar in distribution to measles, but the spread is more rapid, and the color is less intense. Suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy are particularly common in adults with rubella, and can help with the diagnosis [Cherry 1993]. Other diagnoses to consider include acute HIV (which can present with a maculopapular rash, often involving the upper thorax, collar, and face, and sometimes the scalp and extremities) and parvovirus infection, which is usually seen in school-aged children and usually causes an erythematous malar rash over the cheeks (“slapped cheek”), followed by lacelike rash on trunk and extremities.
