title: 2014 November-December Featured Case: A man in his sixties was seen because of p
history:
2014 November-December Featured Case: A man in his sixties was seen because of persistent erythema and swelling of the left wrist and distal forearm 18 months after carpal tunnel release.
Three months after the surgical procedure, debridement of the left wrist was performed and revealed 'rice bodies'. Histopathological examination of the synovial tissue showed chronic inflammation with small non-necrotizing granulomas. No organisms were seen on gram stain or stains for fungi or mycobacteria, and routine bacterial cultures were negative. Testing for rheumatoid factor was negative and angiotensin converting enzyme and serum calcium levels were normal. After the procedure, he reported persistent wrist swelling with mild redness. On examination, there was crepitus in the palm, without pain associated with the swelling.
Nine months before this evaluation, a course of empiric clarithromycin and rifampin was administered for one month, without improvement. Swelling persisted with progressive deformity of the hand and wrist, resulting in limitation of function, associated with numbness and tingling in the left fourth and fifth digits. He did not have any fever, night sweats or weight loss.

He had hyperlipidemia and a history of carpal tunnel release for ulnar nerve compressive symptoms eighteen months before this presentation.

The patient worked as a dairy farmer. He had not traveled outside the country and he did not have any exposure to tuberculosis. A neighbor had been diagnosed with Q fever.

The patient lived with his wife.

He had no drug allergies.

His only medication was simvastatin.
exam_studies:
He appeared well. The blood pressure was 143/86 mm Hg, pulse 60 beats per minute, temperature 97.4°F (36.3°C), and respirations 16 breaths per minute. The left wrist was markedly erythematous and swollen. There was no lymphadenopathy and the remainder of the examination was normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the wrist was performed, which showed evidence of marked tenosynovitis and innumerable low-densities resembling 'rice bodies', with no joint abnormalities (Figure 1 and 2).
Figure 1. MRI of left wrist (axial T2-weighted view) with low-signal masses.
Figure 2. MRI of the left forearm (sagittal T2-weighted view).

Figure 3. Intraoperative image of the left wrist.
Figure 4. Tissue removed during surgical debridement.
diagnosis:
'Rice body' formation caused by Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) tenosynovitis.

After three weeks, the mycobacterial culture from the tissue grew Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC).

The patient was empirically treated with azithromycin, moxifloxacin, rifampin and doxycycline before the culture results were known.
Susceptibility testing revealed resistance to amikacin (8.0) and rifabutin (0.5), sensitivity to clarithromycin (<4.0) and clofazimine (0.25), and intermediate susceptibility to ciprofloxacin (2.0), rifampin (4.0), ethambutol (5.0) and streptomycin (4.0). When the final culture and susceptibility results were available, doxycycline and moxifloxacin were stopped and ethambutol was started. However, peripheral neuropathy developed; ethambutol was stopped, and levofloxacin was begun.
At follow up, swelling had improved and he had regained range of motion and function of the hand. The sedimentation rate decreased to 9 mm/hr and the level of C-reactive protein was 0 mg/dL. After six months, therapy was changed to azithromycin and rifampin. The patient did well until five months of a two-drug regimen, when his symptoms relapsed. He was referred to the orthopedic surgeon for another debridement.

'Rice body' formation is an uncommon inflammatory disorder associated with systemic disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and tuberculosis infection [Forse et al., 2012]. Rice bodies were first described in 1985 as intra-articular proteinaceous masses composed of fibrin and collagen associated with tuberculosis. Incidence is most common in rheumatoid arthritis, where rice bodies were found in 72% of adult rheumatoid joints upon synovial lavage [Forse et al., 2012]. Musculoskeletal involvement occurs in 5-10% of patients with non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection, which is commonly precipitated by trauma, such as surgery or penetrating injury. The hand and the wrist are the most frequent sites of musculoskeletal involvement for non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection [Chau et al., 2003]. The pathogenesis of rice body formation has not yet been completely determined. Micro-infarction of the synovium with release of tissue into the joint, encasement of fibrin and alteration in viscosity and content of synovial fluid are thought to be contributing factors. Rice bodies have also been isolated from pleural fluid, along tendon sheaths and within bursae, suggestive of a non-synovial origin. [Iyengar et al., 2011].
The symptoms are nonspecific and usually include local pain and swelling, joint stiffness along with constitutional symptoms. The diagnosis of mycobacterial tenosynovitis is often delayed due to insidious onset of symptoms. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level may be elevated in some patients, but blood tests are generally not helpful [Iyengar et al., 2011; Zenone et al., 1999].
Both sonography and MR imaging can reveal the presence of rice bodies. Histologic examination may reveal granulomatous inflammation associated with fibrinous rice bodies. The Ziehl-Neelson stain is usually negative and tissue culture is the most important means of identifying the pathogen, although it may take months to obtain a positive result. Mycobacterium marinum is the most common offending agent; however, other mycobacterial species are known to cause tenosynovitis as well [Zenone et al., 1999]. There has been one case report of candidal septic arthritis with rice body formation reported in the literature [Yeong et al., 2013]. Treatment is usually started empirically and patients often respond to synovectomy and antimycobacterial treatment.
Actinomyces infections can be associated with the production of sulfur granules,
which are yellow granules that can extrude from abscesses.

title: 2015 January February Featured Case: A man in his thirties was admitted 4 months
history:
2015 January February Featured Case: A man in his thirties was admitted 4 months after deceased donor kidney transplantation because of diarrhea and fever, and he was found to have an elevated serum creatinine level of 3 mg/dL (baseline was 1.6-1.8 mg/dL). Cultures of the blood and urine were negative. A course of corticosteroids was administered; a renal biopsy at that time showed no evidence of rejection. The following month, he was admitted for fevers. The serum creatinine had increased to 6 mg/dL. He was treated for a urinary tract infection with levofloxacin.
During the next month, the creatinine level continued to rise, and night sweats and chills occurred. The patient was admitted to the hospital because of a low grade fever and increasing serum creatinine level.

The patient had chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertensive nephropathy and underwent a deceased donor transplant one decade earlier, which eventually failed. Six months before this admission, a second deceased donor renal transplant was performed (donor and recipient both cytomegalovirus positive). The donor of the second transplanted kidney was thought to have neurocysticercosis, based on calcified lesions of the brain, and the recipient received an empiric 7-day course of albendazole as part of his post-operative management. He also had a history of gout.

He was born in Thailand. He traveled to the Central Valley in California about once a month, and had not traveled outside the country recently. He ate cooked pork and chicken, and did not consume raw foods. He did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

He lived with his wife and children in California, and worked in a service industry.

Medications were mycophenolate (750mg twice a day), prednisone (5 mg once daily), and sirolimus (3mg once daily).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and was in no acute distress. The blood pressure was 130/80mm Hg, pulse 90 beats per minute, temperature 101.2°F (38.4°C). The oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. The abdomen was soft with fullness of the right lower quadrant at the site of the transplanted kidney. There was mild tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant, with a well-healed surgical scar, 1+ pitting edema of the feet and a palpable thrill of his left upper extremity at the site of an arteriovenous fistula.

The white blood cell count was 6,400 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4,500-11,000), with 79% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes and 2% eosinophils. The hemoglobin was 7.7 g/dL (ref 14-18), hematocrit 23.3% (ref 40-52), albumin 2.5 g/dL (ref 3.4-4.8); other tests of liver function were normal. The level of creatinine was 17.72 mg/dl.

Results of blood and urine cultures were negative. A renal ultrasound showed no fluid collections in the region of the graft. Hemodialysis was resumed via his arteriovenous fistula.
A biopsy of the kidney was performed; pathological examination of the biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) stain is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Renal biopsy specimen (HE stain).
diagnosis:
Microsporidiosis of the kidney in a renal transplant patient.

A renal biopsy showed interstitial inflammation with minimal (5%) tubulointerstitial atrophy and fibrosis, neutrophilic abscesses and eosinophils, without evidence of rejection. Intracellular organisms consistent with microsporidia, Encephalitazoon species, were identified. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the specimen (Figures 1 and 2) revealed microsporidium spores within the renal tubule. Transmission electron micrography demonstrated a microsporidian spore from the renal biopsy, surrounded by exospores and an endospore with two rows of polar tubule coils seen in cross-section (Figure 3). Figure 4 shows the polar filament of a microsporidian spore by transmission electron micrograph.
Figure 2. Renal biopsy specimen (HE stain) with spores within renal tubule (arrows).
Figure 3. Transmission electron micrograph of a microsporidian spore from renal biopsy.
Figure 4. Transmission electron micrograph of a microsporidian spore showing the polar filament (arrow).

Albendazole (400mg orally twice a day) was administered for treatment of microsporidiosis, and his immunosuppresion was reduced (prednisone dose continued, mycophenolate decreased to 500mg twice daily and sirolimus stopped). To rule out disseminated microsporidiosis, a chest radiograph and a microsporidial stain of the stool were obtained, which were both negative. The patient continued with hemodialysis for a very brief time and then stopped going to his hemodialysis sessions. His urine output increased and four months after starting albendazole, his renal function improved to a creatinine of 3mg/dL.
After three months of treatment, pathological examination of a renal biopsy continued to show microscopic foci of residual microsporidian species. Therefore, albendazole was continued. Of note, the recipient of the other deceased donor kidney was not found to have microsporidiosis.

Microsporidia is a term that is used to describe more than 1200 species of obligate intracellular parasites that are ubiquitous in the environment. These organisms exist in spore form and have a unique polar tubule which is coiled inside the spore. There are at least fifteen microsporidian species that have been identified as human pathogens with Enterocytozoon bieneusi and three Encephalitozoon species (E. cuniculi, E. hellem and E. intestinalis) being the most common. Most human microsporidiosis cases are seen in AIDS patients and cause diarrhea, although ocular, pulmonary and genitourinary infections are also common.
In renal transplant patients who present with persistent renal failure, the differential diagnosis includes allograft rejection in addition to viral etiologies such as polyoma virus (i.e. BK virus), adenovirus and cytomegalovirus. However, infection from microsporidiosis should be considered if the patient is not responding to traditional therapies and the renal biopsy shows no evidence of rejection. Failure to diagnose this specific infection can lead to loss of the renal allograft. The frequency of microsporidiosis in renal transplants patient is unknown but can present similarly to acute rejection of the allograft. Patients can also present with intermittent fevers. Infection can occur either through transplant-transmitted microsporidiosis or through acquired transmission by the transplant recipient via ingestion or inhalation of spores. The symptoms of infection vary depending on the species, site of infection and immune status of the infected host. The most common clinical manifestation is localized disease in the gastrointestinal tract, causing diarrhea and malabsorption.
Diagnosis can be difficult but can be obtained by looking at stool, urine, and sputum samples. The urine can be evaluated for spores as patients will have intermittent shedding of the organism. Renal infection causes acute kidney injury due to spores that are shed into the lumina of the renal tubules. In the case of this patient, tissue from the transplanted kidney was obtained and showed findings of microabscesses, eosinophils and chronic interstitial nephritis. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is the gold standard for diagnosis (given the small size of the spores) and will demonstrate rows of polar tubules coils.
Treatment of microsporidiosis of a renal allograft consists of a combination of reducing immunosuppression and antimicrobial therapy. Determining the species of microsporidiosis is important for treatment of the infection. Albendazole is the drug of choice for infections caused by Encephalitozoon species but is ineffective for infections caused by Enterocytozoon bieneusi. The appropriate duration of therapy in transplant patients is unknown but often long-term therapy is required for microbiological cure.

title: A man in his twenties was referred to a pulmonary outpatient clinic because of i
history:
A man in his twenties was referred to a pulmonary outpatient clinic because of intermittent hemoptysis of 4-months’ duration (productive of dark clotted blood, estimated at up to 100 milliliters per day on his worst days). He reported no fever, shortness of breath, weight loss or gastrointestinal symptoms.
Previous evaluations at another hospital revealed peripheral eosinophilia. Testing for vasculitis was negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed at the other hospital. Microscopic examination of the BAL specimen and cultures for bacteria, fungi, acid-fast bacilli and viruses were negative.

A recent Mantoux (purified protein derivative or PPD) test performed at work was reportedly negative.

The patient had a pet dog. He had traveled one year earlier to a resort in Mexico for one week. The patient reported no consumption of raw pork or fish, or use of any lipid products or petroleum jelly products.

The patient was married.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The body mass index (weight measured in kilograms divided by the square of the height measured in meters) was 27. The vital signs and the physical examination were normal.

The white blood cell count was 12,100 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4300 to 10,800), with eosinophils 28% (reference range <3), total eosinophil count 3370 per cubic millimeter (reference range 0-400). Results of a complete metabolic screening panel were normal. Serological tests for Lyme disease, filaria and fungus (including Aspergillus), an interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) including antibodies to myeloperoxidase (MPO) and proteinase-3 (PR3) were negative. Testing for antibodies to Strongyloides (IgG) was 3.40 (negative < or = 1.49). Testing for stool ova and parasites was negative.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) showed a discrete opacity in the left lung. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed focal consolidation (5.2cm by 3.7cm) in the lingula (Figure 2) and bilateral pleural effusions.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.

A needle biopsy of the lingular mass showed interstitial inflammation with eosinophils. A course of ivermectin was administered because of the positive titer for Strongyloides.
After four months, hemoptysis and the eosinophilia persisted. A repeat chest radiograph showed no change in the lung opacity. Additional history was obtained: the patient recalled ingesting raw crawfish while drinking beer on a float trip in Missouri.
A left thoracoscopy with wedge resection was performed. Pathological examination of the resected specimen is shown in Figures 3 and 4.
Figure 3. Lung tissue, HE stain, 40x magnification.
Figure 4. Lung tissue, HE stain, 200x magnification.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary paragonimiasis caused by Paragonimus kellicotti.

Pathological examination of the wedge resection biopsy specimen of the left lingula revealed an extensive necrotizing granulomatous inflammatory process with associated bronchopneumonia. Within the necrotic tissue there were scattered discrete oval organisms with a birefringent fibrous coat and central proteinaceous material. The organisms were morphologically consistent with a Paragonimus species.
Testing for Paragonimus westermani (IgG) was 1:32 (negative < 1:32). A distorted, fractured egg (consistent in appearance with Paragonimus kellicotti) that has been phagocytosed by a giant cell was seen in the fibrotic, inflamed pleural tissue. A Langhans-type giant cell with peripheral fibrosis and an ovoid body at the center, representing a lung fluke in a cystic structure is shown in Figure 3 (by hematoxylin and eosin (HE) stain, 40x magnification), and cross-sections of the human trematode, P. kellicotti are shown in Figure 4 (HE stain, 200x magnification). The adult worm of P. kellicotti in a chitinous capsule within a cystic cavity is shown in Figure 5 (HE stain, 400x magnification). Figure 6 shows lung tissue with GMS stain.
Figure 5. Lung tissue, HE stain, 400x magnification.
Figure 6. Lung tissue, GMS stain.

A three-day course of praziquantel was administered for paragonimiasis. After the patient was treated, he did not return for follow-up appointments and no further information was available.

This is a case of pulmonary infection by the human trematode, Paragonimus kellicotti. The reddish brown adult worms measure 7 to 16 mm by 4 to 7 mm and usually live in lung parenchyma close to bronchioles.
This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough epidemiological history in diagnosing North American paragonimiasis. Even if the morphological features of an egg is not characteristic of Paragonimus kellicotti, the identity of the infecting Paragonimus species could be deduced from the travel and dietary history. Multiple case reports [MMWR 2010; Procop 2009; Diaz 2013; Madariaga et al. 2007; and Lane et al. 2009] highlight the common thread of symptoms and social history (i.e., young male who ingests raw crawfish while under the influence of alcohol) in patients with this lung fluke. Although this case highlights cross-reactivity between P. westermani and P. kellicotti [Lane et al. 2009] when performing Western blot with P. westermani antigen, using Western blot with P. kellicotti antigen is much more reliable and has higher sensitivity and specificity [Fischer et al. 2013]. (Unfortunately, this latter test was not available at the time of this patient's evaluation and was not performed.)
This case also illustrates the importance of considering Paragonimus species when a pulmonary lesion and peripheral eosinophilia are present. Although Strongyloides stercoralis larvae can be found in the lungs, Paragonimus is the only human parasite in which the adult organism resides in the lung, as demonstrated in this case. Because patients with Paragonimus infections often present with cough, hemoptysis, cavitary changes and live in geographic areas also endemic for tuberculosis, these patients are frequently misdiagnosed as having tuberculosis [Procop 2009].
Paragonimus westermani is the most widely distributed of the many Paragonimus species that are found throughout the world; its range extends from Japan and Southeast Asia to India.
North American paragonimiasis is relatively rare compared to the approximately 20.7 million people estimated to be infected with Paragonimus worldwide [Procop 2009]. Paragonimus kellicotti is found in North America. Paragonimus mexicanus is present in Central and South America.

title: A man in his fifties with a history of an orthotopic liver transplantation 28 da
history:
A man in his fifties with a history of an orthotopic liver transplantation 28 days before admission was admitted to the hospital during the winter because of dyspnea, subjective fever, sore throat, myalgias, and cough with minimal productive yellow sputum for 2 days, as well as volume overload.

The patient had end-stage renal disease for which he was receiving hemodialysis, hepatitis B and C virus infections, and had had an orthotopic liver transplant 28 days before admission. Results of testing for antibodies to cytomegalovirus before transplantation showed that the donor was positive and the recipient was negative (D+/R-).

He had smoked in the past, and reported no illicit drug or alcohol use. He had no sick contacts or recent travel history.

Medications included mycophenolate mofetil (500mg by mouth every 12 hours), tacrolimus (2mg daily), prednisone (20mg daily), entecavir, valganciclovir, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, vancomycin and cefepime.
exam_studies:
The blood pressure was 124/69 mm Hg, pulse 60 beats per minute, temperature 98.4°F (36.9°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The patient appeared to be in minimal distress. A right internal jugular hemodialysis catheter was non-tender, and there was no discharge from the exit site. There was minimal pharyngeal erythema, a distended and non-tender abdomen with a well-healed right upper quadrant surgical scar, and edema of both legs. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory findings included white cell count of 1900 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4000-11,000), absolute neutrophil count 1748 cells per cubic millimeter, hemoglobin 7.3gm/dL (ref 13.5-17.5), platelets 121,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-300,000), and serum levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 89 IU/L (ref 0-55), asparate aminotranferase (AST) 141 IU/L (ref 5-34), and alkaline phosphatase 119 IU/L (ref 40-150); levels of total and direct bilirubin were normal.
A chest radiograph revealed minimal pulmonary edema and a pleural effusion on the right side. Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated normal echotexture of the liver, a small post-operative hematoma that was improving, ascites and a minimal right pleural effusion.

On the 2nd hospital day, the patient declined a nasopharyngeal wash. Liver enzymes worsened. A liver biopsy was performed. Tests of a urine specimen for antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, serogroup 1 were negative.
The next day, dyspnea and liver enzymes worsened. The temperature rose to 39°C. Preliminary pathological examination of the liver biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining demonstrated patchy hepatocellular necrosis, with surrounding hepatocytes demonstrating nuclear atypia, intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions, and macrophages and lymphocytes, suggestive of viral hepatitis (Figure 1). There was no evidence of acute rejection.
Intravenous ganciclovir was started after the preliminary results of the biopsy were known.
Figure 1. Liver biopsy, HE stain.
diagnosis:
Disseminated adenovirus infection with fulminant hepatitis in a patient with a liver transplant.

The pathological examination of the liver biopsy by HE stain demonstrated intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions and patchy necrosis with macrophages and lymphocytes consistent with viral hepatitis, with no evidence of acute rejection (Figure 1). Immunohistochemical staining for adenovirus was positive (Figure 2), and testing was negative for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and hepatitis B and C viruses. Qualitative testing for adenovirus of the blood by PCR (performed at Focus Labs) was positive.
Blood and urine cultures remained negative.
Figure 2. Liver biopsy, immunoperoxidase stain for adenovirus.

On the 4th hospital day, worsening hypoxemia and tests of liver function (AST 3592 IU/L, ALT 1072 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 322 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL) occurred, consistent with fulminant hepatitis. When results of immunohistochemistry staining of the biopsy were known, therapy was changed to intravenous cidofovir and immunoglobulin. Quantitative testing of the blood for cytomegalovirus DNA by PCR was negative.
On the 5th hospital day, septic shock that was refractory to multiple pressors and ventilator dependent respiratory failure occurred. Aggressive care was withdrawn, and the patient expired.

This case demonstrates that adenoviral hepatitis in liver transplant recipients may be progressive and rapidly fatal. It also shows that adenoviral disease mostly involves the transplanted organ [Carrigan 1997]. Physicians must consider adenovirus in the differential diagnosis of an immunocompromised patients who presents with fever and elevated liver enzymes.
Adenovirus affects epithelial cells in the gastrointestinal, genitourinary and respiratory tracts. Adenoviral disease in immunocompromised hosts has a wide range of clinical presentations, including pneumonia, hepatitis, nephritis, and hemorrhagic cystitis with a case fatality of 50%.
There are two possible mechanisms by which active adenoviral infection occurs: reactivation of latent infection secondary to immunosuppression or primary adenovirus infection; the latter may be acquired from either ill contacts or from the donor organ itself. The proportion of immunocompromised patients who develop adenoviral infection from reactivation versus primary infection is unknown [Echaverria 2008].
The role of adenovirus serology is limited in the immunosuppressed host due to its lack of sensitivity and the presence of serum antibodies in the majority of adults from prior exposure. A positive serum adenovirus PCR with clinical and laboratory findings of hepatitis favors a probable diagnosis of adenoviral hepatitis. Definitive diagnosis requires a liver biopsy demonstrating viral inclusions.
The optimal treatment of adenovirus hepatitis is not known. Some of the treatments mentioned in the medical literature [Ronan et al. 2014] include:
• Reduction of immunosuppression
• Agents with in vitro activity against adenoviruses (e.g. ribavirin, cidofovir)
• Intravenous infusion of immunoglobulin
• Liver transplantation
A promising experimental agent is an orally derivative of cidofovir called brincidofovir or CMX001. This drug achieves higher intracellular levels than intravenous cidofovir. In a retrospective study of CMX001 as salvage therapy for adenovirus infection in 13 immunocompromised patients [Florescu et al., 2012], there was a sustained drop in viral load over a 4-week period; the 8 week survival rate was 88.9% for responders and 50% for non-responders. The agent was well-tolerated and did not have major side effects.

title: A Japanese man in his seventies with a history of miliary tuberculosis presented
history:
A Japanese man in his seventies with a history of miliary tuberculosis presented with progressive enlargement of masses in the left side of the neck and right thigh.
Eight months before this presentation, a diagnosis of miliary tuberculosis had been made after acid-fast bacilli (AFB) culture of a sputum specimen was positive. Diagnoses of tuberculous enteritis and tuberculoma of the brain were also made at that time. Isoniazid (300 mg), rifampin (450 mg), ethambutol (750 mg) and pyrazinamide (1000 mg) daily were administered for 8 weeks until susceptibility results returned, and the treatment was changed to isoniazid and rifampin. Seven months before this presentation, ileocecectomy and right hemicolectomy were performed because of hemorrhagic shock and recurrent bleeding from an ileocecal ulcer of tuberculous enteritis.
Five months later, the patient noted a subcutaneous mass in the region of the surgical site. Computed tomography showed an intra-abdominal mass extending to abdominal wall. Debridement of an abscess extending from the subcutaneous to the intra-abdominal tissue was performed. AFB culture of the abscess was negative; pathological examination of the tissue with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining revealed caseating epithelioid granuloma with Langhans’ giant cells (Figure 1). One month before this presentation, his family noted a hard subcutaneous mass on his right thigh, which was painless. Approximately 20 days later, the patient noted progressive enlargement of a left neck mass
Figure 1. Subcutaneous to intra-abdominal abscess, HE stain.

He had a history of miliary tuberculosis as above, and, for 5 years, hypertension.

He lived with his wife in Japan. He had been employed as a manufacturer until his sixties. He had not traveled outside of Japan.

His sister died of a “bone tumor”, and his brother died of a “neck tumor” at age of 45.

He had no allergies.

His medications were isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 450 mg and pyridoxine 30 mg daily. He did not take any anti-hypertensive medications.
exam_studies:
He appeared in mild distress and was oriented to person only. The blood pressure was 105/66 mm Hg, pulse 76 beats per minute, temperature 98.0°F (36.7°C), and respirations 16 breaths per minute. There was a tender left cervical mass (140 mm by 80 mm) that was fixed, warm and slightly erythematous. The abdomen was soft with a stoma on his lower abdomen; the surgical scar was well-healed and there was no tenderness or mass. A subcutaneous mass (40mm by 35mm) on the right thigh was non-tender and without erythema. There was no lymphadenopathy including in the right cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, trochlear or inguinal regions. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 8,700 per cubic millimeter (reference range 3,900-9,800) with neutrophils 89%, band forms 3%, and lymphocytes 3%; the level of hemoglobin was 9.6 mg/dL (reference range 13.5-17.6) and the platelet count was 343,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 130,000-369,000). The serum level of urea nitrogen was 31 mg/dL (reference range 8-20), creatinine 0.93 mg/dL (reference range 0.63-1.03), aspartate aminotransferase 37 IU/L (reference range 11-30), alanine aminotransferase 33 IU/L (reference range 4-30), alkaline phosphatase 255 IU/L (reference range 107-330), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGTP) 104 IU/L (reference range <70), lactate dehydrogenase 165 IU/L (reference range 109-216), and albumin 2.5 g/dL (reference range 3.9-5.1).
Computed tomography (CT) of the neck with the administration of contrast showed a large mass on the left side (Figure 2).
Figure 2. CT of the neck with contrast, coronal view.

Three sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli. The serum concentration of isoniazid (INH) was 4.7 µg/mL (usual therapeutic range 1-7) and rifampin 19.0 µg/mL (usual therapeutic range 4-32). Testing for antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. Biopsy of thigh and neck masses was performed; images of pathological examination of the neck mass (Figure 3) and thigh subcutaneous mass (Figure 4) are shown, both with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining.
Figure 3. Left neck mass, HE stain, high power.
Figure 4. Right thigh mass, HE stain, high power.
diagnosis:
T-cell lymphoma associated with Human T-cell leukemia virus type 1.

Pathological examination of the neck and thigh subcutaneous masses (Figures 3 and 4) showed mixtures of intermediate and large atypical tumor cells. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD3, CD4 and CD8 and negative for CD29 and CD 79a, results that were consistent with T-cell lymphoma. Testing for antibody to human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) was positive.

Additional history was obtained that the patient was born on an island in Japan where HTLV-1 is endemic. The patient's condition deteriorated and he died on the 37th hospital day.

HTLV-1 infects an estimated 20 million people worldwide. Endemic areas include Japan, Africa, the Caribbean islands, and Central and South America.
The route of HTLV-1 transmission includes breast feeding, sexual transmission, tissue donation and injection drug use. One million people are infected in Japan, where vertical transmission by breast-feeding is thought to be the most common route of contagion. Seroprevalence rates are up to 37% and are especially high in the southwestern isles of Shikoku, Kyusyu and Okinawa.
Most infected people remain entirely asymptomatic. However, the HTLV-1 virus infection has been associated with a number of complications, including Adult T-cell Lymphoma/Leukemia (ATL), HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis, and HTLV-1-associated uveitis. Acute ATL is a fulminant disease with poor outcome. Furthermore HTLV-1 infection increases the severity and susceptibility to strongyloidiasis, scabies, leprosy and tuberculosis (TB)
Several studies have investigated the effect of HTLV-1 infection on both infection and disease due to M. tuberculosis. People with HTLV-1 infection have 2- to 4-fold increased risk of acquiring M. tuberculosis. Suppression of delayed-type hypersensitivity to purified protein derivative (PPD) of M. tuberculosis has been demonstrated [Bastos et al., 2012], possibly due to impairment of TNF-alpha production caused by HTLV-1 infection.

title: A man in his fifties was admitted because of progressive rectal pain and urinary
history:
A man in his fifties was admitted because of progressive rectal pain and urinary retention of one-month's duration. He also reported diarrhea, an eight-pound weight loss and intermittent night sweats, with no history of fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, melena or hematochezia.

He had non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus and diverticulosis that had been diagnosed by colonoscopic examination 18 month earlier.

He owned dogs, a bird and snakes. He lived in the southwest United States and had traveled extensively to the Middle East, northern Africa and the western horn of Africa. The most recent trip was 2.5 years earlier to Tunisia, after which he had intermittent diarrhea for approximately 18 months, when his symptoms completely resolved.

The patient lived with his wife and children in an urban area and worked in education. He did not drink alcohol or smoke tobacco.
exam_studies:
The patient did not look acutely ill or toxic. The blood pressure was 121/82 mm Hg, pulse 115 beats per minute, temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C) and respirations 18 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturation 94% while breathing room air. There was borderline tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmurs, and tenderness to deep palpation in the lower mid-abdomen and pelvic area, with no appreciable masses. The remainder of the examination was normal. A urinary catheter was in place due to urinary retention.

The white blood cell count was 21,300 per cubic millimeter (reference range 3400-10,400), eosinophils 14% (reference range 0-5), hematocrit 36.0% (reference range 40.0-51.0 in men), and platelets 694,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-425,000). A complete metabolic panel was normal. The blood level of C-reactive protein was 21.44 mg/dL (reference range <0.6), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 95 mm/hr (reference range 0-20), carcinoembryonic antigen <0.5 ng/ml (reference range in non-smokers 0.0-3.0), and cancer antigen 19-9 8 U/ml (reference range 0-37). HIV serology was non-reactive.
Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large mass involving the proximal rectum and distal sigmoid colon with surrounding inflammatory changes and anterior displacement of the bladder.

The patient was admitted to a general medicine floor. The gastrointestinal service was consulted and flexible sigmoidoscopy was performed. A large atypical circumferential mass was seen approximately 25 to 27 cm from the anal verge. The area was described as congested, friable and granular (Figures 1 and 2). Pathological examination of the surgical biopsies revealed marked mucosal eosinophilic infiltration with occasional lymphoid aggregates and no evidence of fungal elements, other microorganisms, lymphoma, or other malignancy; normal mast cells were present.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen and pelvis (Figure 3) revealed a large soft tissue mass (Arrow A) involving a long segment of the rectosigmoid colon with extension into the anterior soft tissues to the seminal vesicles and prostate and posteriorly into the presacral space. A circumferential mass in the cecum below the ileocecal valve suggestive of cecal carcinoma was noted (Arrow B). In addition, multiple areas of enlarged bilateral external iliac, common iliac, retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy were seen.
Figure 1. Rectal mass before biopsy.
Figure 2. Rectal mass after biopsy.
Figure 3. MRI of the abdomen.
diagnosis:
Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis caused by Basidiobolus ranarum.

Serological testing for coccidioidomycosis, strongyloidiasis and schistosomiasis by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay was negative, as were stool specimens tested for acid fast bacilli. Interferon-gamma release assay and chest radiograph were negative.
CT-guided biopsy of the rectal mass was performed. Pathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed extensive inflammation and fibrosis. Fungal organisms were present, confirmed by hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining (Figure 4) and Grocott’s methenanine silver stain (GMS) ((Figure 5). The morphology of the fungal organisms was consistent with basidiobolomycosis. Several weeks later, a serological test result for basidiolomycosis returned and was positive.
Figure 4. Biopsy results, HE staining.
Figure 5. Biopsy results, GMS staining.

Itraconazole, 200 mg one tablet twice daily, was administered. He tolerated antifungal medication without any undesirable side effects. He was discharged from hospital, with gradual improvement in his symptoms. No surgical intervention was undertaken. He continued to follow up in the colorectal surgery clinic, as well as in infectious disease clinic.
At follow-up almost one year later, the patient had done well and remained symptom-free. An interval MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed complete resolution of rectosigmoid colonic mass with no evidence of active inflammation. Therapy was discontinued after 12 months and symptoms recurred 2 months later. Repeat MRI of the abdomen and pelvis showed worsening inflammation. Itraconazole was resumed, with resolution of symptoms.

The clinical presentation (gastrointestinal mass and eosinophilia), epidemiological history (residing in southwest US) and pathological and microbiological data are very suggestive of gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis. The patient did not have pulmonary symptoms suggestive of disseminated tuberculosis or coccidiodomycosis. Furthermore, there was no evidence of intestinal ulceration, adhesion, fistula or strictures to suggest tuberculous enteritis. Intestinal schistosomiasis usually present with intestinal polyps and ulceration rather than infiltrative masses. Pathological/microbiological data were not consistent with lymphoma.
Basidiobolomycosis is a rare disease caused by the fungus Basidiobolus ranarum. B. ranarum is a microscopic fungus in the order of Entomophtorales of the class of Zygomycetes. This mycosis is found in tropical and temperate areas of South America, Africa and the Arabian Peninsula [Vikram et al. 2012]. It is found in soil, plant, decaying vegetables, feces of reptiles (frogs, toads, lizards) and bats. In the US, most of the cases have been found in Arizona [Lyon et al, 2001; CDC 1999]. In humans, B. ranarum is known to cause chronic subcutaneous nodules of the arm, trunk and shoulder. It also has been reported to cause granulomatous intestinal mass in the gastrointestinal tract of immunocompetent hosts. While traumatic inoculation is the most the common way of acquiring B. ranarum, in this patient acquisition was thought to be through ingestion, leading to gastrointestinal manifestation.
Clinical manifestations of gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis include fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, abdominal mass, abdominal distension and constipation [Alhuraiji et al., 2014]. The fungus has a predilection to involve the colon and rectum, but it can also involve the small bowel, liver, gallbladder and the stomach. Complications of the disease include bowel obstruction, urinary retention, perforation, esophageal varices, duodenobiliary fistula and death [Vikram et al. 2012]. The differential diagnosis includes cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, pyogenic abscess, tuberculosis, lymphatic filariasis or mycetoma [Alhuraiji et al., 2014.]
Risk factors for acquisition of gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis include high risk activities (such as gardening or landscaping), ingestion of contaminated food product, gastric acid suppression, diabetes mellitus, gastrectomy, and residing in an endemic area [Vikram et al. 2012].
The diagnosis of basidiobolomycosis is often based on tissue culture. However, a probable diagnosis can be made based on histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen. A specific serologic immunodiffusion assay is available commercially, but its sensitivity is unknown. Marked peripheral eosinophilia occurs in the majority of patients, although the pathogenesis is poorly understood. The microscopic appearance of B. ranarum in tissue shows sparingly septate, broad, thin-walled hyphae with peaked zygospores. The histopathology of surrounding tissue shows a sheath of eosinophilic infiltration, referred to as the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon [CDC 1999]. Macroscopically on Sabouraud agar, colonies have a waxy, yellowish-to-gray appearance with many radial folds [Lyon et al. 2001].
Treatment of basidiobolomycosis is usually with ketoconazole, itraconazole or voriconazole. In vitro susceptibilities are variable and isolate dependent. In one study, Basidiobolus spp. displayed low minimal inhibitory concentrations (MIC) to all azoles. Another study showed high level resistance to fluconazole, amphotericin B, flucytosine, and capsofungin. Isolates were found to be susceptible to itraconazole, voriconazole and posaconazole. In some cases, surgical intervention is required. The mortality is estimated at 20% [Vikram et al. 2012, Guarro et al. 1999].

title: A man in his sixties with a recently diagnosed HIV infection was admitted becaus
history:
A man in his sixties with a recently diagnosed HIV infection was admitted because of skin lesions progressing up his right arm over a month prior to admission.
Approximately 3 months before this admission, he developed nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and a thirty-pound weight loss. He was admitted to a hospital and was found to be HIV-positive. His CD4 T-lymphocyte cell count was 54 cells cells per microliter (reference range 328–1404) and the HIV RNA level was 602,870 copies per milliliter. During that hospitalization, he was also diagnosed with Campylobacter gastroenteritis, cytomegalovirus (CMV) enteritis and oral candidiasis. On examination, there was a small non-inflamed nodule on the distal interphalangeal joint of his right index finger, which was biopsied. Histopathologic staining of the biopsy revealed acid-fast organisms and the specimen was sent for culture. Emtricitabine-tenofovir, raltegravir, atovaquone, valganciclovir, ethambutol and azithromycin were started. He was discharged with outpatient followup.
During the four weeks following discharge, the lesion on his hand became inflamed, with erythema and swelling, and lesions progressed up his arm toward the axilla. He reported night sweats, but had no fever, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea and was gaining weight.

As noted in the history of the present illness.

The patient was born in Mexico and immigrated to the United States more than two decades earlier. He lived in Arizona where he worked as a landscaper. He reported possibly pricking his right index finger with a thorn in the past. There was no recent travel, animal exposures, use of illicit drugs or new sexual contacts.

As noted in the history of the present illness.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared chronically ill. The blood pressure was 107/68 mmHg, pulse 95 beats per minute, temperature 99°F and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The right index finger was swollen and inflamed in the area of the previous biopsy with patchy inflammatory lesions extended up his arm in a lymphatic distribution (Figures 1 and 2). The lesions were not tender and there was no lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 4,300 per microliter (reference range (ref) 4,500-10,700), hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL (ref 12.4-15.7), creatinine 0.76 mg/dL (ref 0.66-1.25), alkaline phosphatase 76 U/L (ref 56-119), aspartate aminotransferase 37 U/L (ref 17-59), alanine aminotransferase 70 U/L (ref 21-72). A chest radiograph was normal. In the month between the two admissions his CD4 T-lymphocytes had increased from 54 to 84 cells per cubic millimeter and the HIV-RNA level had decreased from 602,870 to 351 copies per milliliter.

The patient was readmitted to the hospital. Cultures from the biopsy performed during the first admission had remained negative. Amikacin, ciprofloxacin and rifampin were administered empirically for possible mycobacterial infection. When the lesions worsened, surgical debridement was performed.
diagnosis:
Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) associated with Mycobacterium haemophilum infection in a patient with HIV/AIDS.

Cultures obtained by biopsy of his right index finger during his first admission eventually grew Mycobacterium haemophilum. Cultures for group A streptococcus, Sporothrix and Nocardia were negative. A diagnosis of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) associated with Mycobacterium haemophilum infection was made based on the clinical presentation and testing results.

Shortly after admission and the diagnosis of IRIS was made, prednisone, amikacin, rifampin and ciprofloxacin were administered. Sensitivity testing of the Mycobacterium haemophilum grown in culture suggested resistance to amikacin and ethambutol and they were discontinued; azithromycin was restarted. Antiretroviral therapy was held and his lesions improved. After 2 weeks, antiretroviral therapy was resumed. Four months later, his lesions had healed, although there was scarring.

This patient’s right arm inflammatory lesions were due to Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), which is defined as the unmasking of a previously unrecognized infection (or malignancy) or paradoxical worsening of a previously existing condition following the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in an HIV-infected person [Shelburne, et al., 2002]. The mechanism for IRIS is presumed to involve reconstitution of pathogen-specific immunity occurring during the rapid increase in CD4 cells and rapid drop in viral load in response to antiretroviral therapy [Crum-Cianflone 2006]. Diagnosis of IRIS requires clinical suspicion since there is no diagnostic test. Management must be individualized; steroids are often used to manage IRIS, as in this patient [Crum-Cianflone 2006].
Mycobacteria are a common group of infectious agents associated with IRIS. This patient developed IRIS caused by a non-tuberculous mycobacterium, Mycobacterium haemophilum, a pathogen increasingly recognized in immunocompromised patients [Saubolle et al., 1996; Shah et al., 2001]. Mycobacterium haemophilum is an environmental mycobacterium that can cause skin and soft tissue infections. Growth in culture requires specialized conditions, e.g. supplementation with hemin or ferric ammonium citrate. In addition, optimal growth is at 30-32°C and the organism grows slowly or not at all at higher temperatures. In this patient, these growth requirements contributed to the slow identification of the acid fast organism.

title: 2015 March-April Featured Case: A man in his thirties was seen in an outpatient
history:
2015 March-April Featured Case: A man in his thirties was seen in an outpatient clinic because of an abdominal skin ulcer that developed after a trip to Brazil.
Approximately two months before this presentation, the patient sustained a superficial abrasion (approximately 25 mm in diameter) on his abdomen while bodysurfing in the ocean while in Brazil. One month later, he noted increasing erythema, drainage and ulceration at the site of the enlarging lesion. Topical over-the-counter antibacterial ointment and an occlusive bandage were applied, without improvement. He saw a physician and cephalexin was administered; however, the lesion continued to worsen, with extension toward his left flank.
He was referred to an outpatient clinic at a hospital. On evaluation, he noted the lesion was initially painless, but had become more tender.

Two months earlier he had traveled for several weeks to Brazil, including the Amazon (where he and his girlfriend reportedly received numerous mosquito bites), Brasilia, and Rio de Janeiro. His girlfriend had recently developed a lesion on her arm. He drank alcohol in moderation and did not smoke or use illicit drugs.

He worked in an office.

He had no allergies.

He took no other medications.
exam_studies:
He was afebrile, with normal vital signs. There was a non-healing ulcer (3-to-5 cm by 8cm) in the lower left quadrant of his abdomen, with minimal purulent drainage and a ring (0.5 cm in width) of erythema and induration (Figure 1). The subcutaneous tissue was exposed, with increased warmth along the surrounding erythema. The abdomen was soft, without distension or tenderness.
Figure 1. Physical finding.

The blood level of globulin was 1.7g/dl (reference range 1.9-4.1) and aspartate aminotransferase was 57 U/L (reference range 10-40). A complete blood count, white cell differential, and levels of electrolytes, glucose, total protein, urea nitrogen, creatinine, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and alanine aminotransferase were normal; a test for HIV-antibodies and p24 was non-reactive.

A skin biopsy was performed and amoxicillin-clavulanate administered. A gram stain showed no organisms and a wound culture was negative. Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining of the biopsy is shown (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of skin biopsy (100x magnification).
diagnosis:
Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania guyanensis.

Pathological examination of the skin biopsy by HE and Giemsa stains (Figures 2 and 3) revealed ulceration with a marked granulomatous reaction and scattered histiocytic aggregates with numerous intracellular organisms. The organisms were ovoid with eccentrically located nuclei and kinetoplasts at the opposite pole, and were seen at the periphery of histiocytes. Taken together, these findings were consistent with the amastigotes of leishmaniasis. Tissue from a punch biopsy was sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for PCR and DNA sequencing and Leishmania culture was positive for Leishmania guyanensis.
Figure 3. Giemsa stain of skin biopsy (100x magnification).

Because of the size of the lesion, the patient was admitted for initiation of a course of liposomal amphotericin B (with daily doses on days 1 through 5, day 10 and day 15). The treatment was complicated by nephrotoxicity that improved with hydration and a nonocclusive thrombosis associated with the peripherally inserted central line, for which he was anticoagulated and received a change in the line. Follow-up images of his skin lesion are shown in Figures 4 and 5.
Figure 4. Follow-up 14 days after treatment.
Figure 5. Follow-up 6 weeks after treatment.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic in more than 70 countries worldwide. Of the approximately 1.5 million new cases each year, 90% occur in Afghanistan, Algeria, Brazil, Pakistan, Peru, Saudi Arabia, and Syria [Tiuman et al., 2011]. The protozoan is transmitted through the bite of female phlebotomine sandflies and leads to either local (cutaneous) or systemic (visceral) infection.
Cutaneous manifestations represent the most common forms, ranging from small cutaneous nodules to gross mucosal tissue destruction. The lesions are normally chronic, developing over weeks to months, and frequently painless. Multiple species of Leishmania exist, often classified by their geographical occurrence into “Old World” and “New World” species. Species identification from skin-biopsy samples is available via PCR ((http://www.cdc.gov/laboratory/specimen-submission/form.html) and recommended for guiding therapy selection.
Treatment options include pentavalent antimonials (IND required), amphotericin B, pentamidine and, more recently, miltefosine. Recommendations on treatment selection and schedules are based on small clinical trials and expert opinions [Blum et al., 2014].
Non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) soft tissue infections can occur following exposure to NTM at sites of cutaneous trauma, including in swimming pools, lakes or the ocean. The local infection often develops as a painless, slowly growing indurated area that can ulcerate after a few weeks. Causative organisms include Mycobacterium fortuitum, M. abscessus, M. chelonae, M. marinum, and M. ulcerans. On histological examination, non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections can be recognized by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with a granulomatous reaction. Acid-fast bacilli may be recognized by special stains.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is endemic in Brazil. The organism typically causes asymptomatic pulmonary infection and then develops into an either acute or chronic form. While the acute form is rare and almost always observed in children or adolescents, the chronic form is more common and develops over month and years, primarily manifesting as pulmonary infiltrates and upper respiratory mucosal lesions, but skin manifestations have been reported in endemic areas. On histological examination, paracoccidioidomycosis can be recognized by a chronic granulomatous dermatitis with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Organisms may be recognized as large round yeast cells with multiple narrow-based buds, giving the appearance of the classical “pilot’s (or mariner’s) wheel.”
Chromoblastomycosis infections are caused by the traumatic implantation of dematiaceous hyphomycetes forms into the skin. Lesions usually start as small scaly, painless papules that can develop into verrucose, wart-like lesions due to increased tissue proliferation. On histological examination, pigmented fungi known as medlar bodies (and described as “copper pennies”) are seen amidst a nonspecific inflammatory response.
The ulcerative form of pyoderma gangrenosum is the most common variant and typically starts as a tender papule that develops on the legs or the trunk, in areas of prior trauma but also on normal-appearing skin. Lesions often develop rapidly and are associated with a significant level of pain. If no superinfection occurred, the lesions are sterile. On histological examination, ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum most typically has a nonspecific inflammatory infiltrate with concomitant abscess formation. The edge of the lesion may show a lymphocytic or neutrophilic vasculitis.
Dermatologic malignancies or metastases have very variable presentations and range from papules, plaques, or nodules to ulceration and/or areas of necrosis. On histological examination, the lesion would show extensive dermal involvement by malignant epithelial or mesenchymal elements.

title: 2015 May-June Featured Case: A man in his fifties was in good health until three
history:
2015 May-June Featured Case: A man in his fifties was in good health until three days before presentation when he reportedly relapsed from a period of abstinence from drug use and injected into his left forearm a single dose of heroin, using an old hypodermic needle he had previously used (but not shared). The injected drug was reportedly boiled in tap water, without alcohol.
The next day, he noted redness of his conjunctiva and itching of the eye, with normal vision. Later that day, nausea, vomiting and increasing fatigue occurred. The following day, one day before presentation, he awoke with periorbital swelling, eyelid erythema, and pain and blurred vision of the left eye. He was seen by local healthcare providers, and ophthalmic preparations of tobramycin, steroids and cyclopentolate hydrochloride were administered. The next day, two days after the onset of his symptoms, his symptoms worsened, pain increased to 9 on a scale of 0 to 10 (where 10 is the most severe) and vision worsened to perception of light only. He went to the emergency department of another hospital for evaluation, where brimonidine and timolol were administered, and he was referred to a hospital specializing in ophthalmology.
He reported no ocular trauma, recent fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, headache, sinus pain, rhinorrhea, ear ache, neck stiffness, chest pain, respiratory symptoms, back pain, diarrhea, rash or skin changes, dysuria, penile discharge, joint pain or swelling, or edema.

He had a past history of injection drug use, reportedly with negative screening tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C virus infection.

He was taking methadone.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 100.0°F (37.8°C), and the remaining vital signs were normal. On ophthalmologic examination, there was corneal edema and chemosis, with very poor view of the anterior chamber, and a hypopyon (3mm in height) in the left eye. He had an afferent pupillary defect. On dilated examination, the retina could not be seen. There was significant vitreal debris and choroidal thickening. There was no evidence of corneal injury or trauma. The right eye and extraocular movements were normal. The injection site in the left arm was clean and dry, without evidence of cellulitis, and the remainder of the examination was normal.

The white blood count was 14,000 per cubic millimeter, (reference range 4500-11,000), with 77.4% polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Toxic screening of the urine was positive for opioids.
Computed tomography (CT) of his orbit, performed with intravenous contrast, showed orbital stranding around and posterior to the globe and around the optic nerve, with some preseptal edema. The aqueous and vitreous compartments of the left globe appeared symmetric in size and attenuation with respect to the right eye and there was mild left proptosis. The extraocular muscles were symmetric in size and attenuation with respect to the right. There was no retrobulbar mass lesion, erosion of the bony structures of the left orbit and, with the exception of mild mucosal thickening in the ethmoid air cells, the paranasal sinuses were clear. Ultrasound of the left eye revealed extensive hyperreflective vitreous opacities.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of valvular lesions.

A diagnosis of endophthalmitis was made. After the administration of local anesthetics, a tap of the anterior chamber (AC) of the left eye was performed; 0.1 cc of fluid was aspirated and cultured. Gram stain of the aspirate showed many polymorphonuclear leukocytes but no organisms
An attempt was also made to tap the posterior chamber vitreous, however no fluid was removed. This procedure was followed by intravitreal injection of vancomycin (1mg), ceftazidime (2mg), and amphotericin (5mcg), and placement of a drop of gatifloxacin. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 68 mm Hg, and decreased to 20 mm Hg after an additional AC tap was performed.
The patient was transferred and admitted to another hospital for further care. Physical findings of the left eye after the anterior chamber fluid aspiration and intravitreal injection are shown in Figure 1 (with hypopyon within the anterior chamber). Medications included drops of moxifloxacin four times daily, timolol 0.5% two times daily, dorzolamide 2% two times daily, and brimonidine tartrate 0.2% three times daily, all to the left eye, and vancomycin, ampicillin, and sulbactam intravenously.
The next day, the culture broth of the anterior chamber aspirate was positive; gram stain of the culture is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings after anterior aspiration.
Figure 2. Gram stain of culture of anterior chamber aspirate.
diagnosis:
Endophthalmitis caused by Bacillus cereus group, not B. anthracis, in a patient with injection drug use.

Cultures of the anterior chamber aspirate grew gram-positive rods, and Bacillus cereus group (but not B. anthracis) was identified. Culture of the organism grown on trypticase soy agar (TSA) with sheep blood is seen in Figure 3 (showing hemolysis); gram stain of the organism is seen in Figure 4.
Figure 3. Bacillus cereus group, not B. anthracis, grown on TSA with sheep blood.
Figure 4. Gram stain of Bacillus cereus group, not B. anthracis.

The day after admission, pars plana vitrectomy was performed, with removal of the lens, membrane peel and injection of antibiotics.
External view of the left eye after surgery (Figure 5) revealed aphakia (lens removal) with synthetic absorbable sutures on the nasal side, extensive corneal edema and no evidence of a hypopyon. Discomfort significantly decreased after the surgical procedure.
During the next month, a tractional retinal detachment and ciliary body detachment developed. Three months after his initial presentation, a repeat vitrectomy was performed, with membrane peel, retinectomy, and placement of silicone oil. However, a combined tractional and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment of the left eye occurred, resulting in persistent loss of vision. Further surgical repair was not possible due to the extensive scarring and fibrosis.
Additional testing during his first admission revealed the presence of hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B surface antibodies and no evidence of hepatitis B surface antigen. The patient declined other serologic testing.
Figure 5. Physical findings on 2nd day, after pars plana vitrectomy.

This patient was diagnosed with endophthalmitis caused by a gram-positive rod, Bacillus cereus group (non-anthracis) after an episode of injection drug use. Bacillus cereus is a spore-forming rod that produces toxins, including multiple enzymes, and has been associated with gastrointestinal illness and asymptomatic fecal carriage [Dobniewski 1993]. Case reports of endogenous endophthalmitis after injection drug use caused by this organism have been published [Kumar et al. 2014; Hatem et al. 1979], but are relatively rare in occurrence. The rapidly progressive nature and poor clinical outcomes associated with eye infections by this organism have been attributed, at least in part, to the production of its destructive enzymes [Drobniewski 1993; Kumar et al. 2014].
More than 90% of cases of infectious endophthalmitis are caused by exogenous sources [Nishida et al. 2015], following exposure to organisms from penetrating trauma, surgery, injection of medications into the vitreous, or from direct extension from a corneal source [Durand 2013; Miller et al. 2008]. Coagulase-negative staphylococcal species, streptococci and Propionibacterium acnes are organisms frequently identified in exogenous infections following surgery and vitreal injections; when Bacillus cereus infections occur, 70% to 87% have been identified after penetrating trauma [Miller et al. 2008]. Endogenous endophthalmitis may occur with bacteremia associated with endocarditis (often caused by gram-positive cocci including Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci), liver abscess (when seen in Asia, caused by gram-negatives bacilli including Klebsiella), and in immunocompromised and/or hospitalized patients with indwelling intravenous catheters (conditions in which candidal infections may be seen).

title: 2015 July-August Featured Case: A man in his thirties with a history of HIV-1 in
history:
2015 July-August Featured Case: A man in his thirties with a history of HIV-1 infection developed a severe bifrontal headache, diffuse body aches, nausea, and vomiting, associated with feeling weak and dizzy. On the 5th day of his illness, he saw his doctor, and then was referred to an emergency department. On evaluation, he reported headache that rated 10 (on a scale of 0 to 10 where 10 is the most severe), photophobia, neck stiffness, and decreased urine output, with no diarrhea.

HIV-1 infection had been diagnosed 8 years earlier; at the time of diagnosis, the CD4 cell count was 173 per cubic millimeter. Routine testing for co-infections was positive for IgG antibodies to cytomegalovirus and toxoplasma, and negative for hepatitis B surface antigen and antibodies, and hepatitis C virus antibodies. The next year, therapy with efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate was begun. Four years later (three years before this presentation), the level of HIV RNA rose to 69,300 per milliliter. HIV genotyping revealed a resistance to first-generation non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and his antiretroviral medications were changed to darunavir, raltegravir, ritonavir, emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. There was a history of intermittent non-adherence to antiretroviral medications during the 6 months before this presentation, reportedly because of insurance issues. Two months before this evaluation, he presented with weight loss, fevers and diarrhea. The CD4 cell count was 17 per cubic millimeter (1.3%) and HIV-RNA level was 74,000 copies per milliliter, and a diagnosis of cytomegalovirus infection, including esophagitis and colitis, was made. He was instructed to resume taking his prescribed antiretroviral medications.
He also had a history of alcohol abuse, with symptoms of withdrawal but no seizures, for which he had attended Alcoholics Anonymous meetings in the past.

He was born in Central America, and moved to the United States 13 years earlier. He had no ill contacts or recent travel, and had worked outdoors, in gardening and construction. He was a former smoker, and reportedly drank alcohol occasionally.

He lived with his wife (who was also HIV positive) and children.

He had no allergies.

Medications included darunavir (800mg daily), raltegravir (400mg twice daily), ritonavir (100mg daily), emtricitabine (200mg daily) and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (300 mg daily); however the patient reported he had been unable to keep his medications down during the previous 4 days because of vomiting. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double-strength tablet daily) and azithromycin (1200mg weekly) had been prescribed 19 days earlier but the patient had not begun taking them. Prochlorperazine and ibuprofen were taken as needed.
exam_studies:
The patient looked ill and pale; the blood pressure was 95/52 mm Hg sitting and 89/52 mm Hg standing, and the pulse rose from 59 sitting to 66 beats per minute standing. Respirations were 20 per minute with 98% oxygen saturation, and the temperature was 97.7°F (36.5°C). The tongue was dry and the skin had decreased turgor. The neck was stiff and painful with motion; the mid-abdomen was mildly tender and soft, with normal bowel sounds and no organomegaly. Fundoscopic examination revealed normal optic discs. There was no rash. The remainder of the examination was normal.

The white cell count was 4500 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4500-11,000, with 43.3% neutrophils, 37.6% lymphocytes, 14% monocytes, 4.7% eosinophils and 0.2% basophils) and the CD4 cell count was 35 per cubic millimeter (2%). The erythrocytes sedimentation rate was 39 mm per hour (reference range 0-13). Blood cultures were sent. Computed tomography of the head without the administration of contrast (Figure 1) revealed a large confluent area of hypoattenuation involving the right temporal and parietal white matter with extension to the external and internal capsule, 4 mm of leftward midline shift, medialization of the right uncus and mild right uncal herniation.
Figure 1. CT of the brain, without contrast.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain images (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and, after the administration of gadolinium, T1-weighted) are shown in Figures 2 through 5.
Normal saline and ondansetron were administered intravenously. After the results of the brain imaging were known, lumbar puncture was deferred and dexamethasone, vancomycin and ampicillin were given. The patient was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and treatment.
Figure 2. MRI of the brain, axial FLAIR image.
Figure 3. MRI of the brain, axial FLAIR image.
Figure 4. MRI of the brain, T1 post gadolinium.
Figure 5. MRI of the brain, T1 post gadolinium.
diagnosis:
Cerebral toxoplasmosis in a patient with HIV infection and a history of antiretroviral non-adherence.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain FLAIR images revealed lesions with surrounding edema (Figures 2 and 3) in the cerebral hemispheres (particularly in the right temporal lobe) and cerebellum. A dominant lesion in the right temporal lobe measured 4.2 by 3.1 by 2.4 cm and a lesion in the left cerebellar vermis measured 1.9 by 1.9 by 1.6 cm. There were additional lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres, bilateral basal ganglia, left thalamus and the cerebellar hemispheres, and peripheral restricted diffusion associated with several of these lesions. Supratentorially, there was approximately 2 mm leftward midline shift, effacement of the ambient cisterns and mild mass effect on the midbrain. Infratentorially, there was marked edema in the cerebellar vermis and mass effect, with partial effacement of the fourth ventricle. There was no evidence of hydrocephalus.
After the administration of gadolinium, the lesions demonstrated target-like enhancement with central enhancement and a peripherally enhancing halo (Figures 4 and 5).
Testing revealed no evidence of Epstein Barr virus (EBV) DNA in the blood; EBV serologies were consistent with prior infection; galactomannan, antibodies to histoplasma, blastomyces, and coccidioides, and cryptococcal antigen were not detected, and testing for 1, 3 beta D glucan and a an interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative. Testing for toxoplasma IgG antibodies was positive and for IgM antibodies was negative. Four sets of blood cultures drawn from different sites and at two different times were sterile.

Additional initial treatment was administered and included sulfadiazine (2gm four times daily), pyrimethamine (200mg once then 75mg daily), and leucovorin (10mg daily). His symptoms rapidly improved, with resolution of headache, nausea and vomiting by the third hospital day. Blood cultures remained negative, and ampicillin and vancomycin were stopped after 3 days. Antiretroviral medications (darunavir, ritonavir, emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) were resumed. Raltegravir was discontinued because resistance testing showed no evidence for clinically significant protease inhibitor mutations.
Medications on discharge included sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, leucovorin, darunavir, ritonavir, emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, azithromycin for prophylaxis and fluconazole for oral candidiasis.
The patient improved after discharge, with intensive medication adherence support from community health center staff. Additional medication adjustments included discontinuation of fluconazole, and administration of dapsone for pneumocystis prophylaxis.
On repeat CT imaging 6 weeks later (Figure 6), there was an interval decrease in the size of innumerable supratentorial and infratentorial enhancing lesions with decreased surrounding edema, consistent with response to treatment for toxoplasmosis infection. No new lesions were identified. The patient later missed subsequent infectious disease clinic appointments and was lost to follow-up.
Figure 6. CT without contrast, 6 weeks follow-up.

This severely immunocompromised patient with HIV infection and a CD4 cell count less than 50 per cubic millimeter presented with severe headache and symptoms suggestive of increased intracranial pressure, and was found to have multiple ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect on MRI scanning of the brain. This presentation is highly suggestive of toxoplasmosis of the central nervous system, the most frequent opportunistic infection identified in immunocompromised patients with HIV infection and focal intracerebral lesions [Porter and Sande, 1993; Pereira-Chioccola et al., 2009]. Additional corroboration of the clinical diagnosis was obtained with positive evidence of anti-toxoplasma IgG antibodies indicating prior exposure and significant symptomatic and radiologic response to treatment for the protozoa Toxoplasma gondii [Cho et al., 2012].
Other diagnoses in patients with HIV-infection and focal brain lesions to consider include central nervous system non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (the second most common cause of intracerebral mass lesions in immunosuppressed HIV-positive patients [Cho et al., 2012] but which is less likely to have multiple lesions or respond to antiretroviral therapy and anti-toxoplasma medications alone) and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (which is less likely to exhibit a mass effect or present with ring-enhancing lesions [DHHS Guidelines 2013]). Examination of a patient with bacterial endocarditis with central nervous system emboli and infarcts would have likely revealed evidence of multiple peripheral emboli, and blood cultures might have been positive, in the absence of antibacterial therapy. Chagasic encephalitis may mimic toxoplasma encephalitis in an HIV-infected individual who has possible geographic exposures, such as in this patient from Central America, and should be considered in a patient who does not respond to appropriate anti-toxoplasma therapy [Lambert et al., 2006].
