title: 2015 September-October Featured Case: A woman in her twenties presented to an em
history:
2015 September-October Featured Case: A woman in her twenties presented to an emergency department because of an enlarging 'lump' on her left flank of 4 days' duration, associated with increasing pain.
She had been in her usual state of health until approximately two months earlier, when discomfort, described as a 'knot', in the left side of her back developed. She rubbed the area and applied both ice and a hot pad, but had no improvement. Two weeks before this evaluation, she noted a swelling on her left flank, associated with some redness.
Four days before this evaluation, the pain increased. The next day, she was seen in the emergency department of another hospital. Ultrasonography reported revealed 'fluid' around the left kidney; a diagnosis of a urinary tract infection, and possible pyelonephritis, was made and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole administered. During the next 3 days, she felt a gradual enlargement of a lump on her left flank, associated with pain that was non-radiating, worse with pressure, and increased in severity, rated up to 6 on a scale of 0 to 10 (where 10 is the most severe). She also developed vaginal symptoms that she attributed to a yeast infection and discontinued the antibiotics. She presented to a second hospital for evaluation.
She reported no fever, chills, rigors, dysuria, hematuria, frequency, hesitancy, urgency, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, and did not feel that these symptoms were like a previous urinary tract infection she had after the birth of one of her children.

She had a history of scoliosis, and had had a urinary tract infection after the birth of one of her two children, for which a short course of oral antibiotics were administered.

She worked indoors, and lived with her two children and other relatives. She smoked one-half pack cigarettes per day and drank alcohol in moderation; she did not use illicit drugs.

Her mother had nephrolithiasis and there was a family history of cholelithiasis.

She had no allergies.

She had taken trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for two days.
exam_studies:
The vital signs were normal. There was an erythematous area on left flank approximately 3 centimeters in diameter (Figure 1), with fluctuance and induration approximately 7cm in diameter. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings, left flank.

The white cell count was 16,050 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4500-11,000), with 82.5% neutrophils, 12.7% lymphocytes and 4.1% monocytes, and the hematocrit was 35.0% (ref 36.0-46.0). Blood levels of electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, urea nitrogen, and creatinine and the estimated glomerular filtration rate were normal. Urinalysis revealed clear yellow urine with pH 7.0, 1+ occult blood, 1+ albumin, and 1+ leukocytes by screening dipstick; the urine sediment showed 10 to 20 white cells and 0 to 2 red cells per high power field, with 1+ bacteria, 1+ renal tubular cells, and squamous cells present. A urine pregnancy test was negative. An electrocardiogram revealed a sinus tachycardia at a rate of 112 beats per minute, and was otherwise normal.

Computed tomography (CT) images of the kidneys, performed with the administration of intravenous contrast, are shown in Figures 2, 3 and 4.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen, axial view.
Figure 3. CT of the abdomen, coronal view.
Figure 4. CT of abdomen, coronal view.
diagnosis:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis caused by Proteus mirabilis infection of the urinary tract.

A urine culture obtained 3 days earlier at the first hospital grew greater than 100,000 colonies of Proteus mirabilis, which was susceptible to ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cefepime, with intermediate sensitivity to imipenem, and resistant to nitrofurantoin. At the second hospital, urine culture grew few (1000-10,000) colonies of mixed flora and multiple blood cultures were negative.
CT of the abdomen (shown above) revealed a staghorn calculus (average of 450 Hounsfield units, approximately 3 cm in length) in the left renal pelvis, with severe calyceal dilatation and extensive perinephric inflammation. There was a small rim-enhancing loculated fluid collection in the subcapsular region that extended into the posterior perinephric region, and formed a fistulous tract from the kidney into the left flank, communicating with a large multiloculated abscess (5 cm in diameter) in the left flank musculature and subcutaneous fat. The findings were thought to be consistent with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Inflammatory changes abutted the left psoas muscle, and a delayed nephrogram of the left kidney was thought to be consistent with impaired left renal function.
An aspirate of the loculated fluid was obtained by interventional radiology, and a left nephro-ureteral catheter and two left flank drains (one subcutaneous and one retroperitoneal) were placed under sedation. Examination by gram stain of the aspirate from the abscess revealed abundant leukocytes, few mononuclear cells and rare gram negative rods (Figure 5); culture grew few Proteus mirabilis (Figure 6).
Figure 5. Gram stain of aspirate.
Figure 6. Overnight growth of Proteus mirabilis on MacConkey agar.

The patient was initially treated with vancomycin, cefepime and metronidazole, and intravenous fluids. When the results of the culture of the aspirate specimen and sensitivities were known, and the patient had been afebrile for more than 24 hours, antimicrobial therapy was changed to oral ciprofloxacin. Evaluation of the left kidney revealed renal function of 6% normal. She was discharged on the 6th hospital day, then re-admitted 4 days later, and a left nephrectomy was performed. Gross pathological examination of the excised left kidney, shown in Figure 7, reveals end-stage xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis and calyceal abscesses.
Figure 7. Gross pathology of excised left kidney.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP) is an uncommon but severe complication of chronic pyelonephritis. Typically, after the development of an obstructive stone, the kidney becomes replaced by lipid-laden macrophages leading to destruction and necrosis. The enlarged (and eventually non-functional) kidney is often misdiagnosed as a malignancy on imaging.
XGP most commonly occurs in women (>85%) who suffer from recurrent urinary tract infections [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008]. The most common age at presentation is in the upper 40s [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008; Goodman et al., 1979]. In one case series, 51% of patients had staghorn calculi and another 23% had obstructing ureteric calculi [Addison et al., 2015]. Individuals with metabolic syndrome, obesity and diabetes have an increase risk of renal stones and also appear to have an increased risk of XGP [Kadlec et al., 2012]. Prior history of recurrent urinary tract infections, renal stones, and multi-parity are also seen in patients with XGP [Goodman et al., 1979].
Typical presenting symptoms in one recent case series (n 41) included pain (97%), lower urinary tract symptoms (73%), fever (67%), and palpable flank mass (45%) [Korkes et al., 2008]. Other symptoms may include abdominal pain, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, chills, dysuria, hematuria and draining flank sinus [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008; Goodman et al., 1979]. On physical examination, costovertebral angle (CVA) or abdominal tenderness is common and a palpable flank or abdominal mass may be detected. Routine blood tests typically reveal leukocytosis and anemia but preserved renal function. Urinalysis frequently shows pyuria, proteinuria, or hematuria.
The differential diagnosis includes renal cell carcinoma, transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis, Hodgkin’s or Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, renal tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess, renal parenchymal malakoplakia, megalocytic interstitial nephritis, and retroperitoneal fibrosis [McDougal and Nickeleit, 1995].
In several case series, Escherichia coli was the most common isolated organism followed by Proteus mirabilis [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008]. Other organisms reported as involved in cases of XGP include Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas, and Candida, as well as polymicrobial infections [Goodman et al., 1979].
Computerized axial tomography (CT) scan typically finds unilateral hydronephrosis, kidney enlargement, poor excretion of contract media, perinephric extension and air in the urinary tract [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008; Zorzos et al., 2003].
On gross pathological examination, the kidney is typically enlarged with a destructive inflammatory process. Histologic examination reveals necrotic yellow (from the Greek, "xanthos" or yellow) material surrounded by orange-colored tissue. Renal stones or staghorn calculi are typically seen. The inflammation often extends beyond the kidney and may lead to fistula formation.
Treatment includes initial targeted antibiotic therapy; however, nephrectomy is the definitive, and often recommended, therapy [Addison et al., 2015; Korkes et al., 2008; Goodman et al., 1979]. Although laparoscopic nephrectomies can be performed in select cases, many cases will require open procedures [Guzzo et al., 2009].

title: A woman in her thirties was admitted to a hospital because of drenching night sw
history:
A woman in her thirties was admitted to a hospital because of drenching night sweats, high fevers and submandibular lymphadenopathy.
The patient was well until one month before admission when submandibular swelling on the right side occurred, associated with chills, drenching night sweats, high fevers, mild cough and myalgias. Four days before admission, azithromycin was administered.

She was born in the Southern United States but had lived in the Northeastern U.S. for 20 years. She had no history of foreign travel. She had stopped smoking a few months earlier, drank alcohol occasionally, and had never used illicit drugs. She lived with her two children, one adult cat, and one kitten, and had no other pets.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared alert and well. The blood pressure was 118/54 mm Hg, pulse 92 beats per minute, temperature 105.0°F (40.5°C), respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing room air. A submandibular lymph node (3-cm in diameter) on the right side was mildly tender, with no fluctuance. There was a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur with regular rate and rhythm and no rubs or gallops. There was mild diffuse tenderness in the posterior right gluteal area, with no spinal tenderness, and there were no skin lesions. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The peripheral white blood cell count was 13,200 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4800-10,800) with neutrophils 77% and no bands; the level of hemoglobin was 9.5 grams per deciliter (reference range 13.0-17.0). C-reactive protein 213 milligrams per liter (reference range 0.00-10.00) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 74 millimeters per hour (reference range 0-15). Blood levels of liver enzymes and routine chemistry tests were normal. A urinalysis was normal and urine culture grew urogenital flora. Multiple blood cultures had no growth.
A chest radiograph was normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck revealed an enhancing submandibular lymph node (2.8 cm by 1.5 cm) on the right side. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed innumerable subcentimeter hypoattenuated lesions throughout the spleen and liver and mild gastrohepatic and peripancreatic lymphadenopathy. An MRI of the abdomen and pelvis performed with the administration of gadolinium revealed the same subcentimeter lesions with T2 hyperintensity and diffusion restriction that were thought to be consistent with microabscesses (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Abdominal MRI with contrast.
Figure 2. Abdominal MRI with contrast.

Testing for HIV infection, an interferon –gamma release assay (IGRA) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transthoracic echocardiogram, respiratory viral panel (RVP) and multiple serologic tests were recommended by Infectious disease team upon consultation.
HIV and RVP testing was negative. The patient's fevers persisted and, consequently, an ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of the right submandibular gland was performed (Figure 3). Bloody purulent fluid (2 milliliters) was removed and bacterial, fungal and acid-fast stains and culture performed. On the 7th hospital day, a diagnostic test result was received.
Figure 3. Ultrasound of the neck with an enlarged right submandibular lymph node (up to 2.86 cm by 1.59 cm).
diagnosis:
Disseminated Bartonella henselae infection complicated by prolonged fever and hepatosplenic disease.

Serologic testing for Bartonella henselae IgG antibodies was positive at greater than 1:1024 dilution, and IgM was positive at 1:80 dilution. Serologic testing for both IgG and IgM antibodies to Bartonella quintana was negative. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the fluid aspirated from the right submandibular gland node was positive for Bartonella henselae.

The patient was treated with a two-week course of oral azithromycin and rifampin. She was evaluated in outpatient follow-up two weeks later and had complete resolution of her symptoms. A follow-up CT scan is scheduled for 4 months after the completion of therapy.

Cat scratch disease, which occurs most often in children, typically presents with localized lymphadenopathy and an associated cutaneous lesion at the site of inoculation. Additional manifestations may include fever of unknown origin, oculoglandular syndromes, hepatosplenic disease and less often osteomyelitis or nervous system involvement [Florin et al., 2008].
This patient had manifestations of disseminated hepatosplenic disease with prolonged fever. This patient had exposure to a kitten and, although she denied a definite scratch, this was thought to be the likely exposure. Disseminated disease may occur in immunocompromised patients but is rare in healthy adults. In healthy adult patients with disseminated cat scratch disease, the prognosis is good and patients typically recover without sequelae [Bieraugel et al. 2015; Garcia et al. 2014; Liston and Koehler 1996].

title: A man in his forties with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus was seen because o
history:
A man in his forties with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus was seen because of a fever and recurrent multiple draining sinuses on his back and left side.
The patient had noted multiple recurrent draining sinuses on his chest and back, associated with intermittent low grade fevers, during the previous four years. On evaluation two years earlier, computed tomography (CT) of the chest reportedly showed a left paraspinal collection (8 cm by 2.4 cm) that extended from the level of the 7th to the 9th thoracic vertebrae, reactive changes in the 7th and 8th ribs, and a collection along the lateral aspect of the 8th vertebra, with erosion of cortical margins. Culture of material draining from one of the sinuses was sterile. Antituberculous treatment, including isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrizinamide, was administered daily for 9 months, without any improvement. One month before this evaluation, swelling in the left axilla developed.
He also reported a 6 kg weight loss during the previous two months.

The patient had poorly-controlled diabetes mellitus.

The patient was a farmer in northeast India.
exam_studies:
The patient was looked unwell. The temperature was 102°F (38.9°C), blood pressure 130/90mm Hg, pulse 130 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. There was swelling (4 cm by 3 cm) in the left axilla (Figure 1) and multiple sinus openings on the left side of chest and back (Figure 2 and Figure 3). The remainder of the examination was normal.

The hemoglobin was 7.9 gm/dl (reference range (ref) 13.5-16.5), the white cell count 6730 per cubic millimeter (ref 4000-11,000) with 82% neutrophils and15% lymphocytes, platelets 120,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-450,000), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 140 mm per hour (ref 0-20). Serum levels of urea were 89 mg/dL (ref 20-40), creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (ref 0.8-1.2), bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL (ref 0.4-1.3), alanine aminotransferase 64 IU/L (ref 10-45), aspartate aminotransferase 79 IU/L (ref 10-35) and alkaline phosphatase 120 IU/L (ref 50-129).
CT of the chest without the administration of contrast showed a soft tissue lesion with few enlarged lymph nodes in the left axilla and a small left pleural effusion. CT of the abdomen without the administration of contrast showed mild hepatosplenomegaly with a small left-sided pleural effusion and left paraspinal collection (Figures 4 and 5).
Figure 1. CT of the chest.
Figure 4. Gram stain of colony growth from blood culture.
Figure 2. CT of the abdomen.
Figure 5. CT of the abdomen.

Blood cultures grew gram negative bacilli with shiny colonies on MacConkey agar (Figures 6 and 7). A skin biopsy from a sinus opening grew coagulase negative staphylococci.
Figure 3. Blood culture growth on MacConkey agar plate.
Figure 6. Blood culture growth on MacConkey agar plate.
Figure 7. Gram stain of colony growth from blood culture.
diagnosis:
Disseminated melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei.

Blood cultures sent on the day of admission grew Burkholderia pseudomallei (Figure 7). CT-guided biopsy of the left paraspinal muscle collection also grew B. pseudomallei.

Ceftazidime (2 g intravenously, three times daily) was administered, for a 14-day course. The patient gradually improved and was discharged in a stable condition. After discharge, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxasole (TMP-SMX) was administered for 3 months. At follow-up at 3 months, the patient was doing well.

Melioidosis is an infection caused by the facultative intracellular gram-negative bacterium, Burkholderia pseudomallei. It is a widely distributed environmental saprophyte in the soil and in fresh surface water in endemic regions, particularly in Australia, Southeast Asia and South Asia, including India [Chaowagul et al., 1989].
Burkholderia pseudomallei is transmitted mainly by percutaneous inoculation and inhalation [Brundage et al., 1968]. Diabetes mellitus, chronic liver disease, chronic renal disease, chronic lung disease and alcoholism are risk factors for the development of melioidosis [Chaowagul et al., 1989]. The incubation period is 1 to 21 days (mean nine days) [Currie et al. 2000].
Most B. pseudomallei infections are subclinical. Pneumonia is the most common clinical presentation [Cheng and Currie 2005]. Melioidosis can also present with many other manifestations, including skin ulcers or abscesses, bacteremia and sepsis, genitourinary disease, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.
Culture is the mainstay of diagnosis. Gram stain of sputum or purulent abscess drainage may reveal the gram-negative bacilli of B. pseudomallei. Generally, melioidosis is initially treated with intravenous antibiotics followed by a prolonged course of oral therapy [Dance 2014]. Intravenous options include ceftazidime, meropenem or imipenem. Oral antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxasole or doxycycline. Leukopenia (particularly lymphopenia), hepatic dysfunction, renal dysfunction and respiratory failure are factors associated with poor prognosis [Chierakul et al., 2005].

title: A woman in her forties, recently diagnosed with HIV, AIDS and cutaneous Kaposi s
history:
A woman in her forties, recently diagnosed with HIV, AIDS and cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma, was admitted to a hospital because of progressive dyspnea.
Three weeks earlier, the patient had been admitted to the same hospital because of dyspnea and fevers. On that admission, she reported no active medications. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and pleural effusions (Figure 1). HIV testing was positive, and diagnostic evaluation revealed no other evidence of bacterial, viral, or fungal causes of pneumonia. Bronchoscopic examination revealed scattered erythematous lesions throughout the tracheobronchial tree, which were suspicious for Kaposi sarcoma. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was begun for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis.
Later, during the same admission, the patient revealed she had been diagnosed with AIDS and Kaposi sarcoma (with positive cutaneous and lymph node biopsies) eight weeks earlier at a different hospital (hospital #1). At that time, she had started taking antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir-emtricitabine-efavirenz). During her hospitalization at the second hospital (hospital #2), the antiretroviral therapy had been stopped (because her HIV history was not initially revealed) and it was noted that her symptoms had rapidly improved.
Repeat chest CT performed at hospital #2 ten days after the initial imaging (Figure 2) demonstrated significant improvement in the bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and effusions.
The patient developed neutropenia, which was attributed to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was stopped, and inhaled pentamidine was administered as alternative prophylaxis. The patient was discharged home off all antiretroviral therapy with a presumptive diagnosis of pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), with plans for close outpatient follow-up with infectious diseases and oncology.
Within the two weeks after discharge, her dyspnea gradually worsened, with no other new symptoms. She was readmitted to the hospital for further management.
Figure 1. Initial CT of the chest.
Figure 2. CT of the chest, ten days later, after stopping antiretroviral therapy.

As noted in the above history.

The patient was born in Liberia and had moved to the U.S. Midwest seven years earlier. She reported no recent travel, animal exposure, use of illicit drugs, or any new sexual contacts.

She worked as a housekeeper.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared acutely ill. The temperature was 38.4°C (101.1°F), blood pressure 99/54 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 91% while breathing 6 liters per minute oxygen by nasal cannula. There was marked bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, no air movement in the lung bases bilaterally and rales in the mid-lung fields. There were pre-tibial darkened plaques consistent with cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma.

The white cell count was 2230 cells per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 3700 - 11,000), absolute neutrophil count 970 cells per cubic millimeter (ref 1450 - 7500), hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL (ref 11.5 - 15.5), platelets 123,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000 - 400,000), serum creatinine 0.79 mg/dL (ref 0.70 - 1.40), and albumin 2.0 g/dL (ref 3.5-5). The level of CD4 T-lymphocytes was 61 cells per cubic millimeter.
A chest radiograph demonstrated increased consolidations in both lower lobes and the right middle lobe. Chest CT demonstrated multifocal diffuse lymphadenopathy, bilateral pleural effusions, and dense bilateral consolidative airspace opacities, which had progressed compared to the interim chest CT (Figure 3).
Figure 3. CT of the chest, on admission.

The patient was admitted to the hospital. Within 36 hours of admission, oxygenation worsened and she was transferred to the medical intensive care unit and the trachea was intubated. Empiric antibiotics for hospital-acquired pneumonia were administered (initially vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and azithromycin) and empiric oseltamivir and intravenous ganciclovir were given for possible viral processes (such as influenza and cytomegalovirus respectively). However, the patient's condition worsened, with increasing oxygen requirements (up to 100% FiO2 and 15 of PEEP on the ventilator) and persistently high fevers to 40.0°C (104°F). Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) (tenofovir, emtricitabine, and lopinavir/ritonavir) was begun again on the fourth hospital day.
A lymph node biopsy or bone marrow biopsy was considered for further evaluation but deferred as the patient’s respiratory status remained too tenuous. The patient developed progressive anemia, thrombocytopenia, and severe hypoalbuminemia during the course of the hospitalization.
diagnosis:
Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus-associated Inflammatory Cytokine Syndrome (KICS) in a patient with visceral Kaposi sarcoma and AIDS.

Repeated bacterial cultures for blood, urine, and sputum did not demonstrate growth. A respiratory viral PCR panel (that included testing for influenza, parainfluenza, and adenovirus, among other tests) was negative. Bronchoscopic examination on the fourth hospital day demonstrated erythematous lesions spread throughout the tracheobronchial tree consistent with Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 4).
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) studies, including Legionella PCR, Pneumocystis jiroveci PCR, and bacterial, fungal, and viral cultures, were negative. Serologic testing for fungi was negative. Thoracentesis was completed on the eighth hospital day. Analysis of the pleural fluid confirmed an exudative effusion; cultures for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi were negative, as was a cytological examination. The serum level of HHV-8 nucleic acid was 1287 copies/mL (reference range (ref) <100), C-reactive protein was 6.7 mg/dL (ref 0.0 - 1.0) and interleukin-6 was 23 pg/mL (ref <= 5).
Figure 4. Bronchoscopic examination of the tracheobronchial tree.

Based on the results of her initial testing and the fact that her previous lymph node biopsy did not show evidence of multicentric Castleman’s disease, the patient was started on empiric treatment for Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus associated Inflammatory Cytokine Syndrome (KICS) on the tenth hospital day. Treatment included high-dose zidovudine (600 mg every 6 hours), ganciclovir (340 mg every 12 hours), and dexamethasone (2 mg every 6 hours) (all intravenously), and the ART was continued. Her fevers rapidly resolved and supplemental oxygen requirements decreased from 100% fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) to 60% FiO2 within 48 hours. Thoracic surgery was then able to obtain an axillary lymph node biopsy. Pathological examination demonstrated Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 5 and Figure 6); no evidence of lymphoma was found.
On hospital day 16, the trachea was extubated, and the patient was transferred to the regular nursing floor the following day. She was discharged home on hospital day 27, without oxygen supplementation and with resolution of her cytopenias and hypoalbuminemia.
Figure 5. Biopsy of lymph node (hematoxylin and eosin stain, 40x magnification), with abnormal spindle cell and vascular proliferation of bland ovoid cells.
Figure 6. Biopsy of the lymph node, with staining for HHV-8.

Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV or HHV-8) associated Inflammatory Cytokine Syndrome (KICS), first described in 2010 [Uldrick et al. 2010], is a severe systemic syndrome seen in patients co-infected with HIV and KSHV. Patients with KICS have elevated levels of KSHV vIL-6, IL-6, and KSHV viral loads but do not have evidence for multicentric Castleman’s disease (MCD).
Clinical manifestations of the syndrome include fevers, wasting, hypoalbuminemia, cytopenias, respiratory symptoms, edema, lymphadenopathy, and body cavity effusions. A working case definition was proposed in 2012 [Polizzotto et al. 2012] with diagnosis based on clinical manifestations (including symptoms, laboratory abnormalities, and radiographic findings), evidence of systemic inflammation (CRP > 3 g/dL), elevated KSHV levels (>100 copies per 100,000,000 cells), and exclusion of MCD via pathological examination of lymph node, bone marrow, or spleen.
Little is known about the natural history of KICS. In the first case series with six patients, it was associated with 50% mortality. It is hypothesized that the syndrome may be associated with worsening of KS after initiation of ART (as was the case with this patient). Unfortunately, based on a limited number of cases, it appears that the underlying Kaposi sarcoma in patients with KICS may be less responsive to oncologic therapy than in KS alone as spindle cell proliferation is thought to be driven by the excess cytokine production that accompanies KICS. There is no standard therapy for KICS. In vitro studies have demonstrated that ganciclovir and zidovudine have synergistic activity against cells with activated KSHV. This therapy has been utilized in patients with KSHV related clinical syndromes (MCD, primary effusion lymphomas, and KICS).

title: 2015 November-December Featured Case: A man in his fifties, who was from Central
history:
2015 November-December Featured Case: A man in his fifties, who was from Central America, was admitted to the hospital because of progressive shortness of breath.
The patient had been well until approximately 10 years earlier, when he developed shortness of breath with strenuous activities. After several years, however, dyspnea occurred with moderate activity, such as climbing stairs. Two months before this presentation, the shortness of breath began to occur when walking more than a few blocks. His symptoms progressed during the following weeks until he was short of breath with minimal movement and when lying flat. He was no longer able to work, and came to the hospital for an evaluation.
On evaluation, he reported a cough productive of white phlegm that had been present for approximately 3 months. The phlegm occasionally contained streaks of blood, but he reported no frank hemoptysis. He had unintentional weight loss of approximately 10 pounds (4.5 kilograms) during the previous year. He did not have any chest pain, pleurisy, fevers, night sweats, or chills.

The patient had previously consumed 2 pints of liquor daily for 20 years, but stopped 4 years before this presentation. At age 12 years, he had an illness characterized by 1 month of high fevers and a productive cough, which resolved without treatment. The patient had no other medical history and had not seen a physician in 30 years.

The patient was born in Central America and had moved to the United States 28 years earlier; he had not been to Central America since. When he lived in Central America, he had resided in a rural area and worked on a family farm, which had chickens and goats. He was only sexually active with his wife.

The patient was married; his wife lived in Central America and visited him twice a year. He worked as a chef in a restaurant and lived with a friend who was also from Central America, and who had last visited the region 2 years earlier. He did not use tobacco or drugs.

His father died of lung cancer, his brother died of gastric cancer, and 2 of his sisters died of tuberculosis 3 years before this presentation. He did not know any further details of his family’s medical history.

He took no medications.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and comfortable at rest, but became slightly short of breath when speaking. He was overweight and did not have signs of rapid weight loss. The temperature was 36.7°C (98.5°F), pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, respirations 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 96% while breathing room air. There was a II/IV systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border of the chest, without radiation. The examination was otherwise normal; he did not have any pulmonary findings, lower extremity edema, abdominal distention, jugular venous distention, lymphadenopathy, or clubbing of the digits.

The white blood cell count was 6,540 per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 3500-10,500), hematocrit 44.6% (ref 34.9-50 0 in men), and platelets 226,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-450,000). The blood level of creatinine was 1.1 milligrams per deciliter (ref 0.6-1.3); other routine laboratory tests were normal, including liver function tests. An HIV test was negative.
A posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph (Figure 1) revealed cardiomegaly with right atrial and right ventricular enlargement, calcified densities in the bilateral upper lungs, and possible noncalcified nodular densities in the bilateral lower lungs. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a mean pulmonary gradient of 72 millimeters of mercury (normal being less than 30), a peak velocity of 5.4 meters per second (normal, less than 3), and near-normal right ventricular function.
Figure 1. Chest radiograph.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest with the administration of intravenous contrast is shown in Figures 2 and 3.
Figure 2. CT of the chest.
Figure 3. CT of the chest.
diagnosis:
Fibrosing mediastinitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest with the administration of intravenous contrast showed spiculated calcified masses in the bilateral apices, scattered calcified granulomata, extensive mediastinal calcifications, pleural and pericardial calcified plaques, and narrowing of the main pulmonary artery (Figures 2 and 3).
Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest was then obtained, which showed (in addition to the above findings) dense calcifications along the ascending aorta and proximal main pulmonary artery with severe stenosis of the main pulmonary artery (Figure 4). Three-dimensional mapping with the CTA showed focal stenosis in the distal main pulmonary artery secondary to a fibrous band encircling the mid ascending aorta and pulmonary artery (Figure 5).
Based on the patient’s characteristic chest imaging findings, the presence of calcified granulomas in his lungs and spleen (signifying a prior granulomatous infection), and his clinical and epidemiologic history, a diagnosis of fibrosing mediastinitis was made.
Due to his chronic cough, additional testing was performed, including serum galactomannan index, (1-3)-beta-D-glucan, serum histoplasma antigen, urine histoplasma antigen, serum histoplasma antibodies, and an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) blood test for detection of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) complex antigens. Of these tests, only the ELISA IFN-gamma test for Mtb complex antigens was positive. Bacterial and fungal sputum cultures were negative, as was a sputum specimen stained for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). A nucleic acid amplification test of a sputum specimen was positive for Mtb genetic material. After approximately 2 weeks, sputum cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Figure 4. CT of the chest with angiography (CTA).
Figure 5. Three-dimensional view of the CTA.

Rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and isoniazid were administered. Cardiac catheterization showed external compression of the right pulmonary artery and no stenosis of the pulmonary valve. Due to his severe stenosis and symptoms, surgical replacement of the pulmonary artery with a pulmonary homograft was performed. Pathological examination of tissue lymph nodes showed non-caseating granulomas and extensive fibrosis; stains were negative for fungal and acid fast organisms, and examination of tissue of the pulmonary artery showed nodular calcifications and no granulomas. The patient did well postoperatively and had significant improvement in his dyspnea.
He was discharged to home 10 days after his surgery in good condition, with plans to receive directly observed tuberculosis therapy from his local health department and to follow up with infectious diseases and cardiothoracic surgery.

Fibrosing mediastinitis is a rare process that is characterized by the proliferation of fibrous tissue in the mediastinum. The fibrosis may be diffuse and result in obstruction, compression, and/or obliteration of mediastinal structures. The disease is thought to be the result of an immune response to an inflammatory stimulus, which leads to uncontrolled collagen formation (Schade et al., 2013). It is hypothesized that host immunity plays a role in the fibrotic response; one study found the risk of fibrosing mediastinitis was three times higher in patients with HLA-A2 antigen (Schade et al., 2013; Ackman et al., 2004; Peebles et al., 2000).
The inflammatory stimulus is usually infectious in nature, with histoplasmosis being most common, followed by tuberculosis (Schade et al., 2013; Ackman et al., 2004). Tuberculosis-related fibrosing mediastinitis is often less severe than histoplasmosis-related disease, but there have been reports of extensive fibrosis (Atasoy et al., 2001). Non-infectious precipitants have also been reported, and include radiation, pulmonary hemorrhage, drugs (for example, methysergide maleate), autoimmune processes, idiopathic fibrotic disorders, and a familial variant (Ackman et al., 2004; McNeeley et al., 2012). The course of the disease is not predictable; many patients progress, but some stabilize, and others improve.
There are no established diagnostic criteria for fibrosing mediastinitis. The disease is usually suggested by imaging, with computed tomography demonstrating calcifications and vascular involvement (an exception is the idiopathic variant, which does not present with calcifications) (Ackman et al., 2004; Atasoy et al., 2001). Tissue pathology will show fibrosis, but a pathologic diagnosis may not be required if a patient has evidence of a prior granulomatous infection, epidemiologic risk factors, and consistent imaging (McNeeley et al., 2012). If the clinical presentation is less clear, tissue is often needed to rule out malignancy, but this may be technically difficult due to the involvement of vascular structures and dense fibrosis. Serologic tests for infectious processes and cultures of sputum and tissue are rarely positive (Parish et al., 2002; Peikert et al., 2011).
There is no definitive treatment for infection-related fibrosing mediastinitis. Treating the infectious precipitant in the absence of a demonstrable active infection has not been found to be efficacious, and while there are some reports of positive results with glucocorticoids, this has not been corroborated in larger case series (Schade et al., 2013; Peikert et al., 2011). Surgery is primarily indicated to relieve significant obstruction of mediastinal structures or to repair fistulas, and is most efficacious in patients with focal disease. While traditionally surgical interventions have been associated with a mortality of approximately 30%, recent data suggest outcomes have improved (Peikert et al., 2011).

title: 2016 January-February Featured Case: A man in his sixties was seen in an emergen
history:
2016 January-February Featured Case: A man in his sixties was seen in an emergency department because of prolonged epistaxis and nasal stuffiness.
The patient had been in his usual health with diabetes mellitus and chronic renal insufficiency until five months earlier when bilateral nasal stuffiness (right more than left) associated with intermittent epistaxis developed. Two days before this evaluation, epistaxis recurred and persisted for 12 hours. He was seen in an emergency department where nasal packing was done, with improvement, and he was discharged. On follow-up with otolaryngologic examination 2 days later, the nasal packing was removed. Anterior rhinoscopic examination revealed bilateral nasal masses.
He reported no dysphagia, dyspnea, anosmia, dysphonia, weight loss, night sweats, or loss of appetite.

The patient had a history of poorly controlled diabetes, chronic renal disease with proteinuria (4 gram per 24 hours), hypertension and coronary artery disease.

He had smoked for 7 pack years, and stopped several years before this evaluation. He was born in Mexico, and immigrated to the Midwestern United States 20 years earlier, but returned to visit Mexico every 2 to 3 years.

Medications included gabapentin, furosemide, hydralazine, carvedilol, and amlodipine.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, while sitting comfortably. The blood pressure was 133/55 mmHg, pulse 61 beats per minute, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and temperature 36.6°C. There was no facial deformity, nasal discharge, lesion in the anterior nares, or oropharyngeal lesions. There were bilateral nasal masses seen by otolaryngological examination. The breath sounds were clear, with no stridor, and there was grade 2 bipedal pitting edema. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

The white blood cell was 8600 (reference range (ref) 3600-10,600) per cubic millimeter, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL (ref 13.4-17.0), hematocrit 35% (ref 40-54), platelets 158,000 per cubic millimeter; the blood level of creatinine was 4.92 mg/dL (ref 0.67 – 1.17) and urea nitrogen was 50 mg/dL (ref 7-18).

A biopsy of the nasal masses was performed. Pathological examination of the biopsy is shown (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Biopsy of nasal mass, H and E stain, 400x magnification.
Figure 2. Biopsy of nasal tissue, Warthin Starry stain, 400x magnification.
diagnosis:
Rhinoscleroma caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.

Pathological examination of the biopsies of the nasal masses by Warthin-Starry, Giemsa, hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) and Gram staining revealed findings consistent with rhinoscleroma, including Mikulicz cells (macrophages with enlarged vacuoles and a foamy characteristics that contain the Gram-negative rod bacteria of Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) as seen in Figures 1 and 2.
Cultures of the mucosa of the right and left nares grew Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (also called Klebsiella pneumoniae ssp. rhinoscleromatis), which was resistant to ampicillin (MIC >=32).

Ciprofloxacin (500mg daily) was administered, and a course of at least 3 months' duration planned. The patient was scheduled to be followed by anterior rhinoscopy and nasal culture for Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.

Rhinoscleroma is a chronic, progressive, granulomatous, infection of the respiratory tract caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (KR) [Hart and Rao, 2000]. It is a rare disease, predominantly found in rural areas and endemic in Central America, Egypt and certain parts of China [Hart and Rao, 2000; DePontual et al., 2008]. Transmission is enhanced by poor hygiene, poor nutrition and crowding. Cases in developed countries are mostly identified in immigrants [Hart and Rao, 2000].
KR has a complex capsule which allows the bacteria to resist phagocytosis. It resists digestion and elimination by neutrophils and macrophages and, in the process, the phagocytic cells die and viable organisms are released back into the subepithelial layer [Canalis and Zamboni, 2001]. As histiocytes engulf the bacteria, their vacuoles enlarge becoming Mikulicz cells (MC) – foamy macrophages with vacuoles containing KR - which are pathognomonic for rhinoscleroma (Figure 1 and 2) [Miller et al., 1979].
There are three stages to the disease. The first catarrhal or atrophic stage presents with non-specific rhinitis symptoms, which may progress to fetid rhinorrhea, crusting, and nasal obstruction. Histologically, there is squamous metaplasia, subepithelial neutrophilic infiltrate and possibly granulation tissue. Most patients are diagnosed during the hypertrophic or granulomatous second stage. These patients have widening of the nasal pyramid, epistaxis, anosmia, granuloma formation and tissue destruction. Other problems arise depending on the area and extent of involvement, including airway obstruction, hoarseness, muffled voice, decreased hearing, loss of vision, and secondary infection. Histologically, there is hyperplasia, chronic inflammation, and MC. The third sclerotic or fibrotic stage is when patients present with worsening deformity and stenosis of nasal and vestibular areas due to scarring. At this stage MC are difficult to find [Hart and Rao, 2000; Zhong et al. 2011].
Biopsy of the mass, usually through endoscopy, is diagnostic. Pathology demonstrates MC by periodic acid-Schiff, Giemsa or Warthin-Starry stains. Cultures of biopsy specimens are positive in approximately 50% of cases [de Pontual et al., 2008]. KR may also be isolated by swabbing the mucosal lesion. KR is not part of normal flora and isolation of the organism suggests the diagnosis. Computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging may demonstrate the extent of mass lesion and obstruction.
Treatment involves administration of antibiotics for a prolonged duration; there is no established duration, but case series report treatment from 6 weeks to 6 months. With eradication as the goal, repeat biopsy with culture may guide treatment duration [Maguina et al., 2006]. A number of antibiotics have been used with varying efficacy, including streptomycin, doxycycline, rifampin and fluoroquinolones [Borgstein et al., 1993]. Surgical management may be indicated for debridement, relief of obstruction or correction of scarring stenosis [Zhong et al. 2011].
Granuloma may regress but patients are often left disfigured with scars that may lead to stenosis. Repeat biopsy with culture may guide duration of treatment [Hart and Rao, 2000]. Relapse occurs in about 30%; thus, close follow up is necessary [Zhong et al. 2011].

title: A man in his twenties was admitted to a hospital in a northeastern city during w
history:
A man in his twenties was admitted to a hospital in a northeastern city during winter because of several days of nausea, vomiting and a diffuse rash.
One week before admission, he was in his usual state of good health. Four days before admission, fever, fatigue, and nausea developed, associated with multiple episodes of non-bloody emesis. During the next three days, rash, headache and severe polyarthralgia developed. The rash initially erupted on his legs, and then ascended, with involvement of his palms and soles. The rash was non-pruritic. The polyarticular pain was asymmetric, involving primarily the left first toe, left ankle, right knee, left wrist and right thumb. He also reported gingival bleeding.
He had noted a poor appetite and some photosensitivity with headache. He reported no dyspnea, cough, abdominal pain, hematochezia, hematemesis, hematuria, dysuria, or bruising. The patient reported no recent insect bites.

The patient reported a possible history of genital warts, but denied a history of other sexually transmitted infections.

The patient worked in a restaurant. He owned two cats and four rats, with which he reported having had close contact, including on the face and mouth, but was unaware of bites or scratches. He was sexually active with his girlfriend of four years. He smoked up to three packs per day of cigarettes for more than 10 years and had recently stopped before admission. He had previously smoked marijuana and had a remote history of cocaine and amphetamine use, with no history of intravenous drug use. He had no recent international or regional travel.

He occasionally used over-the-counter sleep aid for insomnia, and took no prescribed medications or herbal supplements.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared acutely ill and fatigued. The blood pressure was 119/64 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute, and temperature 100.6°F (38.1°C). The oropharynx revealed mildly enlarged tonsils, without exudates. There was no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The neck was supple. There was a regular tachycardia and 1/6 systolic ejection murmur, with no cardiac rubs or gallops. The lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally, without rales or rhonchi. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended with normal bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly. There were no genitourinary lesions or penile discharge. Dermatologic examination revealed a maculopapular, non-blanching slightly palpable rash, with some petechial features. The rash was most prominent over his legs, palms and soles; no enanthem was present in the oropharynx. Multiple joints were warm, erythematous, very tender and moderately swollen, including the right knee, left ankle, and left wrist. Physical examination findings are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 7200 cells/microliter (reference range (ref) 4200-9000), hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (ref 13.7-17.5), platelets 43,000 per microliter (ref 150,000-330,000). The international normalized ratio was 1.0 (ref 1.0-1.2).
The level of sodium was 139 mmol/L (ref 133-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (ref 3.3-5.1), serum creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (ref 0.67-1.17), calcium 7.7 mg/dL (ref 9.0-10.3), venous lactate 0.7 mmol/L (ref 0.5-2.2), fibrinogen 622 mg/dL (ref 172-409), haptoglobin 325 mg/dL (ref 30-200) and ferritin 447 ng/mL (ref 20-250).
Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-1 and -2 antibodies and antigen was negative. HIV-1 PCR was negative. Syphilis screen was non-reactive. Parvovirus B19 IgG was positive and IgM was negative. Epstein-Barr virus IgG was positive and IgM was negative. Testing for cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, anti-nuclear antibody screening and the direct antiglobulin test were negative. Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA amplification of the urine was negative.
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed liver with a span of 16.3 cm and enlargement of the spleen, which measuring 16.2 cm.

After the patient's admission, hematologic consultants reviewed a peripheral blood smear and felt the findings were unlikely to be consistent with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or hemolytic uremic syndrome.
diagnosis:
Rat-bite fever caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis.

Two sets of blood cultures were obtained before the administration of antimicrobials, and an additional two blood cultures were collected in tubes containing sodium citrate (lavender top tubes, not containing sodium polyanethol sulfonate). The blood cultures were negative during the hospitalization. Testing by an outside laboratory detected Streptobacillus moniliformis DNA in the patient’s serum by real-time polymerase chain reaction.

Penicillin G (1 million units every 4 hours intravenously) was administered for a seven-day course. After completion of the penicillin course, oral amoxicillin (500 mg orally, three times daily) was administered for another seven days.
The fever, polyarthritis and thrombocytopenia improved during the first several days of his admission. He was discharged to his home with improvement in his symptoms. At a follow-up visit after completion of therapy, he had some residual fatigue and joint discomfort but otherwise felt well, with a normal physical examination.

Rat-bite fever is a bacterial infection caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis, which is more common in North America, and Spirillum minus, which is more common in Asia. The incidence and prevalence of rat-bite fever are unclear, as the disease is not nationally reportable in the United States.
Rat-bite fever is most often associated with exposure to rats, though other rodents may harbor S. moniliformis, as can carnivores that prey on these rodents. It is believed that rats, including pet and laboratory rats as well as wild rats, are asymptomatic carriers of S. moniliformis [Gaastra et al., 2009]. Exposure to S. moniliformis may involve contact with the rat’s saliva or excreta; an actual bite is not necessary to transmit infection. Groups at higher risk for contracting rat-bite fever include people with exposure to rats and rodents, such as rodent or snake owners, pet store workers, laboratory technicians, and inhabitants of crowded urban dwellings. The incubation period is typically less than 10 days (range 1-22 days).
Rat-bite fever is a systemic illness with several non-specific features, including fever, rigors, migratory polyarthralgia and rash. The rash may involve palms and soles and may be maculopapular, petechial, or purpuric; hemorrhagic pustules may be seen [Cunningham et al., 1998].
Thrombocytopenia was a prominent feature of this patient’s illness. Case reports describe rat-bite fever with associated thrombocytopenia [Center for Disease Control and Prevention, 2005; Center for Disease Control and Prevention, 2014].
S. moniliformis is a highly pleomorphic, filamentous, gram negative rod. Isolation of the causative bacteria in cultures of blood or synovial fluid is the gold standard for diagnosis. Because the organism is fastidious and challenging to grow in culture media, confirmation of the diagnosis microbiologically can be difficult. Sodium polyanethol sulfonate, a component in standard blood culture media, has been shown to inhibit bacterial growth of S. moniliformis [Shanson et al., 1985]. S. moniliformis may be isolated using enriched media containing trypticase soy agar or broth enriched with 20% blood, serum or ascitic fluid [Elliott, 2007]. Polymerase chain reaction has been used to detect S. moniliformis in blister fluid from a pediatric patient [Berger et al., 2001]. Serologic testing for S. moniliformis is not currently available.
Left untreated, rat-bite fever may carry significant morbidity and mortality. Numerous complications have been described, including endocarditis [Madhubashini, 2013], leukocytoclastic vasculitis [Gilroy, 2002] and septic arthritis [Dworkin et al., 2010].
The treatment of choice is intravenous penicillin [Roughgarden, 1965; Elliott, 2007]. Tetracycline may be considered in cases of penicillin allergy [Gilroy and Kahn, 2002]. There are cases where ceftriaxone has been used, such as a 58-year-old male with an epidural abscess due to S. moniliformis [Addidle et al., 2012] and a 9-year-old girl who developed rat bite fever [Cunningham et al., 1998]. Antibiotic susceptibility tests may be useful in guiding antibiotic therapy.

title: A woman in her sixties with a history of melanoma of the right leg, ulcerative c
history:
A woman in her sixties with a history of melanoma of the right leg, ulcerative colitis, and atrial fibrillation, presented with worsening of a chronic ulcerative process on the right leg.
Approximately one year earlier, erythema of the right leg developed in the vicinity of the previous melanomas. She was seen by a dermatology consultant; pathological examination of a skin biopsy was thought to be consistent with Sweet's syndrome.
During the next year, trials of minocycline, topical steroids, dapsone, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and multiple prednisone tapers were administered, with waxing and waning findings. The lower extremity ulcerative lesion worsened after an episode of trauma. During one of the periods of worsening, pathological examination of a repeat skin biopsy was consistent with "granulomatous dermatitis", with no evidence of Sweet's syndrome; bacterial stains, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stains for mycobacteria and methenamine silver stains for fungal organisms were negative. Results of serum and urine protein electrophoreses, serum coccidioides immunodiffusion, cryptococcal antigen, blastomyces antibody, beta-D-glucan, and galactomannan, as well as histoplasma urine antigen, were negative. Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was indeterminate due to lack of reactivity in the positive control.
The lower extremity ulcerative lesion continued to worsen; swabs of the ulcer grew Pseudomonas and Proteus. A repeat IGRA was positive. Colchicine and ciprofloxacin were administered and steroids were stopped, without improvement. Ultimately, she presented to the hospital with worsening right leg pain and redness, as well as new low grade fevers, chills, and anorexia.

A diagnosis of superficial melanoma of the right leg was made three years before this presentation and treated with local excision. One year later, locally metastatic melanoma developed; biopsies of the lymph nodes were negative and the lesion was treated with local excision and skin graft. She also had mild ulcerative colitis and atrial fibrillation.

She had lived in California, except for 3 years in Hawaii, and had traveled extensively internationally, visiting Greece, the Middle East, and South and Southeast Asia within the previous year. She had no history of substance use, was not sexually active, and had never been incarcerated or homeless. She went swimming frequently (usually in pools) and, during her travels, had had extensive ocean water exposure. She had no pets and reported no history of animal exposure.

She had had an unspecified reaction to silver sulfadiazine.

Medications were dronedarone, metoprolol, atorvastatin, rivaroxaban, furosemide, lansoprazole, colchicine and ciprofloxacin.
exam_studies:
The temperature was 98.4°F (36.9°C), pulse 88 beats per minute, and the blood pressure was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy. There was extensive swelling, induration, and ulceration of the skin of the distal right leg below the knee, with red papules extending up to the right thigh, some with necrotic areas (Figure 1 and Figure 2).The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white cell count was 6,600 per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4,000-11,000; with 71% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes, and 2% eosinophils). The hemoglobin was 9.0 gm/dL (ref 13.5-17.5), platelets 361,000 per cubic millimeter (ref 150,000-300,000). Her C-reactive protein (CRP) was 132 milligrams/liter (ref < 10). The serum level of albumin was 2.0 grams per deciliter (ref 3.9-5.1); other blood test results were normal including creatinine, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin.

Pathological examination of a skin biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed a tuberculoid granulomatous dermatitis, while staining for bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast (AFB) organisms was negative (Figure 3 and Figure 4).
Figure 3. Skin biopsy results.
Figure 4. Skin biopsy results.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous Mycobacterium marinum in a patient with malignant melanoma.

One week later, results of universal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the skin biopsy specimen returned positive for Mycobacterium marinum DNA, detected with the rpoB primer set. Two days after this result returned, one of the previously obtained skin biopsies showed rare growth of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) organisms, which were identified to be Mycobacterium marinum (Figures 5 and 6).
Figure 5. Mycobacterium marinum shown with Kinyoun stain after growth in culture from skin biopsy specimen.
Figure 6. Mycobacterium marinum, grown in culture on Middlebrook7H11 agar from skin biopsy.

Treatment with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol were started before the results of the biopsies returned. The patient developed a significant allergic reaction to rifampin that required rifampin desensitization.
After the positive results were known, isoniazid and pyrazinamide were stopped and rifampin and ethambutol were continued, with significant improvement. Four weeks later, formal organism identification from the National Jewish Laboratory confirmed the diagnosis of Mycobacterium marinum in two separate cultures with susceptibility testing indicating the organism was susceptible to both rifampin and ethambutol.
Complications with bacterial superinfection and peripheral vascular disease occurred, but her leg erythema, ulcers, and pain continued to improve with rifampin and ethambutol during the next 3-4 months.

Mycobacterium marinum is a non-tuberculous mycobacterium that is classified as a "slow grower" on AFB culture (≥ 14 days for mature growth on solid culture media). It is a water-borne organism that causes disease in fish and is present world-wide in both fresh and salt water. It is particularly known to cause infections related to exposure to stagnant water such as swimming pools or fish tanks earning the moniker of "fish tank granuloma". Human infection occurs by direct inoculation and thus usually affects the distal extremities. Incubation period is 2-4 weeks.
M. marinum prefers cooler temperature typically causing superficial papules, nodules, plaques, abscesses, or ulcers without invasion into deeper tissues. It can progress in a “sporotrichoid fashion”. Cutaneous infection can spontaneously resolve and there are case reports of this occurring after two years of disease [Aubry et al., 2002]. Joint and bone infections can occur but are less common.
Diagnosis of M. marinum can be difficult. Like some other non-tuberculous mycobacteria, it can cause a positive tuberculosis skin test (PPD). Along with M. kansasii and M. szulgai, it can also cause a positive quantiferon-gold test result due to the presence of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 proteins; this finding is seen in > 50% of subjects with M. marinum infection [Kobashi et al., 2009]. The organism burden in the skin lesions is typically low and as a result AFB smears of the infected tissue are usually negative. If cultured at lower temperature (30-33°C) the organism can be recovered in AFB culture in 75% of cases. Pathology typically shows granulomas.
Treatment of M. marinum is based on results from case series rather than large trials. The organism is typically resistant to isoniazid or pyrazinamide. Drugs of choice are rifampin, ethambutol, or the macrolides [Griffith et al., 2007].Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones are also usually active. In the largest case series looking at drug susceptibilities, the following were the average mean inhibitory concentrations (MICs), ug/ml: rifampin (0.2), rifabutin (0.06), ethambutol (2.0), clarithromycin (0.8), doxycycline (4.0), minocycline (2.0), ciprofloxacin (2.0), amikacin (2.0) [Aubry et al., 2002]. Two drug therapy is generally recommended due to concerns for treatment failure or resistance development with monotherapy.
Treatment duration is usually based on the patient’s clinical response; typically, patients are treated for 1-2 months after resolution of skin lesions and for a total of 3-to-4 months. Surgical debridement can be helpful if there is extensive disease. Outcomes are generally good with an 80-90% cure rate reported with appropriate antibiotic therapy [Aubry et al., 2002; Griffith et al., 2007]

title: 2016 July-August Featured Case: A man in his twenties was admitted to the hospit
history:
2016 July-August Featured Case: A man in his twenties was admitted to the hospital in late summer because of recurrent fevers, foot swelling, dyspnea and bradycardia.
The patient had been well until four weeks before admission when, after walking in a campground in northern New England, he noted a rash (approximately 2cm in diameter) on his right foot with 2 central marks, without known trauma or insect bite. During the next three days, his right foot became erythematous, swollen to double its normal size, and painful. He subsequently developed shaking chills but did not take his temperature. He was seen in the emergency department of another hospital and prescribed cephalexin for one week. During the following week, the foot lesion turned black, with reddish-purple discoloration in the surrounding tissue; the pain worsened and the erythema progressed to halfway up his calf. He was referred to a surgeon and a diagnosis of cellulitis secondary to a spider bite was made; the cephalexin course was extended to a total duration of two weeks.
After completion of antibiotic therapy, the pain, redness and swelling of his right foot initially improved to near-normal appearance. The chills and subjective fevers resolved and he was able to return to work.
Five days before this evaluation, temperatures between 102 and 103°F (38.9°C to 39.4°C) developed at night, and recurred nightly thereafter. The patient took acetaminophen, with transient improvement. There were associated diffuse myalgias; shortness of breath; episodic sharp back pain; right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating; several episodes of diarrhea, and increased right foot swelling; as well as headache, dizziness, and blurry vision that resolved when afebrile. Pain in the right foot persisted. He did not have nausea, vomiting, photophobia, headache in the absence of fever, focal weakness, numbness, dysarthria, sore throat, cough, new rash, arthralgias, dysuria, or hematuria.
One day before this presentation, the patient returned to the outpatient department of the other hospital because of persistent symptoms; additional testing was ordered and an appointment with an infectious disease specialist was made. On the day of this presentation, he was seen at work, and was referred to the emergency department of a tertiary care hospital.

He had previously been in good health.

He drank multiple beers approximately twice weekly and smoked cigarettes. He had no other recent travel. He owned a dog.

The patient lived in New England and worked in retail.

He had no allergies.

He took acetaminophen for fevers, and had completed a two-week course of cephalexin.
exam_studies:
He was in no apparent distress, afebrile, with blood pressure 103/60 mm Hg, pulse in the mid-forties per minute, respirations 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% while breathing room air. The heart rhythm was regular, bradycardic, with normal S1 and S2 heart sounds and no murmurs. There was left upper quadrant tenderness when palpating the right lower quadrant, and no rebound or guarding. The right foot was diffusely swollen, with discoloration over the dorsal surface. There was no erythema, tenderness, skin breakdown, or fluctuance. The remainder of the examination was normal, including no peripheral stigmata or evidence of embolic disease, and no rash.

The white cell count was 8400 per cubic millimeter (reference range (ref) 4500-11,000), with 79% neutrophils, 17% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes, and 2% eosinophils; the hematocrit, hemoglobin and platelet count were normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and renal and liver function tests. The glucose level was 66 mg/dl (ref 70-100), globulin 4.3 g/dl (ref 2.6-4.1), and creatine kinase 56 U/L (ref 60-400). Urinalysis revealed 1+ albumin and trace ketones, with 3 to 5 red cells and few bacteria per high-power field.
An electrocardiogram (EKG) is shown (Figures 1 and 2). A chest radiograph revealed linear opacities at the left base that were suggestive of an early focus of pneumonia.
Figure 1. Electrocardiogram.
Figure 2. Detail of EKG shown in Figure 1.

An additional electrocardiogram (Figures 3 and 4) was obtained 7 minutes after the EKG shown above. The patient was admitted to a cardiac telemetry unit for monitoring.
Figure 3. Repeat electrocardiogram, 7 minutes after EKG shown in Figure 1.
Figure 4. Detail of EKG shown in Figure 3.
diagnosis:
Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi infection, complicated by carditis and complete heart block.

Lyme immunoblot IgG testing revealed greater than 5 reactive antigens. Antibody capture enzyme immunoassay for antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi (the agent of Lyme disease) were positive, with an IgM level greater than 27.8, IgG greater than 17.6 and IgA greater than 16.2 (normal range less than 1), diagnostic of disseminated infection. Test results from the other hospital one day earlier were obtained, with reportedly positive testing for IgM antibodies.
The EKG shown in Figures 1 and 2 revealed complete atrioventricular (AV) dissociation and a ventricular QRS rate between 40 and 49 per minute, normal R-wave progression, and no ST-segment changes or pathological T-wave inversions. The EKG shown in Figures 3 and 4 revealed sinus bradycardia at a rate of 42 beats per minute, with 2nd degree AV block and 2:1 AV conduction.
Blood cultures were sterile. Thick and thin Giemsa smears showed no evidence of intracellular organisms. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the foot showed no evidence of osteomyelitis.

Ceftriaxone (2gm daily) was administered intravenously. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a dilated left atrium (AP dimension 42mm (reference 25-38), and SI 56mm) and a mildly dilated left ventricle 56 (reference 37-53), with no segmental wall motion abnormalities, and a 69% ejection fraction. There was a minimal posterior pericardial effusion and no valvular vegetations or evidence of tamponade.
Four days after admission, a treadmill stress test demonstrated excellent exercise capacity, with sinus rhythm ranging between 66 and 160 beats per minute, and first degree AV block, without 2nd or 3rd degree AV block. The patient was discharged on the 5th hospital day, on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, for a total antibiotic course of three week's duration.
On follow-up one month later, an electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at a rate of a 56 per minute.

Lyme carditis is an uncommon but potentially serious complication of disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection. Studies published after the year 2000 have indicated that this manifestation occurs in 1 to 2% of cases of Lyme disease [Forrester and Mead, 2014; Robinson et al. 2015] and is seen more frequently in men than women [Forrester and Mead, 2014]. As compared to the reported frequency of this complication in studies published before 2000, these more recent studies suggest a decline in the rate [Robinson et al., 2014], perhaps related to the greater frequency of antibiotic administration early in the course of Borrelia burgdorferi infection.
Although approximately 60% of patients diagnosed with Lyme carditis may not recall having had a tick bite, many developed a skin lesion consistent with erythema migrans, suggestive of early Lyme disease. Erythema migrans may occur between 5 to 48 days after infection (median 12 days) and last up to several weeks before spontaneous resolution [Robinson et al. 2015]. Dissemination of disease to other tissues, including the heart, occurs weeks to months after initial infection. Skin and organ involvement can occur concurrently. The conduction abnormalities associated with Lyme carditis may be potentially life-threatening [Forrester and Mead, 2014; Robinson et al. 2015] and require temporary pacemaker insertion if associated with asystole, other hemodynamic instability or severe symptoms [Robinson et al. 2015]; however, the abnormal conduction usually resolves within 6 weeks [Forrester and Mead, 2014; Robinson et al. 20154] and the need for permanent pacing is extremely uncommon. When heart block is present, the degree may vacillate rapidly [Forrester and Mead, 2014], as seen in this patient, whose heart block changed from 3rd to 2nd degree within minutes (seen in Figures 2 and 4 above). Associated symptoms in those presenting with complete heart block include syncope, fever, lightheadedness, dyspnea, weakness, palpitations, chest pain, headache, and arthralgia [Forrester and Mead, 2014; Robinson et al. 20154], many of which were present in this patient.
Pathological examination of cardiac specimens obtained from affected patients may reveal spirochetes of Borrelia burgdorferi dispersed diffusely in the tissue, as well as evidence of inflammation [Robinson et al. 2015].
In this patient, the diagnosis was suggested by his residence in a Lyme endemic area and by the clinical picture, which included skin and cardiac findings. The definitive diagnosis was made by serologic testing, with positive IgM and IgG antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi. The differential diagnosis of infectious etiologies of atrioventricular block with preserved ejection fraction is relatively narrow and includes Lyme disease, aortic root abscess in setting of bacterial endocarditis, and Chagas disease [Bern 2011]. Any infection that causes myocarditis [Fung et al. 2016] may result in atrioventricular block; thus the infectious differential diagnosis expands in the setting of accompanying myocardial dysfunction. Other diseases transmitted by ticks such as babesiosis and anaplasmosis were briefly considered, but these were much less likely given the clinical picture and laboratory test results, including the absence of intracellular organisms on Giemsa staining and normal white cell, hematocrit and platelet counts. Bacteremia with endocarditis was also considered, but disproved with negative blood cultures and echocardiography. Influenza was also less likely given the onset in summer, the associated leg findings and the absence of significant upper respiratory symptoms.

title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A previously healthy man in his twen
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A previously healthy man in his twenties developed skin lesions on his right flank, thighs, feet and left wrist, which were initially small, dark and verrucous. The lesions on the right flank eventually resolved spontaneously and the other lesions enlarged, with associated inflammation and brown, malodorous discharge. Results of two skin biopsies, performed approximately 2 and 3 months after the onset of the lesions, were non-diagnostic. Multiple courses of doxycycline were administered, without improvement.
Approximately 8 months after the onset of the skin lesions, progressive right-sided back pain and left wrist pain occurred, with no associated fevers or constitutional symptoms. He was seen in an emergency department, where a fluid collection was identified in the area of the right flank and drained, after which the patient returned home. Two weeks later, he returned to the emergency department because of worsening back pain. He was admitted to the hospital, and then transferred to a tertiary hospital for further evaluation and management.

The patient had previously been in good health.

The patient smoked cigarettes and occasionally drank alcohol, and had no history of illicit drug use. He was born in China, moved to the United States several years before this presentation, and returned to visit China frequently. He lived in New England, and had previously lived in Illinois. He was sexually active with his girlfriend, worked with computers and was physically active, including outdoor activities.

He was on no medications.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was123/80 mmHg, pulse 60 beats per minute, temperature 98.4°F (36.9°C), respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing room air. There was mild right flank tenderness and swelling. Multiple discrete lesions were present on the thighs and arms (Figures 1 and 2). There was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding on the left posterior thigh.
Figure 2. Physical finding on the anterior right thigh.

The white cell count was 13,200 per microliter (reference range (ref) 4000-11,000) with 76% neutrophils, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 104 mm per hour (ref 0-15) and C-reactive protein 54 mg per liter (ref 0-7.48); the results of other routine laboratory tests were normal.
A chest radiograph was normal. Other radiographic studies revealed multiple abnormalities, including a destructive lesion of the left distal radial metadiaphysis; multiple peripherally enhancing loculated fluid collections in the paraspinal, psoas, and right gluteal muscle groups bilaterally; and evidence of advanced osteomyelitis with lytic lesions and multiple Brodie’s abscesses in the left greater trochanter and lumbar spine (Figures 3, 4 and 5).
Figure 3. Radiograph of left wrist.
Figure 4. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and extremities.
Figure 5. CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine.
diagnosis:
Disseminated blastomycosis with skin, soft tissue and bone involvement.

Needle aspiration of the gluteal collection was performed. Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining (Figure 6) and Grocott methenamine-silver (GMS) staining (Figure 7) of the fluid obtained by needle aspiration revealed broad-based budding yeast consistent with Blastomyces dermatitidis. The same organism later grew on cultures. Blastomyces urinary antigen was positive at a level of 2.80 ng/mL (reference range 0.2-14.7).
Figure 6. Pathological examination of the gluteal aspirate (H and E stain).
Figure 7. Pathological examination of the gluteal aspirate (GMS stain).

Liposomal amphotericin B was administered for 6 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole for approximately 18 months. Dose adjustments were made according to measured levels. The patient improved clinically, with decreasing back pain, fading skin lesions (Figure 8), improvement in the appearance of the radiographic abnormalities, and normalization of blood inflammatory markers. The urinary Blastomyces antigen also became undetectable.
Testing for immunocompromising conditions was unrevealing. The HIV test was negative, CD4 T-cell lymphocyte count was 1125 per cubic millimeter (43.3%) and levels of immunoglobulins were normal. Genetic testing revealed no known pathologic variants in interleukin-12 or interferon-gamma pathway genes. The patient did not require surgery after radiologic drainage of gluteal abscess.
Figure 8. Physical findings 10 months after diagnosis.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic fungus endemic in the United States, predominantly the Mississippi, Ohio and St. Lawrence River Valleys and the Great Lakes regions. It grows as a mold at 25-28°C and a yeast at 37°C with a characteristic broad-based single budding appearance. Endemic/sporadic cases occur most often in normal hosts, but as cellular immunity is the primary host defense mechanism, reactivation can occur in the immunocompromised. The organism is primarily acquired by inhalation, resulting in pneumonia as the most common clinical presentation. Extrapulmonary infection can occur via hematogenous dissemination to the skin/subcutaneous tissue, bone, prostate, central nervous system, or other parts of the body [Bradsher, 2015].
Diagnosis is made by direct visualization of organisms on fungal stains or by positive cultures. Antibody testing lacks sensitivity so is unhelpful in the diagnosis of acute disease. The Blastomyces antigen test can aid with diagnosis and tracking response to therapy [Frost and Novicki, 2015].
Prolonged courses of antifungal therapy are required to achieve cure. Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) treatment guidelines [Chapman et al., 2008] recommend 6-12 months of oral itraconazole for mild to moderate disease. An initial course of liposomal amphotericin B is recommended for those with severe or disseminated disease, or underlying immunocompromise. Vertebral/osteoarticular disease requires even longer courses of therapy – at least one year [Saccente et al., 1998]. The newer azoles are not as well studied but are known to have better central nervous system penetration so are an alternative option in patients with CNS disease.
