title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his sixties developed blurr
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his sixties developed blurred vision in his left eye. On the third day of his symptoms, he presented for evaluation.
He reported having had a flu-like illness 2 months earlier, which was followed one week later with the onset of intermittent fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue and almost daily mild headaches. He had also noted early satiety, decreased appetite, and a 20-pound weight loss. One week before this presentation, his hands and feet became swollen, and he developed occasional tingling and burning sensations. He had no joint pain, skin rashes or painful skin nodules.

He was in good health before the flu-like illness two months earlier.

He was born on an island in the South Pacific and immigrated to the United States many years earlier. He had no recent international or national travel, no sick contacts and no known exposure to tuberculosis. He owned several dogs, with no other recent exposure to animals. He had smoked marijuana daily but stopped one month before this presentation. He had no history of tobacco, alcohol or intravenous drug use.

He lived with his wife and children in Southern California and had worked as a landscaper until this illness, when he became unable to work due to his symptoms.

He took acetaminophen and naproxen as needed for headache and fevers.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 143/67 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats per minute, temperature 101.7°F (38.7°C), respirations 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing room air. His hands and feet were edematous and there were splinter hemorrhages on all finger nails. The remainder of the general examination was normal. An ophthalmologic examination performed in the emergency department revealed branch retinal artery occlusion of left eye.

The white blood cell count was 13,000 cells per microliter (reference range (ref) 4000-10,500), hemoglobin 11g/dL (ref 13.5 -16.9), hematocrit 39.7% (ref 39.5 - 50) and platelets 279,000 per microliter (ref 150,000 - 400,000). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 103 mm/hr (ref 0 - 15) and C-reactive protein 0.4 mg/dl (ref 0 - 1.0). The level of albumin was 3.4 g/dl (ref 4.2 - 5.5), total protein 9 g/dl (ref 6 - 8.3) and other tests of liver function were normal. An HIV test was negative. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria, with 23 red cells per high-power field (ref 0-3). Other routine laboratory test results were normal. A chest radiograph was normal.

Three sets of blood cultures were obtained, followed by the administration of intravenous vancomycin, and the patient was admitted to the hospital.
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), performed on the day of admission, demonstrated trace aortic regurgitation, and was otherwise normal. Vancomycin was subsequently stopped, as the patient appeared clinically well and hemodynamically stable. Multiple additional sets of blood cultures were obtained, and prolonged incubation periods requested to evaluate for possible culture negative endocarditis.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen with the administration of intravenous contrast showed mild diffuse bladder-wall thickening and multiple subcentimeter mesenteric lymph nodes that were thought to represent a reactive process. An extensive rheumatologic evaluation revealed a mildly elevated level of rheumatoid factor at 20 IU/ml (ref <14).
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated a possible very thin (2 mm) nodular thickening on the aortic valve.
The patient was discharged from the hospital with symptomatic improvement along with multiple negative blood cultures, with a plan to repeat the echocardiogram in 1 or 2 weeks. Results of some other serologic studies to look for culture-negative causes of endocarditis were pending at discharge.
One week after discharge, the patient did not attend a scheduled outpatient follow-up appointment. Two weeks later, he returned to hospital because of a 3-to-4 day history of bilateral hand pain, swelling and bluish discoloration (Figures 1 and 2). He appeared otherwise well, with normal vital signs. Physical examination revealed bilateral swollen, cool, dusky fingers and hands. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical findings, on re-admission.
Figure 2. Physical findings, on re-admission.
diagnosis:
Endocarditis with septic emboli caused by Bartonella infection.

Results of serological studies from the previous admission returned and were positive fo r Bartonella henselae IgG antibodies at greater than 1:1024 dilution and IgM antiboidies at 1:256 dilution. Coxiella burnetii IgG titers were also positive (phase I at 1:32 dilution and phase II at 1:128 dilution), which were thought to be false positive due to cross-reaction with Bartonella species antigens. Repeat TEE revealed possibly smaller or unchanged non-mobile small thickening or vegetation on the aortic valve.

A diagnosis of Bartonella endocarditis was made and treatment with gentamicin and doxycycline begun; additional treatment included sildenafil, nifedipine and anticoagulation therapy with intravenous heparin for suspected vasospasm or thromboemboli.
Arterial doppler non-invasive studies were negative. CT angiography of the arms demonstrated patent arteries in the subclavian to digital arch regions. There was persistent cyanosis of all fingers that progressed to dry gangrene. His hospital course was further complicated by sudden onset of an expressive aphasia, with no other focal sensory and motor deficits identified on neurology examination. CT of the head, performed emergently, showed multiple hypo-attenuating foci in the bilateral brain parenchyma concerning for acute cerebrovascular accident (CVA), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain confirmed acute multifocal infarctions (Figure 3). A repeat TEE was unchanged from the previous study.
Pathological examination of a skin biopsy from a finger revealed a vasculopathy with microemboli occluding the small vessels. A 2-week course of gentamicin was administered, and the patient was discharged from hospital to complete a course of oral doxycycline of 3-to-6 months' duration.
The patient was evaluated in outpatient follow-up visits after hospital discharge. His speech improved, and vision in the left eye remained poor, but did not worsen. The digital gangrene increased, and progressed to autoamputation (Figures 4 and 5).
Figure 3. MRI scan of the brain.
Figure 4. Physical findings, on follow-up.
Figure 5. Physical findings, on follow-up.

Bartonella species are gram-negative fastidious intracellular bacilli, responsible for about 3% of culture negative endocarditis [Raoult et al., 2003]. HACEK organisms have been traditionally thought to be the most common agents of culture-negative endocarditis. However, studies have found that HACEK organisms can be easily isolated with current blood-culture systems when incubated for at least five days [Petti et al., 2006; Baron et al., 2005]. The most common causative agents of culture-negative infective endocarditis are fastidious organisms, zoonotic agents and fungi.
There are nearly 40 different Bartonella species with 6 species related to infective endocarditis in humans: B. quintana, B. henselae, B. elizabethae, B. vinsonii, B. koehlerae, and B. alsatica. More than 95 percent of the cases have involved either B. quintana or B. henselae. Data suggest that homelessness, alcoholism, and infestation with body lice are associated with B. quintana endocarditis whereas contact with cats and previous valvular disease serve as the major risk factors for B. henselae endocarditis [Raoult et al., 1996]. Our patient did not have any of those typical risk factors.
Approximately 60 percent of patients with Bartonella endocarditis have involvement of the aortic valve. Most cases involve native valves and are mostly seen in adult males. Clinical manifestations are similar to other patients with subacute bacterial endocarditis, including a wide variety of rheumatologic symptoms. There have been reports of Bartonella vasculitis in the literature [Balakrishnan et al., 2016; Chaudhry et al., 2015]..
Because of the difficulty identifying the organism in pathological specimens or growing it in culture, the diagnosis of B. henselae infection is more commonly made by serologic testing by indirect immunofluorescence and/or by identification of B. henselae nucleic acid by polymerase chain reaction analysis or immunohistochemical analysis of valvular biopsy specimens [Fournier et al., 2002; Ruimy et al., 1994]. In an international study, all but one patient with Bartonella endocarditis had titers ≥1:1600 using a microimmunofluorescence test with a positive predictive value of 0.88 [Raoult et al., 1996]. Studies have shown an immunogenic protein, dihydrolipoamide succinyltransferase protein (SucB) causing cross-reactivity between Bartonella species and Brucella melitensis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Franscisella tularensis, Coxiella burnetii and Rickettsia typhi resulting in false positive immunologic diagnostic tests [Litwin et al., 2004]. In this case, the seropositivity for Coxiella was thought to be false positive due to cross-reaction with Bartonella antigens. It is unlikely that our patient has Coxiella endocarditis based on the pattern of Coxiella serologies. In Coxiella endocarditis, phase I IgG antibodies should be significantly elevated (> 1:800 dilution) and typically higher than phase II IgG antibodies.
There are insufficient data to make any definitive recommendations for treating Bartonella endocarditis. In a retrospective study that included 101 cases of Bartonella endocarditis, it was shown that effective antibiotic therapy should include an aminoglycoside prescribed for a minimum of 2 weeks. The guidelines recommend treating with a regimen consisting of doxycycline for a minimum of six weeks plus 14 days course of gentamicin [Rolain et al., 2004]. Most expert recommend extending doxycycline therapy orally for three to six months.
This case report describes a very unusual presentation of native valve Bartonella endocarditis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of Bartonella endocardits associated with retinal artery occlusion, profound bilateral digital gangrene and acute multifocal cerebral infarctions in a previously healthy person without significant associated risk factors.

title: 2016 November-December Featured Case and 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentat
history:
2016 November-December Featured Case and 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A woman in her thirties developed left hand swelling and fevers. On the fourth day of symptoms, she presented to an emergency department for evaluation.
The patient had previously been well until approximately 1 week earlier when she pricked an unspecified finger on a ‘goathead’ plant (Tribulus terrestris) while weeding in her garden. Two days later she noticed pain and swelling in the 4th finger of her left hand, which spread to involve the left hand over the next 4 days. On the fourth day, a fever occurred, to a maximum temperature of 38.6ºC (101.5ºF), and she sought medical attention.

The patient was born and raised in the Southwestern United States, and was of Native American ancestry. She lived in a rural area, had a large garden and owned pet dogs. She reported no other animal exposures. She did not smoke tobacco, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

She was married and monogamous.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared mildly ill but not toxic. The temperature was 38.4ºC (101.1ºF), blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 94% while breathing room air. The left hand was erythematous and swollen, with an ulcer on the tip of the fourth finger (Figure 1) and no streaking. There were 1-2 centimeter lymph nodes, which were firm and mildly tender, in the left supratrochlear and axillary regions. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.
Figure 1. Physical finding of left hand.

The white cell count was 8000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 4000-10,000), with 80% neutrophils. The hemoglobin was 17 g/dL (reference range 12-16 g/dL in women) and the level of platelets was 123,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-500,000). The serum level of glucose was 285 mg/dL (reference range 80-100), bilirubin 2 mg/dL (reference range 0.3-1.1), albumin 2.0 g/dL (reference range 3.1-4.3) and aspartate aminotranferase 157 U/L (reference range 10-40); the level of alanine transaminase was normal.
Blood cultures were obtained.

Cefazolin (1 gram every 8 hrs) was administered intravenously. The erythema and swelling improved slightly but fevers persisted. Intravenous cefazolin was stopped, and oral cephalexin 500 mg by mouth every 8 hrs given. Despite these measures, she had persistent fevers.
Two days after admission, blood culture bottles were noted to have positive growth. Gram stain of a blood culture is shown (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Gram stain from blood culture.
diagnosis:
Ulceroglandular tularemia complicated by bacteremia and sepsis, caused by Francisella tularensis.

Gram stains from both blood culture bottles were initially reported to be negative. Review of a gram stain showed tiny, faintly staining gram-negative coccobacilli (Figure 2). A sample from the positive blood cultures was plated and, after 48 hours, grew pin-point colonies on blood and chocolate agar, with no growth on MacConkey agar. The specimen was sent to the state laboratory where it was identified as Francisella tularensis, first by direct fluorescent antigen (DFA) testing and then confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Oral ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) was begun. Within 24 hours, she was afebrile and within 72 hours the cellulitis of her hand resolved completely. She was discharged on oral ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily), with instructions to complete a 10-day course. At one month follow-up, her symptoms had completely resolved and she had no further complications from the infection.

Francisella tularensis is a gram negative coccobacilli intracellular pathogen, known for its association with rabbits and as a potential agent of bioterrorism [Carvalho et al., 2014]. The disease is spread through rodents by ticks or deer flies, and to humans when they come in contact with either infected rodents or infected ticks [Carvalho et al., 2014]. Tularemia has six clinical presentations: ulceroglandular, glandular, oculoglandular, oropharyngeal, typhoidal and pneumonic tularemia [Hepburn and Simpson, 2008]. All presentations typically involve fever and regional lymphadenopathy at the point of entry [CDC website, Tularemia, Signs and Symptoms; https://www.cdc.gov/tularemia/signssymptoms/index.html, Accessed:5.7.2016)].
Ulceroglandular disease is the most common clinical presentation of tularemia. This usually occurs after a direct bite by a tick or deer fly, or after handling an infected animal [CDC website, Tularemia, Signs and Symptoms; https://www.cdc.gov/tularemia/signssymptoms/index.html, Accessed: 5.7.2016)]. An ulcer appears at the site of bacterial entry and there is swelling of the regional lymph nodes; isolation of the bacteria from the blood stream is rare [CDC website Tularemia, Clinicians;, https://www.cdc.gov/tularemia/clinicians/index.html Accessed: 5.7.2016)]. Upon repeat questioning about animal exposures, the patient noted that her husband had completed a hunting trip 2 days prior to her injury while gardening, after which she skinned about 50 rabbits. This was thought to be the likely the source of her infection.

title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his fifties presented with
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his fifties presented with a 3-week history of skin lesions that were located on the left forearm and both legs.
Three months before this presentation, the patient was diagnosed with HIV infection after evaluation for oral candidiasis and weight loss. The CD4 T-cell count was 90 cells per microliter and the level of HIV RNA was 573,998 copies per milliliter. Treatment was begun with tenofovir-emtricitabine-efavirenz, as well as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for prophylaxis.
Two months after the initiation of antiretroviral therapy, five lesions appeared on his left arm and his legs. The lesions were initially macular and then developed into hyperpigmented desquamative plaques (approximately 50 mm by 40mm each in size), and were hyperesthesic. The level of CD4 T-cells was 98 per microliter and the level of HIV RNA was 118 copies per milliliter.

HIV infection had been diagnosed three months earlier, as above. At that time, he was diagnosed with HIV-associated peripheral neuropathy.

He had had multiple female partners in the past, and had no known history of other sexually transmitted diseases. He had smoked cigarettes for many years and had stopped alcohol and cocaine use 10 years earlier. He had no animal exposures.

He lived near the coast in Mexico and traveled often to Mexico City.

Medications were tenofovir-emtricitabine-efavirenz daily and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole every other day, as well as amitriptyline 50 mg daily for peripheral neuropathy.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg, pulse 80 beats per minute, temperature 97.7ºF (36.5ºC) and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Pupils were equal, round and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements were intact. The oropharynx was moist, and there was no evidence of thrush. The skin was warm and dry, with erythematous-violaceous desquamative plaques (50 by 40 mm) that were hyperesthesic, on the external left elbow and on both knees and legs (Figures 1 through 5). There was no lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Lesion on the left elbow.
Figure 2. Lesion on the left knee.
Figure 3. Lesion on the left leg.
Figure 4. Lesion on the right knee.
Figure 5. Lesion on the right leg.

The level of hemoglobin was 11.8 grams per deciliter (reference range: 14.5 to 17.7), and red cells were normocytic and normochromic; other routine laboratory test results were normal. VDRL testing was negative, as was testing for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibodies. The HIV RNA level was 2.0 log10 copies per milliliter and the CD4 T-cell count was 98 cells per microliter.
A tuberculosis skin test was negative (0 mm induration) and the chest radiograph was normal. A nerve conduction study reported moderate axonal sensory-motor polyneuropathy with a length dependent pattern.
diagnosis:
Borderline leprosy (type 1 reversal reaction) caused by Mycobacterium leprae presenting as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in a patient with HIV-infection.

A punch skin biopsy was performed. The routine and the mycobacterial cultures of the specimen yielded no growth. The histopathological examination of the tissue with hematolylin and eosin staining revealed a multifocal granulomatous infiltrate with epithelioid histiocytes and giant multinucleated cells in the superficial, mid and deep dermis associated with perineural distribution (Figures 6 through 8). Fite-Faraco and Ziehl-Neelsen stains were positive (Figures 9 and 10). The S-100 immunohistochemical stain was also positive identifying Schwann cells (Figure 11). The slit skin direct smear examination from the earlobes was positive with at least 1 acid-fast bacillus in 10 microscopic fields (Bacterial Index: 2+; Figure 12).
Figure 6. Skin biopsy, hematoxylin and eosin stain, with multifocal granulomatous infiltrate (4x).
Figure 7. Skin biopsy with H and E stain showing epithelioid histiocytes, giant multinucleated cells and interstitial edema (40x).
Figure 8. Skin biopsy with H and E stain showing epithelioid histiocytes, giant multinucleated cells and interstitial edema (40x, oil).
Figure 9. Skin biopsy with Ziehl - Neelsen stain and acid-fast bacilli.
Figure 10. Skin biopsy with Fite-Faraco stain showing acid-fast bacilli.
Figure 11. Positive Immunohistochemical staining for S100 protein.
Figure 12. Slit skin direct smears of earlobes, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, with at least 1 bacillus in 10 microscopic fields (Bacterial Index: 2+)

Based on the clinical presentation and the histological findings, a diagnosis of borderline leprosy (type 1 reversal reaction) as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome was made. Treatment was administered according to the WHO recommendations for Borderline Leprosy: dapsone 100mg/day, clofazimine 50mg/day, rifampin 600mg 1/month and clofazimine 300mg 1/month.

Leprosy or Hansen disease is a chronic infectious disease associated with skin, eye and peripheral nerves damage. The etiological agent Mycobacterium leprae is a gram positive and acid-fast rod-shaped organism that is 1 to 8 μm long and unable to grow in vitro [Reibel et al., 2015].
The clinical spectrum of leprosy depends on the specific host immunity and can be classified as:
-Tuberculoid Leprosy: Vigorous cell-mediated immune response to infection
-Lepromatous Leprosy: Ineffective cell-mediated immune response but high humoral response.
-Borderline Leprosy: Some cell-mediated immune response but often immunologically unstable [Scollard et al., 2006]
All types of leprosy have been reported in patients with HIV infection, although the exact incidence has never been properly estimated [Talhari et al., 2010]. The cutaneous manifestations of leprosy in HIV patients are not different from those in conventional leprosy [Massone et al., 2011]. The granulomatous response in both HIV-negative and HIV-positive leprosy patients is morphologically identical. Skin biopsies of patients with leprosy show well-formed granulomas that contained significant CD4 lymphocytes independent of the low peripheral blood CD4 cells count.
After the introduction of antiretroviral therapy, leprosy has presented as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), typically as paucibacillary leprosy with type 1 reaction.
Patients with leprosy and HIV can present with skin lesions and nerve damage, but the diagnosis of leprosy may be challenging in patients with AIDS because of the variety of presentations such as those seen with unmasking or paradoxical IRIS [Talhari et al., 2010]. Tuberculoid leprosy (borderline tuberculoid) is the clinical form observed most often but patients may present with atypical presentations, such as nodules or hyperkeratotic ulcerated lesions.
Leprosy nerve damage may be confounded by neuropathy associated with HIV or may even act synergistically [Ustianowski et al., 2006].
Dermatological signs are the clinical indicators of leprosy in 90% of patients; 10% present with neurological signs only [Lastoria and Abreu, 2014]. Skin biopsy remains the “gold standard” for making the diagnosis, providing information such as the histological patterns of the host response, involvement of cutaneous nerves and, using the Fite-Faraco and Ziehl Neelsen stains, identification of acid-fast bacilli within nerves.
Another method to diagnose leprosy is polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. PCR sensitivity is close to 100% in patients with a positive bacteriological index, but it is significantly lower in patients with a negative bacteriological index (when bacilli are not observed by the microscopist). On the other hand, serologic testing using phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL1) antigen of Mycobacterium leprae is not recommended because of its low sensitivity [Lastoria and Abreu, 2014].
M. leprae in HIV patients responds to multi-drug treatment. Corticosteroid therapy can be used in cases of IRIS to prevent neural damage. The recommended treatment duration for multibacillary leprosy according to the WHO guidelines is 12 months [WHO, retrieved 2016].

title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his sixties, with a history
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his sixties, with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation, presented with a two-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He also reported mild substernal chest pain and a left-sided facial droop.

He had hypertension and atrial fibrillation.

He lived alone in the U.S. Northeast and had recently retired from a position working outside. He drank six to eight beers weekly, never smoked and did not use drugs. He had not been sexually active for years and had never had an HIV test. He had no exposure to tuberculosis. He had no significant family history, exposures to animals or recent travel. He bought his food and beverages from a grocery store.

He had no allergies.

His medications were digoxin, metoprolol, verapamil, hydrochlorothiazide, warfarin, and lisinopril.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 138/88 mm Hg, pulse 89 beats per minute, temperature 98.7ºF (37.1ºC), and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. He was alert and oriented to self, place and time. He had facial droop, including the forehead and mouth, on the left side. There was no sensory deficit. The gag reflex was present. Power, tone and coordination of extremities, and the remainder of the examination, were normal.

Results of routine blood tests were normal. A chest radiograph revealed mild bibasilar atelectasis. Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed no abnormality.

The patient was admitted to the hospital. A presumptive diagnosis of Bell’s palsy was made and corticosteroids were administered.
On the second hospital day, acute confusion with visual hallucinations developed that was attributed to the steroids. Within the next 24 hours, he became unresponsive and apneic, requiring intubation and transfer to the intensive care unit. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a pH 7.20 (reference range 7.35-7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 81 mm Hg (reference range 35-45), partial pressure of oxygen 76 mm Hg (reference range 80-100), bicarbonate of 30 mEq/L (reference range 22-26). The temperature rose to 105ºF (40.6ºC), hypotension occurred and obtundation persisted. The neurological examination revealed rightward gaze deviation, no gag reflex, and a left facial palsy.
Repeat CT of the head and CT-angiogram of head and neck showed no abnormality.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain without contrast (Figure 1) revealed a 4 mm focal abnormality in the left medulla with a small amount of surrounding hemorrhage and edema. Brain MRI imaging with gadolinium (Figure 2) and post-contrast (Figure 3) were obtained.
Figure 1. Axial T2 MRI scan.
Figure 2. Sagittal T1 MRI scan, VIBE sequence, with reconstruction.
Figure 3. A post-contrast coronal T2 MRI FLAIR image.
diagnosis:
Rhombencephalitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes.

The axial T2 MRI images shown in Figure 1 revealed a 4.27 mm focus of susceptibility centered in the left posterior medulla, which had extensive surrounding T2 prolongation. There was local swelling of the brainstem, but no significant mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Figure 2, a sagittal T1 MRI VIBE sequence with reconstruction, showed the multifocal enhancement in the brainstem. Figure 4, a post-contrast coronal T2 MRI FLAIR image, demonstrated leptomeningeal enhancement scattered over the surface of the frontal lobes. The MRI findings were thought to be concerning for an infectious or metastatic process.
The white cell count was 12,200 cells per cubic millimeter with 90.9% neutrophils, 4.3% monocytes and 4.0% lymphocytes.
A lumbar puncture (LP) was performed and revealed an elevated opening pressure at 29 cm of water. Analysis of the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) revealed a white cell count of 83 per cubic millimeter, with 47% segmented neutrophils, 40% lymphocytes, and 12% monocytes; the level of protein was 250 mg/dl and glucose was 20 mg/dl.
One set of blood cultures and culture of the CSF were positive for gram positive rods, identified as Listeria monocytogenes.
Figure 4. MRI (Figure 3, with arrows added) showing leptomeningeal enhancement in the frontal lobes.

Broad spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin) were administered empirically for suspected meningitis. Gentamicin was added to ampicillin for synergy against possible Listeria monocytogenes when one set of blood cultures revealed gram positive rods. After culture of the CSF confirmed Listeria monocytogenes, the antibiotics were changed to ampicillin and gentamicin only.
Despite therapy, the patient had persistent, severe hypercapneic respiratory failure associated with no gag reflex, a weak cough, and an inability to clear secretions. Despite multiple bronchoscopies, he did not improve and ultimately died.

Central nervous system (CNS) infections with Listeria typically occur in the elderly, those with immunosuppression, neonates and pregnant women, and may rarely impact normal hosts. Meningoencephalitis is the most common CNS manifestation of infection and can range from mild disease with fever and confusion to life threatening coma. Many patients do not have signs of meningeal irritation. Brain abscess and rhombencephalitis (brainstem encephalitis) are less common CNS manifestations. When affecting the brainstem, the pons and medulla are involved 64% of the time [Armstrong and Fung, 1993]. Listeria rhombencephalitis (LRE) may cause febrile illness in previously well adults with abrupt onset of asymmetric cranial nerve palsies and encephalopathy, with rapid progression to a fatal outcome, first described in the literature in 1957 [Eck, 1957]. LRE follows a biphasic course and is associated with a high rate of respiratory failure (41%), mortality (51%) and neurological sequelae (61%) [Armstrong and Fung, 1993; Pospescu et al, 2004]. Prognosis varies depending on the specific brain lesion, and the recovery is very unpredictable [Stankiewics and Pazevic, 1989].
This case of LRE included central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome as a consequence of autonomic respiratory failure, also known as Ondine’s curse, associated with sudden apnea and persistent severe hypercapneic respiratory failure.
Ondine’s curse (OC) is an eponym used to describe a disease entity that prevents autonomic respiration while a person is sleeping. It can be congenital or acquired. The acquired central hypoventilation syndrome is a result of tumorous, traumatic, ischemic, or inflammatory-induced lesions in the brainstem, which directly diminish the ability of the brainstem to maintain respiratory drive during sleep resulting in central sleep apnea [Eckert et al., 2007; Muzumdar and Arens, 2008].
The pathophysiologic explanation of acquired OC is due to the lesion affecting the nuclei responsible for the control of the autonomic respiratory center in the medulla [Giangaspero et al., 1988] adjacent to nuclei of the lower cranial nerves (VIII, IX and X) [Frith et al., 1987]. When the lesion extends to the cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem it results in cranial nerve palsies. The most commonly affected cranial nerve (CN) deficits are CN VI and VII, which correspond to the deficit seen in our patient, who had a CN VII palsy on admission. Our patient had an absent gag reflex (CN IX and X). Patients with OC may also develop nystagmus, dysphagia and dysarthria [Stankiewics and Pazevic, 1989].
The evaluation of patients with suspected LRE requires a thorough history and neurological exam. The differential diagnosis of rhombencephalitis (RE) includes a range of infectious and noninfectious diseases, including but not limited to multiple sclerosis, Bechet’s disease, paraneoplastic syndromes, infarction, Epstein–Barr virus, and tuberculosis. Features that increase suspicion for Listeria infection causing RE include cranial nerve palsies and diminished level of consciousness [Moragas et al., 2011]. Work-up for suspected LRE includes blood cultures, lumbar puncture and MRI of the brain. In the setting of fever and high clinical suspicion for meningitis, empiric treatment with broad spectrum antibiotics including ampicillin should be administered. Diagnosis is based upon cerebrospinal fluid and blood cultures growing Listeria monocytogenes, which should be treated with ampicillin and gentamicin. The diagnostic imaging of choice is brain MRI, as CT is often normal early in the disease process, as it was in this case. MRI with gadolinium was crucial for localizing the brainstem lesion in our patient and enabling the recognition of central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome as the cause of our patient’s sudden respiratory failure and subsequent difficulties with weaning from the ventilator.
One of the most critical complications of Listeria rhombencephalitis is respiratory failure, which occurs at a high rate and has grave consequences as our case highlights. Management strategies in cases of OC include noninvasive ventilation via face mask or nasal mask if less than 12 hours of respiratory support is needed, negative pressure ventilators, and diaphragmatic pacing [Muzumdar and Arens, 2008; Naughton, 2006]. Diaphragmatic pacing involves implanting a pacing electrode around the phrenic nerve and has a success rate of 50-70% in case series [Schestatsky and Fernandes, 2004; McNicholas, 1997]. Phrenic pacing has advantages compared with mechanical ventilation as it provides more natural breathing dynamics, reduces the occurrence of respiratory infection and other complications associated with long-term ventilation and improves quality of life [Velazco et al., 2012]. Pharmacological treatments have been used in OC to activate the remaining respiratory nuclei through the induction of metabolic acidosis. Trazodone, acetazolamide, medroxyprogesterone, protyptilin, clomipramine, tiroxine and caffeine have been used in cases with varying success [Schestatsky and Fernandes, 2004].
Our patient required mechanical ventilation support throughout to manage central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome. He failed extubation twice including a trial of extubation to intelligent volume assured pressure support (iVAPS) prior to proceeding with tracheostomy placement. In our case, the patient was not controlled on iVAPS most likely due to his hemodynamic instability and increased secretions requiring constant suctioning.
Our case highlights the importance of recognizing key clinical features of Listeria rhombencephalitis in a previously healthy patient such as cranial nerve palsies and encephalopathy, to initiate timely antimicrobial treatment, thereby reducing the risk for progression of the brainstem infection and Ondine’s curse. MRI is crucial in the identification of characteristic brainstem lesions. Institution of artificial ventilation in the setting of central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome is vital in the management of accompanying respiratory failure.

title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his twenties developed a di
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his twenties developed a diffuse rash shortly after a two-week trip to Madagascar.
One week before the onset of the rash, when he was on a beach on the southern coast in Madagascar, he developed a frontal headache (rated 4 out of 10, on a scale of 0 to 10 where 10 is the most severe) that increased with movement. At that time, he also noticed a lesion on his left upper arm that appeared to be an insect bite. Two days later, chills and sore throat occurred, and the skin lesion developed a scab and became progressively darker. Six days after the onset of the headache, a rash developed on his arms, chest, legs, and face.
The next day, he took ibuprofen for his symptoms, and went to the hospital where he was admitted. He reported no cough, photophobia, abdominal pain, sweating or dysuria.

The patient reported having had chickenpox when he was child.

He lived in the Northeastern United States and worked in an office. He was sexually active, without use of barrier protection, with two female partners in the previous six months. He drank alcohol socially and did not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. His sibling and friends did not have symptoms.

He took ibuprofen (600 mg orally). He had not taken malaria prophylaxis while traveling.
exam_studies:
He was well nourished and not in distress. The blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature 98.6°F (37°C), and respirations 16 per minute. There were scattered vesiculopapular lesions over the trunk, upper and lower extremities, which spared the palms and soles. The lesions were surrounded by erythema that blanched to palpation. There was an eschar (6 mm in diameter) on his left arm that was non-tender and had an erythematous rim (Figure 1). A mobile non-tender lymph node (1 cm diameter) was palpable in the left axilla. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Figure 1. Skin rash.

The white cell count was 5900 per cubic millimeter (reference range 150,000-450,000), with 48% neutrophils, 33.8% lymphocytes, 17.2% monocytes, and 0.4% eosinophils. The blood level of total bilirubin was 1.6 mg/dL (reference range 0.3-1.2) and direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL (reference range 0.05-0.1). The hematocrit, platelet count, and blood levels of electrolytes, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases were normal. There were no intraerythrocytic or extra-erythrocytic parasites seen on peripheral smear. Cultures of the blood and urine were obtained.
A chest radiograph (Figure 2) was normal.
Figure 2. Chest radiograph.
diagnosis:
Rickettsialpox caused by Rickettsia akari.

The eschar lesion on the left arm was biopsied, and pathological examination of the specimen with hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining showed dense perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates (Figures 3 through 5). Figure 3 (low power field of the skin biopsy) revealed a superficial and deep angiocentric adnexotropic lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with attendant ulceration. Figure 4 (higher power magnification) showed the dominant mononuclear cell nature of the infiltrate and its apposition to vessels and nerves. Figure 5 revealed frank vasculitic changes characterized by an angiocentric lymphohistiocytic infiltrate surrounding and permeating vessels with evidence of vascular injury characterized by fibrin deposition and red cell extravasation. Figure 6 demonstrated concomitant interface dermatitis with lymphocyte tagging along the dermal-epidermal junction and serpentine-like macrophages. These findings were thought to be suggestive of Rickettsialpox.
The skin biopsy specimen was sent to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention where the molecular and immunohistochemical testing confirmed the presence of Rickettsia akari.
Serologic testing for Rocky Mountain spotted fever revealed negative IgG (<1:64) but positive IgM (>1:64). Testing for HIV nucleic acid was undetectable (<20 copies/mL). Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was non-reactive. Varicella zoster serology was consistent with remote immunity with negative IgM and positive IgG. Two sets of blood cultures and a urine culture were negative.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy (H and E stain, low power).
Figure 4. Skin biopsy (H and E stain).
Figure 5. Skin biopsy (H and E stain).
Figure 6. Skin biopsy (H and E stain).

Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily, orally) and valacyclovir (1 g every 8 hours) were administered pending test results. Physical findings after two days of therapy (Figure 7) are shown; the erythema surrounding the left arm eschar had improved.
Valacyclovir was stopped after the varicella zoster virus direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test came back negative. Varicella zoster virus culture was also negative.
The patient completed a 1-week course of doxycycline twice daily. Follow-up 1 month later revealed complete resolution of the skin rash with a hypo-pigmented scar at the eschar site.
Figure 7. Physical findings after two days of therapy.

Rickettsialpox is caused by Rickettsia akari, which is transmitted by the bite of the house-mouse mite Liponyssoides sanguineus [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947; Huebner, Jellison and Pomerantz., 1946]. The disease was named rickettsialpox because of its resemblance to chickenpox [Huebner, Stampls and Armstrong, 1946]. It occurs primarily in urban areas, where the density of mites, mice, and humans is high [Koss et al., 2003]. Huebner and his collaborators first isolated Rickettsia akari from a patient, mites, and a naturally infected house mouse in Queens, New York in 1946 [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947; Huebner, Jellison and Pomerantz., 1946].
Rickettsialpox is almost certainly under-recognized and under-reported [Koss et al., 2003]. The bioterrorism attacks of October 2001 may have led to increased awareness and detection of this disease [Koss et al., 2003]. Prior to that time, these clinical syndromes may have been misdiagnosed, or perhaps the infected persons did not seek medical attention. Since the 1960s, only single case reports and small case series have been published, and most of these cases have occurred in New York City [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947; Huebner, Jellison and Pomerantz., 1946; Koss et al., 2003; Kass et al., 1994], but the disease has also been reported in other large cities in the eastern United States [Koss et al., 2003; Kass et al., 1994] as well as in Europe, South Africa and Latin America [Parola et al., 2013]. The presence of an eschar is a key clinical feature of rickettsialpox [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947]. This develops at the location of a mite bite, followed by the onset of systemic symptoms and a more generalized papulovesicular rash [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947; Huebner, Jellison and Pomerantz., 1946].
The most common disease that mimics rickettsialpox is chickenpox [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946]. However, rickettsialpox characteristically has an eschar whereas chickenpox does not. In addition, in rickettsialpox, the rash consists of papulovesicles whereas in chickenpox the rash is vesicular and appears in crops [Heininger et al., 2006]. Finally, chickenpox usually presents with many more skin lesions than rickettsialpox.
Rickettsialpox has also been confused with cutaneous anthrax. This underscores the importance of clinicians' ability to promptly recognize and definitively diagnose rickettsialpox [Koss et al., 2003]. Patients with cutaneous anthrax characteristically have local edema out of proportion to the size of the lesions and gram stain of these lesions should reveal nonsporulating gram-positive rods [CDC 2001]. Rickettsialpox can also be confused with other rickettsial diseases, including Mediterranean spotted fever caused by Rickettsia conorii [Raoult et al., 1986], African tick bite fever [Owen et al., 2006], Rickettsia parkeri infection [Parola et al., 2013], and scrub typhus [Paddock et al., 2006]. All of these infections may be associated with eschars, but only African tick bite fever has rash that is typically or occasionally vesicular [Owen et al., 2006; Parola et al., 2013]. Rickettsia africae, the agent of African tick bite fever, is endemic in Africa - including Madagascar where our patient had recently travelled [Parola et al., 2013] - which made the diagnosis of our patient challenging.
The diagnosis of rickettsialpox is mainly a clinical one based on characteristic symptoms and signs [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946; Huebner et al., 1947; Huebner, Jellison and Pomerantz., 1946; Koss et al., 2003]. It can be established retrospectively by documenting a fourfold rise in convalescent titers of complement fixation or indirect fluorescent antibodies using spotted fever group antigens [Koss et al., 2003]. Direct immunofluorescence can be used to identify rickettsial organisms in paraffin-embedded biopsy tissue from patients with rickettsialpox [Kass et al., 1994]. A definitive diagnosis can be made by isolation of Rickettsia akari from skin eschars [Paddock et al., 2006], or by a real-time multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) that can specifically identify Rickettsia akari in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded skin biopsy specimens [Denison et al., 2014], as in our case. Such tests are available through most state health departments and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [Koss et al., 2003].
Most patients with rickettsialpox have a mild illness and full recovery can be expected even without treatment [Kass et al., 1994]. The treatment of choice for rickettsialpox is doxycycline (100 mg orally every 12 hours) until the patient has been afebrile and clinically well for 48 to 72 hours [Kass et al., 1994].
In conclusion, rickettsialpox should be considered as a differential diagnosis in the setting of an eschar and a papulovesicular rash. Clinicians should be familiar with the clinical presentation and diagnostic features of rickettsialpox because it may be confused with more serious diseases, such as cutaneous anthrax [Koss et al., 2003] or chickenpox [Huebner, Stamps and Armstrong, 1946]. It is a self-limited disease; however, antibiotics hasten defervescence and provide relief of other systemic symptoms.

title: 2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his thirties was admitted w
history:
2016 IDWeek Fellows' Day Case Presentation: A man in his thirties was admitted with a painful mass in the right lower abdominal quadrant, just above the inguinal ligament, of two days' duration. A diagnosis of necrotizing lymphadenitis was made, and the lesion was debrided emergently in the operating room. An infectious disease consultation was requested for antibiotic recommendations.
On examination, the patient was found to have an incidental mass in right axilla and pruritic rash involving his chest, back and extremities. The rash had reportedly worsened during the previous nine months. He reported suffering from this condition intermittently since age 15. When previously treated with antimycotic agents and topical steroids, the skin lesions would improve but the rash relapsed after cessation of treatment. He had never been given a specific diagnosis.

The patient had had asthma during childhood and had had one episode of bronchitis/pneumonia between 10 months and 18 months of age. He reported retention of primary dentition until age fifteen, recurrent skin rashes and onycholysis of nails. A left groin abscess had been drained a few years earlier, without complication.

He lived in Mississippi and worked in construction. He did not use intravenous drugs or tobacco, and had no history of alcohol abuse. He was of Irish and French Creole (Native-American and French) ancestry.

There was no history of consanguinity or reported cancers. His mother had had similar recurrent rashes on her feet and anterior thighs since childhood, which also improved with antifungal treatment. His pre-teen son had a similar recurrent pruritic rash and reported retention of primary dentition.

He was on no medications.
exam_studies:
On examination, there was a markedly raised papillomaform rash on the upper chest, trunk, and proximal upper extremities and right axilla, which was erythematous and tender with areas of lichenification, scaling and weeping.The axillary mass was exophytic, erythematous and friable (Figures 1 and 2). He also had involvement of the back with thick scaling and crusting and a few scaly papules (one-centimeter in diameter) scattered over both legs, onycholysis of all nails of the left hand and left great toe, a well-healed scar in the left groin from the previous incision and drainage, and evidence of a surgical debridement procedure in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.
Figure 1. Physical findings.
Figure 2. Physical findings.

The white blood cell count was 29,000 per microliter on admission, with 84% granulocytes, 11% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, and 3% band forms. Toxic granulations were present. Testing for HIV and a viral hepatitis panel were negative. Results of other routine laboratory were normal.

A skin biopsy was performed and cultures obtained.
diagnosis:
Chronic and recurrent Trichophyton rubrum deep invasive dermatophytosis secondary to compound heterozygous CARD9 deficiency.

The hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stains of punch biopsies from the chest, right axilla and left thigh showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the epidermis with superficial and deep chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Fungal hyphae and round spore-like elements were present within the stratum corneum, epidermis and were noted to be invading the full thickness of the dermis (Figures 3 and 4). The Gomori methanamine silver (GMS) stain revealed numerous pleomorphic fungal hyphae (Figures 5 and 6).
The specimens were inoculated onto Sabouraud’s dextrose agar (SDA) and incubated. After approximately 14 days, ivory white colonies with a cottony surface were observed. Inspection of the reverse side of the culture plate showed that the colonies produced a deep red pigment characteristic of Trichophyton rubrum.
Confirmation of this identification was performed by microscopic examination of the stained preparation as follows:
-Dermatophytic growth was examined weekly via touch prep and stained with Lacotphenol Cotton Blue
- Isolates were observed with a light microscope under low-power (10 x) and high-power (40 x) lens.
-Fungal identification was based on features of hyphae organization. Microscopy revealed small tear or drop-shaped microconidia arranged along the sides of narrow septate hyphae. These findings are characteristic of Trichophyton rubrum.
The bacterial cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, Streptoccocus pyogenes and Prevotella species within 48 hours. Viral culture of the tissue was negative.
Genetic testing for immunodeficiencies were sent to identify potential mutations or variants of genes associated with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), hyper-immunoglobulin E syndrome (HIES), and caspase recruitment domain-containing protein (CARD9). This included the signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) deficiency, dedicator of cytokinesis 8 deficiency (DOCK8), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and caspase recruitment domain-containing protein (CARD 9) genetic testing. Results revealed compound heterozygous mutations in CARD9 through next generation sequencing. The remainder of testing was negative.

Figure 4. Figure 4: Detail of Figure 3, skin biopsy, H and E stain.
Figure 4: Detail of Figure 3, skin biopsy, H and E stain.

The patient received antibiotics for treatment of his necrotizing lymphadenitis and was begun on oral fluconazole. Improvement began within a few days of anti-fungal treatment. After three weeks of therapy the patient continued to show reduction in size of the skin lesions and decreased hypertrophy of the skin lesions (Figure 7). After 8 weeks of oral anti-fungal therapy, the fungating axillary mass had decreased to nearly 25% of its original size; at 12 months, the mass had completely resolved (Figure 8). Additional therapy was extended for a minimum of three months.

This case has clinical features suggestive of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) including chronically recurring skin lesions that may present as plaques and verrucous growths and onycholysis, all of which responded to anti-fungal therapy at least temporarily [Sandhu, 2016; Kirkpatrick, 1994]. Invasion of the skin by Candida species can cause scaling, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and dyskeratosis but usually remains in the superficial layers of skin and does not pass the stratum corneum. In patients with CMC, there is a gain of function STAT1 gene mutation which leads to deficient Th17 and Th1 immune response and increased invasive fungal infections [Van de Veerdonk et al., 2011]. CMC is an inherited disorder which can result in disseminated infection affecting internal organs and the central nervous system may occur. However, this patient’s histopathology and culture showed that the infection was due to a filamentous organism and cultures ultimately confirmed the diagnosis of invasive Trichophyton rubrum rather than Candida species.
Invasive Trichophyton species infections are rare but are well documented in the literature though most cases have been described in immunosuppressed patients [Blake et al., 1991; Lanternier et al., 2013; Tejasvi et al., 2005; Nir-Paz et al., 2003]. This patient had no clear evidence for generalized immunosuppressive disease. The patient’s complement levels were normal and vaccine titers for both pneumococcal disease and tetanus were determined to be protective. However, IgE levels were found to be elevated to over 3000 IU/ml. A primary immunodeficiency associated with recurrent fungal infections is hyper-immunoglobulin E syndrome (HIES) commonly referred to as Job’s syndrome
Elevated IgE levels can be found in a variety of conditions including HIES which is characterized by a dysfunction in immunity, recurrent dermatitis, cyst-forming pneumonia, elevated IgE levels, retained primary dentition, connective tissue and musculoskeletal abnormalities [Holland et al., 2007; Grimbacher et al., 2005]. The genetic abnormalities associated with this syndrome are autosomal recessive mutations in the DOCK8 gene and an autosomal dominant mutation in the STAT3 gene [Holland et al., 2007]. The infectious diseases triad associated with STAT3 deficiency consists of recurrent staphylococcal skin infections, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, though there are phenotypic variants [Grimbacher et al., 2005; Alves de Medeiros et al., 2016]. The DOCK8 mutation results in a milder form of disease.
The use of the clinical scoring system using both immunologic and non-immunologic features helps create an index of suspicion for HIES. This patient has clinical characteristics consistent with HIES including an elevated IgE level, retention of primary teeth, three to four skin abscesses in his lifetime, one other serious infection, the highest eosinophilia of greater than 800, and presence of onchomycosis. Dermatophyte infections are rare in HIES but there is at least one case described in the literature [Chandesris et al., 2012]. In that case the infection was not extensive as in our patient’s [Capucine Picard, person communication, March 29, 2016]. Our patient’s features give him a National Institutes of Health-HIES score [Grimbacher et al., 2005] of 34 which falls into the indeterminate category.
Elevated IgE levels can also be observed in immunocompetent patients with severe local dermatophyte infections in the absence of HIES [Grimbacher et al., 2005; Alves de Medeiros et al., 2016]. Cure of infection in these cases usually results in normalization of these findings. In our patient, the IgE levels decreased only slightly from 3715IU/ml to 2773 IU/ml after treatment even though his post-treatment biopsy revealed no evidence of recurrent infection in the tissue. This suggests that our patient has intrinsic hyper IgE levels rather than simply reactive hyper IgE elevations.
Recently descriptions of deep dermatophyte infections in patients of North African descent sometimes involving the brain and internal organs led to the discovery of a genetic mutation known as autosomal recessive caspase recruitment domain-containing protein (CARD9) deficiency [Lanternier et al., 2013]. CARD9 is an adaptor protein in the signaling pathway for fungal recognition and immunity [Lanternier et al., 2013]. Deficiency of CARD9 results in a selective defect in host defense resulting in impaired phagocytosis and allowing for invasive fungal infection. Other clinical manifestations of CARD9 include invasive infections of the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract but these are rare [Lanternier et al., 2015]. Our patient does not have North African ancestry. However, a few similar cases of deep dermatophytoses in patients not known to be immunosuppressed have been reported in the United States so it is possible that rare CARD9 mutations may occur in other populations [Chastain et al., 2001]. Preliminary genetic analyses of the CARD9 gene for this patient revealed that he is compound heterozygous for CARD9.
Features of Trichophyton species which may contribute to pathogenicity in these syndromes include the production of haemolysins, manan glycoprotein and dermatophyte derived inhibitor factors not yet identified which suppress human immune responses [Tejasvi et al., 2005; Nir-Paz et al., 2003; Ahmed, 1982; Jones et al., 1974]. Some of the extracellular enzymes such as keratinase allow for diffusion through the cornified layer of skin which allows for deeper infection. The release of chemotactic factors by dermatophytes produce irritation and an allergic contact dermatitis [Lanternier et al., 2013; Tejasvi et al., 2005]. This type of reaction manifests as an erythematous, pruritic rash that can be misclassified as eczema and will often initially respond to topical corticosteroids.
This patient responded very well to prolonged fluconazole treatment and likely will require lifelong suppressive anti-fungal therapy [Nir-Paz et al., 2003]. At the time of writing this paper, the patient continues to be evaluated by the National Institutes for Health.
In summary, this patient has a chronic and recurrent Trichophyton rubrum deep invasive dermatophytosis, which is well described among North African patients with homozygous recessive CARD9 deficiency. This patient is the first to be reported with T. rubrum invasive infection associated with compound heterozygous CARD9 mutations. Of considerable interest is the fact that our patient has some clinical characteristics of HIES including a history of retention of primary dentition and recurrent skin infections. Genetic testing for HIES associated gene variants is still pending.

title: A previously well man in his 40s presented to our Emergency Department (ED) with
history:
A previously well man in his 40s presented to our Emergency Department (ED) with 2 weeks of progressive left eye swelling and redness (Figure 1), which he presumed was due to an insect bite. He had difficulty opening his left eye. A week prior to the ED presentation, a general practitioner commenced him on oral flucloxacillin (similar to cloxacillin) 500mg qid for 7 days, however the swelling and redness continued to progress. The patient denied any pain, visual changes, fevers and nausea.
Figure 1. Left eye swelling at 2 weeks of illness

He was born and raised in Melbourne, Australia, has an office-job and spends time in the Mornington Peninsula (coastal Victoria). There was no significant animal exposure. He had no recent overseas travel. He does not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs and did not have any recent trauma.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. He was afebrile (36.1°C = 97°F), his blood pressure was 117/80 with a pulse rate of 75 beats and respiratory rate of 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. He had periorbital swelling around the left eye involving his upper and lower eyelid (Figure 1). This was erythematous, mildly tender and minimally fluctuant. There was no visible punctum or discharge. His visual acuity was 6/6 m bilaterally and his range of eye movements were normal. There was no pain with eye movements. The remainder of the cranial nerve examination and general examination was normal.

Full/Complete blood count and differential, renal and liver function tests were normal. The C-reactive protein was 9 mg/L (reference range 0-5 mg/L). Computer tomography (CT) scan of the orbits showed left periorbital soft tissue swelling and subcutaneous fat standing with a small curvilinear region of low attenuation measuring 4 x 27 x 16 mm suggestive of a subcutaneous collection (Figure 2). The post-septal tissues and globe were normal with no cortical destruction. Ophthalmic veins and cavernous sinuses were normal and paranasal sinuses were well-aerated.
Figure 2. Figure 2: CT of orbits. Red arrow indicating periorbital soft tissue swelling.
Figure 2: CT of orbits. Red arrow indicating periorbital soft tissue swelling.

Cefazolin 1g 8-hourly was administered intravenously. He had a washout of the left peri-orbital collection where a small abscess close to the lateral margin of the left eye was noted. Gram stain showed 1+ polymorphs, no bacteria were seen and routine bacterial cultures were negative. He was discharged the day after the operation on amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (875/125 mg) twice daily and topical chloramphenicol ointment for his left eye. Despite this, he presented again two weeks later with persistent erythema and swelling and a small ulcer over the lateral left eyebrow (Figure 3). He was taken to the operating room for further biopsy.
Figure 3. Figure 3: Persistent left eye swelling (post-initial surgery) at 4 weeks of illness. Red arrow indicating the ulcer.
Figure 3: Persistent left eye swelling (post-initial surgery) at 4 weeks of illness. Red arrow indicating the ulcer.
diagnosis:
Mycobacterium ulcerans infection causing left eye pre-septal cellulitis.

Mycobacterial stain of surgical biopsy of the lesion revealed acid fast bacilli (Figure 4) and Mycobacterium ulcerans PCR was positive.
Figure 4. Figure 4: Fite’s acid fast stain demonstrating acid fast bacilli (AFB). Red arrow indicating the AFB.
Figure 4: Fite’s acid fast stain demonstrating acid fast bacilli (AFB). Red arrow indicating the AFB.

The patient was treated with clarithromycin 500 mg twice-daily and rifampicin 300mg twice-daily, aiming for a duration of 4 months. At three months of follow-up the patient was significantly improved (Figure 5) with mild residual swelling around the left eye.
Figure 5. Figure 5: Photo at 3 months of follow-up demonstrating significant improvement.
Figure 5: Photo at 3 months of follow-up demonstrating significant improvement.

Discussion of Differential diagnoses:
• The lack of fevers, pain and systemic symptoms make a pyogenic bacterial infection unlikely. Pus is usually seen.
• Orbital mucormycosis could explain a swollen protruding eye, but the area is not usually erythematous. He had no limitations in eye movement, he is a normal host and his CT did not show involvement of the globe.
• Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas can occur anywhere, but most commonly presents as patchy trunk and limb rashes. This is a very rare diagnosis. Histology was negative for malignancy.
• There was no history of contact to account for an allergy.
• Despite popular belief, snakes and scorpions are not commonly found in Melbourne homes! Such a localised and slowly progressive swelling without pain, purpura or systemic toxic symptoms would be unusual.
Mycobacterium ulcerans infection, or Buruli ulcer, is an emerging health problem in parts of the developing world and, increasingly, Australia. First described in sub-Saharan Africa, the disease has now been identified in Japan, Mexico, Central America, and Papua New Guinea (reviewed in (1)). In Australia, the disease occurs in specific endemic areas, particularly the coastal and peninsular areas of temperate climate Victoria (south-eastern state), where it is known as Bairnsdale ulcer after a local town (2). The median incubation period is 4.5 months but can range from 34 to 264 days (3). Recent epidemiological research in Victoria suggests a possible role for mosquitos, other biting arthropods and possums in its transmission (4, 5).
Lesions usually begin as a painless nodule under 5mm in diameter, however they can also present as papules, plaques or edematous lesions (6). Frequently there are no systemic features or regional lymphadenopathy as M. ulcerans produces mycolactone, a toxin that inhibits the immune response (7). Infection commonly occurs on the exposed limbs, although it can present on any part of the body. The initial lesion breaks down over days to weeks forming the classic undermined Buruli ulcer which progresses slowly and painlessly (6).
The diagnosis of M. ulcerans can be difficult due to its fastidious nature and specific growth requirements. The diagnosis is based on the clinical picture, the detection of acid-fast staining (42% sensitive) (8) and PCR (86-98% sensitive) (8, 9). Yield of culture is low. We did not send for AFB culture as Mycobacterium ulcerans culture in Lowenstein-Jensen or liquid media is slow (typically requires 6-12 weeks) and the sensitivity approaches only 50% (8). For ulcerated lesions, a swab under the rim of the undermined ulcer for PCR is recommended; however for non-ulcerative lesions (plaques, edematous lesions, nodules), swab specimens often provide false-negative results and biopsy or fine-needle aspirate are often necessary.
While older reviews and guidelines advocated for surgery with wide excision of margins as the mainstay of M ulcerans management (10, 11), recent randomised and observational studies (12-15) have demonstrated antibiotics to be effective. At the time of this writing in 2017, the recommended antibiotic therapy according to Australian guidelines (2) is rifampicin combined with either clarithromycin (preferred) or a fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin). Antibiotics duration is 8 weeks for simple cutaneous lesions, and 12 weeks for lesions involving deeper structures (ie. joints, bones). Paradoxical reactions occur in up to 20% of patients, with worsening of the lesion in a process known as an immune reconstitution inflammatory reaction (16). This does not represent treatment failure, and severe reactions can be managed with adjunctive oral corticosteroids. As clinical and microbiological cure is achievable with antibiotics, surgery is limited to debridement of necrotic areas, repair of large defects or rare instances where antibiotics is declined or contraindicated and direct closure of a small lesion is preferred. Risk of relapse with surgery alone is high (17). The World Health Organization website has a number of useful resources in the epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment of Buruli ulcers (18).

title: A man in his mid-fifties with known hypertension and osteoarthritis, presented w
history:
A man in his mid-fifties with known hypertension and osteoarthritis, presented with a several-month history of progressively worsening headache, dizziness, blurry vision, ataxia, and vomiting. The patient’s problems began approximately four months prior, soon after he had a tooth extraction done while traveling to Nevada. He received antibiotics after the procedure, and then developed a generalized maculopapular, scaly rash, that was worst on the extremities. The rash failed to resolve with topical lubricants. Over the following weeks, he developed the aforementioned neurological symptoms. His work-up included a head MRI, which showed a two-centimeter mass in the right occiput concerning for abscess versus malignancy. He was referred to a tertiary medical center for further evaluation.

The patient had a history of well-controlled hypertension, osteoarthritis, and chronic sinusitis. Additionally, he had a two-year history of a non-healing occipital scalp wound. Skin biopsies of the wound showed Staphylococcus epidermidis and Histoplasma (unknown species), for which he was prescribed cephalexin and fluconazole. However after approximately three months of treatment, he demonstrated minimal improvement.

The patient lived on a ranch in the rural southwest of the U.S. He took care of multiple animals including horses, goats, sheep and chickens. His previous work involved travel to the east and west coasts, with recent travel to Nevada and Texas.

The patient has an allergy to penicillin, which causes a rash.

Upon admission, the patient was taking metoprolol tartrate; cephalexin 500 mg by mouth, three times daily; and fluconazole 100 mg by mouth, once daily.
exam_studies:
Upon admission to the hospital, the patient was in no acute distress. Temperature was 98.4 ° F (36.9 ° C), heart rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 149/86 mm/Hg, respirations 16 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation 92% on room air. His physical exam was significant for sub-centimeter cervical lymphadenopathy, and decreased air entry in the bilateral lung fields; heart and abdominal exam were unremarkable. Skin exam revealed a 2 cm x 2 cm partially healed ulcer in the occiput (Figure 1). He also had a diffuse, maculopapular, raised, scaly, hypertrophied rash with excoriations (Figure 2). Neurological exam was significant for dysdiadokinesis, without nystagmus.
Figure 1. Non-healing ulcer on occiput
Figure 2. Maculopapular skin rash on left shin.

The patient’s white blood cell count was 12.5 x 10 3 (reference range: 4.0-10.5 x 10 3) per microliter with 84% neutrophils and 0% eosinophils. Complete blood count was otherwise within normal limits, and basic metabolic panel had no abnormalities. The patient’s alanine transaminase was 73 units /L (reference range 10-40 units/L); the hepatic function panel was otherwise normal. HIV and Hepatitis C serology were negative. MRI of the brain with and without contrast showed a dominant 2.1 x 2.4 cm ring enhancing lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, suspicious for abscess (Figure 3). CT of the chest with contrast showed bilateral lower lobe atelectasis, and multiple sub 4-mm pulmonary nodules scattered throughout, with the incidental finding of borderline adrenal hyperplasia. Peripheral blood cultures were ultimately negative for yeast or bacteria.
Figure 3. MRI Brain with contrast showing a ring-enhancing lesion in the R cerebellar hemisphere.

The patient was admitted, and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics with vancomycin, cefepime, and metronidazole. Five days later, the patient underwent brain abscess aspiration with purulent material sent for gram stain, and bacterial and fungal cultures. Dermatology was consulted for the biopsy of the rash and of the occipital wound.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum with right cerebellar abscess

Serologies for Coccidiodes IgG/IgM, Blastomyces antibodies, and urine Histoplasma antigen were all negative. Biopsies of the skin from the upper extremity, and scalp showed yeast consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum (Figures 4, 5). After two-and-a-half weeks brain abscess fungal cultures grew mold, with cotton blue staining consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum (Figure 6). The diagnosis was confirmed by PCR of the brain and skin tissue. Bacterial cultures on the brain tissue remained negative.
Figure 4. Scalp biopsy, GMS stain
Figure 5. Skin of the arm, GMS stain
Figure 6. Brain abscess culture, cotton blue stain.

The patient was treated for disseminated histoplasmosis with CNS involvement. Liposomal amphotericin B was added to the antimicrobial regimen. One week later, he developed acute kidney injury, with an increase in creatinine from 0.7 mg/dL to 2.3 mg/dL (reference range 0.6-1.6 mg/dL). His antibiotics were narrowed to ceftriaxone and metronidazole, and his antifungal therapy was switched to itraconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily. The patient did not achieve therapeutic itrazonazole levels and was switched to voriconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily, with excellent clinical response. Finally, because of the possibility of a bacterial component in the setting of symptoms of systemic infection beginning shortly after a tooth extraction, antibiotics were continued for a total of four weeks.

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that is endemic to North and South America, although it has also been found in parts of East Asia, Southeast Asia, and India [1]. Disease is associated with exposure to decaying guano. The most common manifestations of histoplasmosis are acute pulmonary histoplasmosis, usually a self-limiting infection; and chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis, which typically occurs in older patients [2].
Complications of the disease include disseminated histoplasmosis and CNS involvement. Immunosuppressed patients are the most at risk for development of disseminated disease [2], however, immunocompetent patients are increasingly being identified. Our case highlights the importance of keeping this diagnosis in the differential of immunocompetent patients. Nearly all patients present with neurological symptoms as their chief complaint, including encephalopathy, seizures, blurry vision, and weakness. Definitive diagnosis is through culture of the organism. Serology, particularly a urine Histoplasma antigen, are helpful when positive, with a reported sensitivity of up to 95% in AIDS patients. However, there are limited data regarding sensitivity in immunocompetent patients [2] and a negative result cannot exclude the diagnosis. As such, our case demonstrates the limitations of serological testing.
Current guidelines recommend treating CNS histoplasmosis with liposomal amphotericin B for four to six weeks, followed by itraconazole for at least one year, until clinical resolution of disease [3]. Notably, there are cases where voriconazole has been used successfully. In these instances, the patients recovered well and had no re-activation of disease [4] [5]. Our patient was ultimately transitioned to voriconazole with a planned course of one year. Follow-up MRI at one and three months post-op showed no residual abscess, and his neurological symptoms have completely resolved.
This case demonstrates the importance of maintaining a broad differential in all patients who present with sub-acute neurological symptoms. A detailed history, including exposure history, is critical for a thorough evaluation. Finally, there is a possibility that voriconazole may be an acceptable alternative to itraconazole therapy.
