title: A woman in her forties presented to the emergency department with a one-week his
history:
A woman in her forties presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of progressive myalgias, arthralgias, and severe right ankle pain, accompanied by episodic fevers and sore throat. The day prior to hospitalization, she remained bed-bound with high fever, and was unable to mobilize without a wheelchair due to pain.
Her arthralgias were diffuse and migratory in the upper and lower extremities, especially shoulders, elbows, knees, and ankles. The right ankle had become progressively swollen, red, and painful over the preceding 2 days. She denied rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, cough, or headache. She denied recent travel, sick contacts, or new sexual partners. She denied knowing of any specific trigger for this illness.

She reported a history of hypertension. She was obese with previous laparoscopic banding procedure, and denied any allergies.

The patient lived in an urban home with her husband and daughters, dogs, cats, and domesticated rats. She did not report animal or insect bites. She smoked marijuana, but denied any other illicit drug use, tobacco use, or significant alcohol intake. She had been monogamous in her relationship without new sexual contacts. She did not have significant occupational exposures or recent travel.

The patient increased her use of acetaminophen 300mg/codeine 30mg without relief and was on regular ramipril and desogestrel ethinyl estradiol without recent medication changes.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared sick, but not septic, with fever to 39.6°C, blood pressure 135/80 mmHg, pulse 92 beats per minute, and respirations 20 breaths per minute. All joints and muscles were exquisitely tender to palpation especially the shoulders, forearms, arms, knees, and ankles. No active synovitis was noted other than the right ankle, which appeared erythematous, swollen, and hot. The retropharynx was erythematous without exudates or lymphadenopathy. Cardiac, respiratory, abdominal, neurologic, and dermatologic examinations were unremarkable.

The white blood cell count was 18.0 x 10 9 cells/L (reference range (ref) 4.0 – 11.0), predominantly neutrophils (13.4 x 10 9 cells/L) with associated lymphopenia (1.6 x 10 9 cells/L), hemoglobin 98 g/L (ref 130-165), and platelet count 405 x 10 9 cells/L (ref 150 – 400). Electrolytes, liver enzymes and renal function test results were normal.
The C-reactive protein was extremely elevated at 508 mg/L (ref 1.0 – 7.0). An extensive autoimmune work-up was negative.
Right ankle and chest radiographs were normal.

The patient was admitted to the hospital for further work-up and observation. She was hydrated with intravenous fluids and her pain was controlled with narcotics. Blood cultures were drawn and were negative. Arthrocentesis of the right ankle revealed cloudy straw-colored fluid, and gram stain showed 3+ polymorphonuclear cells but no organisms. Insufficient fluid remained for cell count or biochemistry. Synovial fluid was inoculated in pediatric blood culture media, as well as blood agar and chocolate agar plates. Growth was detected in both the pediatric blood culture bottle and on blood agar plate after 48-hours of incubation. Gram stain at 1000x oil magnification is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Gram Stain (1000x oil immersion) of right ankle synovial fluid
diagnosis:
Rat bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis)

Grey non-hemolytic colonies grew on blood agar plates. Gram stain was performed and described as gram-negative, pleomorphic, filamentous organisms with fusiform characteristics, and characteristic lateral bulbar swellings (Figure 1). The organism was identified as Streptobacillus moniliformis by Matrix Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization Time of Flight (MALDI-TOF) (Bruker, Milton, Ontario, MBT Compass Library RUO6903) and confirmed with 16S ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA) polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) were determined by gradient diffusion using Etest antibiotic strips (bioMérieux, Montréal, Québec). As there are no specific breakpoints for this organism, we inferred antimicrobial susceptibility using the CLSI MIC criteria for “ other non-Enterobacteriaceae ”, which suggested this was susceptible to penicillin (0.125 mg/L), ceftriaxone (0.008 mg/L), imipenem (0.094 mg/L), meropenem (0.032 mg/L), and ciprofloxacin (0.25 mg/L). The isolate was predictably resistant to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Blood cultures remained negative on several occasions.
Following culture results, further clinical history was obtained regarding the domestic rats which was not revealed in the first encounter. She reported purchasing three domestic rats using an online classified website 18 months prior. One died months prior, one was healthy, and the last was recently sick, with weight loss, inactivity, and poor oral intake. In consultation with a veterinarian, the rat was euthanized, but prior to this, the patient “kissed the rat goodbye” on the snout and received 2 soft, non-painful bites on the tongue. The bites occurred 4 days prior to onset of illness, and no local effects were evident. In the absence of localized effects, the patient did not feel significant contact was made with the rat, and did not report this on initial history.

Treatment was initiated empirically with ceftriaxone. After speciation, she was switched to intravenous penicillin G, then back to ceftriaxone due to issues with line access. A few days into admission, she developed severe right shoulder pain with immobility and clinical features of septic arthritis, which was managed conservatively with antibiotics. She continued to have migratory generalized polyarthralgias, and decreased mobility, therefore a 6-week course of antibiotics was planned. The patient ultimately received 5 weeks of antibiotics due to challenges obtaining intravenous access and clinical stability. Transthoracic echocardiography did not show evidence of vegetations. In follow up, she developed asymptomatic T-cell large granular lymphocyte proliferation, which was followed by hematology and resolved without treatment. Her pain slowly improved to baseline over 2 to 3 months.

Rat bite fever is an acute systemic illness characterized by relapsing fever, migratory polyarthralgias, and rash. The predominant pathogen responsible for cases in North America is Streptobacillus moniliformis; Spirillum minus is more common in Asia. While illnesses related to rat bites have been documented back 2,300 years, the incidence of rat bite fever is unknown. Several cases are described annually, predominantly in children and those in close contact with domestic rats (1).
The systemic illness typically manifests less than days 10 days after a bite from an infected rat or after close contact with S. moniliformis colonization in the saliva or excreta. A bite is not necessary for transmission, and up to 30% will have no known source of inoculation. The incubation period varies from 1 to 22 days (1).
The clinical presentation can have striking similarities to rheumatoid arthritis, as the polyarthralgias and arthritis often affects multiple joints, including small and large joints (2). There is a predilection for the ankles, and the presence of tender hemorrhagic vesicles on the hands and feet is strongly suggestive of infection. Other clinical features include abrupt onset of fevers which may be relapsing, profound rigors, pharyngitis, severe myalgias and signs of upper respiratory tract infection. Of special interest, the bite site typically does not become infected, inflamed, or painful and no local effects are suffered. There is generally an absence of lymphadenopathy. While T-cell large granular lymphocytosis has previously been associated with other inflammatory arthropathies, to our knowledge, this is the first case reported following infection with Streptobacillus moniliformis (3). Left untreated mortality rates are high with death occurring in 7-13% of cases (1).
Diagnosis requires a high clinical index of suspicion, appropriate use of culture, and identification by MALDI-TOF or molecular testing. It is a slow growing organism which requires prolonged incubation and careful attention to culture media. Characteristic gram stain results are shown and described in Figure 1. Typically, the gram-negative rod appears straight but may be fusiform, may develop characteristic lateral bulbar swelling, and is usually arranged in chains and loosely tangled clumps (1). Commercial blood culture media contains 0.05% sodium polyanethol sulfonate (SPS), an anticoagulant which inhibits its growth; therefore anaerobic culture bottles, resin bead culture systems, and/or trypticase soy agar and broth should be used for culture (4).
The clinical picture can mimic sepsis from beta-hemolytic streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus; in addition, other bacterial causes should be considered (disseminated gonorrhea, meningococcemia, Lyme disease, ehrlichiosis, brucellosis, and complications of streptococcal diseases like scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, and reactive arthritis). While S. moniliformis typically produces characteristic gram stain findings, some mimickers include Fusobacterium necrophorum (pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli, but not typically branching, and clinically is associated with septic thrombophlebitis of the head and neck), Pasteurella multocida (often pleomorphic gram-negative cocco-bacilli, clinically associated with cat and dog bite site infections), and Leptotrichia buccalis (long and tapering gram-negative bacilli, typically only associated with invasive disease in immunocompromised hosts). While beta-lactam damaged E. coli can take on a variety of morphologies via gram stain, septicemia from E. coli is rarely accompanied by septic arthritis.
Penicillin is the treatment of choice; treatment duration varies based upon response to therapy and presence of complications (5). Ceftriaxone has been used successfully, and tetracycline can be used in the setting of penicillin allergy (1).
In conclusion, a detailed search for epidemiological clues, including exposure to domestic rats is important in diagnosis and appropriate treatment of rat bite fever. The non-specific clinical features and challenges in microbial isolation make diagnosis difficult. When suspected, care should be taken in selecting culture media without the presence of SPS which inhibits growth.
Teaching points:
A detailed review of epidemiological risks is important for patients presenting with a non-specific febrile illness.
Patients with domestic rats, especially after exposures to bites, should be investigated for rat bite fever caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis in the appropriate clinical context.
Rat bite fever typically manifests with relapsing fever, migratory polyarthralgias, and rash.
Growth is inhibited by SPS anticoagulant, commonly found in blood culture bottles.
We describe the first case of T-cell large granular lymphocytosis as a complication of rat bite fever.
The treatment of choice is with penicillin.

title: A woman in her fifties from Cameroon who intermittently visits family in the Uni
history:
A woman in her fifties from Cameroon who intermittently visits family in the United States presented to the Emergency Department, 5 days after arrival, with acute hepatic failure with grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy and an international normalized ratio (INR) of 8.6. The acute hepatic failure was initially attributed to either an antimalarial agent presumably dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (which she had recently received for malaria prophylaxis) or a single dose of commercial Moringa tea, and she was managed and intubated in intensive care. Six days after admission, the primary service noted that she had a rising absolute eosinophil count to 2,200 cells per mcL (19.8%) and consulted the Infectious Diseases service.

Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c of 8%), and uncomplicated malaria treated with an unspecified antimalarial agent taken 4 months prior to admission.

Born and raised in Cameroon. She denied any smoking, alcohol, or illicit drug use.

Amlodipine, valsartan, and sitaglipin. She had also recently received a 3 day course of an antimalarial agent (presumably dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine) for malaria prophylaxis, which she had completed 7 days before admission. She drank Moringa tea.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. She remained intubated and mildly sedated. She was jaundiced and her sclera were icteric. No conjunctival lesions. No lower extremity edema bilaterally. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

The leukocyte count was 11,200 cells per mcL (reference range 4,500 to 10,500) with 53% neutrophils, 11.5% lymphocytes, 14.6% monocytes, and 19.8% eosinophils. The absolute eosinophil count was 2200 cells per mcL (reference range <500). The hematocrit (27.6) and platelet count (123) were abnormally low but stable. The creatinine, alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin were elevated but decreasing. No ova or parasites were seen on three separate stool specimens.
She was HAV and HBV immune; HCV antibody negative; HDV IgM and IgG negative; Schistosoma IgG negative; Strongyloides IgG negative; Toxocara IgG positive; HIV negative. Her stools were negative for ova and parasites.

Another peripheral blood smear was prepared using Knott’s technique (Figure 3).

diagnosis:
Loaisis

The peripheral smear prepared using Knott’s technique revealed a sheathed, 280 micrometer microfilaria with nuclei at the tip of its tapered tail consistent with Loa loa. The microfilarial load was significantly less than 8,000 microfilariae (MF) per mL. The serologic test (OV16 IgG antibody) performed by the National Institutes of Health to evaluate for co-infection with Onchocerca volvulus was negative.

After the patient’s hepatic abnormalities resolved completely, she received a 21 day course of diethylcarbamazine (DEC). Nine days after completing the course of DEC, her peripheral eosinophilia had resolved. She did complain of transient urticaria but a repeat peripheral smear prepared using Knott’s technique was negative for any microfilariae.

The identification of the filarial nematodes requires knowledge of their geographic distribution, clinical presentation, and the microscopic appearance of their progeny, the microfilariae, in peripheral smears. The most commonly encountered agent of lymphatic filariasis (LF), Wuchereria bancrofti, is endemic to tropical areas throughout the world. In contrast, the geographic distribution of the two other agents of LF is more limited: Brugia malayi is endemic to Asia including the Indian subcontinent and Brugia timori is endemic to Indonesia. The other three genera of filarial nematodes, namely Loa, Mansonella, and Onchocerca, share a tropism for subcutaneous and neuro-ocular tissues and if symptomatic, result in localized subcutaneous angioedema and varying degrees of ocular impairment and encephalitis. In addition, these three genera of filarial nematodes also share a geographic distribution and are endemic to central and western Africa. The only exception is Mansonella ozzardi, which is endemic to Latin America.
In regard to the appearance of the microfilariae in peripheral smears, there are three elements to consider: (1) their size, (2) the presence or absence of a sheath, and (3) the morphology of their tail. In general, the microfilariae of Brugia, Loa, and Wuchereria are sheathed whereas the microfilariae of Mansonella and Onchocerca are unsheathed. The sheath is not always easily visible though. For the question accompanying this case: Options (1) B. malayi and (3) M. ozzardi can be discarded immediately because of their geographic distribution. Options (4) Mansonella perstans and (5) Onchocerca volvulus can also be discarded because they are unsheathed and because the size of their microfilariae are different than that of Loa loa measuring 180-225 µm and 300-315 µm, respectively. Furthermore, the tail of L. loa is tapered whereas the tail of M. perstans is blunt and the tail of O. volvulus is frequently bent at a sharp angle.
Loiasis or “African eye worm” is a neglected tropical disease caused by the filarial nematode Loa loa. The first case of Loiasis was reported in 1770 by the French surgeon Mongin who observed subconjunctival migration of adult Loa loa, a symptom termed “eye worm,” in a West African slave in Santo Domingo. In 1895, the Scottish ophthalmologist Douglas Argyll-Robertson first described transient localized cutaneous angioedema, or “Calabar swellings,” caused by the migration of adult Loa loa through the subcutaneous tissues of several patients in Calabar, Nigeria. [Grutzig 1977, van Boagert 1955].
The vector of Loiasis, the Chrysops fly, was identified in 1912 by the British parasitologist Robert Thompson Leiper. Larvae develop in the fly and are transmitted to humans during a blood meal. Adults mature over 6 months and migrate to the subconjunctiva and subcutaneous tissues. Microfilariae are released into the bloodstream during the day because this is when the Chrysops fly feeds. Since the vector of Loa loa is only found in the tropical rainforests of central and western Africa, Loiasis is confined to this region. It is particularly common in Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, and Gabon. The prevalence of Loiasis in endemic areas is 40% [Zouré 2011]. In a survey of 271 patients presenting to GeoSentinel sites with filarial infections, 25% had Loiasis [Saito 2015].
The clinical manifestations of Loiasis differ between travelers and migrants. Travelers are more likely to develop eye worm and migrants are more likely to develop Calabar swellings and urticaria. Peripheral eosinophilia is common among both groups and is present in up to 86% of cases. These symptoms may worsen during treatment [Saito 2015]. Fatal encephalitis is a well-documented phenomenon in patients with very high microfilarial loads receiving antifilarial therapy [Boussinesq 1998, Carme 1991, Gadon 1997, van Boagert 1955].
Diagnosis is made by visualization of adult worms in the subconjunctiva or microfilariae in peripheral blood smears. Adults measure 30-40 mm (male) or 40-70 mm (female). The cuticle (outer layer) is ridgeless but has irregularly spaced protrusions called “bosses.” Microfilariae are sheathed and measure 230-250 µm (Giemsa-stained smears) or 270-300 µm (smears prepared using Knott’s technique). The tail is tapered and contains nuclei [cdc.gov/dpdx]. Giemsa-stained smears are used for screening for microfilariae and, if calibrated, for quantifying the microfilarial load. For increased sensitivity, concentration techniques such as centrifugation and blood lysis in 2% formalin (Knott’s technique) may be used. The optimal time of blood specimen collection is 10:00 to 16:00 [Boussinesq 2012].
The recommended treatment for symptomatic Loiasis is DEC orally for 21 days. DEC is the only agent that is efficacious against adult worms and microfilariae. In contrast, the activity of albendazole (ALB) and ivermectin (IVM) are limited to microfilariae. Recrudescence is common and up to 50% of patients require repeated courses of treatment. Prior to starting DEC, 2 conditions must be met: First, the administration of DEC (and IVM) leads to a rapid decline in the microfilarial load. The rapidly dying microfilariae precipitate an inflammatory response that may result in fatal encephalitis, particularly in patients with microfilarial loads in the tens of thousands [Boussinesq 1998, Carme 1991, Gadon 1997, van Boagert 1955]. Thus, the microfilarial load must be decreased to less than 8,000 MF per mL prior to starting DEC. This may be done by the administration of ALB orally for 21 days or apheresis. ALB has an embryotoxic effect on adult Loa loa and thus decreases the microfilarial load more slowly than DEC or IVM [Boussinesq 2012]. Second, co-infection with Onchocerca volvulus must be ruled-out. Onchocerca volvulus is the filarial nematode that causes “African river blindness.” It shares the same geographic distribution of Loa loa and has similar clinical manifestations [Zouré 2014]. Treatment of Onchocerca volvulus with DEC may precipitate a Mazzottii reaction, an inflammatory reaction caused by rapidly dying microfilariae that results in blindness and cardiopulmonary collapse [Awadzi 1992].

title: A man in his fifties presented with penile ulcers. Approximately one month prior
history:
A man in his fifties presented with penile ulcers. Approximately one month prior to the appearance of the lesions, he had passed a kidney stone and subsequently developed burning with urination. Following a 10 day course of cephalexin, a small white ulcer appeared on the right side of the glans. It began as a single lesion, but over two weeks several more ulcers appeared and eventually conglomerated into one large, eroded area. He denied other symptoms. He has not been sexually active for several years. There was no history of trauma or instrumentation.

Coronary artery disease
Diabetes Mellitus type II (last HbA1C 6.8%)

Smoked a few cigarettes daily for many years. The patient lived in the southeast US.
No recent travel, no animal exposures, no known tuberculosis exposures.

Metoprolol Tartrate; Lisinopril; Insulin (Glargine and Aspart); Metformin; Tamsulosin.
exam_studies:
On exam he was alert, oriented, and appeared stable. Blood pressure was 146/82 mmHg, pulse 91 beats per minute, temperature 97.2 o F (36.2 o C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. Lungs had crackles in the bases, but no wheezing. The penis was uncircumcised, with a diffuse ulcer on the right glans with thick yellow purulent material around the edges (Figure 1). He had multiple individual white-based ulcers on the left glans with scant yellow discharge. Exam was negative for oral ulcers, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or scrotal lesions.
Figure 1. Figure 1: Penile ulcer.
Figure 1: Penile ulcer.

White blood cell count was 9.9 x 10 3 /mcL (reference range 4.8 - 10.5 x 10 3 /mcL).
Inflammatory markers were elevated with C-reactive protein 157.1 mg/L (reference range 0 - 9.9) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr (reference range: males over 50 years = <20 mm/hr).
Blood cultures from time of admission were negative. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures, viral culture, gonorrhea, chlamydia, RPR, and HIV testing were negative. CT abdomen/pelvis was negative for renal calculi or masses, but a pleural based nodular opacity was noted in the posterior-medial right lower lobe. This led to a CT scan of the chest which revealed a diffuse, bilateral, miliary, micronodular lung parenchymal process (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Figure 2a: CT of chest. Nonspecific diffuse bilateral miliary micronodular lung parenchymal process involving the visualized lower lungs.
Figure 2a: CT of chest. Nonspecific diffuse bilateral miliary micronodular lung parenchymal process involving the visualized lower lungs.
Figure 3. Figure 2b: CT of chest. Pleural-based nodular density associated with the posterior medial right lower lobe and mildly enlarged sub-carinal mediastinal lymph nodes
Figure 2b: CT of chest. Pleural-based nodular density associated with the posterior medial right lower lobe and mildly enlarged sub-carinal mediastinal lymph nodes

The ulceration spread to the left glans, and repeat wound cultures showed no neutrophils but grew Clostridium, Finegoldia, Corynebacteriu m, alpha hemolytic Streptococci, and coagulase-negative Staphylococci. ANA, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor were negative. An ophthalmologic exam was negative for uveitis.
A transthoracic echocardiogram was performed that showed severe ischemic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular ejection fraction of 20-25% and no evidence of vegetations. The patient had received ten days of piperacillin/tazobactam without change in clinical course and as no other bacterial etiologies were identified, he was discharged home to follow-up with infectious disease at a later date.
diagnosis:
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Fungal cultures of the superficial wound swab grew Blastomyces dermatiditis after four weeks.
Figure 4. Figure 3a: Plate showing initially white and then light brown mold.
Figure 3a: Plate showing initially white and then light brown mold.
Figure 5. Figure 3b: Plate showing initially white and then light brown mold.
Figure 3b: Plate showing initially white and then light brown mold.

The patient was prescribed treatment with itraconazole 200mg oral twice daily. Several days later (before he started the medication), he was admitted to a different hospital with shortness of breath and was found to be in acute respiratory failure. He developed septic shock and the decision was made to make the patient comfort care, soon after which he expired.

This case was unique in the presentation of cutaneous penile blastomycosis as well as miliary blastomycosis without associated pulmonary symptoms in an immunocompetent host. Pulmonary blastomycosis clinically presents as acute or chronic pneumonia with fever, chills, productive cough, with or without hemoptysis. It can also present as an asymptomatic radiographic abnormality. [1] Miliary blastomycosis or endobronchial spread of infection can cause adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). [2] The patient in this case was admitted for nearly three weeks and remained afebrile with no respiratory decline.
On literature review for penile cutaneous blastomycosis, two abstracts were found, both of which involve cases outside of the United States. A case of South American Blastomycosis describes a patient with a similar presentation of an ulcer in the internal surface of the prepuce that had been present for six months. The author references one other case of penile blastomycosis. [3] The presence of penile ulcerative blastomycosis appears to be rare.
Blastomycosis most commonly is found in the soil of the Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys and is acquired through inhalation. It can cause asymptomatic infection of the respiratory tract with spontaneous resolution, or disseminate and cause fulminant septic shock with spread to the central nervous, cutaneous, or osteoarticular systems. While most commonly diagnosed in the United States at a rate of 1 case per 100,000, highly endemic areas may see a rate as high as 10 to 40 per 100,000. [4] Although it is not unusual to be asymptomatic in the presence of radiographic abnormalities, the progression of both the patient’s pulmonary involvement to a diffuse bilateral miliary process, as well as the extensive nature of his penile lesions, appears to be a unique presentation of blastomycosis.

title: A usually well woman in her seventies presented with 3 days of fatigue and 1 day
history:
A usually well woman in her seventies presented with 3 days of fatigue and 1 day of fever. She participated in a sporting tournament only three days prior, felt extremely fatigued afterwards, but noted no other symptoms. On the day of presentation she felt febrile, measured at 104° F (40° C) and was brought to the emergency department.

Osteoarthritis

She was a keen traveler, and last travelled to Cuba 3 years prior. She had house cats (both outdoor/indoor). She had had dental work performed twice in the last three weeks including a tooth extraction and a crown fitting.

Ibuprofen as needed
exam_studies:
At presentation, she was noted to be confused and febrile, 102.7º F (39.3° C); tachycardic at 106 beats per minute; blood pressure was 127/80 mm Hg; and respiration rate was 18 per minute with a saturation of 94% without supplemental oxygen. Her heart rhythm was irregularly irregular. She was noted to have a 5 mm erythematous papule with central crusted erosion over her right forearm (not shown). On further questioning, she indicated that the lesion started as a papule that then became a pustule 2 months prior. She also had an excoriation on her left forearm with no palpable lymphadenopathy. The rest of her physical exam was normal.

Her admission laboratory studies that included a complete cell count and renal and liver function tests were normal. Chest radiograph did not show a pneumonic process and CT chest showed trace bilateral effusions and enlarged lymph nodes in the right axillary, periportal and aortocaval chains, largest measuring 11 mm (not shown). A transthoracic echocardiogram did not show any valvular abnormalities. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation.

Blood cultures were drawn and testing for Bartonella (serum PCR and serology), Coccidiodomycosis, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Brucella and Q fever were performed. She was empirically started on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam and after one day was switched to levofloxacin. She was also started on metoprolol and apixaban given new-onset atrial fibrillation. She was planned for electrical cardioversion, but spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm and was discharged after 1 day of admission.
The next day she returned due to ongoing fever to 102.2° F (39° C) and fatigue, now accompanied by night sweats. On exam, she was noted to have mild swelling of the right calf. No thrombosis was noted in the lower extremities by Doppler ultrasound.
Given her persistent fevers while on antibiotics, a CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast was performed that showed multiple hypovascular liver lesions, some with rim enhancement and central hypodensity, the largest in the left hepatic lobe measured 23 x 10 mm (Figure 1). The scan also demonstrated multiple small splenic lesions and upper abdominal lymphadenopathy with the largest node measuring 16 mm. An ultrasound confirmed at least three focal hypoechoic liver lesions the largest of which was located in the left lateral segment and measured approximately 12 mm. She was started on ceftriaxone and metronidazole due to concern for hepatic abscess.
Figure 1. Abdominal CT with contrast showed multiple hypovascular liver lesions (arrow), some with rim enhancement and central hypodensity, the largest in the left hepatic lobe measured 23 x 10 mm. The scan also demonstrated multiple small splenic lesions and amorphous upper abdominal lymphadenopathy with the largest node measuring 16 mm.
diagnosis:
Hepatosplenic cat scratch disease

Given concern for malignancy a liver biopsy was performed showing marked mixed inflammation and focal necrosis most consistent with an infectious etiology (Figure 2). Additionally, a biopsy of the lesion on her right forearm demonstrated suppurative granulomatous inflammation characterized by scattered loosely formed granulomas showing central suppuration (Figure 3). The overlying epidermis showed reactive epidermal hyperplasia with focal ulceration. The granulomas were surrounded by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate dominated by plasma cells that were seen periadnexally and perivascularly. All special stains for microorganisms (Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, Gomori methenamine silver, acid-fast bacillus and Steiner) were negative on both the liver and skin biopsy. During her two admissions, multiple blood cultures were negative. On presentation, serology and serum PCR for Bartonella henselae were negative, as well as serology for Coccidiodomycosis, Q fever and Brucella and antigen testing for Cryptococcus and Histoplasma.
Figure 2. Liver biopsy (H&E, 40x) showing mixed inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils and poorly aggregated histiocytes. Multinucleate giant cells were not identified. A few portal areas demonstrate edematous expansion and marked, dense mixed inflammation.
Figure 3. Skin biopsy (H&E, 40x) showing a suppurative granuloma consisting of collections of epithelioid histiocytes with a collection of neutrophils in the center (arrow) and a lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate at the periphery.

Despite her initial negative serology, serum PCR and liver biopsy, given a high clinical suspicion, we decided to switch to doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily to treat hepatosplenic cat scratch disease. After switching, she no longer had fevers. Shortly afterwards a rash ensued, presumed to be due to doxycycline. She was switched to azithromycin 500 mg daily. Bartonella henselae serologies at four and six weeks after presentation were positive with titers of 1:128 and 1:256, respectively. After nearly 6 weeks on azithromycin, she felt well, energy level normalized and she returned to her sporting activities. A repeat CT scan showed nearly complete resolution of all hepatic and splenic lesions.

Early in the case, given the age of the patient and hepatic lesions, malignancy was a major concern, but liver biopsy was not consistent. In the persistently febrile patient, endocarditis is always a concern with multiple splenic and hepatic lesions being embolic manifestations of infective endocarditis (1). Blood cultures and serologic testing for etiologies of culture negative endocarditis were negative and transthoracic echocardiography was also negative for suspicious valvular lesions. Multiple hepatic lesions with fever raised the suspicion for pyogenic liver abscess but the patient had none of the classic identifiable risk factors including biliary disease, biliary instrumentation, diabetes, Asian ethnicity or injection drug use (2) and cultures (blood and liver biopsy) were negative.
The patient’s hand lesion and ipsilateral adenopathy seen on CT raised concern that the hand was a primary inoculation site with subsequent spread of infection to her regional lymph nodes. Specific infectious etiologic agents to account for our patient’s lymphocutaenous presentation included Bartonella henselae, Francisella tularensis, Nocardia spp, Bacillus anthracis, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Rhodococcus equi, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria, Sporothrix shenckii, endemic mycosis (Coccidioides, Blastomyces and Histoplasma), Cryptococcus, Leishmania and viruses (Parapoxvirus and Orthopoxvirus) (3). Nonetheless, with her cat exposure, primary skin lesion, hepatosplenic disease, non-necrotizing granulomas on biopsy and positive serology with rising titers to Bartonella henselae, cat scratch disease (CSD) complicated by hepatosplenic (HS) manifestations was the most likely diagnosis.
Specificity of serology for CSD has been reported to be above 90% (4,5). A recent review of the literature published on CSD-HS among immunocompetent patients identified 33 cases and added three more (6). Published reports identified a specific bite or scratch by a cat in only 35% of cases. The most frequent symptoms and signs reported were fever (86%), constitutional symptoms (50%), abdominal pain (44%) and adenopathy (33%). Imaging showed multiple hypodense lesions in most patients (81%), with both the spleen and liver affected in 39% of cases, and a similar proportion of cases had abdominal adenopathy. In patients who had liver biopsies, 80% had necrotizing granulomatous hepatitis. Only 33% of biopsies that underwent silver stains (Warthin-Starry, Steiner) were positive for rod shaped bacteria. PCR of biopsy samples or blood had a sensitivity of 81% and serologic assays showed an IgG titer against B. henselae >1:128 in 94%.
Treatment of HS-CSD in immunocompetent hosts is not well defined. CSD is typically a self-limited disease and may be immune mediated. In susceptible hosts, a type IV hypersensitivity reaction through IL-12 production may lead to granuloma formation seen in HS disease (7). Given the possible immune nature of the disease, the role of antibiotics is unclear. Nonetheless, in a small study in children (n=19) with CSD-HS and prolonged fever (mean 22 days, range 7-56 days), patients had favorable responses when treated with rifampin alone or in combination with other antibiotics (n=16, mean time to defervesce 2.6 days, range 1-5 days) with an average duration of antibiotic therapy of 3 weeks (8). As no control group was available for comparison it is unknown if defervescence was due to antibiotic therapy. No trials exist in adults and it is unclear how long to treat these individuals.

title: An Arabian woman in her 60s undergoing an evaluation for an adenocarcinoma of th
history:
An Arabian woman in her 60s undergoing an evaluation for an adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon was incidentally found on MRI to have a complex mass within the left gluteus maximus.
She reported first noticing tenderness in her left buttocks three years prior. Since then, she had worsening soreness that extended into the lateral aspect of the leg with associated weakness, which she attributed to her chronic lower back pain. She denied any fevers, chills, night sweats, or rash. She reported weight loss following a sleeve gastrectomy.

Adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon
Obesity status-post sleeve gastrectomy
End-stage renal disease on hemodialysis
Hypothyroidism

The patient is from the Arabian Peninsula and had regular exposure to dogs, sheep, and camels.

Levothyroxine
Sevalamer
Omeprazole

The patient was afebrile and did not appear ill, and her vital signs were all within normal limits. Examination was significant for a 7 x 14 cm mildly tender firm immobile mass protruding on the left buttocks (Figure 1). The skin over the mass was intact and appeared similar to the surrounding skin. Her lungs were clear to auscultation and there was no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
Figure 1. 7x14 cm firm mass protruding from left hip.

Leukocyte count was normal with no eosinophilia. Liver enzymes were within normal limits. Interferon gamma release assay for M. tuberculosis was negative. Echinococcus IgG antibody screening was negative. Ultrasonography (U/S) of the mass revealed a subcutaneous 16 x 8 x 17 cm coarsely echogenic non-calcified capsule containing numerous round anechoic cysts measuring up to 1.2 cm (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Ultrasound of gluteal cyst. Subcutaneous 16 x 8 x 17 cm coarsely echogenic lesion containing numerous round anechoic cysts measuring up to 1.2 cm.
diagnosis:

A dedicated musculoskeletal MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a multi-loculated mass well circumscribed by a thin uniform low-intensity capsule with T2 hyperintense / T1 hypointense rounded foci with similar dimensions seen in the ultrasound (Figure 3a and 3b). CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was done as part of the patient’s colorectal cancer evaluation, and no other cystic lesions were seen.

Intra-operative examination described a capsule of fibrous tissue containing tan, purulent viscous fluid and multiple spherical, intact clear sacs which were consistent with hydatid cysts (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). She was treated with albendazole starting 5 days prior to surgery and continued for 6 months. She returned to her family home in the Arabian Peninsula and was lost to follow-up.

Cystic echinococcosis (CE), or cystic hydatid disease, is most commonly caused by the larval stage of the parasitic cestode Echinococcus granulosus, which is endemic in the area of the Arabian Peninsula. There are other species of echinococcus which may also cause CE in a minority of cases. CE has a worldwide distribution with an incidence of over 50 per person-years in endemic areas, and is most commonly seen in pastoral settings where humans live in close proximity to animals [1]. Canines are the definitive hosts for the adult E. granulosus, and the intermediate hosts include sheep, goats and camels, which are prevalent in the Middle East. Humans are exposed to the parasite through fecal ingestion, and are aberrant or accidental hosts. Clinical presentation varies based on the site of infection with the liver being affected in 68-75% of cases followed by the lung in 17.2-22% [1,2]. Lesions are typically solitary, but inoculation of other sites does occur especially following trauma to the primary cyst. Muscle involvement in the absence of hepatic or pulmonary disease as in our patient is very rare, and has only been reported in between 0.2-2.2% of cases even in endemic areas [2]. The antigens contained within hydatid cysts are well known to cause anaphylaxis, which is occasionally the initial presentation, and therefore cystic echinococcosis should be considered in the differential for painless cystic lesions in endemic areas before biopsy or fine needle aspiration that may disrupt the cyst is attempted [3].
The diagnosis and staging of CE is based on characteristic imaging findings [4]. U/S, in addition to being more widely available in endemic areas than CT and MRI, has been shown to have a sensitivity and specificity ranging from 88-99% and 93-100% respectively [5] with very low inter-observer variability [6]. For muscular involvement, such as in our patient, MRI is preferred for the evaluation of anatomic relationships and neurovascular involvement needed to plan surgical excision [7]. Staging of cysts is based on pathognomonic morphologic characteristics on U/S and defined by the 2001 WHO criteria: active, transitional and inactive [2]. Our patient’s cyst was classified in the transitional stage based on degeneration of cysts and no histological evidence of echinococcosis noted.
Serological testing is less reliable for E. granulosus than related species, such as E. multilocularis, with sensitivities only reaching 83-89% [4, 8]. Fluid extracted from hydatid cysts serves as a source of antigen in ELISA-based serologic testing for detection of host anti-echinococcus antibody. However, cross-reactivity with other parasites such as E. multilocularis and Taenia solium may confound test results [9]. Aspiration of the cyst for diagnostic purposes is not recommended due to the risk of spilled cyst contents causing and anaphylactic reaction or spreading to other sites. Protoscolices may be seen developing within cysts during the active stages. However, since the cysts disintegrate over time as they transition to the inactive stage, protoscolices may not always be seen, as depicted in our case. The inactive stage cyst is fibrotic and calcified. Consequently, the diagnosis is secured based on epidemiologic exposure of the patient, clinical presentation, and surgical morphological findings of cysts.
Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the cyst. Perioperative anthelmintic therapy with benzimidazoles (mebendazole or albendazole) started one week before surgery and continued for up to 6 months following the operation is used to prevent recurrence and/or the spread of E. granulosus to other sites should there be spillage from the cyst during its removal. For inoperable cases, monotherapy with antihelmintics may be attempted, but has a cure rate of only around 30%, and is only appropriate in patients in whom surgery is contraindicated. Percutaneous-aspiration-injection-reaspiration (PAIR), which is often used for the hepatic and pulmonary infections that are more complicated to reach surgically, is rarely used for muscular hydatid disease [3]. Finally, watchful waiting may be appropriate for stable, calcified, and asymptomatic cysts [2].
Regarding the other possible diagnoses included in the differential, toxoplasmosis of skeletal muscles caused by Toxoplasmosis gondii is rare and classically seen only in immunocompromised conditions such as HIV. Clonorchis sinesis is the Chinese river fluke, whose geographic distribution is restricted to Southeast Asia and does not form cysts in muscle or soft tissue. Extraneural cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium is typically found in muscle or soft tissue, and most often appears as calcified “cigar-shaped calcifications”. Stool examination for ova and parasites is insensitive in these patients as the intestinal tapeworm may not still be present by the time of diagnosis. Serologic testing is available, but not performed in this patient as the ultrasound was diagnostic. Rhabdomyosarcomas are typically much more aggressive.

title: The patient is a Gravida 3, Para 2 woman in her thirties with a 4 month history
history:
The patient is a Gravida 3, Para 2 woman in her thirties with a 4 month history of abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her menstrual cycle was previously regular at 28 days, albeit with heavy flow. She first noted lower abdominal pain 4 months prior to admission and presented to primary care. There she was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection and treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days with some improvement in her pain. A month later her pain returned and she was again seen in primary care. At that visit it was noted that she had an intrauterine device in place, which had been placed 5 years earlier. She was referred to Obstetrics/Gynecology for intrauterine device removal. After removal she had relief of her abdominal pain and was placed on an oral contraceptive pill.
One month following removal of her intrauterine device she began passing blood clots followed by heavy menstrual bleeding. She was seen in Obstetrics/Gynecology clinic where her cervical exam was notable for purulent discharge. Fluid was obtained for culture. She underwent a pelvic ultrasound, which showed heterogenous and asymmetrically thickened myometrium suggesting adenomyosis. She underwent a cervical pap smear, which was non-diagnostic and showed only blood and inflammation. The next week she called reporting increased abdominal pain limiting her ability to ambulate. She was directly admitted to the hospital for an expedited workup.
She described her pain as 9/10 with movement, but 0/10 when stationary. It was located around her umbilicus without radiation. She reported a loss of appetite and a 12lb (5.4kg) weight loss over the prior 4 months. She had no fevers, chills, rigors, or night sweats. She had intermittent burning with urination, but no increased frequency.

Urinary tract infections
High grade squamous intraepithelial lesion with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia II/III with loop electrode excision 6 years prior

She has a family history of breast cancer and is monogamous with her male partner for more than a decade. She does not use condoms. She endorses anogenital and urogenital sexual practices.

Norgestrel-ethinyl estradiol
exam_studies:
Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F (37°C), heart rate 103 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air.
Abdomen: not distended, active bowel sounds, tenderness in the left lower quadrant and around the umbilicus with a firm mass palpated just below the umbilicus with focal warmth.
Vaginal: yellow mucopurulent discharge, thickened appearing cervix, no obvious mass.
The rest of her examination was unremarkable.

The white blood cell count was increased at 14.78 x10³ cells/uL (reference range: 4-10) with 81.3% neutrophils (RR 48-76%). A urine HCG was negative. Her urinalysis had 1+ white blood cells with 17 cells per high powered field on microscopy (normal 0-2 cells per high powered field). An antibody test to HIV-1 and -2 was negative.
diagnosis:
Acute and chronic endometritis due to Actinomyces spp. in association with an intra-uterine device.

Endometrial biopsy and endometrial curette showed acute and chronic endometritis with necrosis and ulceration. There was no viral cytopathic effect but small organisms were seen. Actinomyces colonies were present; Methanamine silver stain and gram stain were positive (Figures 1-3).
Pelvic MRI showed a mass involving the full length and near total circumference of the cervix, concerning for cervical malignancy, with multiple prominent lymph nodes bilaterally.
Figure 1. Hematoxylin and eosin stain of endometrial biopsy (40x)
Figure 2. Gram stain of endometrial biopsy (40x)
Figure 3. Methenamine silver stain of endometrial biopsy (40x)

With evidence of Actinomyces on biopsy and cervical culture, she was started on penicillin G 4 million units IV every 4 hours. Her abdominal pain quickly improved while on antibiotic therapy and she was discharged home. She followed up in Infectious Disease clinic 1 month later and her pain had completely resolved. A repeat MRI at that time showed marked interval improvement in the inflammatory changes previously seen, now with only residual edema in the anterior abdomen, pelvic periuterine soft tissues and cervix; her inguinal, external iliac and mesorectal lymphadenopathy persisted. After 6 weeks of intravenous therapy she was transitioned to amoxicillin 1 gram twice daily and probenecid 500 milligrams twice daily. Six months later her probenecid was discontinued, but she remained on amoxicillin 1 gram twice daily. After 12 months of treatment a repeat pelvic MRI was obtained that showed mild residual changes from her prior pelvic infection with no evidence of active suppurative actinomycoses. Her amoxicillin was discontinued.

At the time of initial consultation we were aware of the endometrial biopsy results with evidence of acute and chronic endometritis with Actinomyces colonies present. Despite this, we thought that it was important to rule out other causes of endometritis, cervicitis and urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) while starting treatment for Actinomyces. PID is a spectrum of inflammatory disorders of the upper female genital tract, including any combination of endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess and pelvic peritonitis. Acute PID (symptoms < 30 days) is often due to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma genitalium, and can be polymicrobial with enteric pathogens such as Escherichia coli, Bacteroides fragilis, Campylobacter spp. and group B streptococci. STIs account for over 85% of all acute presentations of PID.[1] Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease can be caused by indolent and difficult to culture organisms, like Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Actinomyces spp.[1] Her vaginal swab was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis PCR and urine culture was negative.
Actinomyces is an anaerobic, gram-positive organism that is known to colonize the female genital tract and can often colonize intrauterine devices.[2] The initial description of Actinomyces causing an ascending pelvic infection was published in 1895, with additional reports over the next 100 years describing infections in the setting of intrauterine foreign bodies.[3] Despite this association, diagnosis of Actinomyces pelvic infection is difficult. Actinomyces -like organisms can be seen on Pap tests in up to 7% of women with intrauterine devices, but true infection and abscess formation is rare.[4] When an abscess forms, the radiographic appearance can often be mistaken for malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, or appendicitis.[5] Actinomyces is an indolent organism and, thus, many women may not have symptoms of infection, but will instead present with an abdominal mass that may mimic malignancy.[6] Therefore, a combination of symptoms, radiographic appearance, culture and immunohistochemistry are used to make the diagnosis of Actinomyces pelvic infection.
Intrauterine device removal is critical in management of Actinomyces pelvic infections; surgery is reserved for extensive disease, given the risk of infertility.[6] Antimicrobial therapy with a beta-lactam is considered the mainstay of treatment for Actinomyces pelvic infections and usually includes an induction with intravenous therapy followed by prolonged oral treatment.

title: A woman in her 70s, originally from Ethiopia, was brought into the emergency dep
history:
A woman in her 70s, originally from Ethiopia, was brought into the emergency department (ED) after developing respiratory distress at a subacute rehabilitation center; upon arrival in the ED, she had rapid respiratory deterioration requiring intubation. The patient had a history of a left frontal glioblastoma multiforme resected 3 months ago; she was subsequently treated with adjuvant radiotherapy and dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, complicated by steroid-induced diabetes. She also had Clostridium difficile colitis 3 weeks ago, and was on a 6-week tapering course of oral vancomycin.
On admission, she was in septic shock with a high lactic acid level of 2.27 mmol/L (normal range, 0.5-2.0 mmol/L), systolic blood pressures of 60s and tachycardia. She was noted to have significant loose watery stools. She was started empirically on intravenous vancomycin, ceftazidime and metronidazole and enteric vancomycin and intravenous dexamethasone.

Hypertension on aldactone; gastroesophageal reflux disease

She had immigrated to the US nearly 10 years ago from Ethiopia. She does not use alcohol, tobacco or illicit drugs.

Dexamethasone; Lacosamide (anti-epileptic); Enteric Vancomycin taper
exam_studies:
She was intubated and ventilated. Maximum temperature over 24 hours 37.4°C (99.3°F); blood pressure 100-110/60-70s; pulse 98, respiratory rate 32; FIO2 50%/PEEP 5. She had marked bilateral crepitations throughout her lung fields and especially prominent at the bases. She had no cardiac murmurs. Her abdomen was distended but soft with hypoactive bowel sounds. Rectal tube was in situ with copious watery clear stool. There was diffuse pitting edema of her trunk, arms, and legs.

Chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral infiltrates (Figure 1). Colonic gaseous distension (primarily in the sigmoid colon) was seen on abdominal X-ray (Figure 2).
She had a normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 7.7 g/dL (normal range, 11.4-14.4) and MCV of 94 fl. Her white cell count was normal with a normal differential. She had mild electrolyte abnormality with a slightly low sodium, potassium and calcium. Liver function tests were normal.
Respiratory Viral PCR, stool Clostridium difficile toxin and blood cultures were negative. Urine culture revealed E. coli. Bronchoalveolar lavage (performed by a catheter without a bronchoscope or camera) showed 27,111 cells (97% PMNs, 3% macrophages, no squamous cells); cultures showed no growth.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed small non-occlusive acute pulmonary emboli and diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities with ground glass opacifications and architectural distortion most severe in the right upper lobe (Figures 3 and 4). The abdomen had dilated fluid-filled descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum with mild wall thickening consistent with mild colitis. CT brain showed changes consistent with left frontal tumor resection.
Figure 1. Admission portable chest radiograph with widespread bilateral bronchogenic opacities.
Figure 2. Admission abdominal radiograph showing extensive colonic gaseous distension primarily in the sigmoid colon.
Figure 3. CT scan of chest (axial view) showing diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities with ground-glass opacities.
Figure 4. CT scan of chest (coronal view) showing diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities with ground-glass opacities.
diagnosis:
Strongyloides stercoralis Hyperinfection in an immunocompromised patient on chronic steroids

Stool ova and parasite testing was positive for Strongyloides stercoralis (Figure 5). Given her immunocompromised state (on chronic steroids), stool evidence of Strongyloides, extensive pulmonary infiltrates and septic shock, there was concern for Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome. The BAL ova and parasite testing was also positive for Strongyloides sterocoralis (Figure 6). Her serum Strongyloides IgG by Elisa was negative. Although she never had peripheral eosinophilia during this admission, in retrospect she demonstrated eosinophilia of 16% four months ago (prior to surgery and steroids).
Figure 5. Stool ova and parasites showing Strongyloides
Figure 6. BAL showing Strongyloides

She was treated with oral ivermectin and albendazole and her BAL and stools were negative for Strongyloides after one week. Unfortunately she developed progressive worsening respiratory status, hemodynamic instability, and died several weeks into her hospitalization.

Strongylodies stercoralis is a parasitic nematode endemic in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Sub-Saharan African, and parts of the Southeast United States.[1] It is estimated that 30-100 million people are infected worldwide.[2] Symptoms of Strongyloides infection can range from asymptomatic to a hyperinfection syndrome, the latter of which can carry mortality up to 90%.[3] Impaired host immunity, such as corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, can lead to an overwhelming number of larvae. Despite this, in hyperinfection syndrome, peripheral eosinophilia is often absent.[3]
Signs and symptoms that can be seen with Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome include gastrointestinal manifestations (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, ileus, obstruction, peritonitis) and pulmonary manifestations (coughing, wheezing, consolidations on chest imaging, respiratory failure). Other manifestations include neurologic complications (aseptic or gram negative meningitis) and recurrent gram negative bacteremia/sepsis from larvae carrying bacteria that penetrate mucosal walls. Skin manifestations, including maculopapular or urticarial rash, can be found anywhere on the skin but usually on the buttocks, perineum and thighs.[3] Autoinfection is a unique characteristic of Strongyloides in which it is able to reenter the host’s circulation (via the perianal mucosa) allowing for continuous multiplication.
The Centers for Disease Control recommends consideration of screening for Strongyloides in patients with the following conditions: HTLV-1 infection; hematologic malignancies (including leukemias and lymphomas); organ transplant recipients or candidates; persistent or unexplained eosinophilia; recent or remote travel histories to endemic areas; those who are on, or about to begin, corticosteroid therapy or other immunosuppressants.[3] The sensitivity of serologic testing in chronic intestinal Strongyloidiasis is approximately 90% but there is potential for false positive results.[5] False positive results can occur with cross-reaction with other filarial parasites. In Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome, there is possibility for false-negative results in immunocompromised patients.[5] While eosinophilia may serve as a clue to underlying parasitic diseases, the peripheral eosinophil count is rarely elevated in patients with Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome.[5]
The diagnosis of Strongyloides stercoralis infection requires a high index of suspicion. The prompt diagnosis of hyperinfection syndrome is of utmost importance due to high patient mortality. Strongyloides should be considered in patients from endemic areas who are immunocompromised, especially if on corticosteroids, and even in those who lack peripheral eosinophilia. Strongyloides is often treated with ivermectin.[3] Treatment of Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome includes stopping or reducing immunosuppressive therapy, if possible, and enteric ivermectin daily until stool and/or sputum examinations are negative for 2 weeks.[3] Parenteral ivermectin is FDA approved for veterinary use only. There are case reports of improved efficacy of combination treatment with ivermectin and albendazole.[4]
Lessons learned from this case include considering Strongyloides in the differential diagnosis of patients from endemic areas; screening patients from endemic areas prior to starting immunosuppressive agents (including corticosteroids); and that serum eosinophilia may be absent, and Strongyloides serology may be negative, in hyperinfection syndrome.

title: An immunosuppressed man in his sixties on adalimumab, methotrexate and prednison
history:
An immunosuppressed man in his sixties on adalimumab, methotrexate and prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis presented with 3 weeks of generalized weakness and fatigue, palpitations and confusion preceded by 3 days of dry cough. He reported chills during the first few days but no fever or night sweats. He had no headache, blurry vision, chest pain, diarrhea, rash, dysuria, weight loss. He reported recent constipation.
He was noted to be in atrial fibrillation (AF) with rapid ventricular rate of 120 per minute, and was sent to a tertiary care center emergency room where he was admitted to the cardiology service for anticoagulation and rate control. He reported a self-resolving episode of post-operative AF and had had an acute myocardial infarction many years ago, which was complicated by mitral regurgitation necessitating valve replacement. His dry cough apparently occurred annually which he attributed to allergies. He experienced no rhinorrhea or post nasal drip.

1. Rheumatoid arthritis on adalimumab (TNF-alpha blocker) every two weeks, methotrexate 15mg oral tablet weekly, and prednisone 10mg oral tablet daily
2. Skin squamous cell carcinoma

He is a teetotaler, is married and in a monogamous relationship. He works in construction and lives in Tennessee. He has a dog and cats; all of them stay primarily indoors. He has no known exposure history to tuberculosis. There was no significant recent travel.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared comfortable but paused to take a breath after every 2-3 words. His blood pressure was 101/63 mm Hg, pulse was irregular at 89 beats per minute, temperature 98.4°F (Max 100 ° F earlier that day), and respirations 24 breaths per minute. Despite him pausing to take breaths as above, he did not appear to be in distress, nor was he using accessory muscles of respiration. He was oriented but easily distracted. While most of his speech was intact, he would occasionally utter an incomprehensible word. This mental status was noted to be improved according to family who noted confusion prior to his admission. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. The only other positive finding on examination was some tenderness to palpation over his prior adalimumab injection sites at the left lower abdominal quadrant.

The white cell count was 11.2 x 10³ cells per cubic milliliter (normal range, 3.9-10.7) and platelet count of 110 x 10³ cells per cubic milliliter (135-371). Other abnormal initial laboratory findings included a creatinine of 1.72 milligrams per deciliter (0.72-1.25) and a calcium level of 12.7 milligrams per deciliter (8.4-10.5), ionized calcium of 6.38 milligrams per deciliter (4.48-5.28). The albumin level was 2.3 grams per deciliter (thus with a corrected calcium level of 14.1 milligrams per deciliter).
The parathyroid hormone (PTH) level was 4 picograms per milliliter (normal range, 16-77), 25-hydroxy vitamin D level was 44 nanograms per milliliter (25-80), and the 1,25 dihydroxy-vitamin D level was 177 picograms per milliliter (19.9-79.3). PTH related protein was below the detectable range. Serum and urine protein electrophoreses were normal. Blood cultures were negative.
Computed tomography of the chest revealed multiple mildly enlarged nodes in the mediastinum, supraclavicular region, mesentery and retroperitoneum, the largest measuring 1.5 centimeters (see Figure 1).
Figure 1. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest demonstrating enlarged mediastinal, supraclavicular, mesenteric, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, the largest of which was 1.52 cm in diameter (red arrow).

Patient’s mental status and constipation resolved with improvement in the calcium level after intravenous hydration. Given that this symptomatic hypercalcemia appeared to be driven by an elevated 1,25 dihydroxy-vitamin D, diagnostic studies aimed at elucidating its etiology were planned. During hospital stay, he developed worsening shortness of breath.
diagnosis:
Symptomatic hypercalcemia secondary to histoplasmosis

An ultrasound guided right supraclavicular lymph node core biopsy was performed. A DiffQuik -stained touch preparation showed macrophages with numerous small (3-4 microns) intracytoplasmic yeast forms consistent with histoplasmosis. This was confirmed on Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) and Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-diastase stained samples. The biopsy revealed significant granulomatous inflammation (see Figure 3).
His urine and serum histoplasma antigen returned positive at 2.42 ng/mL and 13.5 ng/mL, respectively.
Figure 2. A Diff-Quik stained specimen from a right supraclavicular lymph node core biopsy at 40X magnification reveals macrophages with numerous small (3-4 microns) intracytoplasmic yeast forms consistent with histoplasmosis (red arrow).
Figure 3. H&E stain of the right supraclavicular lymph node core biopsy demonstrating granulomatous inflammation (red arrow) and giant cells (blue arrow). (40x)

He was started on liquid itraconazole loading dose of 200 mg three times a day for three days, followed by maintenance dose of 200 mg twice a day, with plans to treat for at least a year.
He was seen in Infectious Diseases Clinic a month later for follow up. He noted a significant improvement in his respiratory symptoms. His rheumatologist discontinued adalimumab. The urine and serum histoplasma antigen levels were noted to slowly be decreasing.

Histoplasma are common endemic fungi, found most abundantly in the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys in the United States [1]. They are dimorphic, found in the soil as mold, usually in soil contaminated with bird and bat droppings [1]. When its spores are inhaled, it transforms into its yeast form in the host tissue [2]. Most patients exposed to Histoplasma infection either remain asymptomatic or experience a self-limiting non-specific flu-like syndrome [2]. Occasionally, patients become symptomatic with pulmonary histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis can disseminate in certain patients, especially those with a compromised immune system (about 1 in 2000 cases) [3]. This can result in systemic symptoms such as low-grade fevers, weight loss, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy. Rarely, hypercalcemia can be seen with this infection, which is attributed to increased production of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D in the granulomas [4]. Symptomatic hypercalcemia as the initial presentation of this infection is extremely rare, and can result in a diagnostic dilemma [4-12].
Only 9 previous reported instances of disseminated histoplasmosis presenting with hypercalcemia have been reported in the literature [4-12]. Among these, only two cases were on immunosuppressive medications: one was a 56-year-old male who was status-post splenectomy and was on steroid therapy [5]; the other was a 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on infliximab, methotrexate, and prednisone, similar to the case presented here [10]. TNF-alpha, a pro-inflammatory cytokine, is required for the efficient clearing of intracellular pathogens and in the formation of granulomas [13]. Thus, the use of TNF-alpha inhibitors may increase the chance of developing chronic granulomatous infections such as histoplasmosis [14].
In our case, his initial presentation of dehydration, constipation, and confusion resolved quickly with intravenous hydration and correction of the hypercalcemia. Further workup revealed that the hypercalcemia was not mediated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), given his suppressed PTH level. With his constellation of symptoms and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on imaging, malignancy was high on the differential. Thus, a PTH related protein (PTHrP) was checked, which was negative. The next step was to look at the levels of both 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D and 25 hydroxy vitamin D – usually elevated in granulomatous inflammation and the use of supplements, respectively. The elevated 1,25 vitamin D level pointed towards a granulomatous inflammatory process such as sarcoidosis, histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, etc. The biopsy and the urine histoplasma antigen helped to confirm the diagnosis of histoplasmosis. Sensitivity of the urine histoplasma antigen is higher in more severe disease as well as in immunocompromised patients. A multicenter study in 2011 found that in disseminated infection, antigen testing sensitivity was 91.8% and 100% when tested in urine and serum respectively. Specificity was noted to be 99% among healthy subjects and in patients with nonfungal infections. However, cross-reactivity was noted in patients with blastomycosis [15].
Given the involvement of multiple non-contiguous lymph nodes, the infection was disseminated. He was assessed to have mild-to-moderate disease given his hemodynamic stability. He was treated with itraconazole, in accordance with guidelines [16], and responded to this medication
This case highlights the importance of the need for a high index of suspicion for atypical presentations of relatively common endemic infections. These can mimic other conditions such as malignancy, thus delaying accurate diagnosis and, potentially, life-saving therapy.

title: A man in his forties with HIV/AIDS diagnosed one year ago (nadir CD4 of 25 cells
history:
A man in his forties with HIV/AIDS diagnosed one year ago (nadir CD4 of 25 cells/uL and a current CD4 count of 55 cells/uL) was admitted to the hospital with a new tonic-clonic seizure and altered mental state. He was on tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz as well as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and azithromycin as prophylaxis but had been non-adherent for the last 6 months and had been lost to follow-up.

He had no other past medical history. No drug allergies.

The patient was born, bred and was living in Paraguay. He reported no domestic or international travel. He denied injection drug use or history of blood transfusions. He is a heterosexual but has not been sexually active in the last year. He had no animal exposures.
exam_studies:
On examination, the patient was cachectic, responsive, but oriented to person only. His blood pressure was 105/70 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats per minute, temperature 96.8ºF (36.0 º C), and respirations 22 breaths per minute. He was able to follow simple commands and exhibited mild dysarthria. The reminder of the physical examination was normal.

The white cell count was 2410/uL (reference range 4500–11000), lymphocyte count was 650/uL (1000-4800), CD4 was 55 cells/uL (5%), and HIV viral load 95,350 copies/mL. The remainder of the blood work was unremarkable.
A non-contrast CT scan of the head showed a lesion in the medial frontoparietal region which was centrally hypodense, peripherally hyperdense, and with surrounding edema (Figure 1).
Figure 1. CT Brain (non-contrast) at admission demonstrating a large hypodense lesion in medial frontoparietal area with peripheral enhancement and surrounding edema (red arrow).

A lumbar puncture was performed which showed a clear cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with a normal opening pressure of 100 millimetre of water (reference range 60-200), white blood count of 13 cells/uL (100% lymphocytes), elevated protein level of 87 mg/dL (15-45), and low glucose level of 37 mg/dL (50-80); serum glucose was 106 mg/dL (<100).
diagnosis:
Meningoencephalitis and chagoma, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi

Direct examination of CSF showed numerous flagellar organisms, consistent with trypomastigote form of Trypanosoma cruzi (Figures 2a and 2b, Video 1). India ink staining was negative for Cryptococcus. Result of serum Trypanosoma cruzi enzyme linked immunoassay (ELISA) was positive and anti-Toxoplasma IgG was negative.
Figure 2. Figure 2a. Direct microscopic exam of CSF (10x) demonstrating a Trypanosoma cruzi trypomastigote (red arrows showing its kinetoplast and flagellum)
Figure 2a. Direct microscopic exam of CSF (10x) demonstrating a Trypanosoma cruzi trypomastigote (red arrows showing its kinetoplast and flagellum)
Figure 3. Follow-up CT Brain (non-contrast) at 10 months demonstrating A) calcification of the lesion in the medial frontoparietal area with an area of encephalomalacia and B) a right calcified frontal lesion that was not apparent in the initial imaging study.
Figure 2b. Direct microscopic exam of CSF (10x) demonstrating a Trypanosoma cruzi trypomastigote (red arrows showing its nucleus, kinetoplast and flagellum)

The patient was started on benznidazole 5mg/kg/day (divided in 2 doses). Antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz and prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were also re-started. The patient's mental status improved within 72 hours, and he was discharged home to complete 60 days of benznidazole. Five months after diagnosis, the patient had steady neurological improvement with decreased frequency of convulsive episodes; repeat CD4 count was 248 cells/uL and HIV viral load was undetectable. A follow-up CT scan done 10 months after the diagnosis of Chagas meningoencephalitis revealed calcification of the lesion in the medial frontoparietal region with an area of encephalomalacia and a right calcified frontal lesion that was not apparent in his initial imaging study (Figure 3).
Figure 4. Follow-up CT Brain (non-contrast) at 10 months demonstrating A) calcification of the lesion in the medial frontoparietal area with an area of encephalomalacia and B) a right calcified frontal lesion that was not apparent in the initial imaging study.

Chagas disease, or American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi (T. cruzi).[1] It is primarily transmitted by hematophagous “kissing bugs” insects of the family Reduviidae and subfamily T riatominae, also known as vinchuca (Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, and Paraguay), barbeiro (Brazil), chipo (Venezuela), and chinche (Central America).[2] The vectors live in cracks and holes of rustic homes and acquire the trypomastigote forms of the parasite after feeding on blood from infected humans or animals (armadillos, marsupials, domestic animals).[2]
The ingested trypomastigotes transform into epimastigotes in the triatominae’s midgut where they multiply and differentiate into metacyclic tripomastigotes. Humans become infected when the vector defecates during or immediately after its blood meal and fecal material containing metacyclic trypomastigote is inoculated through mucosal membranes or skin breaks.[3] The metacyclic trypomastigotes invade cells from tissues and inside the cells they can transform in amastigotes which can continue intracellular replication or be released into the circulation as bloodstream trypomastigotes.[4] Chagas disease transmission can also occur via consumption of contaminated food or drink, transfusion of blood products, organ transplantation, intravenous drug use or by the transplacental route.[1] Current estimates suggest that 5-18 million people are infected. Previously confined to rural areas of Central and South America where the vector is endemic, the present distribution includes areas of the United States and Europe due to migration.[5]
The clinical manifestations of Chagas disease vary according to whether the infection is acute, chronic, or a reactivation of chronic infection. The acute phase of Chagas disease infection can be subclinical or associated with nonspecific systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, anorexia) and inflammatory reaction at the inoculation site (known as chagoma).[6] Trypomastigotes may be visualized in the blood during 8-12 weeks of the acute phase. Approximately 70% of patients will progress to a chronic “indeterminate” phase, during which individuals are asymptomatic and anti- T. cruzi antibodies can be detected in the absence of parasitemia.[6] Thirty percent of patients will develop clinical manifestations of chronic infection such as gastric motility disorder and cardiomyopathy.[1]
Reactivation of chronic T. cruzi infection is rare, but may occur in immunosuppressed individuals.[7] In HIV-infected patients with chronic T. cruzi, reactivation can lead to high morbidity and mortality. In patients with a CD4 count < 200 cells/uL, meningoencephalitis or focal cerebral abscess (chagoma) is the most common reported manifestation of reactivation.[8,9] Clinical and radiographic CNS manifestations during reactivation are nonspecific and can mimic other opportunistic infections, such as toxoplasmosis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcosis, or neoplastic processes. Because it shares significant epidemiological, clinical, and radiographic similarities with Toxoplasma gondii, cerebral T. cruzi should be considered in the differential diagnosis of meningoencephalitis syndromes and CNS lesions in HIV-infected patients with substantial exposure to endemic areas or pertinent risk factors in whom cerebral toxoplasmosis is suspected.
Diagnosis of Chagas reactivation is achieved by direct visualization of the parasite by microscopy of fresh anticoagulated blood or buffy coat.[1] In cases of meningoencephalitis, trypomastigotes may be seen in direct examination of the cerebrospinal fluid and amastigotes may be found on histological examination of brain tissue.[10,11] Because T. cruzi meningoencephalitis is relatively uncommon, most cases are initially misdiagnosed as toxoplasma encephalitis. In the appropriate epidemiological setting, parasitological or histopathological studies for diagnosis of T. cruzi reactivation should be considered at the time of patient’s initial presentation and among those with inadequate response to toxoplasma therapy to avoid delay or erroneous treatment.
The optimal treatment in immunocompromised individuals with Chagas disease reactivation remains uncertain.[1] Treatment with benznidazole or nifurtimox are currently used; both drugs that have proven to be efficacious in non-immunocompromised patients.[12] Because of the better side effect profile and the reportedly better clinical outcomes in a small series of treated HIV-infected patients with T. cruzi infection, standard dose of benznidazole 5 mg/kg daily divided into two doses for 60 days is commonly used as first line treatment.[6,8] Reported adverse effects include dermatitis, peripheral neuropathy, and bone marrow suppression. There are no well documented cases of Chagas-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in patients infected with HIV following initiation of antiretroviral therapy; therefore, the current recommendation is to start antiretroviral therapy as soon as the patient is clinically stable.[14]
The appropriate follow up evaluation for monitoring response to treatment in patients with CNS Chagas reactivation has not been formally evaluated. Clinical evaluation and direct examination of blood or buffy coat can be used to monitor treatment failure.[1] The role of radiologic monitoring after initiation of treatment is unclear. A small number of case reports have described partial regression of brain lesions, calcification, and encephalomalacia in neuroimaging studies obtained after initiation of therapy.[3,15]
In conclusion, T. cruzi should be considered as a differential diagnosis in HIV-infected patients presenting with meningoencephalitis or space-occupying CNS lesions who are from endemic areas or have relevant risk factors. Clinicians should be familiar with clinical manifestations and diagnostics of T. cruzi CNS reactivation because it may mimic opportunistic infections commonly found in immunosuppressed persons. Delay in diagnosis can lead to neurologic sequelae or mortality.[3]
