title: A previously well woman in her fifties, presented with fatigue, confusion and fe
history:
A previously well woman in her fifties, presented with fatigue, confusion and fever for 3 days. Her family physician prescribed azithromycin, but later that day, she was brought to the emergency room with worsening confusion and word finding difficulty. She felt that her thinking was not normal. She denied headache, cough, dysuria, or changes in bowel or bladder function.

She lived in a town in Midwestern US. She was an avid outdoors person and was frequently out in wooded areas. She had a desk job and did not use alcohol or illicit drugs.
She had a 40 pack-year smoking history.

Sulfonamide (rash)
exam_studies:
The patient appeared somnolent. Her blood pressure was 135/72 mmHg, pulse 115 beats per minute, temperature 38.5°C (101.3 ° F), and respirations 24 breaths per minute. She was awake, alert, but oriented only to self with limited attention span. There were faint palpable pink papules over the abdomen and anterior thighs (Figure 1). Heart sounds were normal with no murmurs, and respiratory and abdominal exams were normal. She had no neck stiffness, and no motor or sensory changes.
Figure 1. Erythematous papular rash over anterior right thigh. The patient had the same rash over her back, abdomen, and bilateral thighs.

The complete blood count including platelets and white cell differential were normal. Other routine lab results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. CT of the head without contrast showed no acute intracranial abnormality.

She was started empirically on vancomycin, ceftriaxone and acyclovir. Lumber puncture (LP) was performed after initiation of antimicrobials. Two hours after the LP was performed, a rapid response team was called for worsening somnolence and tachypnea (respiratory rate > 40 breaths/min). She was transferred to the neurologic intensive care unit and was intubated for airway protection. The infectious disease service was consulted, and meropenem and doxycycline were added 24 hours after hospital admission.
Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that was obtained 10 hours after antibiotics showed elevated total nucleated cell count of 146/uL (9% neutrophils, 56% lymphocytes, and 35% monocytes/ macrophages), 14 erythrocytes/uL, a normal glucose of 70 mg/dL (plasma glucose was 140 mg/dL), and an elevated protein of 109 mg/dL (reference range 0-35). Gram stain was negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on hospital day 2 showed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the left caudate and thalamus and marked leptomeningeal enhancement involving the cerebellum and basal ganglia (Figure 2, 3).
Figure 2. MRI brain without contrast at initial presentation. Axial T2 FLAIR showed T2 hyperintensity at the left thalamus (arrow).
Figure 3. MRI brain with gadolinium contrast at initial presentation. Axial T2 FLAIR showed T2 hyperintensity at the left substantia nigra (arrow) and leptomeningeal enhancement in the temporal horn of the left lateral ventricle (asterisk).
diagnosis:
Powassan meningoencephalitis

CSF gram stain, fungal smear, bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. CSF PCR tests for herpes simplex 1 and 2, Epstein-Barr virus, Varicella Zoster virus, West Nile virus, Cytomegalovirus, Tropheryma whipplei, Borrelia burgdorferi, B. mayonii, and B. garinii were negative. CSF was positive for immunoglobulin M (IgM) against Powassan virus (POWV) via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Additional CSF was sent to Centers for Disease Control (CDC) for Prevention for Plaque Reduction Neutralization Testing (PRNT), which returned positive.
Nasopharyngeal swab was negative for influenza. Blood cultures were negative. Serum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Anaplasma phagocytophilum and Ehrlichia spp. were negative.

CSF studies for Streptococcal pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenza, and HSV-1, and 2 were negative on hospital day 2, so broad spectrum antibiotics and acyclovir were discontinued. A trial of IV methylprednisolone was initiated on hospital day 3 for possible post-viral encephalitis. Repeat brain MRI on hospital day 5 showed interval improvement. She was extubated on hospital day 13. Patient was transferred out of the ICU on hospital day 18, but she remained abulic, and had residual flaccidity of the right arm accompanied by signs of Parkinsonism. She underwent percutaneous endoscopic gastrotomy (PEG) tube placement for nutrition and was transferred to inpatient rehabilitation unit for a month prior to being discharged to a skilled nursing facility. Unfortunately, she developed additional complications and died a few months after her first presentation to the hospital.

When possible, clinicians are encouraged to distinguish between meningitis syndromes and encephalitis syndromes both to help narrow the differentials and to guide empirical therapy. Typically patients with meningitis present with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and fever. An acute presentation of a meningitis syndrome (1-2 days) is more typical for bacterial causes, 3-10 days more typical of viral meningitis while subacute and chronic headaches raises the possibility of tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis and other fungal and parasitic causes. A brain abscess should be considered particularly in those presenting with focal neurological deficits. In this case, the lymphocytic predominance in the CSF and it being culture negative goes against bacterial causes, although the previous use of antibiotics may affect CSF bacterial cultures.
In contrast, an encephalitis syndrome as seen here is typified by confusion and fevers. A wide variety of viruses can infect the central nervous system, and the treatment for most is supportive. Enterovirus is the most common cause of viral encephalitis. HSV encephalitis should be treated with acyclovir.
Host risk factors, epidemiologic and clinical clues are important in determining the exact pathogen. In this case, the patient was an avid outdoor person living in Midwestern U.S. and presented with symptoms during the fall season; she had several risk factors for mosquito and tick exposure, hence raising concern for CNS infection caused by arboviruses. In the U.S., there is an arbovirus surveillance system managed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state public health departments. In 2015, West Nile virus was the most common cause of arboviral disease (2175 of 2282 cases, 95%). Seven cases of Powassan virus infection were reported – variously from Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Wisconsin (Krow-Lucal, Lindsey et al. 2017).
Powassan virus (POWV) was first isolated in Powassan, Ontario in 1958. Powassan meningoencephalitis is rare, with approximately 100 cases reported since 1958 (Birge and Sonnesyn 2012). POWV is an arbovirus in the family of Flaviviridae. It is transmitted by Ixodes scapularis, Ixodes cookei, and other Ixodes tick species. There are two distinct genetic lineages of POWV that have been recognized: lineage I is transmitted by I. cookei, and lineage II is by I. scapularis (Hermance and Thangamani 2017). POWV can be transmitted within 15 minutes following attachment to the host (Ebel 2010). The incubation period ranges from 1 to 5 weeks (Ebel 2010, Birge and Sonnesyn 2012). Presenting symptoms of Powassan virus meningoencephalitis include fever, confusion, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. Rash and gastrointestinal symptoms may also be present.
Pathogenesis is related to the perivascular and parenchymal infiltrate of lymphocytes, more often involving the gray matter (Gholam, Puksa et al. 1999). CSF analysis usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and elevated protein. Diagnosis is made by clinical findings with positive IgM antibody against Powassan virus in serum or CSF, and the positive test is confirmed at CDC with PRNT. (Johnson, Staples et al. 2010, Raval, Singhal et al. 2012).
Cases in the United States have been reported in the Northeastern and Midwestern states. Of cases reported, 10-15% cases are fatal, and 50% of survivors have residual neurologic deficits. Treatment is supportive. Empiric treatment with high dose corticosteroids or IVIG have been given to patients with POWV encephalitis but their role in changing outcomes is uncertain (Piantadosi, Rubin et al. 2016). In summary, evaluation of viral encephalitis should include CNS imaging and CSF examination with additional testing based on epidemiologic and clinical clues, and clinicians should consider POWV as a cause for viral encephalitis in patients hailing from or travelling through the Great Lakes region.

title: A man in his twenties from Jordan visited the emergency department (ED) due to g
history:
A man in his twenties from Jordan visited the emergency department (ED) due to gradual onset of diffuse abdominal pain with weight loss over 3 months. He described the pain as colicky and slightly worse on the right side. He was afebrile. Laboratory testing, including complete blood count and liver function tests, were normal and he was discharged with ibuprofen.
His abdominal pain continued to worsen and he came back to the ED three weeks later. At that time, computed tomography (CT) of abdomen and pelvis showed multiple cystic lesions in his liver and mesentery. A general surgeon reviewed the patient, referred him to infectious diseases clinic and planned a surgical resection of the mesenteric cyst for diagnostic purposes and to avoid the risk of rupture.
He was seen in ID clinic three weeks later, just prior to his planned surgery and complained of worsening abdominal pain in the last 3 days, inability to lie supine and new night sweats without fever.

None

He was born and raised in the Middle East and moved to United States a few years before this presentation. He was not currently working. He had no significant animal or occupational exposure, no recent travel, and no significant outdoor activities. He was an omnivore but avoided pork.

None
exam_studies:
On examination, his temperature was 37.0ºC, blood pressure 132/58 mmHg, pulse rate 89 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. He was not cachectic or icteric but looked uncomfortable due to his abdominal pain. His abdomen was soft and non-distended with generalized tenderness but there was no rebound. He had no organomegaly, palpable masses or skin lesions. His bowel sounds were slightly decreased. He had no palpable lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Complete blood count showed mild microcytic anemia [Hb 12.6 g/dL (normal range, 12.9-16.8), MCV 79.3 fl (81.9-97.8)]. There was no leukocytosis, but he had developed a new eosinophilia of 18.2% (0.4-5.8) and a raised CRP of 9.9 (normal < 0.5) and ESR 64 (normal <14). Liver function tests were normal.
Hepatitis A IgM, IgG, Hepatitis B sAg, cAb, sAb, Hepatitis C Ab, and 4th generation HIV test were all negative. Both QuantiFERON-TB Gold and Echinococcus IgG Ab (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay reflex to western blot, Quest diagnostics) were negative.
Chest X-ray showed no significant abnormality. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe (77x86x 83mm) and caudate lobe (49x58x54mm) (Figure 1a and b). There was a large unilocular thin-walled cystic lesion in the mesentery (67x100x85mm) (Figure 1c, arrow).
Figure 1. Figure 1a. Coronal section of CT abdomen. Arrows indicate two large hypoechoic liver lesions; the regular walls are consistent with cystic lesions. Also indicated: a large cystic lesion in the small bowel mesentery.
Figure 1a. Coronal section of CT abdomen. Arrows indicate two large hypoechoic liver lesions; the regular walls are consistent with cystic lesions. Also indicated: a large cystic lesion in the small bowel mesentery.
Figure 2. Macroscopic picture of ruptured mesenteric cyst
Figure 1b. Axial section of CT abdomen.
Figure 3. Microscopic features of the ruptured mesenteric cyst (at low power) demonstrating multiple layers of parasite-derived cyst wall
Figure 1c. Axial section of CT abdomen.

Cystic Echinococcosis was strongly suspected but the Echinococcus IgG Ab was negative. Oral albendazole was started and the patient was admitted for laparotomy and excision of mesenteric cyst, which he had the next day.
diagnosis:
Cystic Echinococcosis with mesenteric hydatid cyst

During the operation, a substantial amount of turbid fluid was noted in the peritoneal cavity upon entry. The ruptured cyst wall was partially removed (some was adherent to the intestinal wall and unable to be removed) and sent for pathology. The abdominal cavity was copiously irrigated with saline.
The removed cyst wall (Figure 2) consisted of a tan rubbery soft tissue fragment measuring 85x60 mm and ranging from 3 to 6mm with attached fibro-adipose tissue measuring 40x35x6 mm. One surface was tan, smooth and the opposite was hemorrhagic and nodular. Microscopic examination revealed laminated cyst wall and fragments of cyst wall (Figure 3) with granulomatous foreign body reaction, chronic inflammation and fibrosis (Figure 4), consistent with Echinococcal cyst wall.
Figure 4. Microscopic features of the ruptured mesenteric cyst (at high power)
Figure 5. Microscopic features of the ruptured mesenteric cyst (at low power) demonstrating multiple layers of parasite-derived cyst wall
Figure 6. CT abdomen at 7 months of follow- up demonstrating compromised integrity of the cyst consistent with transitional phase

Surgical pathology confirmed the diagnosis of Cystic Echinococcosis (Echinococcus granulosus). He was continued on oral albendazole and Puncture-Aspiration–Injection–Reaspiration (PAIR) procedure was done to the right hepatic lobe cyst 4 months later (Figure 5). The other hepatic cyst was too close to the portal vein and deemed unsafe for surgical intervention. Given the incidence of mesenteric cyst rupture and remaining hepatic cyst, the plan is to continue oral albendazole for at least 12 months. His liver cysts demonstrated compromised integrity of the cyst consistent with transitional phase (as per WHO classification [1]) 7-months post-treatment (Figure 6).
Figure 7. PAIR (Puncture-Aspiration–Injection–Re-aspiration) of the right hepatic lobe cyst via CT guidance
Figure 8. CT abdomen at 7 months of follow- up demonstrating compromised integrity of the cyst consistent with transitional phase

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common cause of cystic echinococcosis. The Mediterranean, Central Asia and South America are known to be highly endemic regions [2]. Humans are infected by ingestion of eggs. Positive serology is useful to make a diagnosis, but sensitivity is 80-90% in liver disease and less for other lesions [3]. For this reason, the diagnosis should not be ruled out by a negative serology. The most common sites of infection are liver and lung, however other sites of involvement including the mesentery are reported [4].
Eosinophilia is uncommon unless the cyst ruptures [5]. In this case, worsening of abdominal pain with new eosinophilia was likely due to recent cyst rupture.

title: A male in his thirties from West Africa presented with a right corneal ulcer. In
history:
A male in his thirties from West Africa presented with a right corneal ulcer. Initial symptoms started approximately three weeks prior to evaluation with tearing, erythema, swelling and progressive vision loss over a period of one week. He was initially evaluated in West Africa and failed empiric therapy consisting of topical vancomycin, tobramycin and natamycin drops. This prompted him to seek care in the United States.

The patient’s medical history was unremarkable. Active medications included the ones prescribed in West Africa. He is a non-smoker and denied any allergies to medications. He reported no history of ocular disease, contact lens use, or ocular trauma.
exam_studies:
Pertinent findings in physical exam included a dry papular rash on the right side of his forehead, ptosis of right eye, and reduced visual acuity. Slit lamp examination revealed diffuse scleritis and complete corneal opacification by a dense white purulent infiltrate (figure 1).
Figure 1. Appearance at presentation showing diffuse dense corneal infiltration with severe scleral injection and a large hypopyon.

The white blood cell count was 14.28 per deciliter. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 49 IU/L (ref 14-40 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 79 IU/L (10-54 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase 303 IU/L (36-180 IU/L). HIV Antibody/Antigen combo was negative.
diagnosis:
Pythium insidiosum keratitis

Frozen tissue from corneal biopsy stained with Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) demonstrated broad long, sparsely septated hyaline hyphae (Figures 2a and b).
On potato dextrose agar, the surface of the slowly growing colonies was white to colorless with an irregular radiating pattern (Figure 3). The lactophenol cotton blue stain preparation of the culture revealed long broad sparsely septated hyphae arranged at right angles projecting off the main cell body (Figure 4a) and zoospore (Figure 4b). These features were morphologically suggestive of Pythium insidiosum infection. The isolate was sent to University of Texas for sequence identification and was later confirmed as P. insidiosum.
Importantly, P. insidiosum is more closely related to algae than fungi, making antifungal therapy ineffective [1]. Although there are no established breakpoints [2], susceptibilities demonstrated resistance to all antifungals with no synergy.
Figure 2. Figure 2a. Frozen tissue from corneal biopsy stained with GMS demonstrated broad long, sparsely septated hyaline hyphae at 40X augmentation.
Figure 2a. Frozen tissue from corneal biopsy stained with GMS demonstrated broad long, sparsely septated hyaline hyphae at 40X augmentation.
Figure 3. Plate cultures on potato dextrose agar (PDA). The surface of the slowly growing colonies were white to colorless with an irregular radiating pattern.
Figure 2b. Frozen tissue from corneal biopsy stained with GMS demonstrated broad long, sparsely septated hyaline hyphae at 100x augmentation.
Figure 4. Plate cultures on potato dextrose agar (PDA). The surface of the slowly growing colonies were white to colorless with an irregular radiating pattern.
Figure 5. Figure 4a. Lactophenol cotton blue stain preparation of the PDA plate culture revealed long broad sparsely septated hyphae arranged at right angles projecting off of the main cell body at 200X augmentation
Figure 4a. Lactophenol cotton blue stain preparation of the PDA plate culture revealed long broad sparsely septated hyphae arranged at right angles projecting off of the main cell body at 200X augmentation
Figure 6. Figure 4b. Lactophenol cotton blue stain preparation of the PDA plate culture revealed a zoospore at 400X augmentation.
Figure 4b. Lactophenol cotton blue stain preparation of the PDA plate culture revealed a zoospore at 400X augmentation.

The initial suspicion was for fusarium keratitis based on the preliminary pathology result which indicated a filamentous fungal infection. Patient was started on empirical antifungal therapy with topical amphotericin B, voriconazole, natamycin and ultimately systemic therapy with posaconazole was begun, with the intention to achieve optimal eye penetration.
While on therapy, patient underwent penetrating keratoplasty (PK). Intraoperatively, he was noted to have a perforated corneal ulcer with complete corneal melt requiring oversized corneal transplant to close the perforation.
In the meantime, internal sequencing found that the organism was consistent with Pythium insidiosum. While awaiting confirmation from the reference laboratory, we added intravenous micafungin 150mg daily as this particular organism has poor response to azoles due to their lack of ergosterol.
At follow-up examination twenty days post penetrating keratoplasty, there was poor corneal graft re-epithelialization and diffuse scleral injection. The patient developed total limbal stem cell failure, inability of corneal epithelium to repair and renew itself; for this reason, enucleation was considered given lack of response and risk of extraocular spread.
Once result from sequencing and susceptibilities were received, the decision was made to discontinue all systemic antifungals and start intravenous tigecycline. The rationale for starting this antibacterial was based on recent in vitro studies that have shown activity of glycylcyclines, macrolides, aminoglycosides and tetracyclines against P. insidiosum.[3] After starting therapy with tigecycline, there was gradual but progressive reduction of the scleritis (Figure 5). Tigecycline was discontinued after a 10 week course secondary to thrombocytopenia and worsening liver function tests. Although the cornea became opaque, no further thinning or perforation occurred and the surface gradually epithelialized with conjunctiva 6 weeks after completing antibiotics.
Figure 7. Appearance of right eye 4-months after penetrating keratoplasty. Conjunctival surface has covered the cornea but notably absent is the severe diffuse scleritis seen at presentation.

Pythium insidiosum is an aquatic oomycete found in tropical and subtropical environment, usually found in wet swampy areas and has been reported to cause disease in mammals, particularly in horses, dogs and humans. P. insidiosum is a fungus-like organism and its cell wall contains cellulose and beta glucans but not chitin or ergosterol thus rendering it resistant to azoles. This organism develops motile zoospores which serve as the infective propagules and seem to be chemotactically attracted to injured tissue. [4]
Several cases of P. insidiosum infection have been reported in Thailand and India. Cutaneous, vascular, ocular and disseminated forms of Pythiosis have been described. In a case series published in 2013, contaminated water, particularly rainwater and/or floodwater, was the main risk factor for the occurrence of Pythium keratitis.[5] Morbidity is high because response to medical treatment is poor. [4] In a cohort of 11 cases of ocular pythiosis in Thailand, 91% of cases required enucleation.[6]
Failure to identify the organism leads to progression of pythiosis and poor outcomes. Zoospore formation is an important diagnostic tool for identification of Pythium species. Delay in zoospore formation and culture failure are the main challenges in the diagnosis of Pythium spp.. Unlike fungi, Pythium spp. show poor or no staining with PAS stain given their cell wall characteristics. Mittal et al recently developed a simple, quick and inexpensive stain to differentiate the oomycete Pythium spp. from fungal organisms based on potassium iodide sulfuric acid.[7]
The rationale for the use of tigecycline was based on two previously published in vitro susceptibility studies where this agent was found to be promising.[3,8] There is no standard treatment for Pythium insidiosum keratitis. A multidisciplinary approach including penetrating keratoplasty and antimicrobials is important in achieving an optimum outcome.

title: A man in his fifties with a history of deceased-donor renal transplant for diabe
history:
A man in his fifties with a history of deceased-donor renal transplant for diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy presented with two weeks of progressive shortness of breath, fatigue, and bilateral lower extremity swelling. The patient’s renal transplant was two years prior to his presentation. He was originally from Western Africa and had moved to the U.S. over a decade ago.

Primary hypertension
Coronary artery disease status post percutaneous coronary intervention
Insulin dependent diabetes mellitus type II

Non-smoker. He was previously a white-collar worker.

Aspirin, Carvedilol, Mycophenolate mofetil (360 mg twice daily), Tacrolimus (2 mg twice daily), Prednisone (5 mg daily), Nifedipine, Simvastatin.
exam_studies:
Heart Rate: 76 beats per minute and regular, Respiratory Rate: 20 breaths per minute, Temperature 98.6°F (37°C), Blood Pressure 145/95 mmHg, Oxygen Saturation: 100% on room air. He was not distressed and spoke in full sentences. There was no jugular venous distension, murmurs or gallop present. He had good air entry bilaterally with no wheezing or crackles. There was mild 1+ pitting edema in his lower limbs. There was no rash or lymphadenopathy.

There was a small ill-defined nodule in the right mid-lung and a 3cm round mass in the left perihilar region on Chest X-Ray (Figure 1). CT chest without contrast revealed multiple bilateral round nodules involving all lobes some with central cavitation, with the largest in the left hilum, measuring 3.1 x 2.9 x 1.8 cm (Figures 2a and b). A lytic lesion was noted in the L1 vertebral body.
Figure 1. Chest X-Ray showed a 3cm mass near the left hilum and an ill-defined opacity in the right mid lung
Figure 2. Chest CT showed multiple bilateral nodular opacities some with cavitation. The largest nodule was seen in the left hilum (arrow), measuring 3.1 x 2.9 x 1.8 cm.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma var. duboisii, in a renal transplant patient.

Bronchoscopy with fine needle aspiration biopsy of the left upper pulmonary node was performed. Thick-walled, budding yeast were observed upon microscopic examination (Figure 3 and 4) and Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii was recovered from the tissue culture (Figure 5). His Histoplasma urine antigen was weakly positive. Cryptococcal antigen was negative in both serum and CSF; Blastomyces and Coccidiodes serum antibodies were negative; (1,3)-beta-D-glucan and Aspergillus galactomannan serum markers were undetectable.
Figure 3. Silver stain of left perihilar and left upper lobe nodes demonstrating budding yeast (arrow)
Figure 4. Direct tissue-KOH preparation demonstrating a thick-walled yeast with a diameter of 11.43 µm
Figure 5. GMS Stain from culture plates of left hilar node demonstrating thick walled conidia resembling Histoplasma var. duboisii

He was started on oral itraconazole 200 mg twice daily and referred to Infectious Diseases clinic for follow-up. Due to a lack of clinical and radiological response with standard itraconazole therapy, he was switched to posaconazole 300 mg daily. His respiratory symptoms improved and a repeat Chest CT after 4 months showed a decrease size of the left peri-hilar mass and left upper consolidations (Figure 6). Figure 6. Follow-up CT chest without contrast at 4 months demonstrating decrease in size of the left hilar mass
Figure 6. Follow-up CT chest without contrast at 4 months demonstrating decrease in size of the left hilar mass

The clinical presentation of Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii exhibits some differences from that caused by H. capsulatum var. capsulatum. African histoplasmosis usually involves the skin, subcutaneous tissues, lymph nodes and bones unlike classical histoplasmosis, which generally involves lungs and mucosa and less commonly cutaneous or bone lesions. The predilection of duboisii histoplasmosis for the bone, particularly the elements of marrow is characteristic of the disease [1]. Two forms of African histoplasmosis are typically described as a localized chronic form that involves skin, subcutaneous tissue, bones, or lymph nodes; and a disseminated rapidly evolving form, which can also involve the spleen, liver, lungs, and abdominal viscera through hematogenous invasion [2]. African histoplasmosis is not commonly reported in immunosuppressed hosts, however reports in HIV-infected individuals are emerging [3-4]. We did not find any previous reports of African histoplasmosis in solid organ recipients.
Fungal culture remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of histoplasmosis [5]. Differentiating this organism from Cryptococcus is not difficult based on morphology and antigen testing. The cryptococcal encapsulated yeast size diameter is about 5 to 10 µm, and is usually surrounded by empty spaces that reflect the capsule while the yeast form of Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii is typically larger (diameter up to 15 µm). Blastomyces dermatididis is similar in size to H. capsulatum var. duboisii and both exhibit a thick cell wall. However, the diagnosis of blastomycosis requires identification of broad-based buds and/or multiple nuclei compared to Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii which has a narrow-based bud and is uni-nucleated [6]. Histoplasma var. duboisii is also unique in that in vivo it appears similar to B. dermatitidis but in vitro it grows with mycelia similar to H. capsulatum with large, thick-walled round tuberculate macroconidia. Histoplasma antigen detection in serum and urine is a sensitive test but has been developed only for the variety capsulatum, and is not validated for species duboisii [7]. PCR assays have been developed but are not yet routinely used [8].
The treatment of moderate pulmonary histoplasmosis as per the IDSA 2007 clinical practice guidelines is with oral itraconazole; in case of disseminated disease, amphotericin followed by itraconazole is the recommended regimen [9]. Posaconazole has been successfully used as salvage therapy in a pediatric patient with disseminated African histoplasmosis [10,11].

title: A man in his 40s presented with progressive edema and pain of the right lateral
history:
A man in his 40s presented with progressive edema and pain of the right lateral forefoot for one month on a background of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by diabetic neuropathy, erectile dysfunction and diabetic retinopathy. He denied any recent trauma to the foot but recalled dropping a heavy object on his right foot 16 years ago which resulted in a laceration that required suturing. About a month prior to presentation, he noticed pressure and tightness around his right lateral forefoot. The swelling and pain progressed to the point where he had to stop playing soccer as his foot would not fit into his usual shoes. Several days prior to admission, he squeezed the area of swelling and expelled turbid whitish fluid. He consulted his primary care doctor who ordered plain films of the right foot and referred him to the Emergency Department for further work-up.

He has hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and insulin (recent hemoglobin A1C 9.6%). He previously tested positive on tuberculin skin testing decades ago but is unclear if he received isoniazid prophylaxis. Twenty years ago, he developed a right cranial nerve V and cranial nerve VII palsy for which there was no clear diagnosis despite a lumbar puncture and nerve biopsy (also negative for acid fast bacilli). He has no known allergies.

The patient was born and raised in Guatemala. He immigrated to the US about 20 years ago. He lives in the Northeast US and returns to Guatemala every few months with no other significant travel. He recalls being bitten by insects in Guatemala but denies any insect or tick bites in the US. He is a non-smoker. He has no pets.

Medications were amlodipine, lisinopril, simvastatin, aspirin, gabapentin, metformin, short- and long-acting insulin. He was only intermittently adherent.
exam_studies:
On exam, the patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 138/86 mmHg, pulse 89 beats per minute, temperature 37.3 °C (99.2 °F). His right foot showed edema and tenderness to palpation in the area of the 5th toe (Figure 1). There was a small, scabbed skin defect overlying the 5th metatarsophalangeal joint. Active and passive motion in the 5th toe was limited by pain. There was an old, hypopigmented scar on the dorsal midfoot over the 2ndmetatarsal.
Figure 1. Photograph of the right forefoot.

Plain film of his right foot demonstrated diffuse soft tissue swelling of the 5th toe and lateral foot as well as cortical irregularity of the lateral aspect of the 5thmetatarsal shaft and head (Figure 2). Routine laboratory tests, including white blood cell count and C reactive protein, were normal except for hyperglycemia. A hemoglobin A1c was 9.6% (reference range 4.3-6.4%). Uric acid was normal. A T-spot interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative. An HIV screening test had been negative. Figure 2. Plain XR film of the right foot. Arrows indicate: diffuse soft tissue swelling of the 5th toe and lateral foot; cortical irregularity of the lateral aspect of the 5th metatarsal shaft and head
Figure 2. Plain XR film of the right foot. Arrows indicate: diffuse soft tissue swelling of the 5th toe and lateral foot; cortical irregularity of the lateral aspect of the 5th metatarsal shaft and head

An MRI with intravenous contrast of the foot was performed (Figures 3 and 4) which demonstrated an enhancing, infiltrative appearing soft tissue mass involving the proximal phalanx of the right 5th toe. This also extended into and around the tendon sheath and along the dorsum of the foot, around the extensor tendons and the subcutaneous fat. There was also patchy marrow enhancement in the more proximal 5th metatarsal shaft consistent with osteomyelitis.
Figure 3. Figure 3: MRI of the right foot - T1 sagittal (post-contrast). Arrows indicate: infiltrative soft tissue mass centered within 5th toe; patchy marrow edema in the metatarsal shaft suggestive of osteomyelitis
Figure 3: MRI of the right foot - T1 sagittal (post-contrast). Arrows indicate: infiltrative soft tissue mass centered within 5th toe; patchy marrow edema in the metatarsal shaft suggestive of osteomyelitis
Figure 4. MRI of the right foot – T1 short axis (post- contrast). Arrow indicates: infiltrative soft tissue mass centered within 5th toe, traversing multiple compartments
diagnosis:
Eumycetoma due to infection with Biatriospora (Pyrenochaeta) mackinnonii

An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the mass was obtained. Histology showed granular mycelial growth of pigmented hyphae with a granular-histiocytic inflammatory response (Figure 5) diagnostic of eumycetoma (maduromycosis). Speciation of the fungal organism based on histologic appearance was not possible. Several weeks after the initial encounter with our patient, a fungal organism grew on culture that was characterized as a dematiaceous (melanized) mold and eventually identified as Biatriospora (previously Pyrenochaeta) mackinnonii.
Figure 5. Histopathology of soft tissue biopsy from right foot. Giemsa stain (40x). Arrows indicate: granular mycelial growth of pigmented hyphae fungi with a granulo-histiocytic inflammatory response

The patient was started on voriconazole that he has tolerated well. A voriconazole trough level has been therapeutic. There is only sparse evidence, mainly on the case-report level, guiding the treatment of eumycetoma. Therapy usually consists of several months to years of antifungal treatment and may involve surgery depending on extension of disease and clinical trajectory. One year after initiation of treatment, our patient had mild persistent pain in the foot, and on imaging showed some improvement of the soft tissue inflammation, however, bone involvement had progressed and, in addition to stable disease on the 5th proximal phalanx, there was now near complete marrow replacement in the 5th metatarsal. A 5th ray amputation has been discussed with the patient, to which he has agreed. In addition to surgery, we are planning to continue the antifungal treatment and monitor the patient clinically.

There are over 100 species of dematiaceous or melanized (pigmented) fungi (mostly molds) which are known to cause human disease. They have a worldwide distribution and are mostly found in soil or associated with plant matter. Biatriospora (previously Pyrenochaeta) mackinnonii is one of the rarer dematiaceous molds, and is also a soil, wood and plant matter organism. More common examples of dematiaceous molds include Madurella spp., Fonsecaea spp., Cladiosporium spp. and Alternaria spp.. There are a few specific clinical syndromes which are attributed to dematiaceous fungi, such as mycetoma and chromoblastocyosis, both seen predominantly in the tropics, and phaeohyphomycosis and other conditions such as sinusitis, allergic reactions or central nervous system infections.
Mycetoma represents a chronic progressive granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue.[1] It has been described worldwide but is much more common in the tropics and subtropical areas.[2,3] It is characterized by the triad of local edema (typically painless), sinus tracts and discharge with granules or grains (often visible).[4] Clinically, bacterial mycetoma (actinomycetoma, most commonly caused by Nocardia brasiliensis) is indistinguishable from fungal mycetoma (eumycetoma, most commonly caused by Madurella spp. and Pseudallescheria boydii, an anamorph of Lomentospora (previously Scedosporium) apiospermum).[6]
Eumycetoma has been described as a “deep tissue infection, usually of the lower extremities, characterized by the presence of mycotic granules.”[8] There is a male predominance (5:1). In most cases, the feet are affected. Small injuries when walking barefoot in the tropics can lead to inoculation with these fungal organisms that are usually not very virulent.[5] The formation of grain-like structures filled with densely packed organisms protects the fungi from the immune response. The lesions are typically firm and nontender and there usually is no erythema.
Chromoblastomycosis (also called chromomycosis or verrucous dermatitis) is a term used for fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, in most cases caused by one of only a few species of dematiaceous fungi that produce characteristic sclerotic bodies in tissue and is usually seen in tropical areas.[8] Since it primarily affects the skin, it tends to be more superficial and, in contrast to eumycetoma, there is mostly visible skin involvement with lesions that appear patchy, nodular, or scar-like (and can therefore clinically resemble other diseases of the skin). Whereas eumycetoma and chromoblastomycosis are predominantly local infections, phaeohyphomycosis is a term generally reserved for the remainder of clinical syndromes caused by melanized fungi, including disseminated infections.
Besides actinomycetoma, the differential includes tuberculous osteomyelitis, atypical mycobacterial infection, and malignancy. Further evaluation is important to guide the choice of treatment. Unless the diagnosis can be confirmed by the secretion of the typical granules with elements of melanized mold, given the broad differential, usually a biopsy is required to distinguish eumycetoma from other, non-fungal infections and malignancy. Histology usually shows the densely packed fungi.
On microscopy, bacterial mycetoma can be distinguished from eumycetoma. Fungal cultures with speciation and susceptibility testing help to guide the choice of an antifungal regimen. Typically, azoles such as voriconazole, posaconazole or itraconazole are used.[7] Surgery for debulking is considered on an individual basis, depending on the extension of tissue destruction (like bony involvement), and the fungal species and sensitivities. Medical treatment with antifungals is often continued for extended periods (3-24 months) which is mainly based on case studies in the absence of randomized controlled trials.[9]

title: A man in his forties with HIV who was virologically suppressed on antiretroviral
history:
A man in his forties with HIV who was virologically suppressed on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with a recent CD4 of 736 cells/uL (37%) presented with 7 days of diffuse, constant headaches, poor sleep and generalized irritability. He denied fevers, chills, night sweats, neck stiffness, photophobia or phonophobia, skin or genital lesions. He also complained of a "lump" in his rectum associated with painful defecation.
He was diagnosed with HIV about 10 years ago, and is currently on emtricitabine, tenofovir and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir. He had had several unprotected encounters with male partners recently and had a history of primary syphilis treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G three years ago.

He had a 15 pack-year cigarette smoking history and also smokes crystal methamphetamine and marijuana. He has not travelled recently.

Sulfamethoxazole (rash).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. Blood pressure was 115/82 mm Hg, pulse 65 beats per minute, temperature 97.5°F (36.3°C), and respirations 18 breaths per minute. Head, eyes, ear, nose, and throat exam (including fundoscopic exam) was unremarkable. Cardiac and pulmonary exam was normal. There was no neck stiffness. Abdominal examination revealed mild right upper quadrant (RUQ) tenderness not associated with rebound, guarding, nor a positive Murphy’s sign. Genitourinary and rectal examinations were unremarkable. There was no rash.

Liver enzymes were elevated, with aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 56 IU/L (reference range 12-38 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase 132 IU/L (10-45), alkaline phosphatase 496 IU/L (25-100). Total bilirubin was elevated at 2.7 mg/dl (0.2-1.3). Rectal PCR was negative for chlamydia and gonorrhea.
His white blood cell count was 7,800 per mm3 with normal differential. Four sets of blood cultures were negative. Hepatitis B DNA and Hepatitis C viral RNA were not detectable by PCR method. Tuberculin skin test and serum interferon gamma release assay (Quantiferon TB gold test) were negative. Beta-d-glucan, serum histoplasma antigen and antibody screen, serum cryptococcal antigen and aspergillus galactomannan tests were negative. MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed minimal parenchymal volume loss without evidence of focal lesions.
An ultrasound liver revealed an ill-defined hypoechoic mass (Figure 1). MRI of the abdomen showed an ill-defined 2.8-cm rim enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left lateral hepatic segment (Figures 2a and 2b), corresponding to the ultrasound lesion and several smaller lesions were seen scattered throughout the liver and spleen; there was mild retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
CT-guided biopsy of the left hepatic lobe lesion was performed.
Figure 1. Ultrasound of the liver demonstrating an ill-defined hypo-echoic mass in the left lateral segment of the liver (arrow).
Figure 2. Figure 2a. MRI of abdomen demonstrating a 2.8 cm rim-enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left lateral hepatic segment (T1 weighted post contrast).
Figure 2a. MRI of abdomen demonstrating a 2.8 cm rim-enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left lateral hepatic segment (T1 weighted post contrast).
Figure 3. Figure 2b. MRI of abdomen demonstrating a 2.8 cm rim-enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left lateral hepatic segment (diffusion sequence).
Figure 2b. MRI of abdomen demonstrating a 2.8 cm rim-enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left lateral hepatic segment (diffusion sequence).

Two weeks after the liver biopsy was performed the patient returned with a new complaint of a non-pruritic, maculopapular rash, spread throughout his trunk, abdomen, upper and lower extremities (Figure 3). A single lesion was also seen on his left palm (Figure 4). He also complained of intermittent night sweats, feeling “feverish”, chills, myalgia and RUQ pain exacerbated by taking a deep breath. Figure 3. Maculopopular rash seen on the upper back. Figure 4. Papular lesion seen on the left palm.
Figure 4. Maculopopular rash seen on the upper back.
Figure 5. Warthin-Starry silver stain of liver biopsy (60x) demonstrating a spiral-shaped organism (arrow).
diagnosis:
Syphilis with CNS involvement, hepatic abscess, and splenic nodules in a HIV-infected man

Serum Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) titer was newly elevated at 1:256. Core biopsy of the liver lesion revealed acute inflammation, consistent with necrotic abscess. Spiral shaped organisms were noted on Warthin-Starry silver staining (Figure 5). Aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and AFB cultures were negative as was the flow cytometry and cytology.
Given his ongoing headache, lumbar puncture was performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 20 white blood cells (92% lymphocytes), normal glucose and normal protein level. CSF bacterial culture was negative. The fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS) in the CSF was positive but CSF VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) was negative. He had a colonoscopy performed to investigate the ‘rectal lump’ which revealed a hyperplastic cecal polyp, colonic tubular adenoma and diverticulosis.
Figure 6. Warthin-Starry silver stain of liver biopsy (60x) demonstrating a spiral-shaped organism (arrow).

The patient was diagnosed with syphilis associated with CNS involvement, hepatic abscess and splenic nodules. He was treated with 14 days of intravenous penicillin G at a dose of 24 million units per day. Liver function tests normalized within three weeks of completion of therapy. RPR, repeated four months after treatment, decreased to a titer of 1:4. There was complete resolution of his headache, proctitis and skin rash following treatment. Repeat liver ultrasound four months after therapy showed a decrease in the size of the left hepatic lobe lesion from 2.8 cm to 1.0 cm.

Syphilis is caused by the spirochete, Treponema pallidum. The primary stage of syphilis presents as a single or multiple ulcerative lesion(s) at the point of entry, usually as genital ulcerative disease. If left untreated, syphilis progresses to the secondary disseminated stage and one third of these patients may silently develop latent stage syphilis, characterized by cardiovascular and/or CNS complications or gummatous destructive lesions over the ensuing 5-30 years. However, it is interesting to note that idea of distinct phases of primary, secondary and tertiary syphilis is being challenged, particularly in the HIV-infected population.
The incidence of syphilis in the US is increasing. Between 2015 and 2016, the number of reported primary and secondary cases in the United States increased by 18%, and there were 27,814 primary and secondary syphilis cases reported in 2016. Most (58%) of these cases were among men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM). It is recommended MSM should be screened for STI at least annually and every 3-6 months for those at high-risk (eg. those with multiple or anonymous sexual partners). This is particularly true since many STIs, including primary syphilis, may be asymptomatic and may go unrecognized [1-3].
Syphilis infection is an independent risk factor for future HIV acquisition [8]. Rectal gonococcal or chlamydia infection can increase the risk of HIV seroconversion by up to eight times [9]. Therefore, all patients with syphilis should also be offered HIV screening [10].
The role of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in the rise of the syphilis epidemic is currently debated [11]. Kojima et al. have reported that MSM populations taking PrEP for HIV prevention are up to 44.6 times more likely to contract syphilis infection than MSM population not on PrEP with other studies pending [12]. The use of doxycycline chemoprophylaxis against syphilis has been proposed as a prevention tool in high risk MSM [13], but this remains controversial.
The spirochetemia seen in secondary syphilis results in diverse clinical manifestations. This is illustrated in our patient who was found to have liver, spleen and CNS involvement. Syphilitic hepatitis often occurs with syphilitic ulcerative proctitis perhaps because spirochetes from the rectal area are thought to directly invade the portal circulation [2- 3, 4- 5, 6].
To our knowledge, hepatic abscess with concomitant extrahepatic visceral involvement has not been previously reported in patients with secondary syphilis, although syphilitic hepatitis has been well described. Unexplained cholestasis should alert the clinician to screen for syphilis in at-risk patients because it is a reversible cause of liver dysfunction with appropriate antimicrobial therapy [5]. The most prominent laboratory abnormality at the time of presentation is unexplained anicteric or icteric cholestasis with a marked elevation of alkaline phosphatase [3,5,7], mild elevations in liver transaminase levels and modest hyperbilirubinemia. Gamma glutamyl transferase and lactate dehydrogenase may be elevated as well.
The diagnosis of syphilitic hepatitis is made by the combination of relevant symptoms with cholestasis or other liver function test abnormalities and serological evidence for syphilis such as a positive RPR titer and a reactive FTA-Abs result or microhemagglutination assay result positive for T. pallidum (MHA-TP) [3, 7]. Spirochetes are often not readily visualized in tissue samples. In a case series of 7 HIV- infected patients with syphilitic hepatitis, a relationship between the RPR titer and the absolute CD4+ T lymphocyte count was noted [3]. The inference is that patients with higher CD4+ T-cell counts may be more likely than others to manifest clinical hepatitis as a result of a more robust inflammatory response in the periportal region [3]. Key histological findings in cases of syphilitic hepatitis include non-specific periportal hepatocyte necrosis, peri-cholangiolar inflammation and occasional visualization of spirochetes [3]. The relatively high CD4 cell count in our patient might have led to more intense inflammatory reaction to spirochetes with the resulting hepatic abscess.
The current recommended treatment for secondary syphilis is a single 2.4 MU of intramuscular benzathine penicillin [14]. Almost all patients with syphilitic hepatitis reported in the literature were treated successfully with penicillin. The reported duration of the therapy varied from 1 dose of intramuscular penicillin to 14 days of aqueous penicillin depending on the accompanying symptoms. Liver enzyme levels, in general, quickly normalized in syphilitic hepatitis even after one dose or a week of penicillin [5]. Diagnosis of neurosyphilis is rather challenging; it should be based on clinical and serologic findings. Typically, a positive CSF VDRL or positive FTA-ABS along with an elevated CSF protein and mononuclear pleocytosis are seen [15]. Lumbar puncture is necessary to establish the diagnosis especially in the context of neurologic, ocular and otic signs. Our patient received a total of 14 days of treatment because of the meningeal involvement.
To conclude, syphilis rates are rising across the US, especially among MSM. High risk MSM should be screened more frequently as signs and symptoms of syphilis can often be subtle and go unrecognized. Hepatic involvement due to spirochetemia is not uncommon, although liver abscess due to syphilis is rare. Physicians should have a low threshold to obtain a lumbar puncture to rule out neurosyphilis if clinical suspicion is high. MSM with symptoms of proctitis should be tested for STIs, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, HSV and syphilis.

title: A man in his thirties with HIV diagnosed 3 years ago (nadir CD4 T-cell count 4 c
history:
A man in his thirties with HIV diagnosed 3 years ago (nadir CD4 T-cell count 4 cells/mm³), currently virally suppressed on tenofovir/lamivudine/efavirenz with a CD4 of 503 cells/mm³ presented with a three-year history of a slowly enlarging, and now massive perianal mass.

He reported having sex with men and women and did not use barrier protection regularly. He drank alcohol socially and did not smoke cigarettes or use any illicit drugs.

Lamivudine, tenofovir and efavirenz once daily
exam_studies:
The patient looked well and vital signs were normal. He had a 12 x 18 cm mass covering the perianal area (Figure 1) accompanied by papillomatous lesions in the scrotal area (Figure 2) and base of the penis. The rest of his physical exam was unremarkable.
Figure 1. 12 x 18 cm buttock mass covering the perianal area
Figure 2. Sub-centimeter papillomatous lesions seen over the scrotum

His HIV-1 RNA level was undetectable and CD4 count was 287 cells/mm³. Proctosigmoidoscopy did not show any intraluminal extension of the mass. The abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous and rectal contrast revealed a large, well-demarcated, hyperdense, enhancing mass arising from the anal region, extending exteriorly as a lobulated verrucous mass. It measured 9.0 x 12.0 x 13.1 cm in its greatest dimension. This mass caused a near-total luminal obstruction of the anorectal region. There were also multiple, enlarged, heterogenous lymph nodes seen in the bilateral inguinal regions and external iliac chains. The largest lymph node was on the right with a measurement of 1.5 cm across. The urinary collecting structures and urinary bladder were normal (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Abdominopelvic CT scan with intravenous (IV) and rectal contrast. Large 9 x 12 x 13cm hyperdense mass seen arising from the anal region extending exteriorly, causing near-total luminal obstruction. Lymphadenopathy noted. Urinary collecting systems were normal.
diagnosis:
Buschke–Löwenstein tumor in a man with HIV.

He underwent left inguinal lymph node biopsy, excision of genital and perianal warts, and electrocauterization of the warts at the penis and scrotum. A post-operative photograph of the anal area is shown (Figure 4).
The inguinal lymph node biopsy did not show any tumor while the histopathology of the excised perianal mass did not show any atypia or cancer cell nests. The base of the lesion was sharply defined without signs of invasion into the underlying connective tissue (Figure 5) while the surface epithelium showed koilocytosis (Figure 6). The squamous epithelium was thickened with areas of hyperkeratosis and had ordered maturation. The final histopathologic diagnosis was condyloma acuminata.
Figure 4. Post-operative photograph of anal area
Figure 5. H&E stain of anal tissue (low power) revealed a lesion with a sharply-defined base (arrow). There were no signs of invasion into the underlying connective tissue, differentiating it from a carcinoma.
Figure 6. H&E stains of anal tissue (high power).The surface epithelium shows koilocytosis (HPV related cellular changes), as demonstrated by the wrinkled hyperchromatic nuclei (arrow), perinuclear halos (box) and multinucleated cells (circle)

Two months after the surgery, physical exam revealed anal strictures and recurrence of the perianal lesion (Figure 7). He was treated with electrocautery and serial anal dilation but the lesions persisted. Figure 7. Photograph of anal area two months after surgery
Figure 7. Photograph of anal area two months after surgery

Buschke–Löwenstein tumor (BLT), also known as giant condyloma acuminata (GCA) is believed to be a transition between condyloma acuminata and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).[1] Often, verrucous carcinoma and BLT are used interchangeably. This may be misleading as the former has a tendency for metastasis while BLT is benign.[2] Human papilloma virus (HPV) types 6 and 11 have been identified as the etiologic agent in the majority of cases of condyloma acuminata and BLT, while types 16 and 18 have been more frequently associated with a higher degree of dysplasia and carcinoma.[1,2]
As seen in this patient, perianal mass is the most common symptom of BLT. Other symptoms include pain, abscess, fistula and bleeding. [3-5] Also, anal stricture as a sequela of surgery is a common complication of BLT. [3,6] Histopathologic findings such as the absence of atypia and cancer cell nests are compatible with BLT. Furthermore, the sharply defined base with no invasion of the underlying connective tissue, the koilocytosis in the surface epithelium, papillomatous and hyperkeratotic growth all support the diagnosis of BLT.[6]
To date, there are no established treatment guidelines for BLT. Surgery is still favored by many [7] and has a curative rate of 61%.[3] However, surgery is associated with a high recurrence rate, difficult wound healing due to secondary infection, and high morbidity due to a large soft tissue defect. Spillage of residual tumor during the operation is proposed as leading to the high recurrence rate after radical surgery. [1,3,5] Our patient’s tumor was managed with surgical excision coupled with electrocautery. Similar to other reports, our patient also experienced recurrence.
BLT tends to persist in HIV-infected patients probably due to immune system dysregulation resulting in the inability to control the expression and replication of HPV. [8] The low number of anal tissue Langerhans cells in HIV-infected patients may also contribute to relapse. Other factors that may contribute to relapse include co-infection with gonorrhea, syphilis, HSV and CMV infections. [9]
It has also been shown that patients with HIV and HPV co-infection have a higher risk of developing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), subsequently resulting in anal cancer. [5, 9]. The 4-year incidence of developing a HSIL among HIV-infected men was 49% compared to 17% in HIV-negative men. Other risk factors for progression to malignancy include a lower CD4 level of less than 500 cells/mm³, persistent anal HPV infection, anal infection with multiple HPV types, high-level HPV infection with the more oncogenic HPV types, and a higher HPV load in the affected tissue. [5,8,10]
The impact of antiretroviral therapy (ART) on HPV infection and HPV-related abnormalities has been inconsistent and controversial. [8,11] Antiretroviral therapy has not consistently been shown to reduce the incidence of HPV-related cancers. Our patient had been on ART but still developed BLT. The progression of the patient’s anal mass while he was receiving ART and having an increase in his CD4 cell count suggests the possibility that the BLT was exacerbated by immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, as has been previously reported.[12]
Although BLT is a benign lesion, its ability to infiltrate and invade surrounding tissues may lead to disfiguring outcomes. The higher risk of recurrence and propensity for malignant transformation of BLT for people living with HIV warrant close attention and pro-active treatment, and monitoring for progression in the setting of ART-induced immune reconstitution.

title: A gravida 2, para 1 (G2P1) woman in her thirties with a past medical history of
history:
A gravida 2, para 1 (G2P1) woman in her thirties with a past medical history of a left breast fibroadenoma excised several years ago presented with a 3-week history of an enlarging, painful left breast mass. Two months prior to presentation, the patient had an asymptomatic ectopic pregnancy for which she received methotrexate without complication. Approximately five weeks later, she developed focal swelling and tenderness of her left medial breast without any antecedent trauma. This swelling evolved into a painful, palpable mass with associated nipple retraction, but no fevers, chills, or overlying erythema. She was not breastfeeding and denied any weight loss, cough, or sick contacts. Her last menstrual period was normal and ended just prior to the onset of her symptoms.

A few years previously, she delivered a healthy baby and was no longer breastfeeding. She had received isoniazid as a child for a positive tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) test.

The patient was originally from Asia and immigrated to the United States as a teenager. She was married and lived with her husband and child. She denied any recent travel or sick contacts, including contact with persons known to have tuberculosis (TB). She denied use of tobacco, drugs, or alcohol and had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

Prenatal vitamins
exam_studies:
At presentation, the patient was well-appearing with a temperature of 98.2ºF (36.8ºC), blood pressure of 104/71, heart rate of 80, and respiratory rate of 16. Her breast examination was notable for a 2-3cm mass on the medial aspect of the left breast that was tender to palpation and poorly circumscribed. There was no overlying erythema or peau d’orange change noted. The left nipple was slightly retracted, but there was no nipple discharge. The right breast was normal, and no infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy was appreciated. Her physical examination was otherwise normal.

Her leukocyte count was 10.7 K/uL (reference range (RR): 4.0-10.0 K/uL) with 75.2% neutrophils. Hemoglobin, platelet count, chemistries, and liver function testing were all normal. C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 6.5 mg/L (RR: 0.0-3.0 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal. Ultrasound of the left breast revealed an irregular, thick-walled complex fluid collection approximately 3cm medial to the nipple (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Ultrasound image of left breast mass

Incisional biopsy and left breast abscess drainage were performed with tissue sent for microbiologic studies and routine pathology (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2. Breast biopsy, H&E stain (4x)
Figure 3. Figure 3: 40x H&E stain of breast tissue with dense neutrophilic infiltrate surrounding the cystic area
Figure 3: 40x H&E stain of breast tissue with dense neutrophilic infiltrate surrounding the cystic area
diagnosis:
Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis associated with C. kroppenstedtii infection

Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 6mL of purulent fluid and gram stain returned 4+ polys, no epithelial cells, and few Gram-positive rods. Routine cultures grew 1+ Corynebacterium species susceptible to doxycycline and amoxicillin/clavulanate, later identified as C. kroppenstedtii by 16s rRNA sequencing. In spite of a one-week course of cephalexin, followed by a three-month course of doxycycline for suspected cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (CNGM), she remained symptomatic. Doxycycline was transitioned to amoxicillin/clavulanate, with no change in her breast pain and induration despite another three months of this treatment. Therefore, the patient underwent an incisional biopsy and left breast abscess drainage with histopathology that returned consistent with CNGM (Figures 2 and 3). Gram-positive rods consistent with Corynebacterium spp. were visualized on gram stain of the breast tissue histopathologic specimen. Routine, anaerobic, fungal, acid fast bacilli (AFB), and modified AFB stains and cultures returned negative. Additional studies including interferon-gamma release assay for TB and Bartonella serologies were negative and 1,3 beta-D-glucan and angiotensin converting enzyme were within normal limits.

Given inadequate response to a prolonged (> 6 months) course of antibiotic therapy prior to the incisional biopsy, she was treated with prednisone 40mg oral daily for two weeks, followed by a slow taper over two months with complete resolution of her residual breast mass and tenderness. She remains asymptomatic one year later.

This case demonstrates the classic clinical and pathologic findings of cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, which is associated with Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii infection. Granulomatous mastitis is a rare inflammatory condition more common in parous, reproductive-aged women and usually presents as a unilateral, painful breast mass.[1-3] A broad array of infectious and non-infectious conditions have been implicated in the development of granulomatous mastitis, including tuberculosis, bartonellosis, fungal infections, sarcoidosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.[4,5] Granulomatous mastitis can mimic breast carcinoma, and requires histologic examination for diagnosis.[3,4,6]
Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (CNGM) is a distinct type of granulomatous mastitis featuring lipogranulomas rimmed by neutrophils on histopathology (Figures 2 and 3), often with gram positive organisms visualized within the vacuoles.[2,4,7,8] This histologic pattern is associated with Corynebacteria infection, particularly infection with Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii. [1,4,8,9] Although identification of C. kroppenstedtii from breast tissue or abscess culture should prompt strong suspicion of CNGM, it is not entirely clear whether this organism is a causative agent or rather a secondary colonizer in these cases.[10] C. kroppenstedtii lacks a mycolic acid in the cell envelope, which makes it lipophilic, and well-suited for growth in breast tissue; it is infrequently isolated from other sites.[1,10] CNGM is typically seen in parous women who have developed lipid-rich mammary glands.[4] Several cases of Corynebacterium associated granulomatous mastitis have also been reported in nulliparous women with hyperprolactinemia, suggesting that lactational changes triggered by prolactin may increase risk of CNGM.[11] The role for therapy that reduces prolactin in treatment of CNGM remains unclear.
Management of CNGM can be challenging, with many patients undergoing multiple rounds of incision and drainage, repeated courses of antibiotics, and occasionally even immunosuppression as part of therapy.[4] Most antibiotics are hydrophilic, and therefore do not penetrate well into lipid-rich areas of the breast tissue.[12] Doxycycline is lipid soluble and has good activity against Corynebacterium, so is recommended for initial therapy.[7,12] Second-line agents include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clarithromycin, clindamycin, and rifampin, which are lipophilic and active against C. kroppenstedtii.[12] C. kroppenstedtii is also generally susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid, but is often resistant to beta-lactams.[12] While fluoroquinolones are used for other granulomatous infections, their low lipid solubility makes them less effective for CNGM.[13]
Corticosteroid therapy is another option for patients who do not respond to antibiotic therapy. In an observational, prospective, single-center cohort summary of women with idiopathic granulomatous mastitis 100% (44/44) of women who received steroids reported an initial response to therapy within two weeks.[3] Of these women, 35/44 (80%) achieved complete symptom resolution.[3] However, median time to resolution was 5.3 months, and one in four women experienced symptom recurrence within a year.[3] Lumpectomy and mastectomy are reserved for patients with antibiotic- and steroid-refractory disease.[3]
In summary, cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis is associated with C. kroppenstedtii infection and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of subacute unilateral breast swelling in women of reproductive age without clear epidemiologic risk factors for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, or malignancy. Treatment options include lipophilic antibiotics active against Corynebacteria (e.g. doxycycline), surgical drainage, and corticosteroids.

title: A man in his forties presented 2 months after renal transplantation for diabetes
history:
A man in his forties presented 2 months after renal transplantation for diabetes nephropathy with 1 week of unprovoked knee pain followed by painful skin nodules on his upper limbs and fevers. The knee pain was not associated with any reported swelling, redness or decreased range of motion. The skin lesions started as small red raised lesions that later evolved to larger, deep, hyperpigmented lesions that were tender to touch. He subsequently developed fevers which prompted his presentation. He had no history of rheumatologic or dermatologic diseases.
He had type 1 diabetes complicated by end-stage renal failure requiring hemodialysis. He had delayed graft function for a few weeks post transplantation and required further hemodialysis. He received Alemtuzumab (CD52 monoclonal antibody) and was on Prednisone 5 mg daily, tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily and Mycophenolic acid 360 mg orally twice daily. There had been no recent changes in the doses of immunosuppressants. Both donor and recipient were positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) antibodies.

Essential Hypertension
Coronary Atherosclerotic Heart Disease with Coronary artery bypass grafting

He did not have recent travel or history of alcohol or illicit drug use.

Prednisone 5 mg daily, Tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, Mycophenolic acid 360 mg orally twice daily
Valganciclovir and Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis
Insulin, Metoprolol, Simvastatin, Aspirin
exam_studies:
Temperature: 36.7° C (98.1° F); Blood Pressure: 141/69; Respiratory Rate: 16/min; Body Mass Index was 20. He had 20 – 30 erythematous, hyperpigmented, tender nodules on the dorsal forearms and upper arms which were noted to be deep-seated (Figures 1 and 2). No nodules were noted on the legs. Both of his knees were tender to gentle palpation at the patella. The knees were not warm, red or swollen and the range of motion was full. All his other joints were normal. He had a well healing abdominal surgical scar with a non-tender graft.
Figure 1. Skin lesions on bilateral upper arms
Figure 2. Close-up view of the skin lesion

His white cell count was normal with a normal differential. He had a mild normocytic anemia and mild thrombocytosis. CRP was elevated at 212 (reference range 0-5 mg/L) and ESR was high at 48 (1-33) mm/hr. He was hyperglycemic with a blood glucose of 522 (= 140 mg/dL). Renal function, liver enzymes and chest plain-radiograph were within normal limits.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Mycobacterium chelonae infection involving skin, bone and bloodstream.

Serum cryptococcal antigen and urine blastomycosis antigen were negative.
Two punch biopsies from the right forearm were obtained: acid fast stains were positive. Gram stain and Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain were negative. Acid fast bacilli (AFB) were also isolated in blood cultures 6 days after culture incubation. This organism was later identified as Mycobacterium chelonae. Interpreted drug susceptibilities include susceptibility to amikacin (MIC ≤ 8), kanamycin (MIC ≤ 8), tobramycin (MIC ≤ 2), doxycycline (MIC ≤ 1), tigecycline (MIC ≤ 0.25), clarithromycin (MIC ≤ 0.25), azithromycin (MIC ≤ 16) and clofazamine (MIC ≤ 0.25) ug/ml. The organism tested resistant to cefoxitin (MIC > 128), ciprofloxacin (MIC=8), moxifloxacin (MIC > 4), amoxicillin/ clavulanic acid (MIC > 32/16) and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole ((MIC > 4/76) and showed intermediate susceptibility to imipenem and linezolid (both MIC = 8 micrograms/ml).

X-rays of the knees were normal. MRI of lower extremities showed marked marrow edema throughout both patellae with mottled areas of marrow edema in the trochleae and more focal marrow edema involving the lateral aspect of the left lateral femoral condyle suspicious for osteomyelitis. Rheumatoid factor, anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide, anti-nuclear antibodies were all negative.
Transthoracic echocardiogram and a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) were negative. The patient was treated with imipenem, linezolid and azithromycin. He developed severe bone marrow suppression that was thought to be secondary to linezolid; this drug was switched to intravenous tigecycline. No new lesions appeared after starting the treatment and further blood cultures have been negative for AFB. The planned treatment course is at least 12 months.

Rapidly growing mycobacteria are a group of environmental non-tuberculous mycobacteria associated with various human diseases. The three rapidly growing AFB species most commonly associated with human disease are Mycobacterium abscessus, Mycobacterium chelonae, and Mycobacterium fortuitum. They are ubiquitous environmental organisms which are notorious for causing biofilms on water-exposed instruments (1).
M. chelonae primarily presents as skin, soft tissue and bone disease (2) with reports of disseminated disease in immunosuppressed patients (3-5). Pedicure-associated mycobacterial furunculosis due to M. chelonae was reported in North Carolina (6), and prior reports have linked outbreaks of M. chelonae infection to tattooing (7). In immunosuppressed patients, such as those with organ transplants, disseminated M. chelonae has been reported to present as multiple cutaneous painful nodules with a predilection for the extremities, a feature that was also noted in our patient. Dissemination into the bloodstream may result from primary catheter-associated bloodstream infections (8) or from hematogenous spread of a primary lung infection.
M. chelonae is characterized by the high prevalence of drug resistance. Treatment should be based on in vitro susceptibilities (9) and clinical response. While monotherapy with a macrolide may be sufficient for localized skin infection, disseminated disease caused by M. chelonae necessitates combination therapy (10). Macrolides constitute the backbone of therapy and are used in combination with other drugs (9). Treatment failure and drug related adverse events are very common during treatment (11). One cohort study showed that using tigecycline for over a month, as part of a salvage multi-drug regimen, tended to improve clinical outcomes (12). Removal of infected indwelling lines and devices is crucial for clearance of the infection (8) and additional aggressive surgical debridement may be needed for recurrent and drug-resistant infections (9).

title: A man in his fifties with HIV (current CD4 cell count 57 cells/microliter) prese
history:
A man in his fifties with HIV (current CD4 cell count 57 cells/microliter) presented with several months of generalized malaise, poor appetite, weight loss (13.6 kg, 30 lb). He had also developed scattered hypopigmented patches on his trunk. Over the month prior to evaluation, he developed fevers, chills, sweats, diffuse lymphadenopathy and abdominal bloating.
He had migrated to the United States from South Asia a few weeks prior to presentation having lived in a refugee camp for several decades.
He denied shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis, vomiting, diarrhea, joint pain or muscle pain. He had no sick contacts but reported numerous insect bites in his country of origin. The common water source at the camp was a well. He has had no other recent travel.

He had been diagnosed with HIV about 6 years ago; at that time, his CD4 cell count was 19 cells/microliter. He had been receiving therapy with tenofovir-lamivudine-efavirenz and was virologically suppressed. He was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis several years ago; details of that treatment were unknown.

He had been married for many years. He had worked as a farmer with exposure to goats and other farm animals. He had never used tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs.

Tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz, trimethroprim-sulfamethoxazole.
exam_studies:
The patient was in mild distress. He appeared diaphoretic with increased work of breathing. The blood pressure was 118/71 mmHg, pulse of 88, temperature of 98.7°F (37.1°C), weight of 62.6 kg (138 lb). His examination was notable for extensive tender lymphadenopathy in his posterior and anterior cervical chain, axilla, inguinal canal, and epitrochlear area, measuring 1-2 cm. Cardiopulmonary examination was notable for soft left upper lobe crackles. Abdominal exam was notable for a liver edge palpable 2cm below the costal margin and a palpable spleen tip. His skin exam revealed numerous hypopigmented macules and papules on his face, neck, and trunk (Figure 1a and 1b). The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Figure 1a. Image of hypopigmented rash on face
Figure 2. Chest X-ray at presentation. Scarring and bronchiectasis seen within the left upper lobe likely secondary to prior tuberculosis infection.
Figure 1b. Image of hypopigmented rash on trunk

The white blood cell count was 1.27 x10³ cells per microliter (reference range, RR, 4-10.4). Absolute neutrophil count was 890 cells per microliter (RR 2200-8850) and total lymphocyte count was 300 cells per microliter (RR 1090-3300). The CD4 count was 57 cells/uL. The HIV RNA level was undetectable. The creatinine was 1.25 mg per dL (RR 0.66-1.25). Liver function tests were notable for AST of 53 U/L (RR 15-46), alkaline phosphatase 284 U/L (RR 38-126) and albumin 2.6 g per dL (RR 3.4-4.9). The chest x-ray revealed areas of scarring and bronchiectasis in the left upper lobe (Figure 2). Three sputum specimens were negative for acid fact bacilli (AFB) by smear; a sputum AFB culture performed 3 months prior had been finalized as no growth.
Figure 3. Chest X-ray at presentation. Scarring and bronchiectasis seen within the left upper lobe likely secondary to prior tuberculosis infection.

He was referred to otolaryngology for an excisional biopsy of a posterior auricular lymph node (1.5 x 0.9 x 0.5 cm). The gram stain is shown in Figures 3a and 3b.
