Figure 3a. Gram stain of lymph node (50x)
Figure 5. Figure 3b. Gram stain of lymph node (100x)
Figure 3b. Gram stain of lymph node (100x)
diagnosis:
Visceral Leishmaniasis by Leishmania donovani

Sputum TB PCR was negative. Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial blood cultures were negative.
The posterior auricular excisional lymph node biopsy was sent for pathology as well as bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures. Pathology demonstrated sheets of histiocytes with numerous intracytoplasmic amastigotes. Giemsa stain of touch imprints revealed numerous organisms with kinetoplasts consistent with leishmania amastigotes. Silver stain for fungus was negative. All cultures were negative. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis.
The dermatology team performed a shave biopsy of the rash on his back. The dermis demonstrated granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes containing numerous organisms some with identifiable kinetoplasts, consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis.
A portion of the lymph node was sent to the CDC reference lab for Leishmania PCR. This returned positive for Leishmania donovani which is endemic in his home country in South Asia.

He was admitted for initiation of IV therapy with liposomal amphotericin B. He was treated with 4mg/kg IV daily on days 1 through 5, then days 10, 17, 24, 31, and 38. The patient responded well to treatment with resolution of his constitutional symptoms. He gained 11 kg (22 lbs). His white blood cell count increased to 2.97 x10 3 cells per microliter. His absolute neutrophil and lymphocyte count increased to 1700 and 600 per microliter, respectively. His CD4 count increased to 122 cells/microliter at 3 months after presentation. His ART was changed to a fixed dose combination of efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Because his CD4 count remained below 200 cells/microliter he received prophylactic therapy with infusion of liposomal amphotericin B 5mg/kg IV every 4 weeks.

Leishmaniasis reflects a variety of pathogenic processes caused by different species of the protozoan parasite in the genus of Leishmania. It has a dimorphic lifecycle with an amastigote stage in the sand fly which is transmitted to humans when the insect takes a blood meal. The amastigote is phagocytosed and becomes a promastigote. It survives and is able to multiply intracellularly (2). It develops a kinetoplast as an outpouching of DNA at a right angle to its nucleus which aids in identification. Visceral leishmaniasis (also called Kala-Azar) is widely distributed in Africa, Asia, South and Central America. The reservoir for the organism is small mammals. Visceral leishmaniasis presents with a wide spectrum of disease from mild or asymptomatic infection to fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. Renal involvement can occur. Immunosuppressed hosts and people with HIV are typically more severely affected. Leishmaniasis is emerging as an under-recognized cause of disease in developing countries. A hypopigmented rash can occur with leishmaniasis which can be macular, papular, or nodular (3). This can manifest even after the completion of treatment when it is called post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis.
Leishmania donovani is endemic in the region of South Asia, where his refugee camp was located (1) and is an emerging pathogen particularly in persons with HIV, with 40% of all cases of Leishmania donovani worldwide occurring there (4).
Laboratory diagnosis consists of identification of the organism in infected tissues including lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow (5). PCR-based testing to confirm the diagnosis and to speciate the organism are available at the CDC. Other identification methods include culture and antibody titers.
For the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis, liposomal amphotericin B is the drug of choice in the US (6). In people with HIV, ART should be started immediately. Combination therapy with amphotericin B and miltefosine is an option for refractory cases (6).
Relapse rates are high in HIV-infected patients with low CD4 counts (<200 cells/uL). In an early case series of 78 patients, 100% of patients with AIDS treated for leishmaniasis relapsed after stopping amphotericin B (7). In HIV-infected patients (all CD4 counts), secondary prophylaxis with amphotericin B decreased relapse from 80% to 50% at 12 months (8). In a prospective series of 27 HIV-infected patients with an initial diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis, patients with a CD4 of less than 100 cells/mL were at risk for relapsed disease despite being maintained on secondary prophylaxis while those with a CD4 of more than 200 cells/mL did not experience any relapses (9). Our patient was started on secondary prophylaxis to reduce his risk of recurrence with the plan to continue until his CD4 count was consistently above 200 cells/mL for 3 months.

title: A woman in her forties with systemic lupus erythematosus who had her second rena
history:
A woman in her forties with systemic lupus erythematosus who had her second renal transplantation 1 year ago, presented with a swollen right hand. She recalled a sliver being lodged in the tip of her right middle finger 10 months ago while gardening with her bare hands. Since then, she developed swollen lumps on her right middle and ring fingers and along the extensor surface of her right wrist. These areas drained pus occasionally and she received various courses of antibiotics including clindamycin with no improvement. At no time did the patient have fever, chills or night sweats.

Splenectomy and previous BK virus nephritis.

Tacrolimus (Advagraf) 2 mg daily; Prednisone 10 mg daily, Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 80/400 mg three times a week
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. The examination was otherwise normal.
The right hand demonstrated a fusiform enlargement of the third proximal interphalangeal joint (PIPJ) with distinct subcentimeter nodules and a few pustules (Figure 1). There was a 1 cm nodule at the dorsal aspect of the right fourth metacarpophalangeal (MCP) area. Another nodule measuring less than 1 cm was present just proximal to the dorsum of the right wrist (Figure 2). There was no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Her renal graft was non-tender. The rest of her examination were unremarkable.
Figure 1. Figure 1: Right hand at presentation
Figure 1: Right hand at presentation
Figure 2. Figure 2: Extensor surface of the right wrist at presentation
Figure 2: Extensor surface of the right wrist at presentation

X-ray of her right hand showed a dense fusiform soft tissue mass at the level of the PIP of the right third finger and a small soft tissue mass over the 3rd MCP area (Figure 3). MRI of her hand (Figure 4) showed 4 complex subcutaneous cystic masses. There was a 0.9 x 0.5 x 0.9 cm T2 hyperintense and T1 hypointense subcutaneous soft tissue nodule on the palmar aspect of the distal phalanx of the middle finger. There was a 2.3 x 1.4 x 5.8 cm mass in the dorsal aspect of the middle finger, overlying the proximal and middle phalanges. There was a lobulated, T2 hyperintense lesion with internal T2 hypointense septations. It was predominantly T1 hypointense. This encased the extensor digitorum longus tendon. There was another lesion, measuring 1.8 x 1.6 x 2 cm at the dorsal aspect of the fourth MCPJ, extending medially into the interspace between the heads of the third and fourth metacarpals. There was an ill-defined T1 hypointense and T2 intermediate signal, in the region of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon, just distal to the ulnar styloid process which showed some enhancement post gadolinium. Figure 3: X-ray of the right hand Figure 4: MRI of the right hand
Figure 3. Figure 3: X-ray of the right hand
Figure 3: X-ray of the right hand
Figure 4. Figure 4: MRI of the right hand
Figure 4: MRI of the right hand
diagnosis:
Exophiala oligosperma soft tissue infection

An incisional biopsy of the right middle finger nodular mass demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and hyphal forms consistent with fungal infection. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Methanamine silver stains for fungal organisms revealed numerous branching closely septated hyphae that are moniliform-like in nature. (Figure 5). Dark olive-black velvety colonies with a dark reverse side were cultured on Sabouraud Dextrose and horse blood agar (Figures 6 and 7). Photomicrography showed septate hyphae with ellipsoidal conidia (Figure 8). The organism was identified as Exophiala oligosperma by molecular testing.
Figure 5. Figure 5: Periodic acid-Schiff stain demonstrated septated fungal hyphae (black arrows)
Figure 5: Periodic acid-Schiff stain demonstrated septated fungal hyphae (black arrows)
Figure 6. Figure 6: Sabouraud's dextrose agar with an olive-black velvet colony and a black reverse
Figure 6: Sabouraud's dextrose agar with an olive-black velvet colony and a black reverse
Figure 7. Figure 7: Horse blood agar (left) and Sabouraud agar (right) – Growth after 4 days showed velvety gray colonies with a black reverse.
Figure 7: Horse blood agar (left) and Sabouraud agar (right) – Growth after 4 days showed velvety gray colonies with a black reverse.
Figure 8. Figure 8: Photomicrography showed septate hyphae with ellipsoidal conidia
Figure 8: Photomicrography showed septate hyphae with ellipsoidal conidia

The patient was treated with itraconazole. She had elevation of her serum creatinine probably related to drug interaction between itraconazole and tacrolimus. Her tacrolimus dose was adjusted and the trough level was monitored on a weekly basis.
After 10 months of antifungal therapy, the right third finger fusiform swelling was markedly reduced in size (Figure 9) and the patient had full function of her finger. The nodule along the dorsum of the right fourth MCP joint was also reduced in size. The nodule on the dorsum of the right wrist became punctate in size.
Figure 9. Figure 9: Photograph of the right hand 10 months after treatment.
Figure 9: Photograph of the right hand 10 months after treatment.

A broad differential including opportunistic infections is important when considering unusual presentations in immunosuppressed individuals. Obtaining tissue diagnosis is particularly critical. Cutaneous nocardiosis and unusual fungal infections including sporothrichosis can all present in this manner. Cutaneous aspergilloma is relatively uncommon, but should be considered. Mycobacterium marinum infection may occur in those with water exposure.
Phaeohyphomycosis is an emerging fungal infection particularly in solid organ transplant recipients and immunosuppressed individuals (1). Phaeohyphomycosis (phaeo- etymology (Greek) for gray) is produced by various black (melanized) fungi (sometimes referred as “dematiaceous”) such as Exophiala, Alternaria, or Bipolaris species. These species may cause pleomorphic infections ranging from allergic diseases (mostly involving the respiratory tract) and superficial subcutaneous infections to fatal disseminated diseases.
Black yeasts of the genus Exophiala are potential agents of human and animal mycoses. Exophiala is a genus of anamorphic fungi in the Herpotrichiellaceae family. Exophiala spp. are common environmental fungi often associated with decaying wood and soil enriched with organic wastes. Although Exophial a species are environmental fungi, they should not be disregarded as contaminants when they are isolated from clinical specimens (2). These fungi are causative agents of skin and subcutaneous tissue infections and of systemic infections, such as prosthetic valve endocarditis, dialysis-associated peritonitis, and disseminated infections, especially in immunocompromised patients (2).
In Exophiala spp. infections, the most common sites of involvement were the subcutaneous tissue of distal limbs, usually with a history of local trauma in the weeks or months before appearance of the lesions (3). Disseminated disease is relatively uncommon. The optimal antifungal agent in the treatment of Exophiala infections is unknown (4). Recent data suggest that antifungal susceptibility differs between species, and some suggest obtaining in vitro susceptibilities although it is unclear if this leads to better clinical outcomes. Azole therapy, especially itraconazole and posaconazole, in combination with surgical excision has been associated with improved clinical outcome.

title: A man in his early twenties who was diagnosed with HIV, cerebral toxoplasmosis a
history:
A man in his early twenties who was diagnosed with HIV, cerebral toxoplasmosis and Kaposi’s sarcoma 16 weeks ago, presented with increasing shortness of breath and dry cough in the setting of a recent change in antiretroviral therapy (ART).
Approximately 16 weeks prior to this second readmission, he presented with seizures and left hemiparesis and was found to have a right parietal, ring-enhancing lesion on head CT. He was started empirically on TMP-SMX 400/80 mg IV every 12 hours and clindamycin 600 mg IV every 6 hours. A biopsy of the brain lesion demonstrated cerebral toxoplasmosis. A follow-up brain CT at 2-weeks showed no improvement and prednisone 40 mg oral daily was added. He was also found to have violaceous nodular skin plaques consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS). His CD4 T-cell count was <20 cells/uL and his HIV viral load was >100,000 copies/mL and he was commenced on ART: dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Approximately 5 weeks after this initial admission, he was discharged home on ART and advised to continue treatment for toxoplasmosis and to taper his steroids.
Eight weeks prior to this second admission, the patient was evaluated at an outpatient clinic where he was changed to pyrimethamine 75 mg oral daily, sulfadiazine 1.5 g oral every 6 hours and folinic acid 10 mg oral daily. ART was changed to combination elvitegravir/ cobicistat/ emtricitabine/ tenofovir alafenamide to decrease his pill burden. His CD4 T-cell count had improved to 35 cells/uL and his HIV RNA had decreased to 195 copies/ml.
Four weeks prior to this second admission, he was reevaluated as an outpatient. He revealed that he had not decreased his prednisone doses as his mother was concerned about seizure recurrence. The CD4 T-cell count continued to improve to 50 cells/uL and the HIV RNA was 28 copies/ml.
He presented 16 weeks after he first initiated ART (8 weeks after the change in ART regimen) complaining of having developed new skin lesions on his scalp over the past 3 weeks and 2 weeks of progressive shortness of breath. The dyspnea was associated with dry cough, night sweats, chills and fever. He had no hemoptysis, weight loss or sick contacts. There was no headache or confusion and no other localizing symptoms.

He did not use alcohol or recreational drugs and does not smoke. He had been sexually active with men for many years without condom use.

Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide 1 tablet oral daily,
Prednisone 30 mg oral twice a day, pyrimethamine 75 mg oral daily, sulfadiazine 1.5 g oral every 6 hours, folinic acid 25 mg oral daily, azithromycin 1,200 mg oral weekly, levetiracetam 1,000 mg oral twice a day
exam_studies:
The patient appeared acutely ill. He was not in acute respiratory distress but had signs of fatigue while talking. The blood pressure was 116/66 mm Hg, pulse 92 beats per minute, temperature 99.8°F (37.7°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. He had expiratory wheezing and decreased air entry at both bases. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was present and he had multiple raised violaceous lesions on his skin that had increased in size (Figure 1a and 1b). There was a new hard palate violaceous hyperplastic lesion seen. (Figure 2). The remainder of his examination were normal.
Figure 1. Bluish/violaceous, hard, firm and nodular lesions seen on his a) left arm and b) left leg
Figure 2. Figure 2: Violaceous hyperplastic lesions seen on the hard palate
Figure 2: Violaceous hyperplastic lesions seen on the hard palate

His current CD4 count was 22 cells/uL and HIV RNA was 160 copies/mL. The WBC was 2.18 x 10 3 /mL (reference range 4-11 10 3 /mL); Polymorph 57%, Lymphocytes 14 %, Bands 10 %. Hematocrit was 45%, LDH was 1037 U/L (reference range 225- 335 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 58 U/L (reference range < 41 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 30 U/L (reference range < 40 U/L), INR was 0.92 (reference range 0.90 – 1.20). Other routine laboratory investigations including urea and electrolytes were normal. Toxoplasma and Histoplasma IgM and IgG were negative.
Chest CT scan showed extensive bilateral axillary, hilar, pericardial, mediastinal and porta hepatis lymphadenopathy with associated compression of bronchi, large bilateral pleural effusions and bilateral central consolidation (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Figure 3: Chest CT (without contrast) demonstrated extensive bilateral axillary/hilar/pericardial/mediastinal/porta hepatis lymphadenopathy with associated compression of bronchi, large bilateral pleural effusions and bilateral central consolidation
Figure 3: Chest CT (without contrast) demonstrated extensive bilateral axillary/hilar/pericardial/mediastinal/porta hepatis lymphadenopathy with associated compression of bronchi, large bilateral pleural effusions and bilateral central consolidation

He was placed on airborne precautions and sputa were collected daily for acid fast bacilli smears. He was also started on vancomycin, cefepime, and azithromycin and changed from sulfadiazine to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
diagnosis:
HIV/AIDS with pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma and possible KS-IRIS

A bronchoscopy showed purpuric raised lesions on the bronchial mucosa (Figure 4). Sampling of these lesions was not performed as they seemed prone to bleeding. Biopsy of his inguinal lymph node confirmed KS (Figure 5 and 6).
Figure 4. Figure 4: Bronchoscopy image showed a raised purple lesion on the bronchial mucosa
Figure 4: Bronchoscopy image showed a raised purple lesion on the bronchial mucosa
Figure 5. Inguinal lymph node, core needle biopsy (H&E, 400X). There were abundant macrophages seen within an atypical lymphoid background. The vascular lesion was consistent with KS – seen as intertwined, and proliferating vascular spaces (shown with thickened endothelial lining) and stained positive for CD31.
Figure 6. Anti-HHV8 stain of inguinal lymph node showed the typical strong, nuclear but granular staining. (1000x)

The patient’s condition continued to deteriorate with progressive respiratory distress requiring intubation. Given the extensive KS lesions seen in his skin, lymph node, oral mucosa and on bronchoscopy, he was started on daunorubicin but unfortunately went into cardiorespiratory arrest and died.

Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignant disease first described on 1872 by Moritz Kaposi (1). It is an important complication in patients with AIDS, especially in men who have sex with men (2). The incidence of KS has significantly decreased since the introduction of ART (3), but there is an increasing recognition of KS exacerbation as a part of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) (4,5). Pulmonary KS has been linked with higher incidence of KS-IRIS, which is associated with increased mortality in patients with AIDS (6). Optimal timing for the initiation of ART in patients with HIV and KS has not been well defined although earlier initiation has been associated with a higher incidence of IRIS (7).
This case is of importance for the medical community as it illustrates the complexity in the diagnosis and treatment of an HIV-infected patient presenting with multiple complications at the time of diagnosis. He was started on steroids, due to a brain lesion that was not responding to antibiotic therapy, but steroids have been associated with KS progression and KS-associated mortality (8). Our case also illustrates progression of complications despite the use of ART that could be secondary to the inability of the immune system to be reconstituted (ie. persistent immunodeficiency) or dysfunctionally reconstituted as in KS-IRIS.

title: A man in his fifties was referred to infectious disease clinic for progressive l
history:
A man in his fifties was referred to infectious disease clinic for progressive left corneal ulcer. Several weeks prior to his initial presentation to ophthalmology, he had two eye injuries. The first occurred when removing insulation from an attic and the second when mowing his lawn and his left eye was struck by plant debris. Fluorescein stains of his left eye demonstrated a corneal ulcer and he had ongoing follow-up with ophthalmology (Figures 1 and 2 taken on day 30 of initial presentation). On day 40, he complained of complete loss of vision in the left eye.

Diet-controlled diabetes mellitus and hypertension.

He lives with his wife and dog, and has had no recent fresh water or small rodent exposures. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes a day.
exam_studies:
T 99°F (37.2°C), P 61 beats per minute, BP 141/78 mmHg. He was in no acute distress. His right eye was normal. On the left, his cornea was completely opacified (figure 3) suggestive of progressive keratitis. His dentition was poor. He had no palpable cervical or pre-auricular lymphadenopathy and the remainder of the exam was normal.
Figure 3. Figure 3: Photograph of left eye taken on day 40 of presentation. Rapid progression seen with complete opacification of the cornea suggestive of progressive keratitis
Figure 3: Photograph of left eye taken on day 40 of presentation. Rapid progression seen with complete opacification of the cornea suggestive of progressive keratitis

Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count were within normal ranges.
diagnosis:
Purpureocillum (previously Paecilomyces) lilacinus fungal keratitis.

Corneal scrapings taken at his initial presentation (day 1) grew a white mold on Sabaroud culture plate (Figure 4); this was later identified as Paecilomyces lilacinus (recently renamed Purpureocillum lilacinus). Subsequent cultures from corneal scrapings on days 8 and 21 also showed Paecilomyces spp., with the latter also positive for Candida glabrata.
He underwent a left eye penetrating keratoplasty and corneal transplant on day 40 (figure 5). Intraoperative specimens grew Paecilomyces spp. and Candida albicans. The MIC for P. lilacinus were: Amphotericin >16, Fluconazole >64, Flucytosine >64, Itraconazole 4, Voriconazole 0.5 (μg/ml).
Figure 4. Figure 4: SAB plate with a powdery white mold on day 5 of culture
Figure 4: SAB plate with a powdery white mold on day 5 of culture
Figure 5. Figure 5: Photograph of left eye on day 41 after presentation (1 day after his first corneal transplant)
Figure 5: Photograph of left eye on day 41 after presentation (1 day after his first corneal transplant)

He received intraocular and topical voriconazole and topical natamycin eye drops and systemic voriconazole. Despite this, 14 days after his first corneal transplant (day 54 of presentation), recurrence of an infiltrate was noted in the inferior aspect of the temporary cornea graft, necessitating further surgery (figure 6).
He became intolerant of systemic voriconazole with intractable nausea and vomiting after two months and transitioned to systemic posaconazole for six months on day 92 (with confirmed therapeutic levels). On day 275, he was transitioned to isavuconazole in the hope of improved tissue penetration and better tolerability. Despite this, he continued to have recurrent fungal infection of all six of his transplanted corneas. He ultimately underwent enucleation of the infected eye.

The evaluation of ocular inflammation includes determining the affected compartment(s), consideration of typical pathogens and non-infectious etiologies, and determination of need for emergent treatment.(1) Keratitis involves the cornea, may be caused by foreign body exposure with incomplete lid closure, ultraviolet radiation, or infection with bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa.(2) The patient discussed in this case had a severe and progressive fungal keratitis. Fungal keratitis is most often associated with ocular trauma, may be complicated by endophthalmitis, and has a higher rate of corneal perforation than bacterial keratitis. Patients with keratitis often complain of eye pain and report a history of foreign body or trauma.
Uveitis is classified as anterior (anterior chamber), posterior (chorioretinal inflammation), intermediate (cells in the vitreous), or pan-uveitis, which involves anterior, vitreous, and posterior chambers. Endophthalmitis is the term used by convention to describe such inflammation when it is caused by bacterial or fungal infection, while uveitis is the term used by convention to describe such inflammation when it is caused by viral, parasitic, or noninfectious processes. Endophthalmitis is a medical emergency and may be due to exogenous (external sources including trauma) or endogenous seeding (via hematogenous spread).
In keratitis, examination with fluorescein may delineate the extent of corneal involvement. Other examination findings may include hypopyon (leucocytic infiltrate seen as a milky white fluid level in the inferior part of the anterior chamber) or corneal infiltrate. The presence of branching, dendritic ulcers in the cornea suggests HSV keratitis.
Paecilomyces spp. are an uncommon cause of fungal infections in humans. They are generally found as an environmental mold in food, soil, air and wood (3). The organism grows rapidly on standard agar and forms velvety whitish, olive or tanned colonies (3). Speciation is important as case series have described distinct antifungal susceptibilities. For example, P. variotii is typically resistant to voriconazole, while P. lilacinus may be resistant to most antifungals other than newer triazoles like voriconazole and posaconazole.(4) Based on whole genome sequencing Paecilomyces lilacinus has been separated from the Paecilomyces family and recently renamed as Purpureocillum lilacinus (5).
A review of published cases of Paecilomyces reported many presented with devastating oculomycosis that required enucleation in 35% of cases.(3) The remainder of reported cases were cutaneous or subcutaneous infections or rarely disseminated infection.(3) Treatment of Paecilomyces keratitis is challenging and often requires surgery, though there is one case report of successful treatment with posaconazole despite the lower intraocular drug-levels anticipated with this drug.(6,7) The organism appears to be susceptible to echinocandins in vitro but this has not been confirmed in vivo. It typically has high MICs to amphotericin, fluconazole, flucytosine and itraconazole. (6-8)

title: A teenage girl with a background history of cystic fibrosis and tracheomalacia p
history:
A teenage girl with a background history of cystic fibrosis and tracheomalacia presented with persistent moist cough of 6 weeks’ duration that had little response to oral antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate and azithromycin sequentially; sputum was negative for any bacteria). Prior to this episode, she did not have a daily cough. She had no fever, dyspnea or weight loss. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Her spirometry revealed pulmonary function deterioration: her forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1) dropped from 2.62 L (94% predicted) six months earlier to 2.39 L (81% predicted) and forced vital capacity from 2.87 L (91% predicted) to 2.59 L (78% predicted). She was subsequently hospitalized for intravenous antibiotic therapy and intensive airway clearance.
The patient had been well until 3 years earlier when she required hospitalization for intravenous antibiotics for her first hospitalized pulmonary exacerbation. Her previous sputum cultures and annual cough swabs isolated Aspergillus fumigatus and Candidia spp. Pseudomonas aeruginosa had not previously been isolated from her sputum.

She had meconium ileus soon after birth and her cystic fibrosis genotype was homozygous for delta F508, with pancreatic insufficiency. She had a functional endoscopic sinus surgery for nasal polyps a year earlier. She has no known allergies.

She was born in Western Australia and moved to our center in Queensland, Australia 2 years earlier. She has no sick contacts, recent travel or household tobacco smoke exposure.

She was on both inhaled and oral medications for cystic fibrosis.
Inhaled medications: Dornase alfa (rhDNAse), mannitol, hypertonic saline and salbutamol.
Oral medication: Pancrealipase, vitamins A, D, E and K, salt.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well with no dyspnea or tachypnea. Her body mass index was 19kg/m². Her cough was wet. She had no digital clubbing. Her chest was clear. Remainder of other examination was unremarkable.

The peripheral blood white blood cell count was 6.3x10 9 /L (reference range 4.5-13.0) with neutrophils 3.11 (49%), lymphocytes 2.19 (35%), monocytes 0.50 (8%), eosinophils 0.47 (8%) and basophils 0.03 (0%). The hemoglobin, platelets, electrolytes and liver function test were normal.
A chest radiograph showed increased bilateral perihilar markings.

On day 13 of the admission, a chest CT scan was undertaken (Figures 1 & 2) because she still had a productive cough and a single sputum (on admission) isolated Mycobacterium abscessus. This showed incomplete anterior segmental collapse and mucus plugging with mild bronchiectasis of the right upper lobe (Figure 1) and moderate lingular cylindrical bronchiectasis with peribronchial thickening and the adjacent tree-in-bud opacification (Figure 2). Given the CT findings and the possibility of Mycobacterium abscessus disease, a bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was then performed and demonstrated viscous yellowish mucus plug obstructing the anterior segment of the right upper lobe (Figure 3). The tenacious plug was subsequently removed bronchoscopically via repeated suctioning (Figures 4 & 5).
Figure 1. CT scan of the chest showed incomplete anterior segmental collapse and mucus plugging with mild bronchiectasis of the right upper lobe.
Figure 2. CT scan of the chest showed moderate lingular cylindrical bronchiectasis with peribronchial thickening and the adjacent tree-in-bud opacification.
Figure 3. Bronchoscopic examination demonstrated viscous yellowish mucus plug obstructing the anterior segment of the right upper lobe.
Figure 4. Bronchoscopic removal of the mucous plug.
Figure 5. Bronchoscopic examination of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe post mucus plug removal.
diagnosis:
Allergic or non-allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in a patient with cystic fibrosis

The BAL total cell count was 80x10 6 /L and the differential cell count showed airway neutrophilia (62%) but no eosinophilia (0%). The BAL cultured Aspergillus fumigatus, no acid-fast bacilli or mycobacteria. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for respiratory viruses were negative.
Her total immunoglobulin E (IgE) was elevated - 165 kU/L on admission (was 55kU/L six months earlier). Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) for Aspergillus fumigatus reported as high positive. Serum Aspergillus precipitins was positive in one line.

She was started on oral prednisolone and itraconazole. At follow up a month post treatment, she reported complete resolution of her respiratory symptoms. Prednisolone was gradually tapered off.

Aspergillosis is a mycotic disease caused by Aspergillus spp., a filamentous fungus that is commonly encountered in organic waste, dust, compost and rotted materials. There are approximately 300 species of Aspergillus but only a few are known to be pathogenic in humans. 80% of clinical infections are caused by Aspergillus fumigatus complex. Its spores measure only 2-3 microns in diameter, therefore easily reach the terminal airways and alveoli where they can grow at body temperature [Chabi et al., 2015].
Pulmonary aspergillosis manifests as a wide spectrum of diseases, from simple aspergilloma to allergic or invasive disease [Soubani and Chandrasekar, 2002]. A more well-recognized form, simple aspergilloma usually occurs in a pre-existing cavitating lung disease. While invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is more commonly encountered in immunocompromised individuals, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), driven by an allergic reaction to Aspergillus antigens, almost exclusively seen in patients with asthma and cystic fibrosis (CF). Though these disease entities appear distinct, occasionally one may transform to another, or different forms can co-exist [Tunnicliffe et al., 2013].
The prevalence of ABPA in asthma ranges from 1-3.5% and in CF from 2-15% [Agarwal et al., 2013]. ABPA is clinically characterized by impaired mucociliary clearance, mucoid impaction with airway obstruction, and pulmonary infiltrates. The pathogenesis of ABPA is complex; it involves a non-invasive growth of Aspergillus spp. aided by poor airway clearance and a hypersensitive response via T-helper 2 (Th 2) pathway in genetically predisposed individuals. The release of fungal enzymes along with the sensitization lead to persistent airway inflammation and subsequent lung damage [Stevens et al., 2003; Thia and Lynn, 2009].
There is no single test, nor universally applied diagnostic criteria, for ABPA. The diagnostic approach has evolved over the past few decades, made on combination of clinical, radiological and immunological findings. Recently, a working group of ‘ABPA in asthmatics’ formed by the International Society of Human and Animal Mycology (ISHAM) proposed new diagnostic criteria to improve the accuracy in diagnosing ABPA [Agarwal et al., 2013]. These criteria include predisposing condition (asthma or cystic fibrosis) associated with both obligatory criteria and at least two out of three of other criteria. Obligatory criteria are positive skin test or elevated specific IgE to Aspergillus fumigatus and raised total IgE of >1000 IU/ml (equivalent to 1000 kU/L). Three other criteria are presence of precipitins or elevated serum IgG for Aspergillus fumigatus, radiographic changes consistent with ABPA and eosinophilia of >500 cells per microliter. The child did not meet all the criteria of ABPA but there is on-going debate on the diagnostic criteria, including the threshold for IgE [Greenberger et al., 2014].
Making a definite diagnosis of ABPA in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) can be challenging as clinical and laboratory features overlap. Bronchiectasis and mucus plugging that may account for the chest symptoms commonly seen in ABPA are often present at baseline in CF. Central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction involving predominantly the segmental and subsegmental bronchi of upper lobes typically described in ABPA may also occur in CF without ABPA [Kaur and Sudan, 2014]. Suspicion of ABPA should be raised if a patient fails to respond to intravenous antibiotics. Our patient did not fulfill all the diagnostic criteria of ABPA but given the supportive tests, her poor response to multiple courses of antibiotics and no other etiology encountered, bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was the most likely diagnosis.
Bronchoscopic examination of the tracheobronchial tree has diagnostic and therapeutic value, as illustrated in this patient. The tenacious mucoid impaction was described as plastic bronchitis, a syndrome of pulmonary aspergillosis but this is controversial as there remains disagreement [Chetty, 2003].
Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstays of therapy to reduce the inflammation and the immunological activity. Antifungal agents act as steroid sparing agent with attenuation of the antigen burden arising from fungal colonization [Patterson and E, 2014]. Early recognition and treatment of Aspergillus infection may prevent progressive lung damage particularly in those with pre-existing lung disease.

title: A man in his 30s with well-controlled HIV infection (CD4+ T-cells > 1000 cells/u
history:
A man in his 30s with well-controlled HIV infection (CD4+ T-cells > 1000 cells/uL) presented with one week of intermittent abdominal pain and cramping. He reported reduced appetite in the week preceding presentation, as well as intermittent nausea, vomiting and watery diarrhea. The patient denied any blood in his stool, and fevers, chills, and rigors.
The patient did not recall any sick contacts and had not recently travelled. He reported that he was last sexually active 2 weeks prior to presentation (reciprocal oral sex with a male partner), but denied any recent oral-anal contact.
He had dental work three months ago for which he received clindamycin prophylaxis.

The patient reported history of well-controlled HIV without recent change in antiretroviral regimen. He also had gastro-esophageal reflux disease.

Medications were emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide, etravirine and ranitidine.
exam_studies:
The patient’s blood pressure was 123/82, pulse rate 69 bpm and oral temperature 36.7°C (98.1°F).
On physical examination the patient appeared comfortable. His abdomen was soft and non-tender. Bowel sounds were normal and there was no rebound or guarding. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations were normal. There was no cervical, axillary, nor inguinal lymphadenopathy.

A complete blood count was notable for white blood cells of 13,000 cells per microliter of which 55% were neutrophils; he was not anemic and he had normal platelet count. He had normal renal function and hepatic function.
diagnosis:
Shigellosis with decreased susceptibility to azithromycin

A stool culture was positive. (Figure 1)
Microbiology
Given the patient’s diarrhea, a stool culture was performed. After 24 hours of incubation a translucent, flat bacterial colony that appeared to spread across the plate was seen on the blood agar plate (Figure 1). Similar colorless colonies were seen on MacConkey and Hektoen enteric agar plates indicating this organism did not ferment lactose, salicin, or sucrose (Figures 2 and 3). Oxidase, indole, and motility testing were negative. An acetate series which included an acetate slant, mucate broth, andrades xylose, andrades salicin, and a citrate slant were also negative. Triple sugar iron agar (TSI) and lysine iron agar (LIA) slants were created. The TSI slant revealed an alkaline reaction in the top and an acidic reaction in the butt of the slant, suggesting glucose fermentation (Figure 4). No gas or hydrogen sulfide was seen. The LIA slant had a purple reaction in the top and a red reaction in the butt of the slant indicating the organism was both lysine deaminase and lysine decarboxylase negative (Figure 5). Based on the above findings, serologic testing for specific Shigella spp. antigens was done via an agglutination assay and identified the organism as Shigella spp. serogroup D. This was confirmed using an automated gram negative identification card (Vitek 2) which gave an excellent identification of Shigella sonnei. Presumptive identification of Shigella sonnei was made and the organism was sent to the State Department of Public Health where the identification of Shigella sonnei was confirmed. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed and identified the organism as resistant to ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. An antimicrobial gradient test strip for azithromycin was performed and resulted in a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) > 256 ug/ml (epidemiological cut-off for wild type Shigella sonnei is ≤ 16 ug/ml).
Figure 1. Growth of the organism on a blood agar plate after 24 hours of incubation. A translucent flat colony that spreads across the plate is seen.
Figure 2. Growth of the organism on a MacConkey agar plate after 24 hours of incubation. Translucent colonies are seen.
Figure 3. Growth of the organism on Hektoen enteric agar plate after 24 hours of incubation. Translucent colonies are seen.
Figure 4. Triple sugar iron (TSI) agar slant of the organism after 24 hours of incubation. This slant contains glucose, sucrose, and lactose. The top portion of the slant is considered the aerobic portion due to its exposure to air and the butt of the slant is considered the anaerobic portion. Glucose fermentation is indicated by the presence of an acidic (A) reaction in the butt of the slant. Sucrose and lactose fermentation is identified by the presence of an acidic (A) reaction in the top of the slant. Shigella ferment glucose but not sucrose or lactose. Therefore, they produce a characteristic alkaline/acidic (K/A) reaction on TSI as seen here. Sodium thiosulfate is also present in this medium for the detection of hydrogen sulfide (H2S). If present, a black color forms in the slant. Shigella spp. do not produce H2S as evidenced by the lack of a black color on this slant. Finally, Shigella spp. do not produce gas so there are no bubbles seen in the TSI slant.
Figure 5. Lysine iron agar slant of the organism after 24 hours of incubation. This slant is used for the detection of lysine deaminase and lysine decarboxylase. If lysine deaminase is present, the top of the slant will turn a red color and if lysine decarboxylase is present the butt of the slant will turn a purple color. Shigella spp. are negative for both lysine deaminase and lysine decarboxylase producing a purple/yellow (K/A) slant. Sodium thiosulfate is also present in this medium for the detection of hydrogen sulfide (H2S). As stated above, Shigella spp. do not produce H2S and do not produce gas.

He was prescribed empirical azithromycin which was ceased when he improved. Interestingly, antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed a concerning resistance profile.
Azithromycin >256 ug/mL (No interpretation)
Ciprofloxacin 4 ug/mL (Resistant)
Ampicillin ≥32 ug/mL (Resistant)
Ceftriaxone ≤1 ug/mL (Susceptible)
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole ≥320 ug/mL (Resistant)

Shigellosis is characterized by acute-onset diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal cramps. (1) Stools often contain blood, although some patients present with watery diarrhea without blood. Rarely, severe shigellosis may be associated with gastrointestinal complications including rectal prolapse, intestinal obstruction and colonic perforation. Reactive arthritis may also be seen rarely one to two weeks after infection.
Shigella species are highly infectious; as few as 10 organisms may be sufficient to cause disease.(2) Contact with infected individuals or contaminated food is most frequently implicated in transmission. As an emerging sexually-transmitted infection in men who have sex with men (MSM) populations, shigellosis is associated with direct or indirect oral-anal contact. (3) In patients with normal immune function the disease is generally self-limited, resolving after seven days on average; however, patients remain infectious for up to four weeks as pathogens continue to be shed in feces. As such, this is a reportable illness and documentation of stool culture clearance is required in food-handlers. (4) In other populations including healthcare workers, antibiotic therapy is recommended to reduce the duration of disease and decrease the risk of continued transmission. (5)
Shigellosis is the third most common enteric bacterial infection in the United States (6) and the most common bacterial cause of diarrheal deaths in under 5 year-olds worldwide. (7) There are four species of Shigella that cause acute gastrointestinal infection: S. dysenteriae, S. flexnerii, S. boydii and S. sonnei. (8) S. dysenteriae was historically responsible for large epidemics but is now rare. S. flexneri and S. sonnei are common globally, with the former traditionally seen in resource-limited settings and the latter in resource-rich settings however S. sonnei is now emerging in resource-limited settings too. S. sonnei, along with S. flexneri serotypes 2a and 3a, are the strains most frequently implicated in outbreaks in MSM populations. (1)
S. dysenteriae, particularly serotype 1, produces shiga toxin and is considered the most virulent species. However, shiga toxins produced by other species including E. coli can be transferred via a lambda bacteriophage to non-toxin producing Shigella species including S. sonnei. Interspecies transfer of virulence factors in S. sonnei has been reported in a number of recent outbreaks. (9, 10)
Shigella species are often intrinsically resistant to multiple antibiotics including ampicillin, trimethroprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones, and reduced susceptibility to azithromycin is now being reported around the world.(11) Approximately 20% of Shigella isolates tested in New York City during 2013–2015 displayed decreased susceptibility to azithromycin. (12) Targeted therapy and improved surveillance will be important factors in limiting the further spread of resistant Shigella strains.

title: Previously healthy man in his 30s presents to a New England hospital in the summ
history:
Previously healthy man in his 30s presents to a New England hospital in the summertime with three days of headache, fatigue, myalgias and a rash.
He reports he developed a bright red rash on his trunk which began on the day prior to admission, and over the next 24 hours spread up to his head and face and down his extremities. About 12 hours into illness, he states “water bubbles broke out” on top of his areas of redness.
He reports he felt well until 5 days prior to presentation, on which day he went to the beach where he was exposed to full sun for 4-5 hours. Thereafter, he felt tired, and developed a frontal headache which he attributed to being dehydrated. He awoke the next morning with slight myalgias, and fatigue, but no arthralgias. He did not take his temperature during this time but may have "felt a little warm." He did have chills, then developed the rash. Denied anorexia, ocular symptoms, runny nose, sore throat nor cough. He denied sick contacts or other exposures.

None

He lives in New England. He is a nonsmoker without pets.

None
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. He had a temperature of 100.6 degrees Fahrenheit, blood pressure of 140/75 mm Hg, pulse of 75 beats per minute. The examination was notable for the truncal rash shown in Figure 1. On his trunk, there were scattered confluent raised erythematous and pruritic red plaques with vesicles atop plaques, many at the same stage. Few had erupted and ulcerated down his arms and legs, sparing palms and soles. His rash extended over the face into his scalp. His back was notable for a confluent rash, erythematous plaques with papules and vesicles. In his mouth, he had 3 small ulcers inside of his lower lip.
Figure 1. Figure 1a. Confluent raised erythematous and pruritic red plaques with vesicles atop plaques densely clustered on patient’s back.
Figure 1a. Confluent raised erythematous and pruritic red plaques with vesicles atop plaques densely clustered on patient’s back.
Figure 2. Immunofluorescent stain of varicella zoster virus from a vesicular lesion (60x). Using the fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) filter, VZV infected basal and/or parabasal epithelial cells will appear yellow-gold in color (white arrow).
Figure 1b. Close-up of clustered plaques with vesicles atop plaques
Figure 3. Figure 1c. Well-demarcated dense lesions separated from cleared skin at the line of patient’s swim trunks
Figure 1c. Well-demarcated dense lesions separated from cleared skin at the line of patient’s swim trunks

His labs were notable for a WBC 3.5 K/uL (normal 4.5-11) with 57% neutrophils, 24% lymphocytes, and 17% atypical lymphocytes. His hematocrit was 40% (normal 41-53%), and his platelets were 95 K/uL (normal 150-400 K/uL). Otherwise, his liver function tests and renal panel were normal. He had blood cultures collected which did not grow any organisms.
diagnosis:
Actinic Varicella

A vesicular lesion on the patient’s posterior left shoulder was unroofed and the vesicle base was sampled along with vesicular fluid, using a nylon flocked swab. The swab was submitted to the virology laboratory for direct detection of Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) antigen using fluorescent monoclonal antibodies (DFA= Direct Fluorescent Antibody).
After specimen centrifugation and staining, examination using a fluorescent microscope revealed nuclear and cytoplasmic fluorescence, indicating the presence of VZV antigen (see Figure 2). In addition, VZV IgM and IgG antibody testing was obtained with a positive and negative result respectively, a pattern potentially consistent with primary VZV infection. As lesions were mainly present in sun-exposed areas of the patient’s body, a diagnosis of photolocalized or actinic varicella was made.
Figure 4. Immunofluorescent stain of varicella zoster virus from a vesicular lesion (60x). Using the fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) filter, VZV infected basal and/or parabasal epithelial cells will appear yellow-gold in color (white arrow).

He was supportively managed with antipyretics, and with diphenhydramine for itching. Upon diagnosis, he was started on valacyclovir therapy with plan to complete 1-2 weeks of therapy until lesions were crusted over and no new lesions were identified. He was maintained on airborne precautions through his course. He recovered quickly.

Primary Varicella zoster virus infection, or chicken pox, classically produces a syndrome of fever, malaise and pruritis with an exanthematous rash of maculopapular, vesicular, and papular lesions which erupt in clusters and are present in varying stages at the same time. Varicella most commonly infects unimmunized children and is spread via respiratory route, but with introduction of childhood vaccination, the incidence has fallen [1].
In this case, an adult man presented with lesions consistent with varicella but arising in the same stages simultaneously, after sun exposure. Through skin scrapings and direct fluorescence antibody testing, the diagnosis of photolocalized or actinic varicella was confirmed.
Actinic varicella is a rare presentation of primary varicella zoster virus infection. It has been described only rarely in case reports, more commonly in infants than in adults [2-9]. Initially described as part of a larger category of accentuated viral exanthems in areas of inflammation (such as, diaper areas, feet) [10], it is thought that sun exposure produces a specific unique form of disease. One hypothesis is that exposure to the varicella zoster virus shortly followed by extensive sun exposure allows rapid proliferation of virus into UV-irradiated areas of skin that suffer from local cutaneous inflammation, increased capillary permeability, and the subsequent localized eruptions [11-12]. Other hypotheses suggest that areas of UV exposure are locally immunocompromised which allow for a more severe presentation [13].
In this patient, a particular curiosity was the patient’s age, as well as history later collected that he had been varicella IgG positive previously, although he noted neither primary varicella as a child, nor immunization, leading the team to suspect that this may have been a false positive result. Repeat testing at the time of presentation revealed a negative varicella IgG.
The differential diagnosis at the time of presentation included such concerning diagnoses as smallpox and measles. While smallpox was highly unlikely given lack of occupational exposure or risk of exposure, the question of varicella versus smallpox in this setting with atypical natural history of rash for primary varicella, was very important to differentiate. Hence, the rapid diagnostic of direct fluorescence antibody proved critically important. Regarding measles, the pattern of rash development was not in the classic head down to toe fashion, and the oral lesions did not precede the exanthema nor were they classic Koplik’s spots. He did not have conjunctivitis, coryza, nor cough. The appearance of the rash was not classic either, and the patient had been immunized with MMR.

title: A man in his fifties with a history of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy who und
history:
A man in his fifties with a history of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy who underwent an orthotopic heart transplantation (CMV donor positive/ recipient negative) about a decade ago, who is currently on tacrolimus 1mg/0.5 milligrams daily, mycophenolate 1500 milligrams twice daily, presented to the hospital with fever, night sweats, and fatigue.
One week prior to admission, he saw his primary care doctor for evaluation of a superficial right thigh nodule and right inguinal lymphadenopathy that had been present for about 4 weeks. He was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a presumed soft tissue infection. He subsequently noted fevers of 38°C (100.4°F) over the next week associated with fatigue and chills. Due to the persistence of fevers, he presented to the emergency department and was admitted to the hospital. Blood cultures were obtained, and the patient was initiated on empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam.

Atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease stage 3

The patient lives in South-eastern USA, does office work, and has not travelled overseas. He has never smoked or used illicit drugs and only drinks alcohol occasionally. He has not had recent sick contacts. He and his wife have outdoor cats.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. He was ambulant and had no exertional dyspnea. Temperature was 38°C (100.4°F), blood pressure 103/66, pulse 90, respiratory rate 17, pulse oximetry 98% on room air. Cardiac exam was notable for a systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Skin exam was notable for a 1 cm right medial thigh nodule with induration but no surrounding fluctuance or erythema (Fig. 1). There was no drainage, and the nodule was not tender to palpation. He had an enlarged, 2 cm nontender right inguinal lymph node. No other palpable lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the exam was normal.
Figure 1. Right medial thigh nodule.

At admission, the white blood cell count was 4.7 x10 9 /L (reference 3.2-9.8): 58% neutrophils (reference 37-80%), 25% lymphocytes (reference 10-50%), 14% monocytes (reference 0- 1%). Hemoglobin 16.4 g/dL (reference 13.7-17.3), platelets 202 x10 9 /L (reference 150-450). Creatinine was 1.9 mg/dL (reference 0.6-1.3). Aspartate transaminase was 55 U/L (reference 15-41), alanine transaminase was 60 U/L (reference 17-63), alkaline phosphatase was 87 U/L (reference 24-110), total bilirubin was 0.7 mg/dL (reference 0.4-1.5).
Two sets of blood cultures from admission showed no growth after five days. Urinalysis demonstrated no evidence of infection. Chest radiograph demonstrated no cardiopulmonary abnormality. Transthoracic echocardiogram noted mild left ventricular hypertrophy without evidence of vegetation or valvular dysfunction. Ejection fraction was 55% with normal diastolic function.
Bedside incision and drainage of the right thigh nodule had a negative Gram stain, bacterial, and fungal culture.

He continued to have fevers as high as 39.4°C (102.9°F) and developed progressive fatigue and night sweats.
Liver function tests continued to increase during admission: aspartate transaminase increased from 55 to 86 U/L, alanine transaminase from 60 to 127 U/L, total bilirubin from 0.7 to 1.0 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase from 87 to 165 U/L. HIV serology was negative and cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus quantitative PCR were negative. Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrated no gallstones or evidence of cholecystitis. A 1.4 cm hyperechoic lesion was seen in the posterior aspect of the left liver lobe consistent with a hemangioma.
Review of a peripheral blood smear demonstrated multiple atypical lymphocytes, raising concern for hematologic malignancy. Positron emission tomography scan was performed. This demonstrated hypermetabolic retroperitoneal, pelvic, left adrenal, and right inguinal lymphadenopathy along with diffuse splenic uptake.
Bartonella serologies (IgG and IgM) were negative (reference ranges <1:320 and <1:100 titers, respectively) and serum toxoplasma PCR was negative. Serum cryptococcal antigen and urine histoplasma antigen were also negative.
The nodule and his inguinal lymph node were biopsied. Skin biopsy of the thigh lesion revealed dense acute and chronic inflammation. Special stains did not reveal an infectious etiology.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Bartonella henselae infection

Inguinal lymph node biopsy revealed suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis (Fig 2) and no evidence of malignancy. Warthin-Starry stain showed rod-shaped organisms (Fig 3). Serum qualitative Bartonella henselae PCR was positive. Bartonella henselae PCR of the inguinal lymph node tissue subsequently returned positive.
Figure 2. H&E stain of right inguinal lymph node biopsy (10x) showing suppurative granulomas (arrows).
Figure 3. Warthin Starry Stain of right inguinal lymph node (40x) showing black rod-shaped organisms (arrows)

The patient was started initially on oral azithromycin 500 mg for three days, which was then decreased to 250 mg daily, and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Fevers rapidly improved, and he was discharged within the next 48 hours. He was seen in clinic 3 weeks after discharge and was feeling clinically improved. He was seen again in clinic 3 months after discharge and was back to his baseline energy level. His antibiotics were stopped at that appointment.

The Bartonella species are gram-negative bacilli, of which Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana are the most common in North America. Human infection is typically associated with cat and flea exposure, particularly young cats. [1] Individuals with intact immune systems typically present with a localized and self-limited lymphadenitis near the site of inoculum, referred to as cat scratch disease. [2] Bartonella has also been identified as an etiology of culture-negative endocarditis, especially in adult patients with prior valvular disease. [3] However, individuals who are immunosuppressed, particularly patients with HIV/AIDS and organ transplant recipients, are at increased risk of disseminated infection. [4] Infection in the HIV/AIDS population typically presents with vasoproliferative lesions. Bacillary angiomatosis most commonly manifests as cutaneous lesions, while bacillary peliosis presents as vascular lesions of the liver and spleen. [5] In contrast, transplant recipients present more frequently with granulomatous and suppurative lesions. There is not a clear correlation between type or duration of immunosuppression and the development of vascular versus granulomatous infection. [6]
In the solid organ transplantation population, there is an increased frequency of cases of bartonellosis reported in renal transplant recipients, followed by liver, then lung and heart transplant recipients, likely due to the proportion of each of these transplants performed annually. Time from transplantation to infection has been reported anywhere from 1 month to 14 years. Patients often present with disseminated infection earlier in their post-transplant course, while those with localized cat scratch disease typically present later (likely due to decreases in immunosuppression over time). [7] Most cases are transmitted by feline exposure, although there have been reported cases of transmission of infection from the transplanted organ. [8] Immunosuppression can also cause reactivation disease.
Solid organ transplant recipients with disseminated bartonellosis often present with non-specific symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and headache, though some have clinical evidence on exam of hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Diagnosis can be made by serology, polymerase chain reaction, culture, and histopathology. [9] Serology is usually positive but can be negative early in the disease course. Cultures can also be negative early on, as Bartonella is a fastidious, slow-growing organism. Pathology often shows granulomas, and the Warthin-Starry silver stain highlights the Bartonella bacilli. The Warthin-Starry stain is a silver-nitrate based staining method that picks up organisms not well detected on traditional Gram stain, such as spirochetes and small bacilli.
Treatment patterns vary based on the degree of dissemination of the infection. Localized cat-scratch disease in an immunocompetent host often does not require treatment, as it is self-limited. If antibiotics are prescribed, the first-line agent is usually azithromycin, which can expedite improvement in lymphadenopathy. [10] No specific guidelines exist for immunocompromised hosts with disseminated bartonellosis. Clinical practice is guided by case reports and expert opinion. Macrolides are often used as monotherapy or in combination with doxycycline. [7, 11, 12] Patients may also benefit from a reduction in immunosuppression. Duration of therapy ranges from a few weeks to several months, depending on the degree of dissemination and clinical response.

title: A man in his sixties presented with left eye painless vision loss, scotomas, int
history:
A man in his sixties presented with left eye painless vision loss, scotomas, intermittent flashes of light and pressure behind the eye over the past 24 hours, 3 months after allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT) for primary myelofibrosis.
He was diagnosed with primary myelofibrosis approximately two years prior to this admission and was treated with hydroxyurea followed by ruxolitinib. He underwent radiation therapy for splenomegaly 3 months prior to his SCT. Approximately 3 months prior to admission, he underwent a fludarabine/melphalan-conditioned unrelated donor allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplant. His donor was CMV-positive, while he was negative for both CMV and Toxoplasma gondii.
His post-transplant course was complicated by CMV reactivation without end organ disease and gastrointestinal graft-versus host-diseases (GvHD). CMV viremia was detected on pre-emptive monitoring and treated successfully with valganciclovir which he completed on day 82. He was then transitioned back to acyclovir prophylaxis with continued preemptive monitoring. He received tacrolimus and methotrexate for primary GvHD prophylaxis but developed GvHD on day 54 thus necessitating high dose systemic steroids and beclomethasone. He was on pentamidine for Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis as his persistent post- transplant pancytopenia precluded the use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. He was given posaconazole as antifungal prophylaxis while on high dose steroids for GvHD. On day 100 his steroids were reduced, and he no longer received fungal prophylaxis. He was discharged approximately 1 month after transplant.
He denied fevers, chills, headaches, hearing changes, neck pain, weight loss, weakness, chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

Chronic hepatitis B on lamivudine

He lives in northwest USA and previously had worked with shipping containers. He had traveled to Asia. He drinks 3-4 beers per day and had a 50-pack year smoking history but quit 3 years ago.

valganciclovir (discontinued D+ 82); acyclovir prophylaxis 800 mg BID; posaconazole (discontinued D+ 100); monthly IV pentamidine for PJP prophylaxis; tacrolimus 2 mg BID for GvHD; prednisone 15 mg daily for GvHD
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well, and not in acute distress. His vital signs were unremarkable with a temperature of 97°F (36.1°C), HR 97, BP 135/67, RR 12, and oxygen saturations of 100% on room air. His lungs were clear and heart sounds were regular. There was no lymphadenopathy or skin rashes.
The external appearance of both eyes were normal without injected sclera, ptosis, or proptosis. Extraocular muscles were intact bilaterally but there was pain associated with inferior movement of the left eye. Both pupils were reactive to light, but the left eye was noted to have an afferent pupillary defect. He was unable to discern the shape of objects and his visual deficits included upper hemispheric deficiencies. He did not have visual deficits in the right eye. Visual acuity on the left was 20/40 and on the right was 20/20. Cranial nerves I-VII were intact.
The ophthalmologist’s exam revealed a normal intraocular pressure of 18 (normal 12-22 mm Hg). The slit exam revealed diffuse WBC and haziness in vitreous chamber. The fundus exam showed inferior edema continuous with retinal inflammation. There was retinal whitening with punctate hemorrhages noted in the macula (Figures 1 and 2).
Figure 1. Figure 1: Left Eye Fundus and Retinal Exam with Fluorescein (color).
Figure 1: Left Eye Fundus and Retinal Exam with Fluorescein (color).
Figure 2. Figure 2: Left Eye Fundus and Retinal Exam with Fluorescein (black and white).
Figure 2: Left Eye Fundus and Retinal Exam with Fluorescein (black and white).

Laboratory findings revealed a white blood cell count of 1500/mm 3 (reference range 3.5-10.8) with a differential of 84% neutrophils and an absolute neutrophil count of 1200. Hemoglobin was 7.1g/dL (reference range 13.5-17.5) and platelets of 24,000//mm 3 (reference range 150,000-400,000). CD4 cell count was 40/mm 3 (reference range 212-1391). Liver function tests were normal.
Chest x-ray was clear without evidence of nodules or consolidations. Computed tomography of the chest revealed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules located throughout the right lung and the left upper lobe that measured between 3mm and 11mm (Figure 3). MRI of the brain with and without contrast revealed a 5 mm ring enhancing lesion in the right precentral gyrus as well as left periorbital edema and enhancement (Figure 4).
Additional laboratory evaluation included negative serum Toxoplasma gondii IgM and IgG, negative serum aspergillus galactomannan, negative plasma cytomegalovirus PCR, negative serum cryptococccal antigen, negative rapid plasma reagin, and negative serum T. gondii PCR.

diagnosis:
Ocular and cerebral toxoplasmosis

Left eye vitreous samples were obtained and sent for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, CMV and Toxoplasma gondii PCR, and broad range 16S ribosomal PCR. The T. gondii PCR was positive and the 16S ribosomal PCR was also positive for T. gondii.
The patient was negative for T. gondii antibodies pre-transplant and the donor’s T. gondii serostatus was not known.

Initially the ophthalmology unit performed intravitreal injections of voriconazole, clindamycin, and foscarnet until a diagnosis was made. He was also started prednisolone eye drops. Once the diagnosis of Toxoplasmosis was made, he was treated with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin.
He subsequently developed acute kidney injury while on these medications and sulfadiazine was discontinued. Atovoquone was substituted and he was continued on daily pyrimethamine, leucovorin, and prednisone. He received induction therapy dosing for approximately 6 weeks followed by maintenance therapy for another 6 weeks. Repeat MRI of the brain 2 months later showed that there was a slight decrease in the rim-enhancing lesion. Repeat CT chest showed that the pulmonary nodules had decreased in size. His T. gondii IgM and IgG were repeated and remained negative.

Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite. It typically remains latent in a normal host but, when there is a T-cell deficiency, fulminant disease can occur. It occurs worldwide and is acquired by ingestion of undercooked or raw meat containing viable cysts or through food and water contaminated with oocytes [1, 2].
Toxoplasmosis in those with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is a rare but potentially life-threatening infection if untreated. Infection typically occurs within the first 6 months post-transplant and the mortality rate is high if unrecognized. Data show that with appropriate treatment 60% of patients show clinical improvement. Infections that occur later after HSCT may have a better prognosis, which could be related to improved immunity over time [3]. Survival is highest in those with ocular and/or isolated cerebral toxoplasmosis but lower in those with disseminated infection [3, 4].
Toxoplasmosis primarily occurs as reactivation of dormant infection and therefore pre-transplant recipient serostatus determination is an important tool in assessing risk for post-transplant disease. Other predisposing factors for developing toxoplasmosis after HSCT include not receiving prophylaxis active against toxoplasmosis such as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, intensification of immunosuppression for GvHD, and low CD4 cell count (<200/mm 3) [3]. This patient had all these risk factors.
Typically, recipients who develop toxoplasmosis after SCT will be seropositive prior to transplant. Toxoplasmosis is rarely considered in patients post-HSCT if they have had negative T. gondii serology prior to transplant [4]. To our knowledge, the fact that our patient was diagnosed with ocular and cerebral toxoplasmosis in the setting of negative pre-transplant T. gondii serology is unusual. There have been a few reports of patients with isolated cerebral or ocular toxoplasmosis in the setting of negative pre-transplant serology, but it is rare [4, 5]. Possible explanations for a negative serology include his low immunoglobulins or donor-to-recipient transmission [6, 7]. The donor’s serology results were not available. PCR testing of serum, CSF, or vitreous samples can aid in providing a diagnosis. There is a higher sensitivity of PCR on aqueous or vitreous humor in the immunocompromised versus immunocompetent patients [6].
Toxoplasma IgG assays typically have a high negative and positive predictive value. IgM serologic assays have negative predictive values around 98% with a more variable positive predictive value between 45-85% [8]. This is important to recognize as a positive IgM in a setting of low prevalence could lead to an unnecessary invasive work up and treatment.

title: A Colombian man in his seventies presented with a history of weight loss, fever,
history:
A Colombian man in his seventies presented with a history of weight loss, fever, decreased appetite, night sweats, and new cutaneous ulcerations involving his arms, legs, and abdominal wall over a period of 4 weeks on a background of multibacillary leprosy 30 years prior, which had been treated with dapsone and rifampin for 1 year. He also reported numbness and paresthesia in the upper and lower extremities and 3-4 weeks of cough productive of yellow sputum. He denied hemoptysis.
He has insulin-requiring diabetes.

He worked in healthcare in Columbia and is now retired. He has no pets and no travel history outside of Columbia.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 160/80 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats per minute, respirations 22 breaths per minute, and temperature 102.2°F (39°C) during initial hospitalization. Lungs revealed bibasilar crackles and coarse breath sounds anteriorly.
Skin exam revealed multiple ulcerated lesions on the elbows, abdomen, and chest wall with surrounding erythema (Figures 1 and 2). Both lower limbs had multiple hypopigmented confluent macules and he had deformed ankle and feet joints consistent with Charcot joints (Figure 3). Neurological exam revealed decreased sensation in the bilateral upper and lower extremities (including temperature, light touch, vibratory, and proprioception) and decreased reflexes in bilateral upper and lower extremities. He also had thickened palpable nerves in the epitrochlear fossae bilaterally and in the neck. The exam was negative for hepatosplenomegaly and cervical, axillary, or submandibular lymphadenopathy. His exam was otherwise normal.

His chest X-ray revealed a miliary pattern (Figure 4). He tested negative for HIV and HTLV-1. Figure 4: Chest X-ray at presentation demonstrated a miliary pattern
Figure 4. Figure 4: Chest X-ray at presentation demonstrated a miliary pattern

diagnosis:
Mycobacterium leprae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis co-infection

His sputum was smear positive with 3+ acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Molecular PCR and culture from sputum was positive for M. tuberculosis (susceptible to rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).
Histopathological examination of skin biopsies demonstrated the occurrence of a Type 2 reaction in a patient with previous history of treated multibacillary disease. Skin biopsy showed a high bacillary index, prominent neutrophilic infiltrate and AFBs were present in the perineurium (Figures 5 and 6). A PCR from the skin biopsy (sent to National Hansen's Disease Program, Carville, Louisiana) was positive for M. leprae.
Figure 5. Figure 5: Fite-Faraco stain of skin biopsy demonstrating very large numbers of acid fast organisms (arrow) within histiocytes, cutaneous nerves, and in epithelial cells. The bacillary index was 6+. (400x)
Figure 5: Fite-Faraco stain of skin biopsy demonstrating very large numbers of acid fast organisms (arrow) within histiocytes, cutaneous nerves, and in epithelial cells. The bacillary index was 6+. (400x)
Figure 6. Figure 6: H&E stain of skin biopsy showing prominent neutrophils (arrow), consistent with erythema nodosum leprosum. (400x)
Figure 6: H&E stain of skin biopsy showing prominent neutrophils (arrow), consistent with erythema nodosum leprosum. (400x)

The patient was initially treated with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol plus clofazimine via directly observed therapy in addition to dapsone 100 mg daily. Sputum cultures remained positive for tuberculosis at 2 months. Pyrazinamide and ethambutol were later discontinued after his AFB smear and culture converted to negative. Isoniazid is currently being continued for a total of 7 months (with rifampin) to complete tuberculosis treatment. Rifampin, dapsone, and clofazimine are being continued for a minimum of 2 years for treatment of leprosy, with plans to obtain repeat skin biopsy to assess for decreasing bacillary load. He also received a prednisone taper beginning at 80 mg daily (with close glucose monitoring) later decreased to 20 mg daily for treatment of a type 2 leprosy reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum).

Our patient was diagnosed with acute pulmonary tuberculosis and a Type 2 leprosy reaction, also known as erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). Leprosy reactions are immunological reactions that occur frequently among patients with Hansen’s disease (leprosy) at any point, including prior to the initiation of multidrug therapy, during therapy, or even years after completion of therapy, often producing significant neurologic sequelae. A type 1 reaction, also known as a reversal reaction, occurs due to an intensification of cell-mediated immunity (1). This presents as increased acute erythema, warmth, edema, and occasional ulceration of pre-existing cutaneous plaques and nodules, without systemic involvement and is usually paucibaciliary (1). Type 2 reactions (ENL) result from antigen-antibody complex deposition, leading to new subcutaneous nodules which are painful, and tender and are accompanied commonly by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise and lymphadenitis (1). This is characterized by a neutrophilic infiltrate (as seen here) accompanied by vasculitis and/ or inflammation of the subcutaneous layer of fatty tissue (panniculitis) (1).
Leprosy remains an important neglected tropical disease in Colombia. Leprosy can lead to long-term complications which most commonly involve the peripheral nerves and skin. It can also affect the eyes, bones, testes, and mucous membranes (2). As this case illustrates, co-infection of M. leprae with other mycobacterial infections, such as tuberculosis, may facilitate the occurrence of late leprosy reactions or possibly clinical relapses of leprosy (3,4). Recent evidence suggests that the occurrence of severe leprosy reactions or severe forms of leprosy including Lucio’s leprosy may be due to co-infection between M. leprae and other mycobacteria including Mycobacterium lepromatosis (5-7). Lucio’s leprosy is uncommon and is characterized by hemorrhagic plaques due to mycobacterial invasion of endothelia (1), and this type of leprosy did not occur in our case. Co-infected patients require long-term clinical monitoring for severe neurologic sequelae, late leprosy reactions, and adverse effects of long-term anti-inflammatory use.
According to WHO guidelines, no additional laboratory tests are recommended if a patient meets one of three common signs: (i) definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch; (ii) thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of the muscles supplied by that nerve; or (iii) presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear (8). Steroids were utilized to prevent further sensory loss in our case and are often initiated to prevent further nerve injury (1). Clofazamine was included in the current recommended regimen but is commonly added as a steroid-sparing agent (1). In Colombia, the rate of drug-resistant tuberculosis is 1.2% in 2016 (9). Prospective monitoring of patients with Hansen’s disease may help define the impact of mycobacterial co-infections on the severity and spectrum of disease of leprosy.
