Blood pressure 114/85 mm Hg, heart rate 136 beats per minute, respiratory rate 36 respirations per minute, oxygen saturation 100% on 3 liters per min of supplemental oxygen.
The cranial incision site was non-tender, non-erythematous, without any pus or swelling. The pupils were equal and reactive to light. There was no nuchal rigidity. The tone in both upper and lower limbs was reduced. Tympanic membranes were non-erythematous and non-bulging bilaterally. A mastoid exam was not documented. Auscultation of the lungs showed good equal air entry bilaterally without any adventitious sounds. Cardiovascular exam revealed normal heart sounds, no gallops or murmurs. Capillary refill was less than 2 seconds and skin turgor was normal. The abdomen was soft, non-tender and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. There was no lymphadenopathy. There were no rashes, Janeway lesions or Osler nodes.

The white blood cell count was 15 200/µL (normal 6 000-17 000/µL) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12 750/µL (normal 1500-8500/µL). The patient also had a sodium level of 125 mM (baseline 139 mM; normal 135-145 mM).
A CT head with contrast showed bilateral small frontal hygromas which were expected postoperative changes, without evidence of empyema or other acute intracranial pathology.
In the context of persistent fever, new-onset vomiting, lethargy and a recent intracranial surgery, a lumbar puncture was performed to rule out meningitis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear. CSF analysis revealed a white blood cell count of 35/µL (normal 0-5/µL), with 50% monocytes and 44% neutrophils, 0 erythrocytes, protein of 1.2 g/L (normal 0.15-0.45 g/L) and a glucose of 0 mM (2.4 – 4.4 mM). diagnosis:

A blood culture obtained on the seventh post-operative day was positive for gram positive cocci in chains. After the lumbar puncture was performed, the patient was started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin at meningitic dosing to provide coverage for the most common bacteria causing meningitis in this age group, namely Streptococcus pneumoniae (including ceftriaxone-resistant strains) and Neisseria meningitidis. Corticosteroids were not administered empirically. CSF gram stain showed 4+ gram-positive diplococci. Cultures of blood and CSF grew penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, confirming the diagnosis of healthcare-associated pneumococcal meningitis. The organism’s antibiogram with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) obtained by E-test for penicillin, ceftriaxone and meropenem are shown in Table 1. As susceptibility testing confirmed ceftriaxone sensitivity, vancomycin was discontinued, and the patient was kept on ceftriaxone.

Unfortunately, after 3 days of ceftriaxone, the patient spiked a new fever, was still lethargic and developed abnormal right-sided upper and lower extremity movements. A head MRI was ordered to rule-out an intracranial collection, and ceftriaxone was changed to meropenem to cover possible nosocomial multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacilli causing a superimposed central nervous system (CNS) infection. The MRI showed lesions suggestive of either small vessel vasculitis secondary to bacterial meningitis – a rare complication – or central pontine myelinolysis due to rapid correction of hyponatremia documented a few days prior. Given the absence of a new focus of infection, meropenem was discontinued and ceftriaxone was restarted. In addition, given the uncertain etiology of the cerebral lesions, the patient received a 10-day course of intravenous corticosteroids and one dose of intravenous immunoglobulins as treatment of cerebral small vessel vasculitis.
A repeat lumbar puncture performed after 11 days of antibiotics to document CSF sterility revealed normal CSF parameters and a negative CSF bacterial culture. The patient subsequently developed post-infectious hydrocephalus for which a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt was inserted. She received a total of 21 days of appropriate antibiotic therapy (adequately covering penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae at meningitic doses). The treatment duration was prolonged in her case pending repeat head imaging which showed no intracranial abscesses and the placement of a VP shunt.
The patient’s infection resolved but she had neurologic sequelae that are improving.

The incidence of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in high-income countries is estimated at 1 to 3 cases per 100,000 individuals, all ages included (1, 2). However, the incidence in young children is significantly higher, ranging from 2 to 80 cases per 100,000 individuals depending on the age group (1). Specifically, pneumococcal meningitis has a worldwide incidence of about 17 cases per 100,000 individuals in children less than 5 years of age (1, 3). As for healthcare-associated bacterial meningitis, incidence rates are derived from neurosurgical patient populations and range between 0.5% and 8% (4). Given that bacterial meningitis tends to affect young children and that the signs and symptoms are non-specific in this age group, a high index of suspicion is required to make the diagnosis.
Causal organisms also vary according to age. Children younger than 6 weeks are at increased risk of meningitis due to pathogens present in the maternal genitourinary flora such as Streptococcus agalactiae and Enterobacteriaceae, whereas Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis predominate in children older than 6 weeks. Overall, the most common pathogen in children less than 5 years of age is S. pneumoniae (5). This epidemiological data helps to inform appropriate empiric antimicrobial treatment choices when faced with a suspected case of bacterial meningitis.
Prompt initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for bacterial meningitis. Empiric antibiotics are chosen according the usual antibiotic susceptibility patterns of the most likely pathogens. In the context of bacterial meningitis, the MIC of key antibiotics must be determined to inform specific therapy. The MIC is defined as the concentration of antibiotic at which growth of 90% of isolates is inhibited. (6). An additional challenge for CNS infections is that the concentration of antibiotic in the CSF is much lower than in the serum due to the blood brain barrier (BBB). As such, in order to achieve therapeutic concentrations of antibiotics in the CSF, a higher concentration of antibiotic must be administered in the blood stream. MIC breakpoints are therefore lower when the isolate is grown in the CSF as compared to non-meningeal sites as illustrated in the table presented in this case.
Global surveillance of pneumococcal susceptibility patterns has shown that rates of penicillin non-susceptibility have been increasing over the past 30 years worldwide (6). Whereas penicillin was frequently part of empiric antibiotic regimens for bacterial meningitis in the past, the increasing incidence of penicillin non-susceptible S. pneumoniae has led to its replacement by third generation cephalosporins. Third generation cephalosporins have adequate CSF penetration and good activity against the usual pathogens causing bacterial meningitis, including S. pneumoniae. However, there has also been a trend towards increasing cephalosporin resistance in pneumococcal isolates worldwide (7). Although the absolute rates of resistance remain low (8), the dramatic outcomes associated with inappropriately treated meningitis have led to recommending the addition of vancomycin in the empiric regimen of bacterial meningitis in certain guidelines (9, 10). Ultimately, the decision to add vancomycin should be guided by local antimicrobial resistance patterns (12).
Corticosteroids also play a role in the treatment of bacterial meningitis. Current evidence suggests that adjunctive dexamethasone reduces rates of hearing impairment in H. influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis in children. Its benefit in pediatric pneumococcal meningitis, however, is less clear and experts vary in recommending its use. In addition, beneficial effects of adjunctive corticosteroids have not been observed in low-income countries (13). Moreover, corticosteroids have no benefit in meningitis caused by other organisms and are not recommended in the context of healthcare-associated meningitis (13).
The advent of vaccination against several causal pathogens of bacterial meningitis has significantly contributed to the reduction of mortality and morbidity related to both community-acquired and nosocomial bacterial meningitis over the last decades (1, 14, 15). Furthermore, several routine practices such as hand-hygiene (16) and perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis (17) have been shown to further help prevent nosocomial meningitis. Despite all these efforts, the fatality rate has remained virtually unchanged at around 14% (1).
In cases where prevention fails, prompt initiation of appropriate empiric antimicrobial treatment guided by local epidemiological data and susceptibility patterns is essential to prevent mortality and morbidity. As illustrated by the case described here, even non-lethal cases can be quite devastating.

title: A woman in her thirties with diabetes and psychiatric disease was admitted to an
history:
A woman in her thirties with diabetes and psychiatric disease was admitted to an inpatient ward in a general hospital in Lima, Peru with five days of crampy and generalized abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting. She was noted to be drowsy for two days and developed persistent vomiting. She denied any fevers, dysuria and urinary frequency. She was brought to the hospital by her mother due to the persistence of symptoms and inability to tolerate her usual medications.

She has a history of admissions to psychiatric centers for psychiatric disease.

Metformin, Valproic acid, Risperidone, Clonazepam
exam_studies:
The patient looked unwell and pale. Her skin was dry. Her vital signs were: BP 120/70 mmHg, pulse rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 22 bpm, temperature 37°C (98.6°F), and oxygen saturation 95% at room air. She had cool extremities. There was no rash. She was tender in the hypogastric area and right hypochondriac and right renal angle. There were no masses and Murphy’s sign was negative.
On neurological assessment, she was drowsy and disoriented to time and place. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable.

White blood cell count (WBC): 15,300 cells/mL (reference range 4000-10,000) with neutrophils 76% and 5% bands; hemoglobin: 9 g/dL, blood glucose: 1,050 mg/dL (reference range 70-110 mg/dL), sodium 135 mEq/dL (reference range 135-145), potassium 4.1 mEq/dL (reference range 3.5-4.5), chloride 89 mEq/mL (reference range 87-110), urea: 28 mg/dL (reference range 10-45), serum creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL (reference range 10-45), plasma osmolarity: 330 mOsm/Kg, amylase: 36 U/L (reference range 30-60), lipase: 386 U/L (reference range 30-90). Arterial blood gas was normal.
Her urine dipstick was positive for leucocytes (Figure 1). Urinalysis showed >100 leukocytes/hpf, 2 – 3 RBCs/hpf, bacteria ++. Blood cultures were negative. Urine culture grew more than 100,000 colony forming units of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
The chest radiograph showed no pulmonary infiltrates or effusion. Renal ultrasound: kidneys with parenchymal inflammatory process in both kidneys and preserved cortical thickness, no stones or urolithiasis were found.

The patient was treated for a hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state based on laboratory findings with the possibility of pyelonephritis as the triggering factor. Empirical therapy with Ceftriaxone 2 grams daily was started. Her fevers persisted over the next five days and her WBC continued to rise, thus, this was changed to Meropenem 1 gram every 8 hours.
diagnosis:

The full antibiogram demonstrating meropenem resistance became available two days after the commencement of meropenem by which time she had improved with resolution of her fevers and normalization of her WBC. Meropenem was continued for 10 days and she recovered completely.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common gram-negative pathogen associated with nosocomial infections. Over the last two decades, multi-drug resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa has become a problem, particularly the strains that produce MBLs (1). There have been several reports of outbreaks of (MDR) P. aeruginosa isolated from urine but the appropriate therapeutic regimen to combat infection with the organism have not been well established (1,2).
Risk factors associated with MBL-producing P. aeruginosa infections are insertion of ureteral stent; urologic diseases; end stage renal disease; female sex; advanced age (>60 years); previous beta-lactam, fluoroquinolone or carbapenem use; diabetes; previous hospitalization, and admission into an intensive care unit. (3, 4) Her multiple admissions to a psychiatric care facility may have played a role in the development of this event. (4) Eveillard et al. reported that the main multiple-drug resistant bacteria in psychiatric facilities were methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, followed P. aeruginosa, where patient-to-patient transmission was suspected (5).
One of the emergent problems in nosocomial transmission of P. aeruginosa infection is the transference of plasmids including MBLs (6). In Peru, the knowledge of the molecular epidemiology of these multidrug- resistant microorganisms is scarce. However, in one local study it was found that the most frequent mechanism of resistance to carbapenems among Pseudomonas was the production of MBLs (7,8).
We highlight the potential utility of a phenotypic method for the presumptive identification of MBL’s in P. aeruginosa. This test relies on combination disk testing using Imipenem and EDTA disks and is easy to perform and accessible. It shows a sensitivity of close to 93% and specificity of 100% in comparison with PCR (9). It should be noted, however, that this method is not endorsed by Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) or the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) for the detection of MBL. The reference methods such as PCR are not systematically applied to characterize MBL-producers in our setting, due to their high cost (10). We implemented these alternative techniques in our setting to enable antibiotic stewardship and reduce nosocomial transmission (10, 11).
These pathogens leave us with scarce options for treatment. Current guidelines recommend the use of high dose carbapenems or colistin, fosfomycin, tigecycline or aminoglycosides, depending on the organism’s susceptibility (12).
The new beta-lactam with beta-lactamase combinations, like ceftolozane/tazobactam, ceftazidime/avibactam and meropenem/vaborbactam, are not active against MBL but may be active against strains of Pseudomonas spp. that harbor other resistance mechanisms. (13, 14) Ceftolozane-tazobactam is the only combination available in Peru. It is not affordable by many of our patients and it is not available at our hospital.
In the present case, MIC quantification for carbapenems was not performed and the patient presented significant improvement only with the use of high doses of Meropenem.

title: A young man with rheumatoid arthritis receiving methotrexate and a tumor necrosi
history: A young man with rheumatoid arthritis receiving methotrexate and a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor presented with several months of non-healing lesions of the fingers. The lesions initially occurred after an injury to the hand while in a pond. Shortly thereafter, he developed erythema and swelling. Despite multiple courses of cephalexin and clindamycin, the lesions did not improve.
exam_studies:
On exam, he had an erythematous ulcerated lesion overlying the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint on the right fourth finger. An additional erythematous lesion was also noted on the dorsal aspect of the third phalanx.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the hand revealed soft tissue thickening with increased T2 signal dorsal to the fourth PIP joint and third middle phalanx. No synovitis or osteomyelitis was seen.

A small amount of purulent material was expressed from one of the lesions and was sent for fungal smear and culture as well as mycobacterial smear and culture.
The direct smears for fungi and mycobacteria were negative. On day 14 of incubation at 30°C, the mycobacteria growth indicator tube (MGIT) was positive for growth. Solid medium culture was also positive at 30°C (chocolate agar slant). No growth was found in the MGIT at 37°C, on the Lowenstein Jensen (LJ) media, or the fungal culture. Ziehl-Neelson staining of the MGIT broth revealed acid fast bacilli with cord formation (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Ziehl-Neelsen stain of the 30°C broth culture after 14 days of incubation. Acid fast bacilli with cord formation are seen.
diagnosis:
A DNA probe for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex performed from the MGIT broth was negative. Subcultures were prepared on solid media (Middlebrook 7H11) and ultimately grew a rough, white colony (Figures 2 and 3). The organism was identified as Mycobacterium marinum based on matrix assisted laser desorption time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF).
Mycobacterium marinum is a slow growing nontuberculous mycobacterium often found in association with fresh or saltwater environments (1). Cutaneous infections such as the one above can occur due to direct inoculation of a cut with the organism and subsequent exposure to contaminated water. The lesions can be nodular, pustular, or ulcerated and infection of the deeper tissues, joints, and bones can occur (1, 2).
Diagnosis of M. marinum infection is often made via isolation of the organism on culture. Growth of the organism is slow, requiring growth time of more than 7 days. Growth temperature is lower than that of many other mycobacterial species, with the optimal temperature ranging from 28 to 30°C (1). A Ziehl-Neelsen smear of the broth can reveal cord formation (Figure 1); a feature which is most commonly seen with the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, however, it has also been described with M. marinum (3). Colonies of M. marinum are rough and white (Figures 2 and 3) and become pigmented upon exposure to light. Formal identification of M. marinum can be made using MALDI-TOF as was done in this instance.

title: A female in her twenties, originally from Central America, presented with an 8-w
history:
A female in her twenties, originally from Central America, presented with an 8-week history of dizziness and headache. She described her dizziness as a spinning sensation and endorsed unsteadiness and subjective weakness in her legs. She complained of a daily headache which was sharp in quality and frontotemporal in distribution, made worse with neck flexion and bending down. This was associated with nausea, vomiting and photophobia.
She endorsed visual disturbance, describing objects jumping across her visual field. She otherwise denied fever, weight loss, cough, abdominal pain, changes in bladder or bowel habits, rash, arthralgia/myalgia, seizures or gait disturbance. Denied sick contacts.

She immigrated from Central America where she lived on a farm. She is an omnivore. No travel in the past year otherwise.
exam_studies:
Patient appeared uncomfortable, retching intermittently, with a bedpan on her lap. Vitals: blood pressure 111/57, pulse 63, temperature 98.1ºF (36.7ºC), respiratory rate 16, SpO 2 98% on room air.
She was alert and oriented and following commands. Her neurological examination revealed intact cranial nerves though the neurology service appreciated mild papilledema in the right eye and was unable to visualize the optic disc on the left. Her peripheral strength was normal and sensation intact. There were no cerebellar signs and reflexes were equal. Her gait was slow and hesitant but otherwise she was able to walk unassisted. There was no meningismus with forward flexion.

Her Complete Blood Count was notable for a Hemoglobin of 11.7 K/uL (Reference: 12-16) and Hematocrit of 34.2% (Reference: 36-46) with no leukocytosis. Her chemistry was unremarkable. Microbiology studies notable for recent negative HIV and Hepatitis B serologies.
Her MRI Brain (Figure 1) was notable for evidence of acute hydrocephalus with diffuse ventricular and cerebral aqueduct dilatation, with an irregular multiloculated cyst along the floor of the fourth ventricle.
Figure 1. Fig 1: MRI Brain at presentation. Sagittal section, FIESTA series. Irregular, cystic-appearing multi-loculated debris is seen at the base of the fourth ventricle with associated upstream ventricular enlargement. The cyst is interposed between the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle and is noted to be T2 isointense to CSF.
Fig 1: MRI Brain at presentation. Sagittal section, FIESTA series. Irregular, cystic-appearing multi-loculated debris is seen at the base of the fourth ventricle with associated upstream ventricular enlargement. The cyst is interposed between the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle and is noted to be T2 isointense to CSF.

Given the hydrocephalus and ventricular lesion, the patient was admitted to the Neurosurgery service with plan for surgical evacuation of cyst and decompression.
diagnosis:
Intraventricular Neurocysticercosis of the 4th ventricle

She underwent a suboccipital craniotomy and evacuation of the cyst. The operative report noted that the fourth ventricle was opened with moderate pressure of cerebrospinal fluid. Yellow cystic material was appreciated immediately underneath this opening, which slid out with very gentle pressure (Figure 2). The ventricle was irrigated and the walls of the fourth ventricle appeared yellowish and gliotic. Ultrasound navigation confirmed that the fourth ventricle was decompressed and there were no obvious cysts remaining.
Pathology confirmed the presence of non-viable, degenerated, hyalinized material recognizable as a neurocysticercosis cyst wall with a cuticular layer, middle cellular layer and an inner reticular layer (Figures 3-5). Adjacent brain showed chronic inflammation and reactive gliosis. She tested positive for serum IgG antibodies against Taenia solium (T solium) glycoproteins.
Figure 2. Fig 2: A fluid-filled cyst evacuated intra-operatively from the ventricular system, measuring almost 3cm in diameter. (Contributed by Dr. Pamela Jones)
Fig 2: A fluid-filled cyst evacuated intra-operatively from the ventricular system, measuring almost 3cm in diameter. (Contributed by Dr. Pamela Jones)
Figure 3. Fig 3. Histopathology of cyst (100x) showing cyst lining, of which some is necrotic (black arrows). (Courtesy of Dr Nathan Clements)

Figure 5. Fig 5: Three layers of the cyst wall is shown: inner reticular (blue), middle cellular (red), and outer layer with tegument and glycocalyx lining (black) 400x. (Courtesy of Dr Nathan Clements)

Postoperatively, MRI spine was performed and detected no additional cysticerci. With no intra-parenchymal or spinal disease, her disease was categorized as purely intraventricular, and she was considered cured after surgical removal of the cyst. Thus, antiparasitic therapy was deferred and follow-up MRI ordered in 6 months to ensure resolution.
At a follow-up visit one month after discharge, she expressed resolution of her dizziness, headache, and nausea, and her surgical wounds were healing well.

Neurocysticercosis (NCC) remains an important cause of central nervous system (CNS) infection in the developing world, with an estimated prevalence of 50 million infected worldwide. [1] The causative microbe is the parasite Taenia solium and the disease has two manifestations depending on where humans interact with the life cycle: egg versus cyst. Ingestion of eggs shed into the feces of a human tapeworm carrier leads to cysticercosis, characterized by systemic tissue deposition of cysts harboring the larvae. NCC is a subtype of cysticercosis where the site of cyst deposition involves the brain and spinal cord. [2] Pigs represent the other major hosts outside humans for larval cysts. Ingestion of pork infected with these cysts leads to the second disease entity, tapeworm infection in the gut, known as Taeniasis. When cysts find their way into the human gut, they undergo development into adult tapeworms and establish infection to continue the life cycle.
NCC is further characterized by its distribution within the CNS and can be separated into intra-parenchymal and extra-parenchymal disease. Intra-parenchymal NCC is the most common form of cysticercosis and often presents clinically with seizures. [3] Extra-parenchymal disease can be further sub-divided into intraventricular, subarachnoid, spinal, and ocular lesions, which more commonly present with symptoms related to hydrocephalus and mass effect. The diagnosis of NCC is made primarily on clinical and radiographic grounds and can be reinforced with serologies. Both CT and MR imaging should be performed where possible when NCC is suspected. CT imaging performs well at identifying parenchymal cysts and calcifications, while MRI can detect edema around lesions, degenerative changes, as well as scolices (head of cyst facilitating attachment to bowel wall) within lesions. [4]
Serologies can support the diagnosis of NCC when imaging is suggestive but not pathognomonic. Enzyme-linked immunotransferase blot (EITB) has replaced ELISA as the test of choice for cysticercosis as it demonstrates higher sensitivity and specificity in serum, with sensitivity approaching 100% in patients with multiple parenchymal lesions or with disease in the ventricles or subarachnoid space. [5] Indeed, our patient tested positive for serum IgG antibodies against T solium glycoproteins. In our patient case, we were fortunate to have pathology confirming the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis. The other differential diagnoses like tuberculoma and toxoplasmosis were less likely given her negative T-SPOT during this admission and HIV-negative status during recent prenatal screening. While Echinococcus can also cause cystic disease, her positive serologies against T solium lent additional support to the diagnosis.
The management of NCC varies by the site of disease. In 2017, the Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) published consensus guidelines for the management of NCC. [5] In our patient case, intraoperative findings along with head and spine imaging confirmed that her disease was confined to the 4th ventricle without parenchymal involvement. Cystic obstruction of the 4th ventricle led to hydrocephalus and symptoms consistent with increased intracranial pressure. Per IDSA guidelines, the recommended management of intraventricular NCC confined to the fourth ventricle is surgical removal rather than medical therapy where possible. Preoperative antiparasitic therapy was not provided given the concern that treatment can disrupt cyst integrity and complicate surgical removal. [6] Moreover, we had yet to exonerate any spinal involvement, and case reports demonstrate the potential for treatment to cause cystic degeneration and a robust inflammatory response which, in the confines of the spinal canal, can cause irreversible damage. [7]
The major clinical question following successful removal of our patient’s intraventricular cyst was whether to provide adjunctive postoperative antiparasitic therapy. IDSA guidelines recommend adjunctive treatment for intraventricular NCC only if complete cyst removal is not possible and shunt insertion is performed instead. In this subset of patients, antiparasitic therapy may reduce the likelihood of subsequent shunt failure. [4, 8] In our patient case, pre- and post-operative MRI of the head and spine confirmed disease confinement to the fourth ventricle, and thus surgery was deemed curative. Medical treatment with anti-parasitics (albendazole and/or praziquantel) are used in patients with intra-parenchymal disease that has not calcified, or in patients with extra-parenchymal disease where cysts cannot be removed surgically. Anti-parasitics are often used with corticosteroids to minimize damage secondary to the inflammatory response.
At one month after discharge, the patient endorsed resolution of her headache and dizziness and her surgical site was healing well. She will undergo repeat MRI in six months post-discharge to confirm resolution and stability.

title: A young male returning traveler in his twenties presented to the emergency depar
history:
A young male returning traveler in his twenties presented to the emergency department (ED) with a three-week history of a pruritic migrating serpiginous rash on his right foot (Figure 1, when he first noticed the lesion). The rash appeared while he was in Thailand, about ten days into his trip. The patient also noted having a nonproductive cough for two weeks with occasional wheezing. He denied other skin lesions, dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest and abdominal pain, or changes in bowel habits. Fig. 1: Right foot cutaneous lesion when it was first noticed (ie. three weeks before presenting to the emergency department)
Figure 1. Fig. 1: Right foot cutaneous lesion when it was first noticed (ie. three weeks before presenting to the emergency department)
Fig. 1: Right foot cutaneous lesion when it was first noticed (ie. three weeks before presenting to the emergency department)

The patient is not known to have any chronic medical problems.

The patient had recently returned from a one-month vacation where he travelled to Laos, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore. Travel activities included hiking, swimming in freshwater, and sunbathing. He admitted to contact with animals including elephants, monkeys, and water buffaloes, but denied eating any raw meat or fish or drinking tap water. He is a non-smoker, does not use recreational drugs, and denied sexual activities while travelling.

The patient was not using any medications. He recently used atovaquone/proguanil (250 mg/100 mg PO daily for 3 weeks) for malaria prophylaxis while on a trip to Southeast Asia, but discontinued it upon return, a few days before presenting to the ED.
exam_studies:
Patient appeared well, with no signs of systemic toxicity or respiratory distress. Vital signs were the following: Temperature 36.4°C (97.5°F), Blood Pressure 135/80, Heart Rate 97, RR 18, Oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The cutaneous lesion (Figure 2) was located over the right foot fifth metatarsal. It was a raised vesiculobullous serpiginous lesion measuring 3 cm in length and about 2 mm in width. Significant swelling and redness surrounded the lesion. According to earlier pictures taken by the patient, the lesion has been migrating proximally leaving burrows behind its leading edge. The lesion moved about 4 cm in the last 3 weeks.
Chest expansion was symmetrical and without accessory muscle use. There was no dullness to percussion over either lung field. Expiratory rhonchi were auscultated in both hemithorax. The examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 2. Fig. 2: Right foot cutaneous lesion two weeks after it was first noticed
Fig. 2: Right foot cutaneous lesion two weeks after it was first noticed

Chest X-ray (Figure 3) showed increased patchy central opacities in the right and left lower lung zone. There was no evidence of pulmonary edema or pleural effusion.
His white blood count was raised at 15.3 x10^9/L (reference range: 4.5-11) with 31% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count, 4.75 x10^9/L (ref 0-0.45)). Hemoglobin and platelets were normal. IgE was high at 917 ug/L (ref 0-240). Renal and liver function tests were normal.
Figure 3. Fig. 3: Chest X-Ray at presentation. Patchy central opacities noted in the right and left lower lung zone.
Fig. 3: Chest X-Ray at presentation. Patchy central opacities noted in the right and left lower lung zone.

Based on the CXR findings, cutaneous eruption and the recent travel history, he was referred to a tropical medicine specialist.
diagnosis:
Loeffler’s syndrome secondary to helminthiasis.

Filaria serology: negative
Strongyloides serology: negative
Strongyloides stool culture: negative
Stool ova/parasites: negative

The patient was prescribed ivermectin 15 mg PO QD for 3 days. After taking the medication, the cutaneous lesion gradually disappeared and the respiratory symptoms resolved. He completed a repeat blood test and microscopy a few weeks later. The results showed a normal eosinophil count and no ova/parasite in his stool. The repeat Chest X-ray was normal (view Figure 4). Cutaneous larva migrans (CLM) results from the migration of a non-human animal hookworm in human skin. Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, or other nematodes of the hookworm family are the common causative organism. This usually occurs in the context of a person in an endemic area (such as Southeast Asia) walking barefoot or sitting on a beach contaminated with an infected animal’s stool. Given that the human is an accidental host, the hookworm lacks the proteases necessary to penetrate below the skin’s basement membrane. As a result, unlike Ancylostoma duodenale or other human hookworm infections, the larva cannot enter the lymphatics or bloodstream. Thus, it migrates through the epidermis for weeks to month until it is eventually disintegrated by immune defenses. Clinically, this manifests as a creeping eruption, a highly pruritic migrating serpiginous rash that may have a vesiculobullous quality (1).
Cellular and humoral immune defense against multicellular parasites is largely mediated by eosinophils and IgE antibodies. The resultant eosinophilia, if persistent, can have a number of consequences on various organ systems, collectively termed secondary hypereosinophilic syndromes (2). The patient presented in this case was diagnosed with Loeffler’s syndrome, an eosinophilic pneumonia secondary to a parasitic infection (3).
The pathogenesis by which CLM leads to Loeffler’s syndrome is not fully elucidated. Some postulate that it occurs as a hypersensitivity reaction to the parasitic antigens, others believe that on rare occasions, CLM can lead to visceral larval migration through lung parenchyma. This has been described with A. caninum (1, 4). Alternatively, the patient may have been infected with two separate hookworm larvae, one cutaneous (non-human) and one visceral (human). The normal route of a human larval hookworm infection consists of skin penetration, lymphatic spread, hematogenous dissemination, lung infiltration and migration up the airways to the oropharynx. The larva is then swallowed and implants itself in the intestines (5). The transpulmonary phase of its migration, and resultant pulmonary eosinophilia, can present with a cough. However, the primary clinical manifestations of a visceral hookworm infections are gastrointestinal, namely, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting (6). The lack of gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms and negative stool ova/parasite analysis in the patient can either be seen as evidence for the absence of a visceral hookworm, or as evidence that the visceral parasite was eradicated during the pulmonary phase of the disease (prior to GI implantation).
The major diagnostic dilemma involved in the case was differentiating the patient’s presentation from strongyloidiasis. Strongyloides stercoralis parasitic infections have a high incidence in Southeast Asia and can be acquired from stepping in contaminated, usually humid, soil. The condition can present with a serpiginous pruritic rash called larva currens. It is distinguished from CLM by its rapid rate of migration (five or more cm per hour) and its tendency to form urticarial bands (7). Strongyloides is uncommonly associated with Loeffler’s syndrome. Its pulmonary symptoms usually arise in the context of chronic infection or acute hyperinfection in an immunocompromised host (8). This diagnostic possibility was further excluded when the serology result was negative.
Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE), caused by filarial nematodes such as Wuchereria bancrofti, was also included as a differential diagnosis. The mosquito-borne illness is endemic to Southeast Asia, can present with striking eosinophilia, and has notable pulmonary symptoms. However, filariasis typically presents with pronounced adenolymphangitis, skin abscesses, and elephantiasis. Contrary to a transitory Loeffler’s syndrome, TPE is a long-lasting mixed obstructive-restrictive lung disease with possible progression to pulmonary fibrosis. Occasionally, it can present with constitutional symptoms such as fever, malaise, and weight loss (9). Filarial serology was also shown to be negative.
Paragonimiasis, or lung flukes, were lower on the differential diagnosis. Although they are endemic to Southeast Asia, they are typically acquired through the ingestion of raw meat or fish, an exposure that the patient denied. Once ingested, the flukes migrate from the duodenum through the peritoneum and diaphragm into the lungs. Thus, symptoms usually consist of pleuritic pain preceded by GI disturbance. Their migration is sometimes associated with pneumothorax and pleural effusions (8).
A community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) was also considered in the diagnostic evaluation. However, the recent travel history, comorbid CLM, and peripheral eosinophilia made CAP unlikely. The fact that the respiratory and skin symptoms both resolved after taking antihelminthic medications (ivermectin) further cemented the likelihood of a parasitic etiology.

title: An elderly lady presented with rapidly growing and painful lesions on her left f
history:
An elderly lady presented with rapidly growing and painful lesions on her left forearm over a week. The lesions had initially started as an erythematous plaque; the area grew and subsequently formed bluish-black tender ulcers. This occurred on a background of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (on long-term prednisolone) and IgM monoclonal paraproteinemia of uncertain significance.
She denied any history of trauma but noted a large hematoma on the left upper arm prior to the lesions appearing. She could not recall any trigger to the hematoma. She denied any fevers, rigors or recent illness but reported some generalized symptoms of headache, weakness and lethargy.

As noted in the history, above. Also, rheumatoid arthritis and emphysema.

She lived at home with her husband and was legally blind. There was no recent travel of note.

Medications included Prednisolone 30 mg (weaning dose).
exam_studies:
The patient appeared systemically well. The blood pressure was 150/70 mmHg, pulse 70 beats per minute. She was saturating at 96% on room air with no signs of respiratory distress and was afebrile with temperature of 37.0ºC (98.6ºF).
There was a 3 cm x 7 cm area with necrotic ulcerations on the extensor surface of the left forearm (Figure 1). These lesions were tender on palpation and movement. There was also some generalized bruising over both arms.
Figure 1. Figure 1: Photograph of left forearm
Figure 1: Photograph of left forearm

Her labs were notable for a white blood cell count of 22.6 x10 9 /L (normal 4 x10 9 – 10 x10 9) with neutrophils of 14.15 x10 9 /L (normal 2 x109 - 7 x10 9). Her platelets were 46 x10 9 /L (normal 150 x10 9 – 410 x10 9) and hemoglobin was 83 g/L (normal 120 – 150). The C-Reactive protein was <2 mg/L (normal <5).
The renal function tests showed mild renal impairment with a creatinine of 144 micromol/L (normal 45 – 90) and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 (normal >90). Her coagulation studies were essentially normal except for a D-dimer of 0.8 mg/L (normal <0.5).
diagnosis:
Cutaneous mucormycosis

2 X 3 mm punch biopsies were taken and sent for culture and histopathology.
Histopathology showed enlarged non-septate thickened branching hyphae consistent with Mucor species as seen in Figure 2. Periodic Acid-Shiff and Grocott’s methenamine silver stains for fungi were positive. Unfortunately, the organism was not cultured in the laboratory.
Figure 2. Figure 2: H&E stain of skin biopsy showing non-septate thickened branching hyphae (400x magnification)
Figure 2: H&E stain of skin biopsy showing non-septate thickened branching hyphae (400x magnification)

The patient was planned for debridement and for post-operative commencement of liposomal amphotericin B. Unfortunately, the patient developed chest sepsis from a hospital acquired pneumonia prior to debridement and decision for palliation was made given her comorbidities.

Mucormycosis is a fungal infection of the Mucorales order of the class of Zygomycetes that typically affects immunocompromised patients and can manifest as rhinocerebral, cutaneous, pulmonary, gastrointestinal or disseminated infection. [1] The most common predisposing factors include hematologic malignancies (as was the case with this patient) as well as diabetes [1].
Cutaneous mucormycosis typically presents as an indurated erythematous plaque that rapidly progresses to a necrotic eschar. A French study in 2014 reported that the incidence of mucormycosis increased by 7.3% per year, especially in patients with neutropenia. [2] The mortality rates of localised infection vary from 4% to 10% and can be as high as 43% with deep extension. [3] Hence, early diagnosis is paramount which can be challenging and depends on clinical and histopathological signs as demonstrated in the images with this case. Fungal cultures are positive in approximately 50% of cases. [3] Treatment involves surgical debridement and antifungal therapy. Until recently, amphotericin B has been the agent of choice. However, isavuconazole, a novel broad spectrum antifungal triazole, is gaining increasing popularity with a small single-arm, open label study matched to historical controls suggesting it to be as effective as amphotericin in the treatment of mucormycosis. [4]
Cutaneous anthrax is usually painless which was not the case here. Additionally, cutaneous anthrax typically presents as a boil like lesion that eventually develops into a necrotic eschar and given the lack of contact with livestock with this patient, it is extremely unlikely. [5]
Ecthyma gangrenosum is an uncommon but severe cutaneous infection usually associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa typically affecting immunocompromised, neutropenic patients. The characteristic lesions are hemorrhagic pustules that then develop into necrotic appearing ulcers. [6] Given that this patient did not appear septic and blood cultures were negative, ecthyma gangrenosum seemed unlikely. However, ecthyma gangrenosum is an important differential to rule out in an unwell patient with cutaneous necrotic appearing lesions – early blood cultures, skin biopsy and tissue cultures are of critical importance here. The characteristic histology for ecthyma gangrenosum would show necrotizing hemorrhagic vasculitis with surrounding bacilli.
Cutaneous nocardia typically results from traumatic inoculation of nocardia into the skin and characteristically presents as cellulitis, pustules and abscess formation under the skin which is not consistent with this case. [7]
The history and the clinical findings are not typical of pyoderma gangrenosum which is usually associated with immune-mediated conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. However, it has been associated with hematological malignancies and can present as necrotic appearing lesions making this an important diagnosis to exclude.

title: A previously well man in his sixties presented with 3 months of exertional dyspn
history:
A previously well man in his sixties presented with 3 months of exertional dyspnea associated with occasional chest pain. His exercise tolerance decreased from one mile to 100 feet. He denied orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower extremity edema. He also reported anorexia, 50-pound weight loss, and frequent night sweats but denied fevers and chills. He was hospitalized and found to have diffuse lymphadenopathy and hypercalcemia and was diagnosed with Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (ATLL) secondary to human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV)-1 infection.

He was born in the Caribbean and moved to the mid-Atlantic United States as a young adult. He had over a 100-pack-year smoking history. He drank about 36 ounces of beer and a pint of liquor a day. He smoked marijuana several times a week.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared fatigued and chronically ill. His temperature was 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure was 106/64 mmHg, pulse 101 beats per minute, respiration was 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 100% on room air. He had no lymphadenopathy. His lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. He had normal active bowel sounds. His abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended, with negative Murphy’s sign, no rebound tenderness, and no hepatosplenomegaly. The exam was otherwise normal.

The white blood cell count was 13,000/microliter (reference range (RR) 4.5-11), with 21% neutrophils, 62% lymphocytes, 8% atypical lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 0% eosinophils, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL (RR 13.9-16.3) and platelets 208,000/mm 3 (RR 150-350). His blood urea was 72 mg/dL (RR 7-22), creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (RR 0.6-1.3), calcium 16 mg/dL (RR 8.4-10.5), and ionized calcium 1.68 mmol/L (RR 1.13-1.32). His albumin was 4.5 g/dL (RR 3.5-5.3), aspartate aminotransferase 69 U/L (RR 0-37), alanine aminotransferase 104 U/L (RR 0-40), and alkaline phosphatase 130 U/L (RR 30-120). His parathyroid hormone was 14 mg/mL (RR 10-65), parathyroid hormone-related peptide 36 pg/mL (RR 14-27), 25-hydroxy vitamin D 29 ng/mL (RR 30-100), 1-25 vitamin D < 8 pg/mL (RR 18-72), and lactate dehydrogenase 607 U/L (RR 118-273).
He tested negative for HIV and Hepatitis A, B and C. Other routine laboratory test results were normal.
A chest x-ray on presentation showed clear lung fields (Fig. 1). CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 5mm right upper lobe nodule, homogenous liver, and normal-sized spleen without lymphadenopathy.
Figure 1. Figure 1: CXR on presentation showing clear lung fields
Figure 1: CXR on presentation showing clear lung fields

On the first hospital day, the patient was started on cyclophosphamide, vincristine, etoposide, and high dose prednisone. On day 2, he developed new right upper quadrant pain and rebound tenderness with an abdominal plain film showing dilated loops of small bowel consistent with small bowel obstruction. On day 3, the patient had increased oxygen requirement with a chest x-ray showing diffuse pulmonary opacities (Fig. 2). His hemoglobin decreased from 10 to 5 g/dL with no evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding.
In this setting, he was transitioned to comfort care, and he passed away shortly thereafter.
Figure 2. Figure 2: CXR on hospital day 3 showing diffuse pulmonary opacities
Figure 2: CXR on hospital day 3 showing diffuse pulmonary opacities
diagnosis:
Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma secondary to Human T-Lymphotrophic Virus-1 with Strongyloides hyperinfection

An autopsy demonstrated ATLL involving the bone marrow, lymph node, spleen, kidneys and liver. In addition, he was found to have Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome with dissemination involving the larynx, trachea, heart, bilateral lungs, esophagus, stomach, small bowel, large bowel, liver, pancreas, spleen, testes, scrotum, thyroid gland, lymph nodes, skeletal muscle, nervous tissue, and skin. There was extensive hemorrhage and congestion in the lungs, along with a dusky and dilated small bowel. Figures 3A and 3B demonstrate larvae in the small bowel in an area of thickened and edematous bowel. Figure 4 shows larvae involvement of the heart, and Figure 5A and 5B are representative of a hilar lymph node involved by ATLL with “floret cells” and larvae.
Figure 3. Figure 3: H&E stain of small bowel a) showing larvae within the mucosa (40x) and b) within the muscularis propria (200x)
Figure 3: H&E stain of small bowel a) showing larvae within the mucosa (40x) and b) within the muscularis propria (200x)
Figure 4. Figure 4: H&E stain of cardiac muscle showing Strongyloides involvement (200x)
Figure 4: H&E stain of cardiac muscle showing Strongyloides involvement (200x)
Figure 5. Figure 5: H&E stain of hilar lymph node a) showing ATLL and larvae (40x) and b) “floret cells” and larvae (200x)
Figure 5: H&E stain of hilar lymph node a) showing ATLL and larvae (40x) and b) “floret cells” and larvae (200x)

Human T-Lymphotrophic Virus-1 (HTLV-1) was the first human onco-retrovirus discovered (1). It is found in sub-Saharan Africa, South America, Caribbean basin, northern Iran, Japan, central Australia (1). Roughly 10 million people are infected with HTLV-1 (1). The virus is transmitted by breast feeding, by sexual contact, or by contaminated blood supply or needles (2). Although the majority of HTLV-1 infections are asymptomatic, up to 5% are associated with Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (ATLL), which usually presents in the fifth decade after being infected in childhood (1,2). HTLV-1 primarily infects CD4 T-lymphocytes and is different than other retroviruses in that it creates new cell clones by cell-to-cell contact via “virologic synapses.”. Even with early initiation of chemotherapy, ATLL carries a poor prognosis (1).
S. stercoralis is an intestinal nematode that infects between 30-100 million people worldwide mostly in the tropical regions, including areas in southeastern United States and southern Europe (3,4,5,6). The life cycle can be divided into the free-living cycle and the parasitic cycle. The filariform larvae from the environment enter through the human skin, move into the circulation and to the lungs where they penetrate alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and arrive at the duodenum where they become adult female worms and lay eggs in the intestinal mucosa. The rhabditiform larvae are then released into the intestinal lumen. At this point, the larvae are either passed in the feces and develop into free-living adult worms, or they mature in the large intestine into filariform larvae and penetrate the intestinal mucosa or perianal skin, repeating the parasitic cycle in the same host, known as autoinfection (7). S. stercoralis is the only helminth that can complete its whole life cycle in a single host (6). Risk factors for acquiring S. stercoralis include visiting endemic regions, gardening, and working in agriculture (4). S. stercoralis may lay dormant and continue its life cycle in the human host until there is a disruption in homeostasis, leading to hyperinfection and dissemination of larvae. Risk factors for hyperinfection include patients receiving immunosuppression (such as steroids), solid organ transplant recipients and patients with hematologic malignancies, diabetes, alcoholism, and HTLV-1 coinfection (4,8).
There is a wide spectrum of S. stercoralis clinical presentations. Most commonly, patients are asymptomatic. Cutaneous manifestations (eg, larvae currens) are found early in the disease course. Chronic infections are usually asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic with vague gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal bloating. Rarely, patients may have hyperinfection with dissemination (2,4). With hyperinfection, symptoms occur at sites of highest larvae burden, typically the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts. Symptoms can be severe and include vomiting, obstruction, and pulmonary hemorrhage (4), all of which occurred with our patient. Another presentation to be aware of is gram-negative bacteremia and meningitis, where the filariform larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and carry with them gram-negative organisms into the blood stream and, at times, the central nervous system (4).
Diagnosis of S. stercoralis can be made via several modalities. Definitive non-invasive diagnosis is made by stool examination for ova and parasites. Due to the intermittent shedding of larvae, at least 3 stool samples are required to increase the sensitivity of the test (7). Another common method is serum enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), which is 90% sensitive but can cross-react with other parasites (7). In cases of hyperinfection, diagnosis is much less difficult given the severe presentation and large number of larvae that can be found in stool, CSF, or BAL fluid (4,7). However, a clinician needs to have a strong clinical suspicion and consider epidemiologic factors in order to arrive at the correct diagnosis.
Ivermectin is the treatment of choice for strongyloidiasis, with duration depending on severity of infection (4,6,7). For uncomplicated acute and chronic strongyloidiasis, ivermectin 200 ug/kg (single dose orally for 1-2 days) is recommended (6,7). Alternatively, albendazole 400mg orally twice daily for 3-7 days can be used (6,7). For Strongyloides hyperinfection and dissemination, recommendations are to use ivermectin 200 ug/kg per day orally for at least 2 weeks after stool parasitic exams are negative. Equally important is to stop or reduce immunosuppression if possible (6,7). Patients from sub-Saharan Africa with suspected concomitant Loa loa infection should not receive ivermectin due to the risk of fatal encephalopathy caused by rapid microfilaricidal activity (7). Unfortunately, decreased treatment efficacy has been noted with co-infected HTLV-1/ S. stercoralis patients (2). Follow-up stool examination for Strongyloides should be performed several weeks after treatment to document infection clearance. If parasites are still seen, retreatment is warranted (7).
S. stercoralis and HTLV-1 share some endemic regions such as Japan, Jamaica, and parts of South America (8,9,10). HTLV-1 infected patients have a greater risk of acquiring strongyloidiasis and developing severe infections with Strongyloides (2). Patients that are co-infected have a modified immune response that allows for increased autoinfection. Separately, HTLV-1 creates a Th1-response with high production of interferon-gamma (IFN-g), whereas patients infected with S. stercoralis have a Th-2 immune response with elevated levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IgE, and increased mast cells and eosinophils, all of which help in the defense against helminths (2). However, co-infection leads to a unique imbalance of immune responses. Decreased IL-4 and IL-13, the absence of IgE antibodies against Strongyloides, and decreased IL-5 lead to reduced elimination of larvae in the stool, inhibition of mast cell degranulation, and decreased number and function of eosinophils, respectively. As a result, this immunologic switch from Th-2 to Th-1 response impairs parasite killing and predisposes to hyperinfection and dissemination (2,11). In turn, there are reports that S. stercoralis can influence the development of ATLL (12,13). This case highlights the importance of screening for S. stercoralis i n patients with ATLL secondary to HTLV-1 who are candidates for immunosuppression, especially those with epidemiologic risk factors.
This case also illustrates how patients can be asymptomatic from their parasitic infection with normal eosinophil counts due to the HTLV-1 downregulation of the Th-2 response, and that the clinician should have a high index of suspicion in order to diagnose Strongyloides hyperinfection. Soon after immunosuppression, our patient developed abdominal pain and ileus and had pulmonary hemorrhage. He had risk factors for hyperinfection such as having co-infection with HTLV-1, receiving high dose steroids, and extensive alcohol use. Patients should be screened for S. stercoralis if they have intermediate or high-risk exposure to S. stercoralis (from endemic area, long trips to endemic area), known HTLV-1 infection, receiving immunosuppression or are candidates for immunosuppression (steroids, pre-transplant evaluation in certain situations), or with unexplained eosinophilia (7,14).

title: A middle-aged otherwise healthy woman was admitted with fever and rash. About on
history:
A middle-aged otherwise healthy woman was admitted with fever and rash. About one month prior to presentation, she had a vesicular rash on the left upper abdomen. She was diagnosed with herpes zoster and treated with famciclovir for seven days with near resolution of rash. A few days later, she developed post-herpetic neuralgia, for which she was started on lidocaine patch, gabapentin, and as needed ibuprofen.
Two weeks prior to presentation, she went on a cruise. On returning home, she felt fatigued, which she initially attributed to the cruise and recent shingles. On the morning prior to admission, she noticed a few bumps on her forehead and face. Towards the evening, she experienced chills and was febrile to 102.4°F. Over the next 24 hours, the rash progressed cephalo-caudally to involve the torso, the back, and all four extremities prompting her to present to her primary care physician who decided to admit her to the hospital for further evaluation. Review of systems was positive for nausea, fatigue, and lack of appetite. She denied headaches, confusion, neck stiffness, cough, coryza, sore throat, dysphagia, dyspnea, myalgias or arthralgias, chest or abdominal pain, or changes in bowel or bladder habits.

Recent zoster

She was born and raised in New England, USA and had not traveled elsewhere previously. She is a life-long non-smoker and denied alcohol or recreational drug use. She had no pets or sick contacts and no exposures to ticks or mosquitoes. She said she was up-to-date with all vaccinations.

Gabapentin, topical lidocaine and as needed ibuprofen
exam_studies:
Temperature 97.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 128/82 mm Hg, pulse 81 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate of 18 per minute. She was a good historian, lucid, alert and fully oriented. She looked uncomfortable and had mild conjunctival injection. The posterior oropharynx was erythematous but without vesicles or ulcerations. Dermatological exam was notable for a generalized eruption consisting of discrete 1-2 mm blanching macules and papules on the palms, soles, trunk, and extremities coalescing into confluent patches on the face, ears, and neck (Figures 1-5). There was mild ear and facial edema, without targetoid lesions, no blistering, and no ulcerations. She did not complain of pruritus or skin tenderness. There was hyperpigmented scarring seen at site of prior zoster. The rest of the examination was normal.

Relevant laboratory findings included leukopenia with bandemia and thrombocytopenia; white blood cell count was 2,080/uL with 16% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 24% bands (reference range 4,400 – 11,300/uL) and platelets were 85 K/uL (reference range 150 – 450 K/uL). There was an increase in both aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase, which were 91 IU/L (reference range 11 – 40 IU/L) and 155 IU/L (reference range 4 – 35 IU/L) respectively. C-reactive protein was 22.4 mg/L (reference range <5.0 mg/L). Other routine laboratory test results were normal. Chest x-ray showed no acute cardiopulmonary process.
diagnosis:
Measles infection

She had a negative Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) test. Hepatitis A, B, C serologies were negative. Lyme C6 peptide screen was negative. Babesia and anaplasmosis smears were negative. Parvovirus B19 IgM was negative and IgG was mildly positive. Mumps IgG was positive. Rubella IgG was negative. Coxsackie IgM and IgG were negative. Antinuclear antibodies and anti-DNA were negative. Blood cultures remained sterile. Punch biopsy of the skin revealed folliculitis with mild superficial perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate compatible with a viral exanthem. Lack of eosinophils on biopsy argued against a drug reaction. Measles IgM and IgG antibodies resulted positive at 1.61 AU/ml (reference range 0.79 AU/ml or less) and >300.00 AU/ml (reference range 24.9 AU/ml or less) respectively. Nasopharyngeal swab for measles polymerase chain reaction (PCR) came back positive for measles virus confirming the diagnosis.

Immediately after initial suspicion of measles, patient was placed on airborne isolation and supportively managed with rest and hydration. On day 2, the diagnosis was confirmed. She improved clinically with fading of rash on day 3 of hospitalization. After speaking with State Department of Public Health, she was discharged on day 4. En route from hospital to home, she was asked to wear a regular surgical mask per infection prevention team. She did well on follow-up appointment with complete resolution of symptoms by day 7.
Further investigations revealed that one of the other members on the cruise had also been infected with measles.

Measles is a negative-stranded RNA virus that belongs to the genus ‘ Morbillivirus ’, hence the term morbilliform rash. The virus emerged more than 1000 years ago when our human ancestors domesticated cattle. In 1954, measles virus was first isolated from an infected boy in Children’s Hospital, Boston. In 1963, measles vaccine was licensed (inactivated killed). In 1967, our patient was born and received the vaccine at 11 months. In 1968, a more potent measles vaccine was developed (live attenuated). In 1971, MMR combination vaccine was developed. In 1978, our patient received the booster dose of MMR vaccine at 10 years of age. In 2000, endemic measles was eliminated from the United States (U.S.).[1]
From January to September of 2019, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported >1,200 cases of measles, making it the greatest number of cases reported in the U.S. since 1992. [2] Measles occurs in the U.S. following virus importations, primarily among unvaccinated children and young adults. It is spread via droplet nuclei when an infected person coughs or sneezes. It is the most contagious of the vaccine-preventable diseases with secondary attack rate in susceptible household contacts being 90%. Incubation period is 7-21 days. Patient is infectious from 4 days before until 4 days after onset of rash. Measles virus spreads first to local lymphoid tissue and is then disseminated throughout the blood stream through infected lymphocytes, infecting cells in almost all organ systems. The disease course begins with a prodrome of fever, malaise, Koplik’s spots, and “3 Cs” (cough, coryza and conjunctivitis). This is followed by a maculopapular rash with cephalocaudal and centrifugal spread. Complications such as laryngitis, otitis media, pneumonia, and diarrhea are seen in ~30% of cases. Subacute sclerosing pan-encephalitis (SSPE) is rare, but potentially fatal. On initial suspicion of measles, mask and promptly isolate the patient in a negative pressure room. Measles is diagnosed by IgM serology or nasopharyngeal/throat swab PCR. Treatment is usually supportive; patients typically improve less than 48 hours after rash onset. Airborne isolation is recommended for at least 4 days after rash onset. [3] Cherry et al. found that vaccine failure measles cases were less ill (as was seen in our patient) than cases that occurred in people who had not been vaccinated. [4] Clinicians should keep measles in their differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with fever and rash who is unvaccinated, has recently traveled internationally, or may have been exposed to a measles outbreak. Adherence to published vaccination schedules should be encouraged. During outbreaks, prompt reporting to health departments is crucial to prompt additional steps to protect the community. Until measles is eliminated globally, we will need to remain vigilant to contain outbreaks when they occur.

title: A female in her fifties with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) was admitted to the
history:
A female in her fifties with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) was admitted to the hospital for an acute lymphoid blast crisis. She was treated with hyper-CVAD (cyclophosphamide/ vincristine sulfate/ doxorubicin hydrochloride/ dexamethasone). Eighteen days after initiation of chemotherapy, she began to feel generally unwell with abdominal discomfort and diarrhea coinciding with her first day of count recovery. Over the next three days, she developed a diffuse macular rash and fever.

Type II diabetes

She lived with her husband in a community outside the city, they have no pets at home. She had no history of travel outside of North America. She had many family members who came to visit her throughout her admission. She denied any smoking, alcohol use or illicit drugs.

Vancomycin 1g IV q12h (day 1 of therapy); Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375g IV q6h (day 9 of therapy); Acyclovir 400mg PO q12h (prophylaxis); Fluconazole 400mg PO daily (prophylaxis)
exam_studies:
The patient appeared generally frail, with a low mood but no acute distress. Her blood pressure was 144/78, pulse 96 beats per minute, respirations 16 per minute with normal oxygen saturation. Temperature was 38.1°C (100.5°F), with maximal temperature of 39.1°C (102.2°F) two days prior to assessment. Cardiac and respiratory exam were within normal limits. The site of her indwelling peripheral vascular access had some erythema without fluctuance or purulent drainage. She had a diffuse papular erythematous rash on her posterior scalp which was non-tender and blanchable (Fig 1). This rash was also present on her abdomen, chest and thighs, though more petechial in appearance (Fig 2).

The total white blood cell count was less than 0.1 x 10^9/L (reference range (RR) 3.5-10.5), hemoglobin was 82 g/L (RR 115-155). Her platelets were less than 10 x10^9/L (RR 130-380). Electrolytes were normal, creatinine 89 umol/L (RR 22-75) or 1.01 mg/dL (RR 0.5-1.0). Her aspartate aminotransferase was 101 U/L (RR 15-37), alanine transaminase was 88 U/L (RR 17-62), alkaline phosphatase was 328 U/L (RR 50-136), gamma-glutamyl transferase was 352 U/L (RR 5-55) and total bilirubin 8 umol/L (RR 3-17) or 0.47 mg/dL (RR 0.2-1.2).
A chest radiograph revealed no acute intrathoracic pathology. Computed tomography of the chest showed mild interstitial pulmonary edema, but no infective focus in the lungs and no pulmonary embolism. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed fluid-filled distended loops of large bowel, with normal caliber small bowel loops. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed normal echogenicity of the liver and a normal biliary tree, with a moderate amount of ascites in the pelvis.

After development of the rash, piperacillin-tazobactam was discontinued as it was suspected she had a drug eruption. She progressed to develop anemia (hemoglobin below 80 g/L) requiring two units of packed red blood cells, as well as progression of her diffuse papular facial rash. She underwent routine bone marrow aspiration and biopsy on day 3 as part of her chemotherapy reinduction protocol for treatment refractory ALL. Repeat induction chemotherapy (idarubicin and fludarabine) was initiated on illness day 6, and within the next week she developed severe fatigue, oligoarthritis (right ankle), progressing to polyarthritis (including the joints of her hands), as well as a purpuric rash on her legs (Fig 3). As her neutropenia worsened post-reinduction, she underwent septic work-up multiple times for fevers without an identifiable source. She required six more transfusions of packed red blood cells for anemia, as well as intermittent platelet transfusions for thrombocytopenia.
diagnosis:
Chronic parvovirus B19 infection in immunocompromised host

Initial microbiology results:
o Blood cultures: Negative after 5 days of growth
o Clostridium difficile assay: negative
o Nasopharyngeal swab: negative for influenza virus A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, enterovirus, parainfluenza viruses 1-4, rhinovirus, and coronavirus NL63 and 229E
Bone marrow biopsy (done on day 3 as part of chemotherapy protocol) results:
o Hypocellular marrow with persistent leukemia and severely reduced erythroid precursors. These are abnormally large with prominent nuclear inclusions suspicious for viral inclusions (Fig 4-5).
Additional microbiology results drawn after bone marrow biopsy:
o Parvovirus B19 PCR (drawn on day 4): DNA detected
o Parvovirus B19 serology (drawn day 10): Parvovirus B19 IgG antibody reactive, Parvovirus B19 IgM antibody non-reactive
o Parvovirus immunohistochemistry positive on bone marrow biopsy (Fig 6)
o CMV serology: IgM non-reactive, IgG positive
o HIV serology: non-reactive
o Hepatitis B core total antibody non-reactive, surface antigen non-reactive, surface antibody 307 IU/L
o Hepatitis C virus antibody: non-reactive
Figure 4. Figure 4: Wright-Giemsa stain of bone marrow aspirate showing large parvovirus B19 erythroblast
Figure 4: Wright-Giemsa stain of bone marrow aspirate showing large parvovirus B19 erythroblast
Figure 5. Figure 5: Trephine hematoxylin and eosin staining showing parvovirus inclusion body
Figure 5: Trephine hematoxylin and eosin staining showing parvovirus inclusion body
Figure 6. Figure 6: Parvovirus immunohistochemistry positive on bone marrow biopsy
Figure 6: Parvovirus immunohistochemistry positive on bone marrow biopsy

On further questioning, the patient’s daughter had been diagnosed with “slapped cheeks” around the time of a recent visit, ten days preceding the development of symptoms, while the patient was neutropenic. This daughter had multiple young children, and according to the patient, at least half of them had a rash in the preceding week.
Intravenous immunoglobin was initiated on illness day 4 and repeated on illness day 11 and 18. Repeat parvovirus B19 PCR post-intravenous immunoglobulin remained positive (day 23), and the patient had ongoing symptoms including arthralgias, papular rash, severe fatigue, and ongoing neutropenia post-reinduction chemotherapy. This improved somewhat when her counts recovered on illness day 35.
Repeat bone marrow aspiration after count recovery did not show presence of inclusion bodies but did have non-specific staining of some trabecular cells for parvovirus B19. She was discharged home in morphological clinical remission.
She was assessed in outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic one month after discharge from hospital (day 67 of illness), with ongoing symptoms of significant fatigue but resolution of her arthralgias, fever and rash. Her parvovirus B19 PCR remained positive at this time.

Humans are the only known host of parvovirus B19, which is an erythroid virus transmitted by respiratory route through close contacts (1). The initial phase of symptoms is generally non-specific (fever, malaise, diarrhea, rash) and coincides with viral replication in upper respiratory tract and concomitant viremia. The second phase of symptoms is immune-complex mediated, correlating with entry of virus into erythroid progenitor cells of the bone marrow (2, 3). In immunocompetent hosts, infection is often asymptomatic but can also include erythema infectiosum (“Fifth disease”) and transient arthropathy. Infection in immunocompromised hosts can present with transient aplastic crisis and pure red cell aplasia with persistent viremia (4, 5). Some patients may have mild elevation in markers of end-organ function, though severe end-organ damage is rare (6). Children most commonly exhibit cutaneous manifestations of disease, whereas arthralgias and arthropathy are more predominant in adults (7).
Chronic infection is often seen in patients with dysfunctional adaptive immunity, most commonly reported in patients with HIV not receiving antiretroviral therapy, patients with congenital immunodeficiency, and patients with underlying hematologic malignancies (3, 8-10). Ongoing symptoms correlate with lack of host immunoglobulin and inability to clear immune complexes.
The diagnosis of parvovirus B19 is often clinical. Serology may not always be positive in patients with immunodeficiency or may be confounded by administration of intravenous immunoglobulin (1). Serum PCR for viral DNA may be performed, and special staining can be performed on tissue biopsy (such as bone marrow aspirate and biopsy) to detect viral inclusion bodies (3).
Treatment of parvovirus B19 infection is supportive, and in cases of chronic infection there is some evidence supporting the value of pooled population intravenous immunoglobulin to assist with clearance of immune complexes, especially in cases of pure red cell aplasia (6, 11). It is recommended that patients with persistent viremia and associated immunodeficiency be maintained on respiratory droplet precautions (12). Generally, the rash of parvovirus B19 disappears within a few weeks in immunocompetent hosts, and immune recovery is pivotal for symptom improvement. There are case reports of recurrent erythema and viremia many months after the initial illness (13). Many patients will develop fatigue after infection, characterized by ongoing arthralgias despite optimal therapy.

title: A previously well man in his sixties was urgently transferred to our hospital fo
history:
A previously well man in his sixties was urgently transferred to our hospital for consideration of ventriculoperitoneal shunting after initially seeking medical care 21 weeks prior.
He first developed fevers, sweats, myalgias and sinus congestion shortly after returning from Arizona and was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. His symptoms then progressed to include fevers and a new cough. Two weeks after symptom onset, he was diagnosed with a bibasilar pneumonia and was treated with levofloxacin. However, he then developed unrelenting headaches followed by diplopia and was admitted to an outside hospital 12 weeks after symptom onset.
There, he underwent a lumbar puncture (LP) which revealed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) white blood cell count 402 (reference range 0-5) of which 71% were lymphocytes and 4% were neutrophils. His CSF glucose was undetectable (reference range 40 - 70 mg/dL) and total protein was 460 mg/dL (reference range 12 - 60 mg/dL). Bacterial and fungal CSF culture showed no growth. Serum Coccidioides IgG was negative and Cryptococcal antigen was negative. He was discharged with a peripherally inserted central catheter for receipt of intravenous ceftriaxone for treatment of presumed Lyme meningitis despite testing negative for Lyme disease both in the serum and in CSF. He was readmitted to the same hospital with deep venous thrombosis and relentless headaches and underwent another LP which revealed 581 white blood cells in the CSF of which 73% were lymphocytes and 10% were neutrophils. CSF glucose was 23 mg/dL (reference range 40 - 70 mg/dL) and total protein was 509 mg/dL (reference range 12 - 60 mg/dL). Quantiferon Gold assay was negative and CSF Lyme antibody was again negative.
Magnetic resonance imaging of his brain revealed abnormal enhancement of the perimesencephalic cisterns. Positron emission tomography (PET) revealed mild 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose avid paratracheal, axillary and hilar nodes. A lymph node biopsy was performed showing non-necrotizing granulomas and stains for acid fast, fungal and bacterial organisms (AFB, GMS, and gram stains) were negative. Flow cytometry of the lymph node biopsy specimen was normal. He was diagnosed with multisystem sarcoidosis and prescribed 60 mg of prednisone daily as an outpatient. Shortly thereafter, he developed altered mental status and was readmitted to the outside hospital where he was found to have acute hydrocephalus and was transferred to our hospital for urgent ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. The infectious diseases service was consulted.

Hypertension and benign prostatic hypertrophy

He was a life-long non-smoker, does not use illicit drugs nor consume alcohol regularly. He lived in the north east USA. He visited India for about 2 weeks a few years ago, Arizona a few months prior to admission and Louisiana 1 year prior to admission. He owned several cats and dogs but no birds.
exam_studies:
Our initial physical exam was notable for a temperature of 101.1ºF (38.3ºC). His blood pressure was 108/67 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats per minute, respirations 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation was 91% on 4 liters per minute by nasal cannula. He had meningismus on neck exam. Scattered crackles were appreciated on pulmonary exam. He was sleepy but rousable and oriented only to self. He was not oriented to year. He could not convey his history accurately but otherwise had a normal neurological exam. Right frontal ventriculoperitoneal shunt was present, and the rest of the examination was otherwise unremarkable.

His initial complete blood count was notable for a white blood cell count of 10,500/uL (reference range 4.0 - 10.0 K/uL) with 90.9 % neutrophils (reference range 34 - 71%). Complete blood count was otherwise unremarkable. His 4th Generation HIV Antigen/Antibody Assay was negative.
Interventional radiology guided lumbar puncture was performed: CSF tube 1 had 73 total nucleated cells (reference range 0-5), 539 red blood cells (reference range 0-5), 37% neutrophils, 55% lymphocytes, 7% plasma cells. Tube 4 had 272 total nucleated cells (reference range 0-5), 104 red blood cells (reference range 0-5), 40% neutrophils, 51% lymphocytes, 8% plasma cells. Total protein was 1260 mg/dL (reference range 15-45). Glucose was 4 mg/dL.
Chest computed tomography (Figure 1) revealed extensive reticulonodular opacities which were seen diffusely throughout his lungs measuring 2 mm. No consolidations were seen. Prominent mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymph nodes were seen.

diagnosis:
Disseminated coccidioidomycosis

Bronchoscopy with bronchioalveolar lavage revealed spherules that were consistent with Coccidioides. (Figure 2)
Coccidioides antibody in the CSF was elevated at 1:8 (reference range <1:1), Coccidioides antibody to F antigen (IgG) was positive.
Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen were negative. Fungal blood culture ultimately grew Coccidioides immitis/posadasii.
While the CSF collected from the first lumbar puncture at our hospital had no growth, a repeat lumbar puncture was performed and CSF culture grew Coccidioides immitis/posadasii.

He was started on fluconazole 800 mg daily and IV liposomal amphotericin 400 mg daily. He was intubated for airway protection and hypoxemia but his mental status continued to worsen with loss of brainstem reflexes. He ultimately passed away. Autopsy showed diffuse nodularity of the lung pleural surfaces (Figure 3). Axial cross section of both lungs revealed widespread micronodular discoloration of the parenchymal surfaces (Figure 4). Microscopy revealed pathognomonic spherules involving the lung parenchyma (Figure 5). Further autopsy findings included prominent para-aortic, peritracheal, and peribronchial lymph nodes and markedly enlarged axillary lymph nodes (1.8 - 6.5 cm) with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and confluent necrosis (Figure 6). The thyroid, adrenals, liver and spleen also showed evidence of disseminated Coccidioides infection.
Brain autopsy findings were notable for disseminated Coccidioides infection diffusely involving the leptomeninges with severe lymphoplasmocytic inflammation (Figure 7, 8). Multifocal parenchymal involvement with microabscesses measuring up to 0.2 cm were seen in the frontal, insular, parietal and temporal cortexes, hippocampus, and cerebellum. The lateral ventricle, choroid plexus, and third ventricle were also involved. There was a fungal abscess at the cerebellopontine angle measuring up to 1.0 cm. Multifocal septic emboli involving the frontal cortex, parietal cortex, basal ganglia, medulla, and cerebellum, measuring from 0.1-0.5 cm were also noted.
