Coccidioidomycosis is colloquially referred to as Valley fever, which alludes to the San Joaquin valley (located in central California) where Coccidioides is highly endemic. Neighboring areas of Arizona, Nevada and New Mexico are also endemic for Coccidioides along with parts of South America. There are 2 species of Coccidioides - immitis and posadasii. They cause similar disease and cannot be differentiated by serology [1-3]. All 3 major endemic fungi in the United States -- Coccidioides, Blastomyces, and Histoplasma -- were actually initially misidentified as protozoa [4]. Coccidioides exists in the environment in the saprobic life cycle as a mycelium or mold composed of septated hyphae which can form spores called arthroconidia [5]. This is the infectious particle, which is easily aerosolized and inhaled. Each arthroconidia is capable of either forming more mycelia or infecting mammals to form spherules. Coccidioides is unique among the pathogenic thermally dimorphic fungi since it does not form single yeast cells but rather conglomerates of endospores within a spherule. Each endospore can form another spherule and spherules are refractory to phagocytosis [6].
Diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis is often difficult. A serum immunodiffusion antibody test against Coccidioides sent at the outside hospital during this patient’s initial hospitalization for meningitis was negative. There are 3 antibody tests for Coccidioides; the immunodiffusion and complement fixation assays are very specific for this disease but less sensitive than the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) [7]. The 2016 IDSA guidelines estimate that the ELISA for Coccidioides is about twice as sensitive as the immunodiffusion or complement fixation tests, especially early in the course of disease and is the recommended initial test [8]. Immunodiffusion helps detect infection in the early phases of disease correlating with the IgM response and complement fixation is better in later phases and therefore correlates with IgG [7]. However, negative serological testing does not rule out disease, but a positive test is highly suggestive of an active infection since these serologies will generally revert back to negative after the infection has cleared.
Coccidioidomycosis is a granulomatous disease that induces a T helper 1 response which leads to a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction when it is injected intradermally which is the basis behind the skin test for Coccidioides [9]. Historically, 99% of otherwise healthy patients were shown to convert their Coccidioides skin test within 3 weeks of symptoms of primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis. This test was recently approved again by the FDA after being discontinued in the 1990s, and has been shown to have a sensitivity and specificity of >98% [10]. An RT PCR diagnostic was recently approved by the FDA that is reported to have 100% sensitivity and between 94% - 100% specificity both retrospectively and prospectively with the caveat that it has only been FDA approved for broncheoalveolar lavage specimens [11].
This patient had coccidioidal meningitis which is notoriously challenging to diagnose. As in this case, diagnosis is usually made by detection of antibodies against Coccidioides in the CSF. CSF in coccidioidal meningitis usually displays a lymphocytic pleocytosis with high total protein and low glucose. CSF Coccidioides antigen testing to diagnose meningitis was recently described [12]. In this study, fungal culture of CSF was only positive in 7% of the cases. However, they showed that CSF Coccidioides antigen had a sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 100%, respectively. Historically, intrathecal amphotericin B was the gold standard of care for coccidioidal meningitis for many decades until a pivotal, albeit uncontrolled, trial published in 1993 changed the field [13]. It showed that treatment with oral fluconazole compared favorably to historical outcomes achieved with intrathecal amphotericin B. Treatment with oral fluconazole daily remains the recommendation in the guidelines published by the Infectious Diseases Society of America in 2016 [8].
Unlike coccidioidal meningitis, which has high mortality if left untreated, there is no evidence that treatment of primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis actually improves outcomes or prevents complications in most patients, as shown by two prospective observational studies [14, 15]. It is estimated that between 20-30% of community-acquired pneumonia in endemic regions is caused by Coccidioides and primary infection is usually self limited and results in lifelong immunity [1, 16].
Coccidioidal meningitis presents with sub acute to chronic symptoms that may be seen in a variety of infectious and non-infectious conditions. Clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion in those with a compatible clinical syndrome and epidemiological risk factors, especially in non-endemic areas. The CSF immunodiffusion antibody test and CSF complement fixation antibody test each have a sensitivity of about 70% for diagnosing Coccidioidal meningitis [12]. Clinical suspicion needs to remain high in non-endemic areas as more cases are being diagnosed where these fungi are not typically described and rates of endemic Coccidioides infections continue to increase [17-19].

title: A girl in her late teens with systemic lupus erythematosus and celiac disease pr
history:
A girl in her late teens with systemic lupus erythematosus and celiac disease presented during the winter season with ten days of dry cough. Over the few days before admission, her cough worsened and became productive with yellow, thick sputum. She denied having fevers, night sweats, hemoptysis, runny nose, chest pain or shortness of breath. She lost 40 lbs (18 kg) of weight in three months and reported a few episodes of diarrhea over the last few weeks. Her family attributed her weight loss to depression. She denied sick contacts, including anyone with tuberculosis.

-Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE)
-Depression.

She is a college student. She drinks city water and has not had recent contacts with hot tubs, swimming pools or gardening. She has not been homeless or incarcerated and has not traveled outside the US. She smokes a half pack of tobacco per day. She denied illicit drug use.

-Hydroxychloroquine
-Fluoxetine
-Received one dose of methylprednisolone (80mg) for SLE flare 2 weeks ago.
exam_studies:
Vital signs: Blood pressure 98/56mmHg, pulse 110 beats per minute, temperature 99.8° F (37.7°C), and respirations 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation: 95% on room air. Patient appeared thin with muscle wasting. No respiratory distress. She had a flat affect. There were coarse breath sounds bilaterally. Heart sounds were dual with no murmurs. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender with no hepatosplenomegaly. There was no lymphadenopathy. Her ankles and wrists were tender to palpation with no appreciable synovitis. The rest of examination was normal.

The white cell count was 6,200/μL (ref 3.7 - 11 K/μL) with lymphopenia of 0.12 K/μL (ref 1 - 4 K/μL) and a left shift, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL (ref 11.5 - 15.5 g/dL) and a platelet count 218,000/μL (ref 150 - 400 K/μL). Serum chemistry showed creatinine 0.43 mg/dL (ref 0.58 - 0.96 mg/dL), sodium 133 (136 - 144 mmol/L), ALT 9 (ref 7 - 38 U/L), AST 57 (ref 13 - 35 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 173 (ref 34 - 123 U/L), albumin 2.1 (ref 3.9 - 4.9 g/dL). Rest of chemistry was normal. A chest radiograph showed prominent opacity in the right paratracheal region (Figure 1).
A chest computed tomography (CT) with contrast (Figure 2a and 2b) showed a 4 cm focal consolidative process in the medial right upper lobe with a large central area of necrosis and early cavitation that extended from the right lung apex to anterior of the right hilar region. There was also evidence of patchy nodular opacities surrounding the cavitary lesion. There were a few small mediastinal and hilar nodes. CT abdomen/pelvis showed evidence for hepatic steatosis.

Figure 2. Figure 2: a) Axial CT chest revealed a 4 cm focal consolidative process in the medial right upper lobe with large central area of necrosis and early cavitation; b) Coronal CT chest revealed focal necrotizing consolidation with cavitation that extends from the right lung apex to the anterior of the right hilar region
Figure 2: a) Axial CT chest revealed a 4 cm focal consolidative process in the medial right upper lobe with large central area of necrosis and early cavitation; b) Coronal CT chest revealed focal necrotizing consolidation with cavitation that extends from the right lung apex to the anterior of the right hilar region

Sputum stain/culture studies for bacterial, mycobacterial and fungi were ordered however the patient was not able to produce good sputum samples. Legionella urine antigen was negative. No antibiotics were started as she remained stable and the pulmonary team was consulted for a bronchoscopy. C-reactive protein 12.9 (<0.9 mg/dL), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 66 (0 - 20 mm/hr), C4 level 10 (13 - 46 mg/dL), C3 level 41 (86 - 166 mg/dL), dsDNA antibodies 859 IU/ml (<30 IU/ml), ANCA negative, proteinase-3 antibody negative, and myeloperoxidase antibody negative. Blood cultures were negative. QuantiFERON - TB Gold PLUS was indeterminate (and there was no prior TB screening documented). 4th generation HIV test was non-reactive. Serum galactomannan was negative. Serum complement fixation antibodies were negative for Aspergillus, Histoplasma and Coccidioides, but positive for Blastomyces at 1:16.
diagnosis:
Legionella pneumophila cavitary pneumonia

A bronchoscopy was performed but there were no endobronchial lesions or secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) were done. Gram stain and culture were negative on the BAL but showed moderate neutrophils. Pneumocystis jirovecii polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from BAL was negative. Legionella pneumophila PCR from BAL came back positive.

The patient was started on oral levofloxacin 750 mg once per day with improvement of symptoms. Oral prednisone (10mg daily) was started for concomitant SLE flare.
Legionella culture from BAL were negative. Histoplasma urine antigen and serum blastomyces immunodiffusion antibody were negative. BAL and TBNA studies for AFB stain/culture, Nocardia, fungal stain/culture, and cytology were negative. BAL galactomannan was negative. Histopathology showed evidence of acute inflammation and granular proteinaceous material. Tissue acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stains, Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain and gram stains were negative.
Patient was discharged with a plan to complete additional 14 days of levofloxacin. She was seen in infectious disease clinic one month later and reported resolution of her respiratory symptoms. A repeat CT chest (Figures 3 a and 3b) performed 1 month after completion of treatment showed complete resolution of right upper lobe necrotizing pneumonia with a residual 2.0 x 2.5 cm thin-walled cystic space.
Figure 3. Figure 3 a and b: Sagittal and coronal CT chest 1 month post completion of treatment revealed residual thin-walled cystic space
Figure 3 a and b: Sagittal and coronal CT chest 1 month post completion of treatment revealed residual thin-walled cystic space

Legionella cavitary pneumonia is an atypical presentation of Legionnaire’s disease and more commonly described in patients with impaired cellular immunity secondary to corticosteroids (particularly high-dose steroid therapy), immunosuppressive therapy, organ transplant, and HIV infection.[1,2,3,4,5].
Cavitation has been associated with L pneumophila serotypes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 as well as other Legionella species (L. micdadei, L. bozemanae, L. dumoffii, and L. longbeachae).6,7 L. pneumophila serotype 1 is the main agent of Legionnaire’s disease. Infections by L pneumophila non-serotype 1 and non-pneumophila Legionella species occur in severely immunocompromised hosts.[4,6,7,8,9]
Our patient presented in winter and was not receiving an intensive immunosuppressive therapy when compared with two prior cases of SLE patients complicated with Legionella pulmonary abscess.[10,11,12] However, her lupus was active and complicated with lymphopenia which may have predisposed her for this severe presentation.
Legionella urinary antigen and culture were negative in our patient. In some settings, Legionella PCR is becoming a preferred test for the diagnosis of Legionnaires' disease due to its rapid turn-around time and better performance regardless of Legionella species and serotypes.[13] Our institution’s laboratory developed a Legionella PCR which detects different serotypes of L. pneumophila by targeting the mip (macrophage infectivity potentiator) gene and it has not shown cross-reactivity in our validation studies with other non- pneumophila species.[14]
Other etiologies for cavitary pneumonia include mycobacteria, fungi, nocardia, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella, anaerobes, cancer and vasculitis.[9] The positive Blastomyces serology was most likely a false positive result. TBNA initially showed possible hyphae however fungal stain/cultures were negative suggesting possible contamination.
Treatment of Legionnaires' disease in immunocompromised patients is longer (14 to 21 days) than for many other causes of pneumonia due to risk for both severe infection and relapse.[6] Our patient had rapid resolution of symptoms and marked radiological improvement after treatment with Legionella-specific therapy. This case highlights the importance of having a high suspicion for Legionella infection in the differential diagnosis of cavitary pneumonia in immunocompromised patients to assure prompt diagnostic work-up and treatment.

title: A male in his sixties with a living-related kidney transplant more than a decade
history:
A male in his sixties with a living-related kidney transplant more than a decade ago, complicated by diabetes and moderate chronic allograft nephropathy, presented with a 2-week history of intermittent diplopia, nausea and vomiting. Upon further questioning, he described a subacute history of disequilibrium and forgetfulness.

Hypertension.
Kidney failure of unknown etiology.
Living-related kidney transplant.
Post-transplant diabetes mellitus.
Chronic allograft nephropathy, Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and IgA nephropathy.

No history of tobacco, illicit drugs or alcohol abuse. No contact with pets.
Born in Mexico, migrated to US >20 years before. No recent travel history.
Previous laborer but retired for over 2 years.

Aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, hydrochlorothiazide, insulin, pioglitazone, mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg twice a day, and tacrolimus 2 mg twice a day.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared ill. The blood pressure was 163/83 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, pulse oximetry 99% on room air and temperature 98.1°F (36.7°C). Eye exam revealed right-sided internuclear ophthalmoparesis (INO) as evidenced by right medial rectus palsy and abducting nystagmus on the left eye, without ptosis, anisocoria or papilledema. He had bilateral patellar hyperreflexia and ankle clonus. The rest of examination was normal.

Initial laboratory tests showed creatinine of 3.3 mg/dL (reference range (RR) 0.6-1.4) (increased from a baseline of 2.7 mg/dL 1 year before), urea 28 mg/dL (RR 8-20), hemoglobin 9.7 mg/dL (RR 12.9-16.8). The rest of routine laboratory findings, including HIV and syphilis screening and serum tacrolimus levels were within normal reference ranges.
Computed tomography (CT) of the head (Figure 1A and B) and chest demonstrated obstructive hydrocephalus with tectum and midbrain edema and a 1.1 cm, noncalcified pulmonary nodule in the left lower lobe posteriorly (Figure 2).

The patient was admitted to the hospital and was scheduled for a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the brain. On day 2 his neurological status rapidly deteriorated. diagnosis:
Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.

Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive to 1:512 dilutions. Serum Cytomegalovirus (CMV) PCR showed a positive DNA of 1122 IU/mL (reference range < 200 IU/mL). An external ventricular drain (EVD) was placed revealing moderately increased intracranial pressure. CSF analysis showed clear fluid, glucose of 10 mg/dL (RR 50-70), protein of 23 mg/dL (RR 20-50), leukocytes of 1/µL (RR 0-5) and erythrocytes < 1/µL (RR 0-5). CSF cryptococcal antigen was positive 1:>8192 dilutions. Encapsulated yeasts were seen on India Ink staining. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, HSV and CMV PCR were all negative on CSF. After 2 days of incubation, CSF culture revealed Cryptococcus neoformans growth.

The patient was switched to intravenous liposomal amphotericin and flucytosine on day 3 after serum cryptococcal antigen showed positivity. Acyclovir was changed to ganciclovir given initial concern for CMV infection (later discontinued after CMV PCR was negative on CSF). The EVD was removed after 5 days, showing normal intracranial pressure. Subsequently, serial CT scans of the head were done which showed no progression of the hydrocephalus. Unfortunately, the patient’s neurological function continued to deteriorate. Repeat MRI of the brain after 14 days of treatment revealed findings consistent with multiple scattered ischemic lesions throughout both cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, deep white matter, subcortical white matter and cortex with involvement of dorsal midbrain (Figure 4a and b). He died shortly after.
Figure 4. Figure 4: Follow up MRI brain without contrast at 14 days. (A) Sagittal FLAIR images showing scattered areas of hyperintensity in corpus callosum, deep white matter, subcortical white matter and cortex. (B) Diffusion-weighted imaging showing high-signal areas in both cerebral hemispheres and cortex. There was no definite corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient changes.
Figure 4: Follow up MRI brain without contrast at 14 days. (A) Sagittal FLAIR images showing scattered areas of hyperintensity in corpus callosum, deep white matter, subcortical white matter and cortex. (B) Diffusion-weighted imaging showing high-signal areas in both cerebral hemispheres and cortex. There was no definite corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient changes.

Cryptococcus infection is the third most common invasive fungal infection and the most common cause of central nervous system (CNS) fungal infection in solid organ transplant recipients (1,2). Kidney and liver transplant patients appear to have the highest risk compared to other solid organ transplants (3). The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis can be challenging as it commonly presents with a subacute onset and nonspecific symptoms and signs. Neuro-ophthalmologic dysfunction is common. Papilledema and cranial nerve (CN) III and VI involvement are the most frequent presentations (4); specific syndromes such as INO are very rare.
INO is one of the most discrete localizing signs in medicine and is usually of considerable value in predicting multiple sclerosis or stroke. Some reports have suggested higher frequency of other causes such as infection or trauma, reaching up to a quarter of all causes. Based on a 2005 review, up to 28% of all cases of INO are due to unusual causes. However, only 4% were associated with infections and even fewer with cryptococcal meningoencephalitis (5). Several theories have been postulated to explain the pathophysiology behind this finding. Cryptococci are thought to physically block CSF drainage across the arachnoid villi and subarachnoid spaces leading to increased intracranial pressure with compression of nerve structures and tracts. Inflammation and direct invasion of cranial nerves is also thought to contribute to the pathogenesis of cranial neuropathies (2,6). Unilateral INO due to involvement of the medial longitudinal fasciculus on one side of the pons is usually vascular or demyelinating in nature. Phlebitis and arteritis have been demonstrated in pathological examination of human brains infected with Cryptococcus (7). Reports of reversibility of the ocular findings with treatment supports the vasculitic nature of the phenomenon.
Amphotericin B (AmB) remains the cornerstone of therapy for cryptococcal meningitis. Liposomal preparations of AmB are preferred as first-line therapy in organ transplant recipients due to the frequency of reduced renal function in such patients (9). Flucytosine is recommended as adjunct therapy as the combination has shown reduced rates of treatment failures (10), and direct survival benefits have also been reported (11). Fluconazole maintenance therapy should be continued for at least 6-12 months. During the early treatment phase of cryptococcal meningitis, control of increased intracranial pressure with external drainage is critical (8), either by repeated lumbar punctures or by ventricular or lumbar drains. In conclusion, cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is a detrimental infection in solid organ transplant recipients and it should be suspected in patients with any combination of fever, headache and focal neurological signs.

title: A Ugandan gentleman with HIV in his thirties presented to a hospital in Uganda w
history:
A Ugandan gentleman with HIV in his thirties presented to a hospital in Uganda with an eight-month history of a slowly-progressive ulcerating facial lesion (Figure 1). The patient initially noted three small dark “bumps” on his face about eight months prior to admission: one on the left side of his forehead, one on the tip of his nose, and one just under the left side of his nose. While the lesions on his forehead and nose remained stable, the lesion under his nose slowly grew, ulcerated, and began to drain purulent material. The patient was treated by multiple local physicians with numerous courses of both intravenous and oral antibiotics as well as systemic steroids without any improvement. Given his lack of response to therapy, he was referred to otolaryngology clinic for further evaluation.
In the otolaryngology clinic, the patient underwent a biopsy of the forehead lesion as well as the leading edge of the larger ulcerating lesion. The ulcerated lesion showed only granulation tissue with fibrinosuppurative membrane. However, the forehead biopsy showed proliferating spindle cells associated with vascular clefts concerning for Kaposi sarcoma (KS) so he was referred to oncology clinic.
Upon presentation to oncology clinic, the patient noted subjective fevers and night-sweats but denied any other systemic symptoms. He denied any history of facial trauma or any insect or animal bites to the face and had no other lesions elsewhere on the skin. Given his systemic symptoms and extensive facial wound, the patient was admitted to the inpatient oncology ward for ongoing management.
Figure 1. Figure 1: Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion upon presentation to the oncology clinic
Figure 1: Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion upon presentation to the oncology clinic

The patient was diagnosed with HIV two months after the skin lesions initially appeared. CD4 cell count and HIV RNA at the time of diagnosis are unknown. He was started on antiretrovirals (lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/efavirenz) but only took them for 2-3 months before self-discontinuing the medications. About one month prior to hospital admission, he restarted his antiretrovirals (ARVs) and was taking them consistently at the time of admission.

The patient lives in a city in Uganda and works as a manual laborer. He had visited a few cities in Northern Uganda 4 months prior to the lesion formation. During this trip, he did not travel outside of city limits. He has no other travel history. He has no exposure to rural or forested areas. He owns a cat but does not recall any prior bites or scratches. Chickens, goats, and dogs are present in his neighborhood but he has no direct contact with these animals.

Lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/efavirenz
exam_studies:
Upon presentation to the oncology clinic, the patient was diaphoretic, appeared to be in pain, and was in mild distress. His vital signs were: axillary temperature: 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse rate: 133 bpm, blood pressure: 134/91 mmHg, and oxygen saturation: 96% on room air.
He had a large central facial lesion measuring 9.5 x 12.2 cm spreading from the bridge of his nose to his chin and covering the lateral aspects of his cheeks bilaterally (Figure 1). The lesion had an eschar over a majority of the surface and there was significant loss of his nasal architecture. The edges of the lesion had a “punched-out” quality and several small satellite lesions were seen on the left inferior aspect of the face and on the chin (Figure 1). Soft tissue edema and tenderness to palpation was noted inferior to the orbits. Purulent discharge could be seen at the wound edges. Oral exam showed no evidence of lesions or ulcerations on the palate. No dental decay was noted and no intraoral tenderness or dental abscesses observed. There was a non-tender 2 cm hyperpigmented nodule noted on his left forehead with a well-healing biopsy site.
On neurologic exam, his pupils were equal and reactive to light and he had full visual acuity. There were no limitations to intraocular muscle movement and all cranial nerves remained intact. Nuchal rigidity was not noted.
Further skin exam revealed no skin rashes or lesions on the trunk or extremities. The rest of his physical exam was within normal limits.
Figure 1: Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion upon presentation to the oncology clinic

White blood cell count (WBC): 10,330/uL (reference range (RR): 4,000-10,000/uL) with an absolute neutrophil count of 8,080/uL (RR 2,000-7,000/uL), absolute lymphocyte count of 1,240/uL (RR 600-3,400/uL) and an absolute eosinophil count of 30/µL (RR 0-700/uL); hemoglobin: 13.9 g/dl (RR 12.2-18.1 g/dl); platelets: 313,000/mm 3 (RR 140,000-400,00/mm 3).
Chemistries were sodium: 130 mmol/L (RR 136-145 mmol/L), potassium: 5.1 mmol/L (RR 3.5-5.1 mmol/L), chloride: 98 mmol/L (RR 98-107 mmol/L), urea: 5.8 mg/dL (RR 2.5-6.7 mmol/L), creatinine: 0.78 mg/dL (RR 0.3-1.2 mg/dL).
Liver function tests were alanine aminotransferase: 64 U/L (RR 0-55 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase: 29 U/L (RR 5-34 U/L), alkaline phosphatase: 151 U/L (RR 40- U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase: 181 U/L (RR 9-6 U/L), total protein: 6.8 g/dL (RR 6.4-8.3 g/dL), albumin: 3.1 g/dL (RR 3.5-5.2 gd/L).
Patient’s CD4 count was 259 cells/mm 3 with a non-detected viral load one month prior to presentation.
Chest radiograph showed no evidence of focal infiltrates, hilar adenopathy, or pleural effusions.

The patient was admitted and started on intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Lamivudine/tenofovir-disoproxil fumarate/efavirenz was continued. Cultures of the purulent drainage were obtained and positive only for diphtheroids and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus.
Over the first four days of his hospital stay, the patient continued to experience subjective fevers, his orbital swelling increased, and the wound edges slowly advanced. Consequently, empiric IV amphotericin deoxycholate and high-dose oral acyclovir were initiated. Plastic surgery was consulted and he underwent unroofing of his eschar with some improvement in the purulent drainage (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion after eschar debridement.
diagnosis:
Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis

Skin biopsies of the leading edge of the lesion revealed significant acanthosis of the epidermis with a dense dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, and macrophages on H&E stain (Figure 3). The macrophages were parasitized by small ovoid basophilic organisms consistent with Leishmania. No histologic features of KS were seen.
Figure 3. Skin, H&E stain, 40X (Courtesy of Diana Basemera)

With the diagnosis of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, the patient was continued on amphotericin deoxycholate, which was readily available at the hospital. Given the concern for renal toxicity with the anticipated prolonged course of amphotericin needed for treatment, the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DND i) was contacted and liposomal amphotericin B was procured through a charitable donation. In total, the patient received 21 days of amphotericin (11 days of amphotericin deoxycholate and 10 days of liposomal amphotericin) for the treatment of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. Renal function was closely monitored throughout his treatment course and he tolerated the amphotericin without any adverse events. Given the concern for superimposed bacterial infection, the patient received a 14-day course of IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole with resolution of all purulent drainage prior to hospital discharge. At the time he left the hospital, wound edges demonstrated evidence of healing. At the recommendation of dermatology, wound care was maintained with topical petroleum jelly 2-4 times daily to prevent excessive drying and scar tissue development.
Since discharge, the patient has followed in infectious diseases clinic every 2-3 weeks to monitor for any evidence of disease relapse. Serial exams demonstrated steady improvement with significant disease-resolution six weeks after completion of therapy. He did note some mild purulent drainage from the lesion after returning home which resolved with topical mupirocin ointment. He is currently being followed by plastic surgery for management of his wound and planning of future reconstructive surgery.
Given the initial concern for KS, the original skin biopsy was obtained. Upon review, the forehead biopsy also demonstrated macrophages which were parasitized by small ovoid basophilic organisms, thus consistent with a diagnosis of leishmaniasis. No evidence of KS was seen on the original or subsequent biopsies.
Figure 4. Figure 4: Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion six weeks after completion of therapy
Figure 4: Photograph of the patient’s facial lesion six weeks after completion of therapy

Mucosal leishmaniasis (ML), characterized by progressive destruction of the mucous membranes due to infection with Leishmania parasites, most commonly affects the nasal or oral mucosa, and is one of the least common clinical presentations of leishmaniasis (1, 2). When mucosal disease occurs in conjunction with cutaneous lesions it is referred to as mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL). New World ML primarily occurs in the Amazon Basin and is caused by parasites in the Leishmania Viannia subgenus, particularly L.V. braziliensis. Patients with New World ML typically experience a self-limiting cutaneous lesion several months to years prior to development of progressive mucosal disease. The clinical presentation of Old World ML, caused by L. L. major, L. L. infantum, L. donovani, or L. aethiopica, is more variable. Mucosal lesions may develop without history of cutaneous disease, appear concurrently with primary skin lesions, or result from direct extension of a local cutaneous lesion (1-3). The progression of our patient’s cutaneous lesion leading to significant destruction of nasal mucosa is consistent with a diagnosis of MCL.
Diagnosis of ML can be challenging. Since mucosal lesions have a low parasite burden, cultures of lesion aspirates and histologic examination are often negative (1,2). Although sensitivity of serologic studies with indirect immunofluorescence assay (IIFA) or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in patients with cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) can be low (20-80%), those with ML have higher rates of positivity (4,5) and often become serologically negative with successful treatment (6). Consequently, serology can play an important diagnostic role in patients with suspected ML whose direct diagnostic studies are negative.
Since our patient had no history of travel to other countries, he must have acquired his disease within Uganda. There is currently little data regarding the epidemiology of leishmaniasis in Uganda (7, 8). Transmission of visceral leishmaniasis due to L. donovani has been described in the northeastern Karamoja region (7), cutaneous leishmaniasis due to L. aethiopica is known to occur on the eastern and south-eastern slopes of Mount Elgon near the border of Kenya (7), and cases of equine leishmaniasis due to L. L. major occur in the Ssesse Islands in northern Lake Victoria (8). Cases of severe mucosal lesions caused by L. donovani have been described in Sudan (9) and, given the strong geographic and trade ties between Uganda and Sudan, it is possible that the catchment area for L. donovani has shifted further south to include northern Uganda where the patient was working around the time of symptom development. Further speciation of the patient’s leishmaniasis may assist in identifying the specific location of his disease transmission.
This case serves to highlight the importance of recognizing HIV/leishmaniasis co-infection. In people with HIV, leishmaniasis may present with severe, widely-disseminated visceral or cutaneous disease (10-13). Skin manifestations are more common and can occur in infections with Leishmania species which are not traditionally considered “dermatotropic”. Skin disease may also present in atypical forms including nodular, cheloid, or plaque-like lesions and can include significant mucosal involvement. Reports of rapid cutaneous or mucosal progression due immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) have been described after initiation of antiretroviral therapy, particularly in those with low CD4 cell counts (10-13). This may have contributed to our patient’s presentation since his lesion seemed to worsen around the time he was first started on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and again worsened when he restarted his ARVs.
As illustrated in our case, patients with HIV/leishmaniasis co-infection are frequently misdiagnosed even when biopsies are obtained (13). Common misdiagnoses include KS, leprosy, and autoimmune disease. As noted, this patient was misdiagnosed with KS on initial pathology evaluation. Histopathology in KS shows dermal proliferation due to spindle cell proliferation of endothelial cells that form sinuous vascular spaces. In leishmaniasis, dermal infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells can be seen in histopathology. Diagnosis of leishmaniasis in those with HIV can also be difficult since serology may be negative even in widely disseminated disease, particularly in those with low CD4 cell counts (1,2).
Management of ML can be challenging and disease relapse is not uncommon. Systemic therapy with pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate) or amphotericin should be used (14, 15). Since people with HIV experience higher rates of complications with antimonials and case reports have demonstrated improved ML cure rates with the use of amphotericin (16), we opted to use amphotericin B when treating our patient. Although most of the studies of leishmaniasis therapy were done using amphotericin deoxycholate, liposomal amphotericin poses fewer side effects, demonstrates good efficacy and is considered equivalent for treatment purposes (14, 15). Small studies using oral miltefosine either alone or in combination with amphotericin for New World ML caused by L.V. braziliensis demonstrated good response (17-18) but the use of miltefosine has not been studied in Old World ML. Since patients with HIV are slower to respond to treatment and experience higher relapse rates, close clinical monitoring after treatment is important to ensure all skin lesions continue to resolve. Determination of cure is based solely on clinical response (14,15). Complete reepithelization and resolution of ulcer base induration should occur within three months and total lesion regression should be seen by six months after treatment. If these criteria are not met, the patient should be re-treated with a full course of systemic therapy, either with the same or an alternate treatment regimen. There is no data to support use of secondary prophylaxis to prevent disease relapse in ML, even in patients with HIV (15).
As seen in the photos (Figure 4) our patient’s lesions continue to epithelize and heal. He will be regularly monitored for complete disease resolution over the next six months and is currently being followed by plastic surgery in order to determine optimal timing of any necessary reconstructive surgery.

title: An African American heterosexual male in his 40s with a history of HIV presented
history:
An African American heterosexual male in his 40s with a history of HIV presented to a local emergency room with complaints of a worsening skin rash. His rash had reportedly been progressing over the past few weeks with involvement of his face, scalp, torso, and legs. Review of systems was also positive for a mild cough, nasal congestion, and a recent nosebleed but was otherwise unremarkable.

The patient’s medical history was significant for HIV, diagnosed about 5 years prior to presentation. He was initially on coformulated efavirenz/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine, but it was discontinued due to nightmares. He was not taking ART until about two months prior to admission when an outside provider had re-initiated therapy with darunavir/cobicistat and tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine. Pre-ART laboratory data demonstrated an HIV RNA of 2.13 million copies/mL and an absolute CD4 count of 4 cells/cubic mm.

The patient had previously been incarcerated until release a few months prior to admission. No reported travel outside the United States. He is a current smoker but denies alcohol or illicit drug use.

Darunavir/cobicistat, tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine, and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim
exam_studies:
The patient was thin and chronically ill-appearing. Temperature 100.6 degrees Fahrenheit, BP 105/63, HR 117, respiratory rate of 29. Pertinent findings on physical examination included a diffuse rash with hyperkeratotic plaques on the forehead, bilateral cheeks, nose, and upper lip with erosions and hemorrhagic crusting. (Figures 1-3). Erosions were also noted on the hard palate, tongue, and buccal mucosa bilaterally. No organomegaly or lymphadenopathy was appreciated on examination. Figure 1. Face, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions Figure 2. Chest, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions Figure 3. Legs, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions
Figure 1. Face, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions
Figure 2. Chest, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions
Figure 3. Legs, appearance at presentation with diffuse papulonodular lesions

The patient had a white blood cell count of 4.9 TH/cmm (normal value: 4.0-10.00 TH/cmm) with an absolute lymphocyte count of 0.18 TH/cmm (normal value: 1.0-3.0 Th/cmm). Hemoglobin was 6.8 g/dL (normal value: 13.0- 17.0 g/dL). Platelet count was 3 TH/cmm (normal value: 150-400 TH/cmm). ESR was elevated to 119 mm/hr (normal value 0.0-10.0 mm/hr), and CRP was 11.5 mg/dL (normal value: 0.0-0.5 mg/dL). Liver function tests, aside from albumin (2.6 g/dL; normal value: 3.5-5.5 g/dL) were unremarkable.

On admission, the patient was started empirically on broad spectrum antibiotics, acyclovir, and fluconazole with minimal improvement of skin lesions. The infectious diseases team recommended the addition of oral ivermectin while awaiting workup results that included HIV RNA, RPR, serum Cryptococcus antigen, urine Histoplasma and Blastomyces antigens. Dermatology and otolaryngology were consulted and performed multiple skin biopsies. ART was continued with bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine.
diagnosis:
Histoplasmosis -Associated Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome

An updated HIV RNA was 202 copies/mL, and the patient’s absolute CD4 count was 20 cells/cmm (14%). A urine Histoplasma antigen was positive at >23 ng/mL. A Histoplasma antibody test was positive with a titer of 1:128. A urine Blastomyces antigen was also positive at 12.45 ng/mL, which we suspect was the result of cross-reactivity between the Histoplasma and Blastomyces antigen tests. The Blastomyces antibody was negative along with negative serum Cryptococcal antigen, RPR, and HTLV-1/2 antibody testing. Pathologic evaluation of all skin biopsies (right earlobe, right forearm, and lip) showed evidence of Histoplasma infection (Figure 4 and 5). The organism also grew on fungal culture several weeks after collection. The isolate was sent to a fungal reference laboratory and confirmed to be Histoplasma capsulatum.
Figure 4. Histoplasmosis, H&E stain 40x: Numerous intracytoplasmic yeast forms are present inside histiocytes
Figure 5. Histoplasmosis, GMS stain 40x: Highlighting many oval-shaped uniform fungal yeasts, morphologically consistent with Histoplasma.

Urine Histoplasma antigen returned positive and the pathology report described yeast-like organisms consistent with disseminated Histoplasmosis (figure 4 and 5). All other antimicrobials were discontinued, and the patient was started on intravenous amphotericin B. Due to steady improvement over a 2-week period, he was transitioned to oral itraconazole for continued management. By the time of discharge, the patient had experienced modest improvement in his skin lesions, and outpatient follow up was arranged.
Two weeks after discharge, the patient was re-admitted with nausea and intractable abdominal pain. CT imaging demonstrated a 5-cm mass in the right lobe of the liver. Biopsy revealed hepatocellular proliferation, sinusoidal dilation, and congestion. No microorganisms were identified by staining and cultures from the liver mass were negative. The patient was discharged home after significant symptomatic improvement to continue ART and antifungal therapy.
Less than two weeks after the second admission, the patient returned with complaints of shortness of breath at rest and on exertion, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 15%. An EKG was significant for a QTc of 551. The patient subsequently improved after intravenous diuresis and was discharged home on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with plans to transition from itraconazole to posaconazole after his QTc improved with outpatient follow up with Infectious Disease and Cardiology. During this admission it was noted that the findings on prior liver biopsy were secondary to hepatic congestion from heart failure.

In people with HIV, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is characterized by an exaggerated or atypical inflammatory response following initiation of ART manifested as either paradoxical worsening of a previously known infection or unmasking of a previously unrecognized one. IRIS has been observed both in ART-naïve patients initiating therapy for the first time as well as treatment-experienced patients who are re-initiating ART after a period of being off therapy. Criteria that support the diagnosis of IRIS include: (1) a temporal relationship between ART initiation and clinical deterioration with symptoms of an infectious or inflammatory condition, (2) symptoms not explained by a newly acquired infection, predicted course of a previously diagnosed infection, or adverse effects of drug therapy, and (3) evidence of virological response to ART with >1-log decrease in HIV RNA often with an associated increase in CD4 cell count[1]. In our patient, the temporal relationship between ART initiation and development of symptoms after previously being asymptomatic along with his rapid virological response evidenced by a 4-log decrease in viral load support the diagnosis of an unmasking IRIS.
In patients with IRIS, memory T cells are redistributed from lymphoid tissue to organs, and the number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells increases faster than that of regulatory T cells, resulting in an imbalance in the immune system [2,3]. This disproportionate inflammatory response has been linked to a number of infectious pathogens [1,4]. Histoplasmosis -associated IRIS appears to be rarely reported in the literature with an estimated incidence rate of 0.74 cases per 1000 HIV-infected person-years and may present months after initiation of ART [4-7]. Asymptomatic dissemination beyond the lungs is fairly common but usually only becomes clinically apparent in patients with impaired cellular immunity in conditions like HIV as seen in our patient [6]. Reactivation of latent infections may occur long after the primary infection has taken place [7,8]. Some evidence suggests increased incidence in endemic regions like the Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys after ART initiation [4-7].
Immune reconstitution in the setting of disseminated Histoplasmosis is classically characterized by fever, fatigue, and a combination of respiratory and/or gastrointestinal symptoms. Central nervous system and cutaneous involvement appear to be far less commonly reported [6]. In the United States, for instance, less than 10% of all cases of disseminated Histoplasmosis present with cutaneous manifestations, and reports of cutaneous manifestations in the absence of involvement of other organ systems are exceedingly rare [9-12]. Cutaneous manifestations of Histoplasma are most often described as diffuse papuloulcerative lesions with crusting, followed by pustular or nodular lesions as witnessed in our patient’s case and can easily be mistaken for other infectious etiologies highlighting the importance of culture and pathology in making a diagnosis [9,10].
Once diagnosed, management of Histoplasmosis -associated IRIS focuses on treatment of the underlying infection since rates of mortality are high [6,7]. The natural disease course is progressive and fatal over a few months time if untreated, and due to the significant morbidity and mortality associated with untreated disease, some literature even propose a role for implementation of screening for latent and subclinical Histoplasmosis prior to initiation of ART therapy for patients in endemic regions [5]. Antifungal agents such as amphotericin and itraconazole (for consolidation and long-term suppression) are the mainstays of therapy [6,7]. For patients intolerant of itraconazole, oral posaconazole and voriconazole have been demonstrated to be effective against Histoplasma and are alternatives for patients who are only moderately ill [7].
While our patient was able to continue ART and remain virologically suppressed throughout his treatment course, the potential adverse effects of antifungal therapy must always be considered. Triazoles may have drug-drug interactions, and gastrointestinal symptoms are the most commonly reported side effects seen in patients receiving itraconazole. However, evidence suggests an association between congestive heart failure and itraconazole use, likely due to the drug’s direct negative inotropic effect [13, 14]. Therefore, itraconazole has a warning advising against its use in individuals with a history of congestive heart failure or in those who develop signs or symptoms of heart failure during its administration [14]. We suspect that our patient’s newly-diagnosed heart failure was either caused by, or at least exacerbated by, the itraconazole he was receiving, so we opted to change his treatment regimen. This black box warning has not been issued with other triazoles although concerns about drug absorption and need for QTc monitoring remain relevant for the majority of the drug class.
Here we present a case of disseminated Histoplasmosis after re-introduction of ART in a treatment-experienced HIV-positive patient. As the efficacy and tolerability of ART continue to improve, IRIS has become an increasingly more commonly recognized early complication observed after ART initiation. This patient’s presentation, characterized primarily by cutaneous lesions, highlights the need for clinicians to: 1) keep a broad differential diagnosis when evaluating immunocompromised hosts that may have atypical manifestations, 2) involve additional consulting services when needed to assist in obtaining a timely diagnosis to guide antimicrobial therapy that may reduce morbidity and mortality, and 3) monitor for potential adverse effects of antimicrobial therapy that may require use of alternative treatment regimens.

title: A man in his 50s presented with dry cough, intermittent fever, progressive dyspn
history:
A man in his 50s presented with dry cough, intermittent fever, progressive dyspnea on exertion and fatigue of 1-week duration. One day prior to presentation he also developed non-bloody diarrhea without abdominal cramping, pain, nausea and vomiting. He was diagnosed with Covid-19 five days prior to presentation by a nasopharyngeal viral PCR that was positive for SARS-CoV-2. A chest radiograph revealed patchy infiltrates in the bilateral perihilar region and bases, right greater than left [Fig 1]. He was admitted for supportive care and monitoring. On day 5 of hospitalization he developed progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. A follow up chest radiograph revealed worsening infiltrates bilaterally. He was given tocilizumab intravenously at 600 milligram every 8 hours for a total of 3 doses and 200 milliliters of convalescent plasma. His sputum culture obtained at the time of intubation grew methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus for which intravenous cefazolin was started. After extubation on hospitalization day 14, he developed a new fever and elevated white blood cell count.
Figure 1. Chest Radiograph single view shows patchy infiltrates in the bilateral perihilar region and bases, right greater than left

Diabetes Mellitus Type 2. Hypertension

Patient’s wife and children also recently had Covid-19. No pets at home and no recent travel.

Metformin, Lisinopril.
exam_studies:
Patient appeared pale, anxious and was in mild respiratory distress. He had a temperature of 38.5C [101.3F]. His respiratory rate was 28 per minute, pulse 110 per minute, blood pressure 121/65 mm Hg and saturating 96% on 4 liters of oxygen. Chest examination revealed bilateral rales with no accessory muscle use. Examination otherwise unremarkable.

White blood cell count of 25,010 cells/microliter (reference range 4000 – 10800 cells/microliter) and absolute neutrophils 15,780 cells/microliter (reference range 1800 – 7800 cells/microliter). His platelet count was 282,000 cells/microliter (reference range 140,000 – 400,000 cells/microliter). His serum creatinine was 0.79 milligram/deciliter (reference range 0.60 – 1.30 milligram/deciliter). His hemoglobin A1C was 9.9% (reference range 4.1% – 5.6%). Liver function tests were normal. A CT angiography of thorax revealed peripheral ground glass opacification as well as more dense consolidation in the superior segments of bilateral lower lobes with bubbly appearance on the right concerning for necrotizing pneumonia [Fig 2]. A sputum culture was obtained.
Figure 2. CT Angiography of the Thorax shows dense consolidation in the superior segments of bilateral lower lobes with bubbly appearance on the right concerning for necrotizing pneumonia
diagnosis:
Probable Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis in a Person with Covid-19

He was continued on cefazolin with no significant change in clinical status. Two days later his sputum culture grew the organism shown in lactophenol cotton blue stain [Fig 3].
The sputum culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus. Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen resulted with an index value of greater than 1.110 (reference range >0.5 – patients with an index value of greater than or equal to 0.5 are considered to be positive for galactomannan antigen). Beta-D Glucan was negative at less than 31 picogram/milliliter (reference range <80 picogram/milliliter). Histoplasma and Blastomyces serologies were negative. A bronchoscopy was deferred due to patient’s tenuous respiratory status. A diagnosis of probable invasive pulmonary aspergillosis was made based on CT findings, microbiological data and positive galactomannan antigen.
Figure 3. Lactophenol cotton blue stain from sputum culture shows Aspergillus fumigatus

He was started on oral voriconazole with initial loading dose of 400 milligram twice a day followed by maintenance dosing of 200 milligram twice a day. Voriconazole is planned to be continued for a total of 12 weeks. He was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and slowly improved. He remained afebrile and was completely weaned off of oxygen at the time of discharge.

Critically ill patients with Covid-19 have a high risk of secondary infections. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is increasingly reported as a co-infection in people with Covid-19 pneumonia (1,3). IPA is a well described complication of severe influenza (1,2), though the exact rate of IPA in Covid-19 patients is yet to be known; in some series, the rate is 30%, similar to influenza (2). In a study from France, 33% out of 27 patients was found to have putative IPA (4) and Koehler et al have published a study from Germany that shows a prevalence of 26% out of 19 critically ill patients (1).
The highly aggressive nature of SARS CoV-2 causing bilateral alveolo-interstitial lesions increases the risk of infections acquired through inhalational route specifically aspergillosis. Less ciliary clearance, elevated IL-6 levels and IL-1 pathway activation promoting fungal growth are possible factors in Covid-19 associated IPA. Immune dysregulation associated with Covid-19 affecting Th1 and Th2 responses could be a risk factor for IPA (5).
Our patient had no host risk factors similar to the other reported cases of Covid-19 with IPA. There is a high risk of missed diagnosis if the diagnosis of probable or proven IPA is made based on the existing consensus definitions like European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer/Mycoses Study Group EORTC/MSG and AspICU algorithm.
Diagnosis of IPA by these definitions require a positive histopathology for invasive disease, typical host risk factors, Aspergillus growth in lower respiratory tract culture and/or positive biomarker assays for Aspergillus antigen. Absence of host factors was also apparent in influenza-associated disease, in which 57% of patients could not be classified based on AspICU algorithm for patients in ICUs. A retrospective multicenter cohort study showed that influenza infection was an independent risk factor for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (2). Diagnosis of IPA is crucial and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) has an important diagnostic role. However, bronchoscopy and BAL in Covid-19 are limited due to risk of aerosolization. Serial measurements of fungal markers including serum galactomannan and serum beta D-glucan can be valuable in the diagnosis along with radiographic and microbiological data from sputum, endotracheal aspirate and/or BAL cultures.
Since mortality rates are higher in untreated IPA, treatment is warranted in patients with high suspicion for IPA. Voriconazole is the first line antifungal for IPA and patients should be treated for a total of 12 weeks with adequate follow up with serum galactomannan and imaging. Until we gain crucial insights into IPA and Covid-19 lung, patients with Covid-19 who are critically ill with evidence for Aspergillus infection should receive antifungal therapy to prevent increased mortality (5).

title: A woman in her twenties with a prior diagnosis of relapsed refractory primary me
history:
A woman in her twenties with a prior diagnosis of relapsed refractory primary mediastinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in partial remission after undergoing chimeric antigen receptor T-cell immunotherapy (CAR-T) 6 months prior to presentation was admitted to the hospital with complaints of left knee pain and swelling for the past 10 days. She also reported fever to 102.8ºF for two days prior to admission. She denied any trauma, animal scratches or bites to the affected knee. Patient denied any respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary symptoms or rash.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) complicated by recurrent bilateral malignant pleural effusions and malignant ascites, in partial remission at the time of presentation.

Patient was born in South America. She moved to Florida 10 years prior to presentation. She has a dog. She denies history of tuberculosis or known exposure. She has not been sexually active in the recent past. Patient reported no history of recent travel.

Acyclovir, Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, Levothyroxine
exam_studies:
Tmax 102.9 F, pulse 110 beats/minute, blood pressure 125/75, respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute. She appeared alert, oriented and in no acute distress. Significant physical examination findings were limited to left knee joint that appeared warm and swollen [Figure 1]; there was associated tenderness on palpation along the joint line as well as limited range of motion with passive and active range of motion. Rest of musculoskeletal examination was normal. No rashes were seen on skin examination.
Figure 1. Ongoing swelling of the Left Knee 12 Weeks from Initial Presentation

White blood cell count 11.41 k/uL (normal range 4.00 to 10.90), hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (normal range 11.4 to 15.0), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 51 mm/hr (normal range 0-20), C-reactive protein 7.82 mg/dL (normal range 0-0.49). Immunoglobulin levels of IgG, IgM, and IgA were all below detectable levels.

Once blood and urine cultures were collected, patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics with ceftriaxone plus vancomycin for suspected infectious arthritis. Patient was evaluated by an orthopedic service and left knee joint aspiration was performed. The joint synovial fluid aspirate revealed 62,390 cells, 54% of which were neutrophils; no crystals were seen. Gram stain of the synovial fluid aspirate was negative for organisms. Blood cultures were negative on a preliminary review. On hospital day 2, ceftriaxone was changed to cefepime due to on-going fever and vancomycin was continued.
diagnosis:
Septic arthritis due to Ureaplasma urealyticum

Due to high synovial fluid white cell count with neutrophil predominance and concerns for septic arthritis, patient underwent left knee joint debridement and irrigation on hospital day 2. During surgery, yellow tinged fluid was extruded from the knee, but no overt purulence was observed. Additional samples for standard bacterial, fungal and acid fast bacilli cultures were sent to the microbiology lab for investigation. Intra-operative synovial fluid sample was sent for Bacterial Detection by PCR assay to an outside laboratory. Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae by amplified detection were negative. Left knee joint pain and swelling improved after surgery but did not resolve.
Despite broad-spectrum antibiotic use, patient continued to have intermittent fever. All cultures returned negative for bacterial growth, therefore, patient’s antibiotics were discontinued after 10 days of therapy. It was felt that on-going fever may have been related to recent immunotherapy; in addition, relapse of lymphoma was considered. At that point, patient was given systemic steroids that resulted in a resolution of the fever and improvement in symptoms associated with the left knee. Patient was discharged home on hospital day 11.
In the course of the next four weeks, patient continued to have persistent left knee effusion and pain. In addition, she gradually developed pain in other joints, including the left ankle, small joints of left hand, and right shoulder.
Given her progressive symptoms, she was re-evaluated. The previous synovial fluid Bacterial Detection by PCR assay returned back positive for Ureaplasma urealyticum. All her prior cultures, including bacterial/fungal/acid fast bacilli, were finalized as negative. Urogenital Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma Species by PCR testing was performed on a urine sample; results were positive for the presence of Ureaplasma species. Based on this information, patient was diagnosed with disseminated Ureaplasma infection with left knee septic arthritis.

Treatment with daily azithromycin was initiated. Patient received 12 weeks of treatment with azithromycin, at which point, urine Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma Species by PCR testing was negative. However, our patient continued to have significant left knee joint pain and joint effusion as well as other joint involvement (See figures 1 and 2). This was associated with continuous elevation of inflammatory markers that prompted a consideration of presence of reactive arthritis in addition to an original infectious etiology.
Due to poor clinical response, azithromycin was stopped and patient was started on the combination of levofloxacin and doxycycline. Patient also received monthly intravenous immune globulin therapy due to low monthly immunoglobulin G levels. The regimen resulted in a significant improvement in her joint symptoms (see figure 3) as well as normalization of her inflammatory markers. Patient remains in complete remission from her lymphoma.
Figure 2. Left 4th metacarpophalangeal joint involvement 12 weeks after initial presentation
Figure 3. Improved swelling of the left knee 16 Weeks after initial presentation

Acute monoarthritis in association with fever warrants a comprehensive evaluation in order to rule out septic arthritis. In a young adult, gonococcal infection is high on a differential diagnosis along with other bacterial causes (eg, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae). Mycobacterial and fungal infections of the joint are uncommon and typically occur in patients with compromised immune system.
We present a rare case of Ureaplasma urealyticum septic arthritis in a patient with a prior diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma status post CAR-T cell immunotherapy. Ureaplasma species are known causative agents of various genitourinary infections in immunocompetent host; however, this pathogen can cause severe infections in immunocompromised patients (1). Septic arthritis with Ureaplasma species has been described in the literature, specifically in patients with severe hypogammaglobulinemia, similar to our patient (2, 3).
Diagnosis of Ureaplasma infection remains challenging as a specialized culture is required for detection of this pathogen, which is typically not performed unless a provider has high index of suspicion for this particular infection. As illustrated in our case, two sets of synovial fluid cultures were negative for any bacterial growth and the diagnosis was made only after a synovial fluid PCR assay was performed.
Our case also highlights treatment challenges as our patient initially had a very poor response to a single agent treatment with azithromycin that prompted us to use combination therapy with doxycycline and levofloxacin. In addition, correction of her severe hypogammaglobulinemia likely played a critical role in her clinical improvement.

title: A man in his fifties with end-stage renal disease status post living related ren
history:
A man in his fifties with end-stage renal disease status post living related renal transplant about 2 years before admission (complicated by graft rejection) presented with a 3-week history of a linear nodular skin rash over his left lower extremity. He reported developing a nodule and erythema over the medial aspect of his left shin after performing yard work that included cleaning a stack of old decaying wood. He did not recall any physical contact with the wood at the time of his yard work, but reported a mechanical fall when he sustained a small wound over the left distal anterior shin that had healed. His physician prescribed a 7-day course of cephalexin one week later for suspected cellulitis. He did not respond to antibiotics, but instead developed new skin nodules distally and proximally in a sporotrichoid pattern over the next few weeks. Some of his lesions broke down and started to drain a yellowish fluid. He denied any fevers, chills, cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or abdominal symptoms.

The patient lived in the northeast US with no recent travel, or animal exposures.

Mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily, Tacrolimus 6 mg twice daily, Prednisone 5 mg daily
exam_studies:
The patient’s vital signs were normal at the outpatient clinic visit: Temperature 97.3ºF (36.3ºC), blood pressure 150/82 mm Hg, pulse 85 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. He was well-appearing and in no acute distress. The exam was notable for multiple nodules of approximately 1-2 cm in diameter distributed in a string-like pattern along medial aspect of LLE associated with some ulcerations, a small amount of purulent discharge, tenderness, and mild erythema as well as hyperpigmentation (Figure 1A). The rest of his exam was within normal limits.
Figure 1. Figure 1A. Image of the patient’s leg demonstrating skin lesions with sporotrichoid pattern before treatment with voriconazole.
Figure 1A. Image of the patient’s leg demonstrating skin lesions with sporotrichoid pattern before treatment with voriconazole.

The complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 1.6 per microliter of blood (reference range 3.4-11.2) and an absolute neutrophil count of 0.9 per microliter of blood (reference range 1.8-7.0), hemoglobin of 9.1 grams per deciliter (reference range 13.3-17.7), and normal platelets. His serum creatinine was 3.51 milligram per deciliter (reference range 0.64-1.27), and his electrolytes and liver function tests were otherwise normal. Blood cultures were negative.
A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left lower leg demonstrated circumferential subcutaneous edema but otherwise no discrete abscesses, osteomyelitis, or other abnormal findings.

After his symptoms progressed, he presented to the emergency room where clindamycin was started and Dermatology consulted. A punch biopsy was obtained and sent for histopathology and culture (Figure 2). He was then discharged with a 10-day course of Linezolid and referred for outpatient Infectious Diseases consultation.
diagnosis:
Scedosporium skin and soft tissue infection in an immunocompromised patient.

Tissue obtained from a skin punch biopsy showed a necrotizing neutrophilic and granulomatous inflammatory reaction associated with a fungus that appeared as irregular septated hyphae and yeast forms (Figure 2). Fungal wound cultures eventually grew Scedosporium apiospermum.
Figure 2. Figure 2A. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. Hematoxylin and eosin staining demonstrates a focus of necrotizing neutrophilic and granulomatous inflammation at the base of the biopsy (20x magnification)
Figure 2A. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. Hematoxylin and eosin staining demonstrates a focus of necrotizing neutrophilic and granulomatous inflammation at the base of the biopsy (20x magnification)
Figure 3. Figure 2B. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. A fungus is discernible on periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain (40x magnification)
Figure 2B. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. A fungus is discernible on periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain (40x magnification)
Figure 4. Figure 2C. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy showing PAS stain at 100x magnification
Figure 2C. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy showing PAS stain at 100x magnification
Figure 5. Figure 2D. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. Grocott Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain with the fungus appearing as irregular septated hyphae and yeast forms (100x magnification)
Figure 2D. Representative histopathology from the skin biopsy. Grocott Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain with the fungus appearing as irregular septated hyphae and yeast forms (100x magnification)

The patient was initially treated with itraconazole for suspected sporotrichosis prior to the result of his cultures. With identification of Scedosporium apiospermum on fungal wound cultures, itraconazole was changed to voriconazole. His neutrophils gradually recovered and he was no longer neutropenic. The doses of his immunosuppressants were not changed. He was treated of a total of 7-8 months with voriconazole. At his 7-month follow-up, his skin lesions had markedly improved (Figure 1B).
Figure 1A. Image of the patient’s leg demonstrating skin lesions with sporotrichoid pattern before treatment with voriconazole.
Figure 6. Figure 1B. Image of the patient’s leg with resolved skin lesions after treatment with voriconazole.
Figure 1B. Image of the patient’s leg with resolved skin lesions after treatment with voriconazole.

Scedosporium species are ubiquitous environmental fungi found in the soil and polluted waters worldwide [1]. The two clinically important species in the genus are Scedosporium apiospermum and Scedosporium prolificans [2]. These species are considered emerging opportunistic pathogens, capable of causing local and invasive diseases in humans which range from cutaneous and subcutaneous tissue infections to disseminated infections in immunocompromised hosts [2]. Other sites of infections include the central nervous system, eyes, sinuses, lungs, abdomen, blood, and other locations [2]. Infection can occur through inhalation of spores or traumatic inoculation of the fungus [2]. In patients who present with skin infections, scedosporiosis can manifest with a sporotrichoid rash. The increasing incidence of Scedosporium infections is thought to be related to the increased use of immunosuppressive agents, such as antineoplastics and corticosteroids, and antifungal agents in the immunocompromised host that have activity against Candida and Aspergillus species but limited or no activity against Scedosporium [2,3]. Diagnosis of Scedosporium species is typically made by detecting the fungus from clinical specimens through direct microscopic examination or histological analysis and by culture on the appropriate media [3]. This could be challenging as it may be difficult to distinguish Scedosporium species from species of Aspergillus or Fusarium, as they may all present with dichotomous branching, hyaline hyphae, and regular hyphal septation [3, 4]. New approaches of diagnostics with non-culture-based molecular methods, such as mass spectroscopy and nucleic acid sequencing, are being pursued to improve the diagnosis of this fungal disease [3]. Treatment of Scedosporium infections could also be challenging because of its intrinsic resistance and reduced susceptibility to some of the commonly used antifungal agents. Scedosporium species are typically resistant to polyenes and the triazole fluconazole. They also demonstrate reduced susceptibility to echinocandins, such as micafungin [3,5]. Most guidelines recommend voriconazole as first-line therapy [3]. While not United States Food and Drug Administration-approved, isavuconazole has shown good in vitro activity, though clinical experience is limited [3,6]. In patients with invasive disease, combination therapy with several antifungal agents and reversal of immunosuppression are often considered [3, 7]. In our case, the patient had a localized skin and soft tissue infection with Scedosporium that was successfully managed with voriconazole. However, given his initial neutropenia which later recovered, it should be acknowledged that the recovery of the neutrophils may have been as important as the antifungal medication to this patient’s healing process. Given the increasing incidence of Scedosporium and other invasive fungal infections in the immunocompromised population along with the intrinsic antimicrobial resistance of Scedosporium species, we suggest clinicians consider obtaining clinical specimens through a tissue biopsy, when available, for routine cultures and pathologic analysis when treating an immunocompromised patient who has failed prior antibiotic therapy for a persistent rash. We also recommend that Scedoporium species be considered in the differential diagnosis of a sporotrichoid rash.
