title: A female in her seventies presented to the emergency department with one day of
history:
A female in her seventies presented to the emergency department with one day of fever and chills associated with myalgia and epigastric pain. She was hospitalized the week before for work-up of myelodysplastic syndrome requiring a bone marrow biopsy. Blood cultures done on this admission were positive for gram-positive rods in three out of four bottles (Figure 1-2) for which infectious disease was consulted.
She reported epigastric pain with no radiation or association with food. She denied having dysphagia or odynophagia. She denied pain at the site of the bone marrow biopsy. There was no recent trauma and no known skin infections. She has a history of fishbone stuck in her esophagus requiring surgical removal seven years ago.
Figure 1. Gram stain, Blood: 100x Oil immersion: predominantly gram-positive rods, non-spore forming.
Figure 2. Blood Culture showing small grey alpha hemolytic colonies at 48 hours.

Diabetes, Hypertension

Immigrated to the U.S.A from China more than 10 years ago. Lives alone, no pets, no recent travel. Patient does not eat raw food; reported eating fish daily. Patient denied consumption of unpasteurized dairy or probiotic use.
exam_studies:
At the time of consult, the patient had a temperature of 97.7F (36.5C), blood pressure of 142/75 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute, and respiration rate of 18 breaths per minute with a saturation of 100% on room air. She appeared uncomfortable. No skin or mucosal lesions. Tender epigastric region without rebounding or guarding. Tender lumbar spine, which was reported to be chronic. The rest of the exam was normal.

Laboratory investigations were significant for white blood cell count of 14.8 k/ul (range 4-11 k/ul) with hemoglobin of 8.8 g/dl (range 11-15 g/dl), which was her baseline. C-reactive protein was 102.60 mg/dl (range 0-7.48 mg/dl). Electrolytes, kidney function, and liver function tests were normal. Urinalysis showed no pyuria, and urine culture was negative. Blood cultures from admission showed gram-positive rods in three out of four bottles (Figure 1-2). Subsequent blood cultures, drawn a day after, were negative. Chest X-ray (CXR) showed no infiltrate (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Chest X-Ray (CXR) on admission.

The patient remained afebrile with hemodynamic stability; examination remained stable, with no evidence of heart failure. Blood cultures flagged for an organism on our matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry on day six of admission. VITEK -2 flagged positive for the same organism on day eight of admission. The organism was oxidase-negative, catalase-negative, non-motile, non-spore-forming, and alpha-hemolytic on blood agar. The blood culture plate was sent out for confirmation, as these machines at our hospital have not been validated for identification for this organism. While awaiting confirmation, the patient was kept on antibiotics, and a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was obtained.
diagnosis:
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae bacteremia with native aortic and tricuspid valve endocarditis

The blood culture came back as Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae. TTE showed multiple large vegetations on the tricuspid valve with possible small vegetation on the aortic valve. This finding was confirmed with a trans-esophageal echocardiogram (TEE), which showed thickened tricuspid leaflets with multiple large mobile tricuspid valve vegetations, moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation (Figure 4). Moderately thickened aortic valve. Small mobile echo-density 0.5 cm in length on the ventricular surface of the aortic valve, likely a vegetation (Figure 5). Moderate aortic regurgitation. No vegetation on the mitral or pulmonic valve seen.
Figure 4. Transesophageal Echocardiogram image of vegetation on Tricuspid Valve.
Figure 5. Transesophageal Echocardiogram image of vegetation on Aortic Valve.

On further questioning, she reported daily consumption of unsold fish from the market. She mentioned having cooked it well with no injuries on the skin while preparing food; however, she stated she might have missed removing the smaller bones while preparing the fish. She did not remember any fishbone being stuck in her throat. Also, on examination, we did not find any skin lesions, but she did complain of epigastric pain on admission, which could have been due to an injury from the fishbone. We obtained chest imaging which did not show any signs of esophageal perforation.
The patient was initially on intravenous vancomycin and ampicillin/sulbactam while awaiting the culture results. She was then switched to intravenous penicillin G once confirmation of the organism was obtained. The patient remained hemodynamically stable with no respiratory or neurological symptoms. She was seen by cardiothoracic surgery after her echocardiography results and was planned for surgery.
She underwent aortic and tricuspid valve replacement. In the operating room, it was noted that she had multilobulated vegetations involving all three leaflets of the tricuspid valve. Also, the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles contained vegetations. The inspection of the aortic valve demonstrated that each of the three leaflets had vegetations on the ventricular side. Pathology of the valves showed acute endocarditis on the aortic valve and acute fibrinous endocarditis with bacterial colonies on the tricuspid valve. Gram stain showed gram-positive colonies.
The patient was discharged on penicillin. She had subsequent imaging of her chest, which showed emboli to lungs likely septic in origin, raising suspicion for repeat endocarditis on the newly placed tricuspid valve. She underwent repeat TEE and was ruled out for endocarditis. The patient completed six weeks of intravenous penicillin. She is being followed in the infectious disease clinic and is recovering well at five months after her initial presentation.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a catalase-negative, indole-negative, non-motile, non-spore-forming, facultative anaerobic gram-positive bacillus. It is commonly alpha-hemolytic on blood agar and may be misidentified as a viridans streptococcus (1). Erysipelothrix and Bacillus species may be differentiated by the absence and presence of spores, respectively. Unlike other gram-positive non-sporulating rods (Lactobacillus species, Listeria monocytogenes, Arcanobacterium species), Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae produces hydrogen sulfide on triple sugar iron media (2). Moreover, Listeria and Arcanobacterium species are beta-hemolytic. Listeria also is a catalase-positive and motile organism.
Erysipelosthrix rhusiopathiae is ubiquitous in nature and has been reported to be a colonizer of swine, fish, shellfish, birds, and even insects, with the pig being the main reservoir (1). In humans, it is primarily associated with occupational exposure - butchers, slaughterhouse workers, farmers, and fish handlers have the highest risk of acquiring the infection (2). Infections following the ingestion of contaminated frozen fish and pork have also been documented (3). People with cirrhosis, alcohol use disorder, poorly controlled diabetes are at higher risk.
There are three well defined clinical categories of human disease. The most common form of infection is a localized cutaneous form called erysipeloid, which occurs as a result of direct inoculation with the infected animal or fish. The second form is rare, a diffuse cutaneous eruption with systemic symptoms. The third form is a systemic infection, predominately bacteremia, often associated with endocarditis (4). It is noteworthy that previously, bacteremic infection, with or without endocarditis, was considered most commonly a primary infection rather than dissemination from localized cutaneous lesions (1). Recent literature shows an increasing rate of bacteremia starting from localized cutaneous lesions (3).
E. rhusiopathiae infection may occur more commonly than reports suggest. It is likely underdiagnosed and under-reported because of the resemblance it bears to other infections and the problems that may be encountered in isolation and identification of this pathogen. Furthermore, gram-positive rods cultured from the blood are often dismissed as diphtheroids and not fully identified.
The definitive diagnosis of infection with E. rhusiopathiae requires isolation of the organism from a biopsy specimen, blood, or other sterile body fluid. Standard methods for culturing blood or biopsy tissue should suffice if incubation is continued up to 7 days (4). It is noteworthy that MALDI-TOF has been shown to accurately and rapidly identify Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (5).
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is different from other bacteria, as it tends to affect normal native heart valves with peculiar tropism seen for aortic valve (1). E. rhusiopathiae is exquisitely susceptible to penicillin and carbapenems but has intrinsic resistance to vancomycin. Even with the administration of appropriate drugs, 36% of patients need valve replacement due to significant valve destruction. The complications, such as mycotic aneurysm, valve perforation, and myocardial abscess, are the same among patients with E. rhusiopathiae as other organisms, but the mortality rate is much higher (38% versus 20%) (1). Intrinsic resistance to vancomycin could be contributing to higher mortality seen with E. rhusiopathiae, as vancomycin is often the first choice for empiric coverage of gram-positive rod bacteremia. Treatment for endocarditis is typically intravenous penicillin for four to six weeks.
Our case demonstrates Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae bacteremia with aortic and tricuspid valve endocarditis without any evidence of skin lesions. We postulate that she had bacteremia after ingestion of contaminated fish followed by gastrointestinal colonization, which allowed the organism to gain access to the patient’s circulation. The purpose of this case report is to emphasize the subtle microbiological differences between different gram-positive rods and the importance of full workup of gram-positive rod bacteremia and not dismissing them as contaminants. Providers should think about Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae in the right setting i.e., patients with high-risk exposures and risk factors; potential of having bacteremia in the absence of skin findings, and associated endocarditis even in the absence of murmur. It is important to note that this organism causes significant valve destruction of native valves, thereby increasing the need for valve replacement. E. rhusiopathiae has intrinsic resistance to vancomycin, and infection with this organism has been associated with a higher mortality rate.

title: A healthy male in his thirties was in his usual state of health until 5 days pri
history:
A healthy male in his thirties was in his usual state of health until 5 days prior to presentation when he developed fever, chills and vomiting. Three days prior to presentation he went to urgent care, where he was given baloxavir for possible influenza. Two days prior to presentation he developed severe headache, pain in left occipital region, neck stiffness, paresthesia over the left side of his body, and unsteady gait. The day before his admission, he presented to a different ho­­­­­spital, underwent a CT Head which was unremarkable, received intravenous hydration and was discharged. The morning of admission he developed dysphagia, hoarseness of voice, and slurring of speech, leading to index hospitalization.

No past medical history or allergies.

He was born in eastern Europe and moved to the United States 10 years ago. He works in finance and lives in the northeast. He is in a monogamous heterosexual relationship. He frequently travels for business, and eats frequently outdoors. Occasional use of marijuana. He saw his dentist 2 months prior to presentation.
exam_studies:
On presentation the patient was febrile to 39.4C, moderately tachycardic at 105 beats/minute. He was ill appearing and diaphoretic. His cardiovascular, pulmonary, GI and skin exam was otherwise normal. His neurologic exam was notable for mild dysarthria although speech was fully intelligible. He exhibited direction changing nystagmus in all directions. He had decreased facial sensation in V2 and V3 distributions on the left. His soft palate did not show elevation on the left side. There was subtle pronation on the left when arms were extended. His sensation was decreased in the left upper and lower extremity to a greater degree distally than proximally. Romberg sign was positive with patient falling towards the right side. A wide-based unsteady gait was observed with patient unable to perform heel-to-toe walking.

His complete blood count was notable for mild neutrophilic predominance leukocytosis: White blood cell count 9,700 [normal range: 4,000 – 10,000/uL], neutrophils 76% [normal range: 34 - 71 %]. Rest of the complete blood count, basic metabolic profile and liver function studies was within normal limits. Urine microscopy revealed 13 red blood cells [normal range: 0 - 5 /hpf] and trace protein and was otherwise normal. Two sets of blood cultures were negative. Influenza A/B PCR as well as HIV antigen/antibody testing 4th generation were negative. A CT head without contrast showed no intracranial findings. Subsequent lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid with 460 nucleated cells (79% lymphs, 9% neutrophils), glucose of 72 mg/dL (serum glucose 124 mg/dL) and protein 68 mg/dL. Gram stain revealed many WBCs, but no organisms were seen and culture remained without growth. The meningitis/encephalitis panel by Filmarray BioFire ® was negative. A chest X-ray suggested a subtle ill-defined right upper lung opacity (Figure 1). 1. An MRI of the brain revealed an expansile T2/FLAIR signal abnormality centered in the left dorsal medulla, in the expected location of the vagus nerve nucleus, and extending along the visualized portions of the upper cervical spine, of indeterminate etiology. There was an area of abnormal tubular enhancement coursing through the center of the lesion. Imaging findings were considered indeterminate with differential diagnosis including demyelination syndrome, vasculitis (such as Behcet's disease), and less likely neoplasm (Figure 2A).

The patient was treated empirically for community meningitis with vancomycin, ceftriaxone and acyclovir and initially received steroids for suspicion of bacterial meningitis. Patient defervesced but had worsening leukocytosis to 13,500. He reported symptomatic worsening with more difficulty on the left side, diplopia and worsening of his voice.
Neurologic examination also worsened with substantial dysarthria, falling immediately to the left side on Romberg and abnormal finger-to-nose with slowness and mild tremor. An MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine performed on hospital day #2 re-demonstrated the expansile lesion centered in the left right dorsal medulla, with enhancing component descending inferiorly to the level of the tip of the dens and associated cord signal abnormality predominately involving the left posterior horn to the level of C2-3. Evidence of restricted diffusion within the enhancing component was noted that was not seen on the prior examination, and increased the likelihood of infectious process with abscess formation (Figure 2B).
On hospital day #4 the patient became lethargic and desaturated requiring intubation. For the first time after admission, he developed a fever to 38.6C. A repeat MRI brain and cervical spine is shown in Figure 3. There was interval worsening and patchy new areas of enhancement in the pons and medulla in addition to the previously known tubular peripheral ring enhancing lesion which was primarily involving the left side of the dorsal part of the medulla and upper cervical spinal cord.
diagnosis:
Listeria Rhomboencephalitis and Brainstem Abscess

Extensive work up in the cerebrovascular fluid (CSF) sample including evaluation for tuberculosis, fungal infections, and viral infections was negative. Cytology was negative for malignancy and flow cytometry had no evidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Paraneoplastic panel was negative. After second episode of fever, repeat CSF revealed 206 nucleated cells (63% neutrophils, 31% lymphocytes, glucose 77 and protein of 72). Repeat PCR evaluation of the CSF was positive for Listeria monocytogenes which also grew in the CSF cultures and blood cultures within the next 48 hours.

He was treated with ampicillin and gentamicin. He underwent a tracheostomy and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. Five days after diagnosis he experienced worsening ataxia. Repeat CSF revealed a lower number of WBCs (58 nucleated cells/cumm; 96% lymphocytes), normal glucose and decreasing protein (29 mg/dL). Repeat MRI showed increased enhancement within the brainstem and cerebellum consistent with evolving rhomboencephalitis with no appreciable interval change in the size of the tubular abscess. Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was added to the regimen. He was discharged to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 1 month after admission. His neurological exam on discharge was notable for fluent speech, limited extraocular movements, asymmetric face, dysmetria on the left. Repeat MRI brain/cervical spine prior to discharge showed interval involution of the previously noted peripherally enhancing thin tubular abscess involving the dorsal brainstem/upper cervical cord, decreasing amount of FLAIR hyperintense signal and edema involving the dorsal brainstem and left cerebellum. He was treated with 3 weeks of ampicillin, gentamicin and 8 weeks of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
Figure 5. MRI brain/C-spine. Decreasing amount of FLAIR hyperintense signal and edema involving the dorsal brainstem and left cerebellum.

The term rhomboencephalitis was first described in 1951 referring to the inflammatory disease affecting the hindbrain (brainstem and cerebellum). In 1957 the first case of brainstem encephalitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes was reported and since then many other cases of rhomboencephalitis with a variety of etiologies have been described (1), with Listeria monocytogenes remaining the most frequently identified microorganism detected. Although the disease typically affects elderly patients with immunocompromising conditions, invasive neurolisteriosis has been described in immunocompetent adults (1). In the largest prospective evaluation of invasive Listeria spp. infections in France, among 252 patients with neurolisteriosis, 87% had encephalitis-associated symptoms and 13% had meningeal involvement without encephalitis. Clinical involvement of the brainstem, although frequently considered indicative of neurolisteriosis, was observed in only 17% of 252 patients and brain abscesses were observed in only 2% of the patients (2). Less than half of patients with neurolisteriosis survive, the majority with significant neurologic sequalae, including motor deficits and cerebellar symptoms. Combination therapy with beta-lactams and aminoglycosides or bactrim may be associated with increased survival (2).

title: A male in his forties with past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthr
history:
A male in his forties with past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis-related interstitial lung disease on significant immunosuppressive medications including mycophenolate mofetil, infliximab, and daily prednisone presented to an outside hospital with syncope and gastrointestinal bleeding. He arrived at our institution approximately five days later secondary to worsening acute hypoxic respiratory failure and worsening abdominal pain. He underwent an emergent exploratory laparoscopy with small bowel resection secondary to a duodenal perforation. The infectious diseases team evaluated the patient due to incidentally discovered cavitary nodules in the setting of an elevated serum galactomannan. There was concern for pulmonary aspergillosis. Further history revealed that the patient had been experiencing subjective fevers, chills, weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, dyspnea, productive cough with white sputum, and a slowly enlarging painful tongue ulcer over the past 4-6 months.

His past medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis-related interstitial lung disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and history of pericarditis.

The patient lived with his wife in southern US and works in an office setting. He denied any travel or any outdoor hobbies. He owned dogs. He denied any exposure to or history of tuberculosis. He denied any tobacco, alcohol, or drug use currently or in the past.

Medications included mycophenolate mofetil 1500 milligrams by mouth every 12 hours, prednisone 20 milligrams by mouth once daily, and infliximab 100 milligrams intravenously every 6 weeks. His last dose of infliximab was 6 weeks prior to presentation. He was also taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160-800 milligrams and azithromycin 500 milligrams by mouth on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays as primary prophylaxis.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared critically ill and was in mild distress. The blood pressure was 168/89 mm Hg, pulse 91 beats per minute, temperature 100.3° Fahrenheit (37.9° Celsius), respirations 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on 40 liters of high flow nasal cannula. The examination was notable for a 2 cm ulcerated lesion on the right lateral tongue (Figure 1). He had coarse rhonchi bilaterally with accessory muscle use. The rest of the examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Physical exam finding of the right lateral tongue ulcer.

The hemoglobin was 8.5 grams/deciliter (reference range 13.5-17), hematocrit 27.0% (reference range 39-50), alanine aminotransferase was 70 units/L (reference range 7-52), aspartate aminotransferase 46 units/L (reference range 12-39), and serum Aspergillus galactomannan was 0.564 index (reference <0.499). The other routine laboratory test results were normal and routine blood cultures were negative. A high-resolution non contrast chest computed tomography revealed multifocal nodules and opacities in both lungs with some of the opacities demonstrating a surrounding ground glass halo and partial cavitation (Figure 2). diagnosis:
Disseminated histoplasmosis with gastrointestinal perforation

The urine histoplasma antigen was elevated at >19 nanograms/milliliter (reference range 0.4-19). Fungal isolator blood cultures initially revealed mold, which was ultimately identified as Histoplasma capsulatum 12 days after the cultures were obtained. He underwent a biopsy of his tongue ulcer which revealed numerous Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain positive yeast forms compatible with Histoplasma species (Figure 3). Furthermore, the pathology report from the proximal jejunum (taken at the time of the surgical exploration for small bowel perforation) revealed non-necrotizing granulomas with numerous microorganisms consistent with Histoplasma and negative acid-fast bacilli stains (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain and GMS stain of the proximal jejunum. A) Submucosal inflammation and granulomas B) Granuloma C) Higher magnification of the granuloma to show histoplasmosis microorganisms D) GMS special stain for fungi, low magnification E) GMS special stain for fungi, high magnification. A) Submucosal inflammation and granulomas B) Granuloma C) Higher magnification of the granuloma to show histoplasmosis microorganisms D) GMS special stain for fungi, low magnification E) GMS special stain for fungi, high magnification. The patient was started on intravenous amphotericin B lipid complex during his hospitalization with clinical improvement. He was transitioned to oral itraconazole at discharge with resolution of dyspnea and cough. He has continued to follow with the infectious diseases clinic in the outpatient setting and continues to do well overall 18 months post diagnosis.

Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by a dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum predominantly found in the soil and endemic to the midwestern and southeastern US, central Canada, and parts of Central and South America. Infection with H. capsulatum can manifest broadly, ranging from asymptomatic self-limited disease to a potentially fatal disseminated presentation. Disseminated histoplasmosis occurs in about 1 in 2000 patients with acute infection. Risk factors for disseminated disease include acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, solid organ transplantation, tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor use, and prolonged steroid use. Diagnosis of histoplasmosis include antigen detection as well as histopathology and cultures of the affected tissues. False positive Aspergillus galactomannan assays have been described in the literature in solid organ transplant patients with histoplasmosis and can cloud the diagnosis.
This case highlights a rare complication of disseminated histoplasmosis presenting as a small bowel perforation. One study showed that approximately 70% of patients with disseminated histoplasmosis were found to have gastrointestinal involvement although only less than 10% of those patients had gastrointestinal symptoms. A high index of suspicion is needed in order to diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis. Recognizing common and uncommon presentations of histoplasmosis, identifying patients at highest risk, and understanding diagnostic tests can aid in the correct diagnosis.

history:
A female in her thirties (G1P1) with recent urinary tract infection (UTI), cholecystitis status post laparascopic cholecystectomy four days prior to transfer, and emergent C-section at 32 weeks presents with acute liver failure.
On days 0 to 3, the patient, who was in her third trimester of pregnancy, was admitted to an outside hospital for complicated UTI, for which she was initially treated with piperacillin/tazobactam and discharged on amoxicillin/clavulanate. She represented on day 5 with abdominal pain diagnosed as cholecystitis and underwent an uncomplicated laparascopic cholecystectomy. Aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) were noted to be elevated at >300 units/L and 170 units/L, respectively. On day 7, she developed fever, tachypnea, and bandemia with signs of fetal distress on monitoring, so an emergent C-section was performed. Liver enzymes continued to increase. Intraoperatively, her liver was noted to be firm and inflamed. She remained intubated post-operatively and was transferred to a tertiary hospital for evaluation and treatment of acute liver failure.

Lives with husband, no travel, unknown history of alcohol/drug use

Due to progressive deterioration and worsening liver and neurologic function, she received a liver transplant on day 11. Following transplant, her neurologic status failed to improve. diagnosis:
Herpes Simplex Virus Hepatitis

Hepatitis panel was nonreactive. Computed tomography (CT) of chest, abdomen, and pelvis was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and anasarca. Liver ultrasound showed a recanalized umbilical vein. Liver explant revealed widespread hepatocellular necrosis with evidence of viral cytopathic effects. HSV-1 and HSV-2 immunostains were positive, consistent with HSV hepatitis. Figure 1. Patient sadly passed before treatment or follow up.

This patient’s rapidly progressive acute liver failure in the setting of pregnancy is most consistent with HSV hepatitis. The leading non-infectious diagnosis on the differential was HELLP syndrome, for which the patient met two out of three criteria (thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes); however, there was no laboratory evidence of hemolysis, including a normal haptoglobin. Furthermore, HELLP syndrome typically resolves after delivery of the child. With respect to other infectious possibilities, CMV, hepatitis A, and toxoplasmosis may all cause acute hepatitis, but the severity of this patient’s illness – in combination with the fulminant onset and rapid time course – is most consistent with HSV hepatitis. Furthermore, the patient had no known exposures concerning for hepatitis or toxoplasmosis.
HSV is a double-stranded DNA virus most typically associated with herpes labialis, keratitis, genital herpes, and encephalitis, among other entities. In rare cases, HSV can cause acute liver failure, though it is responsible for less than 1% of all acute liver failure (Schiødt 2003). Hepatitis can be triggered by primary infection or reactivation of latent virus (Kaufman 1997). Classically, HSV hepatitis presents in immunocompromised persons and during the third trimester of pregnancy (Peters 2000).
Prognosis is better in pregnant patients versus non-pregnant patients: this may be attributable to the fact that pregnant patients typically undergo early evaluation for fever and regular genital examinations (Peters 2000).
HSV hepatitis classically presents as an anicteric hepatitis with AST > ALT (mean peak aminotransferase 4927) (Norvell 2007). Fever, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy are each observed in more than 80% of patients. Lab abnormalities include mild hyperbilirubinemia (mean 6.0), cytopenias (leukopenia 71%, thrombocytopenia 94%), and evidence of acute kidney injury (65%) (Norvell 2007). The diagnosis of HSV hepatitis is often missed because of its rarity and non-specific symptoms (Peters 2000). Many cases lack typical cutaneous herpetic lesions (30-50%) (Norvell 2007; Peters 2000); the absence of herpetic skin findings should not rule out this diagnosis.
Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis, though it is often not feasible in the setting of coagulopathy or significant ascites. The liver explant from our patient revealed the typical cytopathic effects of HSV infection in the hepatocellular parenchyma that should trigger further tissue interrogation with immunostaining, thus yielding a definitive diagnosis. Notably, most cases of HSV hepatitis are diagnosed at autopsy due to difficulty obtaining tissue or lack of diagnostic certainty (Norvell 2007); HSV PCR on blood is typically used first-line to identify viremia. Notably, HSV-2 is more commonly detected than is HSV-1 (61% vs 39%, respectively) (Norvell 2007). HSV serologies may play an adjunctive role in the diagnosis (Peters 2000; Rimawi 2015). In the case of pregnant patients, there is a risk of vertical transmission, so neonates should be assessed for seroconversion or frank HSV infection (Calix 2020) (as was done in this case).
The first-line treatment of HSV hepatitis is high-dose acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 10 to 14 days), adjusted for renal function (Peters 2000). There is a low threshold for empiric trial of acyclovir, as HSV hepatitis is a rapidly progressive entity and delayed initiation of antiviral therapy is associated with increased mortality (Allen 2005). The survival rate without transplant with acyclovir is reported to be about 51%, though most cases are missed (Norvell 2007), leading to high mortality and rates of transplant (rate of death or transplant: 88% among untreated, 74% among treated and untreated) (Norvell 2007). If refractory to acyclovir, foscarnet can be tried (Natu 2017).
Our patient demonstrates both the rapidly progressive nature and elusive diagnosis that is HSV hepatitis in pregnant women. Given the importance of early antiviral therapy in these patients, we suggest a low diagnostic threshold for the initiation of empiric acyclovir in pregnant or recently-pregnant patients presenting with acute liver failure. Furthermore, we recommend early HSV PCR testing for evaluation in the appropriate clinical context.

title: A man in his thirties presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute lowe
history:
A man in his thirties presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute lower extremity weakness. He woke up that morning with urinary incontinence and could not stand up due to the weakness. He also reports pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with green sputum for two months as well as night sweats and weight loss of about 30 pounds in the past month.

None

Smoking history of 5 pack-years, no drug or alcohol use, no pets at home. Works at a food company. No recent travel and no other significant exposure. No close contacts with tuberculosis. No history of incarceration.

None
exam_studies:
T: 97.8°F, BP: 135/82, HR: 83, RR: 25, O2 saturation: 100% on room air. Well appearing patient in no acute distress. Chest: Lungs clear to auscultation. Mouth: poor dentition with periodontal disease. Neurologic: cranial nerves normal. Bilateral upper extremity strength intact. Strength 0/5 in left lower extremity (LE) in both flexors and extensors. 1/5 in right lower extremity. Absent pinprick and vibration sensation down from Left T5 dermatome. Absent knee and ankle reflex in bilateral LE. Brisk bilateral biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes. Rectal exam shows decreased perianal sensation, absent to minimal rectal tone. Rest of exam unremarkable.

Figure 1. Chest radiograph. Right upper lobe opacity, effacement of 3rd right rib.
Figure 2. Chest CT scan. Large lesion at the right lung apex with associated numerous spiculated nodules throughout the bilateral lungs.
Figure 3. Spine MRI. Paravertebral soft tissue component extending into spinal canal causing severe canal narrowing and cord compression.
Figure 4. H&E stain (A,C) and GMS stain (B), 10x.
Figure 5. H&E stain, 10x. Sulfur granule with filamentous organisms inside.

Patient underwent interventional radiology (IR)-guided lung mass biopsy, was started on empiric radiation therapy and dexamethasone. A few days later while awaiting biopsy results then he continued to have signs of worsening cord compression. For this he was taken to operating room for laminectomies of T2 and T3, posterior instrumented fusion of C5-T7 and resection of the epidural tumor.
Intraoperatively, there was a finding of purulent fluid around T3 with caseous necrosis. IR lung biopsy and surgically obtained soft tissue and bone were sent for pathologic examination and culture.
diagnosis:
Pulmonary and vertebral actinomycosis

Biopsy of lung and vertebral tissue revealed gram-positive filamentous organisms morphologically suggestive of Actinomyces as well as structures compatible with sulfur granules. AFB and fungal stain negative.
Cultures from vertebral tissue grew Actinomyces meyeri, Eikenella corrodens and Fusobacterium nucleatum.

The patient received 2 weeks of intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam before being switched to amoxicillin-clavulanate to complete 12 months of therapy, along with receiving physical therapy. He is now able to stand and walk short distances with a walking aid device.

Actinomycosis is caused by species of anaerobic bacteria, most commonly Actinomyces israelii, that that normally colonizes the mouth, colon, and vagina. Actinomyces cause an indolent infection at sites where there is disruption of mucosa. These lesions generally have a purulent nucleus surrounded by dense fibrosis.
Actinomycosis is a diagnostic challenge even in the age of technological advances because of its varied clinical presentation, and it is often confused with malignancy. Actinomyces should be considered on the differential diagnosis whenever there is chronic, progressive disease that crosses tissue boundaries and has mass-like features, when there is a development of a sinus tract, or when there is a relapsing or refractory infection after a short course of therapy. The mass-like lesions can cause severe destruction of tissue and cross several tissue planes as in the case of this patient: presumably he developed an infection in the lung (perhaps from an oral source) which then slowly invaded the spine. Based on information from case reports, 70-80% of Actinomycosis have coinfection with other bacteria, very commonly Fusobacterium and Eikenella spp. Bacterial synergy and symbiosis are thought to facilitate the growth of Actinomyces.

history:
A male in his thirties with HIV/AIDS who did not have stable housing presented with generalized body aches and enlarged lymph nodes in his neck, axilla, and groin. The lymph nodes became rapidly enlarged and very painful over the past 10 days. He also had progressively worsening chest pain and shortness of breath that started one day prior to admission. He noted a new diffuse, red-spotted rash on his arms and legs that emerged in the past week as well as occasional fever and chills for the past few weeks.

HIV/AIDS, Neurosyphilis

Lives on the west coast of the US; no recent travel; unstable housing.

Daily smoker, daily alcohol use (3-4 drinks), uses methamphetamines but no injection drug use. Not sexually active currently. Previously sexually active with female partners.

Non-adherent with medications

The patient was cachectic and in mild distress from diffuse body pain. Blood pressure was 90/56 mm Hg, heart rate was 125 beats per minute, temperature was 98.4°F (36.9°C) and respiratory rate was 21 breaths per minute. There were tender enlarged cervical lymph nodes with two large protuberant lymph nodes at the left mandibular angle with skin ulceration. Tender, large oozing axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were palpated. There was also a 2 cm red, ulcerated lesion on the dorsum of his right hand. Heart sounds were distant, tachycardic.

diagnosis:
Disseminated Cryptococcal Infection in a patient with AIDS involving lymph nodes, pericardium, cavitary lung lesion, skin and fungemia

CT chest abdomen pelvis showed moderate pericardial effusion, extensive lymphadenopathy of the mediastinum and retroperitoneum, and left upper lobe cavitary lung lesion.
CT neck showed exuberant adenopathy throughout bilateral cervical regions and into the supraclavicular region, largest cervical node measured 4.3 x 2.2 cm.
Fungal blood culture: Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcal Antigen Titer: 1:131,072
Left axillary biopsy showed adipose tissue with abundant fungal organisms consistent with Cryptococcus. Grocott’s methenamine silver stain (GMS) and mucin stains were confirmatory.
Right hand lesion biopsy showed ulcer and granulation tissue with dermal yeast forms identified. GMS stain highlighted numerous dermal yeast forms with morphology with high suspicion for Cryptococcus.
Lung lesion biopsy showed increase in alveolar foamy macrophages with numerous yeast forms consistent with Cryptococcus (confirmed by GMS stain).
Pericardial window and biopsy of the pericardium was performed for the large pericardial effusion. Fungal culture of the pericardial fluid was positive for Cryptococcus neoformans. Pathology showed fungal forms present and GMS stain highlighted spherical fungal forms involving pericardial tissue (Figure 4).
Figure 4. GMS special stain, 600x, demonstrates scattered yeast forms in the pericardium.

He was started on Amphotericin and Flucytosine for disseminated Cryptococcal infection as well as Atovaquone for pneumocystis prophylaxis. After 14 days, he was transitioned to oral Fluconazole for consolidation therapy as he wanted to leave the hospital against medical advice. There was mild improvement of the size of the lymph nodes on subsequent imaging. Chest pain and shortness of breath had resolved completely. He followed up in the HIV clinic about 3 weeks after discharge and was doing well on Fluconazole. He was started on antiretroviral therapy at that time but was unfortunately lost to follow up.

Cryptococcosis is a fungal infection common in people with advanced AIDS and which has a high rate of mortality if left untreated (1). Spores are inhaled from the environment and can spread from the lungs to the central nervous system or other areas such as lung and lymph nodes in immunocompromised patients (2). Disseminated cryptococcosis is frequently reported in immunocompromised patients but the extensive nature of this patient’s disease involving pericardium, lungs, skin, and lymph nodes and cryptococcemia is notable. There are only a few cases of pericarditis and pericardial effusion due to Cryptococcus neoformans reported and usually involve organ transplant patients on immunosuppressive medications (3). The differential diagnosis for AIDS patients with exuberant lymphadenopathy can be extensive and should include disseminated cryptococcal infection. Treatment involves initiation of antifungal therapy followed by antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function (1).

title: A male in his fifties with history of insulin-dependent diabetes and deceased do
history:
A male in his fifties with history of insulin-dependent diabetes and deceased donor kidney transplant, presented with acute on chronic ascending paralysis. He received his transplant 7 months prior to admission with alemtuzumab induction. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) status was high risk with the patient being CMV negative and the donor being CMV positive. His maintenance immune suppression was primarily tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone 5 mg and consistently had CMV viremia (mid-2s log IU/mL) with wild-type genotype on recent testing.
Three months prior to admission he had Klebsiella graft pyelonephritis complicated by native mitral valve endocarditis, and he was treated with 6 weeks of oral ciprofloxacin. After this admission he developed lumbar back pain and mild weakness in his feet and lower legs.
Six weeks prior to admission he was admitted for malaise, was found on imaging to have a right lower lobe focal opacity, and was treated for 7 days initially with piperacillin/tazobactam and then amoxicillin/clavulanate.
Four weeks prior to admission he was admitted for bilateral lower extremity weakness. MRI of the lumbar and thoracic spine with and without gadolinium was negative though severely limited by motion. With lack of improvement of brain abscesses after 2 weeks of treatment linezolid was added for a 6 week course of a triple drug regimen. His course has since been complicated by now resistant CMV viremia and he has regained some of the motor function he lost.

In solid organ transplant recipients, the differential diagnosis for pulmonary-brain syndromes encompasses a wide variety of pathogens. Pulmonary-brain syndromes begin with the colonization or infection of the respiratory track with subsequent dissemination to the central nervous system. Besides Nocardia, other potential pathogens are tuberculosis, Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Mucormycosis spp., dimorphic fungi, Cryptococcus, and Toxoplasma (1, 2). This patient prior to admission also had CMV viremia. CMV of the central nervous system can rarely present with a syndrome of transverse myelitis with CSF demonstrating pleocytosis with neutrophilic predominance, high-protein and hypoglycorrhachia on lumbar puncture—though the cell count is not typically as high as seen in this case(3). Most cases of CMV myelitis have been documented in the HIV/AIDS literature as opposed to the transplant literature. Finally, thought this patient had positive HTLV-1 IgG prior to transplant and he had slowly progressive weakness and back pain, he otherwise does not meet the clinical presentation of tropical spastic paraparesis of hyperreflexia and clonus(4).
He had received alemtuzumab, which is a recombinant humanized monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 that targets CD52 surface antigen, present on 95% of B and T cells as well as macrophages, mature and immature dendritic cells(5). Alemtuzumab causes prolonged and profound immune suppression, including mature B cell, CD4+ T cell and Th17 cell depletion(6, 7). Alemtuzumab has been associated with an increased risk of CMV viremia and disseminated fungal infection compared with basiliximab or anti-thymocyte globulin(8). It has also been associated with autoimmunity, most often Grave’s disease—though this is most often seen in the multiple sclerosis literature(9). Alemtuzumab is used often in younger patients with a lower predicted risk for rejection.
Nocardia in solid organ transplant recipients most often affects the lungs. On imaging Nocardia presents as nodules in about 70% of patients though it can also present as a cavitation (30%), consolidation (40%), pleural effusion (25%) or interstitial involvement (12%)(10). Disseminated infection is the next most common manifestation. Nocardia also has a propensity for the central nervous system and skin(10). The species of Nocardia can assist with empiric antibiotic choice as antibiotic sensitivities can take weeks to return. Nocardia farcinica may be resistant to third-generation cephalosporins and minocycline, variably resistant to imipenem and 0.5-6% of isolates resistant to the mainstay of Nocardia therapy, which is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole(11). A two or three-drug regimen is recommended initially for central nervous system disease and continued for at least 12 months with clinical and radiographic monitoring for at least 1 year after completion of therapy to detect late relapses(11).

history:
A male in his fifties developed red, small, papules on his right forearm that disappeared on their own over the course of a month. Two months after these initial lesions resolved, multiple papules and pustules appeared over his face in both malar regions. He was given levofloxacin with mild improvement.

The patient had a history of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) for which he underwent a living unrelated kidney transplant about 10 years prior to admission to the hospital. This allograft had failed due to due to rejection so he had a second living related kidney transplant one month prior to admission to the hospital. He received induction with anti-thymocyte globulin, basiliximab and intravenous steroids. His surgery had no complications, and he was discharged on tacrolimus 3 mg PO every 12 hours, mycophenolate 720 mg PO every 12 hours and Prednisone 20 mg PO daily. Infection prophylaxis included Dapsone 50 mg PO daily and Valganciclovir 900 mg PO daily.
One month after transplantation he noticed the lesions in his face were more numerous, so he visited a dermatologist where he underwent biopsy of the skin lesions. Biopsy results reported a dense lymphohistiocytic infiltrate located in the dermis. He was admitted to the hospital for further workup.

Patient was born in the United States of America. He has lived in the southeast US for most of his life. Had served in the military with deployments to the Middle East. Lived alone, no pets, no exposure to farm animals, no hunting, no camping, no tick bites.
exam_studies:
The patient was afebrile, hemodynamically stable and with a SpO2 of 98% when breathing room air. Physical exam was notable for multiple pink erythematous papules scattered over his bilateral malar area and surrounding his nares, with desquamation and scattered yellow crusting associated with some of the lesions.

Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis of 13 K/uL with lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count of 600/uL), hemoglobin was 9.3 gr/dL and platelets 355 K/uL. Kidney and liver function were normal.
A computed chest tomography was also done which revealed a macronodule in his right middle lobe (Figure 1).
Biopsies of the skin lesions were repeated and sent for bacterial, fungal and acid-fast bacilli cultures with gram stains, KOH prep and acid fast smears being negative
A bronchoscopy with alveolar lavage (BAL) was recommended
Figure 1. Computed tomography of the chest without contrast demonstrates a right sided middle lobe solid pulmonary nodule.

Therapy was held for a week after hospital admission as the differential diagnosis was considered broad. At this time repeat examination of his skin showed striking worsening on the previous lesions in his face and new nodular, violaceous lesions on both his upper and lower extremities (Figure 2). Due to concern for systemic infection decision was made to start therapy with Rifabutin 300 mg PO daily, Isoniazid 300 mg PO daily, Linezolid 600 mg PO daily, Ethambutol 15 mg kg PO daily, Cefoxitin 3 gr IV q 6 h and Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily in order to target most mycobacterial species. diagnosis:
Disseminated Mycobacterium haemophilum Infection involving the lung and skin in a kidney transplant patient

Skin biopsy showed acid fast bacilli. On hospital day 14, mycobacterial culture of the skin biopsy detected a Mycobacterium. Broad base PCR from University of Washington from skin biopsy was positive for Mycobacterium haemophilum.
Acid fast bacilli smear from BAL was positive for rare organisms, with Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR from the same sample resulting negative. Culture would later result positive for Mycobacterium haemophilum

Repeat physical exam revealed that the papulopustular lesions were resolving but crusting and erythema was now more evident (Figure 2). A diagnosis of disseminated Mycobacterium haemophilum involving the lung and skin was made and antimicrobial regimen was changed to Levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily and Rifabutin plus Azithromycin as dosed previously.

Nontuberculous mycobacteria are ubiquitous environmental organisms often found in soil and water which can cause localized or disseminated disease.
Nontuberculous mycobacterial infections seem to be increasing in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed hosts. As an example, incidence of infection in the general population was reported at 0.7 per 100,000 when estimated between 1980-1990 while a more recent review of cases found an incidence rate of 2 per 100,000 between 2000-2009. However, precise estimation of clinical morbidity and mortality is hard to define as infection with these organisms is not reportable and it can be difficult to distinguish colonization from infection.
Reviews of case reports and case series in solid organ transplant recipients in the United States and Europe have helped characterize some aspects of this infection in this particular population.
Incidence reported in case series seems to indicate the highest burden is in thoracic organ recipients specifically lung (4.4%) followed by heart (2.8%). In abdominal organ recipients, reported incidence rates are higher in kidney recipients (0.16-0.55%) as opposed to liver recipients (0.04%).
Clinically infection tends to be localized in the graft or pleural space for lung transplant recipients. Other organ recipients have skin and soft tissue or osteomuscular infection as their predominant presentation. Median time to onset of infection varies but has been estimated to be around 13 months from transplantation for lung recipients and between 27-33 months for non-lung transplant recipients.
Skin infection is characterized by subacute to chronic clinical presentation of a diverse number of lesions including papules, pustules, nodules, and ulcers. Some organisms, such as Mycobacterium marinum and Mycobacterium haemophilum, might present in an acral distribution and/or lymphangitic pattern as their optimal growth occurs in cooler areas of the body.
Gold standard for diagnosis continues to be pathological samples of lesions with positive acid fast smears coupled with culture. Some organisms have special requirements for growth such as cooler temperatures (28-30 C for M marinum, M haemophilum) or special media requirements (iron for M haemophilum and mycobactin for M genavense); for this reason, communication with microbiology is essential if there is suspicion of a particular mycobacteria.
This case reminds the reader to always include mycobacteria in the differential diagnosis of any new skin lesion of solid organ transplant recipients, particularly if clinical presentation is subacute or chronic. Furthermore, given the multitude of organisms that comprise this group of pathogens and specific requirements for growth, close communication with microbiology laboratory is encouraged.

Culture from the excisional biopsy grew Francisella tularensis. Her serum Francisella tularensis IgG/IgM from the regional hospital also returned positive at 1:320. She was discharged on a 10-day course of streptomycin injections for ulceroglandular tularemia.
The patient’s fevers resolved, but she suffered a fall after discharge and returned to the hospital. MRI brain (Figure 2: B, C) showed multiple small, peripherally enhancing lesions throughout both cerebral hemispheres, the largest being 6 mm in size. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms were negative for vegetations and repeat blood cultures were negative. She had previously undergone a lumbar puncture (LP) with normal CSF studies at the local hospital, so this was not repeated.
Figure 2. B shows axial T1 weighted post-contrast MRI image depicting multiple enhancing cerebral lesions consistent with disseminated tularemia. Figure 2C shows a sagittal view T1 weighted post-contrast MRI depicting multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Figure 2D is from the final MRI showing residual lesions after completed therapy.

She completed the 10-day streptomycin course at the regional hospital and was discharged home with plans for a follow-up MRI brain at a later date.
The patient presented to our hospital three weeks later due to persistent weakness, fatigue, gait instability, dizziness and headaches. Repeat MRI brain showed slightly decreased size of all cerebral lesions, the largest now 5 mm in diameter, and improved vasogenic edema. CSF studies showed 1 WBC per microliter, 1 RBC per microliter, total protein 30 mg per deciliter and glucose 47 mg per deciliter with a negative gram stain and cultures. Intravenous gentamicin was initiated. Doxycycline was not recommended due to prior allergy. The patient tolerated an oral ciprofloxacin dose-escalation challenge after a previous intolerance was reported. She was discharged on dual gentamicin and ciprofloxacin therapy.
At her 3-week follow-up appointment, she had developed arthralgias concerning for fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis and mild left-sided hearing loss concerning for aminoglycoside-associated ototoxicity. MRI brain revealed further decreased size of all lesions by 1-2mm. Ciprofloxacin was discontinued, and the patient elected to continue gentamicin. Otolaryngology evaluation confirmed mild, left ear high-frequency hearing loss. Her dizziness, gait and strength improved with physical and vestibular therapy. Her 6-week follow-up MRI brain demonstrated improvement in the size and radiographic density of all lesions, the largest now 2 mm, and gentamicin was discontinued (Figure 2D).

Francisella tularensis, a gram-negative coccobacillus, is the causative agent of tularemia. Infected animals, arthropod vectors, soil and water serve as reservoirs. Transmission can occur by direct contact, ingestion and inhalation. It is considered a grade A bioterrorism agent due to its low infectious dose, ease of distribution and ability to cause fatal disease [1].
In the United States (U.S.), tularemia is most common in south central U.S., the Pacific Northwest and Massachusetts. There are two biovars of F. tularensis. Biovar A (F. tularensis subspecies tularensis) causes the majority of U.S. cases and accounts for more severe presentations. Biovar B (F. tularensis subspecies palearctica) causes milder cases in Europe and Asia [2].
Tularemia incubation is usually 3-5 days but can extend up to 14 days. Symptoms often include fever, malaise, chills and headache. Ulceroglandular, glandular, oropharyngeal and oculoglandular presentations typically occur via direct inoculation and present with fever and regional lymphadenopathy. Pneumonic tularemia typically occurs after inhalation of aerosols and presents with fever and pulmonary infiltrates. Typhoidal tularemia is rare and presents with fever and a variety of symptoms. Less common but more complicated forms of tularemia include pleuropneumonia, meningitis and endocarditis [1].
Francisella tularensis infection presenting with cerebral abscesses is extremely rare, with only two cases reported in the medical literature. In 2006, Gangat reported a case of cerebral microabscesses complicating tularemia meningitis in a 51-year-old female from Kansas. She presented with a one-month history of fever, headache and abdominal pain after eating wild rabbit that progressed to respiratory distress and encephalopathy. MRI brain demonstrated multiple 6-8 mm cerebral microabscesses. CSF studies revealed 2926 WBC per microliter, protein 1890 mg per deciliter, glucose 33 mg per deciliter, and culture grew F. tularensis. She was treated with 10 days of streptomycin followed by one year of doxycycline, but overall outcome was unknown [3].
Van de Beek et al (2007) described tularemia-associated brain abscesses in 2007. A 51-year-old female presented with fever, headache, blurred vision and altered consciousness after eating wild rabbits. CSF examination revealed 450 WBC/uL and a positive CSF culture for F. tularensis. MRI brain demonstrated three lesions with restricted diffusion. She was treated with streptomycin and doxycycline and her outcome at one year was poor [4].
Tularemia can be diagnosed by many different methods. Culture of blood, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage or lymph node tissue has poor sensitivity [2]. PCR antigen detection, direct immunofluorescence antibody testing, immunohistochemical staining and RNA hybridization with 16S ribosomal probe have all been described. Acute and convalescent serologies with a 4-fold rise in antibody titer are the most common means of diagnosis with sensitivity approaching 85% [2]. Diagnosing tularemia can be difficult, in part due to the broad differential diagnoses of lymphadenopathy such as HIV, Epstein-Barr Virus, cytomegalovirus, mycobacterium, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, histoplasmosis, coccidiomycosis, cryptococcosis, sarcoidosis, Castleman disease and malignancy. A high index of suspicion for tularemia remains the most essential component of diagnosis.
Treatment of tularemia consists of doxycycline or ciprofloxacin for mild and moderate disease and streptomycin or gentamicin for severe disease. Duration of treatment is typically 7-10 days. Meningitis treatment is extended to 14-21 days and includes a combination of an aminoglycoside plus ciprofloxacin, doxycycline or chloramphenicol [1].
Most bacterial brain abscesses require 6-8 weeks of antimicrobial therapy [5]. In our case, gentamicin was chosen over streptomycin due to the availability of drug level testing. Doxycycline was avoided due to the patient’s previous Stevens-Johnson-like reaction. Ciprofloxacin was started to provide more optimal combination therapy.
Unfortunately, aminoglycosides and fluroquinolones produce their own therapeutic challenges. Aminoglycosides often have dose-dependent toxic effects [6]. Adverse effects of fluoroquinolone use include, but are not limited to, Clostridioides difficile -associated diarrhea, liver injury, seizures, prolonged QT interval, tendinitis, tendon rupture, phototoxicity, aortic aneurysm rupture and renal failure [7]. Our patient developed tendinitis necessitating cessation of ciprofloxacin, left-sided ototoxicity, mild nephrotoxicity and vestibular toxicity. Fortunately, her lesions substantially improved, and a 6-week gentamicin course was tolerated.
The rarity of disseminated tularemia causing brain abscesses limits the availability of evidence-based recommendations to guide treatment. Combination aminoglycoside therapy with doxycycline, ciprofloxacin or chloramphenicol may offer the greatest likelihood of successful treatment for complicated tularemia cases. This case demonstrated initial treatment with streptomycin alone, followed by combination gentamicin and ciprofloxacin and then gentamicin monotherapy, highlighting how tailoring a treatment regimen to each patient is essential to a successful outcome.

title: A male in his twenties was brought in by his family for two days of worsening me
history:
A male in his twenties was brought in by his family for two days of worsening mental status. He was seen several times at outside Emergency Departments for several weeks of progressive abdominal pain, nausea with emesis, frontal headache, myalgias, fever and facial rash. Prior evaluation included a lumbar puncture that was negative for pleocytosis, hypoglycorrhachia or elevated protein. Ten days prior to hospitalization, a HIV Antigen/Antibody test returned positive, and he was instructed to follow up with Infectious Diseases as an outpatient.

None

Patient was born in the East Coast US but lived in Mexico during his childhood. He was living in the United States for the past two years and had no recent travel. He is sexually active with men only and occasionally uses condoms. He does not use tobacco or injection drugs. He works at a poultry farm.

None

None
exam_studies:
He was hypothermic at 31.9 degrees Celsius. His blood pressure was 92/75 mm Hg. Heart rate was 98 beats per minute. He was tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 33 breaths per minute but was not hypoxic. Overall, he was toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, and in mild distress. The exam was notable for a diffusely tender abdomen and scattered hyperpigmented macules on his torso and lower extremities. His left shoulder had two violaceous red papules with central crusting and umbilication (see figure 1). There was a scabbed lesion on the right nasal tip and crusting along the left nasal ala (see figure 2). He was oriented to person and place but not to time. The rest of the exam was normal.
Figure 1. Fig 1A. Physical exam finding of left shoulder violaceous red papule. Fig 1B. Physical exam finding of left shoulder violaceous red papules with central crusting.
Fig 1A. Physical exam finding of left shoulder violaceous red papule. Fig 1B. Physical exam finding of left shoulder violaceous red papules with central crusting.
Figure 2. Fig 2. Physical exam finding of right nasal tip scab with left nasal ala crusting.
Fig 2. Physical exam finding of right nasal tip scab with left nasal ala crusting.

The lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 7 mm Hg, 1 WBC, 7 RBCs, protein 34mg/dL (reference range 14-47mg/dL), glucose 45mg/dL (reference range 48-79mg/dL). Platelets were 86 x 10 9 /L (reference range 150-440 x10 9 /L). Sodium was 123mmol/L (reference range 135-145mmol/L), creatinine 1.86mg/dL (reference range 0.60-1.10mg/dL). Total bilirubin was 6.2mg/dL (reference range 0.3-1.2mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 256 U/L (reference range <=34U/L), alanine transaminase 93 U/L (reference range 10-49U/L), and alkaline phosphatase 223 U/L (reference range 46-116). Lactate dehydrogenase was 1,887 U/L (reference range 120-246 U/L). The remainder of other routine laboratory tests were normal. Cryptococcal antigen testing was negative. CD4 count was <10 cells/µL (reference range 510-2,320 cells/µL), with HIV RNA 776,495 copies/mL. Nasopharyngeal swab for Influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. A contrasted computed tomography (CT) of the head had no acute abnormality. Contrasted CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed mild splenomegaly, enlarged mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph nodes and normal appearing gastrointestinal tract. Contrasted CT of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass and nodular opacities (see figure 3).
Figure 3. Fig 3. Contrasted computed tomography of the chest. Axial view demonstrating diffuse bilateral ground glass and nodular opacities.
Fig 3. Contrasted computed tomography of the chest. Axial view demonstrating diffuse bilateral ground glass and nodular opacities.

While in the Emergency Department, he developed worsening metabolic acidosis and was subsequently intubated for increased work of breathing and airway protection. He required vasopressor support for hypotension and was placed on continuous renal replacement therapy. Serial labs demonstrated increased transaminases, electrolyte derangements, worsened thrombocytopenia, and anemia. He underwent EGD for acute upper GI bleed and left gastric artery embolization for severe gastritis.
diagnosis:
Disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma capsulatum

Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen returned positive at 4.26 (reference <0.5), however bronchial Aspergillus galactomannan was normal. Histoplasma antigen was elevated in the urine at > 25 ng/ml. Histoplasma capsulatum eventually grew from bone marrow, bronchial lavage, skin punch and gastric biopsies (see figure 4). Cryptococcus neoformans grew from bone marrow and blood culture (see figures 5 and 6). Cryptococcal antigen tests on CSF and serum were repeated and were negative. Patient was also found to have a positive Herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR skin swab, biopsy proven Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, as well as Shigella diarrheal illness.
Figure 4. Fig 4. Tape prep with lactophenol cotton blue stain at 40x magnification on bronchial lavage fungal culture showing hyphae with tuberculate, thick-walled macroconidia consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum.
Fig 4. Tape prep with lactophenol cotton blue stain at 40x magnification on bronchial lavage fungal culture showing hyphae with tuberculate, thick-walled macroconidia consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum.
Figure 5. Fig 5. Gram stain at 100x magnification from bone marrow biopsy growth in bottle demonstrating yeast.
Fig 5. Gram stain at 100x magnification from bone marrow biopsy growth in bottle demonstrating yeast.
Figure 6. Fig 6. GMS stain at 40x magnification on bone marrow biopsy demonstrating small budding yeast, unable to distinguish between Cryptococcus and Histoplasma.
Fig 6. GMS stain at 40x magnification on bone marrow biopsy demonstrating small budding yeast, unable to distinguish between Cryptococcus and Histoplasma.

The patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B for empiric antifungal coverage. Flucytosine was added once Cryptococcus was identified in bone marrow and blood, as there was also concern for central nervous system involvement. Treatment was complicated by ongoing nausea, emesis and poor oral intake from his severe gastritis. He was transitioned from 5-flucytosine (administered via nasogastric tube) to IV fluconazole once he was no longer able to take oral medications. After the induction phase, he was started on itraconazole maintenance therapy but there was difficulty obtaining therapeutic levels with multiple drug adjustments. He completed twelve days of acyclovir for cutaneous HSV infection, and several weeks of ganciclovir for CMV colitis. Eventually he was switched to posaconazole with adequate levels upon discharge. At outpatient follow up, the patient was doing well. He was switched back to itraconazole and was started on antiretroviral therapy.

This case demonstrates the pervasiveness of opportunistic infections that co-exist within immunocompromised patients. While Cryptococcus and Histoplasma are both found within the environment, they rarely co-infect individuals. In this case, induction with amphotericin and 5-flucytosine was given for nearly four weeks, given concern for CNS involvement of Cryptococcus despite negative CSF cultures. Itraconazole was selected over fluconazole for its improved efficacy in Histoplasmosis (1). This case was also particularly puzzling as the patient had several negative serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) tests. Cryptococcal antigen test targets glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), which is the main polysaccharide component of the cryptococcal capsule (2). Often, the CrAg acts as a surrogate biomarker for Cryptococcus, as it has >95% sensitivity and specificity in CSF, serum and blood (2-3). However, false negative CrAg tests can be encountered in several situations: low fungal load, hypocapsular or acapsular strains of Cryptococcus, postzone reaction secondary to high antigen titers, or immune complex deposition preventing release of glucuronoxylomannan (4). In our patient, Cryptococcus was found in both bone marrow and blood, so we suspected a high fungal load. Serial dilution of our sample was performed, and a negative CrAg was again obtained, thus ruling out the possibility of a postzone reaction. India ink staining was not available and thus could not be used to quickly identify the presence of a capsule. We therefore proceeded with mixing studies to evaluate for the presence of an inhibitor. A 0.5 McFarland broth was created of the patient’s Cryptococcus strain and a third-party Cryptococcus strain. Both were inoculated into third-party serum (negative for Cryptococcus) as well as our patient’s serum. These mixing studies were subjected to our standard Cryptococcal antigen lateral flow immunoassay. Results were compared to evaluate for the presence of an inhibitor. In this study, a two-fold or more change in antigen-titer would indicate a significant change in antigen load that would be concerning for an inhibitor. Our patient’s Cryptococcus strain mixed with a third-party serum yielded a positive antigen-titer, thus confirming the presence of a GXM polysaccharide capsule. While there were slight differences in antigen titers between third-party serum and our patient’s serum spiked by third-party or our patient’s Cryptococcus, nothing was greater than one titer difference in either direction, thus eliminating the possibility of a serum inhibitor. But why was our patient’s original CrAg test negative? Above mixing studies did not co-incubate Histoplasma with the patient’s Cryptococcus and thus did not account for this co-infection. We hypothesize that in vivo incubation with both Histoplasma and Cryptococcus may have created an immune complex deposition preventing release of glucuronoxylomannan thus giving a false negative lateral flow assay. Interaction between Histoplasmosis and the capsule of Cryptococcus has been previously documented. Capsular strains of Cryptococcus are composed of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) which functions in inhibition of phagocytosis and dysregulation of immune responses, as well as interference in antigen presentation. Prior mice studies have demonstrated that Histoplasma can acquire and incorporate GXM from Cryptococcus into the yeast cell surface. This functions to reduce intracellular killing and phagocytosis of the Histoplasma by macrophages, which in turn, increases virulence of this yeast (5). Thus, synchronous infection increases virulence and morbidity in mice models and may also explain the severity of disease in co-infected humans. As demonstrated in this case, in instances where disseminated Histoplasmosis is found, one may not be able to rely on serum or CSF CrAg testing to make the diagnosis of Cryptococcus.
