title: A teenaged female presented to our hospital with complaints of vision changes in
history:
A teenaged female presented to our hospital with complaints of vision changes in the left eye. She started having pressure like sensation in the left eye 3 days prior to presentation. She had pain with movement of the eye to the right. She initially had developed dark spots in the vision that progressed to blurring and decreased vision. She also had decrease in the color vision in the central fields. She denied having any change in the vision in the right eye. She was seen at an outpatient optometry office and was found to have macular edema. She was referred to the hospital where she was seen by the ophthalmologist and was confirmed to have optic neuritis.

Polycystic Ovarian Disease and Hypertension both diagnosed when she was a teenager

She was born in the East Coast of the United States and had lived in various East Coast states. She denied having any sick contacts. At the time of history, she worked part time and her job mostly involved desk work. She is unmarried and sexually active with 1 male partner. She has cats at home. She vapes occasionally and denies any illicit drug use.

None
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. Her vitals were stable with temperature 98.6 °F (37 °C), pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure of 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate of 19 breaths per minute. She had pain in the left eye on rightward gaze with relative afferent pupillary defect in left eye. There was a loss of visual fields in the left eye left superior and lower fields. Rest of the exam including neurological exam was negative.

The hematocrit was 39.2% (reference range 37.7 – 47.9%), white blood cell count was 10,770 cells/µL (reference range 4600-10,200/µL), C-Reactive Protein was 1.34 mg/dl (reference range 0.01-0.5 mg/dl), Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 48 mm/hour (reference range 0-20 mm/hour). Other laboratory test results including electrolytes, renal function, liver function, vitamin B12, folate level, Human Immunodeficiency Virus Antigen/ Antibody test, Treponemal Antibody, Bartonella Antibodies, Anti-nuclear antibody screen, Toxoplasma antibody were negative. MRI Brain and MRI Orbit were performed and revealed no acute findings.

Ophthalmology service was consulted, and dilated fundus exam was performed that showed massive 360° optic nerve head elevation with vessel obscuration, hemorrhages, and blurring of the disc margins with edema spanning into macula. There were no macular exudates or macular star. Findings were consistent with optic neuritis (Figure 1). Since the patient had macular edema associated with disc elevation suspicion was high for neuroretinitis caused by entities such as Cat Scratch. While awaiting results of Bartonella serologies, the patient was empirically started on Doxycycline orally 100 mg twice a day as per the recommendations from Infectious Disease service.
Figure 1. Fig 1. Dilated fundus exam of left eye showed optic disc edema with blurring of the disc margins (shown by arrow)
Fig 1. Dilated fundus exam of left eye showed optic disc edema with blurring of the disc margins (shown by arrow)
diagnosis:
Bartonella henselae Neuroretinitis

Three days later, ophthalmology service repeated dilated fundus exam and the patient was found to have macular edema with exudates adjacent to nerve nasally in half macula star configuration (Figure 2) reinforcing clinical suspicion for Bartonella neuroretinitis. However, Bartonella antibodies test returned negative at this point.
Figure 2. Fig 2. Dilated fundus exam of left eye showed macular edema with exudates adjacent to nerve nasally in half macula star configuration (shown by arrow)
Fig 2. Dilated fundus exam of left eye showed macular edema with exudates adjacent to nerve nasally in half macula star configuration (shown by arrow)

Patient requested to be discharged from the hospital. Infectious disease service recommended a course of oral Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day and oral Rifampin 300 mg twice daily for a total of 4 weeks. She was then seen after 3 weeks in the ophthalmology clinic in her hometown and a thorough work up was performed, and Bartonella serologies were repeated. The Macular Ganglion Cell Complex (GCC) available in OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography) showed mild thinning nasally and temporally in the left eye (Figure 3). OCT Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) showed swelling of the layer in the left eye which was 125 µm average thickness compared to the right eye which was 91 µm average thickness (Figure 4). She followed up for routine visit 3 weeks later. By this time, she had completed the antibiotics and was off the medications. Her repeat Bartonella henselae IgG returned as 1:2048 (reference range <1:128 titer) and Bartonella henselae IgM >1:20 (reference range <1:20 titer). Bartonella quintana antibodies were negative. Patient’s vision continued to improve off the medications. Her dilated fundus exam of the left eye revealed normal disc, few macular star exudates, normal vessels and normal periphery (Figure 5).
Figure 3. Fig 3. The Macular Ganglion Cell Complex (GCC) available in OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography) showed mild thinning nasally and temporally in the left eye
Fig 3. The Macular Ganglion Cell Complex (GCC) available in OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography) showed mild thinning nasally and temporally in the left eye
Figure 4. Fig 4. OCT Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) showed swelling of the layer in the left eye (125 µm average thickness) compared to the right eye (91 µm average thickness).
Fig 4. OCT Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) showed swelling of the layer in the left eye (125 µm average thickness) compared to the right eye (91 µm average thickness).
Figure 5. Fig 5. Dilated fundus exam of the left eye revealed normal disc, few macular star exudates, normal vessels, and normal periphery (shown by arrow)
Fig 5. Dilated fundus exam of the left eye revealed normal disc, few macular star exudates, normal vessels, and normal periphery (shown by arrow)

Ocular manifestations of Cat Scratch Disease (CSD) include Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, papillitis, optic neuritis, and focal retinochoroiditis [1]. Cats are usually asymptomatic carriers. Transmission to humans occurs through a cat’s scratch or bite, and less commonly, through mucous membrane contact [2]. Among all patients with CSD, about 1 to 2 percent develop neuroretinitis, which is a syndrome of acute visual loss from optic nerve edema associated with macular exudates. Bartonella PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) on the blood is usually negative. Direct identification of Bartonella henselae using microbiological cultures is difficult owing to the bacterium’s slow growth rate. There is no gold standard for conclusive CSD diagnosis and as such serological test and rising titers of IgG and elevated IgM is considered gold standard for diagnosis [3,4,5]. Patients with neuroretinitis typically present with fever, malaise, and unilateral blurred vision. On examination patients usually have unilateral involvement, with decreased visual acuity, often associated with an afferent pupillary defect as seen with our case. Retinal findings may include hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and multiple discrete lesions in the deep retina. Some patients develop a stellate macular exudate (known as a "macular star") [3]. Macular stars are due to vascular leakage from the optic-disc edema, not by a retinal process, so the optic-nerve edema precedes the macular star. At first glance, the macroscopic star could be missing. It typically resolves 1–12 weeks following the beginning of optic-disc edema. The key role of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) in retinal cells’ metabolism might influence the recovery potential of the retina, as already revealed by research regarding degenerative retinal conditions [6]. The macular star disappears after four weeks but could remain for almost a year and impede the recovery of visual acuity [7]. The extreme sensitivity of macular cells must be considered as an important factor in the recovery of the macula. In our patient, we noticed improvement of the macular star, but it persisted at the 6 weeks follow up in the clinic post discharge from the hospital. Fundus imaging, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and fluorescence angiography (FA) can aid in the diagnosis and treatment of CSD [8]. Late leakage from the optic disc is the most frequently observed finding on FA. Peripapillary angiomatosis and peripapillary serous retinal detachment are additional FA observations [9,10]. Although neuroretinitis is a well-described complication of B. henselae infection, angiomatous lesions remain uncommon. In previous studies, neovessels were discovered during an OCT angiography of a Bartonella focal chorioretinitis. It may assist in differentiating Bartonella lesions from other noninfectious or infectious fundus lesions because Bartonella spp. have a unique vascular proliferative characteristic [11]. In neuroretinitis, optic-disc edema causes serous retinal detachment, resulting in immediate unilateral vision loss, followed by macular exudates organized in a partial or full star pattern around the fovea [12,13]. OCT may show subretinal fluid in all eyes with Bartonella neuroretinitis, while ophthalmoscopy or fluorescein angiography may not. According to Parikh et al. [14], OCT may be helpful in detecting intraretinal edema associated with optic-disc inflammation preceding serous retinal detachment and subsequent macular-star formation. B. henselae -induced ocular inflammation is often benign and self-limiting, with good visual outcomes. Most patients with neuroretinitis appear to have a good long-term prognosis, although patients with macular exudates may have residual defects that include optic disk pallor, diminished contrast sensitivity, and altered color vision. Lee et al. state that antimicrobial treatment reduces the duration of the disease symptoms and that, therefore, patients should be treated with antibiotics until the laboratory testing is completed [15]. On the other hand, Bhatti asserts that therapy has no effect on the cure rate [16]. Given the rarity of Bartonella neuroretinitis, recruiting participants for a randomized clinical study would be very challenging and would require multicenter research [17]. Reed et al. [18] found that antibiotics resulted in a faster visual recovery and a shorter duration of illness. Chiu et al. [19] found no difference in visual results between treated and untreated patients (antibiotics, corticosteroids, or both). There is insufficient evidence to support the advantages of specific antibiotic treatment in immunocompetent individuals with uncommon CSD manifestations [20]. Numerous antibiotic treatments, particularly gentamicin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, doxycycline, and rifampin, were utilized in atypical CSD, alone or in various combinations. Due to their deep penetration of the central nervous system, the majority of researchers and doctors advise a protocol of doxycycline and rifampin for 10–14 days [21], with a treatment course of 2–4 weeks in immunocompetent individuals and four months in immunosuppressed patients

title: A male in his seventies presented with 5-day history of nonproductive cough, dys
history:
A male in his seventies presented with 5-day history of nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and fevers as high as 102.0 ºF. He also had fever, headaches, myalgias, and chills for two weeks which preceded his respiratory symptoms. Prior to onset of symptoms, patient had visited a local zoo. He was also noted to be cleaning his vehicle which he leaves outside often with the windows down.

Hypertension and dyslipidemia

Patient denied illicit substance use, tobacco use, or any alcohol use. He resides in Southern California in the mountain wilderness. He leaves his vehicle outside with the windows down which requires him to frequently clean his dashboard and upholstery. He has no domestic pets, but his home is surrounded by rodents, deer, sheep, raccoons, and other wildlife. He denied staying in any hotels, using a hot tub, or being around any fountains. He also denied any history of recreational hunting, animal skinning, insect bites, or being around farm animals. Patient had no other travel history outside the country or known sick contacts.

None
exam_studies:
The patient was noted to be in mild respiratory distress. The blood pressure was 141/80 mm Hg, pulse 94 beats per minute, temperature 97.7 ºF, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation was 93% on 6 L of high-flow oxygen by nasal canula. Respiratory exam demonstrated mild rhonchi at the lung bases. The examination was otherwise normal.

The white blood cell count was 19.3 K/uL (reference range 3.8-10.8 K/uL), hemoglobin was 18.4 g/dL (reference range 14-18 g/dL), hematocrit was 52.6% (reference range 42.0-54.0% in men), and platelet count 102.0 K/uL (reference range 150-450 K/uL). Procalcitonin 0.219 ng/mL (reference range < 0.499 ng/mL). Manual differential was significant for atypical lymphocytes 4.8 K/uL (reference range 1.2-3.7 K/uL) and metamyelocytes 0.4 K/uL (reference range 0-0 K/uL). Basic metabolic panel and liver function tests were normal. Albumin 2.6 g/dL (3.5-5.7 g/dL). Troponins were <0.017, <0.008, and <0.008 ng/ml (reference range <0.029 ng/ml). Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, HIV-1/2, Q fever, and Cocciodioides serologies were negative. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila urine antigen were negative. Respiratory panel was negative (Figure 1). COVID-19 test was negative. A chest imaging demonstrated hazy ground-glass opacities in the upper and lower lobes bilaterally (Figure 2). Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated hazy ground glass densities in the lower lobes bilaterally, greatest in the superior segments, and more ground glass opacities in the upper lobes posteriorly (Figure 3). He was noted to have small bilateral effusions. Transthoracic echocardiogram was unremarkable.
Figure 1. Figure 1: Respiratory panel obtained via nasopharyngeal swab
Figure 1: Respiratory panel obtained via nasopharyngeal swab
Figure 2. Figure 2: Chest X-ray demonstrating ground-glass opacities in the upper and lower lobes consistent with pneumonia.
Figure 2: Chest X-ray demonstrating ground-glass opacities in the upper and lower lobes consistent with pneumonia.
Figure 3. Figure 3: Chest CT: Hazy ground glass densities in the lower lobes bilaterally with bilateral pleural effusions.
Figure 3: Chest CT: Hazy ground glass densities in the lower lobes bilaterally with bilateral pleural effusions.

Patient was initially admitted with diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia. He was started on azithromycin and ceftriaxone. He was initially requiring minimal supplemental oxygen, however, his respiratory status worsened requiring high flow nasal canula at 20 L with fractional inspired oxygen of 80% saturation (FiO2%) during the initial course of the hospitalization. Infectious disease and Pulmonary services were consulted for further assistance.
diagnosis:
Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS)

CT-guided right sided thoracentesis demonstrated removal of only 100 ccs yellow colored transudative fluid. Body fluid cultures were negative. Hantavirus IgG and IgM serologies were positive.

On day 7 of hospitalization, Hantavirus immunoglobulin IgG and IgM studies returned positive. At this point, patient’s respiratory status had significantly improved without requirement of any supplemental oxygen. Antibiotics were discontinued prior to discharge. Once the diagnosis was made, county public health department was notified. Patient was educated about Hantavirus in-regards to steps to prevent infection. Patient followed up outpatient Infectious Disease clinic 4 weeks later and had no complaints.

Hantavirus is a negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus in the Bunyaviridae family. Infection occurs from aerosolized excretions from infected rodents. The virus is associated with two forms of major illness which include hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) often referred to as the hantaviruses of the New and Old Worlds, respectively [1]. We present a case of HCPS in a patient who presented with rapidly progressive hypoxic respiratory failure after having exposure to rodent droppings. Our patient met the CDC clinical case definition for cardiopulmonary syndrome which consists of being febrile >38.3° Celsius, having bilateral interstitial infiltrates, and requiring oxygen within 72 hours of hospitalization. A diagnostic dilemma commonly arises when a patient with pneumonia presents from the community as the etiology is often assumed to be bacterial or a common virus. Given the chest radiographic findings which included patchy ground glass infiltrates, atypical bacterial microorganisms such as Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila were in the differential [2]. Given the ongoing pandemic, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) was also a consideration. Our patient also resided in Western United States where Coccidioidomycosis should also be suspected in patients who present with respiratory symptoms and diffuse pneumonia findings on imaging. Given our patient’s exposure to wild animals, specifically rodents, one must also consider leptospirosis pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome and tularemia. This case reiterates the importance of taking a careful history which includes identifying animal exposure and understanding the patient’s living conditions. Rapid detection of hantavirus infections is not always possible; therefore, one must have a high index of suspicion as early diagnosis is critical to prevent respiratory deterioration.

title: A female in her twenties presented with sore throat and fever in the summer. COV
history:
A female in her twenties presented with sore throat and fever in the summer. COVID-19 and rapid strep tests were negative, herpes simplex virus (HSV) throat swab returned positive at urgent care. A few days later she developed abdominal pain and presented to hospital, where she was still febrile and labs revealed transaminitis (ALT 1208, AST 1929) and leukopenia (White blood cell count 1.1). Her urine toxicology screen was negative and acetaminophen level was undetectable.

No significant past medical history

Occupation: Works with young children in day care Substance use: No tobacco or recreational drug use; drinks alcohol socially Travel: Born and bred in Northeast United States, no recent travel; Central America a few years prior. Sexual: Had protected intercourse with a new male partner two weeks prior Living: Lives near a city in the Northeast US Vaccinations: Completed childhood vaccinations

Oral contraceptive pill
exam_studies:
The patient was ill-appearing and flushed, but not jaundiced. Temperature was 102.7 F, BP: 121/81, HR: 100, RR: 22, O2 saturation: 97% on room air. She was alert and oriented to time, place and self, but was taciturn. Abdominal exam revealed no tenderness or hepatosplenomegaly. There was no palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and there were no oral or external genital ulcers. The remainder of the exam was normal.

WBC 2.2 K/uL (4.0-10.0), Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL (11.2-15.7), Platelets 54 K/uL (150-400) Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.4-1.1), Sodium 136 mEq/L (135-147), Potassium 3.8 mEq/L (3.5-5.4) ALT 2595 IU/L (0-40), AST 5761 IU/L (0-40), Alkaline phosphatase 90 IU/L (35-105) Bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL (0-1.5), INR 1.3 (0.9-1.1) Ferritin 82401 ng/mL (13-150), Triglycerides 356 mg/dL (0-149), Fibrinogen 102 mg/dL (180-400)
Hepatitis B surface antibody, surface antigen and core antibody were negative. Hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis C antibody were negative. HIV 1/2 screen, Lyme antibody, RPR were negative. Blood cultures were negative. Outside hospital herpes simplex virus throat swab was positive (unclear if culture or PCR). Vaginal chlamydia and gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification tests were negative. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a hypoechoic liver parenchyma consistent with hepatitis, patent portal vein vasculature, mild gallbladder wall edema secondary to hepatitis. There was mild splenomegaly measuring up to 13.5 cm.

None
diagnosis:
HSV hepatitis with HLH-like syndrome secondary to primary HSV-1 infection; co-existent EBV reactivation

Serum HSV 1 level > 2 million copies/ml Serum HSV 2 level <100 copies/ml HSV 1 and 2 IgM positive HSV 1 and 2 IgG negative Serum Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) level 35 654 copies/ml EBV IgM negative, EBV IgG positive, EBNA positive VZV IgG positive Serum CMV DNA undetectable Anaplasma IgM/IgG negative Parasite smear negative NK cell count 12 cells/uL (70-760) Soluble interleukin-2 (IL2) receptor 11663 pg/mL (175.3-858.2) Bone marrow biopsy with histocytes demonstrating hemophagocytes

The patient was started on acyclovir 10 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours with improvement in transaminases. However, on hospital day 3 she developed altered mental status. MRI brain with contrast was negative for acute changes and lumbar puncture was done, with cerebrospinal fluid containing 2 total nucleated cells/uL, lymphocytes 95 %, protein 33 mg/dL, HSV1 PCR 28624 copies/ml. Thus, HSV encephalitis was thought to be the cause of her change in mental status. Given the fevers, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypofibrogenaemia, hemophagocytes on bone marrow biopsy, low NK cell activity, elevated ferritin and elevated IL2 receptor levels, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) was suspected. Due to her clinical deterioration, dexamethasone was started and a dose of etoposide, followed by rituximab, was given, as part of HLH treatment protocol. The patient improved rapidly thereafter, with return of normal mental status and rapid decline in liver enzymes, improvement in cell counts, and decline in ferritin, as well as a decrease in serum HSV levels. Ultimately, she received two weeks of IV acyclovir, alongside one dose of etoposide, four doses of rituximab (spaced one week apart), and a two-month-long dexamethasone taper. Full HLH protocol was deferred due to the rapid improvement and risks of etoposide therapy. It was thought that she had a syndrome on the HLH spectrum, but perhaps not true HLH, due to the rapid recovery after a single etoposide dose. The two-week parenteral acyclovir course was followed by four months of high dose valacyclovir (1 gram orally three times per day), then four months of valacyclovir 1 gram oral daily. On discharge (hospital day 11) the patient was ambulating well and was asymptomatic. By three months post discharge the patient had undetectable serum HSV levels, normal liver enzymes and normal ferritin. EBV levels also became undetectable. She was back to her usual activity.

Hepatitis is a rare manifestation of herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, accounting for <1 % of causes of liver failure and <2 % of viral causes of liver failure overall [1]. Risk factors for this disease include immunosuppression, in the form of HIV, bone marrow or solid organ transplantation, malignancy, steroid use, and pregnancy [1,2,3]. However, it can also occur in immunocompetent individuals, in which scenario it is usually caused by a primary HSV infection [1]. Frequently, patients with HSV hepatitis do not have mucocutaneous lesions, and so the diagnosis is often delayed or missed [1]. The rate of progression to acute liver failure, and death, is high - up to 90 % mortality according to some sources [3]. Timely initiation of high-dose acyclovir therapy dramatically reduces mortality [1]. Therefore, the clinician should have a high suspicion for HSV hepatitis in a patient presenting with fever and transaminase elevation, even without typical herpetic skin lesions, and should have a low threshold to start acyclovir. In a case series by Norvell et al, factors associated with mortality were advanced age, immunocompromise, ALT level >5000, platelets <75,000, encephalopathy, coagulopathy and failure to start antiviral therapy [1]. The optimal duration of high dose acyclovir therapy is unclear, but should be for at least 7 days, and guided by clinical response [2]. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is an even rarer complication of HSV infection and few case reports of this phenomenon exist in literature [4,5,6,7,8]. Again, it is associated with immunocompromise, or sometimes an underlying genetic mutation, particularly affecting interferon signalling and NK cell/ T cell function [4,9]. This entity also carries a high mortality. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is similarly known to trigger HLH, but in this case was thought not to be playing a key role, with the modestly elevated serum levels attributed to reactivation in the setting of acute illness [10]. In our patient, a basic outpatient immunologic work-up and testing for GATA2 deficiency, and other mutations associated with HLH, was negative. More detailed immunologic and genetic work-up is pending.

title: A woman in her sixties with 5 months of weight loss, poor appetite, and increase
history:
A woman in her sixties with 5 months of weight loss, poor appetite, and increased abdominal girth was referred to gynecology after being found to have a large right adnexal mass (7x6x6 cm), masses in liver and peritoneum, cardiophrenic and retroperitoneal nodes, ascites and elevated CA-125. Gynecology requested a consultation for granulomatous inflammation noted from the peritoneal biopsy. GMS and AFB stains were negative. There was no evidence of malignancy. She also reports 7 months of intermittent dry cough. She reported no fever.

1. Hypertension 2. Treated for latent tuberculosis infection with isoniazid about 30 years ago 3. Asthma

1. Originally from Pacific islands 2. Moved to the US in early 2000’s 3. Spent a few months in Southern and Western states within the past 10 years

Lisinopril
exam_studies:
Tmax: 37.5°C, BP: 146/96, HR: 68, RR: 109, O2 saturation: 97% on room air. Pleasant. In no distress. Not ill-appearing. Remainder of exam normal.

White blood cell count 9.6 (Eosinophil 3.3 (34%)). Hemoglobin 11.9. Platelets 395,000. Calcium 10.5. Parathyroid hormone 3 (nl 12-88). 1, 25-OH-Vitamin D 136 (nl 12-72). Rest of the chemistries were normal. Liver enzymes normal. CA-125 556 U/ml (normal < 35).
diagnosis:
Disseminated TB with pulmonary, hepatic, and peritoneal involvement

Negative studies: HIV screening, histoplasma urine antigen, serum aspergillus galactomannan, coccidioides antibodies, schistosomiasis antibody, strongyloides antibody, ANA, ANCA, stool ova and parasites, AFB blood culture, fungal blood culture, midnight blood smear for microfilariae. Positive studies: TB quantiferon, TB growth from sputum at 13 days (smear and PCR negative), TB growth from repeat peritoneal biopsy at 16 days. The TB isolate was pan-susceptible to rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE) regimen. BAL aspergillus galactomannan 4.15 (normal <0.5).
Figure 1. Fig 1. Initial abdominal CT. A large heterogeneously enhancing centrally cystic irregular 7.1 x 6.4 x 6.4 cm soft tissue mass is seen in the rectouterine space, just right of midline. Extensive peritoneal nodularity and omental caking, with large ill-defined soft tissue mass is seen all around the liver, especially in the porta hepatis. Retroperitoneal and bilateral anterior cardiophrenic lymphadenopathy. Multiple liver lesions are also identified. Small right pleural effusion. Mild ascites.

Extensive peritoneal nodularity and omental caking, with large ill-defined soft tissue mass is seen all around the liver, especially in the porta hepatis. Retroperitoneal and bilateral anterior cardiophrenic lymphadenopathy. Multiple liver lesions are also identified. Small right pleural effusion. Mild ascites.
Figure 2. Fig 2. Initial chest CT. Patchy bilateral upper lobe centrilobular nodules, concerning for active endobronchial tuberculosis or, less likely, atypical mycobacterial infection or endobronchial bacterial pneumonia. Small right pleural effusion and small pericardial effusion. Indeterminate anterior mediastinal lymphadenopathy, peritoneal nodularity, hypodense hepatic lesions.
Fig 2. Initial chest CT. Patchy bilateral upper lobe centrilobular nodules, concerning for active endobronchial tuberculosis or, less likely, atypical mycobacterial infection or endobronchial bacterial pneumonia. Small right pleural effusion and small pericardial effusion. Indeterminate anterior mediastinal lymphadenopathy, peritoneal nodularity, hypodense hepatic lesions.

The patient finished 6 months of RIPE, then was switched to INH/RIF standard treatment, which she tolerated well. She gained 20 lbs and both CA-125 elevation and eosinophilia resolved. Subsequent CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis showed much decreased size of pulmonary, perihepatic, abdominal and pelvic masses.
Figure 3. Fig 3. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis after treatment. Interval decrease in the size of cavitary right upper lobe nodule and the extent of the bilateral upper lobe predominant centrilobular nodules, multiple hypoattenuating hepatic lesions, and soft tissue mass surrounding the falciform ligament, porta hepatis, and right perihepatic space.
Fig 3. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis after treatment. Interval decrease in the size of cavitary right upper lobe nodule and the extent of the bilateral upper lobe predominant centrilobular nodules, multiple hypoattenuating hepatic lesions, and soft tissue mass surrounding the falciform ligament, porta hepatis, and right perihepatic space.

Before the final diagnosis, we considered tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, and lymphatic filariasis for her syndrome of infection with eosinophilia [1-7]. These are based on her epidemiological risk factors. We also considered non-infectious causes, such as autoimmune diseases, but the ANA and ANCA were negative and the patient did not have other symptoms associated with autoimmune disorders. We then discussed that TB can be associated with peripheral eosinophilia, although not as common as infections with helminth or fungi [2, 3]. The patient did spend some time in Southern and Western states. Coccidioidomycosis can be associated with peripheral eosinophilia [1], but peritoneal infection is very rare [4, 5], and most patients were reported with positive antibody by immunodiffusion. We were surprised to see the positive BAL aspergillus galactomannan, as the patient’s presentation was not consistent with aspergillus infection. After literature review, we found that histoplasmosis (present in the Pacific Islands but the true burden is unknown) can cross react with aspergillus galactomannan test and yield false positive results [8-10]. Pelvic histoplasmosis is rare in immunocompetent patients, but has been reported [11]. We excluded the possibility of disseminated histoplasmosis based on a strong alternative diagnosis, negative urine histoplasma antigen, and response to anti-TB treatment. Finally, very rarely lymphatic filariasis (endemic in the Philippines) can cause tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, lung lesions, and pelvic lesions [6, 7]. However, the patient had not returned to the Philippines for more than 10 years. It was thought unlikely to sustain a parasitic life cycle, and that the extent of the disease was difficult to be explained by filariasis. We then discussed the nonspecific association between CA-125 elevation and ovarian cancer, given that the patient was initially referred to a gynecologic oncologist [12, 13]. It is also interesting that one study reported potential clinical utility of CA-125 in monitoring treatment effect of pulmonary TB, especially in females, and those with more significant pulmonary involvement [14].

title: A teenaged female presented with eight days of progressively worsening fever, mi
history:
A teenaged female presented with eight days of progressively worsening fever, mid-epigastric abdominal pain, and body aches. Three days prior to presentation, she first noticed a nonpruritic, flat, faint pink rash over her entire body including the palms and soles. Three days prior to presentation, she had transient conjunctival injection and edema to her hands and feet. Two days prior to presentation, she had non-productive cough and shortness of breath. Initially, her symptoms improved with antipyretics. However, on the day of presentation her home temperature increased to 103.9 degrees Fahrenheit. She also noted progressive dyspnea which prompted her to seek care. On day of presentation, she endorsed one episode of non-bloody emesis. Three weeks prior to presentation, the patient had a mild upper respiratory tract infection that was self-limited. Her family member tested positive for COVID-19 a week prior to presentation.

Mild intermittent asthma

She lived in the Pacific United States. A few months ago, patient noted a flea infestation in some clothing. She denied sexual activity, drug use, or travel.

None
exam_studies:
Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 91/41, heart rate 125, respiratory rate of 47, oxygen saturation was 88% on room air. Her temperature was 102.6 degrees Fahrenheit. She appeared tired. Eyes showed clear conjunctiva, pupils equal and reactive to light. The oral exam noted strawberry tongue and mildly erythematous cracked lips. No thrush or oral ulcers were noted. The neck exam did not show lymphadenopathy. Cardiac was normal rhythm, no murmurs. The pulmonary exam demonstrated fine crackles at bilateral bases. Her abdomen was slightly distended with mild epigastric tenderness to palpation without rebound or guarding. Her extremities were without edema and normal peripheral pulses. Her skin had a faint erythematous macular rash on her face, arms and legs, trunk, and palms of hands (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Fig 1. Faint erythematous macular rash on face, arms and legs, trunk, and palms of hands
Fig 1. Faint erythematous macular rash on face, arms and legs, trunk, and palms of hands

Her complete blood count showed hemoglobin of 11.5 gm/dL (reference range 11.4 - 16.0 gm/dL), white blood cells 5.5 x10 3 mcL with left shift (reference range 4.8 - 10.8 x10 3 mcL), and platelets 92 x10 3 mcL (reference range 130 – 440 x10 3 mcL). Procalcitonin was 3.51 ng/mL (reference range <.10 ng/mL). C-reactive protein was 19.3 mg/dL (reference range <0.7 mg/dL). Lactate was 1.7 mmol/L (reference range 0.5 -2.2 mmol/L). Her metabolic panel resulted with sodium 133 mmol/L (reference range 135-145 mmol/L), otherwise, creatinine and other electrolytes were within normal limits. Liver function testing showed aspartate transaminase 241 U/L (reference range 11-41 U/L), alanine transaminase 160 U/L (reference range 5-63 U/L), alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin were within normal limits. Brain natriuretic peptide was 622 pg/mL (reference range <99 pg/mL). D-dimer was 10.5 mcg/mL (reference range < 0.99 mcg/mL). Troponin was within normal limits. Ferritin was 1,431.2 ng/mL (reference range 10 – 291 ng/mL). Triglycerides were 255 mg/dL (reference range <149 mg/dL). Urinalysis demonstrated 1+ protein, 1+ ketones, 3+ hemoglobin with 11-25 red blood cells, trace leukocyte esterase and no bacteria. SARS-CoV-2, influenza A + B, and respiratory syncytial virus nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction tests were negative.
A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral basilar infiltrates. (Figure 2). Computed tomography scan of the abdomen demonstrated mild fluid of the left lower quadrant and splenomegaly. Computed tomography scan of the chest demonstrated bilateral airspace opacities of the posterior lungs and moderate pulmonary edema (Figure 3). The echocardiogram showed mildly dilated left ventricle with normal systolic function, no coronary artery aneurysms, and trace pericardial effusion.

Over the next three days, she developed worsening hypoxia and increasing pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiographs. She was treated with intravenous immune globin, methylprednisolone, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, clindamycin, and azithromycin. She had intermittent temperature elevation to 102.4 degrees Fahrenheit. Her thrombocytopenia resolved. She developed leukocytosis with white blood cell count increasing to 14.2 x10 3 mcL with left shift (reference range 4.8 - 10.8 x10 3 mcL).
diagnosis:
Murine Typhus with multiorgan involvement

Her murine typhus IgM titer was >1:256 (reference range <1:64). Her murine typhus IgG titer was 1:64 (reference range <1:64). Her repeat SARS-COV-2 polymerase chain reaction test was negative in addition to negative nucleocapsid and spike antibody. Blood cultures demonstrated no growth. Group A Streptococcus DNA and antistreptolysin O titer were both negative. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serologies were negative. Leptospirosis antibody was negative. Human immunodeficiency virus testing was negative. Urine legionella and urine pneumococcal antigen were negative.

She was treated with doxycycline for murine typhus. Two days after she started doxycycline, she was afebrile and saturating well off supplemental oxygen. She was discharged from the hospital four days later and completed a fourteen-day course of doxycycline. At outpatient follow-up visit five days after hospital discharge, she had continued symptomatic improvement. She did report significant fatigue. At outpatient follow-up visit one month after hospital discharge, she had completely recovered without any residual symptoms. Repeat laboratory studies and chest radiograph were normal.

This patient presented with a multisystem inflammatory process that closely mimicked multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children secondary to SARS-CoV-2 infection with fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, respiratory symptoms, and mucous membrane involvement with elevated C-reactive protein. Prior studies have shown that 2% of patients diagnosed with multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children have negative results on both SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction test and serology [1]. However, this case demonstrates the importance of including a broad differential diagnosis and obtaining a detailed social history which revealed her contact with fleas. Murine or endemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi. It is typically transmitted by the rat flea, and less commonly transmitted by the cat flea or mouse flea. Murine typhus has worldwide distribution; within the United States most cases occur in Texas, California, and Hawaii. The most common clinical manifestations include faint maculopapular rash on the trunk, fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, headache, and myalgias [2]. It is usually self-limiting and therefore likely underdiagnosed [3]. This case presents the rare manifestations of severe disease in patients with delayed initiation of treatment for murine typhus. Her clinical presentation included respiratory disease with bilateral infiltrates. She also had gastrointestinal involvement with epigastric pain, splenomegaly, and elevated liver function tests. She demonstrated mucocutaneous involvement with maculopapular rash, transient conjunctivitis, and strawberry tongue. Other manifestations of severe murine typhus that have been previously documented include meningoencephalitis [4] and renal dysfunction [5]. Murine typhus should be considered in patients in appropriate geographic locations presenting with multisystem inflammatory syndrome or other syndromes of abnormal immune activation.

title: A male in his forties was referred from a neighboring East African country for e
history:
A male in his forties was referred from a neighboring East African country for evaluation of recurrent abdominal pain. One and a half months earlier, he had presented to the referring institution with abdominal pain and features of bowel obstruction leading to a right hemicolectomy for suspected cecal malignancy following which his symptoms resolved briefly. He presented there again five days prior to referral with recurrence of abdominal pain, without signs of bowel obstruction. On arrival, he reported the abdominal pain as constant, worse on the right compared to the left. There was subjective fever, loss of appetite and significant unquantified weight loss but he denied nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention or difficulty in passing flatus and stool.

His past medical history was unremarkable apart from the recent hemicolectomy.

He was a member of the military posted to the neighboring Eastern African country five months prior to onset of symptoms. He did not smoke, consume alcohol or use illicit drugs. There was no animal exposure, sick contacts or family history of malignancy.

He had received intravenous ceftriaxone, crystalloids and analgesics prior to referral.
exam_studies:
The patient was appeared unwell and was cachectic. The blood pressure was 130/72 mmHg, pulse 63 beats per minute, temperature 97.1°F (36.2°C), and respirations 16 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation was 98% in ambient air. Abdominal examination revealed a scaphoid abdomen with a healed extended midline scar. There was generalized tenderness worse on the right without guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds were present and digital rectal examination revealed hard stools in the rectum. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examination was normal. Accompanying the patient was the hemicolectomy specimen in formalin for histopathologic exam.

Investigations done at admission revealed a mildly elevated white blood count (WBC) at 10.32 x 10 9 /L (reference range, 4-10 x 10 9 /L) with relative and absolute eosinophilia of 9.1% (reference range, 1-6%) and 0.94 x 10 9 /L (reference range, 0.02-0.5 x 10 9 /L) respectively. Hemoglobin level was borderline low at 12.9 g/dL (reference range 13-18) but platelet count was normal at 250 x 10 9 /L (reference range, 150-450 x 10 9 /L). Renal function and liver function tests were within normal limits. Carcinoembryonic antigen was < 0.5 ng/mL (reference range 0-10 ng/mL) and HIV ELISA was negative (reference range, negative).
Computerized tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen done after administration of oral and intravenous contrast revealed evidence of cecectomy and partial right colectomy with ileocolic anastomosis. There was a long segment thickening of the residual right colon and proximal transverse colon spanning 16 cm with a maximum wall thickness of 2.4 cm with regional lymphadenopathy. A 4.8 cm x 2.8 cm hypoattenuating mass that demonstrated progressive post contrast enhancement was seen in hepatic segment III (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Fig 1. Axial (Image A) and coronal (Image B) reformatted images showing diffuse long segment colonic mural thickening in the residual ascending and transverse colon (arrows).
Fig 1. Axial (Image A) and coronal (Image B) reformatted images showing diffuse long segment colonic mural thickening in the residual ascending and transverse colon (arrows).

A presumptive diagnosis of metastatic colon carcinoma was made based on the history and imaging findings and the patient was receiving supportive therapy awaiting histopathologic results. During that interval, the abdominal pain persisted despite analgesia and spread to involve the epigastric region. Repeat CT scan of the abdomen revealed increased extent of colonic thickening and size of previously seen liver lesion with interval development of a new lesion in segment VIII. Contrasted CT scan of the chest was unremarkable. Laboratory testing at this point revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 89 mm/hour (reference range 0-15 mm/hour), elevated C reactive protein of 300 mg/L (reference range, 0-5 mg/L), an elevated IgE level at 2,564 IU/mL (reference range, 0-100 IU/mL) and rising WBC and absolute eosinophil count at 15.43 x 10 9 /L and 1.39 x 10 9 /L respectively. The hemicolectomy specimen grossly revealed a solid, endo-exophytic mass within the cecum and involving the appendix measuring 75 x 65 x 43 mm that was firm and tan-colored on cut surface. Microscopic analysis showed severe inflammation of the submucosa extending to the subserosa, attended by innumerable eosinophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells to a lesser extent. Admixed was foreign-body type granulomatous inflammation, with occasional multinucleated giant cells noted to contain phagocytosed fungal zygospores with a thin eosinophilic outer wall and foamy cytoplasm. Additionally, numerous broad, infrequently septate hyphae surrounded by strongly eosinophilic material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) were observed both on hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains. There were no features of neoplasia. Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative for acid fast bacilli (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Fig 2. A, Severe granulomatous inflammation. The arrow shows a foreign-body type multinucleated giant cell engulfing fungal zygospores, characterized by a thin eosinophilic wall and foamy cytoplasm. B, Broad infrequently septate hyphae (arrow) surrounded by strongly eosinophilic material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) in a background of mixed leukocytic infiltrate attended by numerous eosinophils, and to a lesser extent lymphoplasmacytic cells. (Both hematoxylin & eosin X 400).
Fig 2. A, Severe granulomatous inflammation. The arrow shows a foreign-body type multinucleated giant cell engulfing fungal zygospores, characterized by a thin eosinophilic wall and foamy cytoplasm. B, Broad infrequently septate hyphae (arrow) surrounded by strongly eosinophilic material (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) in a background of mixed leukocytic infiltrate attended by numerous eosinophils, and to a lesser extent lymphoplasmacytic cells. (Both hematoxylin & eosin X 400).
diagnosis:
Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis

A repeat laparotomy was done for source control and to obtain specimen for fungal culture. Intra-operatively a large complex mass involving the ileocolic anastomosis, loop of jejunum and greater curvature of the stomach was noted along with multiple scattered liver lesions. The mass and segment of diseased liver were resected and sent for histopathologic analysis and fungal culture (Figure 3). Histopathologic examination of the liver and ileocolonic anastomosis site showed severe necrotizing granulomatous inflammation attended by numerous eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells and histiocytes. Once again, broad, infrequently septate hyphae surrounded by an eosinophilic sheath (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) were identified on both the H&E and PAS stains (Figure 3). Culture on chloramphenicol Sabouraud dextrose agar (CSDA) grew waxy, cream colonies, with deep radiate fissures in 7- 10 days at room temperature. Lactophenol blue preparation revealed characteristic oval to clavate conidia suggestive of Basidiobolus ranarum (Figure 3). This was confirmed in a reference laboratory using VITEK-MS MALDI-ToF® as Basidiobolus ranarum.
Figure 3. Fig 3A-B. A, Surgical resection specimen showing mural thickening of the colon with an adjacent circumscribed mass (asterisk) and necrotic area (arrow). B, Histopathologic examination of colon showing broad, infrequently septate hyphae surrounded by an eosinophilic sheath (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (periodic acid–Schiff stain X 400)
Fig 3A-B. A, Surgical resection specimen showing mural thickening of the colon with an adjacent circumscribed mass (asterisk) and necrotic area (arrow). B, Histopathologic examination of colon showing broad, infrequently septate hyphae surrounded by an eosinophilic sheath (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (periodic acid–Schiff stain X 400)
Figure 4. Fig 3C-D. C, Fungal culture on chloramphenicol Sabouraud dextrose agar showing waxy cream colonies with radiate fissures surrounded by large mucoid enteric colonies. D, Lactophenol blue preparation of culture showing characteristic clavate conidia.
Fig 3C-D. C, Fungal culture on chloramphenicol Sabouraud dextrose agar showing waxy cream colonies with radiate fissures surrounded by large mucoid enteric colonies. D, Lactophenol blue preparation of culture showing characteristic clavate conidia.

Pre-operatively, the patient was started on oral itraconazole at a dose of 200 mg twice a day administered two hours after proton pump inhibitors that were being administered for gastritis. The patient was transitioned to intravenous voriconazole post-operatively followed by oral voriconazole at a dose of 200mg three times a day once he was able to feed orally. He demonstrated clinical improvement on voriconazole therapy with resolution of abdominal pain. Laboratory testing showed resolution of eosinophilia and reduction in IgE levels to 315.6 IU/mL. Therapeutic drug monitoring of voriconazole was not available in our set up. Repeat imaging showed complete resolution of the diffuse colonic wall thickening and hepatic abscesses. The patient was discharged on oral voriconazole 200mg twice daily to complete 6 months of treatment.

Basidiobolus ranarum is a saprotrophic fungus found in soil and organic matter in the hot and humid climates of the tropics and subtropics. It is also found in the gastrointestinal tracts and droppings of reptiles and amphibians and on insects which act as host carriers. Hyphae are broad, hyaline coenocytic (aseptate) or infrequently septate and produce sticky asexual conidia that are forcibly discharged. Sexual zygospores have a characteristic beaked appearance. B. ranarum is the etiologic agent of basidiobolomycosis, cases of which concentrate in tropical and subtropics. It predominantly affects children and young adults and males are more frequently affected than females which is a reflection of exposure to the causative agent as a result of social and occupational activities [1]. The usual site of infection is the subcutaneous tissue following inoculation of spores into broken skin, manifesting as painless, erythematous nodular swellings on the limbs, thighs and buttocks. Infrequently, it can cause infections of the gastrointestinal tract (gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis) following ingestion of food, soil or other organic matter contaminated by conidia followed by tissue invasion at sites of mucosal breaks [1,2]. The characteristic response in immunocompetent hosts to B. ranarum infection is an eosinophilic inflammatory response with a blanket of eosinophilic granular material surrounding the hyphae, termed Splendore-Höeppli phenomenon. This occurs as a result of activation of Th2 response to the invading fungal hyphae and is common to basidiobolomycosis and conidiobolomycosis which together constitute entomophthoramycosis, but can also be seen in infections due to Oomycota and parasites. It is however absent in infections due to Mucorales (mucormycosis) which morphologically also have broad coenocytic hyphae similar to Entomophthorales and hence can be used to differentiate the two in histological specimens from immunocompetent individuals [1]. Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis predominantly affects immunocompetent young males residing in hot and humid areas. Although rare, it is increasingly being recognized and at last review, 102 cases had been described worldwide, mainly from the Middle East with two cases from Africa [3]. Subsequently, a series of seven cases has been published from Sudan [4]. Abdominal pain is the most common presenting feature. Other symptoms include weight loss, fever, constipation, abdominal distention, vomiting, diarrhea and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The most common examination finding is a palpable mass in the abdomen followed by hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal eosinophilia in majority of patients and elevated IgE levels. The most common organs involved is the colon followed by the small bowel, liver and stomach with occasional pancreatic involvement. Majority of patients receive an erroneous preliminary diagnosis, most commonly malignancy and inflammatory bowel disease but can include appendicitis, lymphoma, diverticulitis, tuberculosis and amebiasis [3]. The diagnosis becomes apparent during histopathologic examination of surgical or biopsy specimens from affected gastrointestinal organs. Characteristic histologic findings are of tissue eosinophilia, granulomatous inflammation attended by multinuclear giant cells, histiocytes and lymphocytes as well as thin walled, hyaline, coenocytic hyphae surrounded by a blanket of eosinophilic material (Splendore-Höeppli phenomenon). Fungal zygospores may also be seen [1,3]. Definitive diagnosis can be made by culture but specimens are not often submitted for microbiologic studies following initial surgical intervention due to lack of clinical suspicion for an infective cause of the symptoms. Specimens sent for culture should be inoculated on SDA and incubated at room temperature and 37°C. Colonies grow rapidly at 37°C but slower at room temperature and appear flat, waxy, grey-yellow with radial folds. In the absence of culture, fungal deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) present in formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissue can be detected using molecular methods. The role of serology in diagnosis is limited by low sensitivity [1,3]. The mainstay of treatment is a combination of surgery followed by systemic antifungal therapy. The optimal drug and duration of therapy has not been established but azoles are generally considered first line agents and treatment duration is usually at least six months. Itraconazole the most widely used azole but there is increasing recent use of voriconazole reported in the literature with good outcomes [3]. In summary gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis is an increasingly recognized manifestation of infection by B. ranarum that is frequently misdiagnosed as malignancy and inflammatory bowel disease. It should be suspected in otherwise healthy young patients from tropical and subtropical regions presenting with abdominal pain, weight loss and fever with radiologically detected thickening or masses of the gastrointestinal tract and peripheral eosinophilia. This will allow a timely and appropriate diagnostic work up and prompt initiation of antifungal therapy, for which azoles are currently the mainstay.

title: A man in his fifties presented with one week of subjective fever and malaise. He
history:
A man in his fifties presented with one week of subjective fever and malaise. He was in his usual state of health until one week prior to presentation when he developed subjective fever, palpitations, and left-sided facial pain involving the jaw and temple. He reported persistent tachycardia noted by his health-monitoring watch. Six days prior to presentation, he sought evaluation at an emergency department, and amoxicillin was empirically administered for odontogenic infection of an upper left molar. Three days prior to presentation, the molar was extracted, and the left-sided facial pain resolved. Subjective fever and tachycardia continued despite adherence to amoxicillin. These symptoms were accompanied by malaise, night sweats, chills, and dark urine. He denied rigors, joint pain, rash, dysuria, diarrhea, cough, and dyspnea. Due to persistent fever and malaise, he again presented to the emergency department.

None

He had one remote episode of treated gonorrhea and no prior contact with active tuberculosis cases..

He worked at an office job and lived in the northeastern United States. He had no significant travel history aside from trips to Western Europe. He was in a monogamous relationship with one female partner but was not sexually active in recent months. No animal exposures aside from contact with his partner’s pet dog. He reported 1-2 standard drinks daily and did not use other substances. No history of incarceration, or homelessness.

None

Amoxicillin
exam_studies:
He was non-toxic appearing, flushed, and supplemental oxygen was being delivered via nasal cannula. The blood pressure was 137/77 mm Hg, pulse 102 beats per minute, temperature 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37.8 degrees Celsius), and respirations 20 breaths per minute (pulse oximetry with oxygen saturation 95% on 5 liters nasal cannula). There were several dental fillings, but no tenderness to palpation or swelling was noted along gingival surfaces. No thrush was visualized in the oropharynx. There was palpable anterior cervical lymphadenopathy in addition to a palpable, mobile lymph node in the left axilla. Cardiac examination was notable for tachycardia. Pulmonary examination identified bibasilar crackles. There were faint macules noted across the chest, abdomen, and back. The examination was otherwise normal.

A basic metabolic panel noted normal renal function. Total bilirubin was 1.5 mg/dL (reference range 0.0-1.0), with a direct component of 1.1 mg/dL (reference range 0.0-0.4). Aspartate transaminase and alanine transaminase were 235 U/L (reference range 10-40) and 346 U/L (reference range 10-55), respectively. The alkaline phosphatase was 250 U/L (reference range 45-115). Complete blood count with differential identified hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL (reference range for men 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelets 130,000/mcL (reference range 150-400 x 10 3 /mcL), and white blood cells 6790/mcL (reference range 4.5-11 x 10 3 /mcL) with 17% atypical lymphocytes (reference range 0%). The N-terminal pro-hormone brain natriuretic peptide was 868 pg/mL (reference range 0-900 pg/mL). A chest radiograph identified pulmonary interstitial edema. Computed tomography scans of the neck and face were performed with intravenous contrast and identified prominent palatine tonsils with a right-sided 6 mm low-attenuation region in addition to several enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Computed tomography scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were also performed with intravenous contrast and identified multifocal groundglass and consolidative opacities within both lungs, small volume bilateral pleural effusions, and mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted. A respiratory pathogen polymerase chain reaction panel was negative, as was polymerase chain reaction-based testing for SARS-CoV-2. A respiratory sputum culture grew normal flora, and no organisms were visualized on Gram stain. Serological tests for hepatitis A virus and hepatitis B virus were negative. A real-time polymerase chain reaction test for hepatitis C virus found an undetectable viral load. Urine legionella and histoplasma antigen tests were negative. Two sets of blood cultures were collected and did not demonstrate growth after seven days of incubation.

In the emergency department, he was placed on supplemental oxygen due to hypoxemia. Azithromycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and vancomycin were empirically administered. Antimicrobial therapy was transitioned to ceftriaxone and doxycycline on hospital day one. The following day, antimicrobial therapy was narrowed to doxycycline, and diuresis with furosemide was initiated. The same day, a mildly pruritic, morbilliform rash (Figure 1) developed on the chest (Figure 2), back (Figure 3), abdomen, upper arms, and upper thighs.
Figure 1. Physical exam finding. Dense, erythematous, maculopapular eruption
Figure 2. Physical exam finding. Morbilliform eruption along chest wall and abdomen
Figure 3. Physical exam finding. Morbilliform eruption along back and flanks
diagnosis:
Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection

Two days after the morbilliform eruption, serological testing for Epstein-Barr virus resulted with positive viral capsid antigen IgM (>160.00 U/mL; reference range >43.99 U/mL positive, <36.00 U/mL negative), negative viral capsid antigen IgG (<18.00 U/mL; reference range <18.00 U/mL negative), and negative nuclear antigen IgG (<18.00 U/mL; reference range <18.00 U/mL negative). A diagnosis of primary Epstein-Barr virus infection was made. Earlier in the admission, serological testing for cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM was negative, as was serum polymerase chain reaction for cytomegalovirus. A fourth-generation screening test for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. Due to concern for drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), a human herpes virus-6 viral load was also checked and not detected.

Doxycycline was discontinued after diagnosis of primary Epstein-Barr virus infection. Topical steroid therapies and oral anti-histamine agents were used for the morbilliform rash. He received one dose of vancomycin on hospital day five after blood cultures (collected on hospital day two) grew Gram positive cocci in 1 of 4 bottles, but vancomycin was discontinued due to clinical suspicion for a contaminant. Indeed, the bacterium was subsequently identified as Staphylococcus capitis. Due to ongoing hypoxemia requiring nasal cannula, intravenous diuresis was continued. A transthoracic echocardiogram identified normal biventricular function, and a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram did not identify a pulmonary embolus. After several days of intravenous diuresis and supportive therapies, he was discharged on hospital day thirteen without need for supplemental oxygen.

The diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis was strongly suggested by the symptom constellation (fever, fatigue, generalized lymphadenopathy, etc.) and laboratory findings (atypical lymphocytosis, mild transaminitis) at presentation, and further reinforced by the subsequent morbilliform eruption after use of amoxicillin. These symptoms were preceded by an odontogenic infection, which proved to be a red herring. In general, the differential diagnosis for infectious mononucleosis includes acute Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, and human immunodeficiency virus. There were no reports of uncooked meat or extensive animal exposure to suggest acute toxoplasmosis, and the patient had no risk factors elicited on history for recent acquisition of human immunodeficiency virus. Cytomegalovirus was considered due to its lower seroprevalence in the adult population (estimated >50% of adults age 40 and above in the United States) [1], but the serological diagnosis was found to be primary EBV infection. This is uncommonly encountered in middle aged adults given that >90% of adults worldwide are estimated to be seropositive for EBV. [2] The patient’s hypoxemic respiratory failure was ultimately attributed to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and may have represented capillary leak in the setting of systemic inflammation. EBV pneumonitis has been reported, but it is exceedingly rare. [3] Importantly, DRESS can also present with the same constellation of symptoms; however, the time course from drug initiation to eruption was deemed too short to be compatible with this diagnosis (DRESS usually occurs at minimum 14 days after drug initiation). Additionally, a human herpesvirus-6 viral load, which can be positive in the setting of DRESS [4], was checked and not detected.
Interestingly, the patient developed the classic morbilliform rash after use of an aminopenicillin in the setting of primary EBV infection. [5] He received other beta-lactam agents (piperacillin-tazobactam and ceftriaxone) before the morbilliform rash emerged, but his recent use of amoxicillin was the most likely culprit. The mechanism of this phenomenon has not been definitively established, but some theorize it is mediated by temporary loss of immune tolerance to aminopenicillins due to ongoing immune stimulation driven by EBV. Historical reports on EBV-associated aminopenicillin rash estimated its occurrence in 90-100% of pediatric cases of acute EBV in which ampicillin was administered. More recent datasets have identified markedly lower numbers. [6,7] For example, one pediatric series reported the incidence of antibiotic-associated rash as 29.5% (compared to the historical ≥90%) in children who received amoxicillin during acute EBV. In general, the rash is not perceived to be a true drug allergy, and most patients are able to tolerate the medication in the future.

title: A woman in her forties with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) associated
history:
A woman in her forties with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) associated with HIV who previously declined antiretroviral therapy (ART) presented with 4 months of progressive ataxia.
She developed unsteadiness with ambulation 4 months before admission. She reported that her symptoms began abruptly and slowly progressed in severity. Over the next 4 months, her progressive imbalance required using a cane, and then later, a walker, to even stand up. She also noted mild coordination impairment in her upper extremities and reported frequently dropping objects. She had no loss of strength or sensory deficit in her extremities.
On review of symptoms, the patient denied cognitive decline, dysarthria, visual or hearing deficits, bowel or bladder incontinence, fever, constitutional symptoms, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, or rash.

She was diagnosed with HIV infection during pregnancy. She briefly took ART during her previous pregnancies but otherwise had not been on therapy. She had no history of ART resistance and had been off antiretrovirals or chemoprophylaxis for opportunistic infections for years.

The patient was born in the Northeastern United States and lived there with her son and cat, for whom she cleaned the litter box. She was not sexually active. The patient had a distant history of heavy alcohol use; she did not smoke and denied recreational drug use.

None

None
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. Her blood pressure was 167/95 mm Hg, pulse 79 beats per minute, temperature 36.8° C (98.3° F), and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were normal. Extremities were without edema, and no rash was noted on the skin.
On neurologic exam, she was alert and oriented, her speech was fluent, and her short-term memory was not significantly impaired. Her cranial nerve exam was within normal limits; no nystagmus was noted, but she did have mild dysarthria. Her strength was normal in all extremities, and her sensation was intact to light touch, vibration, and position. She had appendicular dysmetria with abnormal finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin tests bilaterally. She also had bilateral dysdiadochokinesia and truncal ataxia with a wide-based gait. Her deep tendon reflexes were brisk and symmetric.

Laboratory findings were notable for a normal metabolic panel, white blood cell count 4.2 K/uL [reference range 4.0-10.0 K/µL] with 69.3% neutrophils [reference range 48-76%], and 19.4% lymphocytes [reference range 18-41%]. HIV plasma viral load was 89,300 copies/ml, CD4+ lymphocyte count was 48 cells/µL (6.1%) [reference range 441-2,156 cells/µL (10-40%)], and HIV genotyping did not evidence of resistance.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without contrast did not show acute infarct, mass, hemorrhage, or abnormal enhancement but did demonstrate disproportionate cerebellar parenchymal volume loss (Figure 1). A CT neck obtained 6 years before for an unrelated odontogenic infection is shown (Figure 2) to provide a better comparison of the parenchymal volume loss. A spine MRI with and without contrast showed non-specific faint leptomeningeal enhancement along the cauda equina nerve roots.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed 4 total nucleated cells [reference range 0 - 5 /uL] with 0% neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, and 16% monocytes. The total protein was elevated at 78.2 mg/d [reference range 10.0 - 44.0 mg/dL], and glucose was 55 mg/dL [reference range: 40 - 70 mg/dL].
Figure 1. Figure 1, Brain MRI with contrast. Parenchymal volume loss, disproportionately involving the cerebellum, appears increased compared to CT neck performed 6 years earlier.
Figure 1, Brain MRI with contrast. Parenchymal volume loss, disproportionately involving the cerebellum, appears increased compared to CT neck performed 6 years earlier.
Figure 2. Figure 2, Neck CT without contrast. Performed 6 years earlier, shown for comparison.
Figure 2, Neck CT without contrast. Performed 6 years earlier, shown for comparison.
diagnosis:
Cerebellar atrophy due to JC virus granule cell neuronopathy in a patient with HIV/AIDS.

CSF studies showed a non-reactive VDRL and negative cryptococcus antigen. CSF PCR was negative for herpes simplex type 1 and 2, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, varicella-zoster, and Toxoplasma gondii, but positive for JC virus (JCV). JC virus PCR in blood was also detectable. CSF cytology, paraneoplastic, and autoimmune panels were negative.
Based on her clinical presentation, radiologic findings, and the presence of the JC virus in blood and CSF, a final diagnosis of JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV-GCN) was determined.

The patient agreed to resume antiretroviral therapy and was started on Bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide. Cessation of alcohol intake was also recommended. She was seen in the clinic 2 weeks after restarting antiretrovirals. Her cerebellar symptoms did not progress, and she noted a mild improvement in her balance and functional status. A repeat HIV PCR showed a significant decline to 91 copies/ml. A repeat brain MRI obtained after three months of therapy did not show significant changes in cerebellar atrophy.

There are several clinical syndromes associated with the reactivation of JC virus in the central nervous system. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is the more classical presentation characterized by a lytic infection of glial cells resulting in areas of demyelination in the brain parenchyma (1). Importantly, JCV can infect cells other than oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, leading to the description of novel neurological presentations, including JCV-associated encephalopathy, JCV-associated meningitis, and JCV-GCN (2,3).
JC-GCN is characterized by cerebellar granule cell destruction with sparing of Purkinje cells and may occur in isolation or in conjunction with classic PML findings (3,4). It has been proposed that specific mutations in the VP1 capsid gene of the virus are responsible for its unique tropism (5). The destruction of granule cell neurons causes a subacute to chronic presentation characterized by cerebellar dysfunction, with symptoms including incoordination, gait ataxia, and dysarthria (2).
While JC-GCN appears to be relatively rare, this syndrome may be under-recognized. Cases of previously unexplained cerebellar atrophy in patients with HIV may not have been attributed to JCV infection (6), as not all previously reported cases underwent cerebellar biopsy or JCV studies. Since its original description in patients with HIV infection (3), JCV-GCN has been reported in other immunosuppressive conditions unrelated to HIV infection, including primary immunodeficiencies (7), autoimmune conditions (8), and associated with rituximab (9) and natalizumab treatment (10,11).
MRI characteristically shows bilateral and diffuse cerebellar atrophy and may demonstrate confluent T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the cerebellum without contrast enhancement or diffusion restriction (12). Similar concomitant lesions within the cerebellar peduncles and the pons have also been reported (13).
A confirmatory diagnosis can be established by cerebellar biopsy, showing JCV-mediated lytic infection of the granule cell neurons; however, JC-GCN is generally diagnosed in the proper clinical and radiological setting, with the concurrent detection of JCV DNA by PCR in the CSF (2,13), as this patient had. In addition, the patient possibly had a component of concomitant alcohol-induced cerebellar ataxia, even though her alcohol consumption history and acuity of symptoms are not conclusive.
Currently, no JCV-targeted treatment is available; treatment mainly focuses on reversing the underlying immunosuppressive conditions. In patients with HIV infection, rapid initiation of antiretroviral treatment is considered the cornerstone of treatment (14).
This case report highlights the clinical and radiological presentation of JC-GCN, a unique neurologic presentation associated with JCV infection, and a likely underreported cause of cerebellar disorders in patients with advanced HIV and other immunosuppressive conditions. Infectious disease providers should be aware of its distinctive presentation and have a high index of suspicion in the correct clinical setting. Isolated cerebellar disease in an immunocompromised patient should suggest the possibility of JC-GCN even in the absence of typical findings of PML.

history:
A woman in her 40s presented with a 2-month history of epigastric pain. She also reported a loss of appetite, weight loss of almost 10 kg, and a low-grade fever. The patient denied experiencing any symptoms of jaundice. She had been treated with multiple courses of proton-pump inhibitors without improvement. The patient was referred to the university hospital for further investigation and treatment.

Well controlled essential hypertension

The patient was residing in eastern Thailand and was employed as a laborer. She reported consuming traditional Thai food frequently, which often included uncooked vegetables and freshwater animals.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. Her temperature was 37.8° C. The blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg and heart rate of 80 beats per minute. No anemia and jaundice were noted on examination. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly; the liver was palpated 5 cm below the right costal margin and the liver span was 15 cm. No clinical signs of ascites or splenic dullness were present.

The patient's hemoglobin level was 11.5 g/dL, white blood cell count was 14,600 cells/mm 3 (reference range 4500-11000), and platelet count was 493,000 cells/mm 3. The differential count of white blood cells was neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 18%, monocytes 4%, and eosinophils 26% (with an absolute eosinophil count of 3,796 cells/mm 3). Liver enzymes included an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level of 438 U/L (reference range 30-130 U/L), without elevated AST (SGOT), ALT (SGPT), or bilirubin levels. Abdominal CT revealed hepatomegaly with a 9.6 x 16.3 x 7.1-cm lobulated hypodense mass involving both hepatic lobes, with more prominence in the left lobe. No dilatation of the intrahepatic or common bile duct was observed. diagnosis:
Eosinophilic liver abscess due to Fascioliasis

Multiple blood cultures were negative.
Multiple stool examinations revealed no parasitic eggs.
Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy showed dense eosinophil infiltration with Charcot-Laden crystals. (Figure 2)
No microorganisms were found on Gram, AFB, modified AFB, GMS, and PAS strains.
Culture from the biopsy liver tissue was negative for aerobic bacteria, anaerobic bacteria, fungus, and mycobacteria.
PCR from the biopsy liver tissue was negative for Mycobacterium spp. Both 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA amplification tests were negative.
Serum tests for Entamoeba histolytica and melioidosis antibodies were negative.
In-house PCR for pan-nematodes was negative.
Serum anti-Fasciola antibodies were positive by immunoblot test.
Figure 3. Figure 2: The microscopic pathological study of the liver biopsy tissue found dense eosinophilic infiltration with Charcot-Laden crystals

The patient was treated with triclabendazole 10 mg/kg/day for 2 doses. The patient’s symptoms improved in term of abdominal pain, appetite, and fever. On follow-up, the patient’s weight increased back to her baseline. The follow-up CT abdomen taken 5 months later showed slightly decrease in size of liver lesions. (Figure 3)

Liver abscess is a common illness in clinical practice. In Asia, the common etiologies of liver abscess are pyogenic liver abscess (PLA), including melioidosis, and amoebic liver abscess (ALA). Eosinophilic liver abscess is commonly defined as a typical liver lesion along with peripheral blood eosinophilia. 1,2
The etiologies of eosinophilic liver lesions include parasitic infection, fungal infection, autoimmune diseases, and malignancy. A study from Korea reported that most patients had unidentified causes, followed by malignancy and parasitic infections. 1 Many parasites have been reported as causes of eosinophilic liver abscess, for example, fascioliasis, toxocariasis, and sparganosis. 1,2
Fascioliasis is a foodborne trematode, Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica. Humans can be infected by ingestion of contaminated water or raw freshwater wild plants. After ingestion, the immature flukes excyst in the human duodenum and then penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate through liver parenchyma to the biliary duct, causing tract-like liver lesions. 3,4
Right upper quadrant abdominal pain is the most frequent pressing symptom, with a mean duration of 1.5 months prior to diagnosis. Fever and weight loss are less common, occurring in only about one-third of patients. Eosinophilia is presented in more than 90% of patients. 5 The typical liver lesion seen on CT is a tract-like hypodense lesion. 4
Diagnosis of human fascioliasis requires a high index of suspicion and careful history taking, especially regarding exposure risk. Eosinophilia and a typical liver lesion are clues to the diagnosis. Stool testing has low sensitivity, as less than 10% of patients have positive Fasciola eggs in their stool. 4 Serological diagnosis is the most helpful test, with high sensitivity and specificity. 3,4,5
The drug of choice for human fascioliasis is triclabendazole which shows promising outcomes. 3,6,7 However, even with treatment, the duration to radiographic resolution was reported at median of 270 days (interquartile range: 180-480 days) and radiographic resolution is only achieved in two-thirds of patients. 4,5
In conclusion, we here present a case of biopsy-proven eosinophilic liver abscess with fascioliasis. We highlight the importance of taking a detailed history of exposure risk and eating habits. Triclabendazole is the treatment of choice in case of human fascioliasis but the radiologic resolution is commonly delayed.
