title: A woman in her 50s with a history of heart transplant (CMV D-/R+, EBV D-/R+, tox
history:
A woman in her 50s with a history of heart transplant (CMV D-/R+, EBV D-/R+, toxo D-/R-) about two years prior to presentation was admitted to the hospital with three months of diarrhea, fatigue, cognitive slowing, and weight loss. She also had one week of anorexia with shortness of breath and congestion, and one day of fevers. The patient denied cough, urinary symptoms, and abdominal pain.

- Heart transplant due to non-ischemic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, thought to be due to viral myocarditis in the past.
- Listeria brain abscess, one month following transplant, initially treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for 4 months, and then with TMP-SMX alone for 2 additional months. The patient then took suppressive TMP-SMX for 6 months (12 months of therapy total). The patient had stopped TMP-SMX about a year prior to the current presentation.
- Allergic to TMP-SMX with a history of rash, convulsions as a child. The patient had been desensitized to TMP-SMX before receiving it for treatment of Listeria. She had stopped TMP-SMX about a year prior to the current presentation.
- One prior episode of rejection, approximately one year ago, treated with pulse dose steroids.

- Born in South America; she had pre-transplant travel to Asia.
- Post-transplant travel included Southern California, recent camping in the Midwest.
- Dog and a cat at home. The patient was in contact with new cats around one month prior to presentation.
exam_studies:
Hemodynamically stable, fatigued and cachectic but in no acute distress. Alert and oriented x3 although slow to respond, without focal neurologic abnormalities. Cardiac exam regular rate and rhythm without murmur, no edema. Breathing comfortably on room air, lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. A retinal exam conducted by Ophthalmology was normal.

WBC 8.6 x 10 3 cells/µL (eosinophils 2440 cells/µL, lymphocytes 840 cell/µL) Na 130 mmol/L, AST 137 U/L, ALT 57 U/L, CRP 42 mg/L, LDH 1112 U/L, pro-BNP 31,097 pg/mL (normal range <125). hsTrop 16,740 ng/L (normal range <14) initially; troponin peaked at 20,150 before down-trending to 17,000. Total IgG 370 mg/dL. Two blood cultures on admission were negative for growth, urine culture negative, multiplex respiratory viral nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) panel negative, CMV and EBV NAAT serum negative, stool multiplex gastrointestinal pathogen panel by NAAT notable only for Enteropathogenic E. coli.
CT chest showed upper lobe fine pulmonary nodules, multifocal subsolid and groundglass nodules throughout, with more dense ground glass opacities in the lower lobes. CT abdomen and pelvis did not show evidence of enterocolitis or cholecystitis. MRI brain demonstrated extensive supra- and infratentorial ring enhancing brain lesions consistent with abscesses, some of which were present in the deep grey nuclei.

diagnosis:
Disseminated toxoplasmosis

A cardiac biopsy showed Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoites with surrounding inflammation. Serum toxoplasma quantitative PCR was 38,000 copies, although the patient’s toxoplasma IgG negative. Bronchoscopy was grossly normal, with negative bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures. Other negative BAL studies included PJP immunofluorescence, aspergillus antigen, HSV NAAT, VZV NAAT. CMV NAAT was positive on BAL but negative in blood. Toxoplasma NAAT from BAL fluid was also positive. Lumbar puncture showed 4 WBC/µL (47% lymphocytes, 43% monocytes, glucose 102 mg/dL, protein 87 mg/dL), CSF toxoplasma NAAT positive. CSF bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures negative.

Given the diagnosis of disseminated toxoplasmosis and her prior allergy to TMP-SMX, she was transferred to an intensive care unit for desensitization and started on IV TMP-SMX with goal of 10mg/kg total per day, renally adjusted. She developed worsening mental status, oriented only to self, possible seizure like activities in the days following initiation of therapy. Following evaluation by Neurology, she was found to have new onset seizures. Given concern for an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)-like response to lysing of toxoplasma, she was started on dexamethasone 2 mg every 4 hours with improvement in mental status, which was weaned to 2 mg every 8 hours after 2 days, and stopped after 2 additional days. Following improvement in mental status, she was changed to oral TMP-SMX which was continued for approximately 12 weeks at which time repeat MRI brain appeared back to prior baseline. She was then transitioned to suppressive TMP-SMX 1 DS tab daily, which will continue indefinitely.

Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite with a latent phase that is often asymptomatic in immunocompetent patients but can lead to severe disease in immunocompromised patients, either during primary infection or during reactivation (1).
Disseminated toxoplasmosis can lead to a wide variety of clinical presentations and, in this case, included cerebral abscesses (often visualized as multiple ring enhancing lesions), myocarditis mimicking rejection, pneumonitis (which may resemble pneumocystis on cross-sectional imaging) and likely gastroenteritis (1, 2).
Possible mechanisms of infection in solid-organ transplant (SOT) recipients include graft transmission, reactivation of latent infection, and new exposure (from cat feces or undercooked meat, especially wild game). In this case, it was likely contact with cats. Heart transplant recipients are at a higher risk for donor derived transmission of toxoplasmosis compared to other SOT recipients as the parasite is encysted in muscle; however, given the timeframe and donor/recipient serostatus here, this case is more likely due to new primary infection. As cardiac toxoplasmosis can mimic rejection, misdiagnosis and administration of steroids is a risk for worsening dissemination (1, 3). In immunocompromised patients at high risk of toxoplasmosis (due to positive serostatus in patients with HIV/AIDS or D+/R- in patients who have had a heart transplant), TMP-SMX or pyrimethamine with dapsone and leucovorin are effective in preventing disease (1, 4).
Toxoplasma IgG is often used as an initial screening test for toxoplasmosis, as it has high negative and positive predictive value; however it is less reliable in patients who are immune suppressed, including those with hypogammaglobulinemia or in acute infection prior to seroconversion (5). The toxoplasma IgM antibody is also notable for its poor performance as well, with false positives being common (1, 6). In SOT patients with a high index of suspicion, a negative antibody screen should not be used to rule out disease. Diagnosis may be obtained by histopathology as well as specific NAAT testing on involved tissue, fluid or blood (1, 5, 6).
Although traditionally first line treatment of toxoplasmosis consisted of pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid, given recent drug availability concerns, there is increasing evidence of successful treatment with TMP-SMX, including for CNS disease (4). In the setting of HIV, treatment is typically administered for 6 weeks with secondary prophylaxis continued until the CD4 cell count is >200/microliter for 6 months; however, given slow improvement in our case we elected to treat until radiographic and clinical resolution (12 weeks) and continue secondary prophylaxis indefinitely, given the patient will continue to be immunocompromised.

title: A woman in her 40s with a history of multiple sclerosis on rituximab, hyperammon
history:
A woman in her 40s with a history of multiple sclerosis on rituximab, hyperammonemia, and hypogammaglobulinemia presented with joint swelling and pain. The patient had suffered from joint pain for over 10 years. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis about 10 years prior via MRI and started on rituximab the following year. An IUD was placed a few years prior to presentation. There were concerns for peritonitis and peritoneal abscess soon after IUD insertion. The patient underwent an exploratory laparotomy; culture data was reportedly inconclusive. She was hospitalized a few months later for altered mental status and was noted to have hyperammonemia; she was referred for specialist evaluation given concerns of a potential urea cycle disorder. She continued to have joint pains and swelling. She predominantly noted swelling and pain associated with warmth and erythema in the right wrist, right sternoclavicular join, right hip, left wrist, left knee, and lower back. These symptoms had progressively worsened over the past year. She denied history of fevers, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, nausea, or rashes.

Multiple Sclerosis
Hyperammonemia
Hypogammaglobulinemia

The patient resided in the southern United States. She was in a monogamous relationship with a man. The patient reported no travel outside of the United States or travel to northeastern or southwestern United States. She denied alcohol or illicit drug use. She gardens and has a cat. She denied known tick exposures.

Rituximab
Prednisone (5 mg daily)

She was thin and chronically ill-appearing. Head and neck exam did not reveal thrush or oral ulcers. Cardiovascular exam was notable for regular rhythm and no murmurs. Respiratory exam was notable for clear auscultation in bilateral lung fields. Skin exam was notable for erythematous nodule at bilateral wrists (Figure 1); effusions noted at bilateral knees, right sternoclavicular joint (Figure 2), and left elbow. Abdominal exam notable for normal bowel sounds and no distention or tenderness. The remainder of his physical exam was unremarkable. Following admission, the patient’s leukocytosis fluctuated from 10.4 X 10 3 /mcL to 45.6 x 10 3 /mcL (ref range 3.9-10.7x10 3 /mcL). She remained afebrile throughout admission. She underwent multiple joint aspirations including both knees and right wrist. She received five days of empiric vancomycin and ceftriaxone with no changes in clinical status.
Regarding her multiple joint aspirations, no growth was demonstrated on standard bacterial, fungal, or AFB cultures. Multiple sets of blood cultures and an AFB blood culture remained negative. Further negative studies included urine and synovial Chlamydia and Gonorrhea PCR, Bartonella serologies and serum PCR, Treponemal IgG, serum Cryptococcus antigen, serum, and urine Histoplasmosis and Blastomyces antibodies, serum 1-3, beta-D-glucan, serum Coccidioides antigen. Immunoglobulin testing showed low levels of IgA, IgD, and IgG. Blood flow cytometry detected no B cells (which was expected given rituximab history).
diagnosis:
Ureaplasma urealyticum native joint polyarticular septic arthritis in a patient with multiple sclerosis on multiple immunosuppressive agents and hypogammaglobulinemia

A synovial fluid culture of the knee reported growth of 1,5000,000 CFU/mL of Ureaplasma urealyticum confirmed by PCR. A subsequent synovial fluid collection of the wrist confirmed Ureaplasma urealyticum by 16S rDNA PCR analysis.

The patient elected to not undergo any irrigation and debridement of her afflicted joints and wanted to pursue antimicrobial therapy with close follow-up with her Infectious Diseases physician. An empiric regimen of moxifloxacin and doxycycline was decided upon. Ongoing consideration for surgical intervention was recommended upon discharge to the patient. She tolerated her antimicrobials upon the remainder of her hospital stay, but an extended course of antimicrobial therapy was recommended on discharge in the setting of her immunocompromised status and the extent of infection. Upon telephone communication a few weeks later, the patient noted mild improvement.

Ureaplasma urealyticum is a pathogen belonging to the Mycoplasmatacea family, along with Mycoplasma species, that is typically associated with genitourinary infections. These pathogens are also associated with infectious arthritis – especially in the setting of immunocompromising conditions 1. Hypogammaglobulinemia is one such immunocompromising status that has been directly associated with both Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma related infectious polyarthritis 2. Moreover, immunosuppressive therapies that encompass prolonged B-cell depletion, like rituximab, are also associated with this disease process 3. In the absence of antibody-mediated immune protection, these organisms can survive within neutrophils and readily colonize mucosal surfaces. Disseminated disease can develop thereafter when infected neutrophils transport these pathogens to sites of inflammation and active neutrophil recruitment 4.
Cases of disseminated Ureaplasma urealyticum infection appear to mimic the manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis – particularly rheumatoid nodules 5. The presence of hyperammonemia can suggest disease due to IgA protease production by Ureaplasma. Diagnosis is often difficult given the challenges in microbiologic analysis and negative initial work-up. Specialized media of culture growth are performed in few reference laboratories within the United States. Advancements in molecular biological techniques, such as 16S rRNA polymerase chain reaction, microbial cell-free DNA, and specific PCR have allowed for improved diagnosis 1.
Treatment of Ureaplasma can be difficult given the ineffectiveness of common antimicrobial agents. For example, the absence of peptidoglycan cell wall and lack of folic acid synthesis render beta-lactams and sulfonamides/trimethoprim ineffective, respectively. Commonly utilized antimicrobial classes include macrolides, quinolones, and tetracyclines. Treatment durations rely on the degree of infection, host immune status, and response to treatment 1,3.

title: An 83 year old man was seen in the infectious disease clinic due to a persistent
history:
An 83 year old man was seen in the infectious disease clinic due to a persistent periaortic collection and right psoas abscess after aortic aneurysm rupture requiring endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) over 2 years prior.
The patient initially presented 2 years prior with acute abdominal pain and was found to have a perforated aortic ulceration requiring placement of graft via EVAR. On surveillance imaging six months later (1.5 years prior to presentation), there was soft tissue enhancement surrounding the aorta, extending to the right psoas muscle (Fig 1). The patient was asymptomatic then, and the decision was made to monitor clinically. A year later (6 months prior to presentation), he sought medical care due to right-sided abdominal pain, prompting a CT abdomen that demonstrated new focal collections in the right psoas (Fig 2) which were aspirated, yielding 15 cc of purulent material with negative gram stain and bacterial culture. After a two week course of empiric amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, repeat imaging showed near resolution of the collections (Fig 3); however, surveillance imaging 3 months later (3 months prior to presentation) revealed significant increase in size of the right psoas collection (19 x 9 x 4 cm, Fig 4) with PET/CT showing intense hypermetabolic soft tissue along the distal abdominal aorta and right psoas muscle concerning for an abscess with extent to the aortic stent (Fig 5). Repeat aspiration was attempted but unsuccessful. The patient was deemed to be a poor surgical candidate and was referred to infectious diseases clinic for further diagnostics and antimicrobial guidance.
On evaluation, the patient reported generalized fatigue, malaise, significant weight loss (40 lbs over one year), and intermittent night sweats in addition to chronic, stable lower back pain of 10 years duration. He denied fevers, chills, abdominal or urinary symptoms.

Born and raised in southeastern USA. He has lived in the southwest and California. No incarcerations, known contacts with TB, no homeless shelter exposures. No major zoonotic exposure.
exam_studies:
Blood pressure 111/53 mmHg, pulse 86, temperature 37°C, respirations 16 breaths per minute. The examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Notable for mild leukocytosis (12,000) with monocytosis (1380) as well as mild persistent elevation of inflammatory markers (ESR 84, CRP 2.8) of 2 years duration. The remainder of the complete blood count and the complete metabolic panel were unremarkable. Abdominal imaging was repeated (Fig 6), revealing significantly worse periaortic collection with large right psoas collection. Blood cultures (bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal) were collected, in addition to serologic testing for Brucella, Bartonella, Q fever, Salmonella, and rickettsial diseases, HIV Ag/Ab test, RPR and interferon gamma release assay (IGRA).
diagnosis:
BCG aortitis with psoas abscess

Initial testing was unrevealing so plasma cell free microbial DNA was sent which revealed detection of M. tuberculosis complex. The patient was hospitalized and had repeat aspiration of abscess with 100 cc purulent material drained; the fluid was Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear (+), Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR-positive. Blood AFB smear, Urine AFB smear, Sputum AFB smear were all negative.

The patient was started on treatment with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol pending culture results. He was seen in clinic a few weeks afterwards doing well. MTB complex culture with subsequent whole genome sequencing testing identified Mycobacterium bovis (BCG). Susceptibility testing showed resistance to rifampin and pyrazinamide. The regimen was adjusted accordingly. Unfortunately, several months later, the patient had another rupture from graft and eventually passed away.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex is comprised of 9 species that cause disease in humans and animals. M. bovis can be mistaken clinically with M. tuberculosis but molecular methods including whole genome sequencing can distinguish between the two. The former generally causes zoonotic disease (cattle), causing up to 1% of tuberculosis cases in the United States, and the latter only affects humans [1]. A modified, attenuated, strain of M. bovis named Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) was developed by French physicians in the early 20th century for use as a vaccine against tuberculosis. More recently, it has been used as immunotherapy for high grade non-muscle invasive bladder cancer as adjuvant therapy to tumor resection with a 5% complication rate, including disseminated infection and very rarely mycotic aneurysms [2]. In our patient, given the lack of other high-risk factors for mycobacterial infection, we suspected that his infection was secondary to prior intravesical BCG infusions.
Approximately 60 cases of arterial aneurysms following BCG immunotherapy have been reported in the literature since the first described case in 1988 [3]. A review of such cases, found that the majority involve the abdominal aorta (71.7%) of which 54.2% presented with arterial rupture and 32.2% with associated abscesses, as seen in our case. Management was mostly surgical (90%) with medical treatment including a prolonged combination of rifampin, isoniazid and ethambutol. Mortality was around 14% after 1 month with a 56% recurrence rate [4].
Despite the rare incidence of BCG-related complications, we believe it is important to report these types of cases to raise awareness for other infectious diseases clinicians. This case also highlights the importance of the timely use of molecular methods as an aid for diagnosis of complicated cases.

title: A woman in her 40s presented with six weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea, s
history:
A woman in her 40s presented with six weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea, seven kilograms (about 15 pounds) of weight loss and subjective fevers. She denied any other symptoms including no joint or back pain or swelling, gastrointestinal upset or visual changes.
A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension and an aortic valve vegetation. She was admitted for further evaluation.

No recent hospitalisations, surgeries, antibiotics.

This patient lived in rural Australia with her husband and dog. She had a 30-pack-year history of smoking and consumed approximately six standard drinks per day. She had never used recreational drugs nor travelled outside Australia or to the Northern Territory. She denied recent camping or caving, recent insect or animal bites or exposures.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well and had a blood pressure of 126/74, a regular heart rate of 82 and was saturating 98% on room air with 14 breaths per minute. On admission, she had a single fever to 38.5°C (101.3°F) but subsequently was afebrile. She had poor dentition and marked clubbing of her nails, but no Janeway lesions or Osler’s nodes. There was a single splinter haemorrhage on the third right toe. She had a waterhammer pulse, her heart sounds were dual with pansystolic murmur at the apex and diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Auscultation of the chest was clear. Her abdominal examination was unremarkable, with no palpable organomegaly. She had no peripheral oedema.

On admission, the patient was thrombocytopenic 98 x 10 9 /L (reference range 150-450), with haemoglobin within normal limits 117g/L (reference range 115-165), C-reactive protein 52 mg/L (reference range <3). She had normal liver enzymes and renal function. Five sets of blood cultures were all negative at five days incubation. A transoesophageal echocardiogram (Figure 1) demonstrated:
- Large vegetation on aortic valve with severe aortic regurgitation and moderate to severe mitral regurgitation secondary to AMVL prolapse
- Large pedunculated mass 36 x 0.7 mm attached to aortic valve. Multiple smaller masses or vegetation attached to all coronary cusps with destruction of aortic valve architecture
Figure 1. Figure 1: Transoesophageal echocardiogram demonstrating a large, pedunculated aortic valve vegetation in the mid-oesophageal aortic valve long axis view (left) and the mid-oesophageal aortic valve short axis view (right).
Figure 1: Transoesophageal echocardiogram demonstrating a large, pedunculated aortic valve vegetation in the mid-oesophageal aortic valve long axis view (left) and the mid-oesophageal aortic valve short axis view (right).

After 5 blood cultures were taken, when the large aortic valve vegetation was discovered, she was commenced on intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone and IV benzylpenicillin for culture negative endocarditis and transferred to a larger hospital for operative management.
diagnosis:
Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis

Further workup revealed:
- HIV Antigen/Antibody and Treponema pallidum Antibody negative
- Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) negative, Hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) negative, Hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) negative
- Hepatitis C Antibody screen negative
- Antinuclear antibody (ANA), extractable nuclear antibody (ENA), double stranded DNA (dsDNA), rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-citrullinated protein (anti-CCP), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) antibodies all negative, C3, C4 within normal limits
- Negative cryoglobulins
- Anti-phospholipid antibodies negative
- Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella, Mycoplasma, Legionella serologies negative
- Urine casts negative
- CT brain, chest, abdomen and pelvis: Wedge infarcts in kidneys bilaterally, no evidence of malignancy.

The patient continued antibiotics and underwent aortic valve replacement 10 days after presentation. Intra-operative findings were as follows:
- Aortic valve almost completely destroyed with large vegetations on all leaflets - Ulcerated area of infection at septum under right coronary cusp - Anterior mitral valve leaflet prolapse with tethering of secondary chord and small vegetations on leaflet and chordae
Conventional bacterial culture was negative at five days. Histopathology of the aortic valve revealed “vegetations and valvular destruction, consistent with endocarditis. Both the aortic valve and mitral chordae also show numerous foamy histiocytes containing granular PAS-D-positive material of uncertain significance, and the possibility of Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis (Whipple disease) cannot be excluded.”
Considering these findings, the patient underwent small bowel biopsy to assess for classic Whipple’s disease, and the team organised 16S rRNA gene sequencing on valve culture. 16S rRNA gene sequencing on valvular tissue identified Tropheryma whipplei.
The patient received 2 weeks of IV ceftriaxone 2g daily, followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800mg twice daily to complete a total of six months of antibiotic therapy. At four months follow up the patient remains clinically well with normal cardiovascular function. Duodenal biopsy subsequently returned negative for PAS-D staining and Tropheryma whipplei culture.

The differential diagnosis for culture negative endocarditis is broad. In this immunocompetent, previously well patient with minimal antibiotic or healthcare exposure and no overseas travel, the main differentials are pathogens from environmental exposure such as Coxiella burnetti, Legionella, Mycoplasma, HACEK organisms given her poor dentition and less likely, Tropheryma whipplei. Fungal or mycobacterial pathogens are less likely given she is immunocompetent and does not have relevant exposures. Non-infective causes are possible, but she did not have any evidence of autoimmune disease or solid organ malignancy.
Tropheryma whipplei is an environmental, slow-growing gram-positive rod [1,2]. It can be found in soil and is thought to be common in the human gut, where it is taken up and replicates in macrophages. However, only a small percentage of carriers develop infection. Illness typically occurs in Caucasian people and is rare in Asian and African populations despite common carriage, which is thought to be due to HLA genotype and other genetic differences [2,3].
Whipple’s disease is rare, with prevalence thought to be three in one million based on duodenal biopsy prior to PCR. Since 1999, the organism has been more readily isolated in other specimens, and the incidence is now estimated to be one to six new cases per ten million worldwide [1]. Whipple’s disease typically presents in mid-life (age 48 to 54 years), with a male preponderance of 8:1, largely associated with occupations in farming, building or outdoor exposure, or exposure to animals and soil. In more recent studies, women now account for 25% of diagnoses.
There are 4 clinical syndromes [1,3]:
1. Classic Whipple’s disease which is characterized by diarrhoea, weight loss and joint pain
2. Localized chronic infection
3. Acute infection, often diarrhoeal disease or pneumonia
4. Asymptomatic carriage
Localised chronic disease including endocarditis, osteoarticular disease and encephalitis, has been increasingly recognized since increased availability of polymerase chain reaction (PCR). These patients do not develop systemic involvement, so as with our case, stool, saliva specimens and duodenal biopsy are often negative [4]. Whipple’s endocarditis is reported to contribute to 1.9 to 6.3% of culture negative infective endocarditis cases. It involves intracellular infection of the valves as opposed to biofilm-like superficial colonization [5]. Diagnosis is most commonly by PCR of valvular tissue [6]. As in this case, Periodic acid-Schiff (PASD) stain, used to detect polysaccharides (glycogen) and mucosubstances (glycoproteins, glycolipids, mucin) can be positive (Figures 2,3). However, it is non-specific for Whipple’s, as it can also be positive in infections with fungi, mycosis fungoides, and Mycobacterium avium [1, 5].
Optimal treatment is not known, but recommendations include initial intravenous phase with ceftriaxone then switch to oral cotrimoxazole and sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine [6].

history:
A woman in her 50s presented with headache, chills, lack of appetite and self-described “flu like symptoms”. Her symptoms started 6 days prior to presentation with dyspnea and right sided pleuritic chest pain. She was seen at an urgent care where a chest x-ray was suggestive of pneumonia. The patient was prescribed azithromycin and cefpodoxime, without improvement. She then developed a fever to 101.9F with shortness of breath prompting presentation to the emergency room.

- Acute myeloid leukemia status post allogeneic matched unrelated donor hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Cytomegalovirus donor negative, recipient positive) two years prior
- Aplastic anemia status post 5 cycles of cyclosporine and antithymocyte globulin completed 8 months prior
- Hypogammaglobulinemia receiving monthly intravenous immunoglobulin therapy

Patient lives with her husband in the Midwest region of the United States. No recent travel outside of the Midwest. She has cats. Her husband cleans their litter box. She works at a school. Occasionally drinks alcohol, no recreational drug use, no tobacco use.

Penicillin (rash)

- Atovaquone 1500mg suspension by mouth daily
- Valacyclovir 500mg tablet by mouth daily
- Posaconazole 300mg tablet by mouth daily
- Cyclosporine 60mg solution by mouth 2 times daily
- Eltrombopag 125mg tablet by mouth daily
- Deferasirox 360mg tablet by mouth daily
- Prednisone 4mg tablet by mouth daily

Nocardia species are aerobic gram-positive and partly acid-fast bacteria that are a normal part of the soil microflora, salt, and fresh-water aquatic environments. Nocardia is found in common sources such as tap water, house dust, and beach sands [1]. Given the ubiquitous nature of the bacteria, infections are mostly noted in immunocompromised hosts however approximately one-third of infections occur in immunocompetent individuals. Although the mechanism of pathogenicity is not entirely understood, it is believed that Nocardial species can evade or neutralize the microbicidal activities of the host [2]. Infections are typically insidious with onset of symptoms coursing over weeks. Sites of infection can be localized to point of entry or the organism can disseminate to other organs via the bloodstream and form abscesses in the brain, skin, and lung as well as other sites For this reason, it is important to evaluate for disseminated disease with brain and lung imaging [3]. Nocardial colonization is uncommon so when the bacteria are identified, it is usually considered pathogenic [4]. Diagnosis involves microbiologic identification from suspected sites of infection. However, laboratory personnel should be notified that Nocardia is suspected as it can be difficult to culture and requires special growth media (BCYE) and longer incubation period [5]. Molecular tests, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or whole genome sequencing are also methods utilized in identifying the pathogen. Treatment is guided by antimicrobial susceptibility testing although most isolates are susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) [6]. Susceptibility patterns vary between Nocardia species and as such, empiric coverage with two or three agents is preferred practice in patients with severe infection. Duration of treatment varies depending on extent of disease and underlying host factors, ranging from 3 to 12 months, and in some cases followed by lifelong suppressive therapy.
Although cutaneous Nocardia lesions comprise 5-22% of all Nocardiosis cases, Nocardia as a cause of muscle abscess is a rare complication. The likely mechanism is hematogenous spread from a pulmonary lesion. There are nine case reports of muscle abscesses due to Nocardia species, one in an immunocompetent cattle inspector due to Nocardia farcinica, with no direct trauma [7].
In establishing a diagnosis, the non-invasive serological testing and bronchoscopy with BAL were all negative. Sputum or BAL samples can be adequate for diagnosing pulmonary Nocardial infection. In one observational study, expectorated sputum was diagnostic in 45 of 51 individuals who had pulmonary Nocardial infection [8]. A pulmonary biopsy was suggested in this case, but patient did not wish to pursue this. The diagnosis was established due to the presence of a fluctuant mass in the patient’s right calf which subsequently underwent biopsy and culture. This specimen yielded Nocardia arthritidis, identified by 16S ribosomal rRNA sequencing. Prior to knowledge of the calf abscess, cell free DNA sequencing of plasma (Karius Test TM) was performed. The infection had clinically metastasized to various parts of the body and there were fragments of non-encapsulated microbial DNA in the plasma at significant levels, which were detected by the Karius Test TM, however, this type of testing was not able to differentiate between Nocardia exalbida, Nocardia gamkensis, Nocardia arthritidis.

title: The patient was in his usual state of health until, three months prior to admiss
history:
The patient was in his usual state of health until, three months prior to admission, he experienced a syncopal episode upon standing up from his bed in the morning. Over the next few days, he developed shortness of breath, lower extremity edema, and non-exertional, intermittent chest pain, causing him to present for evaluation to a primary care physician (PCP). He denied fevers, weight loss, night sweats, rash, headaches, vision changes, hearing loss, focal neurological changes, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dysuria at time of presentation. He could recollect no previous illnesses within the preceding weeks nor any significant illnesses throughout his life. He was not taking any prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal medications. His PCP referred him to a cardiologist.
Two months prior to admission, the patient was seen by the cardiologist. Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus rhythm with possible left atrial enlargement and no ST segment or T wave abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated an ejection fraction of 50%, moderate aortic valve stenosis and regurgitation, severe mitral stenosis and regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and bi-atrial enlargement. He was diagnosed with presumed rheumatic heart disease and was prescribed diuretics. Despite this therapy, his symptoms worsened over the following 4 weeks.
Three weeks prior to admission, he presented to a local hospital for worsening dyspnea. Cardiac angiography revealed elevated right-sided pulmonary and left atrial pressures as well as 40% atherosclerotic disease of his left anterior descending coronary artery. Unfortunately, his social situation compelled him to leave that hospital before undergoing planned valve replacement surgery.
After discharge from the local hospital, our patient’s dyspnea continued to worsen, leading him to present to our hospital. He completed pre-operative evaluation and, on hospital day 17, underwent aortic and mitral valve replacement with mechanical valves and tricuspid valve repair via ring annuloplasty. The cardiothoracic surgery team described thickened, calcified aortic and mitral valves but a normal myocardium and aortic root.
His initial post-operative course was unremarkable. However, on post-operative day (POD) 2, the Infectious Diseases service was consulted because the preliminary pathology report of the mitral valve tissue (which is routinely performed on all excised heart valves at our hospital) described necrosis with acute and chronic inflammatory cells consistent with abscess (Figure 1).

diagnosis:
Mitral valve endocarditis due to Treponema pallidum

The Treponema pallidum antibody (TPA) test was positive as was the reflexive reactive plasma reagin (RPR) test (titer 1:32). In the setting of no prior knowledge of syphilis (confirmed by both the patient and the local health department), he was given one dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular (IM) benzathine penicillin G, and two additional weekly doses were planned for late, latent syphilis. The remaining serologic workup was negative, as described above. Next generation sequencing (NGS) of the mitral valve tissue was positive for Treponema pallidum (NGS coverage 59%) and Bacillus licheniformis (NGS coverage 28%).
Given the unclear timeline of history and stage of syphilis (with concern for tertiary syphilis), we planned to pursue a lumbar puncture to rule out neurosyphilis. However, our patient was unable to undergo lumbar puncture due to his elevated INR related to therapeutic warfarin required to protect his mechanical heart valves. Thus, rather than simply completing the 3 weekly doses of IM benzathine penicillin G recommended for tertiary syphilis, we treated with 10 days of intravenous (IV) aqueous crystalline penicillin G 4 million units every 4 hours. Treatment with IV penicillin began after the patient had already received two IM injections of benzathine penicillin G and therefore adequately treated tertiary syphilis as well. After receiving a pacemaker for frequent post-operative bradycardia, he was discharged on post-operative day 21 and remained in good health at clinic follow up several months later.

Treponema pallidum is the causative agent of syphilis. It may be transmitted sexually or from mother-to-child. Historically, syphilis is classified based on duration of infection and symptoms into the following categories: primary, secondary, early latent, late latent, tertiary, and neurosyphilis. Twenty-five percent of untreated people with T. pallidum infection will develop tertiary syphilis 1 - a term denoting symptomatic late syphilis. The cardiac manifestations of tertiary syphilis are feared because of their significant associated morbidity and mortality. Classically, the pathology of cardiac syphilis is related to dissemination of T. pallidum via the aortic vasa vasorum, leading to inflammation (i.e., vasculitis) and compromise of the blood supply of the aortic wall. Broadly, five categories of cardiovascular syphilis are described. 2 First, uncomplicated syphilitic aortitis, which occurs at time of primary infection in 70-80% of patients and typically involves the transverse aorta and aortic arch. Second, aortic aneurysm, where endarteritis of the vasa vasorum results in fibrous replacement of the elastic tissue of the aortic wall, weakening it and allowing for “ballooning.” 3 Third, aortic insufficiency, due to aortic root enlargement dilating the aortic valve annulus and widening the commissures. Fourth, coronary ostial stenosis, which occurs in 29% of cases of syphilitic aortitis when inflammation extends to the coronary ostium. 4 Fifth, syphilitic myocarditis, which was described by the well-known pathologist Dr. Warthin as a common end-stage complication of syphilis with a spectrum of manifestations ranging from “microscopic areas of...plasma cell and lymphocyte infiltrations up to more diffuse areas of interstitial myocarditis.” 5 Regarding manifestations of cardiac syphilis outside of these historic categories, several reports of endocarditis of the aortic valve attributed to T. pallidum infection are published. 6,7 From our literature review, it appears that our case is the first report of T. pallidum infection of the mitral valve confirmed by molecular testing, suggesting that T. pallidum may cause additional types of cardiac disease that have not yet been well-described.
Diagnosis of syphilis
As T. pallidum cannot be grown in culture, direct (e.g., dark field microscopy, histological examination of tissues, and molecular) and indirect (e.g., serologic) methods of detecting T. pallidum are utilized for syphilis diagnosis. The original gold standard of syphilis diagnosis was the rabbit infectivity test (first used for T. pallidum in 1907). 8 In modern times, improved indirect treponemal tests (first developed 1949) and nontreponemal (e.g., rapid plasma reagin [RPR], developed in 1957) are used. These tests are reliable for syphilis diagnosis if used as a two-step algorithm, which should include each of the following:
• A treponemal test like T. pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA), which detects antibodies to Treponema species and is highly sensitive (94.5-96.4%) and specific (99.0-100.0%) but does not differentiate between past and current T. pallidum infection. 9
• A non-treponemal test like RPR, which detects antibodies to lipoidal antigens and is considered less specific (81-96%) but is reported in titers and can therefore be used to assess treatment response. 10 Notably, non-treponemal tests may be negative in up to 30% of tertiary syphilis cases. 11
Molecular tests such as nucleic acid amplification (NAAT) and next generation sequencing (NGS) are newer methods for the diagnosis of syphilis, although their cost and complexity prohibit common use and widespread availability. NAATs are invariably highly specific (98-100%) but with variable sensitivity by specimen source, stage of disease, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) target (0-95%). 12 In latent syphilis, detection ranged from 0-44%. 12-14 Data for NGS are limited; some reports describe the utility of NGS for diagnosis of early-stage syphilis. 15 NGS has proven useful in other cases of culture-negative endocarditis, with reports of 85.9-100% sensitivity and a positive predictive value of 97% when testing heart valve tissue. 16 Molecular testing can be a useful tool for diagnosis of challenging cases, particularly with organisms that are difficult to culture or when little tissue is available, such as in the case presented here. In our case, the diagnosis of mitral valve endocarditis due to T. pallidum is supported by (1) the atypical endocarditis presentation (effectively ruling out pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus), (2) extensive negative workup (e.g., blood and valve cultures and serologic tests for other organisms known to culture-negative endocarditis), (3) pathology definitively showing findings consistent with bacterial infection, (4) T. pallidum being the only organism present (via RPR and NGS), and (5) NGS validity in endocarditis diagnosis with high positive predictive values.
Rheumatic heart disease and Treponema pallidum infection
Rheumatic fever is caused by the host immune response to untreated group A Streptococcus infection, which can cause damage and scarring of the heart valves, leading to a host of cardiac complications including aortic, mitral, and (less commonly) tricuspid valve stenosis and regurgitation, years to decades after initial infection. Rheumatic heart disease increases the patient’s risk of developing infective endocarditis; 15-55% of endocarditis cases are reported to occur in patients with rheumatic heart disease in countries reporting higher rheumatic heart disease prevalence. 17-18 Heart valves damaged by rheumatic fever provide an ideal surface on which circulating bacteria can adhere to and form vegetations. No robust studies have investigated the interaction between T. pallidum and rheumatic heart disease. Authors of one pre-antibiotic era study of 6 cases with both rheumatic and syphilitic cardiovascular disease hypothesized that T. pallidum infection may exacerbate underlying, asymptomatic rheumatic heart disease, 7 but little data are available to support this theory. Rather than “exacerbating” or “re-activating” pre-existing rheumatic heart disease, we suspect that T. pallidum may utilize the damaged heart valve as a nidus of infection, as can other indolent bacterial agents of culture-negative endocarditis. Data to support these theories are sparse as tertiary syphilis is relatively rare due to widespread availability and use of antibiotics. However, syphilis rates are high, 19 so we may see more tertiary syphilis in the future.

title: A man in his 70s presented to the emergency department for several months of wor
history:
A man in his 70s presented to the emergency department for several months of worsening headaches. In the past two days, he also began to experience issues with coordination and weakness in his left hand. He has had worsening of his chronic left foot drop, and new gait instability.
He reported no systemic symptoms of fevers or chills, but did describe a recent 5-pound weight loss and some mild nausea. He had no cough, chest pain, or changes in his baseline dyspnea or exercise tolerance. He reported no visual changes or photosensitivity, no genitourinary symptoms, and no complaints of abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea, The remainder of his review of symptoms was negative.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation; hyperthyroidism. No known drug allergies.

The patient smokes cigarettes (>50 pack-year history); he does not drink alcohol or inject drugs. He has no known tuberculosis exposure history, and no history of homelessness. He lives in a house he remodeled and gardens. He has no pets or routine animal exposures. Other than traveling across the country in the past, he has not left the northeastern United States. Decades ago, he lived in Vietnam for several years.

Albuterol inhaler; medical therapy for heart failure; methimazole.

Disseminated Nocardia farcinica in a presumed immunocompetent patient, found to have anti-granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating-factor autoantibodies.

He was transferred to our hospital for neurosurgical evaluation and subsequently underwent left occipital craniectomy. Intra-operative findings revealed a cerebellar abscess which was drained with cultures sent. Gram-positive rod bacteria grew from the aerobic blood culture bottle (figure 4). Cultures of the chest wall abscess and brain abscess grew Gram-positive rod bacteria.
Gram-positive rod bacteria in the aerobic blood culture bottle were identified as Nocardia farcinica by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF). Tests for antimicrobial susceptibility by broth microdilution methodology were performed at the New York State Department of Health and University of Texas at Tyler reference laboratories (figure 5).
Given the unusual presentation of disseminated nocardiosis in an apparently immunocompetent patient, an anti-cytokine autoantibody panel was sent to the National Institutes of Health and revealed that the patient plasma was positive for neutralizing antibody activity to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (figure 6).

The transferring hospital microbiology lab reported trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) resistance by E-test. Linezolid and imipenem were reported as susceptible by E-test and amikacin was reported as susceptible by disk diffusion. The patient was started on imipenem, linezolid, and amikacin and the Nocardia isolate was sent to two reference labs for Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) approved susceptibility testing by broth microdilution (BMD).
BMD susceptibilities from the two reference labs at the New York State Department of Health (NYS-DOH) and the University of Texas (UT) at Tyler both confirmed TMP-SMX susceptibility. UT Tyler reported intermediate susceptibility to imipenem. Imipenem was discontinued and TMP-SMX started. Amikacin and linezolid were continued. He had steady clinical improvement over the next 6 weeks and was discharged to a subacute rehabilitation facility on maintenance TMP-SMX and reduced dose linezolid, two antibiotics with high central nervous system penetration. At two months follow-up in the clinic, his left-sided arm and leg weakness had improved. At five months, he continued tolerating both antibiotics, had regained his balance, and his left-sided weakness had resolved.

We present a case of disseminated nocardiosis in a patient with no known prior history of immunodeficiency or other typical risk factors such as pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. His initial presentation of subacute pneumonia, bacteremia, and hematogenous dissemination to the brain and skin prompted further testing for autoantibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which returned positive. Our case also highlights challenges in obtaining reliable CLSI-validated BMD susceptibilities for Nocardia farcinica, a multi-drug resistant and virulent Nocardia species.
Nocardia is an aerobic Gram-positive rod with “delicate” filamentous branching and is positive on modified acid-fast staining due to cell wall mycolic acid. It is a ubiquitous environmental saprophyte. Clinical disease often affects people with immunocompromising conditions, especially recipients of solid organ transplants and patients with chronic granulomatous disease. Syndromes caused by Nocardia include pulmonary disease (approximately 63-86% of cases) from direct inhalation from the environment, cutaneous disease (8-31%) from direct primary inoculation or secondary hematogenous seeding, and central nervous system (CNS) disease primarily in the form of abscess (2-26%) and rarely as meningitis (1). When Nocardia is identified, brain imaging is often performed to screen for CNS involvement. Combination antibiotic therapy as induction therapy is recommended for cases of disseminated disease with brain involvement (2).
Patients with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) are also at high risk of pulmonary nocardiosis. PAP is a disease syndrome characterized by poor clearance and accumulation of pulmonary surfactant. It has been associated with the presence of autoantibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating-factor (GM-CSF), a cytokine important in alveolar surfactant homeostasis (3). Loss of GM-CSF activity reduces alveolar macrophage phospholipid catabolism and leads to accumulation of surfactant. However, there is an emerging literature reporting patients who do not have a diagnosis of PAP but who have detectable anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies and develop disseminated nocardiosis, like in this patient (4). The presence of anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies has also been implicated in disseminated cryptococcal disease (5).
This case highlights the importance of sending Nocardia isolates to reliable reference laboratories. The transferring hospital microbiology lab used the E-test method for TMP-SMX, linezolid, and imipenem and the disk diffusion method for amikacin. E-test and disk diffusion are not validated for Nocardia. CLSI recommends using broth microdilution (BMD) performed by reference laboratories. Performance and interpretation of susceptibility testing require expertise with BMD for this organism and knowledge of the differing susceptibility patterns of Nocardia species. Laboratories which infrequently encounter Nocardia should send isolates to reference laboratories validated for these procedures and in interpreting these results. For example, certain Nocardia species grow slowly and make reading at the 72-hour mark difficult, and growth in the control well may also be poor and lead to uninterpretable MIC results (6).
Imipenem susceptibility testing can be particularly challenging as in our case where two reference laboratories reported divergent susceptibility results for this antibiotic (figure 6). Therapeutic options are limited by the multi drug-resistant nature of Nocardia farcinica and this patient’s disseminated disease. Notably, imipenem instability likely contributes to the high MIC observed in susceptibility testing for this antibiotic during prolonged incubation of Nocardia (7,8). Ultimately, confirmatory antimicrobial testing by BMD reported susceptibility to TMP-SMX, which was used in conjunction with reduced-dose linezolid as consolidation therapy with good therapeutic effect.
Testing for anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies should be considered in patients with unexplained disseminated nocardiosis and no history of overt immunodeficiencies or pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP).

title: A man in his 70s with intestinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving chemoth
history:
A man in his 70s with intestinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving chemotherapy presents with fever, chills, and multiple mass-like lesions throughout his body over a 3-month duration. Prior to these symptoms, he had noticed a bruise on his flank with an underlying palpable mass. He had initially attributed this finding to his lymphoma because after his chemotherapy it had decreased in size. However, one day prior to presentation, he bumped himself, leading to purulent drainage from the skin lesion. Throughout this course, he also noticed similar lesions on his mid-scapula and his opposite shoulder, both of which had progressively increased in size despite chemotherapy.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the bowel, status post R-CHOP, intrathecal chemotherapy, and CAR-T therapy.

The patient lives on a ranch in the desert, located in the Southwestern region of the United States. He has worked with tractors and soil in the past. He owns cattle, dogs, and previously owned horses. He drinks alcohol occasionally and denies ever using tobacco or recreational drugs.

Acyclovir, lenalidomide, ondansetron

diagnosis:
Rhodococcus equi bacteremia and multifocal abscesses

Wound culture from the patient’s incision and drainage procedure grew Rhodococcus equi (R. equi). One day later, his blood culture from admission also grew Rhodococcus equi as well.

After initial cultures grew Rhodococcus equi, the patient was started on azithromycin, vancomycin and imipenem. The blood cultures had initially cleared immediately; however, several days later he had recurrent Rhodococcus equi bacteremia. His chest port was removed. A CT head (with and without contrast) and chest (with contrast), transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE), and transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) were performed to help identify additional sources of infection. However, they were all unremarkable. Given his persistent bacteremia, the patient underwent aspiration of his right scapular lesion with eventual placement of a drain. After return of the Rhodococcus culture sensitivities, he was discharged on ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin for an anticipated two-month course dating from his first negative blood culture. The patient finished his antibiotic course, and on follow up he had significant improvement but incomplete resolution of abscesses. Around 3 months after being discharged, he had repeated incision and drainage of the right lower abdominal quadrant abscess and right upper back abscess, with negative wound cultures and blood cultures.

Risk factors for R. equi infection include immunosuppressive states, including from HIV infection, chemotherapy use, organ transplantation, and diabetes. However, R. equi can notably cause disease in both immunocompromised and immunocompetent hosts (5).
There are different manifestations of R. equi infection. R. equi is a facultative intracellular pathogen that infects macrophages and survives inside lysosomes, and thus can cause chronic infection. R. equi infects a variety of tissues, including the lung, blood, brain, skin, lymph nodes, and bone (1). Most commonly, it causes pneumonia. Complications include development of lung abscess, pleural effusion, empyema; it can also cause complications such as pneumothorax, pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, and mediastinitis (2). Extrapulmonary infections manifest as wound infections, traumatic septic arthritis, and endophthalmitis after ocular injuries. With extrapulmonary infections, the infection usually remains localized at the primary site.
The treatment of R. equi can be difficult (5). R. equi is usually susceptible to vancomycin, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, rifampin, teicoplanin, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, and linezolid. In animal studies, vancomycin, imipenem, and rifampin were the most active antibiotics (3). R. equi is often resistant to penicillins. Monotherapy is generally not recommended because resistance can develop while on therapy. There is some evidence to suggest that combination therapy is more effective than monotherapy, with most experts recommending combination therapy (4). Some experts suggest using a combination of antibiotics with bactericidal and intracellular killing properties for initial reduction of bacterial load (4).
Our patient’s case is a reminder of the importance of obtaining a thorough history. The patient’s demographic history was significant for ranch and horse exposure, which were likely the sources of his infection. Our case also highlights this pathogen’s ability to infect a variety of tissues and the difficulties in management of the infection, as this patient required multiple rounds of debridement.

title: An elderly immunocompromised man with untreated small lymphocytic lymphoma prese
history:
An elderly immunocompromised man with untreated small lymphocytic lymphoma presented with 3.5 weeks of scattered pruritic nodules over his body. He reported that the first lesion developed on his chin, starting out as a mildly pruritic bump, then progressed to an ulcer that then became an eschar (Image 1). He did not apply anything to these lesions or take any medication, and nothing seemed to make them worse.
Other lesions started the same as the first one, and developed over his chest, abdomen, back, upper arms, thighs, nose and forehead (Image 2).
His review of systems was negative. He denied new medications. He had no known allergies to medications.

Image 1: Ulcerated lesion of the chin, most advanced lesion at time of presentation
Figure 2. Image 2: Lesion on nose of patient, stage prior to eschar formation
Image 2: Lesion on nose of patient, stage prior to eschar formation

Patient was born and raised in the mountains of the central southwest US, on a ranch, where he currently lives. He served in the military in the US.
Growing up and after discharge from the military, he raised cattle, horses, and dogs, but sold them all >5 years prior to presentation. He denies attended any animal births. He endorsed hunting and fishing, but last time was decades ago. He currently has rabbits, but denies close contact or skinning any of them.

Atorvastatin; clopidogrel; ferrous sulfate; furosemide; levothyroxine; metoprolol
exam_studies:
VS: temperature 36.6, Heart rate 76, Blood pressure 123/48
Patient appeared well. He had numerous subcutaneous, mobile, flesh-colored, nontender nodules scattered over his chest, back, upper arms, thighs, and face. The most prominent lesion was on his chin; that lesion had ulcerated and developed an eschar. Other nodules had ulcerated but not yet scabbed over. Exam was otherwise normal.

Emergomycosis is an emerging endemic fungal infection. Emergomyces is thermodependent dimorphic, soil dwelling yeast. Emergomyces canadensis has only been isolated in North America, with only 6 previous cases having been reported. Formerly classified as Emmonsia, other members of the Aiellomycetacae family include Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Paracoccidiodies.
Assumed to be an inhalation inoculation, there have been outbreaks of other species in southern Africa, eastern Europe and China. All 7 patients (including the one in this report) who developed symptomatic Emergomycosis in North America have been immunocompromised (HIV infection, post-transplant, or hematological malignancies). An early clue that pointed away from histoplasmosis in this patient was the negative result of the sensitive histoplasmosis urine antigen test.
Unique features of the fungi on tape preparation seen on light microscopy helped differentiate Emergomyces from Histoplasma. The tape preparation showed conidiophores that branched from hyphae at right angles and formed clusters of conidiophores bearing a single small round conidia. Comparatively, Histoplasma demonstrates 8 to 15 µm ovoid macroconidia, with finger-like cell walls and 2 to 4 µm microconidia. On histopathology, Emergomyces stains with Grocott–Gömöri's methenamine silver stain and appears as 2 to 7 µm round/oval yeast with narrow-based buds, often surrounded by granulation issue. Histoplasma is also often surrounded by granulation tissue and stains with Grocott–Gömöri's methenamine silver stain as 2 to 4 µm spores. These similarities explain why, on histopathology, Emergomyces has been mistaken for Histoplasma.
Clinical manifestations of Emergomycosis have included acute onset of cutaneous lesions, fever, cough, and weight loss. Cutaneous manifestations include umbilicated papules, nodules, ulcers, verrucous lesions, crusted hyperkeratotic plaques and erythema. Of note, polymorphic skin lesions can be found in a single patient. In the Emergomyces canadensis cases, evidence of infection has been found in lung and endocervical tissue, skin and blood.

title: A man in his 40s with a history of untreated HIV presented to the emergency depa
history:
A man in his 40s with a history of untreated HIV presented to the emergency department for subacute, progressive cough and shortness of breath. He reported associated fatigue, headache, and generalized weakness.
He was initially diagnosed with HIV one year prior to presentation but declined to start antiretroviral therapy. Two months prior to presentation he was admitted due to respiratory failure and multifocal pneumonia. At that time HIV RNA and CD4 count were 981,000 copies/mL and 20 cells/µL, 3%, respectively. He was hospitalized and treated empirically for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone. Bronchoscopy was recommended but was not completed. Initiation of antiretroviral therapy was deferred due to concern for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, and he did not follow up in infectious disease clinic to start antiretroviral therapy. He returned to an emergency department one month later with persistent symptoms. He was again prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone for presumed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

HIV/AIDS
Multifocal pneumonia
Late latent syphilis, treated
Thrush

Injection methamphetamine use.
No tobacco or alcohol use.
Previously lived in the Mountain States region and Southeast US.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 2 double strength tablets by mouth three times daily
Prednisone 80 mg by mouth daily
exam_studies:
The patient appeared thin and cachectic. Blood pressure was 119/81 mmHg, pulse 116 beats per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees C (97.9 degrees F), respirations 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 4 L by nasal cannula. He was noted to be coughing on exam with moderate increased work of breathing. His lung sounds were diminished to auscultation with bilateral apical wheezing. He was noted to have non-tender purple papules on the anterior trunk. The remainder of the physical exam was within normal limits.

The white blood cell count was 10.3 x 10 9) cells/L (reference range 4.4-11.1 x 10 9 cells/L), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL (reference range 14.3 – 18.1 g/dL), platelet count 318 x 10 9 /L (reference range 150-400 x 109/L). Complete metabolic panel was normal. Lactic acid was
2.0 mmol/L (reference range 0.5-2.2 mmol/L), lactate dehydrogenase was 270 U/L (reference range 124-271 U/L), 1-3-beta-D-glucan was negative (reference range negative), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii antigen serum was negative (reference range negative). HIV quantitative polymerase chain reaction showed 678,000 copies/mL (reference range 0 copies/mL), CD4 T-cell count was 18 cells/microliter with 3% (reference range 425-1,860 cells/microliter, 25-62%). Urine legionella and streptococcus pneumonia urine antigens were negative (reference range negative). Treponemal antibody was reactive (reference range not detected) and rapid plasma reagin was non-reactive (reference range non-reactive). Histoplasma and Blastomyces urine antigens were not detected (reference range not detected). Coccidioides antibodies by immunodiffusion and complement fixation were both negative (reference range negative). Chest x-ray showed multifocal ground glass and consolidative opacities scattered throughout the lung fields. Respiratory pathogen panel by polymerase chain reaction was negative (reference range negative). Cytomegalovirus quantitative blood polymerase chain reaction was 80,500 IU/mL (reference range 0 IU/mL), EBV PCR was <2000 IU/mL (reference range 0 IU/mL). CT chest (Figure 1) with intravenous contrast showed bilateral multifocal findings with consolidation in the lower lobes without pleural effusion or cavitary changes. Blood cultures were negative. Bacterial cultures grew mixed normal respiratory flora, and respiratory fungal and acid-fast bacilli cultures were negative. Respiratory polymerase chain reaction testing for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative (reference range not detected). On admission the patient was started on ceftriaxone 2 grams IV daily and doxycycline 100 mg by mouth twice daily for empiric treatment of bacterial pneumonia. The prednisone dose was tapered from 80 to 40 mg. He had progressively increasing oxygen requirements, and on hospital day 5 was placed on high flow nasal cannula and transferred to the medical intensive care unit. IV ceftriaxone was changed to IV piperacillin-tazobactam and IV ganciclovir added for cytomegalovirus viremia. His respiratory status continued to decline, and he was intubated on hospital day 7. IV Liposomal amphotericin B was added for empiric antifungal coverage and prednisone was weaned to 30 mg daily. He continued to have rising oxygen requirement and was cannulated for extracorporeal membranous oxygenation on hospital day 9.
diagnosis:
Respiratory failure secondary to HIV/AIDS associated visceral Kaposi sarcoma

Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no evidence of valvular abnormality or vegetation to suggest infective endocarditis. Dermatologic pathology of the anterior chest wall lesion demonstrated elongated spindle shaped cells and immunohistochemical testing was positive for human-herpesvirus-8. Bronchoscopy was completed and pathology of lung tissue demonstrated spindle cell neoplasm consistent with Kaposi sarcoma with immunohistochemical testing positive for human-herpesvirus-8. Bronchoscopic cultures and pathologic staining for fungus and acid-fast bacilli were negative.

He was started on antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide on hospital day 6. Following pathologic confirmation of Kaposi sarcoma diagnosis on skin and bronchoscopic biopsy, oncology was consulted and he was initiated on chemotherapy with intravenous doxorubicin (hospital day 8). He received a 10-day course of intravenous piperacillin tazobactam for treatment of pneumonia. Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B was discontinued after 3 days in the absence of confirmed fungal infection. Intravenous ganciclovir was stopped on hospital day 15 after cytomegalovirus virus blood polymerase chain reaction resulted below the limit of quantification (reference range not detected). He was decannulated from extracorporeal membranous oxygenation on hospital day 16 and extubated on hospital day 19. He received his second dose of intravenous doxorubicin on hospital day 29.
He was discharged to home on hospital day 31 with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide for antiretroviral therapy and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Following discharge, he moved to a different state and transferred his care to a new health system. Five months following his discharge he has completed 5 cycles of intravenous doxorubicin and continues on bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide for antiretroviral therapy with HIV quantitative polymerase chain reaction showing 167 copies/mL (reference range < 20 copies/mL).

This patient with advanced HIV presented with subacute respiratory failure after treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone for presumed Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. In the setting of his advanced HIV, he was at risk of AIDS-associated opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, tuberculosis, and endemic fungal infections. Physical exam of the patient’s trunk rash was suspicious for cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma and this was subsequently confirmed with skin biopsy. Additional testing for pneumocystis, cryptococcus, tuberculosis, and endemic fungal infections was negative. In the presence of cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma, there was concern for more advanced Kaposi sarcoma with pulmonary involvement. Bronchoscopic biopsy of lung tissue confirmed pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is a mesenchymal tumor of blood and lymphatic vessels caused by the oncogenic human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) in the context of immunosuppression. 1-2 HIV/AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma typically appears with multifocal, cutaneous, brownish plaques. 2 Visceral Kaposi sarcoma is a less common variant that most often involves the stomach, spleen, bowels, liver, and lungs. 2 Pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma typically manifests as cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. In the era of effective antiretroviral therapy the incidence of HIV/AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma has rapidly declined, and as a result is often associated with delayed diagnosis. 1-3
The differential diagnosis for hypoxic respiratory failure and multifocal pneumonia in people with advanced HIV/AIDS is broad; however, diagnosis can be challenging and patients are often presumed to have pneumocystis pneumonia and started on steroids. Glucocorticoid use in persons with Kaposi sarcoma has been associated with worsening disease and mortality, with up to a four-fold increase in mortality associated with steroid use. 1-3 This patient’s clinical course complicated by extended high-dose glucocorticoid use prior to presentation may have accelerated progression of Kaposi sarcoma.
This case demonstrates the successful use of veno-venous extracorporeal membranous oxygenation (VV-ECMO) for respiratory failure secondary to pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma. VV-ECMO has been previously used in multiple cases of respiratory failure in other AIDS associated opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. 4-5 The use of VV-ECMO for respiratory failure secondary to disseminated Kaposi sarcoma has only been documented in two case reports previously. 6,7 This case represents a successful use of VV-ECMO for respiratory failure due to AIDS-associated visceral Kaposi sarcoma.

title: A sailor in his 30s with no significant medical history was admitted to hospital
history:
A sailor in his 30s with no significant medical history was admitted to hospital with an 8.2 cm hepatic abscess within the right lobe of the liver. Symptoms started two weeks prior to presentation with fevers, chills and night sweats that progressed to right-upper abdominal quadrant pain. The patient had no headache, neck stiffness, chest pain, shortness of breath, diarrhea, hematochezia, dysuria, extremity swelling or rashes.

No significant medical history.

The patient was born and lived in Nepal until he was a young adult. He immigrated to the United States (U.S.) and lived in the northeast until joining military in his late 20s. His only subsequent travel outside the U.S. was to South Asia a few years prior for one month, and then more recently to the island of Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean for a military deployment. He had just returned to the U.S. several weeks prior to the onset of symptoms above. He reported multiple stops in Asia on his return trip but noted staying only in hotels. He did report adventurous eating.

None
exam_studies:
He had fever (38.1°C) and tachycardia (106 beats-per-minute) with otherwise normal vital signs and exam notable for abdominal distention and right upper abdomen pain with palpation. No other exam abnormalities were identified.

Initial lab work revealed leukocytosis of 13.6 x10 3 white blood cells/µL (85% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, <1% eosinophils), aspartate transaminase 56 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 356 U/L and total bilirubin 0.74 mg/dL. Computed Tomography scan of the abdomen with contrast revealed the hepatic abscess (Figure 1). Figure 1b: Coronal images of Computed Tomography of the abdomen with contrast demonstrating an 8.2 cm abscess in the right lobe of the liver.

diagnosis:
Amebic Liver Abscess

Initial infectious work-up included blood cultures, hepatic abscess cultures (bacterial and fungal), amebiasis antibodies, and echinococcal antibodies. Hepatic abscess fluid was obtained by Interventional Radiology who placed a drain in the abscess with 25 mL of fluid output (Figure 2). Subsequently, a stool culture and stool multiplex GI PCR panel was ordered, the latter of which returned with a positive result for Entamoeba histolytica. At this point the patient’s abscess fluid was separately run on the same assay, which also was positive for E. histolytica.
Figure 3. Figure 2: Fluid obtained after drain placement with Interventional Radiology demonstrating red-brown fluid with typical "anchovy paste" appearance.
Figure 2: Fluid obtained after drain placement with Interventional Radiology demonstrating red-brown fluid with typical "anchovy paste" appearance.

The patient was started on ceftriaxone and metronidazole on admission. After identification of E. histolytica via multiplex GI PCR panel, and with no growth noted on any bacterial culture, the patient was transitioned to monotherapy with metronidazole for 10 days followed by one week of paromomycin for luminal clearance. The patient demonstrated excellent recovery with no recurrence of any symptoms at three months post-treatment.

Hepatic abscesses can be severe and life-threatening infections and the ability to differentiate between bacterial, fungal, and parasitic etiologies quickly is vital to appropriate management. This patient presented for care in an E. histolytica non-endemic region with hepatic abscess and plausible exposure history for E. histolytica. His parasite was rapidly identified by stool test with a multiplex GI PCR panel leading to early changes to his treatment regimen with excellent outcome. While stool PCR has frequently been used to diagnose acute gastrointestinal illness from E. histolytica (3), the use of stool multiplex PCR testing to diagnose amebic liver abscess (ALA) is not clearly established. It is well-established that only 15-35% of patients with ALA have concurrent gastrointestinal symptoms or amebic colitis (4), and as a result older diagnostics like stool microscopy and stool antigen detection are thought to be less helpful for diagnosis of ALA (5). An apparent gap in the literature, however, is data describing the concurrent rate of luminal amebiasis in patients with ALA. Presumably, patients with sequelae of disseminated E. histolytica infection like ALA should still have concurrent luminal infection, whether symptomatic or not. It could then be reasonably extrapolated that in regions non-endemic for E. histolytica the identification of luminal infection in a patient with undifferentiated hepatic abscess would be strongly predictive of ALA.
In recent decades, stool PCR has become the gold standard for diagnosis of intestinal amebiasis with general sensitivity greater than 90% and specificity approaching 100% (1,6). Molecular testing has additional advantages of rapid turn-around time and ability to combine multiple targets into a single assay. In the case above the BioFire® FilmArray® GI Panel was used for diagnosis. This multiplex PCR panel was initially approved in 2014 with 22 separate targets including 4 parasites (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Entamoeba histolytica, and Giardia lamblia) (7). Regarding E. histolytica specifically, this assay has been shown to be 100% sensitive and 89-100% specific for detection of the parasite in stool. This is comparable to other currently FDA approved multiplex PCR panels like the BD MAX® Enteric Parasite Panel and the Luminex xTAG® GI Pathogen Panel, which also can test for E. histolytica (6).
Another consideration in cases like the one presented is potential utilization of multiplex GI PCR panels to test abscess fluid from an undifferentiated hepatic abscess that has been drained or aspirated. Multiple case reports (2,8) have reported successful identification of E. histolytica by testing liver abscess fluid on multiplex PCR panels that otherwise are designed for stool analysis, leading to rapid adjustment of therapy with good outcomes. Other studies have examined non-multiplex PCR in assessing liver abscess fluid. Othman et al reported positive real-time PCR detection of E. histolytica for 23 of 30 liver abscess fluid samples, with 6 of the 7 negative samples having positive bacterial cultures, indicating both high sensitivity and specificity of real-time PCR for this purpose (9). Ghelfenstein-Ferreira et al examined 12 liver abscess samples for E. histolytica with quantitative PCR noting a positive test for all five ALA patients and a negative test for all seven non-ALA patient (10). While multiplex PCR panels are not generally FDA-approved for testing liver abscess fluid, there are relatively clear data that in certain clinical circumstances this type of analysis can have a meaningful and positive impact on infection management.
In E. histolytica non-endemic regions the likelihood of incidental luminal amebiasis is low, so identification of the parasite by stool PCR on a multiplex GI PCR panel in the setting of an undifferentiated hepatic abscess should be highly predictive of ALA. If stool PCR testing for E. histolytica is available, then a practical approach could include two components. First, in patients with undifferentiated hepatic abscess and a plausible exposure history for E. histolytica for whom abscess fluid can be obtained we would recommend consideration of testing the fluid on a multiplex GI PCR panel. Alternatively, in patients with undifferentiated hepatic abscess and a plausible exposure history for E. histolytica in whom obtaining abscess fluid is not possible (abscess too small or in a high-risk location for drainage), we would recommend consideration of testing stool on a multiplex GI PCR panel. The positive and negative predictive value of this testing strategy should provide rapid and useful information to assist with management decisions.
