title: A man in his 70s presented with cough and weight loss for a month with new onset
history:
A man in his 70s presented with cough and weight loss for a month with new onset-hemoptysis. He denies chest pain, dyspnea, fevers, or chills.

The patient has a history of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) treated with a transurethral bladder tumor resection (TURBT) about 6 years prior to admission, followed by intravesical BCG installation a few years prior to admission, remote squamous cell carcinoma of the neck treated with radiation, hypertension, and a recently diagnosed proximal aortic arch pseudoaneurysm for which he was undergoing evaluation for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) with a graft.

The patient was born and raised in the southwestern United States, and currently lives in the rural Pacific northwest. He had traveled in Asia. He enjoys gardening and fishing. He has no history of tobacco, alcohol, or injection drug use. He lives with his wife and dogs.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. He had a temperature of 99.1 F/ 37.3 C, blood pressure of 189/95 mmHg, and heart rate of 76 beats/minute. On auscultation, he was noted to have diminished breath sounds in the left upper lung field and intermittent cough. The rest of the physical exam was otherwise normal.

The routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic profile were within normal limits. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed a descending aortic arch pseudoaneurysm measuring 1.2 x 1.0 cm. He was also noted to have a left upper lobe lung infiltrate measuring 4.4 x 2.9 cm, adjacent to the pseudoaneurysm and micronodules in the left upper and lower lobes. No microbiologic studies were done at that time.

Due to the suspicion that a fistula between the pseudoaneurysm and bronchus was causing his hemoptysis, the patient underwent an urgent thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) with a graft, and no fistula was found. Hemoptysis resolved soon after this procedure.
A follow-up CT two months after the TEVAR showed persistence of the left upper lobe infiltrate, now resembling a mass, demonstrating this was not due to the aortic pseudoaneurysm. The patient underwent work-up for a suspected malignancy. Cystoscopy was negative for malignancy. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET) scan showed increased metabolic activity within the left upper lobe, left first rib at the costovertebral junction, left transverse process of the T1 vertebrae, and T2 to T4 thoracic vertebral bodies (Figures 1 and 2). A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed multiple punctate foci of enhancement in the supratentorial and infratentorial areas of the brain. He also underwent infectious workup at this time including serologies for a variety of endemic fungal, atypical/zoonotic infections (including Brucella spp., Coxiella spp., Toxoplasma gondii), bacterial blood cultures, cryptococcal antigen testing, and fungal blood cultures, all of which were negative.
Bronchoscopy with fine-needle aspiration (FNA) and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed to evaluate the mass. Microscopic examination of the biopsies showed necrotizing mucosa and caseating granulomatous inflammation with no malignant cells. Bacterial cultures from the BAL samples grew Streptococcus salivarius and alpha-hemolytic Streptococci. No acid-fast bacilli (AFB) or fungal organism was identified.
CT-guided biopsy of the vertebral body was performed, and it showed non-necrotizing granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes without evidence of malignancy. Bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures and smears of the bone biopsy were negative.
After an exhaustive workup, he had a follow-up CT scan five months after TEVAR that showed an enlarging left upper lobe mass measuring about 3.2 x 5.2 x 8.1 cm, increased in size craniocaudally to 8.1 cm from 4.6 cm on prior examination (Figure 3).

Figure 1: FDG PET scan; Increased metabolic activity in posterior medial left upper lobe mass; extending into L hilar region.
Figure 2. Figure 2: FDG PET scan; Multiple foci of metabolic activity involving the T1-T4 four vertebral bodies.
Figure 2: FDG PET scan; Multiple foci of metabolic activity involving the T1-T4 four vertebral bodies.
Figure 3. Figure 3: CT scan of the chest without contrast; Left upper lobe infiltration closely related to aortic stent graft, measuring ~ 3.2 x 5.2 x 8.1 cm, increased in size from prior study.

diagnosis:
Disseminated Mycobacterium bovis - BCG infection

He underwent resection of the lung mass five months after initial presentation and during the surgery, it was noted that the mass was densely adherent to the aortic arch. The lung parenchyma down to the hilum was necrotic with purulent material within it. Pathology demonstrated coalescing necrotizing granulomas with fibrosis and vascular erosions (Figure 4). While bacterial and fungal cultures were negative, AFB smears were positive (Figure 5).
Molecular testing for mycobacterial DNA (GeneXpert MTB-RIF) and 16S rRNA sequencing on the purulent material identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. No rpoB gene mutation was detected. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that the organism was resistant to pyrazinamide but susceptible to rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and streptomycin. Given his history of BCG therapy, the diagnosis of disseminated Mycobacterium bovis - BCG infection was strongly considered, and the isolate was sent for further sequencing to the Centers for Disease control (CDC) reference lab. Sequencing confirmed M. bovis -BCG strain and demonstrated no additional resistance.
Figure 4. Figure 4: Pathology; Lung, 1.25x. Coalescing necrotizing granulomas with fibrosis and vascular erosion (Courtesy of Dr. David Sauer).
Figure 4: Pathology; Lung, 1.25x. Coalescing necrotizing granulomas with fibrosis and vascular erosion (Courtesy of Dr. David Sauer).
Figure 5. Figure 5: Pathology Lung, AFB stain, 40x. Multiple aggregates of acid-fast bacilli on AFB stain (Courtesy of Dr. David Sauer).
Figure 5: Pathology Lung, AFB stain, 40x. Multiple aggregates of acid-fast bacilli on AFB stain (Courtesy of Dr. David Sauer).

Infectious Diseases was formally consulted when the AFB were isolated from the surgical cultures, about five months after initial presentation. The patient was initially placed on empiric therapy for disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE). After the susceptibility testing showed that the isolate was resistant to pyrazinamide, it was stopped. This susceptibility pattern in the setting of previous BCG exposure suggested that this organism was M. bovis - BCG rather than M. tuberculosis.
Treatment was complicated first by rash and oral mucosal ulcers thought to be a drug eruption related to ethambutol. He later developed severe thrombocytopenia requiring steroids and intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), ultimately diagnosed as rifampin-induced immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). He was ultimately switched to therapy with isoniazid and levofloxacin for disseminated M. bovis - BCG infection with a plan for a minimum of 12 months of treatment.
The patient presented again to the hospital about 6 months after starting treatment with repeat episodes of hemoptysis. Upper endoscopy was performed, and the findings were consistent with aorto-esophageal fistula, thought to be associated with the disseminated M. bovis BCG infection. The treatment for this would involve esophagectomy along with aortic resection. Due to the high risk of this procedure, the patient declined further treatment.

Mycobacterium bovis - BCG is typically a nonpathogenic species of M. bovis which was developed in the 1920s from over 200 re-cultures of M. bovis. It was initially produced as a tuberculosis vaccine and has since also become a standard immunotherapeutic treatment for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer [1]. This treatment is typically well tolerated, but local and systemic BCG infections can occur. The incidence of BCG infection following bladder instillation varies from 1%-4.3% in different studies. About half (34.4%-56.1%) of these cases involve disseminated infections [2-4]. The BCG organism can remain in the urinary tract for over a year and disruption of the urothelial barrier from instillation soon after transurethral resection of the bladder, traumatic catheterization, or urinary tract infection may lead to hematogenous spread of the organism [4]. This patient underwent TURBT prior to BCG instillation, which is a known predisposing factor for disseminated infection.
M. bovis is part of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which is a group of closely genetically related species including M. tuberculosis, M. bovis (including M. bovis - BCG), M. africanum, M. microti, and M. caprae. These species can all cause disease in humans but differ in epidemiology and drug resistance [5]. Initial molecular testing in this patient’s case identified M tuberculosis complex, and did not discriminate between species within the complex. While infection caused by M. bovis and M. tuberculosis can present similarly, M. bovis is more likely to cause extrapulmonary disease. Due to this patient’s travel history, M. tuberculosis could not be completely ruled out, and therefore therapy with empiric treatment with RIPE was started. M. bovis is intrinsically resistant to pyrazinamide due to a single point mutation in the pcnA gene from C to G at position 169, which impedes the ability of the enzyme pyrazinamidase to convert pyrazinamide into its active form, pyrazinoic acid [6]. Therefore, the empiric regimen for M. bovis excludes pyrazinamide from the standard RIPE therapy for M. tuberculosis. Evidence supporting treatment regimens for M. bovis is overall limited, especially in instances of drug resistance or intolerance.
In this patient with toxicity from rifampin, one of the treatment cornerstones, we must rely on data for multi-drug resistant M. tuberculosis treatment, expert consultation, and individual sensitivities [9,10]. Fluoroquinolones can be used for rifampin resistant M. tuberculosis with demonstrated sensitivity to fluoroquinolones, but data for the efficacy of M. bovis treatment is lacking [11]. This case demonstrates a relatively rare complication of BCG instillation for the treatment of bladder cancer and highlights the paucity of evidence to inform treatment of M. bovis (including M. bovis - BCG), especially if complicated by drug resistance or intolerance.

title: A woman in her early 60s with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy leading to end-stage h
history:
A woman in her early 60s with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy leading to end-stage heart failure and a history of Hodgkin's lymphoma (treated with radiation therapy many years ago) underwent a heart transplant. Several months post-transplant, she presented with progressively worsening abdominal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) and rash.

Nonischemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure reduced ejection fraction secondary to chemotherapy for Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Born in and raised in the United States; has resided in the Midwest for the past 25 years. No current pets, but previously owned dogs and cats and had a bird many years ago. Never smoker, social alcohol use, no illicit substances.

Tacrolimus, Mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, valganciclovir.
exam_studies:
The patient appeared well. The blood pressure was 128/78, pulse 97 beats per minute, temperature 97.8F (36.5C), and respirations 18 breaths per minute. Exam was remarkable for pruritic maculopapular rash on her trunk and buttocks. Abdomen was soft, non-distended, and tender to palpation in epigastrium. No rebound or guarding. The examination was otherwise normal.
Figure 1. Abdominal skin rash

Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL (reference range 11.5-15.5), hematocrit 31.4% (reference range 36-46%), platelets 314 k/uL (reference range 150-400), white cell count 3.7 k/uL (reference range 3.7-11.0), with 29% neutrophils, 14% lymphocytes, 43% eosinophils. Serum electrolytes and chemistries were normal except for a creatinine of 1.46 mg/dL (reference 0.58-0.96). C-reactive protein 3.4 mg/dL (reference range < 0.9).
Computed tomography (CT) Abdomen/Pelvis demonstrated borderline to mildly dilated loops of small bowel in the lower abdomen with suggestion of wall thickening, possibly enteritis. No pneumatosis, portal venous gas, or free intraperitoneal air. CT Chest showed new diffuse lung opacities, differential including including pulmonary edema, atypical pneumonia, or alveolar hemorrhage.
Figure 2. Skin, abdomen punch biopsy
Figure 5. Skin, abdomen punch biopsy

Pre-transplant screening was unremarkable, including negative Strongyloides IgG. The patient received standard immunizations. She had minimal travel history outside of the U.S., with a past trip to Mexico over 20 years prior. Post-transplant she was placed on standard immunosuppressive therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. She was also on valganciclovir and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. She had undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) approximately 2 weeks post-transplant for dysphagia and odynophagia with evidence of many superficial esophageal ulcers. Pathology demonstrated active esophagitis with granulation tissue, with special stains negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV) and PAS/D. She was discharged with pantoprazole which was continued until re-admission 2 months later.
Initial workup, including stool pathogen panel, blood cultures, and CMV and EBV DNA levels, was negative. On hospital day 4, an EGD revealed erosive gastropathy and a CT A/P raised concern for ileus. Empiric ganciclovir was started due to concern for tissue invasive CMV infection. That evening, the patient became confused and developed hypoxia, necessitating transfer to the ICU and intubation with mechanical ventilation. Blood cultures obtained at this time were positive for gram negative rods, which were subsequently identified as Enterobacter cloacae.
diagnosis:
Donor-derived Strongyloidiasis Hyperinfection Syndrome with cutaneous involvement.

EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy)
Small bowel, duodenum, biopsy: Acute duodenitis with Strongyloides organisms. CMV, HSV and adenovirus immunohistochemistry negative (Figure 3)
Stomach, antrum, biopsy: Positive for Strongyloides organisms. Portions of oxyntic and antral type gastric mucosa with chronic inactive gastritis. Negative for Helicobacter pylori organisms on routine staining. Negative for intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia
Skin abdomen punch biopsy (Figure 2)
Orthokeratosis overlying an essentially unremarkable epidermis. Within the superficial and deep dermis, there is a mildly dense perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with numerous admixed eosinophils. Additionally, there are basophilic exogenous structures, consistent with nematode larvae, percolating between collagen bundles within the dermis and subcutaneous tissues.
Bronchoscopy with BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage):
Cell count and differential: 13,350 RBCs, 48 nucleated cells with 33% neutrophils, 19% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, 37% macrophages and 6% eosinophils.
BAL O&P: rare Strongyloides stercoralis
Lumbar puncture:
Cell count and differential: 9 RBCs, 3 nucleated cells (7% neutrophils, 92% lymphocytes, 1% monocytes)
Protein 41, glucose 169
Bacterial Culture: Vancomycin resistant Enterococcus faecium
Right ventricle, endomyocardial biopsy:
Foci of interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrates with numerous eosinophils. There is one biopsy fragment with a granuloma containing an elongated wrinkled eosinophilic structure with numerous faint blue nuclei. In the setting of disseminated Strongyloides infestation, the morphology of this structure is consistent with a degenerated Strongyloides larva.
Figure 3. Small bowel, duodenum, biopsy. Acute duodenitis with strongyloides organisms.
Figure 4. Stool Ova & Parasite test
Figure 6. Stool Ova & Parasite test

Strongyloides was identified on duodenal biopsy, prompting immediate initiation of oral ivermectin. Because pre-transplant screening of the patient for Strongyloides IgG was negative, there was concern for donor-derived infection which was later confirmed in another recipient from the same donor. A stool O&P confirmed presence of Strongyloides.
Prednisone dosing was reduced and ESBL Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia was treated with meropenem. Despite initial therapy, the patient’s condition worsened, requiring intensive care unit admission for respiratory failure and intubation. Bronchoscopy with BAL demonstrated diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) and O&P of BAL fluid confirmed presence of Strongyloides larvae, leading to the diagnosis of hyperinfection syndrome. Due to persistent encephalopathy, a lumbar puncture was obtained, with E. faecium on culture which was treated with linezolid.
The abdominal maculopapular rash noted on admission became progressively more purpuric and spread to involve her periumbilical region, bilateral flanks and bilateral proximal anterior thighs (Figure 1). Dermatology was consulted due to high suspicion of cutaneous strongyloidiasis. A punch skin biopsy was obtained and histological examination showed basophilic exogenous structures, consistent with nematode larvae, percolating between collagen bundles within the dermis and subcutaneous tissues (Figure 2).
Patient was initiated on oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day the same day that the EGD results were reported. Due to the development of ileus with concern for impaired enteric absorption, an Investigational New Drug (IND) application was submitted and approved by the FDA for subcutaneous administration of a veterinary preparation of ivermectin, which was started on hospital day 9, at which point her PO ivermectin was discontinued. She finished a course of meropenem for ESBL Enterobacter bacteremia. Stool O&Ps were performed every 3 days while on subcutaneously administered ivermectin. O&P became negative after 12 days of ivermectin (9 days of subcutaneous ivermectin) and she was transitioned back to oral ivermectin once bowel function returned.

This case highlights the potential for donor-derived Strongyloides infection in heart transplant recipients, underscoring the need for vigilant screening in high-risk populations. Early recognition and treatment with ivermectin are critical in preventing progression to hyperinfection syndrome.
Additionally, this case demonstrates both disseminated disease in which there is spread of organism to organs outside of the normal life cycle as well as hyperinfection syndrome, characterized by an accelerated autoinfection.
Treatment challenges exist and include ileus or poor gastrointestinal absorption of ivermectin. In this case, it prompted an IND application for subcutaneous administration of ivermectin.
Cutaneous manifestation of disseminated strongyloidiasis are rare, but periumbilical purpura resembling thumbprints can be a pathognomonic physical exam finding to aid in early diagnosis.

title: A man in his forties with past medical history of eosinophilic esophagitis prese
history:
A man in his forties with past medical history of eosinophilic esophagitis presented with fever, shortness of breath on exertion and worsened cough. His shortness of breath and cough had been present for the past month. He had been prescribed 2 courses of oral antibiotics for presumed pneumonia with failure to improve. There was associated 20 pound weight loss, fever to 102 degrees F, and night sweats. He denied any sick contacts, household pets. He filled a bird feeder. He denied any substance use. His work involved a desk job.

Eosinophilic esophagitis

• 1 month prior he had traveled to Midwest for cave exploration
• Also has history of travel to East Asia and Europe

Omeprazole
exam_studies:
• BP 120/70, HR 87, Afebrile, RR 25
• SpO2 84% on room air
• General: Well-built male, visibly fatigued and with labored breathing
• Lungs: Bilateral crackles at lung bases
• Abdomen: Soft non-tender, non-distended abdomen
• Extremities: lower extremities without any significant edema
• Skin: violaceous nodule on right lower leg and left upper chest

• CBC: WBC 25.2k (87% neutrophils), Hb 13.5, PLT 170k
• CMP: Creatinine 0.9. Liver enzymes within normal limits
• Lactic acid 1.7 • Procalcitonin 0.21
Figure 1 (CT Chest): “Extensive consolidative opacities within right lung with regions of central cavitation”
Figure 1. Initial CT from 2022

Hospital Course
The patient was started on Vancomycin and Piperacillin/Tazobactam. He was requiring 3-5L of supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula. Further workup of his pneumonia included a bronchoscopy. During his bronchoscopy, fungating tracheal lesions were noted and a biopsy was done. These slides are shown below:
Figure 2. Pathology Slide 1(H&E stain)
Figure 3. Pathology Slide 2 (GMS) - Respiratory viral panel (Negative)
diagnosis:
Disseminated blastomycosis complicated by pulmonary alveolar proteinosis

- Streptococcus pneumoniae urine Ag (Negative)
- Urine Legionella Ag (Negative)
- Interferon gamma release assay (Negative)
- Blood cultures (Negative)
- Serology for Histoplasma, Blastomycosis, Aspergillus, Coccidoides were negative
- 1, 3 Beta D Glucan 127pg/mL(< 60 pg/ mL normal)
- Urine histoplasma Ag (positive >15ng/ mL)
- Urine Blastomycosis Ag (positive above the limit of quantification, >14.7 ng/mL)
Bronchoscopy
• Fungal culture Blastomyces spp
• Routine culture w/ gram stain Negative
• AFB culture Negative
• Pathology from the tracheal biopsy displayed numerous fungal yeast forms compatible with Blastomyces species
With the presence of moderate to severe pulmonary symptoms, skin lesions and tracheal lesions, the patient was diagnosed with disseminated blastomycosis and was started on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B. A few days later he was noted to develop a headache and agreed to a lumbar puncture. His CSF analysis revealed WBC 1, RBC 3, Protein 28, Glucose 68 and positive Blastomyces Ag 1.59 (0.2-14.7 ng/mL). There were negative fungal, routine, and AFB CSF cultures. An MRI Brain also was unrevealing for any signs of meningitis or focal abscess.
Primary Diagnosis: CNS Disseminated Blastomycosis

Patient was administered intravenous liposomal Amphotericin B for 2 weeks and then transitioned to oral voriconazole. He had therapeutic serum levels throughout treatment. He continued voriconazole for seven months when he developed visual symptoms and a skin rash. He was then switched over to oral itraconazole. He continued itraconazole with therapeutic serum levels. Over the year the patient continued to improve clinically yet his Blastomyces antigenuria persisted despite antifungal treatment. CT chest done 1 year later displayed improvement of the consolidation with residual fibroatelectasis (Figure 4).
While on treatment for Blastomycosis, he was noted to develop new ground glass opacities bilaterally on chest CT(Figure 5). At that time, he displayed no symptoms of dyspnea, cough, fever, night sweats, or fatigue. Work-up for atypical pneumonia was negative. A repeat CT chest few months later showed persistence of these ground glass opacities and a crazy-paving pattern (Figure 6). Patient underwent repeat bronchoscopy, which showed normal airways and no endobronchial lesions. Bronchial cultures showed rare Aspergillus niger and Penicillium species, both of questionable significance. Bronchial Blastomyces antigen and beta D-glucan were negative. Patient was switched to posaconazole when 4 months after these imaging findings he started to complain of shortness of breath on exertion, dry cough and fatigue. During this interval he also had a workup done for immunodeficiency which was non-reactive for HIV and negative for complement or IgG deficiency and his CD4 count was 1184. A repeat CT (Figure 7) displayed further worsening of the ground glass opacities and interlobular septal thickening. Patient became hypoxic requiring oxygen supplementation at rest. He underwent VATS-assisted lung biopsy of the right middle and lower lobes. The pathology displayed granulomatous inflammation and fungal organisms consistent with blastomycosis. There were features consistent with alveolar proteinosis such as eosinophilic proteinaceous material filling the alveolar spaces(Figure 8 and 9). Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis(PAP).
He was re-initiated on IV Amphotericin B and completed a 30-day course after which he was switched back to itraconazole. Antibody testing for granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was positive, suggesting an autoimmune etiology for the alveolar proteinosis. Our patient was thus started on treatment with whole lung lavage and GM-CSF replacement therapy and has had some relative improvement in CT imaging although continues to require oxygen. His oxygen requirement varies with level of exertion and his treatment is ongoing.
(Figure 8 and 9) Pathology: “ Alveolar spaces are filled with proteinaceous material consistent with alveolar proteinosis. There are also patchy areas of granulomatous inflammation in which multinucleated cells contain fungal structures. The fungal structures are compatible with blastomycosis ”
Second diagnosis: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
Figure 4. 1 year into treatment (2023)
Figure 5. Early 2024, 1st instance of worsening
Figure 6. 2 months later
Figure 7. 2025, prior to VATS guided biopsy
Figure 8. Alveolar spaces are filled with proteinaceous material consistent with alveolar proteinosis.
Figure 9. Alveolar spaces are filled with proteinaceous material consistent with alveolar proteinosis.

Although there has been documentation of infections associated with development of PAP (for example, nocardia, non-tuberculous mycobacteria and even fungal infections such as Histoplasma, Aspergillus, and cryptococcus), there had been only one other case of blastomycosis documented in 1995 (1).
That was a case of a middle-aged female who was diagnosed with blastomycosis and PAP simultaneously, yet the diagnosis of PAP was made only after she continued to have non-resolving changes on imaging leading to a biopsy. Her severity of disease, serology, and antigen test results were not discussed (2).
Our case is noteworthy because it raises many questions on the pathophysiology and natural course of infection with blastomycosis. This case describes a patient with disseminated blastomycosis, who seemingly improved but subsequently developed radiological changes suggestive of a new pathology. His urinary antigen declined but did not become undetectable. He subsequently had an increase in the urine antigen titer (Figure 10).
Blastomycosis is a fungal infection characterized by a granulomatous reaction. It has a dimorphic nature that allows it to present as mold in the environment, and yeast form at body temperature. Blastomyces causes infection by the inhalation of conidia from the environment and has many virulence factors. Some of these factors include its thermotolerance and intracellular survival. With the inhalation of the conidia, the alveolar macrophages engulf the organisms which facilitate the development of the yeast form of the fungus. These yeast forms develop a protein known as BAD-1 (Blastomyces-adhesin-1) on the cell wall. This protein inhibits the production of TNF-alpha by macrophages and neutrophils; this impairs the immune response, which permits survival of yeast. In addition, BAD-1 also inhibits CD4 T lymphocyte activation. Pulmonary infection is usually the primary source of entry for the fungus (3).
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is a syndrome characterized by alveolar surfactant accumulation. The most common type of PAP is primary, most commonly, autoimmune PAP, which involves antibodies against granulocyte macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF) resulting in a decrease in functional macrophages (4). Both Blastomyces and PAP cause dysfunctional macrophages (5). Treatment of PAP often consists of whole lung lavage with or without anti-GM-CSF antibodies.
Our case is the second documented case of blastomycosis associated pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. Furthermore, it is the only known, documented case of disseminated blastomycosis associated with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. This case highlights a few important points giving insight into management of the disease as well as some interplay between the two disease states. It can be observed that the urinary antigen titers create an excellent test to monitor response to treatment. In our patient when the blastomycosis infection was at the forefront of the pulmonary disease we can see that we had significantly elevated titers. With appropriate therapy, we saw a reassuring decline in urinary antigen levels and symptomatic improvement, indicating the effectiveness of the treatment. When a new onset of respiratory symptoms occurs, more than one year into treatment, it is important to note that there is no concurrent rise in urinary antigen titers. Retrospectively, it can be concluded that this was an accurate translation of the fact that there was not a relapse in infection. Rather, it was the persistence of the Blastomyces yeast form, allowing for a persistently low-level urine titer. In this case, addressing the new onset pulmonary findings with a lung biopsy was the right approach as a new disease process needed to be considered. Additionally, the recognition of this association between pulmonary blastomycosis and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis will allow for better awareness of this potential complication.

title: A man in his late 60s was referred to the hospital by his primary care physician
history:
A man in his late 60s was referred to the hospital by his primary care physician due to a significant change in cognition and behavior as well as an unintentional weight loss of 40 lbs over several months. The patient was noted to have become forgetful and confused and had made delusional statements. He was noted by his daughter to have developed difficulty performing activities of daily living and behavioral changes. He additionally reported malaise, intermittent headache, neck pain, and occasional muscle spasms. He denied fever or chills. He had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection a few weeks prior based on dysuria and pelvic discomfort and these two symptoms had resolved with antibiotic treatment.

The patient's medical history included well-controlled HIV, genital herpes simplex virus, hepatitis C virus that cleared without treatment, cleared hepatitis B virus, remote deep vein thrombosis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and chronic pain. His surgical history included penetrating keratoplasty, vitrectomy, and corneal transplant several years prior related to an open globe injury.

He had last smoked cigarettes and used substances thirty years prior, with no substance use since that time. Twenty years prior to presentation, he had been incarcerated for one year and received tattoos during that time. He previously worked as a painter. He denied animal exposure or international travel. He lived in a house in the mid-Atlantic United States. He had not been sexually active in many years.

His most recent antiretroviral regimen included darunavir, ritonavir, lamivudine, and doravirine. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis. He had also been recently treated for a urinary tract infection with ciprofloxacin.
exam_studies:
On presentation, the patient was nontoxic but appeared mildly frustrated. His vital signs were within normal limits. He did not display nuchal rigidity though restricted mobility of the neck with tight muscles was noted. He was oriented to person and place, but not to time. Cranial nerves were normal aside from asymmetric and irregular pupils. Muscle tone, strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, cerebellar testing, and gait were normal. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score was 11 out of 30 points, including deficits in visuospatial function, naming, abstraction, and delayed recall. The examination was otherwise normal.

He was mildly anemic with hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL (reference range 13.9-16.3 g/dL), with otherwise unremarkable blood counts. Complete metabolic panel showed chronically elevated creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL (reference range 0.6-1.3 mg/dL), which was at baseline, and was otherwise unremarkable. Urinalysis showed small leukocyte esterase (reference range: negative) with 6 white blood cells per high powered field (reference range < =5 per high powered field). Urine toxicology screen was consistent with adherence to prescribed oxycodone. His ammonia level was normal. His CD4+ cell count was 1,121/mm^3 with undetectable HIV viral load. Cerebrospinal fluid collected via lumbar puncture contained 1 white blood cell/cu mm (reference range 1-5/cu mm), normal glucose of 51 mg/dL (reference range 50-75 mg/dL), and elevated protein of 56.8 mg/dL (reference range 15-45 mg/dL).
Computed tomography of his head showed mild areas of periventricular and subcortical white matter hypoattenuation in the brain. Computed tomography angiogram of the neck showed multilevel degenerative changes in the cervical spine most pronounced at C5-6 where there was moderate canal and severe bilateral foraminal stenosis. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unrevealing.
Electroencephalography showed rhythmic slow activity and intermittent generalized periodic discharges bilaterally. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse cortical restricted diffusion in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres sparing the mesial temporal lobes, insular cortices, and posterolateral frontal lobes associated with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) hyperintensity without associated enhancement (Figure 1, Figure 2).
Figure 1. Signal hyperintensity in the bilateral cerebral cortex on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI).
Figure 2. Signal hyperintensity in the bilateral cerebral cortex on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR).
diagnosis:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease

There was concern for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease based on the appearance of his brain magnetic resonance imaging. He underwent a second lumbar puncture to obtain additional studies. Cerebrospinal fluid studies showed 1 white blood cell/cu mm (reference range 1-5/cu mm), normal glucose of 63 mg/dL (reference range 50-75 mg/dL), elevated protein of 49.3 mg/dL (reference range 15-45 mg/dL), a markedly elevated 14-3-3 protein level of 21194 AU/mL (reference range: less than 30-1999 AU/mL), elevated T-tau protein level of 5377 pg/mL (reference range: 0-1149 pg/mL), and positive real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC, a highly sensitive and specific test for prion disease), consistent with prion disease. Additional microbiologic testing from cerebrospinal fluid was negative, including for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, JC virus, venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), cryptococcal antigen, toxoplasma antibodies, and bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures. Blood cultures and Treponema pallidum antibody were negative.

The patient was connected to palliative and supportive home services. He was ultimately enrolled in hospice care as he experienced progressive, expected decline. He passed away three months after discharge.

The differential diagnosis of infectious causes of cognitive and behavioral changes in persons living with HIV is broad and includes opportunistic processes such as cryptococcosis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and toxoplasmosis. In patients without depressed CD4+ cell counts, however, non-opportunistic pathogens must be considered. Late neurosyphilis, HIV-associated dementia, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease can cause progressive cognitive and psychiatric deterioration, though the latter is rare. A cerebrospinal fluid profile that includes elevated protein with normal glucose and absence of pleocytosis can be seen in all three conditions, though pleocytosis can be seen in neurosyphilis and HIV-associated dementia (1,2). CSF VDRL may be positive in neurosyphilis, though sensitivity is poor (1).
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a uniformly fatal cause of neuropsychiatric deterioration. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as behavior changes, memory deficits, mood changes, or psychotic or delusional features, occur in all cases. Myoclonus is often, but not always, present. This patient developed right upper extremity myoclonus two months after his initial diagnosis after experiencing further neurologic decline. Pyramidal, extrapyramidal, or cerebellar symptoms may also occur (3).
There are multiple categories of prion disease. The most common is the sporadic form, but genetic and acquired forms also exist. Iatrogenic CJD, a subset of acquired CJD, has been reported after cadaveric pituitary hormone administration, neurosurgical procedures including grafting of dural mater, and corneal transplant (3).
Our patient had undergone corneal transplantation seven years prior to diagnosis, raising concern for iatrogenic CJD. Iatrogenic CJD related to corneal transplant has been reported in the literature, though without diagnosis of CJD in the donor, the possibility of the much more common sporadic CJD cannot be ruled out (4).
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is typically non-inflammatory with normal glucose and can demonstrate increased protein in about one-third of patients (5). 14-3-3 or tau protein are commonly elevated, though neither is disease-specific (6). More recently, real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) has become available as a superior test with 92% sensitivity and 100% specificity for prion disease (7). In RT-QuIC, shaking induces a conformational change in recombinant prion protein by the disease-associated prion protein (PrPSc) in a chain reaction, resulting in aggregation of misfolded proteins which bind to fluorescent dye and are quantified in real time.
MRI frequently demonstrates signal hyperintensity in the cerebral cortex (“cortical ribboning”) or caudate/putamen on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), as demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2 on our patient's MRI (8). “Hockey stick sign,” formed by medial and pulvinar thalamic hyperintensity, can be seen in variant CJD. On EEG, periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) or generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) can be seen (9).
Definite diagnosis of CJD requires neuropathologic confirmation. The probable diagnosis of CJD can be ascertained from a positive RT-QuIC test plus neuropsychiatric features. If RT-QuIC is not available, the CDC defines a probable diagnosis as progressive dementia with two of four characteristic clinical features (akinetic mutism, myoclonus, visual/cerebellar signs, or pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs), a consistent diagnostic test (EEG with PSWCs, positive 14-3-3 assay in a patient with less than 2 years of symptoms, or brain magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showing increased signal in the caudate/putamen or at least two cortical regions), and lack of diagnostics that suggest an alternative diagnosis (8).
There is no effective treatment for CJD. Management is focused on supportive and palliative care. Genetic testing can be offered to family members for genetic forms of the disease, though appropriate counseling should be provided. Prognosis is poor and most patients pass away within one year of diagnosis. To our knowledge, there have been 7 prior cases reported of confirmed or probable CJD in persons living with HIV; data is therefore limited in this population (10-15).

history:

Initially presumed to be an insect bite, the lesion progressed to ulceration with surrounding erythema (Figure 1); treatment with a 5 day course of cephalexin and topical antibiotics provided no improvement. Subsequently he presented to his primary care provider with persistence of the lesion and localized pain. Doxycycline was initiated for 10 days, again with no improvement. Roughly three weeks after the initial presentation, dermatologic evaluation noted a healing violaceous plaque at the original site (Figure 2A) and a new pustular lesion distal to it (Figure 2B), along with a tender, enlarging subcutaneous nodule on the medial left elbow. Dermatology consultation was pursued, and punch biopsies of the dorsal hand and medial elbow lesions were performed, with specimens sent for culture and histopathologic evaluation. Wound swabs were also collected for herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), and Mpox testing.
diagnosis:
Cutaneous Mycobacterium marinum infection with sporotrichoid spread.

Hand radiographs showed mild soft tissue swelling without evidence of fracture or foreign body. Bacterial cultures demonstrated no growth. Histopathology of the hand lesion revealed a mixed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate with rare acid-fast bacilli identified on Fite and AFB stains. The elbow biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation, consistent with a ruptured follicular process. AFB cultures were negative; however, PCR testing confirmed the presence of Mycobacterium marinum DNA via hsp65 probe. PCR testing for HSV, VZV, and Mpox was initially ordered but canceled following the biopsy findings. Laboratory studies, including Complete Blood Count, Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), ANCA, SPEP, and IFE, and HIV were within normal limits. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold test was positive, prompting referral to Infectious Diseases. He was evaluated by Infectious Diseases approximately six weeks after symptom onset.

Initial empiric therapy following biopsy results included ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, and ethambutol. After PCR confirmation, the regimen was narrowed to doxycycline, azithromycin, and continued ethambutol. Surgical debridement was not required. At 11 weeks, re-epithelialization and resolution of nodules were noted. Treatment was concluded based on the clinical appearance and resolution of the lesions, and the patient was advised to continue close monitoring.

The patient’s ulcerative lesion and lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics prompted consideration of both non-infectious and infectious etiologies. Among non-infectious causes, pyoderma gangrenosum was considered due to its characteristic painful ulcers with undermined borders. Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma was also on the differential, as it can present with solitary or multiple skin lesions and requires histopathologic and immunohistochemical analysis for diagnosis. Infectious causes were also explored. Sporothrix schenckii, typically associated with traumatic inoculation, can present with nodular lymphangitis and was a plausible consideration.
Cutaneous tuberculosis was considered due to the violaceous ulceration, surrounding erythema, and lymphatic spread. Nocardia species, particularly N. brasiliensis, can cause ulcerative skin lesions and pustules; however, this is more common in immunocompromised individuals, which did not fit this patient's immune profile. Cutaneous leishmaniasis was considered, given its potential to cause chronic ulcerative lesions with indurated borders, though less likely without relevant endemic travel.
Lastly, Bacillus anthracis was included in the differential due to its ability to cause ulcerative lesions with prominent edema; confirmation would require lesion culture and PCR testing. PCR testing ultimately confirmed Mycobacterium marinum infection.
Notably, AFB cultures failed to yield growth, likely due to the organism’s distinct temperature requirements. While standard AFB cultures are incubated at 35–37°C, M. marinum grows optimally at approximately 30°C, and may not grow at typical incubation temperatures—leading to potential false-negative results. This underscores the importance of clinical suspicion and appropriate laboratory conditions when M. marinum is part of the differential diagnosis.
Although commonly associated with aquatic exposure, M. marinum infections can also arise in the absence of such contact; exotic pets (iguanas and African pygmy hedgehog) are an underrecognized potential source. The incubation period is variable and may be prolonged—ranging from 3 weeks to 9 months—making exposure history difficult to pinpoint. Additionally, false-positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold results may occur due to shared RD1 antigens with M. tuberculosis. There is no standardized treatment regimen for M. marinum; prolonged combination antibiotic therapy is often required. Surgical intervention should be tailored to the individual patient, though early clinical improvement may permit conservative, non-surgical management. This patient’s likely source of infection was his pet ferrets who had died a few weeks prior. Ferrets are known to be a species more innately susceptible to mycobacterial infections and have been used as animal models in studying these infections.

title: A woman in her 80s presented with a 2-week history of bilateral wrist pain, swel
history:
A woman in her 80s presented with a 2-week history of bilateral wrist pain, swelling, erythema and purulent drainage. Three weeks prior to admission, she developed visual disturbances and was diagnosed with giant cell arteritis (GCA), for which she was initiated on high-dose corticosteroids. Approximately one week later, she developed bilateral wrist pain, erythema, and edema, more pronounced on the right. A blister subsequently formed on the right wrist, which ruptured and began draining purulent fluid. She also reported systemic symptoms including fevers and chills. She presented to the hospital following a fall after a syncopal episode and was found to have bilateral segmental/subsegmental pulmonary emboli.

Right open distal radius fracture many years ago with hardware placement. Right wrist septic arthritis several years ago; at the time, the hardware was removed and she received a course of antibiotics.

No recent travel or animal exposures. She had a recent dental cleaning.

Prednisone 20 milligram (mg) once daily. Apixaban.

The right upper extremity exam revealed edema and erythema from distal phalanges to distal forearm. A 1.5 cm (about 0.59 in) open wound was noted over the radial dorsal hand draining purulent fluid. Tenderness was noted at the distal radius. No motor, sensory or perfusion deficits were noted. The left upper extremity exam revealed mild edema from distal phalanges to wrist, tenderness at distal radius. No motor, sensory or perfusion deficits were noted.

Biopsy revealed acute and chronic osteomyelitis of the right distal radius, scaphoid, and lunate, with granuloma containing yeast and hyphal fungal forms (see Figure 1 and 2).

Antibiotics were discontinued, and voriconazole was initiated at 400 mg twice daily for two doses, followed by 200 mg twice daily. Therapeutic drug levels were confirmed after one week. Despite treatment, the patient had persistent right wrist drainage with worsening findings of osteomyelitis on magnetic resonance imaging (see Figure 3). One month later, she underwent repeat debridement, with noted intraoperative purulence and a sinus tract. Micafungin 100 mg IV daily was added to voriconazole for salvage therapy. She was discharged on this dual antifungal regimen and later transitioned to oral olorofim monotherapy (via emergency use of expanded access).
Ongoing drainage from the incision site in the right upper extremity (see Figure 4) led to discontinuation of corticosteroids, and antifungal therapy was escalated to a combination of triple antifungal agents including posaconazole 300 mg twice daily for two doses, then 300 mg daily, and high-dose micafungin 150 mg IV daily, while continuing olorofim. After a subsequent I&D, micafungin was reduced to 100 mg daily due to intolerance. Posaconazole was discontinued after fifteen days due to transaminitis. Despite being on dual therapy with IV micafungin and olorofim, transaminitis persisted; therefore, IV micafungin was discontinued after a six-week course, and she continued olorofim monotherapy. See Figure 5 for a summary of the treatment course.
Her course was complicated by central retinal artery occlusion secondary to a relapse of GCA, necessitating resumption of high-dose steroids. At four months on olorofim, the left wrist had healed fully, while the right wrist had mild serous drainage, pending surgical closure (see Figure 6). The patient remained clinically stable with plans to complete at least a six-month course of olorofim from the date of her last debridement.

In an immunosuppressed patient presenting with subacute bilateral wrist swelling, erythema, and purulent drainage, the differential diagnosis for an infectious process is broad.
Bacterial septic arthritis is the most common etiology, particularly in older adults. However, the subacute course, negative blood cultures, and lack of clinical improvement with empiric antibiotics prompted consideration of less common pathogens (1).
Fungal arthritis is rare but increasingly recognized in immunocompromised hosts. In this case, bone tissue cultures revealed Scedosporium boydii, a mold notable for its intrinsic resistance to multiple antifungal classes and potential for deep tissue invasion (2-3).
Mycobacterial arthritis, several species of nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are linked to bone and joint infections. However, the cultures and biopsies did not show NTM infection.
Scedosporium boydii is a rare, multidrug-resistant mold that poses significant treatment challenges and often requires prolonged antifungal therapy and aggressive surgical source control (2-3). Olorofim, a novel orotomide antifungal, demonstrated sustained clinical activity in this case and represents a promising option for salvage therapy in refractory mold infections (4-5). Olorofim has been associated with abnormal liver enzyme levels. When used in combination with other antifungal agents, close monitoring of liver function tests is recommended due to the risk of drug-induced liver injury (6). This case underscores the value of broad-range fungal PCR and susceptibility testing in guiding targeted antifungal therapy when conventional agents fail (7). Timely surgical intervention remains critical in managing invasive fungal arthritis, particularly when structural involvement or drainage persists 8. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for atypical pathogens in immunosuppressed patients with refractory joint infections.

title: A woman in her 50s presented to the Emergency Department with cough, myalgias, f
history:
A woman in her 50s presented to the Emergency Department with cough, myalgias, fever (102°F), and pleuritic chest pain. Three days before presentation, the patient tested positive for influenza A and diagnosed with pneumonia based on chest radiograph. At that time, she was started on oseltamivir, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and azithromycin. Two days prior to presentation, she was prescribed a methylprednisolone taper due to persistent symptoms.

• Hypertension
• Obesity

The patient was born in Eastern Europe and moved to the United States decades ago. She lives with her husband. The patient recently returned from one-week vacation to Southeast Asia. In Singapore, she visited city areas and gardens. No rainforest or jungle excursions. Ate halloumi cheese at a "street market" and shortly after had diarrhea that self-resolved.

• Lisinopril 10mg daily
• Triamterene-hydrochlorothiazide 37.5-25mg daily
exam_studies:
• Vital signs: BP 167/106, HR 114 bpm, Temperature 36° C, RR 28 bpm, Weight 114 kg, SpO2 67% on room air, BMI 44.85 kg/m²
• General: In acute distress, ill-appearing
• Cardiac: Tachycardic, no murmur
• Pulmonary: Tachypneic, accessory muscle use, respiratory distress present, rales auscultated
• The remainder of the physical exam was within normal limits.

Initial complete metabolic panel was significant for sodium 128 mmol/L, bicarbonate 13 mmol/L, BUN 43 mg/dL, creatinine 2.76 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 171 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 75 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 83 U/L. The remainder of the complete metabolic panel was within normal limits. Complete blood count was normal and without leukocytosis. Arterial blood gas revealed a pH of 7.301, PaCO2 39.9 mmHg, and PaO2 103 mmHg. Lactic acid was 7.0 mmol/L. Brain natriuretic peptide was elevated to 510 ng/L. Troponin level was within normal limits. Blood cultures were collected. Repeat complete respiratory pathogen panel was positive for influenza A H1N1-2009. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia.
Figure 1. CT Chest without contrast

The patient’s clinical course deteriorated rapidly upon presentation to the hospital. She experienced worsening hypoxia necessitating endotracheal intubation in the emergency department. Piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin were initiated. Repeat chest radiography revealed a new pleural effusion, and a thoracentesis was performed with pleural fluid sent for cultures. She also developed new atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and a newly reduced ejection fraction of 30%. Coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary artery disease. An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed. However, due to progressive decompensation (Figure 1) and worsening multi-organ dysfunction, cannulation for veno-arterial extracorporeal membranous oxygenation (VA-ECMO) was performed. A bronchoscopy was completed at the time of VA-ECMO cannulation, and clear airways without significant secretions were noted. At 24 hours, blood cultures were growing gram-negative rods, and the Infectious Disease consultation service was consulted.
diagnosis:
Melioidosis

• Initial blood cultures were speciated as Burkholderia cepacia via commercial antimicrobial susceptibility test system (Figure 2, Figure 3)
• Given lack of patient risk factors for B. cepacia including no history of chronic pulmonary disease or immunocompromising conditions, the infectious disease team referred the blood culture isolate to the state health department for further testing. As the patient had recently traveled to Southeast Asia, Burkholderia pseudomallei (B. pseudomallei) was suspected.
• Repeat molecular testing at the state public health department identified the blood isolate as B. pseudomallei via polymerase chain reaction methods
• Pleural fluid cultures also grew B. pseudomallei at 48 hours, and sputum cultures grew B. pseudomallei at 50 hours
Figure 2. Figure 2: Photos taken on day 5 on Chocolate agar
Figure 2: Photos taken on day 5 on Chocolate agar
Figure 3. Photos taken on day 5 on blood agar

Piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin were discontinued, and the patient was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Due to concerns about inadequate antimicrobial monotherapy in the setting of the VA-ECMO circuit and while awaiting confirmatory testing, the patient was started on meropenem to provide dual coverage. The course of oseltamivir was completed. The state’s Department of Public Health Laboratory identified the isolate as B. pseudomallei. An isolate was also sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for whole-genome sequencing with data available at NCBI under biosample SAMN45894604. The isolate, 3101412784, was likely originating from Singapore due to the multi-locus sequence type (MLST) being attributed to ST-423 which is comprised of previous isolates from Southeast Asia as well as the finding that it grouped with multiple B. pseudomallei genomes from Singapore based on high resolution single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis. Unfortunately, the patient’s prolonged hospital course was complicated by fungemia, cerebrovascular accident, gastrointestinal bleed, and multi-limb ischemia secondary to vasopressor-induced soft tissue complications requiring amputations to three extremities. Her family ultimately made the decision to withdraw care and compassionately extubate.

Melioidosis is caused by B. pseudomallei, a gram-negative rod-shaped bacterium endemic to Southeast Asia, Northern Australia, Thailand, and some areas within the Americas. This illness is typically contracted by direct contact, inhalation, or ingestion from soil or water. Though diagnosis can be difficult given nonspecific signs and symptoms, early recognition of this underlying illness is imperative. Aside from recent travel to an endemic area, the patient did not have typical risk factors for melioidosis, and her pre-hospitalization presentation featured non-specific symptoms. B. cepacia tends to have a predilection for infecting severely immunocompromised individuals with prior pulmonary disease, which was not present in the current case. Recent methylprednisolone exposure may have contributed to her relatively immunosuppressed state at the time of infection. A link between influenza or SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of melioidosis has been investigated, but a definitive association has not been found. Finally, prior research has demonstrated the potential for mis-speciation of Burkholderia species using typical protocols available in clinical laboratories.
This case demonstrates the need for a high index of suspicion of melioidosis in patients who present with nonspecific symptoms and have a history of travel to endemic areas. Additionally, an automated instrument’s “expert rule” noted the blood culture isolate, initially identified as B. cepacia, to be resistant to amoxicillin-clavulanate on initial speciation. Proper recognition of B. pseudomallei is imperative given the risk of transmission to laboratory personnel. Direct contact with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the state’s Department of Public Health were of utmost importance to further characterize this patient’s condition.

title: A man in his seventies presented with a non-painful left index finger ulcer that
history:
A man in his seventies presented with a non-painful left index finger ulcer that had been present for several years. The lesion began as a superficial scratch that occurred while working on a tractor. The scratch did not improve after using over the counter antibiotic cream. He then developed an ulceration that slowly enlarged over several years. He was then diagnosed with giant cell arteritis and started on high-dose prednisone and other oral immunosuppression. He noted initial improvement in the ulceration but then it rapidly worsened.
He denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, congestion, hoarseness, odynophagia, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. No other skin lesions were present.
He was referred to infectious disease for further evaluation.

• Giant cell arteritis
• Hyperlipidemia

He previously worked as an ecologist and retired years ago. Monogamous with his wife. Currently lives in a rural area in the South-Central United States. He has hobbies including birding, woodworking, gardening, fishing, and hunting. He does not ingest unpasteurized dairy products or undercooked food. He has traveled previously to South and Central America several years before the finger ulceration appeared with additional trips afterwards. He previously had dogs, no other direct contact with animals except as above.

• Adalimumab
• Metronidazole cream 0.75%
• Minocycline 100mg twice daily
• Mycophenolate 1000mg twice daily
• Pimecrolimus 1% cream
• Prednisone 7mg daily (tapered from 60mg daily)
exam_studies:
He was well appearing. His temperature was 98.1 degrees Fahrenheit, heart rate was 64, blood pressure was 117/83, respiratory rate was 18, and O2 saturation was 100% on room air. An ulcerated plaque was present on the left index finger with cribriform scarring and some areas of overlying granulation tissue with extension of the ulcer into the interweb space and onto the base of the middle finger. Rolled borders were present around the lesion. A few erythematous papules were present on the acral aspect of the left middle finger. Otherwise, examination was normal.
A few erythematous papules were present on the acral aspect of the left middle finger (Figure 3)
Figure 1. Skin lesion after 9 months
Figure 2. Skin lesion after 3 years
Figure 3. Skin lesion after 4.5 years

• Wbc 8.39K/uL with 72.2% neutrophils and without eosinophilia. Hemoglobin and platelets were normal.
• Creatinine was normal.
• ALT was elevated to 49 (reference range 4-45 IU/L). AST, LDH, alkaline phosphatase, GGT, Total bilirubin were normal.
• Interferon-gamma release assay was negative.
• X-ray of the left hand was without acute findings. No bony erosions, joint spaces were well maintained, no significant soft tissue swelling seen.

He had been evaluated by dermatology who performed numerous biopsies. Pathology on a wedge biopsy performed after being started on immunosuppression showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. Multiple fungal and AFB cultures were negative.
He had also previously received an empiric trial of itraconazole for blastomycosis without improvement.
He had ongoing follow-up with dermatology with leading diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum. Trials of topical clobetasol, topical sodium cromoglycate, intra-lesional kenalog, dapsone, minocycline, and adalimumab did not demonstrate any improvement (Figures 1-3).
diagnosis:
Cutaneous Leishmaniasis

Repeat biopsy with dermatology was pursued. Tissue culture grew skin flora. AFB and fungal cultures were negative.
Pathology showed an ulcer with mixed inflammation, granulation tissue, dermal necrosis, and poorly formed necrotizing granulomata. Another area that was biopsied showed a focal epidermal ulceration with underlying acute and lymphohistiocytic inflammation. PAS and FITE stains were negative.
Bacterial DNA 16S PCR testing was positive for Leishmaniasis braziliensis complex.

He was admitted to the hospital and started on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B 3mg/kg daily for 6 days. Due to acute kidney injury further doses were delayed. A week later he was started back on amphotericin 3mg/kg twice weekly for another 2 weeks. Due to clinical improvement treatment was then stopped.
Otolaryngology performed an endoscopy and no evidence of mucosal leishmaniasis was found.
Figure 4. Skin lesion after 2 weeks of treatment
Figure 5. Skin lesion after 1 month of treatment
Figure 6. Skin lesion after 1.5 months of treatment
Figure 7. Skin lesion after 3 months of treatment

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection transmitted by bites from the sand fly. There is a diverse spectrum of disease depending on the infecting species residing in specific geographic locations. Leishmaniasis braziliensis is in the New World subgenus and is most commonly found in Central and South America [1, 2]. Our patient most likely acquired his infection in one of these regions during his travels. As the incubation period can be weeks to months, it is difficult to identify the precise timing or location of his infection. The most common skin findings are painless, chronic ulcerative lesions with well-defined indurated borders. This species can be associated with mucosal involvement, although none was found in this case [1, 2].
Biopsy with histology, culture with special media to promote promastigote formation, and PCR testing are all recommended to improve yield of diagnosis. As demonstrated in this case, it can be difficult to diagnose Leishmaniasis braziliensis with histology alone due to scant number of organisms in the tissue. Even if amastigotes are not seen, granulomas with lymphocytic infiltration should raise concern for this diagnosis [1]. Culture is also more likely to be negative in lesions present for greater than 12 months. PCR is the most sensitive test, although can be limited due to poor sampling or presence of inhibitors of the sample [1, 2, 3].
Uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis can heal without treatment, which might have occurred in our patient if he had not been started on immunosuppression which then led to worsening disease. Complicated infections require systemic therapy. This includes lesions greater than 5 cm, lesions on the fingers, infections in those who are immunocompromised, or infections with a species associated with mucocutaneous involvement. Amphotericin B is most widely used for treatment due to accessibility and shorter treatment durations [1, 2, 5]. As with this patient, the skin lesions are rarely fully healed at completion of treatment. There is a period of increased local inflammation at the beginning of treatment followed by gradual improvement over the subsequent weeks to months. Relapse of cutaneous or mucosal disease can be seen, thereby necessitating clinical follow-up for one to two years following treatment [1, 4]. Our patient has remained symptom free for several years after completing treatment.
